# Mistakes found in published sources

The atlas's workers read papers and books line by line to extract and plan their mathematics, and they record every mistake they find in them: misprints (slips whose intended meaning is clear), errors (false statements or steps that fail) and gaps (steps asserted without an adequate proof). A finding counts as confirmed once an independent reviewer has checked it at its locator. Each finding says where its worker looked for an existing correction; a new one is not corrected in any erratum or later version they found. Nothing here has been sent to the authors.

Collected by `scripts/errata.py` from the paper extractions and blueprint packets (research/blueprint/PROTOCOL.md, section 18); the data is in `data/source-issues.json`.

604 new mistakes confirmed · 3452 awaiting review · 236 already corrected in print · 18 rejected on review · 0 extractions and packets not yet checked.

- **Misprint** at §7.1, Proposition 7.1(ii): arXiv v3 p. 35; published p. 940.. - **Misprint** at §7.3, proof of Lemma 7.4: arXiv v3 p. 38; published p. 945.. The source says `π_2 of Y − {y_0}`; it should be `'… because the π_2 of Y vanishes': the relevant group is π_2 of the base of the fibration, not of its fibre.`. The fibration is the second map of (7.5), (Y² − Δ, y) → (Y, y_0), (y, y') ↦ y', whose fibre over y_0 is Y − {y_0}. Its long exact sequence reads π_2(Y) → π_1(Y − {y_0}) → π_1(Y² − Δ) → π_1(Y) → π_0, so injectivity on the left is governed by π_2 of the base Y; π_2 of the fibre enters the sequence one step earlier and is irrelevant to it. The conclusion is correct because Y is a closed surface of genus ⩾ 2, hence aspherical, so π_2(Y) = 0 — and in any case only the middle exactness, which gives the normality of Γ in Γ̃^geom that the argument goes on to use, is needed. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-DESIGN-LV`. - **Error** at §8.3, Lemma 8.2: arXiv v3 p. 42; published p. 951. (it affects a stated result). The source says `[e_1], …, [e_k]`; it should be `Require e to be nonseparating in Y, equivalently [e] ≠ 0 in H_1(Y; Q).`. A simple curve bounding a disk away from the branch point is permitted by the paper’s definition. Its q inverse images bound disks, so all q homology classes are zero, contradicting the claimed independence and primitive rank q−1. For a nonseparating curve one can choose the one-face CW decomposition used in the proof; the lifted edge classes are independent and transfer supplies the single relation after primitive projection. The required distinguishing curves can be chosen nonseparating, including curves with q-cycle monodromy; they are not all liftable curves in the paper’s special sense. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-DESIGN-LV`. - **Error** at §8.3, Lemma 8.3: arXiv v3 p. 42; published p. 951. (it affects a stated result). The source says `rank(Mon(D_e^M) − Id)`; it should be `Take a nonseparating simple closed curve e in Y−{y} and a positive sufficiently divisible M (for example a positive multiple of the order of Cov(e), and of the relevant stabilizer indices). Then the rank is k−1, where k is the number of cycles of Cov(e).`. The lemma is deduced from Lemma 8.2, which needs e nonseparating (finding E13), and it fails without that hypothesis. If e bounds a disk in Y − {y} then Mon(D_e^M) = Id and the rank is 0, while Cov(e) = 1; if e is nonseparating with Cov(e) a q-cycle then k = 1 and the rank is again 0. Two different conjugacy classes give the same rank, so the rank does not determine the class. With e nonseparating the three possible cycle types in Aff(q) — (1^q), (q) and (1, r, …, r) — have k = q, 1 and 1 + (q − 1)/r cycles respectively, all distinct, and the lemma holds. The applications, in the proof of Lemma 8.9, are to nonseparating curves. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-DESIGN-LV`. - **Misprint** at §2.3, Lemma 2.3: arXiv v3 p. 9, standing notation p. 8; published pp. 902–904. Applications in §§3.4, 4.3, 6. (it affects the proof). The source says `ρ is unramified outside S`; it should be `Use a finite set T = S ∪ {w : w divides p} in the finiteness lemma and its applications; impose its Frobenius weight and integrality conditions away from T.`. The standing S excludes every place above p. Good reduction makes p-adic cohomology crystalline there, but does not make it unramified. For example H²_et(P¹,Q_p)=Q_p(−1) is ramified at p although P¹ has good reduction. The finiteness argument allows any fixed finite ramification set: enlargement to T is harmless. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-DESIGN-LV`. - **Error** at End of §8.3: arXiv v3 p. 43; published p. 951. (it affects the proof). The source says `D_e`; it should be `Use D_e^{q−1}, or a suitable further positive multiple in the common cover stabilizer. Its lift is D_{e+}^{q−1}D_{e−}; it induces a nontrivial transvection on primitive homology.`. For a liftable e the multiplier of Cov(e) generates F_q^×. A dual curve meeting e once has its abelian multiplier changed by this generator under D_e. Conjugation in Aff(q) preserves multipliers, so D_e does not stabilize the cover. The preceding lifting formula instead applies to the (q−1)-st power. If u is the primitive projection of [e+], then the projection of [e−] is −u and the lift acts by x↦x+q⟨u,x⟩u, up to the intersection-sign convention. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-DESIGN-LV`. - **Error** at §2.4, Lemma 2.8: arXiv v3 p. 12; published p. 908. (it affects a stated result). The source says `η²|_{K_v^*} = χ · Norm_{K_v/Q_p}^w`; it should be `The identity holds on the local units: η²|_{O_{K_v}^*} = χ · Norm_{K_v/Q_p}^w with χ of finite order. Counterexample: K = Q (which has no CM subfield, so every finite place is friendly), v = p, η = χ_cyc^{-1}. Then η is ramified only at p, locally algebraic there, and pure of weight w = 2, since geometric Frobenius at ℓ acts by ℓ. As an idele class character η(p) = 1, because the local Artin image of a uniformizer acts trivially on μ_{p^∞} in either normalisation; so η²(p) = 1 while Norm_{Q_p/Q_p}(p)^w = p², and χ(p) = p^{-2} has infinite order. On units η(u) = u and η² = Norm², so the identity does hold there. The proof cannot give more: local algebraicity is the hypothesis that η_p 'agrees, in a neighbourhood of the identity, with the Q_p-points of an algebraic homomorphism' (p. 12), and the closing step — 'any Q_p-rational character of (Res_{E/Q} G_m)^1 is trivial upon pullback to E_v^*' — is a statement about that algebraic character, hence controls η only on an open subgroup of E_v^*, not on a uniformizer. For the proposition as stated at p=2, replace the whole residue disk by finitely many smaller congruence disks and carry out the argument on each. No counterexample to Proposition 5.3 is asserted.`. Friendliness ensures K_v/Q_p is unramified, but does not imply p>2. The quoted estimate for flat sections is |z|<p^(−1/(p−1)). At p=2, points with |z|=1/2 in a residue disk are on its boundary, so that estimate does not justify §6’s assertion that the analytic domain contains the entire residue disk. Subdivision into disks modulo 4 avoids this issue. The original claim that other primes above p must be good for crystallinity at v was incorrect: v∉S already supplies good reduction at v. ### André, "Le lemme d'Abhyankar perfectoïde", Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS (2018) (`PAPER-ANDRE-18`)

- **Error** at Published §2.2.4 p.13; Lemme 2.4.1(2) p.22; Lemme 2.4.2 proof p.24; discussion after Théorème 3.4.1 p.41. (it affects a stated result). The source says `« au plus une norme spectrale » (p.13); the surrounding assertion imposes completeness, but no fixed topology. Its proof replaces two norms by their maximum.`; it should be `Keep uniqueness for a fixed topology. If both norms are complete, a continuous identity in one direction suffices by open mapping. Delete the automatic-invariance parenthesis in Lemme 2.4.1(2), or require continuity of the finite-group action; retain its explicit norm-invariance hypothesis. Reprove applications using their additional hypotheses.`. Let F be the algebraic closure of Q_p inside C_p. It is dense and properly contained in C_p. Extend t from C_p minus F to a transcendence basis over F. The automorphism of the rational function field sending t to pt and fixing the other basis elements and F extends to an automorphism σ of its algebraic closure C_p. Thus ν(x)=|x| and ν′(x)=|σ(x)| are distinct complete multiplicative Q_p-algebra norms, with ν′(t)=p^(-1)ν(t). For a_n in F tending to t in ν, the same sequence tends to p^(-1)t in ν′. It is Cauchy for max(ν,ν′) but cannot have a limit for that norm. There is also an actual finite-group counterexample to the parenthesis of Lemme 2.4.1(2): put B=C_p×C_p with N(x,y)=max(ν(x),ν′(y)), let G=C_2 swap factors, and give A=B^G=diagonal C_p its induced norm max(ν,ν′). B is complete and spectral; A is uniform normed, exactly as allowed in §2.4.1, though incomplete. The swap takes (t,0), of norm ν(t), to (0,t), of norm p^(-1)ν(t). The proposed old repair from (2.11) is invalid: that formula determines max_γ N(γb), not N(b), and its proof of individual equality uses G-invariance. The prior extraction also missed the invocation on p.24. For a finite projective algebra over a complete A, its given complete Banach topology agrees with the canonical module topology: choose finite generators, use the continuous surjection A^n→B and open mapping. A-linear isomorphisms are then continuous, so fixed-topology uniqueness applies to p.24 and p.41. This does not repair the general parenthesis on p.22, where A need not be complete. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-PAPER-ANDRE-18`. ### Bakker–Klingler–Tsimerman, "Tame topology of arithmetic quotients and algebraicity of Hodge loci", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020) (`PAPER-BAKKER-KLINGLER-TSIMERMAN-20`)

- **Error** at Theorem 4.1, JAMS p.928, proof p.929; author p.13–14 (it affects a stated result). The source says `"Theorem 4.1. Let V be a polarized variation of pure Hodge structures of weight k over the punctured polydisk (∆*)^n, with period map Φ: (∆*)^n → S_{Γ,G,M}. Then Φ is R_an,exp-definable." (∆ is the unit disk; see §1.3.)`; it should be `Replace the whole-unit-polydisk assertion by a local assertion after shrinking to (∆*_ρ)^n for a sufficiently small 0<ρ<1, with the Hodge-compatible fixed maximal compact. In §4.1 choose such smaller charts around every point of the compactification and then a finite subcover. Do not justify the several-variable step by calling the remaining punctured annular pieces compact. This correction specifies the necessary domain change; it does not discharge the separate proof gaps recorded below.`. with τ(z)=2i+ε exp(−(1+z)/(1−z)), take ε>0 small enough that its image lies in a quotient-injective disk for Γ(3)\H. The trivial integral rank-two local system, its holomorphic weight-one Hodge line and the standard polarization give a PVHS; transversality is automatic in weight one. The fibre at π(2i+ε/e) is EXACTLY {2πin/(2+2πin):n∈Z\{0}} on ∆*. Solving the exponential equation proves equality, not just containment; it is infinite and discrete with accumulation only at the excluded outer boundary. A definable discrete subset of R² is finite. The y>1 strip in the proof covers only |q|<exp(−2π), and Lemma 4.2 explicitly permits shrinking. Confirmed for the literal whole-disk statement. Repaired the original insufficient 'contains' argument and removed the several-variable compact-annulus shortcut. This does not refute Theorem 1.3. - **Gap** at Appendix A.3 proof of Proposition A.2, JAMS pp.935–936 (it affects the proof). The source says `relatively compact`; it should be `Choose smaller semialgebraic corner boxes whose closures lie inside larger analytic charts. On the compact matching graph for two closed boxes, cover by finitely many neighborhoods carrying analytic transition extensions, restrict each to bounded boxes, and use finite unions and projections to obtain definable overlaps and transitions. F(x)=x+(x²/4)sin(1/x) on (0,1) is an analytic diffeomorphism to a bounded interval because F′=1+(x/2)sin(1/x)−(1/4)cos(1/x)>1/4. The zero set of F−id is exactly {1/(nπ):n≥1}, so F is not definable in an o-minimal structure. Two analytic charts on an arc of a compact circle can have this transition despite bounded semianalytic domains. Confirmed that the immediate compatibility inference needs more control. Checked the buffered-box repair via a finite cover of the compact matching graph by analytic transition germs; compactness alone is not asserted to imply definability. - **Error** at §3.2 surjective case, JAMS p.928 (it affects the proof). The source says `S_(Γ′,G′,M′) = S_(Γ′∩G,G,M′∩G) × S_(Γ′∩H,H,M′∩H)`; it should be `Do not identify the quotient by an arbitrary compact M′ with the product of quotients by its intersections with the normal factors. Supply an argument for the compact-stabilizer quotient map (for example factoring through the full preimage of the target stabilizer), in addition to the finite-index arithmetic step. This review verifies the displayed product's failure, not a complete replacement proof.`. Take G′=PSL₂(R)×PSL₂(R), projection to the first factor, Γ′=Γ₁×Γ₂ with torsion-free arithmetic factors, and M′ the diagonal SO₂. Its intersections with the two normal factors are trivial. The left-hand quotient has real dimension 5, whereas the displayed product of intersection-stabilizer quotients has dimension 6. Passing to finite-index arithmetic subgroups does not fix that discrepancy. The corrected morphism theorem may still hold; this literal intermediate equality does not. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-PAPER-BAKKER-KLINGLER-TSIMERMAN-20`. The source says `"Consider for each positive integer m and real number c the function f_{m,c} which we obtain from f by setting z_1 = mz_2 + c. The required bounded-width Schmid/CKS/Kashiwara inputs are not verified by this review; a wider-sector formulation alone is not a completed repair.`. Independent domain check in Definition 4.4 and the printed induction: x_1=mx_2+c>1 for c≥1 and 0<x_2<1, while for c=0 the original domain requires x_2<1/m. Thus the stated curve hypothesis on Σ_n cannot simply be applied on all of Σ_(n−1) as printed. Confirmed as a gap in this step, not as a counterexample to Lemma 4.5. Revised the correction/reason so that the stronger bounded-width input and its application are explicitly requirements, not an independently completed repair. - **Error** at §5, JAMS pp.933–934, definition of the target Hodge locus. The source says `union of special subvarieties`; it should be `For the exceptional Hodge locus, use proper Mumford–Tate-drop subdata relative to the generic Hodge datum, not the union of every special image including the identity. Supply the correspondence with exceptional Hodge tensors. The proof's stronger assertion that the inverse image of each special subvariety is algebraic is compatible with this correction; Theorem 1.6 is not refuted.`. As defined immediately above, a special image may be the image of the identity Hodge morphism. Including it makes the union the whole target, whose pullback is all S, whereas §1.4 defines HL(S,V) using exceptional Hodge tensors. The extraction uses proper special images; the correspondence remains G6. (cc-442dc5) Reclassified to affect nothing: §1.4 defines the Hodge locus through exceptional Hodge tensors, i.e. proper Mumford–Tate-drop special images; including the identity image in §5's description is a slip that the statement of Theorem 1.6 does not use. - **Gap** at Theorem 4.12 and proof, JAMS p.933 (it affects the proof). The source says `smooth complex algebraic manifold S×S_(Γ,G,K)`; it should be `Restrict the displayed argument to smooth S, or add the singular-source reduction and algebraicity-descent argument (for instance using a resolution or stratification with the required analytic comparison). The theorem quantifies an arbitrary complex algebraic variety S, while the proof applies Theorem 1.3 and the stated smooth-source definable Chow theorem to S itself. - **Error** at §4.5, JAMS p.933; author p.18. The source says `Published p.933: “then b will also be (e, C″)-reduced for some C″ = C″(e, e′, C′) > 0.” Author copy/arXiv v2 p.18: the same clause has C″(e, C, e′, C′).`; it should be `The ordered-basis conclusion cannot hold as printed. At a minimum it must allow finitely many permutations of e (and retain dependence on the condition-(3) constant C). The following paragraph already allows finitely many orderings. The counterexample verifies the necessity of this correction, not every estimate in the general basis-change argument.`. Take e′ = (e_1, e_2), e = (e_2, e_1) and b = diag(1, T) with T ≥ 1. Then b is (e′, 2)-reduced and satisfies condition (3) for e (b(e_2)b(e_1) = T = det b), but condition (2) for e would need T = b(e_2) < C″b(e_1) = C″ for all T. The proof immediately adds 'we may assume (2) as there are only finitely many orderings of the basis', which is the corrected form, so Theorem 1.5 is unaffected. The source says `“It identifies G(R)/M with the image p(G(R))”`; it should be `Remove the asserted identification by the M-invariant polynomial map. ### Bakker–Tsimerman, "p-torsion monodromy representations of elliptic curves over geometric function fields", Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), no. 3 (`PAPER-BAKKER-TSIMERMAN-16`)

- **Misprint** at Proof of Proposition 23, p.735, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 709–744 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 814976ee…f40a). The source says `"dd^c(f∘χ) = −(1/2π) dd^c log(|1 − z w̄|² − |z − w|²) + dd^c log|z − w|² = −(1/2π) dd^c log[(1 − |z|²)(1 − |w|²)] + [Δ_D] = (1/4π) ω_{D×D} + [Δ_D]."`; it should be `The coefficient in the first two lines is −1: f∘χ = log|z − w|² − log(|1 − z w̄|² − |z − w|²), so dd^c(f∘χ) = −dd^c log[(1 − |z|²)(1 − |w|²)] + [Δ_D] = (1/4π) ω_{D×D} + [Δ_D].`. With f(s) = log(s/(1 − s)) and χ = |z − w|²/|1 − z w̄|², f∘χ is the stated difference of logarithms with coefficient 1; the final line is consistent with the paper's d^c normalization only with coefficient −1 in front of the first term. - **Gap** at Published Lemma 5 proof, p.718, its upper-bound matrix witness; arXiv v2 Lemma 5 p.9, with the compactification condition on p.8 (it affects the proof). The source says `The trace bound is attained by γ=[[1−p²,p],[-p,1]], and “The result then follows.”`; it should be `The upper bound for the radius defined using loops nontrivial in the compactification requires a short element of Γ(p) whose image in π₁(X(p)) is nontrivial. The displayed element cannot supply it. Keep the trace lower bound, but supply a different upper-bound witness or a separate geometric argument compatible with that homotopy condition. This review has not supplied that missing argument.`. The displayed γ factors exactly as [[1,p],[0,1]]·[[1,0],[-p,1]]. Both factors are peripheral unipotents in Γ(p), killed when cusps are filled: the first is a p-th power of the standard cusp generator and the second a conjugate of its inverse. Therefore their product also maps to the identity in the compactified fundamental group. Although γ is hyperbolic with |tr γ|=p²−2, its geodesic is excluded by the definition immediately above Lemma 5. The published proof itself identifies the kernel with the group generated by these unipotents. Thus the exhibited matrix proves an upper bound for the ordinary nonperipheral systole, not the compactification-nontrivial systole being used. The defect remains after inserting E8’s factor one-half. No counterexample to the eventual asymptotic theorem is asserted; the missing upper-bound argument remains open in this review. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-PAPER-BAKKER-TSIMERMAN-16`. - **Gap** at Published proof of Corollary 8, p.720; arXiv v2 pp.10–11 (it affects the proof). The source says `“γ can be within (log p)/2 of at most one cusp, as ℓ_X(p)(γ) ≤ 2 log p + O(1).”`; it should be `Distinguish the closed-geodesic length ℓ(γ)=2ρ_X(p) from the injectivity radius. Even granting the intended upper bound ρ_X(p)≤2 log p+O(1), the available length bound is 4 log p+O(1). Rework the cusp-avoidance argument to control all cusp neighborhoods visited, with a total O(1) length-comparison error; replacing 2 by 4 alone does not justify the asserted one-cusp claim. This review does not claim to close that geometric step.`. The compact definition p.718 sets ρ to half the shortest closed-geodesic length, and the last line of this same proof explicitly uses ℓ(γ)=2ρ_X(p). Its preliminary upper-bound argument therefore provides only ℓ(γ)≤4 log p+O(1), not the quoted estimate. The proof then uses the stronger estimate to reduce its detour and integration to one cusp. Lemma 6’s separation >2 log p−O(1), together with the corrected length bound, does not imply this one-cusp assertion. A bounded-number-of-cusps replacement may repair the strategy but needs a proof controlling visits and detours. The claim confirmed here is the missing justification in this step, not a counterexample to Corollary 8. It is separate from the inadmissible witness in E12. - **Misprint** at Proof of Proposition 4.1, p.3, in the authors' erratum (B. Bakker and J. Tsimerman, Erratum, 5 pp., https://benjamin-bakker.github.io/P.torsion.erratum.pdf, SHA-256 db8effa1…acc1). The source says `"mult_{CM−∩Δ̄}(T*_m C) ≪ … ≪ vol(T*_m C ∩ B(Δ̄, ε)) ≪ (sinh(ρ_{X(p)}/2)/sinh(ε)) vol(T*_m C)"`; it should be `The factor is sinh(ε)/sinh(ρ_{X(p)}/2): Proposition 3.1 gives vol(C ∩ B(Δ̄,ε)) ≤ (sinh ε/sinh R) vol(C ∩ B(Δ̄,R)) for 0 < ε < R < ρ/2, and letting R ↑ ρ_{X(p)}/2 gives the small factor.`. Proposition 3.1 says (1/sinh r)·vol(C ∩ B(Δ̄,r)) increases with r, so the small ball has at most the proportion sinh ε/sinh R of the large one. The printed reciprocal is a large factor (ρ_{X(p)} ~ 2 log p) and would not give the p^{−1} saving the next line states, (p^{−2δ₂} + d₃p^{−1}) Deg(C). - **Gap** at Proof of Lemma 15, pp.726–727, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 709–744 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 814976ee…f40a) (it affects the proof). The source says `"Since M′² = −1, it follows that M′ is either equal to t̃ or −t̃" … "Thus g = a + b(0 1; −1 0), … and (x,y) lies on T_m where m = det g = a² + b²."`; it should be `For the order-three lift actually printed, t₀=[[0,1],[-1,−1]], use t̃²+t̃+I=0. A conjugate M′ in the centralizer algebra is t̃ or −I−t̃ (exclude scalar roots using conjugacy when the polynomial splits modulo p). Lifting the small-coefficient identities still shows M_x,M_y normalize the same elliptic torus, and their positive determinant forces them into its centralizer. In the concluding degree calculation use g=aI+bt₀ and m=a²−ab+b². Equivalently one may replace t₀ by −t₀ and use the trace +1 relation and a²+ab+b², but that change of lift must be explicit.`. The displayed square relation and Gaussian norm apply only to the order-four lift. The separate order-three matrix on p.725 has trace −1 and determinant 1. Its Cayley–Hamilton relation and direct determinant expansion yield the correction above. Its centralizer is the Eisenstein quadratic algebra, and the same positive-determinant normalizer argument works. The earlier errata correction implicitly changed to the negative lift without saying so. The source proof needs this branch; no counterexample to the Heegner-only conclusion is asserted. The source says `"Its discriminant is Δ_a = 64(a_a b_a c_a)² = (2⁸/g⁶)(n+id)²(n+jd)²(n+(2j−i)d)²."`; it should be `Δ_a = 16(a_a b_a c_a)² = (2⁶/g⁶)(n+id)²(n+jd)²(n+(2j−i)d)².`. For y² = x³ + a₂x² + a₄x, Δ = 16a₄²(a₂² − 4a₄). For E_a: Y² = X(X−a)(X+c), a₂ = c − a and a₄ = −ac, so Δ = 16a²c²(a+c)² = 16(abc)² since a+b+c = 0; with b_a = −2(n+jd)/g this is 2⁶/g⁶ times the product. - **Misprint** at Theorem 6, pp.376–377, and Case 1 of the proof of Proposition 8.2, pp.377–378, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 191 (2020), 355–392 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 3920a7524a37870942fe3591ac858db23cb604f4331bccd2a6dc5f11a1671fbf) Compared with arXiv:1709.01022v1, pp.19–20.. The source says `“Let π_i be characters of conductor q_i for 1 ≤ i ≤ r”, later applied with “ψ … principal of conductor M₂”.`; it should be `Use modulus q_i in Theorem 6 and modulus M₂ for the principal character. The first factor retains its explicit primitivity requirement. No extra M₂=1 case is missing: allow r=s, so the product of principal factors is empty.`. A principal Dirichlet character has primitive conductor 1 regardless of its ambient modulus; the application itself says modulus for the factors. The original errata additionally objected that M₂=1 forces a missing nontrivial principal block, but the source never requires r>s. When r=s, condition (d) applies to the last primitive factor. Pack the odd prime factors into blocks between B=k^(7/32) and B², leaving at most one short primitive block (including any 2-part) and one short principal block; discard empty blocks. The first block is odd and at least B. If M₂=1, the second collection is empty and the same construction applies. The printed r−2 count remains sufficient. The source says `"… every zero of every Dirichlet L-function corresponding to a primitive character of modulus q ≤ T (where T ≥ 2) necessarily has real part β satisfying β < 1 − c/log T, with at most a single exception"`; it should be `Restrict the zero β+it to |t|≤T. This is the classical Landau–Page statement required in the addendum; no claim that the stronger all-height assertion is known false is made.`. The standard Landau–Page region depends on log(Q(1+|t|)), as in Ford–Green–Konyagin–Maynard–Tao, Long gaps between primes, Lemma 7.1, published p.96, https://www.ams.org/journals/jams/2018-31-01/S0894-0347-2017-00876-2/S0894-0347-2017-00876-2.pdf. With Q=T and |t|≤T this yields the stated strip after changing the absolute constant. No such fixed strip for all heights follows. The paper’s (41) uses exactly the bounded-height form. (it affects a stated result). The source says `"Proposition 12.2. If q ≤ Q = k⁴ and q ∉ Q(k), then Σ_{k/2<m≤k} χ(m)·Λ(m) ≪ k/log k."`; it should be `Add that χ is a primitive nonprincipal character modulo q.`. The character is not specified in the proposition. - **Misprint** at §12, proof of Proposition 12.2, p.387, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 191 (2020), 355–392 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 3920a7524a37870942fe3591ac858db23cb604f4331bccd2a6dc5f11a1671fbf) The §12 addendum is absent from arXiv:1709.01022v1.. The source says `The explicit formula is truncated at |t| ≤ T, but the bound is then written for "Σ_{L(β+it,χ)=0, β>0, |t|≤Q} k^ρ/ρ" and finished with "(k/(log k)³) Σ 1/|ρ| ≪ k/log k; here, the last inequality follows from the standard proof of the Prime Number Theorem in Arithmetic Progressions".`; it should be `Replace |t|≤Q by |t|≤T in both zero sums. The claimed additional gap concerning small zeros is rejected: q∉Q(k) and the functional equation already control them.`. Put δ=3 log log k/log k. For a primitive character of conductor q∉Q(k), all zeros with |γ|≤T have δ≤β≤1−δ, by reflection in the functional equation. Thus the zeros with |γ|≤1 contribute at most N(1,χ)/δ≪log(2q)/δ to Σ1/|ρ|. For 1<|γ|≤T, partial summation of N(u,χ)≪u log(q(u+2)) gives O(log(2q)log T+(log T)²). Since q≤k⁴ and log T=O(log k/log log k), the total is O((log k)²), as required. Bennett–Martin–O’Bryant–Rechnitzer, arXiv:1802.00085, p.11 and Proposition 2.5 p.14, explicitly provide the reflection and zero-counting input cited by the paper. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-PAPER-BENNETT-SIKSEK-20`. - **Error** at Theorem A(ii), published p.4, and Theorem 3.16(ii), published p.55, author-hosted journal PDF; corresponding arXiv 1801.00872v3 / Wittenberg-manuscript pp.4,48. (it affects a stated result). The source says `of dimension d ≥ 1`; it should be `For the even-genus equivalence in part (ii), add dim(X) ≥ 2 or X(R) = ∅. A simpler sufficient restriction is dim(X) ≥ 2. In the excluded case dim(X)=1 with X(R) nonempty, Pic descent is always surjective and the equivalence holds precisely when X itself has even genus. This finding does not require restricting part (i).`. Use the smooth projective completion E of y²=x³−x over R. The cubic discriminant is 4 (Weierstrass discriminant 64); the point [0:1:0] is real and nonsingular, and E is geometrically integral of genus 1. Coherent H²(E,O_E)=0. Since E(C) is connected, H⁰_G(E(C),Z)=Z, generated by the codimension-zero cycle class [E]; hence the real integral Hodge conjecture for 1-cycles holds. The only reduced geometrically irreducible closed curve in E is E, so no even-genus curve exists. A real point splits Br(R)→Br(E); the low-degree Hochschild–Serre sequence therefore gives Pic(E)≅Pic(E_C)^G and hence the same isomorphism on 2-primary torsion. For the repair, Proposition 3.9 supplies even-genus curves when dim(X)≥2 and X(R)≠∅. If X(R)=∅, Theorems 3.3/3.6 apply without that dimension restriction; for curves this is exactly Lemma 3.7. ### Bhargava–Shankar–Taniguchi–Thorne–Tsimerman–Zhao, "Bounds on 2-torsion in class groups of number fields and integral points on elliptic curves", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020) (`PAPER-BHARGAVA-SHANKAR-TANIGUCHI-ETAL-20`)

- **Misprint** at Taniguchi author copy dated 18 February 2017, proof of Theorem 2.1, p.4, volume display; also arXiv:1701.02458v1, p.4. Author-copy page image independently inspected.. The source says `sqrt(pi) |Disc(K)|^(1/(2n)) |alpha|_v^(-1/m)`; it should be `For every complex place, square the whole displayed factor: its disc contributes pi R_v^2, not sqrt(pi) R_v. The body volume is 2^r pi^s sqrt(D_K)/N(I).`. A complex coordinate is two real dimensions. With K=Q(i), I=O_K and alpha=1, the radius is sqrt(2); the disc area is 2pi rather than sqrt(2pi). The latter is below the Minkowski threshold 4 in the ordinary metric, whereas the correct area is above it. The existing balanced-body item already uses the corrected formula, so the theorem and its route are unchanged. The source says `where |A| <= |Disc(K)|^(1/3), B <= |Disc(K)|^(2/3), and C <= |Disc(K)|`; it should be `State two-sided bounds |A| << D_K^(1/3), |B| << D_K^(2/3), |C| << D_K, with fixed-degree constants. - **Misprint** at arXiv:1701.02458v1, Remark 7.2, p.10 (page image independently inspected); collated with the 18 February 2017 Taniguchi author copy, Remark 7.2, p.11.. The source says `|Pic^0(C)(k)| = |k|^g log|k| Res_(s=1) zeta_C(s)`; it should be `|Pic^0(C)(k)| = |k|^g (1 - |k|^(-1)) log|k| Res_(s=1) zeta_C(s).`. Write zeta_C(s) = Z(|k|^(-s)) with Z(T) = P(T)/((1-T)(1-|k|T)) and P(1) = |Pic^0(C)(k)|. The pole at s = 1 comes from the factor 1 - |k|T, and the residue is P(|k|^(-1))/((1 - |k|^(-1)) log|k|); the functional equation P(1/(|k|T)) = |k|^(-g) T^(-2g) P(T) at T = 1 gives P(|k|^(-1)) = |k|^(-g) P(1). Hence P(1) = |k|^g (1 - |k|^(-1)) log|k| Res, and the printed identity omits 1 - |k|^(-1). That factor lies in [1/2, 1), so the remark, which only compares growth in g, is unaffected. - **Misprint** at arXiv:1701.02458v1, Remark 7.3, p.10 (page image independently inspected); collated with the 18 February 2017 Taniguchi author copy, Remark 7.3, p.11.. The source says `Pic^0(C)(k)[2] subset Pic^0(C)(kbar)[2] and the latter group has size 2^(2g), or 2^g if the characteristic is 2`; it should be `... or at most 2^g if the characteristic is 2.`. Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 2 the 2-torsion of a g-dimensional abelian variety is (Z/2)^f with f the 2-rank, 0 <= f <= g; f = g characterises the ordinary case and a supersingular Jacobian has f = 0. Only the upper bound is used: the remark compares |k|^g with 2^(2g) in odd characteristic and with 2^g in characteristic 2, and concludes that the first bound of Theorem 7.1 wins only for k = F_3. - **Gap** at Taniguchi author copy dated 18 February 2017, §4, p.6, index-two case; independently collated with arXiv:1701.02458v1, p.6. (it affects the proof). The source says `by genus theory, the 2-torsion in the class group of K is bounded by the 2-torsion in the class group of F multiplied by O(2^t) … we obtain a bound of O_ε(|Disc(K)|^{1/4+ε})`; it should be `A verified sufficient replacement is Klüners–Wang, arXiv:2003.12161v2, Theorem 2.1: h_2(K) ≤ 4^{e-1} h_2(F)², where t counts all ramified places including infinite ones and e = max(t,1), not simply t. Use this in a strong induction on n = [K:Q] rather than with Brauer–Siegel. If m = [F:Q] = n/2 ≥ 3 and the lower-degree case of the theorem gives exponent 1/2 - 1/(2m) + η, then D_F² ≤ D_K and 4^{e-1} ≪_{n,η} D_K^η give exponent 1/2 - 1/n + O(η), which is stronger than the 1/2 - 1/(2n) + ε the theorem needs. For n = 4, quadratic genus theory for F gives D_K^ε directly. This replacement neither proves nor refutes the printed one-factor relative bound, and it reaches the theorem's exponent without the printed D_K^{1/4+ε} claim for this case.`. The displayed one-factor estimate has no derivation or precise citation in either preprint, and it is not what genus theory delivers. Genus theory for a quadratic K/F is the ambiguous class number formula, which bounds the Gal(K/F)-invariant classes: |Cl(K)^G| = h_F 2^{t-1} / [E_F : E_F ∩ N K^×] ≤ h_F 2^{t-1}. Passing from those to the 2-torsion costs a second factor: on Cl(K)[2] the map c ↦ c·σ(c) lands in Cl(K)^G and has kernel Cl(K)[2]^G, so the standard route gives only |Cl(K)[2]| ≤ |Cl(K)^G|², and genus theory bounds neither Cl(K)[2]^G nor Cl(K)^G by O(2^t)·h_2(F). That missing step is the whole of the gap, and it is load-bearing here: it is exactly what lets the printed argument finish by applying Brauer–Siegel to F, since h_2(F) ≪_ε |Disc F|^{1/2+ε} ≤ |Disc K|^{1/4+ε}. With the squared estimate that route gives only |Disc K|^{1/2+ε}, which is the trivial bound. Klüners–Wang Theorem 2.1 and its proof give the squared estimate h_2(K) ≤ 4^{e-1}h_2(F)², with Remark 2.2 improving it when the base 2-rank is zero; no statement in the literature gives the one-factor form. A weaker known upper bound is not evidence that the printed bound is false, and none is claimed here: the finding is that the step is asserted without proof or citation, not that it is refuted. The source says `if C admits a degree n map to P¹ over k, then |Pic⁰(C)(k)[2]| ≪_n |k|^{(1−1/n)g}`; it should be `The cited argument does not establish the epsilon-free, n-only second bound. The published Acta Arithmetica 181.4 (2017), p.321, also retains epsilon and prints an implied constant depending only on d and epsilon, not q. That printed uniformity cannot hold for the stated full range: on Y=X^2 with I={degree<=2 polynomials}, |I|=q^3 and |S|=q^2, so at epsilon=1/12 the ratio to |I|^(1/2+epsilon) is q^(1/4). Thus q-independent use of the cited bound needs an additional repair or restricted range. Neither this constant issue nor the epsilon endpoint is addressed in BSTTTZ's one-sentence reduction. This supports a gap in that deduction, not falsity of the desired torsion bound. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-PAPER-BHARGAVA-SHANKAR-TANIGUCHI-ETAL-20`. ### Bhatt et al., "Globally +-regular varieties and the minimal model program for threefolds in mixed characteristic", Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS (2023) (`PAPER-BHATT-ETAL-23`)

- **Error** at Lemma 2.56, second assertion, p.101 of the published version; the same wording is arXiv v1 Lemma 2.37 (p.20), v2 Lemma 2.50 (p.26) and v3 Lemma 2.56 (p.29) (it affects a stated result). The source says `"More generally, let D be a fixed divisor and let A be a semiample Q-Cartier Q-divisor such that A ∼_Q M + Λ, where M is an effective Cartier divisor with no exceptional curve of Y → X in its support, and −δD ≤ Λ ≤ δD for δ > 0. Take x ∈ F ∩ M of multiplicity k ∈ Z_{>0} in M. Then ε_sa(A; x) converges to k when δ → 0."`; it should be `Only a lower bound holds. For every rational γ with 0 < γ < k there is δ₀ > 0, depending only on f, D and γ, such that ε_sa(A; x) = ε(A; x) ≥ k − γ for all δ < δ₀ and all such A, M, Λ and x. Equivalently, liminf_{δ→0} ε_sa(A; x) ≥ k, uniformly. This follows by the printed strategy after correcting its intersection estimate as in E9; the strategy provides no upper bound.`. Counterexample with Λ = 0. Let k be a field of characteristic p > 0, X = A²_k, and f: Y → X the blow-up of the origin with exceptional curve E = F. Let M be the sum of the strict transforms of the two axes. Then M ∼ −2E, so M is effective, Cartier, globally generated over X (O_Y(−E) = m·O_Y) and has no exceptional component. Let x = E ∩ (strict transform of the y-axis), so mult_x M = 1 = k. Blow up x, with exceptional curve G and strict transform E′. Then E′² = −2, G² = −1, E′·G = 1 and π*M − tG ∼ −2E′ − (2+t)G, which has degree 2 − t on E′ and t on G. Hence ε(M; x) = 2. At t = 2 the ideal (x, y²) pulls back to O(−E′ − 2G) (charts x = ab, y = b, then a = c, b = cd, giving c²d, and a = ef, b = f, giving f²). So π*M − 2G ∼ −2E′ − 4G is globally generated and ε_sa(M; x) = 2. Taking A = M and Λ = 0 (any D), ε_sa(A; x) = 2 for every δ, not converging to k = 1. The proof aims to show that π*A − (k − γ)E is nef; its coefficient estimate must first be repaired as in E9. The consumers need only the lower bound: Proposition 8.15 (p.173) uses the first assertion ε_sa(M; x) ≥ 1, which is correct, and Claim 8.21 (p.178) needs ε_sa > 2 for k = 3. So the paper's results are unaffected. Checked on the page image and by exact arithmetic. The source says `"Let Δ ≥ 0 be a Q-divisor on X such that (X, Δ) is globally +-regular (completely purely globally +-regular over R, resp.). Suppose that Δ_Y ≥ 0, where K_Y + Δ_Y = f*(K_X + Δ). Take R = k[[t]] with k of characteristic p, X = Y = Spec R, f = id and Δ = S = V(t). Then (X, S) is purely globally +-regular. For a finite normal R′ ⊇ R with uniformizer s and ramification e, the map R → s^{1−e}R′ splits because R′ is R-free and 1 ∉ t·s^{1−e}R′ = sR′. But (X, S) is not globally +-regular: already for the identity cover, a splitting of O_X → O_X(S) = t^{−1}R would send 1 = t·t^{−1} into tR. The cited proof (Proposition 6.26, which applies because R is complete, together with Lemma 4.27 with B′ = B_Y) proves the pure conclusion. The consumer in Theorem 7.14 (p.165) uses the pure conclusion. In arXiv v3 the qualifier is visibly garbled as "( ly globally +-regular, resp.)", so the published wording is a typesetting slip. The source says `Hence the map κ is an isomorphism (Lemma 2.36)`; it should be `Use the following stronger form of Lemma 2.36: for a proper birational f:Y→X of normal integral Noetherian schemes, let D_X be a Q-Cartier integral Weil divisor and D_Y an integral Weil divisor with f_*D_Y=D_X and D_Y≥floor(f*D_X). Then f_*O_Y(D_Y)=O_X(D_X); D_Y need not be Q-Cartier. Apply this to D_X=ceil(L), D_Y=ceil(π*L+A_Y).`. The target divisor in Lemma 4.20 need not be Q-Cartier because Y is only normal. The stronger form is proved by sections as rational functions: if div(g)+D_X≥0, pullback gives div(g)+f*D_X≥0, and integrality gives div(g)+floor(f*D_X)=floor(div(g)+f*D_X)≥0. Thus D_Y≥floor(f*D_X) gives a section upstairs. Conversely push the effective divisor div(g)+D_Y down; normality identifies the resulting sections with O_X(D_X). Then X is smooth affine of genus zero and its boundary has degree two, so it is parabolic by the paper’s definition. The point 0 lies in X(Q) and induces a geometric Galois section. There is no rational boundary point, hence no cuspidal section by the definition on published p.129. The section at 0 is also t-b.l.: after extending to Q(t), the local parameter at 0 supplies the usual birational lift. Thus even restricting the printed cuspidality assertion to t-b.l. sections does not fix it. Schmidt, Homotopy Rational Points of Brauer-Severi Varieties, arXiv 1503.08108v1, Theorem A p.2, provides splitting/existence of rational points for the relevant open variety; it does not turn a degree-two boundary into rational cusps. The source says `“by hypothesis it is cuspidal”; later, ι_U(s) ∈ P_{U,x} for every U ⊂ X.`; it should be `First use the hypothesis that each image is geometric or cuspidal. On the hyperbolic X, it determines a unique associated rational point x of the smooth completion, using geometric-section injectivity together with Stix Theorem 17(1) and (3). If x lies inside X, an open U containing x receives the geometric section at x, not a section in a cuspidal packet indexed by x. Removing x is cofinal among opens, so it does not change the function-field inverse limit. Once x is outside U, disjointness of geometric and cuspidal sections and uniqueness of the associated point force the image to lie in P_{U,x}. The compatibility maps for these packets are the ones already used by the printed inverse-limit argument. Stix, On cuspidal sections of algebraic fundamental groups, Theorem 17 and Remark 18, author PDF p.8, https://www.math.uni-frankfurt.de/~stix/research/preprints/STIXcuspsec20120802homepage.pdf, were directly read. Its injectivity hypothesis holds over finitely generated extensions of Q and their finite extensions: rational points of abelian varieties are finitely generated, hence have no nonzero divisible subgroup; the standard Abel–Jacobi injectivity argument and finite étale neighborhoods give the corresponding geometric-point uniqueness on a hyperbolic curve. - **Misprint** at Lemma 9 proof: published p.140; arXiv 2108.13397v3 p.10, polynomial lift and finite étale extension paragraph. Both directly read.. The source says `“any lifting” q ∈ R[t] of q̄; R′ = R[t]/(q).`; it should be `Choose q̄ monic and q a monic lift of the same degree. Write z=f(p) for the closed point of A¹_k occurring here, and use q̄ to present k(z); this avoids confusing it with the original point p of X_k.`. For R=Q[u]_(u), q̄=T and q=uT²+T, reduction modulo u is indeed q̄. But T and uT+1 are comaximal, since (uT+1)−uT=1, so R[T]/(q) ≃ R×R[1/u] = R×Q(u), which is not finite over R and has more than one maximal ideal. In contrast, a monic lift of the same degree gives a finite free R-algebra, and separability of q̄ makes its discriminant a unit. It is therefore finite étale; its special fiber is the field k(z), so it is local, and an étale local algebra over a DVR is a DVR. This is exactly the extension needed for the curve through z, whose inverse image has a component through the original p. The intended choice is clear and leaves the lemma unchanged. ### Burungale–Kobayashi–Ota, "Rubin's conjecture on local units in the anticyclotomic tower at inert primes", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 3 (`PAPER-BURUNGALE-KOBAYASHI-OTA-21`)

The source says `"(ii) The number of supersingular points in X₀(N)(F_{p²}) that correspond to supersingular elliptic curves over F_{p²} with the Frobenius trace a_{p²} = 2p or −2p and the j-invariant different from 0 and 1728 is at least µ(⌊(p−1)/12⌋ − 3/2 + (−3/p) + ½(−1/p)). That is, a_{p²} = 2p gives parameter p, and a_{p²} = −2p gives parameter −p.`. By (i), φ_q = ±p on A̅ when a_q = ±2p. For a Lubin–Tate group with parameter π, [π] reduces to the q-power Frobenius. So π = φ_q = ±p, not ∓p. The paper's own set-up confirms this. §5.0.1 takes E/Q with a_p = 0, whose reduction has a_{p²} = a_p² − 2p = −2p, and states that Ê ≅ F, the Lubin–Tate group with parameter −p; the printed (ii) would give +p. Honda's type p − a_p x + x² for E/Z_p is x² + p there, whereas the printed (ii) would give −x² + p. The pairing of types with parameters in (ii) is right; only the link to the sign of a_q is reversed. Only "Â is Lubin–Tate" is used afterwards (p.958), so nothing is affected. ### Burungale–Tian, "A rank zero p-converse to a theorem of Gross–Zagier, Kolyvagin and Rubin", Annals of Mathematics 203 (2026), no. 1 (`PAPER-BURUNGALE-TIAN-26`)

- **Error** at Theorem 2.1 and footnote 3, p.4, in arXiv 2506.03465v2 (11 October 2025), the version read; the passage is the same in v1 (4 June 2025) (it affects a stated result). The source says `"Theorem 2.1. Let the notation be as above. Then we have ξ(h²_Q) = ξ((h¹/z)_Q), an equality of ideals in Z_p[[G_{p∞f}]]⊗Q." Footnote 3: "The formulation in Theorem 2.1 is then identical with the one in [11, §7.2]."`; it should be `ξ((h¹/z)_Q) = ξ(h²_Q)·∏_{𝔩|f, 𝔩∤p} ξ(Z_p[[G_{p∞f}/D_𝔩]]_Q), D_𝔩 the decomposition group of 𝔩; equivalently ξ((h¹/z)_Q) = ξ(H²_Q) with H² = lim_{K'} H²(O_{K'}[1/pf], Z_p(1)), which is the module of Johnson-Leung–Kings §7.2. The printed equality holds when every prime factor of f lies above p, and after localizing at height-one primes on components ramified at every 𝔩|f with 𝔩∤p.`. z is generated by the elliptic units of the single modulus p^n f (Kato §15.5), whose projection to a character χ carries ∏_{𝔩|f,𝔩∤p}(1 − χ(𝔩)Frob_𝔩^{−1}) (Johnson-Leung–Kings Lemma 7.7); JLK accordingly pair it with H² over O_K[1/pf]. BT's h² is the class-group limit, which Kato (15.6.2) identifies at height one with H² over O_K[1/p]. By purity, 0 → H²(O[1/p]) → H²(O[1/pf]) → ⊕_{𝔩|f,𝔩∤p} Z_p[[G/D_𝔩]] → 0, and since D_𝔩 has Z_p-rank one each term is torsion but not pseudo-null. On the trivial-character component 1 − Frob_𝔩^{−1} is a non-unit even after inverting p, so the printed equality fails whenever f has a prime factor not above p, and footnote 3's "identical" is false for h². The same imprecision is in Kato's quotation of Rubin (Astérisque 295, Theorem 15.2(2)); Rubin's elliptic units include all moduli g|f. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-PAPER-BURUNGALE-TIAN-26`. Kato's Lemma 15.13 (Astérisque 295, p.264) opens with "assume K is not contained in Q(ζ_{p^∞})". It also assumes that 2 and the order of Δ are invertible in the residue field of p, which is the hypothesis the footnote secures. The excluded case is exactly where the paper applies Theorem 2.6. Theorem 1.2 uses p = 2 and the congruent number curve, with K = Q(i) = Q(ζ_4). Remark 3.6(i) uses p = 3 and K = Q(ζ_3). Kato's 15.14 states the modified lemma, and his proofs of 15.15 and Proposition 15.17 say they go through with it. The equality step of E2 uses only the conclusions of the lemma, so it goes through too. The pullback θ=j*Θ is nef and big because j is generically finite onto its image, and is ample when j is a closed immersion (the nonhyperelliptic case). Now K≡θ+(g−3)V gives all the stated cases. The source says `"Given an integer m, let Ψ^{[m]} = (Ψ^{[m]}_1, ..., Ψ^{[m]}_n) be the power series expansion of the morphism [m] : A → A of multiplication by m in terms of t." "From [11] III.5.3 Proposition 2(i) we get Lemma 7.4. The terms of degree less than m in Ψ^{[m]}_j vanish for each j = 1, ..., n." "Log^t_j(y) = Σ_{m≥1} ((−1)^m/m) · Ψ^{[m]}_j(y), Exp^t_j(x) = Σ_{m≥1} (1/m!) · ψ^{[m]}_j(x)", with ψ^{[m]}_j the homogeneous part of degree m of Ψ^{[m]}_j.`; it should be `Replace the multiplication-map series by the coefficientwise finite differences Δ_m(t) = Σ_{i=0}^m (−1)^(m−i) binom(m,i)[i](t), for m≥1. These formulas have identity linear term, are mutual inverses, and satisfy the claimed denominator bounds. This repair is verified here by formal polynomial interpolation; no claim is made to have directly read Bourbaki III.5.3–5.4.`. For the printed definition, [m](t) has linear term mt in every characteristic-zero formal group. Thus Lemma 7.4 fails and the proposed logarithm’s linear terms are (−1)^m t, which do not tend to zero. To verify the repair at all orders, let L and E be the normalized formal logarithm and exponential over K. The degree-d part of [z](t)=E(zL(t)) is polynomial in z of degree at most d. Newton interpolation at z=0 gives [z]=Σ_m binom(z,m)Δ_m coefficientwise. Differentiating at zero gives L=Σ_m(−1)^(m−1)Δ_m/m. The leading z^m coefficient in degree m is E_m(t), so [Δ_m]_m=m!E_m and Δ_m has no terms of degree below m. Since Δ_m is an integral linear combination of integral [i], these identities prove the bounds of Lemmas 7.5–7.6. Exact computation through degree four with L(t)=t+at²+bt³+ct⁴ verifies both identities; the printed exponential’s cubic coefficient is 6a²−4b, whereas E has 2a²−b. The all-order interpolation argument, not that finite check alone, establishes the repair. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-PAPER-CARO-PASTEN-23`. ### Česnavičius, "Purity for the Brauer group", Duke Mathematical Journal (2019) (`PAPER-CESNAVICIUS-19`)

- **Gap** at Proposition 2.2, proof of (2.2.2), p.4 of arXiv 1711.06456v4 (1 December 2018, SHA-256 a62a12bbe26595aec89d31d24d46774a1ee3eff73c08da0febf5a2b472118709); same passage in the author manuscript dated 27 November 2018, served at both the old Paris-Saclay and current Sorbonne sites (SHA-256 4187331ead5a5246acba1c032a2574ffd6ac9ee6fe1a72bb09d46e2e9f9b97a1). Duke Math. J. 168 (2019), 1461–1486, DOI 10.1215/00127094-2018-0057, remains uncollated. (it affects the proof). The source says `“so, by [Gir71, III.3.2.2], the map” H¹_et(V,G) → H¹_et(V,Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′})) “is injective.”`; it should be `For full injectivity, restrict Proposition 2.2 to commutative G; this covers both uses, Proposition 2.3 and Corollary 2.4. Alternatively, retain arbitrary affine smooth G but weaken the conclusion to triviality of the fibre over the trivial torsor. To retain the original full noncommutative statement, supply surjectivity of (^P H)(V) → (^P X)(V) for every G-torsor P over V, where H=Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′}), X=H/G, the groups are twisted by conjugation and X by the induced G-action.`. Affineness gives X(R)=X(V), and H¹(R,G)=1 lifts each X(R)-point to H(R). Thus H(V)→X(V) is surjective. The torsor boundary sequence identifies H(V)\X(V) with only the neutral fibre of H¹(V,G)→H¹(V,H). For a torsor P the fibre through [P] instead identifies with (^P H)(V)\(^P X)(V): twisting sends [P] to the trivial torsor. These twists are initially defined over V, and no extension of them to affine R-schemes is established. If P itself extended, hypothesis (2) would make it trivial, leaving precisely the other fibres untreated. This fibre calculation is also explicit for group cohomology in Serre, Galois Cohomology, I.§5.3 Proposition 35 and §5.4 Proposition 36, Corollaries 1–2, pp.49–51 (the inherited §5.5 Corollary 2 citation was incorrect). If G is commutative, so is H; the H¹ map is a group homomorphism, so its trivial kernel proves injectivity. Proposition 2.3 applies this to the commutative quotient Res(T)/T, and Corollary 2.4 to the torus T. Therefore this gap does not obstruct these applications or their downstream purity arguments. No counterexample to the geometric proposition is asserted. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-PAPER-CESNAVICIUS-19`. ### François Charles, "Birational boundedness for holomorphic symplectic varieties, Zarhin's trick for K3 surfaces, and the Tate conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), no. 2 (`PAPER-CHARLES-16`)

- **Error** at Corollary 2.8 and its proof, pp.499–500, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 487–526 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 3425f269…40e2) (it affects a stated result). The source says `"If p > 0, we can find nonnegative integers λ and t such that 0 < λ ≤ v² and |disc(NS(X))| = p^t λ |disc(NS(M_H(v)))|." Proof: "… we have a natural injection of lattices with torsion cokernel Zv ⊕ (v^⊥ ∩ N(X)) ↪ N(X). Since the discriminant of Zv ⊕ v^⊥ is v² disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X)), this implies by the same argument that |disc(N(X))| ≤ v² |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))|."`; it should be `λ need not be an integer. With I = [N(X) : Zv ⊕ (v^⊥ ∩ N(X))], one has |disc NS(X)| = p^t (v²/I²) |disc NS(M_H(v))| with t ≥ 0. So λ = v²/I² is a positive rational number with λ ≤ v², and I divides v² because v is primitive. For p ∤ v², for example v² = 2 and p ≥ 3 as in the applications, λ is still a p-adic unit, which is what the later arguments use.`. Take v = (1, 0, −1), the Mukai vector of ideal sheaves of length-two subschemes, so M_H(v) = X^[2]. It satisfies condition (C): it is primitive, of rank 1, v² = 2, and gcd(1, 0, −1) = 1. Then v^⊥ ∩ N(X) = NS(X) ⊕ Z(1, 0, 1) with (1, 0, 1)² = −2, so |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))| = 2|disc NS(X)|. The proof's first step gives |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))| = p^r |disc NS(M_H(v))|. Hence |disc NS(X)| = ½ p^r |disc NS(M_H(v))|, which is not of the form p^t λ with λ a positive integer when p is odd. The proof passes from the equality disc(Zv ⊕ K) = I² disc N(X) to an integer multiplier without controlling I, here I = 2. The inequality stated for p = 0 is correct. Checked on the page image. The source says `"Proposition 2.9. Let d be a positive integer, and let Λ be a rank 2 positive definite sublattice of Λ_2d. There exists a positive integer N and nonzero integers a, b such that if m is any positive integer satisfying (i) m = 1[N]; (ii) m is prime to a and b, and both a and b are quadratic residues modulo m; then there exists a primitive embedding of Λ into Λ_2md." It is primitive, since (x, y, z) ↦ (z, y − z) retracts it, and its Gram matrix [[2, 1], [1, 2dk²]] is positive definite.`. The proof starts from a primitive embedding Λ ⊂ Λ_2d, which the statement does not provide, and the statement fails for non-primitive Λ. In Λ_2 = ⟨2⟩ ⊕ U, the sublattice Λ generated by 2h and 2(e + f) has Gram matrix diag(8, 8). Take m = 1, which satisfies (i) and (ii) for every N, a, b. A primitive embedding of Λ into Λ_2 would give a 2-dimensional subspace of Λ_2/2Λ_2 = F_2³ on which the half-norm Q(x, y, z) = x² + yz vanishes, since Λ has all half-norms even. The nonzero zeros of Q are (0,0,1), (0,1,0) and (1,1,1), and each pairwise sum has Q = 1, so no such plane exists. Noted by the extraction (items 38–41), which also gave the primitive choice above. ### William Y. Chen, "Nonabelian level structures, Nielsen equivalence, and Markoff triples", Annals of Mathematics 199 (2024), no. 1 (`PAPER-CHEN-24`)

- **Error** at §5.6, p. 83, Proposition 5.6.1(a) (arXiv v2). The source says `There is a unique unramified point in f^{−1}(0). Every other point is ramified with index 3, so |f^{−1}(0)| = (p(p+3)−3)/3 if p ≡ 1 mod 4, (p(p−3)−3)/3 if p ≡ 3 mod 4`; it should be `|f^{−1}(0)| = 1 + (deg f − 1)/3 = (p(p+3)+2)/3 for p ≡ 1 mod 4 and (p(p−3)+2)/3 for p ≡ 3 mod 4.`. The printed expression is never an integer: deg f = |X*(p)| = p(p±3) ≡ p² ≡ 1 (mod 3) for every prime p ≠ 3, so 3 never divides deg f − 3. The sentence preceding the display gives the correct count, one unramified point together with (deg f − 1)/3 points of ramification index 3. Computing the γ₀-orbits on X*(p) directly confirms it: for p = 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 the fibre has 14, 10, 30, 70, 114, 102, 154 points and γ₀ has exactly one fixed point in each case, matching (deg f + 2)/3 = 14, 10, 30, 70, 114, 102, 154 and not (deg f − 3)/3 = 37/3, 25/3, 85/3, 205/3, 337/3, 301/3, 457/3. Subgroups of the cyclic group ⟨z′⟩ form a chain, so a nontrivial intersection lies in every nontrivial subgroup of ⟨z′⟩. A concrete configuration: in ℤ/27 × ℤ/3 with ℓ = 3, k = 3, j = 1, z′ = (1,0) and u′ = (3,1), |u′| = 9 = ℓ^{k−j}. By Theorem 2.5.2(4) the coarse fibre of M → M(1) over j ≠ 0, 1728 is O/⟨γ_{−I}⟩ for the orbit O = Out⁺(Π)·ϕ, as in the proof of Theorem 4.10.5 and in Corollary 4.12.5, which states the congruence for orbits on Epi^ext/⟨γ_{−I}⟩. The corrected point has multiplicities n_v(10)=1,n_v(9)=0,n_v(8)=2, as needed there. ### Jean-Marc Couveignes, "Enumerating number fields", Annals of Mathematics 192 (2020), no. 2 (`PAPER-COUVEIGNES-20`)

- **Misprint** at §3, published p.493 (PDF p.7), Annals of Mathematics 192 (2020), 487–497; arXiv 1907.13617v1/v2 p.5; HAL hal-02375397v1 PDF p.7 (manuscript p.6).. The source says `We set L = 𝓛 ⊗_Q R as the underlying R-vector space`; it should be `L = 𝓛 ⊗_Z R, the real span of 𝓛 in V_R (equivalently (𝓛 ⊗_Z Q) ⊗_Q R).`. The preceding definition makes 𝓛 the kernel of integral polynomial evaluation in the finite free Z-module V_Z. Its rank ℓ = C(d+r,d) − n is positive: the standing assumptions give ℓ ≥ nr ≥ 1. A basis vector of a nonzero finite free Z-module is not divisible by 2, so this Z-module admits no compatible Q-module structure. Thus the displayed tensor product needs Z as its base ring. Extending the integral evaluation matrix to R identifies 𝓛 ⊗_Z R with its real kernel and real span in V_R. This supplies the space used for orthogonality and successive minima. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-PAPER-COUVEIGNES-20`. The source says `"For a cusp [𝒜] ∈ C₀(𝔠, 𝔫), the normalized constant term c_𝒜(0, W_k(ψ_𝔓, 1)) equals 𝔱 · τ(ψ)/N𝔠₀^k · sgn(N(−c)) ψ(𝔠_𝒜) · L(ψ^{−1}, 1−k)/2^n · ∏_{𝔭|𝔓}(1 − ψ(𝔭)/N𝔭^k) · ∏_{𝔩∈J_𝔱}(1 − ψ(𝔩)) · ∏_{𝔩∈J_𝔱^c}(1 − N𝔩^k)."`; it should be `Delete the leading 𝔱: c_𝒜(0, W_k(ψ_𝔓, 1)) = τ(ψ)/N𝔠₀^k · sgn(N(−c)) ψ(𝔠_𝒜) · L(ψ^{−1}, 1−k)/2^n · ∏_{𝔭|𝔓}(1 − ψ(𝔭)/N𝔭^k) · ∏_{𝔩∈J_𝔱}(1 − ψ(𝔩)) · ∏_{𝔩∈J_𝔱^c}(1 − N𝔩^k).`. The auxiliary ideal 𝔱=∏_{𝔩∈T}𝔩 in §8.1 is not a scalar. More decisively, applying Proposition 8.4 to Definition 8.2 gives the common scalar prefactor times Σ_{𝔪|𝔱} μ(𝔪)∏_{𝔩∈J_𝔪}ψ(𝔩)∏_{𝔩∈J_𝔪^c}(N𝔩)^k. - **Gap** at Equation (2) and the paragraph after it, p.2, and Corollary 1.3, p.3; compared with Marshall 2012, §2.1, equation (4), in arXiv 2201.11190v2 (15 February 2024, SHA-256 d71e9d3f…2614), the version the extraction read; the published Annals text (200 (2024), 123–152) was not collated (it affects the proof). The source says `"… the Eichler–Shimura isomorphism summarized as dim_C H_c^{r1+r2}(Y(K_f), W_k) = 2^{r1} dim_C S_k(K_f) (2) in [Mar12]." "This space corresponds to the first compactly supported cohomology …" Corollary 1.3: "dim_C H^n_c(Y(K_f), W_k) ∼_{K_f} k" for n = 1, 2.`; it should be `In [Mar12] H_c denotes cuspidal cohomology (inside ordinary cohomology), which is what (2) describes. For compactly supported cohomology, Corollary 1.3 needs a boundary estimate: for c cusps and n = 1, 2, |dim H^n_c − dim H^n| ≤ 3c (a cusp-torus Koszul computation with dimensions (1,2,1)), with the trivial coefficient system treated separately.`. Fu attributes (2) to Marshall but reads Marshall's H_c as compactly supported cohomology. The difference is a boundary term bounded in terms of the number of cusps, so the two-sided growth in Corollary 1.3 survives, but the paper does not supply that step. Converted from the extraction's older-form finding S1 ("source-convention mismatch; boundary proof required"): finding: Marshall defines H_c as cuspidal cohomology inside ordinary cohomology, whereas Fu describes it as compactly supported. Marshall also states the displayed dimension identity for nontrivial coefficient systems. Resolution recorded there: Use the cuspidal injection for the upper bound. For the full compact-support interpretation retain an explicit boundary long-exact-sequence calculation and Poincare-Lefschetz comparison, treating the trivial coefficient separately. The two-sided Bianchi result uses the specified base-change lower-bound level class. The continuation gives a cusp-torus Koszul argument with dimensions(1,2,1) and resulting |dim H_c^i−dim H^i|<=3c for i=1,2 and c cusps; its geometric and chain-comparison imports remain explicit. The source says `"So assume 9|k, in which case (3,0,0) is a non-singular solution modulo 9 and so lifts to solutions modulo 3ⁿ, n ≥ 2." … "So assume k ≡ 1 (mod 4) and we find the non-singular solution (1,0,0) modulo 4 … This then lifts to higher powers of 2."`; it should be `The two lifts exist only in part of the stated classes: every x ≡ (3,0,0) mod 9 has M(x) ≡ 9 mod 27, and every x ≡ (1,0,0) mod 4 has M(x) ≡ 1 mod 8. Complete the argument with further points. For p = 2 and k ≡ 5 mod 8, use (x₁, 0, 2) with x₁² = k − 4 ≡ 1 mod 8, a 2-adic square. For p = 3, use (3,0,0) when k ≡ 9 mod 27; when k ≡ 18 mod 27, use (3y, 3, 0) with y² = (k − 9)/9 ≡ 1 mod 3; when 27 | k, use (3, 3, x₃) with x₃ a root of x₃² − 9x₃ + 18 − k, whose discriminant 9 + 4k = 9(1 + 4k/9) is a 3-adic square. Each is an exact ℤ_p-point, since the required square roots exist in ℤ₂, resp. ℤ₃.`. The gradient of M at (3,0,0) is 6 and at (1,0,0) it is 2, so the lifting needs M(a) ≡ k modulo 27, resp. 8 (Hensel's lemma in the form ‖F(a)‖ < ‖F′(a)‖²). A direct check confirms the two failing classes, k ≡ 18 mod 27 and k ≡ 5 mod 8 (e.g. k = 18, 5). Counting solutions modulo 3⁴ and 2⁶ confirms that Proposition 6.1 itself holds in every admissible class. Confirmed by `REV-PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22`. The source says `Theorem 4.4(2): "The Tits index Δ_0(G) is the smallest subset of Δ(G_{F_s}) which is stable under the ⋆-action of Gal(F_s/F) and such that Δ_0(G) ⊂ Δ_0(G_{F_U}) for each U ∈ U and Δ_0(G) ⊂ Δ_0(G_{F_P}) for each P ∈ P." Corollary 4.5(2) is worded the same way. The proof defines Θ by the same condition and uses "Θ ⊂ Δ_0(G_{F_U}) so that Z(F_U) ≠ ∅".`; it should be `After the stated identifications of simple roots, Δ₀(G) is the smallest ⋆-stable subset Θ containing every relevant local Δ₀(G_L). Use Δ₀(G_L) ⊂ Θ, not Θ ⊂ Δ₀(G_L), to deduce Par_Θ(G)(L) ≠ ∅. Apply this correction to all four HAL statements and their proofs, and to the arXiv counterparts.`. In the paper’s order-preserving convention, Δ₀(G) is the type of a minimal parabolic. Par_Θ(G)(L) has a point iff Δ₀(G_L) ⊂ Θ (with Θ stable over L); extension of fields can shrink this type. Let Θ be the smallest global ⋆-stable set containing the local types. The global type contains them, so Θ ⊂ Δ₀(G). The corrected local criterion and part (1) give a global Par_Θ point, hence Δ₀(G) ⊂ Θ. The printed smallest set contained in every local type would be empty, including when the group is anisotropic. ### Hacon–Witaszek, "On the relative minimal model program for fourfolds in positive and mixed characteristic", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2023) (`PAPER-HACON-WITASZEK-23`)

- **Error** at Lemma 2.2, second paragraph, p.5 of the published version (arXiv v2 Lemma 2.2, p.6) (it affects a stated result). The source says `index of K_X`; it should be `Use the local Cartier index of K_X + S at P, rather than the index of K_X. This is the log index of the localized plt surface pair; it gives the denominator of the different and kills local Weil divisor classes.`. Over k = F_7, take X = Spec k[x,y,z]/(xy-z²), S = V(x,z), and P the vertex. The two resolution charts (u,uv²,uv) and (st²,s,st), in coordinates (x,y,z), are crepant and have one exceptional (-2)-curve E. Thus K_X is Cartier. The strict transform S′ meets E once, and f*S=S′+E/2; the snc pullback S′+E/2 proves that (X,S) is plt. Since div(x)=2S and (x,z) needs two generators at P, S is not Cartier. Adjunction gives different P/2. Hence the printed m=1 fails, whereas index(K_X+S)=2 works. More generally, for the plt surface chain with determinant d, the different coefficient is 1-1/d and d annihilates local divisor classes, forcing the log index to equal d. This is the surface adjunction calculation, not a claim about the canonical index. Lemma 4.2 only needs the standard-coefficient different. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-PAPER-HACON-WITASZEK-23`. - **Error** at Lemma 2.16, p.13 of the published version (arXiv v2 Lemma 2.16, p.14) (it affects a stated result). The source says `all these discrepancies`; it should be `For the version needed in Proposition 2.15, fix a finite set I ⊂ [0,1), require coeff(B) ⊂ I, and formulate both the bound of m distinct exceptional log discrepancies and the conclusion on the minimal resolution of the surface germ. The printed statement says minimal log resolution; the source proof and this repair concern the minimal resolution. No finiteness theorem for all discrepancies on all higher models is asserted.`. On the A1 surface over F_7, put B=bC for the ruling C=V(x,z) and rational 0<b<1/2. Its one-curve minimal resolution is also a log resolution of this pair, and K_{S′}+bC′+(b/2)E=f*(K_S+bC). Thus the exceptional discrepancy is -b/2 (log discrepancy 1-b/2), varying infinitely even for b=1/n, n≥3. The snc model is 1/2-lc. There is one exceptional value, so m=1 under the exceptional convention; if strict boundary components are counted, the uniform bound m=2 still disproves the statement. For the repaired minimal-resolution version, write T=f^{-1}_*B and a_i for exceptional log discrepancies. Minimality and negativity give 0≤1-a_i. Adjunction gives T.C_i=2r_i+a_i C_i²-Σ_{j≠i}(1-a_j)C_j.C_i<2r_i≤8. With finite I these nonnegative sums of integer multiples of positive elements of I lie in a finite set. Together with the source’s bounded intersection coefficients, convexity and compression of constant runs on the at-most-three-legged graph, only finitely many bounded-size linear systems remain. Negative definiteness gives uniqueness. The fixed boundary of a flip sequence supplies I, so this repair addresses the cited use in Proposition 2.15. Merely bounding arbitrary real right-hand sides would not prove finiteness. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-PAPER-HACON-WITASZEK-23`. The remaining generic vertex Z is closed in T and disjoint from that fibre, so codim(Z∩X,X)≥3. The ruling D=V(x,z) is Cartier on T\Z, restricts to a Cartier divisor on X, and does not contain X. Over K=Frac(R), use the small resolution xt=zs, wt=ys in N×P¹. On its charts z=ux,y=uw and x=vz,w=vy, with v=1/u, the strict transform of D has equations x and z. The source says `𝒜|_X = A`; it should be `Choose Q-Cartier representatives with 𝒜|_X ≡ A and ℋ|_X ≡ H; clear denominators when constructing sections. For large m choose a primitive section of a divisible multiple of mℋ+𝒜, giving an effective 𝒟 that omits X and has 𝒟|_X ≡ mH+A. Theorem 6.1 defines N¹ as Pic⊗Q modulo numerical equivalence. Its surjectivity supplies rational numerical classes, not specified line bundles or integral representatives of prescribed classes. The proof of (2a), p.31, correctly uses ≡; p.33 uses literal equality. The needed construction can be made numerically: H is nef and big on X, hence its lift is nef and big on the generic fibre; choose m so mℋ+𝒜 is generically big. For a sufficiently divisible multiple L, the nonzero finite torsion-free R-module H⁰(𝒳,L) has a primitive section. The kernel of restriction to X is πH⁰(𝒳,L), so the primitive section does not vanish identically on X. Its divisor restricts with the desired numerical class and is negative on the chosen ray because H.Σ=0 and A.Σ<0. The fixed-resolution hypothesis permits a sufficiently small boundary coefficient. These steps require neither completeness nor H²(X,O_X)=0. They do not by themselves identify the prescribed special flop or prove numerical descent after the perturbed step; those are separate proof obligations. The finding is retained as a local proof gap, not a counterexample to the theorem. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-PAPER-HACON-WITASZEK-23`. ### Harpaz–Wittenberg, "Zéro-cycles sur les espaces homogènes et problème de Galois inverse", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020) (`PAPER-HARPAZ-WITTENBERG-20`)

- **Gap** at Remarque4.5, author manuscript and arXiv1802.09605v2, PDF17; compare standing assumptions at the start of §4, PDF15, and Theorem4.2, PDF16–17. Journal wording unverified. (it affects the proof). The source says `le théorème 4.2 (i)`; it should be `Make explicit the generalization of Theorem4.2(i) used here: the printed theorem carries a rationally connected generic-fibre hypothesis which the remark has not established. Adding rational connectedness of X is a sufficient restricted repair, not a demonstrated necessary hypothesis for the original implication. To retain the full implication, justify the section-based fibration variant; Proposition3.3(i) already provides a geometric section without rational connectedness.`. Theorem4.2 inherits the rational-connectedness assumption fixed for §4 on PDF15. In Remark4.5 the new fibration π′ compactifies universal torsors of V; after geometric base change such a torus torsor is birational to V times a split torus. The remark does not establish rational connectedness for these fibres. This verifies a literal theorem-application scope mismatch. It does not disprove the implication. Proposition3.3(i), PDF14, obtains a section by splitting a free character-module sequence and has no rational-connectedness hypothesis. Moreover Sko90 Theorem1 uses a geometric section condition along general lines, rather than rational connectedness itself. Thus the earlier assertion that the missing rational-connectedness condition changes a stated result was too strong; a fully stated extension of the cited fibration argument is the remaining proof obligation. Demarche BMgroupes.pdf §8, PDF26, explicitly defines Q_(2^n) for n≥2 and discusses n=2 as a valid rational case. At m=2 the presentation gives x²=1 and y²=x, hence x=y², y⁴=1 and the group C4; it is deliberately included, not a reason to exclude m=2. At m=1 the exponent 2^(m−2) is not an integer, so that presentation does not define Q2. The earlier correction m≥3 and its appeal to the known cases m≤4 unnecessarily discarded Demarche’s cyclic endpoint. No weak-approximation conclusion for the actual quaternion groups is changed. For p = 2, (Z/2)^× = (Z/1)^× is trivial and the proof shows the action is trivial (n ≤ 3 by Lemma 4.6; 4 ≤ n ≤ 6 because M^{−1} is conjugate to M), so e = 1, not 2; the divisibility step holds only for odd p. The lemma is used only to make the cyclotomic character χ : G → (Z/e)^× trivial when μ_p ⊂ k and to choose L ⊇ μ_e, which is unchanged for e = 1 since μ₂ ⊂ k; the main theorems are unaffected. For v real and p = 2, the proof of Proposition 5.3 goes through: the split case is group theory, and in the non-split case H¹(R, Hom(P/Z, μ₂)) × H¹(R, P/Z) → H²(R, μ₂) is perfect (Tate duality over R), so cup product with [γ] is onto.`. The global argument needs local solvability at every place, but Proposition 5.3 is stated only for non-archimedean fields; the real places with p = 2 need an argument, which is short. Noted by the extraction (items 91, 117). Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-PAPER-HARPAZ-WITTENBERG-23`. A general criterion still requires its own hypotheses to be proved; replacing the citation alone is not a proof.`. The cited survey theorem assumes a shrunken alcove. In split adjoint A2 take λ=ω2∨, x=s2s1, y=1. The published construction gives J=∅, J′={s1}, x′=s2, z=s1, γ=λ, y′=1 and a=s1s2. On the negative base alcove u<0, v<0, u+v>−1, w sends (u,v) to (v−1,1−u−v), with positive-root ranges (−2,−1),(1,2),(0,1). The seed a t^γ sends it to (1−u−v,u), whose second coordinate lies in the critical strip (−1,0). Both finite factors have full support. This disproves applicability of the cited theorem, not nonemptiness or the main result. The extraction’s stronger claim that every nonregular γ causes failure is false and is not retained. The corrected formula matches direct counts in all 2,816 tested cases (p ∈ {3, 5, 7} with all unit u_1, u_2, u_3 and m ≤ 3, and p = 2 with q_0 ∈ {xy, x² + xy + y²}), and the printed one fails in 2,112 of them; the lemma feeds the p | ω formulas of Proposition B.5. - **Error** at published version, Forum Math. Pi 14 (2026) e14 (Cambridge repository and publisher PDFs; full hashes in the companion report); Remark 4.1.5(2), p.31. The source says `Consider the normal surface X = Spec k[x, y, x]/(x² + xyz).`; it should be `X = Spec k[x, y, z]/(x² + xyz), which is not normal: x² + xyz = x(x + yz), so X is the union of two smooth surfaces meeting along x = yz = 0, and its local ring at the origin is not a domain.`. In k[x,y,z]/(x(x+yz)), the two factors give nonzero zero divisors even in the local ring at the origin; a normal local ring must be a domain. Both components are graphs isomorphic to A². Since the defining equation has initial term x², the tangent space has dimension 3 and the reduced tangent cone is the plane x=0. In the domain k[[t]], f(f+gh)=0 forces f=0 or f=-gh; with g,h in (t), f has no linear term. The y- and z-axis arcs span exactly that plane. The source says `Hence, the base change of c by the map Ŵ(R_G/𝔞_G) → Ŵ(k[[u]]) → Ŵ(k[ε]) induced by a*_(2): R_G → k[[u]] → k[ε] preserves the tensors s̃_a.`; it should be `The base change of c by the map Ŵ(R_G/𝔞_G) → Ŵ(k[ε]) induced by a*_(2): R_G → k[[u]] → k[ε], which factors through R_G/𝔞_G.`. There is in general no factorization of the chosen a*:R_G→k[[u]] through R_G/𝔞_G. On the smooth GL₂ Grassmannian chart R_G=W(k)[[x]], the curve x↦u sends x²∈𝔞_G to u²≠0. By contrast a*_(2) sends it to ε²=0 and kills π_E, so it always factors through R_G/𝔞_G. Functoriality of Zink's Witt rings then gives the single map to Ŵ(k[ε]) already used in the preceding tensor-product formula. Constant curves can factor through the quotient; the defect is the asserted intermediate arrow for an arbitrary chosen curve, not nonexistence for every possible curve. - **Error** at Published proof of Lemma 7.2.8, p.79, definition of Bil_Hc(V) and assertion that U_σ is open; arXiv v3 p.82. (it affects the proof). The source says `Bil_Hc(V) is the space of all invariant F-bilinear forms; the subset U_σ consisting of polarization forms is then asserted to be open.`; it should be `Work in Alt_Hc(V), the F-linear subspace of invariant alternating forms. Its real extension is the product of the corresponding local alternating-form spaces. Each polarization cone U_σ is nonempty and open in that subspace, and the rational points of Alt_Hc(V), viewed as a Q-vector space, are dense in its real extension. Thus choose Ψ there with all components polarizations and take Tr_(F/Q)Ψ as in the paper. The conclusion of Lemma 7.2.8 is unchanged.`. Take F=Q, G=GSp₂≅GL₂ with its usual Shimura datum, Hc=SL₂, and the fundamental Hodge embedding on V=Q²⊗Q² where G acts on the first factor and trivially on the multiplicity factor. With J the standard alternating form, invariant bilinear forms are J⊗A for arbitrary A∈M₂(Q). Such a form is alternating iff A is symmetric; with compatible sign convention the polarization cone is A symmetric positive definite. This is open in Sym₂(R), not in M₂(R): arbitrarily small nonsymmetric perturbations of I leave the cone. In general, h_σ(U(1))⊂Hc_(R,σ) makes b(x,h_σ(i)y) symmetric for invariant alternating b; positive definiteness is open there. Nonemptiness is supplied by the Cartan-involution polarization argument cited in the paper. Deligne 1979 §1.1.10 (p.253) explicitly requires symmetry after applying h(i); §1.1.18(a) (p.256) provides existence, not automatic alternation of every invariant bilinear form. Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-PAPER-KISIN-PAPPAS-ZHOU-26`. The source says `"Lemma 5.2.5. Let y ∈ M_λ(F_q) and assume ṫ_λ ∈ G(F_q[[t]]). Then there exists g ∈ G(F_q[[t]]) such that g ṫ_λ L^+G = y in FL_G."`; it should be `"… assume ṫ_λ ∈ G(F_q((t))) …"`. ṫ_λ lifts the translation t_λ of the Iwahori–Weyl group, and for λ ≠ 0 it is not in the positive loop group G(F_q[[t]]). The proof works with G(k[[t]]) ∩ ṫ_λ G(k[[t]]) ṫ_λ^{−1} ⊂ G(k((t))). The application in the proof of Proposition 5.2.3 chooses "the lift ṫ_λ ∈ G(F_q((t)))". Noted by the extraction (item C08). Confirmed by `REV-ERRATA-PAPER-KISIN-ZHOU-25`. ### Koymans–Pagano, "On Stevenhagen's conjecture", Acta Mathematica (`PAPER-KOYMANS-PAGANO`)

- **Misprint** at §1 (pp. 1–3), §2.1 (p. 11), §3.2 (pp. 23, 24, 26): typographical slips (arXiv v1). The source says `(a) p. 1: "Unbeknownst of the work of these Indian mathematicians"; (b) p. 2: "𝒟⁻(X) ≫ X/(log X)^{0.62}"; (c) p. 3: "Gerth's [21] extension fo the Cohen–Lenstra heuristics"; (d) p. 11: "The final conclusion is now a trivial consequences of such a splitting"; (e) p. 23: "This leaves two possibilities for the character χ from the larger group G₂"; (f) p. 24: "Suppose that that there exists a place w"; (g) p. 26, twice: "w(α_{1,A}) · Art(v, L(ψ₂)/ℚ))." and "Art(v, L(ψ₂)/ℚ)) if v ∈ R̃am(ℚ(χ₁)/ℚ)"`; it should be `(a) "Unbeknownst to"; (b) "|𝒟⁻(X)| ≫ X/(log X)^{0.62}"; (c) "extension of"; (d) "a trivial consequence"; (e) "two possibilities for the co-restriction of χ to the larger group G₂"; (f) "Suppose that there exists"; (g) "Art(v, L(ψ₂)/ℚ)" with one closing parenthesis`. 𝒟⁻(X) is defined on p. 2 as a set of integers, and the bound is on its cardinality, as in the limits |𝒟⁻(X)|/|𝒟(X)| just above. In (e), χ is a given character of the index-2 subgroup G₁; the next sentence says that equation (3.2) 'forces the co-restriction of χ to be in the set {χ′, χ′ + ε}'. The others are a wrong preposition, a dropped letter, a stray plural, a doubled word and an unmatched parenthesis. All are harmless. Confirmed by `REV-PAPER-KOYMANS-PAGANO`. - **Misprint** at §4, Remark 4.3, p. 29 (arXiv v1). The source says `To see this, fix some j ∈ [s] and apply the operator d_{x₀} to equation (4.2). Then we get ∑_{∅≠T⊆[s]−{i}} χ_{{p_k(1)p_k(2):k∈T}}(σ) · (−1)^{|T|+1+χ_{x₀}(σ)} · (∑_{x∈C_T} ψ_{s−|T|}(x)(τ)) by Proposition 2.9. Now evaluate the resulting expression at (σ, τ) satisfying χ_{p_j(1)p_j(2)}(σ) = 1 and χ_{p_k(1)p_k(2)}(σ) = 0 for all k ∈ [s] − {i, j}. This gives ∑_{x∈C_{{i,j}}} ψ_{s−2}(x) = 0.`; it should be `fix some j ∈ [s] − {i} … ∑_{∅≠T⊆[s]−{i}} χ_{{p_k(1)p_k(2):k∈T}}(σ) · (−1)^{|T|+1+χ_{x₀}(σ)} · (∑_{x∈C_{T∪{i}}} ψ_{s−1−|T|}(x)(τ)) = 0 for σ with χ_{p_i(1)p_i(2)}(σ) = 0; evaluate at such σ that also satisfy χ_{p_j(1)p_j(2)}(σ) = 1 and χ_{p_k(1)p_k(2)}(σ) = 0 for k ∈ [s] − {i, j}`. Equation (4.2) is ∑_{x∈C_{p_i(2)}} ψ_{s−1}(x) = 0, a sum over the (s − 1)-dimensional face C_{p_i(2)}, so Proposition 2.9 on that face produces its sub-faces C_{T∪{i}} and the index s − 1 − |T|, and the left side is d_{x₀} of 0. Proposition 2.9 needs the p(1)-vertex of the summed cube as base point, and x₀ ∉ C_{p_i(2)}; extending the family by 0 to C adds only terms with i ∈ T, which vanish when χ_{p_i(1)p_i(2)}(σ) = 0. - **Gap** at §4, the sentence before Lemma 4.5 (p. 29) and Lemma 4.5(ii) (p. 30) (arXiv v1). The source says `p. 29: 'When we apply Lemma 4.5 later, Proposition 4.4 will guarantee that the decomposition groups of the field ℚ({√x : x ∈ S}) are indeed cyclic.' p. 30, Lemma 4.5(ii): 'Then the ramification index of p in ∏_{x∈S} L(ψ_{k+1}(x)) equals 2. Now assume that all decomposition groups of K/ℚ are cyclic. Then, if p ramifies in ℚ(√x) for every x ∈ S, the residue field degree of p in ∏_{x∈S} L(ψ_k(x)) equals 1.'`; it should be `'Now assume that the decomposition group of p in K/ℚ is cyclic' (equivalently, ℚ_p(√x) is the same field for all x ∈ S). This local statement is what Proposition 4.4 provides, and it is what the conclusion uses; the global claim on p. 29 is false at a prime p_i(h), where the decomposition group of the whole of K need not be cyclic. The ramification index in the first sentence does equal 2, so nothing is wrong there.`. The applications check cyclicity only at p, via Proposition 4.4: S = C − {x₀} with p | d₀, S = C_{p_i(2)} with p = p_i(2) and S = C_{(p_i(1),p_j(2))} with p = p_i(1) (pp. 32–33), and S = C with p | a (p. 37). For S = C − {x₀} and s ≥ 2, K contains √x₀ and √(p_i(1)p_i(2)), so its decomposition group at p_i(1) is cyclic only if d₀p_i(2)∏_{j≠i}p_j(1) is a square modulo p_i(1), which Definition 4.2 does not impose. The local hypothesis suffices: Up(p) is 2-torsion in the narrow class group, so ψ_k(x) = 2ψ_{k+1}(x) pairs trivially with it and i_p(L(ψ_k(x))) ⊆ ℚ_p(√x), one ramified quadratic field for all x. 'Equals 2' fails for trivial raw cocycles (L(0) = ℚ); only e ≤ 2 is ever used. Confirmed by `REV-PAPER-KOYMANS-PAGANO`. For s = 1 the base set {χ_{p_j(1)p_j(2)} : j ∈ [s] − {i}} of the 4-tuple on p. 33 is empty, but Theorem 3.2 assumes |A| = n ≥ 1, its proof uses n ≥ 1 at ∞ (p. 26), and with A = ∅ one has L(ψ) = M(ψ), so its Artin symbols in Gal(L(ψ)/M(ψ)) ≅ 𝔽₂ make no sense. Moreover for s = 1, M(E) = ℚ(√a), so the first half of (4.7) is exactly the splitting of p₁(1) to be proved, while the 'equivalent' condition over sets T of size 2 is vacuous.
