- **Misprint** at Published §4.1, definition of a partial modification, p.85. The source says `M′ := M[T_1, …, T_i]_{≤n}/(m_{i+1} − Σ_1^i x_j T_j) · M[T_1, …, T_i]_{≤n−1}`; it should be `M′ := M[T_1, …, T_i]_{≤n}/(m_{i+1} − Σ_1^i x_j T_j) · B[T_1, …, T_i]_{≤n−1}: the degree-one element F = m_{i+1} − Σ x_j T_j of M[T] is multiplied by polynomials with coefficients in B.`. M is only a B-module, so the product of F ∈ M[T] with an element of M[T]_{≤n−1} is not defined. M[T] is a B[T]-module, and the definition Heitmann and Ma recall from Hochster 2002 (arXiv:1703.08281v2 §1.2) is M′ = M[X_1,…,X_s]_{≤N}/F · R[X_1,…,X_s]_{≤N−1}. The source says `It implies that the sequence (a_n)_{n∈N} becomes stationary. … Thus, the coefficients of x must belong to A, and this implies that the limit x belongs to Ã.`; it should be `Justify both steps. (1) x_n = u·y_n^{−1} with y_n^{−1} = Π x_P/x_P(0) ∈ K[z] of constant term 1, so ord_z(x_n) = ord_z(u) for every n. (2) By Proposition 4.5 with n = 1, u ∈ z^a F_q[z]_(z) T_z(K∞), and y^{−1} = lim y_n^{−1} ∈ T_z(K∞); so x = z^a h/f with f ∈ F_q[z], f(0) ≠ 0 and h ∈ T_z(K∞). ### Anschütz–Le Bras, "Prismatic Dieudonné Theory", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2023) (`PAPER-ANSCHUTZ-LEBRAS-23`)

- **Misprint** at Theorem 4.9.5 (published: Theorem 4.90), the statement; present in arXiv v4 and in the published version. The source says `Then the prismatic Dieudonné functor M_Δ(−) : BT(R) → DM^adm(R) from the category of p-divisible groups over R to the category of admissible prismatic Dieudonné crystals over R is essentially surjective.`; it should be `… to the category of admissible prismatic Dieudonné modules over R …`. R is assumed quasi-regular semiperfectoid and the displayed functor is the non-calligraphic M_Δ(−), which Definition 4.42 (arXiv Definition 4.2.8) defines as Ext^1_{(R)_qsyn}(G, O^pris) with values in prismatic Dieudonné modules over R; DM^adm(R) is used for both categories by the deliberate overloading of Definitions 4.8 and 4.19 (arXiv Definitions 4.1.8 and 4.1.15), but the words in the statement name the wrong one. The proof settles it: it begins 'let M ∈ DM^adm(R)' and speaks of 'a descent datum for expressing that it comes from an admissible prismatic Dieudonné module over R (namely, M)'. The crystal version of the same statement is Theorem 4.74 (arXiv Theorem 4.6.10), for a general quasi-syntomic ring. Recorded as `PAPER-ANSCHUTZ-LEBRAS-23/E1`; looked for an existing correction in: the arXiv listing and submission history of arXiv:1907.10525, read 22 September 2026: v1 (24 July 2019), v2 (6 February 2020), v3 (14 May 2021) and v4 (11 October 2022), the version read, whose comment records that the notion of filtered prismatic Dieudonné crystal was replaced by the equivalent notion of admissible prismatic Dieudonné crystal and that the proof of full faithfulness was corrected and simplified following a suggestion of Akhil Mathew; there is no later preprint version and no version carrying the erratum; the published version, doi:10.1017/fmp.2022.22 (Forum of Mathematics, Pi 11 (2023), e2, open access on Cambridge Core), read 22 September 2026, including its 'A correction has been issued for this article' notice; the erratum itself, Prismatic Dieudonné Theory – ERRATUM, doi:10.1017/fmp.2024.30 (Forum of Mathematics, Pi 13 (2025), e3, published 7 February 2025), read 22 September 2026: it is the only correction listed for the article; the numbering of the preprint against the numbering of the published version, statement by statement, in all six sections and the appendix; the two agree except that arXiv Remark 5.1.7, on Cartier duality for finite locally free group schemes, has no counterpart in the published version.

The source says `Recall the following definition, which already appeared in Proposition 4.26 before.`; it should be `Recall the following definition, which already appeared in Definition 4.24 before.`. The definition that follows is the definition of a Breuil–Kisin module over a prism and of the minuscule ones, repeated verbatim; it appeared as Definition 4.24 (arXiv Definition 4.1.24). Proposition 4.26 (arXiv Proposition 4.1.26) is the Cais–Lau equivalence between windows over the frame A_d and BK_min(A), which uses the definition but does not state it. - **Misprint** at Example 6.0.4 (published: Example A.4), the displayed chain of equalities; present in arXiv v4 and in the published version. The source says `p^{i}x_{i,0}=p^{i}fx_{i,1}=\ldots = f^{i}x_{i,i}\neq 0`; it should be `p^{i}x_{i,0}=p^{i−1}fx_{i,1}=\ldots = f^{i}x_{i,i}\neq 0`. The relations imposed are p x_{i,j} = f x_{i,j+1}. Substituting once gives p^i x_{i,0} = p^{i−1}(p x_{i,0}) = p^{i−1} f x_{i,1}, and each further substitution trades one p for one f, so that the chain is p^i x_{i,0} = p^{i−1}f x_{i,1} = p^{i−2}f^2 x_{i,2} = … = f^i x_{i,i}: the total degree in p and f is i throughout. As printed, the second term has degree i+1 and is in fact equal to f^{i+1}x_{i,i+1} = 0, since x_{i,i+1} = 0, which would contradict the assertion that the chain is non-zero. The next sentence, p^{i+1}x_{i,0} = f^i p x_{i,i} = 0, is correct. ### Antieau–Mathew–Morrow–Nikolaus, "On the Beilinson fiber square", Duke Mathematical Journal (2022) (`PAPER-ANTIEAU-MATHEW-MORROW-ETAL-22`)

- **Misprint** at Example 7.3, the two stated ranges in the computation of the cyclic homology of k over W(k); in arXiv v2, the version read (the published version could not be consulted). The source says `Using the filtrations of [antieauperiodic], we conclude for i ≤ 2p−1, π_i HC(k/W(k)) ≅ W(k)/p^{s+1} if i = 2s ≥ 0, 0 otherwise. … Thus, in the range 0 ≤ i ≤ 2p−2, we deduce that π_i HC((W(k),(p)/W(k)) ≅ p^{s+1}W(k) if i = 2s, 0 if i is odd.`; it should be `The two ranges should be i ≤ 2p−4 and 0 ≤ i ≤ 2p−4 (equivalently i ≤ 2p−3, since the odd groups vanish).`. Both formulas are read off from the sentence immediately before them, that LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥s} ≅ W(k)/p^s for s ≤ p−1, applied with s+1 in place of s: π_{2s}HC(k/W(k)) = LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥s+1}. That needs s+1 ≤ p−1, i.e. i = 2s ≤ 2p−4. At the first excluded value, i = 2p−2 and s = p−1, the formula would give W(k)/p^p, but LΩ_k here is the p-completed divided power envelope of (p) ⊆ W(k) — that is, W(k) itself — and its Hodge filtration is the divided power filtration, whose p-th step is generated by γ_p(p) = p^p/p!, of p-adic valuation p − 1 since v_p(p!) = 1. So LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥p} = W(k)/p^{p−1} and π_{2p−2}HC(k/W(k)) ≅ W(k)/p^{p−1}, not W(k)/p^p; correspondingly the relative group is p^{p−1}W(k), not p^pW(k). The conclusion of the example is unaffected: it is drawn in the range 1 ≤ i ≤ 2p−5, where the odd degrees used are i = 2s+1 ≤ 2p−5, so s ≤ p−3 and s+1 ≤ p−2, well inside the range where the de Rham formula holds. ### Atobe–Kondo–Yasuda, "Local newforms for the general linear groups over a non-archimedean local field", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2022) (`PAPER-ATOBE-KONDO-YASUDA-22`)

- **Error** at Published Theorem9.1/Definition9.2 pp48–50; arXiv v4 pp52–54 (it affects a stated result). The source says `There exists a unique function`; it should be `Replace the unique-choice definition by a solution-set/existence interface pending a repaired theorem with extra conditions. The two printed test conditions alone do not determine a vector for n=m=2. Also remove the assertion that all restricted Speh vectors lie in Pi.`. For n=m=2, G'=GL2,V'=1,T'=id and all formal W^0 are left-N'-invariant. With u=[[1,varpi^-1],[0,1]], f=1_(uK')-1_K' is a nonzero right-K'-invariant compact function annihilated by every test integral by left translation (det u=1). Extend f to D=V iota(G') using Psi. Lapid–Mao20 Cor3.13/3.15 supplies a Shalika vector with this restriction; right averaging preserves f. Adding it to the L=1 essential vector gives a second solution. The proof's character claim fails explicitly: (I+tE13)(I+bE32)(I-tE13)=I+bE32+tbE12, so Psi changes by psi(tb). See report for full argument and limits. The continuation verifies the compact-induction hypothesis directly against Lapid–Mao Cor3.13/3.15 and obtains infinitely many independent perturbations using u_r=I+varpi^-r E12. These vectors satisfy precisely the printed right-iota(Kprime) condition; no K^(c_pi)-invariance is claimed. (cc-442dc5) Rechecked. For n = m = 2, V′ = 1, V″ = V and Ψ(g) = ψ(g_12 + g_34). Conjugating V by ι(u′) = 1 + zE_13 sends E_32 to E_32 − zE_12, so Ψ is not preserved, and the step 'φ_Ze(u′g′) = Ψ(u′)φ_Ze(g′)' in the uniqueness proof fails. If it held, every W∘ι (W ∈ W_Sh(σ)) would be left N′-invariant and square-integrable on GL_2 (Theorem 8.2), hence zero. That contradicts Lapid–Mao's Corollary 3.15, which the paper uses in its own existence proof. ### Bakker–Klingler–Tsimerman, "Tame topology of arithmetic quotients and algebraicity of Hodge loci", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020) (`PAPER-BAKKER-KLINGLER-TSIMERMAN-20`)

- **Error** at Theorem 4.1, JAMS p.928, proof p.929; author p.13–14 (it affects a stated result). The source says `"Theorem 4.1. Let V be a polarized variation of pure Hodge structures of weight k over the punctured polydisk (∆*)^n, with period map Φ: (∆*)^n → S_{Γ,G,M}. Then Φ is R_an,exp-definable." (∆ is the unit disk, p.4.)`; it should be `Definability holds only after shrinking. For some radius 0 < ρ < 1, the restriction of Φ to (∆*_ρ)^n is R_an,exp-definable, and then for every ρ < 1 by compactness of the remaining annular pieces. The reduction in §4.1 must use charts whose shrunken polydisks still cover the compactification.`. Counterexample (n = 1, trivial monodromy). Let f(z) = exp(−(1+z)/(1−z)) on the unit disk, so |f| < 1, and τ = 2i + εf with ε small, so that τ(∆) lies in a disk on which π: H → Γ\H is injective (Γ torsion-free, e.g. Γ(3)). τ is the period map of a polarized weight-one integral VHS. But Φ^{−1}(π(2i + ε/e)) contains the points z_n = 2πin/(2 + 2πin), n ≠ 0, where f = 1/e. These form an infinite discrete set accumulating at 1, which is impossible for a fibre of a definable map. The proof itself allows for this: it says 'after maybe shrinking the polydisk' (p.14), and its Siegel set S_H (y > 1) covers only |q| < e^{−2π}. Theorem 1.3 is unaffected, since §4.1 can use finitely many shrunken charts. Checked numerically: |f(z_n) − 1/e| < 1e−8 for 0 < |n| ≤ 2000. Noted by the extraction (item local-outer-boundary-obstruction). (cc-442dc5) Rechecked: the proof on p.929 says 'after maybe shrinking the polydisk', so the intended statement is the shrunken one, and §4.1 needs only finitely many shrunken charts; Theorem 1.3 is unaffected. The printed statement for the whole punctured polydisk is still false, so the finding keeps 'a stated result'. - **Gap** at Appendix A.3 proof of Proposition A.2, JAMS pp.935–936 (it affects the proof). The source says `relatively compact`; it should be `Choose smaller semialgebraic corner boxes whose closures lie inside larger analytic charts. Prove definability of the compact matching graph and cover it by finitely many neighborhoods of analytic transition extensions. Mere boundedness of the smaller domains is insufficient.`. Analytic coordinate changes between relatively compact domains need not be R_an-definable: F(x)=x+(x²/4)sin(1/x), 0<x<1, has derivative greater than 1/4 and maps diffeomorphically to a bounded interval. If F were definable, the zero set of F(x)−x, containing exactly x=1/(nπ), n≥1, would contradict o-minimality. Reparametrize an analytic arc in a compact circle by F. Thus a buffer in larger charts is necessary for the printed immediate inference. The new buffered-transition-graph item supplies a proof of the theorem, not a counterexample to its conclusion. The source says `S_(Γ′,G′,M′) = S_(Γ₁,G,M₁) × S_(Γ_H,H,M_H)`; it should be `A product decomposition of the semisimple group does not decompose an arbitrary compact stabilizer. Take G′=PSL₂(R)×PSL₂(R), projection to the first factor, Γ′=Γ₁×Γ₂ with torsion-free arithmetic factors, and M′ the diagonal SO₂. Its intersections with the two normal factors are trivial. The left-hand quotient has real dimension 5, whereas the displayed product of intersection-stabilizer quotients has dimension 6. Passing to finite-index arithmetic subgroups does not fix that discrepancy. The corrected morphism theorem may still hold; this literal intermediate equality does not. ### Benoist–Wittenberg, "On the integral Hodge conjecture for real varieties, I", Inventiones Mathematicae (2020) (`PAPER-BENOIST-WITTENBERG-20`)

- **Error** at Inventiones mathematicae 222 (2020), Theorem 3.16 (ii), p. 55, and its introduction form Theorem A (ii), p. 4 (it affects a stated result). The source says `dim(X) > 0`; it should be `Part (ii) needs dim(X) ≥ 2 whenever X(R) ≠ ∅. The hypothesis dim(X) > 0 of Theorem 3.16, and the hypothesis d ≥ 1 of Theorem A, are too weak: the case dim(X) = 1 with X(R) ≠ ∅ must be excluded. Part (i) is not affected by this counterexample.`. Take X = E the elliptic curve y^2 = x^3 - x over R = ℝ, with its rational point at infinity. All the printed hypotheses hold: dim(X) = 1 > 0; H^2(X,O_X) = 0 because X is a curve; and the real integral Hodge conjecture for 1-cycles is the codimension-0 case, which holds trivially, since X is geometrically irreducible, so H^0_G(X(ℂ),ℤ(0)) = ℤ and the class of the codimension-0 cycle [X] generates it. The left-hand side of (ii) fails: the only integral closed subscheme of dimension 1 in a curve is the curve itself, and E has geometric genus 1, which is odd, so X contains no geometrically irreducible curve of even geometric genus. The right-hand side holds: by Hochschild–Serre, Pic(X) → Pic(X_ℂ)^G is injective with cokernel embedding in Br(ℝ), and that obstruction is killed by the real point, so the map is an isomorphism and is in particular onto on 2-primary torsion. Hence (ii) is false as printed. The proof combines Theorems3.3 and3.6 with Proposition3.9, whose real-point argument assumes dimension at least2. Prior worker checked the published and arXiv statements; retained here without an independent-review verdict. (cc-442dc5) Rechecked against Theorem A (p.4) and Theorem 3.16 (p.55): for a curve the only integral curve is X itself, so the genus-one real curve makes the left side of (ii) false and the right side true. ### Beuzart-Plessis–Chaudouard–Zydor, "The global Gan-Gross-Prasad conjecture for unitary groups: the endoscopic case", Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS (2022) (`PAPER-BEUZARTPLESSIS-CHAUDOUARD-ZYDOR-22`)

- **Gap** at §10.1.6, proof of Proposition 10.1.6.1, p. 321 (it affects the proof). The source says `Let ξ_Π be the infinitesimal character of Π. By [BPLZZ21, Theorem 4.12 (4)], for every h ∈ ℋ° and (U_h, σ) ∈ 𝔛^h_0, the base-change of the infinitesimal character of σ is ξ_Π.`; it should be `The infinitesimal-character statement is true, but the cited proof does not give it in this case. Take it from Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu Theorem 4.14(4) (the Annals numbering) with its Proposition 4.13(1) repaired: suppose 𝔇(G′, 1)^♥_{χ′} = ∅ and isolate with Theorem 3.19 instead of Theorem 3.6 (PAPER-BEUZARTPLESSIS-LIU-ZHANG-ETAL-21/E1). Alternatively deduce it from Mok and Kaletha–Mínguez–Shin–White, where the base change is strong at archimedean places (BPLZZ Remark 4.15), at the cost of making the proof of Theorem 1.1.5.1 depend on them.`. The cited result is BPLZZ Theorem 4.14(4): if the weak base change of π exists and is hermitian, the base change of χ_{π_∞} is χ_{BC(π)_∞}. Its proof reduces to BPLZZ Proposition 4.13(1), whose argument by contradiction only rules out 'weak base change does not exist'. When the weak base change exists but is not cuspidal, the T-character χ′ is CAP, Theorem 3.6 does not apply, and nothing in the printed argument reaches the archimedean component. This paper applies the theorem to σ whose weak base change is a Hermitian Arthur parameter Π. In the endoscopic case, the one the paper is about, Π is not cuspidal. The common infinitesimal character is needed to choose the multipliers μ^h with μ^h(σ) = 1 for all (U_h, σ) ∈ 𝔛^h_0, compatible with μ(Π) = 1 under base change, which (10.1.6.6) uses. Theorems 1.1.5.1 and 1.1.6.1 remain true (by the repaired argument), so only the proof is affected. The top form (det h)^{−1}∧dh_{ij} is not invariant under translation for n ≥ 2: left multiplication by g scales ∧dh_{ij} by det(g)^n. The invariant form is (det h)^{−n}∧dh_{ij}, the local measure the paper itself uses in §9.1.2 (dx = ∏dx_{ij}/|det x|^n). It is also the one for which (2.3.2.2) holds: vol(GL_n(O_v)) = |GL_n(𝔽_q)|q^{−n²} = ∏_{i=1}^n(1 − q^{−i}) = L_{H,v}(0)^{−1} for L_H(s) = ζ_F(s + 1)⋯ζ_F(s + n). ### Bhargava–Shankar–Wang, "Squarefree values of polynomial discriminants I", Inventiones Mathematicae (2022) (`PAPER-BHARGAVA-SHANKAR-WANG-22`)

- **Error** at §1, p.4 (arXiv v3). The source says `"Then p² strongly divides ∆(f) if and only if f modulo p has at least two distinct multiple roots in F̄_p, or has a root in F_p of multiplicity at least 3; and p² weakly divides ∆(f) if p² | ∆(f) but f modulo p has only one multiple root in F_p and this root is a simple double root."`; it should be `This holds for odd p. For p = 2, 4 always divides Δ(f) strongly when 2 | Δ(f), so W^{(2)}_m is empty for even m.`. By Stickelberger's congruence, the discriminant of a monic integer polynomial is ≡ 0 or 1 mod 4, so 2 | Δ(f + 2g) implies 4 | Δ(f + 2g) for every g. For example f = x² + 1 ≡ (x + 1)² mod 2 has a single simple double root, yet Δ(x² + a_1x + a_2) = a_1² − 4a_2 ≡ 0 mod 4 whenever a_1 is even. A brute-force check over all f mod p confirms the criterion for p = 3 (n ≤ 5) and p = 5 (n ≤ 4), and finds failures at p = 2 for every n = 2, …, 5. The proofs only use the implication "two multiple roots or a triple root ⇒ strong", which holds at p = 2 as well (in Proposition 2.2), and the tail estimates concern large primes, so nothing else changes. ### Bhatt, "On the direct summand conjecture and its derived variant", Inventiones Mathematicae 212 (2018) (`PAPER-BHATT-18`)

- **Error** at Bhatt arXiv:1608.08882v2, Proposition 6.2, p. 11; rendered page checked. Published full text not collated. (it affects a stated result). The source says `proper morphism such that f[1/p] is finite étale`; it should be `Require the generic finite étale map to be surjective; state the mixed-characteristic setting used in the proof.`. Take mixed-characteristic perfectoid K, A=K°×K°, Y=Spec(K°) as the first component. The morphism is finite, proper and étale, but the unit A→K° is projection. The second idempotent is nonzero even in the m_p-almost category, since multiplication by every p-root on its K° component is nonzero. A projection with this kernel has no almost left inverse. The proof explicitly upgrades to an almost finite étale cover and needs faithfulness. Let k be a field of characteristic p > 0, X = A²_k, and f: Y → X the blow-up of the origin with exceptional curve E = F. Let M be the sum of the strict transforms of the two axes. So π*M − 2G ∼ −2E′ − 4G is globally generated and ε_sa(M; x) = 2. Taking A = M and Λ = 0 (any D), ε_sa(A; x) = 2 for every δ, not converging to k = 1. The proof only shows that π*A − (k − γ)E is nef. - **Gap** at Theorem 1.19 of the introduction (= Theorem 7.3), and Remark 7.4(2) (arXiv v4, the version read) (it affects a stated result). The source says `Fix a complete and algebraically closed nonarchimedean field K. Let A be a classical affinoid K-algebra of dimension d. Fix a prime ℓ and let F be an ℓ-power torsion étale sheaf on Spec(A). If A is smooth or if ℓ is not the residue characteristic of K, then H^i(Spec(A)_ét, F) = 0 for i > d.`; it should be `The disjunct 'if A is smooth' is not proved in the paper at this generality. Theorem 7.3, which Theorem 1.19 is labelled as, proves the vanishing above degree d only for ℓ prime to the residue characteristic; the smooth case is claimed only in Remark 7.4(2), only for constant coefficients, and only as an adaptation: 'The algebraization method used to prove Lemma 7.8 below can be adapted to prove this statement when A is smooth (in the sense of rigid spaces) and F is constant, thanks to [Elkik, Theorem 7 and Remark 2 on page 587].' Either the introduction should restrict the smooth case to constant coefficients and point at Remark 7.4(2), or the adaptation should be written out for arbitrary ℓ-power torsion sheaves.`. Theorem 7.3 as printed has two parts: (1) H^i = 0 for i > d + 1 for every torsion sheaf, and (2) H^i = 0 for i > d when F is ℓ-power torsion with ℓ prime to the residue characteristic. Neither mentions smoothness of A, and Remark 7.4 opens 'We would expect that part (2) of Theorem 7.3 holds for arbitrary torsion sheaves', listing the smooth constant-coefficient case as one of two special cases that are 'within reach'. No proof of the smooth case for non-constant ℓ-power torsion sheaves appears in Section 7, and the reduction of Theorem 7.3 to constant coefficients runs through Proposition 7.9 for the two cases actually stated there, not for the smooth case. - **Misprint** at §5.2, display before Lemma 5.3, p. 21 (arXiv v2 §5.2; identical in both versions). The source says `Recall that the latter is defined as an equalizer: F_p(i)(A) = eq(N^{≥p−1}Δ_A{p−1}/p ⇉ Δ_A{p−1}/p)`; it should be `F_p(i)(A) = eq(N^{≥i}Δ_A{i}/p ⇉ Δ_A{i}/p), the equalizer of can and φ_i in weight i.`. Take X = Spec Z_p[x, y]/(xy − p), regular and semistable over Z_p, at the point x = y = p = 0. Then x ∈ R[1/p]^× because xy = p, but x ∉ p^Z·R^×, since v_x(x) = 1 ≠ 0 = v_y(x). For i = 2, the same bilinearity trick applied to each t_k repairs the case: 1 + πa is a product of elements 1 + t_k w with w ∈ R^×, and {1 + t_k w, −t_k w} = 0. - **Misprint** at Lemma 15 and proof, (34)–(35), p.11 (published version). The source says `"S(X ∩ B², ε) ≤ (2^m/c(m)) vol(X)·ε^{−2m}" … "vol(X ∩ B_p) ≥ c(n)(ε/2)^{2m}"`; it should be `S(X ∩ B², ε) ≤ (2^{2m}/c(m)) vol(X) ε^{−2m}, from vol(X ∩ B_p) ≥ c(m)(ε/2)^{2m}.`. Take L = ∂_t, which is Fuchsian: its only singular point ∞ is regular singular (∂_t = −z(z∂_z), z = 1/t). Then φ(s) = κs gives φ*L = κ^{-1}∂_s and inf_φ ‖a₀(φ*L)‖ = 0. Here L + 1 = ∂ + 1 has an irregular singularity at ∞. Theorems 1–8 are unaffected. - **Misprint** at Lemma 9.1(i), p. 51 (arXiv v2). The source says `"Suppose that ψ is surjective, even after restriction to π_1(Y_{F̄_q}, η_Y). Z_{ψ,φ} is defined on p. 50 as Isom_{Y_K,H}(X_φ, X_ψ), the scheme of isomorphisms of two H-torsors over the curve Y_K, so it is finite étale over Y_K, not over K. ### Boxer, Calegari, Gee and Pilloni, "Abelian surfaces over totally real fields are potentially modular" (arXiv:1812.09269) (`PAPER-BOXER-CALEGARI-GEE-PILLONI-21`)

- **Misprint** at §7.6, the proof of Corollary 7.6.3 (published version p. 406; arXiv:1812.09269v3); in the LaTeX source the statement is \begin{lem}\label{thm:TWprimes} at line 13222 of abeliansurfacesmodular.tex and the citation is at line 13308. The source says `By Proposition 7.2.1 and Theorem 7.6.1, the claim holds with g instead equal to …`; it should be `"Theorem 7.6.1" should read "Lemma 7.6.1"`. 7.6.1 is a Lemma — the statement constructing Taylor–Wiles data for a vast ρ̄ — and is headed "Lemma 7.6.1" in both PDFs; the string "Lemma 7.6.1" occurs exactly once in each and the string "Theorem 7.6.1" exactly once, in this sentence. The cause is visible in the source: the statement carries the label thm:TWprimes although its environment is lem, and the reference is written out as Theorem~\ref{thm:TWprimes} rather than with \Cref, so the automatic name is not used. A mechanical check of every cross-reference in the paper against the environment carrying its target label found this to be the only such mismatch. - **Misprint** at Corollary 6.4.3, its statement and the spectral sequence in the first line of its proof (published version pp. 338–339; §6.4 of arXiv:1812.09269v3). The source says `Then the map e(U^I)H^i(𝓧_{K(I,p^n)}(ε), ω^κ(−D)) → e(U^I)H^i(𝓧_{K(I,p^n)}(ε), 𝓕^{κ,w} ⊗ (det ω_𝓖)^2(−D)) is an isomorphism for i = 0 and injective if i = 1 … Proposition 6.4.2 gives a spectral sequence E_1^{p,q} = ⊕_{s∈W^{(p)}} H^q(𝓧_{K(I,p^n)}(ε), 𝓕^{s•κ,w} ⊗ (det ω_𝓖)^2(−D))`; it should be `both occurrences of 𝓕^{κ,w} and 𝓕^{s•κ,w} should read 𝓕^{κ,w^-} and 𝓕^{s•κ,w^-}`. The sheaf 𝓕^{κ,w^-} = colim_{w'<w}𝓕^{κ,w'} is defined immediately before Proposition 6.4.2, which resolves ω^κ(−D) by the 𝓕^{s•κ,w^-} and not by the 𝓕^{s•κ,w}; the sentence between Proposition 6.4.2 and Corollary 6.4.3 says that the Hecke operators act on 𝓕^{κ,w^-} ⊗ (det ω_𝓖)^2(−D); and within the proof of Corollary 6.4.3 itself the differentials θ_{s,s'} are written between the 𝓕^{s•κ,w^-}. So the spectral sequence of that proof is the one attached to a resolution by the w^- sheaves, and the map in the statement of the corollary is the first map of that resolution. The slip is exactly the one the authors correct in the source they are citing: the proof of Proposition 6.4.2 says in parentheses that in Andreatta–Iovita–Pilloni §7.2 "one needs to replace 𝓕^{κ,w} with 𝓕^{κ,w^-} as defined above". The distinction is visible in both PDFs, where the minus is typeset in the exponent of Proposition 6.4.2 and of the sentence after it, and is absent in the statement and the spectral sequence of Corollary 6.4.3. - **Misprint** at Remark 5.8.5, the sentence announcing the proof of the strengthened vanishing (published version p. 315; §5.8 of arXiv:1812.09269v3), against Proposition 5.9.1 and Remark 5.9.2 on p. 316. The source says `In the case p>3, we will sketch a proof of this result in §5.9 using Fourier–Jacobi expansions, but since a complete argument in the case p=3 would involve developing considerably more of the details of toroidal compactifications than we need in the rest of the paper, we have decided not to give the details.`; it should be `the hypothesis should read "in the case p > 3 and [F:Q] > 1"`. What §5.9 actually proves is Proposition 5.9.1, which assumes both p > 3 and [F:Q] > 1, and Remark 5.9.2 immediately afterwards says in as many words that for F = Q, as for p = 3, the authors have only a sketch: "We also have a sketch of an argument for F = Q." So the case F = Q is in exactly the same position as the case p = 3, and Remark 5.8.5 names only the latter. Nothing depends on this: §5.9 opens by saying that the result "partially strengthens Corollary 5.4.5 but is not needed in this paper", and the doubling theorem actually used, Theorem 5.8.4, is proved for all p ≥ 3 and all totally real F from Corollary 5.4.5 alone. ### Boxer–Pilloni, "Higher Hida theory for Siegel modular forms", Inventiones Mathematicae (2026) (`PAPER-BOXER-PILLONI-26`)

- **Misprint** at §1.1, p. 2. The source says `"We fix a point h ∈ 𝓗_g corresponding to a map h : Res_{ℂ/ℝ}(𝔾_m) → G_ℝ. We let µ be the Hodge cocharacter associated to h, P_µ be the Siegel parabolic of G associated to µ, and M_µ be the unipotent radical of P_µ."`; it should be `"… and M_µ be the Levi of P_µ." Here M_µ is the Levi subgroup containing T, which is the centralizer of µ. With µ(z) = diag(Id_g, z·Id_g) it is isomorphic to GL_g × 𝔾_m. This is how §3.1, p. 33 defines it.`. The page image confirms the printed sentence word for word: "M_µ be the unipotent radical of P_µ". Every other use of M_µ in the paper, including the next sentences, treats it as the Levi of P_µ.

(i) p. 2: "Let us fix a maximal torus and a Borel T ⊆ B ⊆ P_µ ⊆ G. Let Rep(M_µ) be the category of finite dimensional algebraic representations of M_µ. Irreducible representations are labeled by M_µ-dominant weights κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M_µ,+}. The tower of Shimura varieties carries a natural M_µ-torsor". The unipotent radical of the Siegel parabolic is the commutative vector group Sym² of dimension g(g+1)/2. In characteristic 0 its only irreducible algebraic representation is the trivial one, and it contains no maximal torus of G. So a labelling by dominant weights of T makes no sense for it. The automorphic vector bundles ω^κ come from representations of the Levi GL_g × 𝔾_m.

(ii) p. 2, §1.2: "the unipotent subgroup of the Borel of M_µ(ℤ_p)". This only makes sense if M_µ is reductive.

(iii) p. 3, §1.3: "W_M be the Weyl group of M_µ". Also ^MW is the set of minimal length representatives of W_M\W.

(iv) p. 4, §1.3.7: K_∞ ⊆ G(ℝ), the stabilizer of h, "is a real form of M_µ". K_∞ is compact modulo centre (a unitary group in g variables, with similitudes). It is a real form of GL_g × 𝔾_m, never of a unipotent group.

(v) §3.1, p. 33 sets up the notation correctly: "Let M_µ = M be the Levi and U_P be the unipotent radical." It also gives dominance "for the Levi M" as k_1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ k_g and says "W_M be the Weyl group of the Levi M". p. 36 says "We recall that M = M_µ is the Levi of P_µ = P."

So the words "unipotent radical" in §1.1 are a slip for "Levi". The paper's own conventions do not support the printed reading. Because §3 re-defines M_µ correctly and all proofs and results use it as the Levi, the slip affects nothing beyond this sentence of the introduction. - **Misprint** at §1.4, Proposition 1.4.7, p. 5: the definition of κ and the right-hand side of the display. §5.4, Remark 5.4.3, p. 57: the definition of κ. The 2024 preprint has the same text in Proposition 1.4.7 (p. 5) and in Remark 5.4.3 (p. 55).. The source says `Proposition 1.4.7 (p. 5): "For any ν = ν_{alg}χ : T(ℤ_p) → ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n})^×, with ν_{alg} ∈ X^⋆(T)^+ and χ a finite order character, and for κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν + ρ) − ρ, we have: M^•_w ⊗_{Λ,−ν} ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}) = RΓ(S^{tor}_{K^pK_p}, ω^κ)^{ord} ⊗_{ℚ_p} ℚ_p(ζ_p^n)[χ]". Remark 5.4.3 (p. 57): "For any ν = ν_{alg}χ : T(ℤ_p) → ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n})^×, with ν_{alg} ∈ X^⋆(T) and χ a finite order character, and for κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν + ρ) − ρ, we have: M^•_w ⊗_{Λ,−ν} ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n}) = RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ)."`; it should be `In Proposition 1.4.7, read "for κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν_{alg} + ρ) − ρ, we have: M^•_w ⊗_{Λ,−ν} ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}) = RΓ(S^{tor}_{K^pK_p}, ω^κ)^{ord} ⊗_{ℚ_p} ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n})[χ]". In Remark 5.4.3, read "for κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν_{alg} + ρ) − ρ, we have: M^•_w ⊗_{Λ,−ν} ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n}) = RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ)". This is the definition of κ that the paper itself fixes at the end of §5.3, p. 56.`. (1) The coefficient field in Proposition 1.4.7. The left-hand side of the display is over ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}). On the right-hand side, however, the exponent n is printed on ζ_p (ζ_p^n) instead of in the subscript. Read literally, ζ_p^n is the n-th power of a primitive p-th root of unity. Then ℚ_p(ζ_p^n) ⊆ ℚ_p(ζ_p): it equals ℚ_p(ζ_p) if p ∤ n and ℚ_p if p | n. For n ≥ 2 this field is strictly smaller than ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}), which has degree p^{n−1}(p−1) over ℚ_p. The two sides of the stated equality would then not have the same scalars. The field is meant to be ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}) on both sides: χ takes values in ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n})^×, and on the same page Theorem 1.4.3(4) and (5) and Remark 1.4.6 all extend scalars to ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}). This slip does not recur in Remark 5.4.3 on p. 57, where the coefficients are correctly printed as ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n}).

(2) The weight κ in Proposition 1.4.7 and Remark 5.4.3. Both passages form κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν + ρ) − ρ from ν = ν_{alg}χ.

The sheaf ω^κ is defined only for an algebraic weight κ ∈ X^⋆(T)^{M,+} (§5.3.1, p. 55; compare Theorem 1.4.3(4), p. 5). Likewise, the notation RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ) is introduced on p. 56 only for κ formed from the algebraic part ν_{alg}. But ν = ν_{alg}χ is a character of T(ℤ_p) with values in ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n})^×, and it is the restriction of an algebraic character only when χ is trivial. The reason is that a character of T that is algebraic and has finite order on the Zariski-dense subgroup T(ℤ_p) is trivial. So for χ ≠ 1 the printed κ is only locally algebraic. Then ω^κ is not defined, and κ is not a weight for which RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ) has been given a meaning.

The finite-order part χ is already accounted for elsewhere. In Proposition 1.4.7 it enters through the χ-isotypic part [χ]. In Remark 5.4.3 it enters through the definition RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ) = RHom_{T(ℤ_p)}(ν, RΓ_w(K^p) ⊗ ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n})).

The paper states the intended formula in its definitions at the end of §5.3, p. 56: "Let ν = ν_{alg}χ : T(ℤ_p) → ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n})^×, with ν_{alg} ∈ X^⋆(T) and χ a finite order character. Let κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν_{alg}+ρ)−ρ." In the regular-weight case, Theorem 1.4.3(4) applies the same formula to an algebraic ν ∈ X^⋆(T)^+. In the 2024 preprint, the corresponding definition (p. 54) also read κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν + ρ) − ρ. The revision corrected it to ν_{alg} there, but not in Proposition 1.4.7 or in Remark 5.4.3.

Both slips are notational, and the intended statements are clear from p. 56 and from Theorem 1.4.3. The rest of the paper takes κ algebraic and treats χ separately, for instance in Proposition 6.2.6 (p. 61) and Theorem 6.2.9 (p. 62). Nothing later uses the misprinted forms. These are therefore misprints, and the mathematics is unaffected. Recorded as `PAPER-BOXER-PILLONI-26/E10`; looked for an existing correction in: The authors' version on V. - **Gap** at §4.5.6, proof of Theorem 4.5.2. The theorem is stated on p. 51. The E_1 decomposition and the sentence introducing Proposition 4.5.8 are on p. 52, and the proof of Proposition 4.5.8 ends on p. 53. The January 2024 preprint has the same text (its §4.5.6, "proof of the main result", pp. 50–51). (it affects the proof). The source says `Theorem 4.5.2 (p. 51): "(1) ⊕_{w∈C(κ), ℓ(w)=p} H^{p+q}_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ) ⇒ H^{p+q}(S^{tor}, ω̃^κ)^{t−ord}" (and similarly for (2) and the Nebentypus versions). Proof, p. 52: "We see by lemma 2.9.3 and lemma 4.5.7 that RΓ_c(F̂_p \ F̂_{p−1}, ω̃^κ) = ⊕_{w,ℓ(w)=p} RΓ(S^{tor}, lim_m lim_n ω̃^κ(−mD_{−,w})/𝓘^n_{Z,>w−1}). ... The key proposition which implies theorem 4.5.2 is the following (given that the ordinary part of the right hand side is RΓ_w(K_pK_{w,p,P}, κ) by corollary 2.3.11):"`; it should be `Replace the parenthetical with the following argument, applied to each w with ℓ(w) = p. Also, "K_p" printed as a subscript should be the superscript K^p. Below, s indexes the truncations mod p^s (this index is written n in Proposition 4.5.8), and n is the level of K_{p,n}, as in Proposition 4.1.13. (a) Comparison. By Corollary 2.3.11, the right-hand side of Proposition 4.5.8 is lim_s RΓ_{D_{−,w},D_{+,w}}(S^tor_{Z/p^s}, ω̃^κ/p^s). Modulo p^s, the complement of D_{+,w} ∪ D_{−,w} in S^tor is the stratum 𝔖^tor_w (Proposition 4.1.13(2), Corollary 4.1.14). By Lemma 4.2.11, (C_t^tor, S^tor, p_1, p_2, D_{+,w}, D_{−,w}) mod p^s is a dynamic compactification of (ℭ^tor_{t,w}, 𝔖^tor_w) mod p^s, though not necessarily a strict one. The strict dynamic compactification of Proposition 4.4.4 is made of the closures of the stratum, and it maps to this one by a strict map made of closed immersions. So Proposition 2.2.11 (through Lemma 2.2.8) identifies the two cohomologies with partial support, compatibly with the Hecke operators. Theorem 2.5.1(1) then lets one pass between the two orders of support. On 𝔖^tor_w the divisors Z_{i,>w_i} and Z_{i,<w_i} are empty, so Proposition 4.1.13(1) gives Z_i = V(p^{n w_i}) there. So ω̃^κ = p^{n k' Σ_i w_i} ω^κ on 𝔖^tor_w, and this is the same scalar on both sides of the correspondence. Under the resulting identification of ω̃^κ with ω^κ, t̃ therefore corresponds over ℭ^tor_{t,w} to the restriction of t. By Remark 4.3.12 (with w' = w), this restriction is p^{n_w} t_w, and n_w = 0 for w ∈ C(κ). (b) Case w ∈ C(κ). The operator is t_w. With Lemma 2.4.4(1), the ordinary part of the right-hand side of Proposition 4.5.8 is RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ) as defined in §4.4 (p. 51). By that proposition, it is also the ordinary part of the w-summand of the E_1 term. (c) Case w ∉ C(κ). The ordinary part of the w-summand is 0. Since t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p), Remark 4.3.12 gives n_w > 0. Modulo p^s the operator is therefore p^{n_w} t_w, and its s-th power p^{s n_w} t_w^s vanishes. So each level is a module over the polynomial ring Z/p^s[t_w], and in that ring the image p^{n_w} t_w of t is nilpotent. Inverting it gives the zero ring, so the level has zero ordinary part by Definition 2.4.2 (as in case (1) of the proof of Lemma 2.4.3). The limit then has zero ordinary part by Lemma 2.4.4(1). The relation t = p^{n_w} t_w holds only over ℭ^tor_{t,w}, where t_w is defined. So the vanishing has to be read off on the right-hand side of Proposition 4.5.8 and carried over to the E_1-summand by that proposition. This works because Proposition 4.5.8 holds for every w. Its proof (pp. 52–53) uses only Lemma 4.3.14, Corollary 4.4.3, Lemma 2.4.4 and the equality (p) = 𝓘_{Z,>w−1} over 𝔖^tor_w, and it never uses w ∈ C(κ). Case (c) is what cuts the E_1 term down from all w with ℓ(w) = p to w ∈ C(κ), as Theorem 4.5.2 states. The same argument applies to the cuspidal and Nebentypus variants.`. The Cousin filtration F_i = ∪_{ℓ(w)≤i} Z_{>w−1} and Lemma 4.5.7 (p. 52) run over all of ^MW. So the E_1 term RΓ_c(F̂_p \ F̂_{p−1}, ω̃^κ) = ⊕_{w,ℓ(w)=p}(…) is a sum over every w with ℓ(w) = p. Theorem 4.5.2 (p. 51), however, sums only over w ∈ C(κ). The only justification given for identifying the summands is the parenthetical before Proposition 4.5.8, which cites Corollary 2.3.11. That corollary (p. 17) only rewrites the colim_r lim_m of twisted cohomologies as cohomology with partial support along D_{−,w}, D_{+,w}. It says nothing about ordinary parts. RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ) is defined differently (p. 51): through the closure compactification of Proposition 4.4.4, with the sheaf ω^κ and the operator t_w of Proposition 4.3.9. The right-hand side of Proposition 4.5.8 uses instead ω̃^κ = ω^κ(−k'ΣZ_i) on all of S^tor. Its operator is the single t̃ extending the t of Proposition 4.3.11, which is normalized by ⟨−w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)−ρ, t⟩ for w ∈ C(κ). The proof supplies neither the comparison of the two compactifications nor the comparison of (ω̃^κ, t̃) with (ω^κ, t_w).

The first comparison is routine. It needs no strictness over all of S^tor and no change of support conditions of the kind treated in §2.11. Definition 2.1.9 (p. 7) does not require X to be dense in X̄, and Lemma 4.2.11 (p. 45) shows that D_{+,w} is expanded and D_{−,w} is contracted. So the toroidal pair is a dynamic compactification of (ℭ^tor_{t,w}, 𝔖^tor_w) mod p^s, and the Proposition 4.4.4 compactification maps strictly to it. Proposition 2.2.11 (p. 15) then gives the equivariant identification, exactly as in the proof of Theorem 2.11.4(2) (p. 32).

The second comparison changes the statement. On 𝔖^tor_w both Z_{i,>w_i} and Z_{i,<w_i} are empty, so Z_i = V(p^{n w_i}) there (Proposition 4.1.13(1), p. 42). The twist by −k'ΣZ_i is therefore the same scalar on both sides. But by Remark 4.3.12 (p. 48), t restricted to ℭ^tor_{t,w} equals t_w only for w ∈ C(κ). For w ∉ C(κ) and t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p) it equals p^{n_w} t_w with n_w > 0. For such w the operator is nilpotent modulo each p^s, so the ordinary part of the w-summand is 0.

On the other hand, RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ) is defined for every w ∈ ^MW. §4.4 uses the t_w of Proposition 4.3.9, which exists for all w, and T(Z_p) acts through ν = −w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)−ρ (Proposition 4.4.5, Remark 4.4.6). In general this complex is nonzero. For example, take g = 1 and w = Id. Then RΓ_Id computes Hida's ordinary p-adic modular forms of weight κ. By Hida's theory, an ordinary family of a given tame level specializes to a nonzero ordinary p-adic modular form in every weight of its component of weight space, and that component contains weights with C(κ) = {s}. In such a weight the Id-summand of the E_1 term has ordinary part 0, while RΓ_Id ≠ 0. So if the parenthetical is read as applying to every summand of the sum displayed just above it, it is false for w ∉ C(κ). What holds for those summands is that the ordinary part vanishes.

The needed vanishing is stated nowhere. C(κ) does not occur anywhere in §4.5.6 (pp. 52–53). Remark 4.3.12 is never cited in the paper, although its last sentence, "If t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p), n_{w'} > 0 for w' ∉ C(κ)", is exactly what is needed here.

Why this is a gap and not an error. The parenthetical is correct for the w that Theorem 4.5.2 keeps, namely w ∈ C(κ). For the other w, the statement the proof needs, the vanishing, is true. What is missing is a proof of each, and every ingredient is in the paper:
- Remark 4.3.12;
- Proposition 4.5.8, which holds for every w because its proof never uses w ∈ C(κ);
- Definition 2.4.2, with the argument of case (1) in the proof of Lemma 2.4.3;
- Lemma 2.4.4(1);
- the comparison above.
So the missing step is short, and Theorem 4.5.2 is correct as stated.

Corollaries 4.5.4 and 4.5.5 (C(κ) = {w}) need exactly this vanishing, for all lengths, so that the spectral sequence reduces to a single term. Corollary 4.5.5 is the classicality in regular weight listed as item (4) of Theorem 1.4.3, and Remark 1.4.5 says the spectral sequence degenerates because #C(κ) = 1. With the step supplied, these results stand. The same text is in the January 2024 preprint (pp. 50–51), so the omission was already there and the revision did not fix it. - **Misprint** at §4.5, Corollaries 4.5.4 and 4.5.5, p. 52 (it affects a stated result). The source says `Corollary 4.5.4. Let κ ∈ X⋆(T)⁺ be such that C(κ) = {w}. There is a canonical isomorphism: RΓ_w(K^p K_{w,p,P}, κ) ≃ RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ)^{t−ord} ... Corollary 4.5.5. Let κ ∈ X⋆(T)⁺ be such that C(κ) = {w}. Let ν = −w⁻¹w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ. There is a canonical isomorphism: RΓ_w(K^p K_{w,p,P}, κ) ⊗ Q_p(−ν) ≃ RΓ(S^tor_{Q_p}, ω^κ)^{ord} ...`; it should be `In both corollaries, read "Let κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M,+} be such that C(κ) = {w}". This is the M-dominant cone k_1 ≥ ··· ≥ k_g. It is written X⋆(T)^{+,M} on p. 34, and κ ranges over it from p. 48 onward ("Let κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M,+}", just before Proposition 4.3.9).`. The page image confirms the printed hypothesis: the superscript in both corollaries is a bare "+", with no M.

Conventions (p. 34). X⋆(T)⁺ is the dominant cone "0 ≥ k_1 ≥ ··· ≥ k_g". X⋆(T)^{+,M} is the M-dominant cone "k_1 ≥ ··· ≥ k_g". Also ρ = ½Σ_{α∈Φ⁺} α. P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩, so the positive roots are e_i − e_j (i < j), −(e_i + e_j) and −2e_i. Summing them gives ρ = (−1, −2, …, −g), which is dominant and regular, as it should be.

On p. 48, C(κ) = {w ∈ ^M W : w⁻¹w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) ∈ X⋆(T)⁻_Q}; the introduction (p. 3) gives the equivalent form −w⁻¹w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) ∈ X⋆(T)⁺.

Take κ ∈ X⋆(T)⁺. Then κ + ρ = (k_1 − 1, …, k_g − g) is strictly decreasing and negative, so it is dominant regular. Since W acts simply transitively on regular chambers, w⁻¹w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) is antidominant only when w⁻¹w_{0,M} = w_0, that is, when w = w_{0,M}w_0. This element lies in ^M W: it is its longest element, of length g² − g(g−1)/2 = g(g+1)/2. So for every κ ∈ X⋆(T)⁺ we have C(κ) = {w_{0,M}w_0} automatically. As printed, the hypothesis "C(κ) = {w}" is therefore empty, and the corollaries only cover the top-degree theory w = w_{0,M}w_0.

Example, g = 1 (checked by direct computation). Here ρ = −1 and ^M W = {1, s}. Every κ ∈ X⋆(T)⁺ (k_1 ≤ 0) has C(κ) = {s}. The weights with C(κ) = {1} are exactly k_1 ≥ 2, which are M-dominant but not in X⋆(T)⁺. So the printed statement does not even contain the degree-0 (classical Hida) control theorem.

The intended hypothesis is clear from the rest of the paper:
- On p. 48, κ is fixed in X⋆(T)^{M,+} before Proposition 4.3.9. The ω̃^κ of Theorem 4.5.2 is defined in that setting.
- Theorem 4.5.2 is the spectral sequence ⊕_{w∈C(κ), ℓ(w)=p} H^{p+q}_w ⇒ H^{p+q}(S^tor, ω̃^κ)^{t-ord}. When C(κ) = {w}, it has a single column and degenerates, for any κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M,+}. So the proof of the corollaries needs no G-dominance.
- Theorem 1.4.3(4) on p. 5 is labelled "(Classicality in regular weight 4.5.5)". It takes ν ∈ X⋆(T)⁺ and κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν+ρ) − ρ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M_µ,+} for arbitrary w ∈ ^M W. One checks −w⁻¹w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) = ν + ρ, which is dominant regular, so C(κ) = {w}.
- Remark 1.4.5 says point 4) is the case #C(κ) = 1 of point 5), where 5) is stated for κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M,+}.

The corrected statement follows from Theorem 4.5.2 by the same one-line degeneration argument.

Consequences. As printed, the two corollaries are true but much weaker than intended. They do not support the uses made of them:
- Theorem 1.4.3(4), classicality for every w.
- The interpolation Proposition 1.4.7 (p. 5), which combines the specialisation formula of §5.4 (p. 57) with κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν_alg+ρ) − ρ for arbitrary w.
With the M-dominant hypothesis these results are fine. Recorded as `PAPER-BOXER-PILLONI-26/E101`; looked for an existing correction in: The authors' version on V. Theorem 2.9.7 then gives a spectral sequence, equivariant for t, that converges to H^*(S^tor, ω̃^κ). Its E_1 page has one extra column: RΓ_c(S^tor_{Q_p}, ω̃^κ) = RΓ(S^tor, j_! j^* ω̃^κ), where j : S^tor_{Q_p} → S^tor. Apply Corollary 2.3.4 with X̄ = S^tor. Let the special fibre S^tor_{F_p} = V(p) play the role of the divisor of §2.3.1, and let multiplication by p : O_{S^tor} → O_{S^tor} play the role of O(−D) → O. Corollary 2.3.4 then gives this column as the derived limit of the tower ··· → RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ) → RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ), in which every map is multiplication by p. S^tor is proper over Z_p and ω̃^κ is coherent, so RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ) is a perfect complex of Z_p-modules, and this derived limit is 0. The extra column vanishes, and the spectral sequence is the one printed. Equivalently, the printed E_1 terms give a spectral sequence that converges to H^*(F̂_{g(g+1)/2}, ω̃^κ) (first triangle of Lemma 2.9.6, for l = 0, …, g(g+1)/2). By Lemma 2.9.3, with the special fibre defined by the ideal (p), RΓ(F̂_{g(g+1)/2}, ω̃^κ) = lim_n RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ/p^n). By the same perfectness this equals RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ). The same argument applies to ω̃^κ(−D) on S^tor, and to ω̃^κ(χ) and ω̃^κ(χ)(−D) on S^tor_{Z_p(ζ_{p^n})}, which is proper over Z_p(ζ_{p^n}). Here D is the boundary.`. The proof of Theorem 2.9.7 needs Z_d = X. With U_l = X \ Z_l, it filters RΓ(X, F) = RΓ_c(U_{−1}, F) by the subcomplexes RΓ_c(U_l, F) for l = −1, …, d−1. The second triangle of Lemma 2.9.6 identifies the graded pieces with the RΓ_c(Ẑ_l \ Ẑ_{l−1}, F). The last piece, RΓ_c(U_{d−1}, F), equals RΓ_c(Ẑ_d \ Ẑ_{d−1}, F) only because U_d = ∅.

In §4.5.6, X = S^tor is a scheme over Z_p, and the filtration of §4.1.16 stops at the special fibre, so U_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{Q_p} is not empty. So the printed E_1 terms are the graded pieces of RΓ(F̂_{g(g+1)/2}, ω̃^κ) = lim_n RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ/p^n). This is the cohomology of the p-adic completion. It is not, a priori, RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ).

The two can differ, and here it is properness that makes them agree. Take X = A^1_{Z_p}, F = O and the filtration ∅ ⊆ X_{F_p}. The same construction gives H^0 = lim_n (Z/p^n)[T] = Z_p⟨T⟩, but H^0(X, O) = Z_p[T].

In the paper's setting the two do agree. S^tor is proper over Z_p: it is a blow-up (Proposition 4.1.13) of the proper integral toroidal model of §4.1.1. The sheaf ω̃^κ = ω^κ(−k′ Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i) (p. 49) is coherent. So RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ) is a perfect complex of Z_p-modules. Now let M be a finitely generated Z_p-module and consider the tower M ← M ← ⋯ in which each map is multiplication by p. Every term of a compatible sequence lies in ∩_n p^n M = 0, so the limit of the tower is 0. Its lim^1 is also 0: for any sequence (a_n), the series m_n = Σ_{k≥0} p^k a_{n+k} converges and satisfies m_n − p m_{n+1} = a_n. By the Milnor sequence, the derived limit of the corresponding tower of perfect complexes vanishes. This is the vanishing of the extra column. Equivalently, RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ) → lim_n RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ/p^n) is an isomorphism.

One could read X as the formal completion 𝔖^tor of §4.1.5, whose underlying space is the special fibre, but that does not avoid the problem. Theorem 2.9.7 is stated for schemes. Theorem 4.5.2 and Corollary 4.5.4 state the abutment for the scheme S^tor. Corollary 4.5.5 inverts p to reach RΓ(S^tor_{Q_p}, ω^κ), which requires the algebraic cohomology. So on either reading the two cohomologies must be compared. The paper has the tools for this (Lemma 2.9.3, Remark 2.9.4, Corollary 2.3.4), but it never makes the comparison. §4.5.6 does not address the abutment. Neither does the proof of Proposition 4.5.8, which ends on p. 53 and treats only the E_1 terms.

The spectral sequence as stated is true, and the missing argument is short. So this is a gap in the proof, not an error. The step cites a theorem whose hypotheses the filtration does not meet. It also never uses the fact that makes the conclusion hold, namely that S^tor is proper over Z_p. Once the step is added, the proof of Theorem 4.5.2 is complete. The results deduced from it are then also proved: Corollaries 4.5.4 and 4.5.5 and Theorem 1.4.3 (4) and (5) (p. 5). The 2024 preprint has the same text. - **Gap** at §4.5.6, proof of Proposition 4.5.8, pp. 52–53 (the sentence at the top of p. 53 that justifies the triangle at the foot of p. 52), citing Corollary 4.4.3 on p. 50. The 2024 preprint has the same text. (it affects the proof). The source says `p. 53: "This follows from the property that the original cohomological correspondence factors into p⋆_2 ω̃^κ → O_{C_t^{tor}}((k′ − k) Σ_{i=1}^g p⋆_2 Z_i − Σ_{i=1}^g p⋆_1 Z_i) ⊗ p⋆_2 ω̃^κ → p^!_1 ω̃^κ by lemma 4.3.14, and an application of corollary 4.4.3 (at this place we choose k′ large enough)." The cited Corollary 4.4.3 (p. 50) reads: "Let i ∈ {1, 2}. There exists m ∈ Z≥0 (depending on w and i) such that the canonical map O_{C_t^{tor}} → O_{C_t^{tor}}(m(p⋆_2 Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i − p⋆_1 Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i)) can be factored over p_i^{−1} S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} through maps: O_{p_i^{−1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}} → O_{p_i^{−1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}}(p⋆_1 D_{w,+} + p⋆_2 D_{w,+}) → O_{p_i^{−1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}}(m(p⋆_2 Σ Z_i − p⋆_1 Σ Z_i))." On p. 50 the locus is defined as "S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1}".`; it should be `Corollary 4.4.3 should be stated over p_i^{-1}(Z_{>w−1}), for any closed-subscheme structure on that set, and in particular over V(p_2^{-1}I_{Z,>w−1}·O_{C_t^{tor}}). This set contains p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}. The proof is unchanged except for the support comparison. It only needs supp(p_1^⋆D_{w,+}+p_2^⋆D_{w,+}) ⊆ supp(p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i), and this inclusion holds on all of p_i^{-1}(Z_{>w−1}) (see the argument below). Then take k′ ≥ k + m, with m the constant for V(p_2^{-1}I_{Z,>w−1}). This m does not depend on n or on the twist m in D_{−,w}, because every I^{n−1}_{Z,>w−1}/I^n_{Z,>w−1} is killed by I_{Z,>w−1}. No restriction to the complement of p_2^⋆D_{−,w} is needed, and no argument through the limit over m.`. Checked from the definitions of §4.1, using Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}) and D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n), where n is the level. On the open stratum S̃_{=w′} we have Z_i = V(p^{n w′_i}). Hence Z_{>w−1} = ∩_i Z_{i,>w_i−1} contains every stratum S_{F_p,w′} with w′_i ≥ w_i for all i. By contrast, S_{(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i(Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1}) meets only the stratum S_{F_p,w}.

Explicit case, g = 2 and w = (1,1), i.e. Gr_3 multiplicative and Gr_4 étale:
- Z_{1,>0} = D_3 and Z_{2,>0} = D_3 + D_4. So Z_{>w−1} = supp D_3, which contains S_{F_p,(1,2)}, the locus where Gr_3 and Gr_4 are multiplicative.
- Z_2 − V(p^{2n}) = −(D_1 + D_2). So Z_{2,<2} = D_1 + D_2, and this vanishes on S_{F_p,(1,2)}. Hence S_{F_p,(1,2)} ∩ S_{(w−1,w+1)} = ∅.
- D_{+,w} ⊇ Z_{1,<1} = D_2 ≠ 0. So the required factorization is not vacuous.

The sheaves ω̃^κ(−mD_{−,w}) ⊗ I^{n−1}_{Z,>w−1}/I^n_{Z,>w−1} are supported on all of Z_{>w−1}. So "an application of corollary 4.4.3" does not, as stated, give the factorization on the whole support of p⋆_2 of these sheaves. The missing extension is short: either the support argument in (a), or the extension-by-zero argument in (b). For (b) one uses that Z_{>w−1} ∖ D_{−,w} ⊆ S_{(w−1,w+1)}. Here is why. At a special-fibre point x off Z_{i,>w_i}, we have Z_{i,>w_i+1} − Z_{i,<w_i+1} = −Z_{i,<w_i} − V(p^n) near x. If x were not in Z_{i,<w_i+1}, an effective divisor would equal an anti-effective one containing V(p^n), which is impossible at a point where p is not a unit.

This is an omitted argument, not a false statement. The factorization in the proof of Proposition 4.5.8 is applied to p_2^⋆(ω̃^κ(−mD_{−,w}) ⊗ I^{n−1}_{Z,>w−1}/I^n_{Z,>w−1}). This is a module over O/p_2^{-1}I_{Z,>w−1}, so it lives on p_2^{-1}(Z_{>w−1}), where Z_{>w−1} = ∩_i Z_{i,>w_i−1} (§4.1.16). The divisor D_{+,w} of p. 52 is the D_{w,+} of p. 50.

Corollary 4.4.3 only gives the factorization over p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}. Here S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1}. Page 50 prints Z_{i,>w_i+1}, which is a slip: with it the set would not contain S^{tor}_{F_p,w}, which the proof of 4.4.3 requires. So S_{(w−1,w+1)} = Z_{>w−1} ∩ ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1}, and this is in general strictly smaller than Z_{>w−1}.

- On S̃_{=w′} one has Z_i = V(p^{nw′_i}). Together with Lemma 4.1.17(1), this shows that S^{tor}_{F_p,w′} ⊆ Z_{>w−1} exactly when w′_i ≥ w_i for all i.
- S^{tor}_{F_p,w′} misses Z_{i,<w_i+1} whenever w′_i > w_i.
- Example: for g = 2 and w = (0,1), the strata w′ = (1,1) and (1,2) lie in Z_{>w−1} but not in S_{(w−1,w+1)}.
- The excess Z_{>w−1} \ S_{(w−1,w+1)} lies in D_{−,w}.

So the sheaves in question are not covered by Corollary 4.4.3 as stated, and no other statement in the paper covers them. For g = 1 the problem does not arise (either D_{w,+} = ∅ or the two sets coincide).

Why this is only a gap. The proof of Corollary 4.4.3 uses two things:
- the scheme is quasi-compact;
- supp(p_1^⋆D_{w,+}+p_2^⋆D_{w,+}) ⊆ supp(E), where E = p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i.

The inclusion is what gives f_i^n = h_i g_i; the reverse inclusion is never used. This inclusion holds on all of p_i^{-1}(Z_{>w−1}):
1. By Propositions 4.2.14(1) and 4.2.15(3), the complement of supp E is ∪_{w′} C^{tor}_{t,w′}, where C_{t,w′} = p_1^{-1}S_{w′} ∩ p_2^{-1}S_{w′}.
2. If such a point lies over Z_{>w−1}, then S_{w′} meets every Z_{i,>w_i−1}. This forces w′_i ≥ w_i for all i: otherwise Z_{i,>w_i−1} ≤ Z_{i,>w′_i} by Lemma 4.1.17(1), and Z_{i,>w′_i} misses S_{w′} by definition.
3. Then Z_{i,<w_i} ≤ Z_{i,<w′_i} also misses S_{w′}, so the point lies on neither p_1^⋆D_{w,+} nor p_2^⋆D_{w,+}.

Hence the proof of Corollary 4.4.3 goes through verbatim over the fixed closed subscheme V(p_2^{-1}I_{Z,>w−1}), with a single m that serves all n. Composing O → O(p_2^⋆D_{w,+}) → O(p_1^⋆D_{w,+}+p_2^⋆D_{w,+}) → O(mE) → O((k′−k)E) then gives the claimed factorization. Proposition 4.5.8, Theorem 4.5.2 (item (5) of the introduction) and Corollaries 4.5.4–4.5.5 are unaffected.

On the scheme structure: the paper takes (p) ⊆ I_{Z,>w−1} (last sentence of the proof, p. 53), so these graded pieces are killed by p. The argument does not depend on this in any case. - **Misprint** at §5.1, Remark 5.1.2 and proof of Theorem 5.1.4, p. 53. The source says `Remark 5.1.2, p. 53: "Let t_0 = diag(1_g, p1_g). Let K_{p,P} be a decomposable compact. For n large enough, t_0^{−n} K_{p,P} t_0^{n} ⊆ P′(Z_p)." Proof of Theorem 5.1.4, p. 53: "Also, if the theorem is satisfied by a compact open subgroup K_{p,P}, it is satisfied by any conjugate by t_0 = diag(1_g, p1_g) and for r large enough, t_0^{−r} K_{p,P} t_0^{r} ⊆ K′_{p,P}."`; it should be `Remark 5.1.2 should read: for n large enough, t_0^{n} K_{p,P} t_0^{−n} ⊆ P′(Z_p). In the proof of Theorem 5.1.4 it should read: for r large enough, t_0^{r} K_{p,P} t_0^{−r} ⊆ K′_{p,P}. Equivalently, keep the printed exponents and replace t_0 by t_0^{−1} = diag(1_g, p^{−1}1_g).`. Conventions (§3.1, pp. 33–34). Matrices act on column vectors. P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩, and x^{−1}Px is described as the stabiliser of x^{−1}⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩. So P is block lower triangular and U_P is the lower-left g×g block. The Borel B ⊆ P is upper triangular on the diagonal blocks, and its unipotent radical is N = N_M·U_P.

The definition of T^+(Q_p) on p. 34 is v(t_{g+1}) ≥ … ≥ v(t_{2g}) ≥ v(t_1) ≥ … ≥ v(t_g). This is exactly the condition that v(t_i) ≥ v(t_j) for every entry (i, j) of N, that is, that n ↦ tnt^{−1} maps N(Z_p) into itself. The dominant cone 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ … ≥ k_g on the same page gives the same picture. With row vectors, B would be upper triangular, and for g ≥ 2 neither condition would cut out the chamber of B or of its opposite.

By Lemma 3.4.3 and the paragraph after it (p. 36), P′(Q_p) has the group structure of P(Q_p), with M(Q_p) acting on U_P(Q_p)(1) by the usual conjugation. Also P′(Z_p) = M(Z_p) ⋉ U_P(Z_p)(1) (Remark 3.4.6).

Computation. t_0 = diag(1_g, p1_g) is a similitude with factor p. It is central in M and lies in T^+(Q_p). For u ∈ U_P and an entry (i, j) with i > g ≥ j, (t_0^{a} u t_0^{−a})_{ij} = p^{a} u_{ij}. So conjugation by t_0^{a} fixes M and scales U_P by p^{a}. Hence t_0^{−n}(·)t_0^{n} enlarges the unipotent part.

The printed inclusions are false. Let K = K_{p,P}. Since K is open in P′(Q_p), U_K = K ∩ U_P(Q_p)(1) is a nonzero compact open subgroup. Then t_0^{−n}Kt_0^{n} ∩ U_P(Q_p)(1) = p^{−n}U_K, and this is not contained in U_P(Z_p)(1) once n is large. So Remark 5.1.2 fails for every K and all large n. The group K′_{p,P} = wK″_pw^{−1} ∩ P(Q_p) is compact, so t_0^{−r}Kt_0^{r} ⊆ K′_{p,P} also fails for all large r.

Example: take g = 1 and w = 1. Then M = T and B = P. K = P′(Z_p) = T(Z_p) ⋉ U_P(Z_p)(1) is decomposable, and K′_{p,P} = P(Z_p). But t_0^{−n}Kt_0^{n} contains the unipotent element with lower-left entry p^{−n}. So both inclusions fail for every n, r ≥ 1.

The corrected inclusions hold. By condition (1), t_0^{r}Kt_0^{−r} = M_K ⋉ p^{r}U_K. By condition (3), M_K lies in the Iwahori subgroup of M(Q_p) with respect to B ∩ M = B_w ∩ M. That subgroup is contained in M(Z_p) and equals wK″_pw^{−1} ∩ M. For r large, p^{r}U_K ⊆ pU_P(Z_p) ⊆ wK″_pw^{−1} ∩ U_P, since elements of pU_P(Z_p) reduce to 1 mod p. Hence t_0^{r}Kt_0^{−r} ⊆ P′(Z_p) and t_0^{r}Kt_0^{−r} ⊆ K′_{p,P}. Conjugation by t_0 also preserves decomposability.

Why this is a misprint and not an error. As printed, both inclusions are false in every case, not only in an edge case. But the intended statement is unambiguous. "For n large enough" can hold only for the conjugation that contracts U_P. The proof of Lemma 3.4.8 (p. 37) conjugates by the same central element diag(1,…,1,p,…,p) of M(Q_p) for exactly this purpose ("to have K_{p,U_P} ⊆ U_P(Z_p)(1)"), without stating a direction. For t_0 ∈ T^+, the map x ↦ t_0xt_0^{−1} fixes M and shrinks U_P ⊆ N (Remark 5.1.3: N_{K_{p,P}} = N_{M_{K_{p,P}}} × U_{K_{p,P}}). The fix is the same change of sign in both places.

Consequences: none. In the proof of Theorem 5.1.4, the theorem holds for t_0^{r}Kt_0^{−r} ⊆ K′_{p,P} by Proposition 4.4.4 and Lemma 2.1.34. It then holds for K, which is the conjugate of t_0^{r}Kt_0^{−r} by t_0^{−r}. The proof invokes invariance under conjugation by t_0, and this applies equally to t_0^{−1}: both lie in T(Q_p) ⊆ M(Q_p), so both commute with t ∈ T_w(Q_p)^{++} ⊆ T(Q_p). The later appeal in the proof of Proposition 5.2.5 (p. 54), "by conjugating by t_0, we may assume that K_{p,P} ⊆ P′(Z_p)", states no direction and is correct in the corrected one. Theorem 2.6.10 (§2.6.9, p. 22) assumes a finite abelian group G acting linearly on the coherent sheaf. The cohomological correspondence must commute with this action, and the sheaf must be flat over A[G]. The only natural way to realise G = T_w(Z_p)/T_{w,K_{p,P}} is as the deck group of IG_{K^pK_{p,P}} → IG_{K^pT_w(Z_p)K_{p,P}}. This needs T_w(Z_p) to normalise K_{p,P}.

The definition of "decomposable with respect to w" (§5.1, p. 53) does not require this. It asks for: (1) K = M_K ⋉ U_K; (2) an Iwahori decomposition K = N_{w,K} × T_{w,K} × N̄_{w,K}; (3) M_K inside the Iwahori subgroup of M with an Iwahori decomposition. Remark 5.1.1 stresses that the class is broad.

Counterexample, checked by direct computation. Take g = 2, w = Id and p ≥ 5, with the pairing ⟨e_1,e_4⟩ = ⟨e_2,e_3⟩ = 1. Then P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_3,e_4⟩, and U_P consists of the lower-left blocks X. Such a block is symplectic exactly when x_{31} = x_{42}. Use the coordinates a = x_{41}, b = x_{32}, m = x_{31}. The element t = diag(t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4) with t_1t_4 = t_2t_3 = c scales them by c t_1^{-2}, c t_2^{-2} and c(t_1t_2)^{-1}.

Let M_K = {g ∈ M(Z_p) : g ≡ 1 mod p} and U_K = {a ≡ b mod p}. U_K is stable under Z_p^× (so it is Galois-stable) and contains pU_P(Z_p). M_K acts trivially modulo p, so K = M_K ⋉ U_K is a compact open subgroup of P′(Z_p). It satisfies (1)–(3) with N_K = N_{M_K}U_K and T_K = T(1+pZ_p).

Now take s = diag(1,2,1/2,1) ∈ T(Z_p), which is symplectic with c = 1. Conjugating u = (a,b,m) = (1,1,0) ∈ U_K by s gives (1,1/4,0). This is not in U_K, since 1 ≢ 1/4 mod p for p ≥ 5. So T(Z_p) does not normalise K, and s carries IG_{K^pK} to a different Igusa variety. Moreover U_K ∩ sU_Ks^{-1} = {a ≡ b ≡ 0 mod p}, of index p in U_K. So the Hecke correspondence [KsK] has degree p and is not an automorphism. The paper nowhere shows that the operators [KsK] with s ∈ T(Z_p) give a group action on the ordinary part.

Hence neither the T_w(Z_p)/T_{w,K}-module structure nor its perfectness follows from Theorem 2.6.10 for such K. The statement survives, by reduction through Proposition 5.2.5 to a T(Z_p)-normalised compact with the same torus part. Proposition 5.2.7, the only place Proposition 5.2.3 is cited, can be run with such a compact. So only the proof is affected. Printed text checked on the page image of p. 54, and in the 2024 preprint, p. 52.

What Theorem 2.6.10 needs. The setting of §2.6.9 (p. 22) is a finite abelian group G acting linearly on the coherent sheaf. The cohomological correspondence must commute with G, and the sheaf must be flat over A[G]. For F = O on IG_{K^pK_{p,P}}, the only available action of G = T_w(Z_p)/T_{w,K_{p,P}} is by deck transformations. That action exists only if T(Z_p) normalises K_{p,P}.

What decomposability gives. Conditions (1)–(3) of §5.1 (p. 53) require:
- K = M_K ⋉ U_K;
- an Iwahori decomposition N_{w,K} × T_{w,K} × N̄_{w,K};
- M_K inside the Iwahori subgroup of M, with its own Iwahori decomposition.

None of these forces T(Z_p) to normalise U_K. The paper treats a product decomposition U_K = ∏K_α as an extra assumption (Remark 3.4.11, p. 37). Remark 5.1.1 stresses that the class of decomposable compacts is broad.

Counterexample, checked by direct computation. Take g = 2, w = Id and p ≥ 5, with the conventions of p. 34:
- B ⊂ P is upper triangular on the diagonal blocks;
- P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_3, e_4⟩;
- e_i pairs with e_{5−i}.

Then U_P consists of the lower-left blocks X, and such a block is symplectic exactly when x_{31} = x_{42}. Use the coordinates a = x_{41}, b = x_{32}, m = x_{31}. The element t = diag(t_1, t_2, t_3, t_4) with t_1t_4 = t_2t_3 = c scales them by c t_1^{-2}, c t_2^{-2} and c(t_1t_2)^{-1}.

Let M_K = ker(M(Z_p) → M(F_p)) and U_K = {a ≡ b mod p}. Then U_K contains pU_P(Z_p), is Z_p^×-stable, and is M_K-stable, since M_K acts trivially mod p. So K = M_K ⋉ U_K is a compact open subgroup of P′(Z_p). It satisfies (1)–(3) with:
- N_K = N_{M_K}U_K;
- T_K = T(1+pZ_p), so that T(Z_p)/T_K = T(F_p);
- N̄_K = N̄_{M_K}.

Now take s = diag(1, 2, 1/2, 1). It sends (1, 1, 0) ∈ U_K to (1, 1/4, 0) ∉ U_K. In fact, the normaliser of K in T(Z_p) is {t_1^2 ≡ t_2^2 mod p}, which has index (p−1)/2 in T(F_p). So T(F_p) does not act on IG_{K^pK}.

The correspondence of Lemma 5.2.2 for s has p_1 of degree [K : K ∩ sKs^{-1}] = [U_K : U_K ∩ sU_Ks^{-1}] = p. Moreover, the coset decompositions coming from the Iwahori decomposition give [KtK][KsK] = p[KtsK] in the Hecke algebra of K, for every t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p). So the correspondences attached to T^+(Q_p) ⊇ T(Z_p) do not multiply like the monoid T^+(Q_p). The T(Z_p)-part of the asserted T(Q_p)-structure can therefore only be the extension of the invertible T^{++}-action, which no finite group acting on the sheaf induces. For this K, Theorem 2.6.10 gives neither the T(Q_p)-structure nor perfectness over Z_p[T(F_p)]. Similar examples exist for p = 3 with congruences mod 9.

Defence considered. When T(Z_p) normalises K_{p,P}, as for K_{w,p,P}, the proof goes through as in the correction. So the statement is fine in the cases the paper actually needs. Without that hypothesis, it is at best recoverable through Proposition 5.2.5. The same caveat applies to the T(Q_p)-module structure asserted without proof in §5.3.1 (p. 55) for general decomposable K_{p,P}.

Consequences. Proposition 5.2.3 is cited only in the proof of Proposition 5.2.7, which can be run with a T(Z_p)-normalised K_{p,P}. Later results (Theorem 5.3.5, Lemma 5.4.1, …) use only RΓ_w(K^p). So only the proof is affected. The proposed hypothesis is correct and is the minimal natural one. K′_{p,P}) with {M ∈ P′(Z_p), M mod p^nZ_p ∈ B(Z/p^nZ)} for n large enough."`; it should be `Replace "B(Z/p^nZ)" with "B̄_w(Z/p^nZ)". For n large, both N_w-parts equal the congruence subgroup (N_w ∩ P′)(p^nZ_p), which serves as the common N″. Both groups are again decomposable: (1) We have B̄_w ∩ P = T·(N̄_w ∩ M)·(N̄_w ∩ U_P), so the congruence condition splits into an M-part and a U_P-part. (3) B_w ∩ M = B ∩ M, so B̄_w ∩ M = B̄ ∩ M. Hence M_{K″} = N_{M_K}(p^n) × T × N̄_{M_K} still lies in the Iwahori subgroup of M and has an Iwahori decomposition. There is one other consistent repair: use B_w, mirror the claim to N_{w,K} × T × N̄″, and swap the roles of traces and pull-backs in the rest of the proof. That changes more text. B̄_w is the one-symbol fix that leaves the claim and the rest of the proof as printed.`. Conventions of the paper. P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩ (p. 34), so its unipotent radical U_P is the lower-left block. B ⊆ P is "upper triangular on the diagonal g × g blocks" (p. 35), so U_P ⊆ B and N = N_M·U_P. Remark 5.1.3 (p. 53) confirms this: N_{K_{p,P}} = N_{M_{K_{p,P}}} × U_{K_{p,P}} and N̄_{K_{p,P}} = N̄_{M_{K_{p,P}}}.

The printed condition, for w = Id and g ≥ 2. Here B_w = B. Write k = n t n̄ with n t ∈ B(Z_p) and n̄ ∈ N̄_{M_K}. Then k mod p^n ∈ B(Z/p^n) iff n̄ ≡ 1 mod p^n. So K ∩ {M mod p^n ∈ B} = N_K × T_K × (N̄_{M_K} ∩ N̄_M(p^nZ_p)). Its N-part is unchanged and its N̄-part is cut down. Take for example K = K_{p,1} ∩ P(Q_p), the Iwahori-level group of Lemma 4.1.7 (p. 42) with w = Id, and take n ≥ 2. Then N̄_{M_K} consists of matrices with entries in pZ_p, so it is strictly cut down. The result is not of the form N″ × T × N̄_{w,K}. Also K″ and K‴ keep the different N-parts N_K and N′_K, so they share no common N″.

For general w, the printed condition cuts only N̄_M = N̄_w ∩ M. It never touches the root groups of U_P ∩ N̄_w, because U_P ⊆ B. So for w ≠ Id it does not even give a common N̄_w-part. Swapping the roles of N_w and N̄_w in the claim therefore does not save the printed recipe.

The rest of the proof needs the claim exactly as stated. For t ∈ T^{++}, direct computation shows that v(t_i) − v(t_j) > 0 on every root of B, using v(t_{g+1}) > … > v(t_{2g}) > v(t_1) > … > v(t_g) (p. 35). So x ↦ t x t^{−1} contracts N, and for t ∈ T_w^{++} it contracts N_w. Hence K_{n,0} = K ∩ t^nKt^{−n} cuts down only the N_w-part. The chain K″_{n,0} ⊆ K_{m,0} ⊆ K″_{l,0} ⊆ K_{r,0} with trace maps (p. 55) therefore compares groups that differ only in their N_w-part, as in the stated claim. The pull-back step for K″ and K‴ compares groups that differ only in their N̄_w-part. With B̄_w in place of B, everything fits.

The claim itself is true, and Proposition 5.2.5 holds as stated. Proposition 5.2.7 uses only the statement and its method. So nothing downstream changes. Conventions (pp. 33–35).
- P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩, so U_P is the lower-left block.
- B ⊆ P is upper triangular on the diagonal blocks, so U_P ⊆ B.
- This matches the stated dominance conditions. Φ^+ contains the U_P roots t_i/t_j (i > g ≥ j), which forces v(t_{g+1}) ≥ … ≥ v(t_{2g}) ≥ v(t_1) ≥ … ≥ v(t_g) for T^+ and 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ … ≥ k_g for X*(T)^+.
- So t ∈ T^{++} satisfies |α(t)| < 1 for every α ∈ Φ^+, and x ↦ t x t^{−1} contracts N. Likewise t ∈ T_w^{++} = wT^{++}w^{−1} contracts N_w. This is Casselman's A^-, the monoid used in §4.2 via [Cas].
- Remark 5.1.3 gives the B-decomposition K = N_K × T × N̄_K with N̄_K = N̄_{M_K} and N_K = N_{M_K} × U_K.

The printed recipe does not give the claimed shape.
- Case w = Id. Write k = n t n̄ with n t ∈ B. Then k mod p^n ∈ B iff n̄ ≡ 1 mod p^n, so K ∩ {mod p^n ∈ B} = N_K × T × N̄_K(p^n). The N-part is unchanged and the N̄-part is cut down. This is the mirror image of the claim.
- Concrete example, checked by direct computation. Take g = 2 and K = {M ∈ P′(Z_p) : M mod p ∈ B}, the w = Id group from the proof of Theorem 5.1.4. The element diag([[1,0],[p,1]], [[1,0],[−p,1]]) lies in N̄_{M_K} ⊆ N̄_{w,K}. For n ≥ 2 it is not in the printed K″. So K″ is not of the form N″ × T × N̄_{w,K} for any N″.
- Also K″ and K‴ keep the different N-parts N_K and N′_K, so there is no common N″.
- Case w ≠ Id. The printed condition cuts only N̄_M = N̄_w ∩ M. It never touches U_K ∩ N̄_w, which is nontrivial for w ≠ Id and depends on K, because U_P ⊆ B. So K″ and K‴ share neither their N_w-part nor their N̄_w-part. Reading the claim the other way round therefore does not rescue the printed recipe.

The claim as printed is the shape the rest of the proof needs (p. 55).
- For m large, K_{m,0} = K ∩ t^mKt^{−m} = t^m N_{w,K} t^{−m} × T × N̄_{w,K}. So the chain K″_{n,0} ⊆ K_{m,0} ⊆ K″_{l,0} ⊆ K_{r,0} with trace maps requires K″ to have N̄-part exactly N̄_{w,K}.
- K″ and K‴ then differ only in their N̄_w-part, which the pull-back step handles.
- With B̄_w the chain holds. N″ = (N_w ∩ P′)(p^nZ_p) is stable under conjugation by t, lies in N_{w,K}, and t^c N_{w,K} t^{−c} ⊆ N″ for c large.

The one other use of this construction in the paper is correct. The proof of Theorem 5.3.5 (p. 56) deliberately intersects with B(Z/p^n) to cut the N̄-side, with limit B_{K_{p,P}}. That is presumably where the letter B came from.

- **Misprint** at §5.3.4, proof of Theorem 5.3.5, p. 56. The subscript slip is in the display after "It follows that". The ω_{0,M} slip is in four formulas: the inline map to the lowest weight vector, the display after "It follows that", and both lines of the display after "We then check that". The January 2024 preprint has the same text on p. 54.. The source says `(i) Lowest-weight projection: "It induces a surjective map which is thought of as the projection to the lowest weight vector: ω^κ → (π⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{N_{K_{p,P}}}} ⊗ ω_{0,M}κ)^{T_{w,K_{p,P}}}." (ii) After "It follows that": "RΓ(𝔍𝔊^{tor}_{K^pB_{K_{p,P}}}, ω^κ)^{ord} = RΓ(𝔍𝔊^{tor}_{K^pB_{K_{p,P}}}, (π⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{K^pU(ℤ_p)}} ⊗ ω_{0,M}κ)^{T_{w,K_{p,P}}})^{ord}." (iii) After "We then check that": "RHom_{T_{K_{p,P}}}(ν, RΓ_w(K^p)) = RΓ(𝔍𝔊^{tor}_{K^pB_{K_{p,P}}}, (π⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{K^pN_{K_{p,P}}}} ⊗ w^{−1}ω_{0,M}κ)^{T_{K_{p,P}}})^{ord}" (iv) "= RΓ(𝔍𝔊^{tor}_{K^pB_{K_{p,P}}}, (π⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{K^pN_{K_{p,P}}}} ⊗ ω_{0,M}κ)^{T_{w,K_{p,P}}})^{ord}" All four places print a Greek omega. In (iii) it comes right after a Roman w^{−1}. The next paragraph uses Roman w: "ν = −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ becomes −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ)".`; it should be `In (ii), read π⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{K^pN_{K_{p,P}}}} for π⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{K^pU(ℤ_p)}}, where π : 𝔍𝔊^{tor}_{K^pN_{K_{p,P}}} → 𝔍𝔊^{tor}_{K^pB_{K_{p,P}}}. In (i), (ii) and (iv), read w_{0,M}κ for ω_{0,M}κ, and in (iii) read w^{−1}w_{0,M}κ for w^{−1}ω_{0,M}κ. Here w_{0,M} is the longest element of W_M (p. 3). The corrected (ii) is RΓ(𝔍𝔊^{tor}_{K^pB_{K_{p,P}}}, ω^κ)^{ord} = RΓ(𝔍𝔊^{tor}_{K^pB_{K_{p,P}}}, (π⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{K^pN_{K_{p,P}}}} ⊗ w_{0,M}κ)^{T_{w,K_{p,P}}})^{ord}.`. The omega. The page shows a Greek ω in all four places, while the nearby text writes Roman w_{0,M}. The symbol ω_{0,M} is never defined and occurs nowhere else in the paper. By contrast, w_{0,M} is defined on p. 3 as the longest element of W_M and is used throughout. What is tensored in is a character of the torus: the lowest weight w_{0,M}κ of V_κ. Compare p. 46, where ω^κ = π⋆𝒪_{M_dR}[−w_{0,M}κ]. Several things confirm this reading:
- The closing paragraph of the proof says that ν = −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) − ρ becomes −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ), in Roman type.
- In (iii) a Roman w^{−1} is followed directly by the Greek ω_{0,M}.
- Remark 5.4.3 (p. 57) gives the same construction in families. There T_w(ℤ_p) acts on Λ through the character w_{0,M}κ^{univ}, again in Roman type.
- The signs agree. RHom_{T_{K_{p,P}}}(ν, −) twists by −ν = w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) + ρ. Once the ρ-shift is absorbed by the normalisation of the trace, this is w^{−1}w_{0,M}κ, as in (iii). Conjugating by w, using T_{K_{p,P}} = w^{−1}T_{w,K_{p,P}}w, turns it into the character w_{0,M}κ of T_{w,K_{p,P}}, as in (iv).

The subscript. By Remark 5.1.3 (p. 53), K_{p,P} = N_{K_{p,P}} × T_{w,K_{p,P}} × N̄_{K_{p,P}}, so B_{K_{p,P}} = N_{K_{p,P}} × T_{w,K_{p,P}}. In this proof, π : 𝔍𝔊^{tor}_{K^pN_{K_{p,P}}} → 𝔍𝔊^{tor}_{K^pB_{K_{p,P}}} is therefore a T_{w,K_{p,P}}-torsor, and the T_{w,K_{p,P}}-invariants in (i)–(iv) are taken on this torsor. Display (ii) is derived from the vanishing of the ordinary cohomology of the kernel of the map in (i). Its right-hand side must therefore be the target of (i), which is built from 𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{N_{K_{p,P}}}}. Also, (ii), (iii) and (iv) form one chain, and the proof closes only if the right-hand side of (ii) equals (iv), which is written with 𝔍𝔊_{K^pN_{K_{p,P}}}. The surrounding lines agree:
- the "by definition" display uses π⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊^{tor}_{K^pN_{K_{p,P}}}};
- (i) uses 𝔍𝔊_{N_{K_{p,P}}};
- (iii) and (iv) use 𝔍𝔊_{K^pN_{K_{p,P}}};
- Remark 5.4.3 (p. 57) writes π⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊^{tor}_{K^pN_{K_{p,P}}}}, with T_w(ℤ_p) acting as the diagonal torus of B_{K_{p,P}}.

The symbol U(ℤ_p) comes from the notation of §1 (p. 3, K_p = U_{K_p} × T_{K_p} × Ū_{K_p}) and of §4.3.5 (p. 47), where U is the unipotent radical of B. In §5 that group is called N (§5.1, p. 53). There U_{K_{p,P}} denotes the U_P-part of K_{p,P}, with N_{K_{p,P}} = N_{M_{K_{p,P}}} × U_{K_{p,P}} (Remark 5.1.3). For a general decomposable K_{p,P}, the group N_{K_{p,P}} = N ∩ K_{p,P} differs from U(ℤ_p). In fact 𝔍𝔊_{K^pU(ℤ_p)} does not even lie over 𝔍𝔊_{K^pB_{K_{p,P}}} unless U(ℤ_p) ⊆ K_{p,P}. U(ℤ_p) occurs nowhere else in the proof. The only other U in the proof is in 𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_{p,P}}}}, in the map 𝒪_{M_dR} → 𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_{p,P}}}} from Proposition 5.3.3. That map uses the M_{K_{p,P}}-torsor and plays a different role.
