- **Misprint** at §5.4, Remark 5.4.3, p. 57 (propagates to §6.2.11, Proposition 6.2.13 and Theorem 6.2.15(1), pp. 63–64; compare Proposition 1.4.7, p. 5). The source says `Remark 5.4.3 (p. 57): "M_w^• = RΓ(IG^{tor}_{K^pB_{K_{p,P}}}, (π_⋆O_{IG^{tor}_{K^pN_{K_{p,P}}}} ⊗ Λ)^{T_w(Z_p)})^{ord}. Let ν^{univ} : T(Z_p) → Λ^× be the universal character. Let κ^{univ} be defined by the formula κ^{univ} = −w_{0,M}w(ν^{univ} + ρ) − ρ. In this last formula, T_w(Z_p) acts on π_⋆O_{IG^{tor}_{K^pN_{K_{p,P}}}} since T_w(Z_p) is the diagonal torus of B_{K_{p,P}}. It acts on Λ = Z_p[[T(Z_p)]] via the character w_{0,M}κ^{univ} (this is the composition of T_w(Z_p) →^{w^{−1}} T(Z_p) →^{w^{−1}w_{0,M}κ^{univ}} Λ^×). For any ν = ν_{alg}χ : T(Z_p) → Z_p(ζ_{p^n})^×, with ν_{alg} ∈ X^⋆(T) and χ a finite order character, and for κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν + ρ) − ρ, we have: M_w^• ⊗_{Λ,−ν} Z_p(ζ_{p^n}) = RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ)."`; it should be `Normalise the universal character as ν^{univ}(t) = [t^{−1}], not as the tautological t ↦ [t]. The paper gives no formula for ν^{univ}. Read ⊗_{Λ,ψ}, for a character ψ of T(Z_p), as base change along the ring map [t] ↦ ψ(t). Write c = −ρ − w^{−1}w_{0,M}ρ. With these conventions: - In the sheaf formula, T_w(Z_p) acts on Λ through t ↦ [w^{−1}tw]·c(w^{−1}tw). So the formula agrees, as Λ-modules, with the definition M_w^• = RHom_{T(Z_p)}(1, RΓ_w(K^p)⊗̂Λ), where T(Z_p) acts on Λ by t ↦ [t]. - ⊗_{Λ,−ν} is base change along [t] ↦ ν(t)^{−1}. This map sends ν^{univ} to ν, and the base change gives RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ), as printed. In §6.2.11, ν_A is the restriction of this ν^{univ}. The map ν: A → O_C on p. 64 is the one sending ν_A to ν. With this convention, no sign needs to change in Proposition 1.4.7, Remark 5.4.3, Proposition 6.2.13 or Theorem 6.2.15. Alternatively, keep ν^{univ}(t) = [t] and make two changes: - In the sheaf formula of the remark, T_w(Z_p) must act on Λ through t ↦ [w^{−1}tw]·c(w^{−1}tw). - "M_w^• ⊗ A/p^n" in Proposition 6.2.13 and "M_w^• ⊗_Λ A" in Theorem 6.2.15(1) must be formed along Λ → A composed with the involution ι: [t] ↦ [t^{−1}] of Λ. This alternative changes a displayed formula and two stated results. The normalisation above changes none of them.`. Write T for T(Z_p). The remark identifies T_w(Z_p) with T through w^{−1}, i.e. t ↦ w^{−1}tw. For a character ψ: T → R^×, read ⊗_{Λ,ψ} as base change along the ring map Λ → R, [t] ↦ ψ(t). So ⊗_{Λ,−ν} is base change along [t] ↦ ν(t)^{−1}. For a character ψ, RHom_T(1, X⊗ψ) = RHom_T(ψ^{−1}, X).

Conventions of the paper.
- RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ) = RHom_T(ν, RΓ_w(K^p)⊗Z_p(ζ_{p^n})) is the ν-isotypic part (p. 56). Compare Remark 4.4.6 (p. 51), where T acts through ν_{alg}χ.
- The proof of Theorem 5.3.5 (p. 56) gives RHom_T(ν, RΓ_w(K^p)) = RΓ((π_⋆O ⊗ w^{−1}w_{0,M}κ)^T)^{ord}. Here w^{−1}w_{0,M}κ = −ν + c, where c = −ρ − w^{−1}w_{0,M}ρ is the factor "absorbed by the normalization of the trace map". So the normalised action of T on RΓ_w(K^p) is the geometric action on π_⋆O twisted by c.

The definition. M_w^• = RHom_T(1, RΓ_w(K^p)⊗̂Λ) (p. 56, and p. 5). The paper does not say how T acts on Λ. Of the two actions t ↦ [t] and t ↦ [t^{−1}], only t ↦ [t] makes the last display of the remark hold, so take that one. Base change along θ: Λ → R gives RHom_T(ψ^{−1}, RΓ_w(K^p)⊗R), where ψ(t) = θ([t]). Along −ν this is the ν-isotypic part RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ), which is what the last display of the remark states. Proposition 1.4.7 combines this identity with the classicality theorem, Theorem 1.4.3(4). In sheaf form, the definition has T acting on Λ through t ↦ c(t)[t].

The sheaf formula of the remark. Here T acts on Λ through w^{−1}w_{0,M}κ^{univ} = −ν^{univ} + c, i.e. through t ↦ c(t)ν^{univ}(t)^{−1}. Base change along θ commutes with the invariants and with the ordinary part. It gives the complex in the proof of Theorem 5.3.5 for the character θ∘ν^{univ}, i.e. the θ∘ν^{univ}-isotypic part of RΓ_w(K^p). This is RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ) when θ∘ν^{univ} = ν.

With the usual universal character ν^{univ}(t) = [t], the two displays of the remark contradict each other.
- The sheaf formula has T acting on Λ through c(t)[t]^{−1}, not c(t)[t]. So it is M_w^• with its Λ-structure twisted by ι: [t] ↦ [t^{−1}].
- Specialised along −ν, it gives the ν^{−1}-isotypic part RΓ_w(K^p, −w_{0,M}w(−ν_{alg}+ρ)−ρ, χ^{−1}), not RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ).
- A toy case shows this. Take T = Z/5, replace Λ by F_11[T] (F_11 contains the 5th roots of unity), take c trivial and let ν be a nontrivial character. Let V = ν⊕ν. Its ν-isotypic part has dimension 2 and its ν^{−1}-isotypic part is 0. Along −ν, the definition gives (V⊗ν^{−1})^T, of dimension 2. The remark's formula gives (V⊗ν)^T = 0. Along +ν, the remark's formula gives (V⊗ν^{−1})^T, of dimension 2.

Resolution. The pair (Λ, t ↦ [t^{−1}]) also represents continuous characters of T, so ν^{univ}(t) = [t^{−1}] is a legitimate universal character.
- With this choice the sheaf formula has T acting on Λ through c(t)[t], as the definition does.
- ⊗_{Λ,−ν} then sends ν^{univ} to ν. Both displays of the remark hold, and they agree with the definition.
- §6.2.11 (p. 63) takes ν_A to be the restriction of the universal character, with κ_A = −w_{0,M}w(ν_A+ρ)−ρ and F^{ν_A} = (π_⋆O⊗̂A)^{B_{K_{p,n}} = −w_{0,M}κ_A}. The (−w_{0,M}κ_A)-eigenspace of π_⋆O⊗̂A is the torus invariants of π_⋆O⊗A, where the torus acts on A through w_{0,M}κ_A. So on the torus this is the remark's sheaf formula base-changed to A. Under the same normalisation, Proposition 6.2.13 ("follows from the definition. See remark 5.4.3") and Theorem 6.2.15(1) need no change of sign.
- The sign matters in only one other place, the phrase "a continuous character inducing a map ν: A → O_C" (p. 64). It must mean the map sending ν_A to ν. The phrase only names the sheaf F̃^{ν,n}. Theorem 6.2.15(2) and Corollary 6.2.16 are asserted for every A and every ν. As A runs over all quasi-compact opens, they do not depend on this sign.

If instead ν^{univ}(t) = [t] is kept, the last display of the remark and Proposition 1.4.7 still follow from the definition. Proposition 6.2.13 and Theorem 6.2.15(1) then hold once M_w^• ⊗ A is formed along Λ → A composed with ι.

Either way, the context fixes the intended meaning: the definition of M_w^•, and the "−ν" in Proposition 1.4.7 and in the remark itself. The slip is a sign, namely an unstated, non-standard normalisation of the universal character, or equivalently of the character through which T_w(Z_p) acts on Λ. So this is a misprint.

Consequences. Remark 5.4.3 is cited by number only in the proof of Proposition 6.2.13. Proposition 1.4.7 refers to section 5.4 as a whole. Through Proposition 6.2.13 the remark feeds Theorem 6.2.15(1), and from there Corollary 6.2.17 and Theorem 1.4.3(3). Those amplitude bounds do not depend on the sign: ι is an automorphism of Λ, and the opens Spa(A[1/p],A) and their images under ι both cover weight space. With the normalisation above, no stated result needs a change of sign. The January 2024 preprint has the same text (Remark 5.4.3, p. 55; Proposition 6.2.13, p. 61; Proposition 1.4.7, p. 5). - **Misprint** at §5.5, proof of Theorem 5.5.1, p. 57. The source says `Statement: "RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ) ⊗ RΓ_{w_{0,M}ww_0}(K^p, −w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_{nc}, w_0χ^{−1}, cusp) → Z_p(ζ_{p^n})[−d]". Proof: "By theorem 2.7.4, the duality is a perfect pairing RΓ(IG^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,P}}, ω^κ)^{ord} ⊗ RΓ(IG^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,P}}, ω^{κ−2ρ_{nc}})^{−,ord} → Z_p(ζ_{p^n})[−d] where on RΓ(IG^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,P}}, ω^{κ−2ρ_{nc}})^{−,ord} the ordinary part is taken with respect to the map T^−(Q_p) → T(Q_p) →^w M(Q_p). … We deduce that conjugation by w_{0,M} induces an isomorphism RΓ(IG^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,P}}, ω^{κ−2ρ_{nc}})^{−,ord} ≃ RΓ(IG^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,P}}, ω^{κ−2ρ_{nc}})^{ord}." (IG is Fraktur on the page; the exponent reads κ−2ρ_{nc} with no minus sign or w_{0,M} in front, and there is no (−D), in all four places.)`; it should be `In all four places in the proof, replace ω^{κ−2ρ_{nc}} by ω^{−w_{0,M}κ−2ρ_{nc}}(−D). This is the Serre dual of ω^κ, and it matches the weight −w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_{nc} and the "cusp" in the second factor of the statement.`. The page image confirms the printed text. Theorem 2.7.4 (p. 24) pairs RΓ(X, F) with RΓ(X, D_X(F)), where D_X(F) = F^∨ ⊗ p^!O_S. For F = ω^κ we have F^∨ = ω^{−w_{0,M}κ}, because the dual of the irreducible M-representation of highest weight κ has highest weight −w_{0,M}κ. By Remark 4.3.3 (p. 47), ω_A has weights (e_i; −1), Lie(A) has weights (−e_i; 1), and ω_{A^t} has weights (e_i; 1). By Kodaira–Spencer, Ω^1(log D) is the symmetric part of ω_A ⊗ ω_{A^t}, with weights (e_a+e_b; 0) for a ≤ b. Its determinant has weight (g+1,…,g+1; 0).

P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩, so the root of the entry (g+a, b) of u_P is t_{g+1−a}^{−1}t_b^{−1}. Hence Φ^{+,M} = {(−e_a−e_b; 0) : a ≤ b}. Checked by direct computation, this is consistent with the dominant cone 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ … ≥ k_g on p. 35. It gives 2ρ_{nc} = (−(g+1),…,−(g+1); 0), so the canonical bundle Ω^d(log D)(−D) is ω^{−2ρ_{nc}}(−D). The Serre dual of ω^κ is therefore ω^{−w_{0,M}κ−2ρ_{nc}}(−D), which is exactly what the statement asserts. The cuspidal complexes are defined with O(−D) on p. 54.

Checks:
- For g = 1 the statement gives the classical pairing of ω^k with ω^{2−k}(−D). The printed proof would give ω^{k+2}.
- The statement is internally consistent. Take w′ = w_{0,M}ww_0 and κ′ = −w_{0,M}κ−2ρ_{nc}. Since −w_{0,M}ρ = ρ−2ρ_{nc}, we get κ′+ρ = −w_{0,M}(κ+ρ). Then ν′ = −w′^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ′+ρ)−ρ = −w_0ν, using w_0ρ = −ρ. This agrees with the adjoint t ↦ w_0t^{−1} and the character w_0χ^{−1}.
- The printed κ−2ρ_{nc} agrees with the correct weight only when −w_{0,M}κ = κ.
- Conjugation by w_{0,M} ∈ M(Z_p) preserves the weight of the equivariant sheaf, so the corrected sheaf belongs on both sides of the final isomorphism.

One small refinement to the reported justification: the weight (g+1,…,g+1) comes from the Kodaira–Spencer form ω_A ⊗ ω_{A^t}. Literally, det Sym^2 ω_A differs from it by a similitude twist, which does not change the conclusion.

Nothing else depends on the slip. Theorem 5.5.2 ("follows as in the previous theorem") and Theorem 1.4.8 carry no weights, and the argument goes through verbatim with the corrected sheaf. For w = Id the passage from support conditions to ordinary sheaf cohomology is correct, because D_− = ∅. In the length-one case D_{w,−} = Z_{2,>1} is non-empty, and the printed sentence silently drops the support condition along it, which amounts to taking k_− = 0.

The paper's own formalism does not allow this. The Hecke operator extends over the compactified correspondence only after a twist by −nD_− (Proposition 2.3.13). The ordinary parts of the twisted cohomologies are only shown to agree with the ordinary part with support for k_± ≥ m (Lemma 2.5.3, Proposition 2.5.4; also Theorem 2.11.4(4)). This is also why §4.3 works with ω̃^κ = ω^κ(−k′ΣZ_i), k′ large (Proposition 4.3.13, Lemma 4.3.14). So with k_− = 0 the operator need not act on RΓ(S̄ \ D_{w,+}, ω^κ(−cusp)), and even when it does, nothing shows that its ordinary part equals RΓ_w⊗Z/pZ.

The support condition also cannot be dropped as harmless. RΓ_{D_+,D_−} is a limit over k of twisted cohomologies, and such a limit can acquire lim^1 terms even on an affine scheme. For example, on A^1 over a field k, R lim_m t^m k[t] = (k[[t]]/k[t])[−1], checked by direct computation from 0 → t^m k[t] → k[t] → k[t]/t^m → 0.

The fix is the twisted statement above, which the paper's Proposition 2.5.4 supplies directly (Theorem 2.11.4 is not needed). The amplitude [0,1] = [0, ℓ(w)] then follows, provided the paper's cohomological-dimension step (itself only sketched) is applied to the twisted sheaf. So Proposition 5.6.3, and item (2) of Theorem 1.4.3 (p. 5), which quotes it, are unaffected. The only defect is in the proof. The page image confirms the printed text.

By §4.4 and Proposition 2.6.2, RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ, cusp)⊗Z/pZ is the ordinary part of RΓ_{D_{w,+},D_{w,−}}(S̄, ω^κ(−cusp)), where S̄ = S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}. By Definition 2.2.4 and Corollary 2.3.11 this complex is RΓ(S̄ \ D_{w,+}, (j_−)_!ω^κ(−cusp)) = R lim_n RΓ(S̄ \ D_{w,+}, ω^κ(−cusp)(−nD_{w,−})). So it has compact support towards D_{w,−}. For w = Id the paper notes that D_− = ∅, so usual cohomology is correct there. In the length-one case D_{w,−} = Z_{2,>1} is non-empty, and the printed sentence silently drops the support condition, which amounts to taking n = 0.

Possible defences, and why they fail:
(a) The notation does not hide a support condition. The parenthesis in the w = Id case explicitly contrasts D_− = ∅ ("so we consider usual cohomology") with the general case.
(b) The paper's own formalism does not allow n = 0.
- The Hecke operator extends over the compactified correspondence only after a twist by −nD_− (Proposition 2.3.13). For the Siegel correspondence, Proposition 4.3.13 and Lemma 4.3.14 likewise twist by −k∑Z_i.
- The ordinary parts of the twisted cohomologies are identified with the ordinary part with support only for k_± ≥ m (Lemma 2.5.3, Proposition 2.5.4, Theorem 2.11.4(4)).
- Theorem 2.11.4(3) would allow no twist, but only if T factors through p̄_1^!F(−D_−) with no pole along D_−. This is not verified for this correspondence.
- So nothing in the paper shows that the operator acts on RΓ(S̄ \ D_{w,+}, ω^κ(−cusp)) at all, or that its ordinary part there equals RΓ_w⊗Z/pZ.
(c) The support condition cannot be dropped as harmless, because an R lim of complexes in degrees [0,1] can have cohomology in degree 2 (lim^1). Already on an affine scheme a lim^1 appears. For example, on A^1 over a field k, the sequences 0 → t^m k[t] → k[t] → k[t]/t^m → 0 give R lim_m t^m k[t] = (k[[t]]/k[t])[−1], which is non-zero in degree 1 (checked by direct computation). So a degree bound for the limit does not follow from cohomological dimension 1.

With the twisted statement in the correction, which the paper's own Proposition 2.5.4 and Lemma 2.4.4 supply, the complex is a direct summand of the cohomology of a single coherent sheaf on S̄ \ D_{w,+}. The amplitude [0,1] = [0, ℓ(w)] then follows, provided the cohomological-dimension step is applied to the twisted sheaf. That step is only sketched in the paper (it concerns the map from S̄ \ D_{w,+}, inside the blown-up toroidal model, to the p-rank ≥ 1 locus of the minimal compactification). If it is read as a property of the scheme S̄ \ D_{w,+}, it covers the twisted sheaf automatically. If it is read as sheaf-specific, as in the w = Id case, where it rests on [Lan17] thm. 8.6, then it is unproved for both the untwisted and the twisted sheaf. So this correction introduces no new difficulty.

Consequences. The passage is used only in this proof: the cuspidal length-one case for g = 2, and through the duality of Theorem 5.5.2 the non-cuspidal case paired with it. Proposition 5.6.3 is quoted as Theorem 1.4.3(2) on p. 5. With the correction these statements stand, so only the proof is affected.

The nested case treated in the proof uses the hypothesis only through one fact: the limit set of the larger pair lies in the smaller pair. That fact is what gives ∩_{m,n} 𝒰′_m ∩ 𝒵_n ∩ 𝒰^c = ∅. Now go in two steps: - From (𝒰, 𝒵) to (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵): L ⊆ 𝒰, and L = L′ ⊆ 𝒰′. - From (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵) to (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′): the limit set of (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵) is contained in L, and L ⊆ 𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′. The same two steps work for (𝒰′, 𝒵′). So both finite slope parts are canonically quasi-isomorphic to that of (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′). In fact every pair in these chains has limit set exactly L, so the nested case applies even in its printed form, with equal limit sets. The union pair can be used only when the mixed sets 𝒰_∞ ∩ 𝒵′_∞ and 𝒰′_∞ ∩ 𝒵_∞ lie in L, and in general they do not. Here 𝒰_∞ = ∩_m 𝒰_m and 𝒵_∞ = ∩_n 𝒵_n. With this change the statement of Proposition 6.1.7 stands.`. The printed text on p. 59 is as quoted: the pair is (U ∪ U′, Z ∪ Z′), with ∪ in both places.

Why the union reduction fails. The proof must compare (U, Z) and (U′, Z′) with the union pair. Its own special case U ⊆ U′, Z = Z′ uses equality of the limit sets: the step "∩_{m,n} U′_m ∩ Z_n ∩ U^c = ∅" needs L′ = L ⊆ U. So the union pair would need limit set L, and nothing guarantees that.
- Since T(Ū) ⊆ U and T^t(Z) ⊆ Z°, the sets U_m and Z_n decrease.
- T commutes with unions.
- For decreasing sequences, ∩_m (A_m ∪ B_m) = (∩A_m) ∪ (∩B_m).
So the union pair has limit set (U_∞ ∪ U′_∞) ∩ (Z_∞ ∪ Z′_∞) = L ∪ (U_∞ ∩ Z′_∞) ∪ (U′_∞ ∩ Z_∞). The hypothesis L = L′ says nothing about the two mixed terms.

Counterexample, checked by direct computation:
- Setup: X̄ = three points {a, b, c}, C̄ = X̄, p̄_1 = p̄_2 = id, so T = T^t = id and every pair of subsets is a quasi-compact support condition. Let (U, Z) = ({a,b}, {a,c}) and (U′, Z′) = ({a,c}, {a,b}).
- Limit sets: both pairs have limit set {a}, but the union pair (X̄, X̄) has limit set X̄.
- Cohomology: for F = O, the finite slope parts are one-dimensional for the two pairs and three-dimensional for the union pair. So neither pair can be compared with the union pair.

In finite discrete models (directed graphs, with U closed under successors and Z under predecessors), the union pair changed the limit set in 1349 of 12662 random instances with L = L′. The intersection pair never did.

The statement itself survives. The intersection pair (U ∩ U′, Z ∩ Z′) always has limit set L, by the compactness argument in the correction, which is the same argument the proof already uses. So this is a gap in the proof, not an error in the result.

Downstream use: Proposition 6.1.7 is not cited by number later. Implicitly, it is what identifies the degree-defined support conditions of Proposition 6.1.10 (used in Theorems 6.2.9 and 6.2.15) with the Hodge–Tate ones of Proposition 6.1.11. Both have limit set S_w^tor. The deductions of Corollaries 6.2.10, 6.2.16 and 6.2.17 from [BP21] go through that identification. Since the proposition holds with the repaired proof, none of these results is affected. The page image of p. 59 shows the text as quoted, with ∪ in both entries of the pair. The 2024 preprint (p. 57) has the same words.

**What the reduction needs.** To pass to nested pairs, the proof must compare (𝒰, 𝒵) and (𝒰′, 𝒵′) with (𝒰 ∪ 𝒰′, 𝒵 ∪ 𝒵′), using the two nested special cases. The nested case (p. 59) needs the limit set of the larger pair to lie in the smaller pair: "we know that ∩_{m,n} 𝒰′_m ∩ 𝒵_n ⋂ 𝒰^c = ∅", which follows from L′ = L ⊆ 𝒰. So the union pair would need limit set L.

**Why that fails.** Since T(𝒰̄) ⊆ 𝒰 and T^t(𝒵) ⊆ 𝒵°, the sequences 𝒰_m and 𝒵_n decrease. T and T^t commute with unions, and for decreasing sequences ∩_m(A_m ∪ B_m) = (∩A_m) ∪ (∩B_m). Hence the limit set of the union pair is L ∪ (𝒰_∞ ∩ 𝒵′_∞) ∪ (𝒰′_∞ ∩ 𝒵_∞). The hypothesis says nothing about the two mixed terms. Replacing 𝒰 by 𝒰_m or 𝒵 by 𝒵_n (Proposition 6.1.4) does not change any limit set, so shrinking first does not help.

**Counterexamples** (checked by direct computation). In both, the conclusion of the proposition holds for the two given pairs, but the union pair has different finite slope cohomology. So neither given pair can be compared with the union pair: the route through the union fails, it is not merely left unproved.
- (a) Take 𝒳̄ = 𝒞̄ = three points {a, b, c}, p̄_1 = p̄_2 = id, so T = T^t = id, and F = O with the identity correspondence. Let (𝒰, 𝒵) = ({a,b}, {a,c}) and (𝒰′, 𝒵′) = ({a,c}, {a,b}). Both are quasi-compact support conditions with limit set {a}, and each finite slope part is 1-dimensional. The union pair (𝒳̄, 𝒳̄) has limit set 𝒳̄ and a 3-dimensional finite slope part.
- (b) Take 𝒳̄ = 𝒞̄ = P^1 over Q_p, p̄_1 = id, p̄_2(z) = z^2, and F = O, so T acts by f ↦ f(z^2). Let (𝒰, 𝒵) = ({|z| < p^{-1}}, {|z| ≥ p^{-1}}) and (𝒰′, 𝒵′) = ({|z| > p}, {|z| ≤ p}). Both pairs have empty support 𝒰 ∩ 𝒵, hence zero cohomology. The union pair has 𝒵 ∪ 𝒵′ = P^1, and on its cohomology the functions constant on each of the two discs are eigenvectors of T with eigenvalue 1. So its finite slope part is non-zero.

In random finite models (a relation on a finite set, with 𝒰 stable under T and 𝒵 stable under T^t) whose two pairs have equal limit sets, the union pair changed the limit set in about 6% of cases. The intersection pair, and the intermediate pair (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵), never did.

**Defence tried.** No convention in §6.1 makes the union step valid. Nor do the cited [BP21] results. Theorem 5.3.7 of [BP21] concerns one fixed pair. Corollary 5.3.8 is a sandwich criterion (T^{m+s}(𝒰) ∩ (T^t)^n(𝒵) ⊆ 𝒰′ ⊆ T^m(𝒰), and similarly for the supports). It cannot apply to the union pair, because in (a) and (b) the cohomologies really differ.

**The statement survives.** The repair in the correction is sound. That the intersection pair has limit set exactly L follows from the compactness argument already in the proof. That argument gives m0, n0 with 𝒰_{m0} ∩ 𝒵_{n0} ⊆ 𝒰′ ∩ 𝒵′. Now take x ∈ L:
- For each m, write x as the end of a T-chain of length m + m0 that starts in 𝒰. The chain's point at step m0 lies in 𝒰_{m0} ∩ 𝒵_{n0} ⊆ 𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′. So x ∈ T^m(𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′).
- Symmetrically, x ∈ (T^t)^n(𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′) for each n.

So this is a gap, not a false result. The claimed reduction to nested pairs is achievable, but not by the route given.

**Consequences.** Proposition 6.1.7 is not cited by number later. It is the implicit link between two kinds of support conditions:
- the degree-defined ones of §6.1.8 and Proposition 6.1.10, used in Theorems 6.2.9 and 6.2.15;
- the Hodge–Tate-defined ones of Proposition 6.1.11, which are those of [BP21].

Both kinds have limit set the closure of S_w^tor. This identification is what transfers the results to the cohomology of [BP21]: Corollaries 6.2.10, 6.2.16 and 6.2.17, and the remark after Corollary 6.2.10 that yields Theorem 1.5.1. The proposition claims an equality: the limit set ∩_{m,n} T^m(π^{-1}]X_w[) ∩ (T^t)^n(π^{-1}\overline{]Y_w[}) equals \overline{S^tor_w}. The proof ends as soon as it has shown that the (m,n)-th set lies in π^{-1}(]C_w[_{m,\bar n}K_{p,n}).
- It never intersects over m and n.
- It never identifies the result with \overline{S^tor_w}: S^tor_w is not mentioned and Lemma 4.1.6 is not invoked.
- It never addresses the reverse inclusion.

Nothing cited fills the gap. [BP21] lem. 3.5.10 (checked on p. 46 of [BP21]) gives only the upper bounds used here, and [BP21] does not state this limit set anywhere.

Defence considered. The missing steps are routine and the stated equality is true: the argument in the correction proves it from Lemma 4.1.6, [BP21] coro. 3.3.14 and [BP21] thm. 4.5.2. But the reverse inclusion does not follow formally from what is written. On p. 60 the paper uses only the inclusion T(π^{-1}A) ⊆ π^{-1}(A·KtK). The reverse inclusion needs the equality form of Hecke equivariance together with w·t^{±1} = w in P\G.

Downstream use. Proposition 6.1.7 needs the two limit sets to be equal. With Proposition 6.1.10, whose limit set is also \overline{S^tor_w}, this identifies the finite-slope cohomology for the support condition (U_{≥w−ε}, Z_{<w+ε}) of Theorem 6.2.9 with the [BP21] cohomology for (π^{-1}]X_w[, π^{-1}\overline{]Y_w[}). Corollary 6.2.10 (Conjecture 5.9.2 of [BP21] in the Siegel case) uses this identification without citing it, and so do the remark after it and hence Theorem 1.5.1. Since the equality holds, none of these results is affected; only the proof of Proposition 6.1.11 is incomplete.

- **Gap** at §2.1.1, proof of Lemma 2.1.6, p. 7. The 2024 preprint (also p. 7) has a different proof. It takes "an arbitrary extension of 𝒢 to X̄ by [Sta22], TAG 01PE", performs "a suitable blow-up X̄′" and cites [RG71], thm. 5.2.2 (flattening by blow-up), whose hypotheses hold here. The preprint's statement also does not ask for strict maps. So the issue was introduced in the revision. (it affects the proof). The source says `Lemma 2.1.6. Let 𝓕 be a locally free sheaf of finite rank over X. The set of compactifications (j_X : X ↪ X̄) with the property that 𝓕 extends to a locally free sheaf over X̄ is cofinal among compactifications, with maps being strict maps. Proof. Let X̄ be a compactification. We can take a coherent 𝓕̄ extension of 𝓕 to X̄ by [Sta22], Tag 0G41, and then perform a suitable blow-up so that the strict transform of 𝓕̄ is locally free by [Sta22], Tag 0ESN.`; it should be `Replace the reference to Tag 0ESN by flattening by blow-up (Raynaud–Gruson [RG71], Thm. 5.2.2 = [Sta22], Tag 0815), applied to 𝓕̄ on X̄ with U = X. This is what the 2024 preprint cites. It gives a U-admissible blow-up X̄′ → X̄ (centre disjoint from X) after which the strict transform of 𝓕̄ is flat and of finite presentation, hence finite locally free, and restricts to 𝓕 on X. Because the centre misses X, the map X̄′ → X̄ is an isomorphism over X and hence strict. Alternatively, Tag 0ESN can be kept after one preparatory step. Replace X̄ by the disjoint union of the scheme-theoretic closures in X̄ of the finitely many open-and-closed pieces X_r ⊂ X on which 𝓕 has constant rank r. This map is strict, and X_r is scheme-theoretically dense in its closure. Then blow up the r-th Fitting ideal on each piece. Passing first to a compactification with Cartier boundary (Lemma 2.1.5) is another way to get density, but the constant-rank splitting is still needed.`. Tag 0ESN is Lemma 31.36.3 of the Stacks Project. It reads: "Let X be a scheme. Let 𝓕 be a finitely presented O_X-module. Let U ⊂ X be a scheme theoretically dense open such that 𝓕|_U is finite locally free of constant rank r." It then concludes that the blow-up in the r-th Fitting ideal is U-admissible and that the strict transform is locally free of rank r. In the proof, X̄ is an arbitrary compactification, and Definition 2.1.2 asks only for a proper X̄ with an open immersion of X. So X need not be scheme-theoretically dense, or even dense, in X̄. Also, 𝓕 is only locally free "of finite rank", so its rank may vary from one connected component of X to another. The proof does not reduce to the case covered by the lemma, and without these hypotheses the lemma's conclusion fails. Two examples over S = Spec k, checked by direct computation:
(i) Density. Take X = A¹, X̄ = P¹ ⊔ Spec k[ε]/(ε²), 𝓕 = O_X, and 𝓕̄ = O_{P¹} on the first piece and k = k[ε]/(ε) on the second. The module k is cyclic, so Fit_1(𝓕̄) = O_X̄. The blow-up in Fit_1 is therefore the identity, and the strict transform is 𝓕̄ itself, which is not locally free at the extra point.
(ii) Constant rank. Take X = A¹ ⊔ A¹, X̄ = P¹ ⊔ P¹, 𝓕 = O ⊔ O², and 𝓕̄ = (O ⊕ k_∞) ⊔ (O² ⊕ k_∞). Here X is scheme-theoretically dense. Fit_1(𝓕̄) is zero on the second P¹, so blowing it up deletes that component and the blow-up is not X-admissible. Fit_2(𝓕̄) is the unit ideal on the first P¹, so blowing it up leaves O ⊕ k_∞ there, which is not locally free.
So the cited lemma does not give the asserted step for an arbitrary compactification. The lemma itself is true: repair (a) or the routine reductions in (b) prove it. Strictness is not a separate problem. Once a blow-up with centre disjoint from X is available (Tag 0ESN(1), or U-admissibility in Raynaud–Gruson), strictness is immediate, and Lemma 2.1.4 also gives it once X is dense. Stacks Tag 0ESN (Divisors, Lemma 31.36.3) reads: "Let X be a scheme. Let 𝓕 be a finitely presented O_X-module. Let U ⊂ X be a scheme theoretically dense open such that 𝓕|_U is finite locally free of constant rank r. Then the blowup of X in the rth Fitting ideal of 𝓕 is U-admissible [and] the strict transform 𝓕′ ... is locally free of rank r ...". The proof applies it with U = X inside an arbitrary compactification X̄. Neither hypothesis is checked there, and neither holds in general.

(a) Density. X need not be scheme-theoretically dense in X̄, and without density the conclusion can fail. Example: let X̄ be P¹_k with an embedded point at ∞, with local ring k[t,e]/(te, e²) there. Let X = X̄ − {∞} = A¹ and 𝓕 = O_X. The coherent extension 𝓕̄ = O_X̄/(e) has Fit₁(𝓕̄) = O_X̄, so the Fitting-ideal blow-up is the identity. The strict transform is then 𝓕̄ itself, which is killed by e ≠ 0 and has fibre k at ∞, so it is not locally free there. Blowing up the reduced point ∞ does remove the embedded point and makes the pull-back O_{P¹}. So a suitable blow-up exists, but not by the cited lemma as stated.

(b) Constant rank. The lemma assumes 𝓕 has finite rank, not constant rank, and X may be disconnected. Example: two P¹'s meeting in a point, with X the complement of the node. If 𝓕 has rank 1 on one component of X and rank 2 on the other, then Tag 0ESN does not apply for any single r.

Defence considered. The statement of Lemma 2.1.6 is true, and both defects are easy to repair. The preceding Lemma 2.1.5 produces Cartier boundary, and the complement of an effective Cartier divisor is scheme-theoretically dense ([Sta22], Tag 07ZU). Taking scheme-theoretic closures of the constant-rank pieces is a strict map. Strictness is automatic once a result of this kind applies: part (1) of Tag 0ESN (or the U-admissibility in Raynaud–Gruson) puts the centre off X, so the blow-up is an isomorphism over X. Part (3) (K|_U = 0) shows that the strict transform restricts to 𝓕. The word "suitable" does not supply these steps, and the proof does not mention them. So this is a genuine but minor gap in the proof, not an error in the statement.

Consequences. Lemma 2.1.6 is used only in the proof of Theorem 2.7.4 (p. 24), together with Lemmas 2.1.12 and 2.1.30. That proof needs a strict map so that Lemma 2.1.29 transfers the dynamic structure. Both repairs above give strict maps, so Theorem 2.7.4 and everything after it is unaffected.

Raynaud–Gruson flattening needs neither density nor constant rank. The preprint's Lemma 2.1.6 also did not claim strictness. The revision added the strictness clause, replaced [RG71] by Tag 0ESN, and dropped [RG71] from the bibliography. Computation (checked directly). Z_i = Σ_{k≤i} D_{g+k} is the degree divisor of H_{g+i}. By Proposition 6.2.2, Z_{i,>a} − Z_{i,<a} = Z_i − V(p^{na}), and the two divisors have disjoint support. So at a generic point of the special fibre where Z_i = V(p^{nd}), we get Z_{i,<a} = n·max(0, a−d)·V(p) and Z_{i,>a} = n·max(0, d−a)·V(p). Fix w′ ∈ ^M W. On the nonempty open piece C_{t,w′}^tor = p_1^{-1}S_{w′}^tor ∩ p_2^{-1}S_{w′}^tor (Proposition 4.2.4), we have p_1^⋆Z_k = p_2^⋆Z_k = V(p^{n w′_k}) (§4.1.3 and Lemma 4.1.6 with the convention of §3.1, and Proposition 4.2.14 (2)). The blow-up does not change this, because over the ordinary strata the ideals being blown up are generated by powers of p. With D_{+,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} and D_{−,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ} (the printed w_j is a slip for w_i), we get on C_{t,w′}^tor:
- p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} − p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} = −n(ϵ−ϵ′)·#{k : w′_k < w_k}·V(p);
- p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ} − p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ′} = −n(ϵ−ϵ′)·#{k : w′_k > w_k}·V(p).

Since ϵ′ < ϵ (§6.2.1), neither difference is effective as soon as w′_k < w_k (respectively w′_k > w_k) for some k. For g = 1, the convention of §3.1 gives w_1 = 1 for w = Id and w_1 = 0 for w_0.
- For (2), take w = Id on C_{t,w_0}^tor. There Z_1 = 0, so p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} = n(1−ϵ)V(p), which is strictly less than p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} = n(1−ϵ′)V(p).
- For (3), take w = w_0 on C_{t,Id}^tor. There Z_1 = V(p^n), so p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ} = n(1−ϵ)V(p), which is strictly less than p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ′} = n(1−ϵ′)V(p).

In every genus, (2) fails for w = Id and (3) fails for the w with all w_i = 0. The argument does not need nϵ or nϵ′ to be integers. In these examples the supports agree, which is consistent with the set-theoretic inclusions.

Why the inclusions hold. On the adic generic fibre, the complement of the support of D_{+,ϵ} is U_{≥w−ϵ}. Take a point with p_1 outside the support of D_{+,ϵ}. Since T(U_{≥w−ϵ}) ⊆ U_{≥w−ϵ′}, p_2 of that point lies outside the support of D_{+,ϵ′}. The argument for D_− is the same, using T^t(U_{≤w+ϵ}) ⊆ U_{≤w+ϵ′}.

Why nothing downstream is affected. Proposition 6.2.3 is never cited by number. It enters the proof of Theorem 6.2.9 in two places:
- Through Proposition 2.10.4 (p. 30). Its hypotheses are the set-theoretic inclusions p̄_1^⋆D_+ ⊇ p̄_2^⋆D′_+ and p̄_2^⋆D_− ⊇ p̄_1^⋆D′_−.
- Through Theorem 2.11.4 (3) (p. 32). This needs the maps p_2^⋆O(D_+) → p_1^⋆O(D_+) and p_2^⋆O(−D_−) → p_1^⋆O(−D_−), which are the true first halves, together with (4).

No stated result depends on the false divisor inequalities. How to read the symbol. In Proposition 6.2.3, "≥" means an inequality of divisors. That is true in (1) (Lemma 4.1.17), in the first halves of (2) and (3) (Lemma 4.2.11), and in (4), where s·p_1^⋆D_+ ≥ p_2^⋆D_+ with s ∈ ]0,1[ makes sense only for divisors. The paper writes set inclusions of closed subsets as ⊆ or ⊇ (Proposition 2.10.4, §2.11).

Readings that would save the statement, and why they fail:
- Reading the second halves only over C_t^tor \ p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ}, as in (4), would make them trivial (0 ≥ 0). But (2) and (3) are stated on all of C_t^tor.
- Swapping ϵ and ϵ′ gives p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} ≥ p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ}, which is a true divisor inequality by (1) and Lemma 4.2.11. But it needs no Proposition 6.1.9, and it gives only the inclusion that is of no use for Proposition 2.10.4.

Setting up the computation (checked by direct computation). Z_i = Σ_{k≤i} D_{g+k} is the degree divisor of H_{g+i}. By Proposition 6.2.2, Z_{i,>a} − Z_{i,<a} = Z_i − V(p^{na}), and the two divisors have disjoint supports. Hence at a generic point of the special fibre where Z_i = V(p^{nd}), we have Z_{i,<a} = n·max(0, a−d)·V(p).

Fix w′ ∈ ^M W. On the open piece C_{t,w′}^tor = p_1^{-1}S_{w′} ∩ p_2^{-1}S_{w′}:
- Each Gr_{g+k} is multiplicative (D_{g+k} = V(p^n)) or étale (D_{g+k} = 0), by §4.1.3, §4.1.8 and the convention for (w_1,…,w_g) in §3.1.
- So p_1^⋆Z_i = p_2^⋆Z_i = V(p^{n w′_i}) (Proposition 4.2.14 (2)).
- The blow-up changes nothing there, because the ideals being blown up are principal.

This gives, on C_{t,w′}^tor:
- p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} − p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} = −n(ϵ−ϵ′)·#{i : w′_i < w_i}·V(p);
- p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ} − p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ′} = −n(ϵ−ϵ′)·#{i : w′_i > w_i}·V(p).

Since ϵ′ < ϵ (§6.2.1), neither difference is effective as soon as such an i exists.

Concrete cases for g = 1:
- For (2), take w = Id (w_1 = 1). On C_{t,w_0}^tor we have Z_1 = 0, so p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} = V(p^{n(1−ϵ)}), which is strictly less than p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} = V(p^{n(1−ϵ′)}).
- For (3), take w = w_0 (w_1 = 0). On C_{t,Id}^tor we have Z_1 = V(p^n), so p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ} = V(p^{n(1−ϵ)}), which is strictly less than p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ′} = V(p^{n(1−ϵ′)}).

These opens are nonempty. For example, when H is étale, the quotient by the multiplicative subgroup of order p again has étale image of H. More generally:
- (2) fails whenever some w_i > 0 (compare with the all-étale stratum).
- (3) fails whenever w ≠ Id (compare with w′ = Id).
So for every w at least one of the two fails. In these examples the two supports coincide, which is consistent with the corrected inclusions.

Why the inclusions hold. Let η be a generic point of a component of the special fibre of C_t^tor, and x_η the corresponding rank-1 point. Then η lies in supp p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} if and only if p_2(x_η) ∉ U_{≥w−ϵ′}. By the choice of ϵ′ (Proposition 6.1.9 (1)), this forces p_1(x_η) ∉ U_{≥w−ϵ}, that is, η lies in supp p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ}. Supports are unions of such components. The argument for D_− is the same, using T^t(U_{≤w+ϵ}) ⊆ U_{≤w+ϵ′}.

What uses the passage. Proposition 6.2.3 is never cited by number. It enters the proof of Theorem 6.2.9 (p. 62) in three ways:
- Through Proposition 2.10.4 (p. 30). This gives t̃ : RΓ_{D_{+,ϵ′},D_{−,ϵ}} → RΓ_{D_{+,ϵ},D_{−,ϵ′}}, whose hypotheses are the set inclusions above.
- Through Theorem 2.11.4 (pp. 31–33), with D″_± = D_{±,ϵ} and D′_± = D_{±,ϵ′}. Here Remark 2.11.2 again invokes Proposition 2.10.4, and the proof uses T : RΓ_{D′_+,D_−} → RΓ_{D″_+,D_−}. Both need only the inclusions. The corresponding hypotheses in §2.11 are printed with p̄_1 and p̄_2 interchanged; this is a separate slip.
- Through Theorem 2.11.4 (3). This needs the maps p_2^⋆O(D_+) → p_1^⋆O(D_+) and p_2^⋆O(−D_−) → p_1^⋆O(−D_−), which are the true first halves, together with (4).

Theorem 6.2.15 is proved "similarly". No stated result needs the false divisor inequalities. - **Misprint** at §6.2.1, Proposition 6.2.2 (1)–(2) and the paragraph after its proof defining D_±, D_{±,ϵ}, D_{±,ϵ′}, p. 61. The source says `Proposition 6.2.2 (p. 61): "(1) for all 0 ≤ i ≤ g we have effective divisors Z_{i,>w_j} and Z_{i,<w_j} on S̃^{tor} with disjoint support, and Z_{i,>w_j} − Z_{i,<w_j} = Z_i − V(p^{nw_j}). (2) for all 0 ≤ i ≤ g and all η ∈ {ϵ, −ϵ, ϵ′, −ϵ′}, we have effective divisors Z_{i,>w_j+η} and Z_{i,<w_j+η} on S̃^{tor} with disjoint support, and Z_{i,>w_j+η} − Z_{i,<w_j+η} = Z_i − V(p^{n(w_j+η)})." Paragraph after the proof: "We change our notation and let S^{tor} be S̃^{tor}. We let D_+ = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_j}, D_− = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_j}, D_{+,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_j−ϵ}, D_{−,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_j+ϵ} D_{+,ϵ′} = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_j−ϵ′}, D_{−,ϵ′} = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_j+ϵ′}." (There is no comma before D_{+,ϵ′} in the printed text.)`; it should be `Replace the subscript w_j by w_i throughout. Then Z_{i,>w_i} − Z_{i,<w_i} = Z_i − V(p^{nw_i}) and Z_{i,>w_i+η} − Z_{i,<w_i+η} = Z_i − V(p^{n(w_i+η)}). The divisors become D_+ = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_i}, D_− = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_i}, D_{+,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ}, D_{−,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ}, D_{+,ϵ′} = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ′} and D_{−,ϵ′} = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ′}. A comma is also missing before D_{+,ϵ′}.`. At high magnification the page shows the subscript w_j in every place quoted above. The index j is never bound. In the definitions of D_± and D_{±,ϵ}, D_{±,ϵ′} the sum runs over i only. This is the only place in the paper where w_j occurs. §6.2 fixes only w ∈ ^MW and t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p) (p. 61), and w_1, …, w_g is the sequence attached to w at the end of §3.1.

Several parts of the paper require w_i:
(a) Proposition 4.1.13(1) (p. 42) gives Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}) for 0 ≤ j ≤ i. Proposition 6.2.2 says its proof "is identical to the proof of proposition 4.1.13". Taking j = w_i is allowed there, because 0 ≤ w_i ≤ i.
(b) §4.4.1 (p. 50) sets D_{w,−} = ∪ Z_{i,>w_i} and D_{w,+} = ∪_i Z_{i,<w_i}. §4.5.6 (p. 52) recalls "D_{−,w} = Σ_{i=1}^g Z_{i,>w_i} and D_{+,w} = Σ_{i=1}^g Z_{i,<w_i}".
(c) §6.1.8 (p. 60) defines U_{≥w−ϵ} by deg H_{g+i}(x) ≥ n(w_i − ϵ) for all i.
(d) §6.2.8 (p. 62) writes "Z_{<w+ϵ} = ∩Z_{i,<w_i+ϵ}" and "U_{≥w−ϵ} = S^{tor} \ D_{+,ϵ}".

With w_i, the support of Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} is the locus where deg H_{g+i} < n(w_i − ϵ). So S^{tor} \ D_{+,ϵ} is the locus where deg H_{g+i} ≥ n(w_i − ϵ) for all i, which is U_{≥w−ϵ} of §6.1.8, as §6.2.8 requires. No reading with one fixed j fits the sums over i.

The slip is purely notational and does not affect anything. Everything after it (Propositions 6.2.3–6.2.7 and Theorem 6.2.9, pp. 61–62) uses D_±, D_{±,ϵ}, D_{±,ϵ′} only in the w_i sense, as §6.2.8 makes explicit. The arguments cited for them (Proposition 6.1.9, Lemma 4.2.11, Lemma 4.4.2) are all stated with w_i. No result or proof changes. - **Gap** at §6.2.1, Proposition 6.2.2(2) and its one-line proof, p. 61. The earlier preprint (build of 15 Jan 2024) has the same text.. The source says `Proposition 6.2.2. There exists a blow-up π : S̃^{tor} → S^{tor} satisfying the following properties: ... (2) for all 0 ≤ i ≤ g and all η ∈ {ϵ, −ϵ, ϵ′, −ϵ′}, we have effective divisors Z_{i,>w_j+η} and Z_{i,<w_j+η} on S̃^{tor} with disjoint support, and Z_{i,>w_j+η} − Z_{i,<w_j+η} = Z_i − V(p^{n(w_j+η)}). ... Proof. This is identical to the proof of proposition 4.1.13.`; it should be `Choose an integer q ≥ 1 with q·n(w_i+η) ∈ Z for all i and all η ∈ {±ϵ, ±ϵ′}. Read V(p^{n(w_i+η)}) as the Q-Cartier divisor n(w_i+η)·V(p), and read Z_{i,>w_i+η} and Z_{i,<w_i+η} as effective Q-Cartier divisors. When n(w_i+η) ≤ 0, which happens only if w_i = 0 and η < 0, take Z_{i,<w_i+η} = 0, because the difference is already effective. Otherwise, apply Proposition-construction 4.1.11 to the Cartier divisors qZ_i and V(p^{q n(w_i+η)}). Locally this is the blow-up along (f^q, p^{qn(w_i+η)}), where f is a local equation of Z_i. Divide the two resulting divisors by q. Equivalently, keep the two Cartier divisors themselves: they have the same supports, and the identity holds after multiplying by q. The subscripts w_j in (1), (2) and in the definitions of D_±, D_{±,ϵ}, D_{±,ϵ′} should read w_i. This is a separate index slip. The reported correction is right and essentially minimal. The one addition needed is the case n(w_i+η) ≤ 0, where the "apply 4.1.11" form would involve a negative power of p.`. The model S^{tor} is a scheme over Spec Z_p: in 4.1.1, p. 41, it is defined as a normalisation of a product of the A_{g,d_i} × Spec Z_p. In §6.2.1 the numbers ϵ ∈ ]0,1[∩Q and ϵ′ ∈ ]0,ϵ[∩Q are arbitrary, and the level n is any element of Z_{≥0} (p. 41). Take n = 1. Then for every η ∈ {±ϵ, ±ϵ′} the exponent n(w_i+η) = w_i + η is not an integer, because the w_i are integers and 0 < |η| < 1. So p^{n(w_i+η)} is not a function on S^{tor}, and V(p^{n(w_i+η)}) is not an effective Cartier divisor in the sense of p. 7 (a closed subscheme V(I) with I invertible). Therefore no pair of effective Cartier divisors can satisfy the printed identity. The same happens for any n whenever nη is not an integer. Passing to Z_p(ζ_{p^n}), the ring used for the Nebentypus, does not help: its value group is (1/(p^{n−1}(p−1)))Z, and ϵ is an arbitrary rational.

The proof says it is "identical to the proof of proposition 4.1.13". That proof (p. 42) applies Proposition-construction 4.1.11, which is stated for effective Cartier divisors, to Z_{k+1} and V(p^{nj}) with j an integer. It does not cover a rational exponent. The missing step is to scale by a common denominator q as in the correction. On the blow-up of the ideal locally generated by (f^q, p^{qn(w_i+η)}), where f is a local equation of Z_i, one of the two generators divides the other, and the quotients generate the unit ideal. This gives E_>, E_< with disjoint support, and dividing by q gives the Q-divisors.

This intended reading fits the rest of the paper. The adic definition on p. 60 already uses rational exponents: U_{≥w−ϵ} is defined by |f_{g+i}|_x ≤ |p^{n(w_i−ϵ)}|_x. Rational multiples of divisors also appear without comment in Lemma 4.4.2 ("there exists 0 < s < 1 such that s p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i} ≥ p_2^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}") and in Proposition 6.2.3(4) (s ∈ ]0,1[∩Q). Later the divisors D_{±,ϵ} and D_{±,ϵ′} are used only through their supports (U_{≥w−ϵ} = S^{tor} \ D_{+,ϵ}, and cohomology with supports) and through the inequalities of Proposition 6.2.3. Both make sense for Q-divisors, or after replacing each divisor by q times itself. So the statement as printed is not meaningful, and its cited proof does not apply literally, but the repair is routine and no result changes. Why the statement is not meaningful as printed:
- The w_i are integers (bottom of §3.1, recalled before Corollary 4.1.14).
- ϵ is an arbitrary rational in ]0,1[. Theorem 6.2.9 is stated for every such ϵ.
- ϵ′ is not free either. By Proposition 6.1.9(1) the admissible ϵ′ fill an interval ending at ϵ, but that interval need not contain a point of (1/n)Z. For n = 1, no ϵ in ]0,1[ has nϵ ∈ Z at all.
- So n(w_i+η) is in general not an integer.
- S^tor is a scheme over Z_p: it is the normalisation in §4.1, and with a nebentypus the base is Z_p(ζ_{p^n}). A rational power of p is not a function on it, so V(p^{n(w_i+η)}) is not a closed subscheme.
- In the paper, "divisor" always means a closed subscheme, Cartier or locally principal (§2.1.14). The only rational coefficients the paper allows are in the relation D ≤ sD′ of Definition 2.1.15(2). It never defines Q-divisors.
- Every other occurrence of V(p^·) in the paper has integer exponent nj with 0 ≤ j ≤ i: Proposition 4.1.13, its proof, and Lemma 4.2.11.

Why the cited proof does not literally cover it: the proof of Proposition 4.1.13 applies Proposition-construction 4.1.11 "to the divisors Z_{k+1} and V(p^{nj})". Proposition-construction 4.1.11 is stated only for effective Cartier divisors D_1, D_2. So "identical to the proof of proposition 4.1.13" does not apply as written.

The defence, and why it succeeds only as a repair. The intended meaning is clear from §6.1.8, where U_{≥w−ϵ} is defined by |f_{g+i}|_x ≤ |p^{n(w_i−ϵ)}|_x. That is a meaningful condition on rank-one points. The repair described in the correction works:
- Blowing up (f^q, p^m) with m = qn(w_i+η) gives disjoint-support Cartier divisors whose difference is qZ_i − V(p^m).
- Point (3) survives. By the proof of Proposition 4.1.13, Z_i = V(p^{nw_i}) on the open S̃_{=w_1,…,w_g}. There the ideal (f^q, p^m) is generated by a power of p times a unit, so the extra blow-up is an isomorphism over it.

What later uses the passage:
- The divisors D_{±,ϵ} and D_{±,ϵ′} defined just below it on p. 61.
- Proposition 6.2.3(1)–(3). These inequalities follow as in Lemma 4.2.11, either with Q-coefficients or after multiplying by q, which is compatible with Definition 2.1.15(2).
- The open C_t^tor \ (p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} ∪ p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ}) in Proposition 6.2.7.
- Z_{<w+ϵ} and U_{≥w−ϵ} = S^tor \ D_{+,ϵ} in §6.2.8.
- The support conditions RΓ_{D_{+,ϵ},D_{−,ϵ′}} in the proof of Theorem 6.2.9.

All of these use only the supports of the divisors, or inequalities that are unchanged by rescaling. Lemma 2.10.2 and Proposition 2.10.4 need only closed subschemes and containments of supports. The integral model ω̃^κ(χ) = ω^κ(χ)(m(D_+ − D_−)) and Proposition 6.2.3(4) use only D_±, which are built from the integers w_i. So Theorem 6.2.9 and Corollary 6.2.10 are unaffected.

Classification: this is an unjustified step with a routine repair, and no result changes. Hence a gap that affects nothing. - **Misprint** at §6.2.8, definition preceding Theorem 6.2.9, p. 62. The source says `Let RΓ_{𝒵_{<w+ϵ}∩𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}}(𝒰_{≥w+ϵ}, ω^κ(χ))^{int} = lim_s RΓ_{Ẑ_{<w+ϵ}∩U_{≥w−ϵ,ℤ/p^sℤ}}(U_{≥w+ϵ,ℤ/p^sℤ}, ω̃^κ(χ)).`; it should be `Replace 𝒰_{≥w+ϵ} by 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ} on the left and U_{≥w+ϵ,ℤ/p^sℤ} by U_{≥w−ϵ,ℤ/p^sℤ} on the right: "Let RΓ_{𝒵_{<w+ϵ}∩𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}}(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, ω^κ(χ))^{int} = lim_s RΓ_{Ẑ_{<w+ϵ}∩U_{≥w−ϵ,ℤ/p^sℤ}}(U_{≥w−ϵ,ℤ/p^sℤ}, ω̃^κ(χ))."`. Checked on the page image of p. 62. The left-hand side is printed with calligraphic letters (the adic generic fibre) and the right-hand side with roman letters (the integral model), as transcribed above. The same page gives the definition in the form it needs. §6.2.8 introduces only U_{≥w−ϵ} = S^{tor} \ D_{+,ϵ} ↪ S^{tor} and î′ : Ẑ_{<w+ϵ} ∩ U_{≥w−ϵ} ↪ U_{≥w−ϵ}. It then considers RΓ_{Ẑ_{<w+ϵ}∩U_{≥w−ϵ,ℤ/p^sℤ}}(U_{≥w−ϵ,ℤ/p^sℤ}, ω̃^κ(χ)) = RΓ(U_{≥w−ϵ,ℤ/p^sℤ}, î′_⋆(î′)^! ω̃^κ(χ)) and places it in the exact triangle with RΓ(U_{≥w−ϵ,ℤ/p^sℤ}, ω̃^κ(χ)) and RΓ(U_{≥w−ϵ,ℤ/p^sℤ} \ Z_{<w+ϵ}, ω̃^κ(χ)). No integral U_{≥w+ϵ} or U_{≥w+ϵ,ℤ/p^sℤ} is defined in §6.2, and this line is the only place where either symbol appears. Theorem 6.2.9 (1) and (3), which this line is meant to define, read "RΓ_{𝒵_{<w+ϵ}∩𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}}(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, ω^κ(χ))^{int}". The proof also works only with U_{≥w−ϵ,ℤ/p^sℤ}: the change-of-support maps from Lemma 2.10.1, the same triangle, and the limits lim_s RΓ(U_{≥w−ϵ,ℤ/p^sℤ}, ω̃^κ(χ)) ⊗ ℚ_p = RΓ(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, ω^κ(χ)) and lim_s RΓ(U_{≥w−ϵ,ℤ/p^sℤ} \ Z_{<w+ϵ}, ω̃^κ(χ)) ⊗ ℚ_p = RΓ(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ} \ 𝒵_{<w+ϵ}, ω^κ(χ)). The parallel definition before Theorem 6.2.15 (p. 64) reads RΓ_{𝒵_{<w+ϵ}∩𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}}(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, 𝔉̃^{ν_A,n})^{int} = lim_r RΓ_{Ẑ_{<w+ϵ}∩U_{≥w−ϵ,ℤ/p^rℤ}}(U_{≥w−ϵ,ℤ/p^rℤ}, 𝔉̃_r^{ν_A,n}), with w−ϵ in both places. One nuance: §6.1.8 (p. 60) defines the adic open 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ} for every ϵ ∈ ℚ. Read that way, 𝒰_{≥w+ϵ} would be the locus where deg H_{g+i} ≥ n(w_i+ϵ) for all i. But 𝒵_{<w+ϵ} is the union over ϵ′ < ϵ of the closures of 𝒰_{≤w+ϵ′}, where deg H_{g+i} ≤ n(w_i+ϵ′) < n(w_i+ϵ). So that locus does not contain the support 𝒵_{<w+ϵ} ∩ 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, and the literal reading makes no sense. The sign is therefore a typographical slip. With the correction, the definition agrees with Theorem 6.2.9 and its proof, and nothing later changes: Corollary 6.2.10 and Theorem 6.2.15 only use the object as Theorem 6.2.9 states it. This record rests on the authors' version (PDF of 5 Nov 2025); the published text could not be checked. - **Gap** at §6.2: Corollary 6.2.10 and its proof, p. 62; Corollary 6.2.16, the sentence before it and its proof, p. 64. Theorem 1.4.10 on p. 6 (introduction) states the same result. The January 2024 preprint has the same corollaries and proofs word for word (pp. 60 and 62 there), and Theorem 1.4.10, worded almost identically, is on p. 5 there. (it affects the proof). The source says `p. 6: "Theorem 1.4.10. The lower bounds on slopes of conjectures 5.9.2 and 6.8.1 in [BP21] hold true." p. 62: "Corollary 6.2.10. Conjecture 5.9.2 of [BP21] holds in the Siegel case. Proof. The conjecture is the statement that elements t ∈ T^+(Q_p) acting on the finite slope cohomology have bounded below slope by a precise bound. This slope bound is equivalent to the property that the normalized action of t stabilizes a lattice. It is also enough to check this for all t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p) as they generate T(Q_p) as a group. This follows from theorem 6.2.9. □" p. 64: "In conjecture 6.8.1 of [BP21], we conjectured that the slopes of t ∈ T^+(Q_p) are nonnegative on finite slope locally analytic overconvergent cohomologies, or equivalently that these operators preserve a lattice. Corollary 6.2.16. Conjecture 6.8.1 of [BP21] holds in the Siegel case. Proof. It suffices to check this for t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p) which then follows from 6.2.15 (2). □"`; it should be `(1) Reduction to T^{++}. Replace "as they generate T(Q_p) as a group" with a cone argument. Let λ be a character of T^+ on the finite slope cohomology. For Conjecture 5.9.2 put β = w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)+ρ, and for Conjecture 6.8.1 put β = 0. Let f(t) = v(λ(t)) − ⟨v(t), β⟩. Then f is additive on T^+. Take t ∈ T^+ and t_0 ∈ T^{++}. For every m ≥ 1, v(t^m t_0) = m·v(t) + v(t_0) is regular dominant, so t^m t_0 ∈ T^{++}. Theorem 6.2.9 (resp. 6.2.15(2)), applied with t^m t_0 as the element of T^{++} fixed in §6.2, gives m·f(t) + f(t_0) ≥ 0 for all m, and hence f(t) ≥ 0. Put differently, f(t) = ⟨v(t), v(λ) − β⟩ is a linear form in v(t) that is ≥ 0 on v(T^{++}). The positive multiples of v(T^{++}) are dense in the closed dominant cone, which contains v(T^+), so the form is ≥ 0 on v(T^+). (2) The cuspidal '+' theories. Before the two corollaries, state the cuspidal analogues of Theorems 6.2.9 and 6.2.15. These are the same statements for ω̃^κ(χ)(−D) and F̃^{ν_A,n}(−D), with the cuspidal higher Hida theory as ordinary part, and they are proved in the same way. Here D is the boundary divisor of the toroidal compactification, as in the definition of cuspidal higher Hida theory in §4.4; it is not one of the divisors D_± of §6.2. Together with the theorems as printed, these analogues give part (1) of [BP21] Conjectures 5.9.2 and 6.8.1 (the bound for characters of T^+ on the '+' theories), for both the non-cuspidal and the cuspidal theories. (3) Part (2). Add the deduction of part (2) of both conjectures (the bound for characters of T^− on the '−' theories) from part (1), using the Serre duality of [BP21]: Theorems 5.7.1–5.7.2 in the coherent case, and 6.7.1–6.7.2 in the locally analytic case. Put κ^∨ = −2ρ_nc − w_{0,M}κ. The pairing H^i_w(K^p,κ,χ,cusp)^{±,fs} × H^{d−i}_w(K^p,κ^∨,χ^{-1})^{∓,fs} → F is perfect on generalized eigenspaces, and t is adjoint to t^{-1}. So a character λ of T^+ on one side corresponds to a character λ' = λ∘inv of T^− on the other, and v(λ') = −v(λ). Since w_{0,M}ρ = 2ρ_nc − ρ, we have κ^∨ + ρ = −w_{0,M}(κ+ρ). Hence the part (1) bound at κ is exactly the part (2) bound at κ^∨, and conversely ([BP21] Remark 5.9.5). For Conjecture 6.8.1 both bounds are 0, and duality turns v ≥ 0 on T^+ into v ≤ 0 on T^−. Duality pairs cuspidal with non-cuspidal theories, so (2) is needed here. Without it, the printed theorems give part (2) only for the cuspidal '−' theories. (4) The proof of Corollary 6.2.10 and the sentence before Corollary 6.2.16 should stop describing each conjecture as a statement about T^+ alone.`. [BP21] is cited as arXiv:2110.10251. Version v1 (19 October 2021) is used here, and its numbering matches every [BP21] reference in §6.2.

What is conjectured. Conjecture 5.9.2 of [BP21] has two parts, and each is asserted for both the non-cuspidal and the cuspidal theory:
(1) every character λ of T^+ on RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ)^{+,fs} or RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ,cusp)^{+,fs} satisfies v(λ) ≥ w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)+ρ;
(2) every character λ of T^− on RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ)^{−,fs} or RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ,cusp)^{−,fs} satisfies v(λ) ≤ w^{-1}(κ+ρ)−ρ.
Conjecture 6.8.1 makes the same four assertions for RΓ_{w,an}(K^p,ν)^{±,fs} and its cuspidal version, with bounds v(λ) ≥ 0 and v(λ) ≤ 0. By [BP21] Remark 5.9.3, both parts are lower bounds on slopes: part (2) means v(λ(t)) ≥ ⟨v(t), w^{-1}(κ+ρ)−ρ⟩ for all t ∈ T^−. So Theorem 1.4.10 ("The lower bounds on slopes of conjectures 5.9.2 and 6.8.1") claims both parts in full. It is not a narrower statement.

What the proofs cover. The proof on p. 62 describes the conjecture as a statement about t ∈ T^+ only, and so does the sentence before Corollary 6.2.16 on p. 64. Both proofs appeal only to Theorems 6.2.9(3) and 6.2.15(2). Those give a lattice in the cohomology of ω^κ(χ), resp. F̃^{ν,n}, with the '+' support condition (U_{≥w−ε}, Z_{<w+ε}) and with t ∈ T^{++} acting. Propositions 6.1.7, 6.1.10 and 6.1.11 compare this cohomology with the '+' theory of [BP21]. There is no (−D) twist, so this is the non-cuspidal '+' theory. Section 6 contains no '−' support condition, no T^− and no cuspidal sheaf. Remark 6.2.18 uses duality, but only for vanishing. So as written, each proof establishes one of the four assertions of its conjecture: part (1) for the non-cuspidal theory. In the same way, the proof of Corollary 6.2.17 (p. 64) derives the amplitude of M^•_{w,cusp} ⊗ Q_p "from 6.2.15", although 6.2.15 is stated only for the non-cuspidal sheaf. There too the cuspidal case is left implicit.

Duality supplies only some of part (2). The locally analytic pairing of [BP21] Theorems 6.7.1–6.7.2 behaves in the same way as the coherent one. In the coherent case, w_{0,M}ρ_M = −ρ_M and w_{0,M}ρ_nc = ρ_nc, so w_{0,M}ρ = 2ρ_nc − ρ. Hence (−2ρ_nc − w_{0,M}κ) + ρ = −w_{0,M}(κ+ρ). Now take κ^∨ = −2ρ_nc − w_{0,M}κ and s = t^{-1} ∈ T^−. In the form of Remark 5.9.3, the part (2) bound at κ^∨ is v(λ'(s)) ≥ ⟨v(s), w^{-1}(κ^∨+ρ)−ρ⟩. This reads v(λ(t)) ≥ ⟨v(t), w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)+ρ⟩, which is part (1) at κ. Since ρ_nc is W_M-invariant, κ ↦ κ^∨ is an involution of X^*(T^c)^{M_μ,+}, so every weight is covered. However, the pairing matches cuspidal '±' with non-cuspidal '∓'. From the printed theorems it therefore yields part (2) only for the cuspidal '−' theories. Theorems 6.2.9 and 6.2.15 as stated do not cover the cuspidal '+' case of part (1), nor therefore, through duality, the non-cuspidal '−' case of part (2). Both need the cuspidal analogues of those theorems. The paper never states these analogues. They follow by the same argument, because the integral models and the higher Hida theory of §4.4–§5 are also set up for cuspidal cohomology.

The reduction to T^{++}. The stated reason does not justify the reduction. Suppose a lower bound on slopes holds for t_1 and t_2. That says nothing about t_1 t_2^{-1}. And every t ∈ T^+ with v(t) on a wall of the dominant cone has this form with t_1, t_2 ∈ T^{++}: take any t_2 ∈ T^{++} and t_1 = t·t_2. [BP21] §5.9 defines the slope v(λ) of a T^±-character by extending λ to T(Q_p) ("recall that T(Q_p) is generated by the monoids T^±"). So group generation does show that v(λ) is a linear form determined by its values on T^{++}. But the inequality needs one more fact: the positive multiples of v(T^{++}) are dense in the closed dominant cone. The bound then passes to T^+ by linearity and continuity, as in (1) of the correction. The sentence on p. 62 does not say this, and the proof of Corollary 6.2.16 gives no reason at all. The reduction itself cannot be skipped, since §6.2 fixes t ∈ T^{++} (p. 61) and builds its integral models from that choice. So Theorems 6.2.9 and 6.2.15 say nothing directly about t on a wall.

Why only the proof is affected. Later statements use the corollaries at full strength:
- Theorem 1.4.10 (p. 6), and the paragraph after it. That paragraph replaces "strongly small slope" by "small slope" in [BP21] 5.12.3, 6.8.4 and 5.12.20.
- The remark after Corollary 6.2.10 (p. 62). It replaces "strongly small slope" by "small slope" in [BP21] Theorems 5.12.3, 5.12.5 and 5.12.11. All three are stated for both signs ±. Theorems 5.12.3 and 5.12.5 cover cuspidal and non-cuspidal coherent cohomology, and 5.12.11 covers ordinary, compactly supported and interior Betti cohomology. Theorem 1.5.1 is deduced from these on p. 62.
- The remark after Corollary 6.2.16 (p. 64). It improves [BP21] Corollary 6.8.4 and Theorem 6.9.3(2). Corollary 6.8.4 includes a '−' morphism and the cuspidal versions (see [BP21] Remark 6.8.5).
All the missing steps are routine: the cone argument, the cuspidal analogues, and then duality. With them, the two corollaries and all of these consequences hold, so no stated result is lost. - **Misprint** at §6.2.8, proof of Theorem 6.2.9, last sentence, p. 62. The statement of Theorem 6.2.9(3) is on the same page. The 2024 preprint has the same sentence on p. 60, where (3) was still stated for the finite slope part.. The source says `Theorem 6.2.9(3): "… the image of RΓ_{𝒵_{<w+ϵ}∩𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}}(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, ω^κ(χ))^{int} in RΓ_{𝒵_{<w+ϵ}∩𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}}(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, ω^κ(χ))^{≤h} is a ℤ_p-lattice. (Here the superscript ≤ h means the slope ≤ h part for any t ∈ T^{++}(ℚ_p) and h ∈ ℚ. This is a finite dimensional ℚ_p-vector space.)" The proof ends: "That this gives a lattice in the finite slope part of cohomology is a consequence of [BP21] lem. 5.9.10 (which explains how to construct lattices)."`; it should be `Replace "a lattice in the finite slope part of cohomology" by "a ℤ_p-lattice in the slope ≤ h part of cohomology, for every h ∈ ℚ". The sentence then reads: "That the image of RΓ_{𝒵_{<w+ϵ}∩𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}}(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, ω^κ(χ))^{int} in RΓ_{𝒵_{<w+ϵ}∩𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}}(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, ω^κ(χ))^{≤h} is a ℤ_p-lattice for every h ∈ ℚ is a consequence of [BP21] lem. 5.9.10 (which explains how to construct lattices)." More precisely, it follows from the first step of that lemma's proof, which works one slope ≤ h part at a time.`. The proof's last sentence names a different space from the one in the statement. Theorem 6.2.9(3), as printed on p. 62, is about the slope ≤ h part, and the statement itself notes that this part is a finite-dimensional ℚ_p-vector space. The 2024 preprint stated (3) for the finite slope part (superscript fs) instead. The statement was later changed, but this sentence of the proof was not.

The two spaces differ. Proposition 6.1.4 takes the finite slope part from [BP21], sect. 5.1.1, where it is the projective limit of the slope ≤ h parts over all h. This space is in general infinite-dimensional: already for g = 1 it contains the finite slope overconvergent modular forms of a given weight. So there cannot be a ℤ_p-lattice there in the sense of (3), meaning a finitely generated submodule that spans the space.

The best defence of the wording is that [BP21] Lemma 5.9.10 is itself stated for the finite slope part. It says that the image there is an "open and bounded submodule". On that reading, "a lattice in the finite slope part" can only mean that the projection of the integral cohomology to every slope ≤ h part is a lattice, which is (3) for every h. This is also the order of the argument in the cited proof. It first shows, for each h, that the image in the slope ≤ h part is open and bounded (a lattice, since that part is finite-dimensional), and only then "passes to the limit over h".

So the intended meaning is clear and the mathematics is unaffected. The slope ≤ h form for every h is also all that Corollary 6.2.10 uses, since every eigenvalue of t on the finite slope cohomology occurs in some slope ≤ h part. Theorem 6.2.15(2), whose proof is "similar to the proof of theorem 6.2.9", was changed from the finite slope part to the slope ≤ h part in the same way, and the corrected sentence covers it too. The citation still supplies what the statement needs: the proof of [BP21] Lemma 5.9.10 first shows, for every h, that the image in the slope ≤ h part is open and bounded, and only then passes to the finite slope part. So the intended meaning is clear, and nothing depends on the wording. Recorded as `PAPER-BOXER-PILLONI-26/E127`; looked for an existing correction in: The authors' version on V. - **Misprint** at §6.2.11 (Big sheaves), definition of 𝓘𝒲_n, p. 63. The 2024 preprint has the same text (p. 61).. The source says `We let 𝓘𝒲_n → Spa(Q_p, Z_p) be the group defined by 𝓘𝒲_n(C, C^+) = {x ∈ M(C^+), x mod p^n ∈ M_{K_{p,P}}}.`; it should be `𝓘𝒲_n(C, C^+) = {x ∈ M(C^+) : x mod p^n lies in the image of M_{K_{p,P}} ⊆ M(Z_p) in M(Z/p^nZ) ↪ M(C^+/p^nC^+)}.`. x mod p^n is an element of M(C^+/p^nC^+). On p. 37, M_{K_{p,P}} is defined as K_{p,P} ∩ M(Q_p), a compact subgroup of M(Q_p). Since K_{p,P} = wK_{p,n}w^{−1} ∩ P(Q_p) and K_{p,n} ⊆ G(Z_p), this subgroup lies in M(Z_p). So the printed membership does not make sense as written. The intended reading is 'lies in the reduction of M_{K_{p,P}}', parallel to the definition of 𝒯_n one sentence earlier, which inserts T(Z/p^nZ) ↪ T(C^+/p^nC^+) explicitly. The corrected definition is consistent. K_{p,n} is the full preimage of B(Z/p^nZ), so M_{K_{p,P}} contains the kernel of reduction mod p^n and is determined by its image mod p^n. Also M_{K_{p,P}} ∩ T = T(Z_p), so the torus of 𝓘𝒲_n is 𝒯_n, as the text asserts ('with torus 𝔗_n'). This is a mild, common abuse of notation rather than a substantive slip, which is why confidence is only medium that it deserves recording. - **Misprint** at §2.1, proof of Lemma 2.1.5, p. 7. The source says `"We have D = V(ℐ). We let X̄′ be the blow-up of X at the ideal ℐ. Then by [Sta22], Tag 02OS, X ↪ X̄′ is a compactification mapping to X ↪ X̄."`; it should be `"We let X̄′ be the blow-up of X̄ at the ideal ℐ." The blow-up should be of the compactification X̄, not of the open subscheme X.`. On the page image, the bar is on X̄′ but not on the X in "the blow-up of X", while the surrounding sentences do distinguish X from X̄ ("the closed complement of X in X̄", "mapping to X ↪ X̄"). So this is not a text-layer artefact. In this proof, X is the open subscheme, D is the closed complement X̄ \ X with its reduced structure, and ℐ is the ideal sheaf in O_X̄ with D = V(ℐ). This matches the sentence just before Lemma 2.1.5, which takes ℐ as "a sheaf of ideals in O_X̄". Taken literally, the printed sentence does not work: ℐ is not an ideal sheaf of O_X, and its restriction to X is the unit ideal O_X. So "the blow-up of X at ℐ" is either undefined or equal to X itself, which is generally not proper. The cited result fits only the corrected reading. Stacks Tag 02OS (Lemma 31.33.4) states: "Let X be a scheme. Let Z ⊂ X be a closed subscheme. The blowing up b : X′ → X of Z in X has the following properties: 1. b|_{b⁻¹(X∖Z)} : b⁻¹(X∖Z) → X∖Z is an isomorphism, 2. the exceptional divisor E = b⁻¹(Z) is an effective Cartier divisor on X′, …". Apply this to the ambient scheme X̄ with Z = D. Then b : X̄′ → X̄ is an isomorphism over X̄ \ D = X, so X embeds as an open subscheme of X̄′. Also X̄′ \ X = b⁻¹(D) is an effective Cartier divisor. X̄′ is proper over S because it is projective over the noetherian scheme X̄, which is proper over S. X is dense in X̄′ because it is the complement of an effective Cartier divisor, so Lemma 2.1.4 gives strictness, exactly as the proof goes on to say. The intended argument is therefore clear and correct once the bar is restored. Lemma 2.1.5 and everything that relies on it are unaffected. Since w is a minimal length representative of W_M\W, w^{−1} sends the positive roots of M to positive roots. So for w ≠ 1 there is a root α of U_P with w^{−1}α < 0. Then K_{p,P} meets U_α in U_α(p^nZ_p), whereas K_{p,n} ∩ P(Q_p) contains U_α(Z_p). Here n ≥ 1, since n is large in §6.2.11.
The symbol U_{K_p} is not defined in §6 either. In §1 (pp. 3, 5) it denotes the unipotent factor of an Iwahori decomposition K_p = U_{K_p} × T_{K_p} × Ū_{K_p} of a subgroup of G(Q_p), which is a different object.
π′ is the push-out of the M_{K_{p,P}}-torsor π along M_{K_{p,P}} → 𝔍𝔚_n, and a push-out keeps its base. So the base is 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P}} = 𝔖^{tor}_w and the total space is 𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_{p,P}}} ×^{M_{K_{p,P}}} 𝔍𝔚_n. The text confirms this in three places:

- Proposition 6.2.13 takes cohomology of ℱ_r^{ν_A,n} on S^{tor}_{w,Z/p^rZ};
- the proof of Proposition 6.2.14 (p. 64) speaks of "the 𝔍𝔚_n-torsor on 𝔖^{tor}_w".
The subscript in M_{K_{p,n}} does no mathematical harm. With the convention M_K = K ∩ M(Q_p) of p. 37, M_{K_{p,n}} is the depth-n Iwahori subgroup of M(Z_p), that is, the set of m with m mod p^n ∈ B_M. This is the same group as M_{K_{p,P}} = wK_{p,n}w^{−1} ∩ M(Q_p). Indeed, m ∈ M(Z_p) lies in wK_{p,n}w^{−1} if and only if m mod p^n ∈ wBw^{−1} ∩ M, and wBw^{−1} ∩ M = B_M because w^{−1} sends the positive roots of M to positive roots. The notation is still inconsistent with that of π.

(2) The group B_{K_{p,n}} in the definition of 𝔉^{ν_A}. The symbol is defined, but it names the wrong group. The Iwahori decomposition K_{p,n} = B_{K_{p,n}} × U^{op}_{K_{p,n}} on p. 61 gives B_{K_{p,n}} = B(Z_p). The group that acts on the sheaf π_⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_{p,P}}}} over 𝔖^{tor}_w is the structure group M_{K_{p,P}} of π (Proposition 3.4.9(5), p. 37). So the invariance condition must be for a subgroup of M_{K_{p,P}}. B(Z_p) is not one. It is not contained in M(Q_p), and for w ≠ 1 it is not even contained in K_{p,P}. Indeed, for the root α of (1), U_α(Z_p) ⊂ B(Z_p) but w^{−1}U_α(Z_p)w = U_{w^{−1}α}(Z_p) ⊄ K_{p,n}. The intended group is B_M(Z_p) = B ∩ M_{K_{p,P}}, the image in M of B ∩ K_{p,P}. In §5 the corresponding group is written B_{K_{p,P}} and acts through this image: Remark 5.4.3 (p. 57) calls T_w(Z_p) "the diagonal torus of B_{K_{p,P}}". As with the subscripts in (1), K_{p,n} is written where K_{p,P} is meant.

(3) ℱ_r^{κ_A,n}. The sheaves reduced modulo p^r are the two just defined, 𝔉^{ν_A,n} and 𝔉^{ν_A}. The notation ℱ_r^{ν_A,n} is used from then on:
- in both diagrams of Proposition 6.2.12 and its proof;
- in Proposition 6.2.13 and its proof (the map ℱ_r^{ν_A,n} → ℱ_r^{ν_A});
- in Proposition 6.2.14.
The superscript κ_A is a slip, presumably prompted by the weight κ_A = −w_{0,M}w(ν_A+ρ)−ρ that appears in the invariance conditions.

(4) 𝔘_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]}. This symbol and its blow-up 𝔘̃_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]} occur only in Proposition 6.2.14 and the first line of its proof. They are defined nowhere, and the paper uses no other interval subscript 𝒰_{[·,·]}, U_{[·,·]} or 𝔘_{[·,·]}. The only sets defined by degree conditions are:
- the opens 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ} and 𝒰_{≤w+ϵ} and the closed sets 𝒵_{<w+ϵ} and 𝒵_{>w−ϵ} (§6.1.8, p. 60);
- integrally, U_{≥w−ϵ} = S^{tor} ∖ D_{+,ϵ} and Ẑ_{<w+ϵ} (§6.2.8, p. 62).
The proof cites [BP21] (Higher Coleman theory), Lemma 6.6.2, which does not supply the notation. Its proof builds formal models of π_{HT}^{−1}(U) for affinoid opens U ⊆ ]C_{w,k}[_{n,n}K_p of the flag variety, not for opens cut out by degree conditions.
The statement does not say over which part of C_t^{tor} the correspondences and their factorisation through D_± live.
The phrase "For ε sufficiently small" puts a new condition on the ϵ already fixed in §6.2.1 (p. 61, "Let ϵ ∈ ]0,1[∩Q"). It is also printed with a different glyph (ε, against ϵ in the subscripts). Theorem 6.2.15 uses the same ϵ with no smallness condition. Yet its complex RΓ_{𝒵_{<w+ϵ}∩𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}}(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, 𝔉̃^{ν_A,n})^{int} makes sense only when 𝔉̃^{ν_A,n} exists, that is, only for such ϵ.
The intended meaning can be recovered. The reading 𝔘 = 𝔖^{tor} ∖ (D_{+,ϵ} ∪ D_{−,ϵ}) is the one the notation and its uses require. Here D_{+,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} and D_{−,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ} (p. 61), with Z_i as in §4.1.12 (p. 42). The following checks use Proposition 4.1.13 and Corollary 4.1.14 (p. 42) and the definitions and results on pp. 59–62.
- Generic fibre. Proposition 6.2.2(2) gives Z_{i,>w_i+η} − Z_{i,<w_i+η} = Z_i − V(p^{n(w_i+η)}), with disjoint supports. So off Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} we have Z_i ≥ V(p^{n(w_i−ϵ)}), and off Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ} we have Z_i ≤ V(p^{n(w_i+ϵ)}). These are the conditions deg H_{g+i} ≥ n(w_i−ϵ) and deg H_{g+i} ≤ n(w_i+ϵ) of §6.1.8. So the generic fibre of 𝔘 is 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ} ∩ 𝒰_{≤w+ϵ}, matching U_{≥w−ϵ} = S^{tor} ∖ D_{+,ϵ} in §6.2.8.
- 𝔘 contains 𝔖^{tor}_w. By Proposition 4.1.13(2) and Corollary 4.1.14 (p. 42), 𝔖^{tor}_w is the open where all Z_{i,>w_i} and Z_{i,<w_i} vanish, so the degrees there are exactly nw_i, that is, Z_i = V(p^{nw_i}). Hence Z_{i,>w_i−ϵ} − Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} = V(p^{nϵ}) there. Since the two divisors have disjoint supports, Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} vanishes on 𝔖^{tor}_w, and likewise Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ}. So D_{+,ϵ} and D_{−,ϵ} vanish there, and "extends" makes sense.
- The support in the definition before Theorem 6.2.15 lies in 𝔘. The supports of Z_{i,<w_i+ϵ} and Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ} are disjoint, so Ẑ_{<w+ϵ} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+ϵ} misses D_{−,ϵ}. Hence Ẑ_{<w+ϵ} ∩ U_{≥w−ϵ} is a closed subset of U_{≥w−ϵ} that lies inside 𝔘. By excision, RΓ_{Ẑ_{<w+ϵ}∩U_{≥w−ϵ,Z/p^rZ}}(U_{≥w−ϵ,Z/p^rZ}, ℱ̃_r^{ν_A,n}) is meaningful even though its sheaf lives only on 𝔘̃: it is cohomology on 𝔘̃ with support in the preimage.
- The domain of the correspondences. Only supports matter here. By Proposition 6.2.3(1), supp D_{+,ϵ} ⊆ supp D_{+,ϵ′} and supp D_{−,ϵ} ⊆ supp D_{−,ϵ′}. The choice of ϵ′ in §6.2.1 gives T(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}) ⊆ 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ′} and T^t(𝒰_{≤w+ϵ}) ⊆ 𝒰_{≤w+ϵ′}. So supp p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} ⊆ supp p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} and supp p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ′} ⊆ supp p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ}. These are the second statements of Proposition 6.2.3(2) and (3), read as inclusions of supports. Hence supp p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ} ⊆ supp p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} and supp p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ} ⊆ supp p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ}. So p_1^{−1}(𝔘) ∩ p_2^{−1}(𝔘) = C_t^{tor} ∖ (p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} ∪ p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ}), which is exactly the open of Proposition 6.2.7. The domain therefore follows from the definition and fits the rest of §6.2.
Shrinking ϵ does no harm. By Proposition 6.1.10 (p. 60), ∩_{m,n} T^m(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}) ∩ (T^t)^n(𝒵_{<w+ϵ}) is the closure of 𝒮^{tor}_w for every ϵ ∈ ]0,1[∩Q. So by Proposition 6.1.7 (p. 59) the finite-slope parts do not depend on ϵ. The ordinary part is M_w^• ⊗_Λ A for every such ϵ, by Theorem 6.2.15(1), whose input Proposition 6.2.13 does not involve ϵ.

Kind and reach. Each item is a slip of notation, an omitted definition or an omitted standing assumption, and in each case the surrounding text fixes the intended meaning. None is a false statement or a missing argument. The passage is used by the definition before Theorem 6.2.15 and by Theorem 6.2.15 (p. 64). - **Misprint** at §6.2.11, proof of Proposition 6.2.14, second paragraph, p. 64. The 2024 preprint has the same slip (proof of Proposition 6.2.14, p. 61), printed there without tildes on either side: $p_2^\star\mathscr F_r^{\nu_A,n}(-mD_-) \to p_1^!\mathscr F^{\nu_A,n}(mD_+)$. The revision added the tildes but still left out the subscript r on the right.. The source says `We now tensor with the fundamental class to get a map $p_2^\star\tilde{\mathscr F}_r^{\nu_A,n}(-mD_-) \to p_1^!\tilde{\mathscr F}^{\nu_A,n}(mD_+)$ for some $m \geq 0$.`; it should be `$p_2^\star\tilde{\mathscr F}_r^{\nu_A,n}(-mD_-) \to p_1^!\tilde{\mathscr F}_r^{\nu_A,n}(mD_+)$: the target sheaf should carry the subscript r.`. On p. 63 the paper defines the script sheaves $\mathscr F_r$ only as reductions modulo $p^r$ ('We let $\mathscr F_r^{\kappa_A,n}$ and $\mathscr F_r^{\nu_A}$ be the sheaves obtained by reduction modulo $p^r$'). The integral extended sheaf is the fraktur $\tilde{\mathfrak F}^{\nu_A,n}$. A script $\tilde{\mathscr F}^{\nu_A,n}$ with no subscript r is never defined. The map in question comes from reducing the integral map $p_2^\star\tilde{\mathfrak F}^{\nu_A,n} \to p_1^\star\tilde{\mathfrak F}^{\nu_A,n}$ modulo $p^r$ and tensoring with the fundamental class, so it has the same level r on both sides. This matches the source $p_2^\star\tilde{\mathscr F}_r^{\nu_A,n}(-mD_-)$, the next sentence's remark that m is independent of r, and the conclusion a few lines later, the cohomological correspondence $p_2^\star\tilde{\mathscr F}_r^{\nu_A,n} \to p_1^!\tilde{\mathscr F}_r^{\nu_A,n}$ (also the form in the statement of Proposition 6.2.14 on p. 63). The intended meaning is therefore clear, and restoring the subscript r leaves the argument unchanged.
