- **Gap** at §2.1.1, the paragraph after Definition 2.1.2, p. 7; also Lemma 2.1.13, p. 8, and Lemma 2.1.32, p. 10. The 2024 preprint has the same omission. There, p. 6 says only "Moreover, the category is cofiltered." with no argument. Lemma 2.1.13 (p. 7) is glossed the same way, with the proof "We can take X̄″ = X̄ × X̄′ and C̄″ = C̄ × C̄′". The revision replaced these products by closures. Lemma 2.1.31 (p. 10, numbered 2.1.32 in the revision) is also glossed the same way. Neither version addresses parallel maps.. The source says `p. 7 (§2.1.1, after Definition 2.1.2): "Compactifications of X form a category, with maps ξ : (j_X : X ↪ X̄) → (j′_X : X ↪ X̄′) being given by maps of S-scheme ξ : X̄ → X̄′, extending the identity of X. Moreover, the category is cofiltered: given compactifications X̄ and X̄′ we may take the closure of the diagonal X in X̄ ×_S X̄′." p. 8, Lemma 2.1.13: "The category of compactifications of (C, X, p1, p2) is cofiltered, with maps being strict maps: if (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2) and (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′1, p̄′2) are two compactifications, there exists a compactification (C̄″, X̄″, p̄″1, p̄″2) with strict maps (C̄″, X̄″, p̄″1, p̄″2) → (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2) and (C̄″, X̄″, p̄″1, p̄″2) → (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′1, p̄′2). Proof. We can take X̄″ to be the closure of X in X̄ × X̄′ and C̄″ to be the closure of C in C̄ × C̄′." p. 10, Lemma 2.1.32: "The category of dynamic (resp. strict dynamic, resp. compact dynamic) compactifications of (C, X, p1, p2, ) where maps are non strict maps is cofiltered: if (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2, D+, D−) and (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′1, p̄′2, D′+, D′−) are two dynamic (...) compactifications, there exists a dynamic (...) compactification (C̄″, X̄″, p̄″1, p̄″2, D″+, D″−) with maps (C̄″, ...) → (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2, D+, D−), (C̄″, ...) → (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′1, p̄′2, D′+, D′−)."`; it should be `The fix is to add the equalizer condition for parallel maps. Let ξ1, ξ2 : X̄ ⇉ X̄′ be two maps of compactifications. Let E ⊆ X̄ be their equalizer, the pull-back of the diagonal of X̄′ ×_S X̄′ along (ξ1, ξ2). - E is a closed subscheme, because X̄′ is separated over S. - X ⊆ E, because ξ1∘j_X = ξ2∘j_X = j′_X. - E ∩ X = X, so X is open in E. Hence E is a compactification, and E ↪ X̄ is a strict map with ξ1|_E = ξ2|_E. Equivalently, one can use the scheme-theoretic closure X̄″ of X in X̄. Since j_X is quasi-compact, X is scheme-theoretically dense in X̄″. Two maps to the separated X̄′ that agree on X therefore agree on X̄″. For compactifications of correspondences (Lemma 2.1.13), take the equalizers E_C ⊆ C̄ and E_X ⊆ X̄ of the two components. Then p̄_i maps E_C into E_X. Also E_C ×_{E_X×E_X} (X×X) = E_C ×_{C̄} C = C. So (E_C, E_X) is a compactification with a strict map to (C̄, X̄) that equalizes the two maps. For dynamic compactifications (Lemma 2.1.32), pull D± back to E_X. By Lemma 2.1.29 the result is dynamic (resp. strict dynamic, resp. compact dynamic), and the inclusion is a strict map. Non-emptiness holds by Remark 2.1.3 and Lemma 2.1.11. For dynamic compactifications it is the standing assumption of §2.5.`. At all three places the paper claims "cofiltered", but the argument only builds a common refinement of two objects. The second axiom of a cofiltered category, equalizing parallel maps, is never addressed.
This axiom is not automatic. Definition 2.1.2 does not require X to be dense in X̄; Lemma 2.1.4 adds density as a separate hypothesis. So maps of compactifications need not be unique. Example: X = A^1_k over a field k, X̄ = P^1_k ⊔ Spec k and X̄′ = P^1_k, with X embedded in the P^1 component of X̄. Proper over k: yes. A map X̄ → X̄′ extending the identity of X must be the identity on the P^1 component, since X is dense there and P^1 is separated. The extra point, however, may go to any k-point of P^1. So there are distinct parallel maps ξ1 ≠ ξ2 (for example, sending the point to 0 or to ∞). Such a pair is equalized, for example, by the closed immersion of the P^1 component, but that needs an argument.
The argument above (the equalizer is a closed subscheme containing X, and the inclusion is strict) was checked directly, and it goes through in all three settings. So the claims are true as stated.
The omission touches no stated result. The later uses rely only on common refinements: §2.5.6 (p. 20), "By lemma 2.1.13, we can therefore assume that (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2) = (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′1, p̄′2)". The same holds for the remark after Theorem 2.5.1 (p. 19), "(recall that the category of strict dynamic compactifications is cofiltered by lemma 2.1.32)". The equalizer axiom is what makes identifications obtained through different refinements agree. A cofiltered category, in the standard sense, satisfies three conditions:
1. it is non-empty;
2. any two objects receive maps from a common object;
3. any two parallel maps are equalized by some map into their source.

The sentence on p. 7 establishes only condition 2, and so do the glosses after the colons in Lemmas 2.1.13 and 2.1.32.

Condition 3 is not automatic. Definition 2.1.2 does not require X to be dense in X̄, and Lemma 2.1.4 adds density as a separate hypothesis. So maps of compactifications need not be unique. Example over a field k: take X = A^1, X̄ = P^1 ⊔ Spec k and X̄′ = P^1. A map X̄ → X̄′ extending the identity of X may send the extra point to any k-point of P^1. Parallel strict maps also exist. Take X̄′ = P^1 ⊔ P^1, with X in the first copy. The extra point may go to ∞ or to any k-point of the second copy. With C = X, p1 = p2 = id and C̄ = X̄, the same happens in the categories of Lemma 2.1.13.

The best defence is that the glosses show the authors use "cofiltered" to mean only condition 2. Under that reading, all three statements are proved correctly. The closure of X in X̄ ×_S X̄′ is a compactification with strict maps to both factors, since the graph of j′_X is closed in X × X̄′.

However, the property is used only once, in the remark on p. 19: "The theorem implies that the ordinary cohomology depends only on the data (C, X, p1, p2) (recall that the category of strict dynamic compactifications is cofiltered by lemma 2.1.32) … We simply denote it by RΓ(X, F)^{C−ord}". Section 2.5.6 (p. 20) uses Lemma 2.1.13 only for common refinements. Common refinements show that two choices give quasi-isomorphic complexes. They do not show that the quasi-isomorphism is independent of the maps chosen. Those maps are built from pull-backs along ξ (Lemma 2.2.7, Proposition 2.2.11), so a priori they depend on ξ. Condition 3 closes the gap. Let e : E → C′ be a strict map that equalizes ξ1, ξ2 : C′ ⇉ C. Then e*ξ1* = e*ξ2*, and e* is a quasi-isomorphism by Theorem 2.5.1(3). Hence ξ1* = ξ2* on ordinary cohomology, given the evident compatibility of these quasi-isomorphisms with composition. So the paper asserts the property, needs it for the canonical identification it uses, and does not prove it. That makes this a genuine but minor gap.

The missing condition holds by the equalizer argument in the correction. Direct verification confirms each step: E is closed, contains X, and meets X in X; E_C ×_{E_X×E_X} (X×X) = C; Lemma 2.1.29 applies to the strict inclusion. Condition 1 holds for schemes and for correspondences. For dynamic compactifications it can fail. Example over a field: X = A^1 and C = A^1 ⊔ A^1, with (p1, p2) given by x ↦ (x, 0) on the first copy and x ↦ (0, x) on the second. This correspondence has no dynamic compactification: a boundary point can lie in neither D+ nor D−. But §2.5 assumes that a strict dynamic compactification exists.

Lemmas 2.1.13 and 2.1.32 are cited only on pp. 10, 19 and 20, and no other argument uses condition 3. The stated results stand, and the proposed fix is correct and minimal. - **Misprint** at §2.1.14, Lemma 2.1.17(1), p. 8 (the 2024 preprint has the same text, Lemma 2.1.17(1), p. 8). The source says `(1) If D and D′ are Cartier divisors, then D ≤ D′ implies that there exists n₀ ∈ ℤ_{≥0} such that we have a canonical injective map: 𝒪_X̄(−n₀D′) → 𝒪_X̄(−n₀D).`; it should be `… there exists n₀ ∈ ℤ_{>0} (i.e. n₀ ≥ 1) such that (𝒥′)^{n₀} ⊆ 𝒥^{n₀}, that is, a canonical injective map 𝒪_X̄(−n₀D′) → 𝒪_X̄(−n₀D). Here D = V(𝒥) and D′ = V(𝒥′).`. With n₀ = 0 both sheaves equal 𝒪_X̄ and the identity map satisfies the conclusion. As printed, the statement therefore holds for any pair D, D′ and says nothing. The intended value comes from Definition 2.1.15(2): D ≤ D′ is the case s = 1 of D ≤ sD′, so (𝒥′)^p ⊆ 𝒥^q with p/q = 1. Since s > 0 forces q ≥ 1, this gives p = q = n₀ ≥ 1, and that is the n₀ the proof uses ("by definition there exists n₀ such that Af′^{n₀} ⊆ Af^{n₀}"). The lemma is applied on p. 33 as "after replacing D₊ and D₋ by a multiple nD₊ and nD₋ for n ∈ ℤ_{>0}", which needs n₀ ≥ 1. The same "p, q ∈ ℤ_{≥0}" appears in Definition 2.1.15(2), but it does no harm there because s > 0 already forces p, q ≥ 1. The printed statement is literally true but empty, and the intended one is clear from the proof and from how the lemma is used. - **Error** at §2.1, Example 2.1.21, p. 9. The source says `Example 2.1.21. Let S = Spec F_p. We consider the Frobenius correspondence. Namely, C̄ = X̄, and we let p_2 = F : X̄ → X̄ be the Frobenius map and p_1 : X̄ → X̄ be the identity. Then for any closed subscheme D, we have p̄⋆_2 D = p p̄⋆_1 D, so D is strictly contracted.`; it should be `Replace "we have p̄⋆_2 D = p p̄⋆_1 D" by "we have p̄⋆_1 D ≤ (1/p) p̄⋆_2 D". The reason: write D = V(I). Then p̄⋆_1 D = D, and p̄⋆_2 D = F⋆D = V(I^{[p]}), where I^{[p]} is the ideal generated by the p-th powers of local sections of I. Since I^{[p]} ⊆ I^p, Definition 2.1.15(2), applied with 1/p = 1/p (numerator 1, denominator p), gives p̄⋆_1 D ≤ (1/p) p̄⋆_2 D. So D is strictly contracted, with s = 1/p. The equality p̄⋆_2 D = p p̄⋆_1 D, meaning I^{[p]} = I^p, holds when D is locally principal. It fails in general, although it can hold for some other D. One can also note that p̄⋆_2 D ≤ s' p̄⋆_1 D holds for every rational s' > p, but not for s' = p.`. The printed text on p. 9 matches the quotation above. The paper writes p̄⋆D for the preimage (fibre product) of a closed subscheme, as with ξ⋆X on p. 7. So p̄⋆_1 D = V(I), and p̄⋆_2 D = F⋆D has ideal F^{-1}(I)·O = I^{[p]}. The paper defines multiples nD only for locally principal subschemes, through O(−nD). The natural meaning of p·p̄⋆_1 D is V(I^p).

The equality fails as soon as D is not locally principal. Take D = V(x, y), the origin of A^2 over F_p, or a closed F_p-point of P^2, where the local computation is the same. Then F⋆D = V(x^p, y^p). The monomial x^{p−1}y has total degree p, so it lies in (x, y)^p. It is not divisible by x^p or by y^p, so it does not lie in (x^p, y^p). Hence V(I^{[p]}) ≠ V(I^p).

The equality also fails in the weaker two-sided sense of the preorder ≤ of Definition 2.1.15(2). The relation p̄⋆_2 D ≤ p·p̄⋆_1 D would need (x, y)^{pb} ⊆ (x^p, y^p)^b for some b ≥ 1. But x^{pb−1}y lies in (x, y)^{pb} and in none of the generators x^{pi}y^{p(b−i)}. This was checked by direct computation for p = 2, 3, 5, 7 and b = 1, …, 4, and it holds for all p and b by the divisibility argument just given.

Only the inequality p̄⋆_1 D ≤ (1/p) p̄⋆_2 D is needed for strict contraction (Definition 2.1.19(5)). It holds because (I^{[p]})^1 ⊆ I^p. So the conclusion of the example is correct. Nothing in the paper cites Example 2.1.21, and the later uses of Frobenius (§3.4, pp. 38–39) do not rely on it. The error is confined to this illustrative example.

One refinement to the proposed correction: the equality can hold for some D that are not locally principal. For example, take I = (x, y) in F_p[x, y]/(x, y)^2; there I^p = 0 = I^{[p]}. So "holds when D is locally principal, but not in general" is more accurate than "holds only for locally principal D". The printed text on p. 9 is as quoted. The paper writes p̄⋆D for the scheme-theoretic pull-back of a closed subscheme (compare ξ⋆X on p. 7 and the pull-backs of Cartier divisors in Lemma 2.1.29). For the graph of Frobenius, p̄⋆_1 D = V(I) and p̄⋆_2 D = F^{-1}(D) = V(I^{[p]}). The paper defines a multiple nD of a closed subscheme only when D is locally principal, through O(−nD) (§2.1.14, p. 8). Otherwise the only scaled notion is the relation "D ≤ sD′" of Definition 2.1.15(2): D = V(I), D′ = V(I′), s = a/b and (I′)^a ⊆ I^b.

Defence considered. Under every reading the paper supports, the printed equality is false once D is not locally principal.
(i) As ideals, the equality reads I^{[p]} = I^p. Take D = V(x, y), the origin in A^2 over F_p, or a closed F_p-point of P^2, where the local picture is the same. Then x^{p−1}y lies in (x, y)^p but not in (x^p, y^p).
(ii) Read as a two-sided relation in the preorder of Definition 2.1.15(2), the equality needs p̄⋆_2 D ≤ p·p̄⋆_1 D. That means (x, y)^{pb} ⊆ (x^p, y^p)^b for some b ≥ 1. But the monomial x^{pb−1}y lies in (x, y)^{pb}, while ⌊(pb−1)/p⌋ + ⌊1/p⌋ = b − 1 < b, so it does not lie in (x^p, y^p)^b. Checked by direct computation for p = 2, 3, 5, 7 and all b ≤ 29, and the argument covers all p and b.
(iii) The most charitable reading is asymptotic. I^{[p]} is a reduction of I^p: every product of p generators has its p-th power in (I^{[p]})^p. So p̄⋆_2 D ≤ s′ p̄⋆_1 D holds for every s′ > p. For I = (x, y), checked by direct computation, the least admissible exponent ratio is (pb + p − 1)/b, which tends to p. So the equality is true "up to ε". The paper never defines such an equivalence, however, and at s = p the relation fails.
Locally principal D (I = (f) locally) do satisfy I^{[p]} = (f^p) = I^p, and that is presumably the case the authors had in mind. The example, though, says "for any closed subscheme D".

The conclusion survives. Strict contraction (Definition 2.1.19(5)) needs only p̄⋆_1 D ≤ s p̄⋆_2 D for some 0 < s < 1. Here s = 1/p works because I^{[p]} ⊆ I^p. (The correspondence is admissible because the graph of F is a closed immersion, X̄ being separated.)

Consequences. Nothing in the paper cites Example 2.1.21. Strict contraction is established later only in Lemma 4.4.2 (p. 50), by a direct local computation with generators of Cartier divisors. The Frobenius lifts of §3.4 (pp. 38–39) play no role in any contraction argument. So the error is confined to this illustrative example. - **Misprint** at §2.1, proof of Lemma 2.1.17(3), second diagram, bottom-left vertex, p. 9. The source says `In the second commutative diagram of the proof of Lemma 2.1.17 (p. 9), the top row reads "A --a^k f^q--> A --f^{(k−1)q−k′q′}--> A". The vertical arrows are labelled "(f′)^{k′p′}", "f^{(k−1)q}" and "f^{k′q′}". The bottom row reads "A(f′)^{kp′} ⟶ A(f)^{(k−1)q} ⟶ A(f)^{k′q′}". The diagram is introduced by the sentence "We now let k′ = k p/p′ (for k large enough and divisible by p′). The above diagram yields the new diagram:"`; it should be `The bottom-left vertex should read A(f′)^{k′p′}, which equals A(f′)^{kp}. It should not read A(f′)^{kp′}.`. The proof sets s = p/q and s′ = p′/q′, and then defines k′ = kp/p′, so k′p′ = kp. The second diagram is said to be obtained from the first. The first diagram's left column is the multiplication map A → A(f′)^{kp}, given by (f′)^{kp}. In the second diagram that arrow is correctly relabelled "(f′)^{k′p′}", which is again (f′)^{kp}. Its target must therefore be the ideal A(f′)^{k′p′} = A(f′)^{kp}. The printed vertex A(f′)^{kp′} is a different ideal in general: kp′ = k′p′ only if p = p′. The printed vertex also contradicts the arrow label directly beneath it.

I checked the rest of the diagram by direct computation. First, (k−1)q = k′q′ · (p′q/(pq′)) · ((k−1)/k) ≥ k′q′ for k large, because p′q/(pq′) = s′/s > 1. So the right square, with f^{(k−1)q} = f^{k′q′} · f^{(k−1)q−k′q′}, commutes. Second, the left square commutes because (f′)^{kp} = a^k f^q f^{(k−1)q}. The bottom row therefore gives A(f′)^{k′p′} → A(f)^{k′q′}. This matches the next sentence, "We now change p′ to k′p′ and q′ to k′q′", and the conclusion O_X̄(−p′D′) → O_X̄(−q′D) with the ratio still equal to s′.

The rendered page and a zoomed image both show the superscript as kp′, so this is not an artefact of the text layer. The slip is confined to one vertex label. The arrow label, the ratios, the renaming and the conclusion of Lemma 2.1.17(3) are all correct as printed, so nothing downstream depends on the misprint. - **Misprint** at §2.1.25, Lemma 2.1.30, p. 10 (the 2024 preprint has the same text as Lemma 2.1.29, p. 9). The source says `There exists a dynamic (resp. strict dynamic, resp. compact dynamic) compactification 𝒞′ = (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′₁, p̄′₂, D′₊, D′₋) and a strict map 𝒞′ → 𝒞 with the property that D′₊ and D′₋ are Cartier divisors on X̄′ and p̄⋆_i D′₊, p̄⋆_i D′₋ for i = 1, 2 are Cartier Divisors in 𝒞′.`; it should be `… D′₊ and D′₋ are Cartier divisors on X̄′, and (p̄′_i)⋆D′₊, (p̄′_i)⋆D′₋ for i = 1, 2 are Cartier divisors on C̄′.`. D′₊ and D′₋ are subschemes of X̄′. They can only be pulled back along the maps p̄′_i : C̄′ → X̄′, which the statement itself names inside 𝒞′. The unprimed p̄_i go from C̄ to X̄ and cannot be applied to D′±. "In 𝒞′" should be "on C̄′", because 𝒞′ denotes the whole tuple and not a scheme. The proof gives the corrected statement. X̄′ is the blow-up of X̄ along 𝒥𝒥 (the product of the ideals of D₊ and D₋), so the pullbacks D′± are Cartier. C̄′ is the blow-up of C̄″ = C̄ ×_{X̄×X̄} (X̄′ × X̄′) along the union of the four pulled-back divisors, so the ideal of that union becomes invertible on C̄′. A product of ideals is invertible only if each factor is, so each of the four pullbacks is Cartier on C̄′. The proof also writes p̄⋆_i for the unnamed projections C̄″ → X̄′, so the dropped prime is a notational slip. The intended statement is unambiguous. - **Gap** at §2.1.33, proof of Lemma 2.1.34, p. 11 (it affects the proof). The source says `"Proof. We let X̄′′ and C̄′′ be compactifications of X′ and C′. We let X̄′ be the closure of X′ in X̄′′ × X̄ and C̄′ be the closure of C′ in C̄′′ × C̄. We claim that X̄′ ×_X̄ X = X′. Indeed, the natural map X′ → X̄′ ×_X̄ X is both an open immersion and a proper map (since X′ → X is assumed to be proper). Similarly, we see that C̄′ ×_C̄ C = C′. We thus deduce that C′ = C̄′ ×_{X̄′×X̄′} X′ × X′. We have a diagram:" This is followed by a displayed diagram with C̄′ at the top, arrows p̄′2 and p̄′1 from C̄′ to the two copies of X̄′, a vertical arrow t : C̄′ → C̄, arrows p̄2, p̄1 : C̄ → X̄, and r : X̄′ → X̄ on both sides.`; it should be `Replace the first sentence with: "We let (C̄″, X̄″, p̄″1, p̄″2) be a compactification of the correspondence (C′, X′, p′1, p′2), which exists by Lemma 2.1.11." Keep X̄′ and C̄′ as the closures of X′ and C′ in X̄″ × X̄ and C̄″ × C̄. Let t : C̄′ → C̄ be the second projection. Define p̄′i : C̄′ → X̄′ as the restriction of p̄″i × p̄i : C̄″ × C̄ → X̄″ × X̄. The rest of the proof then goes through unchanged, because p̄i ∘ t = r ∘ p̄′i. An equivalent fix, following the pattern of the proof of Lemma 2.1.11: take C̄′ to be the closure of C′ in C̄″ × C̄ × X̄′ × X̄′, and let t, p̄′1, p̄′2 be the projections.`. The printed page matches the quoted text. The gap is real under the paper's own conventions.

**Why the maps are missing.** In Definition 2.1.2, a compactification of C′ is just a proper scheme containing C′ as an open subscheme. The paper uses the phrase "compactifications of X and C" in exactly this sense in the proof of Lemma 2.1.11 (p. 8). There it takes the closure of C in C̄′ × X̄ × X̄ precisely so that the projections p̄1 and p̄2 exist. In the proof of Lemma 2.1.34 the closure is taken only in C̄′′ × C̄. That space carries t : C̄′ → C̄ but no map to X̄′. So the arrows p̄′1 and p̄′2 in the displayed diagram are never constructed. The earlier sentence "C′ = C̄′ ×_{X̄′×X̄′} X′ × X′" already assumes these arrows exist.

**Counterexample: the maps can fail to exist.**
- Work over a field. Let X = C = X′ = C′ = A², with every map the identity.
- Let X̄ = C̄ = P² and p̄1 = p̄2 = id. Then C̄ ×_{X̄×X̄} (X × X) = A².
- Let D+ be the line at infinity and D− = ∅. This is a dynamic compactification.
- Choose X̄′′ = P¹ × P¹ and C̄′′ = P².
- Then X̄′ is the closure of the graph of the rational map P² ⇢ P¹ × P¹, [x:y:z] ↦ ([x:z],[y:z]). This is P² blown up at [1:0:0] and [0:1:0].
- C̄′ is the diagonal of P² × P², so it is P².
- A morphism C̄′ → X̄′ extending the identity of A² would give a morphism P² → P¹ × P¹ extending this rational map. The rational map is undefined at [1:0:0]: near that point it is (y,z) ↦ [y:z]. So no such morphism exists.

**The correction works.** Checked directly:
- C′ is open and dense in the new C̄′.
- C′ → C̄′ ×_C̄ C is an open immersion and is proper, because C′ → C is proper. Hence C̄′ ×_C̄ C = C′.
- X̄′ ×_X̄ X = X′, so (r × r)⁻¹(X × X) = X′ × X′.
- Using p̄i ∘ t = r ∘ p̄′i: C̄′ ×_{X̄′×X̄′} (X′ × X′) = t⁻¹(C̄ ×_{X̄×X̄} (X × X)) = t⁻¹(C) = C′.
- r⁻¹(D+ ∪ D−) = X̄′ \ X′.
- Pullbacks of (strict or compact) expansion and contraction go through t exactly as printed.

**Effect.** Only the proof is affected; the statement of Lemma 2.1.34 is true. The lemma is used in the proof of Theorem 5.1.4 (p. 53), which remains valid. **The printed text is as quoted.** The proof never builds the arrows p̄′1 and p̄′2 in its diagram, and with the choices as printed they need not exist.

**Defences tried.**
- (i) Could "compactifications of X′ and C′" mean a compactification of the correspondence (C′, X′, p′1, p′2)? The paper's usage does not support this. Definition 2.1.2 defines a compactification of a scheme. The proof of Lemma 2.1.11 (p. 8) uses the same phrase, "Let X̄ and C̄′ be compactifications of X and C", in exactly that sense: there the two compactifications are unrelated. That is why the proof then takes the closure of C in C̄′ × X̄ × X̄, so that the projections p̄1 and p̄2 exist. By contrast, when the proof of Lemma 2.1.13 (p. 8) takes closures in C̄ × C̄′ and X̄ × X̄′, both factors are already compactifications of correspondences, with maps between them.
- (ii) Could the arrows exist anyway? Not in general. The closure C̄′ ⊂ C̄″ × C̄ maps to C̄ and to C̄″, but nothing given maps C̄″ to X̄″, so nothing maps C̄′ to X̄′.

**Counterexample.** It satisfies the lemma's hypotheses in the dynamic case.
- Work over a field. Let X = C = X′ = C′ = A², with all maps the identity.
- Take the dynamic compactification C̄ = X̄ = P², p̄1 = p̄2 = id, D+ = ∅, D− = the line at infinity. Then D+ is expanded, D− is contracted, and X̄ \ X = D− ∪ D+.
- Choose X̄″ = P¹ × P¹ ⊃ A² and C̄″ = P². Then C̄′ is the diagonal of P² × P², isomorphic to P².
- Any p̄′i compatible with the correspondence must be the identity on A². Compose it with X̄′ → X̄″ = P¹ × P¹ and then with the second projection. This gives a morphism P² → P¹ extending (x, y) ↦ y, which is not constant.
- But every morphism P² → P¹ is constant, since two distinct fibres would be disjoint curves in P².
- So the diagram in the proof does not exist for this admissible choice. The same failure breaks the step "C′ = C̄′ ×_{X̄′×X̄′} X′ × X′" and the pull-back step (p̄′2)⋆D′+ ≤ s(p̄′1)⋆D′+, since both need p̄′i with p̄i ∘ t = r ∘ p̄′i.

**Why the correction works.** Checked directly.
- Both sides of p̄″i ∘ j_{C′} = j_{X′} ∘ p′i agree, and p̄i ∘ j_C ∘ (C′ → C) = j_X ∘ (X′ → X) ∘ p′i. So (p̄″i × p̄i) maps C′ into X′. Hence it maps the schematic closure C̄′ into the closed subscheme X̄′, and p̄i ∘ t = r ∘ p̄′i holds by construction.
- The map C′ → C̄′ ×_C̄ C is an open immersion. It is proper because C′ → C is proper. So C̄′ ×_C̄ C = C′.
- Likewise X̄′ ×_X̄ X = X′, and so (p̄′1 × p̄′2)⁻¹(X′ × X′) = t⁻¹((p̄1 × p̄2)⁻¹(X × X)) = t⁻¹(C) = C′. So (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′1, p̄′2) is a compactification of (C′, X′, p′1, p′2). It is proper because C̄′ is proper and X̄′ is separated.
- r⁻¹(D+ ∪ D−) = X̄′ \ X′.
- (p̄′j)⋆r⋆D± = t⋆p̄j⋆D±. Inclusions, the ideal inequalities (I′)^p ⊆ I^q, and interiors all behave correctly under pull-back by t, since t⁻¹(int T) ⊆ int t⁻¹(T). So the dynamic, strict dynamic and compact dynamic conditions carry over exactly as the proof says.
- The first correction changes only the choice in the first sentence and adds the definition of p̄′i, so it is minimal.

**What uses the lemma.** Lemma 2.1.34 is cited once, in the proof of Theorem 5.1.4 (p. 53), to pass from the level K′_{p,P} (handled by Proposition 4.4.4) to smaller decomposable K_{p,P} ⊆ K′_{p,P}. That proof uses only the lemma's statement, which is true. So Theorem 5.1.4 and everything after it stand. - **Gap** at §1.2 (Hida theory), last sentence of the paragraph beginning "In [Pil20], we considered the case g = 2", p. 2. The 2024 preprint does not contain this sentence: its §1.2 says only "Results in this direction have already appeared in [Pil20], [BCGP21], [LPSZ19], [BP20] for g = 1 and g = 2". The whole paragraph describing the complex M^0 → M^1 of [Pil20], this sentence included, was added in the revision.. The source says `In the current paper we show that the modules M^0 and M^1 actually extend over the entire weight space : they are higher Hida theories for H^0 and H^1 (interpolating regular weight cohomology).`; it should be `Replace the sentence with one that says only what the paper proves: "In the current paper we construct higher Hida theories for H^0 and H^1 over the entire weight space. These are the complexes M^•_w for w = Id and for the element w_1 of length one of ^MW (§5.2, §5.4). They interpolate ordinary H^0 and H^1 in the regular weights with C(κ) = {Id}, resp. {w_1} (Corollary 4.5.5, Proposition 1.4.7). In the singular weights ω^{(k,2)} we have C(κ) = {Id, w_1}. There the Cousin spectral sequence (Theorem 4.5.2) computes the ordinary part of H^0 and H^1 at Iwahori level from their specialisations, which is the role that M^0 → M^1 plays in [Pil20]." The claim that the complex of [Pil20] is itself a restriction of M^•_Id and M^•_{w_1} should either be dropped or be stated and proved separately. Such a statement would have to pass from Iwahori level to Klingen level (see the reason).`. The sentence on p. 2 says that the paper shows that the terms M^0 and M^1 of the complex of [Pil20], which is built along the one-variable line of weights ω^{(k,2)}, extend over the whole weight space. The body never states or proves such a comparison. [Pil20] is cited in the body only twice, and neither citation concerns its complex M^0 → M^1. On p. 56, in the proof of Theorem 5.3.5, the ordinary cohomology of a kernel vanishes "as in [Pil20], sect. 10.7". On p. 63, in the proof of Proposition 6.2.13, the proof says "Compare with [Pil20], sect. 10.7". The weights ω^{(k,2)} and the singular line never reappear after p. 2.

The best defence is to read the sentence loosely, and in that sense the intended content is proved. The complexes M^•_Id and M^•_{w_1} are defined over Λ = Z_p[[T(Z_p)]] (§5.2, §5.4). They specialise in every locally algebraic weight (Theorem 5.3.5, Remark 5.4.3), and they interpolate regular-weight H^0 and H^1 (Corollary 4.5.5, Proposition 1.4.7). For κ = (k,2) we have C(κ) = {Id, w_1}, and the Cousin spectral sequence (Theorem 4.5.2) builds the ordinary H^0 and H^1 from their two specialisations. The notions of ordinarity also agree on Hecke parameters. By [Pil20] (the discussion of the T-operator before its §7.1), for r = 2 ordinarity for the Klingen operator diag(p², p, p, 1) is equivalent to Newton = Hodge, i.e. α_p β_p is a unit. That is also the condition of Definition 1.3.5.

The literal claim still needs an argument that is not formal and that the paper does not give. The objects differ as follows:
- **Level and ordinary projector.** [Pil20] works at Klingen level with the projector of the single operator U. The present paper works at (deep) Iwahori level with the T^{++}(Q_p)-ordinary projector.
- **Coefficients and support.** [Pil20] uses a sheaf F^κ over Z_p[[Z_p^×]] on the p-rank ≥ 1 locus, and its two terms come from the ordinary locus and from local cohomology along the p-rank-one locus. The paper uses Igusa towers with the support conditions of §§4–5.

The levels really do give different answers. Take an unramified π_p with slopes (0, 0, k+1, k+1) and α_p ≠ β_p:
- On the Klingen invariants of π_p (dimension 4), the Klingen U has eigenvalues proportional to α_pβ_p, α_pγ_p, β_pδ_p and γ_pδ_p. Only the first is a unit, so π_p contributes once to the complex of [Pil20].
- The stabiliser of the singular ν+ρ has order 2, so π_p has two characters that are ordinary in weight κ (orderings (α, β, γ, δ) and (β, α, δ, γ)). So π_p contributes twice to the Iwahori-level abutment.

Hence the specialisations of M^•_Id and M^•_{w_1} along the line are not literally the terms of the complex of [Pil20]. At best that complex is a Klingen-level descent or direct factor of them, which the paper does not construct.

The paper also proves only that M^•_{w_1,cusp} has amplitude [0, 1] (Proposition 5.6.3). So even its restriction to the line is not shown to be a module in degree 1, as M^1 is in [Pil20].

Consequences: the passage is used nowhere later in the paper. No numbered statement and no proof depends on it, and Theorems 1.4.3, 1.4.8 and 4.5.2 are unaffected. The rewording given in the correction describes accurately what the paper proves, and it is the minimal fix. The kind is a gap because the sentence asserts a comparison with the complex of [Pil20] that is nowhere proved; it affects nothing because no later statement or proof uses it. We see that for all l ≥ 0, (p̄⋆₂(t̂₁, ⋯, t̂_{d′}))^q + √0_V)^l ⊆ (p̄⋆₂(t̂₁, ⋯, t̂_{d′}))^{q(l−r)}.`; it should be `((p̄⋆₂(t̂₁, ⋯, t̂_{d′}))^q + √0_V)^l ⊆ (p̄⋆₂(t̂₁, ⋯, t̂_{d′}))^{q(l−r)}. Optionally, say "for all l ≥ r", or state that non-positive powers of an ideal mean the unit ideal.`. The display has two opening and three closing parentheses, so the outer parenthesis before p̄⋆₂ is missing. The inclusion is correct once it is restored. Write J = p̄⋆₂(t̂₁, …, t̂_{d′}) and N = √0_V with N^r = 0. Then (J^q + N)^l = Σ_{k=0}^{min(l,r−1)} J^{q(l−k)}N^k ⊆ J^{q(l−r+1)} ⊆ J^{q(l−r)} for l ≥ r. For 0 ≤ l < r the exponent q(l − r) is negative. With the usual reading of a non-positive power as the whole ring, the inclusion is trivial there, so "for all l ≥ 0" does no harm, and only large l is used on p. 12 ("For l large enough, pl < q(l−r)"). The same missing parenthesis is in the 2024 preprint. There the exponent was printed as ql − r, which does not hold in general: for A = k[x, ε]/(ε³), J = (x), N = (ε), q = 2, r = 3, the term ε²x^{2l−4} lies in (J² + N)^l but not in (x^{2l−3}). The revision corrected the exponent to q(l − r) but left the parenthesis unbalanced. Recorded as `PAPER-BOXER-PILLONI-26/E20`; looked for an existing correction in: The authors' version on V. - **Misprint** at §2.2.9, Proposition 2.2.10 (second diagram of the statement) and its proof, p. 14 (the January 2024 preprint has the same text on pp. 13–14) (it affects a stated result). The source says `Proposition 2.2.10, p. 14: "The map T induces endomorphisms T_𝒞 of RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, ℱ) and RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, ℱ) as follows:" First diagram, for RΓ_{D₊,D₋}: RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₂D₊,p̄⋆₂D₋}(C̄, p⋆₂ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₊,p̄⋆₂D₋}(C̄, p⋆₂ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₊,p̄⋆₂D₋}(C̄, p!₁ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₊,p̄⋆₁D₋}(C̄, p!₁ℱ) → RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, ℱ). Second diagram, for RΓ_{D₋,D₊}: RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X, ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₂D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊}(C, p⋆₂ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊}(C, p⋆₂ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊}(C, p!₁ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₁D₊}(C, p!₁ℱ) → RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X, ℱ). In this diagram C and X are printed without bars throughout. Proof: "We only do the first case. The maps RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₂D₊,p̄⋆₂D₋}(C̄, p⋆₂ℱ), RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₊,p̄⋆₁D₋}(C̄, p!₁ℱ) → RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, ℱ) are given by lemma 2.2.7. The maps RΓ_{p̄⋆₂D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊}(C̄, p⋆₂ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊}(C̄, p⋆₂ℱ), RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊}(C̄, p!₁ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₁D₊}(C̄, p!₁ℱ) are given by lemma 2.2.6. The middle map RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊}(C, p⋆₂ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊}(C, p!₁ℱ) is produced by T as we now explain. We consider the chain of open immersions: C →(j_{C,−}) C̄ \ p̄⋆₁D₊ →(j_{C,+}) C̄. We deduce from T a map: (j_{C,+})⋆(j_{C,−})!p⋆₂ℱ → (j_{C,+})⋆(j_{C,−})!p!₁ℱ which induces the middle map RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊}(C, p⋆₂ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊}(C, p!₁ℱ)."`; it should be `Statement, second diagram. It should read RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₂D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊}(C̄, p⋆₂ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₂D₋,p̄⋆₁D₊}(C̄, p⋆₂ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₂D₋,p̄⋆₁D₊}(C̄, p!₁ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₁D₊}(C̄, p!₁ℱ) → RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, ℱ). The indices 1 and 2 on the two middle terms are swapped, and C and X should be C̄ and X̄. As in the first diagram, the D₊-set is enlarged first, then T is applied over C, and then the D₋-set is shrunk. Proof, which treats the first case. The two Lemma 2.2.6 maps should be RΓ_{p̄⋆₂D₊,p̄⋆₂D₋}(C̄, p⋆₂ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₊,p̄⋆₂D₋}(C̄, p⋆₂ℱ) and RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₊,p̄⋆₂D₋}(C̄, p!₁ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₊,p̄⋆₁D₋}(C̄, p!₁ℱ). The middle map appears twice: where it is introduced and in the final sentence. Both times it should be RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₊,p̄⋆₂D₋}(C̄, p⋆₂ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₊,p̄⋆₂D₋}(C̄, p!₁ℱ). So in the two Lemma 2.2.6 maps and in both occurrences of the middle map, + and − are interchanged in the subscripts, and in the middle map C should also be C̄. The Lemma 2.2.7 maps are correct as printed, and so is the construction of the middle map through (j_{C,+})⋆(j_{C,−})!.`. Conventions. Definition 2.2.4 (p. 12) defines two groups: RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, ℱ) = RΓ(X̄, (j₊)⋆(j₋)!ℱ) and RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, ℱ) = RΓ(X̄, (i₋)!(i₊)⋆ℱ). In each, the first subscript is the outer operation and the second is the inner one. The D₊-type set always carries ⋆ and the D₋-type set always carries !. The sheaf must be given on X̄ \ (D₊ ∪ D₋). By Remark 2.2.5 (p. 12), a sheaf on a larger open can be used after restricting it.

Lemma-construction 2.2.6 (p. 12) gives maps RΓ_{D₊,D₋} → RΓ_{D′₊,D′₋} and RΓ_{D₋,D₊} → RΓ_{D′₋,D′₊}. It assumes D′₋ ⊆ D₋ and D₊ ⊆ D′₊, and it needs the sheaf on X̄ \ (D′₋ ∪ D₊). That open contains both X̄ \ (D₊ ∪ D₋) and X̄ \ (D′₊ ∪ D′₋). The construction involves only the complementary opens, so inclusions of the underlying sets are enough.

Definition 2.1.24 (p. 9) requires D₊ to be expanded and D₋ to be contracted. By Definition 2.1.19(1) and (4) (p. 9), this means p̄⋆₂D₊ ⊆ p̄⋆₁D₊ and p̄⋆₁D₋ ⊆ p̄⋆₂D₋. These inclusions are set-theoretic (Remark 2.1.20). Take X = X̄ \ (D₊ ∪ D₋) and C = C̄ ×_{X̄×X̄} (X × X), as in Definition 2.1.9 (p. 7). Then C = C̄ \ (p̄⋆₁D₊ ∪ p̄⋆₂D₋). Proposition 2.10.4(2) (p. 30) takes C to be exactly this open, and the proof's chain C → C̄ \ p̄⋆₁D₊ → C̄ assumes it. The sheaves live on the following opens:
- p⋆₂ℱ on p̄₂⁻¹(X) = C̄ \ (p̄⋆₂D₊ ∪ p̄⋆₂D₋);
- p!₁ℱ on p̄₁⁻¹(X) = C̄ \ (p̄⋆₁D₊ ∪ p̄⋆₁D₋);
- T only on C.

The first diagram is correct. Its three opens are p̄₂⁻¹(X), C and p̄₁⁻¹(X). Both of its Lemma 2.2.6 steps satisfy the hypotheses: the first uses p̄⋆₂D₊ ⊆ p̄⋆₁D₊, and the second uses p̄⋆₁D₋ ⊆ p̄⋆₂D₋. Each sheaf is given where it is needed.

The printed second diagram is not correct. Both middle terms RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊} use the open U = C̄ \ (p̄⋆₁D₋ ∪ p̄⋆₂D₊). This open contains both p̄₁⁻¹(X) and p̄₂⁻¹(X), and in general it is strictly larger than C. The first arrow does satisfy the inclusion hypotheses of Lemma 2.2.6, but it needs p⋆₂ℱ on U, and p⋆₂ℱ is given only on p̄₂⁻¹(X). The middle arrow would need T on U. The last Lemma 2.2.6 arrow would likewise need p!₁ℱ on U. U is strictly larger than p̄₂⁻¹(X), and so also than C, as soon as p̄⋆₂D₋ is not contained in p̄⋆₁D₋ ∪ p̄⋆₂D₊. Nothing in the hypotheses rules this out.

Example. Work over S = Spec 𝔽₃; §2.2 assumes that all schemes are of finite type over ℤ. Take X̄ = C̄ = ℙ¹, p̄₁ = id, p̄₂(z) = z², D₊ = {∞} and D₋ = {1}. As sets, p̄⋆₁D₊ = p̄⋆₂D₊ = {∞} and p̄⋆₁D₋ = {1} ⊆ p̄⋆₂D₋ = {1, −1}. So (C̄, X̄, p̄₁, p̄₂, D₊, D₋) is a dynamic correspondence. Put X = ℙ¹ \ {1, ∞} and C = p̄₁⁻¹(X) ∩ p̄₂⁻¹(X) = ℙ¹ \ {1, −1, ∞}. Then the data form a dynamic compactification (Definition 2.1.26, p. 10) of the correspondence (C, X, p₁, p₂), where p₁ is the inclusion and p₂(z) = z². The printed middle open U = ℙ¹ \ {1, ∞} contains −1, where neither p⋆₂ℱ nor T is given.

The printed second row is exactly the first row with D₊ and D₋ interchanged in every subscript. That moves the index 1 onto D₋ and the index 2 onto D₊, which is the wrong way round.

With the corrected indices, the middle terms RΓ_{p̄⋆₂D₋,p̄⋆₁D₊} live on C̄ \ (p̄⋆₂D₋ ∪ p̄⋆₁D₊) = C. Both uses of Lemma 2.2.6 are then legitimate. The first uses p̄⋆₂D₊ ⊆ p̄⋆₁D₊ with the sheaf on p̄₂⁻¹(X). The second uses p̄⋆₁D₋ ⊆ p̄⋆₂D₋ with the sheaf on p̄₁⁻¹(X). The endpoints must be RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, ℱ), since Definition 2.2.4 defines these groups on X̄ and the proposition's own sentence names RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, ℱ).

The proof says it does "the first case". The sentence of the statement names RΓ_{D₋,D₊} first. But the proof's Lemma 2.2.7 pair and its construction of the middle map both belong to the first diagram, for RΓ_{D₊,D₋}. Its Lemma 2.2.6 pair and its middle map, however, are the terms of the printed second diagram: they carry that diagram's supports (p̄⋆₁D₋, p̄⋆₂D₊), and the middle map even has that diagram's C in place of C̄. The construction that follows belongs to the first case. On the chain C → C̄ \ p̄⋆₁D₊ → C̄, j_{C,−} extends by zero across p̄⋆₂D₋, and j_{C,+} pushes forward across p̄⋆₁D₊. By Definition 2.2.4 and Remark 2.2.5, (j_{C,+})⋆(j_{C,−})! therefore computes RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₊,p̄⋆₂D₋}(C̄, ·). This is the middle term of the first diagram, not the printed RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊}(C, ·). The corrected outer maps are exactly the ones Lemma 2.2.6 provides, by the two inclusions above.

The later use agrees with the correction. The proof of Proposition 2.10.3 (p. 30) treats the RΓ_{D₋,D₊} case using only the composite RΓ_{p̄⋆₂D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊}(C̄, p⋆₂ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₁D₊}(C̄, p!₁ℱ). It factors this composite through cohomology of C̄ \ (p̄⋆₁D₊)° with support in the closed set C̄ \ ((p̄⋆₂D₋)° ∪ (p̄⋆₁D₊)°). This set is the formula for C with interiors. Like the corrected row, it pairs p̄⋆₂ with D₋ and p̄⋆₁ with D₊. No later result uses the misprinted intermediate terms. The January 2024 preprint has the same statement and proof (pp. 13–14).

Kind and reach. The intended construction is clear from the first diagram, from the proof's own chain of immersions and from its later use, so this is a misprint. Part of it is in the statement. As printed, the second diagram of Proposition 2.2.10 is not defined: its middle terms live on an open where p⋆₂ℱ and T are not given. So it affects a stated result. The endpoints of both diagrams and the intended endomorphism T_𝒞 are unchanged. Recorded as `PAPER-BOXER-PILLONI-26/E21`; looked for an existing correction in: The authors' version on V. - **Misprint** at §2.2, Proposition 2.2.11 and the commutative diagram in its proof, p. 15. The 2024 preprint has the same diagram on p. 14.. The source says `Statement: "Let 𝒞 = (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2, D+, D−) → 𝒞′ = (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′1, p̄′2, D′+, D′−) be a strict map of dynamic compactifications (definition 2.1.28)." The diagram in the proof has six columns and is printed on two lines. The top row belongs to 𝒞′ and the bottom row to 𝒞. Top row: RΓ_{D′+,D′−}(X̄′, 𝓕) → RΓ_{(p̄′2)⋆D′+,(p̄′2)⋆D′−}(C̄′, (p̄′2)⋆𝓕) → RΓ_{(p̄′1)⋆D′+,(p̄′2)⋆D′−}(C̄′, (p̄′2)⋆𝓕) → RΓ_{(p̄′1)⋆D′+,(p̄′2)⋆D′−}(C̄′, (p̄′1)^!𝓕) → RΓ_{(p̄′1)⋆D′+,(p̄′1)⋆D′−}(C̄′, (p̄′1)^!𝓕) → RΓ_{D′+,D′−}(X̄′, 𝓕) Bottom row: RΓ_{D+,D−}(X̄, 𝓕) → RΓ_{(p̄2)⋆D+,(p̄2)⋆D−}(C̄, (p̄2)⋆𝓕) → RΓ_{(p̄1)⋆D′+,(p̄2)⋆D′−}(C̄, (p̄2)⋆𝓕) → RΓ_{(p̄1)⋆D+,(p̄2)⋆D−}(C̄, (p̄1)^!𝓕) → RΓ_{(p̄1)⋆D+,(p̄1)⋆D−}(C̄, (p̄1)^!𝓕) → RΓ_{D+,D−}(X̄, 𝓕) Vertical maps in columns 1 to 6: ‖, ↑ (from the C̄-term up to the C̄′-term), ‖, ‖, ↓ (from the C̄′-term down to the C̄-term), ‖. The primes on D′+ and D′− in the bottom-row entry of column 3 are unambiguous on the page.`; it should be `(a) The bottom-row entry of column 3 should read RΓ_{(p̄1)⋆D+,(p̄2)⋆D−}(C̄, (p̄2)⋆𝓕). (b) The direction of the map must match the vertical arrows. There are two ways to fix this. - State the proposition for a strict map 𝒞′ → 𝒞. This is the direction used in Definition 2.1.28 and Lemma 2.1.30, and with it the printed arrows are correct. - Or keep 𝒞 → 𝒞′ and reverse the two vertical arrows that are not equalities. Column 2 then has the pull-back ↓ from RΓ_{(p̄′2)⋆D′+,(p̄′2)⋆D′−}(C̄′, (p̄′2)⋆𝓕) to RΓ_{(p̄2)⋆D+,(p̄2)⋆D−}(C̄, (p̄2)⋆𝓕). Column 5 has the trace ↑ from RΓ_{(p̄1)⋆D+,(p̄1)⋆D−}(C̄, (p̄1)^!𝓕) to RΓ_{(p̄′1)⋆D′+,(p̄′1)⋆D′−}(C̄′, (p̄′1)^!𝓕). Correction (a) is needed with either choice.`. 1. What the statement means. On p. 8, a map of compactifications (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2) → (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′1, p̄′2) consists of maps C̄ → C̄′ and X̄ → X̄′ that are the identity on C and X and make the obvious diagrams commute. Definition 2.1.28 (p. 10) writes a map of dynamic compactifications as ξ: 𝒞′ → 𝒞 with D′± ⊇ ξ⋆D±, and calls it strict when D′± = ξ⋆D±. So the stated map 𝒞 → 𝒞′ is a pair ξ: C̄ → C̄′, ξ: X̄ → X̄′ with the following properties:
- p̄′i∘ξ = ξ∘p̄i;
- D± = ξ⋆D′±;
- ξ⁻¹(X) = X, so ξ: X̄ → X̄′ is strict in the sense of p. 7. This follows from the previous property, because X̄ \ X = D+ ∪ D− and X̄′ \ X = D′+ ∪ D′− (Definition 2.1.26, p. 10).
Both maps ξ are proper, since they are maps between proper S-schemes.

2. The primes in column 3 are a slip. D′+ and D′− are closed subschemes of X̄′, but p̄1 and p̄2 map C̄ to X̄. So (p̄1)⋆D′+ and (p̄2)⋆D′− are not defined. Every other subscript in the bottom row uses D±. In particular, column 4, RΓ_{(p̄1)⋆D+,(p̄2)⋆D−}(C̄, (p̄1)^!𝓕), is reached from column 3 by the map induced by T. That map does not change the supports. Strictness gives (p̄1)⋆D+ = ξ⋆(p̄′1)⋆D′+ and (p̄2)⋆D− = ξ⋆(p̄′2)⋆D′−. So the unprimed entry is exactly the pull-back of the top-row entry above it, which is what the equality in column 3 asserts.

3. The four columns marked ‖ are correct.
- Columns 1 and 6: the open part is X̄ \ (D+ ∪ D−) = X (Definition 2.1.26, p. 10).
- Columns 3 and 4: the open part is C̄ \ ((p̄1)⋆D+ ∪ (p̄2)⋆D−). D+ is expanded and D− is contracted (Definitions 2.1.19 and 2.1.24, p. 9). So (p̄2)⋆D+ ⊆ (p̄1)⋆D+ and (p̄1)⋆D− ⊆ (p̄2)⋆D− as sets. Hence the open part is p̄1⁻¹(X) ∩ p̄2⁻¹(X), which is C by Definition 2.1.9 (p. 7). The same holds on C̄′, and strictness gives ξ⁻¹(C) = C.
Over these open parts ξ is the identity, so Lemma 2.2.8 (p. 14) gives the equalities.

4. Column 2 is a pull-back, and it points down. Here the open part is U = p̄2⁻¹(X). It is the preimage of U′ = (p̄′2)⁻¹(X) ⊆ C̄′. U contains C but can be larger, and ξ: U → U′ is proper but need not be an isomorphism. Since p̄′2∘ξ = ξ∘p̄2 and ξ is the identity on X, we have ξ⋆(p̄′2)⋆𝓕 = (p̄2)⋆𝓕. So Lemma 2.2.7 (p. 13) gives a pull-back from the C̄′-term to the C̄-term, which is ↓.
Lemma 2.2.7 gives a map ↑ only as a trace. A trace would need the sheaf ξ^!(p̄′2)⋆𝓕 on U, and this is not (p̄2)⋆𝓕 in general. For example, take X̄′ = X̄ with ξ the identity and D′± = D±. Let C̄ be the blow-up of C̄′ at a closed point of U′ \ C near which C̄′ is a smooth surface. This is a strict map of dynamic compactifications: the expanded and contracted conditions pull back, and C = C̄ ×_{X̄×X̄} (X × X) still holds because the centre is not in C. Near the exceptional curve E we have ξ^!(p̄′2)⋆𝓕 = (p̄2)⋆𝓕 ⊗ 𝒪(E). For a nonzero locally free 𝓕 the two sheaves differ: (p̄2)⋆𝓕 is trivial on E, because p̄2 contracts E, while 𝒪(E) restricts to 𝒪(−1) on E.

5. Column 5 is a trace, and it points up. Here the sheaf is (p̄1)^!𝓕 on p̄1⁻¹(X). On that open part, ξ^!(p̄′1)^!𝓕 = (p̄′1∘ξ)^!𝓕 = (ξ∘p̄1)^!𝓕 = (p̄1)^!𝓕, because ξ is the identity on X. So Lemma 2.2.7 gives the trace from the C̄-term to the C̄′-term, which is ↑. The printed arrow is ↓.

6. The printed arrows fit a map in the other direction. For a strict map ξ: C̄′ → C̄, that is 𝒞′ → 𝒞, the pull-back goes from the C̄-term to the C̄′-term (↑) and the trace goes from the C̄′-term to the C̄-term (↓). This is exactly what is printed. It is also the direction of Definition 2.1.28 and of Lemma 2.1.30 (p. 10), which builds a strict map 𝒞′ → 𝒞. Unlike the ‖ in columns 3 and 4, the maps in columns 2 and 5 are not quasi-isomorphisms in general, so their direction matters.
The statement in the 2024 preprint (p. 14) has the same map 𝒞 → 𝒞′, and its diagram has the same arrows and the same primed entry in column 3. There the definition of a map of dynamic compactifications (p. 9) is written 𝒞 → 𝒞′, which matches the statement but not the arrows. In the authors' version, Definition 2.1.28 is written 𝒞′ → 𝒞, which matches the arrows but not the statement.

7. Nothing else is affected. With either fix, each square commutes by functoriality of the pull-back, trace and change-of-support maps (Lemma-construction 2.2.6 and Lemma 2.2.7). The square between columns 3 and 4 commutes because both rows use the same T on C. The conclusion says that the canonical quasi-isomorphisms RΓ_{D+,D−}(X̄, 𝓕) = RΓ_{D′+,D′−}(X̄′, 𝓕) and RΓ_{D−,D+}(X̄, 𝓕) = RΓ_{D′−,D′+}(X̄′, 𝓕) intertwine T_𝒞 and T_𝒞′. This is symmetric in 𝒞 and 𝒞′. Both later uses work with either reading: p. 19 (§2.5.2, with the map 𝒞′ → 𝒞 from Lemma 2.1.30) and p. 20 (§2.5.6, with a strict map 𝒟 → 𝒞). - **Misprint** at §2.3.1, the recalled formula for lim_n F̄(−nD) just before Proposition 2.3.2 (p. 15); proof of Proposition 2.3.2 (pp. 15–16); §2.4.1, first paragraph (p. 18). The January 2024 preprint has the same text as pp. 15–16 on its pp. 14–15, except that its final display writes ⊗_A and ⊗_{A[X]} for the solid tensor products. The p. 18 sentence and its footnote 2 are not in the preprint (§2.4.1, p. 17), so that slip entered in the revision.. The source says `p. 15 (§2.3.1): "We recall that lim_n F̄(−nD) = cone(∏_n F̄(−nD) → ∏_n F̄(−nD))[1] where the map sends (m_n)_n to (m_n − m_{n+1})_n." p. 15 (proof of Proposition 2.3.2): "By definition ([CSb], lecture VIII) j_!M = M ⊗_{(A[X],A)■} A((X^{−1}))/A[X]. Moreover, it is true that j_!M = M̄ ⊗_{(A,A)■} A[X]/(Xf − 1) ⊗_{(A[X],A)■} A((X^{−1}))/A[X]." p. 16 (end of the same proof): "Therefore, j_!M = M̄ ⊗_{(A,A)■} A((X^{−1}))/A[X] ⊗_{(A[X],A)■} A[X]/(Xf − 1) = cone(M̄[[X^{−1}]]X^{−1} →^{1−Xf} M̄[[X^{−1}]]X^{−1})[1]" p. 18 (§2.4.1): "Indeed, we can replace² M by the quasi-isomorphic cone(M ⊗_A A[X] →^{X−T} M ⊗_A A[X])[1] (where X is a formal variable that we rename T)." For comparison, p. 16 (proof of Proposition 2.3.5), about the levelwise surjection of inverse systems (M, ·f) → (f^nM), whose kernels are the M[f^n]: "The cone is given by (lim_n M[f^n])[1]".`; it should be `The paper's own conventions are the standard ones: K[1]^i = K^{i+1}, and cone(K → L) has K in degree −1 and L in degree 0. Under them the shifts change as follows. (1) p. 15: lim_n F̄(−nD) = cone(∏_n F̄(−nD) → ∏_n F̄(−nD))[−1]. This is the fibre of (m_n) ↦ (m_n − m_{n+1}), with H^0 = lim and H^1 = lim^1. (2) p. 15: j_!M = M ⊗_{(A[X],A)■} (A((X^{−1}))/A[X])[−1]. This is the cited definition ([CSb], Lecture VIII, Observation 8.11). The same [−1] belongs in the "Moreover" display and in the first line of the display on p. 16. (3) p. 16: j_!M = cone(M̄[[X^{−1}]]X^{−1} →^{1−Xf} M̄[[X^{−1}]]X^{−1})[−1]. This is the fibre of 1 − Xf. For M̄ a module, it is a two-term complex in degrees 0 and 1. (4) p. 18: M is quasi-isomorphic to cone(M ⊗_A A[X] →^{X−T} M ⊗_A A[X]), with no shift. For M a module, that is the two-term complex M ⊗_A A[X] → M ⊗_A A[X] with differential X − T, in degrees −1 and 0. To fix the p. 15 display alone, replace [1] by [−1]. For the proof of Proposition 2.3.2 to be right line by line, (2) and (3) are also needed. Fixing (1) and (3) without (2) leaves the step from the first to the second line of the p. 16 display off by one shift. The statement of Proposition 2.3.2 is unchanged, with lim the usual derived limit, and so is every later result.`. Conventions. The paper does not state its conventions for shifts or cones. It grades cohomologically throughout (H^i, and amplitudes such as [0, ℓ(w)] in Theorem 1.4.3, p. 5). It uses the standard conventions: K[1]^i = K^{i+1}, and cone(φ: K → L) has K in degree −1 and L in degree 0. Three passages show this.
- Theorem 1.4.8 (p. 5) gives a pairing into Λ[−d] and says it is compatible with classical Serre duality. Classical Serre duality pairs H^i with H^{d−i} through a trace map on H^d. So Λ[−d] sits in degree d. The same reading applies to the pairings into Z_p(ζ_{p^n})[−d] and Λ[−d] in Theorems 5.5.1–5.5.2 (p. 57).
- In the proof of Proposition 2.3.5 (p. 16), the cone of the levelwise surjection (M, ·f) → (f^nM), whose kernels are the M[f^n], is written (lim_n M[f^n])[1]. So a surjection with kernel K has cone K[1], with the kernel in degree −1.
- Remark 2.9.4 (p. 28) writes the triangle j_!j*F → F → î_*î*F as lim_n I^n ⊗ F → F → lim_n F ⊗ O_X/I^n. This is R lim applied to the levelwise triangles I^n ⊗ F → F → F ⊗ O_X/I^n. So it needs the limit of the constant system F to be F, in degree 0. It also identifies j_!j*F with lim_n I^n ⊗ F with no shift, which is what Proposition 2.3.2 intends.
With these conventions, let φ: P → Q be a map of modules in degree 0. Then cone(φ) has H^{−1} = ker φ and H^0 = coker φ. cone(φ)[1] lives in degrees −2 and −1. The fibre cone(φ)[−1] has ker φ in degree 0 and coker φ in degree 1.

(1) p. 15. The derived limit of an inverse system (P_n) is the fibre of (m_n) ↦ (m_n − m_{n+1}) on ∏P_n, with H^0 = lim and H^1 = lim^1. Read literally, the printed formula gives (R lim)[2].
Example: take the constant system A with identity transitions. The map on ∏A has kernel the constant sequences, which is ≅ A. It is surjective: put m_1 = 0 and m_{n+1} = m_n − b_n. So cone(∏ → ∏) is A in degree −1, and the printed cone(∏ → ∏)[1] is A in degree −2. The limit is A in degree 0. Even if "cone" is read as the fibre, the printed [1] puts A in degree −1.
Geometric check: X̄ = P^1 over a field k, D = ∞, F̄ = O. For n ≥ 1, H^0(P^1, O(−n)) = 0 and H^1(P^1, O(−n)) has dimension n − 1, with surjective transition maps. So lim_n RΓ(P^1, O(−n)) is concentrated in degree 1, as H^1_c(A^1, O) ≅ k((T^{−1}))/k[T] should be. The printed formula would put it in degree −1.
The printed formula also contradicts how lim is used afterwards. In the proof of Proposition 2.3.5, Mittag-Leffler gives H^i(X̄, j_!F) = lim_n H^i(X̄, I^nF̄) in the same degree i.

(2) p. 15. The cited definition carries the shift.
- [CSb], Lecture VIII, Observation 8.11 defines j_! as M ↦ M ⊗^L (A_∞/A)[−1], with A = Z[T] and A_∞ = Z((T^{−1})).
- Observation 8.12 applies this to products: j_!(∏_I A) = ∏_I (A_∞/A)[−1].
- For A = R[T], the proof of Proposition 11.4 in Lecture XI has f_!M = M ⊗^L_{(A,R)■} R((T^{−1}))/R[T][−1], and f^!R = RHom_R(R((T^{−1}))/R[T], R)[1] ≅ R[T][1].
The shift is forced. A((X^{−1})) is an idempotent (A[X],A)■-algebra that becomes 0 in (A[X],A[X])■. So j_!M is the fibre of M → M ⊗ A((X^{−1})). Since A[X] → A((X^{−1})) is injective, this fibre is M ⊗ (A((X^{−1}))/A[X])[−1]. Over a field this is the compactly supported cohomology of the affine line, k((X^{−1}))/k[X] in degree 1. The formula quoted "by definition" on p. 15 drops the [−1].

(3) p. 16. Put N = M̄[[X^{−1}]]X^{−1} = ∏_{n≥1} M̄X^{−n}. X acts by (Xm)_n = m_{n+1}, since the X^0 term dies in A((X^{−1}))/A[X]. So (1 − Xf)(Σ m_n X^{−n}) = Σ (m_n − f m_{n+1}) X^{−n}.
Locally F̄(−nD) = M̄, with multiplication by f as the transition maps. So 1 − Xf is exactly the map (m_n) ↦ (m_n − m_{n+1}) of the p. 15 display. Its kernel is lim(⋯ →^f M̄ →^f M̄) and its cokernel is lim^1.
Xf − 1 has constant term −1, so it is a nonzerodivisor on A[X]. Hence A[X]/(Xf − 1) ≃ [A[X] →^{Xf−1} A[X]] in degrees −1 and 0. So N ⊗_{(A[X],A)■} A[X]/(Xf − 1) ≃ cone(N →^{1−Xf} N), up to the sign of the differential, with no shift. The printed second equality therefore does not follow even from the printed first line: it adds a spurious [1].
With the [−1] from (2), j_!M = cone(1 − Xf)[−1]. Its H^0 is the limit and its H^1 is lim^1, so j_!M = R lim_n F̄(−nD), which is Proposition 2.3.2.
Example: take A = M̄ = k[f] over a field k. The system k[f] ←^f k[f] ←^f ⋯ has lim 0 and lim^1 = k[[f]]/k[f]. So j_!O sits in degree 1, as the [−1] predicts.

(4) p. 18. X − T is injective on M ⊗_A A[X] = M[X]: compare leading coefficients in X. Its cokernel is M, via Σ m_i X^i ↦ Σ T^i m_i, and X acts on it as T. This works degreewise when M is a complex. So cone(X − T) ≃ M, while the printed cone(X − T)[1] ≃ M[1].

No single convention makes all four passages correct.
- Reversing the direction of [1] makes (1) and (3) correct. But it contradicts the Λ[−d] duality and the cone (lim_n M[f^n])[1] in the proof of Proposition 2.3.5.
- Reading "cone" as the fibre makes (4) correct. It also makes the last step on p. 16 agree with the printed line before it. But it contradicts the proof of Proposition 2.3.5, and it leaves (1) in degrees −1 and 0.
- On pp. 15–16, cone(…)[1] seems to be meant as the two-term complex in degrees 0 and 1. Read that way, the p. 18 formula gives M[−1].
- A homological grading is ruled out by the paper's cohomological notation.
- The j_! formula misquotes [CSb] under every convention.
Still, the intended meaning of each passage is clear. (1), (2) and (4) recall standard facts, and their wording says so ("We recall", "By definition ([CSb])", "the quasi-isomorphic"). (3) is the step that is to be matched with (1) to give Proposition 2.3.2. Every slip is in a shift: a [−1] is dropped in (2), and [1] stands in place of [−1] in (1) and (3) and in place of no shift in (4). So these are misprints.

Consequences: none. The p. 15 display is used only in the proof of Proposition 2.3.2, where the final display on p. 16 is matched against it. As printed, each side is its true value shifted by [2]. The printed values are cone(1 − Xf)[1] and cone(∏ → ∏)[1], and the true values are cone(1 − Xf)[−1] and cone(∏ → ∏)[−1]. So the printed comparison still gives the right identification j_!F ≅ lim_n F̄(−nD). With the corrected shifts the computation proves Proposition 2.3.2, and Remark 2.9.4 (p. 28) agrees with it. Later uses of Proposition 2.3.2 need only its statement, with lim the ordinary derived limit: Corollary 2.3.4 and Proposition 2.3.5 (p. 16), Corollary 2.3.11 (p. 17), and the proof of Proposition 2.7.2 (p. 23). The p. 18 sentence serves only to view M as an object of D((A[T],A)■) before Definition 2.4.2. The text says that the replacement is quasi-isomorphic to M, and the shift plays no role later. - **Misprint** at §2.3, Proposition 2.3.5, p. 16. The source says `Proposition 2.3.5. Assume that S = Spec A with A an artinian ring. Assume that 𝓕 is a coherent sheaf and assume that X̄ is proper. We let 𝓘 be the ideal of D. Then H^i(X, j_!𝓕) = lim_n H^i(X̄, 𝓘^n 𝓕).`; it should be `Then H^i(X̄, j_!𝓕) = lim_n H^i(X̄, 𝓘^n \overline{𝓕}), where \overline{𝓕} is a coherent extension of 𝓕 to X̄ (Remark 2.3.3). This is what the last line of the proof states.`. On the page image, the statement on p. 16 prints "H^i(X, j_!𝓕)": the X has no bar. The right-hand side is printed "lim_n H^i(X̄, 𝓘^n 𝓕)", also without a bar over 𝓕. So the reported quote is slightly off: it puts \overline{𝓕} on the right-hand side, but the statement prints plain 𝓕 there. The proof does use \overline{𝓕} in its last line.

The paper's own conventions in §2.3 settle the point. In §2.3.1 (p. 15), j : X → X̄ is the open immersion with X̄ \ X = D, 𝓕 lives on X, and \overline{𝓕} is a chosen object on X̄ with j^*\overline{𝓕} = 𝓕. Proposition 2.3.2 gives j_!𝓕 = lim_n \overline{𝓕}(−nD) as an object on X̄. So j_!𝓕 is a sheaf on X̄, and its cohomology is taken on X̄. Corollary 2.3.4 writes RΓ(X̄, j_!𝓕), and the proof of 2.3.5 ends "hence H^i(X̄, j_!𝓕) = lim_n H^i(X̄, 𝓘^n \overline{𝓕})" (image checked).

Read literally, H^i(X, j_!𝓕) would mean cohomology on the open X of j^*j_!𝓕 = 𝓕, which is H^i(X, 𝓕). That is not the intended group. Remark 2.3.6 identifies the right-hand side with Hartshorne's cohomology with compact support, which is not the ordinary cohomology of 𝓕 on the non-proper X. The X without a bar is therefore a genuine misprint, not an artefact of the text layer. The plain 𝓕 on the right-hand side is a second, smaller slip of the same kind.

The argument is sound once corrected. The cone of the map of inverse systems is controlled by the systems M[f^n], which stabilise, so lim \overline{𝓕}(−nD) → lim 𝓘^n\overline{𝓕} is a quasi-isomorphism. Since X̄ is proper over an artinian ring, the H^i(X̄, 𝓘^n\overline{𝓕}) are finite A-modules, so the system is Mittag-Leffler and the limit passes to cohomology. This proves the corrected statement.

Nothing later cites Proposition 2.3.5. Its label and Hartshorne's [Har72] occur only here and in the bibliography, so no later result or proof is affected. The source says `Corollary 2.3.14. Assume that we have maps p̄⋆₂𝒪_X̄(D₊) → p̄⋆₁𝒪_X̄(D₊) and p̄⋆₂𝒪_X̄(−D₋) → p̄⋆₁𝒪_X̄(−D₋). Proof. We have maps p̄⋆₂𝒪_X̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋) → p̄⋆₁𝒪_X̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋). Equivalently, both maps lie over the maps to O_C̄. Locally they are induced by the ideal inclusions p̄⋆₁I₊ ⊆ p̄⋆₂I₊ and p̄⋆₂I₋ ⊆ p̄⋆₁I₋. To pass to the colimit over k₊ and the limit over k₋, these maps must commute with the transition maps 𝓕̄(k₊D₊ − …) → 𝓕̄((k₊+1)D₊ − …), induced by s₊, and 𝓕̄(… − (k₋+1)D₋) → 𝓕̄(… − k₋D₋), induced by t₋. The hypothesis as printed ("Assume that we have maps") imposes nothing of the kind, and the one-line proof ("We simply twist …") does not address it.

A counterexample, checked by direct computation. Take S = Spec k with k a field. Let (C, X, p₁, p₂) = (𝔸¹, 𝔸¹, id, id), compactified by (ℙ¹, ℙ¹, id, id), with D₊ = {∞} and D₋ = ∅, where 𝒪(−D₋) = 𝒪 → 𝒪 is the identity. This is a dynamic compactification in the sense of Definition 2.1.26: the maps are proper, D₊ is expanded, D₋ is contracted, and X̄ \ X = D₊ ∪ D₋. Take 𝓕 = 𝒪_X, T = id, 𝓕̄ = 𝒪_ℙ¹ and n = 0. Then every map in the diagram of Proposition 2.2.10 is the identity. So T_𝒞 is the identity of RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, 𝓕) = colim_{k₊} H⁰(ℙ¹, 𝒪(k₊)) = k[x].

(a) Let α₊ = 0 and α₋ = id. The maps at every level k₊ ≥ 1 are zero, so they induce the zero map on k[x], not T_𝒞 = id.

(b) Let α₊ = λ·(canonical map) with λ ∈ k^×, λ ≠ 1. The level-k₊ map is λ^{k₊}·id on H⁰(ℙ¹, 𝒪(k₊)). Follow the section 1 ∈ H⁰(𝒪). Applying the level-0 map and then the transition gives 1; applying the transition and then the level-1 map gives λ. So the maps are not a morphism of direct systems and induce no map on the colimit.

In both cases the conclusion of the corollary fails, so the printed statement is false for arbitrary maps. It holds once the compatibility above is added. Restricted to C, compatible maps are the identity under the identification 𝒪(±D±)|_C = 𝒪_C, so the twisted maps restrict to T.

The intended maps are the natural ones: the proof speaks of "the" twisted maps, and Lemma 2.1.17(3) explicitly provides diagrams compatible with the maps to the ideals. The corollary is not cited by number elsewhere. The same twisting is carried out in the proofs of Lemma 2.5.3 and Proposition 2.5.4 with the canonical maps of Lemma 2.1.17, which satisfy the condition. So no later result is affected; only the corollary's statement needs the extra hypothesis. **Why the hypothesis is too weak.** To pass to lim over k₋ and colim over k₊, the level maps must form a map of systems. So they must commute with the transition maps F̄(aD₊ − bD₋) → F̄((a+1)D₊ − bD₋), which come from s₊, and F̄(aD₊ − (b+1)D₋) → F̄(aD₊ − bD₋), which come from t₋.

For the twisted maps this holds when α₊ ∘ p̄⋆₂s₊ = p̄⋆₁s₊ and p̄⋆₁t₋ ∘ α₋ = p̄⋆₂t₋. It fails in general, and the printed hypothesis asks nothing of the maps. That hypothesis is even vacuous, since the zero maps always exist.

**Why the charitable reading fails.** Under the paper's own conventions "maps" cannot silently mean "the canonical maps". By §2.1.14, O_X̄(−D) is a chosen invertible sheaf with a map to O_X̄, and it is not unique. Moreover, Lemma 2.1.17 says "canonical" explicitly where it means it; Corollary 2.3.14 has no such qualifier.

**Counterexample (checked by direct computation).** Take:
- S = X = X̄ = C = C̄ = Spec Z, with p₁ = p₂ = id;
- D₊ = D₋ = ∅, with O(−D±) = O → O the identity (allowed by §2.1.14);
- F = O and T = id, so n = 0;
- α₊ = −1 and α₋ = 1.

The twisted level map on RΓ(Spec Z, O) = Z is multiplication by (−1)^{k₊}, while all transition maps are the identity. So the level maps do not form a map of systems, and nothing is induced on the colimit. Yet T_C is the identity.

A non-degenerate version of the same example:
- X̄ = C̄ = P¹_Z and X = C = A¹_Z;
- D₊ = ∞ and D₋ = ∅;
- α₊ = −1.

On H⁰(P¹, O(k)) the level map is (−1)^k. The transition map is multiplication by the section vanishing at ∞, which is injective. The two paths around the square differ by 2ι(f) ≠ 0.

Taking α₊ = 0 also fails: the level maps vanish for k₊ ≥ 1 but not for k₊ = 0.

The proof ("We simply twist …") does not address any of this. With compatible maps, the remaining identification of the limit map with T_C through Corollary 2.3.11 and Lemma 2.2.7 is routine but also unwritten.

So M^ord is functorial in (M, T), and the cone of X − T realises this equivalence. With the standard cone, the displayed shift [1] should be dropped. 3. Lemma 2.4.4. The forgetful functor to D(A■) preserves limits and colimits, so the first line of the proof and part (1) then hold as printed. Parts (2) and (3) follow as written. 4. Applications. Each application must supply this coherence. In §2.5 it does. - The sheaves F(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋) and their transition maps form a diagram of coherent sheaves, so the diagram is canonically coherent. - The operators of Lemma 2.5.3 and Corollary 2.3.14 are one morphism p̄⋆₂F(−nD₋) → p̄!₁F(nD₊) in D(O_{C̄,■}), tensored with maps of invertible sheaves and composed with transition maps, followed by the adjunction unit and the trace. All of these are natural transformations. - With the colimit–limit of Corollary 2.3.11 taken in the ∞-category, the operators therefore form an endomorphism of the diagram. The same holds for the later uses (Theorem 2.7.4, p. 24; p. 53). One refinement to the proposed wording: the operators are not maps of sheaves, since p̄!₁F is a complex. They are a single morphism twisted by maps of invertible sheaves.`. The paper says it works in "a triangulated category of solid O_X-modules" (p. 12). Footnote 2 admits that turning an endomorphism into an A[T]-module is not canonical there. The following checks show exactly what survives in the triangulated setting and what does not.

(a) Objects survive. Let T be an endomorphism of M in D(A■). By adjunction, X − T : M ⊗_A A[X] → M ⊗_A A[X] is a well-defined morphism of D((A[X],A)■). So its cone is determined up to isomorphism, and so is M^ord ≅ cone(X − T on M ⊗_{A■} A[X^{±1}]■). Definition 2.4.2 therefore makes sense for objects, though not canonically or functorially.

(b) Invertibility statements survive. Let f : M → N commute with T in the homotopy category. Apply Hom(−, Ñ) to the triangle M ⊗ A[X] → M ⊗ A[X] → M̃. This shows that f lifts to a morphism M̃ → Ñ in D((A[T],A)■), but only up to morphisms that the forgetful functor kills. Every object Ñ of D((A[T],A)■) is the cone of T ⊗ 1 − 1 ⊗ T on N ⊗_A A[T]. So such a morphism factors through the connecting map, and by adjunction a composite of two of them is zero. Lifts are therefore unique modulo an ideal of square zero, and whether a lift becomes invertible on ordinary parts does not depend on the lift chosen. So this step of Lemma 2.4.4(2) and Proposition 2.5.4 (p. 20) holds even in the triangulated setting: T invertible on ordinary parts forces the horizontal maps, the vertical maps and T′ to be invertible.

(c) The colimit–limit step does not survive. The step that fails is "We have that M = colim_i lim_j M_{i,j} in D((A[T],A)■)" (proof of Lemma 2.4.4). In a triangulated category, colimits and limits of diagrams exist only up to non-unique isomorphism. Endomorphisms T_{i,j} that commute with the transition maps up to homotopy do not determine the induced endomorphism of the colimit–limit: for a sequential colimit it is unique only modulo lim¹ Hom(M_i[1], M). Nor do they give a diagram in D((A[T],A)■) whose colimit–limit is (M, T). The paper gives no such lift, and footnote 2 concerns only the non-uniqueness of the cone. Lemma 2.4.4(1) needs the lift, and (2) and (3) use (1). Through (1) the lift is needed by Proposition 2.5.4 and Theorem 2.5.1 (pp. 19–20; "canonically quasi-isomorphic" also needs it), by Theorem 2.7.4 (p. 24) and by p. 53.

The defence succeeds only in the ∞-categorical setting, which the cited source supplies. There:
- modules over the induced analytic ring (A[T],A)■ are A[T]-modules whose underlying A-module is A■-complete, since completeness is tested by adjunction against A■[S];
- modules over the free algebra A[T] are exactly objects with an endomorphism.
So the paper's lemma holds for coherent diagrams, and §2.5 produces coherent diagrams, as explained in the correction. No stated result changes. But the paper declares a triangulated framework, and in footnote 2 the authors say that an ∞-categorical treatment "might be desirable". So the step as printed is asserted without adequate proof: a genuine gap in the proofs.

Preprint. The text of January 2024, p. 17, has only "Let T be an operator acting on M so that we can view M as an object of D((A[T],A)■)", with no justification and no footnote. The gap is therefore already there. The revision added the cone construction and footnote 2, which flag the problem but do not resolve it. An object of D(A■), or of D((A[T],A)■), whose cohomology groups are all discrete is itself discrete: the natural map to it from the discrete complex of its underlying values is an isomorphism on every H^i. So C, with the action of T_C, is a discrete complex of A[T]-modules. The functor − ⊗_{(A[T],A)■} A[T,T^{-1}]■ preserves colimits and sends A[T] to A[T,T^{-1}]. Discrete complexes of A[T]-modules are generated from A[T] by colimits and shifts. So on discrete complexes this functor is the ordinary localization − ⊗^L_{A[T]} A[T,T^{-1}]. Case (2) of the proof of Lemma 2.4.3 uses the same fact. This localization is exact, so H^i(C^ord) = H^i(C) ⊗_{A[T]} A[T,T^{-1}]. Since H^i(C) has finite length and T acts A-linearly on it, this is the Fitting summand of H^i(C) on which T is bijective. It is a direct factor of H^i(C), and its complement is the summand on which T is nilpotent. Hence H^i(M^ord) ≅ H^i(C^ord) is a finite A-module. The step can also be proved with the paper's own lemmas. For a ≤ b, the truncation τ^{[a,b]}C is a bounded complex with finite cohomology on which T_C acts, so Lemma 2.4.3 applies to it. For a ≤ i ≤ b it gives H^i((τ^{[a,b]}C)^ord) = the T-bijective summand of H^i(C). D(A■) is left complete, because countable products of solid A-modules are exact. Filtered colimits are exact. The proof of Lemma 2.4.3 needs a bounded complex. It uses that the A-subalgebra B of End(M) generated by T is finite over A, so that B is a product of local algebras. Definition 2.4.5 puts no boundedness condition on C. The paper says "bounded" explicitly when it means it: in Lemma 2.4.3, Lemma 2.4.4(3) and Theorem 2.5.1(2). The paper's own use of the definition also allows unbounded C. In the proof of Proposition 2.10.3 (p. 30), the finite rank of T_C comes from factoring the map RΓ_{p̄₂^⋆D₋,p̄₂^⋆D₊}(C̄, p₂^⋆F) → RΓ_{p̄₁^⋆D₋,p̄₁^⋆D₊}(C̄, p₁^!F) through RΓ_{C̄∖(p̄₂^⋆D̊₋ ∪ p̄₁^⋆D̊₊)}(C̄∖p̄₁^⋆D̊₊, p₂^⋆F). There F ∈ D(O_{X,■}) is only assumed to have coherent cohomology groups, and Lemma 2.10.1(4) gives only finite cohomology groups. When F is unbounded, this complex is in general unbounded too.

For unbounded C the finiteness used in the proof of Lemma 2.4.3 fails, even within the hypotheses of Lemma 2.4.6. Under the convention of §2.2, schemes are of finite type over Z, so an artinian local A is a finite ring. Take A = k = F_p (any field works). Let C = ⊕_{n≥1} (k[x]/(x^n))[n], with T_C acting as multiplication by x on the n-th summand. Every H^i(C) is finite. Since T_C = T_C∘id, T_C is a finite-rank endomorphism of M = C. D(k) → D(k■) is fully faithful, and over a field Hom_{D(k)}(V[n], W[m]) = 0 for n ≠ m. Each summand is compact. Hence End(C) = ∏_n End_k(k[x]/(x^n)). A polynomial that kills T_C is divisible by x^n for every n, so it is zero. Thus B ≅ k[x], which is not finite over k, and the argument of Lemma 2.4.3 cannot start. Taking C = ⊕_{n≥1} (k[x]/(f_n))[n], with f_n pairwise distinct monic irreducible polynomials other than x, gives an example in which T_C is invertible.

The assertion made in the step is nevertheless true, by the argument in the correction. In the first example, H^i(C) ⊗_{A[T]} A[T,T^{-1}] = 0 for all i, so C^ord = 0. The earlier steps of the proof are sound for unbounded C as well. Write a : M → C and b : C → M, with b∘a = T_M and a∘b = T_C. On ordinary parts, a has the left inverse T_M^{-1}∘b and the right inverse b∘T_C^{-1}, so M^ord → C^ord is an isomorphism. So the step is asserted without adequate justification, but it is not false, and Lemma 2.4.6 holds as stated.

The gap is confined to this proof. No later proof cites Lemma 2.4.6 or Proposition 2.10.3. The finiteness of ordinary cohomology in Theorem 2.5.1(2) and Proposition 2.5.4 (pp. 19–20) comes from Lemma 2.4.4 applied to the bounded complexes RΓ(X̄, F̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋)). The sentence just before it reduces to the case D′+ ⊇ D+ and D′− ⊇ D−. That is exactly the case where the identity of (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2) is a map C′ → C in the sense of Definition 2.1.28 (p. 10). That definition requires D′+ ⊇ ξ⋆D+ and D′− ⊇ ξ⋆D−, and Theorem 2.5.1(3) is stated for such maps. The natural way to split this case into two steps is to pass through the intermediate pair (D′+, D−). The first step, (D+, D−) against (D′+, D−), is the printed first case: D′+ ⊇ D+ and D′− = D−. The second step, (D′+, D−) against (D′+, D′−), keeps D+ fixed and enlarges the minus-divisor. The printed text makes sense only if one silently swaps which compactification carries the primes in the second step. The next sentence keeps the original naming ("concentrate on the case D′+ ⊇ D+ and D′− = D−"), so no such swap is intended. The sign is therefore a slip. It is harmless. What is being proved is that two ordinary cohomologies are quasi-isomorphic, and that statement is symmetric in C and C′, so either inclusion gives the same case after renaming. The second case is also never written out ("the other is similar"). The argument that is written out uses only D′+ ⊇ D+ with D′− = D−: it uses D′+ ≤ aD+ + bD− and the chain of maps with k+ ≥ m and k− ≥ m + bk+. That argument is unaffected. The printed text on pp. 22–23 was checked against the rendered pages. In [CSb], Prop. 11.4 (Scholze, Lectures on condensed mathematics, Lecture XI) proves two things: that f^! ≅ f^!R ⊗^L f^* when f has finite Tor-dimension, and that g′^*f^! ≅ f′^!g^* when the base change g is flat. On p. 25 the paper itself cites this proposition as "flat base change", in a setting where p₁ and p₂ are assumed flat.

In §2.6.12 neither hypothesis is available. The relevant base change is along X′ → X, the pullback of the finite map S′ → S, which is not flat in general; in the application on p. 51 it is Spec Z/p^s → Spec Z/p^{s+1}. Nor is p₁ assumed to have finite Tor-dimension. Here C′ = C ×_X X′. Since O_{X′} = O_X ⊗^L_A A′, one gets O_C ⊗^L_{O_X} O_{X′} = O_C ⊗^L_A A′. So the square C′/C over X′/X is tor-independent exactly when C and S′ are tor-independent, and the hypothesis on X alone does not imply this.

Counterexample to the identification, under all the stated hypotheses:
- Take A = F_p[x], A′ = A/(x²), X = S = Spec A, C = Spec A/(x), and p₁ = p₂ the closed immersion.
- This is a correspondence with the strict dynamic compactification X̄ = X, C̄ = C, D₊ = D₋ = ∅.
- X and S′ are tor-independent, and 𝓕 = O_X is A-flat. Also C′ = Spec F_p = C.
- p₁^!O_X = RHom_A(A/x, A) = F_p[−1] by the Koszul complex, so g_C^*p₁^!O_X = F_p[−1].
- (p′₁)^!O_{X′} = RHom_{A′}(F_p, A′) = xA′ ≅ F_p in degree 0, since A′ = F_p[x]/(x²) is self-injective.
- Checked by direct computation: these differ, and every map F_p[−1] → F_p is zero. So no base-change isomorphism g_C^*p₁^!𝓕 ≅ (p′₁)^!𝓕′ exists under the stated hypotheses.

The proof of Proposition 2.6.13 only identifies the two complexes. It then "applies ordinary projectors" without checking that T ⊗ 1 corresponds to T′, which depends on how T′ is defined.

Limits of this finding:
- In the example T = 0 (Hom(O_C, O_C[−1]) = 0), so the example refutes the construction, not the formula.
- When p₁ is finite, T factors through H⁰, and a compatible T′ can still be defined from the map p₁*p₂^*𝓕 → 𝓕.
- In the uses on p. 51 and p. 54 the correspondences have finite flat projections and are flat over the base (Prop. 3.4.9), so the corrected hypotheses hold there.

What remains is a gap in Proposition 2.6.13 at the generality stated. No downstream result fails. To construct T′ one needs a map g′⋆p₁^!𝓕 → (p′₁)^!g⋆𝓕 for the cartesian square C′ = C ×_X X′ over g : X′ → X. The cited [CSb], Prop. 11.4 (Scholze, Lectures on condensed mathematics, Lecture XI) proves g′⋆f^! ≃ f′^! g⋆ only when g is flat and f has finite Tor-dimension. There the map is built from f^! g⋆ ≃ g′⋆ f′^!, which is adjoint to proper base change, and [CSb] notes (in the footnote to its proper base change statement) that in the coherent setting a square that is not Tor-independent needs derived schemes. Here g is the base change of the finite map S′ → S, which is in general not flat; in the applications S′ → S is Spec Z/p^{s−1} → Spec Z/p^s. Under the stated hypothesis O_{X′} = O_X ⊗^L_A A′, so O_C ⊗^L_{O_X} O_{X′} = O_C ⊗^L_A A′. The relevant square is therefore Tor-independent exactly when C and S′ are Tor-independent over S, and the Tor-independence of X and S′ does not give this. In the analogous place, Lemma 2.2.2(2) on p. 12, the paper does record the needed condition: "note that C̄ and X are tor-independent".

Example (checked by direct computation). Take A = F_p[x], A′ = A/(x²), X = S, C = Spec A/(x), and p₁ = p₂ the closed immersion. Then (C, X, ∅, ∅) is a strict dynamic compactification, X and S′ are Tor-independent, 𝓕 = O_X is A-flat, and C′ = Spec F_p. Now p₁^!O_X = RHom_A(A/(x), A) = F_p[−1], and its pullback to C′ is F_p[−1]. But (p′₁)^!O_{X′} = RHom_{A′}(F_p, A′) = xA′ ≅ F_p in degree 0, because A′ is self-injective. So the base-change identification the text relies on fails under the stated hypotheses; indeed Tor₁^A(A/(x), A′) ≅ F_p ≠ 0. In this example Hom(O_C, O_C[−1]) = 0, so T = 0 and the formula holds trivially. The example shows that the construction of T′ is unjustified, not that the displayed formula is false.

The stupid truncation is not an operation on the derived category: it depends on the complex K chosen to represent p̄^!O_S, and the proof never specifies that complex. The final sentence is about σ≤m(K|_X), because (p^!O_S)_{σ≤m} is what Proposition 2.3.2 produces from j⋆((p̄^!O_S)_{σ≤m}). Smoothness of p only says that K|_X has cohomology in the single degree −d.

Take m > −d. Then K|_X is exact in degree m, so H^m(σ≤m K|_X) = K^m/d(K^{m−1}) = K^m/ker d^m ≅ d^m(K^m). Hence σ≤m(K|_X) ≃ p^!O_S holds if and only if d^m vanishes on X. For example, this fails for any representative whose restriction to X is a complex of injectives that is unbounded above. Nothing in the proof arranges d^m|_X = 0, and "since p is smooth" does not give it.

The truncation is used exactly when p̄^!O_S is unbounded above; otherwise a bounded representative makes σ≤m harmless. That case does occur under the hypotheses of Proposition 2.7.2, which allow any A and do not require X̄ to be flat over S. Checked by direct computation:
- Take A = F_p[x,y]/(x,y)^2, which is not Gorenstein, and m_A its maximal ideal.
- Replace the chart A[t] of P^1_A by Spec B, with B = A[t] + m_A t^{-1} ⊂ A[t, t^{-1}]. The result X̄ is finite over P^1_A, hence proper.
- X = X̄ \ V(t) ≅ A^1_A is smooth over S, and V(t) is Cartier because t is a non-zero-divisor on B.
- B contains m_A t^{-1} ≅ k^2 as an A-module summand. So Tor_i^A(B, E) ≠ 0 for all i, where E is the injective hull of k: indeed Tor_i^A(k, E) ≅ Hom(Ext^i_A(k, A), E) and A has infinite injective dimension.
- Hence p̄^!O_S = RHom(Lp̄^*E, p̄^!E) is unbounded above.
So the step can fail precisely in the case the truncation was introduced for.

The first three equalities in the display are fine: K = lim_m σ≤m K, since the system is termwise surjective and termwise eventually constant. The repair above yields the stated isomorphism D_X̄(j⋆F) = j_! D_X(F).

Theorem 2.7.4 (p. 24) uses Proposition 2.7.2, and Theorem 5.5.1 (p. 57) uses Theorem 2.7.4. Because the statement of Proposition 2.7.2 remains true, only the proof is affected. This was checked on the page image of p. 23.

The defence fails for the following reasons.

1. A stupid truncation is not an operation on the derived category. It depends on the complex K chosen to represent p̄^!O_S, and the proof never names one.

2. For Proposition 2.3.2 to give the printed equality, one needs j⋆(F̄^∨ ⊗ σ≤m K) = F^∨ ⊗ σ≤m(K|_X). So the object written (p^!O_S)_{σ≤m} must be σ≤m(K|_X), the stupid truncation of the restricted complex, not a truncation of the one-term complex Ω^d_{X/S}[d]. Smoothness of p says only that K|_X has cohomology in the single degree −d.

3. For m ≥ 0, exactness of K|_X at m gives H^m(σ≤m(K|_X)) = K^m/d(K^{m−1}) = K^m/ker d^m ≅ d^m(K^m) on X. So σ≤m(K|_X) ≃ p^!O_S exactly when d^m vanishes on X. This holds for all large m exactly when the terms K^i vanish on X for all large i. Nothing in the proof arranges this.

4. The claim fails for some legitimate representatives. Take any coherent sheaf Ḡ with G = Ḡ|_X ≠ 0. Adding to K the acyclic complex ⊕_{m≥0}(Ḡ →id Ḡ), placed in degrees m and m+1, gives another bounded below complex of coherent sheaves representing p̄^!O_S. For it, σ≤m(K|_X) ≃ p^!O_S ⊕ G[−m] for every m ≥ 0.

5. Choosing a bounded representative rescues the sentence only when p̄^!O_S is bounded, and then the truncation is superfluous. The truncation matters exactly when p̄^!O_S is unbounded above. That case does occur under the hypotheses of Proposition 2.7.2, which allow any A and do not require X̄ to be flat over S. The following example was checked by direct computation.
- Let A = F_p[x,y]/(x,y)^2, which is not Gorenstein.
- Let X̄ be P^1_A with the chart Spec A[t] replaced by Spec B, where B = A[t] + m_A t^{−1} ⊂ A[t,t^{−1}].
- X̄ is finite over P^1_A, hence proper. D = V(t) is Cartier, because t is a non-zero-divisor on B. X = X̄ \ D ≅ A^1_A is smooth. F = O_X extends to O_X̄.
- The A-module B has m_A t^{−1} ≅ k^2 as a direct summand. Let E be the injective hull of k. Then Hom(Tor_i^A(k,E), E) ≅ Ext^i_A(k,A), so Tor_i^A(B,E) ≠ 0 for infinitely many i.
- Hence p̄^!O_S = RHom(Lp̄^⋆E, p̄^!E) is the dual, with respect to the dualizing complex p̄^!E, of a complex that is unbounded below. So it is unbounded above.
There, every representative has infinitely many nonzero terms. The printed step would need one whose high-degree terms are supported on D. The proof neither chooses such a representative nor shows that one exists.

The rest of the argument is sound.
- K = lim_m σ≤m K, since the system is termwise surjective and termwise eventually constant.
- σ≤m K is a bounded complex of coherent sheaves, so Proposition 2.3.2 applies.
- The limit argument in the correction closes the gap for every representative. So the statement of Proposition 2.7.2 is true as printed.

Consequences. Proposition 2.7.2 is used in the proof of Theorem 2.7.4 (p. 24). Theorem 2.7.4 is used in the proof of Theorem 5.5.1 (p. 57; stated in the introduction as Theorem 1.4.8). These results are unaffected because the statement of Proposition 2.7.2 stands. In addition, the artinian coefficient rings relevant to Theorem 5.5.1 are quotients of Z_p[ζ_{p^n}] by powers of p. These are Gorenstein, so there p̄^!O_S is a dualizing complex, hence bounded, and the printed argument works with a bounded representative.
