The second diagram is the periodic zig-zag of the maps (p_2^{(n+1)})^⋆ : RΓ′_n → RΓ′_{n+1} and (p_1^{(n+1)})_! : RΓ′_{n+1} → RΓ′_n, as the sentence on p. 26 describes.

(1) Every other vertex of this diagram is some RΓ′_k. The last down-arrow has the same label (p_1)_! as the other labelled down-arrow, RΓ′_1 → RΓ′_0, and the diagram repeats with period two, so its target is also RΓ′_0. The unprimed RΓ_0 is something else. Since C^{(0)} = X and C^{(1)} = C (p. 24), RΓ_0 = RΓ(X, O_X)^{C−ord}, the ordinary part. It belongs to the first diagram, in the statement of the proposition, whose bottom row RΓ_0, RΓ_0, RΓ_0 is correctly printed. So the printed RΓ_0 is a dropped prime.

(2) On p. 25 the paper defines T_n : (p_2^{(n)})^⋆O_{C^{(n−1)}} → (p_1^{(n)})^!O_{C^{(n−1)}}. This is a cohomological correspondence for (C^{(n)}, C^{(n−1)}, p_1^{(n)}, p_2^{(n)}). It acts on the cohomology of C^{(n−1)}, that is on RΓ′_{n−1}, by pulling back along p_2^{(n)} and tracing down along p_1^{(n)}. The operator in the sentence starts at RΓ′_n, goes up to RΓ′_{n+1} along (p_2^{(n+1)})^⋆ and comes back along (p_1^{(n+1)})_!. It comes from the correspondence C^{(n+1)} over C^{(n)}, so it is the operator of T_{n+1}. It is also the operator that defines RΓ_n = RΓ(C^{(n)}, O_{C^{(n)}})^{C^{(n+1)}−ord} on p. 25 via Theorem 2.5.1. The paper's later text agrees. On p. 26 comes the square introduced by "By construction, the following square commutes". In its top row, the first arrow (p_1^{(n+1)})_!(p_2^{(n+1)})^⋆O_{C^{(n)}} → (p_1^{(n+1)})_!(p_1^{(n+1)})^!O_{C^{(n)}} is labelled T_{n+1}. The arrow labelled T_n in its bottom row is induced by T_n : (p_2^{(n)})^⋆O_{C^{(n−1)}} → (p_1^{(n)})^!O_{C^{(n−1)}}, as in the definition. The final diagram on p. 27 computes the endomorphism of RΓ′_n through (p_1^{(n+1)})_!(p_2^{(n+1)})^⋆O_{C^{(n)}}. So "T_n" is an off-by-one index slip, not a different convention.

Neither slip affects the argument. The proof shows that the square (2.8.A) commutes, using the proper base change identity (p_1^{(n+1)})_!(p_2^{(n+1)})^⋆ = (p_2^{(n)})^⋆(p_1^{(n)})_!. By (2.8.A), for n ≥ 1 the two composites RΓ′_n → RΓ′_{n+1} → RΓ′_n and RΓ′_n → RΓ′_{n−1} → RΓ′_n both equal the operator of T_{n+1}, which is invertible on the ordinary part RΓ_n. That is what "if we can prove the commutativity, we conclude" relies on. With the vertex read as RΓ′_0 and the index as n+1, the argument reads as intended. The statement of Proposition 2.8.2 is correctly printed. Its only later citation is on p. 54: there the maps in a diagram of the cohomologies RΓ_w(K_{i,j}) are quasi-isomorphisms "by proposition 2.8.2". That use relies on the statement alone. - **Error** at §2.9.8 and Proposition 2.9.9 with its proof, pp. 28–29 (see also Definition 2.1.8, p. 7, and §2.9.5, p. 28). The 2024 preprint has the same text, with §2.9.8, Proposition 2.9.9 and its proof all on p. 27 there. (it affects a stated result). The source says `p. 28: "2.9.8. Action of a correspondence on the spectral sequence. Let (C, X, p_1, p_2) be a correspondence. Let T : p_2^⋆𝓕 → p_1^!𝓕 be a cohomological correspondence. Let Z_{−1} = ∅ ⊆ Z_0 ⊆ Z_1 ⊆ Z_2 ⊆ ··· ⊆ X = Z_d be a filtration by closed subschemes on X. Proposition 2.9.9. Assume that p_1^⋆(Z_l) ⊆ p_2^⋆(Z_l) for all 0 ≤ l ≤ d (set theoretically). Then we have an action of T on RΓ(Ẑ_l, 𝓕), RΓ_c(U_l, 𝓕)and RΓ_c(Ẑ_l \ Ẑ_{l−1}, 𝓕) for all i, compatible with the natural morphisms. The spectral sequence of theorem 2.9.7 is T-equivariant." p. 29: "Proof. We need to explain how we can attach to T a map of triangles:" [a diagram from p_2^⋆(j_l)_!j_l^⋆𝓕 → p_2^⋆𝓕 → p_2^⋆(î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆𝓕 → to p_1^!(j_l)_!j_l^⋆𝓕 → p_1^!𝓕 → (p_1)^!(î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆𝓕 →, with middle vertical arrow T]. The proof then builds the left vertical arrow and ends: "... this map is just given by the co-unit of the adjunction (p′_1)_!(p′_1)^! → Id." Definition 2.1.8 (p. 7): "A correspondence is a quadruple (C, X, p_1, p_2), where X and C are separated, finite type schemes over S, coming with two projections p_1, p_2 : C ⇒ X and such that p_1 × p_2 : C → X × X is a proper map." §2.9.5 (p. 28): "We now let X be a scheme ..."`; it should be `Add to §2.9.8 (or to Proposition 2.9.9) the hypothesis that p_1 is proper, as Definition 2.1.24(1) (p. 9) requires for dynamic correspondences. For example, this holds when X is proper over S. Then the first projection pr_1 : X ×_S X → X is proper, and so is p_1 = pr_1 ∘ (p_1 × p_2). In particular it holds for a compactification (C̄, X̄, p̄_1, p̄_2) (Remark 2.1.10). With this hypothesis, let G be (j_l)_!j_l^⋆𝓕, 𝓕 or (î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆𝓕. The action of T on RΓ(X, G) is the composite RΓ(X, G) → RΓ(C, p_2^⋆G) → RΓ(C, p_1^!G) = RΓ(X, (p_1)_!p_1^!G) → RΓ(X, G). - The first arrow is pullback along p_2. - The middle arrow is the matching vertical arrow of the map of triangles built in the proof. - The equality uses (p_1)_⋆ = (p_1)_!, which holds because p_1 is proper. The last arrow comes from the counit (p_1)_!p_1^! → Id. It is the trace map of Lemma 2.2.7 (p. 13) with D_+ = D_− = ∅. The three middle arrows form a map of triangles, and the outer arrows are natural. So the three endomorphisms are compatible with the triangle RΓ_c(U_l, 𝓕) → RΓ(X, 𝓕) → RΓ(Ẑ_l, 𝓕) →. The action on RΓ_c(Ẑ_l \ Ẑ_{l−1}, 𝓕) then comes from the triangles of Lemma 2.9.6, as the paper intends.`. Proposition 2.9.9 is stated for any correspondence (C, X, p_1, p_2) in the sense of Definition 2.1.8, and §2.9 puts no properness condition on X (§2.9.5: "We now let X be a scheme"). Definition 2.1.8 asks only that p_1 × p_2 be proper. That does not make p_1 proper.

By §2.9.5 and Lemma 2.9.6 (p. 28), each complex in the proposition has the form RΓ(X, G) for a complex G on X:
- RΓ(Ẑ_l, 𝓕) = RΓ(X, (î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆𝓕);
- RΓ_c(U_l, 𝓕) = RΓ(X, (j_l)_!j_l^⋆𝓕), implicit in the triangle RΓ_c(U_l, 𝓕) → RΓ(X, 𝓕) → RΓ(Ẑ_l, 𝓕) → of §2.9.5;
- RΓ_c(Ẑ_l \ Ẑ_{l−1}, 𝓕) = RΓ(X, (î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆(j_{l−1})_!(j_{l−1})^⋆𝓕).

The proof builds only a map of triangles on C. It goes from p_2^⋆ of the triangle (j_l)_!j_l^⋆𝓕 → 𝓕 → (î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆𝓕 → to p_1^! of the same triangle. Apart from some notational slips, this part is correct and needs no properness: it uses only the adjunction between (p_1)_! and p_1^! and the counit for p′_1.

Turning this into an endomorphism of RΓ(X, G) takes two further steps. The first is to pull back along p_2, which is always possible. The second needs a map RΓ(C, p_1^!G) = RΓ(X, (p_1)_⋆p_1^!G) → RΓ(X, G), and the proof does not supply one. The formalism provides only the counit (p_1)_!p_1^! → Id. That counit gives the required map when (p_1)_⋆ = (p_1)_!, which holds when p_1 is proper.

Elsewhere in §2 the paper imposes exactly this condition. Lemma 2.2.7 (p. 13) says "If p̄ is proper, we also have canonical trace maps". The action of T on cohomology is otherwise built from a dynamic correspondence (Proposition 2.2.10, p. 14; Proposition 2.10.3, p. 30). Definition 2.1.24(1) (p. 9) requires of a dynamic correspondence that "p̄_1 and p̄_2 are proper maps". The support hypothesis of Proposition 2.9.9 says that each Z_l is contracted in the sense of Definition 2.1.19(4) (p. 9), as D_− is in a dynamic correspondence. But §2.9.8 does not carry over the properness of p_1.

Without this hypothesis the missing step fails. Here is an example.
- Setup: S = Spec k for a field k, X = C = A¹_k with coordinate t, p_2 = id, and p_1 the constant map with value 0. Then p_1 × p_2 is the closed immersion x ↦ (0, x), so (C, X, p_1, p_2) is a correspondence, but p_1 is not proper.
- The claim: take 𝓕 = O_X, d = 0 and Z_0 = X. The support hypothesis holds trivially and Ẑ_0 = X, so the proposition claims an action of T on RΓ(X, O_X) = k[t].
- T can be nonzero: write p_1 = i ∘ q, with q : A¹_k → Spec k and i the inclusion of the origin. Then i^!O_X = k[−1] and q^!k = Ω¹[1], so p_1^!O_X ≅ Ω¹_C. Hence T = dt : O_C = p_2^⋆O_X → Ω¹_C = p_1^!O_X is a nonzero cohomological correspondence.
- There is no nonzero trace: (p_1)_⋆p_1^!O_X = i_⋆V with V = k[t]dt in degree 0, and Hom(i_⋆V, O_X) = Hom(V, i^!O_X) = Hom(V, k[−1]) = 0. So every map (p_1)_⋆p_1^!O_X → O_X is zero. For every T, completing the construction of the proof with such a map gives only the zero endomorphism of k[t].

Read literally, the zero endomorphism is "an action" compatible with all the natural maps, so the wording of the proposition is not strictly contradicted. But in this generality T induces no nonzero action in this way. A genuine action induced by T is what the proposition is meant to provide and what §4.5.6 uses. So Proposition 2.9.9 needs the extra hypothesis that p_1 is proper.

Proposition 2.9.9 is used once, in §4.5.6 (p. 52): "We have an action of t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p) on the spectral sequence by proposition 2.9.9 and corollary 4.2.10." There X = S^tor, which is proper over Z_p. By §4.2.1 (p. 43), C_t^tor is the normalization of S^tor × S^tor in C^tor_{t,Q_p}, so it is finite over S^tor × S^tor. Hence p_1 is proper and the argument works. Theorem 4.5.2 and Corollaries 4.5.4 and 4.5.5 are unaffected. - **Gap** at §2.10, Lemma 2.10.1(3) and its proof, p. 29; applied in Lemma 2.10.2 (pp. 29–30) and Proposition 2.10.3 (p. 30) (it affects the proof). F)", and î : Ẑ → Y is "the closed subset of the locale".`; it should be `In (3), the inclusion U ⊆ Z has to hold scheme-theoretically: j_U must factor through i. Equivalently, the ideal of Z must vanish on U, so that Z ∩ U = U as open subschemes. Then j_U^⋆ i_⋆ i^! F = F|_U. The first arrow is the map adjoint to the identity of F|_U, and the three maps compose to the change-of-support map (j_U)_! j_U^⋆ F → (j_{U′})_! j_{U′}^⋆ F. In Lemma 2.10.2, the closed set X̄ ∖ (D′_+° ∪ D_−°) inside Y = X̄ ∖ D′_+° must be given a closed-subscheme structure that contains U = Y ∖ D_− scheme-theoretically. The same applies to C̄ ∖ (p̄_2^⋆D_−° ∪ p̄_1^⋆D_+°) in Proposition 2.10.3. Either of two choices works: - V(J^n) for any ideal J defining the set and n large. J|_U lies in the nilradical of the noetherian, quasi-compact scheme U, so J^n|_U = 0. - The scheme-theoretic union of the reduced structure with the scheme-theoretic closure of U. The underlying set does not change, so the set stays proper and Lemma 2.10.1(4) still gives finiteness in Proposition 2.10.3. On p. 29, in Lemma 2.10.2, the middle term is printed without a hat: RΓ_{X̄\(D′_+° ∪ D_−°)}(X̄ \ D′_+°, F).

Where the proof fails: by Definition 2.1.15(1) (p. 8), "D ⊆ D′" means that D is a subset of D′. In Lemma 2.10.2 the set Z = X̄ \ (D′_+° ∪ D_−°) is the complement of interiors, a purely topological set. It is given no scheme structure, and U = (X̄ \ D′_+°) \ D_− is contained in it only as a set. The "standard adjunction" gives Hom((j_U)_! j_U^⋆F, i_⋆ i^!F) = Hom(F|_U, (i_U)_⋆ (i_U)^! F|_U), where i_U : Z ∩ U → U. When i_U is a proper nilpotent thickening, this has no canonical map compatible with the counit to F.

Counterexample, checked by direct computation: A = k[ε]/(ε²) with k = F_p (A = Z/p² works the same way), Y = Spec A, Z = V(ε), U = U′ = Y. Then U ⊆ Z ⊆ U′ as sets. RΓ(Y, (j_U)_! j_U^⋆ O) = A has length 2. A is self-injective, so RΓ_Z(Y, O) = RHom_A(k, A) = εA ≅ k in degree 0, of length 1. Also RΓ_Ẑ(Y, O) = A, since Y \ Z = ∅. The map RΓ_Z → RΓ_Ẑ of (1) is the inclusion εA ⊆ A. For the factorization in Proposition 2.10.3 the composite must be the change-of-support map, here the identity of A. The identity of a module of length 2 cannot factor through a module of length 1. The literal statement (3) survives only through trivial "natural maps" such as zero, which are useless for Lemma 2.10.2 and Proposition 2.10.3.

The non-reduced case is in scope. §2 allows any scheme of finite type over Z and artinian bases (Proposition 2.3.5, Lemma 2.4.6 on finite rank over an artinian local ring, Theorem 2.6.8), and §6 works over Z/p^s.

The scheme-theoretic RΓ_Z cannot simply be swapped for RΓ_Ẑ in Proposition 2.10.3. Finiteness (4) is stated for RΓ_Z, and RΓ_Ẑ need not be finite: for Y = A^1_k and Ẑ = {0}, H^1 = k[x, x^{-1}]/k[x]. So the thickening is needed.

The corrected map is right: when Z ∩ U = U, j_U^⋆ i_⋆ i^! F = F|_U. A reduced Y needs no change, because a nil ideal on reduced U is zero.

Downstream: Proposition 2.10.3 is not cited anywhere else. Proposition 2.10.4 (p. 31) and Theorem 6.2.9 (p. 62, which writes RΓ_Ẑ explicitly) need only the maps, and these exist through RΓ_Ẑ with set-theoretic containment. All stated results remain true once the scheme structure is chosen as above.

This is a gap rather than an error: the lemma asserts only "natural maps", and the defect is an unstated scheme-theoretic hypothesis plus an unspecified choice of scheme structure where the lemma is applied. Attempted defences.

(a) Read "U ⊆ Z" scheme-theoretically, as saying that the open U is a subscheme of Z. Then (3) is correct as stated. But this is not the paper's convention: Definition 2.1.15(1) (p. 8) reads "We write D ⊆ D′ when D is a subset of D′". More importantly, the lemma is applied in Lemma 2.10.2 to Z = X̄ ∖ (D′_+° ∪ D_−°), which is defined only as a set and given no scheme structure. There U = (X̄ ∖ D′_+°) ∖ D_− lies inside Z only as a set. The middle term in Lemma 2.10.2 carries no hat, so it is the scheme-theoretic RΓ_Z. On p. 27 the authors note that a closed subset becomes a subscheme only "for the choice of some ideal J". Here the choice matters and is never made. The only canonical choice, the reduced structure, fails whenever X̄ is non-reduced along U.

(b) Route everything through the locale. With set-theoretic containment the maps RΓ(Y, (j_U)_! j_U^⋆F) → RΓ_Ẑ(Y, F) → RΓ(Y, (j_{U′})_! j_{U′}^⋆F) do exist and compose correctly. By the triangle î_⋆î^!F → F → j_⋆j^⋆F on p. 27, j_U^⋆ î_⋆ î^! F = j_U^⋆F whenever U does not meet Y ∖ Z. This does not rescue Proposition 2.10.3, which needs a middle term with finite cohomology. Lemma 2.10.1(4) supplies that only for the scheme-theoretic RΓ_Z. RΓ_Ẑ is not finite in general: for Y = P^1_k and Z = {0}, H^1 = k[y]/k.

Why the first arrow fails. Adjunction gives Hom((j_U)_! j_U^⋆F, i_⋆i^!F) = Hom(F|_U, (i_U)_⋆ i_U^! F|_U), where i_U : Z ∩ U → U. When i_U is a proper nilpotent thickening, this has no canonical element compatible with the counit to F.

Counterexample (checked by direct computation). Take A = k[ε]/(ε²), Y = Spec A, Z = V(ε) = Spec k and U = U′ = Y, so that U ⊆ Z ⊆ U′ as sets.
- RΓ(Y, (j_U)_! j_U^⋆ O_Y) = A, of length 2.
- The resolution … → A → A → A → k, with every map multiplication by ε, gives RΓ_Z(Y, O_Y) = RHom_A(k, A) = εA ≅ k in degree 0, of length 1.
- RΓ_Ẑ(Y, O_Y) = A because Y ∖ Z = ∅, and the map of (1) is the inclusion εA ⊂ A.
- The change-of-support map is the identity of A, which cannot factor through a module of length 1.
Natural maps A → εA do exist, such as multiplication by ε, but their composite is multiplication by ε, not the identity. More generally, taking F = O_Y shows that a factorization compatible with the counit forces the ideal of Z to vanish on U.

Non-reduced schemes are within the scope of §2 (finite type over Z, artinian bases in Lemma 2.4.6 and Theorem 2.5.1(2)), and §6 works over Z/p^s.

Consequences.
- Lemma 2.10.2 builds both lines by "applying lemma 2.10.1" twice.
- Proposition 2.10.3 uses "By lemma 2.10.2 … the following factorization". A factorization requires the composite to equal the original map, and finiteness then comes from 2.10.1(4) for the scheme-theoretic RΓ_Z.
- Proposition 2.10.4(5) uses "By lemma 2.10.2, we have a commutative diagram" whose horizontal arrows are change-of-support maps.
- Theorem 6.2.9 (p. 62) cites Lemma 2.10.1 but factors only through RΓ_Ẑ, so it is covered by (b).
- Theorem 2.11.4 (p. 33) uses an RΓ_c middle term, not this lemma.
- Proposition 2.10.3 and Lemma 2.4.6 are not cited later.

With the scheme structure chosen as in the correction, every stated result survives. The defect is an unstated hypothesis, together with a missing choice where the lemma is applied. - **Misprint** at §2.9, proof of Proposition 2.9.9, p. 29. The January 2024 preprint has the same text with the same slips (p. 27).. The source says `"We have that p_2^⋆(U_l) ⊆ p_1^⋆(U_l). Let us write C_{U_l,1} = p_1^⋆(U_l) and C_{U_l,2} = p_2^⋆(U_l). Let j_{C_{U_l,k}} : C_{U_l,k} ↪ X be the open immersions for k = 1, 2. We have a chain of maps: (j_{C_{U_l,2}})_! j^⋆_{C_{U_l,2}} p_2^⋆𝓕 → (j_{C_{U_l,2}})_! j^⋆_{C_{U_l,2}} p_1^!𝓕 → (j_{C_{U_l,1}})_! j^⋆_{C_{U_l,1}} p_1^!𝓕. We observe that thanks to the base change theorem we have: (j_{C_{U_l,2}})_! j^⋆_{C_{U_l,2}} p_2^⋆𝓕 = p_2^⋆(j_l)_! j_l^⋆𝓕. On the other hand, we claim that we have a map (j_{C_{U_l,1}})_! j^⋆_{C_{U_l,1}} p_1^!𝓕 → (p_1)^!(j_l)_⋆(j_l)^⋆𝓕. By adjunction this map is equivalent to a map (p_1)_!(j_{C_{U_l,1}})_! j^⋆_{C_{U_l,1}} p_1^!𝓕 → (j_l)_⋆(j_l)^⋆𝓕. Since (p_1)_!(j_{C_{U_l,1}})_! j^⋆_{C_{U_l,1}} p_1^!𝓕 = (j_l)_!(p'_1)_!(p'_1)^!(j_l)^!𝓕 for p'_1 : C_{U_l,1} → U_l, this map is just given by the co-unit of the adjunction (p'_1)_!(p'_1)^! → Id."`; it should be `Read "Let j_{C_{U_l,k}} : C_{U_l,k} ↪ C be the open immersions for k = 1, 2." In the sentences beginning "On the other hand" and "By adjunction", replace (j_l)_⋆ by (j_l)_! (once in each). The claimed map is then (j_{C_{U_l,1}})_! j^⋆_{C_{U_l,1}} p_1^!𝓕 → (p_1)^!(j_l)_!(j_l)^⋆𝓕. By adjunction it is equivalent to a map (p_1)_!(j_{C_{U_l,1}})_! j^⋆_{C_{U_l,1}} p_1^!𝓕 → (j_l)_!(j_l)^⋆𝓕.`. Target of the immersions. In §2.9.8 (p. 28), (C, X, p_1, p_2) is a correspondence, so p_1, p_2 : C → X (Definition 2.1.8, p. 7), and T : p_2^⋆𝓕 → p_1^!𝓕. So C_{U_l,k} = p_k^⋆(U_l) = p_k^{−1}(U_l) is an open subscheme of C, not of X. Every later use of j_{C_{U_l,k}} needs target C:
- the functors (j_{C_{U_l,k}})_! j^⋆_{C_{U_l,k}} are applied to p_2^⋆𝓕 and p_1^!𝓕, which are objects on C;
- the base change identity (j_{C_{U_l,2}})_! j^⋆_{C_{U_l,2}} p_2^⋆𝓕 = p_2^⋆(j_l)_! j_l^⋆𝓕 compares objects on C;
- the composite (p_1)_!(j_{C_{U_l,1}})_! only makes sense when j_{C_{U_l,1}} maps into C.
So the printed "↪ X" is a slip.

(j_l)_⋆ versus (j_l)_!. The proof has to supply the left vertical arrow in the map of triangles displayed at the top of p. 29. That arrow is p_2^⋆(j_l)_! j_l^⋆𝓕 → p_1^!(j_l)_! j_l^⋆𝓕, with (j_l)_! in both the source and the target: the bottom row is p_1^! applied to the triangle (j_l)_! j_l^⋆𝓕 → 𝓕 → (î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆𝓕. Base change identifies the start of the displayed chain with the source of this arrow. So the chain has to be completed by a map (j_{C_{U_l,1}})_! j^⋆_{C_{U_l,1}} p_1^!𝓕 → p_1^!(j_l)_! j_l^⋆𝓕.

The argument in the proof produces exactly this map. Since C_{U_l,1} = p_1^{−1}(U_l), we have p_1 ∘ j_{C_{U_l,1}} = j_l ∘ p'_1. The square is even Cartesian, but only this equality is used. Also j^⋆ = j^! for open immersions. Together these give (p_1)_!(j_{C_{U_l,1}})_! j^⋆_{C_{U_l,1}} p_1^!𝓕 = (j_l)_!(p'_1)_!(p'_1)^!(j_l)^!𝓕, which agrees with the printed identity. The co-unit (p'_1)_!(p'_1)^! → Id then gives a map to (j_l)_!(j_l)^!𝓕 = (j_l)_!(j_l)^⋆𝓕. The adjunction (p_1)_! ⊣ p_1^! turns this into the required map into p_1^!(j_l)_!(j_l)^⋆𝓕.

As printed, with (j_l)_⋆, the argument only yields the composite of this map with p_1^! applied to the natural map (j_l)_!(j_l)^⋆𝓕 → (j_l)_⋆(j_l)^⋆𝓕. That composite lands in p_1^!(j_l)_⋆(j_l)^⋆𝓕, which is not a vertex of the triangle. The diagram at the top of the page has (j_l)_! in this position, so the (j_l)_⋆ in the text is a slip.

With both slips corrected, this step of the proof builds the left vertical arrow as intended. The slips affect neither the statement of Proposition 2.9.9 nor its use in §4.5.6 (p. 52). - **Error** at §2.10, Lemma 2.10.1(4) and the last sentence of its proof, p. 29. The only place it is used is the last line of the proof of Proposition 2.10.3, p. 30. The January 2024 preprint has the same text word for word (Lemma 2.10.1(4) on p. 27, its proof on p. 28 there), so the problem was there from the start. (it affects a stated result). The source says `Setup (p. 29): "If Y → Spec A is a scheme, i : Z ↪ Y is a closed subscheme of Y, and if F ∈ D(O_{Y,■}), we let RΓ_Z(Y, F) = RΓ(Z, i^!F)." Lemma 2.10.1: "(4) If Z is proper and if F has coherent cohomology groups, RΓ_Z(Y, F) has finite cohomology groups." Proof: "For the last point, we observe that if F has coherent cohomology groups, the same holds for i^!F and one uses the finiteness of the cohomology of proper schemes."`; it should be `Add a bounded-below hypothesis. The corrected statement: (4) If Z is proper and 𝓕 is bounded below with coherent cohomology sheaves, then RΓ_Z(Y, 𝓕) has finite cohomology groups. Proof: Y is noetherian, so i^!𝓕 = RHom_{𝒪_Y}(𝒪_Z, 𝓕) is again bounded below with coherent cohomology. Locally, resolve 𝒪_Z by finite free modules. Because 𝓕 is bounded below, each cohomology sheaf of i^!𝓕 involves only finitely many terms of that resolution. Then use the finiteness of coherent cohomology of the proper scheme Z. Another fix is to keep 𝓕 unbounded but assume that 𝒪_Z has finite Tor-dimension over 𝒪_Y near Z, for example Y regular. Then i^! has bounded amplitude and Z has finite cohomological dimension. Proposition 2.10.3 needs a matching repair. Its statement can stay as it is for 𝓕 bounded below with coherent cohomology, in particular for a coherent sheaf. Only the proof needs one more step. Near the closed set Z = C̄ \ (p̄₁⋆D̊₊ ∪ p̄₂⋆D̊₋), the target p₁^!𝓕 is bounded below, say in D^{≥a}. So T factors through τ^{≥a} p₂⋆𝓕. The bottom arrow of the diagram on p. 30 then factors through RΓ_Z(C̄ \ p̄₁⋆D̊₊, τ^{≥a} p₂⋆𝓕), and this complex has finite cohomology by the corrected (4). No flatness of p̄₂ is needed. Requiring p₂⋆𝓕 itself to be bounded below near Z (for example 𝓕 bounded and p̄₂ flat there, or 𝓕 perfect) also works, but it is stronger than necessary.`. Nothing in the statement or its setup requires F to be bounded: F is any object of D(O_{Y,■}) with coherent cohomology. Without boundedness, both the statement and the step "the same holds for i^!F" fail.

Counterexample, checked by direct computation. Let A = k be a field (e.g. F_p), R = k[x]/(x²), Y = Spec R, and Z = V(x) = Spec k, which is proper over Spec k. Let F = ⊕_{m≥0} k[m], where k = R/(x). Then H^{-m}(F) = k for every m ≥ 0, so every cohomology sheaf is coherent, but F is unbounded below.

To compute i^!F = RHom_R(k, F), resolve k by the free complex P: ⋯ → R → R → R → k, with every differential multiplication by x. P is a bounded-above complex of free modules, so the Hom complex Hom_R(P, F) computes RHom_R(k, F) for any F, bounded or not. Its degree-0 term is ∏_{n≥0} Hom_R(P^{-n}, F^{-n}) = ∏_{n≥0} k. All its differentials vanish, because x acts by 0 on F and F has zero differential. Hence H^0(i^!F) = ∏_{n≥0} k.

Another way to see it: in each degree F has only one nonzero summand, so F ≅ ∏_m k[m]. Products are exact, so RHom(k, ∏_m k[m]) = ∏_m RHom(k, k)[m], and its H^0 is ∏_m Ext^m_R(k, k) = ∏_{m≥0} k.

Since Z is a point, RΓ_Z(Y, F) = i^!F, and its H^0 is infinite-dimensional, so not a finite A-module. The same computation goes through in solid modules: products are exact there, and internal Hom out of R is the identity. The resulting H^0 is the product ∏_N k, which is still not finite.

The step that fails is "the same holds for i^!F". O_Z = R/(x) is pseudo-coherent but not perfect over R, so RHom(O_Z, −) keeps cohomology coherent only on bounded-below complexes. The second step, finiteness of cohomology on a proper scheme, is fine once i^!F is bounded below with coherent cohomology.

The paper watches for this elsewhere. Remark 2.6.3 (p. 21) notes that its hypothesis ensures the relevant object "is again a coherent sheaf (and in particular is bounded below)". Lemma 2.10.1(4) has no such hypothesis.

Consequences. Proposition 2.10.3 applies (4) to the derived pullback p_2^⋆F. For non-flat p_2 this can be unbounded below even when F is a coherent sheaf: for the closed point Spec k → Spec k[x]/(x²), the pullback of k is k ⊗^L_R k, which has nonzero Tor_n for every n. So the proof of Proposition 2.10.3 has a gap unless boundedness is added. Proposition 2.10.3 is not cited later in the paper, and part (4) of the lemma is not used anywhere else. The later uses of Lemma 2.10.1 (Lemma 2.10.2, and the proof of Theorem 6.2.9, p. 64) use only parts (1)–(3). So the fix is a missing hypothesis and does not affect the main theorems. 1. The statement is false as printed. Counterexample, checked by direct computation:
- Take A = k = F_p (finite type over Z, as §2.2 requires), Y = Spec k[x]/(x²), and Z = Spec k, which is proper over Spec k.
- Take 𝓕 = ⊕_{m≥0} k[m], a discrete object of D(𝒪_{Y,■}). Its cohomology sheaves are H^{-m}(𝓕) = k for m ≥ 0, all coherent. Its global cohomology groups H^{-m}(Y, 𝓕) = k are also finite, so the example works under either reading of "coherent cohomology groups".
- Each degree of this complex has only one nonzero term, and sums and products are exact and computed termwise. So 𝓕 ≅ ∏_{m≥0} k[m].
- Hence i^!𝓕 = RHom_{k[x]/(x²)}(k, 𝓕) = ∏_m RHom(k, k)[m].
- The periodic resolution ⋯ → R →x R →x R → k gives Ext^m(k, k) = k for every m ≥ 0.
- So H⁰(RΓ_Z(Y, 𝓕)) = H⁰(i^!𝓕) = ∏_{m≥0} k. This is not a finite k-module, which contradicts (4).
- The failing step is "the same holds for i^!𝓕": H⁰(i^!𝓕) = ∏ k is not coherent. The second step, finiteness of cohomology on proper Z, is not what breaks.

2. The defence does not work.
- The lemma allows any 𝓕 ∈ D(𝒪_{Y,■}), the unbounded solid derived category. The paper states boundedness explicitly where it wants it, for example "𝓕 ∈ D⁻(𝒪_{X,■})" in Theorem 2.9.7 on p. 28.
- One could charitably read 𝓕 as bounded. That reading does not cover the only application. In the proof of Proposition 2.10.3 the lemma is applied to the derived pullback p₂⋆𝓕.
- The paper itself describes p̄₂⋆𝓕 only as "pseudo coherent" (proof of Proposition 2.3.13, p. 18), that is, bounded above.
- When p̄₂ is not of finite Tor-dimension near Z, p₂⋆𝓕 is unbounded below even for a coherent sheaf 𝓕. For instance, pulling k back along Spec k → Spec k[x]/(x²) gives exactly the complex ⊕_m k[m] above.
- So as written, the proof of Proposition 2.10.3 rests on a false lemma.

3. Consequences.
- Part (4) is used only in Proposition 2.10.3.
- The later citations of Lemma 2.10.1 use only parts (1)–(3), the change-of-support maps. These are the proof of Lemma 2.10.2 (pp. 29–30) and the proof of Theorem 6.2.9.
- Proposition 2.10.3 is not cited anywhere else in the paper.
- For 𝓕 bounded below with coherent cohomology (the case of interest), the conclusion of Proposition 2.10.3 is recovered by the truncation argument in the correction. That argument uses the standard fact that the twisted inverse image p₁^! of a bounded-below complex with coherent cohomology is bounded below.
- No main result of the paper is affected. The stated result that is false as printed is Lemma 2.10.1(4) itself, together with the proof of Proposition 2.10.3 as written. - **Misprint** at §2.11, standing hypotheses before Remark 2.11.1, p. 31 (it affects a stated result). The source says `"We also assume that p̄⋆1D′+ ⊆ p̄⋆2D′′+ and that p̄⋆2D′− ⊆ p̄⋆1D′′−." (p. 31, last sentence of the setting paragraph of §2.11, just before Remark 2.11.1)`; it should be `"We also assume that p̄⋆2D′+ ⊆ p̄⋆1D′′+ and that p̄⋆1D′− ⊆ p̄⋆2D′′−." In both inclusions p̄1 and p̄2 are interchanged. This is the hypothesis of Proposition 2.10.4 for the pair D′′ ⊆ D̊′.`. Conventions (Definitions 2.1.19 and 2.1.24, p. 9). D is expanded if p̄⋆2D ⊆ p̄⋆1D and compactly expanded if p̄⋆2D lies in the interior of p̄⋆1D. D is contracted if p̄⋆1D ⊆ p̄⋆2D. In a dynamic correspondence D+ is expanded and D− is contracted. The setting of §2.11 (p. 31) has D′′± ⊆ D̊′± ⊆ D′± ⊆ D̊± ⊆ D±.

(1) Proposition 2.10.4 (p. 30) takes pairs with D± ⊆ D̊′± ⊆ D′± and assumes "p̄⋆1D+ ⊇ p̄⋆2D′+ and that p̄⋆2D− ⊇ p̄⋆1D′−". The smaller divisor goes with p̄1 on the + side and with p̄2 on the − side. Remark 2.11.2 (p. 31) says the (D′+, D′−) and (D′′+, D′′−) compactifications are compact dynamic "by proposition 2.10.4". This needs the proposition for the pair D′′ ⊆ D̊′, and so needs p̄⋆2D′+ ⊆ p̄⋆1D′′+ and p̄⋆1D′− ⊆ p̄⋆2D′′−. Nothing is assumed that would let one use the pair (D′, D) instead.

(2) The proof of Theorem 2.11.4(3) (p. 33) uses maps "T : RΓ_{D′+,D−}(X̄,F′′) → RΓ_{D′′+,D−}(X̄,F′′)" and "T : RΓ_{D−,D′+}(X̄,F′′) → RΓ_{D−,D′′+}(X̄,F′′)". These are built as in the proof of Proposition 2.10.4 (p. 31): pull back along p̄2, change support by Lemma 2.2.6, apply T, then trace along p̄1. Lemma 2.2.6 (p. 12) gives RΓ_{A+,A−} → RΓ_{A′+,A′−} only when A+ ⊆ A′+ and A′− ⊆ A−. The change-of-support step goes from RΓ_{p̄⋆2D′+,·} to RΓ_{p̄⋆1D′′+,·}, so it needs p̄⋆2D′+ ⊆ p̄⋆1D′′+.

(3) §6.2 is where the theory is applied. Proposition 6.2.3 (p. 61) has (1) "D+ ≥ D+,ϵ′ ≥ D+,ϵ and D− ≥ D−,ϵ′ ≥ D−,ϵ", so D′ = D±,ϵ′ and D′′ = D±,ϵ. It also has (2) "p⋆1D+,ϵ ≥ p⋆2D+,ϵ′" and (3) "p⋆2D−,ϵ ≥ p⋆1D−,ϵ′". These are exactly the corrected inclusions. Item (4) is stated "over C_t^tor \ p⋆1D+,ϵ ∪ p⋆2D−,ϵ", which is C′′. The proof of Theorem 6.2.9 (p. 62) then applies Proposition 2.10.4 and Theorem 2.11.4. Nothing in §6 checks the printed inclusions.

(4) The printed form is degenerate. Checked by direct computation: p̄⋆1D′′+ ⊆ p̄⋆1D′+ ⊆ p̄⋆2D′′+ ⊆ p̄⋆1D′′+, using D′′+ ⊆ D′+, then the printed inclusion, then the fact that D′′+ is expanded. Also p̄⋆2D′′+ ⊆ p̄⋆2D′+ ⊆ p̄⋆1D′+, since D′+ is expanded. So all four sets p̄⋆1D′+, p̄⋆2D′+, p̄⋆1D′′+ and p̄⋆2D′′+ coincide. D′′+ can then be compactly expanded only if this common closed set is also open. The − side behaves the same way. Such a hypothesis cannot hold for the Hecke correspondences of §6.

Scope. Because D′± and D′′± are expanded or contracted, the printed inclusions imply the corrected ones: p̄⋆2D′+ ⊆ p̄⋆1D′+ ⊆ p̄⋆2D′′+ ⊆ p̄⋆1D′′+, and likewise p̄⋆1D′− ⊆ p̄⋆2D′− ⊆ p̄⋆1D′′− ⊆ p̄⋆2D′′−. So Remark 2.11.2 and Theorem 2.11.4 are not false as printed. They are stated under a stronger hypothesis that holds only in degenerate cases. The proofs use only the corrected inclusions, and the application in Theorem 6.2.9 supplies only those. As printed, Theorem 2.11.4 therefore does not cover its one use. The correction weakens the standing hypothesis of a stated theorem to the form that is proved and used. - **Misprint** at §2.11: Theorem 2.11.4(3), p. 32, and the last paragraph of the proof of Theorem 2.11.4, p. 33. The 2024 preprint has the same text in both places (theorem on p. 30, proof on p. 31, with the four items numbered the same way).. The source says `Theorem 2.11.4(3), p. 32, final display: "RΓ_{D″₊,D″₋}(X̄, 𝓕″)^{ord} = RΓ_{D″₋,D″₊}(X̄, 𝓕″)^{ord} → RΓ(X̄, 𝓕)^{C−ord}." Proof of Theorem 2.11.4, last paragraph, p. 33: "Regarding the last point, by lemma 2.5.3 and lemma 2.1.17, after replacing D₊ and D₋ by a multiple nD₊ and nD₋ for n ∈ ℤ_{>0}, there exists m ≥ 0 such that the twisted map T : (p″₂)^⋆𝓕″(mD₊ − mD₋) → (p″₁)^!𝓕″(mD₊ − mD₋) satisfies the factorization of (2) and such that we have maps (p″₂)^⋆𝒪_{X″}(D₊) → (p″₁)^⋆𝒪_{X″}(D₊) and (p″₂)^⋆𝒪_{X″}(−D₋) → (p″₁)^⋆𝒪_{X″}(−D₋). The last point is now a direct consequence of (2)."`; it should be `In Theorem 2.11.4(3), the target should be RΓ(X, 𝓕)^{C−ord}, not RΓ(X̄, 𝓕)^{C−ord}. In the proof of (4), both occurrences of "(2)" should read "(3)": "... satisfies the factorization of (3) and such that ... The last point is now a direct consequence of (3)." Point (2) is then used to identify RΓ(X, 𝓕)^{C−ord} with RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, 𝓕)^{ord}, which is the target in (4).`. (a) The target in (3). In the setting of §2.11 (p. 31), 𝓕 is the restriction of 𝓕″ from X″ to X = X̄ \ (D₊ ∪ D₋), so it is defined only on X. For a sheaf on an open subscheme, the paper defines cohomology over X̄ only with partial supports, as RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, ·) and RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, ·) (Definition 2.2.4 and Remark 2.2.5, p. 12). An unsupported RΓ(X̄, 𝓕) is therefore not defined in the paper for this 𝓕. The notation RΓ(X, 𝓕)^{C−ord} for the ordinary cohomology of the correspondence (C, X, p₁, p₂) is introduced right after Theorem 2.5.1 (p. 19). Item (2) of the same theorem writes "RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, 𝓕)^{ord} = RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, 𝓕)^{ord} = RΓ(X, 𝓕)^{C−ord}", with X unbarred. By (1) and (2), the ordinary part of the diagrams in (1) links RΓ_{D″₊,D″₋}(X̄, 𝓕″)^{ord} to RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, 𝓕)^{ord} = RΓ(X, 𝓕)^{C−ord}. The target in (4) is likewise RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, 𝓕)^{ord}. The bar printed in (3) is the short bar used for the compactification X̄. It is not the wide bar that the proof of (2) uses for the closure of X in X̄, so the formula does not refer to that closure. Unsupported cohomology of 𝓕 would not be defined on the closure either, since 𝓕 lives only on X.

(b) The reference in the proof of (4). Item (2) contains no factorization. It only asserts that (C, X, p₁, p₂) admits a strict dynamic compactification, and identifies the ordinary parts. The proof relies on two things: a factorization of T, which can only be the one assumed in (3), through (p″₂)^⋆𝓕″(D₊) and (p″₁)^!𝓕″(−D₋); and the maps (p″₂)^⋆𝒪_{X″}(D₊) → (p″₁)^⋆𝒪_{X″}(D₊) and (p″₂)^⋆𝒪_{X″}(−D₋) → (p″₁)^⋆𝒪_{X″}(−D₋), quoted word for word from (3). Together these are exactly the hypotheses of (3). Item (4) follows by applying (3) to the twisted correspondence on 𝓕″(mD₊ − mD₋). This sheaf restricts to 𝓕 on X, because D₊ and D₋ do not meet X. Replacing D± by nD± does not change the supports, because Definition 2.2.4 depends on D₊ and D₋ only through the open subschemes X̄ \ D₊ and X̄ \ D₋. The result is the quasi-isomorphism RΓ_{D″₊,D″₋}(X̄, 𝓕″(mD₊ − mD₋))^{ord} = RΓ_{D″₋,D″₊}(X̄, 𝓕″(mD₊ − mD₋))^{ord} → RΓ(X, 𝓕)^{C−ord} = RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, 𝓕)^{ord}, where the last equality is (2). This is exactly the statement of (4). So the result being invoked is (3), not (2).

Neither slip changes the intended mathematics. Theorem 2.11.4 is cited later only in the proof of Theorem 6.2.9 (p. 62), where it identifies the ordinary parts with RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ) ⊗_{ℤ_p} ℤ/p^sℤ, and that use is unaffected. - **Error** at §1.3.7, Theorem 1.3.8, p. 4. The January 2024 preprint has the same statement as Theorem 1.3.7 (§1.3.6, p. 3 of the preprint), with (𝔭, K∞) in place of (𝔭_µ, K∞). The mistake was therefore already in the preprint and was not fixed in the revision. (it affects a stated result). The source says `Theorem 1.3.8 ([Har90], thm. 3.4). Let κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{Mµ,+} and w ∈ C(κ). There exists a unique non degenerate limit of discrete series representation π∞(κ, w) of G(R), with the property that π∞(κ, w) ⊗ Vκ has (𝔭_µ, K∞)-cohomology in degree ℓ(w).`; it should be `Drop the claim that the cohomological degree characterises the representation. A correct form: "Let κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{Mµ,+} and w ∈ C(κ). There is a non-degenerate limit of discrete series π∞(κ, w) of G(R), determined by κ and w, such that π∞(κ, w) ⊗ Vκ has (𝔭_µ, K∞)-cohomology in degree ℓ(w)." Here κ fixes the Harish-Chandra parameter λ = −w_{0,M}(κ + ρ). The element w fixes the Weyl chamber w·C⁺, where C⁺ is the dominant chamber; the closure of w·C⁺ contains λ. π∞(κ, w) is the representation of G(R) induced from the limit of discrete series of G(R)^+ with these data. The degree ℓ(w) alone determines π∞(κ, w) only when no other element of C(κ) of the same length gives a different representation. For G(R) = GSp_{2g}(R) this fails for every g ≥ 4. In the other direction, distinct elements of C(κ) give distinct limits of discrete series of G(R)^+, but not necessarily distinct representations of GSp_{2g}(R). The elements w and w_{0,M} w w_0 give the same representation of G(R) whenever both lie in C(κ). This happens exactly when κ = −w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc on the derived group. The simplest case is g = 1 in weight one: the weight-one limit of discrete series of GL_2(R) contributes to both H^0 and H^1.`. Conventions of §3.1 (pp. 33–34). X⋆(T)^+ is given by 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ … ≥ k_g, and Mµ-dominance by k_1 ≥ … ≥ k_g. The positive roots are e_i − e_j and −e_i − e_j (i < j) and −2e_i, with simple roots −2e_1 and the e_i − e_{i+1}. So ρ = (−1, −2, …, −g) on the derived group. The roots of M are the e_i − e_j, W_M = S_g, and d = g(g+1)/2. Put λ = −w_{0,M}(κ + ρ). The definition on p. 3 then reads C(κ) = {w ∈ ^MW : w(ν + ρ) = λ}. Since κ + ρ is strictly decreasing, λ is regular for the roots of M. So every w ∈ W with w(ν + ρ) = λ lies in ^MW, and C(κ) is a coset of the stabiliser of ν + ρ.

Counterexample for g = 4. Take κ = (3,3,3,3; k) with k even; this is parallel weight 3. Then κ + ρ = (2, 1, 0, −1), λ = (1, 0, −1, −2) and ν + ρ = (0, −1, −1, −2). The stabiliser of ν + ρ is generated by the reflections in −2e_1 and e_2 − e_3 and has order 4. So C(κ) has four elements:
- x ↦ (−x_2, x_1, x_3, x_4), of length 2;
- w: x ↦ (−x_2, −x_1, x_3, x_4), of length 3;
- w′: x ↦ (−x_3, x_1, x_2, x_4), of length 3;
- x ↦ (−x_3, −x_1, x_2, x_4), of length 4.
Each sends ν + ρ to λ and maps the dominant cone into the Mµ-dominant cone. The positive roots made negative are −e_1 − e_2, −2e_1, −2e_2 for w, and e_1 − e_3, e_2 − e_3, −2e_3 for w′. So ℓ(w) = ℓ(w′) = 3.

Identify the compact Cartan of K∞ with T, so that the compact roots are the roots of M. As in [Har90], each u ∈ C(κ) corresponds to the limit of discrete series π(λ, uC⁺) of G(R)^+ with Harish-Chandra parameter λ and chamber uC⁺. Here π(λ, uC⁺) ⊗ Vκ has (𝔭_µ, K∞)-cohomology in degree ℓ(u) and in no other degree. π(λ, uC⁺) is non-degenerate because λ is regular for every compact root. By Knapp–Zuckerman, π(λ, wC⁺) ≅ π(λ, w′C⁺) would require an element of W_K = W_M that fixes λ and carries wC⁺ to w′C⁺. Since λ is M-regular, that element is trivial, so the two representations of G(R)^+ are inequivalent.

The same holds for G(R) = GSp_8(R). K∞ lies in G(R)^+, which has index 2. An element δ of similitude −1 normalises K∞ and inverts its compact Cartan. Hence δπ(λ, uC⁺) ≅ π(λ*, w_{0,M}uw_0·C⁺) with λ* = −w_{0,M}λ = (2, 1, 0, −1), which is not W_M-conjugate to λ. So each π(λ, uC⁺) induces to an irreducible representation of G(R) whose restriction to G(R)^+ is π(λ, uC⁺) ⊕ δπ(λ, uC⁺). The inductions for w and w′ are non-isomorphic, because π(λ, w′C⁺) is neither π(λ, wC⁺) nor δπ(λ, wC⁺).

For u = w or w′, the δ-constituent belongs to the Serre-dual weight κ* = −w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc = (2,2,2,2) and to the element w_{0,M}uw_0 ∈ C(κ*), of length 10 − 3 = 7. Its cohomology is against V_{κ*}, and it has none against Vκ, because its parameter λ* is not W_M-conjugate to λ. So G(R) has two non-isomorphic non-degenerate limits of discrete series, each with (𝔭_µ, K∞)-cohomology against Vκ in degree 3 = ℓ(w) = ℓ(w′), and in that degree only. This contradicts the uniqueness asserted in the theorem.

If instead the parameter attached to κ is normalised as κ + ρ = λ*, each π(λ, uC⁺) is replaced by its δ-conjugate, and the representations of G(R) are the same. The weights (2,2,2,2) and (2,2,2,0) give further examples for g = 4: in each, C(κ) has lengths 6, 7, 7, 8 and λ ≠ −w_{0,M}λ.

Every g ≥ 4. Take κ = (3,3,3,3,0,…,0; k) with k even. Then ν + ρ = (0, −1, −1, −2, −5, −6, …, −g) and λ = (g, …, 6, 5, 1, 0, −1, −2). The stabiliser of ν + ρ is generated by the commuting simple reflections in −2e_1 and e_2 − e_3. So C(κ) is m times this group of order 4, with m of minimal length in the coset, and its lengths are ℓ(m), ℓ(m) + 1, ℓ(m) + 1, ℓ(m) + 2. For example they are 7, 8, 8, 9 for g = 5. Since −2 is an entry of λ and 2 is not, λ* is not W_M-conjugate to λ, and the argument above applies unchanged.

Small g.
- For g ≤ 2 the lengths on ^MW (0, 1, resp. 0, 1, 2, 3) are pairwise distinct, so the question does not arise.
- For g = 3 the lengths on ^MW are 0, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6. The two elements of length 3 are x ↦ (−x_2, −x_1, x_3) and x ↦ (−x_3, x_1, x_2). Both lie in C(κ) only when ν + ρ = (0, b, b) with b < 0. Then λ = (−b, 0, b) = −w_{0,M}λ. An example is κ = (2,2,2), where C(κ) has lengths 2, 3, 3, 4.
- The involution w ↦ w_{0,M} w w_0 of ^MW has no fixed points, because w_0 = −1 is central in W and w_{0,M} ≠ w_0. So in this case it exchanges the two elements of length 3. Their limits of discrete series of G(R)^+ are δ-conjugate, and together they form one irreducible representation of GSp_6(R). For κ = (2,2,2), Blattner's formula gives their lowest K-types as (1, 1, −2) and (2, −1, −1), and x ↦ −w_{0,M}x exchanges them.
So for G(R) = GSp_{2g}(R) the uniqueness holds for g ≤ 3 and fails for every g ≥ 4. For G(R)^+ or Sp_{2g}(R) it already fails for g = 3.

The paper itself allows several elements of C(κ) of the same length. Theorem 1.4.3(5) (p. 5) and Theorem 4.5.2 (p. 51) sum over the w ∈ C(κ) of a given length (ℓ(w) = a, resp. ℓ(w) = p).

Classification. The uniqueness is a substantive claim, false as printed, and not a slip whose intended meaning is clear from context; so this is an error. What is false is the numbered Theorem 1.3.8 itself, so the error affects a stated result. Its reach ends there. Theorem 1.3.8 is a recollection in the introduction, and limits of discrete series appear nowhere else in the paper. The sentence after it (π_f ↪ colim_K H^{ℓ(w)}) is indexed by w ∈ C(κ) and does not use uniqueness. The same holds for the Cousin spectral sequence (Theorem 1.4.3(5), Theorem 4.5.2). Earlier in the same paragraph the notation is fixed as: "We have a decomposition Φ⁺ = Φ⁺_M ∐ Φ^{+,M} where Φ⁺_M accounts for the positive roots in 𝔪 = Lie(M) and Φ^{+,M} for the positive roots in 𝔲_P = Lie(U_P)."`; it should be `"… or equivalently by the condition w⁻¹Φ⁺_M ⊆ Φ⁺" (equivalently Φ⁺_M ⊆ wΦ⁺; stated with the roots of U_P instead, every α ∈ Φ⁺ with w⁻¹α ∉ Φ⁺ lies in Φ^{+,M}). The first condition, wX⋆(T)⁺ ⊆ X⋆(T)^{+,M}, and the definition as minimal-length representatives are correct as printed. The proposed attribution of the corrected condition to §3.1 of Boxer–Pilloni's "Higher Coleman theory" could not be checked against that paper, so it is left out here.`. The printed page confirms the text layer: the second condition uses Φ^{+,M}, and a few lines earlier on p. 34 the paper defines Φ^{+,M} as the positive roots in 𝔲_P = Lie(U_P), not the roots of M.

(1) The first condition is correct and matches minimal length. Since ⟨wλ, α^∨⟩ = ⟨λ, (w⁻¹α)^∨⟩, taking λ regular dominant shows that wX⋆(T)⁺ ⊆ X⋆(T)^{+,M} holds iff w⁻¹α ∈ Φ⁺ for every α ∈ Φ⁺_M. By the exchange property ℓ(s_α w) > ℓ(w) ⟺ w⁻¹α > 0, this holds iff w has minimal length in W_M w.

(2) The printed condition cuts out W_M, not ᴹW. M normalises U_P, so W_M preserves Φ^{+,M} and every element of W_M satisfies it. Conversely, write w = uv with u ∈ W_M and v ∈ ᴹW. Then w⁻¹Φ^{+,M} = v⁻¹Φ^{+,M}. If this lies in Φ⁺, then together with v⁻¹Φ⁺_M ⊆ Φ⁺ (from (1)) we get v⁻¹Φ⁺ ⊆ Φ⁺. So v = 1 and w ∈ W_M.

For g = 1: G = GL₂, M = T, W_M = 1, so ᴹW = W = {1, s}. But s⁻¹Φ^{+,M} = {−β}, where β is the positive root, and this is not in Φ⁺. So the printed condition keeps only the identity.

(3) Checked by direct computation in the paper's own conventions for g = 1, 2, 3, 4. The conventions are: B consists of the root spaces E_{xy} with x before y in the order g+1, …, 2g, 1, …, g; the Weyl group acts by w·e_i = e_{w(i)}, from w(diag(t_i)) = diag(t_{w⁻¹(i)}); and the dominant cone reproduces the paper's 0 ≥ k₁ ≥ … ≥ k_g. Three sets coincide: the minimal-length coset representatives, the set cut out by wX⋆(T)⁺ ⊆ X⋆(T)^{+,M}, and the set cut out by w⁻¹Φ⁺_M ⊆ Φ⁺. They have 2, 4, 8 and 16 elements. The printed condition gives exactly W_M, with 1, 2, 6 and 24 elements.

(4) Nothing later depends on the slip. The paper consistently uses the correct set:
- Definition 1.3.1 (p. 3) defines ᴹW as minimal-length representatives.
- §1.3.3 (p. 3) states X⋆(T)^{M,+} = ∪_{w∈ᴹW} wX⋆(T)⁺.
- p. 34 gives the length function ℓ: ᴹW → [0, g(g+1)/2] and FL = ∐_{w∈ᴹW} C_w.
- The proof of Lemma 4.3.8 (p. 48) uses w⁻¹w_{0,M}ρ + ρ = Σ_{α∈(w⁻¹Φ^{+,M})∩Φ⁺} α. Writing A = w⁻¹Φ^{+,M} ∩ Φ⁺ and B = w⁻¹Φ^{+,M} ∩ Φ⁻, the condition w⁻¹Φ⁺_M ⊆ Φ⁺ gives Φ⁺ = w⁻¹Φ⁺_M ⊔ A ⊔ (−B). Hence 2ρ = 2w⁻¹ρ_M + ΣA − ΣB and 2w⁻¹ρ_nc = ΣA + ΣB. Since w_{0,M}ρ = ρ_nc − ρ_M, the identity follows. Under the printed condition the intersection with Φ⁺ would be redundant; for g = 1 and w = s both sides are 0, which needs s ∈ ᴹW.

So this is an isolated notational slip, Φ^{+,M} written for Φ⁺_M, in a parenthetical reformulation. - **Error** at §3.1, concrete description of ᴹW, p. 34 (it affects a stated result). The source says `Finally, ᴹW is the subset of w such that w⁻¹(g + 1) < w⁻¹(g + 2) · · · < w⁻¹(2g).`; it should be `^MW is the set of w ∈ W such that w^{−1}(g+1) ≺ w^{−1}(g+2) ≺ ··· ≺ w^{−1}(2g). Here ≺ is the total order g+1 ≺ g+2 ≺ ··· ≺ 2g ≺ 1 ≺ 2 ≺ ··· ≺ g. This is the order in the description of T^+(Q_p) on p. 34 and the order of the Iwahori flag H_{g+1} ⊆ ··· ⊆ H_{2g} ⊆ H_1 ⊆ ··· ⊆ H_g on p. 41. Equivalently: in the list w^{−1}(g+1), …, w^{−1}(2g), the entries > g come first in increasing order, followed by the entries ≤ g in increasing order. A related slip two lines earlier: "w^{−1}Φ^{+,M} ⊆ Φ^+" should read w^{−1}Φ^+_M ⊆ Φ^+.`. The page image of p. 34 confirms the printed sentence. It follows the definition of ᴹW as the minimal-length representatives of W_M\W.

**Conventions.** On p. 34, B ⊆ P is block lower triangular with upper-triangular diagonal blocks. So the root t_a/t_b, whose root space is E_{ab}, is B-positive exactly when a ≺ b. This agrees with the dominance condition for T⁺(Q_p) printed on the same page, and with the cone 0 ≥ k₁ ≥ ··· ≥ k_g. The stated action is w·diag(t_i) = diag(t_{w⁻¹(i)}), which is conjugation by the permutation matrix e_i ↦ e_{w(i)}. It gives w(t_a/t_b) = t_{w(a)}/t_{w(b)}.

**The correct condition.** An element w is minimal in W_M w if and only if w⁻¹ sends the simple roots t_{g+i}/t_{g+i+1} of M to positive roots. That is, w⁻¹(g+i) ≺ w⁻¹(g+i+1) for 1 ≤ i ≤ g−1. The printed condition uses the usual order 1 < ··· < 2g. That would be Kostant's condition for the upper-triangular Borel, which lies in P^std, not for B ⊆ P.

**Why the printed set is wrong.** Both conditions pick exactly one element from each coset, because a coset is determined by w⁻¹{g+1,…,2g}. They disagree on every coset where this set meets both halves of {1,…,2g}. That is 2^g − 2 of the 2^g cosets.

**Counterexample for g = 2.** Take w = (2 3). Then w⁻¹(3) = 2 < 4 = w⁻¹(4), so w satisfies the printed condition.
- In coordinates (k₁,k₂;k), w changes the sign of k₂.
- It makes three of the four positive roots (1,−1), (−1,−1), (0,−2), (−2,0) negative, so ℓ(w) = 3.
- The other element of its coset is w′ = s_α w, where α = (1,−1); w′⁻¹ is (3,1,4,2) in one-line notation. w′ has ℓ(w′) = 2 and satisfies the ≺ condition, but not the printed one.
- dim C_w = #{α > 0 : wα ∈ −Φ^{+,M}} = 2 ≠ ℓ(w).
- The identity in the proof of Lemma 4.3.8 (p. 48), w⁻¹w_{0,M}ρ + ρ = Σ_{α∈(w⁻¹Φ^{+,M})∩Φ⁺} α with ρ = (−1,−2;0), gives (−3,−1;0) on the left and (−2,0;0) on the right. For w′ both sides are (−2,0;0).
- In general, w⁻¹w_{0,M}ρ + ρ is the sum of the positive roots in w⁻¹(Φ^{+,M} ∪ Φ⁻_M). So the identity holds exactly for Kostant representatives.

**Further checks by direct computation.** For g = 2, 3, 4 the ≺-increasing element is the unique minimal-length element of each coset. The lengths in the printed set are {0,2,3,3} for g = 2, and include 7 > g(g+1)/2 = 6 for g = 3. So the printed set is incompatible with ℓ: ᴹW → [0, g(g+1)/2] and ℓ(w) = dim C_w, both on p. 34. It is also incompatible with "the length one element" of §5.6 on p. 58: the printed set has no element of length 1.

**Scope.** Every later use goes through the definition (minimal length, Kostant's condition) or through coset invariants, which are unaffected: the set w⁻¹{g+1,…,2g}, the sequence (w_i), C_w and the strata. So later results stand. The false statement is the concrete description itself.

**Related slip.** The equivalent condition two lines earlier, "w⁻¹Φ^{+,M} ⊆ Φ⁺", should read w⁻¹Φ⁺_M ⊆ Φ⁺. As printed it fails for w_{0,M}w₀ ∈ ᴹW, and it holds for all of W_M. **The paper's conventions (p. 34).** P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩, so it is block lower triangular. B ⊆ P is upper triangular on the diagonal g×g blocks.
- The root t ↦ t_a/t_b has root space spanned by E_{ab}. So it is B-positive exactly when a ≺ b, for the order g+1 ≺ ··· ≺ 2g ≺ 1 ≺ ··· ≺ g.
- The paper confirms this order three times:
  - the dominant cone 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ ··· ≥ k_g, whose simple roots are t_j/t_{j+1} and t_{2g}/t_1 (= t_1^{−2} in the (k;k) coordinates);
  - the condition v(t_{g+1}) ≥ ··· ≥ v(t_{2g}) ≥ v(t_1) ≥ ··· ≥ v(t_g) for T^+(Q_p);
  - the Iwahori flag on p. 41, with H_{g+i} corresponding to ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{g+i}⟩.
- The natural order < is the positivity order of the upper triangular Borel. That Borel lies in P^std, not in P. For it the dominant cone would be k_1 ≥ ··· ≥ k_g ≥ 0, which contradicts the paper.
- Switching between a left and a right action of W on characters only exchanges w and w^{−1}. It never turns ≺ into <. So no faithful reading of the conventions makes the sentence true.

**The correct condition.** Since w·diag(t_i) = diag(t_{w^{−1}(i)}), w sends t_a/t_b to t_{w(a)}/t_{w(b)}.
- The simple roots of M are t_{g+i}/t_{g+i+1} for 1 ≤ i ≤ g−1.
- So w is minimal in W_M w (w^{−1}Φ^+_M ⊆ Φ^+, equivalently wX*(T)^+ ⊆ X*(T)^{+,M}) if and only if w^{−1}(g+i) ≺ w^{−1}(g+i+1) for all i.
- A coset W_M w is determined by S = w^{−1}{g+1,…,2g}. Its g! elements correspond to the orderings of S as w^{−1}(g+1),…,w^{−1}(2g).
- Both rules pick one element from each coset. They disagree exactly when S meets both halves of {1,…,2g}, which happens for 2^g − 2 of the 2^g cosets.

**Counterexample, g = 2.** Take w = (2 3), so w(1)=1, w(2)=3, w(3)=2, w(4)=4. It satisfies the printed condition, because w^{−1}(3) = 2 < 4 = w^{−1}(4).
- In coordinates (k_1,k_2;k), w changes the sign of k_2. It makes t_1/t_2, (t_1t_2)^{−1} and t_2^{−2} negative, so ℓ(w) = 3.
- The other element w′ of W_M w has w′^{−1} = (3,1,4,2) in one-line notation. It has ℓ(w′) = 2 and satisfies the ≺ condition.
- This contradicts three statements on p. 34:
  - ℓ(w) = dim C_w fails, since dim C_w = dim C_{w′} = 2;
  - w sends the dominant weight (−1,−3;0) to (−1,3;0), which is not M-dominant, so w violates the defining condition wX*(T)^+ ⊆ X*(T)^{+,M};
  - for g = 2 the printed set has lengths {0,2,3,3}. It has no element of length 1, but §5.6 on p. 58 argues with "the length one element".

**Checked by direct computation for g = 2, 3, 4:**
- The ≺-increasing element is the unique minimal-length element of each coset. It also equals the "entries > g first" description in the correction.
- The printed set has lengths up to 7 for g = 3 and 12 for g = 4. This exceeds the range [0, g(g+1)/2] asserted for ℓ on p. 34.
- The literal condition w^{−1}Φ^{+,M} ⊆ Φ^+ cuts out exactly W_M, since it says w^{−1}Pw ⊇ B. This confirms the related slip.

**Defence attempted.**
- The sentence is not a paraphrase of the definition. It is an independent concrete claim, and it is false.
- Its intended content cannot be recovered by fixing an index or a sign: a different order is needed.
- So it is an error rather than a misprint.

**What later uses the passage.** Later arguments use ^MW either through its definition (minimal length, Kostant) or through quantities that are the same for every element of a coset. So no later result depends on the false description.
- **Quantities that do not depend on the representative:**
  - the set w^{−1}{g+1,…,2g}, the sequence (w_i), and C_w;
  - the strata in 4.1.3 and Lemmas 4.1.6 and 4.1.9;
  - the filtration and Z_{>w−1} in 4.1.16 and 4.5;
  - the sets w^{−1}Φ^{±,M} in Proposition 4.2.4.
- **Places that need the Kostant representative:**
  - Lemma 4.3.4, which needs w(v(t)) to be M-dominant;

  - Proposition 4.3.9, C(κ), and ν = −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) − ρ;
  - X*(T)^{M,+} = ∪ wX*(T)^+ on p. 3;
  - the use of ℓ(w) in Theorem 4.5.2, Conjecture 5.6.1 and Proposition 5.6.3.
- All of these hold with the definition. They would fail if the printed description were used instead.
- The duality involution w ↦ w_{0,M}ww_0 preserves both sets.

**Scope.** The proposed correction is right and minimal. The false statement is the concrete description of ^MW itself. No numbered lemma, proposition or theorem is affected. The source says `An isomorphism ξ : (A, λ, η) → (A′, λ′, η′) is a quasi-isogeny ξ : A → A′ for which η′ = H₁(ξ) ∘ η and ξ^D λξ = rλ for some r ∈ ℚ_{>0}.`; it should be `ξ^D λ′ ξ = rλ for some r ∈ ℚ_{>0}. Here λ′ is the quasi-polarization of the target, and the composite A → A′ → A′^D → A^D is compared with rλ : A → A^D. This is the usual condition that the quasi-isogeny respects the quasi-polarizations up to a positive rational scalar.`. The page image at high resolution shows "ξ^D λξ = rλ" with no prime on the first λ. The line just above prints the target triple as (A′, λ′, η′) with a clearly visible prime, so the missing prime is in the source and not an artefact of the text layer. The paper's own conventions make the printed formula ill-typed. By item (2), λ : A → A^D. Since ξ : A → A′, its dual is ξ^D : A′^D → A^D. For ξ^D ∘ λ ∘ ξ to make sense, the middle map has to go from A′ to A′^D, which λ does not do unless A′ = A. Reading the composition left to right does not help either: then ξ is followed by λ, but ξ lands in A′ and λ starts from A. So the only sensible reading is ξ^D λ′ ξ = rλ, which has the correct type A → A^D on both sides. This is the standard condition for an isomorphism of polarized abelian schemes up to isogeny with level structure. The paper states the analogous conditions for the Igusa tower in words on p. 35 ("matching λ and λ′ up to an element in ℤ^×_{(p),>0}", and in the quasi-isogeny formulation "up to an element in ℚ_{>0}"), and there the target polarization λ′ is used. The formula is only a recollection of the standard moduli interpretation of the Siegel Shimura variety. Nothing later in the paper uses it: the Hecke correspondences (§4.2) are defined through the universal quasi-isogeny p₁^⋆A → p₂^⋆A over the Shimura variety of level tK_{p,n}t^{-1} ∩ K_{p,n}, with no reference to this formula. Multiplicative part first:
- §1.3.9 (p. 4): "A[p^∞] ≃ µ^g_{p^∞} ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)^g".
- §3.4.1 (p. 35), including the displayed λ_can.
- The matrix in the proof of Lemma 3.4.3 (p. 36).
- The proof of Proposition 3.4.9 (p. 38): "x : µ^g_{p^∞} → A[p^∞]^m, y : (Q_p/Z_p)^g → A[p^∞]^e … (x^D, y^D) ∘ λ ∘ (x, y) = cλ_can".
- Remark 3.4.18 (p. 39).

Étale part first: §3.4.17 (p. 39), which sits between these passages. It calls j "the isomorphism (Q_p/Z_p)^g ⊕ µ^g_{p^∞} → A[p^∞]", although j has source X_ord, and sends it to "Z_p^g ⊕ Z_p^g(1) = Z_p^{2g} → T_p(A)".

Only the étale-first order fits the paper's group-theoretic conventions:
- On p. 33, P = P_µ is the stabiliser of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩ and P^std is the stabiliser of ⟨e_1,…,e_g⟩.
- On p. 35, π_HT(A, Ψ) = P g(Ψ)^{-1}, where Ψ(⟨g(Ψ)(e_{g+1}),…,g(Ψ)(e_{2g})⟩) = Lie_A(1).
- For ordinary A, the Hodge–Tate map kills the Tate module of the multiplicative part, since the ω of its Cartier dual (Q_p/Z_p)^g is 0. Hence T_p(A[p^∞]^m) ⊗ C = Lie_A(1).
- So a map that is P(Q_p)-equivariant and lands over the base point P of FL, as §3.4.17 states, must send e_{g+1},…,e_{2g} to the multiplicative part.
- The proof of Lemma 4.1.6 (p. 41) uses the same normalisation: "e_{w^{-1}(i)}, g+1 ≤ i ≤ 2g span the multiplicative part of the Tate module".

In the printed multiplicative-first coordinates, the displayed Aut(X̃_ord) is block upper triangular, so it lies in P^std, and Hom(X̃_et, X̃_m) is the upper-right block U_{P^std}. Lemma 3.4.3 instead says that M(Q_p) acts on U_{J_ord} as on U_P(Q_p), and Remark 3.4.6 describes J^int_ord as M(Z_p) ⋉ U_P(Z_p)(1). These two do not match, checked by direct computation:
- For m = diag(A, D) ∈ M, conjugation sends the lower-left block C of U_P to DCA^{-1} and the upper-right block B of U_{P^std} to ABD^{-1}.
- The element z = diag(1_g, p·1_g) is in G with similitude p and is central in M.
- So z acts by p on U_P and by p^{-1} on U_{P^std}. Directly on Hom(X̃_et, X̃_m) it is f ↦ 1∘f∘p^{-1} = p^{-1}f.

Hence, with M embedded block-diagonally in the printed coordinates, the M-module in Lemma 3.4.3 is U_{P^std}, not U_P. Lemma 3.4.3 holds only if the Levi is identified through the étale-first coordinates. Equivalently, one conjugates by the Weyl element swapping the two blocks, which normalises M and exchanges U_P and U_{P^std}. §3.4.17 makes this swap without saying so.

The proposed correction is consistent. Suppose the isocrystal is normalised through the rational Tate module, so that µ_{p^∞} (Tate module Z_p(1)) gets Frobenius p^{-1}, as for D_cris(Q_p(1)), with similitude p^{-1} matching the Weil pairing. Then the printed b_ord = diag(p^{-1}Id_g, Id_g) is written in the multiplicative-first order. In the étale-first order it becomes diag(Id_g, p^{-1}Id_g) = µ(p)^{-1}. The automorphism matrix then becomes block lower triangular, inside P.

No stated result is affected. Every later use is phrased with P and the étale-first normalisation of §3.4.17, namely:
- K_{p,P} = P(Q_p) ∩ xK_px^{-1};
- Lemmas 3.4.20 and 4.1.7;
- Proposition 4.2.4;
- the map T(Q_p) → P′(Q_p).

The local replacement is the minimal fix. Redefining M_{K_{p,P}} everywhere as the image would make condition (1) of §5.1 and Remark 3.4.7 need rewording.`. Page 37 was checked on the rendered image. The paper allows any prime p ("We now fix a prime p", §3.3, p. 34). It also allows every compact open subgroup of P'(Q_p). By p. 36 these are the compact open subgroups of P(Q_p) that are stable under the Galois action, where Galois acts trivially on M and by χ_cycl on the unipotent radical. The splitting K = M_K ⋉ U_K is proved only for p > 2: the argument needs σ with χ_cycl(σ) − 1 ∈ Z_p^×, and no such σ exists when p = 2. Even so, the next paragraph uses the "exact sequence" 1 → U_K → K → M_K → 1 with no condition on p, and Proposition 3.4.9(5) relies on it.

The counterexample was checked by hand and by direct computation modulo 16. Since K below contains the kernel of reduction mod 4, a check modulo 16 decides the question over Z_2. Take p = 2 and g = 1, so G = GSp_2 = GL_2. Here P, the stabiliser of ⟨e_2⟩ (p. 33), is the lower triangular Borel and M = T is the diagonal torus. Galois acts by σ(a 0; c d) = (a 0; χ(σ)c d).
- Let K₀ = {(a 0; c d) : a ≡ d ≡ 1 mod 4, c ≡ 0 mod 2}. This is the preimage of a normal subgroup of B(Z/4), so it is normal in B(Z_2). It is Galois-stable.
- Let g₀ = (1 0; −1 −1). Then g₀ ∈ B(Z_2) and g₀² = 1, so g₀ normalises K₀ and K = K₀ ∪ g₀K₀ is a compact open subgroup.
- K is Galois-stable, because g₀^{-1}σ(g₀) = (1 0; χ(σ)−1 1) ∈ K₀.
- Every element g₀(a 0; c d) = (a 0; −a−c −d) of g₀K₀ has an odd lower-left entry. So K ∩ T = K₀ ∩ T ≅ (1+4Z_2)², which is torsion-free.
- The image of K in T contains diag(1,−1), an element of order 2.

So K/U_K is not K ∩ M(Q_p), not even as an abstract group, and the printed sequence is not exact. The fibres of 𝔍𝔊_{K^pU_K} → 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK} are torsors under K/U_K. The subgroup M_K = K ∩ M(Q_p) has index 2 in K/U_K here, so it acts freely but not transitively on those fibres. Hence Proposition 3.4.9(5) is false as printed for this K.

The authors appear aware of the issue elsewhere:
- Remark 3.4.7 states the bijection only for p > 2.
- Condition (1) of §5.1 (p. 53) imposes K_{p,P} = M_{K_{p,P}} ⋉ U_{K_{p,P}}, "automatic if p > 2".
- The proof of Lemma 3.4.8 uses the "Levi quotient K_{p,M}", which is the image.

No later result is affected:
- Where Proposition 3.4.9 is used later (§3.4.13 on p. 39, the proof on p. 48, Remark 3.4.10), only finite flatness or the profinite étaleness of the map is needed, not the name of its group.
- §4 uses K_{p,P,w} = wK_{p,n}w^{-1} ∩ P(Q_p) (Lemma 4.1.7, p. 41), with K_{p,n} of Iwahori type. §6 (p. 63) uses subgroups of the same kind. All of these are semidirect products.
- §5 works only with decomposable subgroups, and §5.3.2 (p. 55) restates the exact sequence for those.

The defect is therefore confined to Proposition 3.4.9(5) and the sentence before it, for p = 2. No defence works:
- The paper allows p = 2. It fixes an arbitrary prime in §3.3 (p. 34). The paper itself says p > 2 is needed for the splitting (p. 37, Remark 3.4.7, and §5.1(1) "automatic if p > 2").
- The paper allows every compact open subgroup of P'(Q_p). Remark 3.4.6 explicitly includes every finite-index subgroup of P'(Z_p). By p. 36 these are the compact open subgroups of P(Q_p) stable under Galois, where Galois acts trivially on M and by χ_cycl on U_P.
- M_{K_{p,P}} cannot be read as the quotient K/U_K. Two lines earlier it is defined as K ∩ M(Q_p) = K^{Gal}, which is the group of Q_p-points of the twisted group K. The map from K^{Gal} to the Galois-fixed points of K/U_K can fail to be surjective, because of H^1(Gal, U_K), and it does fail for p = 2. The proof of Lemma 3.4.8 uses a separate symbol K_{p,M} ("Levi quotient") for the image.
- The splitting argument needs some σ with χ_cycl(σ) − 1 ∈ Z_p^×. For p = 2 there is no such σ.

Counterexample, checked by hand and by direct computation modulo 16. The group below contains the level-4 congruence subgroup of B(Z_2), so this computation decides the question.
- Take p = 2 and g = 1, so G = GL_2. P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_2⟩, the lower triangular Borel, and M = T. The Galois action is (a 0; c d) ↦ (a 0; χ(σ)c d).
- Let K = {(a 0; c d) ∈ GL_2(Z_2) : c ≡ (a−1)/2 mod 2}.
- K is a subgroup. The product has lower-left entry ca' + dc' ≡ c + c' mod 2, and (aa'−1)/2 ≡ (a−1)/2 + (a'−1)/2 mod 2.
- K is open and Galois-stable, since χ(σ) is odd.
- The image of K in T is all of T(Z_2).
- K ∩ T = {diag(a,d) : a ≡ 1 mod 4} has index 2 in that image. For example, (−1 0; 1 1) ∈ K, but its Levi component diag(−1,1) is not in K.

So K → M(Q_p) does not land in M_K, and the displayed sequence is not exact. The construction g_0 = (1 0; −1 −1), K = K_0 ∪ g_0K_0 with K_0 = {a ≡ d ≡ 1 mod 4, c even} gives another counterexample, checked in the same way.

Why (5) fails for this K:
- By (2), 𝔍𝔊_{K^p} → 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK} is a \overline{K}-torsor.

- M_K acts freely on the fibres but not transitively, since it has index 2. The two groups are not even abstractly isomorphic: their 2-torsion subgroups have orders 2 and 4.

Example. Take g = 1, so G = GL_2, and P, the stabiliser of ⟨e_2⟩, is the lower triangular Borel. Take p odd and x = 1. Let K_p = {γ ∈ GL_2(Z_p) : γ_11, γ_22 ∈ 1+pZ_p, γ_12 ∈ p²Z_p, γ_21 ≡ (γ_11−1)/p mod p}. This is a compact open subgroup:
- (γδ)_11 ≡ γ_11δ_11 mod p² and (γδ)_21 ≡ γ_21+δ_21 mod p;
- it contains 1+p²M_2(Z_p);
- closure under products was also checked by direct computation mod p² for p = 3, 5.
Then K_p ∩ P(Q_p) = {(a 0; c d) : a, d ∈ 1+pZ_p, c ≡ (a−1)/p mod p}. Its intersection with M(Q_p) is {a ≡ 1 mod p²}, which has index p in its image (1+pZ_p)² in M(Q_p). So it is not the semi-direct product of its M- and U_P-parts. It is not Galois-stable either: c ↦ χ_cycl(σ)c does not preserve it when χ_cycl(σ) ≢ 1 mod p. So Proposition 3.4.9, as cited for normality in the proof of Lemma 3.4.24, does not cover this level. Defence: the claim is true. Over Z_p^cycl, with Z_p(1) = Z_p fixed, each element of P(Q_p) gives a Z_p^cycl-point of J_ord. Let K ⊆ P(Q_p) be compact open.
1. U_K = K ∩ U_P(Q_p) is a Z_p-lattice, so it is Galois-stable.
2. K ∩ M(Q_p) is open in the image K̄ of K, so it contains an open subgroup M_1 that is normal in K̄.
3. K_1 = M_1 ⋉ U_K is open and normal in K, comes from P′(Q_p), and satisfies K/K_1 ≅ K̄/M_1.
4. The closure of a coset kK_1 is the translate k·\overline{K_1}. These translates are disjoint, since they have different images in M(Q_p)/M_1. Hence \overline{K}/\overline{K_1} is the constant group K/K_1.
5. So IG_{K^pK,Z_p^cycl} is the quotient of IG_{K^pK_1} ×_{Spf Z_p} Spf Z_p^cycl, which is smooth by 3.4.9(3), by a free action of a finite constant group. It is therefore smooth over Z_p^cycl, in particular normal.

- the proof of Proposition 4.2.4 (p. 43), at K_{p,P,w} ∩ w(t)K_{p,P,w}w(t)^{−1}.
Both groups have Iwahori factorisations: they are semi-direct products whose U_P-part is a Z_p-lattice, so they come from P′(Q_p) and Proposition 3.4.9 applies directly. Levels that are not semi-direct products do occur in the proof of Proposition 4.2.4, for the components x ≢ 1. Then P(Q_p) ∩ wx(K_{p,1} ∩ tK_{p,1}t^{−1})(wx)^{−1} = {(a 0; c d) : a, d ∈ Z_p^×, c ∈ pZ_p, a−d ≡ −pc mod p³} (checked by direct computation). Its M-part {a ≡ d mod p³} has index p in its image {a ≡ d mod p²}. These components enter only through their generic fibres, and they are discarded. So no stated result is affected. - **Error** at §1.3.7 (Archimedean representation theory and limits of discrete series), the paragraph after Theorem 1.3.8, p. 4. The 2024 preprint has the same text in §1.3.6, after Theorem 1.3.7, p. 3.. The source says `Let π = π∞(κ, w) ⊗ πf be an automorphic representation. Then πf ↪ colimK H^{ℓ(w)}(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, ω^κ) ⊗ ℂ. When w = Id, π∞(κ, Id) is a holomorphic limit of discrete series and the representation π is generated by holomorphic modular forms.`; it should be `Add the word "cuspidal": "Let π = π∞(κ, w) ⊗ πf be a cuspidal automorphic representation. Then πf ↪ colim_K H^{ℓ(w)}(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, ω^κ) ⊗ C." This is the standard statement from Harris: cusp forms of ∂̄-cohomology type give classes in the coherent cohomology of the canonical extension. The failure only happens when ℓ(w) ≥ 1. For w = Id, a holomorphic automorphic form of moderate growth is a section of ω^κ over the toroidal compactification, and H^0 is left exact. So the degree-0 case, and the following sentence about w = Id, hold for every automorphic π.`. The paper sets G = GSp_{2g}, and nothing in this recollection excludes g = 1. Take g = 1, so G = GL_2. M_µ is then the torus, ^M W = {Id, w_0}, and ℓ(w_0) = 1. Fix k ≥ 3 and the weight κ with ω^κ = ω^{2−k} in classical notation. Then C(κ) = {w_0}, and π∞(κ, w_0) is the antiholomorphic discrete series D_k^- (after matching the central character by a twist). This is the representation that computes H^1(X, ω^{2−k}) by Dolbeault cohomology.

(1) A non-cuspidal π of this type exists. A holomorphic Eisenstein series of weight k (for example E_4 at level SL_2(ℤ), or a weight-k Eisenstein series of level Γ_1(N)) generates the automorphic representation D_k^+ ⊗ πf. At every unramified ℓ, πf has the component Ind(|·|^{(k−1)/2}, |·|^{−(k−1)/2}), up to a twist; this is irreducible because k − 1 ≠ ±1. Its T_ℓ eigenvalue is 1 + ℓ^{k−1}, so the normalized Satake parameters are {ℓ^{(k−1)/2}, ℓ^{−(k−1)/2}}. The complex conjugate of this Eisenstein series, twisted by a power of |ν| if needed, generates an automorphic representation π' = D_k^- ⊗ π'_f. Here π'_f is a twist of the contragredient of πf, so its Satake parameters at ℓ still have ratio of absolute value ℓ^{±(k−1)}. Hence π' has the form π∞(κ, w_0) ⊗ π'_f, with π' automorphic but not cuspidal.

(2) Such a π'_f cannot occur in H^1. On the compactified modular curve, Kodaira–Spencer gives Ω^1 = ω^2(−D). Serre duality then gives H^1(X_K, ω^{2−k})^∨ ≅ H^0(X_K, ω^k(−D)) = S_k(K), compatibly with Hecke correspondences up to a twist by a character. So colimK H^1(X_K, ω^{2−k}) ⊗ ℂ is a character twist of the smooth dual of colimK S_k(K) ⊗ ℂ = ⊕ σ_f, the sum over cuspidal σ of weight k. Every irreducible subrepresentation is therefore σ_f^∨ ⊗ χ for a cuspidal σ. At unramified ℓ, its Satake parameters have ratio of absolute value 1: this follows from Deligne's theorem, or already from the Hecke bound |a_ℓ| = O(ℓ^{k/2}) against ℓ^{k−1} for large ℓ, since k ≥ 3. So π'_f does not embed into colimK H^1(S^{tor}_K, ω^κ) ⊗ ℂ, and the printed statement fails for w = w_0.

For w = Id the non-cuspidal statement does hold, because holomorphic Eisenstein series lie in H^0(X, ω^k) for the canonical extension. That is presumably why the slip goes unnoticed in the next sentence. The statement is an introductory recollection and is not used later in the paper, so no result depends on it. As printed, the statement is false for non-cuspidal π. Counterexample: take g = 1 and G = GL2, so that M_µ = T, ^MW = W = {1, s} and ℓ(s) = 1. Take k = 4 (any k ≥ 3 works). Let κ be the weight with ω^κ = ω^{2−k} = ω^{−2} in classical notation, with the matching similitude component. Then ν + ρ is regular and C(κ) = {s}. The representation π∞(κ, s) of Theorem 1.3.8 is the antiholomorphic discrete series of weight k (or the full discrete series D_k, if G(R)-representations are meant). Now take the automorphic representation π generated by the complex conjugate of the level-one Eisenstein series E_4 (or by E_4 itself, in the G(R) reading). Its archimedean component is π∞(κ, s). Its finite part πf is unramified everywhere, with T_ℓ-eigenvalue 1 + ℓ^3, so the ratio of its Satake parameters at ℓ is ℓ^{±3}. The hypothesis of the sentence is therefore satisfied.

On the other side, look at the compactified modular curve with the canonical extension. There Ω^1 = ω^2(−D) (Kodaira–Spencer), so Serre duality gives H^1(X_K, ω^{2−k}) ≅ H^0(X_K, ω^k(−D))^∨ = S_k(K)^∨, compatibly with Hecke operators. Hence colim_K H^1(X_K, ω^{2−k}) ⊗ C is, up to a twist by a character, the smooth dual of the space of weight-k cusp forms. Every irreducible subrepresentation of it is a twist of the contragredient of the finite part of a cuspidal representation. For such a representation the ratio of Satake parameters at unramified ℓ has absolute value 1 (Deligne), and neither twisting nor taking contragredients changes that. So πf does not embed, and does not even occur as a subquotient; this was checked by direct computation of the Satake ratios above.

Attempted defences, none of which works:
(a) The paper never defines "automorphic representation" as cuspidal. In §1.1 it refers to [Su24] for computing coherent cohomology by automorphic forms, which suggests general automorphic forms.
(b) That comparison does not rescue the claim. (p,K)-cohomology is not left exact in positive degree, so a subrepresentation π of the space of automorphic forms need not inject on H^{ℓ(w)}; the example above is exactly such a case.
(c) The citation [Har90, thm. 3.4] supports only the archimedean statement (Theorem 1.3.8). The embedding is Harris's result for cusp forms.
The intended meaning is almost certainly "cuspidal", and with that word added the sentence is correct. As printed, though, it is a false statement, not a slip that the context repairs.

Remark 3.4.10 (p. 37) then spells out the argument: "The point (6), implies that the completed local rings at a closed point x … is isomorphic to \mathscr{O}_{\hat T_{K_{p,P}}}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_p} W(k(x)). By (5), for any closed point x ∈ \mathfrak{IG}_{K^pK_{p,P}} and any x′ above x", the completed local ring at x, after completed base change to W(k(x′)), is the completed local ring at x′. That completed local ring is a power-series ring over W(k(x′)). Regularity descends along the faithfully flat map W(k(x)) → W(k(x′)), for both the ring and its reduction mod p. So the completed local ring of \mathfrak{IG}_{K^pK_{p,P}} at x is a power-series ring over W(k(x)). Together with finite type, this gives smoothness, which is (3). The step therefore uses (6) and (5), not (4). The paper's own wording ("This implies (3)", with "This" referring to (6)) and Remark 3.4.10 show that the intended reference is (6). Point (4) only enters indirectly, because it defines the space that appears in (6). No quotient argument of the kind used for (4) could supply smoothness: a quotient by a finite flat group scheme need not preserve smoothness. The error is a wrong item number. The statement (3) and its proof stand once the reference is corrected. Later uses of Proposition 3.4.9 rely on (7) and on Remark 3.4.11: the Hecke projections in 3.4.13 on p. 39 and the proof on p. 48. None of these depends on the mis-cited item.
