- **Error** at §3.4.19 (the definition of A_{g,δ}, the decomposition 𝔄^{ord}_{g,d} = ∐_δ 𝔄^{ord}_{g,δ}, and Lemma 3.4.20), p. 40 of the author version. The 2024 preprint has the same text on p. 38. (it affects a stated result). The source says `"We let A_{g,δ} → A_{g,d} be the locally closed substack where the kernel of the polarization is isomorphic, locally in the étale topology, to ∏_{i=1}^g Z/δ_iZ × μ_{δ_i}. By definition, we have A_{g,δ,Q} = S_{K_δ,Q}. [...] We let 𝔄_{g,δ} be the p-adic formal completion of A_{g,δ} and we let 𝔄^{ord}_{g,δ} be the ordinary locus. We have 𝔄^{ord}_{g,d} = ∐_δ 𝔄^{ord}_{g,δ}. Lemma 3.4.20. We have 𝔄^{ord}_{g,δ} = 𝔍𝔊_{K_{δ,P}} where K_{δ,P} = K^p_δ(K_{δ,p} ∩ P(Q_p)). Proof. Clear from the definition."`; it should be `Replace "locally in the étale topology" with "locally in the fppf topology". The two conditions agree over Z[1/d], so A_{g,δ,Q} = S_{K_δ,Q} is unaffected. With this definition, a point of 𝔄^ord_{g,d} lies in 𝔄^ord_{g,δ} exactly when the étale quotient of the p-primary part of the kernel has type (p^{v_p(δ_i)})_i, and Lemma 3.4.20 becomes the intended statement. The displayed equality 𝔄^ord_{g,d} = ∐_δ 𝔄^ord_{g,δ} must then be read as an equality of underlying topological spaces: for g ≥ 2 it is not an equality of formal schemes (see the reason). Defining A_{g,δ} instead as the schematic closure of A_{g,δ,Q} in A_{g,d} does not work.`. The failure already shows for g = 1 and d = p. The case p | d is the one the paper needs: in 4.1.1 the degrees are d_i = p^{2ng−2in}. Every polarization of degree p² on an elliptic curve is p times the principal one. So δ = (p) is the only type, the kernel is E[p], and A_{1,(p)} should be all of A_{1,p}.

(1) The printed locus is not locally closed. Let E be ordinary over a separably closed field L of characteristic p. Then E[p] ≅ Z/p × μ_p exactly when the connected–étale sequence splits, that is, when E has an étale subgroup C of order p. In that case the dual of E → E/C is purely inseparable of degree p, hence a Frobenius, so E ≅ (E/C)^{(p)} and j(E) ∈ L^p. Conversely, if j(E) = a^p, then E ≅ E'^{(p)} for some E' with j(E') = a, and E'^{(p)} contains the étale group ker V_{E'}.

Now take the generic point of the ordinary locus of the special fibre (on an étale atlas, for example level N ≥ 3 prime to p). Its function field K is separable over F_p(j). A p-th root of j in K^sep would be both separable and purely inseparable over F_p(j), so it would lie in F_p(j). That is impossible, since j ∉ F_p(j^p). So the condition fails at this generic point. It holds at every ordinary closed point, because the residue field is finite and its separable closure is perfect. The locus therefore meets the special fibre in infinitely many closed points but not in the generic point. Such a set is not constructible, so the locus is not a locally closed substack.

(2) The same happens formally. Over the Serre–Tate deformation ring W(k̄)[[t]] of an ordinary point, E[p] is the extension of Z/p by μ_p whose Kummer class is q = 1 + t. This class is not a p-th power even modulo p, since p-th powers in k̄[[t]] are series in t^p. The ring is strictly henselian, so E[p] does not split étale-locally either. As defined, then, 𝔄^{ord}_{1,(p)} contains no formal neighbourhood of any ordinary point. So 𝔄^{ord}_{1,p} = ∐_δ 𝔄^{ord}_{1,δ} fails.

(3) Lemma 3.4.20 fails too. Its right-hand side 𝔍𝔊_{K_{δ,P}} is a smooth formal scheme. Here K_{δ,p} ∩ P(Q_p) = diag(p,1)P(Z_p)diag(p,1)^{-1} is T(Q_p)-conjugate to P(Z_p), so 𝔍𝔊_{K_{δ,P}} is the whole ordinary locus.

(4) With the fppf condition everything works. On the ordinary locus, the p-primary part of the kernel is an extension of an étale group by a multiplicative group, and such an extension splits fppf-locally (extract p-power roots of the Kummer class). The type δ is determined by the étale quotient, which is locally constant. So the loci are open and closed in the ordinary locus, and the decomposition and Lemma 3.4.20 hold.

A_{g,δ} is used later only through these ordinary loci, in the proof of Lemma 3.4.24. The integral models in 3.4.19–3.4.23 and 4.1.1 are normalizations of A_{g,d_i}, not of A_{g,δ}. So correcting the definition changes nothing further. (1) The printed condition fails. Take g = 1 and d = p. A polarization of degree p² on an elliptic curve is p times the principal one, so its kernel is E[p]. Then δ = (p) is the only type, and K_{δ,p} is GL_2(Z_p) conjugated by diag(p,1), so A_{1,(p),Q} = A_{1,p,Q}. On the ordinary locus, E[p] is (étale-locally) an extension of Z/p by μ_p. Since E[p] is killed by p, its class lies in H^1_fppf(R, μ_p), which is R^×/R^{×p} for local R. Over the Serre–Tate deformation ring W(k)[[t]] of an ordinary curve (k = F̄_p), the class is that of q = 1 + t, which is not a p-th power even modulo p. That ring is strictly henselian, so E[p] is not étale-locally ≅ Z/p × μ_p on the formal neighbourhood of any ordinary point.

Over a field k of characteristic p, E[p] splits iff E has an étale subgroup of order p, iff E is a Frobenius twist, iff j(E) ∈ k^p. Separable extensions do not help, because k ∩ (k^sep)^p = k^p. So the condition holds at every closed point of the ordinary locus of A_{1,p} ⊗ F_p (their residue fields are perfect) but fails at its generic point (j is not a p-th power there). The set of points satisfying the printed condition is therefore not constructible, so there is no locally closed substack "where" the condition holds.

Lemma 3.4.20 also fails with the printed definition. Here P is the stabilizer of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩ (p. 33), so K_{δ,p} ∩ P(Q_p) = {(a 0; c d) : a, d ∈ Z_p^×, c ∈ p^{-1}Z_p}. This group is conjugate by diag(1,p) ∈ T(Q_p) to P(Z_p). Hence 𝔍𝔊_{K_{δ,P}} is the whole ordinary locus of 𝔄_{1,1} ≅ 𝔄_{1,p}, which the étale-local locus is not.

(2) Defence. The words work only if the condition is tested at geometric points, where "étale-locally" says nothing, and the locus is given its reduced structure. The text does not say this, and "locally in the étale topology" is a condition on families. The scheme structure matters, because Lemma 3.4.20 compares 𝔄^ord_{g,δ} with a formal scheme. The reference [dJ93] is cited only for A_{g,d}, not for A_{g,δ}.

(3) The fppf repair and what it gives. For g = 1 the class of E[p] dies fppf-locally, so A_{1,(p)} = A_{1,p} minus the supersingular points and Lemma 3.4.20 holds. In general, on 𝔄^ord_{g,d} the p-part K of ker λ is an extension of an étale group K^et by a multiplicative group K^m, and the Weil pairing gives K^m ≅ D(K^et). So each point has a type that can be read from K^et, and the fppf locus is the intended one.

However, such extensions need not split fppf-locally over non-reduced bases: Ext^1(Z/p, μ_p) contains μ_p(R). Also, 𝔄_{g,d} can be non-reduced at ordinary points. Example: g = 2, d = p², and x = (A_0, pλ_0) with A_0 ordinary and λ_0 principal. Put Q(α,β) = q(α, λ_0β), where q is the Serre–Tate parameter. By Katz's lifting criterion, pλ_0 lifts iff Q(e_1,e_2)^p = Q(e_2,e_1)^p. So the complete local ring at x is W[[x_11, x_22, x_12, x_21]]/((1+x_12)^p − (1+x_21)^p). Its reduction mod p is k[[…]]/((x_12 − x_21)^p) (checked by direct computation), which is not reduced. Near x:
- The type-(p,p) locus is x_12 = x_21, the locus where λ_0 itself lifts.
- The fppf type-(1,p²) locus lies in the generic fibre, so it does not meet the p-adic completion.
- Hence ∐_δ 𝔄^ord_{2,δ} ⊊ 𝔄^ord_{2,p²}: the two have the same underlying space but are different formal schemes.

The branches 1+x_12 = ζ(1+x_21) with ζ ≠ 1 carry characteristic-0 polarizations of type (1,p²). So x lies in the closures of both A_{2,(p,p),Q} and A_{2,(1,p²),Q}. With the schematic-closure definition, the ordinary loci would therefore overlap. For p odd, the closure of the type-(1,p²) locus at x is Spf W[[…]]/(((1+x_12)^p − (1+x_21)^p)/(x_12 − x_21)), whose special fibre is k[[…]]/((x_12 − x_21)^{p−1}). So it is not smooth over Z_p there, whereas 𝔍𝔊 is smooth by Prop. 3.4.9(3).

(4) Later use. The decomposition itself is not used later. Lemma 3.4.20 enters only in the proof of Lemma 3.4.24 (p. 40), through the finite maps 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_{p,P}} → ∏ 𝔄^ord_{g,δ_i} with normal source. The fppf version of Lemma 3.4.20 supplies these maps, and normalization ignores nilpotents. So Lemma 3.4.24, Lemma 4.1.7 (p. 41) and Proposition 4.2.4 (p. 43) stand once the definition is corrected. - **Misprint** at §4.1, first line, p. 40. The source says `4.1. The Siegel variety of Iwahori level. Let n ∈ ℤ_{≥0}. Let K_{p,n} ⊆ G(ℚ_p) be the Iwahori subgroup of matrices in G(ℤ_p), reducing modulo p^n to B(ℤ/p^nℤ).`; it should be `Replace "Let n ∈ ℤ_{≥0}" with "Let n ∈ ℤ_{≥1}", i.e. n ≥ 1. No other text needs to change.`. The page image shows "Let n ∈ ℤ_{≥0}" (subscript ≥0), so this is not a text-layer artefact. For n = 0 the definition gives the reduction modulo p^0 = 1 to B(ℤ/ℤ), which is the trivial group. So K_{p,0} = G(ℤ_p), the hyperspecial maximal compact subgroup, not an Iwahori subgroup. Several statements of §4.1 then fail, as checked by direct computation.

(i) Flag and filtration. In §4.1.1 (p. 41), Ker(A_g → A_{g+i}) is a subgroup of A[p^0] = 0. Every H_i and every Gr_i = H_i/H_{i−1} is therefore the trivial group scheme, which is both étale and multiplicative.

(ii) Strata and Remark 4.1.4. For each w ∈ ^MW, the stratum S^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},F_p,w} of §4.1.3 is the locus where Gr_{w^{-1}(i)} is multiplicative for i = g+1, …, 2g. For n = 0 this is the whole special fibre. Remark 4.1.4 (p. 41) says: "Clearly, S^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},F_p,w} is included in the ordinary locus". That is false at n = 0, because the special fibre of the Siegel variety at hyperspecial level has non-ordinary points (for example supersingular ones).

(iii) Lemmas 4.1.6, 4.1.7 and 4.1.9. G(ℤ_p) acts transitively on FL(ℚ_p) = G(ℤ_p)/P(ℤ_p). So for n = 0 every w·K_{p,0} equals FL(ℚ_p). The proof of Lemma 4.1.6 says π_HT^{-1}(FL(ℚ_p)) is the closure of the ordinary locus, but the lemma would make it the closure of S^tor_w, which is the whole space. Lemma 4.1.7 (S^tor_w equals an ordinary Igusa variety) fails for the same reason. The divisors D_i of §4.1.8 are all zero (D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^0)), so Lemma 4.1.9 gives the whole special fibre for every w. That contradicts Remark 4.1.4 again.

(iv) The rest of the paper also needs n ≥ 1:
- The Casselman algebra map t ↦ [K_{p,n} t K_{p,n}] of §4.2 (p. 43) needs a subgroup with an Iwahori decomposition.
- Remark 4.1.2 takes n = 1 as the usual Iwahori level.
- The support conditions deg H_{g+i} ≥ n(w_i − ε) of §6.1.8 (p. 60) are empty conditions when n = 0.

So the authors clearly mean n ≥ 1, and ℤ_{≥0} is a slip in the range. No later result needs K_{p,0}. The other statements that allow n ∈ ℤ_{≥0} (Theorem 1.4.3 (4),(5) on p. 5, Theorem 5.1.4 on p. 53) use a different parameter: a congruence level for T_{K_p}, or reduction modulo p^n. They do not use the group K_{p,n} of §4.1. Correcting the range therefore changes nothing downstream. The published Springer text could not be compared. The page image shows "ℤ_{≥0}", so this is not an extraction artefact.

Defence tried. Could n = 0 be a harmless degenerate case, or be excluded by the words "the Iwahori subgroup"? At n = 0 the condition is reduction modulo p^0 = 1 into B(ℤ/ℤ), which is trivial, so K_{p,0} = G(ℤ_p). This is the hyperspecial maximal compact subgroup, not an Iwahori subgroup. The phrase "the Iwahori subgroup", the title of §4.1 and Remark 4.1.2 ("When n = 1, S^tor_{K^pK_{p,1}} is the usual integral model of Iwahori level") all show that the authors mean n ≥ 1. So the range ℤ_{≥0} is a slip, not a deliberate inclusion. At n = 0 the statements of §4 are not vacuous; they are false:
- p. 41: Ker(A_g → A_{g+i}) ⊆ A[p^0] = 0. So every H_i and every Gr_i is the trivial group scheme, which is both étale and multiplicative. By §4.1.3, the stratum S^tor_{K^pK_{p,0},F_p,w} is then the whole special fibre for every w. This contradicts Remark 4.1.4 ("Clearly, S^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},F_p,w} is included in the ordinary locus"), because the special fibre at hyperspecial level has non-ordinary (e.g. supersingular) points.
- G(ℤ_p) acts transitively on FL(ℚ_p). So w·K_{p,0} = FL(ℚ_p) for every w, and Lemmas 4.1.6 and 4.1.7 fail for the same reason.
- By §4.1.8, "D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n)" becomes the zero divisor, so every D_i = 0. In Proposition 4.1.13 (2), every Z_i and V(p^{nj}) is then 0. So S̃_{=j_1,…,=j_k} is the whole space even when some j_i − j_{i−1} ∉ {0,1}, although (2) says it is then empty.
- §4.2, p. 43: the map t ↦ [K_{p,n} t K_{p,n}] from [Cas] lem. 4.1.5 is an algebra map only for groups with an Iwahori decomposition. For g = 1 at level GL_2(ℤ_p), with t = diag(1,p), one has [KtK]^2 = [Kt^2K] + (p+1)[K pI K] (degrees (p+1)^2 = (p^2+p) + (p+1), checked by direct computation). So the map is not multiplicative.
- Proof of Proposition 6.1.11, p. 61: it uses "the Iwahori decomposition K_{p,n} = B_{K_{p,n}} × U^{op}_{K_{p,n}}". G(ℤ_p) has no such decomposition: U(ℤ_p)T(ℤ_p)Ū(ℤ_p) misses the Weyl element. The same proof also pulls back ]X_{w,F_p}[, which is K_{p,n}-stable for n ≥ 1 but not G(ℤ_p)-stable.

Nothing later uses n = 0. Every later use of K_{p,n} relies on the flag H_i, the divisors D_i or the Iwahori decomposition:
- §4.2–4.5;
- the Nebentypus of §4.3.5;
- §6.1.8–6.1.11 (whose conditions deg H_{g+i} ≥ n(w_i − ε) are empty at n = 0);
- §6.2.

The other places where the paper writes "n ∈ ℤ_{≥0}" use a different parameter:
- Theorem 1.4.3 (4),(5), p. 5: the conductor of T_{K_p}, where K_p must admit an Iwahori decomposition, which G(ℤ_p) does not;
- Theorem 5.1.4, p. 53: reduction modulo p^n.

So these statements never involve K_{p,0}. The corrected range n ≥ 1 is right and minimal, and no stated result or proof changes. (§4.1.1, p. 41; wording and exponents checked on the page image)`; it should be `"... equipped with a polarization of degree p^{2ng−2in} = d_i² for 1 ≤ i ≤ g", so d_i = p^{n(g−i)}. The map is then S_{K^pK_{p,n},ℚ} → ∏_{i=0}^{g} A_{g,p^{n(g−i)}}, with d_0 = 1 as printed (the i = 0 factor uses the principal polarization of A itself).`. On p. 40 (§3.4.19) the paper says: "We let A_{g,d} → Spec Z be the moduli stack of abelian varieties of dimension g, with a degree d² polarization (see [dJ93]). For any δ = (δ_1, …, δ_g) ∈ Z^g_{≥0} with (δ_1 | δ_2 | ⋯ | δ_g) and ∏_{i=1}^g δ_i = d …". The kernel is then locally ∏ Z/δ_iZ × μ_{δ_i}, of order d². So in the paper, "degree" means the order of the kernel, and the index d of A_{g,d} is its square root.

Recomputed directly: H_{g+i} = Ker(A_g → A_{g+i}) is a totally isotropic subgroup of A[p^n], locally isomorphic to (Z/p^nZ)^i, so it has order p^{ni}. The polarization λ_{g+i} on A_{g+i} = A/H_{g+i} comes from descending p^nλ, so π^∨ ∘ λ_{g+i} ∘ π = p^nλ. Taking degrees gives p^{ni} · deg λ_{g+i} · p^{ni} = p^{2ng}, so deg λ_{g+i} = p^{2n(g−i)}. Equivalently, its kernel H_{g+i}^⊥/H_{g+i} has order p^{2ng−ni}/p^{ni}. The kernel is locally (Z/p^nZ)^{g−i} × μ_{p^n}^{g−i}, so the type is δ = (1, …, 1, p^n, …, p^n), with i ones and g−i entries equal to p^n, and ∏δ_j = p^{n(g−i)}.

So the printed degree p^{2ng−2in} is right, but it equals d_i², not d_i. The point (A_{g+i}, λ_{g+i}) lies in A_{g,p^{n(g−i)}}. Read literally, d_i = p^{2n(g−i)} would require a polarization with ∏δ_j = p^{2n(g−i)}, and there is no natural one. An integer multiple mλ_{g+i} has ∏δ_j = m^g p^{n(g−i)}, which fails already for g = 2, i = 1, n = 1, since m² = p has no integer solution. The two readings agree only for i = g, where d_g = 1, and for i = 0, where d_0 = 1 is set separately. The text layer is not the cause: the page image shows the same "p^{2ng−2in} = d_i" and "A_{g,d_i}".

No later result depends on this. The d_i only name the auxiliary spaces A_{g,d_i} used in the normalization that defines the integral model. Remark 3.4.21 already says the model depends on these auxiliary choices. The later statements (Remark 4.1.2, Lemma 4.1.7 via Lemma 3.4.24, Proposition 4.1.13) use only the chain of isogenies, the flag H_i, and the independence of the ordinary locus from the choices. Equivalently, read indices mod 2g with H_0 := H_{2g}, and take H_g to mean 0 = Ker(A_g → A_g) when it sits at the start of the chain, as in the paper's own sentence "For 0 ≤ i ≤ g, the group Ker(A_g → A_{g+i}) …" with i = 0.`. I checked the text against the rendered page. The flag is indexed g+1, …, 2g, 1, …, g, and the same sentence states explicitly that A[p^n] = H_g. Read literally, "Gr_i = H_i/H_{i−1}" fails at two indices. (a) At i = g+1 it gives H_{g+1}/H_g = H_{g+1}/A[p^n]. That is not a quotient, because A[p^n] is not contained in H_{g+1}. (b) At i = 1 it gives H_1/H_0, and H_0 is never defined in the paper.

The intended meaning is clear from the next sentence, which says every Gr_i has order p^n and Gr_{2g−i+1} = Gr_i^D. I checked both claims by direct computation with the corrected convention. H_{g+j} has order p^{nj} and H_j has order p^{n(g+j)}, so every step of the flag has order p^n. The flag is self-dual: H_{g+j}^⊥ = H_{g−j}, and H_{2g−i+1}^⊥ = H_{i−1}. The Weil pairing then gives H_i/H_{i−1} = H_{2g−i}^⊥/H_{2g−i+1}^⊥ ≅ (H_{2g−i+1}/H_{2g−i})^D. The endpoint cases also check out. For i = 1: Gr_1 = H_1/H_{2g} = H_{2g−1}^⊥/H_{2g}^⊥ ≅ Gr_{2g}^D. For i = g: Gr_g = A[p^n]/H_{g−1} = A[p^n]/H_{g+1}^⊥ ≅ H_{g+1}^D = Gr_{g+1}^D.

The revision changed the wording to "the generically étale finite flat group scheme Gr_i as in [Far10], sect. 2, déf. 3". (it affects the proof). The source says `p. 41, before 4.1.3: "We let 0 ⊆ H_{g+1} ⊆ H_{g+2} ⊆ ··· ⊆ H_{2g} = H_{2g}^⊥ ⊆ H_1 ⊆ H_2 ⊆ ··· ⊆ A[p^n] = H_g be the full flag of subgroups of A[p^n], given by the kernel of the maps A → A_{g+i}, and we let Gr_i = H_i/H_{i−1}. They are finite flat group scheme of order p^n over the interior of the Shimura variety and Gr_{2g−i+1} = Gr_i^D." p. 41, 4.1.8: "Cartier divisors. For all 1 ≤ i ≤ 2g, we let D_i be the effective Cartier divisor on S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n}} associated to the generically étale finite flat group scheme Gr_i as in [Far10], sect. 2, déf. 3. The complement of D_i is the locus where Gr_i is étale. We have D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n) ([Far10], sect. 2, lem. 3)." p. 47, proof of Lemma 4.3.6: "We first argue that the group schemes Gr_i extend to finite flat group schemes over S^{tor}_{Z_p(ζ_{p^n})} \ Σ_{i=1}^d D_i ∩ D_{2g+1−i}."`; it should be `Over the whole of S^tor, let Gr_i be the kernel of the i-th isogeny f_i: A_{i−1} → A_i in the chain of semi-abelian schemes from p. 41, which comes from [FC90], I, 2.7. This kernel is quasi-finite and flat but in general not finite, and over the interior it equals H_i/H_{i−1}. Define D_i as the divisor of the determinant of its co-Lie complex [ω_{A_i} → ω_{A_{i−1}}], that is, the zero locus of det Lie(f_i). This is essentially the preprint's formulation. - D_i is an effective Cartier divisor, because S^tor is normal and Z_p-flat and det Lie(f_i) becomes invertible once p is inverted. - On the interior it is Fargues' divisor. - Its complement is the locus where f_i, equivalently Gr_i, is étale. The identity D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n) needs its own argument at the boundary. It holds on the interior by [Far10], and both sides are trivial on the generic fibre. Since S^tor is normal, it follows on all of S^tor once one knows that no irreducible component of the special fibre lies in the boundary. Alternatively, it follows from a local computation with the Raynaud extension, splitting into torus, abelian and étale parts. This density statement, or the local computation, should be stated and justified. Taking the schematic closure of the divisor on the interior would not be enough on its own, because one would still have to show that the closure is Cartier.`. Fargues' construction ([Far10], sect. 2) attaches an effective Cartier divisor to a generically étale finite locally free group scheme. The paper states only that Gr_i is finite flat over the interior (p. 41). Near the boundary, Gr_i is a subquotient of kernels of isogenies of semi-abelian schemes. Such a kernel is only quasi-finite flat, and in general Gr_i admits no finite flat extension at all. So 4.1.8 applies a construction outside its hypotheses and gives no argument at the boundary. Checked by direct computation for g = 1:

(1) n = 1, at the cusp where A = Tate(q) and H_2 = μ_p. Here A_2 = Tate(q^p), and the second step Tate(q^p) → Tate(q) is the quotient by ⟨q⟩. Its kernel Gr_1 has order p for q ≠ 0. On the boundary fibre q = 0 the map is the identity of G_m, so the kernel is trivial there. The order drops from p to 1, so Gr_1 is quasi-finite flat but not finite. In this case a different finite flat extension (the constant group Z/p) happens to exist.

(2) n = 2, at a cusp where H_2 ∩ μ_{p^2} = μ_p. H_2 = Gr_2 is cyclic of order p^2, generated by x = u·q^{1/p} with u a primitive p^2-th root of unity. It is defined over Q_p(ζ_p)((q)). The cusp has width 1: A/H_2 ≅ Tate(u^p q), and near the cusp S^tor is Z_p[ζ_p][[q]], with q a local equation of the boundary. The automorphism q^{1/p} ↦ ζ_p q^{1/p} fixing u lies in the inertia at q = 0 and sends x to ζ_p x = x^{1+pk} ≠ x. So Gr_2 is ramified along the boundary. It therefore has no finite flat extension even at the characteristic-0 boundary points, since there such an extension would be finite étale and hence unramified.

The divisors are then used on the boundary: in Lemma 4.1.9 and Proposition 4.1.13, in the normality argument of Corollary 4.2.10, and in Lemma 4.3.6. The proof of Lemma 4.3.6 has to show separately that the Gr_i extend to finite flat group schemes off Σ D_i ∩ D_{2g+1−i}. This confirms that no such extension was available when D_i was defined. The missing step is routine: use the determinant of f_i^* on invariant differentials of the semi-abelian schemes, which is essentially the preprint's co-Lie-complex definition applied to the quasi-finite kernel, together with a codimension-one argument. After this repair no stated result changes. The paper says itself (p. 41) that the Gr_i are finite flat only over the interior. §4.1.8 then defines D_i on the toroidal compactification by Fargues' construction for finite flat group schemes, and cites Fargues' Cartier-duality lemma for D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n). Neither applies at the boundary. There the groups H_i/H_{i−1} are kernels of isogenies of semi-abelian schemes: they are quasi-finite and flat, not finite, and Gr_{2g+1−i} = Gr_i^D no longer makes sense.

Example, g = n = 1 (the modular curve X_0(p)). At the cusp 0, with parameter q^{1/p}, the subgroup ⟨q^{1/p}⟩ of the Tate curve G_m/q^Z has trivial fibre at the cusp, so it is not finite. The proof of Lemma 4.3.6 (p. 47) has to build finite flat extensions of the Gr_i by hand, which shows the authors know this.

Defence. The definition itself extends routinely. The paper constructs the chain of isogenies f_i of semi-abelian schemes over S^tor just before §4.1.8. The co-Lie complex of the kernel of an isogeny of smooth commutative group schemes is [ω_{A_i} → ω_{A_{i−1}}] with or without finiteness, so D_i := V(det Lie f_i) is defined on all of S^tor and has the stated étale-locus property. The 2024 preprint phrased §4.1.8 in exactly this co-Lie form. In the example, near the cusp 0:
- the isogeny E_q → E_{q^{1/p}} is the identity on G_m at the cusp, so D_2 is empty there;
- the isogeny E_{q^{1/p}} → E_q is x ↦ x^p, with kernel μ_p, so D_1 = V(p);
- hence D_1 + D_2 = V(p). A direct computation gives the same at the cusp ∞.

So the stated properties are true. What is missing is the boundary step for D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n), where Fargues' lemma does not apply. The natural argument is Hartogs on the normal scheme S^tor. It needs the codimension-1 points of the special fibre to lie in the interior, which the paper never states. The paper assumes the same thing implicitly in the proof of Corollary 4.2.10 (p. 45): it reduces to generic points of the special fibre and treats the group schemes there as finite flat. So this is a genuine but fillable gap. It is not a false statement.

Uses. Every later result relies on the D_i near the boundary:
- Lemma 4.1.9 (its proof also uses Gr_{2g+1−i} = Gr_i^D);
- the blow-up of Proposition 4.1.13, whose proof uses D_g + D_{g+1} = V(p^n), for example to get Z_{1,<1} = D_g;
- Corollary 4.1.14 and the filtration in 4.1.16–4.1.18;
- Lemma 4.2.12, which begins "Granting that D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = (p^n)";
- Lemma 4.2.13 and Propositions 4.2.14 and 4.2.15;
- Lemma 4.3.6, Propositions 4.3.11 and 4.3.13, and Lemma 4.3.16;
- the divisors D_{w,±} in §§4.4–4.5, and so the control theorem 4.5.2.

All of these survive once the extension is justified, so the gap is in the proof, not in any stated result. - **Error** at §1.4, Theorem 1.4.8, p. 5. The body version is Theorem 5.5.2, p. 57: "We have a perfect pairing M^•_w ⊗ M^•_{w_{0,M}ww_0,cusp} → Λ[−d], for which the adjoint of t is w_0t^{−1}". Here the tensor has no subscript and the Λ-structure is not specified. The 2024 preprint has the same text: Theorem 1.4.8 on p. 5, which differs only in reading "for some prime ℓ ≠ p", and Theorem 5.5.2 on p. 56. The mistake was therefore already in the preprint and was not fixed in the revision. (it affects a stated result). The source says `Theorem 1.4.8 (Serre duality 5.5.1). There is a perfect pairing M^•_w ⊗_Λ M^•_{w_{0,M}ww_0,cusp} → Λ[−d], for which the adjoint of t ∈ T(Q_p) is w_0t^{−1} and the adjoint of [K_ℓgK_ℓ] is [K_ℓg^{−1}K_ℓ] for any prime ℓ ≠ p such that K_ℓ = G(Z_ℓ) and g ∈ G(Q_ℓ). This pairing is compatible with the classical Serre duality when specializing to locally algebraic dominant weights.`; it should be `Twist the Λ-structure of the second factor by the involution ι of Λ = Z_p[[T(Z_p)]] induced by t ↦ w_0t^{−1}. For GSp_{2g} this involution is t ↦ c(t)^{−1}t, where c is the similitude character. The corrected statement is: there is a perfect pairing M^•_w ⊗_Λ ι^*M^•_{w_{0,M}ww_0,cusp} → Λ[−d]. Equivalently, ⟨λx, y⟩ = ⟨x, ι(λ)y⟩ = λ⟨x, y⟩, so that M^•_{w_{0,M}ww_0,cusp} ≅ ι^*RHom_Λ(M^•_w, Λ)[−d]. The adjoint of t ∈ T(Q_p) is w_0t^{−1}, as printed. In the compatibility clause, the first factor is specialized at ν and the second at ν∘ι: the weights (κ, χ) and (−w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc, w_0χ^{−1}) of Theorem 5.5.1. The same reading should be given to the unsubscripted ⊗ of Theorem 5.5.2.`. 1. The paper defines M^•_w and M^•_{w,cusp} for every w by the same formula, RHom_{T(Z_p)}(1, RΓ_w(K^p, cusp/∅) ⊗̂_{Z_p} Λ) (p. 5 and §5.4, p. 56). On these invariants, the action of t ∈ T(Z_p) through the cohomology factor equals multiplication by a fixed unit λ_t ∈ Λ, which is [t] or [t]^{−1} depending on the convention for the T(Z_p)-action on Λ. The same recipe gives the same λ_t for every w. For central t the twist of the T(Q_p)-action by w (p. 55) plays no role.

2. Take z = a·1_{2g} central with a ∈ Z_p^×. Then w_0z^{−1} = z^{−1}. The notation ⊗_Λ means the pairing is balanced, so ⟨zx, y⟩ = ⟨λ_z x, y⟩ = ⟨x, λ_z y⟩. The stated adjoint rule gives instead ⟨zx, y⟩ = ⟨x, z^{−1}y⟩ = ⟨x, λ_z^{−1}y⟩. The pairing is perfect, so λ_z² − 1 would act as zero on M^•_w, and its specialization at any ν with ν(z)² ≠ 1 would vanish. By Proposition 1.4.7 (p. 5) that specialization is the classical ordinary cohomology RΓ(S^tor, ω^κ)^ord ⊗ Q_p(ζ_{p^n})[χ]. This group is not zero for all weights whose central character has infinite order: for example, with g = 1 and w = Id, ordinary cusp forms exist in infinitely many such weights. So the pairing cannot be both Λ-balanced and have adjoint w_0t^{−1}.

3. The paper's own finite-level statement gives the same conclusion. Theorem 5.5.1 (p. 57) pairs RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ) with RΓ_{w_{0,M}ww_0}(K^p, −w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc, w_0χ^{−1}, cusp). Here κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν_alg + ρ) − ρ (p. 56). Using w_{0,M}ρ = −ρ_c + ρ_nc and w_0ρ = −ρ, the partner weight corresponds to the character ν' = (−w_0ν_alg)·(w_0χ^{−1}) = ν∘ι. This was checked by direct computation for g = 1, 2, 3 and every w in the Weyl group. On the centre, ν' = ν^{−1}. A Λ-bilinear pairing M ⊗_Λ N → Λ[−d] specializes at ν to a pairing of the two specializations at the same ν, which is not the classical duality.

4. The correction is consistent with both facts. Under ι, ⟨λ_z x, y⟩ = ⟨x, λ_{ι(z)}y⟩ = ⟨x, (w_0z^{−1})y⟩, and the specialization of ι^*N at ν equals the specialization of N at ν∘ι. The formula ι(t) = c(t)^{−1}t for GSp_{2g} was also checked by direct computation. 1. How T(Z_p) acts. Both factors are defined in the same way (p. 5; §5.4, p. 56): M^•_w = RHom_{T(Z_p)}(1, RΓ_w(K^p) ⊗̂_{Z_p} Λ), where T(Z_p) acts diagonally, and M^•_{w,cusp} is defined in the same way. T(Q_p) acts through its action on RΓ_w(K^p). This is the action used in every "T(Q_p)-equivariant" statement and in the diamond operators of Proposition 1.4.7. On the diagonal invariants, t ∈ T(Z_p) acting on the first factor is the same as multiplication by the unit [t]^{−1} ∈ Λ. So on M^•_w and on M^•_{w',cusp} (w' = w_{0,M}ww_0), every t ∈ T(Z_p) ⊂ T(Q_p) acts by the same scalar of Λ.

2. What a Λ-balanced pairing forces. If the pairing is balanced over Λ with these structures, then ⟨[t]^{−1}x, y⟩ = ⟨x, [t]^{−1}y⟩, so each t ∈ T(Z_p) is its own adjoint.

3. Why this contradicts the adjoint clause. Use the conventions of §3.1 (p. 33): W is the set of permutations w with w(i) + w(2g+1−i) = 2g+1, and T = {diag(t_i) : t_i t_{2g+1−i} = c}. Then w_0 is i ↦ 2g+1−i, so w_0(t) = c(t)t^{−1} and w_0t^{−1} = c(t)^{−1}t. For a scalar z ∈ Z(Z_p) we get w_0z^{−1} = z^{−1} ≠ z. Combining step 2 with the stated adjoint gives ⟨x, ([z] − [z]^{−1})y⟩ = 0 for all x, y. Since the pairing is perfect, [z]^2 − 1 would annihilate the cohomology of M^•_{w',cusp}. Its specializations would then vanish at every weight ν with ν(z)^2 ≠ 1. By Proposition 1.4.7 (the cuspidal case), these specializations are classical ordinary coherent cohomology, which is nonzero in weights with nontrivial central weight. For example, take g = 1, w = Id and w' = w_0: the specializations are Serre-dual to ordinary cusp forms, whose central characters vary with the weight.

4. The paper's own Theorem 5.5.1 (p. 57) points the same way. It pairs weight (κ, χ) of w with weight (−w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc, w_0χ^{−1}) of w'. Write κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν+ρ) − ρ and use w_{0,M}ρ = ρ_nc − ρ_M and −w_0ρ = ρ. Then −w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc = −w_{0,M}w'(ν'+ρ) − ρ with ν' = −w_0ν, that is, ν'(t) = ν(w_0t^{−1}). This identity was checked by direct computation for all w ∈ W when g = 1, 2, 3. The finite part matches as well: χ' = w_0χ^{−1} = χ∘ι. So the dual factor is the specialization of M^•_{w'} at ν∘ι, not at ν. In the coordinates of §3.1, ι fixes the k_i and changes k to −k. A ⊗_Λ pairing specializes both factors at the same point, so it can agree with Theorem 5.5.1, as the last sentence of Theorem 1.4.8 claims, only at weights that are trivial on the centre.

5. The defence fails. The Λ-structure on M^• is fixed by its definition, and nothing in the paper twists it on the second factor. A reading in which T(Z_p) acts trivially on M^• contradicts the T(Q_p)-action the paper uses. Theorem 5.5.1, the specialized statement, is correct. The proof of Theorem 5.5.2 "as in the previous theorem" produces the ι-twisted pairing, so the fix is the twist.

6. What depends on it. Remark 5.6.2 and the length-two case in the proof of Proposition 5.6.3 (p. 58, "prove the dual statement for the non-cuspidal cohomology") use the duality only for amplitudes, checked at all residual characters. ι^* is an exact autoequivalence of perfect Λ-complexes: it preserves amplitude and permutes the residual characters. So these arguments are unaffected. Remark 6.2.18 uses the duality of Lemma 5.4.2, not Serre duality. The Hecke operators t ∉ T(Z_p) and the prime-to-p adjoints are unaffected. Only the statement of Theorem 1.4.8, and the unsubscripted Theorem 5.5.2 if read as Λ-bilinear, needs correcting. - **Error** at §4.1.12, Proposition 4.1.13(2) and its proof, p. 42 (it affects a stated result). The source says `(2) For any increasing sequence j_1 ≤ ··· ≤ j_k, we can consider the open subset S̃^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n},=j_1,···,=j_k} = ∩_{i=1}^k Z^c_{i,>j_i} ∩ Z^c_{i,<j_i} of S̃^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n}}. This open subset is empty unless j_i − j_{i−1} ∈ {0,1} (where j_0 = 0 by convention). The map S̃^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n},=j_1,···,=j_k} → S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n}} is an open immersion, and the image of S̃^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n},=j_1,···,=j_k} identifies with the open sub-scheme where Gr_{g+i} is multiplicative if j_i − j_{i−1} = 1, and étale if j_i − j_{i−1} = 0. [Proof, same page: "... and Z_{k+1,>j} = S̃^{tor}_{k,=j_1,···,=j_k} for j < j_k, Z_{k+1,<j} = S̃^{tor}_{k,=j_1,···,=j_k} for j > j_k + 1."]`; it should be `Replace "This open subset is empty unless j_i − j_{i−1} ∈ {0,1}" with "Its special fibre S̃^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n},=j_1,…,=j_k} ×_{Spec Z_p} Spec F_p (equivalently, the corresponding open formal subscheme of the p-adic completion) is empty unless j_i − j_{i−1} ∈ {0,1} (j_0 = 0)". An equivalent form: when the condition fails, the open subset equals the preimage of the generic fibre S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n},Q_p}. That preimage is never empty. The proof needs the same qualification. On S̃_{k,=j_1,…,=j_k}, the "equalities" Z_{k+1,>j} = S̃_{k,=j_1,…,=j_k} (for j < j_k) and Z_{k+1,<j} = S̃_{k,=j_1,…,=j_k} (for j > j_k+1) hold only as equalities of supports inside the special fibre. There, Z_{k+1,>j} = V(p^{n(j_k−j)}) + D_{g+k+1} and Z_{k+1,<j} = V(p^{n(j−j_k−1)}) + D_{g−k}. This is the smallest change that is correct. The rest of (2) and all of (3) can stay as printed.`. The printed text is confirmed on the page image of p. 42. Here S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n}} is a normal scheme over Spec Z_p whose generic fibre is non-empty (§4.1.1, p. 41, following §3.4.23, p. 40). S̃^{tor} is a blow-up of it. The proposition calls S̃_{=j_1,…,=j_k} an open subset of S̃^{tor} and says it maps to S^{tor} by an open immersion. Corollary 4.1.14 takes "× Spec F_p" as a separate step. So the paper has no convention under which "empty" refers only to the special fibre.

(a) Every Z lies in the special fibre. Section 4.1.8 (p. 41) gives D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n) with both divisors effective. So supp D_i ⊆ V(p), and the same holds for every Z_i = Σ_{l≤i} D_{g+l}. On the generic fibre, V(p^{nj}) is also empty. By (1), Z_{i,>j} and Z_{i,<j} have disjoint supports and Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}). This difference restricts to 0 on the generic fibre. If two effective divisors are equal and have disjoint supports, both are 0. So every Z_{i,>j} and Z_{i,<j} is supported in the special fibre. The blow-up also changes nothing over the generic fibre, because the ideals (O(−Z_{k+1}), O(−V(p^{nj}))) are the unit ideal there. Hence every S̃_{=j_1,…,=j_k} contains the preimage of the generic fibre, which is isomorphic to S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n},Q_p} and so non-empty.

(b) A counterexample. Take g ≥ 2, k = 2 and (j_1, j_2) = (0, 2). This sequence is admissible (j_i ≤ i as (1) requires) and has j_2 − j_1 = 2. By (a) the open set is non-empty, so the printed claim is false. For g = 1 the claim is vacuous.

(c) The special-fibre version holds (checked by direct computation). On the open set, Z_{i,>j_i} and Z_{i,<j_i} are both absent, so Z_i = V(p^{nj_i}) there for i ≤ k (with Z_0 = 0 and j_0 = 0). Hence D_{g+i} = V(p^{n(j_i−j_{i−1})}) and D_{g+1−i} = V(p^n) − D_{g+i} = V(p^{n(1−(j_i−j_{i−1}))}). If j_i − j_{i−1} ≥ 2, this effective divisor would have local equation p^{−n(d−1)} with d − 1 ≥ 1. That is impossible at any point where p is not a unit. So the special fibre of the open set is empty. The inductive step of the proof needs only that the blow-up is an isomorphism over S̃_{k,=j_1,…,=j_k}. That holds, because there Z_{k+1} − V(p^{nj}) is effective for j ≤ j_k and anti-effective for j ≥ j_k+1.

(d) Nothing downstream uses the literal claim. Corollary 4.1.14 (p. 42) base-changes to F_p. The filtration F_i of §4.1.16 and Lemma 4.1.18 (p. 43) live inside S^{tor}_{F_p}. Lemma 4.2.11 (p. 44) uses only the disjoint supports in (1). So the stated result is wrong as printed, but the proof and later results are unaffected. A separate index slip appears in the same proof: "−D_{g−k−1} = −Z_{k+1,<j_k+1}" should read −D_{g−k}, as in statement (3), since D_{g+k+1} + D_{g−k} = V(p^n). No convention in the paper saves the printed claim. Section 4.1.1 (p. 41) defines S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n}} as a scheme over Spec Z_p: a normalization of an object that lives over Q_p. Its p-adic formal completion is introduced separately in §4.1.5. The proposition speaks of a blow-up of this scheme, of an "open subset", of an open immersion and of an "open sub-scheme". Corollary 4.1.14 (p. 42) takes "× Spec F_p" as a separate step, which shows that S̃_{=w_1,…,=w_g} is not itself inside the special fibre.

(a) Every divisor involved lies in the special fibre. Section 4.1.8 (p. 41) gives D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n) with both divisors effective, so supp D_i ⊆ V(p). The 2024 preprint says it outright on p. 40: D_i is "supported on the special fiber". Hence every Z_i and every V(p^{nj}) is supported in V(p). By (1), Z_{i,>j} and Z_{i,<j} are effective with disjoint supports, and Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}). This difference restricts to 0 on the generic fibre. Two equal effective divisors with disjoint supports are both 0, so Z_{i,>j} and Z_{i,<j} are also supported in V(p). The ideals blown up are generated by O(−Z_{k+1}) and O(−V(p^{nj})), and these are the unit ideal on the generic fibre. So the blow-up is an isomorphism there. Therefore every S̃_{=j_1,…,=j_k} contains the preimage of S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n},Q_p}, which is non-empty.

(b) A counterexample. Take g ≥ 2, k = 2 and (j_1, j_2) = (0, 2). This sequence is allowed, because (1) only requires 0 ≤ j_i ≤ i. It has j_2 − j_1 = 2, yet by (a) the open subset is non-empty. For g = 1 the claim is vacuous.

(c) The special-fibre version is true (checked by direct computation). On U = S̃_{=j_1,…,=j_k}, the divisors Z_{i,>j_i} and Z_{i,<j_i} restrict to 0. Hence Z_i|_U = V(p^{nj_i}) for i ≤ k (with Z_0 = 0 and j_0 = 0). Therefore D_{g+i}|_U = V(p^{nd}) with d = j_i − j_{i−1}, and D_{g+1−i}|_U = V(p^n) − V(p^{nd}). If d ≥ 2, the local equation h of this effective divisor satisfies h·p^{n(d−1)} = unit, where p is a non-zero-divisor because everything is Z_p-flat. So p is invertible on U, and U lies over the generic fibre. The proof's intended mechanism gives the same result. On S̃_{k,=j_1,…,=j_k}, the divisor Z_{k+1,>j} (for j < j_k), respectively Z_{k+1,<j} (for j > j_k+1), has support equal to the whole special fibre of that open set, so the next open set misses the special fibre. The rest of the proposition is correct on the whole scheme. That includes the open immersion, the description of the image (in characteristic 0 every finite flat group scheme is both étale and multiplicative) and item (3).

(d) What later uses the passage. Nothing uses the false emptiness claim. The only later use of the sets S̃_{=j} is Corollary 4.1.14 (p. 42). It takes the sequence (w_1,…,w_g) of w ∈ ^MW, which by the end of §3.1 has jumps in {0,1}, and it uses only the image description, followed by base change to F_p. The filtration F_i of §4.1.16, Lemma 4.1.17 and Lemma 4.1.18 (p. 43) live in S^{tor}_{F_p}, where the corrected statement holds. Lemma 4.2.11 (p. 44) and the argument of §5 use only the disjoint supports in (1). Proposition 6.2.2, whose proof is "identical to the proof of proposition 4.1.13", makes no emptiness claim. So a numbered result is false as printed, but nothing that depends on it is harmed.

A separate slip sits in the same proof: "Z_{k+1} − V(p^{n(j_k+1)}) = −D_{g−k−1}" should read −D_{g−k}, as statement (3) has it, since D_{g+k+1} + D_{g−k} = V(p^n). - **Error** at Section 4.1.12, Proposition 4.1.13 (2) and its proof, p. 42. The 2024 preprint has the same statement and proof (Proposition 4.1.13, p. 40). (it affects a stated result). The map S̃^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},=j_1,···,=j_k} → S^tor_{K^pK_{p,n}} is an open immersion, and the image of S̃^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},=j_1,···,=j_k} identifies with the open sub-scheme where Gr_{g+i} is multiplicative if j_i − j_{i−1} = 1, and étale if j_i − j_{i−1} = 0. [The proof ends:] It follows that the map S̃^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},k+1} → S̃^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},k} induces an isomorphism S̃^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},k+1} ×_{S̃^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},k}} S̃^tor_{k,=j_1,···,=j_k} → S̃^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},k,=j_1,···,=j_k}.`; it should be `In (2), the claim that S̃^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},=j_1,…,=j_k} → S^tor_{K^pK_{p,n}} is an open immersion onto the stated open is true for the final blow-up S̃^tor_{K^pK_{p,n}} = S̃^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},g} only when k = g or k = g − 1. For general k, it holds once S̃^tor_{K^pK_{p,n}} is replaced by the k-th stage S̃^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},k} of the tower built in the proof; this is what the induction actually proves. For g ≥ 3 and k ≤ g − 2 it can fail on the final blow-up; a counterexample is g = 3, n = 1, k = 1, j_1 = 0. Three things stay true for every k: the set-theoretic image, the emptiness assertion (read in the special fibre), and parts (1) and (3), with pulled-back divisors. Later the paper uses only the case k = g: in Corollary 4.1.14, and in Proposition 6.2.2(3), whose proof is said to be identical. So no later result is affected.`. This reads Z_k = Σ_{i=1}^k D_{g+i}, as in the proof. At each step the induction proves only that S̃_{k+1} → S̃_k is an isomorphism over S̃_{k,=j_1,…,=j_k}. That gives (2) on S̃_k, and on the final blow-up S̃ = S̃_g only for k ≥ g−1. The later blow-ups, along O(−Z_{k'}) and p^{nj} with k' ≥ k+2, need not be isomorphisms over this locus.

Counterexample: g = 3, n = 1 (the Iwahori model), k = 1, j_1 = 0.
- Since Z_{1,>0} = D_4 and Z_{1,<0} = 0, the set S̃_{=0} is the preimage in S̃ = S̃_3 of U = S^tor \ D_4, the locus where Gr_4 is étale.
- On U we have Z_2 = D_5 and Z_3 = D_5 + D_6. Locally write D_5 = V(x_5), D_6 = V(x_6) and D_2 = V(y_5). Then x_5·y_5 = p·(unit), because D_5 + D_2 = V(p).
- The ideals (x_5, p^j) are principal, so S̃_2 → S is an isomorphism over U.
- At the third stage, for j = 1, the ideal is (x_5x_6, p) = x_5·(x_6, y_5).

Now take the point P given by A = E × E_1 × E_2 with the product principal polarization. Here E is ordinary, E_1 and E_2 are supersingular, and K_i ⊂ E_i[p] is the subgroup of order p. The flag is:
- H_4 = E[p]^ét,
- H_5 = H_4 × K_1,
- H_6 = H_4 × K_1 × K_2, which is Lagrangian,
- H_1 = H_4 × K_1 × E_2[p],
- H_2 = H_4 × E_1[p] × E_2[p].

Gr_4 is étale, so P ∈ U. Move (E_1,K_1) and (E_2,K_2) along the two components of the special fibre of Y_0(p), which meet at supersingular points. This gives two points that specialize to P:
- Q, with (Gr_4, Gr_5, Gr_6) = (étale, multiplicative, multiplicative);
- Q', with (étale, étale, étale).

Q lies on D_6 but not on D_2, because Gr_2 = Gr_5^D is étale there. Q' lies on D_2 but not on D_6. So in the local ring at P neither x_6 nor y_5 divides the other.

In a local ring, if (a,b) is invertible then it equals (a) or (b). Hence (x_6, y_5) is not invertible at P, and neither is x_5·(x_6, y_5). So S̃_3 → S̃_2 ≅ S is not an isomorphism over any neighbourhood of P in U. This map is proper and is an isomorphism on the dense generic fibre, so it is surjective onto U. A surjective open immersion would be an isomorphism, so S̃_{=0} → S^tor is not an open immersion. This contradicts (2) for k = 1.

For k ≥ g−1 the argument in the proof is valid. Later arguments use only the case k = g (Corollary 4.1.14). So the false case of the stated proposition does not propagate. Notation: S = S^tor_{K^pK_{p,n}}, S̃_k is the k-th stage of the tower in the proof, and S̃ = S̃_g. For a sequence (j_1,…,j_k), U(j) ⊂ S is the open set where Z_i = V(p^{nj_i}) for i ≤ k. This is the same as saying that Gr_{g+i} is multiplicative or étale, as prescribed in (2).

1. What the proof proves. In the step from k to k+1 (p. 42), U(j_1,…,j_k) is identified with S̃_{k,=j_1,…,=j_k}. On this set Z_k = V(p^{nj_k}). So Z_{k+1} − V(p^{nj}) equals D_{g+k+1} + V(p^{n(j_k−j)}) when j ≤ j_k, and −D_{g−k} − V(p^{n(j−j_k−1)}) when j > j_k. Hence every ideal blown up at stage k+1 is invertible there, and S̃_{k+1} → S̃_k is an isomorphism over this set. This gives (2) for sequences of length k on S̃_k, and on S̃_{k+1}. In particular it gives (2) on S̃ for k = g − 1 and k = g.
The proof does not show that the later maps S̃_{k'+1} → S̃_{k'} with k' ≥ k + 1 are isomorphisms over U(j_1,…,j_k). Over that set, Z_{k'+1} = V(p^{nj_k}) + D_{g+k+1} + … + D_{g+k'+1}, which has at least two unconstrained summands. So the induction hypothesis "S̃_k satisfies the properties for all indices i ≤ k" is not carried over to S̃_{k+1} for sequences shorter than k.

2. Counterexample: g = 3, n = 1, k = 1, j_1 = 0.
- Here Z_{1,>0} = D_4 and Z_{1,<0} = 0. So S̃_{=0} is the full preimage of U = S \ D_4, the locus where Gr_4 is étale. Since a blow-up is surjective, (2) would say that S̃ → S is an isomorphism over U.
- Over U, the map S̃_2 → S̃_1 = S is an isomorphism, by step 1 with k = 1.
- The map S̃_3 → S̃_2 blows up, among other ideals, (O(−Z_3), p). On U, Z_3 = D_5 + D_6. Since D_5 + D_2 = V(p), we have p = x_5·y_5 up to a unit, where x_i is a local equation of D_i and y_5 is a local equation of D_2. So (O(−Z_3), p) = x_5·(x_6, y_5).
- If S̃ → S were an isomorphism over U, this ideal would be invertible on U. Then (x_6, y_5) would be invertible too, because x_5 is a nonzerodivisor. By Nakayama, in each local ring it would then be generated by x_6 or by y_5. Since S is normal, this would mean that D_6 ≤ D_2 or D_2 ≤ D_6 at every height-one prime through the point.

3. A point where this fails.
- Let E_1 be ordinary, with C_1 ⊂ E_1[p] its étale subgroup. Let E_2, E_3 be supersingular, with C_i = ker F for i = 2, 3.
- Let x be the point given by A = E_1 × E_2 × E_3 with the product polarization, H_4 = C_1, H_5 = C_1 × C_2, H_6 = C_1 × C_2 × C_3, and the dual chain. Then Gr_4 = C_1 is étale, so x ∈ U.
- The product of three Deligne–Rapoport models of X_0(p) is normal and flat, so it maps to the normalization S, and the product point goes to x. Both components of the special fibre of X_0(p) pass through every supersingular point. So x is a limit of ordinary points of type (Gr_4, Gr_5, Gr_6) = (étale, multiplicative, multiplicative). It is also a limit of ordinary points where all three are étale.
- The points of each type form an open subset of the special fibre: the complement of D_4 ∪ D_2 ∪ D_1, and the complement of D_4 ∪ D_5 ∪ D_6. So x lies on special-fibre components C and C' whose generic points have these two types.
- Along C: Gr_1 = Gr_6^D is étale, so D_6 = V(p) − D_1 has positive multiplicity. Gr_2 = Gr_5^D is étale, so D_2 has multiplicity 0.
- Along C': D_6 has multiplicity 0, and D_2 = V(p) − D_5 has positive multiplicity.
- So neither x_6 nor y_5 divides the other in O_{S,x}. Hence (x_6, y_5) is not principal, S̃ → S is not an isomorphism over x ∈ U, and S̃_{=0} → S is not an open immersion.

4. Second check, by direct computation. The complete local ring of the product of modular curves at this point is W[[u, s_2, t_2, s_3, t_3]]/(s_2t_2 − p, s_3t_3 − p). Here s_3 cuts out the branch where C_3 is multiplicative, and t_2 the branch where C_2 is étale. The pullbacks of D_6 (the divisor of C_3) and of D_2 (the divisor of C_2^D) are cut out, up to units, by s_3 and t_2. These two elements are independent in m/m², so the pulled-back ideal (s_3, t_2) needs two generators.

5. Consequences. The inductive construction itself uses (2) only for sequences of length k on S̃_k. Part (1), which Lemma 4.2.11 uses, is unaffected. Part (3) holds on S̃ with pulled-back divisors. Corollary 4.1.14 and Proposition 6.2.2(3) use only complete sequences (k = g), where the claim holds. So only the printed statement of (2) for g ≥ 3 and k ≤ g − 2 is false. There is no clash there, and it matches the correction.

The corrected statement is true under the paper's definitions.

(a) Each point has a sequence a_j with differences 0 or 1. Take a point x of the special fibre of the blow-up. In its local ring, let f_j be the local equation of Z_j = Σ_{k≤j} D_{g+k}. By Prop. 4.1.13(1), the ideal (f_j, p^{nm}) is invertible, so in the local ring one of f_j, p^{nm} divides the other. Hence x ∈ Z_{j,>m} if and only if f_j ∈ p^{nm}·m_x. Put a_j(x) = max{m : x ∈ Z_{j,>m−1}}, with a_0 = 0. Since f_{j−1} divides f_j, we get a_j ≥ a_{j−1}. Now write f_j = f_{j−1}d_j. Because D_{g+j} + D_{g+1−j} = V(p^n), we have d_j e_j = p^n. Suppose f_j ∈ p^{n(m+1)}m_x with m = a_{j−1}. Cancelling d_j gives f_{j−1} ∈ p^{nm}e_j·m_x ⊆ p^{nm}m_x, a contradiction. So a_j − a_{j−1} ∈ {0,1}, and a(x) is the sequence of a unique w ∈ ^MW. There are 2^g such sequences, and each one occurs.

(b) Z_{>w−1} is an up-set. By Lemma 4.1.17(1), x ∈ Z_{>w−1} if and only if a(x) ≥ w componentwise.

(c) The length formula. ℓ(w) = g(g+1)/2 − Σ_j w_j. This was checked by direct computation of the Coxeter lengths of the minimal coset representatives in W_M\W for g ≤ 4, using the positive system fixed by T^+ on p. 30. It also agrees with ℓ(w) = dim C_w and w_j = dim(L ∩ ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{g+j}⟩), since Σ_j w_j is the codimension of the Schubert cell in the Lagrangian Grassmannian. So ℓ is decreasing for the componentwise order.

Hence x ∈ F_i if and only if ℓ(a(x)) ≤ i, and F_i \ F_{i−1} = {x : ℓ(a(x)) = i}, which is the corrected formula. Only the name of a bound variable changes, so nothing downstream is affected. - **Misprint** at §4.2.3, proof of Proposition 4.2.4, pp. 43–44 (the displayed decomposition at the foot of p. 43 and the two products on p. 44) (it affects the proof). The source says `p. 43, last display: "We have a unique decomposition P(Q_p)wK_{p,n} = P(Q_p)w ∏_{α∈w^{-1}Φ^{-,M}∩ϕ^+} U_{α,n} ∏_{α∈w^{-1}Φ^{-,M}∩ϕ^-} U_{α,0}". p. 44: "where U_α is the root group corresponding to α and U_{α,n} is the subgroup of elements reducing to 1 modulo p^n. Let us take x ∈ ∏_{α∈w^{-1}Φ^{-,M}∩ϕ^+} U_{α,n} ∏_{α∈w^{-1}Φ^{-,M}∩ϕ^-} U_{α,0}. We have wxt = wtw^{-1}wt^{-1}xt. We deduce that wxt ∈ P(Q_p)wK_{p,n} if and only if t^{-1}xt ∈ ∏_{α∈w^{-1}Φ^{-,M}∩ϕ^+} U_{α,n} ∏_{α∈w^{-1}Φ^{-,M}∩ϕ^-} U_{α,0}. This is equivalent to x ∈ tK_{p,n}t^{-1}." (The symbol printed is a lower-case ϕ, which is not defined anywhere in the paper.)`; it should be `Exchange the subscripts n and 0 in all three places, reading ϕ^± as Φ^±. The decomposition becomes P(Q_p)wK_{p,n} = P(Q_p)w ∏_{α∈w^{-1}Φ^{-,M}∩Φ^+} U_{α,0} ∏_{α∈w^{-1}Φ^{-,M}∩Φ^-} U_{α,n}. Equivalently, P(Q_p)wK_{p,n} = P(Q_p)w(K_{p,n} ∩ w^{-1}Ū_P w), where Ū_P is the unipotent radical opposite to P, with roots Φ^{-,M}. The same change applies to "Let us take x ∈ …" and "t^{-1}xt ∈ …". Then t^{-1}xt ∈ K_{p,n} ∩ w^{-1}Ū_P w holds if and only if x ∈ tK_{p,n}t^{-1}, which is exactly the next sentence of the proof.`. Conventions of the paper. P = P_μ is the stabilizer of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩ (§3.1, p. 33), so it is block lower triangular. B ⊆ P is upper triangular on the diagonal g×g blocks, and Φ^+ is the set of roots of B (p. 34). So Φ^+ contains the roots of the lower-left block, and Φ^{-,M} (not defined explicitly, but necessarily the roots opposite to Φ^{+,M}) consists of the upper-right block roots. K_{p,n} is the group of matrices in G(Z_p) that reduce mod p^n into B(Z/p^n) (§4.1). Hence K_{p,n} ∩ U_α = U_α(Z_p) = U_{α,0} for α ∈ Φ^+, and K_{p,n} ∩ U_α = U_α(p^nZ_p) = U_{α,n} for α ∈ Φ^-. For n ≥ 1, K_{p,n} has an Iwahori factorization with respect to the parabolic w^{-1}Pw: K_{p,n} = (K_{p,n} ∩ w^{-1}Pw)(K_{p,n} ∩ w^{-1}Ū_P w). The first factor is absorbed into P after conjugation by w. So P wK_{p,n} = P w ∏_{α∈w^{-1}Φ^{-,M}} (K_{p,n} ∩ U_α), and this is unique because P ∩ Ū_P = 1. That gives the corrected formula, not the printed one.

Direct check for g = 1, n = 1, w = 1. Here G = GL_2, P = B is the lower triangular group, Φ^+ = {β} with U_β = (1 0; c 1), and U_{-β} = (1 b; 0 1). The printed right-hand side is P·U_{-β}(Z_p), which contains u = (1 1; 0 1). Now K_{p,1} = {(a b; c d) ∈ GL_2(Z_p) : b ∈ pZ_p}. Suppose u = qk with q ∈ P, and write q^{-1} = (a' 0; c' d'). Then k = (a' a'; c' c'+d'). This forces a' ∈ pZ_p and d' ∈ Z_p, so det k = a'd' ∈ pZ_p, which is impossible. So u ∉ P K_{p,1} = P·U_{-β}(pZ_p). The printed identity is false. In fact it describes the orbits of the opposite Iwahori subgroup.

With the subscripts exchanged the argument works. For t ∈ T^+ (p. 34: v(t_{g+1}) ≥ … ≥ v(t_{2g}) ≥ v(t_1) ≥ … ≥ v(t_g)) we have v(α(t)) ≥ 0 for all α ∈ Φ^+. So t^{-1}U_{α,n}t ⊆ U_{α,n} for α ∈ Φ^-. For α ∈ Φ^+, t^{-1}u_α(a)t = u_α(α(t)^{-1}a) lies in U_{α,0} if and only if v(a) ≥ v(α(t)). Together these give "t^{-1}xt ∈ (product) ⇔ x ∈ tK_{p,n}t^{-1}", which is the equivalence the proof states next. With the printed sets that equivalence fails already for t = 1 and x = u above.

The error is consistent in all three places, so it is a systematic exchange of subscripts (or of ϕ^+ and ϕ^-). It is not an artefact of the text layer: the page images show exactly the printed formulas. Proposition 4.2.4 itself, and everything that uses it later, is unaffected, because the corrected argument proves the stated isomorphism. - **Misprint** at §4.1.16 (definition of Z_{>w−1} and of the filtration F_i), p. 43. The divisors Z_{i,>j} are defined in Prop. 4.1.13(1), p. 42, and the sequence (w_1, …, w_g) at the end of §3.1, p. 34. The January 2024 preprint has the same text: §4.1.16 is on p. 41 there, and Prop. 4.1.13(1), on p. 40 there, has the same range 0 ≤ j ≤ i.. The source says `p. 43: "4.1.16. A filtration. Let w ∈ ᴹW. We let Z_{>w−1} = ∩_{i=1}^g Z_{i,>w_i−1}" and "We construct a filtration by closed subsets: F_{−1} = ∅ ⊆ F_0 ⊆ ··· ⊆ F_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{F_p}, by letting F_i = ∪_{w∈ᴹW, ℓ(w)≤i} Z_{>w−1}." The only definition of these divisors is Prop. 4.1.13(1), p. 42: "for all 0 ≤ i ≤ g and all 0 ≤ j ≤ i we have effective Cartier divisors Z_{i,>j} and Z_{i,<j} on S̃^tor_{K^pK_{p,n}} with disjoint support, and Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj})."`; it should be `Prop. 4.1.13(1) should also cover j = −1, with Z_{i,>−1} = Z_i + V(p^n) and Z_{i,<−1} = 0. These two divisors satisfy Z_{i,>−1} − Z_{i,<−1} = Z_i − V(p^{n·(−1)}) and have disjoint supports, so no further blow-up is needed. As a closed subset, Z_{i,>−1} is then the whole special fibre S^tor_{F_p}. With this convention Z_{>w−1} is defined for every w ∈ ᴹW. Lemma 4.1.17, the equality F_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{F_p} and the inclusion S^tor_{F_p,w} ⊆ ∩_i (Z_{i,>w_i−1} ∩ Z^c_{i,>w_i}) on p. 43 then hold as stated.`. The symbol is undefined. At the end of §3.1 (p. 34), the sequence attached to w ∈ ᴹW satisfies w_0 = 0 and w_i − w_{i−1} ∈ {0,1}. So 0 ≤ w_i ≤ i, and w_i = 0 does occur. For example, w_1 = 0 exactly when g+1 ∉ w^{−1}{g+1,…,2g}. Whenever w_i = 0, the index w_i − 1 in Z_{i,>w_i−1} is −1. But Prop. 4.1.13(1) defines Z_{i,>j} only for 0 ≤ j ≤ i, and the paper gives no convention for j = −1.

This case matters. Let w_max be the longest element of ᴹW (the open cell). Then w_max^{−1}{g+1,…,2g} = {1,…,g}, so every w_i = 0 and every factor of Z_{>w_max−1} is undefined. Every w satisfies w ≤ w_max. Lemma 4.1.17(2) is stated for all w, so it gives F_{g(g+1)/2} = Z_{>w_max−1} = ∩_i Z_{i,>−1}. Hence, given Lemma 4.1.17(2), the stated equality F_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{F_p} holds exactly when each Z_{i,>−1} contains the special fibre.

Example, g = 1. Here ᴹW = {1, s}, with ℓ(1) = 0 and ℓ(s) = 1. For the identity w_1 = 1, and for s, w_1 = 0. We have Z_1 = D_2, and D_1 + D_2 = V(p^n) by §4.1.8 (p. 41). The proof of Prop. 4.1.13 gives Z_{1,>0} = D_2. Also Z_{1,>1} = 0: we have Z_{1,>1} − Z_{1,<1} = Z_1 − V(p^n) = −D_1 ≤ 0, and the two divisors have disjoint supports. So F_0 = D_2 and F_1 = D_2 ∪ Z_{1,>−1}. Thus F_1 = S^tor_{F_p} requires Z_{1,>−1} to contain S^tor_{F_p} \ D_2. By Cor. 4.1.14, this set is the stratum S^tor_{F_p,s}.

The paper's own formula forces the value. Put j = −1 in Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}). This gives Z_{i,>−1} − Z_{i,<−1} = Z_i + V(p^n), which is effective. Now let A and B be effective Cartier divisors with disjoint supports such that A − B is effective. Near any point of the support of B, A is trivial, so −B ≥ 0 there. Hence B = 0. So Z_{i,<−1} = 0 and Z_{i,>−1} = Z_i + V(p^n). By §4.1.8 (p. 41), D_{g+k} + D_{g+1−k} = V(p^n), so each D_{g+k} ≤ V(p^n). Hence Z_i is supported in the special fibre, and Z_i + V(p^n) has support exactly S^tor_{F_p}.

The paper uses the same formula at negative indices elsewhere. Prop. 6.2.2(2), p. 61, asserts divisors with Z_{i,>w_j+η} − Z_{i,<w_j+η} = Z_i − V(p^{n(w_j+η)}) for η ∈ {±ε, ±ε′}, and w_j − ε < 0 when w_j = 0. The paper also identifies such a divisor with the whole special fibre around it. The proof of Prop. 4.1.13 (p. 42) writes "Z_{k+1,>j} = S̃^tor_{k,=j_1,…,=j_k} for j < j_k". On that open Z_k = V(p^{nj_k}), so Z_{k+1,>j} = V(p^{n(j_k−j)}) + D_{g+k+1}, whose support is the whole special fibre there.

With this convention, the surrounding statements hold:
- The formula at j = 0 gives Z_{i,>0} = Z_i and Z_{i,<0} = 0. So Lemma 4.1.17(1) extends to the index −1: for 0 ≤ j ≤ i we have Z_{i,>j} ≤ Z_{i,>0} = Z_i ≤ Z_i + V(p^n), and Z_{i,<−1} = 0. Hence Lemma 4.1.17(2) holds for all w and w′, and F_{g(g+1)/2} = ∩_i Z_{i,>−1} = S^tor_{F_p}.
- Consider the open S̃^tor_{=w_1,…,=w_g}, whose special fibre is S^tor_{F_p,w} (Cor. 4.1.14). On it, Z_{i,>w_i} and Z_{i,<w_i} are trivial, so Z_i = V(p^{nw_i}). For w_i ≥ 1 this gives Z_{i,>w_i−1} − Z_{i,<w_i−1} = V(p^n), so Z_{i,>w_i−1} = V(p^n) there by the disjoint-support argument. For w_i = 0 the convention gives Z_i + V(p^n) = V(p^n) as well. So on this open every Z_{i,>w_i−1} equals V(p^n). This proves the inclusion S^tor_{F_p,w} ⊆ ∩_i (Z_{i,>w_i−1} ∩ Z^c_{i,>w_i}) stated on p. 43.
- The same computation shows two more things over 𝔖^tor_w. First, the closed set Z_{>w−1} is the whole special fibre there. Second, the ideal of Z_{>w−1} obtained from these divisors is (p^n) there, with n the level, and this ideal has the same radical as (p). This is all that the last step of the proof of Prop. 4.5.8 (p. 53) needs: "the inclusion (p) ⊆ 𝓘_{Z,>w−1} is an equality over 𝔖^tor_w". The reason is that the completion lim_m 𝒪/𝓘^m of §2.9.1 depends on 𝓘 only up to radical, since on a noetherian scheme two ideals with the same radical have cofinal powers.
- Lemma 4.1.18 gives the expected strata. For g = 1 it gives F_1 \ F_0 = Z_{1,>−1} ∩ Z^c_{1,>0} = S^tor_{F_p} \ D_2 = S^tor_{F_p,s}. In general its top piece is S^tor_{F_p} \ Z_g, which is S^tor_{F_p,w_max} by Cor. 4.1.14.

So the text uses a symbol it never defines. The paper's own formula allows only one value for it, and that is the value the stated equality F_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{F_p} needs. With that value filled in, the statements above follow from the paper's own arguments with no new step. Nothing false is stated and no argument is missing; the definition simply omits the case j = −1. The filtration and its top step feed the spectral sequence of Theorem 2.9.7 in §4.5.6 (p. 52). Lemma 4.5.7 and Prop. 4.5.8 involve Z_{>w−1} for every w, including those with w_1 = 0. The omission does not affect any of these results, nor Theorem 4.5.2. - **Gap** at §4.2.9: proof of Corollary 4.2.10 (p. 45) and proof of Proposition 4.2.15 (p. 46), in both places the step that invokes Proposition 4.2.8 to conclude that p⋆1 H is a BT_n. The 2024 preprint has the same text (pp. 43–44). (it affects the proof). The source says `Proof of Cor. 4.2.10 (p. 45): "We may therefore apply proposition 4.2.8 and deduce that deg(p⋆2 H_{g+i,x}) ≥ deg(p⋆1 H_{g+i,x}). Moreover, in case t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p) and we have equality, the groups p⋆1 H_{g+i,x} and p⋆1 H_{g+i,x} are BT_n's and their degree is a multiple of n." Proof of Prop. 4.2.15 (p. 46): "We therefore assume that for all g+1 ≤ k′ ≤ k, deg(p⋆2 H_{k′,x}) = deg(p⋆1 H_{k′,x}). We deduce from proposition 4.2.8 that p⋆1 H_{k′,x} is a BT_n. Since this is true for all k′, we deduce that p⋆1 Gr_{k′,x} ≃ p⋆2 Gr_{k′,x} is a multiplicative or an étale BT_n for all k′."`; it should be `Prove only the degree statement; it is all that is needed. Corollary 4.2.10: write the transports of H = p1*H_{g+i,x} along the factorization of §4.2.5 as H = H^(0), H^(1), …, H^(k) = p2*H_{g+i,x}. By Prop. 4.2.8, deg H^(0) ≤ … ≤ deg H^(k). If the two ends have equal degree, every step is an equality. Let j0 be the first step with kernel rank p^s where s = 2g − i; such a step exists by Remark 4.2.6. There Prop. 4.2.8(2) applies to H^(j0) and shows that H^(j0) is a BT_n. Every later step has i + s ≤ 2g, so it is a generic isomorphism, and it has equal degrees, so it is an isomorphism ([Far10], sect. 3, cor. 3, as in the proof of Prop. 4.2.8). Hence p2*H_{g+i,x} ≅ H^(j0) is a BT_n. Its degree is then n times its dimension, so deg p1*H_{g+i,x} = deg p2*H_{g+i,x} ∈ nZ. The claim that p1*H_{g+i,x} is a BT_n should be dropped or given a separate proof. Proposition 4.2.15: apply this for every 1 ≤ k′ ≤ k. By additivity of the degree, deg p1*Gr_{g+k′,x} = deg p2*Gr_{g+k′,x} lies in nZ ∩ [0, n] = {0, n}. So on both sides Gr_{g+k′,x} is étale (degree 0) or multiplicative (degree n), and of the same type. The same passage also contains three small misprints: the second "p⋆1H_{g+i,x}" on p. 45 should be p⋆2H_{g+i,x}; "section 4.2.1" should be 4.2.5; and "for all g+1 ≤ k′ ≤ k, deg(p⋆2H_{k′,x}) = deg(p⋆1H_{k′,x})" should read "for all 1 ≤ k′ ≤ k, deg(p⋆2H_{g+k′,x}) = deg(p⋆1H_{g+k′,x})".`. In §4.2.5 the isogeny p⋆1 A → p⋆2 A is factored as G_0 → G_1 → … → G_k, with kernels L[p^{j+1}]/L[p^j] of rank p^{s_j}. Multiplication by p embeds L[p^{j+2}]/L[p^{j+1}] into L[p^{j+1}]/L[p^j], so s_j does not increase with j. For t ∈ T^{++} the s_j take every value 1, …, 2g−1 (Remark 4.2.6).

The second assertion of Prop. 4.2.8 is about one step: if i + s = h and deg H = deg H′, then the source H of that step is a BT_n. For the flag member of rank p^{in}, this is the step with s = 2g − i.

For i = 1 the proof works. Every step before that one has s = 2g, where H′ = φ(p^{-1}H) is identified with H through G/G[p] ≅ G, so the source really is p⋆1 H.

For g ≥ 2 and 2 ≤ i ≤ g it does not work. The step with s = 2g − i comes after a step with s = 2g − 1, and there i + s > 2g. At that earlier step case (2) applies: the transported group is φ(p^{-1}H ∩ p^{-n}L), and §4.2.5 identifies only its graded piece Gr′ with Gr, not the group with H. At such a step Prop. 4.2.8 gives only deg H′ ≥ deg H. So Prop. 4.2.8 makes an intermediate group a BT_n, not p⋆1 H_{g+i,x}. The step "We deduce from proposition 4.2.8 that p⋆1 H_{k′,x} is a BT_n" (k′ ≥ g+2) is asserted without proof, and Cor. 4.2.10 makes the same claim for p⋆1 H_{g+i,x}.

The conclusions survive. The BT_n statement does transfer forward to p⋆2 H, and the degree argument in the correction gives everything the two results use. A direct computation at ordinary points, where degrees are read off the multiplicative part of the Tate module, found no failure of the p⋆1 claim itself. It used g = 2, t with elementary divisors (1, p^{-1}, p^{-2}, p^{-3}), p = 2, 3 and n = 2, 3, over randomly sampled flags and multiplicative parts. The degrees never decreased along the chain. In every sampled case with equality for i = 2, p⋆1 H_{g+2} was a BT_n, and a degree-preserving case-(2) step never changed the type of the multiplicative part. So what is missing is a proof, not a true statement. Section 4.2.5 factors p1*A → p2*A as G_0 → G_1 → … → G_k. The step G_j → G_{j+1} has kernel L[p^{j+1}]/L[p^j], of rank p^s with s non-increasing in j. The flag is carried step by step: H' = φ(H) if i + s ≤ 2g, and H' = φ(p^{-1}H ∩ p^{-n}L) if i + s > 2g. Proposition 4.2.8 gives deg H' ≥ deg H at every step. So deg p1*H ≤ deg p2*H, and when the two are equal, every step is an equality.

The second part of Prop. 4.2.8 (L is a BT_1 and H is a BT_n) needs i + s = h = 2g. So it applies only at a step whose kernel has rank p^{2g−i}, and only to the group carried to that G_j, not to p1*H_{g+i,x}. For t ∈ T^{++}, every rank p, …, p^{2g−1} occurs (Remark 4.2.6). Hence for i ≥ 2 (so g ≥ 2), a step with 2g − i < s < 2g, for example s = 2g − 1, comes before it. At such a step, φ gives only one relation between H' and H. Multiplication by p maps H' onto H'' = H ∩ p^{-(n-1)}L. That map has kernel G[p]/L, of order p^{2g−s}, and H'' has order p^{ni − (2g−s)} < p^{ni}. The construction of §4.2.5 identifies only the graded pieces Gr_{g+i} and Gr'_{g+i}. Example: g = 2, i = 2, s = 3 with p = 2, n = 2. There H' has order 16, but its image H'' in H has order 8, checked by direct computation. So no statement about H' being a BT_n carries back to H.

Defence attempts:
- The case i = 1 is fine. Every earlier step then has s = 2g and L = G[p], and H' is H under G/G[p] ≅ G.
- The p2 side is fine as well. After the first step with i + s = 2g, every step is a generic isomorphism, and equal degrees make it an isomorphism. So p2*H_{g+i,x} is a BT_n.
- Running the isogeny backwards does not help. At a step with i + s > 2g, H' contains φ(G[p]), which is the kernel of the reverse isogeny. So the hypotheses of Prop. 4.2.8 fail for the reverse step.
- No other statement in the paper supplies the p1 claim. In the setting of Prop. 4.2.15 the claim does hold, but only a posteriori. Once every Gr_{g+k′} is known to be étale or multiplicative, H_{g+k′} is an extension of étale by multiplicative groups of this type, killed by p^n, hence a BT_n. That knowledge comes from the degree argument. In Cor. 4.2.10, where equality is assumed for a single i, the paper does not settle the claim.

So the step "p1*H is a BT_n, by Prop. 4.2.8" is asserted without proof. The consequences it is used for still hold by the degree argument given in the correction.

Later uses need only the degree and support conclusions:
- Prop. 4.2.15(3) in the proof of Prop. 4.3.13 (p. 48);
- Cor. 4.2.10 in the proof of Lemma 4.4.2 (p. 50) and for the action of t on the spectral sequence (p. 52);
- Prop. 4.2.15 in the proof of Prop. 6.1.9 (p. 60), in the form "deg H_{g+i}(p1(x)) ≤ deg H_{g+i}(p2(x)) and if equality holds they are multiples of n".

Every other term in the inequality is integral: p^{−1}H, X and G[p^{n+1}]. The inequality comes from the displayed generic sequence. So the quotient (p^{−1}H × p^{−n}L)/X maps to G[p^{n+1}] by a generic isomorphism, and its degree is at most deg G[p^{n+1}] ([Far10], sect. 3, cor. 3). The final equality deg H′ = deg X − deg L holds exactly, not only as an inequality. L ⊂ G[p] ⊂ p^{−1}H and L ⊂ p^{−n}L, so L_K ⊂ X_K. Since L is finite flat, it is the closure of L_K, so L ⊂ X. The quotient X/L is finite flat. The kernel of X → G′ is X ∩ L = L, so the induced map X/L → G/L = G′ has trivial kernel. It lands in G′[p^{n+1}], so it is a monomorphism of finite V-schemes and hence a closed immersion. Its generic fibre is φ(p^{−1}H_K ∩ p^{−n}L_K). A closed subscheme that is flat over V is the schematic closure of its generic fibre, so H′ = X/L. Additivity of the degree then gives deg H′ = deg X − deg L. Only in the case i + s ≤ h is the map H → H′ merely a generic isomorphism, and there the proof correctly uses [Far10], sect. 3, cor. 3.

Proposition 4.2.8 then makes the group at that step a BT_n, so its degree deg p⋆_1 H_{g+i} is a multiple of n, which is a contradiction. This was checked on the rendered p. 45.

The proof takes V = 𝒪_{C_t^{tor},x} with x a generic point of the special fibre and argues only there. For the inequality that is enough. The 'Moreover' is a containment of closed sets. The support of an effective Cartier divisor on a normal scheme has pure codimension 1, so a point y lies in supp(p⋆₂Z_i − p⋆₁Z_i) exactly when some codimension-one point specialising to y does. The printed argument shows only that generic points x of the special fibre with p₁(x) (or p₂(x)) in ∩_j(Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}) lie in the support. It says nothing about points of the preimage that are not specialisations of such x.

Such points occur. For g = 1, n = 1, i = 1, Proposition 4.1.13 and its proof give Z_{1,>0} = D_2, Z_{1,<0} = 0, Z_{1,>1} = 0 and Z_{1,<1} = D_1, so the set is D_1 ∩ D_2. By Lemma 4.1.9 and Remark 4.1.4 this is the non-ordinary (supersingular) locus of the Iwahori-level model, a finite set of closed points of the two-dimensional S^{tor}; no blow-up is needed when g = 1. The fibres of p₁ and p₂ over these points are finite: over F̄_p a supersingular elliptic curve has a unique subgroup scheme of each p-power order, namely ker F^j. So the preimage in C_t^{tor} has codimension 2, and no generic point of the special fibre maps into it.

The statement is still true. It follows from the valuation argument above, which was checked step by step. For g = 1 it was also checked by direct computation with the Katz–Lubin degrees. For a supersingular E with Hasse valuation h < p/(p+1), the canonical subgroup has degree 1−h and the other subgroups have degree h/p. For h ≥ p/(p+1), every subgroup has degree 1/(p+1). The new subgroup E[p]/L has degree 1 − deg L, which is strictly larger than deg H in every case with 0 < deg H < 1.

Dependence: the 'Moreover' is used in the proof of Lemma 4.4.2 (p. 50). There it shows that, on C_{t,F_p,(w−1,w+1)}, the support of p⋆₂(Z_{i,>w_i}−Z_{i,<w_i}) − p⋆₁(Z_{i,>w_i}−Z_{i,<w_i}) contains p⋆₁Z_{i,>w_i} and p⋆₂Z_{i,<w_i}. For g = 1 and w the identity (w_1 = 1), S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} is D_2 and D_{w,+} = Z_{1,<1} = D_1. So the needed containment is at points lying over D_1 ∩ D_2, exactly the codimension-two case. Lemma 4.4.2 feeds Proposition 4.4.4 (strict dynamic compactifications), on which the complexes RΓ_w and Theorem 4.5.2 rest.

The citation of Corollary 4.2.10 on p. 52, for the action of t on the spectral sequence, needs only the inclusion p₁^{-1}(F_l) ⊆ p₂^{-1}(F_l) that Proposition 2.9.9 requires. That inclusion follows from Lemma 4.2.11, which uses only the first (inequality) part. So the gap does not touch the p. 52 citation.

The statement is true and the repair is short, so only the proof is affected. The proof works only at the local rings 𝒪_{C_t^{tor},x} of generic points x of the special fibre. That shows only this: a generic point x with p_1(x) (or p_2(x)) in T := ∩_{j=0}^{i}(Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}) lies in the support, and so do its specialisations. A point of p_1^{-1}(T) that is not a specialisation of such an x is not covered.

Such points exist. Take g = 1, n = 1, i = 1. By Proposition 4.1.13 and its proof (the blow-up is trivial for g = 1), Z_{1,>0} = D_2, Z_{1,<0} = 0, Z_{1,<1} = D_1 and Z_{1,>1} = 0. So T = D_1 ∩ D_2, the supersingular points of the special fibre of the Iwahori-level model, which are closed points of a two-dimensional scheme. The quasi-isogeny extends over C_t^{tor} (Lemma 4.2.2). Over F̄_p a supersingular elliptic curve has only finitely many finite subgroup schemes of each order (one of each p-power order). So p_1 and p_2 have finite fibres over these points. The preimage therefore has codimension 2, and no generic point of the special fibre maps into it. So the codimension-one argument proves nothing about this set.

A charitable reading does not save the argument. One could read ∩ and ∪ as gcd and lcm of divisors, which would make the codimension-one reduction valid. But then the claim is empty in this example (gcd(D_1, D_2) = 0), and the paper itself uses ∩ of the Z's as intersections of closed sets (§4.1.16, Lemma 4.1.18, §4.4.1). Lemma 4.4.2 needs the set-theoretic claim. Proposition 4.2.15 concerns Σ_{l≤k} Z_l, not a single Z_i, so it does not supply the step. Only its technique does: a valuation ring through an arbitrary point.

The statement itself is true, by the repair above. In the example it was also checked by direct computation with the Katz–Lubin degrees. Let h be the valuation of the Hasse invariant.
- If 0 < h < p/(p+1), the canonical subgroup has degree 1 − h and the other subgroups have degree h/p.
- If h ≥ p/(p+1), every subgroup of order p has degree 1/(p+1).
For H ∩ L = 0 the new level subgroup E[p]/L has degree 1 − deg L. In every supersingular case this is strictly larger than deg H: 1 − h/p > 1 − h, h > h/p, 1 − h/p > h/p, and p/(p+1) > 1/(p+1).

What uses the passage: the proof of Lemma 4.4.2 (p. 50) applies the 'Moreover' on C_{t,F_p,(w−1,w+1)}. It concludes that the support contains p⋆_1 Z_{i,>w_i} and p⋆_2 Z_{i,<w_i}. For g = 1, n = 1 and w = 1 (so w_1 = 1), S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = D_2, D_{w,+} = D_1 and D_{w,−} = 0. The needed containment is then exactly at points over D_1 ∩ D_2, the codimension-two case above. Lemma 4.4.2 feeds Proposition 4.4.4, the complexes RΓ_w, Proposition 4.4.5 and Theorem 4.5.2, and it is also invoked in §6 (pp. 58, 61).

The citation on p. 52 (the action of t on the Cousin spectral sequence) needs only p_1^{-1}(F_l) ⊆ p_2^{-1}(F_l) for Proposition 2.9.9. That follows from Lemma 4.2.11, which uses only the inequality, so that citation is unaffected.

Since the statement is true and the repair is short and uses only Proposition 4.2.8 and Remark 4.2.6, no stated result is affected. Only the proof of Corollary 4.2.10 is incomplete, and with it the justification of the step in Lemma 4.4.2. The text is identical in the 2024 preprint. The fixed isomorphism Z_p(1) ≅ Z_p enters only modulo p^n, so the open immersion descends from Z_p^cycl to Z_p(ζ_{p^n}). It is onto the full preimage of the w-stratum because both sides are T(Z/p^nZ)-torsors over 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P,w}K^p}. The statement itself needs no change.`. The printed proof establishes only the first assertion. It extends the Gr_i to finite flat group schemes off Σ D_i ∩ D_{2g+1−i}, chooses an étale U on which Gr_{w^{-1}(l)} ≅ Z/p^nZ and Gr_{w^{-1}(g+l)} ≅ μ_{p^n}, and concludes that the cover is T(Z/p^nZ) × U over U. That is local triviality of the cover. The Igusa variety 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P,1,w}K^p} never appears in the proof, and nothing identifies the cover over the w-locus with it. No earlier result covers this level:
- Lemma 4.1.7 (p. 41) treats only level K_{p,n}. Its proof says it follows from Lemma 3.4.24 and notes that "here the embedding is defined over Z_p, not only Z_p^cycl".
- Lemma 3.4.24 (p. 40) is stated over Z_p^cycl for models normalised over Z_p^cycl, and Remark 3.4.22 says these are in general not base changes.
- Remark 3.4.18 (p. 39) warns: "In general this map doesn't descend to a map IG_{K^pK_{p,P}} → S_{K^pK_p} because the level structure on both sides are formulated in a different way. One uses isomorphisms with μ_{p^∞}^g ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)^g on the left, and isomorphisms with (Q_p/Z_p)^{2g} on the right." It then points to Section 4.1, which handles only K_{p,n}.
Level K_{p,1,n} over Z_p(ζ_{p^n}) is exactly a case where this descent must be argued: one has to match trivialisations by Z/p^nZ on the Shimura side with trivialisations by μ_{p^n} on the Igusa side.

The assertion itself is correct. Both sides are finite étale T(Z/p^nZ)-covers of a smooth formal scheme, hence normal, and they agree on the generic fibre once ζ_{p^n} is fixed. Checked directly for g = 1. There K_{p,1,n} = {(a b; c d) : a ≡ d ≡ 1, c ≡ 0 mod p^n}, so a K_{p,1,n}-level structure is a point P of exact order p^n (generating the flag subgroup H) together with a generator of A[p^n]/H. On the locus where H is multiplicative (resp. étale), it becomes a trivialisation μ_{p^n} ≅ H and Z/p^n ≅ A[p^n]/H (resp. Z/p^n ≅ H and μ_{p^n} ≅ A[p^n]/H) once ζ_{p^n} is fixed. That is the Igusa level structure for K_{p,P,1,w}.

So the lemma is true, but its second half is asserted without any argument. It is not idle: the nebentypus comparison RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P},κ,χ) = RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ) stated on p. 56 compares the sheaf ω^κ(χ), defined through this normalised cover, with the Igusa tower. That comparison needs this identification. The lemma makes two claims. The printed proof establishes only the first. After extending the Gr_i as finite flat groups, it shows étale-locally on U that the normalisation is T(Z/p^nZ) ×_{Spec Z_p(ζ_{p^n})} U, and it ends there. The Igusa variety 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P,1,w}K^p} does not appear anywhere in the proof, so the second claim ("Moreover, ...") is asserted without argument. Showing that a torsor is trivial étale-locally does not identify it with a particular global torsor.

Defence attempts:
(a) Lemma 3.4.24 (p. 40) gives an open immersion 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_{p,P}} ↪ S_{K^pK_p} for K_{p,P} = P(Q_p) ∩ xK_p x^{-1}, but only over Z_p^cycl, after fixing Z_p(1) = Z_p. Remarks 3.4.18 and 3.4.25 say explicitly that in general this map does not descend, because the Igusa level structure uses μ_{p^∞}^g ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)^g and the Shimura level structure uses (Q_p/Z_p)^{2g}. Remark 1.4.6 (p. 5) says scalars must be extended to Q_p(ζ_{p^n}) for exactly this reason.
(b) Lemma 4.1.7 (p. 41) is the analogue at level K_{p,n}, where the authors do give a justification ("follows from lemma 3.4.24 ... here the embedding is defined over Z_p"). Nothing comparable is given at level K_{p,1,n}, where the descent to Z_p(ζ_{p^n}) is the only non-formal point.
So no nearby statement supplies the step as written.

The claim is nevertheless true, and the missing argument is routine (see the correction). Checked directly: K_{p,1,n} = ker(K_{p,n} → T(Z/p^nZ)), so K_{p,P,1,w} is normal in K_{p,P,w}. The quotient is all of T(Z/p^nZ), because T ⊂ M ⊂ P. The pairing matches Gr_{w^{-1}(l)} (étale) with Gr_{w^{-1}(2g+1−l)} (multiplicative), so the similitude data agree once ζ_{p^n} is fixed.

Later use: the lemma is not cited by number elsewhere. Its second assertion is what underlies the identification on p. 56, "RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ, χ) = RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ)" (itself stated without proof). That identification compares the Shimura-side complexes with Nebentypus (built from O(χ) on p. 47) with the Igusa-side complexes. Through it the lemma supports Theorem 1.4.3(4),(5) and Proposition 1.4.7 for levels with torus part T(1+p^nZ_p) and nontrivial χ. I rendered pp. 48–49 at high resolution, and the subscript clearly reads "2g+i−1". The printed index cannot be right, for three reasons.

1. **Undefined divisors.** In §4.1.8 (p. 41), D_i is defined only for 1 ≤ i ≤ 2g ("For all 1 ≤ i ≤ 2g, we let D_i be the effective Cartier divisor … associated to … Gr_i"). For g ≥ 2 and 2 ≤ i ≤ g, the index 2g+i−1 is between 2g+1 and 3g−1, so D_{2g+i−1} is not defined. For i = 1 the two indices agree (both equal 2g), so for g = 1 the printed formula happens to be correct.

2. **Inconsistency with the rest of the paper.** Everywhere else the relevant locus pairs D_i with D_{2g+1−i}:
   - §4.1.8 states D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n).
   - Lemma 4.1.9 (p. 41) gives ∪_{w∈^MW} S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n},𝔽_p,w} = S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n},𝔽_p} ∖ ∑_{i=1}^g D_i∩D_{2g+1−i}.

   The slip is the transposition "+i−1" for "+1−i".

3. **The corrected set is the right target.** By Lemma 4.2.13, C^{tor}_{t,w} lies in the complement of ∑_{i=1}^g p_1^⋆D_{w^{-1}(i)}. So p_1 maps C^{tor}_{t,w} into the complement of ∑_i D_{w^{-1}(i)}, which by Lemma 4.1.9 is the w-stratum of the special fibre. Hence p_1 maps the stated source into S^{tor}∖∑ D_i∩D_{2g+1−i}.

**Consequences.** None of the later arguments uses the misprinted index. Proposition 4.3.13, Proposition 4.3.18 and Lemma 4.3.14 use the correspondence over C_t^{tor}∖∑ p_1^⋆D_i∩p_2^⋆D_{2g+1−i}, which is printed correctly, and they use Proposition 4.2.15(3). No stated result changes.

A separate slip nearby: Lemma 4.3.16 (p. 49) has ∑_{i=1}^d where ∑_{i=1}^g is meant.
