Equivalently, close it right after (κ + ρ). - Remark 4.3.12 should read n_{w′} = ⟨(w′)^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) + ρ, t⟩ − ⟨w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) + ρ, t⟩. Here the pairing is used additively, as the pairing with v(t). The ρ terms cancel, so n_{w′} = ⟨(w′)^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ), v(t)⟩. - Proposition 4.3.17 should read ⟨−w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ, t⟩t_w^{naive}. This is the normalisation of Proposition 4.3.9, and the one used to define t right after Proposition 4.3.17.`. The parentheses are unbalanced as printed on pp. 48–49, and the 2024 preprint has the same text. Each pairing can be balanced in two ways: close the parenthesis after (κ + ρ), or after the trailing ±ρ. The paper's own normalisations settle which is meant. The second reading makes the Remark's positivity claim false and gives the wrong normalisation in Proposition 4.3.17.

Notation. Write λ = w_{0,M}(κ + ρ). Characters are written (k_1, …, k_g; k) as on p. 33. In these coordinates W acts by signed permutations of (k_1, …, k_g) and fixes k. The conventions on p. 34 are:
- X^⋆(T)^+ is the cone 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ k_g.
- T^+(Q_p) is the set of t with v(t) dominant; T^{++}(Q_p) is the set with v(t) dominant regular. So ⟨α, v(t)⟩ ≥ 0 for every α ∈ Φ^+, strictly for t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p).
- ^MW is defined by the condition wX^⋆(T)^+ ⊆ X^⋆(T)^{+,M}.
C(κ) is defined on p. 48: w ∈ ^MW lies in C(κ) exactly when w^{−1}λ ∈ X^⋆(T)^−_Q. This is the antidominant cone −X^⋆(T)^+_Q; compare the definition of C(κ) on p. 3.

Remark 4.3.12. The intended formula follows from the normalisations:
- By Proposition 4.3.9, t_{w′} = ⟨−(w′)^{−1}λ − ρ, t⟩t_{w′}^{naive}.
- By Proposition 4.3.11, t = ⟨−w^{−1}λ − ρ, t⟩t^{naive} for any w ∈ C(κ).
- On ℭ^{tor}_{t,w′}, the rational map t^{naive} restricts to t_{w′}^{naive}.
So t restricts there to ⟨(w′)^{−1}λ − w^{−1}λ, t⟩t_{w′}. The p-adic valuation of this factor is ⟨(w′)^{−1}λ + ρ, v(t)⟩ − ⟨w^{−1}λ + ρ, v(t)⟩ = ⟨(w′)^{−1}λ − w^{−1}λ, v(t)⟩. That is the printed formula with ")" inserted after (κ + ρ).

Closing the parenthesis after "+ ρ" instead gives ⟨(w′)^{−1}(λ + ρ) − w^{−1}(λ + ρ), v(t)⟩. This adds the term ⟨(w′)^{−1}ρ − w^{−1}ρ, v(t)⟩, which is nonzero in general, and with it the Remark's positivity claim fails.

Example: GSp_4 (g = 2) with κ = (2, −6; k), where k is even (the parity condition of p. 33). Then ρ = (−1, −2; 0) and λ = (−8, 1; k). C(κ) = {w}, where w^{−1}λ = (1, 8; k). Take the w′ ∈ ^MW with (w′)^{−1}λ = (−1, 8; k); it does not lie in C(κ). Then:
- (w′)^{−1}λ − w^{−1}λ = (−2, 0; 0). This is the positive root t ↦ t_4/t_1. The intended value is n_{w′} = v(t_4) − v(t_1), which is > 0 for every t = diag(t_1, …, t_4) ∈ T^{++}(Q_p).
- (w′)^{−1}ρ − w^{−1}ρ = (4, 0; 0), which is −2 times that root. So the other reading gives v(t_1) − v(t_4), which is < 0 for every such t.
For instance, take (v(t_1), …, v(t_4)) = (−1, −2, 2, 1). This t lies in T^{++}(Q_p), since v(t_3) > v(t_4) > v(t_1) > v(t_2). The intended value is 2 and the other reading gives −2.

The positivity claim holds with the intended formula. For w ∈ C(κ), μ = w^{−1}λ is the unique antidominant element of Wλ. Hence σμ − μ is a non-negative rational combination of positive roots for every σ ∈ W, and it is nonzero when σμ ≠ μ. Take σ = (w′)^{−1}w. Then n_{w′} = ⟨σμ − μ, v(t)⟩ ≥ 0 for t ∈ T^+(Q_p). If w′ ∉ C(κ), then (w′)^{−1}λ is not antidominant, so it differs from μ, and n_{w′} > 0 for t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p).

Proposition 4.3.17. The other balancing, ⟨−w^{−1}(w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ), t⟩, gives the weight −w^{−1}λ + w^{−1}ρ instead of −w^{−1}λ − ρ. This is a different normalisation: the valuations differ by ⟨w^{−1}ρ + ρ, v(t)⟩. In the GSp_4 example above, with (v(t_1), …, v(t_4)) = (−1, −2, 2, 1), the intended factor has valuation 12 and the other reading gives 17. The paper excludes that reading in four ways:
- The proof says only "This is analogue to proposition 4.3.9", and Proposition 4.3.9 (p. 48) has ⟨−w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ, t⟩t_w^{naive}.
- The Nebentypus adds no normalisation, since p_2^⋆O(χ) → p_1^⋆O(χ) is an isomorphism (Lemma 4.3.16).
- The definition of t immediately after the proposition (p. 49) uses the balanced factor ⟨−w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ, t⟩. So does Proposition 6.2.6 (p. 61), the correspondence with Nebentypus used in §6.
- Proposition 4.4.5 (p. 51) and Corollary 4.5.5 (p. 52) give the algebraic part of the resulting action as ν = −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ. Remark 4.4.6 (p. 51) says that T(Z_p) acts on the Nebentypus complexes by νχ.

Consequences. Neither Remark 4.3.12 nor Proposition 4.3.17 is cited by number later in the paper. Proposition 4.3.17 supplies the correspondence t_w behind the Nebentypus complexes RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ, χ) of p. 51, and their weight νχ matches the intended normalisation. The Remark's positivity statement is the fact that makes the summands with w′ ∉ C(κ) vanish in the Cousin spectral sequence of Theorem 4.5.2, and it holds for the intended formula. The intended meaning is clear in all three places, so this is a typographical slip that changes no result or argument. - **Misprint** at §1.4, display before Proposition 1.4.7, p. 5. The 2024 preprint has the same display (p. 5). In the preprint, §5.4 (p. 55) also used a plain ⊗. The revision changed §5.4 to ⊗̂ but left the introduction unchanged.. The source says `M^•_w = RHom_{T(Z_p)}(1, RΓ_w(K^p) ⊗_{Z_p} Λ) M^•_{w,cusp} = RHom_{T(Z_p)}(1, RΓ_w(K^p, cusp) ⊗_{Z_p} Λ).`; it should be `M^•_w = RHom_{T(Z_p)}(1, RΓ_w(K^p) ⊗̂_{Z_p} Λ) and M^•_{w,cusp} = RHom_{T(Z_p)}(1, RΓ_w(K^p, cusp) ⊗̂_{Z_p} Λ), with the completed tensor product, as in §5.4.`. §5.4 (p. 56) defines M^•_w and M^•_{w,cusp} with ⊗̂_{Z_p}. The proof of Lemma 5.4.1 (perfectness) rests on RHom_{T′(Z_p)}(1, C^0(T′(Z_p),Z_p) ⊗̂_{Z_p} Λ) = Λ[0], and Lemma 5.4.2 also uses ⊗̂. By Theorem 1.4.3(1) and Definition 1.4.1, RΓ_w(K^p) is represented by a complex whose terms are C^0(T′(Z_p),Z_p)^{n_i}. These terms are not finitely generated over Z_p. The algebraic tensor product C^0(T′(Z_p),Z_p) ⊗_{Z_p} Λ is only the submodule of C^0(T′(Z_p),Λ) = C^0(T′(Z_p),Z_p) ⊗̂ Λ made of functions whose values lie in a finitely generated Z_p-submodule. The invariant function that corresponds to 1 ∈ Λ is x ↦ [x]^{±1}. The group elements [x] are Z_p-linearly independent, so this function is not in the algebraic tensor product. Hence the key identity Λ[0] fails for ⊗. The intended meaning is clear from the pointer to §5.4. - **Misprint** at §4.4.1, definition of S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} (the sentence before the definition of D_{w,±}, just above Lemma 4.4.2), p. 50. The 2024 preprint has the same text (p. 48).. The source says `We let S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1}.`; it should be `We let S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i (Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1}). The second index should be w_i − 1, not w_i + 1. As in Z_{>w−1} = ∩_i Z_{i,>w_i−1} (§4.1.16), a factor whose index lies outside the range 0 ≤ j ≤ i of Proposition 4.1.13 is the whole special fibre and imposes no condition. These factors are Z_{i,>−1} when w_i = 0 and Z_{i,<i+1} when w_i = i. Extending Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}) with disjoint supports gives Z_{i,>−1} = Z_i + V(p^n) and Z_{i,<i+1} = V(p^{n(i+1)}) − Z_i ≥ V(p^n).`. p. 50 reads: "We let S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1}." Notation:
- D_1, …, D_{2g} are the Cartier divisors of §4.1.8, with D_k + D_{2g+1−k} = V(p^n), and Z_i = D_{g+1} + … + D_{g+i} (§4.1.12).
- For 0 ≤ j ≤ i, Z_{i,>j} and Z_{i,<j} are the Cartier divisors of Proposition 4.1.13 (p. 42). They have disjoint supports, and Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}).
- (w_1, …, w_g) is the sequence attached to w at the end of §3.1. The identity has w_i = i.
- All intersections are taken of supports, inside the special fibre.

1. The printed set cannot be what is meant.
- Lemma 4.1.17(1) gives Z_{i,>w_i+1} ⊆ Z_{i,>w_i}.
- By p. 43, S_{F_p,w} ⊆ ∩_i (Z_{i,>w_i−1} ∩ Z^c_{i,>w_i}).
- So the printed set never meets the non-empty stratum S_{F_p,w}.
- In fact the printed set is empty for every w, because each factor Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1} is empty. If w_i < i, then j = w_i + 1 ≤ i, and Z_{i,<j} and Z_{i,>j} have disjoint supports. If w_i = i, the extension in the correction gives Z_{i,>i+1} = 0, since Z_i − V(p^{n(i+1)}) = −V(p^n) − (D_{g+1−i} + … + D_g) is anti-effective.

Lemma 4.4.2, however, says that this set compactifies S_{F_p,w}. By Definitions 2.1.9 and 2.1.26 (pp. 7 and 10), S_{F_p,w} must be open in it, with complement D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}. So Lemma 4.4.2 is false as printed.

Example, g = 1. The proof of Proposition 4.1.13 gives Z_{1,>0} = D_2 and Z_{1,<1} = D_1, and §4.1.8 gives D_1 + D_2 = V(p^n). Hence Z_{1,>1} − Z_{1,<1} = −D_1, so Z_{1,>1} = 0. For w ≠ Id, §3.1 gives w_1 = 0. The printed set is then Z_{1,<1} ∩ Z_{1,>1} = ∅. But S_{F_p,w} = S_{F_p} ∖ D_2 (Lemma 4.1.9) is not empty: it is the locus where H_2 is étale.

2. The corrected set works.
- Let S̃_{=w} = ∩_i (Z^c_{i,>w_i} ∩ Z^c_{i,<w_i}) be the open set of Proposition 4.1.13(2). It is the complement of D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}.
- On S̃_{=w}, Z_i = V(p^{nw_i}) (proof of Proposition 4.1.13). So there Z_{i,<w_i+1} − Z_{i,>w_i+1} = V(p^n) and Z_{i,>w_i−1} − Z_{i,<w_i−1} = V(p^n).
- In each pair the two divisors have disjoint supports. So Z_{i,<w_i+1} and Z_{i,>w_i−1} both contain the whole special fibre of S̃_{=w}, which is S_{F_p,w} (Corollary 4.1.14).
- Hence the corrected set is closed in the proper S^{tor}_{F_p} and contains S_{F_p,w}. Removing D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−} from it leaves exactly S_{F_p,w}.
- For g = 1 and w ≠ Id: the corrected set is Z_{1,<1} = D_1, D_{w,+} = Z_{1,<0} = ∅ and D_{w,−} = Z_{1,>0} = D_2. So D_1 ∖ D_2 = S_{F_p} ∖ D_2 = S_{F_p,w}.

The proof of Lemma 4.4.2 uses exactly these two bounds. Inside the set, it needs Z_{i,>w_i} and Z_{i,<w_i} to lie in ∩_{j=0}^{i}(Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}). This follows from Lemma 4.1.17(1):
- for j ≤ w_i, Z_{i,>w_i} ⊆ Z_{i,>j};
- for j ≥ w_i + 1, the set lies in Z_{i,<w_i+1} ⊆ Z_{i,<j};
- the case of Z_{i,<w_i} is symmetric, using Z_{i,>w_i−1}.

3. The paper itself uses the corrected set.
- The notation "(w−1, w+1)" and Z_{>w−1} = ∩_i Z_{i,>w_i−1} (§4.1.16, p. 43) both point to the lower bound w_i − 1.
- On p. 58 (proof of Proposition 5.6.3, g = 2, w of length one) the paper writes "Concretely, S^{tor}_{(w−1,w+1)} = Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{1,>0}". Here (w_1, w_2) = (1, 1), which matches D_{w,+} = Z_{1,<1} and D_{w,−} = Z_{2,>1} on the same page.
- The corrected definition gives Z_{1,<2} ∩ Z_{1,>0} ∩ Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{2,>0}. Here Z_{1,<2} is the whole special fibre and Z_{1,>0} = Z_1 ⊆ Z_2 = Z_{2,>0}. So it equals Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{1,>0}, exactly as on p. 58. The printed definition would give ∅, since it includes Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{2,>2}.
- The proof of Corollary 4.4.3 uses (∪_{w'} C^{tor}_{t,F_p,w'}) ∩ p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = C^{tor}_{t,F_p,w}. Here p_i maps C^{tor}_{t,F_p,w'} into S_{F_p,w'}. On S̃_{=w'} we have Z_i = V(p^{nw'_i}). So there Z_{i,<w_i+1} − Z_{i,>w_i+1} = V(p^{n(w_i+1−w'_i)}) and Z_{i,>w_i−1} − Z_{i,<w_i−1} = V(p^{n(w'_i−w_i+1)}). Hence the first factor misses S_{F_p,w'} when w'_i > w_i, and the second misses it when w'_i < w_i. So S_{F_p,w'} meets the corrected set only if w'_i = w_i for all i. Since the sequence determines w (§3.1), this means w' = w, so the equality holds for the corrected set. With the printed set the left-hand side is empty.

So the slip is a single index, and the notation and p. 58 fix the intended set. With that set, Lemma 4.4.2 holds as intended. The later uses of the set and of the lemma (Corollary 4.4.3, Proposition 4.4.4 and Proposition 5.6.3) all refer to the corrected set. - **Misprint** at §4.4.1, proof of Lemma 4.4.2, first paragraph (the first sentence and the "In particular" sentence), p. 50. The 2024 preprint has the same text (p. 48).. The source says `"Proof. We first work on C_t. By lemma 4.2.11, we see that p_2^⋆Z_{i,>w_i} ≥ p_1^⋆Z_{i,>w_i} and p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i} ≥ p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}. By corollary 4.2.10, we find that the support of p_2^⋆(Z_{i,>w_i} − Z_{i,<w_i}) − p_1^⋆(Z_{i,>w_i} − Z_{i,<w_i}) contains p_1^⋆ ∩_{j=0}^{i} (Z_{i<j} ∪ Z_{i>j}) and p_2^⋆ ∩_{j=0}^{i} (Z_{i<j} ∪ Z_{i>j}). We now consider this property in C^{tor}_{t,F_p,(w−1,w+1)}. We deduce that the support of p_2^⋆(Z_{i,>w_i} − Z_{i,<w_i}) − p_1^⋆(Z_{i,>w_i} − Z_{i,<w_i}) contains p_1^⋆Z_{i,>w_i} and p_2^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}. (1) The first sentence should end "and p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i} ≥ p_2^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}". This is the second inequality of Lemma 4.2.11 with j = w_i. (2) The "In particular" sentence should end "contains p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}", not "contains p_1^⋆Z_{i,>w_i}". The sentence just before the "In particular" sentence ("We deduce that the support of … contains p_1^⋆Z_{i,>w_i} and p_2^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}") is correct as printed and should stay. Replacing its pair by p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i} and p_2^⋆Z_{i,>w_i} would also give a true statement, but that change is not needed: the printed pair already implies both containments the argument uses (see the reason).`. The 2024 preprint has the same paragraph, with both slips, on its p. 48.

Notation. Fix i and write Z_> = Z_{i,>w_i} and Z_< = Z_{i,<w_i}. As in the proof, f_+ and f_− are local generators of Z_< and Z_>. Lemma 4.2.11 (p. 45) states p_1^⋆Z_{i,>j} ≤ p_2^⋆Z_{i,>j} and p_2^⋆Z_{i,<j} ≤ p_1^⋆Z_{i,<j}. Take j = w_i. Put E = p_2^⋆(Z_> − Z_<) − p_1^⋆(Z_> − Z_<). By Lemma 4.2.11, E = (p_2^⋆Z_> − p_1^⋆Z_>) + (p_1^⋆Z_< − p_2^⋆Z_<) is a sum of two effective divisors. The proof of Lemma 4.2.11 uses Z_> − Z_< = Z_i − V(p^{nw_i}) (Proposition 4.1.13(1)) and p_1^⋆V(p^{nw_i}) = p_2^⋆V(p^{nw_i}). So E = p_2^⋆Z_i − p_1^⋆Z_i, which is why Corollary 4.2.10 applies. Put F = p_1^⋆Z_< − p_2^⋆Z_< + p_2^⋆Z_>. Then F = E + p_1^⋆Z_>. Also, F is the divisor of the function h = p_1^⋆f_+ p_2^⋆f_− / p_2^⋆f_+ that the proof's identity p_1^⋆f_+ p_2^⋆f_− = h p_2^⋆f_+ defines.

(1) The first sentence. As printed, the second inequality compares a divisor with itself, so it says nothing. The inequality that Lemma 4.2.11 gives, and that the proof uses, is p_1^⋆Z_< ≥ p_2^⋆Z_<. This inequality makes F effective, so h is regular. Without it, h is not known to be regular. The end of the proof states the same inequality in strict form: "there exists 0 < s < 1 such that s p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i} ≥ p_2^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}". So the subscript 1 on the right-hand side is a slip for 2.

(2) The "In particular" sentence. The printed claim is that the support of F contains p_1^⋆Z_>. This is trivially true, because F = E + p_1^⋆Z_> with E effective. It is also not what the argument uses. The next sentence says that h vanishes on p_1^⋆Z_<, and this is the property the argument needs. Since Z_> and Z_< have disjoint supports, there are local functions a and b with af_+ + bf_− = 1. Together with p_1^⋆f_+ p_2^⋆f_− = h p_2^⋆f_+, this gives p_1^⋆f_+ = (p_1^⋆f_+ p_2^⋆a + h p_2^⋆b) p_2^⋆f_+. Because h vanishes on p_1^⋆Z_<, so does the factor p_1^⋆f_+ p_2^⋆a + h p_2^⋆b. That gives s p_1^⋆Z_< ≥ p_2^⋆Z_< for some 0 < s < 1. This is the condition of Definition 2.1.19(2) (p. 9) for Z_{i,<w_i}. Summing over i, as the proof does at the end, gives the same condition for D_{w,+}. So the sentence should end with p_1^⋆Z_<.

(3) The sentence just before the "In particular" sentence is true, and it is enough. It says that, on C^{tor}_{t,F_p,(w−1,w+1)}, the support of E contains p_1^⋆Z_> and p_2^⋆Z_<. We have p_1^⋆Z_< − p_2^⋆Z_< ≤ E. So the support of p_1^⋆Z_< = (p_1^⋆Z_< − p_2^⋆Z_<) + p_2^⋆Z_< lies in supp E ∪ supp p_2^⋆Z_<. By that sentence, this union is supp E, and supp E ⊆ supp F. This proves the corrected sentence (2). In the same way, p_2^⋆Z_> ≤ E + p_1^⋆Z_>, and supp E ⊇ p_1^⋆Z_>, so supp E ⊇ p_2^⋆Z_>. This is the input needed for "One argues similarly with Z_{i,>w_i}". There, h' = p_2^⋆f_− p_1^⋆f_+ / p_1^⋆f_− has divisor E + p_2^⋆Z_<, and h' must vanish on p_2^⋆Z_>.

That sentence follows from Corollary 4.2.10 as follows. The definition just before the lemma on p. 50 prints S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1}. As printed, this set is empty, because Z_{i,<j} and Z_{i,>j} have disjoint supports. So the second term should read Z_{i,>w_i−1}. By Lemma 4.1.17(1) (p. 43), Z_{i,>j} decreases and Z_{i,<j} increases as j grows. Hence Z_{i,>w_i} ∩ Z_{i,<w_i+1} ⊆ ∩_{j=0}^{i} (Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}) and Z_{i,<w_i} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1} ⊆ ∩_{j=0}^{i} (Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}). So on C^{tor}_{t,F_p,(w−1,w+1)}, the support of E contains p_1^⋆ and p_2^⋆ of both Z_{i,<w_i} and Z_{i,>w_i}. In particular it contains the printed pair, and also the alternative pair.

Why this is a misprint that affects nothing. Each slip is a wrong subscript, and the intended form is clear. Lemma 4.2.11 and the proof's own final inequality fix the first slip. The sentence that follows fixes the second. With these two corrections, the paragraph's argument goes through. The statement of Lemma 4.4.2 is unaffected, and so is Proposition 4.4.4 (p. 51), which rests on it. - **Error** at §4.4.1, proof of Corollary 4.4.3, p. 50 (it affects the proof). The source says `Proof of Corollary 4.4.3, p. 50: "Over p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}, p_2^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i − p_1^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i and p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+} have the same support. Indeed, the complement of p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+} is C^{tor}_{t,F_p,w}. On the other hand, the complement of p_2^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i − p_1^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i in C^{tor}_{t,F_p} is ∪_{w′}C^{tor}_{t,F_p,w′} and (∪_{w′}C^{tor}_{t,F_p,w′}) ∩ p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = C^{tor}_{t,F_p,w}. We deduce that there exists n such that f_i^n = h_ig_i for some h_i ∈ O_{p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}}(U_i) and for all i. [...] There exists units a_{i,j} and b_{i,j} [...] such that X_i = b_{i,j}X_j and Y_i^n = a_{i,j}Y_j^n. We deduce that f_i = a_{i,j}f_j and g_i = b_{i,j}g_j. It follows that g_j(h_j − b_{i,j}a_{i,j}^{-1}h_i) = 0 [...] We now set m = 2n. It follows that the map defined locally by sending Y_i^m to g_ih_i^2X_i glues to give a map O_{p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}}(−2m(p_2^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i − p_1^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i)) → O_{p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}}(−p_1^⋆D_{w,+} − p_2^⋆D_{w,+})."`; it should be `Replace the first two sentences with: "Over p_i^{-1}S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}, the support of p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+} is contained in the support of p_2^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i − p_1^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i. Indeed, the complement of p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+} contains C_{t,F_p,w}, since S_{F_p,w} ∩ D_{w,+} = ∅." The third sentence then gives the inclusion, and the rest of the proof uses nothing more. That sentence needs S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1}; the definition on p. 50 prints Z_{i,>w_i+1}. Equality of supports would hold only with D_{w,+} replaced by D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}, but the corollary needs D_{w,+}. The same proof has two more slips, both harmless: - 'f_i = a_{i,j}f_j' should read f_i^n = a_{i,j}f_j^n. - The glued map is O(−m(p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i)) → O(−p_1^⋆D_{w,+} − p_2^⋆D_{w,+}) with m = 2n, not O(−2m(…)).`. Setting. By Proposition 4.1.13 (p. 42), Z_i = Σ_{k≤i} D_{g+k}, and Z_{i,>j}, Z_{i,<j} are effective with disjoint support, with Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}). On S_{F_p,w′}, the reduction of S̃_{=w′_1,…,w′_g} (Corollary 4.1.14), we have Z_k = V(p^{nw′_k}) locally. In §4.4.1 (p. 50), D_{w,+} = ∪_i Z_{i,<w_i}, D_{w,−} = ∪_i Z_{i,>w_i}, and S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} is printed as ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1}. As printed, this set misses S_{F_p,w}: it would need w′_k ≤ w_k and w′_k ≥ w_k+2. So it must be read as ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1}. This reading agrees with the GSp4 case on p. 58, where S_{(w−1,w+1)} = Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{1,>0}, D_{w,+} = Z_{1,<1} and D_{w,−} = Z_{2,>1} for (w_1,w_2) = (1,1).

Counterexample to the printed sentences. Take g = 1, n = 1 and w the non-identity element. By §3.1, w_1 = 1 exactly when 2 ∈ w^{-1}{2}, so here w_1 = 0. Then:
- Z_1 = D_2, so Z_{1,>0} = D_2 and Z_{1,<0} = ∅.
- D_2 − V(p) = −D_1, so Z_{1,<1} = D_1 (as also stated on p. 42).
Hence D_{w,+} = ∅, D_{w,−} = D_2, S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = D_1 and S_{F_p,w} = D_1 \ D_2. So p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+} = 0, and its complement is all of p_i^{-1}(D_1). This set contains points x with p_1(x) and p_2(x) supersingular, and such points are not in C_{t,F_p,w}.

By Proposition 4.2.15(3) with k = g = 1, supp(p_2^⋆Z_1 − p_1^⋆Z_1) = p_1^⋆D_1 ∩ p_2^⋆D_2. This contains those supersingular points, for i = 1 and for i = 2. For i = 1 it also contains a component on which p_1^⋆H is étale and p_2^⋆H is multiplicative. That component comes from triples (E, H, L) with E ordinary, H ≠ L both non-canonical, and φ(H) = E[p]/L the canonical subgroup of E/L. So the two supports differ, and both 'have the same support' and 'the complement … is C_{t,F_p,w}' are false. The claims also fail for general w, since the complement of p_j^⋆D_{w,+} includes points over D_{w,−} \ D_{w,+}.

The corollary still holds. To get f_i^n ∈ (g_i) one only needs V(g_i) ⊆ V(f_i), that is, the inclusion of supports. This inclusion holds:
- The divisors in Propositions 4.2.14(1) and 4.2.15(3) coincide after reindexing: both are Σ_j p_1^⋆D_j ∩ p_2^⋆D_{2g+1−j}. So the complement of supp(p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i) in C_{t,F_p} is ∪_{w′} C_{t,F_p,w′}.
- At a point y ∈ S_{F_p,w′}, locally Z_k − V(p^{nj}) = V(p^{n(w′_k−j)}). Hence y ∈ Z_{k,<w_k+1} if and only if w′_k ≤ w_k, and y ∈ Z_{k,>w_k−1} if and only if w′_k ≥ w_k. So S_{F_p,w′} meets S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} only when w′ = w.
- S_{F_p,w} is disjoint from D_{w,+}.
So the paper's own third sentence already gives the inclusion. The corrected statement about complements was checked the same way, using S_{F_p} \ (D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}) = S_{F_p,w} (Proposition 4.1.13(2)).

The two slips:
- Since Y_i^n ↦ f_i^n, the relation Y_i^n = a_{i,j}Y_j^n gives f_i^n = a_{i,j}f_j^n. The printed relation g_j(h_j − b_{i,j}a_{i,j}^{-1}h_i) = 0 follows from exactly this, via h_ig_i = f_i^n = a_{i,j}h_jg_j and g_i = b_{i,j}g_j. With f_i = a_{i,j}f_j it would read a_{i,j}^{-n}.
- Gluing Y_i^{2n} ↦ g_ih_i^2X_i requires g_j(a_{i,j}^2h_j^2 − b_{i,j}^2h_i^2) = 0, which is the printed identity. The composite sends Y_i^{2n} to g_i^2h_i^2 = f_i^{2n}, which is the canonical map. So the source is O(−m(…)) with m = 2n, and the printed −2m is inconsistent, though harmless because m is only asserted to exist.
All of this was checked by direct computation.

Downstream. Corollary 4.4.3 is used only through its statement, in the proof of Proposition 4.5.8 (p. 53). That statement is correct, so only the proof is affected. Setting (pp. 41–42, 50):
- Z_k = Σ_{l≤k} D_{g+l}.
- Z_{k,>j} and Z_{k,<j} are effective, have disjoint support, and satisfy Z_{k,>j} − Z_{k,<j} = Z_k − V(p^{nj}) (Prop. 4.1.13).
- D_{w,+} = ∪_k Z_{k,<w_k} and D_{w,−} = ∪_k Z_{k,>w_k}.
- S_{F_p,w} is the special fibre of S̃_{=w_1,…,w_g} = ∩_k Z^c_{k,>w_k} ∩ Z^c_{k,<w_k} (Prop. 4.1.13(2), Cor. 4.1.14). So S_{F_p,w} is disjoint from D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}.
- Write E = p_2^⋆ΣZ_k − p_1^⋆ΣZ_k, which is effective by Cor. 4.2.10.

Counterexample. Take g = 1 and w = s, the non-trivial element of ^MW = W. By §3.1, w_1 = 0, since 2 ∉ s^{-1}{2}.
- Z_{1,>0} − Z_{1,<0} = Z_1 = D_2 is effective and the two parts have disjoint support, so Z_{1,<0} = 0. Hence D_{w,+} = ∅ and p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+} = 0 has empty support.
- S_{F_p,w} = S_{F_p} \ D_2 is the locus where H = Gr_2 is étale. With the corrected definition, S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = Z_{1,<1} = D_1 (p. 42 gives Z_{1,<1} = D_g).

(a) Supersingular points. Cor. 4.2.10 with i = 1 shows that supp E contains p_1^{-1}(D_1 ∩ D_2) and p_2^{-1}(D_1 ∩ D_2). This set is non-empty: over a supersingular curve A[p^n] is connected, so neither Gr_1 nor Gr_2 is étale. It lies in p_i^{-1}(D_1) for i = 1 and for i = 2.

(b) Points over S_{F_p,w} itself. These do not depend on the misprinted definition, because Lemma 4.4.2 requires S_{F_p,w} ⊆ S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}.
- In the correspondence of §4.2.5, L has order p and meets H trivially, and H′ = φ(H).
- Take E ordinary with H non-canonical, and L ≠ H non-canonical.
- Then φ(H) = E[p]/L is the kernel of the dual isogeny, which is the multiplicative (canonical) subgroup of E/L.
- At the resulting point y, p_1(y) ∈ S_{F_p,w} while p_2^⋆D_2 > 0 = p_1^⋆D_2. So y ∈ supp E.
So over p_1^{-1}S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} the support of E is non-empty, while that of p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+} is empty. This refutes the first sentence. The point y lies in the complement of p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+}, but not in C_{t,F_p,w} = p_1^{-1}S_{F_p,w} ∩ p_2^{-1}S_{F_p,w}. This refutes the second sentence.

The failure is general. For i = 1, any y with p_1(y) ∈ S_{F_p,w} and p_2(y) ∈ S_{F_p,w′}, where w′ ≠ w, gives a counterexample:
- y ∈ supp E by Props. 4.2.14(1) and 4.2.15(3).
- p_2^⋆Z_k ≥ p_1^⋆Z_k forces w′_k ≥ w_k, so p_2(y) ∉ D_{w,+}.
Equality holds only in special cases, such as w = Id, where D_{w,−} = ∅.

Defence. No faithful reading saves the equality. The claim uses D_{w,+} alone, and the point in (b) does not involve D_{w,−}. What is true is this: since S_{F_p} \ (D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}) = S_{F_p,w}, the complement of p_1^⋆(D_{w,+}+D_{w,−}) + p_2^⋆(D_{w,+}+D_{w,−}) inside p_i^{-1}S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} is C_{t,F_p,w}.

Why the corollary survives. The step "f_i^n = h_ig_i" needs only V(g_i) ⊆ V(f_i), that is, the inclusion of supports. The paper's third sentence supplies it:
- The complement of supp E in C_{t,F_p} is ∪_{w′}C_{t,F_p,w′}. After reindexing, the divisors in Props. 4.2.14(1) and 4.2.15(3) agree.
- At a point of S_{F_p,w′}, locally Z_k − V(p^{nj}) = V(p^{n(w′_k−j)}). So the point lies in Z_{k,<w_k+1} if and only if w′_k ≤ w_k, and in Z_{k,>w_k−1} if and only if w′_k ≥ w_k. Hence S_{F_p,w′} meets S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} only when w′ = w.
- This needs the reading Z_{k,>w_k−1}. With the printed Z_{i,>w_i+1}, S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} would miss S_{F_p,w}. The GSp_4 case on p. 58 uses Z_{1,>0} for (w_1,w_2) = (1,1), which agrees with the corrected reading.
- C_{t,F_p,w} avoids p_1^{-1}D_{w,+} ∪ p_2^{-1}D_{w,+}.
Then f_i^n ∈ (g_i), because O(U_i) is Noetherian. The squares h_i^2 make g_ih_i^2 independent of the choice of h_i, so the gluing goes through.

The two slips:
- Only f_i^n = a_{i,j}f_j^n yields the printed g_j(h_j − b_{i,j}a_{i,j}^{-1}h_i) = 0. The printed f_i = a_{i,j}f_j would give a_{i,j}^{-n} instead.
- Y_i^m generates O(−mE). The composite with O(−p_1^⋆D_{w,+} − p_2^⋆D_{w,+}) → O sends Y_i^m to g_i^2h_i^2 = f_i^m, which is the canonical map. So the source is O(−mE), not O(−2mE).
The identities were checked by direct computation.

Downstream. Cor. 4.4.3 is cited once, in the proof of Prop. 4.5.8 (p. 53), and only through its statement. That statement is correct, so only the proof of Cor. 4.4.3 is affected.

- **Misprint** at §4.4.1, proof of Corollary 4.4.3, last paragraph, p. 50. The 2024 preprint has the same text (p. 48).. The source says `There exists units a_{i,j} and b_{i,j} ∈ O_{p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}}(U_{i,j})^× such that X_i = b_{i,j}X_j and Y_i^n = a_{i,j}Y_j^n. We deduce that f_i = a_{i,j}f_j and g_i = b_{i,j}g_j. It follows that g_j(h_j − b_{i,j}a_{i,j}^{-1}h_i) = 0 in O_{p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}}(U_{i,j}).`; it should be `We deduce that f_i^n = a_{i,j}f_j^n and g_i = b_{i,j}g_j.`. Here Y_i is a local generator of O(−(p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i)) with image f_i, and the unit a_{i,j} is defined by Y_i^n = a_{i,j}Y_j^n. Taking images gives f_i^n = a_{i,j}f_j^n, not f_i = a_{i,j}f_j. The corrected relation is the one the next sentence uses. From f_i^n = h_ig_i = b_{i,j}h_ig_j and f_i^n = a_{i,j}f_j^n = a_{i,j}h_jg_j we get g_j(a_{i,j}h_j − b_{i,j}h_i) = 0, i.e. g_j(h_j − b_{i,j}a_{i,j}^{-1}h_i) = 0, exactly as printed. With the printed f_i = a_{i,j}f_j one would instead get g_j(h_j − b_{i,j}a_{i,j}^{-n}h_i) = 0. The later gluing step uses Y_i^{2n} = a_{i,j}^2Y_j^{2n}, which is also consistent with the corrected relation. The rest of the argument is unaffected. It follows that the map defined locally by sending Y_i^m to g_ih_i^2X_i glues to give a map O_{p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}}(−2m(p_2^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i − p_1^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i)) → O_{p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}}(−p_1^⋆D_{w,+} − p_2^⋆D_{w,+}) .`; it should be `… glues to give a map O_{p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}}(−m(p_2^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i − p_1^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i)) → O_{p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}}(−p_1^⋆D_{w,+} − p_2^⋆D_{w,+}).`. Y_i generates O(−(p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i)) on U_i, so Y_i^m generates O(−m(p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i)). The source of the map is therefore the −m twist, not the −2m twist. This twist also matches the statement of the corollary and the dual maps displayed at the start of the proof. The map is compatible with the inclusions into O: Y_i^m has image f_i^{2n} = h_i^2g_i^2, which is the image of g_ih_i^2X_i. The gluing check (Y_i^{2n} = a_{i,j}^2Y_j^{2n}, X_i = b_{i,j}X_j, g_j(h_j^2 − b_{i,j}^2a_{i,j}^{-2}h_i^2) = 0) also applies to this map. Read literally, the −2m twist would need a generator Y_i^{2m}, which the construction does not provide. Only the existence of some exponent matters, so nothing downstream is affected. - **Misprint** at §4.5.1, Remark 4.5.3, p. 51. The 2024 preprint has the same text (p. 50).. The source says `Remark 4.5.3. The differentials and the abutment in the spectral sequence of theorem 4.5.2 depend in principle on the choice of the integral models S^{tor} and w̃^κ. The higher Hida complexes are however canonical.`; it should be `… on the choice of the integral models S^{tor} and ω̃^κ.`. The symbol is printed as a Latin w with a tilde. In the preceding lines of §4.5.1 and in Theorem 4.5.2, the sheaf is a Greek omega with a tilde. The source says `p. 51, proof of Proposition 4.4.5: "In proposition 4.4.4, the construction of a compactification S̄^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ} of S^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ}, with boundary D = D_+∪D_− is independent of the choice of t ∈ T^+(Q_p). We see that RΓ(S^{tor}_{Z/p^s,w}, ω^κ)^{C^{tor}_{t,w,Z/p^sZ}−ord} and RΓ(S^{tor}_{Z_p/p^s,w}, ω^κ)^{C^{tor}_{t′,w,Z/p^sZ}−ord} are direct factors of the cohomology with support RΓ_{D_+,D_−}(S̄^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ}, ω^κ). (a) For each t ∈ T^+(Q_p), the operator T_t is defined on that complex. This part is easy. By Lemma 4.2.11, the tuple (C̄_{t,w}, S̄_w, D_+, D_−) is a dynamic compactification for every t ∈ T^+(Q_p), not only for t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p). Proposition 2.2.10 applied to t_w of Proposition 4.3.9 then gives T_t. (b) A composition law: T_t T_{t′} ≃ T_{tt′} ≃ T_{t′} T_t for all t, t′ ∈ T^+(Q_p). This is the missing step. Proving it requires: - an identification C_{t,w} ×_{S_w} C_{t′,w} ≅ C_{tt′,w}, which is the integral, Igusa-level analogue, via Proposition 4.2.4, of the double-coset identity [K t K][K t′ K] = [K tt′ K] from [Cas], lem. 4.1.5, cited on p. 43; - multiplicativity of the normalizing factors ⟨−w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)−ρ, t⟩; - a proper-base-change argument, as in the proof of Proposition 2.8.2, showing that composing the operators on cohomology with partial support gives the operator of the composite correspondence. Once (b) is available, the deduction is indeed easy.`. Checked against the paper's constructions. The operators on RΓ_{D_+,D_−} come from these results:
- Proposition 4.3.9 (p. 48): for each t separately, the normalized cohomological correspondence t_w = ⟨−w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)−ρ, t⟩ t_w^{naive} on C^{tor}_{t,w}.
- §§2.2–2.3 (Proposition 2.3.13, p. 17): its extension to a dynamic compactification.
- Proposition 4.4.4: the compactification p_1^⋆S̄ ∩ p_2^⋆S̄.

The only justification offered for "T^+(Q_p) acts" is that the compactification S̄^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ} does not depend on t. That gives one endomorphism T_x for each x on a common complex. It says nothing about how these endomorphisms relate to one another.

The relations t^n = t′u′ and (t′)^n = tu hold in the group. They carry information about the operators only through T_{t^n} = T_t^n = T_{t′}T_{u′} (and symmetrically) with commuting operators. Without this, the t- and t′-ordinary projectors on RΓ_{D_+,D_−} are unrelated.

The paper proves no such composition law in this setting:
- §2.8 (Proposition 2.8.2, pp. 25–27) handles only the iterates C^{(n)} of a single correspondence. It does not compare C_t ×_S C_{t′} (or C_t^{(n)}) with C_{tt′} (or C_{t^n}), and it says nothing about the normalizations.
- Casselman's lemma, cited on p. 48, gives the algebra map Z[T^+(Q_p)/T(Z_p)] → C_c(K_{p,n}\G(Q_p)/K_{p,n}, Z). That is multiplicativity in the abstract Hecke algebra, i.e. on cohomology of the generic fibre. It does not cover the mod p^s cohomology with partial support over the strata S^{tor}_w, defined via integral models and integrally normalized maps.

That §2.8 is needed even for iterates of one correspondence shows that such compatibilities are not formal in this framework. The step is therefore asserted without adequate proof.

The result itself is not in doubt, and the gap looks fillable:
- For t, t′ ∈ T^+ the double cosets multiply at level K_{p,n}, so the composite correspondence is C_{tt′} on the generic fibre.
- The normalizing factors are multiplicative in t.
- Maps p_2^⋆ω^κ → p_1^!ω^κ on the normal Z_p-flat integral models are determined by their generic fibre.
- The remaining bookkeeping is of the kind done in Proposition 2.8.2.

As printed, however, "it is easy to deduce" rests on the unproved sentence "We deduce that T^+(Q_p) acts". The multiplicativity is also needed for the asserted T(Q_p)-action, since T(Q_p) is generated by T^{++}(Q_p) acting invertibly on the ordinary part. 1. What the paper actually shows. Independence of the compactification from t gives, for each t, an endomorphism T_t of the one complex M = RΓ_{D_+,D_−}(S̄^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ}, ω^κ). It does not give a monoid action, meaning T_{tt′} = T_t T_{t′} with the operators commuting.

2. Why the argument needs such an action. The relation t^n = t′u′ is useful only if T_t^n = T_{t′}T_{u′} and T_t commutes with T_{t′}.

3. Nothing nearby supplies the composition law. I searched the paper for it and found the following.
- Section 2 constructs the operator of a single dynamic correspondence (Proposition 2.2.10) and checks that it does not depend on the compactification (Proposition 2.2.11).
- Section 2.8 treats only the iterates of one fixed correspondence C, not products C_t ∘ C_{t′} of different Hecke correspondences.
- Section 4.2 cites [Cas] only for the abstract Hecke algebra map Z[T^+(Q_p)/T(Z_p)] → C_c(K_{p,n}\G(Q_p)/K_{p,n}, Z). That map does not transfer to the integral, normalized cohomological correspondences restricted to S_w with partial supports. Transferring it requires checking that the fibre product of the finite flat formal schemes C_{t,w} and C_{t′,w} over S_w matches C_{tt′,w} integrally, and that the fundamental classes and normalizations compose.
- Proposition 4.2.4 and Lemma 4.3.8 contain the right ingredients: the Igusa description, and trace factors additive on T^+ because the sign of α(w(v(t))) is constant there. They are never assembled into a composition statement.
The step is standard and very likely true, so the defence fails only as a matter of written proof.

4. The final deduction does go through once (b) holds, even with commutativity only up to homotopy. By Proposition 2.5.4, H^i(M^{t-ord}) is a finite Z/p^s-module on which T_t is invertible. Then T_{t′} is invertible on it, because T_t^n = T_{t′}T_{u′} with commuting operators. The t′-non-ordinary factor is a Z/p^s[[T]]-module, so T_{t′} acts nilpotently on any finite-length piece of it. Hence the projection of H^i(M^{t-ord}) to the t′-non-ordinary factor vanishes. Symmetrically, the composite of inclusion and projection between the two direct factors is a quasi-isomorphism.

5. The proposed correction is right and essentially minimal. I add only (a), which follows from Lemma 4.2.11, and the note that (b) is exactly what the sentence "T^+(Q_p) acts" presupposes.

6. What depends on this passage.
- The T(Q_p)-action asserted in the statement of Proposition 4.4.5. Its only justification is this sentence, together with inverting T^{++}(Q_p) on ordinary parts, which also needs commutativity.
- Corollary 4.5.5 (an isomorphism of T(Q_p)-modules).
- The definition of RΓ_w(K^pK_{p,P}) on p. 54 ("the argument of proposition 4.4.5 shows that the ordinary part does not depend on the choice of t") and Proposition 5.2.3 (these complexes lie in D(Z_p[T(Q_p)])).
- Through these, the T(Q_p)-equivariance claims in Theorem 1.4.3 and the adjoint statement in Theorem 5.5.1.

- **Error** at Published §4 p.141, paragraph after Corollary 15, and its uses: proof of Lemma 16 p.142 ('We may assume that X is non-parabolic'), the remark after Definition 18 p.144 ('it is immediate to check that t-b.l. sections are quasi-t-b.l.') and the proof of Theorem A p.146; arXiv v3 §4 the same (it affects a stated result). The source says `If X is parabolic affine, every Galois section of X is cuspidal (the only non-trivial case is settled by [18, Theorem A]). Because of this, we can always assume that X is non-parabolic.`; it should be `The sentence holds when the boundary is split (every section of A^1 or G_m lies in each cuspidal packet), and for proper genus-zero curves Schmidt's theorem gives X ≅ P^1 once the section is b.l. It is false for X ≅ P^1_k minus a closed point of degree 2, which has geometric sections but no cuspidal ones. That case of Theorem A needs its own proof, and so does the remark after Definition 18, whose identity-map argument needs X non-parabolic. Over number fields the extraction records a proposed repair (items /169–/177, not in the paper, unreviewed). Over fields of positive transcendence degree no argument is known: Proposition 22 takes quasi-t-b.l. sections as input. Theorem A for non-parabolic curves, and Theorems B and C, which only use hyperbolic curves, are unaffected. Items /96 and /112 state what is proved.`. X = P^1_Q minus V(T²−2) is affine and parabolic, 0 ∈ X(Q) gives a geometric section, and the boundary has no Q-point, so X has no cuspidal section. Schmidt's theorem concerns the splitting of the completion, not rationality of the boundary. The reductions in Lemma 16 and in the proof of Theorem A therefore leave unhandled the t-b.l. sections of such X that are not geometric. - **Error** at Proof of Proposition 10.9, p. 886 (Invent. Math.); same text in arXiv v5 (it affects the proof). The source says `"Let L/K be any wildly ramified extension of degree p. … the same calculation as before shows that rsw_{e′_L}(res_{L/K} A) = [c̄_L ω, 0]_{π_L, e′_L}, where π_L is a uniformiser of L, e′_L = pe′ and c̄_L is some non-zero element of F."`; it should be `Let L/K be a totally ramified extension of degree p, e.g. L = K(π^{1/p}) (K contains ζ_p). Then F_L = F, ω stays non-zero, e′_L = pe′, and the rest of the proof is unchanged.`. With an imperfect residue field, a degree-p extension can be wildly ramified with e(L/K) = 1 and purely inseparable residue extension (ferociously ramified, the paper's own term in the proof of Lemma 10.5). For such L, e′_L = e′, not pe′. Concretely, take L = K(x̃^{1/p}), where x̃ lifts the x in ω = dx/x ∧ dy/y. This is wildly ramified of degree p, and x̃ is a p-th power in L, so res_{L/K}A = (x̃, ỹ)_p = 0 and the claimed rsw_{e′_L}(res A) = [c̄_L ω, 0] with c̄_L ≠ 0 fails (ω also dies in Ω²_{F_L}, since dx = 0 there). The proposition asserts failure for some L, so one totally ramified L suffices and the stated result stands. - **Gap** at Introduction, paragraph before Theorem C, p. 823 (Invent. Math.); same text in arXiv v5 (it affects a stated result). The source says `"Our next result owes its existence to Wittenberg's suggestion that our methods could be used to address Question 1.4. It gives a positive answer to that question, and also shows that the answer to Question 1.3 is no, in general."`; it should be `Theorem C gives a positive answer to Question 1.4 for every V that has good ordinary reduction at some prime of L, for example abelian surfaces and K3 surfaces. In general the positive answer is conditional on the existence of such a prime, conjectured by Serre and recorded by the authors right after Theorem C. The negative answer to Question 1.3 is unconditional, e.g. via K3 surfaces.`. Theorem C assumes a prime 𝔭 of good ordinary reduction, and its proof uses ordinarity through [BK, Theorem 0.7(iii)] to get gr⁰ H²(V̄_𝔭, Q_p) ≠ 0. For a smooth projective V with H²(V, O_V) ≠ 0 (so H⁰(Ω²) ≠ 0 by Hodge symmetry), nothing in the paper supplies such a prime. Ordinarity is geometric and does not change under finite extension of L. The paper itself says, after Theorem C, that ordinary reduction at a positive density of primes is only conjectured in general (Joshi, attributing it to Serre), and known for abelian surfaces and K3 surfaces. So the claim holds only for varieties with an ordinary prime. ### Calegari–Geraghty, "Modularity lifting beyond the Taylor-Wiles method", Inventiones Mathematicae (2018) (`PAPER-CALEGARI-GERAGHTY-18`)

- **Gap** at Abstract (p. 298) and §1 Introduction (p. 305), compared with the §4.1 set-up for Theorem 4.8 (p. 361) and Lemma 4.11 (pp. 364–365). arXiv v2 has the same text ("completely solved", l. 316; same parenthetical on twisting before Thm 4.8). arXiv v1 is also the same: intro, and §3.8 Theorem 3.25 with the same twist-minimal hypothesis. (it affects a stated result). The source says `p. 305 (§1): "In the process of proving our main result, we also completely solve the problem (for p odd) of determining the multiplicity of an irreducible modular representation ρ̄ in the Jacobian J_1(N*)[m], where N* is the minimal level such that ρ̄ arises in weight two. In particular, we prove that when ρ̄ is unramified at p and ρ̄(Frob_p) is a scalar, then the multiplicity of ρ̄ is two (see Theorem 4.8). (In all other cases, the multiplicity was already known to be one—and in the exceptional cases we consider, the multiplicity was also known to be ≥2)." Abstract, p. 298: "Moreover, we also completely solve the problem (for p odd) of determining the multiplicity of an irreducible modular representation ρ̄ in the Jacobian J_1(N), where N is the minimal level such that ρ̄ arises in weight two." p. 361 (§4.1, set-up before Thm 4.8): "Assume that ρ̄ has minimal conductor amongst all its twists at all other primes (one can always twist ρ̄ to satisfy these condition)."`; it should be `In the abstract and introduction, limit the multiplicity claim to ρ̄ that have minimal conductor amongst their twists at primes ≠ p. That is the hypothesis of Theorem 4.8. Twist-minimality at p is automatic in the scalar case, where ρ̄|G_p is unramified. The alternative is to give a separate argument for non-twist-minimal ρ̄. Theorem 4.8 as stated in §4.1 needs no change.`. I rendered pp. 298, 305 and 361–366 and checked them against the text above.

1. The claims do not match. The abstract and introduction claim multiplicity two for every irreducible modular ρ̄ (p odd) at its own minimal weight-2 level. The classical multiplicity-one results cited in Remark 4.9 (Mazur, Gross, Edixhoven, ...) are stated without twist-minimality. Theorem 4.8, however, is proved only under the hypothesis that ρ̄ has minimal conductor among its twists. The only link between the two is the parenthetical "(one can always twist ρ̄ to satisfy these condition)". That remark is true, but it does not show that multiplicity is unchanged by twisting: ρ̄ and ρ̄⊗ψ̄ sit at different levels N(ρ̄)p and N(ρ̄⊗ψ̄)p, with different Jacobians and Hecke algebras.

2. The multiplicity depends on the Hecke algebra. The proof of Theorem 4.8 uses T_pG^0 ≅ T_m and T_pG^e = Hom(T_m, Z_p), so dim J[m] = 1 + (number of generators of ω_{T_m}). Multiplicity two therefore means T_m has type 3. This is a property of T_m, and T_m changes under twisting.

3. A concrete example where T_m changes. Let ρ̄ = ρ̄_0⊗χ̄, with ρ̄_0 twist-minimal and unramified at a prime v ∤ N_0 p, and χ̄ tame of conductor v. Then ρ̄^{I_v} = 0, so every lift has conductor exactly v² and every lift appears at level N(ρ̄)p, with U_v = 0. If ρ̄_0(Frob_v) has eigenvalue ratio ≡ v, then Ribet's level-raised forms (Steinberg at v, level N_0vp) twisted by χ̃ are extra newforms of conductor v² in T_m(ρ̄). They have no counterpart in T_{m_0}(ρ̄_0) at level N_0p. So T_m(ρ̄) corresponds to the unrestricted deformation problem at v, while T_{m_0}(ρ̄_0) corresponds to the unramified one.

4. The proof does not carry over word for word. The proof of Lemma 4.11 lists the non-smooth cases only under twist-minimality. In the example above, R_v ≅ R_v^unrestricted(ρ̄_0|G_v). Its unramified and Steinberg components meet at characteristic-0 points (unramified lifts with eigenvalue ratio v), where H^2(G_v, ad^0ρ) ≠ 0. So "R_v[1/p] formally smooth" fails, and that property is what the text uses when applying Kisin's method to get R̃[1/p] = T[1/p]. The paper's own remark on p. 363 also uses twist-minimality to exclude v ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄^{I_v} = 0.

5. The result is probably still true. R_v is still a complete intersection, and weight-2 points avoid the intersection locus by Ramanujan. So multiplicity two is plausible at non-minimal level too, but the paper gives no argument for it.

Conclusion: this is a gap in the reduction to the twist-minimal case, and it affects the claim in the abstract and introduction. Theorem 4.8 itself, as stated, is correct. Defence tried and failed. (1) The quantity is not twist-invariant by any formal argument. Twisting ρ̄ = ρ̄_0⊗χ̄ (χ̄ of conductor x ≠ p) changes N(ρ̄), N*, the curve J_1(N*) and the Hecke algebra T. (2) If ρ̄ is not twist-minimal at x, then ρ̄^{I_x} = 0. Every lift then has conductor cond(ρ̄|G_x), so every lift of ρ̄|G_x shows up at level Γ_1(N). After twisting back, m at level N(ρ̄)p also sees non-minimal forms for ρ̄_0. Examples are χ-twists of forms that are Steinberg at x (conductor x²) when the level-raising condition holds, or of ramified principal series of p-power type when x ≡ 1 mod p. So T_m is not the twist of T_{m_0} at level N(ρ̄_0)p. When no such extra forms exist, a Chebotarev/trace argument does identify the two Hecke algebras, but not in general. (3) The paper's proof really does use minimality. On p. 362, Φ is 'the only twists' preserving minimal-conductor lifts only under minimality; when x ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄ is non-minimal at x, the characters of Z_p⊗(Z/x)^× also qualify. On p. 363 the paper itself says the twist-uniqueness 'is not true when v ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄ has trivial invariants under I_v' and removes this case by the minimality assumption. Lemma 4.11 lists only the non-smooth cases that can occur for twist-minimal ρ̄. For a non-minimal ρ̄|G_x = χ̄⊗(unramified, Frobenius-eigenvalue ratio ≡ x mod p), R_{x,φ} is isomorphic to the unrestricted fixed-determinant ring of an unramified representation. Its unramified and Steinberg components meet in the generic fibre at the points μ⊕με, where H²(G_x, ad⁰ρ) ≠ 0. So the claim that the generic fibre is formally smooth fails, and with it the stated input to Kisin's R[1/p] = T[1/p]. (4) No nearby statement closes the gap. Remark 4.12 concerns J_H, and the parenthetical '(one can always twist ρ̄…)' only says that a twist-minimal twist exists. The general statement is very plausibly true: the extra local rings are complete intersections of type 1, and modular points avoid the singular locus. But the paper gives no proof of it, so the introduction and abstract claim more than Theorem 4.8 proves. Consequences: §4.1 opens with 'Although this is not needed for our main results', and nothing later cites Theorem 4.8. Only the claim in the abstract and introduction is affected, and the proposed restriction is right and minimal. 2. Absolutely irreducible case: the claim holds. Let J ⊂ I_x be the kernel of I_x → Z_p(1). Then ρ(J) ≅ ρ̄(J). ρ̄|J is still absolutely irreducible because p is odd. So ρ(J) spans M_2(R), and ρ(t_p)^n is a scalar a ≡ 1 with a^2 = det = 1, hence a = 1.

Frobenius adds u^{N+1} = 1 if it swaps the eigenlines, or u^{N−1} = 1 if it fixes them.

Explicit check (python script in work/agents/vK6A/check.py). Take p = 3, k = F_3, R = F_3[e]/(e^2), ρ̄(t) = s = [[0,−1],[1,0]]. The polynomial x^2 + 1 has no root mod 3, so ρ̄|I_x is irreducible over F_3. Put ρ(t) = s(1 + e·s), which has det 1 and order 12.
- Swap case: N = 11 or 23 (≡ −1 mod 12), ρ(Frob) = diag(1,−1) with det −1 ≡ N mod 3.
- Non-swap case: N = 13 or 169 (≡ 1 mod 12), ρ(Frob) = 1.
In all four cases F t F^{−1} = t^N holds (also with N^{−1}), and det ρ = ε on D_x. Yet |ρ(I_x)| = 12 while |ρ̄(I_x)| = 4, so H fails.

The swap case is allowed by (3)(a) as printed. It is not caught by (3)(d), which asks ρ̄|I_x to be reducible. Here ρ̄|D_x is dihedral of order 8, hence absolutely irreducible, so x is a genuine vexing prime. A global example is E[3] of y^2 = x^3 + 11x at 11 over F = Q(√−2). (it affects a stated result). The source says `(5) If v ∈ S(ρ̄), K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} is defined as follows: (a) If ρ̄ is of type S at v, then K_{Q,v} = Γ_0(v). [p. 372: Γ_0(v^c) = {g ∈ PGL_2(O_v) | g ≡ (1 *; 0 *) mod π_v^c}, Γ_p(v^c) = {g ∈ PGL_2(O_v) | g ≡ (1 *; 0 d) mod π_v^c, d has p− power order}. p. 369, condition (6): "P : If x ∈ S(ρ̄), and ρ̄|I_x ≃ ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}, then ρ|I_x ≃ ⟨ψ⟩ ⊕ ⟨ψ⟩^{−1}." p. 374, Conjecture A(2)(b): "If ρ̄|D_v is of type P, so that ρ̄|I_v ≅ ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}, then ρ|I_v ≅ ⟨ψ⟩ ⊕ ⟨ψ⟩^{−1}."]`; it should be `At a type-P prime the level has to cut out the minimal inertial type ⟨ψ⟩ ⊕ ⟨ψ⟩^{−1}. With c equal to the Artin conductor 2a(ψ) of ρ̄|D_v, it does not. Γ_p(v^c) ⊂ Γ_0(v^c), and Γ_0(v^c) fixes the newvector of every π(χ'', χ''^{−1}) with a(χ'') ≤ a(ψ). Then Γ_p(v^{a(ψ)}) sees π(χ, χ^{−1}) only with a(χ) ≤ a(ψ) and χ|O_v^× of prime-to-p order, so χ|O_v^× = ⟨ψ⟩^{±1}; this is the analogue of v1's level. 2. For v ∤ p, a p-power-order character ξ of O_v^× factors through (O_v/π_v)^×, so a nontrivial one exists iff p | N(v) − 1. Put χ″|O^× = ⟨ψ⟩ξ.
- If a(ψ) ≥ 2, then ⟨ψ⟩ξ agrees with ⟨ψ⟩ on 1 + π^{a−1}.
- If a(ψ) = 1, then ⟨ψ⟩ξ is still nontrivial, because the orders of ⟨ψ⟩ and ξ are coprime.
Either way a(⟨ψ⟩ξ) = a(ψ). So π″ = π(χ″, χ″^{−1}) is irreducible with trivial central character and conductor 2a(ψ) = c. By Casselman its newvector is K_0(π^c)-fixed, hence Γ_p(v^c)-fixed.

3. Mackey check (script at work/agents/K6-1-A/mackey.py). Take N(v) = 7, p = 3, ψ quadratic, so c = 2. Double cosets B(O)\GL_2(O)/K_0(7^n) have representatives (1 0; 7^i 1), and the character condition becomes a(χ) ≤ min(i, n − i). For both the minimal χ = ⟨ψ⟩ (order 2) and the non-minimal χ″ = ⟨ψ⟩ξ (order 6):
- n = 1: no coset contributes.
- n = 2: only i = 1 contributes.
So each has exactly a 1-dimensional space of K_0(v²)-fixed vectors.

4. π″ reduces to ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1} on I_v, and T_∅ has no operators at v, so π″ lies in the m∅-part. Moreover ⟨ψ⟩ξ ∉ {⟨ψ⟩, ⟨ψ⟩^{−1}}, because ξ ≠ 1 has p-power order while ⟨ψ⟩ has prime-to-p order. So π″ is excluded by condition (6).

5. Existence of such forms. Take r̄ over Q with trivial character and weight 2, ℓ ≡ 1 mod p split in F, and r̄|I_ℓ = ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}. Lifts of prescribed type exist (Diamond–Taylor 1994; Gee 2011); take a newform f with type ⟨ψ⟩ξ ⊕ (⟨ψ⟩ξ)^{−1} at ℓ and minimal elsewhere. Then BC_F(f) is a cohomological cuspidal π″ at level K_∅. At the Q̄_p-point of T_{∅,m∅} it defines, the specialisation of ρ_m has the traces of r_f|G_F. So it is r_f|G_F, and by Carayol r_f|I_v has the non-minimal type, contradicting A(2)(b). In that case R^min ≅ T_m (Theorem 1.3) fails too, and the theorem survives only because its hypothesis, Conjecture A, is false.

6. §3 avoids this by twisting (p. 310: ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0) together with X_H / U_x at level x^{c_x}, c_x = a(ψ). That route is unavailable in §5, where det = ε is fixed on PGL_2.

7. Types M and H are fine: with fixed determinant ε, a non-minimal lift at a type-M prime needs p | N(v) + 1, which is excluded. A separate case, not checked in detail: when ψ is quadratic, a twisted Steinberg St⊗χ (conductor c) also sits at Γ_0(v^c) whatever N(v) is.

I classify this as an error rather than the candidate's "gap": Conjecture A as formulated at this level is false in cases where π″ occurs. Defence attempts, none of which works:
(1) Γ_p(v^c) is contained in Γ_0(v^c) by definition. Take π'' = π(χ'', χ''^{−1}) with χ''|O^× = ⟨ψ⟩ξ, where ξ ≠ 1 is tame of p-power order. Then π'' has trivial central character and conductor 2a(⟨ψ⟩ξ) = 2a(ψ) = c. By Casselman newform theory, K_0(ϖ^c) acts on the newvector through ω(d) = 1, so the newvector is Γ_0(v^c)-fixed and hence Γ_p(v^c)-fixed. The restriction "d has p-power order" therefore removes nothing here.
(2) Explicit check in the induced model: at PGL-level {a ≡ d, c ≡ 0 mod ϖ^n}, π(χ, χ^{−1}) has vectors on which K_0 acts by χ^{±1}(a/d), and only when a(χ) ≤ n. The p-power restriction does separate ⟨ψ⟩ from ⟨ψ⟩ξ at n = a(ψ), but not at n = 2a(ψ), where both have Γ_0-fixed newvectors. The paper's own §5.5 (p. 380) says the level was chosen as the X_H(N) analogue to exclude such twists. v1's GL_2 version (type 1 ⊕ ψ, c = a(ψ)) does exclude them. Nothing in the hypotheses rules out p | N(v) − 1 at type-P primes: (3)(c) and Theorem 1.3(4) only exclude N ≡ −1 for vexing primes.
(3) Consequence. π'' has I_v-type ⟨ψ⟩ξ ⊕ (⟨ψ⟩ξ)^{−1}, which fails condition (6). If π'' is cohomological at level K_∅ with residual representation ρ̄, it contributes to T_{∅,m} ⊗ Q̄_p. Then Conjecture A(2)(b) for Q = ∅ contradicts local–global compatibility at v, even up to semisimplification.
Such π'' exist. Take the base change to F, with ℓ split, of a classical weight-2 form on Γ_0(ℓ²) with ℓ ≡ 1 mod p and local type ⟨ψ⟩ξ that is congruent to a minimal form of type ⟨ψ⟩; Carayol and Diamond–Taylor give such congruences. So Conjecture A as stated is false for such ρ̄, and Theorems 5.11 and 1.3 are vacuous for them.
Theorem 1.2 is unaffected: semistable minimal ρ has only type-S primes. The proofs of 5.11 and 1.3 use the level only through Conjecture A, so the patching argument survives once the level is corrected. However, the conclusion of Theorem 1.3 as stated, R^min ≅ T_m on H_1(Y_0(N)), is false in these cases.
On kind: I classify this as an error (a wrong definition that makes a stated conjecture false), not a gap. Otherwise, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = Γ_0(v).`; it should be `(4) If v|p, then K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = PGL_2(𝒪_v) (equivalently, the image of GL_2(𝒪_v) in PGL_2(F_v)) if ρ̄|D_v is finite flat. Otherwise, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = Γ_0(v).`. I checked the rendered image of p. 373 (PDF p. 77). Item (4) of §5.2.1 does print "GL_2(𝒪_v)". On p. 372, §5.2 sets G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(2), and K_Q = ∏_v K_{Q,v} is described as an open compact subgroup of G(A) (the text says G(A); it should be G(A^∞)). So each K_{Q,v} has to be a compact open subgroup of PGL_2(F_v), and GL_2(𝒪_v) is literally not one. The rest of the definition is written for PGL_2 throughout:
- Item (3) on the same page uses PGL_2(𝒪_v).
- Γ_0(v^c), Γ_1(v^c) and Γ_p(v^c) on p. 372 are all defined as subsets of PGL_2(𝒪_v), and item (5) uses them.
- §5.5 ("The distinction between GL and PGL") explains why the paper deliberately works with PGL rather than GL.
- In the PGL(n) analogue in §9.1, the authors write "the image in PGL(𝒪_v) of {g ∈ GL_n(𝒪_v) | …}", which shows they distinguish the two groups when they mean the image.

The intended meaning is still clear. 𝒪_v is local, so Pic(𝒪_v) = 0 and PGL_2(𝒪_v) = GL_2(𝒪_v)/𝒪_v^×. That is the image of GL_2(𝒪_v) in PGL_2(F_v), the maximal compact subgroup that stabilises the lattice class [𝒪_v^2]. So the proposed correction to PGL_2(𝒪_v) is right, and it agrees with the finite-flat (unramified, maximal level at p) intent and with item (3) of §9.1 (PGL_n(𝒪_v) for v ∉ S ∪ Q, which includes v|p). The arXiv v2 text (§5.2.1) has the identical wording "GL2 (Ov)", so the slip was never corrected. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

Nothing else in Conjecture A mentions v ∈ Q: (1) covers λ outside S ∪ Q ∪ {v|p}, (2) covers S(ρ̄) and (4) covers v|p. Lemma 5.6 allows any maximal ideal m of T_Q associated to ρ̄. "Taylor–Wiles primes" (§5.1 and Prop. 5.2) only means N(x) ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄(Frob_x) has distinct eigenvalues, which is a condition on ρ̄ and not on m. So nothing ensures U_v mod m ≠ ±1. The proof uses the conclusion of (3) without checking its hypothesis. Without that conclusion, the operators T_α at Q are not linked to ρ_m at all, so "traces generate T_{Q,m}" is not justified. Hensel's lemma alone splits ρ|D_x into two characters, but it cannot identify either character with the Hecke character φ.

I also checked whether the paper excludes such m elsewhere. It does not. Lemma 5.8, like Lemma 3.5 (pp. 305–307), treats only the m containing U_x − α_x. The step showing V[m] = 0 gives x·U_x² = ⟨x⟩, i.e. γ² ≡ α_xβ_x ≡ 1 for the eigenvalue γ of U_x on V. That contradicts γ = α_x (since α_x ≠ β_x), but it is consistent with γ = ±1. So "new at x" torsion with U_x ≡ ±1 (Steinberg type) is not ruled out without local–global compatibility at x, which Conjecture A deliberately leaves out.

The minimality part of the conclusion and the cyclotomic determinant (from (1) plus Chebotarev) do not use (3). Lemma 5.6 is never cited later. Theorem 5.11 repeats the argument itself for m ∋ U_x − α_x, where α_x ≢ ±1, and its step (a) invokes (3) correctly. So the main results are unaffected, and only Lemma 5.6 as stated overreaches. A charitable reading ("there exists m" meaning a suitably chosen m) does not help, because the conclusion is about T_{Q,m} for the given m and no choice of U_x-eigenvalue is specified. Defence tried and failed. (i) The "Taylor–Wiles primes" hypothesis (Prop. 5.2: N(v) ≡ 1 mod p, ρ̄ unramified at v, ρ̄(Frob_v) has distinct eigenvalues) is a condition on ρ̄, not on U_v mod m. It would give U_v ≢ ±1 mod m only through the conclusion ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1}. Then the eigenvalues of ρ̄(Frob_v) are φ̄(Frob_v)^{±1}, which are distinct iff φ̄(Frob_v) ≠ ±1, because ε(Frob_v) = N(v) ≡ 1. But that conclusion is exactly what (3) withholds when φ(Frob_v) ≡ ±1, so the argument is circular. (ii) "Associated to ρ̄" (Def. before Conj. A) constrains only T_λ for λ ∉ S(ρ̄) ∪ Q ∪ {v|p}. (iii) Nothing else in Conjecture A controls U_v mod m. (1) gives ρ_m mod m ≅ ρ̄, but no statement ties φ(Frob_v) to the eigenvalues of ρ̄(Frob_v) in the ±1 case. (iv) No nearby result supplies the step. Lemma 5.8 and the Ihara argument in the proof of Lemma 9.6 deal only with m ∋ U_x − α_x where U_x² − 1 is invertible. They do not show that H_1(Y_1(Q))_m = 0 when U_x ≡ ±1. For torsion classes, nothing rules out "new at x" classes with U_x ≡ ±1. Such classes would be excluded under full local–global compatibility (Steinberg at v would force equal eigenvalues of ρ̄(Frob_v)), but Conjecture A does not assume that. (v) T_{Q,m} is generated by the T_λ, which are traces by (1), together with U_v and the diamond operators at v ∈ Q. The only route to putting U_v in the trace subalgebra is Hensel applied to ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1}, using the fact that the roots φε(σ) and φ^{-1}(σ) are distinct mod m. So for an m with U_v ≡ ±1 mod m, "traces generate T_{Q,m}" is not proved. The rest of the lemma does not use (3). Minimality outside Q holds because R_Q (§5.1) puts no condition at x ∈ Q, and L_{Q,x} is the full H^1. The determinant is cyclotomic by (1) and Chebotarev. Consequences: the paper never cites Lemma 5.6 by number (grep finds only its own statement). Its content is re-derived in the proof of Theorem 5.11 ("Applying Conjecture A to T_{Q_N,m}, we deduce the existence of a surjective homomorphism R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m}", together with step (5a) using part (3)). There m ⊇ (m_∅, U_x − α_x), and by Lemma 5.8, which step (b) invokes, α_x is a root of X² − T_xX + 1 whose two roots are distinct mod m_∅. Since α_xβ_x ≡ 1 and α_x ≢ β_x, we get α_x ≢ ±1, so (3) applies. Theorem 5.11, Theorem 1.3 and §9 (Conjecture B, with m = (m, U_x − α_x) stated explicitly) are therefore unaffected. Only Lemma 5.6, as stated for an arbitrary m, overreaches. - **Misprint** at §5.3, Conjecture A(4), p. 375 (published version) (it affects the proof). The source says `(4) If v|p, then ρ̄|D_v is finite flat, and if ρ̄|D_v is ordinary, then ρ|D_v is ordinary.`; it should be `(4) If v|p and ρ̄|D_v is finite flat, then ρ|D_v is finite flat (that is, (ρ ⊗ T_{Q,m}/m^n)|D_v is finite flat for all n ≥ 1, as in §5.1 condition (3)); and if ρ̄|D_v is ordinary, then ρ|D_v is ordinary. An equivalent phrasing is "If v|p, then ρ|D_v is finite flat if ρ̄|D_v is". Deleting the first bar alone would not fix it. An unconditional "ρ|D_v is finite flat" would force ρ̄|D_v to be finite flat, because finite flat representations are closed under quotients when e = 1 < p − 1 (Raynaud). That contradicts the allowed case where ρ̄ is ordinary but not finite flat.`. I checked the page images at 110 and 250 dpi. Conjecture A starts on p. 374 (PDF p. 78), and part (4) is at the top of p. 375 (PDF p. 79). It reads exactly: "(4) If v|p, then ρ̄|D_v is finite flat, and if ρ̄|D_v is ordinary, then ρ|D_v is ordinary." The first two ρ's have bars and the last one does not. arXiv v2 (p. 58, image checked) has the same text.

As printed, the first clause says something about the residual representation ρ̄ and nothing about ρ = ρ_m. Taken literally, it contradicts the paper's own setup:
- §5.1 hypothesis (2), p. 369: "ρ̄ is either ordinary or finite flat at v|p".
- Theorem 1.3(1): ρ̄ is "either finite flat or ordinary" at v|p.
- §5.2 level condition (4), p. 373: K_{Q,v} = GL2(O_v) "if ρ̄|D_v is finite flat. Otherwise … Γ0(v)".

So the printed conjecture would be false whenever ρ̄ is ordinary but not finite flat. When ρ̄|D_v is finite flat and not ordinary, it says nothing about ρ|D_v.

The conclusion that is missing is exactly what the proofs need. §5.1 deformation conditions (2) and (3), p. 369, require the reductions mod m^n to be finite flat or ordinary, and finite flat whenever ρ̄|G_v is finite flat. These conditions define R_Q and R^min. They are used in three places:
- Lemma 5.6, p. 375: "By Conjecture A, the representation ρ_Q := ρ_m … is such a representation", i.e. a minimal deformation.
- §5.4, p. 378: "Properties (1)–(4) of Conjecture A then imply that ρ_{m∅} gives rise to a homomorphism ϕ : R^min → T_{m∅}".
- §5.4, p. 379: the surjection R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m}, which the proof of Theorem 5.11 uses. Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 are deduced from that result.

Under the printed wording, ρ_m need not satisfy condition (3), so ϕ is not justified. The intended meaning is clear, and the proofs work once (4) is corrected. So this is a misprint in the statement of an assumed conjecture that the proofs depend on. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

A side note on a separate issue: the pdftotext layer drops the ε in part (3). The image shows "ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1}", which is correct as printed. Remark 5.3 and §5.2.2 take (co)homology in the orbifold sense, i.e. group homology of the arithmetic lattices. Under that convention the step is false for p = 3 whenever a component lattice has 3-torsion. My own check of the candidate's example, F = Q(i) (3 is inert) and level PGL2(O_v) everywhere, so Γ = PGL2(Z[i]):
(i) g = [[0,−1],[1,1]] has order 3 in PGL2.
(ii) Its centralizer in Γ is Z[i][g]^×/Z[i]^× = Z[ζ12]^×/μ4 ≅ Z/3 × Z, because Q(ζ12) has unit rank 1.
(iii) h = [[0,1],[1,0]] conjugates g to g^{-1}.
(iv) Γ has 3-rank 1 and vcd = 3 − 1 = 2. By Brown's theorem, Ĥ^4(Γ,Z)_(3) contains Ĥ^4(C,Z)_(3)^{N/C} = H^4(Z/3,Z) = Z/3 ≠ 0. Aut(Z/3) acts trivially on H^4.
(v) By universal coefficients, H_3(Γ,Z)_(3) ≠ 0, so H_3(Γ,F_3) ≠ 0.
Independent cross-check: Fine's amalgam PSL2(Z[i]) = (S3 *_{Z/3} A4) *_{PSL2(Z)} (S3 *_{Z/2} D2) with Mayer–Vietoris gives dim H^3(PSL2(Z[i]),F_3) = 2. This matches Z/3 in integral degrees ≡ 0, 3 mod 4.
The failure does not depend on this particular example. Every allowed level has 3-torsion: Γ_0(x) for Taylor–Wiles x (N(x) ≡ 1 mod 3) and Γ_0(v) for v|3 contain conjugates of g, since g fixes a point of P^1(k_x). The candidate's p ≥ 5 claim and element-order list are also correct.
The localized statement Lemma 5.9(1) is probably still true under the paper's hypotheses, but the printed proof does not establish it for p = 3.

Thm 5.11(b) needs only the H_0 part, which is fine. Thm 1.3 follows from Thm 5.11. Remark 9.3 makes a related unproved claim ("may be verified directly" for GL(2)/F, F imaginary quadratic), but that is outside this item. DEFENCE ATTEMPTS, ALL FAIL.
(i) Convention. Remark 5.3 (p. 372) says explicitly that for every K the cohomology of Y(K) is taken in the orbifold sense, i.e. as the cohomology of the arithmetic lattices. It adds that this can differ from the cohomology of the underlying space. The argument itself needs this convention: the Shapiro isomorphism H_1(Y_0(Q),O[Δ]) ≅ H_1(Y_Δ(Q),O) and the Hochschild–Serre sequences in Prop. 5.10 and Thm 5.11(b) hold for group homology. So H_3 cannot be read as homology of the coarse space.
(ii) Scope. §5.1 and Thms 1.2 and 1.3 take any p ≥ 3 unramified in F. So p = 3 is allowed for F = Q(i), Q(√−2), and so on.
(iii) 3-torsion is present. g = [[0,−1],[1,1]] ∈ SL_2(Z) has order 3 in every PGL_2(O_F). Its characteristic polynomial X²−X+1 splits mod x when N(x) ≡ 1 mod 3, which holds at every Taylor–Wiles prime for p = 3. So Γ_0(x) contains conjugates of g.
  Example: F = Q(i), p = 3, S(ρ̄) = ∅, ρ̄ finite flat at 3. Then Y = Y_0(∅) = PGL_2(Z[i])\H³.
(iv) H_3 ≠ 0 there. The lattice Γ = PGL_2(Z[i]) has vcd 2 and 3-rank 1. The centralizer of ⟨g⟩ is Z[ζ12]^×/Z[i]^× ≅ Z/3 × Z; mod torsion it is generated by 1−ζ12. Conjugation by h = [[0,1],[1,0]] acts as ζ12 ↦ ζ12^5, so N/C = Z/2 inverts both factors. It follows that Ĥ^n(N)_(3) = Z/3 for n ≡ 0, 3 mod 4.
  By Brown's p-rank-one theorem, H^4(Γ,Z)_(3) = Ĥ^4 ≠ 0. Hence H_3(Γ,Z)_(3) ≠ 0 and H_3(Γ,F_3) ≠ 0.
  Cross-check: Fine's amalgam PSL_2(Z[i]) = (S_3 *_{Z/3} A_4) *_{PSL_2 Z} (S_3 *_{Z/2} D_2) with Mayer–Vietoris gives dim H³(PSL_2(Z[i]);F_3) = 2.
  The example is not special to Q(i). For any F, the relative automorphism of F(√−3)/F inverts norm-one units, so Ĥ^4 ⊇ Z/3 for every component lattice with 3-torsion.
(v) Nothing nearby supplies the missing step.
  - Remark 9.3 concerns only low degrees, via the congruence subgroup property.
  - §9 assumes the needed vanishing as Conjecture B(4)(a).
  - Footnote 3 in §3 on X_H(13) shows the authors knew stacky p = 3 classes exist; that class is induced from Q(√−3).

So the printed statement H_3(Y_0(Q),k) = 0 is false, not merely unproved. Under PROTOCOL §18 that is a step that fails, hence "error". The lemma itself is not shown false.

CONSEQUENCES, for p = 3 only:
- Lemma 5.9(1) with i = 3 is left unproved.
- Lemma 5.9(2) is left unproved: its proof uses H_3(μ/ϖ)_m = 0.
- Prop. 5.10 depends on 5.9(2). It needs H_2(Y_0(Q),O)_m to be torsion-free in order to bound dim Tor_1/ϖ by r. This is a real gap, not a formality: unlocalized, H_2(Γ,Z) does have 3-torsion (Z/3 for PSL_2(Z[i])). The displayed Hochschild–Serre exact sequence itself needs only the i = 0 part.
- Thm 5.11(c) depends on Prop. 5.10.
- Thm 5.11(b) uses only the i = 0 vanishing (low-degree Hochschild–Serre terms) and is unaffected. X-K6-10 says (b) relies on the H_3 vanishing; that is slightly off.
- Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 for p = 3 therefore rest on an unproved step. For p ≥ 5 nothing is affected, and §9 is unaffected. - **Misprint** at §5.3.1, proof of Lemma 5.9(2), p. 377 (published version). The source says `Taking cohomology, localizing at 𝔪, and using the vanishing of H_3(Y_0(Q), μ)_𝔪 from part (1), we deduce that H^2(Y_0(Q), μ)_𝔪[ϖ] = 0, hence the result. [The display just before it, printed without a ϖ over the first arrow, is "0 → μ → μ → μ/ϖ → 0". §5.3.1, proof of Lemma 5.9(2), p. 377 = PDF p. 81. arXiv v2 has the same wording.]`; it should be `"Taking homology, localizing at 𝔪, and using the vanishing of H_3(Y_0(Q), μ/ϖ)_𝔪 from part (1) (applied to the finitely generated O[Δ]-module μ/ϖ), we deduce that H_2(Y_0(Q), μ)_𝔪[ϖ] = 0, hence the result."`. I checked the page image of PDF p. 81 (published p. 377), and the text is printed as quoted. Lemma 5.9(2) is about homology: "If μ is p-torsion free, then H_2(Y_0(Q), μ)_𝔪 is p-torsion free." Its only use, in the proof of Prop. 5.10 on p. 378, is also about homology: H_2(Y_0(Q), O)_𝔪 must be O-free. So "cohomology" and the superscript H^2 are slips. Throughout §5.3 the paper writes H_i for homology and H^i for cohomology. Cohomology would also give the wrong sequence: H^1(μ/ϖ) → H^2(μ) → H^2(μ) (the second map multiplication by ϖ) says nothing about H^2[ϖ].

I redid the argument myself. Multiplication by ϖ commutes with the Hecke operators, and localizing at 𝔪 is exact. The homology long exact sequence of 0 → μ → μ → μ/ϖ → 0 (first map multiplication by ϖ) therefore gives, after localizing:
H_3(μ)_𝔪 → H_3(μ)_𝔪 (multiplication by ϖ) → H_3(μ/ϖ)_𝔪 → H_2(μ)_𝔪 → H_2(μ)_𝔪 (multiplication by ϖ).
Hence H_2(μ)_𝔪[ϖ] is the image of H_3(μ/ϖ)_𝔪. If only H_3(μ)_𝔪 = 0, we get H_2(μ)_𝔪[ϖ] ≅ H_3(μ/ϖ)_𝔪, which need not be zero. So the fact actually needed is H_3(Y_0(Q), μ/ϖ)_𝔪 = 0. Part (1) supplies it, because μ/ϖ is a finitely generated O[Δ]-module and part (1) holds for all such modules. Since H_2(μ)_𝔪 is a finitely generated O-module, having no ϖ-torsion means it is p-torsion free.

This is the paper's own pattern done slightly wrong. In the parallel Lemma 3.7(1) (p. 316) the authors correctly use the quotient coefficients: "H^2(X_Δ(Q), L_k) vanishes". Lemma 5.9's proof looks adapted from it, with the words "Taking cohomology" left in and the coefficients left as μ instead of μ/ϖ.

The candidate's correction is accurate. This is not one of the 47 known bracket errors: the "[ϖ]" here correctly means the ϖ-torsion, not a mangled ⟦ ⟧.

On 'affects': the statement of Lemma 5.9(2) is correct, and the corrected proof is immediate from part (1). Prop. 5.10 and §5.4 use only the statement, so nothing downstream is affected. Without the parentheses this is a restrictive clause, i.e. only the Hecke operators that preserve components act by degree, and that version is correct.. The source says `Proof Consider part (1). By Nakayama's Lemma, we reduce to the case when μ = k. Yet H_3(Y_0(Q), k) = 0 and the action of Hecke operators on H_0(Y_0(Q), k) (which preserve the connected components) is via the degree map, and this action is Eisenstein (in the sense that the only m in the support of H_0 are Eisenstein).`; it should be `Minimal fix: make the clause restrictive again, as in v1: "the action on H_0(Y_0(Q),k) of those Hecke operators which preserve the connected components (e.g. T_λ for λ trivial in the component group F^×\A_F^{∞,×}/(A_F^{∞,×})^2 det(L_Q)) is via the degree map, T_λ ↦ N(λ)+1". Such λ are exactly the primes that split completely in the finite abelian (2-power) extension L that corresponds to the component group. So T_λ − 2 ∈ m for every λ outside the level that splits completely in L(ζ_p), and m is Eisenstein in the sense of Def. 5.5. The candidate's alternative is also correct but longer: T_λ[C] = (N(λ)+1)[C·λ], so the eigenvalues are (1+N(λ))χ(λ) with χ a quadratic character of the component group.`. I rendered pp. 373-377 and read them. (a) §5.2.2 on p. 373 says: 'The Hecke operators act on H•(Y(K), O) but do not preserve the homology of the connected components. The group of components is isomorphic, via the determinant map, to F^×\A_F^{∞,×}/A_F^{∞,×2} det(K).' T^univ (p. 376) is generated by the T_α for α trivial at Q ∪ S(ρ̄) ∪ {v|p}, together with the U_x. So it contains T_λ = T(diag(ϖ_λ,1)), where det g = ϖ_λ. (b) Here is a counterexample to the parenthetical. §5.1 lets F be any imaginary quadratic field, with p ≥ 3 unramified in F. Take F = Q(√−5), whose class group is Z/2 = Cl/Cl^2, and p = 7. Let λ = (3, 1+√−5), which has norm 3 and is not principal because a^2 + 5b^2 = 3 has no solution. Assume ρ̄ is unramified at 3; the primes above 3 are not in Q, since Q consists of primes with N(v) ≡ 1 mod 7. We have L_Q ⊆ ∏ PGL_2(O_v), so det(L_Q) ⊆ Ô^×·(squares). Hence A surjects onto F^×\A^{∞,×}/(A^{∞,×})^2 Ô^× = Cl/Cl^2 = Z/2. The class of ϖ_λ maps to the nontrivial element there. So T_λ carries each component to one with a different determinant class: T_λ[C] = 4[C'] with C' ≠ C, because the transfer on H_0 has total degree [K : gKg^{-1} ∩ K] = N(λ)+1 = 4. The parenthetical claim is therefore false, and 'the action is via the degree map' is only true up to this permutation of components. (c) The conclusion still holds. H_0(Y_0(Q), k) = k[A] with p odd, so it decomposes into χ-eigenspaces, and T_λ acts on them by χ(λ^{±1})(1+N(λ)). This equals 2 mod p whenever λ splits completely in F(ζ_p)·(class field of A), an abelian extension of F. That is exactly the form required by Definition 5.5, so the support of H_0 is Eisenstein. The v1 wording, with its restrictive clause, already gave this argument. The published version and v2 added parentheses, which turned the clause into a false general assertion. I classify this as an error in one step of the proof whose conclusion is unaffected; since v1 shows what was intended, one could also argue it is a punctuation-level misprint. The printed parenthetical is false. G = Res_{F/Q} PGL_2, and F is an arbitrary imaginary quadratic field in which p ≥ 3 is unramified (§5.1). Every double-coset representative of K diag(α,1) K has determinant in α·det(K). So T_α translates components by the class of α in the component group F^×\A_F^{∞,×}/(A_F^{∞,×})^2 det(K), which the paper identifies in §5.2.2. That group surjects onto Cl(F)/Cl(F)^2, which is nontrivial for most F (for example Q(√−5)). Then T_λ for a non-principal λ swaps components. The paper itself says so three pages earlier (§5.2.2, p. 373): "The Hecke operators act on H•(Y(K), O) but do not preserve the homology of the connected components."

Defence: the intended meaning is clear, and the argument is complete under it. arXiv v1 has the same sentence without parentheses, as a restrictive clause: only the Hecke operators that preserve components are claimed to act by degree. That is true. It is also enough, because Def. 5.5 only asks that T_λ − 2 ∈ m for almost all λ splitting completely in some fixed abelian extension of F. For λ trivial in the component group, T_λ acts on each component's H_0 = k by its degree N(λ)+1. That equals 2 in k once N(λ) ≡ 1 mod p. So every m in the support of H_0 is Eisenstein, and since m ∩ T^an = m_∅ is non-Eisenstein, H_0(Y_0(Q),k)_m = 0. The parentheses were added in revision (v2 and published) and turned a restrictive qualifier into a false blanket assertion.

This is a slip whose intended meaning is clear from context (v1 and §5.2.2), so it is a misprint rather than an error. The candidate's statement of the fact is right, as is its fix via characters χ, but the minimal correction is simply the restrictive reading.

Downstream: Lemma 5.9(1) feeds Lemma 5.9(2) (vanishing of H_3), Prop. 5.10 (balancedness) and the main §5 modularity argument. Its conclusion is true as stated, so nothing downstream changes. The display reads "q := dim_k H^1_∅(G_F, ad^0 ρ̄)." with no Tate twist. arXiv v2 (cg-v2.txt line 3193) prints the same thing.

The paper's own notation shows this is a slip. In §5.1 (p. 377), H^1_Q(F, ad^0 ρ̄) is defined as the Selmer group, and H^1_Q(F, ad^0 ρ̄(1)) is "the corresponding dual Selmer group". So the printed q is the dimension of the Selmer group H^1_∅(F, ad^0 ρ̄), which is the reduced tangent space of R^min. Proposition 5.1 with Q = ∅ bounds it by dim H^1_∅(F, ad^0 ρ̄(1)) − 1. So it is strictly smaller than the dual Selmer dimension and can be 0.

Under the printed definition the proof does not work:
(i) "q ≥ 1 by Proposition 5.2" fails. Proposition 5.2 proves q ≥ 1 only for q = dim H^1_∅(F, ad^0 ρ̄(1)).
(ii) The Q_N taken from Proposition 5.2 have #Q_N equal to the dual Selmer dimension. Each R_{Q_N} is a quotient of a power series ring in (dual Selmer − 1) variables. So the needed surjections R_∞ = O⟦x_1..x_{q−1}⟧ ↠ R_{Q_N} and Δ_{Q_N} ↠ (Z/p^N)^q, with the counts Proposition 2.3 requires, only work with the dual Selmer q.
(iii) The remark after the proof ("T_{∅,m_∅} is a quotient of a power series ring in q−1 variables by q elements") also uses the dual Selmer q.

The remark and Theorem 1.3's clause "then μ = 1" are therefore correct only when every prime of S(ρ̄) has type S. (Theorem 1.2 only has type S primes and does not claim μ = 1 anyway.) Two ways to repair it: (a) Add that restriction. (b) Replace H by its Δ-invariants, where Δ = ∏_v Γ_0(v^c)/Γ_p(v^c), which is equivalent to working at the literal Γ_0(v^c) level. Δ has prime-to-p order and commutes with T_∅, so H^Δ is a T_m-direct summand of the free module H, hence itself free. Its rank in characteristic 0 is ∏ dim π_v^{Γ_0(v^c)} = 1, and it is nonzero once H⊗Q ≠ 0. This restores "μ = 1" for the space Y_0(N) of literal Γ_0(N) level.
