Rendered PDF p.8 = p.304; the printed text matches the transcription. The same statement appears in arXiv v2. I checked the setup the corollary relies on. Def. 3.1(1) (p.307) fixes det ρ = Teichmüller lift of det ρ̄, and R^min is taken with Q=∅. Theorem 1.4 is proved with X_U = X_1(N)/H, where H is the p-part of (Z/N)^× (§3.3). In §3.9, U_x at x ∈ P(ρ̄) requires d to have p-power order. So T_m only sees forms whose nebentypus has order prime to p.

Redoing the counterexample. Take v ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄|I_v = 1 ⊕ χ̄, χ̄ ≠ 1. Frobenius fixes the trivial isotypic line, so ρ̄|G_v is reducible, v ∈ S−T, and dim ρ̄^{I_v} = 1. Let ρ|I_v = 1 ⊕ [χ̄]θ with θ ≠ 1 of p-power order. Then dim ρ^{I_v} = 1, so (1) holds. Put ψ = det ρ/[det ρ̄], which has p-power order and ψ|I_v = θ. Any twist ρ⊗ε that lifts ρ̄⊗ε̄ with the fixed determinant forces ε = [ε̄]·ψ^{-1/2}, because squaring is bijective on 1+m when p is odd. The standing hypothesis ρ̄^{I_v} ≠ 0 forces ε̄|I_v ∈ {1, χ̄^{-1}}. In both cases (ρ⊗ε)|I_v has characters [ε̄]θ^{-1/2} and [ε̄χ̄]θ^{1/2}, and neither is trivial, so there are no inertia invariants and Def. 3.1(4) fails. So no twist of ρ is a point of any R^min covered by Theorem 1.4. The Hecke side agrees: the twist has conductor v² at v, and the untwisted ρ has non-p'-order nebentypus.

A global example exists. Take p=3, v=13, K=Q(√−14): 13 splits, 3 is unramified, and O_K^× = ±1. Let ψ be a character of order 6 on I_w, unramified at w' and elsewhere. ψ_w(−1) = 1 because 12/6 is even, so ψ extends to a Hecke character. Then ρ = Ind_K ψ is odd, ρ̄ is irreducible (ψ̄ ≠ ψ̄^c at w), ρ is unramified at 3, and (1) holds at 2, 7 (order-2 inertia) and at 13. ρ is modular, but only on X_1(728), not on X_U. So the claimed "immediate" deduction fails for part of the hypothesis. The paper itself says non-minimal lifting is hard (p.304 text after Cor. 1.6).

Corollary 1.5 is not cited again in the paper (grep). Corollary 1.6 assumes minimality, so it is unaffected. The candidate's gap is correct. Its correction's "equivalently" and "only at v ≡ 1 mod p" are overstated, as the correction field explains. I checked the Steinberg case only locally and did not construct a global example. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED AND FAILED. Theorem 1.4 is proved in §3 for R^min as defined in Def. 3.1 with Q = ∅. That ring has a fixed determinant, equal to the Teichmüller lift of det ρ̄ (Def. 3.1(1)), and it requires ρ^{I_x} to be a rank-one direct summand at every x ∈ S−T where ρ̄|G_x is reducible (Def. 3.1(4)). T_m lives on X_U = X_1(N)/H, where H is the p-part of (Z/N)^× (§3.3, p. 2141 of the text). At x ∈ P(ρ̄), the group U_x forces d to have p-power order (§3.9). So T_m sees only forms of conductor dividing N whose nebentypus has no p-part.
The intended deduction runs: twist by ψ^{-1/2}, get a minimal deformation, conclude modularity, twist back. This only works if hypothesis (1) makes some twist of ρ minimal. Two cases show that it does not.

(i) DETERMINANT CASE. Take v ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄|I_v = 1⊕χ̄, χ̄ ≠ 1, and ρ|I_v = 1⊕[χ̄]θ, with θ ≠ 1 of p-power order. The second alternative of (1) holds. Consider any twist ρ⊗ε that lifts ρ̄⊗ε̄ with the fixed determinant. Since squaring is bijective on 1+m, this forces ε = [ε̄]ψ^{-1/2}. On I_v the twist then has characters [ε̄]θ^{-1/2} and [ε̄χ̄]θ^{1/2}, and neither is trivial. So Def. 3.1(4) fails for every such twist.
A global example, which I re-checked: p = 3, K = Q(√−14), in which 13 splits, 3 is unramified and O_K^× = ±1. Take ψ of order 6 on I_w for one prime w | 13; since ψ_w(−1) = 1, ψ extends to a Hecke character. Then ρ = Ind_K ψ is odd, ρ̄ is irreducible (ψ̄ ≠ ψ̄^c), ρ is unramified at 3, and (1) holds at 2, 7 and 13. This ρ is modular (it is dihedral), but no twist of it is a point of T_m.

(ii) UNIPOTENT-REDUCTION CASE. Take x ≡ ±1 mod p with ρ̄|I_x unipotent and nontrivial, so ρ̄(I_x) ≅ Z/p. Let ρ|I_x = ζ⊕ζ^{-1} with ζ of order p. This occurs as a non-split lattice; I checked the lattice explicitly. Here ρ(I_x) ⥲ ρ̄(I_x), so the first alternative of (1) holds, and det ρ|I_x = 1. But ρ^{I_x} = 0 and the conductor is x^2. Any p-power twist still has no inertia invariants, and a prime-to-p twist destroys ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0.
In fact, at a Steinberg-type x the first alternative never yields a minimal ρ. Minimal lifts there have infinite inertia image and satisfy the second alternative instead. I expect global examples to exist (for instance p = 3 tetrahedral or octahedral forms with inertia of order 3 at some prime), but I did not construct a specific one.

In both cases ρ is a non-minimal lift. The paper itself says (p. 304–305) that its method cannot handle such lifts. So the word "immediately" is unjustified for part of the range of hypothesis (1). The conclusion is probably true, as predicted by Fontaine–Mazur, and the examples above are modular by classical results. That makes this a gap rather than a false statement.

CONSEQUENCES. Corollary 1.5 is not used later in the paper. Corollary 1.6 assumes minimality outright, and Theorem 1.4 is unaffected. Only the corollary, as a stated result, is not established in the generality stated. The arXiv v2 footnote 5 (cg-v2.txt l. 2716–2721) has the same wording, "primitive" included.`; it should be `Replace "for some primitive q-th root of unity ζ ≠ 1" with "for some q-th root of unity ζ ≠ 1", i.e. ζ ∈ μ_q \ {1}, taken up to ζ ↔ ζ^{−1}. The paper says "unipotent" elsewhere (e.g. p. 297 text line 205, and §5 conditions), but "nilpotent" here can also be read loosely as "σ − 1 is nilpotent / N is nilpotent", so on its own it is not a mathematical error.`. I redid the computation. Set t^v + t^{−v} − t − t^{−1} = (t^v − t)(1 − t^{−v−1}). So C(T) = T at T = t + t^{−1} exactly when t^{v−1} = 1 or t^{v+1} = 1. C(T) − T is separable of degree v in T: its roots are ±2, (v−3)/2 values from t^{v−1} = 1 and (v−1)/2 values from t^{v+1} = 1. The condition T − 2 ∈ m forces t ≡ 1, so t is a 1-unit root of unity of p-power order. Since v ≡ 1 mod p and p is odd, p does not divide v + 1, so t^{v+1} = 1 gives only t = 1, and t^{v−1} = 1 gives t ∈ μ_q.

The T-values in the residue disc are therefore T = 2 plus ζ + ζ^{−1} for ζ ∈ μ_q \ {1} modulo inversion. That is 1 + (q−1)/2 = (q+1)/2 values, matching the footnote's count. Each ζ ≠ 1 gives one geometric component: σ is regular semisimple with eigenvalues ζ^{±1}, Frobenius lies in its centralizer torus with fixed determinant, and the result is irreducible of dimension 3.

If only primitive ζ were allowed there would be φ(q)/2 = p^{s−1}(p−1)/2 such components, fewer than (q−1)/2 once q = p^s with s ≥ 2. Concrete check: p = 3, v = 19, so q = 9. ζ_3 + ζ_3^{−1} = −1 satisfies T − 2 = −3 ∈ m and is a genuine root, giving 4 = (9−1)/2 non-trivial values against 3 primitive ones.

The sentence itself points the same way. It says "finitely ramified of order dividing q", and "ζ ≠ 1" would be redundant for a primitive q-th root, since q ≥ p > 1. So "primitive" is a slip. The counts (q+1)/2 and (q−1)/2 are correct; only this adjective is wrong. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. (That known defect does appear on the same page in "R_v ≅ O[x1,…,x4]/(r)", which should read O⟦x1,…,x4⟧/(r), but that is separate.) This is confirmed on the page image, and arXiv v2 has the same wording. O[Φ] is the group ring of a finite group, so it is not one of the 47 bracket errors. Both justifications given in the paper fail:
(1) Being local does not force the image into T_{1,m}⊗O[Φ]. Take T_{1,m}=O, Φ=Z/p and O=Z_p[ζ_p]. The ring A={(a_φ)∈⊕O : all a_φ congruent mod ϖ} is local and contains O[Φ]. It also contains (ϖ,0,…,0) = (ϖ/p)Σ[g], which is not in O[Φ] because v_ϖ(p)=p−1≥2.
(2) An injection of ϖ-torsion-free lattices that becomes an isomorphism after ⊗K need not be onto. O[Φ] ⊂ ⊕_φ O is itself an example. Torsion-freeness gives only injectivity.
So the printed reasons prove at most an inclusion of finite index. I checked the candidate's replacement argument myself, including the twisting convention, the images T_l ↦ T_l⊗[l] and ⟨d⟩ ↦ 1⊗[d]^2 for d∈Φ, and that squaring is bijective on Φ. It is correct, apart from the small base-change caveat noted in the correction.
On 'affects', I disagree with the candidate's "nothing". The proof of Theorem 4.8 as printed does not establish the isomorphism, and a different argument is needed, so it affects the proof. Theorem 4.8 still holds, because the intermediate isomorphism is true. Only the multiplicity-two statement of Thm 4.8 uses this step, together with Remark 4.12 ("a similar argument"), and neither is changed. I tried to defend the printed argument and could not.

(1) "Since T_m is local, the image lands inside T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ]" does not follow. A local subring of T_{1,m} ⊗ ⊕_φ O need not lie in T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ]. Take T_{1,m} = O, Φ = Z/p, O = Z_p[ζ_p]. The ring A = {(a_φ) : all a_φ congruent mod ϖ} is local and contains O[Φ]. It also contains (ϖ,0,…,0) = (ϖ/p)Σ_g[g], and this is not in O[Φ] because v_ϖ(p) = p−1 ≥ 2. The containment is true only because of the explicit images of the generators, and the paper never states them.

(2) "Isomorphism after ⊗K + ϖ-torsion free" gives only an injection of lattices of the same rank. O[Φ] ⊂ ⊕_φ O is itself such an injection, and it is not onto.

I looked for other readings:
- a Nakayama argument would need surjectivity onto target/m_{T_m}·target, not just onto the residue field;
- an integral module isomorphism S_2(Γ_1(N*),O)_m ≅ S_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ] would still leave the same generator argument to be made;
- nothing elsewhere in the paper supplies the step (I searched every twisting passage and the 2022 Correction).

The step cannot be skipped. Lemma 4.2 (p. 334) gives CM-ness and the number of generators of ω only for an actual B ⊗_O C, and a finite-index subring of T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ] inherits neither. Without the equality, the proof of dim ω_{T_m}/m = 3, and so of multiplicity two, is incomplete.

I checked the repair myself, including the twisting direction (on S_{φ²}, ⟨d⟩ for d ∈ Φ acts by φ²(d), so it matches 1⊗[d²]) and that U_l = 0 for l | M. The repair is sound, so the stated result is correct.

Consequences: Theorem 4.8 is used nowhere else. §4.1 opens with "Although this is not needed for our main results". Remark 4.12 ("a similar argument shows…") inherits the same step. So the proof of the multiplicity-two case of Thm 4.8 is affected, but no stated result is. I checked the page image (PDF p. 70 = p. 366); the display is exactly as quoted, and arXiv v2 has the same wording. I recomputed the parts. G^0 = T_pG^0 ⊗ Q_p/Z_p has Pontryagin dual Hom(T_pG^0, Z_p) = T_pG^e ≅ ω, so dim G^0[m] = dim ω/m = 3. G^e has dual Hom(T_pG^e, Z_p) = T_pG^0 ≅ T_m (free of rank 1), so dim G^e[m] = 1. Both values are correct. The additivity dim G[m] = dim G^0[m] + dim G^e[m] needs G[m] → G^e[m] to be onto. The obstruction lives in Ext^1_T(k, G^0), which is Pontryagin dual to Tor_1^T(k, ω). That group is nonzero because ω needs 3 generators (T_m is not Gorenstein), so additivity is not automatic, and the proof gives no argument for it. The paper only cites the Tate-module exact sequence from Gross 12.9/12.10. In Gross's multiplicity-one setting only the upper bound is needed, and here the "=" is simply asserted. The equality is true after the fact: the image of G[m] in the 1-dimensional G^e[m] is either 0 or everything, and 0 would force dim G[m] = 3, which is odd and contradicts BLR. So Theorem 4.8 is unaffected. The candidate's correction and its two side remarks are right. I disagree only on 'affects': the printed proof has an unjustified step that is false in general and needs a one-line repair (parity via BLR, or Wiese's d ≥ 2 from Remark 4.9), so I rate it 'the proof', not 'nothing'. No stated result changes. Theorem 4.8 is a standalone application and nothing later depends on it (grep finds only the introduction and Remarks 4.9/4.12). Remark 4.12's "similar argument" would need the same repair. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The page image confirms the display. The two dimensions are right. Pontryagin duality gives G^0[m]^∨ = Hom(T_pG^0,Z_p)/m = T_pG^e/m ≅ ω_{T_m}/m, which has dimension 3. Likewise G^e[m]^∨ = T_pG^0/m ≅ T_m/m, which has dimension 1.

The additivity dim G[m] = dim G^0[m] + dim G^e[m] is the step in question. It holds only if G[m] → G^e[m] is surjective. Dually, T_m/m → T_pG^∨/m must be injective in 0 → T_m → T_pG^∨ → ω → 0, where the obstruction is the connecting map Tor_1^{T_m}(ω,k) → k. That group is nonzero because T_m is not Gorenstein (ω needs 3 generators). So the equality is not formal, and the proof gives no argument for it. Its only input is the Tate-module sequence of Gross, Prop. 12.9/12.10. In Gross's Gorenstein case only the upper bound is needed.

Defence attempts:
(a) Gross's exact sequence is for Tate modules, and those sequences do not stay exact after taking [m].
(b) Nothing in §4.1 splits the sequence of T_m-modules. Ext^1_T(ω, T) can be nonzero, and the Galois structure is not used.
(c) The strongest charitable reading is Remark 4.9, just before the proof. It says Wiese proved multiplicity ≥ 2 and that "our contribution … is to show that the multiplicity is exactly two". With that bound only "≤" is needed. But the proof never invokes it; it asserts "=" and concludes "= 2" from the display alone.
So the printed proof has an unjustified step. It is not an error: the equality is true here by parity or by Wiese's bound, so the stated result is unaffected.

Consequences: I grepped the published text. Theorem 4.8 is used nowhere later. It is cited only in the Introduction (p. 305) and in Remarks 4.9/4.12/4.13. Remark 4.12 (J_H(N*)[m], "a similar argument shows…") inherits the same step and the same one-line repair.

Affects: "the proof" rather than "nothing", because the repair needs an ingredient absent from the proof (BLR parity or Wiese's bound). This is not one of the 47 bracket errors, and the Correction (2022) does not address it. (ii) Replace "a Z_p-extension which is unramified outside primes outside those above S" with "a Z_p^r-extension of L (the image of G_L is 1+εX for X in a compact subgroup of M_2(E), so ≅ Z_p^r) unramified outside the primes above S". (iii) Replace "because G_{L,S} has finite image in G_{F,S} ... because the inflation map is injective" with "because G_{L,S} has finite index in G_{F,S} (take L the fixed field of ker V, so L ⊂ F_S and L/F is Galois), the extension also splits over G_{F,S}, because the restriction map H^1(G_{F,S}, ad V) → H^1(G_{L,S}, ad V) is injective: its kernel is the inflation of H^1(Gal(L/F), ad V), which is 0 because Gal(L/F) is finite and ad V is a Q_p-vector space".`. I rendered PDF pp. 71–72 (pp. 367–368) and the text is exactly as quoted. arXiv v2 (p. 52–53) has the same wording. Each point in the candidate holds.
(a) A Noetherian semi-local ring is not in general the product of its localizations. For example, Z_(p) is not Q × Z_(p). What makes it work is dimension 0. The paper has that one sentence earlier: Spec R[1/p] is in bijection with Spec of a finite product of fields, so every prime is maximal. So "semi-local" names the wrong property, and "finite ideals" is a misprint for "(finitely many) prime ideals". "Direct sum" is harmless because there are finitely many factors.
(b) "G_{L,S} has finite image in G_{F,S}" is literally false: the image is an open subgroup of finite index and is infinite in general. It should say "finite index".
(c) The step needs the restriction H^1(G_{F,S}, ad V) → H^1(G_{L,S}, ad V) to be injective. By inflation–restriction its kernel is H^1(Gal(L/F), (ad V)^{G_L}), which is 0 because the group is finite and the coefficients are in characteristic zero. That is exactly what the paper's parenthetical describes. Inflation is always injective on H^1 and is not the relevant map. Even on a generous reading with an arbitrary L, where G_{L,S} → G_{F,S} factors as a surjection onto a finite-index subgroup, the kernel of H^1 of a finite group comes from restriction.
(d) "unramified outside primes outside those above S" has a doubled "outside". Read literally it contradicts the next clause, "unramified at all primes v|p", because S has no primes above p. Also, the image is Z_p^r, not necessarily Z_p. The step itself is fine: in a torsion-free abelian pro-p extension, inertia at v∤p has finite image and is therefore trivial. So an extension unramified at p is unramified everywhere, hence finite, hence trivial.
I re-checked the rest of the proof and it is correct: R[1/p] → A/m² is surjective since 𝔭 is maximal, and the traces argument goes through. Lemma 4.14 is cited only in the introduction (p. 298, comparison with Buzzard–Taylor) and in the remark right after it. No later theorem uses it. So these are wording slips in a correct proof of a correct lemma, and none of them is one of the 47 known bracket errors. ### Calegari–Geraghty, "Modularity lifting for non-regular symplectic representations", Duke Mathematical Journal (2020) (`PAPER-CALEGARI-GERAGHTY-20`)

- **Gap** at §1, the paragraph before Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.2 itself, pp. 802–803. Compare Theorem 9.1, pp. 878–879; the Koecher principle in §5.2, p. 821; Definition 5.13, pp. 834–835; Definition 6.15, p. 844; the sentence after the definition of e_{α,β}, p. 845; Lemma 7.10, p. 852. arXiv v1 (1907.08691v1) has the same text: intro p. 2–3, Definition 6.15 and the sentence "The assumption that r̄ is Katz modular implies that this space is non-zero after localization at m". (it affects a stated result). The source says `pp. 802–803: "Let Y_1(N) denote the (open) Siegel modular variety of level N = N(r̄) over Spec(O), ... and let ω(j,2) denote the coherent sheaf on Y_1(N) whose complex sections define Siegel modular forms of weight (j,2) ... Let T denote the subring of endomorphisms of eH^0(Y_1(N), ω(j,2) ⊗ K/O) ≃ lim_→ eH^0(Y_1(N), ω(j,2) ⊗ O/ϖ^n) (where e = e_{α,β} is a certain ordinary projection; see Section 6.4) generated by Hecke operators at primes not dividing Np." Theorem 1.2: "... Then there is an isomorphism R^min ~→ T_m, and moreover, the T_m-module eH^0(Y_1(N), ω(j,2) ⊗ K/O)^∨_m is free as a T_m-module." Compare pp. 878–879 (Theorem 9.1): "Furthermore, the space H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^{α,β,∨}_{m_∅} is a free T^{α,β}_{σ,m_∅}-module." And p. 821: "The Koecher principle states that there is an isomorphism H^0(Y, ω(a,b)_M) ≃ H^0(X, ω(a,b)_M)." And p. 845: "The assumption that r̄ is Katz modular implies that this space is nonzero after localization at m."`; it should be `There are two ways to fix it. (a) Minimal fix: state Theorem 1.2 for cusp forms, as Theorem 9.1 does (with Q = ∅). Let T be the image of the prime-to-Np Hecke operators in End_O(e_{α,β}H^0(X_1(N), ω(j,2)(−∞)_{K/O})), where ω(j,2)(−∞) = ω(j,2)^sub. Take m to be a maximal ideal of this T, and conclude R^min ≅ T_m with H^0(X_1(N), ω(j,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^{α,β,∨}_m free over T_m. (b) Keep the printed statement and add a lemma: for m non-Eisenstein, the inclusion e H^0(X, ω(j,2)(−∞)_{K/O})_m ⊂ e H^0(X, ω(j,2)_{K/O})_m is an equality. Then the two localised Hecke algebras agree too. The standard argument: the quotient embeds, through the Siegel Φ-operator/constant terms, Hecke-equivariantly mod ϖ^n into elliptic modular forms and constants on the boundary strata. Its Hecke eigensystems are therefore Klingen/Siegel-Eisenstein, and their Galois representations are reducible. Chebotarev and Brauer–Nesbitt rule this out when r̄_m is absolutely irreducible. The same lemma, or at least its non-vanishing half, is needed for the claim on p. 845 that Katz modularity (η in the full space, Definition 6.15) makes the cuspidal space nonzero at m. That is sourceIssues E65.`. I rendered p. 802, 803, 821, 844, 845, 846, 852, 878 and 879 and checked each point.
(1) Theorem 1.2 is stated for H^0 over the open variety Y_1(N) with K/O coefficients. By the paper's own Koecher statement (p. 821, for any O-module M), this equals H^0(X, ω(j,2)_{K/O}): all forms, not only cusp forms.
(2) Every Hecke algebra in the body is defined on the cuspidal space: Definition 5.13 uses End_O H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O}); §6.4 defines T_σ(Q)^{α,β} on e_{α,β}H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O}). Theorem 9.1, which p. 878 calls "the main result of this paper", asserts R^min ≅ T^{α,β}_{σ,m_∅} and freeness only for H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^{α,β,∨}_{m_∅}. Its proof (p. 879) takes H to be that cuspidal module.
(3) The only comparison of the canonical and subcanonical sheaves is Lemma 7.10 (pp. 852–853), and only after ⊗K, via Harris–Zucker boundary cohomology over C. That says nothing about torsion. A search of the text for canonical/boundary/cusp/Eisenstein turns up no torsion-coefficient comparison anywhere.
(4) Definition 6.15 puts the Katz eigenform η in H^0(X, ω(a,2)_{K/O})[m_∅], the full space. Yet p. 845 asserts without argument that Katz modularity makes the cuspidal e_{α,β}H^0(...(−∞)_{K/O}) nonzero at m.
So Theorem 1.2 as printed is not what the paper proves. Getting from Theorem 9.1 to it needs the fact that the boundary (non-cuspidal) part vanishes after localizing at a non-Eisenstein m with ϖ-torsion coefficients, and the paper never states or proves this.
I believe the missing step is true and standard (q-expansion principle plus the classical Hecke-equivariance of Φ, and reducibility of Klingen/Siegel-type boundary eigensystems). So Theorem 1.2 is almost certainly correct, and this is a minor gap, not an error. It is not a misreading: the intro deliberately works on the open Y_1(N), "whose complex sections define Siegel modular forms", which by Koecher means all forms. The intro is informal in other ways too (level Y_1(N) versus the level K of §6.3), which is why my confidence is only medium that this is a genuine gap rather than a harmless informal restatement. I looked for a defence and found none.

1. **The space is the full one.** On the open variety, the Koecher principle (p. 821: "H^0(Y, ω(a,b)_M) ≃ H^0(X, ω(a,b)_M)" for any O-module M) makes H^0(Y_1(N), ω(j,2) ⊗ K/O) the space of all forms on X_1(N), cuspidal or not. p. 822 makes this the paper's convention: "We may therefore pass freely between the open variety Y and the (any) smooth projective toroidal compactification X ... when dealing with H^0". The paper sometimes drops (−∞) elsewhere (Lemma 6.2, §8), but that cannot rescue the reading here: on Y there is no (−∞) to drop, and the text stresses "(open)".

2. **The body proves only the cuspidal statement.**
   - Definition 5.13 (p. 834) defines T_σ on H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O}).
   - p. 845 defines T_σ(Q)^{α,β} on e_{α,β}H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O}).
   - Theorem 9.1 ("the main result of this paper") concludes only that H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^{α,β,∨}_{m∅} is free over T^{α,β}_{σ,m∅}. Its proof (pp. 879–880) and the balancedness input (Theorem 7.11, H^2 vanishing for ω(−∞) via Theorem 5.1/Assumption 7.7, Serre duality with ω^3(−∞)) are intrinsically subcanonical. The proof does not transfer to the canonical sheaf.

3. **Nothing in the paper bridges the two.** The only comparison is Lemma 7.10 (p. 852), and it holds only after ⊗K. Its proof uses boundary cohomology over C, which says nothing about ϖ-torsion. From Lemma 7.10 one gets only that cusp_m has finite index in full_m over O. Torsion in H^1 of either sheaf could still separate e·full_{K/O,m} from e·cusp_{K/O,m}. The paper also defines no Hecke action on H^0(∂X, ·) with torsion coefficients, and Lemma 8.8 constructs T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2} on the full space but proves nothing about boundary support.

4. **The printed statement is almost certainly true.** The Φ-operator argument in the correction is standard folklore (also used implicitly in [16] in weight 1). So this is an omitted step, not a false claim. That is why I call it a gap rather than an error.

5. **Not a misprint.** The difference between full and cuspidal spaces with K/O coefficients is mathematical content, not a notational slip. The hypothesis is also stated for the full-space algebra ("maximal ideal m of T"), which matches the full-space Katz-modularity condition of Definition 6.15, not a cuspidal one.

6. **What uses the passage.**
   - Nothing later uses the full-space form of Theorem 1.2.
   - Theorem 1.1 needs only a cuspidal eigenform, which Theorem 9.1 supplies directly. Its deduction is not written out anyway (sourceIssues E3).
   - The appendix's "Theorem A.1 follows as in Theorem 1.2 above" (p. 889) reuses the method, not the full-space statement.

So the damage is confined to Theorem 1.2 as printed. That statement is not established by the paper, although the minimal restatement (a) is exactly Theorem 9.1 and the lemma in (b) restores it verbatim. The correction above is right and minimal. The same sentence appears word for word in arXiv:1907.08691v1, p. 7. w_0 is used again in the proof of Theorem 5.5 (pp. 828–829) and in Definition 5.7 (p. 830).. The source says `The longest element of W_G which we denote by w_0 acts via w_0(a,b;c) = (b,a;c).`; it should be `Minimal fix: change "W_G" to "W_M". The sentence then reads: "The longest element of W_M (its unique nontrivial element s_0 = s_{α1}), which we denote by w_0, acts via w_0(a,b;c) = (b,a;c)." Under the p. 809 identification of X*(H_C) with Z^3, this is also the longest (nontrivial) element of the compact Weyl group of K_{∞,1} ≅ U(2). For contrast, the longest element of W_G is s_0 s_1 s_0 s_1, and it acts by (a,b;c) ↦ (−a,−b;a+b+c).`. I checked the page image. p. 808 prints exactly "The longest element of W_G which we denote by w_0 acts via w_0(a,b;c) = (b,a;c)." W_G is defined in the same paragraph as N_G(T)/T, the Weyl group of GSp4, which has order 8.

I recomputed with the paper's conventions: characters diag(t1,t2,νt2^{-1},νt1^{-1}) ↦ t1^a t2^b ν^c, and (wλ)(t) = λ(w^{-1}tw). I enumerated the 8 signed-permutation representatives in GSp4 for the printed J by direct computation. The map (a,b;c) ↦ (b,a;c) is s_0 = s_{α1}, which has length 1. It sends α2 = (0,2;−1) to α4 = (2,0;−1), which is positive, so it is not the longest element of W_G. The unique length-4 element acts by (a,b;c) ↦ (−a,−b;a+b+c). The printed formulas w̃1 = s_1 = s_{α2}: (a,−b;b+c), w̃2 = (b,−a;a+c) and w̃3 = (−b,−a;a+b+c) all check out. So the printed label "W_G" is wrong: the displayed map is the longest (nontrivial) element of W_M = {1, s_{α1}}.

The paper's own formula, however, is the one used later, and every later use agrees with it:
- p. 829: "C_{3−i} = −w_0(C_i)" holds with w_0 = s_0. I checked −s_0(C_0) = C_3 and −s_0(C_1) = C_2.
- p. 829: the displayed "−w_0(−b+2,−a+1;−(a+b+2c)) = (a−1,b−2;a+b+2c)" is exactly the swap followed by negation.
- p. 830, Definition 5.7: μ − w_0(ρ) = (a,b;c) − (1,2;−3/2) = (a−1,b−2;c+3/2). This matches the "(a−1,b−2;c)" in the same definition (chambers do not constrain c) and gives exactly the three listed families (a,2;c), (a,3−a;c) and (1,b;c).
- p. 828: π(λ,C)^* = π(−w_0λ, −w_0C) is the right fact when w_0 is the compact Weyl element, which under the p. 809 identification is the swap t1 ↔ t2.

The objection that "both steps fail" applies only if one substitutes the true longest element of W_G. The paper never does that; it computes with the explicit formula. The error is therefore a one-word mislabel (W_G for W_M). It is a genuine misprint, but "error" and "affects: the proof" overstate it: no proof or result changes.

Separately, the statement of Theorem 5.5 prints "μ = (a−1,b−2;c) ∉ C_i", presumably meaning μ − w_0(ρ). This is not part of this issue. CHECKING THE LABEL. W_G is defined in the same paragraph as N_G(T)/T, the Weyl group of GSp4, which has order 8. I used the printed J, the torus diag(t1,t2,νt2^{-1},νt1^{-1}) and the paper's action (wλ)(t) = λ(w^{-1}tw). A direct computation enumerated the 8 signed permutation matrices in GSp4 and computed each element's action and its length (the number of positive roots α1..α4 sent to non-positive roots). The results:
- (a,b;c) ↦ (b,a;c) has length 1. It is s_0 = s_{α1}.
- (a,b;c) ↦ (a,−b;b+c) has length 1. It is s_1, which matches the printed w̃1.
- The unique element of length 4 acts by (a,b;c) ↦ (−a,−b;a+b+c).
The printed w̃2 = s1s0 and w̃3 = s1s0s1 also check out, but only with s_0 = the swap. The swap fixes the positive root α3 = (1,1;−1), so under no convention can it be the longest element of W_G. The label "W_G" is therefore false as printed.

DEFENCE. The formula is right and the label is wrong. W_M = {1, s_0}, since M is the Siegel Levi GL2×GL1. So the swap is exactly the longest element of W_M. On X*(H_C), the compact Weyl group also acts by t1 ↔ t2: an element h(t1,t2;0) maps to i·diag(t2,t1) in U(2). Every later use of w_0 needs the swap and fails for the true longest element of W_G:
(i) p. 828: π(λ,C)^* = π(−w_0λ, −w_0C) is the standard formula with w_0 the longest compact Weyl element. That element puts −λ back into a chamber with a ≥ b.
(ii) p. 829: C_{3−i} = −w_0(C_i). I checked −swap(C0) = C3 and −swap(C1) = C2. For the longest element of W_G, −w_0 is the identity on the (a,b) coordinates, so this would give C_i.
(iii) p. 829: −w_0(−b+2,−a+1;−(a+b+2c)) = (a−1,b−2;a+b+2c). This is exactly swap followed by negation. With the W_G element one gets (2−b,1−a;2a+2b+2c−3).
(iv) p. 830, Def. 5.7: μ − w_0(ρ) = (a,b;c) − (1,2;−3/2) = (a−1,b−2;c+3/2). This matches the "(a−1,b−2;c)" in the same definition and gives exactly the three listed families (a,2;c), (a,3−a;c) and (1,b;c). With the W_G element it would be μ + (2,1;−3/2), and the families would be different.
So the authors computed throughout with the explicit swap formula, and only the group named is wrong. The intended meaning is clear from the displayed formula and from every use.

CLASSIFICATION. "Misprint, affects nothing" is the right classification. "Error, affects the proof" overstates it: the proof fails only if one substitutes the real longest element of W_G, and the paper never does that. No proof or stated result changes.

Separate misprints nearby (not part of this issue):
- p. 807 prints t_1^a t_2^a ν^c for t_1^a t_2^b ν^c.
- p. 828 prints "C_0,…,C_4" for C_0,…,C_3.
- The statement of Theorem 5.5 prints "μ = (a−1,b−2;c) ∉ C_i". - **Error** at §8.5, p. 863. arXiv v1 p. 46 has the same text ("where α and β have non-negative p-adic valuation").. The source says `"We may write the eigenvalues of this polynomial as α, βp^{k−2}, β^{−1}p^{j−1}, α^{−1}p^{k+j−3}, where α and β have nonnegative p-adic valuation. That means that the coefficient of crystalline Frobenius should have characteristic polynomial X^4 − (α + ···) + (αβp^{k−2} + O(p^{k−1}))X^2 + ··· ."`; it should be `The expansion 'X^2-coefficient = αβp^{k−2} + O(p^{k−1})' holds when α and β are p-adic units, i.e. in the ordinary case. That is the only case used later, in the 'in particular' of Lemma 8.12. For α, β merely integral, Newton-above-Hodge gives only that the X^2-coefficient has valuation ≥ k−2. That still yields the passage's conclusion that the Q_2-eigenvalues are integral.`. I rendered p. 863 and confirmed the text.

**The X^2-coefficient.** The polynomial's X^2-coefficient is e_2 = αβp^{k−2} + αβ^{−1}p^{j−1} + 2p^{k+j−3} + α^{−1}βp^{2k+j−5} + α^{−1}β^{−1}p^{k+2j−4}. When α and β are units, every term after the first is O(p^{k−1}), using j ≥ k ≥ 2. So the claim is fine in the ordinary case.

**Counterexample under the printed hypothesis.** Nonnegative valuations do not suffice. Take (j,k) = (4,4), so the Hodge weights are 0, 2, 3, 5, and take p = 5, α = 2·5, β = 3·5^2.
- The Frobenius slopes are {1, 4, 1, 4}. The Newton polygon has vertices (0,1,2,6,10), which lie on or above the Hodge polygon (0,0,2,5,10), and the pairing condition s1+s4 = s2+s3 = 5 holds.
- A direct computation gives v(e_2) = 2 but v(αβp^2) = 5. So e_2 − αβp^2 has valuation 2, which is less than k−1 = 3.
- The only other labelling with v(α), v(β) ≥ 0 is v(α) = 4, v(β) = 2. It gives v(αβp^2) = 8 and fails in the same way. Labellings with v(β) = −1 are excluded by the printed hypothesis.
- A filtered φ-module with these slopes and Hodge weights exists, since the Newton point lies in B(GSp4, μ).

So the displayed expansion is false in general for non-ordinary forms. The passage's final conclusion, that the Q_2-eigenvalues are integral, still holds, because v(e_2) ≥ s1+s2 ≥ k−2.

**Why it affects nothing.** The passage is heuristic ('One expects', 'should'). Lemma 8.12 is proved directly on formal q-expansions. Its 'In particular' is stated only for ordinary forms, where the expansion is correct. The displayed expansion is false in general, not merely imprecise, so it is recorded as an error in a motivational passage. The classification is the only uncertain point: one could read 'nonnegative valuation' as a slip for 'unit', which would make it a misprint. The mathematics is not in doubt. - **Misprint** at §8.6, Theorem 8.13, statement, pp. 864–865. arXiv v1 (Thm 8.13) has the same text: 'Let A denotes a non-trivial power of the Hasse invariant of weight k'.. The source says `Let m denote the corresponding ideal of the Hecke algebra away from p. Let A denote a nontrivial power of the Hasse invariant of weight k. Then the composite map H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j,2)_{O/ϖ^m})^{α,β}_m --A--> H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j+k, 2+k)_{O/ϖ^m})_m --π_β--> H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j+k, 2+k)_{O/ϖ^m})^β_m is injective, where π_β denotes the projection onto the summand where U − β and Q_2 − αβ (equivalently, Z_2 − αβ) are nilpotent.`; it should be `'Let A denote a suitable power of the Hasse invariant of weight k', i.e. a power A^s of the lift A of h^r from Definition 6.1 with p^{m−1} | s, as in Lemma 6.4. A is a noncanonical lift of h^r, and Lemma 6.4 gets Hecke-equivariance of multiplication by A^s on O/ϖ^m-coefficients only when p^{m−1} | s (it cites [32, Thm 6.2.1]). Two things need that equivariance. First, the composite in the theorem is a map between m-localizations. Second, the proof asserts on p. 865 that 'In both results, all of the corresponding maps are equivariant with respect to Hecke operators away from p' to reduce to the socle. For m ≥ 2 and an arbitrary power this equivariance fails: in the GL_2 analogue, multiplication by E_{p−1} mod p^2 does not commute with T_ℓ. The paper's own usage points to the intended hypothesis. The parallel Lemma 8.14 says 'a suitable power'. Theorem 6.17 applies Theorem 8.13 as 'there exists a power A^s of A', with t = r p^{m−1}(p−1), so s = p^{m−1}. So 'nontrivial' is a slip for 'suitable'. Nothing downstream is affected, for three reasons. The application uses s = p^{m−1}. Everything over k = O/ϖ is fine for any power, since h^{rs} has q-expansion 1. And injectivity on O/ϖ^m can in any case be checked on ϖ-torsion, where A acts as h^{rs}. - **Misprint** at §8.6, proof of Lemma 8.14, p. 866, first lines. arXiv v1 has the identical text ('U 2 − T U + hpi = 0').. The source says `Let U denote the action of T on N. Then U satisfies the polynomial U^2 − TU + ⟨p⟩ = 0 on the image of M, and so M lies inside the ordinary subspace of N, and so inside N_α ⊕ N_β, where N_γ is the factor of N on which (U − γ) is nilpotent.`; it should be `U^2 − UT + ⟨p⟩ = 0 on M, i.e. U^2 F − U(TF) + ⟨p⟩F = 0 for F ∈ M, where T is the weight-one operator T_p acting on M.`. The composition order in 'TU' is wrong, and the correct relation has T applied first. With T = U + ⟨p⟩V on weight-one forms and UV = 1: U(TF) = U^2 F + ⟨p⟩UVF = U^2 F + ⟨p⟩F, so U^2 − UT + ⟨p⟩ = 0 on M. The printed order fails under both possible readings. First, the paper says T acts on N as U, so T(UF) = U^2 F and the relation would give ⟨p⟩F = 0. Second, as formal q-expansion operators, TU = U^2 + ⟨p⟩VU, so U^2 − TU + ⟨p⟩ = ⟨p⟩(1 − VU) ≠ 0. Here VU(Σa_n q^n) = Σ a_{np} q^{np} ≠ F in general. U does not preserve the image of M, so T∘U is not even defined on it. Read as a Hecke polynomial whose coefficient T commutes with U, the intended meaning is clear. The conclusion also holds with the corrected relation: F = ⟨p⟩^{−1}U(TF − UF), so W = M + UM is U-stable with U(W) ⊇ W, hence W is ordinary. This is a notational slip with no effect on the proof. - **Misprint** at §8.6, proof of Lemma 8.14, p. 866; arXiv:1907.08691v1 pp. 48–49. The source says `p. 866, proof of Lemma 8.14: "Note that U is invertible on N_α. Since TF also lies in N_α ⊕ N_β, we deduce that VF lies in N_α ⊕ N_β. Yet UVF = F ∈ N_β, and so VF ∈ N_α, and moreover ⟨p⟩VF = αβU^{-1}F_α." ... "We are thus left with a form F such that [display] TF = (α + β)F, UF = αF, VF = βF. We may now achieve a contradiction based purely on a computation with formal q-expansions. For example, the identity VF = βF is impossible as soon as either β ≠ 1 or F is a cusp form, simply by considering the exponent of the smallest coefficient. Alternatively, a nonformal argument using properties of modular forms would be to note that θVF = 0, and then use the fact that θ has no kernel in low weight (by [45])."`; it should be `"Yet UVF = F ∈ N_α, and so VF ∈ N_α"; the displayed relations should read "TF = (α+β)F, UF = αF, VF = α^{-1}F" (equivalently ⟨p⟩VF = βF); and "the identity VF = α^{-1}F is impossible as soon as either α ≠ 1 or F is a cusp form".`. I checked the page images: the published p. 866 at 110 and 220 dpi, and arXiv v1 p. 48 at 110 dpi. The printed text is as quoted, and arXiv v1 (pp. 48–49) has the same wording.

I redid the computation from the proof's own hypotheses: π_β(F) = (U−α)^m F = 0, so "We are assuming that F = F_α ∈ N_α". U and V are the q-expansion operators, with UV = id and T = U + ⟨p⟩V in weight 1.

(1) Write VF = x_α + x_β in N_α ⊕ N_β. Since U preserves both factors, U(VF) = F ∈ N_α forces Ux_β = 0. U is invertible on N_β because β ≠ 0 (β is an eigenvalue of an invertible matrix). So x_β = 0 and VF ∈ N_α, which is the conclusion the text draws. With "F ∈ N_β" the same step would give VF ∈ N_β instead. So "N_β" must be "N_α".

(2) After the reduction G_α = 0 we have UF = αF. U is injective on N_α and U(VF − α^{-1}F) = F − F = 0, so VF = α^{-1}F. With ⟨p⟩F = αβF this gives ⟨p⟩VF = βF and TF = αF + βF = (α+β)F. That matches the displayed ⟨p⟩VF = αβU^{-1}F_α. The printed VF = βF would force β = α^{-1}, i.e. αβ = 1, since βUF = UVF = F. The reduction explicitly lets ⟨p⟩ act by αβ, which is det ρ̄(Frob_p) and need not be 1. So the ⟨p⟩ has been dropped from the displayed relation.

(3) Write F = Σ a_n q^n. If VF = cF with c ≠ 0, the lowest exponent of VF is p·n0 while that of cF is n0, so n0 = 0 and F is not cuspidal. Comparing constant terms then gives a_0 = c·a_0, so c = 1. With c = α^{-1}, the condition should be "α ≠ 1", not "β ≠ 1".

This correction is right on all three points. As (2) shows, the printed VF = βF is compatible with the rest only when αβ = 1; α = 1 alone is not enough.

The θ argument is unaffected, since θVF = 0 still forces θF = 0. The cusp-form case also still closes. Lemma 8.14 is a warm-up ("a much easier analogue for GL(2)"). The label 8.14 appears nowhere else in the text except at the lemma and its proof heading, and the proof of Theorem 8.13 is separate. So no stated result or later argument changes. The printed VF = βF would need αβ = 1, which the lemma does not assume (it assumes only α ≠ β). The smallest-exponent argument for VF = cF with c ≠ 0 works as corrected. - **Gap** at §8.6, proof of Lemma 8.15, pp. 867–868. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text at Lemma 8.15, p. 49, with "characteristic zero" in place of "characteristic 0". (it affects the proof). The source says `p. 867: "In the first case, by assumption we know that Q_2 − αβ is nilpotent, and so Q_2 induces an isomorphism of M. On the other hand, the operator Q_2 acts via the formal operator Z_2. In weight τ = (j + k, 2 + k), the corresponding operator Q_2 also acts via Z_2, and so we deduce that Q_2 − αβ acts on M ⊂ N and acts nilpotently. Yet Q_2 only acts invertibly on the ordinary part of N, as can be seen by lifting to characteristic 0." p. 868: "Since the left-hand side is an isomorphism, it follows that Z_2^2 M = Z_2 M, and hence that Z_2 acts invertibly on Z_2 M, and as in the previous argument it follows that Z_2 and hence U is invertible on this space."`; it should be `The following replacement argument is correct, and it is minimal because it uses only identities the paper already states. On M, which has weight (j,2), Lemma 8.3 gives T ≡ U + Z mod p. On N, which has weight τ = (j+t, 2+t), it gives T ≡ U, and Lemma 8.12 gives Q_2 ≡ Z_2. For m ∈ M, Um = T_N m lies in N and Tm lies in M, so Zm = Tm − Um lies in W := Σ_{i≥0} U^i M. This W is a finite-dimensional U-stable subspace of N. The formal identity Z_2 = UZ (p. 859) gives Z_2 M ⊂ UW. Z_2 commutes with U (p. 869; formally, a(Z_2 UF, Q) = a(UZ_2 F, Q), because M^{-1}.pQ is always integral). Hence Z_2 W ⊂ UW, and by induction Z_2^n W ⊂ U^n W. For j > 2, M = Z_2^n M lies in U^n W for every n. For (2,2), Z_2 M = Z_2^{n−1}(Z_2 M) lies in U^n W, using the paper's own equality Z_2^2 M = Z_2 M. In both cases the space lies in ∩_n U^n W, which is the part of W on which U is invertible, and so it lies in N_α ⊕ N_β by Lemma 8.16. The rest of the proof is unchanged, including the injectivity of M → Z_2 M, which uses only (αβ)^2 ≠ 1. The first sentence of the p. 867 passage should therefore be replaced by this argument, and "as in the previous argument" on p. 868 should point to it.`. This is a genuine gap. The key step, 'Q2 only acts invertibly on the ordinary part of N', is justified only by 'lifting to characteristic 0', and the case (2,2) reuses that step. I redid the computation. For an eigenform of weight (j',k') with Frobenius slopes s1 ≤ … ≤ s4, where s1 + s4 = s2 + s3 = j' + k' − 3, the Hodge weights are 0, k'−2, j'−1, j'+k'−3. The X^2 coefficient is p^{k'−2}·Q2, so Q2 is a unit exactly when s1 + s2 = k'−2. T is a unit exactly when s1 = 0; this uses k' = 2 + t > 2. The slopes (s, k'−2−s, j'−1+s, j'+k'−3−s) with 0 < s ≤ (k'−2)/2 have partial sums s, k'−2, 2k'+j'−3+s and the correct total, so they lie on or above the Hodge polygon. So a Q2-unit eigenform that is not T-ordinary is not excluded by the Galois side. A residual condition does not exclude it locally either. The GL2 analogue: θ^{p−1}f, for f of weight 1 with ρ̄|G_Qp = unr_α ⊕ unr_β, lifts to a non-ordinary crystalline form of weight p², with Hodge–Tate weights {0, (p+1)(p−1)}. Theorem 6.17 uses Hasse powers t = r p^{m−1}(p−1), which can be arbitrarily large. The heuristic in §8.5 (p. 863) does not close the gap. It parametrises the eigenvalues as α, βp^{k−2}, β^{−1}p^{j−1}, α^{−1}p^{k+j−3} with v(α), v(β) ≥ 0, and writes the X^2 coefficient as αβp^{k−2} + O(p^{k−1}). But the term αβ^{−1}p^{j−1} has valuation s1 + s2, which can equal k−2, so 'Q2 unit ⇒ α, β units' does not follow. The obvious formal shortcut also fails. The paper's identity is Z2 = UZ, and Z2 commutes with U, but ZU ≠ UZ formally: a(UF, R) = 0 for non-integral R, so for example the first term of a(ZUF; n,r,m) needs p | m. So U-nilpotence does not force Z2-nilpotence on N. Likewise 'Z2 and hence U' does not follow, since Z does not act on N. Whether Q2 is invertible only on the ordinary part of all of N remains unproven; the lemma needs only the version on W, which the correction proves. On 'affects': 'nothing' would mean the mathematics is right as intended. Here the intended justification fails and the proof needs a new argument, so the right value is 'the proof'. No stated result changes. Lemma 8.15 as stated is true. Its conclusions are used in Lemma 8.17: the statement 'π_β: Z2M → N_β' and M ⊂ N_α ⊕ N_β (with Lemma 8.16), and on p. 871 'the injectivity of Z2 in Lemma 8.15'. From there they feed Theorem 8.13 and Theorem 6.17, and all of these survive. arXiv v1 has the same passage. I tried to defend the paper and could not.

(1) Charitable reading. "Ordinary part of N" can only mean the U-invertible part. That is how p. 866 uses "ordinary subspace of N" in the GL(2) analogue, and the lemma concludes that U is invertible. The needed claim is therefore: a nonzero generalized Q_2-eigenvalue on N implies U is invertible there.

(2) Lifting to characteristic 0. A lifted eigenform of weight (j+t, 2+t) has Hodge–Tate weights 0, t, j+t−1, j+2t−1. A unit Q_2 means s1 + s2 = t, so the Newton polygon touches the Hodge polygon at vertex 2. Then r|G_Qp has a 2-dimensional crystalline piece V_1 with weights {0, t} and slopes {s, t−s}. Since j−1 ≢ 0 mod p−1, V_1-bar^ss must be unr(α) ⊕ unr(β). U invertible needs s = 0.
- For t = p−1 the defence actually works. Breuil and Berger–Li–Zhu (BLZ) for k = p ≤ p+1 say any positive slope reduces to the irreducible ind(ω_2^{p−1}). The paper supplies none of this.
- But Theorem 8.13 claims every nontrivial Hasse power, and Theorem 6.17 uses t = r·p^{m−1}(p−1), so t can be large.
- For (p²−1) | t and slope s > ⌊(t−1)/(p−1)⌋, BLZ gives V_1-bar = ind(ω_2^t)⊗unr = unr(λ) ⊕ unr(−λ). This is compatible with α = −β, which the hypotheses allow: αβ(α²−1)(β²−1)(α−β)(α²β²−1) ≠ 0 whenever α⁴ ≠ 1.
- Example: p = 5, j = 3, t = 24, α of order 8, β = −α. The slopes are (6, 18, 32, 44) against Hodge (0, 24, 26, 50). The Newton polygon touches at x = 2, so Q_2 is a unit, while v(T) = 6 > 0.

So the Galois side does not rule out Q_2-invertible, non-ordinary eigensystems. Whether they occur globally is still open, and so is the claim for all of N. Hence this is a gap, not an error.

(3) Formal shortcut. Z_2 = UZ, but ZU ≠ UZ. For example, the first term of a(ZUF; n,r,m) needs p | m. And Z does not preserve N. So "Z_2 and hence U" (p. 868) does not follow by itself.

(4) No nearby statement fills the gap. Lemma 8.16 only gives N = N_0 ⊕ N_α ⊕ N_β. The p. 806 introduction and Remark 8.18 concede that non-ordinary forms do appear.

Consequences. Lemma 8.15 as stated is true (by the correction above), so no stated result changes. Where the lemma is used:
- Lemma 8.17: the map "π_β: Z_2M ⊂ N_α ⊕ N_β → N_β" (p. 869); "π_β(F) = 0 implies F = F_α ∈ N_α" in the case j > 2; and on p. 871 "the injectivity of Z_2 in Lemma 8.15".
- §8.8 (p. 874 area, "contradicting the injectivity of Z_2: M → N in Lemma 8.15").
- Through these, Theorem 8.13 and Theorem 6.17.
All of them survive. The intended justification fails and a new argument is needed, so 'affects' is "the proof", not "nothing". arXiv v1 has the same text. (1) h(x+iy) = xI + yJ, so the centraliser of h equals the centraliser of J. Suppose gJ = Jg and g^tJg = νJ. Then g^tJ = νJg^{-1} = νg^{-1}J, so g^tg = νI and ν > 0. I checked this by direct computation, together with h(i) = J. So the paper's own three statements are inconsistent: K^h is the centraliser, K^h = R^×K_∞, and ν is surjective on K_∞. (a) "as above" refers back to the case j > 2 (p. 869). There M ⊂ N_α ⊕ N_β (Lemma 8.15), and the hypothesis is π_β(F) = 0, so F ∈ N_α. In weight (2,2), M is not in the ordinary part: Remark 8.18 (tripling) says that weight (2,2) oldforms produce elements of the kernel of Z_2, which is why N_0 appears. The only hypothesis there is π_β(Z_2F) = 0, i.e. Z_2F ∈ N_α. Z_2 commutes with U, so this gives Z_2F_β = Z_2F_0 = 0, but not F_β = 0.
(b) Even with F_β = 0, the equation Q_2F = αβF only gives X_2F = (αβF_α − (Z_2F)_α, 0, αβF_0). Lemma 8.6 (Z_2X_2 = 0) then gives Z_2(Z_2F) = αβZ_2F, which is already known from Z_2Q_2F = αβZ_2F. It would force (X_2F)_α = 0 only if Z_2 were injective on N_α. The paper proves injectivity of Z_2 only on M and on Z_2M (Lemma 8.15), and (X_2F)_α need not lie in Z_2M. U is not an operator on M, so F cannot be projected to remove F_β either.
(c) The printed G = (… , 0, G_0 − (α+β)F_0) drops a term UF_0. The hypothesis ZF = βF + αF_0 of Theorem 8.22(2) equals TF − UF only if UF_0 = 0. The text states UF_0 = 0 nowhere.

A search of both versions finds no statement of UX_2 = 0 or of X_2F ∈ ker U. The ingredients are printed, however: a(UF, Q) = a(F, pQ) in Lemma 8.3, and a(X_2F, Q) = p·a(F, Q) for Q ≡ 0 mod p in Definition 8.5 (equivalently, "a(X_2F, Q) = 0 if det(Q) ≡ 0" in the proof of Lemma 8.6).

I checked the fill line by line:
- X_2F ∈ N: Q_2F ∈ M ⊂ N, and Z_2 acts on N as Q_2 (Lemma 8.12, since the weight (2+k, 2+k) is not (2,2)).
- U on N is the formal U, since T ≡ U in weight (·, 2+k).
- N = N_α ⊕ N_β ⊕ N_0 by Lemma 8.16 and α ≠ β, αβ ≠ 0.
The component comparison then gives every printed claim. ZF = βF + αF_0 follows from T = U + p^{k−2}Z + p^{k+j−3}V = U + Z + pV at (j,k) = (2,2). This agrees with §8.8's ZF = βF + β^{-1}X_2F, since β^{-1}X_2F = αF_0.

With the added lines, the rest of the proof works: the induction on G, and the step Z_2(T−α−β)F = 0 (an element of M ∩ N_0 is killed by Z_2, because Z_2M lies in the U-invertible part).

CONSEQUENCES. The passage feeds only the weight (2,2) case of Theorem 8.13, through Theorem 8.22(2) (p. 873) and §8.8 (p. 874). §8.8 also uses F ∈ M, which holds by construction but is not stated. A separate §8.8 issue (E121, on "F − X_2F ∈ M") is not part of this issue.

No stated result is false, but the printed proof omits needed steps, so affects is "the proof". "Nothing" would also be defensible, because the fill uses only printed facts. So in weight (2,2), F₀ = (αβ)⁻¹X₂F = 0 (using αβ ≠ 0) and F = F_α, which gives UF = αF and ZF = βF + αF₀ = βF." The rest of the paragraph then ends in a contradiction, and the sentence on p. 874 ("We may therefore assume that a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q of discriminant D prime to p") states the conclusion. The hypothesis "if F ≠ 0" must be kept, since the printed proof uses it. "Misprint" fits better than "gap": the one missing step is a single line from Definition 8.5.`. I rendered p. 859, 872, 873 and 874 and checked the text against the page images.

(1) The claim is printed without its key condition. 'There exists a Q with det(Q) ≢ 0 mod p' says nothing about F, and any Q prime to p satisfies it. What the paragraph proves, as its conclusion on p. 874 states, is that a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some such Q. The clause 'with a(F,Q) ≠ 0' is missing.

(2) 'In particular' is the wrong connective. Suppose there is a Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 and p ∤ det(Q). By Definition 8.5 (p. 859), a(X₂F,Q) ≡ (D/p)a(F,Q) ≠ 0, so X₂F ≠ 0 and F₀ = (αβ)⁻¹X₂F ≠ 0. So the existence claim does not imply F₀ = 0; it contradicts it. F₀ = 0 holds only under the opposite assumption, that every Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 has p | det(Q). In that case every coefficient of X₂F vanishes: either (D/p) = 0 or a(F,Q) = 0, and a(X₂F,Q) = p·a(F,Q) = 0 when Q ≡ 0 mod p. Then X₂F = 0 in characteristic p, so F₀ = 0 because αβ ≠ 0, and ZF = βF + αF₀ = βF.

(3) The same unstated assumption is used again two sentences later. 'By Lemma 8.21, F(Q) consists of a single class [P]' needs (d(Q)/p) = 0 (Lemma 8.21(2), p. 872). That holds for the chosen Q only because of the contrary assumption.

So the printed text states a proof by contradiction without ever stating the contrary assumption, and it misstates what is being proved. Nothing about the conventions makes 'In particular' mean 'suppose not', so this is not a misreading of the text.

On the classification: the missing justification for F₀ = 0 is one line from Definition 8.5 once the assumption is stated. The intended structure is clear from 'we may also assume', from the hint 'F₀ = (αβ)⁻¹X₂F', and from the conclusion on p. 874. That fits the definition of a misprint (a slip whose intended meaning is clear from context) better than 'gap'. Classing it as a minor gap would also be defensible.

The mathematics is unaffected once the assumption is restored. Separate problems in the rest of this proof are recorded under other ids: the reversed display a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q), and the degenerate case d(Q) = 0. Checked on the rendered pages 859 and 872–875 and on arXiv v1 p. 53.

(1) The sentence cannot be read literally. Without "and a(F,Q) ≠ 0", the claim "there exists a Q with det(Q) ≢ 0 mod p" is trivial. The words "In particular ... F₀ = 0" also cannot follow from the intended claim. By Definition 8.5 (p. 859), a(X₂F,Q) = (D/p)a(F,Q) mod p, and we work over k, which has characteristic p. So a Q with p ∤ D and a(F,Q) ≠ 0 would give X₂F ≠ 0, and hence F₀ = (αβ)⁻¹X₂F ≠ 0. Read literally, the connective "In particular" states the opposite of what is true.

(2) The defence fails, but the charitable reading works. The phrase "we may also assume" only makes sense as the contrary hypothesis in a proof by contradiction. In weight (2,2), X₂F = 0 is exactly equivalent to "a(F,Q) = 0 for all Q with p ∤ D". The rest of the paragraph uses this hypothesis without saying so, in both weights. "By Lemma 8.21, F(Q) consists of a single class [P]" needs (D/p) = 0 for the minimal Q, which holds only under the contrary hypothesis. Otherwise Lemma 8.21 allows 0, 1 or 2 classes. The paragraph ends in a contradiction: β²a(F,Q) = 0 when j > 2 and β ≠ 0, or β² = 1 in weight (2,2). The authors then state the conclusion on p. 874: "We may therefore assume that a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q of discriminant D prime to p." So the intended meaning is clear from context. The only step the reader must supply, contrary hypothesis ⇒ X₂F = 0 ⇒ F₀ = 0, follows at once from Definition 8.5 and αβ ≠ 0. This makes it an expository misprint (a missing clause and the wrong connective), not a substantive gap.

(3) Downstream use. The conclusion of this step is used in §8.9 (Theorem 8.22(1), weight (j,2) with j ≥ 4). There, (D/p) = −1 is excluded and "Hence we may assume that (D/p) = 1", which silently needs (D/p) ≠ 0, i.e. p ∤ D, from this step. §8.8 (weight (2,2)) argues on its own through Theorem 8.10 and does not use the conclusion. Theorem 8.22 feeds Theorem 8.13 via Lemma 8.17. Once the passage is read as intended, the mathematics of this step is right, so nothing is affected. The separate issues in the same argument, recorded as other issues, are not part of this finding: the degenerate or minimal-discriminant case, and the ρ(M_Q) versus ρ(M_P)⁻¹ display. - **Error** at §8.7, proof of Theorem 8.22, the display after "By Lemma 8.21, ℱ(Q) consists of a single class [P]", p. 873. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same wording and display on p. 53 (checked on the page image). (it affects the proof). The source says `"Without loss of generality, assume that Q is a p-primitive form of minimal discriminant with a(F,Q) ≠ 0. By Lemma 8.21, ℱ(Q) consists of a single class [P]. It follows that [display] a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) = β · ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q). If P is not p-primitive, then P = pR for some R, and then a(F,R) ≠ 0, contradicting the minimality of Q (note that P and Q have the same discriminant)."`; it should be `Replace the display with β·a(F,Q) = a(ZF,Q) = ρ(M_P)a(F,P), where M_P ∈ 𝒮 and M_P.P = Q. This holds by the identity on p. 872 (Lemma 8.3), because ℱ(Q) = {[P]}. Since β ≠ 0 and a(F,Q) ≠ 0, it gives a(F,P) ≠ 0. The next sentence then works unchanged: if P = pR, then a(F,P) = a(UF,R) = α·a(F,R), so a(F,R) ≠ 0. So does the rest of the proof. M_Q is no longer needed at this point. This is the minimal fix.`. I checked the display on the rendered page image; it reads exactly as quoted.

Conventions, from pp. 856–858: M.Q = (det M)^{-1} M Q M^T. ρ = Sym^{j−k} is extended to a homomorphism M_2(Z) → End(U). Lemma 8.3 gives a(ZF,Q) = Σ_𝒮 ρ(M)a(F, M^{-1}.Q). On p. 872 this becomes a(ZF,Q) = Σ_{[P]∈ℱ(Q)} ρ(M_P)a(F,P) with M_P.P = Q.

I redid the computation. Normalise Q = [[m, r/2],[r/2, n]] with m a unit, p | r and p | n; this is the case (D/p) = 0, where ℱ(Q) has one element. Then:
- P = M_P^{-1}.Q = [[pm, r/2],[r/2, n/p]], with M_P = diag(1,p).
- When P is p-primitive (v_p(n) = 1), M_Q = diag(p,1) gives M_Q.Q = P.
- So M_Q·M_P = pI, as the paper itself says on p. 874 ("ρ(M_Q.M_P) = ρ(p·I) ... zero in higher weight").

With ρ = Sym^{j−2}, the paper's own Z-identity gives ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) = ρ(M_Q M_P)a(F,P) = p^{j−2}a(F,P). In characteristic p and weight (j,2) with j ≥ 4, this is 0. So the first printed equality, a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q), would force a(F,P) = 0. That is exactly the opposite of what the next sentence needs: it uses a(F,P) ≠ 0 to get a(F,R) ≠ 0 when P = pR. No step in the text justifies that equality. It holds only in weight (2,2), where ρ is trivial and ρ(pI) = 1. Even taken at face value, the printed line would not give a(F,P) ≠ 0 when j ≥ 4, because ρ(M_Q) = Sym^{j−2}(diag(p,1)) is singular mod p.

The corrected line βa(F,Q) = ρ(M_P)a(F,P) follows directly from the paper's identity. It gives a(F,P) ≠ 0 in all weights. The later chain β²a(F,Q) = ρ(M_P)a(ZF,P) = ρ(M_Q)ρ(M_P)a(F,Q) is fine, because both M_P M_Q and M_Q M_P equal pI.

Also, [Q] ∈ ℱ(P) (needed to define M_Q) is only cited afterwards. This is harmless: Lemma 8.20 has no p-primitivity hypothesis. It does not affect the finding.

This is a real but local slip. Theorem 8.22, Theorem 8.13 (via Lemma 8.17) and the reduction to Q with D prime to p in §§8.8–8.9 all hold once the one-line fix is made. No later result depends on the wrong identity. arXiv v1 (p. 53) has the same text. I checked the display on the rendered page images, both the Duke version (p. 873) and arXiv v1 (p. 53). It reads exactly as quoted.

The paper's conventions:
- M.Q = (det M)^{-1} M Q M^T (p. 857).
- ρ = Sym^{j−k}, extended to a homomorphism M_2(Z) → End(U) (p. 857).
- Lemma 8.3 gives a(ZF,Q) = Σ_𝒮 ρ(M)a(F, M^{-1}.Q). On p. 872 this becomes a(ZF,Q) = Σ_{[P]∈ℱ(Q)} ρ(M_P)a(F,P), with M_P.P = Q.
- a(F, γ.Q) = ρ(γ)a(F,Q) holds only for γ ∈ Γ̄, not for matrices of determinant p.

Defence attempts. None of them survives.
(a) The identity on p. 872 expresses a(ZF,Q) in terms of a(F,P), not the other way round. Nothing in §8 gives a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q).
(b) One could read the display as a garbled form of the identity at P, namely β·a(F,P) = a(ZF,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q). That needs ℱ(P) = {[Q]}. But this uses P being p-primitive, which the very next sentence derives from the display, so that reading is circular. It also puts β on the other side.
(c) The only other possible source is the Γ̄-equivariance a(F, M_Q.Q) = ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q) applied wrongly to M_Q ∈ 𝒮. That has no Z in it, so it does not produce the display either.

The printed display is false in weight (j,2) with j ≥ 4.
- With ℱ(Q) = {[P]}, the only term in Lemma 8.3 comes from M_P, with P := M_P^{-1}.Q.
- The adjugate pM_P^{-1} is an integral matrix of determinant p, and it sends Q to P. So in the coefficient identity at P we may take M_Q = pM_P^{-1} (writing pM_P^{-1} = s'γ with s' ∈ 𝒮 and γ ∈ Γ̄ gives ρ(s')a(F, s'^{-1}.P) = ρ(pM_P^{-1})a(F,Q)). Then M_Q M_P = M_P M_Q = pI. The paper says the same on p. 874: "ρ(M_Q.M_P) = ρ(p·I) is the identity in weight (2,2) and zero in higher weight".
- Hence ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) = ρ(M_Q M_P)a(F,P) = p^{j−2}a(F,P), which is 0 in characteristic p when j ≥ 3.
- So the first printed equality would force a(F,P) = 0, the opposite of what the next sentence needs (a(F,P) ≠ 0, to get a(F,R) ≠ 0 when P = pR).
- The printed conclusion a(F,P) = β·ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q) does not give a(F,P) ≠ 0 either: ρ(M_Q) = Sym^{j−2} of a matrix of determinant p is singular mod p.

In weight (2,2), ρ is trivial, and the printed line reduces to the true a(F,P) = a(ZF,Q) = β·a(F,Q). So this looks like the weight-2 line with ρ(M_Q) inserted wrongly. It is a false step, not a mere index slip, so I class it as an error rather than a misprint.

Consequences. The corrected line gives a(F,P) ≠ 0 in every weight, and the rest of the proof survives:
- the minimality argument;
- ℱ(P) = {[Q]}, from Lemma 8.20, which has no primitivity hypothesis, and Lemma 8.21;
- the chain β²a(F,Q) = ρ(M_P)ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q), which is 0 for j > 2 and a(F,Q) for j = 2. This is fine because both products are pI, even though the printed order ρ(M_Q)ρ(M_P) is reversed.

Nothing else in the paper uses the wrong identity. §8.8 and §8.9 start from the output of this proof ("a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q of discriminant D prime to p"). Theorem 8.13, which follows via Lemma 8.17, and Theorem 8.22 itself remain true.

On 'affects': "nothing" would understate it, because the printed step actually fails for j ≥ 4. "the proof" is right: the proof is broken as written, it is repaired locally in one line, and no stated result changes. - **Gap** at §8.7, proof of Theorem 8.22 (first step, the minimal-discriminant choice), p. 873. Also the statement of Theorem 8.22 on p. 873, and Theorem 8.13 on pp. 864–865 (it affects the proof). The source says `Theorem 8.22 (p. 873): "Suppose that F = Σ a(F,Q)q^Q is a Siegel modular q-expansion of weight σ = (j,2) in characteristic p, where p − 1 > j. (1) Let σ = (j,2) with j ≥ 4, and suppose that UF = αF and ZF = βF for some α, β with αβ(β^2 − 1) ≠ 0. Then F = 0. (2) Let σ = (2,2), and suppose that F = F_α + F_0, where UF_α = αF_α, X_2F = αβF_0, and ZF = βF + αF_0 for some α, β with αβ(β^2 − 1)(α^2β^2 − 1) ≠ 0. Then F = 0." Proof (p. 873): "… Hence, if F ≠ 0, then there exists a p-primitive form Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0. Without loss of generality, assume that Q is a p-primitive form of minimal discriminant with a(F,Q) ≠ 0. By Lemma 8.21, 𝓕(Q) consists of a single class [P]. It follows that a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) = β·ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q). If P is not p-primitive, then P = pR for some R, and then a(F,R) ≠ 0, contradicting the minimality of Q (note that P and Q have the same discriminant). Hence P is also p-primitive."`; it should be `The minimal fix keeps Theorem 8.22 as stated. Add one line before, or in place of, the minimal-discriminant step: "If a(F,Q) = 0 for every Q with det(Q) ≢ 0 mod p, then ΘF = 0 in weight (2,2), resp. θ1F = 0 in weight (j,2), since both operators multiply the Q-th coefficient by det(Q). Hence F = 0 by Theorem 8.10 (k = 2, p > 3), resp. Theorem 8.11 (p − 1 > j ≥ 4)." This makes the descent over p-primitive forms unnecessary, and it also covers the constant-term case. Both theorems are already in the paper, and their hypotheses are exactly those of Theorem 8.22. Acceptable alternatives: - Add cuspidality to Theorem 8.22, i.e. a(F,Q) = 0 for degenerate Q. This holds in the application, since §6.4 and Theorem 6.17 use H^0(X1(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)). - Take Q of minimal nonzero |d|, and dispose of an F supported on degenerate Q by the Θ/θ1 argument above. Another proposed route, via α ≠ β, is not recommended: - α ≠ β is not a hypothesis of Theorem 8.22. It comes only from Theorem 8.13. - For a smaller Γ̄ the Γ̄-classes of degenerate forms can cycle under Z.`. The printed text matches the page images of pp. 873–874. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has word-for-word the same text (§8.7, Theorem 8.22), and the same undecorated Theorem 8.13.

Where the gap is:
- §8.2 (p. 856) takes the index set X to be all positive semidefinite Q, so degenerate Q are included.
- The statement of Theorem 8.22 assumes only "a Siegel modular q-expansion". It does not assume cuspidality, and it does not assume α ≠ β.
- If some degenerate coefficient is nonzero, the minimal |d| is 0. Then R = P/p also has d = 0, and minimality gives no contradiction.

I checked an explicit example myself. Take S = {diag(1,p), [[p,b],[0,1]]} and P = adj(M).Q, with Q = diag(c,0) and p ∤ c.
- Only M = diag(1,p) gives an integral P, namely P = diag(pc,0) = pQ. So R = Q.
- The relations are then β·a(F,Q) = ρ(diag(1,p))·a(F,pQ) = α·ρ(diag(1,p))·a(F,Q).
- In weight (2,2), ρ is trivial, so this gives (β − α)a(F,Q) = 0.
- In weight (j,2), ρ(diag(1,p)) reduces mod p to the projection onto f1^{j−2}. The stabiliser [[1,b],[0,1]] fixes the same line. So if α = β, the relations are consistent and give no contradiction.
- The hypotheses of Theorem 8.22 are αβ(β^2−1) ≠ 0 in part (1) and αβ(β^2−1)(α^2β^2−1) ≠ 0 in part (2). Neither includes α ≠ β.

The step before this one has the same problem. "If F ≠ 0 there is a p-primitive Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0" fails when only a(F,0) ≠ 0, since 0 = p·0. The lemma 8.14 proof on p. 866 handles the analogous constant-term case explicitly ("β ≠ 1 or F is a cusp form"), but Theorem 8.22 does not. Also, p. 865 prints the space without (−∞), while pp. 845–846 have it.

Impact: the application is cuspidal, so Theorems 8.13, 6.17 and 9.1 are not affected. The alternative fix above also appears to prove Theorem 8.22 as literally stated for genuine forms. So the result stands, but the written proof has an unhandled case. The affects value "the proof" is right.

A separate slip in the same passage: the display a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) is valid only when j = 2. For j > 2 its right-hand side is ρ(pI)a(F,P) = 0. The fact actually needed, a(F,P) ≠ 0, follows instead from a(ZF,Q) = ρ(M_P)a(F,P) = β·a(F,Q) ≠ 0. The printed text matches the page images of pp. 873–874 and is identical in arXiv v1. The defence fails:

1. Degenerate forms are included. §8.2 (p. 856) takes the index set 𝒳 to be all positive semidefinite Q.
2. "Siegel modular q-expansion" occurs only in Theorem 8.22 and is never defined. It must mean the q-expansion of a genuine form, since the proof then uses Theorem 8.10 and Lemma 8.15. Nothing in the statement makes F cuspidal. The spaces M and N (p. 867) and the display of Theorem 8.13 (p. 865) are printed without (−∞).
3. No reading of "minimal discriminant" rescues the step:
   - Minimal |d|: this is 0 whenever some degenerate p-primitive Q has a(F,Q) ≠ 0.
   - Minimal v_p(d), or minimal nonzero |d|: the case where every p-primitive Q in the support is degenerate is still left over.

I checked the failure by direct computation (S = {diag(1,p), [[p,b],[0,1]]}):
- Take p = 5, 7, 11 and Q = c·ℓℓ^T with p ∤ c.
- Exactly one M ∈ S gives an integral P = M^{-1}.Q, as Lemma 8.21 says.
- In every case P = p·R with d(R) = 0 = d(Q). For example, Q = diag(c,0) gives P = pQ.
- So a(F,R) ≠ 0 does not contradict minimality.
- For Q = diag(c,0) the relations reduce to β·a(F,Q) = α·ρ(diag(1,p))·a(F,Q). In weight (2,2) with F0 = 0 this reads (β − α)·a(F,Q) = 0. That is no contradiction unless α ≠ β, and α ≠ β is not among the hypotheses of Theorem 8.22.

The Q = 0 subcase is also not addressed: "a p-primitive Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0" need not exist if only a(F,0) ≠ 0. It is excluded anyway:
- In weight (2,2) with F0 = 0: a(ZF,0) = (p+1)·a(F,0) ≡ a(F,0), so (β − 1)·a(F,0) = 0 and a(F,0) = 0.
- In weight (j,2): a(F,0) is Γ̄-invariant in Sym^{j−2}. That representation is irreducible and nontrivial for SL2(F_p), and Γ̄ surjects onto SL2(F_p) (proof of Theorem 8.11). So a(F,0) = 0.

Consequences. The step's only output is "a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q with p ∤ D" (p. 874).
- §8.8, weight (2,2), does not use it. That argument treats every D directly: (D/p) = −1 is killed by β² ≠ 1, then Θ(F − X2F) = 0, Theorem 8.10 applies, and Lemma 8.15 finishes.
- §8.9 uses it only to meet the hypothesis of Proposition 8.25 (recap on p. 876; "Combining Proposition 8.25 with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11", p. 877). If no Q with p ∤ det Q carries a nonzero coefficient, then θ1F = 0 trivially and Theorem 8.11 still gives F = 0.

So Theorem 8.22 holds as stated for genuine forms, and Theorems 8.13, 6.17 and the main results are unaffected. In the application F is in any case cuspidal (§6.4, p. 845). Only the written proof has an unhandled case.

Remark 8.23 says a Θ-kernel argument would need a new theorem in nonparallel weight. Theorem 8.11 is in fact enough, because ΘF = 0 implies θ1F = 0.

A separate slip in the same passage: a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) holds only for j = 2. For j > 2 its right-hand side is ρ(pI)·a(F,P) ≡ 0. The fact actually needed, a(F,P) ≠ 0, follows instead from β·a(F,Q) = a(ZF,Q) = ρ(M_P)·a(F,P). - **Misprint** at §8.9, first paragraph (part of the proof of Theorem 8.22(1)), p. 874. The source says `8.9. The case σ = (j,2) with j ≥ 4 / We may assume that a(F,Q) ≠ 0, where Q is p-primitive and D = d(Q) is nonzero. If (D/p) = −1, then a(ZF,Q) = 0, contradicting the nonvanishing of a(F,Q) and the identity ZF = βZ. Hence we may assume that (D/p) = 1.`; it should be `"the identity ZF = βZ" should read "the identity ZF = βF". Optionally, "D = d(Q) is nonzero" can be clarified to "D = d(Q) is nonzero mod p (prime to p)". That second change only tidies loose wording; it is not a misprint.`. I rendered p. 874 at 130 dpi and read the page image. The quotation above is exact. The phrase 'ZF = βZ' makes no sense as printed: an operator is set equal to a scalar times an operator, applied to nothing. The argument needs the eigen-identity ZF = βF, which is a hypothesis of Theorem 8.22(1) (p. 873: 'suppose that UF = αF and ZF = βF for some α, β with αβ(β²−1) ≠ 0'). The proof then says 'thus have the equalities UF = αF, ZF = βF.'

I redid the argument. Page 872 gives a(ZF,Q) = Σ_{[P]∈F(Q)} ρ(M_P) a(F,P). Lemma 8.21(1) says that when Q is p-primitive with (D/p) = −1, F([Q]) is empty, so a(ZF,Q) = 0. With ZF = βF this gives β·a(F,Q) = 0. Since β ≠ 0 (from αβ(β²−1) ≠ 0), we get a(F,Q) = 0, the stated contradiction. So the intended text is certainly βF.

On 'D is nonzero': the argument also has to rule out (D/p) = 0 before 'Hence (D/p) = 1'. That is supplied by the first part of the proof (p. 873: 'there exists a Q with det(Q) ≢ 0 mod p') and the recap on p. 874 ('a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q of discriminant D prime to p'). In this characteristic-p setting, 'nonzero' is naturally read as nonzero mod p. So this part is imprecise wording rather than a misprint, and the substance of this entry is the βZ → βF typo.

arXiv:1907.08691v1 (§8.9, p. 54 there) has the identical text: 'D = d(Q) is non-zero … the identity ZF = βZ.'

Effect on results: none. The intended step is correct and immediate from Lemma 8.21(1), the p. 872 identity and the hypothesis ZF = βF with β ≠ 0. Theorem 8.22, and through Lemma 8.17 Theorem 8.13 and the results that depend on it, are unaffected. The source says `If (D/p) = −1, then a(ZF,Q) = 0, contradicting the nonvanishing of a(F,Q) and the identity ZF = βZ.`; it should be `'... and the identity ZF = βF.'`. - **Misprint** at §8.9 (opening paragraph), p. 874; arXiv v1 §8.9, p. 54 has the same sentence verbatim. The source says `We may assume that a(F,Q) ≠ 0, where Q is p-primitive and D = d(Q) is nonzero. [...] Hence we may assume that (D/p) = 1. The action of Γ̄ ⊂ SL2(Z) on binary quadratic forms of discriminant D has a finite orbit which may be identified with a ray class group.`; it should be `'... has finitely many orbits, and the (finite) set of orbits may be identified with a ray class group.'`. Γ̄ is 'the congruence subgroup of SL2(Z) defined in [67]' (p. 857), so it is infinite. The forms here are positive semidefinite with D = r^2 − 4mn ≠ 0, so they are positive definite. The stabiliser in SL2(Z) of a positive definite form is finite (order at most 6), so every Γ̄-orbit is infinite. What is finite, and carries the class-group structure, is the set of Γ̄-orbits (classes). The next paragraph (p. 875) uses exactly that when it says the ray class group 'is partitioned by this process Q → {P,R} into a finite number of cyclic orbits'. The intended meaning is clear, so this is a wording slip. - **Misprint** at §8.8 (The case σ = (2,2)), first paragraph, p. 874. The source says `§8.8 (p. 874): "Let us now assume that σ = (2,2). The coefficient a(X_2F, Q) is equal to (D/p)a(F, R), where D = D_Q is the discriminant of Q. Hence, since ZF = βF + β^{-1}X_2F, we deduce that, if (D/p) = −1, then 0 = a(ZF,Q) = βa(F,Q) − β^{-1}a(F,Q) = (β − β^{-1})a(F,Q). Assuming that β^2 ≠ 1, we deduce that a(F,Q) = 0. It follows that the only Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 has D = det(Q) satisfying (D/p) = 0, 1. In particular, the form F − X_2F ∈ M lies in the kernel of Θ."`; it should be `Read "a(X_2F,Q) is equal to (D/p)a(F,Q)" and "has D = d(Q) (the discriminant r^2 − 4mn = −4det(Q)) satisfying (D/p) = 0, 1". The same mix-up of det and discriminant appears earlier in the paper. In Lemma 8.4 (p. 859), "(det(Q)/p)" should be "(−det(Q)/p)", which equals ((r^2 − 4mn)/p). In Definition 8.5 (p. 859), "D is the determinant of the quadratic form associated to Q" should say "discriminant", unless "determinant" is taken in Gauss's sense b^2 − ac.`. I checked the page images at 130 dpi and the printed text is as quoted above.

(1) a(F,R): nothing called R is defined in §8.8. Definition 8.5 (p. 859) gives a(X_2F,Q) = (D/p)a(F,Q) mod p. The next display also uses a(F,Q) on the right: a(ZF,Q) = βa(F,Q) + β^{-1}(D/p)a(F,Q). So "R" is a plain typo for "Q".

(2) det versus discriminant. By §8.2 (p. 856), Q = [[m, r/2],[r/2, n]], so det(Q) = mn − r^2/4. The paper itself writes "con(Q⊗Q^∨) = r^2 − 4mn = −4det(Q)" on p. 877, and defines d(Q) as the discriminant on p. 872. That gives (det Q/p) = (−1/p)(D/p), which is wrong for p ≡ 3 mod 4. Example: p = 3 and Q = I. Then x^2 + y^2 has no zeros in P^1(F_3), D = −4, (D/3) = −1, but (det Q/3) = +1. The paragraph defines D as the discriminant two lines earlier and relies on Lemma 8.21 (p. 872, stated for d(Q)) to get a(ZF,Q) = 0 when (D/p) = −1. So "D = det(Q)" contradicts its own definition.

I recomputed the Hecke symbol. The rank-one cosets B = λvv^T (λ ∈ F_p^*, v ∈ P^1(F_p)) contribute Σ_v Σ_λ e(λQ[v]/p) = p·#{zeros of Q in P^1(F_p)} − (p+1). This equals −1 + p((r^2−4mn)/p) when Q ≢ 0, and p^2 − 1 when Q ≡ 0. That matches the second expression in Lemma 8.4, so the symbol in X_2 really is the discriminant symbol. This confirms the correction and shows that the paper's first expression (det(Q)/p) is the same slip. One caveat: Definition 8.5 calls D "the determinant", so the §8.8 wording follows that loose usage. The usage is still wrong against p. 877.

arXiv 1907.08691v1 §8.8 has the same text: "is equal to (D/p)a(F, R), where D = D_Q is the discriminant of Q" and "the only Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 have D = det(Q) satisfying (D/p) = 0, 1". The only differences are "have" for "has" and "that" for "then". Definition 8.5 and Lemma 8.4 read the same in v1 as well. - **Misprint** at §8.8 (the case σ = (2,2)), p. 874. arXiv v1 has the same text ('have D = det(Q) satisfying (D/p) = 0, 1').. The source says `The coefficient a(X_2F, Q) is equal to (D/p)a(F,R), where D = D_Q is the discriminant of Q. ... Assuming that β^2 ≠ 1, we deduce that a(F,Q) = 0. It follows that the only Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 has D = det(Q) satisfying (D/p) = 0, 1.`; it should be `'... has D = D_Q = d(Q) (the discriminant r^2 − 4mn = −4 det(Q)) satisfying (D/p) = 0, 1.'`. The paper's own convention is Q = [[m, r/2],[r/2, n]] (p. 856), with det(Q) = mn − r^2/4. Page 877 states explicitly 'con(Q ⊗ Q^∨) = r^2 − 4mn = −4 det(Q)'. So (det(Q)/p) = (−1/p)(d(Q)/p), which differs from (d(Q)/p) when p ≡ 3 mod 4. The vanishing just derived comes from two facts, both governed by the discriminant: F(Q) is empty when (d(Q)/p) = −1 (Lemma 8.21, where D = d(Q)), and a(X_2F,Q) = (D_Q/p)a(F,Q). The same paragraph defines D = D_Q as the discriminant two lines earlier. So 'D = det(Q)' contradicts the paragraph's own D. With det(Q) literally, the claim would say (det(Q)/p) ∈ {0, −1} for p ≡ 3 mod 4, so the printed statement is false for those p. The next step uses only the discriminant reading: F − X_2F is supported on Q with (D_Q/p) = 0, i.e. det(Q) ≡ 0 mod p, so Θ(F − X_2F) = 0. Definition 8.5 also calls D 'the determinant', and Lemma 8.4 equates (det(Q)/p) with ((r^2−4mn)/p). Those are the same slip at other places and do not change this locator.
