- **Error** at §8.8 "The case σ = (2,2)", p. 874. This is the (2,2) case of the proof of Theorem 8.22(2), which gives Theorem 8.13 by the sentence before Theorem 8.22 on p. 873. arXiv v1: §8.8, p. 53. (it affects the proof). The source says `"It follows that the only Q with a(F, Q) ≠ 0 has D = det(Q) satisfying (D/p) = 0, 1. In particular, the form F − X_2F ∈ M lies in the kernel of Θ. Yet this implies that F − X_2F is trivial by Theorem 8.10. But this implies that Z_2F = Z_2X_2F = 0, contradicting the injectivity of Z_2 : M → N in Lemma 8.15." (checked against the rendered image of p. 874. arXiv:1907.08691v1, §8.8, p. 53, has the same text with small wording changes: "F − X_2F trivial by Theorem 8.10", "and this contradicts the injectivity".)`; it should be `Replace "F − X₂F ∈ M" by the statement that F − X₂F is (the q-expansion of) a section of weight (p+1, p+1), and apply Theorem 8.10 with k = p+1. The step works as follows. 1. Lemma 8.12 in weight (2,2) gives X₂F = Q₂F − Z₂F. Here Q₂F ∈ M, and Z₂F is the q-expansion of Q₂(hF) ∈ H⁰(X₁(Q), ω(p+1,p+1)_k), where h is the Hasse invariant: in weight (p+1,p+1) ≠ (2,2), Lemma 8.12 gives Q₂ ≡ Z₂, and Lemma 8.8 gives the action. 2. So F − X₂F is the q-expansion of hF − h·Q₂F + Q₂(hF), a section of weight (p+1,p+1). When A = h this is simply "F − X₂F ∈ N". 3. The coefficients of F − X₂F vanish unless det(Q) ≡ 0 mod p, so Θ(F − X₂F) = 0. 4. Theorem 8.10 applies with k = p+1, since p ∤ (p+1)(2p+1). It gives F = X₂F. Then Z₂F = Z₂X₂F = 0 by Lemma 8.6, which contradicts Lemma 8.15 as printed. 5. The contradiction can also be reached without Lemma 8.15. Formally UX₂ ≡ 0, since a(UX₂F, Q) = p·a(F, pQ). So F = X₂F gives 0 = UF = αF_α, hence F = F₀ = (αβ)⁻¹X₂F = (αβ)⁻¹F, which is impossible because αβ ≠ 1. Replacing M by N alone is not a minimal correction. Theorem 8.13 allows A = h^s for any s ≥ 1, and then N has weight 2 + s(p−1), which is beyond the range of Theorem 8.10 when s ≥ 2. So N has to be taken with A = h, or equivalently one uses the weight-(p+1) section in step 2. Alternatively, reduce Theorem 8.13 to s = 1. Multiplication by h^{s−1} is injective and is the identity on q-expansions, and it commutes with U, with Q₂ = Z₂ and with the Hecke operators away from p. Hence it commutes with π_β, so π_β∘h^s = h^{s−1}∘(π_β∘h).`. Rendered pages checked: p. 874, and for context p. 859, 861, 864, 865, 867 and 868.

1. F ∈ M. The F of Lemma 8.17(2) is obtained inside M by applying Q_2 − αβ and T − α − β. The last sentence of §8.8 uses "injectivity of Z_2 : M → N", which needs F ∈ M.

2. For nonzero F ∈ M, X_2F is never in M. Suppose X_2F ∈ M.
- Z_2X_2 = 0 over k (Lemma 8.6), so Z_2(X_2F) = 0.
- The map M → Z_2M is injective (Lemma 8.15), so X_2F = 0.
- Then a(F,Q) = 0 whenever Q is p-primitive with (D/p) ≠ 0. So ΘF = 0 coefficient by coefficient, and Theorem 8.10 with k = 2 gives F = 0.
So under the proof's standing assumption F ≠ 0, the claim "F − X_2F ∈ M" is false, not just unjustified. Nothing in §8.8 supports it. The only place the paper puts X_2F in M is the proof of Lemma 8.15, under the opposite hypothesis Z_2F = 0.

3. The paper itself expects this. Lemma 8.17(2) writes F = F_α + F_0 with X_2F = αβF_0 ∈ N_0, a part of N (not M) where U is nilpotent. Remark 8.18 says the "tripled" space in weight (p+1, p+1) "contains nonzero elements in the kernel of Z_2".

4. The correction works, and I redid the computations myself:
- Membership: X_2F = Q_2F − Z_2F ∈ N. Lemma 8.12's computation gives Q_2 ≡ p^{j−2}X_2 + Z_2 ≡ Z_2 mod p in weight (p+1, p+1).
- Theorem 8.10 hypotheses: "p + 1 ≥ k, p ∤ k(2k−1) — so in particular k = 2 and k = p+1 are admissible". Theorem 8.10 is used only here, and Remark 8.23 mentions only an analogue of it. This supports the reading that k = p+1 was meant.
- Kernel of Θ: the vanishing of Θ(F − X_2F) holds under the paper's own conventions for (D/p) and det. When p | D we have det ≡ 0, since det = (4mn − r²)/4.
- General powers: the reduction from h^s to h in the last paragraph of the correction is valid. Steps 1–2 of the correction give a more direct alternative. The example Θ(G^p) = 0 in weight (2p, 2p) shows the extra step is needed for s ≥ 2: Theorem 8.10 fails outside k ≤ p+1.

5. The statement of Theorem 8.13 is still true for all nontrivial powers A. Downstream results that depend on it (Theorem 6.17 and the main theorems) are unaffected once the proof is repaired as above. So only the proof is affected.

6. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text on p. 53. Theorem 8.10 there also lists k = 2 and k = p+1 as admissible.

Unrelated misprint in the same paragraph: "(D/p)a(F, R)" should be "(D/p)a(F, Q)". Rendered and read: pp. 859–874 and v1 p. 53.

DEFENCE ATTEMPTS, all of which fail.

(i) X₂ is not an operator on M. Definition 8.5 (p. 859) defines X₂ only as a formal operator on q-expansions. Mod p it is the twist by (D/p) ≡ (−4det Q)^{(p−1)/2}, so it agrees with ±Θ^{(p−1)/2}, which raises the weight. On M only Q₂ = Z₂ + X₂ acts (p. 867: "the operator Q₂ acts on M either as Z₂ or as Z₂ + X₂"). The one place the paper puts X₂F in M is the proof of Lemma 8.15, under the opposite hypothesis Z₂F = 0. In the proof of Lemma 8.17(2) (p. 870) the paper itself writes X₂F = (0, 0, αβF₀) ∈ N₀ ⊂ N, not in M.

(ii) The claim cannot be justified, and the principle it would need is false. Take any F ∈ M.
- If X₂F ∈ M, then Z₂X₂F = 0 by Lemma 8.6, so X₂F = 0 by the injectivity of Z₂ on M (Lemma 8.15).
- But at this point the proof has F with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q whose discriminant is prime to p. Since (D/p) = −1 was just excluded, (D/p) = 1, so a(X₂F,Q) = a(F,Q) ≠ 0.
- So "F − X₂F ∈ M" is equivalent to the contradiction the proof is looking for. It cannot be obtained without already finishing the proof. (Because this is a proof by contradiction, no concrete false instance exists, but the inference fails.)
- Moreover, X₂(M) ⊂ M would force X₂M = 0. Every F ∈ M would then be supported on det ≡ 0, so ΘF = 0, so F = 0 by Theorem 8.10 with k = 2. Hence X₂ preserves M only when M = 0, and M ≠ 0 here.

(iii) Reading "M" as a slip for "N" (the paper views M ⊂ N "by abuse of notation", p. 867) works only when N has weight ≤ p+1, that is when A = h. Theorem 8.10's remark "so in particular k = 2 and k = p+1 are admissible" fits that intent. But Theorem 8.13 allows any nontrivial power, and Theorem 6.17 (pp. 845–846) invokes it with a power of weight t = r·p^{m−1}(p−1). In weight (2p, 2p), Θ is not injective: Θ(G^p) = 0 for G of weight (2,2), since det(pQ) ≡ 0. So an extra step is needed, and the text is not a pure misprint. Since it is not a slip with a clear intended meaning, I class it as an error (a step that fails) rather than a gap; "gap" would also be defensible.

THE REPAIR, checked step by step.
- Lemma 8.12 gives Q₂ ≡ Z₂ + X₂ in weight (2,2), and Q₂ ≡ Z₂ in weight (p+1,p+1), where the p-power terms vanish mod p.
- a(F − X₂F, Q) = 0 when (D/p) = 1 (the two coefficients cancel) and when (D/p) = −1 (a(F,Q) = 0 was just shown).
- D = −4·det, so (D/p) = 0 exactly when det ≡ 0. Hence Θ(F − X₂F) = 0.
- Theorem 8.10 with k = p+1 gives F = X₂F, and the printed ending then goes through.

WHERE IT IS USED. §8.8 is the only place Theorem 8.10 is used; Remark 8.23 refers only to an analogue of it. Through Lemma 8.17(2), §8.8 gives Theorem 8.13 in weight (2,2). Theorem 8.13 feeds Theorem 6.17, which feeds §9 (the weight (2,2) modularity lifting, including the abelian-surface application). With the repair, every stated result stays true.

Both routes in the correction are valid: taking A = h (reducing A^s to A as in its last paragraph), so that F − X₂F ∈ N and Theorem 8.10 applies with k = p+1; and the direct route of steps 1–4 through a section of weight (p+1, p+1).

(a) The defence. Theorem 8.22 comes right after "In light of Lemma 8.17, to prove Theorem 8.13, it suffices to prove the following." The §8.8 proof writes "F − X_2F ∈ M", so it treats F as an element of the §8.6 space M. The paper ends with "this completes the proof of Theorem 8.13". In that use, F comes from Lemma 8.17(2). That F lies in M: the proof starts with F ∈ M and only applies Q_2 − αβ and T − α − β, both of which preserve M. And α and β are as in Theorem 8.13. So Lemma 8.15's injectivity of M → Z_2M applies, and the chain Theorem 8.13 → Theorem 6.17 → main theorems is not affected by this step. (Other steps in the same paragraph are recorded as sourceIssues E121.)

(b) Why it is still a gap. Theorem 8.22(2) is stated for any Siegel modular q-expansion with those identities, with α and β chosen afresh subject only to αβ(β²−1)(α²β²−1) ≠ 0. Lemma 8.15 needs α and β "as in Theorem 8.13", which also requires α ≠ β, α² ≠ 1 and the Galois setting, and it needs F in the localized (α,β)-part M, where "the only generalized eigenvalue of Q_2 is αβ" (p. 868). Neither is a hypothesis of Theorem 8.22(2). The factor α²β² − 1 in 8.22(2) matches the remark on p. 868 that Lemma 8.15 is "the point … which uses (αβ)² ≠ 1". So the authors were relying on Lemma 8.15's argument, but the proof cites the lemma, and the lemma's hypotheses do not hold for a general F.

(c) The repair works; I checked it from the printed formulas.
- Page 859 gives U_2 = −1 + pX_2, a(X_2F,Q) ≡ (D/p)a(F,Q) mod p, and Z_2 = UZ.
- Lemma 8.6 gives Z_2X_2 = 0.
- From these, UX_2 ≡ 0 and X_2³ ≡ X_2.
- Then UF_0 = 0 and Z_2F = αβF_α, which gives (Z_2 + X_2)F = αβF.
- If Z_2F = 0, then F = F_0 and X_2F = αβF, which forces F = 0 since αβ ≠ ±1.
So Theorem 8.22(2) is true as stated, given the rest of its proof. Only the justification of this step is missing for the stated generality.

(d) affects. The printed proof of the stated Theorem 8.22(2) cites a lemma outside its hypotheses, so the gap affects the proof. The stated results, 8.22(2) and 8.13, survive. "nothing" would also be defensible, since the paper's only use of the passage (Theorem 8.13) is covered by Lemma 8.15 as cited.

- **Misprint** at §8.9, paragraph before Lemma 8.24, p. 875; arXiv v1 p. 54 has the same text ('neighbours'). The source says `on which this operation takes a binary quadratic form to its two nearest neighbors (if the orbit has fewer than two elements, this pair of neighbors may have multiplicity).`; it should be `'(if the orbit has at most two elements, this pair of neighbors may have multiplicity)', i.e. 'fewer than three'`. Each class has exactly two neighbours counted with multiplicity (Lemma 8.21(3)), and the relation is symmetric (Lemma 8.20). So each orbit is a cycle, and a class's two neighbours are its two cyclic neighbours. In a cycle of size 1 both neighbours are Q itself; the proof of Lemma 8.21 gives the example of class number 1. In a cycle of size 2, {Q,P}, both neighbours of Q are P. In class-group terms, the neighbours of c are c[𝔭] and c[𝔭]^{-1}, and these coincide when [𝔭] has order 2. So the pair has multiplicity exactly when s ≤ 2. The printed condition 'fewer than two' leaves out s = 2. The printed sentence is not false as it stands (it says 'may'), but its threshold is off by one. The later argument (Lemma 8.24) works for every s, so nothing depends on this. DEFENCE. Two parts of the missing step are routine.
- The Q in the proof is generic. Lemma 8.24 is stated for any Q with (D/p) = 1, and the proof never uses the Q from the hypothesis. So the step from one Q to all Q with (D/p) = +1 can be read charitably.
- The (D/p) = −1 case is in the recap paragraph just before the proposition: a(ZF,Q) = 0, which with ZF = βF gives a(F,Q) = 0.
- With the paper's own printed Prop. 8.9(2), θ₁ Σ a_Q q^Q = Σ det(Q)con(a_Q ⊗ Q) q^Q, the p | d(Q) coefficients would also vanish trivially. So under the paper's printed conventions this would be only a terse omission.

WHY THE DEFENCE FAILS. The det(Q) factor is wrong.
- In Yamauchi (arXiv:1410.7894v5, the cited [75]; v8 is the same), θ₁ = H_{p−1}·θ̃₁, where θ̃₁ is a projection of KS^{-1}∘∇. The q-expansion there is A_G(T) = (1/N)A_f(T) ⊗ T, which is linear in T. Only Θ carries det(T).
- The weight count agrees: first order gives +(0,2), and the Hasse invariant gives +(p−1,p−1).
- The paper's own display on p. 876 also has no det(Q).
- This is recorded as sourceIssues E95.

With the correct formula, a(θ₁F,Q) = con(a(F,Q) ⊗ Q) does not vanish automatically when p | d(Q). For example, con(Y^{j−2} ⊗ X²) = 2(j−2)(j−3)Y^{j−4}, and d(X²) = 0. Nothing in the paper shows these coefficients vanish.
- Theorem 8.22's opening argument only finds some Q with p ∤ D and a(F,Q) ≠ 0.
- Even a(F,Q) itself need not vanish for p-primitive Q with p | D, when F(Q) = {[pR]}.

So the final "θ₁F = 0" is asserted without proof for these Q. That is a genuine gap, and it cannot be closed from the printed text.

THE FIX IS SOUND. The identity con(Sym^{j−2}[M]x ⊗ p^{-1}MPM^T) = p·Sym^{j−4}[M]con(x ⊗ P), for det M = p, is equivariance of the second transvectant: Sym^a ⊗ Sym^2 → Sym^{a−2} ⊗ det². I checked it by direct computation in exact rational arithmetic: 1500 random trials with p ∈ {5, 7, 11, 13}, 0 mismatches. The contraction reproduces the paper's normalisation (4, −2) ∝ (2, −1). The paper's own claim that con(Sym^{j−2}[A]x ⊗ Q^∨) = 0 when AQA^t = p^sQ is a special case of this identity (it gives a factor p^s).

USE LATER. Prop. 8.25 is used only in the last sentence of §8.9: combined with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11 (injectivity of θ₁), it gives the contradiction that proves Theorem 8.22(1), and so Theorem 8.13. The statement of Prop. 8.25 is still true after the repair, so nothing downstream changes. The proof as written, however, does not establish θ₁F = 0.

This issue overlaps with the consequence recorded in sourceIssues E95; case (iii) cannot rest on the det(Q) factor. - **Misprint** at §8.9, proof of Proposition 8.25, second display on p. 877; arXiv:1907.08691v1, p. 55. The source says `Similarly, the contraction mapping on Sym^{j−2} ⊗ Sym^2 for p > j − 2 satisfies con(f_1^i f_2^{j−2−i} e_1^k e_2^{2−k}) = 0 unless 2 ≤ i + k ≤ j − 4. (Checked on the page image, p. 877 at 300 dpi. arXiv:1907.08691v1, p. 55, prints the same text: "con(f_1^i f_2^{j−2−i} e_1^k e_2^{2−k}) = 0 unless 2 ≤ i + k ≤ j − 4.")`; it should be `"unless 2 ≤ i + k ≤ j − 2". Equivalently, the image f_1^{i+k−2} f_2^{j−2−i−k} lies in Sym^{j−4}, so 0 ≤ i+k−2 ≤ j−4. For p > j−2 the contraction is in fact nonzero exactly when 2 ≤ i + k ≤ j − 2.`. The page fixes the convention just before this display (p. 876 to p. 877). On Sym^2 ⊗ Sym^2, con sends e_1^2 f_2^2 and e_2^2 f_1^2 to −2, sends e_1 f_1 e_2 f_2 to 1, and kills all other monomials. So e_1 pairs with f_2 and e_2 pairs with f_1.

Contracting e_1^k e_2^{2−k} against f_1^i f_2^{j−2−i} therefore uses k copies of f_2 and 2−k copies of f_1, leaving f_1^{i+k−2} f_2^{j−2−i−k}. This needs i+k ≥ 2 and i+k ≤ j−2. The scalar is a product of falling factorials of i and j−2−i, which is a unit when p > j−2.

I checked this by direct computation. I used the GL2-equivariant second transvectant φ_xx ψ_yy − 2 φ_xy ψ_xy + φ_yy ψ_xx, with x = f_1, y = f_2 and e_1 ↦ x, e_2 ↦ y in the ψ slot:
- It reproduces the paper's Sym^2 ⊗ Sym^2 values (4, 4, −2) ∝ (−2, −2, 1), and con(Q ⊗ Q^∨) = 8mn − 2r² ∝ r² − 4mn.
- For j = 4, …, 9 the set of i+k with nonzero contraction is exactly {2, …, j−2}. The printed range {2, …, j−4} is empty for j = 4, 5 and too small for every j.

The printed bound also contradicts the paper's own text in two places:
- For j = 4 it makes con identically zero on Sym^2 ⊗ Sym^2, against the displayed con(Q ⊗ Q^∨) = r² − 4mn = −4 det(Q) just above it.
- In case (1) the paper says "the only monomial which f_1^{j−2} contracts nontrivially with is e_2^2" (i = j−2, k = 0, so i+k = j−2). The printed bound would make that contraction zero.

This is a slip in the upper bound (j−4, the degree of the target Sym, written in place of j−2), so it is a misprint, not an error in the argument.

Effect: none. The proof only needs con(f_1^{j−2} ⊗ e_1^k e_2^{2−k}) = 0 for k = 1, 2, because Q^∨ ≡ m e_1^2 + r e_1 e_2 mod p. Here i+k = j−1 or j, both greater than j−2, so the corrected bound gives exactly this. Case (1) also states the needed fact directly and correctly, and case (2) reduces to case (1). Nothing else cites the display: after the proof, Proposition 8.25 is only combined with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11 to finish Theorem 8.13, and it does not rely on this display. This correction is right and minimal. - **Error** at §9, proof of Theorem 9.1, verification of condition (a) of Proposition 3.3, p. 879. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text (p. 57 of v1, same proof).. The source says `(a) The image of S_N in End_O(H_N) is contained in the image of R_∞ because under the Galois representation r_{Q_N} of Theorem 6.17, the image of an element σ ∈ I_x, for x a prime in Q_N, is conjugate to a matrix of the form diag(1, 1, ⟨u⟩, ⟨u⟩) where Art_x(u) = σ. This follows from [64, Corollary 3].`; it should be `Replace the matrix with the shape for the twisted representation: r_{Q_N}(σ) is conjugate to diag(χ(σ), χ(σ), χ(σ)^{-1}, χ(σ)^{-1}), where χ is the character by which I_x acts on V_1 (Definition 4.6(5)) and χ(σ)^{-2} = ⟨u⟩. Equivalently, the matrix is diag(⟨u⟩^{-1/2}, ⟨u⟩^{-1/2}, ⟨u⟩^{1/2}, ⟨u⟩^{1/2}), with ⟨u⟩^{1/2} = ⟨u^{1/2}⟩ the unique square root in the odd p-group Δ. So ⟨u⟩ = χ(σ)^{-2} still lies in the image of R_{Q_N}, and step (a) goes through. The printed diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩) is correct only for the untwisted representation r'_m of Theorem 6.13 and of the proof of Theorem 6.17, before the twist by the inverse square root of ψ_Q̃. The exponent's sign depends on how Art_x and [64] are normalised, but the conclusion does not.`. I rendered p. 879, 815, 842, 845 and 846. Theorem 6.17 (p. 845) says r_Q is "a minimal deformation of r̄ outside Q". By Definition 4.6(1) (p. 815) its similitude is ε^{-(a-1)}, which is unramified at x ∈ Q_N (x ≠ p). So for σ ∈ I_x, ν(r_{Q_N}(σ)) = 1 and det r_{Q_N}(σ) = ν(σ)^2 = 1. But det diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩) = ⟨u⟩^2, and conjugation does not change the determinant. So the printed claim forces ⟨u⟩^2 = 1, and hence ⟨u⟩ = 1 because Δ has odd order. The same thing follows from Definition 4.6(5): inertia acts on V1 by a character and on V2 by its inverse, so the shape diag(1,1,c,c) needs c = 1.

The diamond operators are not trivial in general, and the paper's own results show this. ⟨u⟩ is defined on pp. 833–834 as the deck transformation of X_1(Q) → X_0(Q) and lies in T_σ(Q) (Definition 5.13(2)). Suppose every ⟨u⟩ with u from the inertia at the primes of Q_N were 1. These inertia images generate Δ, so Δ would act trivially on H_N, and H_N ≅ (H_N)_Δ ≅ H ≠ 0. For S = O[Δ] and an S-module M with trivial Δ-action, the base-change five-term sequence gives 0 → M⊗Tor_1^S(O,k) → Tor_1^S(M,k) → Tor_1^O(M,k) → 0, with Tor_1^S(O,k) = I/m_S I ≅ k^q. So d_S(M) ≤ r(1−q), where r = dim_k M/ϖM ≥ 1. That is negative for q ≥ 2 and contradicts Theorem 7.11 (H_N balanced), which step (c) uses.

The paper itself says the untwisted Hecke representation has ramified similitude: Theorem 6.13(1),(4) on p. 842 gives ν∘r = χ_{μ,0}ε^{-w}, and only the twist by √χ_{μ,0} satisfies Definition 4.6(2)–(5). The proof of Theorem 6.17 (p. 846) twists r'_m by the inverse square root of χ_Q. The [64, Cor. 3] shape diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩), with similitude ⟨u⟩, is therefore that of the untwisted representation. As printed, the statement is false for r_{Q_N} whenever ⟨u⟩ ≠ 1.

The step's conclusion survives. The universal deformation's inertial scalar χ^univ(σ) on V1 maps to ⟨u⟩^{-1/2}, so ⟨u⟩ = (χ^univ(σ))^{-2} is in the image of R_{Q_N}. Also ⟨u⟩−1 = (χ^{-1}−1)(χ^{-1}+1) is in the image of ker(R_{Q_N} → R^min), since minimal deformations are unramified at x. So this is a false intermediate statement with a routine fix; the mathematics as intended is right. It sits on the misprint/error borderline: the paper spells out the twist elsewhere (Theorem 6.13(4), proof of 6.17), but the printed claim about r_{Q_N} is literally false, so I classify it as an error. I tried to defend the printed text and could not.

(1) Theorem 6.17, p. 845, says r_Q is 'a minimal deformation of r̄ outside Q'. Definition 4.6(1), p. 815, fixes the similitude ν∘r = ε^{-(a-1)}, which is unramified at x ∈ Q_N (x ≠ p). So ν(r_{Q_N}(σ)) = 1 for σ ∈ I_x.

(2) In the paper's symplectic form, the Siegel Levi is diag(A, λB) with B = S^t A^{-1} S (p. 820). So ⟨e1,e2⟩ and ⟨e3,e4⟩ are dual Lagrangians, and ν(diag(1,1,c,c)) = c. GSp4-conjugation preserves ν, so the printed claim forces ⟨u⟩ = 1. Even if we allow conjugation in GL4, taking determinants gives ⟨u⟩^2 = ν(r(σ))^2 = 1. Since ⟨u⟩ has odd p-power order (Δ ≅ (Z/p^N)^q), again ⟨u⟩ = 1. So the printed claim would make every diamond operator act trivially on H_N.

(3) That is false in the relevant situation. Condition (c), from Theorem 7.11, says H_N is balanced over S_N = O[Δ]. For a nonzero module with trivial Δ-action and q ≥ 2 the defect is negative: for example, M = O has Tor_0 of dimension 1 and Tor_1 of dimension q. So the diamond operators cannot all act trivially.

(4) The paper's own text shows where the printed shape comes from. Theorem 6.13(4), p. 842, says the Hecke-algebra representation satisfies Definition 4.6(2)–(5) only 'after twisting by the unique square-root of χ_{μ,0}'. The proof of Theorem 6.17, p. 846, then twists r'_m by the inverse of a square root of ψ_Q̃, where ν(r'_m) = ε^{-(a-1)}ψ_Q̃. On I_x the central character is the diamond character: the centre z ∈ Z_x^× maps to λ = z under Π(x)/Π(x)^+ ≅ (Z/x)^× (p. 821, ⟨u⟩ as on p. 833). So the untwisted r'_m(σ) ~ diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩), as [64, Cor. 3] gives. This matches a dual-torus check: a tamely ramified character on the Klingen λ gives inertia eigenvalues 1,1,χ,χ on two Lagrangian planes. Twisting by θ^{-1}, where θ^2 = ψ_Q̃ and θ(σ)^2 = ⟨u⟩, gives r_{Q_N}(σ) ~ diag(θ^{-1},θ^{-1},θ,θ). This satisfies Definition 4.6(5) and has similitude 1. The printed statement drops this twist.

No charitable reading works. ⟨u⟩ is the diamond operator (p. 833). 'r_{Q_N} of Theorem 6.17' is the twisted, fixed-similitude representation, because the classifying map R_{Q_N} → T is defined from it.

Consequences: step (a) is used only to apply Proposition 3.3 in the proof of Theorem 9.1, and nothing else repeats the claim. With the correction, ⟨u⟩ = χ(σ)^{-2}. Here χ(σ) ∈ R_{Q_N} is the scalar by which σ acts on the canonical summand V_1 of the universal deformation. So the image of S_N still lies in the image of R_∞. The second half of Proposition 3.3(a), which the paper does not address, also holds: χ(σ)^{-2} − 1 maps to 0 in R^min, since minimal deformations are unramified at x. So Theorem 9.1 and everything downstream stand. The correction above is right and minimal.

It is an error rather than a misprint because the printed statement is false and the intended twisted shape is not obvious from the text. I set affects = nothing because the argument as intended survives with a one-line repair. A strict reviewer could argue for 'the proof', since the stated justification of (a) is false as written.

arXiv v1 (p. 57) has the identical text.

I could not consult [64] (Sorensen, Doc. Math. 15). The finding does not depend on it: it follows from the paper's own Definition 4.6(1),(5), Theorem 6.13(4) and the proof of Theorem 6.17. (a) The image of S_N in End_O(H_N) is contained in the image of R_∞ because under the Galois representation r_{Q_N} of Theorem 6.17, the image of an element σ ∈ I_x, for x a prime in Q_N, is conjugate to a matrix of the form diag(1, 1, ⟨u⟩, ⟨u⟩) where Art_x(u) = σ. By Definition 4.6(2) with Q = ∅, every minimal deformation is therefore unramified at x. So for σ ∈ I_x, the entries of r^univ_{Q_N}(σ) − 1 lie in ker(R_{Q_N} → R^min). That ideal does not change under conjugation, so by the shape above it contains ⟨u⟩ − 1. Now R_∞ ↠ R_{Q_N} is surjective, ker(φ_N) is the preimage of ker(R_{Q_N} → R^min), and the first half of (a) holds. Hence the image of the augmentation ideal of S_N (generated by the [u] − 1) lies in the image of ker(φ_N)." This correction is right and minimal. Note that the matrix entries of r_{Q_N}(σ) − 1 lie in T, not in R_{Q_N}. The kernel statement belongs to the corresponding entries of the universal representation (or to their ideal). Also, whether one uses the printed shape diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩) or the shape after the square-root twist in the proof of Thm 6.17, diag(⟨u⟩^{-1/2},⟨u⟩^{-1/2},⟨u⟩^{1/2},⟨u⟩^{1/2}), the ideal still contains ⟨u⟩ − 1, because ⟨u⟩ − 1 = (⟨u⟩^{1/2} − 1)(⟨u⟩^{1/2} + 1).`. 1. The printed text is confirmed on the rendered pages 812 and 879. Prop. 3.3(a) has two clauses. The second, "and moreover ... augmentation ideal ... image of ker(φ_N)", is needed: in the cited proof ([16, Prop. 2.3] = CG18 Prop. 2.3), it gives ı(𝔞) ⊂ ker(φ_∞) and hence R_∞/ı(𝔞)R_∞ ≅ R. Item (a) of the proof on p. 879 repeats only the first clause, nearly word for word ("The image of S_N ... is contained in the image of R_∞ because ..."), then moves on to (b). Nowhere in the paper is the second clause verified. ker(φ_N) appears only in Prop. 3.3. No statement that R_{Q_N} is an O[Δ_{Q_N}]-algebra with R_{Q_N}/𝔞 = R^min appears in §4 or anywhere else (R_Q is mentioned only on pp. 816–818 and in §9). The analogous proof in CG18 (Thm 3.26, Invent. Math. p. 339–340) does this explicitly: "The second part of condition 5a is a consequence of the following: ... χ_{α_x} ⊕ χ_{β_x} ... we obtain ... a map O[Δ_{Q_N}] → R_{Q_N}. The quotient of R_{Q_N} by the image of the augmentation ideal of O[Δ_{Q_N}] is just R^min." So the omission here is a real missing step, not a convention the authors follow. It is a gap: the proof asserts that the conditions of Prop. 3.3 hold without an argument for part of one.
2. I redid the missing step, and it is routine. Take x ∈ Q_N. Prop. 4.10(3) makes r̄ unramified at x with distinct Frobenius eigenvalues. Def. 4.6(5) gives a canonical splitting V_1 ⊕ V_2 of the universal deformation and a character χ_x : I_x → R_{Q_N}^× on V_1. Def. 4.6(2) with Q = ∅ makes every minimal deformation unramified at x. So χ_x(σ) − 1 ∈ ker(R_{Q_N} → R^min). Its image in End(H_N) generates, together with that of R_∞, the ideal containing ⟨u⟩ − 1. Since ker(φ_N) is an ideal and the first clause holds, the image of the whole augmentation ideal follows.
3. A side point, separate from this gap, but it bears on the correction's wording. The printed shape diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩) has similitude ⟨u⟩, using the pairing 1↔4, 2↔3 of the p-adic shape on pp. 812 and 815. It is the shape of the untwisted r'_m in the proof of Theorem 6.17 (p. 846: "ν(r'_m) = ε^{-(a-1)}χ_Q ... twist r'_m by the inverse of this square root"). The twisted r_{Q_N} of Theorem 6.17 has similitude ε^{-(a-1)}, which is unramified at x, and is conjugate on I_x to diag(⟨u⟩^{-1/2}, ⟨u⟩^{-1/2}, ⟨u⟩^{1/2}, ⟨u⟩^{1/2}), in line with Def. 4.6(1),(5). Both clauses of (a) still hold, because ⟨u⟩ has p-power order and p is odd. This is recorded separately as sourceIssues E129.
4. Scope: the missing clause is true, so Prop. 3.3 applies as the authors intend. Theorem 9.1, Theorem 1.1 and the other results deduced from it, and the appendix's use of them, all stand. Affects: nothing. Defence attempted; it fails. (1) Both halves of Prop. 3.3(a) are confirmed on the page images of p. 812 and 879. Item (a) of the proof restates only the first half ("contained in the image of R_∞ because ...") and goes on to (b). Nothing else in the paper supplies the second half. The word "augmentation" occurs only in Prop. 3.3 itself. Nowhere is R_{Q_N} made an O[Δ_{Q_N}]-algebra with R_{Q_N}/a = R^min: not in §4 (Def. 4.6, the text after Rem. 4.7, Prop. 4.10), not in item (4) of the proof, not in Thm 6.17. (2) The second half cannot be dropped. In the patching proof of the cited result ([16, Prop. 2.3] = CG18 Prop. 2.3), it is what gives ı(a) ⊂ ker φ_∞. Without it, the argument only shows that H is free over R_∞/aR_∞. That ring is the faithful quotient of R acting on H, i.e. T. So one would get only "H is free over T" and lose R^min = T, the main assertion of Thm 9.1 (the proof ends "H is a finite free R-module. Since the action of R on H factors through T, the conclusions ... follow"). The second half is also not a formal consequence of the first half together with (b): showing that R^min acts faithfully on H is exactly what is being proved. (3) The authors' own model proof checks it explicitly. CG18, proof of Thm 3.26, item (a): "The second part of condition 5a is a consequence of the following: ... χ_{α_x} ⊕ χ_{β_x} ... we obtain ... a map O[Δ_{Q_N}] → R_{Q_N}. The quotient of R_{Q_N} by the image of the augmentation ideal of O[Δ_{Q_N}] is just R^min." The omission here is therefore a missing step, not a convention of the authors. It is therefore a gap. (4) Charitable reading: the "because" clause (the shape of r_{Q_N} on I_x, from [64, Cor. 3]) together with Def. 4.6(2) does give the second half at once, by the argument in the correction. I checked that argument: ker φ_N is the preimage of ker(R_{Q_N}→R^min) under a surjection; the entry ideal is conjugation-invariant and the classifying map R_{Q_N} ↠ T is surjective; x ∈ Q_N lies outside S(r̄) ∪ {p} by Prop. 4.10(3) and x ≡ 1 mod p; and [δδ'] − 1 = [δ]([δ'] − 1) + ([δ] − 1), so the augmentation ideal is generated by the [u] − 1. So the gap is routine and true, but it is not stated. (5) Consequences: the passage is used only to apply Prop. 3.3 in the proof of Thm 9.1. From Thm 9.1 follow R^min = T, H free, and through it Theorem 1.1, its corollaries and the appendix. The missing clause holds, so all of these stand. Separate side issue, not part of this gap: the printed shape diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩) is the shape for the untwisted r'_m; after the twist in the proof of Thm 6.17 (p. 846) it becomes diag(⟨u⟩^{-1/2},⟨u⟩^{-1/2},⟨u⟩^{1/2},⟨u⟩^{1/2}). This affects neither half of (a). - **Gap** at §9, proof of Theorem 9.1, item (c), p. 880, applying Theorem 7.11, p. 853. H_N is defined on p. 879 and e_{α,β} on p. 845 (§6.4, before Theorem 6.17). (it affects the proof). The source says `(c) Finally, H_N is finite and balanced over S_N by Theorem 7.11.`; it should be `The proof needs its own argument that the (α,β)-summand is balanced, i.e. d_{S_N}(e_{α,β}M) ≥ 0, where M = H^0(X_Δ(Q_N), ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^∨_{m_N}. Theorem 7.11 gives d_{S_N}(M) ≥ 0 only for M itself. There are two possible repairs, and neither is in the paper. (A) Construct T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2}, hence e_{α,β}, integrally on coherent H^1, or on the complex RΓ(X_Δ(Q_N), ω(a,2)(−∞)). They must be compatible with the Δ-action and the Hochschild–Serre sequence, for example via Pilloni [58] (which p. 860 cites as [56]; see sourceIssues E156). Then rerun the rank count of Theorem 7.11 on e-parts: e·H_1(X_0(Q_N), L)_{m_N} surjects onto Tor_1^{S_N}(eM, O), and one needs rank e·H^1 ≤ rank e·H^0 in characteristic 0. (B) Show that e_{α,β} acts as the identity on the characteristic-0 forms H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_K)_{m_∅}. By Theorem 7.2 these are the same as H^0(X_0(Q_N), ω(a,2)(−∞)_K)_{m_N}, and Theorem 7.2 is T_{p,1}, Q_{p,2}-equivariant. Then r_e := rank(eM)_Δ = r := rank M_Δ. Tor_1(eM,O) is a direct summand of Tor_1(M,O), which is a quotient of H_1(X_0(Q_N),L)_{m_N} ≅ O^r. So d(eM) = r_e − dim Tor_1(eM,O)/ϖ ≥ r − r = 0. Statement (B) would follow from crystallinity and local–global compatibility at p in weight (a,2), plus Fontaine–Laffaille, but §8.5 says crystallinity is known only in regular weight. The right minimal correction is to supply a proof that the (α,β)-summand is balanced.`. Checked on the page images of p. 845, 853, 860, 878, 879 and 880.

(1) What Theorem 7.11 covers. Theorem 7.11 (p. 853) states that the O[Δ]-module H_0(X_Δ(Q), ω(1,3−a))_m = H^0(X_Δ(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^∨_m is balanced, for m "a non-Eisenstein ideal of T_μ(Q)". Definition 5.13 generates T_σ(Q) by T_{x,i} (x ∉ S∪Q∪{p}), U_{x,i} and ⟨u⟩, so it contains no Hecke operators at p. Those operators are in T̃_σ(Q).

(2) What step (c) needs. On p. 879, H_N := H^0(X_Δ(Q_N), ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^{α,β,∨}_{m_N}, with m_N the ideal of Theorem 7.2, a maximal ideal of T_σ(Q_N). That is the dual of e_{α,β}·H^0(...)_{m_N}, where e_{α,β} (p. 845) is built from T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2}. By Lemma 8.8 these commute with the other Hecke operators, including ⟨u⟩. So H_N is an S_N-direct summand of the module in Theorem 7.11. The paper never says it is all of that module. Theorem 6.17 says only that the (α,β)-space "is nonzero after localization at m". Remark 8.18 exhibits nonordinary oldforms. §8.5 says crystallinity at p is known only in regular weight.

(3) Balancedness does not pass to summands. The defect is additive. An example: S = O[(Z/p^N)^2] = O[x,y]/((1+x)^{p^N}−1, (1+y)^{p^N}−1) is a local complete intersection. Its embedding dimension is 3, because the relations lie in m^2 for N ≥ 1, and its codimension is 2. Tate's Poincaré series (1+t)^3/(1−t^2)^2 gives dim Tor_2^S(k,k) = 3 + 2 = 5. So d_S(m_S) = 3 − 5 = −2, d_S(S^2) = 2, and m_S ⊕ S^2 is balanced with defect 0, while its O-free summand m_S is not. (For q = 1 one gets d(m_S) = 0, so the example needs q ≥ 2.)

(4) The proof of Theorem 7.11 does not localize to the summand. It bounds dim Tor_1^S(M,O)/ϖ by the rank of H_1(X_0(Q),L)_m, through the sequence (H_1(X_Δ(Q),L)_m)_Δ → H_1(X_0(Q),L)_m → Tor_1^S(M,O) → 0, and then uses dim H^1 = dim H^0 in characteristic 0. For eM one needs Tor_1(eM,O) to be bounded by the e-part of H_1, since rank(eM)_Δ can be smaller than r. That requires e acting integrally on coherent H^1. Tor_1 is finite torsion, so an action over K does not help. The paper disclaims exactly this on p. 860: "Note that this argument is not sufficient to construct these operators on H^1(X_1(Q), ω(j,k)_{K/O}); however, we have no need to the consider the action of Hecke operators at p on these spaces." The proof defers to [16, Prop. 3.8]. In that weight-one case the patched module is the full m-localization, with no p-idempotent, so that reference does not cover the summand either.

arXiv v1 (1907.08691v1) has the same text: "(c) Finally, HN is finite and balanced over SN by Theorem 7.11.", and the same Theorem 7.11 for the full localized module, with p − 2 > a.

Nothing shows the conclusion is false, and the fix appears to be available from Pilloni's operators, which the paper cites as acting on higher coherent cohomology. So this is a gap in the proof, not an error. It reaches the proof of Theorem 9.1 (Prop. 3.3(c)), hence the proofs of Theorems 1.2 and 1.1 deduced from it. It also reaches Theorem A.1, which "follows as in Theorem 1.2 above" (p. 889). Checked on the page images of p. 845, 851, 853, 854, 855, 860, 878, 879 and 880, and in the text at the start of §7 and in the appendix.

What the cited theorem covers. Theorem 7.11 (p. 853) reads: "let m be a non-Eisenstein ideal of T_μ(Q) ... Then the O[Δ]-module H_0(X_Δ(Q), ω(1,3−a))_m = H^0(X_Δ(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^∨_m is balanced". There is no (α,β) superscript. On p. 851, m is "a non-Eisenstein maximal ideal of T_μ(Q)". That algebra has no Hecke operators at p. T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2} exist only on H^0, through q-expansions (Lemma 8.8). Step (c) applies the theorem to H_N, which is the dual of e_{α,β}H^0(...)_{m_N}. By Lemma 8.8, e commutes with the diamond operators, and the S_N-structure in item (4) already assumes this. So H_N is an S_N-direct summand of the module in Theorem 7.11.

Defences tried, and why each fails.
(1) Read m as a maximal ideal of the larger Hecke algebra that includes T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2}. The proof of 7.11 bounds Tor_1^S(M,O) through (H_1(X_Δ(Q),L)_m)_Δ → H_1(X_0(Q),L)_m → Tor_1^S(M,O) → 0. Localizing that sequence would need the p-operators on H_1, which is dual to coherent H^1. p. 860 says: "this argument is not sufficient to construct these operators on H^1(X_1(Q), ω(j,k)_{K/O}); however, we have no need to the consider the action of Hecke operators at p on these spaces." Nor can an action over K be used: Tor_1 is finite, and e ⊗ K need not preserve the lattice.
(2) Balancedness might pass to direct summands. It does not, because the defect is additive. Over S = O[(Z/p^N)^2] one has d(S) = 1 and d(O) = 1 − q = −1, so S ⊕ O is balanced but O is not. The m_S ⊕ S^2 example given earlier is also right: the Poincaré series (1+t)^3/(1−t^2)^2 gives Tor_2(k,k) of dimension 5, so d(m_S) = −2.
(3) e might equal 1 on the m_N-part. The paper never says so. On p. 845 it says only that the (α,β)-space "is nonzero after localization at m". Theorem 1.2 calls e "a certain ordinary projection". The image of T_σ(Q)_m in End(M) is local, so it contains no idempotents other than 0 and 1. Hence e cannot be expressed in the operators that do act on H_1 unless e = 1.
(4) The alternative "pd ≤ 1 passes to summands" argument after patching would need the full patched module to be S_∞-torsion. That in turn needs a Galois-side dimension bound for the full m-part, which the paper does not have.
(5) The p. 889 appendix step and Lemma A.5 reuse Theorem 7.11 and do not add the missing point.

The resulting repair (B) is a characteristic-0 statement. It is expected to be true but is not proved in the paper. So the claim in (c) is very likely true and the step is unsupported, not false. That makes this a gap, not an error.

What depends on it. Step (c) is hypothesis (c) of Proposition 3.3 in the proof of Theorem 9.1. Theorem 9.1 gives Theorems 1.1 and 1.2. Theorem A.1 "follows as in Theorem 1.2 above" (p. 889). The stated results are expected to hold, so affects = the proof.

A separate slip at the same step, not part of this issue: Theorem 9.1 allows a = p − 2 (p − 1 > a), but Theorem 7.11 as printed requires p − 2 > a, while §7.2 (p. 851) says p > a − 2. - **Gap** at §9, proof of Theorem 9.1, step (c), p. 880. The root of the problem is the hypothesis of Theorem 7.11 (p. 853), which is Assumption 7.7 (p. 851): "The space H^2(X_Δ(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_m is trivial." arXiv v1 has the same text: Assumption 7.7 on p. 38, Theorem 7.11 and its proof on pp. 39–40, hypothesis (6) on p. 56 and step (c) on p. 57.. The source says `(c) Finally, H_N is finite and balanced over S_N by Theorem 7.11.`; it should be `In the proof of Theorem 7.11, Assumption 7.7 is needed only for Δ trivial, i.e. H^2(X_0(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_m = 0. It enters through Lemma 7.9, which is applied to H_1(X_0(Q), L)_m. The stated hypothesis for X_Δ(Q) is never used. So Theorem 7.11's hypothesis should read "Assumption 7.7 holds for X_0(Q)", and step (c) should add that this is given by hypothesis (6) with i = 0 for Q = Q_N. This works for three reasons. Q_N satisfies Assumption 6.12(2) by Proposition 4.10(2),(3). m_N ⊂ T_σ(Q_N) is maximal, contains m_∅, and contracts to the maximal ideal m_∅ of T^an_σ(Q_N). So localizing the finite-dimensional k-space H^2 at m_N gives a direct summand of its localization at m_∅. Another fix would be to require x ≢ 1 mod p^{N+1} in Proposition 4.10. Then p does not divide deg(X_1(Q_N) → X_Δ(Q_N)), and a trace argument gives the vanishing on X_Δ from (6) with i = 1. The first fix is the smaller one.`. Pages 851–853 and 878–880 checked as images.

(1) Step (c) cites Theorem 7.11. That theorem assumes Assumption 7.7 for the fixed Δ, i.e. vanishing of H^2 on X_Δ(Q_N) localized at m_N. Hypothesis (6) of Theorem 9.1 only covers X_i(Q), and §5.2 defines K_i(Q) only for i = 0, 1. Vanishing on X_1 gives vanishing on X_Δ by trace only when p does not divide [X_1(Q_N) : X_Δ(Q_N)] = ∏(x−1)/p^N. Proposition 4.10(2) only gives x ≡ 1 mod p^N, so this can fail. Nothing in the paper checks the hypothesis. Remark 7.8 and Theorem 5.1 cover p ≥ a ≥ 4 only, not a = 2 or 3.

(2) Defence: the proof of Theorem 7.11 never uses the X_Δ vanishing. By Definition 3.1, and since Tor^O_p vanishes for p ≥ 2, d_S(M) = rank_O(M_Δ) − dim_k Tor_1^S(M,O)/ϖ for any finite M. This is the formula printed, with r the rank of M_Δ, which is H_0(X_0(Q), L)_m. Hochschild–Serre gives a surjection H_1(X_0(Q), L)_m → Tor_1^S(M,O). So one needs H_1(X_0(Q), L)_m to be torsion-free, which is Lemma 7.9 with Δ trivial and so needs Assumption 7.7 for X_0(Q). The rest is a characteristic-0 argument on X_0(Q) (Lemma 7.10 and Arthur's classification). Hypothesis (6) with i = 0 supplies exactly this, as explained in the correction. So Theorem 9.1 is fully supported by its own hypotheses. The fault is only that Theorem 7.11 states a hypothesis (X_Δ) other than the one its proof uses (X_0), and that step (c) leaves the check implicit.

(3) Is Theorem 7.11 correct as stated? Vanishing on X_Δ does not formally give vanishing on X_0. The Hochschild–Serre terms H^2(Δ, H^0) and H^1(Δ, H^1) with k-coefficients need not vanish for a p-group Δ. So Theorem 7.11 is proved under the X_0 hypothesis, not under the one it states. Its only use is step (c), where the X_0 hypothesis is available.

(4) One detail needs care. What fails is the trace argument from X_1 to X_Δ; it has not been shown that the vanishing on X_Δ(Q_N) itself fails.

(5) A separate point, not part of this issue and not assessed here: H_N is the (α,β)-ordinary part, while Theorem 7.11 is stated for the whole m-localized module. - **Misprint** at §A.1, Theorem A.2(1), p. 881. The arXiv appendix 1907.08694v1, Theorem 1.2(1), has the same slip: 'in the sense of [CG18] §9.2'. Its [CG18] is also the Invent. Math. 211 (2018) article.. The source says `(1) The representation r̄|_{F(ζ_p)} has enormous image in the sense of [16, Section 9.2].`; it should be `'... enormous image in the sense of [16, Section 9.4]': the opening paragraph of §9.4, 'An approach to Conjecture B part 5', p. 419 of Invent. Math. 211.`. Bibliography entry [16] is F. Calegari and D. Geraghty, Invent. Math. 211 (2018), no. 1, 297–433. I checked the published article (local copy, 137 pp. = pp. 297–433). Its table of contents reads: 9.1 Arithmetic quotients; 9.2 Hecke operators; 9.3 Conjectures on existence of Galois representations; 9.4 An approach to Conjecture B part 5; 9.5 Modularity lifting. §9.2 does not mention enormous image. The term is introduced only at the start of §9.4 (PDF p. 123 = p. 419): 'under a stronger assumption that r has enormous image ... Here, by enormous image, we require (in addition to bigness) the existence of suitable Taylor–Wiles primes x such that r(Frob_x) has distinct eigenvalues.' In the arXiv preprint 1207.4224v2 that material is numbered §9.2 ('9.2. An approach to Conjecture B part 5'), which explains the slip. The section number is wrong for the cited published article, and the intended reference is unambiguous. - **Misprint** at §A.1, Theorem A.1(2) and its conclusion, p. 881. The arXiv appendix 1907.08694v1, Theorem 1.1, is identical. The same undefined 'D_cris(V)' also occurs in the main-text Theorem 1.1(2), p. 802, where r is defined but V is not.. The source says `(2) A is ordinary at p, and if α, β are the unit root eigenvalues of D_cris(V), then (α^2 − 1)(β^2 − 1)(α − β)(α^2β^2 − 1) ≢ 0 mod p. Then H^1_f(Q, asp^0(r) ⊗ Q_p/Z_p) = 0, where asp^0(r) is the 10-dimensional adjoint representation of PGSp(4).`; it should be `State that V = V_p(A) (equivalently H^1_et(A_{Q̄}, Q_p)) is the p-adic Galois representation of A, and that r: G_Q → GSp_4(Z_p) is the associated integral representation (Tate module), with mod-p reduction r̄_p as in §A.3.2. asp^0(r) is r composed with the adjoint action on the 10-dimensional Lie algebra of PGSp_4.`. Neither V nor r is introduced in Theorem A.1. Earlier in §A.1, V denotes an arbitrary pure de Rham representation ('for any pure de Rham representation V'), and r denotes 'a p-adic representation r: G_Q → GL_n(O) coming from M' for an automorphic compatible system M. The intended objects (the p-adic realisation of A and its integral model) are clear from Theorem 9.1(1) and from §A.3.2, where r̄_p is 'the corresponding semisimple representation' of the abelian surface A. The ambiguity between H^1 and the Tate module does not matter. Their crystalline Frobenius eigenvalues differ by x ↦ p/x on H^1 versus x ↦ 1/x after the Tate twist, so the unit roots α, β are replaced by 1/α, 1/β. A direct computation gives (α^{-2}−1)(β^{-2}−1)(α^{-1}−β^{-1})(α^{-2}β^{-2}−1) = unit × (α^2−1)(β^2−1)(β−α)(α^2β^2−1), so the non-vanishing condition is the same either way. This is an omitted definition in a theorem statement whose meaning is clear from context. - **Gap** at §A.1, paragraph after Theorem A.2, parenthetical remark, p. 882. The arXiv appendix 1907.08694v1, p. 3, is identical (with [ACC+18] for [1]).. The source says `(The conclusion of the theorem holds for F if it holds for any extension F′/F, and any symmetric power of E/F is potentially modular over some CM extension F/F in this case by [1].)`; it should be `'(The conclusion of the theorem holds for F if it holds for an extension F′/F for which restriction H^1_f(F, ad^0(r) ⊗ K/O) → H^1_f(F′, ad^0(r) ⊗ K/O) is injective. This holds, for example, if p ∤ [F′:F], or if (ad^0 r̄)^{G_{F″}} = 0 for the Galois closure F″ of F′/F, e.g. F′/F Galois with r̄|G_{F′} absolutely irreducible and p ∤ n, as for the linearly disjoint CM fields supplied by [1] ...)'. The 'F/F' slip is recorded separately.`. Restriction preserves the Bloch–Kato local conditions, so vanishing over F′ implies vanishing over F exactly when restriction on H^1 is injective. By inflation–restriction, the kernel of H^1(F, M) → H^1(F″, M), with M = ad^0(r) ⊗ K/O and F″ the Galois closure, is H^1(Gal(F″/F), M^{G_{F″}}). The kernel to G_{F′} is contained in it. If p ∤ [F′:F], cor∘res = [F′:F] also gives injectivity. M^{G_{F″}} = 0 iff (ad^0 r̄)^{G_{F″}} = 0, since M[λ] = ad^0 r̄. With r̄|G_{F″} absolutely irreducible and p ∤ n, Schur's lemma gives this. These conditions are not automatic for 'any extension': if p | [F″:F] and ad^0 r̄ acquires G_{F″}-invariants, the kernel can be nonzero, and the remark gives no hypothesis excluding this. In the intended example (symmetric powers of a non-CM E, p large, F′ a Galois CM extension linearly disjoint from F(r̄, ζ_p) as potential-automorphy theorems provide), the condition holds, so nothing downstream is affected. This is an unjustified, over-general reduction in an informal remark, not a false theorem. I could not build an explicit counterexample within the theorem's setting, hence low confidence. - **Misprint** at §A.1, Theorem A.2(2)(b), p. 882. The arXiv appendix 1907.08694v1, Theorem 1.2(2)(b), is identical (checked on the rendered arXiv page 2).. The source says `(b) The representations r|_{G_{I_v}} and r̄|_{G_{I_v}} are unipotent. For a topological generator σ_v ∈ I_v of tame inertia, r̄(σ) consists of a single block, namely: dim ker(r̄(σ) − id_n) = 1.`; it should be `'The representations r|_{I_v} and r̄|_{I_v} are unipotent. For a topological generator σ_v ∈ I_v of tame inertia, r̄(σ_v) consists of a single (Jordan) block, namely dim ker(r̄(σ_v) − id_n) = 1.'`. Checked on the 300 dpi render. 'G_{I_v}' is not defined anywhere. Elsewhere the paper writes restriction to inertia as r|I_x (Assumption 4.3, Definition 4.6(3)) and restriction to the decomposition group as r|G_x. The decomposition-group reading is ruled out: r|G_{F_v} is not unipotent for an unramified twist of Steinberg, since Frobenius acts through the twist. So restriction to I_v is meant. The generator is introduced as σ_v but then written σ. 'Single block' is made precise by the displayed condition dim ker = 1, which for a unipotent matrix means a single Jordan block. These are notational slips with clear intended meaning. - **Misprint** at Appendix (Calegari–Geraghty–Harris), §A.1 Introduction, paragraph after Theorem A.2 ("Unlike the case of Theorem A.1, ..."), p. 882. arXiv:1907.08694v1, §1, p. 3 (theorems numbered 1.1/1.2 there).. The source says `"(The conclusion of the theorem holds for F if it holds for any extension F′/F, and any symmetric power of E/F is potentially modular over some CM extension F/F in this case by [1].)"`; it should be `"... is potentially modular over some CM extension F′/F in this case by [1]." That is, F/F should read F′/F, the same auxiliary extension as in the preceding clause.`. I checked this against page images: p. 882 at 110 dpi, plus a 300 dpi crop of the passage. The same sentence first has "extension F′/F" with a visible prime. Two lines later it has "CM extension F/F" with no prime. The phrase "CM extension" occurs nowhere else in the paper.

Theorem A.2 (p. 881) fixes F as a CM field. The remark says the theorem's conclusion over F follows from the conclusion over any extension F′/F. It then says symmetric powers of a non-CM elliptic curve E/F are potentially modular by ACC+18 [1], which gives modularity over some CM extension F′/F. Read as F/F, the extension would be trivial. That would make the "potentially" and the preceding base-change clause pointless, and it would claim more than [1] proves. No convention in the paper gives F/F a meaning, so this is a missing prime and not an intended statement.

The arXiv appendix (1907.08694v1) has the same slip. I rendered its p. 3 and it reads "potentially modular over some CM extension F/F in this case by [ACC+18]."

Impact: the sentence is a parenthetical in the appendix introduction. It explains which examples Theorem A.2 would apply to. It is not a hypothesis or a step in any proof. Theorem A.2 and its proof in §A.3 (p. 888) do not use it, and neither do Theorem A.1 or the main text. - **Error** at §A.2, Relation with special values of periods, p. 883. The arXiv appendix 1907.08694v1, §2, is identical.. The source says `If one chooses a prime p, and supposes that ρ has a model over O, then the finiteness of the Selmer group H^1_f(Q, ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O) is a consequence of the finiteness of the p-class group of Q(ker(ρ)). (The former is a quotient of the latter.)`; it should be `Replace the parenthetical by: '(With L = Q(ker ρ), restriction to G_L maps the former, with kernel inside the finite group H^1(Gal(L/Q), ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O), which is zero if p ∤ [L:Q], into Hom_{Gal(L/Q)}(Cl(L)[p^∞], ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O).)' The finiteness claim itself is correct.`. G_L acts trivially on ad^0(ρ). A Bloch–Kato class restricted to G_L is a homomorphism G_L → ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O that is unramified everywhere. At w | p this holds because H^1_f(L_w, Q_p) = H^1_ur for trivial coefficients. At infinite places nothing is needed since p is odd. So the class factors through Cl(L)[p^∞], and by inflation–restriction the kernel is H^1(Gal(L/Q), M), a finite group since it is |Gal(L/Q)|-torsion and cofinitely generated. This gives finiteness, as the paper says. The parenthetical 'quotient' claim is false as stated. When p ∤ [L:Q] and ρ is unramified at p, the Selmer group equals Hom_{Gal(L/Q)}(Cl(L)[p^∞], ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O), and enlarging K by degree d raises its order to the d-th power, while Cl(L)[p^∞] does not depend on K. Take any case with a nonzero Selmer group, which the paper itself discusses ('there exist such congruences if and only if H^1_f(...) is nonzero'). For a large enough coefficient field its order then exceeds |Cl(L)[p^∞]|, so it cannot be a quotient of that group. The accurate relation is an embedding, up to finite kernel, into a Hom group out of the class group; dually, the Pontryagin dual is roughly a quotient. The error is in an informal justification, and the conclusion drawn is unaffected. - **Gap** at Appendix (Calegari–Geraghty–Harris), §A.2 'Relation with special values of periods', p. 883, second half of the page, in the test-case paragraph about an odd irreducible ρ: G_Q → GL_2(C). arXiv:1907.08694v1 (the appendix preprint), §2, has the same words, citing [CG18] in place of [16].. The source says `The methods of this paper (following [16]) show that, at all primes p > 2 such that ρ is unramified, the Selmer group H^1_f(Q, ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O) is detected by congruences between the modular form f and other Katz modular forms of weight 1 which may not lift to characteristic 0. In particular, there exist such congruences if and only if H^1_f(Q, ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O) is nonzero.`; it should be `"... at all primes p > 2 such that ρ is unramified at p, the reduction ρ̄ is irreducible, and ρ is a minimal deformation of ρ̄ (in the sense of [16, Corollary 1.5(1)]; for example, at all p > 2 with p ∤ N(ρ)·|ρ(G_Q)|, so for all but finitely many p) ...". Adding "ρ̄ irreducible" alone, as an alternative correction does, is necessary but not sufficient: minimality must also be assumed.`. Printed text checked on the rendered p. 883; it matches the transcription.

(1) What [16] gives. [16] is CG18, Invent. Math. 211. I read its Theorem 1.4 (p. 303): 'Suppose that p ≥ 3. Let ρ̄ : G_Q → GL_2(k) be an odd continuous irreducible Galois representation ... Assume that ρ̄ is unramified at p. ... R^min ⥲ T_m'. The theorem needs ρ̄ irreducible, and it covers only minimal deformations. The Taylor–Wiles patching behind it also needs ρ̄ absolutely irreducible. So the methods cited say nothing at a prime p where ρ̄ is reducible (m Eisenstein), or where ρ is not minimal.

(2) Such primes exist. Let H be the splitting field of x³−x−1 (discriminant −23), and let ρ be the 2-dimensional representation of S_3. It is irreducible and odd, and it is ramified only at 23, so it is unramified at p = 3. In characteristic 3 every irreducible representation of S_3 is 1-dimensional, so ρ̄ is reducible. Both stable lattices check this explicitly: on the sum-zero lattice, b1+2b2 is fixed mod 3. So the sentence covers (ρ, p = 3), but [16] does not apply there. Primes of this kind all divide |ρ(G_Q)|, so the exceptions are finite. For p ∤ |ρ(G_Q)|, ρ̄ is irreducible and ρ(I_v) ≅ ρ̄(I_v).

(3) The 'iff' can fail in this example. f = η(z)η(23z) satisfies f ≡ E_1(1, χ_{−23}) (mod 3) coefficient by coefficient: the traces are 2, 0, −1 against 1+χ = 2, 0, 2, and a_23 = 1 on both sides. The constant term h/2 = 3/2 ≡ 0, so the two agree as mod-3 Katz forms by the q-expansion principle. On the other side, H^1_f(Q, ad^0ρ ⊗ Q_3/Z_3) = 0:
- h(H) = 1. The Minkowski bound is ≈ 3.51, and the primes of H above 2 and 3 have norms 8 and 27, because they lie over non-principal primes of Q(√−23).
- So a Selmer class dies on G_H, and the group is H^1(S_3, M) ≅ Ĥ^0(C_3, ad^0 L)^{C_2}.
- I computed this for both stable lattices L. In each case N_{C_3}(ad^0 L) = (ad^0 L)^{C_3}, so the group is 0.
- The local conditions at 23 and 3 add nothing: D_23 = C_2, which has no 3-torsion cohomology, and the classes at 3 are unramified.
So if Eisenstein series count as 'other Katz modular forms of weight 1', the 'iff' is false at (ρ, 3). If only cusp forms count (T in [16] acts on H^1(X_U, ω⊗L_σ), which is dual to cusp forms), I cannot decide the statement at such p. It is simply unproved there. That is why I class this as a gap and not an error.

The authors know these conditions matter: on p. 882 they say they 'do not even know that the representations r̄ are irreducible' and 'whether r is a minimal deformation'. Nothing in §A.2 assumes either condition. The remark is informal and nothing later uses it. The printed text is confirmed from the rendered p. 883. The claim rests on [16] = Calegari–Geraghty, Invent. Math. 2018, Theorem 1.4: "Suppose that p ≥ 3. Let ρ̄ : G_Q → GL_2(k) be an odd continuous irreducible Galois representation ... unramified at p. Let R^min denote the universal minimal unramified-at-p deformation ring of ρ̄ ... R^min ≅ T_m." To read H^1_f(Q, ad^0ρ ⊗ K/O) off R^min = T_m, two things are needed. (i) ρ̄ must be irreducible. (ii) ρ must be a point of R^min, i.e. minimally ramified; this is [16, Cor. 1.5(1)]: "either ρ(I_v) ≅ ρ̄(I_v) or dim ρ^{I_v} = dim ρ̄^{I_v} = 1".

Both conditions can fail at primes p > 2 where ρ is unramified.
(i) Take the S_3 representation cut out by x^3 − x − 1. The discriminant is −23 (computed), and the splitting field is the Hilbert class field of Q(√−23), ramified only at 23. So ρ is odd, irreducible, and unramified at 3. Its reduction mod 3 is reducible: in the reflection representation, (1,1,1) lies in {Σx_i = 0} mod 3 and is S_3-fixed, and Brauer–Nesbitt gives ρ̄^ss = 1 ⊕ ε_{−23}. Here m is Eisenstein, and indeed η(z)η(23z) ≡ E_1(1, ε_{−23}) mod 3. So [16] does not apply.
(ii) Take ρ = Ind_K^Q ψ with K = Q(√−47) (class number 5) and ψ a ring class character of order 15. The order-3 part should have conductor ℓ, with ℓ ≡ 1 mod 3 split in K. Then ρ is unramified at 3, and ρ̄ = Ind ψ̄ with ψ̄ of order 5 is irreducible. But ρ|I_ℓ = ω ⊕ ω^{-1} with ω of order 3, while ρ̄|I_ℓ is trivial. So ρ is not minimal and is not a point of R^min.

Defence attempted, without success. No charitable reading restricts p. The paper's own methods also assume residual irreducibility (big image). The authors are aware of both conditions. On p. 882, about Theorem A.2, they write: "we do not even know that the representations r̄ are irreducible for sufficiently large p. Another is that we do not know whether r is a minimal deformation of r̄ at ramified primes v". §A.2 simply omits these conditions. For p ∤ |ρ(G_Q)| the reduction of the finite image group is injective and preserves irreducibility, so both conditions hold for all but finitely many p. I cannot show that the "iff" statement is actually false at the excluded p; in the S_3 example both sides are nonzero, since the 3-class group of K gives a Selmer class. The fault is an unsupported claim of scope, so the kind is gap, not error.

Consequences: §A.2 is a discussion remark. Nothing in the paper cites it; the text contains no reference to Section A.2, and Theorems A.1 and A.2 and §A.3 do not use it. So affects = nothing. - **Error** at §2.2 (The group GSp4(R)), p. 809, the paragraph after the display defining h = {h(t1,t2;z)}. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text word for word in §2.0.2, pp. 7–8 ("h(t1,t2;t)" on p. 7; the kernel, the "Equivalently" sentence and "K_{1,C}" on p. 8).. The source says `"Then h_C = Lie H_C = {h(t1, t2; t) : t1, t2, z ∈ C} and the surjective map exp : h_C → H_C sends h(t1, t2; z) to exp(z)·[[cos t1, 0, 0, sin t1],[0, cos t2, sin t2, 0],[0, −sin t2, cos t2, 0],[−sin t1, 0, 0, cos t1]]. Thus its kernel is {h(t1, t2; z) : t1, t2 ∈ 2πZ, z ∈ 2πiZ}. We define the lattice X*(H_C) ⊂ h*_C to be the subspace consisting of differentials of (complex analytic) characters of H_C. Equivalently, X*(H_C) is the subset of X*(C^× × H_{1,C}) = {λ ∈ h*_C : λ(ker(exp : h_C → H_C)) ⊂ 2πiZ} consisting of differentials of characters of C^× × K_{1,C} which factor through the multiplication map C^× × H_{1,C} → H_C. We fix an isomorphism {(a, b; c) ∈ Z^3 : a + b ≡ c mod 2} ~→ X*(H_C) by letting (a, b; c) correspond to the linear form h(t1, t2; z) ↦ a t1 i + b t2 i + c z on h_C." (checked on the page image at 250 dpi)`; it should be `The kernel of exp : h_C → H_C is {h(πm, πn; πik) : m ≡ n ≡ k mod 2}. This is the printed lattice (2πZ)^2 × 2πiZ together with its coset h(π,π;πi) + (printed lattice). The printed set is the kernel of h_C → C^× × H_{1,C}, h(t1,t2;z) ↦ (e^z, R(t1,t2)). The smallest fix is to read "Thus the kernel of h_C → C^× × H_{1,C} is {…}". In the "Equivalently" sentence, read X*(C^× × H_{1,C}) = {λ : λ(ker(h_C → C^× × H_{1,C})) ⊂ 2πiZ}, which is Z^3 in the (a,b;c) coordinates, and read "characters of C^× × H_{1,C}" for "C^× × K_{1,C}". Alternatively, keep exp : h_C → H_C, use its true kernel, and note that {λ : λ(ker exp) ⊂ 2πiZ} is X*(H_C) itself. Separately, "h(t1,t2;t)" should be "h(t1,t2;z)". The final isomorphism {(a,b;c) ∈ Z^3 : a+b ≡ c mod 2} ≅ X*(H_C) is correct and needs no change.`. exp(h(t1,t2;z)) = e^z·R(t1,t2), because zI commutes with the rotation part. For t1 = t2 = π and z = πi this is e^{πi}·R(π,π) = (−1)(−I) = I. I checked this numerically with the power series of the actual 4×4 matrix. So h(π,π;πi) lies in ker(exp : h_C → H_C) but not in the printed set. Solving e^z R(t1,t2) = I directly gives sin t1 = sin t2 = 0 and cos t1 = cos t2 = e^{−z}, so the kernel is {(πm,πn;πik) : m ≡ n ≡ k mod 2}.

The paper's own conventions require this larger kernel. H_C is the image of the explicit exp formula in G(C), and the paper itself treats C^× × H_{1,C} → H_C as a multiplication map with kernel {(1,I),(−1,−I)}. Its final answer a+b ≡ c mod 2 is only correct for that quotient. With the printed kernel, {λ : λ(ker) ⊂ 2πiZ} would be all of Z^3.

Check of the final answer: the form (a,b;c) sends (2π,0;0), (0,2π;0) and (0,0;2πi) to 2πia, 2πib and 2πic, so a, b, c ∈ Z. It sends (π,π;πi) to (a+b+c)πi, which lies in 2πiZ iff a+b ≡ c mod 2. The same result comes from requiring the character to be trivial on (−1,−I).

So the 'Equivalently' identity X*(C^× × H_{1,C}) = {λ : λ(ker(exp: h_C→H_C)) ⊂ 2πiZ} is false as written. It holds only with the kernel of h_C → C^× × H_{1,C}; with the true kernel the right-hand side is X*(H_C). 'K_{1,C}' appears nowhere else in either version and is never defined. Read as the complexification of K_{∞,1} ≅ U(2), i.e. GL_2(C), its characters are only powers of det, which would give far too small a lattice. So it is a typo for H_{1,C}. 'h(t1,t2;t)' is also confirmed as a typo for z.

Downstream: only the final isomorphism (a,b;c) ↔ λ is used later (weights of automorphic bundles). That isomorphism is correct, and the faulty kernel statement is used nowhere else. So this correction is right, and nothing downstream is affected. Defence attempted and it fails.

(1) The paper fixes H_C concretely. It says exp : h_C → H_C sends h(t1,t2;z) to exp(z)·R(t1,t2) ∈ G(C), and it calls C^× × H_{1,C} → H_C a "multiplication map". So H_C is the image in GSp4(C), not the abstract product C^× × H_{1,C}. It is also not the universal complexification of H ≅ R_{>0} × H_1; that would be C × (C^×)^2, and its exp-kernel would have z = 0, which does not match the printed set either. Under the paper's own description, e^z R(t1,t2) = I forces sin t1 = sin t2 = 0 and cos t1 = cos t2 = e^{−z}, so the kernel is {(πm, πn; πik) : m ≡ n ≡ k mod 2}. A power-series computation of the actual 4×4 matrix exponential gives exp(h(π,π;πi)) = I exactly, while exp(h(π,0;πi)) = diag(1,−1,−1,1) ≠ I. So h(π,π;πi) is in the kernel but not in the printed set, and "Thus its kernel is …" is false. The pronoun "its" can only refer to exp : h_C → H_C, and the next sentence writes ker(exp : h_C → H_C) explicitly, so no charitable reading rescues it. Over R the printed set would not be the kernel either: the real kernel has z = 0.

(2) The mistake is internally consistent, and this is why the final answer is right. The "Equivalently" sentence uses the same wrong kernel to describe X*(C^× × H_{1,C}). With the printed lattice, {λ : λ(ker) ⊂ 2πiZ} = Z^3, which is the correct X*(C^× × H_{1,C}). Imposing that the character factors through the multiplication map, whose kernel is {(1,I),(−1,−I)}, then gives a+b ≡ c mod 2. Directly: the form a t1 i + b t2 i + c z takes the value (a+b+c)πi on h(π,π;πi), which lies in 2πiZ exactly when a+b ≡ c mod 2. So the paper conflates ker(h_C → H_C) with ker(h_C → C^× × H_{1,C}) in two sentences, but the conclusion is correct. With the true exp-kernel substituted literally, the displayed formula for "X*(C^× × H_{1,C})" would already equal X*(H_C), and the extra factoring condition would be vacuous.

(3) "K_{1,C}" appears nowhere else in either version. Read as the complexification of K_{∞,1} ≅ U(2), i.e. GL_2(C), its characters are powers of det, which gives only a rank-2 lattice. So it is a slip for H_{1,C}. "h(t1,t2;t)" is a slip for z.

Consequences: later text uses only the final identification of X*(H_C) with {(a,b;c) : a+b ≡ c mod 2} ⊂ Z^3 and its extension to C^3 ≅ h*_C. That covers the roots Φ_c^+ = {(1,−1;0)} and Φ_n^+ = {(0,2;0),(1,1;0),(2,0;0)}, all of even parity; Definition 2.2's X*(H_C)^+_{K^h_C} = {a ≥ b}; the weights (0,−1;1) and (1,0;1) of V^∓; and the weights σ = (−b,−a;a+b+2c) in the later chamber lemma. The kernel statement is never used again. (Separately, the later chamber-lemma proof says "we identified X*(H_C) with Z^3", where it should say a sublattice of Z^3. That is harmless there, since only X*(H_C) ⊗ R ≅ R^3 is used, and it is a separate slip.) The correction and the alternative given with it are both right. The minimal fix is to rename the map whose kernel is displayed. Classified as an error, not a misprint, because it is a false mathematical statement about an explicitly given map, not a typographical slip, though its intended content can be recovered. - **Gap** at Appendix A, §A.3.1, Theorem A.4 and its proof, pp. 885–886; setup of r̄_v on pp. 884–885 (it affects the proof). The source says `p. 885: "THEOREM A.4 Suppose that H^i(Y, O/ϖ^n)_m = 0 unless i ∈ [q_0, …, q_0 + l_0]. Let Q be a finite collection of primes x such that r̄(Frob_x) has distinct eigenvalues and N(x) ≡ 1 mod p. Then H^i(Y_1(Q), O/ϖ^n)_{m_α} = 0 for all i ∉ [q_0, …, q_0 + l_0], where" p. 886: "(1) α = {α_x} is a choice of eigenvalues of r̄(Frob_x) for each x dividing Q; (2) the localization takes place with respect to the Hecke algebra T_Q consisting of the Hecke operators prime to p and prime to the level together with U_x − α_x for all x ∈ Q. In particular, the conclusions of this theorem apply for all sufficiently large p. Proof. We first note that the assumption (of absolute irreducibility) on r̄ ensures that the cohomology of the boundary vanishes after localization at m. This is because the cohomology of the boundary may be computed inductively from the cohomology of Levi subgroups and then of GL_{n_i} for n_i < n (see, e.g., Section 3 and in particular Proposition 3.3 of [17]), and so the corresponding Galois representations associated to these classes are reducible. By Poincaré duality (and the discussion above concerning the vanishing of the boundary cohomology localized at m), it suffices to prove the result for i < q_0. Let i be the smallest integer for which the inequality is violated. Then, by the Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence, we deduce that H^i(Y_0(Q), k)_{m_α} ≠ 0. As in [16, Section 9.4] (see also [46, Lemma 6.25(4)]), we deduce that H^i(Y_0(Q), k)_{m_α} ≃ H^i(Y, k)_m. The result then follows by Lemma A.3." Setup, pp. 884–885: "For a prime v of O_E, let r̄_v : G_F → GL_n(k) be the corresponding semisimple Galois representation, and let m denote the corresponding maximal ideal of T." p. 882: "we do not even know that the representations r_λ are irreducible for sufficiently large p."`; it should be `Minimal fix: add one hypothesis to Theorem A.4, or to the §A.3.1 setup: "Suppose moreover that r̄ (= r̄_v) is absolutely irreducible." This is what the proof calls "the assumption", and it matches the parallel coherent Lemma A.6, which does say "Suppose, moreover, that r̄_p is absolutely irreducible." The last sentence then needs a qualifier: "the conclusions apply for all sufficiently large p [for which r̄ is absolutely irreducible]". Lemma A.3 supplies the vanishing hypothesis for large p. It does not supply irreducibility, which p. 882 says is not known. An extra hypothesis at m^∨, as in an alternative correction, is not needed. Absolute irreducibility of r̄ gives it for r̄^∨ as well, so boundary cohomology vanishes at both m and m^∨. Poincaré duality on Y then turns the stated vanishing at m for i > q0+l0 into vanishing at m^∨ for i < q0. [16, Remark 9.3] uses the same "by duality, considering both m and m^*". Alternative fix that keeps the statement as printed: skip the boundary step and run the i < q0 argument on H_c at m_α^∨. Hochschild–Serre and the Taylor–Wiles isomorphism apply to H_c in the same way. Poincaré duality on Y gives H_c^j(Y,k)_{m^∨} = H^{D−j}(Y,k)_m^∨ = 0 for j < q0. Or use the minimal-complex argument over k[Δ_Q]. The application to A.2 still needs the boundary vanishing of [16, Conj. B(4)(b)]. That comes from irreducibility, which A.2(1) supplies.`. Checked on the page images (p. 881, 884–886). The core claim holds:
- Neither Theorem A.4 nor the setup of §A.3.1 assumes r̄ absolutely irreducible. There r̄_v is only "the corresponding semisimple Galois representation", and p. 882 admits that irreducibility for large p is unknown.
- Yet the proof's first step, boundary vanishing at m (needed for the Poincaré duality reduction), uses "the assumption (of absolute irreducibility) on r̄", which the statement does not contain.
- arXiv:1907.08694v1, Theorem 3.2 and its proof, has word-for-word the same text, including "the assumption (of absolute irreducibility) on r".

Another proposed reading says the upper degrees need the hypothesis at m^∨ as well. That is wrong. Given boundary vanishing at m and m^∨ (both follow from absolute irreducibility of r̄), Poincaré duality on Y derives vanishing at m^∨ for i < q0 from the stated vanishing at m for i > q0+l0. So "suffices to prove i < q0" is legitimate, and the added m^∨ hypothesis is redundant.

Impact: downstream results are fine. Theorem A.4 is used only in the proof of Theorem A.2 (pp. 888–889: "we use Theorem A.4 as a substitute for the vanishing assumption required in [16, Conjecture B]"). There, hypothesis (1) (r̄|F(ζp) has enormous image, which includes CHT bigness) forces absolute irreducibility. That application also silently needs the boundary vanishing of [16, Conj. B(4)(b)], which the proof of A.4 supplies under this hypothesis.

Minor side slips:
- The proof ends with "follows by Lemma A.3" where the theorem's own hypothesis suffices.
- Theorem A.2 cites "[16, Section 9.2]" for "enormous", but [16] discusses it in §9.4. Checked on the page images (pp. 881–889) and in arXiv v1.

What is missing:
- Neither Theorem A.4 nor the §A.3.1 setup assumes r̄ is irreducible. r̄_v is only "the corresponding semisimple Galois representation", and p. 882 admits "we do not even know that the representations r_λ are irreducible for sufficiently large p".
- Yet the proof's first step, boundary vanishing at m, rests on "the assumption (of absolute irreducibility) on r̄". The Poincaré-duality reduction to i < q0 uses that step.
- The theorem's last sentence claims the conclusions hold "for all sufficiently large p", which the printed proof does not cover when r̄ is reducible.

Defences tried:
(a) The inherited setting. §A.3.1 works "in [16, Section 9]". In [16] (arXiv 1207.4224v2), §8.5 fixes "a continuous absolutely irreducible representation r̄", and Conjecture B(1)–(5) is stated only for non-Eisenstein m with r̄_m ≅ r̄. A.4 is meant to replace B(4). So the "assumption" is plausibly this imported standing hypothesis. That explains the intent, but it does not make the text correct: §A.3.1 redefines r̄_v for every v as merely semisimple, and the "all sufficiently large p" sentence contradicts p. 882.
(b) The parallel coherent Lemma A.6 (p. 887; v1 Lemma 3.4) states irreducibility explicitly. This confirms the omission in A.4 is a slip.
(c) The conclusion itself is probably true without irreducibility, using the H_c or minimal-complex argument and the same cited inputs. So the statement is not shown false; only the proof's first step relies on the missing hypothesis.

Consequences: Theorem A.4 is used only in the proof of Theorem A.2 (pp. 888–889: "we use Theorem A.4 as a substitute for the vanishing assumption required in [16, Conjecture B]") and in the remark on p. 886.
- In A.2, hypothesis (1) is enormous image, which [16] §9.2 defines as "in addition to bigness".
- Bigness gives H^0(r̄(G_{F(ζp)}), ad^0) = 0. With p ∤ n and r̄ semisimple, this forces r̄ to be absolutely irreducible.
- A.2 also assumes the rest of Conjecture B, which is set in the irreducible case.
So A.2 stands. Theorem A.1 does not use A.4; it uses Lemma A.6. The references to "Theorem A.4" on p. 889 that should read A.1 are a separate slip, already recorded as E151. Lemma A.3 gives this only 'for all sufficiently large v', so citing it literally proves only the final 'In particular' clause. The needed vanishing comes directly from the theorem's own hypothesis, which is word for word the conclusion of Lemma A.3. So the intended meaning is clear and the fix is routine. This is a wrong cross-reference, not a mathematical error or a real gap. State and prove the theorem for the subcover Y_Δ(Q) → Y_0(Q), where Δ is the maximal p-power quotient of Δ_Q (any p-power quotient also works). The Hochschild–Serre lowest-degree argument then goes through word for word, because a p-group acting on a non-zero k-vector space has non-zero invariants. The alternative is to keep Y_1(Q) and add the missing input: the prime-to-p part of Δ_Q acts trivially on H^*(Y_1(Q),k)_{m_α}. That input is local–global compatibility at x ∈ Q, relating diamond operators to inertia, as in [16, Conj. B(2)] and condition (d) of [16, Thm 6.3]. Note that the first option (going through Y_Δ(Q)) proves the statement for Y_Δ(Q), not for Y_1(Q). Getting back to Y_1(Q) again needs the prime-to-p invariants to be non-zero. Coherent case (Lemma A.6). The statement needs no change, only one missing sentence. By p. 821, Π(x)/Π(x)^+ ≅ (Z/x)^× through λ mod x, and this map is onto already on the centre Z_x^×. So the diamond operators are central, and for y ∉ S∪Q∪{p} the operator S_y = T_{y,0} (which lies in the localising Hecke algebra) equals y^w⟨y^{-1}⟩_S⟨y^{-1}⟩_Q. Localising at m_α fixes S_y ≡ s̄_y, the same value as at level X. By Dirichlet (CRT on (Z/Q)^× × (Z/N)^×) every prime-to-p character of Δ_Q in H^*(X_1(Q),·)_{m_α} is trivial. Hence the Δ_Q-invariants are non-zero, compare the main text p. 846: "χ_Q is a finite-order character of p-power order which is unramified outside Q".`. I rendered pp. 884–889 and checked the printed text above against the images; the arXiv v1 appendix reads the same.

(1) Which cover Y_1(Q) is. The appendix never defines Y_1(Q), Y_0(Q), X_1(Q) or X_0(Q); it relies on [16, §9] and the main text. [16] = CG18, §9.1 sets L_{Q,v} ⊂ K_{Q,v} to be "the normal subgroup with quotient group k_v^×", and §9.5 says "Y_1(Q_N) → Y_0(Q_N) with Galois group Δ := ∏_{x∈Q}(O_F/x)^×". The main text, §5.2 (p. 822) and p. 833, says "X_{K_1(Q)} → X_{K_0(Q)} is then finite étale with Galois group Δ_Q := (Z/Q)^×". So in both cases the Galois group is the full ∏(O_F/x)^×. That group is essentially never a p-group: N(x)−1 is even whenever N(x) is odd, so for odd p there is always a 2-part. For example, x = 7 and p = 3 give (Z/7)^× ≅ Z/6.

(2) The step. Let i be the least degree with H^i(Y_1(Q),k)_{m_α} ≠ 0. Hochschild–Serre gives H^i(Y_0(Q),k)_{m_α} ≅ E_2^{0,i} = (H^i(Y_1(Q),k)_{m_α})^{Δ_Q}. For a p-group acting on a nonzero k-vector space, the invariants are nonzero. For Δ_Q = Δ'×Δ_p with |Δ'| > 1 prime to p they need not be. Decompose V = ⊕_χ V_χ over characters of Δ'. Then H^a(Δ_Q, V_χ) = 0 for every a whenever χ ≠ 1. Toy check: Z/6 acting on k = F_3 through the quadratic character has V^G = 0 and no group cohomology at all. So the spectral sequence only brings the χ = 1 part down to Y_0(Q). Components with nontrivial prime-to-p nebentypus in degree < q_0 are left untreated.

(3) Localisation does not remove those components. Theorem A.4(2) defines T_Q explicitly as "the Hecke operators prime to p and prime to the level together with U_x − α_x", so there are no diamond operators, and m_α does not cut out χ = 1. Showing that the χ ≠ 1 components vanish requires local–global compatibility at x for torsion classes (inertia acting through χ, which is nontrivial mod p, would contradict r̄ being unramified at x). The proof never mentions this. Lemma A.6 has the same pattern; its m_α is described only as "any collection of eigenvalues", as in A.4.

(4) Status. The stated results are very probably true, since they follow from local–global compatibility. The p-power subcover version, which is all that [16, §7/§9.5] and Theorem 7.11 need, is proved by the printed argument as it stands. So this is a gap in the proofs of A.4 and A.6 as stated for Y_1/X_1, not a false statement, and Theorems A.1 and A.2 are unaffected.

One minor imprecision: the "[16, Conjecture B(2)]" attribution is loose, because the local–global compatibility needed is really the diamond-operator/inertia link. The gap itself is real. Lowest-degree Hochschild–Serre: when H^b(Y_1(Q),k)_{m_α} = 0 for b < i, we get H^i(Y_0(Q),k)_{m_α} = E_2^{0,i} = (H^i(Y_1(Q),k)_{m_α})^{Δ_Q}. The argument therefore needs these invariants to be non-zero. The appendix never defines Y_1(Q). It takes Y from [16, §9], says 'As in [16, Section 9.4]', and calls Thm A.4 'a replacement for Conjecture B(4) of [16]'. In [16] (arXiv v2, §9.0.1), Y_1(Q) = Y(L_Q), with K_{Q,v}/L_{Q,v} ≅ k_v^×. The Galois group of Y_1(Q) → Y_0(Q) is Δ̃ = ∏_{x∈Q}(O_F/x)^× ([16] §9.3), and this group is not a p-group. The main text uses the same convention for X_1(Q) (p. 822: Galois group Δ_Q := (Z/Q)^×; p. 833). An element of prime order ℓ ≠ p acting on k through a non-trivial character has no invariants. So the step is valid only if prime-to-p characters of Δ_Q cannot occur in the m_α-localisation. The localising algebra T_Q in Thm A.4(2) contains no diamond operators. In PGL_n the centre is trivial (T_{α,n} = 1), so no Hecke operator away from Q controls them. With only A.4's hypotheses (vanishing at level Y), ruling them out needs local–global compatibility at x ∈ Q for torsion classes, and A.4 does not assume it. So the Betti step is a real gap. Charitable reading: Khare–Thorne [46], which the proof cites, define U_1(Q) through the maximal p-power quotient (arXiv:1409.7007v1 p. 41: 'U_1(Q)_v is the pre-image ... of the maximal p-power quotient'). With that reading the proof is correct, but the text points to [16]'s full cover. Defence that succeeds for Lemma A.6: in GSp_4 with Klingen level, the Q-diamond operators are central elements, so the S_y in the localising algebra, together with Dirichlet, kill prime-to-p characters (details in the correction). That part of the issue is only an omitted routine sentence. Consequences: Thm A.4 is used only in the proof of Thm A.2 (pp. 888–889, as a substitute for [16, Conj. B(4)]). The patching in [16] (proof of Thm 9.19) uses only the p-power subcovers Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), for which the corrected argument is complete. Thm A.2 also assumes Conj. B apart from (4), which supplies the missing compatibility. Lemma A.6 feeds Thm A.1 through Assumption 7.7, which concerns X_Δ(Q) with Δ of p-power order (Thm 7.11). Thms A.1 and A.2 are not affected. Only Thm A.4 in the form stated (unconditional, for the full Y_1(Q)) is left without a complete proof.
