Thus it suffices to prove the result in weight μ' := (a',b') := (a+t,b+t)." Later on p. 843: "For part (3), note that Q_p(X) ∈ T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪 factors as (X − d_{p,1})(X − p^{b−2}d_{p,2})(X − p^{a−1}d_{p,1})(X − p^𝐰 d_{p,4}) for units d_{p,i} ∈ T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪." Statement (3), p. 842: "There are units d_{p,1},…,d_{p,4} ∈ T_μ(Q)^β_𝔪 satisfying Q_p(X) = (X − d_{p,1})(X − p^{b−2}d_{p,2})(X − p^{a−1}d_{p,3})(X − p^𝐰 d_{p,4}) ∈ T_μ(Q)^β_𝔪[X]". The arXiv preprint 1907.08691v1 has the same text and numbering (Theorem 6.13, pp. 31–32 there).`; it should be `Replace plain multiplication by A^s with the composite e'_β∘A^s, where e'_β is the β-idempotent in weight μ'. The paper itself does this in Theorem 6.17 (p. 846, "e_β∘A^s") and Theorem 8.13 (π_β∘A). Why the composite works: - It is T_μ(Q)-equivariant. A^s commutes with the operators away from p (Lemma 6.4), and e'_β commutes with T_{μ'}(Q). - It is injective on the β-part. Suppose x ≠ 0 and e'_β(A^s x) = 0, and let y = ϖ^{j−1}x ≠ 0 with ϖy = 0. Then y lies in H^0(…_{O/ϖ^m})[ϖ] = H^0(…_k) (Remark 6.5), in its β-part. - On that ϖ-torsion, A^s acts as h^{rs}. By Lemma 6.2(2), iterated (every intermediate weight has b ≥ 3), h^{rs} commutes with T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2}. So A^s y is in the β-part of weight μ'. - Hence 0 = ϖ^{j−1}e'_β(A^s x) = e'_β(A^s y) = h^{rs}y, which is nonzero by Lemma 6.2(1). This is a contradiction. This gives the surjection T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪 ↠ T_μ(Q)^β_𝔪/I_{μ,m}. Parts (1), (2), (4), (3)(a) and (3)(b) then transfer from weight μ' to weight μ; for (3)(b), ε^t ≡ 1 mod p^m because (p−1)p^{m−1} | t. What still needs an argument or a weaker statement: the part of (3) claiming the identity Q_p(X) = ∏(X − p^{n_i}d_{p,i}) with coefficients in T_μ(Q)^β_𝔪, in weight μ. The surjection does not see operators at p. The image of the weight-μ' polynomial is ≡ (X−d_{p,1})X^3 mod ϖ^m, not the weight-μ Q_p(X). Separately, "Q_p(X) ∈ T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪" is only asserted; a priori T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2} lie in T̃, not in T. Either weaken (3) to the existence of units d_{p,i} with (a) and (b), or add an argument. Remarks on an alternative correction: - With the same replacement, both (3)(a) and (3)(b) transfer, not only the shape (3)(b). - Restricting instead to m ≤ b−2 also suffices for the only application (Theorem 6.17, where b'−2 = t ≥ m), but it weakens Theorem 6.13. The e'_β∘A^s fix is the minimal one.`. I confirmed the printed text from the page images; the arXiv text is identical.

1. The cited lemmas do not cover the step. Lemma 6.2(2) (p. 836) is only about h: H^0(ω(a,b)_k) → H^0(ω(a+p−1,b+p−1)_k), with coefficients in k. Lemma 6.4(2) (p. 837) gives equivariance for A^s mod ϖ^m only for T_{x,i} with x ∉ S∪Q∪{p} and U_{x,i} with x ∈ Q. Remark 6.5 (p. 837) itself extends the map to the tilde algebras only mod Ĩ_{μ,1}, i.e. for m = 1.

2. I redid the commutator computation. By Lemma 8.3 (p. 858), in weight (j,k) we have T = U + p^{k−2}Z + p^{k+j−3}V, where U and Z are given by formulas whose ρ depends only on j−k. The q-expansion of A^s is ≡ 1 mod ϖ^m, since p^{m−1} | s. Since t ≥ m, T^{(μ')}(A^sF) − A^sT^{(μ)}F ≡ −p^{b−2}ZF − p^{a+b−3}VF mod ϖ^m. This is nonzero in general once m > e(b−2); the bound "m > b−2" is the unramified case.

3. The step is not just unjustified; it fails in the GL2 analogue. Take f of level N prime to p and weight k ≥ 2 with a_p = α+β', α a unit and αβ' = p^{k−1}. Take E ≡ 1 mod p^m of weight k'−k. In weight k', T' ≡ U mod p^m. Put g = p^{k−1}Vf. Then T'f ≡ (α+β')f − g and T'g ≡ αβ'f, so (T'−α)(T'−β') = 0 on the span of f and g. Hence e_α f − f = β'(f − αVf)/(α−β'). Comparing q^1-coefficients shows this is nonzero mod p^m for m ≥ k. So Ef is not in the α-part of weight k'.

4. The reduction "it suffices to prove the result in weight μ'" does not handle (3). The coefficients of Q_p(X) (Definition 6.7) involve T_{p,1} and p^{b−2}Q_{p,2}, which lie in T̃ rather than T (Definition 5.13(3)). Listing S_p among these operators outside T would be imprecise: S_p acts by the scalar p^{j+k−6} (proof of Lemma 8.12). The surjection sees no operators at p. The image of the weight-μ' polynomial is ≡ (X−d_1)X^3 mod ϖ^m, not the weight-μ polynomial. The proof also only asserts ("note that") that Q_p(X) lies in T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪.

5. Downstream effect. Theorem 6.13 is used only in Theorem 6.17, applied in weight μ' = (a+t, 2+t). That proof uses only (1), (2), (4), (3)(a) and (3)(b). Those survive the e_β∘A^s fix, so no stated downstream result is affected.

Side issues noticed nearby, recorded separately as sourceIssues E64 (the d_{p,3} slip) and E59 (the definition of e_β):
- On p. 843, "p^{a−1}d_{p,1}" should read d_{p,3}.
- As printed, e_β = lim((T_{p,1}−β̃)(Q_{p,2}−α̃β̃))^{n!} projects onto the part where these operators are units. The text uses it for the part where they are nilpotent (compare Theorem 8.13). I checked the printed text on the page images of pp. 834–847, 857–858 and 864–866. The arXiv v1 text is identical.

Defence attempts, and why each fails:
(i) Cited lemmas. Lemma 6.4(2) (p. 837) gives equivariance of A^s mod ϖ^m only for T_{x,i} with x ∉ S∪Q∪{p} and U_{x,i} with x ∈ Q. Lemma 6.2(2) (p. 836) concerns h on mod-p forms. Remark 6.5 (p. 837) itself extends the map to the tilde algebras only mod Ĩ_{μ,1}, that is, for m = 1. So the paper's own lemmas cover the p-operators only mod ϖ.
(ii) Lemma 8.3 (p. 858). In weight (a,b), T_{p,1} = U + p^{b−2}Z + p^{a+b−3}V, and U, Z, V depend on the weight only through a−b. The q-expansion of A^s is ≡ 1 mod ϖ^m, and T' ≡ U mod ϖ^m in weight μ' because b+t−2 ≥ m. So T'A^s − A^sT ≡ −p^{b−2}Z − p^{a+b−3}V, which does not vanish mod ϖ^m once m > e(b−2).
(iii) The step genuinely fails; it is not merely unjustified. The β-part sits inside the part where T' is a unit, where T'^{n!} acts as the identity for n large. So A^s F ∈ β-part would force U^{n!}F ≡ F mod ϖ^m on q-expansions.
 - GL2 check (by direct computation). Take f = 11a, p = 3, a_3 = −1 (a unit), and E = E_4^3 ≡ 1 mod 9, weight 12. The q^1-coefficient of lim U^{n!}f is a_{3^{n!}} ≡ 4 mod 9. That is ≡ 1 mod 3 but ≠ 1 mod 9. So Ef is not in the ordinary part of weight 14 mod 9.
 - GSp4 analogue. If the claim held for all m, then P_1(U)F = F, i.e. UF = α_pF for a spherical eigenform F. For generic π_p this contradicts the nonvanishing of the spherical vector's components on the non-ordinary Siegel-parahoric U-eigenlines. This part rests on standard facts that I did not re-derive here.
(iv) Reading e_β literally does not rescue the step. As printed, e_β projects onto the part where the operators are units. Under that reading, (3)(a) and p. 843 ("T_{p,1} ≡ β mod 𝔪 … by definition of e_β") would contradict the definition. The intended meaning is the generalized eigenspace, as in Theorem 8.13. That is a separate misprint.

Consequences. Theorem 6.13 is used only in the proof of Theorem 6.17 (p. 846), in weight (a+t, 2+t); p. 863 cites it only as background. That proof uses (1), (2), (4) and (3)(a)/(b): the unramified rank-1 submodules with Frobenius lifting β, and the α-version. All of these survive the e'_β∘A^s fix. The membership of d_{p,i} in T rather than T̃ is also unargued, but in the application it can plausibly be supplied: under Section 4's hypotheses, r̄|G_{Q_p} is a sum of four distinct characters. Theorem 6.17 then feeds R = T on pp. 878–879, which is unaffected.

Only the unused identity clause of (3), in general weight μ, is left unproven. It is not shown to be false.

Side notes: on p. 843, "p^{a−1}d_{p,1}" should read d_{p,3}; S_p is a scalar, so it should not be listed among the operators outside T. - **Gap** at §6.3, Theorem 6.13(3), p. 842, and its proof, pp. 842–843. The relevant definitions are Definition 5.13 (pp. 834–835), Definition 6.7 (p. 838) and Lemmas 6.2 and 6.4 (pp. 836–837). arXiv v1 (1907.08691v1, pp. 31–32) has identical text. (it affects a stated result). The source says `Statement (p. 842): "(3) There are units d_{p,1}, …, d_{p,4} ∈ T_μ(Q)^β_m satisfying Q_p(X) = (X − d_{p,1})(X − p^{b−2}d_{p,2})(X − p^{a−1}d_{p,3})(X − p^𝐰 d_{p,4}) ∈ T_μ(Q)^β_m[X], and such that: (a) we have d_{p,1} mod m = β and d_{p,2} mod m = α; (b) r | G_{Q_p} is conjugate in GSp_4 to a representation of the form: [upper triangular, diagonal λ(d_{p,1}), ε^{−(b−2)}·λ(d_{p,2}), ε^{−(a−1)}·λ(d_{p,3}), ε^{−𝐰}·λ(d_{p,4})]." Proof (pp. 842–843): "This in turns gives rise to a surjective map T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m ↠ T_μ(Q)^β_m/I_{μ,m}. Thus it suffices to prove the result in weight μ′ := (a′, b′) := (a + t, b + t). … For part (3), note that Q_p(X) ∈ T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m factors as (X − d_{p,1})(X − p^{b−2}d_{p,2})(X − p^{a−1}d_{p,1})(X − p^𝐰 d_{p,4}) for units d_{p,i} ∈ T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m."`; it should be `Three repairs are needed. (i) Weight μ′. Here T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m ⊂ ∏ O_{K_i} is reduced. Show that the d_{p,i} and the triangular form (b) are defined over T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m itself. Take a Frobenius lift φ ∈ G_{Q_p} with ε(φ) = 1. By §4, r̄(φ) is upper triangular with eigenvalues α, β, β^{−1}, α^{−1}, and these are pairwise distinct because (α²−1)(β²−1)(α²β²−1)(α−β) ≠ 0. So Hensel's lemma factors the characteristic polynomial of r(φ) over T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m. The ordinary flag of each r_{f_i} is a sum of the matching spectral lines, so it is cut out by projectors in T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m[r(φ)], and d_{p,j} = ψ_j(φ) lies in T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m. Then T_{p,1} = Σ p^{k_j} d_{p,j} and Q_{p,2} also lie in T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m, which gives the displayed identity in weight μ′. (ii) Transport to weight μ. Carry only (3)(a) and (3)(b) down, using the images of the weight-μ′ units in T_μ(Q)^β_m/I_{μ,m}. This works because t = rs(p−1) with p^{m−1} | s, so ε^{t} ≡ 1 mod p^m. The d's are fixed by r, so they agree as m varies. (iii) The displayed identity Q_p(X) = ∏(X − p^{k_j} d_{p,j}) in weight μ is not proved. It also carries the implicit claim T_{p,1}, Q_{p,2} ∈ T_μ(Q)^β_m. Either drop it, or state it only in weights where H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞))_{K/O} = H^0(…) ⊗ K/O, i.e. where the μ′ argument applies directly. An alternative correction, 'state it in T̃_μ(Q)^β_m[X]', does not by itself fix the transport problem. (3)(b) also needs the d's to lie in T_μ(Q)^β_m, not only in T̃.`. Checked against the rendered pages 834–847.

1. **The coefficients are not in T_μ(Q) by definition.** Definition 5.13 generates T^an_μ(Q) from T_{x,i} for x ∉ S∪Q∪{p}. T_μ(Q) adds only U_{x,i} (x∈Q) and ⟨u⟩. T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2} are added only in T̃_μ(Q). Definition 6.7 gives Q_p(X) = X^4 − T_{p,1}X^3 + (pT_{p,2}+(p^3+p)S_p)X^2 − p^3S_pT_{p,1}X + p^6S_p^2. So "Q_p(X) … ∈ T_μ(Q)^β_m[X]" with the d_{p,i} in T_μ(Q)^β_m claims that T_{p,1} and p^{b−2}Q_{p,2} lie in the image of T_μ(Q). The proof never argues this, even in weight μ′, where it just says "note that Q_p(X) ∈ T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m factors as…".

2. **The reduction to weight μ′ does not carry the identity down.** The surjection T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m ↠ T_μ(Q)^β_m/I_{μ,m} comes from multiplication by A^s. Lemma 6.4 makes that equivariant only for T_{x,i} (x ∉ S∪Q∪{p}) and U_{x,i} (x∈Q). Lemma 6.2(2) gives equivariance for T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2} only for h and only mod p. Also, the Hecke polynomials depend on the weight. The X^2 coefficient is p^{b−2}Q_{p,2} in weight μ but p^{b+t−2}Q′_{p,2} in weight μ′. The printed weight-μ factors p^{b−2}, p^{a−1}, p^𝐰 are not images of the weight-μ′ ones: p^{b′−2} = p^{b−2+t} ≡ 0 mod ϖ^m once t ≥ m.

3. **Unnormalized T_{p,1} really fails to match mod ϖ^m.** Take char-0 ordinary eigenforms f (weight μ) and g (weight μ′) that are congruent mod p^m. Their ordinary filtrations give d_i(f) ≡ d_i(g), since ε^t ≡ 1 mod p^m. Then T_{p,1}(f) − T_{p,1}(g) ≡ p^{b−2}d_2 + p^{a−1}d_3 + p^𝐰 d_4 mod p^m. This is nonzero when m > b−2, because d_2 is a unit and b−2 < a−1 < 𝐰.

So in weight μ, where Remark 6.14 admits torsion-freeness is not known, the displayed identity is asserted but not proved. The claim is plausibly true, since Hensel's lemma factors Q_p over T̃_μ(Q)^β_m, but the proof never links those roots to the Galois-side d_{p,i}.

The gap is genuine. The only downstream use of Theorem 6.13 is Theorem 6.17 (p. 846), which uses only the unramified submodules from (3)(a) and (3)(b) in weight μ′. So the main theorems are not affected. Separately, the proof's display repeats d_{p,1} in the third factor and keeps the weight-μ exponents in weight μ′; those are separate misprints, not part of this issue. Defence tried and failed.
(1) Notation. On p. 841, T_μ(Q)^β is defined as the image of T_μ(Q). By Definition 5.13(2), T_μ(Q) is generated by T_{x,i} for x ∉ S∪Q∪{p}, by U_{x,i} for x ∈ Q, and by the ⟨u⟩. It has no operators at p. Definition 5.13(3) puts T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2} = (pT_{p,2} + (p+p³)S_p)p^{2−b} only into T̃_μ(Q). By Definition 6.7, Q_p(X) = X⁴ − T_{p,1}X³ + p^{b−2}Q_{p,2}X² − p³S_pT_{p,1}X + p⁶S_p². So '∈ T_μ(Q)^β_m[X]', together with d_{p,i} ∈ T_μ(Q)^β_m, really claims that T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2} lie in T_μ(Q)^β_m. No convention in the paper makes this automatic.
(2) Weight μ′. The claim is true there by the Frobenius-lift/Hensel argument in the correction. It uses the §4 hypothesis, and I checked that r̄(φ) has four distinct eigenvalues. The proof leaves this out ('It follows from Proposition 6.8 …'), but that is only a gap in the write-up.
(3) The reduction 'it suffices to prove the result in weight μ′' does not reach the displayed identity. Lemma 6.4(2) makes A^s equivariant only for T_{x,i} with x ∉ S∪Q∪{p} and for U_{x,i}. Lemma 6.2(2) gives equivariance at p only for h, and only mod p. The surjection T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m ↠ T_μ(Q)^β_m/I_{μ,m} involves no operators at p. The polynomial also depends on the weight. In weight μ′ it is X⁴ − T_{p,1}X³ + p^{b+t−2}Q_{p,2}X² − …, and since t ≥ p^{m−1}(p−1) ≥ m it is ≡ (X − d′_{p,1})X³ mod ϖ^m. In weight μ, T_{p,1} = d_{p,1} + p^{b−2}d_{p,2} + …. So transporting the polynomial would give the wrong answer, and the authors themselves apply e_β∘A^s in Theorem 6.17 and Theorem 8.13. The only other route is torsion-freeness in weight μ, and Remark 6.14 says explicitly that this is not proved. No cited result supplies the step.
(4) What survives. (3)(a) and (3)(b) transport correctly, with d_{p,i} the images of the weight-μ′ units, since ε^{−t} ≡ 1 mod p^m.
(5) Downstream use. Theorem 6.13 is used only in the proof of Theorem 6.17 (p. 846). There it is applied in weight μ′ = σ + (t,t), and the proof needs only r over T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m, properties (2)–(5) of Definition 4.6, and (3)(a),(b): the unramified line λ(d_{p,1}) with d_{p,1} ≡ β, and its α-analogue. §8.5 (p. 863) cites Theorem 6.13 only for crystallinity of characteristic-0 eigenforms. So no later result is affected. The part left unproved is the displayed identity in (3) for a general regular μ.
Side notes, separate slips: the proof prints '(X − p^{a−1}d_{p,1})' where d_{p,3} is meant. It also writes the exponents b−2, a−1, 𝐰 for the weight-μ′ polynomial, which reads correctly only if a, b are renamed a′, b′. - **Gap** at §6.3, proof of Theorem 6.13, last two paragraphs, pp. 843–844. It checks part (4) of the theorem, stated on p. 842. arXiv v1 (1907.08691) has the same text: pp. 32–33, "To show that r satisfies properties (2)– (5) ... it suffices to show that each r_{f_i} does so ... the required property holds by [Sor10, Corollary 3]", again with no twist. (it affects the proof). The source says `p. 843: "To show that r satisfies properties (2)–(5) of Definition 4.6, it suffices to show that each r_{f_i} does so." p. 844: "Finally, we turn to Definition 4.6(5). Let x ∈ Q, and recall that K_x = Π(x)^+. ... In this case, Definition 4.6(5) certainly holds for r_{f_i}. In the remaining case, where π_x has no nontrivial Π(x)-invariants, we see that Π(x)/Π^+(x) acts through a nontrivial character on π_x^{Π(x)^+}, and the required property holds by [64, Corollary 3]." The statement it proves, Theorem 6.13(4) on p. 842, reads: "After twisting by the unique square-root of χ_{μ,0} which is trivial modulo m, the deformation r of r̄ satisfies properties (2)–(5) of Definition 4.6."`; it should be `Run the verification for r⊗ψ^{-1} and r_{f_i}⊗ψ_i^{-1}. Here ψ is the square root of χ_{μ,0} with ψ ≡ 1 mod 𝔪, and ψ_i = λ_{f_i}∘ψ. The twist must be by ψ^{-1}, the inverse of the square root, as the proof of Theorem 6.17 (p. 846) does explicitly; (4) says "twisting by the square-root" and should be read that way. The missing lines: - (2): at q every lift of r̄ is unramified (the paper's own argument). At any other x ∉ S∪Q∪{p}, ν(r) = χ_{μ,0}ε^{-w} is unramified, so ψ^2|I_x = 1. - (3): at x of type U, r_{f_i}(I_x) is unipotent, so ν(r_{f_i})|I_x = 1 and ψ_i^2|I_x = 1. - In both cases ψ_i|I_x = 1: it is ≡ 1 mod the maximal ideal, so its values on inertia have odd p-power order. - (5), unramified case: π_x is unramified, so ψ_i is unramified at x. - (5), remaining case: [64, Cor. 3] gives r_{f_i}|I_x ≅ 1⊕1⊕χ⊕χ with totally isotropic eigenspaces. Then ν(r_{f_i})|I_x = χ = ψ_i^2|I_x, and after the twist I_x acts by χ^{-1/2} and χ^{1/2}, which are mutually inverse. This correction is minimal. One point is not covered by it: identifying these two eigenspaces with V_1 and V_2 relative to the fixed labelling. This is a separate question and has nothing to do with the twist.`. I rendered p. 815, 820–821 and 841–844 and read them.

1. Definition 4.6(5) forces ν|I_x = 1. The planes V_1 and V_2 are complementary isotropic planes, so the symplectic form gives a perfect pairing V_1 × V_2 → R(ν). If I_x acts by ξ on V_1 and by ξ^{-1} on V_2, then ν(g)⟨v,w⟩ = ⟨gv,gw⟩ = ξξ^{-1}⟨v,w⟩, so ν(g) = 1.

2. For r_{f_i}, Prop. 6.8(1) gives ν = λ_f∘χ_{μ,0}·ε^{-w}. Since x ≠ p, ν|I_x = χ_{μ,0}|I_x.

3. By p. 821, Π(x)/Π(x)^+ ≅ (Z/x)^× via λ mod x, where λ is the top-left entry of the Klingen Levi diag(λ, A, λ^{-1}det A). A scalar zI has λ = z, so Π(x) = Z_x^×·Π(x)^+. Hence Π(x)/Π(x)^+ acts on π_x^{Π(x)^+} through the central character on Z_x^×. By local Langlands, that character corresponds to ν(r_{f_i})|I_x. The proof itself says the same in the type-P case: "By [64, Corollary 3] all such characters have to lift the character ν∘r̄|I_x".

4. So in the "remaining case", where that character is nontrivial, ν(r_{f_i})|I_x = χ_{μ,0}|I_x ≠ 1. By step 1, r_{f_i} then does not satisfy Definition 4.6(5), and neither does the untwisted r. Such x ∈ Q really occur, because x ≡ 1 mod p and χ_{μ,0} is a character of p-power order. The theorem's statement includes the twist for exactly this reason.

5. A local model gives the same answer. Take the Klingen induction χ ⋊ τ with χ tamely ramified and τ unramified. Its L-parameter is φ_τ ⊕ χφ_τ, so inertia acts as 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ χ ⊕ χ. The two characters are mutually inverse only after twisting by ψ^{-1}, where ψ² = χ.

So the proof sets out to show a false statement (untwisted r satisfies (5)) and never mentions the twist that Theorem 6.13(4) asserts. The fix is short and routine: the twist keeps (2)–(4), as in the correction. Theorem 6.13(4) as stated is therefore correct; only its proof is incomplete as printed. Defence tried and failed. Definition 4.6(5) (p. 815) forces ν|I_x = 1 for x ∈ Q. The reason: R^4 = V_1⊕V_2 with V_1, V_2 isotropic, so the pairing V_1×V_2 is perfect, and ⟨gv,gw⟩ = ξ(g)ξ(g)^{-1}⟨v,w⟩ gives ν(g) = 1. The proof's "remaining case" is exactly the case where this fails for the untwisted r_{f_i}.

What [64, Cor. 3] says: I read it in Sorensen's arXiv 0806.4967v1, and the wording there is: "ρ_{π,ι}|I_{F_v} = 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ χ ⊕ χ … one can arrange for the two eigenspaces, for 1 and χ, to be totally isotropic." Since the eigenspaces are complementary Lagrangians, ν(r_{f_i})|I_x = χ ≠ 1. So (5) fails for r_{f_i}: the characters 1 and χ are not mutually inverse.

A second route gives the same answer. By p. 821, Π(x)/Π(x)^+ ≅ (Z/x)^× via λ mod x, and a central zI has λ = z. So Π(x) = Z_x^×Π(x)^+, and the nontrivial character in the proof is the central character on Z_x^×. That character is ramified, so ν∘r_{f_i} = λ_{f_i}∘χ_{μ,0}ε^{-w} is ramified at x. The case is not vacuous: Taylor–Wiles forms with nontrivial diamond character are exactly the ones treated here.

So the sentence "it suffices to show that each r_{f_i} does so", followed by "the required property holds by [64, Cor. 3]", is false if read literally about r_{f_i}. The twist announced in (4) never appears in the proof. With the twist, every check works (see correction), so (4) is true and the gap is routine. The twist must be by ψ^{-1}: tensoring with ψ gives inertial characters χ^{1/2} and χ^{3/2}, which are not inverse because χ has odd order greater than 1.

Downstream uses:
- Proof of Theorem 6.17 (p. 846): it says r′_m satisfies "all … except (1) and (6)". That is equally loose, since r′_m also fails (5). But it then twists by the inverse square root of χ_Q, so the final r_m satisfies (5) and Theorem 6.17 stands.
- Theorem 9.1(a) (p. 879): uses the untwisted inertial shape diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩). That is the related sourceIssues E129.
No stated result changes.

Side note on the labelling: for x ∈ Q both splittings {αβ|γδ} and {αγ|βδ} are Lagrangian. Neither the proof nor the correction says which one the [64, Cor. 3] eigenspaces realise for an arbitrary 𝔪. That is a separate labelling issue. - **Gap** at §6.3, proof of Theorem 6.13, second paragraph, p. 843. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text (proof of Theorem 6.13, v1 PDF p. 32). (it affects the proof). The source says `and hence we may regard T_{μ′}(Q) as acting faithfully on both H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a′,b′)(−∞)) and H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a′,b′)(−∞)_K). Thus we have T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m ↪ ∏_i O_{K_i}, where the K_i's are a finite collection of finite extensions of K, one for each minimal prime ℘_i of T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m. Each such minimal prime corresponds to an eigenform f_i for T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m.`; it should be `Before "Thus we have", add a proof that T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m ⊗ K is reduced. The anemic operators T_{x,i} (x ∉ S∪Q∪{p}) are semisimple. The ⟨u⟩ act through a finite abelian group. At x ∈ Q, take any π contributing to the m-part. By Assumption 6.12(2), x ≡ 1 mod p and Prop. 6.8(5), π_x is an irreducible principal series induced from a regular, tamely ramified character. Via the Klingen Jacquet module, U_{x,1}, U_{x,2} and ⟨u⟩ then act semisimply on π_x^{Π(x)^+}. With that, the embedding into ∏ O_{K_i} follows from torsion-freeness. This correction is right and minimal. An alternative correction (build r over the reduced anemic algebra and push it into T) is enough for Theorem 6.13 as literally stated, because properties (1)–(4) do not involve U_{x,i} or ⟨u⟩. It is not enough for the later use in step (a) of the proof of Theorem 9.1 without further argument.`. By Definition 5.13(2), T_μ(Q) is generated over T^an_μ(Q) by the U_{x,i} (x ∈ Q) and the ⟨u⟩. T_μ(Q)^β is its image in End(H^0(…)^β) (p. 841). The only justification the proof gives for the embedding is "Thus", following faithfulness on H^0(…) and H^0(…)_K.

Faithfulness gives T ⊗ K ↪ End_K(H^0_K), plus torsion-freeness. It does not give T ↪ ∏ over minimal primes of O_{K_i}. That needs T ⊗ K to be reduced, which needs the operators to act semisimply. The prime-to-level T_{x,i} are normal for the Petersson product and the ⟨u⟩ have finite order, so both are fine. Nothing in the paper addresses the U_{x,i} at Klingen-type level Π(x)^+. A search of the text for semisimplicity, reducedness, Petersson and diagonalization finds nothing relevant. Remark 6.14 only discusses torsion-freeness. The cited [20, Prop. 3.4.4] (Clozel–Harris–Taylor) is an argument for an anemic Hecke algebra, which is reduced for free.

Semisimplicity of U-operators at ramified level is not automatic in general (compare semisimplicity of U_p on old forms). The step also carries weight: the descent of ∏ r_{f_i} to T via [29, Lemma 7.1.1], and "it suffices to show that each r_{f_i} does so", both use the embedding.

I believe the claim is nevertheless true. By local–global compatibility, each π_x (x ∈ Q) is a principal series with parameter lifting four distinct characters, so the parameter is regular.
- Unramified case: π_x^{Π(x)^+} = π_x^{Π(x)}. Casselman's map gives an isomorphism onto the M(Z_x)-invariants of the Klingen Jacquet module. That module is a direct sum of 4 principal series with distinct cuspidal supports, each with a 1-dimensional spherical line. Both U_{x,1} (β_{x,1} is P-positive) and U_{x,2} (β_{x,2} is central in the Klingen Levi) act diagonally there.
- Tamely ramified case (Π(x) acting through ξ ≠ 1): the ξ-isotypic space is 1-dimensional.

So this is a fillable omission, not a false statement. It affects the proof, not the stated result. Checked on the rendered p. 843, with Def. 5.13 (pp. 834–835) and §5.1–5.2 (pp. 820–822).

(1) What the step needs. By Def. 5.13(2), T_μ(Q) is generated by the T_{x,i} (x ∉ S∪Q∪{p}), the U_{x,i} = [K_1(Q)β_{x,i}K_1(Q)] for x ∈ Q, where K_{x,1} = Π(x)^+ is Klingen-type, and the ⟨u⟩. Faithful action on the finite free O-module H^0(…) shows only that T is O-torsion-free, so T ↪ T⊗K ⊂ End_K(H^0_K). Landing in a product of the O_{K_i} additionally needs T⊗K to be reduced, i.e. every generator acting semisimply. The text gives no argument for this. The cited [20, Prop. 3.4.4] (CHT) works with an anemic Hecke algebra, where reducedness is automatic, so it does not fill the gap. No other passage does either: a search of the paper for "reduced" and "semisimpl" finds nothing relevant.

(2) Defence: the claim is true, so this is a gap, not an error. By Thm 5.2 the Hecke action on H^0_C factors through ⊕_π π_f^{K_1(Q)}. At x ∈ S and at p the algebra has no operators, so only x ∈ Q matters. For π in the m-part, local-global compatibility (Prop. 6.8(5), since r̄ is absolutely irreducible) and Assumption 6.12(2) give four characters whose Frobenius values are residually distinct. π_x has I(1)-invariants, because I(1) ⊂ Π(x)^+, so π_x is a subquotient of a tamely ramified principal series Ind χ′ with χ′ regular. Because x ≡ 1 mod p, no ratio equals x^{±1}, so π_x = Ind χ′ is irreducible. The Borel–Casselman-type isomorphism π_x^{Π^+} ≅ r_P(π_x)^{M∩Π^+} intertwines U_{x,2} (central in the Klingen Levi M) and U_{x,1} (the GL_2-factor operator diag(1,1,x,x), which is weakly positive) with M-Hecke operators. The four constituents Ind_{B_M}^M(wχ′) of r_P(π_x) are irreducible and have distinct cuspidal supports, since χ′ is regular. So r_P(π_x) is their direct sum. Each constituent has at most a one-dimensional (M∩Π^+, χ)-part, so U_{x,1}, U_{x,2} and ⟨u⟩ are simultaneously diagonalisable. U_{x,2} alone can have a repeated eigenvalue: with α=−γ and β=−δ the relation αδ=βγ holds and αβ=γδ. U_{x,1} still separates those lines, since α+β ≠ γ+δ. The paper has all these ingredients (§6.3 final paragraph, [31, Prop. 3.2.3], [64, Cors. 1, 3]) but never states or proves reducedness. It is not an obvious consequence of torsion-freeness: this is exactly where the Taylor–Wiles conditions enter.

(3) Consequences. Reducedness of T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m is essential and cannot be avoided by using T^red. The proof pushes r forward along the surjection T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m ↠ T_μ(Q)^β_m/I_{μ,m}, whose target may be non-reduced; this is the whole point of passing to high weight (Remark 6.14). Theorem 6.17 is proved through this surjection. Step (a) of the proof of Theorem 9.1 (p. 879) uses that r_{Q_N}(σ) for σ ∈ I_x is conjugate to diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩) in T(Q_N)^{α,β}_{m_N}. That identity is only accessible through the embedding T ↪ ∏ O_{K_i}, with ⟨u⟩ and U_{x,i} included, together with [64, Cor. 3]. So the gap sits in the proof chain of the main theorem. However, the missing statement is true and follows by the standard local argument above, so no stated result is affected. The source says `"For part (3), note that Q_p(X) ∈ T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪 factors as (X − d_{p,1})(X − p^{b−2}d_{p,2})(X − p^{a−1}d_{p,1})(X − p^𝐰 d_{p,4}) for units d_{p,i} ∈ T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪. We also have T_{p,1} ≡ β mod 𝔪 and Q_{p,2} ≡ αβ mod 𝔪 in T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪 (by definition of the idempotent e_β). Since Q_p(X) = X^4 − T_{p,1}X^3 + p^{b−2}Q_{p,2}X^2 − ⋯, we deduce that d_{p,1} ≡ β mod 𝔪 and d_{p,2} ≡ α mod 𝔪." (I checked this against a 300 dpi render of p. 843. The third factor really does print subscript "p,1".)`; it should be `(X − d_{p,1})(X − p^{b−2}d_{p,2})(X − p^{a−1}d_{p,3})(X − p^𝐰 d_{p,4}), so the third root is p^{a−1}d_{p,3}. The proof has already moved to weight μ' = (a',b') = (a+t, b+t). Read strictly, the exponents there should be b'−2, a'−1 and 𝐰' = a'+b'−3, and the next sentence should read "Q_p(X) = X^4 − T_{p,1}X^3 + p^{b'−2}Q_{p,2}X^2 − ⋯". The reason is that Q_{p,2} = (pT_{p,2}+(p+p^3)S_p)p^{2−b} (Definition 5.13(3), p. 835) is normalised using the b of the weight in question. For an eigenform of weight μ', Proposition 6.8(4) gives root valuations 0, b'−2, a'−1, 𝐰'. The unprimed letters are a notational abuse that runs through the whole paragraph. The substantive misprint is d_{p,1} printed where d_{p,3} belongs.`. Page images show the misprint is real.
- **Theorem 6.13(3) (p. 842)** prints Q_p(X) = (X − d_{p,1})(X − p^{b−2}d_{p,2})(X − p^{a−1}d_{p,3})(X − p^𝐰 d_{p,4}), with d_{p,3} also appearing in the matrix of (3)(b).
- **Proposition 6.8(4) (p. 839)** gives four distinct eigenvalues α_p, β_p, γ_p, δ_p with valuations 0, b−2, a−1, 𝐰.
- **The proof (p. 843)** prints d_{p,1} in the third factor and never mentions d_{p,3}, even though it says "for units d_{p,i}". Read literally, it claims the third root equals p^{a−1} times the first. Proposition 6.8(4) does not give this, and it is false in general.

**Redoing the deduction.** Let (A,B) be the working weight, with B ≥ 3 and A ≥ B, and 𝐖 = A+B−3. Take roots d_1, p^{B−2}d_2, p^{A−1}d_3, p^𝐖 d_4.
- From the X^3 coefficient: T_{p,1} = d_1 + p^{B−2}(…) ≡ d_1 mod p.
- From the X^2 coefficient, dividing by p^{B−2}: Q_{p,2} = d_1d_2 + p^{A−B+1}d_1d_3 + p^{A−1}d_1d_4 + p^{A−1}d_2d_3 + … ≡ d_1d_2 mod p. Division is allowed because T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪 embeds into ∏O_{K_i}.
- So d_{p,1} ≡ β and d_{p,2} ≡ α, as the paper says.
- The argument uses only these two coefficients mod 𝔪. It gives the same answer with the misprinted d_{p,1} in the third slot, so the proof is not affected.

**Downstream.** Nothing later uses this displayed line. Theorem 6.17 (pp. 845–846) calls on Theorem 6.13 only through its statement, which is correct, and through the reduction to high weight.

The misprint is in the Duke version and in arXiv v1. This correction is right, including its secondary remark about primed exponents. - **Gap** at §6.4: Definition 6.15(2), p. 844, and the sentence after the definition of e_{α,β}, p. 845. Compare Definition 5.13, p. 834, Lemma 7.10, pp. 852–853, Theorem 7.2, p. 847, and the proof of Theorem 9.1, pp. 878–880. arXiv 1907.08691v1 (§6.4, pp. 33–34) has the same text. (it affects the proof). The source says `p. 844, Definition 6.15: "We say that r̄ is Katz modular of weight σ if there exists a maximal ideal m_∅ of T_σ such that (1) we have r̄_{m_∅} ≅ r̄, and (2) there exists a form η ∈ H^0(X, ω(a,2)_{K/O})[m_∅] such that T_{p,1}(η) = (α+β)η, Q_{p,2}(η) = (αβ)η." p. 845, after Assumption 6.16: "We let m be any maximal ideal of T_σ(Q) containing m_∅. Let e_{α,β} be the idempotent lim_{→n}((T_{p,1} − α̃ − β̃)(Q_{p,2} − α̃β̃))^{n!}, where α̃ and β̃ are lifts of α and β to O, and define H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^{α,β} = e_{α,β}H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O}). The assumption that r̄ is Katz modular implies that this space is nonzero after localization at m." For comparison, p. 834, Definition 5.13(1)–(2): "The anemic Hecke algebra T^an_μ(Q) ⊂ End_O(H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O})) is the O-algebra generated by the operators T_{x,i} for x ∉ S ∪ Q ∪ {p}. … When Q = ∅, we have T^an_μ(∅) = T_μ(∅) and we denote this algebra by T_μ."`; it should be `(i) Either take η cuspidal in Definition 6.15(2), i.e. η ∈ H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})[m_∅], or add a lemma. The lemma: since r̄ is absolutely irreducible, m_∅ is non-Eisenstein, so the m_∅-part of the boundary vanishes mod p and H^0(X, ω(a,2)_k)[m_∅] = H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)[m_∅]. One route is the Siegel Φ-operator: it is Hecke-equivariant and carries non-cuspidal eigenforms to eigensystems with reducible Galois representations. Lemma 7.10 does not supply this, because it holds only after ⊗K. (ii) Restrict "any maximal ideal m of T_σ(Q) containing m_∅" to the ideals of Theorem 7.2, one for each isotropic labelling at each x ∈ Q. Those are the only ones used later. If "any" is kept, the argument must be added. Applying Theorem 7.2 for each labelling handles only these old-type ideals at level X_0(Q). Two more facts are needed. First, the prime-to-p part of Δ_Q acts trivially on the m-part, which follows from local-global compatibility at x, since r̄ is unramified at x. Second, every maximal ideal above m_∅ is old-type, which is the no-newforms consequence of Assumption 7.1. (iii) Separately, read e_{α,β} as the projector onto the generalized (α+β, αβ)-eigenspace. As printed it kills η. This is sourceIssues E59.`. I transcribed p. 834, 844, 845 and 846 from the page images; the text is as quoted above.

(1) Cuspidality. T_σ acts on cusp forms: Definition 5.13 embeds it in End_O(H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})). So does T_σ(Q), and the space made nonzero on p. 845 is cuspidal. Definition 6.15(2) only asks for η in the full space H^0(X, ω(a,2)_{K/O}). "[m_∅]" there makes sense only through the abstract Hecke algebra; the paper spells out this abuse for H^2 in Assumption 7.7 but not here. If η were not cuspidal, m_∅ could lie in the cuspidal support only with other T_{p,1}/Q_{p,2}-eigenvalues. Then H = H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^{α,β,∨}_{m_∅} would be 0.

The paper proves the boundary is Eisenstein only after ⊗K (Lemma 7.10, via Harris–Zucker). It never proves this with torsion coefficients. The statement is true: r̄ is absolutely irreducible, and boundary eigensystems give reducible representations, e.g. via Φ-operator/q-expansion compatibility. It can also be derived from A^s, H^1-vanishing in high weight and Lemma 7.10. So this is a gap, not an error.

(2) Arbitrary m. Katz modularity is a level-K condition. Getting from it to a nonzero (α,β)-part at every m ⊇ m_∅ of T_σ(Q) is a level-raising statement. Pulling back η gives support at only some m, not all. The paper gives no argument at this point. Theorem 7.2, proved later, covers only the m attached to the fixed labelling (U_{x,1} ≡ α_x+β_x, xU_{x,2} ≡ α_xβ_x). Other m need relabelling, plus a Δ_Q-invariants argument that every m is of one of these types.

(3) As printed, the e_{α,β} kills η: η is ϖ-torsion and (T_{p,1} − α̃ − β̃)η = 0. So the sentence can only be read with the corrected idempotent (sourceIssues E59).

Reach. The proof of Theorem 6.17 does not use the nonvanishing. But the Q = ∅ case, H ≠ 0, is needed in Theorem 9.1: if H = 0, Proposition 3.3 gives only "0 is free", and R^min ≅ T^{α,β}_{σ,m_∅} fails. Its only justification in the paper is this sentence. §9 uses only the m_N of Theorem 7.2, so part (2) matters only for the remark as stated. I think the claims are true, so the gap can be filled.

Side note, not checked in detail: for an m whose U_{x,1}-eigenvalue is α_x+γ_x, local–global compatibility would seem to make inertia act by scalars on lifts of {α_x,γ_x} ⊕ {β_x,δ_x}, not the {α_x,β_x} ⊕ {γ_x,δ_x} that Definition 4.6(5) requires. That would also make "any m" questionable in Theorems 6.13 and 6.17. Both texts are confirmed from the page images (pp. 844–845, and v1 p. 33).

(1) Cuspidality. T_σ = T_σ(∅) is defined (Definition 5.13, p. 834) as a subalgebra of End_O(H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O})), i.e. through the cusp forms. The idempotent e_{α,β}, and hence T_σ(Q)^{α,β}, is also defined on the cuspidal space. Definition 6.15(2) instead puts η in the full space H^0(X, ω(a,2)_{K/O}). This looks deliberate rather than a dropped "(−∞)": Lemma 8.8 (p. 860) defines T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2} on the full space H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j,k)_{K/O}), and §1 also uses the full space via the Koecher principle.

For Q = ∅ we have m = m_∅, and the sentence claims e_{α,β}H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})_{m_∅} ≠ 0. That follows from η only if η is cuspidal. The only comparison of the two sheaves in the paper is Lemma 7.10 (pp. 852–853), which is proved after ⊗K via boundary cohomology over C and says nothing about torsion. The missing fact is standard and I believe it is true: η is ϖ-torsion, and its image under restriction to the boundary would be killed by the non-Eisenstein m_∅. But the paper does not state or prove it.

(2) Arbitrary m ⊇ m_∅ for Q ≠ ∅. T_σ(Q) acts faithfully, so H_m ≠ 0 automatically. But T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2} are not in T_σ(Q), so the (α,β)-part at m is not automatic. Different m above m_∅ differ in their U_{x,i} and ⟨u⟩ eigenvalues. The claim is plausibly true: Theorem 7.2 for each of the four isotropic labellings gives the old-type ideals at level X_0(Q), and local-global compatibility together with Assumption 7.1 rules out the others. But none of this appears at p. 845, and Theorem 7.2 is stated only for one labelling.

Defence attempts. §6.3 makes no such claim, and Theorem 6.13 has the same degenerate form at an m where the β-part vanishes (its conclusion is then vacuous). So the "any m" part is at worst an unjustified remark, and Theorem 6.17's proof never uses it.

What uses the passage. §9 (p. 879) applies Theorem 6.17 only with Q = ∅ (m = m_∅) and with Q = Q_N and m = m_N, the ideal of Theorem 7.2. For m_N, nonvanishing follows from (H_N)_Δ ≅ H (Theorem 7.2 and item (b), p. 879), so the "any m" part affects nothing. The Q = ∅ case is different. The proof of Theorem 9.1 concludes from Proposition 3.3 (p. 812; its hypotheses do not force H ≠ 0) that H = H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^{α,β,∨}_{m_∅} is free, and hence that R^min ≅ T^{α,β}_{σ,m_∅}. That step needs H ≠ 0: otherwise T = 0, while R^min, an object of C_O, is not. The only justification of H ≠ 0 in the paper is this sentence with Q = ∅. For a non-cuspidal η, as Definition 6.15 allows, that sentence depends on the missing cuspidality step.

So this gap is not harmless. The gap sits in the proof of Theorem 9.1. The result stands once (i) is supplied. - **Error** at §7.1, Assumption 7.1, p. 846; Theorem 7.2 (definition of R_x, pr_x) and Theorem 7.3, p. 847. The same text is in arXiv:1907.08691v1, pp. 34–35. (it affects a stated result). The source says `Assumption 7.1 (p. 846): "For each x ∈ Q, we have x ≡ 1 mod p, and r̄_{𝔪∅} | G_x is a direct sum of four pairwise distinct characters with Frobenius eigenvalues α_x, β_x, γ_x, δ_x. We assume that the eigenvalues have been labeled so that the plane λ(α_x) ⊕ λ(β_x) is isotropic, and hence α_xδ_x = β_xγ_x." Theorem 7.2 (p. 847): "Let μ and 𝔪∅ be as above, and suppose that Assumption 7.1 holds. Let 𝔪 denote the ideal of T_μ(Q) containing 𝔪∅ together with the elements xU_{x,2} − α'_xβ'_x and U_{x,1} − α'_x − β'_x for each x ∈ Q. Then 𝔪 is maximal and there is an isomorphism pr_Q ∘ i : H^0(X, ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O})_{𝔪∅} ⥲ H^0(X_0(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O})_𝔪 ... Here i is the natural inclusion and pr_Q is defined as follows. For x ∈ Q, let R_x denote the Hecke operator R_x = (xU_{x,2} − α'_xγ'_x)(xU_{x,2} − β'_xδ'_x)(xU_{x,2} − γ'_xδ'_x) ∈ T_μ(Q), and let pr_x denote the idempotent pr_x = lim_{n→∞} (R'_x)^{n!}. Then the pr_x's commute with one another and pr_Q denotes their product." Theorem 7.3 (p. 847) states the same isomorphism pr_Q ∘ i for W^sub_{μ,K/O} under a vanishing hypothesis.`; it should be `Assumption 7.1 needs a further condition on the labelling: α_xβ_x ≠ γ_xδ_x in k. Since ν(r̄)(Frob_x) = 1 for x ≡ 1 mod p, this is the same as (α_xβ_x)² ≠ 1, and also the same as α_x ≠ −γ_x or β_x ≠ −δ_x. Genestier–Tilouine (the paper's [31], §5.1, p. 212) state this very condition in their definition of Taylor–Wiles primes, as "(ᾱ_qβ̄_q)² ≠ 1". A good labelling always exists when the four eigenvalues are pairwise distinct: - the split {α,β}|{γ,δ} clashes exactly when α = −γ; - the split {α,γ}|{β,δ} clashes exactly when α = −β; - if both clashed we would get β = γ, which is excluded. So swapping β_x and γ_x cures a clash. For the application, the labellings chosen in §4 (p. 815) for the primes Q_N of Prop. 4.10 must satisfy the condition, since §6.3–6.4 and §9 reuse them. Assumptions 6.12(2) and 6.16(2) should say the same. Another fix is to replace the third factor of R_x by (U_{x,1} − γ'_x − δ'_x). U_{x,1} separates {α,β} from {γ,δ}: in the clash case the difference of the sums is 2(α+β) ≠ 0. Separately, R'_x in the formula for pr_x is undefined and should read R_x. This is a misprint, and arXiv v1 has it too.`. I checked this on the rendered p. 846 and p. 847 images and on arXiv v1 pp. 34–35. The text is identical in both, including the undefined R'_x. I redid the computation.

(1) Why R_x can lie in 𝔪. The third factor of R_x can be written as xU_{x,2} − γ'δ' = (xU_{x,2} − α'β') + (α'β' − γ'δ'). The first term is in 𝔪 by definition. If αβ = γδ in k, the second term is in ϖO ⊂ 𝔪∅. So R_x ∈ 𝔪. This is pure algebra and needs no knowledge of U_{x,2}-eigenvalues.

(2) When αβ = γδ is allowed. Using αδ = βγ = ν, we get γδ = ν²/(αβ). So αβ = γδ iff αβ = ±ν. The case αβ = ν would force α = γ, which is excluded. The case αβ = −ν is equivalent to α = −γ, and also to β = −δ. Assumption 7.1 and Prop. 4.10(3) (which only asks for "four pairwise distinct eigenvalues") do not exclude it. Concrete check in F_7 with ν = 1: (α,β,γ,δ) = (2, 3, 5, 4), which is (2, −1/2, −2, 1/2). These are distinct, αδ = βγ = 1, and αβ = −1 ≠ ν, so the plane is isotropic. Also αβ = γδ = 6. Then R_x mod 𝔪 = (6−3)(6−5)(6−6) = 0. Since x ≡ 1 mod p and ν(r̄) is a power of the cyclotomic character, ν(Frob_x) = 1. For r̄ with image containing Sp4(F_p), Chebotarev gives such primes x.

(3) Why the theorem then fails. On the 𝔪-part, every element of the finite ϖ^n-torsion is killed by a power of 𝔪. So R_x^{n!} → 0 there, pr_x acts as 0 on the 𝔪-part, and pr_Q ∘ i = 0. But the source H^0(X, ·)_{𝔪∅} is nonzero: T_μ acts faithfully (Def. 5.13) and 𝔪∅ is a maximal ideal. So the claimed isomorphism fails. Theorem 7.3 and Lemmas 7.4–7.6 fail the same way.

(4) Further checks. The first two factors reduce to (αβ−αγ) and (αβ−βδ), which are nonzero since β ≠ γ and α ≠ δ. The swap argument is also right: a clash for the new labelling needs α = −β, and together with α = −γ this gives β = γ, which is excluded.

(5) Where this matters. Theorem 7.2 is used in the patching step (b) of the proof of Thm 9.1 (p. 879), with Q = Q_N from Prop. 4.10, and nothing there fixes the labelling. So a stated result is false as printed in an edge case its hypotheses allow. The main theorems survive once the labelling is chosen correctly, which is always possible. I tried to defend the paper and could not.

(1) R_x lies in 𝔪 in the clash case. The third factor can be written as xU_{x,2} − γ'δ' = (xU_{x,2} − α'β') + (α'β' − γ'δ'). The first term is in 𝔪 by definition. If αβ = γδ in k, the second term lies in ϖO ⊂ 𝔪∅. So R_x ∈ 𝔪. This is pure algebra: it needs no facts about U_{x,2}-eigenvalues and no reading of the undefined R'_x.

(2) The theorem then fails. The target is ϖ-power torsion, and each element is killed by a power of 𝔪. So R_x is topologically nilpotent on H^0(X_0(Q), ·)_𝔪, and lim R_x^{n!} = 0 there. Hence pr_Q∘i = 0 into the 𝔪-part. If 𝔪 were not proper the target would be 0, which also fails.

The source is nonzero. By Def. 5.13 (with Q = ∅), T_μ acts faithfully on H^0(X, ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O}). T_μ is finite over O and so semilocal, and 𝔪∅ is one of its maximal ideals, so the 𝔪∅-part is nonzero. Therefore Theorem 7.2 fails. So do Theorem 7.3 and Lemmas 7.4–7.6, which assert that pr_Q∘i is an isomorphism with inverse d_Q^{-1}tr.

(3) Assumption 7.1 allows the clash. Here ν = 1, so γ = 1/β and δ = 1/α, and αβ = γδ ⇔ (αβ)² = 1. The case αβ = 1 would force β = δ, which is excluded. The case αβ = −1 means α = −γ, which is not excluded.

Example in F_7: (α, β, γ, δ) = (2, 3, 5, 4). These are distinct, αδ = βγ = 1, and αβ = 6 ≠ 1, so {α,β} is isotropic. Also αβ = γδ = 6, and R_x ≡ (6−3)(6−5)(6−6) = 0.

A short computer enumeration over p ≤ 23 checked that:
- R_x ≡ 0 mod 𝔪 exactly in the clash case, since the first two factors are always units;
- the two Lagrangian splittings never both clash.

This kind of Frobenius occurs in the paper itself. Example 4.11 (p. 819) builds the element c·(g,h), with eigenvalues ±(xy)^{1/2}, ±(xy)^{−1/2}. That is {s, −s, 1/s, −1/s}, and its labelling (s, −1/s, −s, 1/s) clashes. Prop. 4.10(3) and the §4 labelling rule (p. 815) ask only for "four pairwise distinct eigenvalues" and isotropic planes.

(4) The cited source has the missing hypothesis. The proof of Thm 7.3 rests on [31, Prop. 11.1.2]. Genestier–Tilouine define Taylor–Wiles primes (§5.1, p. 212) by: "P_{π,q} a quatre racines distinctes ᾱ_q, β̄_q, γ̄_q = β̄_q^{-1} et δ̄_q = ᾱ_q^{-1} dans k, telles que (ᾱ_qβ̄_q)² ≠ 1". Their injectivity proof (p. 282) inverts (α_qβ_q − α_qγ_q)(α_qβ_q − β_qδ_q)(α_qβ_q − γ_qδ_q), which needs exactly this condition. Calegari–Geraghty dropped it, so the citation does not rescue the statement.

(5) Where it is used. Theorem 7.2 feeds step (b) of the proof of Thm 9.1 (p. 879), with Q = Q_N from Prop. 4.10 and 𝔪_N as in Thm 7.2. Nothing in that proof fixes the labelling. Since a non-clashing labelling always exists, the fix is to add the condition and choose labellings accordingly. Only an abstract Hecke-equivariant isomorphism is used in (b), so Thm 9.1 and the main theorems survive.

The steps behind the correction check out:
- β ≠ −δ ⇔ αβ ≠ −ν; the alternative split {α,γ}|{β,δ} fails iff α = −β; and if both splits fail, then α = δ.
- The condition α ≠ −γ and the swap argument are right. That image is the interior cohomology H̄^2 as the paper defines it on p. 824. (2) "a characteristic 0 form of level N = N(r̄)" (the form has weight (2,2)), in place of "of weight N = N(r̄)".`. (1) The paper's own conventions give the direction. On p. 824 (§5.2, checked on the page image) it says "This bundle has extensions V^sub ⊂ V^can to X(C) ... We have V^sub = V^can(−∞)". It then defines the interior cohomology as H̄^i(X(C),V) := Im(H^i(X(C),V^sub) → H^i(X(C),V^can)). On p. 854 it again says "interior cohomology (the image of H^i(ω(a,b)(−∞)) in H^i(ω(a,b)))". There is no natural map from ω^can to ω^can(−D) in the same weight, so "the image of H^2(can) in H^2(sub)" has no meaning under the paper's conventions. With the swap, "the image is zero" is formally weaker than the vanishing H^2(ω(j,2)^sub) = 0 that the same paragraph says is used for j ≥ 4, which is exactly how the sentence presents it. The next sentence of this paragraph also speaks of "an auxiliary Siegel modular form G of the same level also of weight (2,2)". So "weight N = N(r̄)" should read "level". Both slips are only in a speculative remark in the introduction. The hypothesis the proofs actually use is stated correctly with subcanonical sheaves: Assumption 7.7 (p. 851), "H^2(X_Δ(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_𝔪 is trivial", and hypothesis (6) of the main theorem, Theorem 9.1 in §9 (p. 878). Lemma 7.5 (p. 849) and Lemma 7.6 (p. 850): "...is an isomorphism with inverse d_Q^{−1}tr." The proofs of Lemmas 7.5 and 7.6 repeat "with inverse d_Q^{−1}tr" for the auxiliary vertical maps. Each is checked against the page image (display on p. 847 checked at 220 dpi). arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text with the same numbering: Theorem 7.3 on p. 35, Lemmas 7.4 and 7.5 on p. 36, Lemma 7.6 on p. 37.`; it should be `pr_Q∘i is an isomorphism, but d_Q^{−1}tr is not its inverse. Set v_Q := tr∘pr_Q∘i, an endomorphism of H^0(X,·)_{m_∅}. It is a p-adic limit of spherical Hecke operators at the primes of Q, since tr∘[Π g Π]∘i is K-spherical. So v_Q lies in (the completion of) T_{m_∅} and commutes with h, h̃, i, tr, restriction to S and S_0(Q), and the connecting maps. Under Assumption 7.1 (x ≡ 1 mod p, and α_x, β_x, γ_x, δ_x distinct, so the parameter is regular mod ϖ), the value mod m_∅ is d_x·c_x ≡ 4·(1/4) = 1. So v_Q ≡ 1 mod m_∅, and v_Q is a unit. The correct inverse is v_Q^{−1}∘tr = (tr∘pr_Q∘i)^{−1}∘tr, restricted to the m-summand, which is defined over O. In the statements of Theorem 7.3 and Lemmas 7.5 and 7.6, replace d_Q^{−1}tr by this. In Lemma 7.4, drop "mutually inverse" in favour of "the left-hand pr_Q∘i is an isomorphism", and use f = v_Q^{−1}tr(F) = h^t v_Q^{−1}tr(g) in the proof. The proofs then go through unchanged.`. Set-up from the paper. K_{x,0} = Π(x) is the Klingen parahoric (§5.2, p. 822). pr_x is "the idempotent" lim(R'_x)^{n!} (p. 847), so pr_Q∘i sends the spherical vector v0 to its component in one U_{x,2}-eigenline of π_x^{Π(x)}. tr∘i = d_Q, so d_Q^{−1}tr is averaging e_K over GSp4(Z_x)/Π(x). The composite therefore acts by c = (e_K-coefficient of that component). The four c's sum to 1 because v0 is the sum of its components, so c = 1 cannot hold in general.

I redid the computation independently and checked it by direct computation.

(1) GL2 analogue by q-expansions. With U f_α = α f_α, f_α = f − βVf and tr(Vf) = (a/p)f in weight 2, I get (p+1)^{−1}tr(pr_α f) = (αp−β)/((p+1)(α−β))·f. This equals f only if α = pβ, and it is ≡ 1/2 mod (p−1). The Bernstein-presentation model reproduces this exactly (for example −7/6 and 13/6 at q = 5).

(2) GSp4, principal-series module H⊗_A χ of the Iwahori–Hecke algebra (Bernstein relations), with W_J = ⟨s2⟩ (Klingen) and λ = (0,1,2) ↔ β_{x,2}. The θ's commute and are additive (checked). At q = 7, χ = (2,3,5), the four values are c = −5863/2000, 779/200, −11/1000 and 19/400. They sum to 1 and none equals 1. With parameters t = (2,3,5,15/2) the same computation gives 339663/154000, −1083/875, 59/1750, −247/154000, agreeing exactly with an independent computation. At q = 1 every c = 1/4 = |W_J|/|W|. For (p,q) = (13,53), (11,23), (23,47), (7,29), with θ-eigenvalues distinct mod p, every c ≡ 1/4 mod p and (1+q+q²+q³)c ≡ 1 mod p.

(3) Cross-checks. A Macdonald c-function formula, c_C = Σ_{w∈C}∏_{α>0}(1−q^{−1}χ(wα^∨)^{−1})/(1−χ(wα^∨)^{−1}) / P_W(q^{−1}), gives the same numbers. Using the opposite-chamber operator T_{w0}θ_{w0λ}T_{w0}^{−1} (antidominant β_{x,2}) gives the same set of four values, so the result does not depend on conventions. c also varies with χ, so no rescaling of tr can make d_Q^{−1}tr an inverse.

Consequence: for p ≥ 5 the claimed inverse acts as ≡ 4^{−#Q} ≠ 1 on the nonzero 𝔪_∅-part, and for any p it is ≠ 1 for generic Satake parameters. So the printed "explicit inverse" is false.

Dependence. The proof of Theorem 7.2 (pp. 850–851) and everything after it use only that the pr_Q maps are isomorphisms. Lemma 7.6 follows from the five lemma. Lemma 7.4 and the K to K/O step of Theorem 7.3 need some O-integral inverse that commutes with h, and the corrected one qualifies. So the false claims are stated clauses of Theorem 7.3 and Lemmas 7.4–7.6, and nothing downstream breaks. The formulas above, the congruences and the correction all check out. DEFENCE ATTEMPTS, ALL FAILED.
(a) The paper says tr is "the trace map associated to X_0(Q) → X". The map is finite étale of degree [K:K_0(Q)] = d_Q (the Klingen parahoric Π(x), §5.1), so tr∘i = d_Q. No renormalisation of tr is in play.

(b) A convention-free contradiction. Assumption 7.1 fixes only that λ(α_x)⊕λ(β_x) is isotropic, and four labellings satisfy it: (α,β,γ,δ), (α,γ,β,δ), (β,δ,α,γ) and (γ,δ,α,β). Each preserves α_xδ_x = β_xγ_x. The theorem is stated for each of them. The corresponding pr^{(j)} (p. 847: R_x kills the other three products) project onto the four generalized eigenspaces of xU_{x,2} on the old part, taking the products distinct mod ϖ, which is generic. So Σ_j pr^{(j)}∘i = i. If each d_Q^{−1}tr∘pr^{(j)}∘i were the identity, summing would give d_Q^{−1}tr∘i = 4·id. But d_Q^{−1}tr∘i = id, so 3·id = 0 on H^0(X, W_K)_{m_∅} ≠ 0. Hence the claimed inverse fails for some admissible labelling, for every p: over K, and on ϖ^n-torsion for large n.

(c) A GL2 analogue, redone by hand with tr(Vf) = q^{1−k}a_q f and αβ = q^{k−1}. Here (q+1)^{−1}tr(pr_α f) = (αq−β)/((q+1)(α−β))·f. This is ≡ 1/2 mod (q−1), and the two values sum to 1.

(d) A computer implementation of the Casselman–Macdonald formula. It verifies Macdonald's identity Σ_w ∏ c_a(wχ) = Q_W(q^{−1}). At q = 7 and z = (3,5), the four coset values are 1/700, −29/700, −377/700 and 221/140 for W_P = ⟨short⟩. For W_P = ⟨long⟩ they are −8/175, −52/35, −443/700 and 443/140. Each set sums to 1, and no value is 1. For (q,p) = (23,11) and (29,7) with regular parameters, every value is ≡ 1/4 mod p and d·c ≡ 1, for either parabolic. For p ≠ 3 the claim therefore already fails on the nonzero ϖ-torsion. This agrees with the computation in (2) above: each set of four values sums to 1, none equals 1, and for (q,p) = (23,11) and (29,7) every value is ≡ 1/4 mod p.

CONSEQUENCES.
- The explicit inverse is used in the K-to-K/O injectivity step of Theorem 7.3's proof, and in Lemma 7.4's divisibility argument (f = d_Q^{−1}tr(F) = h^t d_Q^{−1}tr(g)).
- Lemmas 7.5 and 7.6 need only that the vertical maps are isomorphisms (the Lemma 7.4 argument, and the five lemma).
- The proof of Theorem 7.2 (pp. 850–851) and its only later use (§9, p. 879: "Combining this with the isomorphism of Theorem 7.2") use only the isomorphism.
- With v_Q^{−1}∘tr as the inverse, every step works: it is O-integral, commutes with h, h̃ and restriction, and is intertwined by h^t across weights. So the isomorphisms in Theorems 7.2 and 7.3 and Lemmas 7.4–7.6 all survive. What is false is the stated "inverse d_Q^{−1}tr" / "mutually inverse" clauses in the statements of Theorem 7.3 and Lemmas 7.4–7.6.

(Aside, not assessed: if αβ ≡ γδ mod ϖ, which is possible when (α,β,γ,δ) = (α,β,−α,−β), then R_x does not separate m from the ideal with U_{x,1} ≡ γ+δ.) - **Misprint** at §7.1, Theorem 7.2, p. 847; arXiv:1907.08691v1 Theorem 7.2, p. 35. The source says `"Here i is the natural inclusion and pr_Q is defined as follows. For x ∈ Q, let R_x denote the Hecke operator R_x = (xU_{x,2} − α'_xγ'_x)(xU_{x,2} − β'_xδ'_x)(xU_{x,2} − γ'_xδ'_x) ∈ T_μ(Q), and let pr_x denote the idempotent pr_x = lim_{n→∞} (R'_x)^{n!}. Then the pr_x's commute with one another and pr_Q denotes their product." (p. 847, checked on the page image rendered at 130 dpi.)`; it should be `pr_x = lim_{n→∞} (R_x)^{n!}. The prime on R_x should be dropped. The primed letters α'_x, β'_x, γ'_x, δ'_x are already used inside R_x for the lifts to O^× of the Frobenius eigenvalues.`. The page image of p. 847 confirms that the displayed idempotent is printed as lim_{n→∞}(R'_x)^{n!}, while only the unprimed R_x is defined, in the display just above it. I searched the full text of the published version and of arXiv v1 for any R'_x or R_x. Each has exactly three hits, all in this passage: the sentence "let R_x denote", the display defining R_x, and the display for pr_x with the prime. So R'_x is never defined. The only sensible reading is R_x itself. The primes in this section mark the lifts α'_x, ..., δ'_x ∈ O^× of α_x, ..., δ_x ∈ k^× (p. 847, first line), and R_x is already built from those lifts. I checked the formula myself. The level K_0(Q) is the Siegel parahoric, m contains xU_{x,2} − α'_xβ'_x and U_{x,1} − α'_x − β'_x, and α_xδ_x = β_xγ_x (Assumption 7.1). The Frobenius-stable Lagrangian planes therefore give the eigenvalues αβ, αγ, βδ, γδ for xU_{x,2}. R_x is the product of the factors for the three eigenvalues other than αβ. lim R_x^{n!} is then the idempotent of the finite Hecke algebra that kills the generalized eigenspaces where R_x is nilpotent and is the identity where R_x is a unit, which is exactly what pr_x is meant to be. No normalization of R_x is needed, because the n! limit is already idempotent. arXiv:1907.08691v1, p. 35, prints the same thing (checked on the rendered image): "pr_x = lim_{n→∞}(R'_x)^{n!}", with R_x defined identically just above. Later text uses only pr_Q: Theorem 7.3, its proof (which cites [GT05, Prop. 11.1.2]), and the diagrams in §7 on pp. 848–851. None of it mentions R'_x or depends on a separately defined primed operator, so the proofs and stated results are unaffected. The diamond operators act trivially on H^0(X_0(Q), ·), and they act unipotently on H^0(X_Δ(Q_N), ·) when Δ is a p-group. Hence all the localizations used later are unchanged. (b) Keep the printed definition and add the missing argument. First, a residual step: by [64, Cor. 3], and because r̄ is unramified at x, ⟨u⟩ ≡ 1 modulo every maximal ideal containing m_∅. So T/m is local with residue field k. Second, an integral step: pass to high weight using the surjections T_{μ'}(Q) ↠ T_μ(Q)/I_{μ,m} of Remark 6.5, together with Chevalley's lemma. In high weight, ⟨u⟩ equals the inertia character on the (γ_x, δ_x)-plane of the T^an-valued Galois representation, as in Theorem 9.1(a). By Definition 5.13(2), T_μ(Q) ⊂ End_O H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O}) is generated over T^an_μ(Q) by the U_{x,i} and the diamond operators ⟨u⟩, u ∈ Δ_Q. In T_μ(Q), m_∅ denotes the pushforward ideal (§6.3, §7.1), and §6.3 says explicitly that it 'need not be maximal'. Modulo the listed ideal, T^an maps onto k and U_{x,1} and xU_{x,2} become constants. The quotient is therefore a k-algebra generated by the images of the ⟨u⟩, which satisfy ⟨u⟩^{|Δ_Q|} = 1 and nothing more a priori. So maximality needs two things: (a) no nontrivial residual diamond character occurs, and (b) ⟨u⟩ − 1 lies in the ideal, not merely in its radical. Neither the proof of Theorem 7.3 nor Lemmas 7.4–7.6 nor the proof on pp. 850–851 mentions maximality or diamond operators. The only other places the ⟨u⟩ appear are Definition 5.13 and §9, step (a). The assertion is therefore unproved as printed. It is not false: the local–global compatibility at x ∈ Q plus Carayol argument sketched in the correction proves it, using results the paper cites elsewhere. So in this setting the quotient is the field k, although a priori such a quotient need not be a field (it could be non-reduced). This is a gap rather than an error, since the claim is true, and only the proof is affected, since every later use needs only the maximal ideal that correction (a) supplies. I confirmed the printed text by rendering p. 834, 846, 847, 851 and 879. As an ideal of T_μ(Q), m_∅ is the extension of the maximal ideal of T^an_μ(Q). The paper itself warns on p. 841 that this extension 'need not be maximal'. Modulo the printed ideal I, the images of T^an_μ(Q), U_{x,1} and U_{x,2} are scalars. The quotient T/I is therefore a finite k-algebra generated by the images of the diamond operators (and U_{x,0}). Such a quotient of k[Δ_Q] can be non-local through the prime-to-p part of Δ_Q, and non-reduced through its p-part (x ≡ 1 mod p). The statement and proof of Theorem 7.2 use the word 'maximal' only in the statement itself. Theorem 7.3 relies on [31, Prop. 11.1.2] for the isomorphism, not for maximality. Lemmas 7.4–7.6 and the five-lemma argument only concern H^0(X_0(Q), ·)_m, on which ⟨u⟩ acts trivially. None of them shows ⟨u⟩ − 1 ∈ I.

The paper states this only for the α,β-ordinary algebra of Theorem 6.17, not for the full T_μ(Q) of Theorem 7.2. No nearby statement or cited source supplies the step. The attribution to Genestier–Tilouine covers only 'sufficiently high weight', and no argument is given for lowering the weight. In the first square the vertical maps are pr_Q∘i, going up. In the second they are d_Q^{-1}tr, going down. The right-hand vertical maps are marked ≅. Then: "In particular, the left-hand vertical maps are mutually inverse isomorphisms." Proof of Lemma 7.4, p. 849: "(Note that since X_0(Q) and X are smooth (and in particular irreducible) over k, multiplication by h is injective on H^0.)" Proof of Lemma 7.5, p. 850: "The lemma now follows by the same argument as Lemma 7.4." arXiv:1907.08691v1 (Lemmas 7.4–7.5, pp. 36–37 there) has the same text: "co-cartesian", the same parenthetical about "smooth (and in particular irreducible)", and "The lemma now follows by the same argument as the previous lemma."`; it should be `Keep "co-Cartesian" as printed: it is true, so it should not be changed to "Cartesian". The genuine slip is the parenthetical on p. 849. It should read: since X_k and X_0(Q)_k are smooth, their connected components are integral, and h is not identically zero on any component, because the ordinary locus is dense. Hence h, and so h^t, is a nonzerodivisor, and multiplication by it is injective on H^0 of the locally free sheaves W^sub. In the proof of Lemma 7.5 the "same argument" also needs h̃^s to be injective on H^0(S, W^sub_{μ,k}) and H^0(S_0(Q), W^sub_{μ,k}). The paper leaves this unstated. It holds for two reasons. First, S = V(h) is a Cartier divisor in a smooth threefold, so it is Cohen–Macaulay of pure dimension 2 and has no embedded points. Second, every irreducible component of S has its generic point in the p-rank-1 locus, where h̃ does not vanish, because the p-rank-0 locus and S ∩ boundary have dimension at most 1.`. I transcribed the text from renders of pp. 847–850.

(1) "co-Cartesian" is not a misprint. Take the upward square: C = H^0(X,W_μ)_{m∅} → D = H^0(X,W_{μ'})_{m∅} along the bottom, A → B along the top, with vertical maps ψ: C → A and φ: D → B, and φ an isomorphism. In an abelian category this square is a pushout iff ψ is epi, and a pullback iff ψ is an isomorphism. The proof explicitly notes that h^t is injective. With that, commutativity gives ψ injective: if ψ(c) = 0, then φ(h^t c) = h^t ψ(c) = 0, so c = 0. The same inputs give τψ = id, where τ = d_Q^{-1}tr. So co-Cartesian plus the noted injectivity already yields "the left-hand vertical maps are mutually inverse isomorphisms". Once the lemma holds, both vertical maps are isomorphisms, and a square with two parallel isomorphisms is both Cartesian and co-Cartesian, so the printed statement is true. So the pushout property, together with the noted injectivity of h^t, does give the conclusion that the left-hand vertical maps are mutually inverse isomorphisms. What the proof shows ("f is divisible by h^t iff F is") is the pullback description, but that does not make "co-Cartesian" false.

(2) "smooth (and in particular irreducible)" is false in the paper's own setting. In §6.3, K_q (and K_x for x of type H) is the full congruence subgroup, so ν(K_q) = 1 + qZ_q. Then π_0(X_{Q̄}) is at least (Z/q)^×, and X is proper and smooth over O, so X_k is disconnected in general, for example whenever μ_q ⊂ k. The conclusion (h is injective on H^0) is still true by the component-wise argument in the correction.

(3) Lemma 7.5 uses the injectivity of h̃^s without saying so. It is true, as argued in the correction.

This is the same "well known" injectivity the paper cites in the proof of Lemma 6.2(1). That lemma is stated only for X_1(Q) and ω(a,b)_k, but its argument works unchanged for X, X_0(Q) and W^sub.`. I rendered p. 849 and confirmed the printed text. First, smooth does not imply irreducible: a disjoint union of two smooth varieties is smooth. Second, X_k is not irreducible in general under the paper's own setup. In §5.2, p. 821 the paper says K is neat, and "This will be the case if S contains a prime x ≥ 3 where K_x is the full congruence subgroup of level x". In that case ν(K) = (1+xZ_x) × ∏_{y≠x} Z_y^×. So π_0(Sh_K ⊗ Q̄) = Q_{>0}\A_f^×/ν(K) = Ẑ^×/ν(K) ≅ (Z/x)^×, which has x−1 ≥ 2 geometric components. Since the level is prime to p, the smooth special fibre has the same component set. Frobenius Frob_q acts on it by multiplication by q, so X_k has (x−1)/ord_x(q) connected components. For example, if q ≡ 1 mod x, X_k has x−1 components. The paper puts no restriction on k (§2: O is the ring of integers of an arbitrary finite extension of Q_p with residue field k). So the parenthetical claim "irreducible over k" is false in general, and the implication behind it is invalid. The same holds for X_0(Q)_k. The conclusion is still true. Each connected component of a smooth k-scheme is integral. The Hasse invariant is nonzero on every component, because prime-to-p Hecke correspondences preserve the ordinary locus and act transitively on components (ν(K_p) = Z_p^×). Multiplying a locally free sheaf by a section of a line bundle that is nonzero on each integral component is injective. So Lemma 7.4 and its proof survive once this one-line justification is replaced. It is a false justifying statement, not a failed step. I call it an error rather than a misprint because the printed word "irreducible" asserts something false, not a typo for something true. It affects nothing. Checked against the p. 849 page image; the printed text matches. The conclusion is right but the reason given is false. Smoothness does not imply irreducibility; it only makes each connected component irreducible. Under the paper's own setup X is not connected in general.

(1) §5.2 (p. 821) requires K to be neat, "the case if S contains a prime x ≥ 3 where K_x is the full congruence subgroup of level x". The level used in §7 (§6.3, pp. 840–841, item (7)) takes K_q to be the full congruence subgroup of level q. Y_K is the standard moduli space of principally polarised abelian surfaces with K-level structure, which is a model of Sh_K(GSp4).

(2) Since Sp4 is simply connected, π_0(Sh_K ⊗ Q̄) = Ẑ^×/ν(K). Here ν(K_q) = 1 + qZ_q, so this group surjects onto (Z/q)^×, which has q−1 ≥ 2 elements. X is proper and smooth over O, so X_{k̄} has the same number (≥ 2) of connected components.

(3) Over the finite field k, Frobenius acts on these components through multiplication by |k|. So X_k is reducible whenever |k| does not generate (Z/q)^×, for instance when k contains μ_q. Nothing in the paper excludes this, and k is normally enlarged freely. The same holds for X_0(Q)_k, since ν is surjective on the Klingen parahoric.

The defence fails: no convention in the paper makes X connected, and the word "irreducible" appears nowhere else for X. The best charitable reading, that each connected component is irreducible, still leaves out the fact that is actually needed: h ≠ 0 on every component. That fact is true and standard: the non-ordinary locus has codimension 1 (Koblitz, Norman–Oort), the ordinary locus is dense in every fibre, and Hecke transitivity on π_0 gives the same. W^sub_{μ,k} = ω(a,b)(−∞)_k is locally free, and H^0 is left exact. So multiplication by h^t is injective on H^0, and the argument of Lemma 7.4 goes through as written. This correction is right. One precision: Lemma 6.2(1) states the injectivity only for X_1(Q) and ω(a,b)_k, so it is better cited as "the well-known injectivity used in the proof of Lemma 6.2".

Later uses: Lemma 7.5 ("same argument as Lemma 7.4"), Lemma 7.6 and the proof of Theorem 7.2 (p. 850) use Lemma 7.4, and the appendix refers back to it. None of them relies on irreducibility, only on the injectivity. One side note, outside this issue: Lemma 7.5 separately needs h̃^s to be injective on H^0(S, ·). The parenthetical does not cover that either; it holds because S = V(h) is reduced and h̃ vanishes only on the 1-dimensional supersingular locus. Since the conclusion is correct, this affects nothing. (1) The step really needs injectivity. The proof of Lemma 7.4 turns "f is h^t-divisible iff F is h^t-divisible" into "the left vertical maps are mutually inverse". That only works because the horizontal maps are injective, which the paper states explicitly on p. 849: "(Note that since X_0(Q) and X are smooth (and in particular irreducible) over k, multiplication by h is injective on H^0.)". Abstractly, let α = pr_Q∘i and α' = d_Q^{-1}tr. Commutativity gives h̃^s(α'α − 1) = 0 and h̃^s(αα' − 1) = 0. To conclude α'α = 1 and αα' = 1 you need h̃^s injective on H^0(S, W_{μ,k})_{m∅} and on H^0(S_0(Q), W_{μ,k})_m. Surjectivity also needs injectivity on the top-left group. So "the same argument as Lemma 7.4" silently needs injectivity of h̃^s on sections over S and S_0(Q). This is not covered by the Lemma 7.4 remark: S is not smooth (it has quadric-cone singularities at superspecial points), and its scheme structure V(h) is never discussed.

(2) Defence attempted. The paper does contain the geometric input, but not the deduction. On p. 849 it cites Boxer [12] for h̃ extending to the boundary and being Hecke-equivariant. It says, calling this "not relevant here", that h̃ vanishes on the 1-dimensional EO stratum to order 2. The proof of Theorem 8.10 (p. 862) says the supersingular locus is a Cartier divisor in the p-rank 1 stratum (Koblitz). Theorem 8.11 uses the same kind of injectivity implicitly: "0 → H^0(Y, ω(j,2)_k ⊗ ω^{-m}) → H^0(Y, ω(j,2)_k) → ...". So the fact is standard and true, and the other ingredients (tr(h̃G) = h̃ tr(G) because h̃ on S_0(Q) is pulled back; Hecke-equivariance at Q from [12, Thm 4.5.4(3)]) are handled. But nowhere does the paper state or prove injectivity on S or S_0(Q). The authors even call the vanishing-locus information irrelevant, although it is exactly what gives injectivity. So this is a genuine omitted step. It is minor and routine to fill.

(3) The fill (checked). S = V(h) is a hypersurface in a regular scheme, hence CM and pure of dimension 2. The boundary divisor is not contained in S, because h restricted to a boundary component is essentially the elliptic Hasse invariant of the abelian part. So S ∩ boundary has dimension ≤ 1. The supersingular locus has dimension 1. So each generic point of S is an interior point of p-rank 1, where h̃ does not vanish, so h̃ is a unit in the Artinian local ring there. Since the associated points of S are exactly its generic points, h̃ is a nonzerodivisor. The same holds for S_0(Q), which is finite étale over S on the interior because the primes in Q are not p.

(Sym^n V)^∨ = Γ^n(V^∨) ≅ Γ^n(V) ⊗ det^{−n}, and the natural map Sym^n V → Γ^n V, which sends x^i y^{n−i} to i!(n−i)! x^{[i]}y^{[n−i]}, is an isomorphism over O when n! ∈ O^×, that is, when n = a−2 < p. The GL_2-equivariant isomorphism (Sym^n)^∨ ≅ Sym^n ⊗ det^{−n} over O (here n = a−2) exists if n! is a unit, but not only then. For n = 2p−1, Sym^n_k = L(p−1) ⊗ L(1)^{[1]} is irreducible of dimension 2p, so the two O-lattices are homothetic and the isomorphism still holds. Only the 'if' direction is used, so this does not matter here. An incidental observation, separate from this issue: the §7.2 preamble assumes p > a−2, but Theorem 7.11 (p. 853) is stated with 'p − 2 > a'. The text of arXiv:1907.08691v1 is the same for Assumption 7.7, Lemma 7.9, Theorem 7.11 with its proof, and Theorem 9.1(6); the only difference is "Suppose Assumption 7.7 holds" in Lemma 7.9.

(2) The hypothesis in the theorem is Assumption 7.7 for its fixed Δ, and nothing in the proof uses it. The proof only uses M, the Tor/Hochschild–Serre sequence, Lemma 7.9 at X_0, Lemma 7.10 and char-0 automorphic input on X_0.

(3) The vanishing on X_0 does not follow formally from the vanishing on X_Δ. X_1(Q) → X_0(Q) is finite étale with group Δ_Q (p. 822), so C = RΓ(X_Δ, ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_𝔪 is perfect over k[Δ] and RΓ(X_0, ·)_𝔪 = C ⊗^L_{k[Δ]} k. If H^2(C) = 0, the Tor spectral sequence gives H^2(X_0, ·)_𝔪 ≅ Tor_1^{k[Δ]}(H^3(X_Δ, ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_𝔪, k). That group need not vanish. For Δ = Z/p, the perfect complex k[Δ] →(σ−1) k[Δ] →N k[Δ] →(σ−1) k[Δ] has H^2 = 0, but its coinvariants have H^2 = k. The group H^3(X_Δ, ω(a,2)(−∞)_k) is Serre dual to H^0(X_Δ, ω(1,3−a)_k). Theorem 5.1 does not kill it for a ∈ {2,3}: parts (1) and (3) need a−b ≥ 2 or b ≥ 4. For a ≥ 4 (Remark 7.8) the vanishing holds at every level, so there is no issue there.

So, read literally, the stated hypothesis does not cover what the proof uses, and the paper gives no argument connecting the two. Only a charitable reading of Assumption 7.7 as holding for all Δ, including Δ = 1, closes the gap. The authors plainly intended the X_0 vanishing, since 9.1(6) assumes it for X_0 and X_1. The main result, Theorem 9.1, is not affected, because (6) with i = 0 supplies the needed vanishing. What needs repair is the proof of Theorem 7.11 together with its hypothesis; I label this "the proof", not "nothing". No later result depends on the X_Δ form of the assumption. This step is essential. Since Tor_1^S(M,O) is a quotient of H_1(X_0)_𝔪, torsion in H_1(X_0)_𝔪 would break the bound dim_k Tor_1^S(M,O)/ϖ ≤ r. Nothing else in the proof uses the X_Δ vanishing: the defect formula, the Hochschild–Serre exact sequence (1)–(2), Lemma 7.10 and the char-0 count all work without it.

- "Suppose that Assumption 7.7 holds" comes right after "Let Δ be a quotient…". So it concerns that Δ.
- Reading 7.7 as a standing assumption for every quotient Δ, including Δ = 1, would cover the step. But then §9(c) would have to check it for X_Δ(Q_N) too, and (6) only states it for X_0 and X_1.
- There is no formal implication either. For a perfect k[Δ]-complex C with H^2(C) = 0, one gets H^2(C⊗^L_{k[Δ]} k) ≅ Tor_1^{k[Δ]}(H^3(C), k). For Δ = Z/p this can be nonzero: take the complex k[Δ] →(σ−1) k[Δ] →N k[Δ] →(σ−1) k[Δ].

(3) However, the stated theorem is still true. The paper's own tools close the gap, though the paper does not do so:
(i) Assumption 7.7 and the ϖ-sequence give H^2(X_Δ, F)_𝔪 = 0 (by Nakayama) and H^3(X_Δ, F)_𝔪[ϖ] = 0.
(ii) In characteristic 0, H^3(X_Δ, F)_𝔪 ⊗ K = 0. The steps:
  - Lemma 7.10, which the paper says "holds in all weights and in all prime-to-p levels", applies at level X_Δ.
  - The inclusion from Theorem 5.2, together with the class (a)–(f) argument of pp. 854–855, shows that every contributing π is tempered at ∞. That argument does not depend on the degree.
  - By Theorem 5.5 with (a−1, 0), this point lies in C_0 and C_1 but not in C_2 or C_3 when a ≥ 2. So nothing contributes in degrees 2 or 3.
(iii) By (i) and (ii), H^3(X_Δ, F)_𝔪 = 0, so H^3(X_Δ, F_k)_𝔪 = 0.
(iv) X_Δ → X_0 is finite étale with group Δ (p. 822). So RΓ(X_Δ, F_k) is perfect over k[Δ], and RΓ(X_0, F_k) ≅ RΓ(X_Δ, F_k) ⊗^L_{k[Δ]} k. The Tor spectral sequence then gives H^2(X_0, F_k)_𝔪 = 0.
So Theorem 7.11 holds as stated, but its proof as written omits (i)–(iv). That makes this a gap, not an error, and it affects the proof only.

(4) Consequences. Theorem 7.11 is used only in §9 step (c) ("H_N is finite and balanced over S_N by Theorem 7.11"), and in the Appendix Lemma A.5 ("a consequence of the proof of Theorem 7.11"), which has no bearing on this hypothesis. Theorem 9.1 is unaffected: (6) with i = 0 gives exactly the vanishing on X_0 that the proof uses.

Aside, outside this issue: §9(c) also never checks the literal hypothesis of 7.11 on X_Δ(Q_N). It follows from (6) with i = 1 by the same argument (i)–(iv). Also, Theorem 7.11 requires p−2 > a, while Theorem 9.1 only requires p−1 > a. - **Misprint** at §1.3 (speculative remarks on geometric doubling), p. 805, last paragraph and display at the foot of the page. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same wording and display: the sentence starts on p. 4 and the display is on p. 5.. The source says `"Let π_p be a smooth admissible irreducible unramified representation of GL_2(Q_p) (over C) which is not trivial. (For example, π_p could be the local constituent of an automorphic representation π associated to a classical modular form.) Let Sph = GL_2(Z_p), and let Iw denote the Iwahori subgroup of Sph. The classical theory of oldforms is a reflection of the fact that dim π_p^{Iw} = 2 = 2 · dim π_p^{Sph}"`; it should be `Replace "which is not trivial" with "which is not one-dimensional" (equivalently "infinite-dimensional" or "generic"). Then π_p is an irreducible unramified principal series Ind_B^G(χ1⊗χ2), with χ1, χ2 unramified and χ1χ2^{-1} ≠ |·|^{±1}, and the display holds. This one-word change is the minimal fix.`. I rendered p. 805 at 130 dpi and read the page image. The printed text is exactly as quoted: the hypothesis is "irreducible unramified … which is not trivial", followed by the unconditional display dim π_p^{Iw} = 2 = 2·dim π_p^{Sph}.

My own check of the dimensions:
- Take a one-dimensional representation π = χ∘det with χ an unramified character of Q_p^× that is not trivial, for example χ = |·| or χ(p) = −1. It is smooth, admissible, irreducible and unramified (GL_2(Z_p) acts trivially), and it is not the trivial representation. It meets every hypothesis as printed. Since Iw ⊂ GL_2(Z_p) acts trivially, π^{Iw} = π^{Sph} = π, which has dimension 1. The display then fails (1 ≠ 2).
- If π is infinite-dimensional, irreducible and unramified, it is a full induced representation Ind_B^G(χ1⊗χ2) with χ1, χ2 unramified. Then dim π^{K} = #(B\G/K) = 1 by the Iwasawa decomposition, and dim π^{Iw} = #(B\G/Iw) = |W| = 2 by the Bruhat decomposition G = BIw ⊔ BwIw. So the display holds exactly for these representations.
- Steinberg twists and other ramified representations have no nonzero GL_2(Z_p)-fixed vector, so "unramified" already excludes them. The only exceptions allowed by the printed hypothesis are the nontrivial unramified characters.

So "not trivial" is too weak and "not one-dimensional" is the right condition. The intended meaning is clear from the parenthetical example (automorphic representations of classical modular forms are generic at every place), and the analogous GSp_4 statement is hedged with "for the Π_p of interest". This is a wording slip, not a mathematical error in any argument, so "misprint" is the right kind.

Why it affects nothing: the passage is explicitly "speculative remarks" in the introduction on whether the geometric doubling of [13]/BCGP could be adapted. No lemma, proposition or theorem refers to this display. The paper's actual Hecke-operator and tripling arguments (§8.4–8.5, Lemma 8.12, Remark 8.18) are carried out independently with q-expansions for GSp_4. I rendered p. 805 (and p. 806 for the GSp_4 continuation) at 130 dpi and read the page images. The text is exactly as quoted.

Counterexample to the printed hypothesis: let π = χ∘det, where χ is a nontrivial unramified character of Q_p^× (for example χ = |·|, or χ(p) = −1). Then π is smooth, admissible, irreducible and unramified, because GL_2(Z_p) acts trivially. It is also not the trivial representation, so it meets every printed hypothesis. But Iw ⊂ Sph acts trivially too, so π^{Iw} = π^{Sph} = π, which has dimension 1. The display "dim π_p^{Iw} = 2" fails.

Positive check: the irreducible admissible unramified representations of GL_2(Q_p) are exactly (a) the irreducible full unramified principal series and (b) the characters χ∘det with χ unramified. Unramified twists of Steinberg have no nonzero GL_2(Z_p)-fixed vector, so they are excluded already. In case (a), dim π^{Sph} = #B\G/K = 1 (Iwasawa) and dim π^{Iw} = #B\G/Iw = |W| = 2 (Bruhat, G = BIw ⊔ BwIw), so the display holds. So the right hypothesis is "infinite-dimensional". "Not trivial" rules out only one member of family (b).

Defence attempted: (i) "trivial" might loosely mean "a twist of the trivial representation", i.e. one-dimensional. That is not the standard meaning, and the text gives no such convention. (ii) The parenthetical example, a local component of a classical modular form, is always infinite-dimensional (generic), so the intended meaning is clear. (iii) The parallel GSp_4 statement on p. 806 is hedged "(for the Π_p of interest)". Points (ii) and (iii) support reading this as a wording slip with a clear intent, so the kind is misprint. The literal statement is false, but its intended meaning is unambiguous, so misprint is a better label than error.

Consequences: the passage is explicitly "speculative remarks". The only back-reference is p. 867 (§8.6): "No doubt (see Section 1.3) there will be better geometric replacements for this argument". That is a general pointer and does not use the dimension count. No lemma, proposition or theorem depends on it. The paper's actual arguments (§8.4–8.5, Lemma 8.12, Remark 8.18) use q-expansions for GSp_4 and are independent of this display. I rendered p. 854 at 110, 600 and 1200 dpi. The subscript reads "(0,0−(a−1),−(a−1))": there is no comma between the second 0 and "−(a−1)". That leaves a 3-tuple, (0, −(a−1), −(a−1)), which cannot be added to 3/2(1,1,1,1) in C^4, so the formula as printed has no meaning.
