(1) Theorem 5.6(2) on p. 829 gives τ = ((a+b−3−w)/2, (a−b+1−w)/2, (−a+b−1−w)/2, (−a−b+3−w)/2) with w = −(a+b+2c). Remark 5.12 on p. 834 takes μ = (a,b;3−a−b), so c = 3−a−b and w = a+b−6. The argument that follows agrees with this value. In case (d), the characters λ|·|^{±1/2} need two parameters that differ by 1, which forces 3/2 − (5/2−a) = a−1 = 1, i.e. a = 2, exactly as the text says. In case (b), the two GL2 pieces must each carry parameters {3/2, 5/2−a}, which differ by a−1, so both are weight-a forms, again as stated. The paper never writes this multiset out; it is what the argument implicitly uses. Theorem 5.6(3) with b = 2 gives λ = (a−1,0;4−a), matching the next paragraph. So the error is a dropped comma, and the correct value is fixed by the explicit "by Remark 5.12".

- **Misprint** at §7.2, proof of Theorem 7.11, p. 855; arXiv:1907.08691v1, p. 41. The source says `"Indeed, since π(λ, C_i) is essentially tempered, the local packet Π_{ψ_∞} (where ψ = π̃ ⊞ 1, in the notation of [3]) is in fact an L-packet by [55, Theorem 2.1]." Checked on a 500-dpi render of p. 855: the symbol is the boxed plus ⊞, not the boxed times ⊠. The arXiv preprint 1907.08691v1 (p. 41) has the same text: "(where ψ = π̃ ⊞ 1, in the notation of [Art04])".`; it should be `ψ = π̃ ⊠ 1. In Arthur's notation for GSp4 this is the general-type (case (a)) parameter μ ⊠ 1 with μ = π̃: the cuspidal symplectic-type representation of GL4 tensored with the trivial 1-dimensional representation of SL2 (written ν(1) or 1).`. 1. The paper never defines ψ; it refers to "the notation of [3]", where [3] is Arthur, "Automorphic representations of GSp(4)". In that notation a global parameter is a formal sum ⊞_i μ_i ⊠ ν_i, with μ_i cuspidal on GL(m_i) and ν_i the irreducible representation of SL2 of dimension n_i, and Σ m_i n_i = 4. The general type is μ ⊠ 1. Brumer–Pacetti–Poor–Tornaría–Voight–Yuen (arXiv:1805.10873v4) use the same convention, citing Schmidt: "type (G) given by the formal tensor µ ⊠ 1, where µ is a cuspidal, self-dual, symplectic, unitary, automorphic representation of GL4(A) and 1 is the trivial representation of SU2(A)".
2. I redid the degree count. π̃ ⊞ 1 is an isobaric sum of the 4-dimensional π̃ with a 1-dimensional character, so it has degree 5. That cannot be a parameter for GSp4, whose dual group GSp4(C) sits inside GL4. It is also not the Sp4/SO5 transfer of a general-type parameter, which would be ∧²π̃ ⊗ χ^{-1}, not π̃ ⊞ 1.
3. The printed version contradicts its own sentence. A sum with two summands would not be case (a) and would have a nontrivial S_ψ, yet the next sentence says "the group S_ψ is trivial in Case (a) of [3]". With ⊠ everything fits: the SL2 factor is trivial, so ψ_∞ is essentially tempered and Π_{ψ_∞} is an L-packet, as the text says.
4. The ⊞ signs in cases (b)–(d) (λ|·|^{1/2} ⊞ λ|·|^{-1/2} ⊞ μ, μ|·|^{1/2} ⊞ μ|·|^{-1/2}, μ1 ⊞ μ2) are correct isobaric sums. They describe the GL4 transfer π̃, not ψ.
5. Those case (b)–(d) formulas are on p. 854, the page before this passage (p. 855).
6. The appendix (proof of Lemma A.5) and BCGP18 Lemma 2.9.1 reuse the argument of this proof but not this formula. BCGP18 Lemma 2.9.1 uses only cases (b)–(f). - **Misprint** at §8.1, display right before Theorem 8.1, p. 856. arXiv v1 (p. 41) has the identical display.. The source says `There is a q-expansion map H^0(Y_1(Q), ω(j,k)_R) → R[[q, q′, ζ]][ζ^{−1}] ⊗_R U.`; it should be `The target should be R[ζ, ζ^{−1}][[q, q′]] ⊗_R U: power series in q, q′ whose coefficients are Laurent polynomials in ζ, i.e. formal sums Σ_{Q∈𝒳} a(F,Q) q^Q. For general L, fractional exponents with a bounded power of L in the denominator must also be allowed; the paper suggests pretending L = 1.`. The paper's own expansion (p. 857) is F = Σ_{n,m≥0, r²−4mn≤0} a_F(n,r,m) q^n ζ^r q′^m. For fixed (n,m) the exponent r runs over |r| ≤ 2√(nm), which is finite, so the q^n q′^m coefficient is a Laurent polynomial in ζ. But r is unbounded below over all (n,m), while every element of R[[q,q′,ζ]][ζ^{−1}] has ζ-exponents ≥ −N for some N. I checked the unipotent argument by hand. With M = (1 k; 0 1) and M.Q = (det M)^{−1} M Q M^T, the form Q = (m, r/2; r/2, n) goes to (m+kr+k²n, (r+2kn)/2; ·, n). Since a(F, M.Q) = ρ(M)a(F,Q) with ρ(M) invertible, and k can be taken in the level of Γ̄ of either sign, any nonconstant F has nonzero coefficients with arbitrarily negative r. So its expansion is not in the printed ring. Concretely, the rank-one forms Q with r = −2t and r² = 4mn carry ζ^{−2t}, and Siegel Eisenstein series have nonzero coefficients there. The intended meaning (the formal q-expansion) is clear, and the later arguments (Lemmas 8.3–8.4 etc.) use only the coefficients a(F,Q). For L = 1, as the paper suggests, the corrected target is exactly R[ζ,ζ^{−1}][[q,q′]] ⊗_R U. - **Error** at §8.1, the displayed q-expansion map and Theorem 8.1 with its one-line proof, p. 856. arXiv v1 has the same text (§8.1, Theorem 8.1, v1 PDF p. 41; proof cites "Prop. 3.2 of [Til06]"). Related setup: §5.2, p. 821 (K neat, list of allowed K_x).. The source says `"There is a q-expansion map H^0(Y_1(Q), ω(j,k)_R) → R[[q, q′, ζ]][ζ^{−1}] ⊗_R U. THEOREM 8.1 The q-expansion map is injective. Proof This is a standard fact (see, e.g., [67, Proposition 3.2])." (and on p. 857: "Here Γ̄ is the congruence subgroup of SL2(Z) defined in [67, p. 807]; ... (It will do the reader little harm to pretend that Γ̄ is just SL2(Z).)")`; it should be `Take a q-expansion at a cusp on each geometric connected component c ∈ π0 = Ẑ^×/ν(K_1(Q)) of Y_1(Q). The coefficients lie in R ⊗_O O′, where O′ = O[ζ_M] and M is the level. Theorem 8.1 should say that the resulting map H^0(Y_1(Q), ω(j,k)_R) → ∏_c (R⊗O′)[[q,q′,ζ]][ζ^{-1}] ⊗ U is injective. This is [67, Prop. 3.2] applied to each component. This is right and minimal. The formal operators of Lemmas 8.3 and 8.4 must then carry a component label: T = T_{p,1} (similitude p) sends the expansion on component c to one on component p^{-1}·c.`. Checked against the page images (p. 821, 856–861) and against Tilouine [67] itself (Doc. Math. Extra Vol. Coates 2006), fetched from the web archive.

(1) Y_1(Q) is necessarily geometrically disconnected. §5.2 (p. 821) lets each K_x (x ∈ S) be one of S(x), Π(x), K(x), Π(x)^+, I(x), or the full congruence subgroup of level x, and assumes K is neat. The torsion element g = diag(1,−1,−1,1) is in GSp4(Q), with similitude ad = bc = 1 for the paper's antidiagonal form. It lies in the torus of GSp4(Z_x), so it lies in every parahoric S(x), Π(x), I(x) and in the paramodular K(x). It lies in Π(x)^+ because its Klingen-Levi λ-entry is 1. It lies in the level-2 full congruence subgroup because g ≡ I mod 2. It also lies in Π(x), Π^+(x) for x ∈ Q and in GSp4(Z_x) outside S. So neatness forces some x ∈ S with x ≥ 3 and K_x the full congruence subgroup of level x. Then ν(K_x) ⊆ 1+xZ_x, so Ẑ^×/ν(K_1(Q)) maps onto (Z/x)^×, which has order ≥ 2. Hence π_0(Y_1(Q)_C) has at least 2 elements.

(2) The cited proof covers only the connected case. [67, §3.1] says "for simplicity, we restrict our attention to one connected component X corresponding to a discrete subgroup Γ ⊂ Sp4(Z). We assume that X has a geometrically connected model over Z[1/N]." It defines "the arithmetic q-expansion (at the ∞ cusp)". Its Prop. 3.2(1) (q-expansion principle) is proved by "The first point follows from the irreducibility of the modular scheme". Its §2 Remark adds: "All schemes above have geometrically connected generic fibers if and only if ν(K) = Ẑ^×."

(3) Counterexample to the literal statement. Take O with ζ_x ∈ O (for example p ≡ 1 mod x), so Y_1(Q)_O is a disjoint union of at least 2 components. With R = O/ϖ, let F = 1_c·h^N, a power of the Hasse invariant (weight (N(p−1), N(p−1))) supported on a component c that does not contain the chosen cusp. Then F ≠ 0, but its expansion there is 0. So a single-cusp map into one copy of R[[q,q′,ζ]][ζ^{−1}] ⊗ U is not injective on H^0(Y_1(Q), ω(j,k)_R). If ζ_x ∉ O, a cusp is not O-rational and the coefficients would lie in R⊗O[ζ_x], not in R.

(4) The paper cannot be tacitly working on one component. Lemma 8.8 and §§8–9 use T_{p,1} = [K β_{p,1} K] with β_{p,1} = diag(1,1,p,p) (p. 830). This operator moves components by p^{±1} mod x. The paper never mentions components.

The fix is standard and all later arguments work componentwise, so the mathematics is right as intended. The statement as printed, and its cited proof, do not cover the geometrically disconnected Y_1(Q) that the paper actually uses. Minor corroboration of the same conflation: p. 849 (v1 p. 36) says "X_0(Q) and X are smooth (and in particular irreducible) over k". The issue could also be described as a "gap" or as an "imprecision"; it affects nothing. The defence fails. (1) The level K_1(Q) is not geometrically connected. §6.3(7) takes K_q to be the full congruence subgroup of level q, and §5.2 gets neatness from such a prime x ≥ 3. That subgroup has ν(K_q) = 1+qZ_q, so π0(Y_{K,Q̄}) = Ẑ^×/ν(K) maps onto (Z/q)^×, which has order q−1 ≥ 2. The moduli problem cited, [57, §4.1] (Pilloni), uses "isomorphismes symplectiques à un facteur de similitude près", so the Weil-pairing root of unity varies and the components are indexed by it.

(2) The cited source covers only one component. Tilouine [67, §3.1] says: "we restrict our attention to one connected component X corresponding to a discrete subgroup Γ ⊂ Sp4(Z). We assume that X has a geometrically connected model over Z[1/N]." His Prop. 3.2(1) "follows from the irreducibility of the modular scheme". His own Remark in §2 says: "All schemes above have geometrically connected generic fibers if and only if ν(K) = Ẑ^×". The Γ̄ of [67, p. 807] that CG cite also belongs to this one-component setting.

(3) As printed, the statement is false in cases the paper allows. Take p = 7 and q = 3, which satisfies q ≢ 1 mod p. Then ζ_3 ∈ O, and Y_1(Q) over O is a disjoint union Y′ ⊔ Y″ of at least 2 components defined over O. A nonzero form supported on Y″ has zero expansion at a cusp of Y′. Such forms exist in every weight where H^0 ≠ 0, because GSp4(Z_q) normalises K_q and permutes the components transitively. When ζ_q ∉ O the standard cusp is not even defined over O, so the target ring should be R⊗O[ζ_q], not R.

(4) Consequences: the downstream arguments hold after rewriting them component by component. T_{p,1}, and hence U, Z and V, shift components by p^{-1} mod ν(K), so Lemmas 8.3 and 8.4 relate an expansion on component c to one on component p^{-1}c.
- Theorem 8.22, first step: minimality and the U-relation work on the tuple (F_c). The j > 2 branch uses ρ(pI) = 0, which is independent of the component.
- Theorem 8.22, (2,2) branch: it needs a_{p^{-2}c}(F,Q) = a_c(F,Q). This holds because the central element acts trivially on the m-part (the Nebentypus mod m is trivial). The paper's single-expansion formula "ρ(pI) is the identity" already assumes the same fact.
- Proposition 8.25: the contraction claim holds for every x, so it is independent of the component.
- Theorems 8.10 and 8.11, and the injectivity of multiplication by the Hasse invariant, are geometric and hold on each component.

So Theorem 8.13 and every stated result survive. A related instance of the same suppression is on p. 849, "X_0(Q) and X are smooth (and in particular irreducible) over k". It is harmless because h is nonzero on each component. "gap" is also a defensible kind, since the cited result proves only the connected case. It is recorded as an "error" because the printed theorem is literally false in allowed cases. - **Misprint** at §8.2 (Explicit formulas), first paragraph, p. 856. arXiv v1 (p. 42) has the identical sentence.. The source says `Let L be the product of the primes in S and Q, so that X_1(Q) has good reduction outside L. Let R be a Z_p-module and thus a Z[1/L]-algebra.`; it should be `'Let R be a Z_p-module and thus a Z[1/L]-module.'`. S and Q do not contain p (§8, opening), so L is a unit in Z_p and every Z_p-module is naturally a Z[1/L]-module. A module is not in general an algebra, so the 'thus' in the printed text is wrong. §8.1 says the R of interest are O/ϖ^n and K/O, and K/O is not a ring. 'Algebra' is therefore a slip for 'module'. The intended meaning (inverting L is harmless on R) is clear, and nothing later depends on R being a ring beyond the paper's general loose notation R[[…]]. - **Misprint** at §8.2, p. 856, definition of 𝒳 after F = Σ_𝒳 a(F,Q)q^Q. arXiv v1 (p. 42) is identical (spelled 'positive semi-definite').. The source says `where 𝒳 denotes the 2 × 2 positive semidefinite matrices which take on Z[1/L]-integral arguments for integral vectors, or equivalently, 𝒳 = ( m ½r ; ½r n ), m, n, r ∈ Z[1/L].`; it should be `𝒳 = { (m, ½r; ½r, n) : m, n, r ∈ Z[1/L], m, n ≥ 0, r² − 4mn ≤ 0 }, the positive semidefinite symmetric matrices that take Z[1/L]-integral values (not 'arguments') on integral vectors.`. The two descriptions called 'equivalent' differ. For Q = (m, r/2; r/2, n), taking Z[1/L]-integral values x^T Q x on all integral x is equivalent to m, n, r ∈ Z[1/L] (m = Q(e1), n = Q(e2), r = Q(e1+e2) − m − n). But the displayed set drops positive semidefiniteness, so read literally it contains, e.g., (−1, 0; 0, 0). The q-expansion on p. 857 sums only over n, m ≥ 0 with r² − 4mn ≤ 0, and the first half of the sentence says 'positive semidefinite', so the intended set is clear. 'Arguments' is also a word slip for 'values'. This is a harmless imprecision in notation. - **Misprint** at §8.2, Remark 8.2, p. 857; arXiv v1 p. 42. The source says `Remark 8.2: "We will assume that either j ≥ 4 or j = k = 2. Since we are most interested in representations with similitude character ν equal to ε^{j+k−3}, the oddness condition forces the congruence j ≡ k mod 2, and so if j > k ≥ 2, then j ≥ 4." (checked on the rendered page image, p. 857). arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same exponent in Remark 8.2 on p. 42 (checked on the rendered page): "…with similitude character ν is equal to ε^{j+k−3}, the oddness condition forces the congruence j ≡ k mod 2…" (with a stray "is").`; it should be `ν = ε^{−(j+k−3)} = ε^{3−j−k}. For forms with nontrivial Nebentypus this holds up to a finite-order character, as in Theorem 6.13(1): ν∘r = χ_{μ,0} ε^{−w}, where w = a+b−3.`. The sign is wrong under the paper's own conventions.
(i) §2, p. 806 sets the convention: "The Hodge–Tate weight of ε | G_{Q_p} is −1."
(ii) Every other place gives the similitude with a negative exponent:
- p. 802: ε^{1−j} for weight (j,2).
- §4, p. 812: ν(r̄) = ε̄^{−(a−1)}.
- Definition 4.6(1), p. 815: ν(r) = ε^{−(a−1)}.
- Prop. 6.8(1), p. 838: ν∘r_f = λ_f∘χ_{μ,0} ε^{−w}, with w = a+b−3.
- Theorem 6.13(1), p. 842: ν∘r = χ_{μ,0} ε^{−w}.
- Proof of Theorem 6.17, p. 846: ν(r′_m) = χ ε^{−(a−1)} χ_Q.
- Theorem 9.1, p. 878: ν(r̄) = ε^{−(a−1)}.
(iii) §8 itself agrees with the corrected sign.
- The weight (j,k) of §8 is the (a,b) of §6: the §8.5 Frobenius eigenvalues on p. 863 are α, βp^{k−2}, β^{−1}p^{j−1} and α^{−1}p^{k+j−3}. These match Theorem 6.13(3) with a = j and b = k.
- The paired eigenvalues multiply to p^{k+j−3}, and Lemma 8.3 has T = U + p^{k−2}Z + p^{k+j−3}V.
- Since φ acts on D_cris(Q_p(1)) by p^{−1}, a similitude with φ = p^{k+j−3} and Hodge–Tate weight 0 + (j+k−3) is ε^{−(j+k−3)} under the paper's convention.
- ε^{j+k−3} would instead have Hodge–Tate weight −(j+k−3), which cannot pair the nonnegative weights 0, k−2, j−1 and j+k−3.
I redid the parity step: ε(c) = −1, so ε^{±(j+k−3)}(c) = (−1)^{j+k−3}. Oddness (ν(c) = −1) then gives j+k even, i.e. j ≡ k mod 2. So j > k ≥ 2 forces j ≥ k+2 ≥ 4. The deduction holds whichever sign is used. - **Misprint** at §2.1 ("The group GSp4"), p. 807, displayed formula identifying X*(T) with Z^3. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text in §2.0.1, p. 6.. The source says `"Let T denote the diagonal torus in GSp4, and let X*(T) denote its character group. We identify X*(T) with the lattice Z^3 by associating to (a, b; c) the character diag(t1, t2, νt2^{−1}, νt1^{−1}) ↦ t1^a t2^a ν^c." I checked this on a 400 dpi crop of p. 807: both exponents are plainly "a". arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text in §2.0.1, p. 6 (400 dpi crop): "diag(t1, t2, νt2^{−1}, νt1^{−1}) ↦ t1^a t2^a ν^c".`; it should be `diag(t1, t2, νt2^{−1}, νt1^{−1}) ↦ t1^a t2^b ν^c`. I redid the checks with d = diag(t1, t2, ν/t2, ν/t1).
(1) As printed, b never appears, so (a,b;c) and (a,b';c) give the same character. The printed map is also not onto X*(T): the root t1/t2 is not of the form t1^a t2^a ν^c. So the printed formula cannot be the intended identification.
(2) With t1^a t2^b ν^c everything that follows checks out:
- Pairing: the cocharacter (α,β;γ): t ↦ diag(t^α, t^β, t^{γ−β}, t^{γ−α}) has t1 = t^α, t2 = t^β, ν = t^γ. The pairing is therefore aα + bβ + cγ, as printed. The printed formula would give aα + aβ + cγ instead.
- Positive roots:
  - E12: d1/d2 = t1/t2 = (1,−1;0) = α1.
  - E23: this lies in sp4 for the given J (I checked E32·J + J·E23 = 0). It gives d2/d3 = t2²/ν = (0,2;−1) = α2.
  - E13: d1/d3 = t1t2/ν = (1,1;−1) = α3.
  - E14: d1/d4 = t1²/ν = (2,0;−1) = α4.
- ρ: the four roots sum to (4,2;−3), so ρ = (2,1;−3/2).
- Coroots: diag(t,t^{-1},t,t^{-1}), diag(1,t,t^{-1},1), diag(t,t,t^{-1},t^{-1}) and diag(t,1,1,t^{-1}) give (1,−1;0), (0,1;0), (1,1;0) and (1,0;0). Each pairs to 2 with its root.
- Dominance: ⟨λ,α1∨⟩ = a−b and ⟨λ,α2∨⟩ = b, so X*(T)+_G = {a ≥ b ≥ 0} and X*(T)+_M = {a ≥ b}.
- The highest weights on p. 808 also check out. The first two basis vectors have weights t1, t2, so the highest is (1,0;0). The last two have weights ν/t2, ν/t1, so the highest is (0,−1;1).
- The Weyl-group formulas on p. 808 check out with s1 = s_{α2} and s0 = s_{α1}: w̃1(a,b;c) = (a,−b;b+c), w̃2(a,b;c) = (b,−a;a+c) and w̃3(a,b;c) = (−b,−a;a+b+c).
Every later use of (a,b;c) needs t2^b, so this is a typographical slip in a single display. It is not an error in content. Separate observation, not part of this issue: p. 808 says the longest element of W_G acts by "w0(a,b;c) = (b,a;c)". That is the reflection s_{α1}, which is the longest element of W_M. The longest element of W_G (−1 on roots) would give (−a,−b;a+b+c). This may be worth a separate check. - **Misprint** at §8.3, Lemma 8.4, display at top of p. 859, with Definition 8.5 on p. 859; the same slip "D = det(Q)" recurs in §8.8 on p. 874. The source says `a(U_2F, Q) = (−1 + p (det(Q)/p)) a(Q) = (−1 + p ((r^2 − 4mn)/p)) a(Q). [p. 859, top display, continuing Lemma 8.4 from p. 858 after "If Q ≢ 0 mod p, then". It is followed by "If Q ≡ 0 mod p, then a(U_2F, Q) = (−1 + p^2)a(Q)." Definition 8.5 on the same page reads: "Explicitly, if Q ≢ 0 mod p, then a(X_2F, Q) = a(F, Q) times (D/p), where D is the determinant of the quadratic form associated to Q, and (D/p) is the Legendre symbol."]`; it should be `For Q ≢ 0 mod p: a(U_2F,Q) = (−1 + p((r^2 − 4mn)/p)) a(Q) = (−1 + p(−det(Q)/p)) a(Q). So the first expression should use −det(Q), i.e. the discriminant d(Q) = r^2 − 4mn. Definition 8.5 is correct only if "determinant of the quadratic form" is read in Gauss's sense, b^2 − ac = r^2/4 − mn = −det(Q). In §8.8 (p. 874), "D = det(Q)" should likewise read D = d(Q). The same passage also has an unrelated slip: "(D/p)a(F,R)" should be "(D/p)a(F,Q)".`. I rendered p. 859 and confirmed the printed display exactly. The paper's convention is Q = (m, r/2; r/2, n) (p. 856, and again p. 876), and it states on p. 877 that r^2 − 4mn = −4 det(Q). So (det(Q)/p) = (−1/p)((r^2−4mn)/p): the two sides of the printed equality disagree whenever p ≡ 3 mod 4 and d(Q) is prime to p.

I redid the computation. The U_2-part comes from the cosets (pI B; 0 pI) with B symmetric of rank 1 mod p; there are p^2 − 1 of these, which matches the printed Q ≡ 0 value −1 + p^2. It contributes Σ_B e(tr(QB)/p). Writing B = λvv^T with λ ∈ F_p^* and v ∈ P^1(F_p), tr(QB) = λ(mx^2 + rxy + ny^2). The sum is then Σ_v [p·1{Q(v)=0} − 1] = −(p+1) + p·N, where N = 1 + ((r^2−4mn)/p) is the number of projective zeros of a nonzero form. That gives −1 + p((r^2−4mn)/p). A brute-force check over all Q mod p for p = 3, 5, 7, 11 (1822 nonzero Q) matched the discriminant formula every time. The det(Q) formula failed in 1522 cases, all with p ≡ 3 mod 4. Example: Q = x^2 + y^2, p = 3 gives −4, not 2.

The second printed expression is right and the first is a sign slip. This is internal to the paper's own conventions: p. 877 fixes det(Q) as the matrix determinant.

Downstream, the argument needs the discriminant. Lemma 8.21 counts F([Q]) by d(Q), and F([Q]) is the set of zeros of Q in P^1(F_p): M^{-1}.Q is p-integral iff Q(v) ≡ 0. §8.8 argues that (D/p) = −1 gives F(Q) = ∅, hence 0 = a(ZF,Q) = (β − β^{-1})a(F,Q), which requires a(X_2F,Q) = −a(F,Q). With det(Q) and p ≡ 3 mod 4 one would get (β + β^{-1}) instead, and the stated hypothesis β^2 ≠ 1 would not suffice. Since the paper defines D in §8.8 as D_Q, the discriminant, the argument goes through. Lemma 8.6 only uses det(Q) ≡ 0, where the sign does not matter.

- **Misprint** at §8.3, proof of Lemma 8.6, p. 859; arXiv:1907.08691v1 p. 44, same wording. The source says `Proof. We have a(X_2F, Q) = 0 if det(Q) ≡ 0 mod p, but a(Z_2F, Q) is a sum over terms of the form a(F, R) with det(R) = 0.`; it should be `"... a sum over terms of the form a(X_2F, R) with det(R) ≡ 0 mod p (in fact det(R) = p^2·det(Q))." Here R = M^{-1}.pQ = p·(M^{-1}.Q), and M^{-1}.Q has the same det as Q. So a(X_2F, R) ≡ (det R/p)·a(F, R) = 0 in k, and hence Z_2X_2 = 0 over k.`. I rendered p. 859 and transcribed the proof exactly as printed. It says "det(R) = 0", while the same sentence uses "det(Q) ≡ 0 mod p" for Q. The paper's convention is fixed on the same page: det(Q) = r^2 − 4mn, as in the display for a(U_2F, Q) on p. 859. I recomputed the determinant of every R in the explicit formula for Z_2 on p. 859: for R = (p^2 n, pr, m), det = p^2 r^2 − 4p^2 mn = p^2(r^2 − 4mn). For R = (n+αr+α^2 m, p(r+2mα), p^2 m), det = p^2(r+2mα)^2 − 4p^2 m(n+αr+α^2 m) = p^2(r^2 − 4mn). A random numeric test with 1000 cases also passed. It confirms that the Z-forms M^{-1}.Q keep det(Q), and that M^{-1}.pQ = p·M^{-1}.Q. So det(R) = p^2 det(Q). That is nonzero whenever Q is nondegenerate, e.g. every positive definite index. Read as an integer equation, "det(R) = 0" is false. The argument only needs p | det(R). Then Definition 8.5 gives a(X_2F, R) ≡ (D/p)a(F, R) = 0 mod p, so every term of a(Z_2X_2F, Q) vanishes in k. So the correction above, with det R = p^2 det Q, is right. One charitable reading exists: since the lemma is "over k", R reduced mod p is a degenerate form over F_p ((0,0,m) or (n+αr+α^2m,0,0)), so its determinant is 0 in k. That is why this is only a notational misprint and not a mathematical error. It is still inconsistent with the explicit "≡ 0 mod p" in the same sentence. arXiv:1907.08691v1 (p. 44, rendered) has word-for-word the same proof, including "det(R) = 0". Downstream, Lemma 8.6 is used only through the identity Z_2X_2 = 0: in the proof on pp. 867–868 (the commutative diagram and Q_2^2F = X_2^2F), on p. 870 ("because Z_2X_2 = 0"), and on p. 874 ("Z_2F = Z_2X_2F = 0"). That identity is true and the corrected proof covers it, so no stated result changes. - **Error** at §8.4, Theorem 8.10 and its proof, pp. 861–862; arXiv:1907.08691v1 Theorem 8.10, p. 45 (it affects a stated result). The source says `THEOREM 8.10. Let p > 3, let p + 1 ≥ k, and assume that p ∤ k(2k − 1)—so in particular k = 2 and k = p + 1 are admissible values of k. Then the map Θ : H^0(X_1(Q), ω(k,k)_{O/ϖ^m}) → H^0(X_1(Q), ω(k+p+1, k+p+1)_{O/ϖ^m}) is injective. In particular, if ΘF = 0, then we must have F = 0. Proof: We may immediately reduce to the case m = 1 and O/ϖ = k. Suppose that F lies in the kernel, so ΘF = 0. After possibly replacing (k,k) by (k − (p − 1), k − (p − 1)), we may assume that F is not divisible by the Hasse invariant. Following [75, Theorem 4.7], it suffices to show that F is not zero on the superspecial locus if it is not divisible by the Hasse invariant. … Hence the restriction to the superspecial points is injective as long has k(p − 1) ≤ p^2 + 1, which holds for k ≤ p + 1. [Checked on the rendered images of pp. 861–862.]`; it should be `The minimal fix is to exclude k = p − 1. The hypotheses become 2 ≤ k ≤ p + 1, k ≠ p − 1 and p ∤ k(2k − 1). Equivalently: 2 ≤ k ≤ p − 2 or k = p + 1, with p ∤ k(2k − 1). The bound k ≥ 2 is already implicit, because Prop. 8.9 only defines Θ for k ≥ 2. With this change the printed proof works as it stands. Either of two alternative fixes also works: - claim injectivity only on forms not divisible by the Hasse invariant; - localize at a non-Eisenstein maximal ideal m, which removes the multiples of h. This is the setting where §8.8 actually uses the theorem.`. k = p − 1 meets every printed hypothesis. p + 1 ≥ p − 1, and k(2k − 1) = (p − 1)(2p − 3) ≡ (−1)(−3) = 3 mod p, so p does not divide it when p > 3.

The spaces H^0(X_1(Q), ω(k,k)) hold all forms, not just cusp forms. §5.2 sets ω(a,b) = Sym^{a−b}E ⊗ det^b E on the toroidal compactification (the canonical extension; the subcanonical one is written W^sub). Definition 6.1 gives the Hasse invariant h ∈ H^0(X, ω^{p−1}_k), and Lemma 6.2 uses it on X_1(Q).

h has q-expansion 1. Yamauchi [75] v5, Prop. 3.11(2) says so, and the paper relies on it on pp. 865–867: multiplication by A "is the identity on q-expansions".

By Prop. 8.9(1), Θ multiplies each coefficient a_Q by det(Q). Yamauchi's own formula in the proof of his Prop. 3.9 has an extra unit factor (2/3)N^{-2}, which changes nothing. The only coefficient of h sits at Q = 0, and det(0) = 0, so Θh has q-expansion 0. The q-expansion principle (Theorem 8.1) then gives Θh = 0 with h ≠ 0, so Θ is not injective in weight (p − 1, p − 1). For m > 1, ϖ^{m−1}h is a nonzero element of H^0(ω^{p−1}_{O/ϖ^m}), since ω is locally free, and Θ also kills it.

Where the proof fails: the step "after replacing (k,k) by (k − (p − 1), k − (p − 1))" turns F = h into F/h = 1, of weight 0. Yamauchi's Theorem 4.7 (v5) does not apply there: it needs k ≥ 2, F nonzero on the superspecial locus and p ∤ k(2k − 1), and p divides 0. His local formula Θ(F)(X) ≡ k(2k − 1)α/9 is 0 at k = 0, matching Θ(1) = 0.

No other value in the range breaks the argument. For 2 ≤ k ≤ p − 2, F/h would have negative weight, so no nonzero form is divisible by h. For k = p + 1, the reduction lands in weight 2, which passes. k = p is already excluded by p ∤ k.

arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same Theorem 8.10 (p. 45) with identical hypotheses and proof. k = p − 1 meets every printed hypothesis:
- p + 1 ≥ p − 1;
- (p − 1)(2p − 3) ≡ (−1)(−3) = 3 mod p, which is nonzero for p > 3;
- Θ is defined in this weight, since Prop. 8.9 needs only k ≥ 2 (take j = k + 2, so j − k = 2 < p − 2 for p ≥ 5).

Two readings that could have rescued the theorem do not apply:
- H^0 means all forms, not cusp forms. Def. 5.3 says ω(a,b) is the canonical extension; cusp forms are written ω(a,b)(−∞).
- The standing weight assumption in Remark 8.2 ("j ≥ 4 or j = k = 2") allows the weight (p − 1, p − 1).

The counterexample:
- Take F = h, the Hasse invariant of Def. 6.1. It lies in H^0(X, ω_k^{p−1}) = H^0(ω(p − 1, p − 1)_k) and pulls back to a nonzero form on X_1(Q).
- Its q-expansion is 1. Yamauchi [75] v5, Prop. 3.11(2), says "H_{p−1}(q) = 1". The paper relies on the same fact on p. 867, where multiplication by a power A of h "is the identity on q-expansions".
- By Prop. 8.9(1), Θh has q-expansion det(0)·1 = 0, so Θh = 0 by Theorem 8.1. For m > 1, ϖ^{m−1}h works the same way.
- This matches the classical picture: Böcherer–Nagaoka give a degree-2 form of weight p − 1 congruent to 1 mod p, and Θ kills it.

Where the proof breaks: the step "replace (k,k) by (k − (p − 1), k − (p − 1))" turns h into the constant 1, of weight 0. There Yamauchi's Thm 4.7 does not apply: it assumes k ≥ 2 and p ∤ k(2k − 1), and p divides 0. His local formula Θ(F)(X) ≡ k(2k − 1)α/9 vanishes at k = 0.

No other value of k in the range fails:
- 2 ≤ k ≤ p − 2: no nonzero form is divisible by h, because the quotient would have negative weight.
- k = p: excluded by p ∤ k.
- k = p + 1: we have Θ(hG) = hΘ(G) on q-expansions, which reduces to weight 2.
- k = 1: Θ is not defined there in the paper.

How far it reaches: the theorem is used only once, in §8.8 on p. 874, where "F − X_2F ∈ M lies in the kernel of Θ … trivial by Theorem 8.10". There M = H^0(X_1(Q), ω(2,2)_k)_m (p. 867, with j = 2), so only k = 2 is used, and that case holds. Theorem 8.13 and the main results are therefore unaffected. In particular, k = p + 1 is not used in §8.8. The correction (exclude p − 1, keep k ≥ 2) is right and minimal. Theorem 8.10 as stated is still false, so affects = a stated result. - **Error** at §8.4, Proposition 8.9(2), p. 861; used in the proof of Proposition 8.25, §8.9, pp. 876–877 (it affects a stated result). The source says `PROPOSITION 8.9. Let p > 3, let j − 2 ≥ k ≥ 2, and let p − 2 > j − k. ... (2) There is a map θ1 : H^0(X1(Q), ω(j,k)_{O/ϖ^m}) → H^0(X1(Q), ω(j + p − 1, k + p + 1)_{O/ϖ^m}) whose action on q-expansions is given by θ1 Σ a_Q q^Q = Σ det(Q) con(a_Q ⊗ Q) q^Q, where con : Sym^{j−k} ⊗ Sym^2 → Sym^{j−k−2} is the natural SL2(Z)-equivariant projection. Proof: The operator Θ is defined in [75, Proposition 3.9], and the operator θ1 is defined in [75, Proposition 3.12]. [Transcribed from the rendered image of p. 861. Proof of Prop. 8.25, p. 876: "a(θ1 Z^s F, Q) = con(Sym^{j−2}[A]a(F,Q) ⊗ Q^∨) + con(Sym^{j−2}[B]a(F,Q) ⊗ Q^∨) ... we deduce that β^s a(θ1F,Q) = a(θ1 Z^s F,Q) = 0, and since β ≠ 0, we have a(θ1F,Q) = 0 and θ1F = 0."]`; it should be `Prop. 8.9(2) should read θ1 Σ a_Q q^Q = Σ con(a_Q ⊗ Q) q^Q, with no det(Q) factor. Here con is the integral SL2-equivariant projection, which is unique up to a p-adic unit. The target weight (j+p−1, k+p+1) is correct as printed. Deleting det(Q) is the right and minimal correction. Consequence for the proof of Prop. 8.25. The proof as written only gives a(θ1F,Q) = 0 when (D/p) = 1, through Lemma 8.24. The case (D/p) = −1 is also fine, because there a(F,Q) = β^{-1}a(ZF,Q) = 0. The case p | d(Q) was covered automatically by the printed det(Q), but the correct formula does not cover it, so it needs its own argument. Fix. Second-transvectant equivariance gives con(ρ(g)x ⊗ gPg^T) = det(g)^2 ρ'(g) con(x ⊗ P). So for det M = p and p-integral P, con(ρ(M)x ⊗ M.P) = p·ρ'(M) con(x ⊗ P) ≡ 0 mod p. By Lemma 8.3, a(θ1ZF,Q) = Σ_S con(ρ(M)a(F,M^{-1}.Q) ⊗ Q) ≡ 0. Hence θ1∘Z ≡ 0 on formal mod-p q-expansions, and θ1F = β^{-1}θ1(ZF) = 0 for every Q at once. With this, Lemma 8.24 and the (D/p) = 1 hypothesis are not needed. Equivalently, case by case. For p-primitive Q with p | D, F(Q) = {[P]} and βa(F,Q) = ρ(M_P)a(F,P), which is killed by the same identity. For Q ≡ 0 mod p, con(· ⊗ Q) ≡ 0.`. Printed text confirmed on the rendered p. 861. arXiv:1907.08691v1 Prop. 8.9(2) has the identical formula. Its proof of Prop. 8.25 is the same, citing [Yam16] = "ArXiv version from August, 2016", which is Yamauchi 1410.7894v5 (submitted 30 Aug 2016).

(1) The cited source. I downloaded Yamauchi v5. θ_i^k = H_{p−1}·θ̃_i^k, where θ̃_1^k is the projection of KS^{-1}∘∇ onto ω(k1, k2+2) under decomposition (3.31) (see (3.34)). The proof of Prop. 3.12 gives G = H_{p−1}·KS^{-1}∘∇(F) with A_G(T) = Σ_n (1/N)A_{F_n}(T)δ_n ⊗ T. This is linear in T. So the q-expansion of θ1 is pr_1(A_F(T) ⊗ T), with no det(T). Only Θ carries a det(T): "Θ(F)(q) = (2/3)Σ(1/N^2) det(T)A_F(T)q_N^T". The same holds in v8 (Prop. 3.13).

(2) Independent reasons.
(a) θ̃1 involves a single application of ∇, and on the Mumford family d(q^T) contributes one factor of T. So the coefficients are linear in Q, whereas det(Q)·con(a⊗Q) is cubic.
(b) Prop. 8.9(1) and (2) as printed are mutually inconsistent. Yamauchi defines Θ̃ = θ̃_1∘θ̃, and θ has coefficients a_T ⊗ T (his Rem. 3.14). So θ1(θF) = H·ΘF, with coefficients ∝ con(T⊗T)a_T ∝ det(T)a_T. The printed (2), applied in weight (k+p+1, k+p−1), which satisfies the hypotheses, would instead give det(T)^2 a_T.
(c) Weight count. con lands in Sym^{j−k−2}det^{k+2}, and adding the Hasse weight (p−1,p−1) gives the printed target. An extra det(Q) is a shift of (2,2), as Θ shows, and 2 ≢ 0 mod p−1.

(3) The paper's own proof of Prop. 8.25 uses the formula without det(Q): a(θ1Z^sF,Q) = con(Sym^{j−2}[A]a(F,Q) ⊗ Q^∨) + .... Its final "θ1F = 0" silently needs the coefficients with p | D. The printed det(Q) supplies them, but the correct formula does not, so as written the proof has a gap. I checked the repair identity con(Sym[M]x ⊗ p^{-1}MPM^T) = p·Sym[M]con(x⊗P) (second transvectant) by exact rational arithmetic: 900 random trials with p = 5, 7, 11 and det M = p, and it held in every case. I also checked that tv2(Q,Q) = 8det(Q).

Affects: Prop. 8.9(2) is a numbered result and is false as stated. Its only use of the q-expansion formula is the proof of Prop. 8.25. The statement of Prop. 8.25 remains true by the repair, and Thm. 8.11 uses [75, Thm. 3.20], not the formula. Thm. 8.13 and Thm. 9.1 are unaffected. Printed text confirmed on the rendered p. 861 and on arXiv v1 p. 45.

Defence attempts, all of which fail:
(i) Conventions. The paper's weight convention (p. 856: U = Sym^{j−k} ⊗ det^k) and the target weight are exactly those of Yamauchi's θ1, so no reinterpretation is available. The proof simply defers to [75, Prop. 3.12], and [75] is arXiv:1410.7894v5 (ref. list; v1 cites "[Yam16], ArXiv version from August, 2016"). In v5, θ1 = H_{p−1}·θ̃1, where θ̃1 is the projection of KS^{-1}∘∇ onto ω(k1, k2+2) (see (3.34)). The proof of Prop. 3.12 computes A_G(T) := Σ_n (1/N) A_{F_n}(T) δ_n ⊗ T, which is linear in T and has no det(T). The only formula with det(T) is Θ: Θ(F)(q) = (2/3) Σ (1/N^2) det(T) A_F(T) q_N^T.
(ii) Weight count. con(a_Q ⊗ Q) lies in Sym^{j−k−2} det^{k+2}, which is weight (j, k+2). Adding the Hasse weight (p−1, p−1) gives exactly the printed target. A det(Q) factor shifts the weight by (2,2), as Prop. 8.9(1) itself shows ((k,k) → (k+p+1, k+p+1)), and 2 ≢ 0 mod p−1 for p > 3. So the printed q-expansion is that of Θ∘θ1F, not of a form of the stated weight.
(iii) The paper's own computation on p. 876 uses the formula without det(Q), so the authors' actual calculation agrees with the correction.

Hence Prop. 8.9(2) is false as stated. It is not only a typographical slip, because deleting det(Q) opens a hole in a later proof. The only place the q-expansion formula is used is the proof of Prop. 8.25. That proof establishes a(θ1F,Q) = 0 only for (D/p) = 1 (Lemma 8.24), and then concludes "θ1F = 0". With the correct formula, the Q with p | d(Q) are no longer killed by det(Q) ≡ 0, so the proof as written has a gap there.

The gap closes with the GL2-equivariance identity above. That identity also underlies the paper's own claim con(Sym^{j−2}[A]x ⊗ Q^∨) = 0 when AQA^t = p^s Q. I checked it in exact rational arithmetic, using the paper's variance (Q ↦ MQM^T paired with ρ(M), as in a(F,M.Q) = ρ(M)a(F,Q)):
- 3000 random trials with p ∈ {5, 7, 11, 13}, Sym degree 2–10 and integral M with det M = p: con(ρ(M)x ⊗ p^{-1}MPM^T) = p·ρ'(M)con(x⊗P) held every time.
- 1000 SL2 trials confirmed the transformation law.
- tv2(Q,Q) = 8 det Q, as expected.

Other uses: Theorem 8.11 uses θ1 only through [75, Thm 3.20] and restrictions to strata, not through the formula. Prop. 8.9 is never cited by number. The statement of Prop. 8.25 remains true, and Theorem 8.13 and everything downstream are unaffected. - **Error** at §8.4, Proposition 8.9 (1) and (2), p. 861; also the statements of Theorem 8.10 (p. 861) and Theorem 8.11 (p. 862). arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text (Prop. 8.9, Thms 8.10–8.11, pp. 44–46, citing [Yam16]). (it affects a stated result). The source says `PROPOSITION 8.9 Let p > 3, let j − 2 ≥ k ≥ 2, and let p − 2 > j − k. (1) There is a map Θ : H^0(X_1(Q), ω(k,k)_{O/ϖ^m}) → H^0(X_1(Q), ω(k + p + 1, k + p + 1)_{O/ϖ^m}) whose action on q-expansions is given by Θ Σ a_Q q^Q = Σ det(Q) a_Q q^Q. (2) There is a map θ_1 : H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j,k)_{O/ϖ^m}) → H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j + p − 1, k + p + 1)_{O/ϖ^m}) whose action on q-expansions is given by θ_1 Σ a_Q q^Q = Σ det(Q) con(a_Q ⊗ Q) q^Q, ... Proof: The operator Θ is defined in [75, Proposition 3.9], and the operator θ_1 is defined in [75, Proposition 3.12]. [Theorem 8.10 (p. 861) and Theorem 8.11 (p. 862) repeat the maps with coefficients O/ϖ^m; their proofs begin 'We may immediately reduce to the case m = 1 and O/ϖ = k' and 'It suffices to work over k = O/ϖ'.]`; it should be `In Proposition 8.9 and Theorems 8.10–8.11, replace the coefficients O/ϖ^m with k = O/ϖ. More generally the results hold over any O-algebra in which p = 0, for example O/ϖ^m with m ≤ e(O/Z_p), by flat base change of Yamauchi's characteristic-p construction. Then drop "We may immediately reduce to the case m = 1" and "It suffices to work over k". When m > e, so that p ≠ 0 in O/ϖ^m (e.g. O = Z_p and m = 2), there is in general no map with weight shift (p+1,p+1) (resp. (p−1,p+1)) acting as stated on q-expansions. A mod-p^m theta operator exists only with a weight shift ≡ 2 mod (p−1)p^{m−1}, which is larger. Stating everything over O/ϖ, i.e. mod p, is right and minimal. For m > e the printed statement is false, not merely unproved.`. I confirmed the printed text from the rendered p. 861. The only justification given is the citation of [75], Yamauchi, 'The weight reduction of mod p Siegel modular forms for GSp4'. That source works mod p: its operators involve the Hasse invariant, which exists only in characteristic p. No construction over O/ϖ^m is given for m ≥ 2 with p ≠ 0 in O/ϖ^m, and the claim is false there.

(a) Elliptic analogue. θ does not send forms mod p^2 of weight k to weight k+p+1. Katz's weight congruences show that θf mod p^m has weight ≡ k+2 mod (p−1)p^{m−1} whenever θf ≢ 0 mod p (Chen–Kiming). I checked this for p=5: θE6 is congruent to a form in M_12 = <E4^3, Δ> modulo 5 but not modulo 25.

(b) The Siegel case, computed directly. I coded the degree-2 Siegel Eisenstein coefficients from Cohen's H(k−1,N), with checks E4: 13440, 30240; E6: 44352, 166320. Level-1 forms of weight w are spanned by monomials in E4, E6, E10 and E12. I took p=5 and F=E6, which is 5-integral. The hypotheses allow this: Thm 8.10 explicitly admits k=p+1=6, and Prop 8.9 holds with j=8. ΘF is not ≡ 0 mod 5: at T=[[1,1/2],[1/2,1]] the coefficient is (3/4)·44352 = 33264 ≡ 4 mod 5.

For each weight I computed the saturated 5-adic span of the weight-w forms restricted to the 477 matrices T with n,m ≤ 6. Failure of this test is a rigorous obstruction, and a positive control passes. Results:
- ΘE6 ≡ a weight-12 form mod 5, consistent with Böcherer–Nagaoka and Yamauchi.
- ΘE6 is not congruent mod 25 to any 5-integral level-1 form of weight 12, and it also fails in weights 28 and 32.
- It passes mod 25 only in weight 48 = 6+2+2·20. This matches the Chen–Kiming-type shift 2+2p^{m−1}(p−1).
So with O=Z_5 and m=2, the map asserted in Prop 8.9(1) and Thm 8.10 cannot exist at level 1.

At any prime-to-p level, including X_1(Q), a weight-(12,12) form mod 25 with this q-expansion would give a function on the irreducible Igusa tower. Ichikawa/Katz-type weight congruences would then force 12 ≡ 8 (the p-adic weight of ΘE6) mod 20, which is false.

(c) Nothing downstream breaks. The proofs of Thms 8.10 and 8.11 immediately reduce to m=1, and all uses (§8.8, Prop. 8.25 with Thm 8.11) are over k. So the mistake is confined to the stated generality of Prop 8.9 and Thms 8.10–8.11. It is best classed as an error, a false statement for m ≥ 2, rather than a gap. The computations in (b) were done by a short computer enumeration. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED AND FAILED.
(a) The cited source works only mod p. Yamauchi arXiv:1410.7894v5, §3, begins: "In this section we will define various θ-operators on the space of mod p Siegel modular forms". Prop. 3.9 reads: "Recall the Hasse invariant H_{p−1} = det A ∈ H^0(S_{N,p}, ω^{p−1}). Put Θ := H_{p−1}·Θ̃ ... (1) Let F ∈ M_k(Γ(N), F_p) ... (a) Θ(F) ∈ M_{k+p+1}(Γ(N), F_p)". Prop. 3.12 says: "If F ∈ M_k(Γ(N), F_p), then θ_1^k(F) ∈ M_{(k1+p−1,k2+p+1)}(Γ(N), F_p)". Here S_{N,p} is a component of S_K(N) ⊗ F_p. So the construction needs the characteristic-p Hasse invariant and the Frobenius splitting. The other reference, [27] Flander, is also "(mod p)". Nothing in the paper or in its sources builds Θ or θ_1 over O/ϖ^m when p ≠ 0 there.
(b) One partial defence holds. If m ≤ e, then O/ϖ^m = k[ϖ]/(ϖ^m) is flat over F_p, and Yamauchi's maps extend by base change. So the statement is true in that case, but not for general m.
(c) For m > e the statement is false. Example: p ≥ 11, O = Z_p, m = 2, F = the degree-2 Siegel Eisenstein series E_4, pulled back to X_1(Q). Take k = 4 and j = 6, which satisfies the hypotheses. Cohen's formula gives a(E_4; n,r,m = 1,1,1) = 13440; direct computation also gives 30240 for (1,0,1). So the coefficient of ΘE_4 at Q = [[1,1/2],[1/2,1]] is (3/4)·13440 = 10080 = 2^5·3^2·5·7, a p-unit, and ΘE_4 ≢ 0 mod p.
- Böcherer–Nagaoka (arXiv:1305.0604, Thm 4.1 and Cor. 4.9) show ΘE_4 ≡ F mod p^m with F of weight k+(p−1)p^{m−1} and ρ = det^2. So ΘE_4 is a p-adic Siegel form of weight k+2.
- Suppose G were a mod-p^2 form of weight k+p+1 with the same q-expansion. By the q-expansion principle on the Igusa tower, G and ΘE_4 would agree there, with G transforming by det^{k+p+1} and ΘE_4 by det^{k+2}. Take t a primitive root mod p^2; then t^{p−1} = 1 + p·u with u a unit. This forces p·ΘE_4 ≡ 0 mod p^2, i.e. ΘE_4 ≡ 0 mod p, a contradiction.
- The same happens for elliptic forms: Chen–Kiming (Mathematika 62, 2016) prove θ mod p^m has weight shift 2 + 2p^{m−1}(p−1), which is optimal in some cases when m ≥ 2.
- A sanity check matches the known mod-p kernel: the coefficients of ΘE_4 above all vanish mod 5 and mod 7, as expected because 4 = p−1 (for p = 5) and 4 = (p+1)/2 (for p = 7).
So the maps in Proposition 8.9 do not exist over O/ϖ^m for m > e. Theorems 8.10 and 8.11 are then ill-posed for such m, since they "reduce to m = 1" a map that does not exist.
CONSEQUENCES. Only the mod-ϖ versions are used later:
- The proof of Theorem 8.13 says (p. 865) "we may work with coefficients over a finite field k = O/ϖ", with M = H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j,2)_k)_m on p. 867.
- §8.8 (p. 874) applies Theorem 8.10 to F − X_2F ∈ M over k.
- Proposition 8.25 is stated "modulo p" and is combined with Theorem 8.11 on p. 877.
- Remark 8.23 only mentions Θ.
Theorem 8.13, Theorem 9.1 and the appendix are unaffected; the appendix never uses Θ. (4) I recomputed the fit with the proof of Theorem 8.11. There (k1,k2) = (j,2) with p−1 > j ≥ 4, so r = j−2 < p and k1−3k2 = j−6. Since |j−6| < p, this is ≡ 0 mod p only when j = 6. That matches "does not apply in weight (6,2)". When j = 6 the F0 and F1 terms vanish, leaving −3 t22 F2|X, which is nonzero for p > 3 once F2|X ≠ 0. That matches "provided that one may assume ... that F2|X ≠ 0". So the intended result is certainly v5 Theorem 4.9.
(5) The statement is word-for-word "Theorem 3.20" in v1, v2 and v3 (p. 28 of v1). It became Theorem 4.9 from v4 onward. The number 3.20 is therefore a stale reference to the 2014 versions.

arXiv v1 of this paper (1907.08691v1, p. 45) has the same error: "Then the result follows directly from Theorem 3.20 of [Yam16]", with "(in the notation of ibid.)" in place of the second occurrence. It also has "Following Theorem 4.7 of [Yam16]" in the proof of Theorem 8.10.

Both follow from one lemma: if a ≥ b and pa − b < 0, then H^0(X, ω(a,b)_k) = 0. Proof of the lemma, using only what the paper already uses: 1. On each supersingular P^1, ω(a,b) = Sym^{a−b}E ⊗ det^b with E = O(−1)⊕O(p) and det E = O(p−1). So it is a sum of line bundles of degree at most pa − b < 0, and a section vanishes on Z. 2. The printed text matches the image of p. 862 word for word. Earlier in the proof the only assumptions are θ1F = 0 and (for the case sent to [75]) that F is nonzero on the superspecial locus. The proof never assumes or proves that F|_Y ≠ 0.

2. The reduction "it remains to show that the restriction of F to the superspecial locus is nonzero" must hold for every nonzero F. A form F = hF' vanishes on V(h), which contains Z and S, so this case has to be ruled out. The proof of Theorem 8.10 does this explicitly: "After possibly replacing (k,k) by (k−(p−1), k−(p−1)), we may assume that F is not divisible by the Hasse invariant." Theorem 8.11 has no such step. The same trick is not available there, because the lowered weight (j−p+1, 3−p) is outside the range of Prop. 8.9 and Theorem 8.11. What is needed instead is the vanishing H^0(X, ω(j−p+1, 3−p)_k) = 0. This is neither proved nor cited.

3. I checked Yamauchi arXiv:1410.7894v5, whose numbering differs from the paper's citation. Its θ1 non-vanishing result (Thm 4.9) assumes that F is not identically zero on S(0,0). Nothing in it treats forms divisible by the Hasse invariant or proves negative-weight vanishing.

5. The second printed sequence ends in H^1(X, ω(j,2)_k ⊗ ω^{−m−(p−1)}), a twist by ω^{−(p−1)}. That is the sequence for 0 → L⊗ω^{−(p−1)} →(h) L → L|_{V(h)} → 0, so Y must be V(h). Theorem 8.10 uses "p-rank 1 strata" in the same loose way for the closure, so this is a clarification, not a separate error.

6. The fix in the correction works. The iteration along Z and V(h) uses only facts the paper already relies on: the Moret-Bailly P^1's, Z Cartier in V(h) (Koblitz), and V(h) reduced (Yamauchi v5 Prop. 3.24). The paper's own unproved "The first term vanishes" needs exactly this vanishing lemma.

7. The claim F|_Y ≠ 0 is in fact true for nonzero F, so Theorem 8.11 as stated is correct. Only the written proof is incomplete. It is used in the proof of Theorem 8.13 ("Combining Proposition 8.25 with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11 ..."), and through it the main modularity theorem, but those results are unaffected once the step is supplied.

8. arXiv:1907.08691v1 (Theorem 8.11, pp. 45–46) has the same text, with "rank one strata ... We are assuming that the restriction of F to Y is nonzero."

The gap is genuine but minor and easy to fill. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED, FAILS.
(a) Nothing earlier in the proof, or in the statement, gives F|_Y ≠ 0. The only assumptions are θ1F = 0 and, for the case sent to [75, Thm 3.20], F|_S ≠ 0. Then "it remains to show that the restriction of F to the superspecial locus is nonzero" must hold for every nonzero F. A form F = hG vanishes on V(h), which contains Z and S. So that case has to be ruled out.
(b) Theorem 8.10 does rule it out (pp. 861–862): "After possibly replacing (k,k) by (k−(p−1), k−(p−1)), we may assume that F is not divisible by the Hasse invariant." Theorem 8.11 has no such step. The same trick is not available there, because the new weight (j−p+1, 3−p) is outside the theorem.
(c) The charitable reading is "forms of weight with negative entries obviously vanish". That is standard in characteristic 0 and for scalar weights (ampleness). For vector-valued weights mod p it needs an argument, and none is given. The same goes for "The first term vanishes", which is asserted bare.
(d) Yamauchi (arXiv 1410.7894v8) Thms 4.7 and 4.9 assume f is not identically zero on S(0,0). Nothing there handles forms divisible by h.
(e) Y must be V(h): the second sequence, with twist ω^{−m−(p−1)}, is the sequence for multiplication by h.

TRUTH. With the paper's convention ω(j,k) = Sym^{j−k} ⊗ det^k (p. 856) and the P^1 data it quotes (E = O(−1)⊕O(p), ω = O(p−1)), the top summand degree of ω(a,b) is pa − b. This reproduces the paper's own jp − 2 for weight (j,2). A short computer enumeration over p ≤ 101 and 4 ≤ j < p−1 confirms pa − b < 0 for both weights. So the lemma above applies. It needs only facts the main argument already uses: Z is a reduced Cartier divisor in V(h) (Koblitz, [70]), and it is the union of P^1s. Theorem 8.11 is therefore true, and the proof is incomplete.

CONSEQUENCES. Theorem 8.11 is used only in the proof of Theorem 8.13 (p. 877: "Combining Proposition 8.25 with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11"). Theorem 8.13 feeds Theorem 6.17 (p. 845) and then the main Theorem 9.1. None of these is affected once the lemma is supplied. - **Gap** at §8.4, proof of Theorem 8.11, p. 862, sentences 4–5 of the proof. arXiv v1 (1907.08691v1) has the same text in the proof of Theorem 8.11 on pp. 45–46. There it reads "Theorem 3.20 of [Yam16] ... (in the notation of ibid.)", and has the extra slip "and thus for there exists".. The source says `provided that one may assume (in the notation of [75, Theorem 3.20]) that F_2|_X ≠ 0, which can be achieved under the action of Γ̄ ⊂ SL_2(Z) for j < p − 1, since the level of Γ̄ is prime to p and so surjects onto SL_2(F_p). The corresponding representation of SL_2(F_p) is irreducible, and thus there exists an element which applied to F has F_i|_X ≠ 0 for any fixed choice of i.`; it should be `Replace the appeal to Γ̄ with a change of the local frame (ω1, ω2) of E at the superspecial point X by some g ∈ SL_2(F_p). This is Yamauchi's own device: in the proof of his Theorem 4.9 (arXiv v5; Theorem 3.20 in v1–v3) he uses ρ_r((1 a; 0 1)) with a ∈ F_p. The components F_i are taken in the basis δ_n = ω1^{r−n} ω2^n (ω1∧ω2)^{k2}, so they move by Sym^{j−2} of the frame change. For j − 2 ≤ p − 1 that representation is absolutely irreducible under SL_2(F_p), and F|_X ≠ 0. So some F_p-rational frame gives F_2|_X ≠ 0. Whether θ1(F) vanishes at X does not depend on the frame. The frame change should be F_p-rational, as in Yamauchi, and not an arbitrary element of GL_2(k). Yamauchi's normal form A(X) ≡ (t11 t12; t12 t22) mod m^2 involves a Frobenius twist g^{(p)}, and F_p-rational frame changes keep it. The rest of the proof is unchanged.`. Checked against the rendered p. 857 and 861–863 and against Yamauchi arXiv:1410.7894 v1–v6. In v5 the cited Theorem 3.20 is Theorem 4.9. It assumes k1 − 3k2 ≢ 0 mod p. The local term of (4.5) at X is −(k1−3k2)/2·t11F0|X − (k1−3k2)/2·t12F1|X − (k1−3)·t22F2|X. In weight (6,2) the first two coefficients vanish and the third is −3, so F_2|_X ≠ 0 is exactly what is needed. The paper's reduction to that case is correct.

Case for the defence. The paper names the right group, SL_2(F_p). The irreducibility argument is correct: if (gv)_2 = 0 for every g, the span of the orbit would be a nonzero invariant subspace inside the hyperplane x_2 = 0. Γ̄ does surject onto SL_2(F_p) because its level is prime to p. Read charitably, "the action of Γ̄" means ρ acting on the coefficients, which mod ϖ factors through SL_2(F_p), and so amounts to a frame change.

Why the justification still fails. On p. 857, Γ̄ is defined only by the q-expansion symmetry a(F, M.Q) = ρ(M)a(F,Q) for M ∈ Γ̄. That symmetry says F is Γ̄-invariant: Γ̄ lies in the level group and acts trivially on X_1(Q) and on F. It gives no action on the fibre of E at a superspecial point in characteristic p. So "applying an element of Γ̄ to F" leaves F_i|_X unchanged in any fixed frame, and the "since the level of Γ̄ is prime to p" clause proves nothing about X. The step actually needed is the frame change. The paper does not state it, but it is standard and appears in the cited source, restricted there to unipotent frame changes. So this is a gap in the exposition, not a false statement. The proposed correction is right and minimal.

Consequences. Theorem 8.11 is used only at the end of the proof of Theorem 8.13 (p. 877: "Combining Proposition 8.25 with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11, we obtain a contradiction"), and Theorem 8.13 feeds Theorem 9.1. Weight (6,2) falls inside the range p−1 > j of Theorem 8.13 once p ≥ 11, so the case matters, but the claim F_2|_X ≠ 0 holds with the frame-change argument. Nothing downstream changes.

Side note, a separate citation slip: "[75, Theorem 3.20]" follows the numbering of Yamauchi v1–v3, while "[75, Theorem 4.7]" and the bibliography (v5) follow v4/v5 numbering, where 3.20 is a Lemma and the result is Theorem 4.9. - **Misprint** at Proposition 1.3.1, parts (i) and (ii), p. 27 (it affects a stated result). The source says `i) Every Poincare object in Pn(D^p(R), Q^{[-n]}) is cobordant to one which is ((-n-a)/2)-connective. ii) Every Lagrangian L -> X of a ((-n-a)/2)-connective Poincare object (X,q) in Pn(D^p(R), Q^{[-n]}) is cobordant relative to X to a Lagrangian L' -> X such that ...`; it should be `Pn(C, Q^{[-n]}) in both places`. The proposition is stated for a general stable infinity-category C: its hypotheses are 'Let C be a stable infinity-category with a bounded t-structure C_{>=0}, C_{<=0}. Let Q be an r-symmetric Poincare structure on C with duality D such that D(C_{<=0}) is contained in C_{>=-d}', and its concluding sentence is 'the canonical map L^{a,b}_n(C,Q) -> L_n(C,Q) is an isomorphism'. There is no ring R in the hypotheses at all, so D^p(R) in parts (i) and (ii) is undefined there. The proof confirms the intended reading, opening 'it suffices to show that every Poincare object (X,q) in Pn(C, Q[-n]) is cobordant to one whose underlying object is ((-n-a)/2)-connective'. What makes this more than cosmetic is that the generality is the whole point: the paragraph immediately preceding the proposition says the argument is cast 'in the setting of a general Poincare infinity-category (C,Q) equipped with a t-structure ... as we shall use this more general setup for a category of torsion modules, which is not itself given by modules over a discrete ring, in Theorem 2.2.4 below'. That application is real and the chain is short: Corollary 1.3.8, which IS stated correctly for a general C, is proved by 'Apply Proposition 1.3.1 in the case of r = infinity, d = 0'; and the proof of Theorem 2.2.4 says 'Hence for both sides of (7) we are in the situation of Corollary 1.3.8', where the two sides of (7) are the direct sum over the primes of S of the perfect derived categories D^p(F_p) of the residue fields, and D^p_S(R), the full subcategory of S-primary torsion perfect R-modules. Neither is D^p(R) - the second is precisely the category of torsion modules the preceding paragraph promised, and the first is a product. So as printed, parts (i) and (ii) fail to cover what Corollary 1.3.8, and through it the devissage Theorem 2.2.4 and hence Theorem 7 and the Berrick-Karoubi conjecture, ask of them. - **Misprint** at Example 2.3.14, p. 47 (it affects the proof). The source says `and again from [Lam05, VI Remark 2.31], we find that the kernel of .<1,3> is additively generated by 2<1> and <1,-2>, and deduce an isomorphism ker( L^s_0(Q_2) --.<1,3>--> L^s_0(Q_2) ) = Z/4 (+) Z/2`; it should be `additively generated by 2<1> and <1,-3>`. The form <1,-2> is not in that kernel. Over Q_2 the form <1,3> is the norm form of the unramified quadratic extension E = Q_2(sqrt(-3)) - which is the same field whose ring of integers the example is about - so for a unit or non-unit scalar a the form a.<1,3> is the scaled norm form, and a.<1,3> = c.<1,3> in the Witt group if and only if a/c is a norm from E. Since E is unramified, its norm group is exactly the set of elements of even valuation. Hence <a,b>.<1,3> = a.<1,3> + b.<1,3> vanishes if and only if a/(-b) is a norm, that is if and only if v(a) + v(b) is even. For <1,-2> that sum is 0 + 1 = 1, so <1,-2>.<1,3> is not zero; for <1,-3> it is 0 + 0, so <1,-3>.<1,3> is zero, as one also sees directly: <1,-3>.<1,3> = <1,3,-3,-9> = <1,-1> + <3,-3> = 0. The failure of <1,-2> can be confirmed a second way, by computing invariants: <1,-2>.<1,3> = <1,3,-2,-6> has rank 4 and discriminant 36, that is 1 modulo squares, and Hasse invariant (3,-2)(3,-6)(-2,-6) = (+1)(-1)(-1) = +1 at the prime 2, whereas the hyperbolic form of rank 4 has Hasse invariant (-1,-1) = -1; and directly, x^2 + 3y^2 = 2(z^2 + 3w^2) forces a valuation-parity contradiction because both bracketed terms are norms from E and so of even valuation, so the form is anisotropic and in particular not hyperbolic. The stated isomorphism type Z/4 (+) Z/2 is nevertheless correct, with 2<1> and <1,-3> as generators: <1> has order 8 in W(Q_2), 2<1,-3> = 4<1> since <1,1,-3,-3> and <1,1,1,1> agree in rank, discriminant and Hasse invariant, and <1,-3> - 2<1> = <-1,-3> has discriminant 3 and so does not lie in the cyclic group generated by 2<1>; the order is confirmed by counting, the image of multiplication by <1,3> having order 4 and W(Q_2) order 32. Since 2 and 3 differ by one glyph and <1,-3> is exactly the right element, this reads as a typographical slip rather than a mistaken computation. It affects only this step: the conclusion of the example, and the L-group table it feeds, are correct. Checked in a rendered clip of p. 47 at 300 dpi, where the entry is unambiguously <1,-2>. - **Gap** at Example 2.3.14, p. 46 (it affects the proof). The source says `The discriminant of K is (3), and as (2) does not divide (3), we deduce that (2) is a prime ideal in R [Neu99, Corollary III.2.12], and hence is the single dyadic prime.`; it should be `the cited criterion gives only that (2) is unramified; that it is prime needs in addition that -3 is not a square modulo 8, equivalently that x^2 + x + 1 is irreducible over F_2`. Not dividing the discriminant gives unramifiedness, not inertia: an unramified rational prime in a quadratic field is either prime or a product of two distinct primes. The printed inference therefore does not follow, as the field Q(sqrt(-7)) shows - its discriminant is -7, the prime 2 does not divide it, and yet (2) splits, because x^2 + x + 2 factors as x(x+1) modulo 2. The conclusion drawn here is true: in Q(sqrt(-3)) the minimal polynomial x^2 + x + 1 of the Eisenstein unit is irreducible over F_2, equivalently -3 is congruent to 5 and not to 1 modulo 8, so (2) is inert and is the unique dyadic prime, and the example's count d = 1 of dyadic primes is right. Only the justification is incomplete, and the cited Neukirch corollary sits in the section on the different and discriminant, where the statement available is the ramification criterion. ### Canning–Larson–Payne, "Extensions of tautological rings and motivic structures in the cohomology of the moduli spaces of stable curves", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2024) (`PAPER-CANNING-LARSON-PAYNE-24`)

- **Misprint** at First sentence of the proof of Theorem 1.5(3), Section 6.2 (arXiv v3; the published version at doi:10.1017/fmp.2024.24 has the same text). The source says `We now show that H_k(M̄_{g,n}) is tautological for even k ≥ 14.`; it should be `for even k ≤ 14.`. Theorem 1.5(3) states that RH^*(M̄_{g,n}) contains H_k(M̄_{g,n}) for even k ≤ 14, and the proof itself uses the opposite inequality two sentences later: 'When g ≥ 3, in all of these cases with k ≤ 14 we know that M_{g,n} has the CKgP'. The proof is correct with k ≤ 14; with k ≥ 14 it would assert the statement in degrees where it is open (Conjecture 1.8 concerns even k ≤ 20) and where the table of known CKgP cases does not apply. ### Castella et al., "On the anticyclotomic Iwasawa theory of rational elliptic curves at Eisenstein primes", Inventiones Mathematicae (2022) (`PAPER-CASTELLA-ETAL-22`)

- **Error** at Introduction §0.3 (Examples), p. 5. The source says `One can proceed similarly for p = 3 (resp. p = 7), taking real quadratic twists of, for example, the elliptic curve y² + y = x³ + x² − 7x + 5 of conductor 91 (resp. y² + xy + y = x³ − x² − 19353x + 958713 of conductor 574).`; it should be `For p = 7 use a curve with good reduction at 7 and a rational 7-isogeny, for example 26b1: y² + xy + y = x³ − x² − 3x + 3 (conductor 26, rational 7-torsion).`. 574 = 2·7·41, and the curve has multiplicative reduction of type I_7 at 7 (PARI: ellglobalred and elllocalred). Since v_7(j) < 0, every quadratic twist has bad reduction at 7, so neither the curve nor any twist satisfies the paper's standing hypothesis that p be a prime of good reduction. The other examples check out: conductors 123, 91, 441 and 1225 are prime to p = 5, 3, 13, 37, and the curves have rational p-isogenies and analytic rank 1. ### Česnavičius, "Purity for the Brauer group", Duke Mathematical Journal (2019) (`PAPER-CESNAVICIUS-19`)

- **Gap** at Proposition 2.2 and its proof, p.4, in arXiv 1711.06456v4 (1 December 2018, the latest version; PDF SHA-256 a62a12bb…8709); the author's copy of 27 November 2018 on his homepage has the same text; the published text, Duke Math. J. 168 (2019), 1461–1486, was not collated (it affects a stated result). The source says `"Proposition 2.2. For a finite, flat map R → R′ of local rings, an open subscheme V ⊂ Spec R, and an affine, smooth R-group scheme G, if (1) Γ(Spec R, O) ≅ Γ(V, O) via pullback; and (2) every G-torsor is trivial over R; then the following pullback is injective: H¹_et(V, G) ↪ H¹_et(V_{R′}, G). (2.2.1)" Proof: "… every element of X(V) lifts to (Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′}))(V), so, by [Gir71, III.3.2.2], the map H¹_et(V, G) → H¹_et(V, Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′})) (2.2.2) is injective."`; it should be `State Proposition 2.2 for commutative G, which covers both of its uses (Proposition 2.3, with G = Res_{R′/R}(T_{R′})/T, and Corollary 2.4, with G = T). For noncommutative G, supply the missing step: for every G-torsor P over V, the twisted map (^P Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′}))(V) → (^P X)(V) must also be surjective.`. Write H = Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′}) and X = H/G. Surjectivity of H(V) → X(V) shows that the fibre of H¹(V, G) → H¹(V, H) over the trivial class is trivial. When G is commutative this is injectivity, because the map is a group homomorphism. For a noncommutative G, H¹ is only a pointed set. The fibre through the class of a torsor P is the orbit set of (^P H)(V) acting on (^P X)(V), for the twists by P (Giraud III.3.2; cf. Serre, Galois Cohomology, I.5.5, Cor. 2). The proof checks only the untwisted case. The twisted forms ^P X live only over V, so hypothesis (1) and the affineness of X give no control of their V-points. If P extends to R it is trivial by (2), so the problem is exactly the torsors on V that do not extend. Proposition 2.2 is used only in the proofs of Proposition 2.3 (G = Res_{R′/R}(T_{R′})/T) and Corollary 2.4 (G = T, an R-torus), where G is commutative, so the main theorems are unaffected. Noted by the extraction (gap G-NONABELIAN, items h1-descent and h1-abelian), which did not claim the statement false; neither is it claimed false here. (cc-442dc5) Reclassified to affect a stated result: Proposition 2.2 is stated for arbitrary affine smooth G, and for noncommutative G the printed proof gives only a trivial neutral fibre, so the statement is not established in that generality. Its two uses (Proposition 2.3 and Corollary 2.4) have commutative G, so the main theorems are unaffected. Recorded as `PAPER-CESNAVICIUS-19/E1`; looked for an existing correction in: Duke Mathematical Journal: Crossref record of DOI 10.1215/00127094-2018-0057, checked 22 September 2026: no erratum or other update is registered; arXiv 1711.06456: v1 (17 November 2017), v2 (24 November 2017), v3 (17 January 2018), v4 (1 December 2018, the latest); the author's copy https://www.imo.universite-paris-saclay.fr/~kestutis.cesnavicius/brauer-purity.pdf (dated 27 November 2018, SHA-256 4187331e…97a1), checked 22 September 2026: Proposition 2.2 and its proof are unchanged, and no erratum is linked; web search for an erratum or correction, 22 September 2026: none found; Rechecked by cc-442dc5 on 23 September 2026: arXiv v4 re-fetched (SHA-256 a62a12bb…, matching); Unpaywall lists only the arXiv copy, so the Duke text could not be collated..

- **Misprint** at Corollary 1.11, last words of the statement (page 3 of the author's copy of the published version); the same sentence in arXiv:1810.04493v2. The source says `there is an open S-immersion X ↪ X̄ into a proper S-scheme X̄ that is Cohen–Macaulay such that X̄ \ X is a (possibly nonreduced) divisor in X.`; it should be `"a divisor in X" should read "a divisor in X̄"`. X̄ \ X is by construction disjoint from X, so it cannot be a divisor in X; the assertion being made is that the boundary of the compactification is a divisor in the compactification, which is what the proof produces by applying Corollary 1.10 to the Nagata compactification. The reading is not an artefact of the text layer: in the content stream of the published PDF each overlined X is typeset as a letter preceded by an explicitly drawn rule, and in this sentence the rule is present before the first X of "X̄ \ X" and absent before the final X, which is therefore the plain X. - **Gap** at Lemma 2.11, its final clause, and the proof of Lemma 2.11 (pages 8–9 of the author's copy of the published version); the same in arXiv:1810.04493v2. The source says `Moreover, if 𝓜 is (S₂) and for each x ∈ closure(Supp(𝓜)) \ Supp(𝓜) of height ≥ 2 in closure(Supp(𝓜)) the punctured spectrum of O_{closure(Supp(𝓜)),x} has no isolated points, then 𝓜' may be chosen to itself be (S₂).`; it should be `the proof should return to this clause; as written its only trace is the parenthesis "(in the (S₂) case, this step is the reason for a direct sum in the statement; in the (S₁) case, no direct sum issue arises …)" in the middle of the dim X ≥ 2 case.`. The body of the proof establishes the first two assertions of the lemma and never mentions the extra hypothesis again, so the final clause is stated without an argument. The argument is short and is clearly what the author has in mind, and the clause is true: after the reductions made at the start of the proof one may assume that X is local with closed point x, that U is the punctured spectrum and that closure(Supp(𝓜)) = X, and the direct sum in the (S₂) case arises only from the summand U₀ of isolated points of U. If dim X ≥ 2 then x has height ≥ 2 and the extra hypothesis says exactly that U₀ = ∅, so no splitting occurs; if dim X = 1 the extension produced in that case is (S₁) and, the support having dimension ≤ 1, therefore also (S₂). A formalisation has to supply these two lines. - **Error** at Proof of Corollary 9.6, first sentence, author PDF p. 28 (the published version p. 27). The source says `Every inner form of SO_n is an SO(E) for a nondegenerate quadratic space E over R of rank n.`; it should be `Every twist of SO_n by an SO_n-torsor is an SO(E) for such an E; these are the only twists the argument uses.`. For even n ≥ 4, inner forms also come from central simple algebras with orthogonal involution. Over R = Q (allowed in Theorem 9.1 with O = Q), take H = (−1,−1) and H′ = (−1,3), non-isomorphic quaternion algebras ramified at {2, ∞} and {2, 3}. Then SO(H ⊗ H′, γ ⊗ γ′) ≅ (SL₁(H) × SL₁(H′))/μ₂ is an inner form of split SO₄. It is not an SO(E): for E of trivial discriminant, SO(E) ≅ (SL₁(C) × SL₁(C))/μ₂ with isomorphic factors. For odd n every form is an SO(E), and the proof only twists by H¹(R, SO_n). As a second check, over the real numbers the example has Lie algebra su(2) ⊕ sl₂(R), with one compact and one split simple factor. A four-dimensional real quadratic space gives so(4) (both compact), so(2,2) (both split), or so(3,1) (real simple), never this mixed pair. Thus the Q-example is not SO(E) even without invoking the full classification of algebras with involution. The unrestricted inner-form assertion fails, while pure-inner twisting suffices for the stated corollary. ### Chang–Chen–Mishiba, "On Thakur's basis conjecture for multiple zeta values in positive characteristic", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2023) (`PAPER-CHANG-CHEN-MISHIBA-23`)

- **Misprint** at Section 2.2, the definition of the power sums, just before Definition 2.2.2 (published version: Section 2.2, before Definition 2.4); present in arXiv v2 and in the published version. The source says `S^{ζ}_{d}(s) := Σ_{a ∈ A_{+,d}} 1/a^{d} ∈ k`; it should be `S^{ζ}_{d}(s) := Σ_{a ∈ A_{+,d}} 1/a^{s} ∈ k`. The exponent must be s, not d: S^ζ_d(s) is the power sum of exponent s over the monic polynomials of degree d. With the printed exponent the symbol would not depend on s at all, and Remark 2.2.12 — which states Carlitz's identity 1/L_d^s = Σ_{a ∈ A_{+,d}} 1/a^s and concludes 𝔏^{Li}_d(s) = 𝔏^ζ_d(s) for 1 ≤ s ≤ q — uses the exponent s. The definition of ζ_A(s) in Section 1.2 likewise sums a^{-s} over monic a. Checked against the published text on Cambridge Core, which prints the same formula. Recorded as `PAPER-CHANG-CHEN-MISHIBA-23/E1`; looked for an existing correction in: the arXiv listing and submission history of arXiv:2205.09929, read 22 September 2026: v1 (20 May 2022) and v2 (11 July 2022), the version read, whose comment is 'added Section 5.4, corrected a few typos'; there is no later preprint version; the published version, doi:10.1017/fmp.2023.26 (Forum of Mathematics, Pi 11 (2023), open access on Cambridge Core), read 22 September 2026: the article carries no erratum, and each finding below was compared with the published text.
- **Misprint** at Remark 1.2.5 (published: Remark 1.6), the displayed upper bound; present in arXiv v2 and in the published version. The source says `dim_{w} Z_{w} ≤ d'_{w}, ∀ w ≥ 1`; it should be `dim_{k} Z_{w} ≤ d'_{w}, ∀ w ≥ 1`. Z_w is a k-vector space and its dimension is taken over k everywhere else in the paper (Conjecture 1.2.2 writes dim_k Z_w = d'_w, and Corollary 1.2.7 writes dim_k Z_{v,w}); 'dim_w' is not defined. ### François Charles, "Birational boundedness for holomorphic symplectic varieties, Zarhin's trick for K3 surfaces, and the Tate conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), no. 2 (`PAPER-CHARLES-16`)

- **Error** at Corollary 2.8 and its proof, pp.499–500, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 487–526 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 3425f269…40e2) (it affects a stated result). The source says `"If p > 0, we can find nonnegative integers λ and t such that 0 < λ ≤ v² and |disc(NS(X))| = p^t λ |disc(NS(M_H(v)))|." Proof: "… we have a natural injection of lattices with torsion cokernel Zv ⊕ (v^⊥ ∩ N(X)) ↪ N(X). Since the discriminant of Zv ⊕ v^⊥ is v² disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X)), this implies by the same argument that |disc(N(X))| ≤ v² |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))|."`; it should be `λ need not be an integer. With I = [N(X) : Zv ⊕ (v^⊥ ∩ N(X))], one has |disc NS(X)| = p^t (v²/I²) |disc NS(M_H(v))| with t ≥ 0. So λ = v²/I² is a positive rational number with λ ≤ v², and I divides v² because v is primitive. For p ∤ v², for example v² = 2 and p ≥ 3 as in the applications, λ is still a p-adic unit, which is what the later arguments use.`. Take v = (1, 0, −1), the Mukai vector of ideal sheaves of length-two subschemes, so M_H(v) = X^[2]. It satisfies condition (C): it is primitive, of rank 1, v² = 2, and gcd(1, 0, −1) = 1. Then v^⊥ ∩ N(X) = NS(X) ⊕ Z(1, 0, 1) with (1, 0, 1)² = −2, so |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))| = 2|disc NS(X)|. The proof's first step gives |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))| = p^r |disc NS(M_H(v))|. Hence |disc NS(X)| = ½ p^r |disc NS(M_H(v))|, which is not of the form p^t λ with λ a positive integer when p is odd. The proof passes from the equality disc(Zv ⊕ K) = I² disc N(X) to an integer multiplier without controlling I, here I = 2. The inequality stated for p = 0 is correct. Checked on the page image. - **Gap** at Charles Lemma 4.5, p. 521 (it affects the proof). The source says `only finitely many prime numbers`; it should be `Lemma 4.5 holds, with the argument below, after replacing k by a finite extension on which −1 is not a Frobenius eigenvalue on H²(X_k̄, Q_ℓ(1)), and with −1 added to the p_i; it needs Frobenius semisimple on the eigenvalue-1 part (item 111). Let g be the characteristic polynomial of Frobenius on the complement V′ of the invariants. The Cayley transform (F−1)(F+1)⁻¹ is skew-adjoint on V′, so det V′ ≡ g(1)g(−1) modulo squares. Hence disc T(X, Q_ℓ) ≡ −g(1)g(−1)·disc NS(X), a rational number independent of ℓ. The p_i are the primes dividing it. Item 113 states and proves this form.`. Each l-adic discriminant is defined modulo l-adic unit squares. A uniform bound on its l-valuation does not compare square classes at distinct primes. A valuation-zero rank-one form can have nonsquare unit coefficient. (cc-442dc5) The repair above supplies the missing rational square class. It is not available over the original k when −1 is an eigenvalue, because the determinant of the (−1)-eigenspace is not fixed by the characteristic polynomial. The finite extension is harmless for Theorems 1.3 and 1.4, since the Tate statement descends (item finite-extension-tate-descent). The finding therefore still affects the proof only. One block of size 2 (r = 2, r′ = 1, K = J_F(U·U) + its e⊥ term): β_Q = ((A − K, −K), (−K, A − K)) has μ_Q = A − 2K for K > 0, while β_{Q′} = A/2 − K, so μ_Q = 2μ_{Q′}. The worker ported the authors' formulas (without_GRH.gp, testfin.gp), checked the port against seven of their certificate values (six digits), and evaluated the displayed elements. In Section 2.4.6 the printed C-values −0.173, −0.198, −0.147 are exactly β_Q(t, t), that is C(x′, x′) for the weights t_1/2; the displayed x (weights t_1/√2) have C ≈ −0.293, −0.321, −0.251. - **Misprint** at §3.2.1, p. 19 (it affects the proof). The source says `There is a natural G_K-equivariant map ι : B̂^+_st → B^+_dR induced by the maps p_ϖ : B̂^+_st → B^+_cr,K, B^+_cr/F^r ≅→ B^+_cr,K/F^r ≅← B^+_cr/F^r, where p_ϖ denotes the map induced by sending T ↦ ϖ. The composition B^+_st → B̂^+_st —ι→ B̂^+_dR is the map ι = ι_ϖ from Section 1.4.2.`; it should be `… B^+_cr/F^r ≅→ B^+_cr,K/F^r ≅← B^+_dR/F^r …, and the composition B^+_st → B̂^+_st —ι→ B^+_dR.`. Two slips in one sentence. The displayed chain has the same ring B^+_cr/F^r at both ends, so it produces no map to B^+_dR and the announced ι : B̂^+_st → B^+_dR is not defined; the third term must be B^+_dR/F^r, which is what the comparison of the graded pieces of A_cr and A_cr,K just quoted from Tsuji (Lemma 4.6.2) identifies with B^+_cr,K/F^r. And B̂^+_dR is defined nowhere in the paper: the target of ι_ϖ in §1.4.2 is B^+_dR. This map is used in the definition of RΓ_syn(X_C,Q_p(r)) and in every fundamental diagram. ### Colmez–Dospinescu–Nizioł, "Cohomologie p-adique de la tour de Drinfeld: le cas de la dimension 1", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020) (`PAPER-COLMEZ-DOSPINESCU-NIZIOL-20-B`)

Pour montrer le (ii), on montre d'abord que l'action de G_j (resp., Ǧ_n) sur O(M^ϖ_n)^* (resp., O(LT^ϖ_j)^*) peut se dériver`; it should be `‘Pour montrer le (i)’, and ‘et de la suite exacte ci-dessus’.`. The first sentence deduces (ii) from (i); the rest of the proof then establishes (i) — that the invariants of the duals vanish — by deriving the action and showing that a functional killed by the Lie algebra is zero. As printed the proof announces twice that it proves (ii) and never that it proves (i). - **Error** at Theorem 1.1(ii), p. 2, against Theorem 5.4(ii), p. 54 (it affects a stated result). The source says `Theorem 1.1(ii): 'In general, the kernel and cokernel of this map are annihilated by p^N for an integer N = N(e,p,r), which depends on e, r, but not on X or n.' Theorem 5.4(ii): 'In general, the kernel and cokernel of this map is annihilated by p^N for an integer N = N(K,p,r), which depends on K, p, r.'`; it should be `The constant depends on K, as Theorem 5.4(ii) says; Theorem 1.1(ii) overstates it as depending only on e, p and r.`. These are the same theorem — §1.1.1 states it, §5.1 proves it — and the proof of Theorem 5.4(ii) obtains the constant by passing to R_i = R(ζ_{p^i}) with i ≥ c(K)+3, where c(K) is the conductor of K, and then descending by Lemma 5.9, whose constant involves the relative ramification index e_1 and the different δ_{K_1/K_0}. None of that is controlled by e alone. Remark 1.7 confirms the reading: the descent introduces 'constants depending on K', and the authors write that 'it seems likely that one could make the constants depend only on the valuation of the different of K and not on K itself' — an expectation, not what is proved. ### Colmez–Nizioł, "On the cohomology of p-adic analytic spaces, II: The C_st-conjecture", Duke Mathematical Journal (2025) (`PAPER-COLMEZ-NIZIOL-25`)

- **Error** at §5.1.2, p. 32 (both displays). The source says `deg(M) := tN(M) − tH(M), and again deg(M) := deg(det M) = tN(M) − tH(M)`; it should be `deg(M) := tH(M) − tN(M)`. The sign is the wrong way round, and it is printed twice — once for rank 1 and once for rank r — so it is a systematic convention rather than a slip of one character. Three independent checks force tH − tN. (a) The paper's own semistability convention, fixed in §3.2.2, is µ(E′) ≤ µ(E) for strict subobjects, so Definition 5.1's 'weakly admissible = semistable of slope 0' means deg(M′) ≤ 0 for all subobjects; Fontaine's weak admissibility is tH(M′) ≤ tN(M′), which is deg(M′) ≤ 0 only for deg = tH − tN. (b) Remark 5.5(ii) asserts that the Harder-Narasimhan slope of E(M,Fil) equals that of (M,Fil) and that H^1(E) = 0 iff (M,Fil) is acyclic, i.e. iff its slopes are ≥ 0. Take M = F with ϕ(e) = pe, so tN = 1, filtered with Fil^0 M_K = M_K and Fil^1 M_K = 0, so tH = 0: then X_st(M,Fil) = (M ⊗ B_st)^{N=0,ϕ=1} = B_st^{ϕ=p^{-1}} = 0 while X_dR = B_dR/B^+_dR ≠ 0, so H^0(E) = 0 and H^1(E) ≠ 0 and M is not acyclic; but the printed formula gives deg = +1 ≥ 0, which would make it acyclic. (c) The proof of Lemma 5.3 requires that shrinking the filtration strictly decrease the degree, and shrinking decreases tH. Definition 5.13, which defines the same two notions over C directly on the bundle, is unaffected and independently fixes the intended sign. ### Disegni, "The universal p-adic Gross–Zagier formula", Inventiones Mathematicae (2022) (`PAPER-DISEGNI-22`)

- **Misprint** at §7.3.6 (Applications to non-vanishing / 2: exceptional families), first sentence of the proof of Theorem G, arXiv:2001.00045v4. The source says `Let E be an imaginary quadratic field, with associated quadratic character η, satisfying the following: p is inert in A, all other primes dividing the conductor of A split in E, and the twisted L-value L(A, η, 1) ≠ 0.`; it should be `"p is inert in A" should read "p is inert in E"`. A is an elliptic curve over Q and "inert in A" is meaningless; E is the imaginary quadratic field being chosen. The rest of the proof requires exactly that p be inert in E: it is what makes A have split multiplicative reduction over E with a Tate parameter q ∈ E_p^×, and it is the hypothesis under which the Bertolini–Darmon rigid-analytic formula quoted immediately afterwards applies. It is also the condition under which, in Remark 7.3.4, condition (★) of the Correction holds for this family. Recorded as `PAPER-DISEGNI-22/E2`; looked for an existing correction in: Appendix B of arXiv:2001.00045v4, whose Errata list only the footnote-12 citation and the symbol in the proof of Lemma 4.1.1; the arXiv abstract page for 2001.00045, which lists no further erratum beyond the Appendix B correction; the text of v4, the latest version, where the sentence is unchanged.
- **Misprint** at Proof of Lemma 6.4.4 (§6.4.6, the vanishing of loc^−_w(𝓟)), last sentence, arXiv:2001.00045v4. The source says `Since H^1(E_w, 𝓜̃^−_w) = lim_n H^1(E_w, 𝓜̃^−_{n,w}) by Proposition 5.2.2, the lemma is proved.`; it should be `"Proposition 5.2.2" should read "Lemma 5.2.2"`. The statement invoked — that continuous cohomology commutes with countable projective limits of admissible modules of finite type over a profinite group satisfying (F) — is 5.2.2, and 5.2.2 is a lemma, not a proposition. In the SMF class used by the paper, theorems, propositions, lemmas and definitions share a single counter within each subsection, so the number 5.2.2 is unambiguous and no other statement can be meant; the only statement of §5.2 that could be confused with it, Proposition 5.2.3, is about supports and specialisation, not about limits. A mechanical audit of the LaTeX source comparing the capitalised word introducing each \ref with the environment carrying the target label found this as the unique mismatch among the 68 typed cross-references of the paper.
