- **Gap** at Appendix B (Correction), the itemised list of the effects of the correction on the main results, arXiv:2001.00045v4. The source says `Theorem A holds for π₀ ⊗ χ under the extra assumption (★). • Theorem B, as well as Theorem B^ord of §7.1.1, hold for Π = π ⊗ χ under the extra assumption (★). • Theorem C is not affected. • … Then Theorem D and Theorem E hold for Hida* families rather than Hida families. • Theorem F is not affected. • Theorem G is not affected, and the related alternative proof of the theorem of Greenberg–Stevens mentioned in Remark 7.3.4 remains valid.`; it should be `The list should also say what happens to Theorem H, the universal Waldspurger formula of §7.2, which is the eighth lettered theorem of the paper and is not mentioned. Theorem H is in fact unaffected.`. The lettered theoA environment is numbered A–H in order of appearance: Theorem A in §1.1.3, B in §1.2.8, C in §1.3.3, D in §1.4.3, E, F and G in §1.5, and H in §7.2; the Correction enumerates A, B, B^ord, C, D, E, F and G and stops. A reader applying the Correction cannot tell from it whether Theorem H is restricted. It is not: §7.2 deduces Theorem H from its specialisations at all classical points satisfying (wt), which are known by modifying Waldspurger's classical formula, and those points are dense by Lemma 3.1.4 — the density of classical points of a fixed weight — not by Lemma 7.1.4, which is the statement the Correction has to replace. Neither the paper on nonsplit primes nor condition (★) enters the proof of Theorem H at any point. The omission is in the enumeration, not in the mathematics. Recorded as `PAPER-DISEGNI-22/E6`; looked for an existing correction in: Appendix B of arXiv:2001.00045v4, read in full; it lists Theorems A, B, B^ord, C, D, E, F and G and no other; §7.2 of v4, whose proof sketch of Theorem H cites only Waldspurger and Theorem B^ord's method, not the paper on nonsplit primes; the arXiv abstract page for 2001.00045, which announces the Appendix B correction and no other erratum.

AKNS §2.9 works with a finitely generated L-structure A in a finite language L, and Proposition 2.28 gives a formula characterizing A among finitely generated L-structures (read in arXiv 1610.04768, p. 20). - **Gap** at Proposition 2, (6.6), and its proof, pp.968–969, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 949–990 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 a67de715…5f61); the author preprint of 29 July 2016 on W. Duke's page has the same text there (it affects a stated result). The source says `"Weyl(⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ, χ) ≪_ε r^C |D|^{13/28+ε}, (6.6) where … φ is any even Hecke–Maass cusp form with Laplace eigenvalue 1/4 + r²." Proof: "Part (6.6) of Proposition 2 follows straight from Theorem 4 and Theorem 5 of [12]."`; it should be `State (6.6) for the unit vector u = φ/‖φ‖: Weyl(u, χ) ≪_ε r^C |D|^{13/28+ε}. It follows from Theorem 4 and [12, Theorem 5] together with the Rankin–Selberg size of ‖φ‖ for the normalization a(1) = 1. It is also what the proof of Theorem 2 uses, since c(φ)⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ = ⟨f, u⟩u.`. The forms φ are normalized by a(1) = 1 in (5.7), p.962, and the Shimura relation in Theorem 4 forces this too. [12, Theorem 5] (Duke 1988, p.85, read on the page image) bounds the coefficients of a spectral weight-1/2 form with eigenvalue 1/4 + t² by |λ|^A ch(πt/2)|n|^{−2/7+ε}. Here t = r/2, so Theorem 4 gives |Weyl(⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ, χ)| ≪ r^C cosh²(πr/4)|D|^{3/4−2/7+ε}. That bound has an exponential factor, which (6.6) omits. The factor cannot simply be dropped. For a(1) = 1, Rankin–Selberg unfolding gives ⟨φ, φ⟩ ≍ L(1, sym²φ)/cosh(πr), so ⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ is about e^{πr/2} times the unit vector u. As printed, (6.6) would therefore make the Weyl integrals of u exponentially small in r, which the cited results do not give. For u the two exponentials cancel: Weyl(u, χ) = ‖φ‖ Weyl(⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ, χ) ≪ L(1, sym²φ)^{1/2} r^C |D|^{13/28+ε}, and L(1, sym²φ) ≪ r^ε. The coefficient bound "c(φ) ≪ |r|^{−A}" used for Theorem 2 on p.969 holds for u, so Theorem 2 stands. Noted by the extraction ("The spectral norm gate"). Reclassified by cc-442dc5 from 'the proof' to 'a stated result': Proposition 2 is a stated result and (6.6) as printed is not established; items /150 and /152 state what the cited results give. The paper's own numbers show the size. At r ≈ 13.78, ⟨φ,φ⟩ = 7.263×10⁻¹⁹ (p.966), and the first example on p.967 has Weyl(⟨φ,φ⟩⁻¹φ, χ) ≈ −1.94×10⁹ for D = 12, which is about e^{πr/2} ≈ 2.5×10⁹. Theorem 2 is unaffected, because its proof needs only the unit-vector bound. - **Misprint** at Lemma 6.6.1(ii), p. 98, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 96. The source says `T(g)^♭ = T(g^†) = T(ḡ).`; it should be `T(g)^♭ = T(g^†); away from p, g^† = ν(g)^{-1}ḡ, so T(g^†) = T(ν(g)^{-1})·T(ḡ), which equals T(ḡ) when ν(g) is a local unit.`. By §6.2.3, g^† = ν(g)^{-1}δ_p^{-1}ḡδ_p; at ℓ ≠ p this is the central element ν(g)^{-1} ∈ Q_ℓ^× times ḡ. The double coset operator of a central element z_ℓ = ℓ^{-k} is not the identity: it acts on a representation through its central character (which is non-trivial in general, e.g. ξ_{π,∞}(t) = t^{a(κ)} forces non-trivial finite components). Defence: for Hecke operators with unit similitude (in particular for the unitary part of the Hecke algebra) the equality holds; it may be intended as an identity up to the central Hecke operators. - **Error** at Lemma 6.6.5(ii), p. 100, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 97–98 (it affects a stated result). The source says `let S_κ(K_r,R)[λ] be the localization of the T_{K_r,κ,R}-module S_κ(K_r,R) at the prime ideal p_λ ⊂ T_{K_r,κ,R} that is the kernel of the character λ; in other words, S_κ(K_r,R)[λ] is the λ-isotypic component of S_κ(K_r,R). Then j_π defines an isomorphism j_π: π_S^{K_S} ⊗ π_p^{I_r}[λ] ⥲ S_κ(K_r,R)[λ] ⊗_R C = S_κ(K_r,C)[λ]. Here π_p^{I_r}[λ] is the subspace of π_p^{I_r} on which each U_{w,j,κ} acts as λ(U_{w,j,κ}).`; it should be `Define π_p^{I_r}[λ] as the generalized eigenspace (the subspace killed by a power of every U_{w,j,κ} − λ(U_{w,j,κ})), matching the localization on the right. Alternatively, keep true eigenspaces on both sides, replace the localization by the λ-eigenspace, and restrict to λ with unit (ordinary) U-eigenvalues or assume the U_{w,j,κ} act semisimply.`. R is a field (a finite extension of E(π)), so localization of the finite-dimensional module S_κ(K_r,R) at the maximal ideal p_λ is the generalized λ-eigenspace, which equals the λ-isotypic (eigen)space only if the Hecke algebra acts semisimply. The U_{w,j} need not act semisimply on Iwahori-type invariants (e.g. for GL_2, U_p on the two-dimensional Iwahori invariants of an unramified principal series with equal Satake parameters is a Jordan block). The two sides differ in general, and not only in exotic cases like equal Satake parameters (the first reading's example). They differ for every π with π_p unramified once r ≥ 3, taking λ with λ(U) = 0. - **Error** at §6.6.8, Theorem 6.6.9 (Hida), p. 101 — whose proof is given in §8.3 (Lemma 8.3.2, Corollary 8.3.3, pp. 128–130) — in arXiv v5; the same mistake at Theorem 6.6.9, p. 101, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 98 (it affects a stated result). The source says `Theorem 6.6.9 (Hida). For any representation π_p of G(ℚ_p), the ordinary eigenspace e_κπ_p^{I_r} ⊂ π_p^{I_r} is of dimension ≤ 1, for any r. … The proof, an adaptation of Hida's, is given in Section 8.3 below.`; it should be `Theorem 6.6.9. For any irreducible admissible representation π_p of G(Q_p) and κ satisfying (166) (κ_{σ,a_σ} + κ_{σc,b_σ} ≥ n for all σ), the ordinary eigenspace e_κπ_p^{I_r} has dimension ≤ 1 for every r.`. The proof in §8.3 (Lemma 8.3.2) uses irreducibility of π_w and inequality (166) to make |κ_norm|_pδ_w^{1/2} regular; without (166) two Weyl conjugates can both give unit eigenvalues (e.g. for GL_2 in weight one, both roots of X² − a_pX + χ(p) can be units, giving a two-dimensional ordinary space of Iwahori-fixed vectors). Defence: the holomorphic π of §6.6 may be tacitly assumed to have κ in the range (166)/sufficiently regular. Independent check: p. 101: 'Theorem 6.6.9 (Hida). For any representation π_p of G(Q_p), the ordinary eigenspace e_κπ_p^{I_r} ⊂ π_p^{I_r} is of dimension ≤ 1, for any r.' Nothing in §6.6 restricts κ beyond dominance ((16) on p. 22 is only dominance; §6.6.8 takes any holomorphic cuspidal π of type (κ,K_r)), whereas the proof in §8.3 (Lemma 8.3.2, Corollary 8.3.3) assumes π_w irreducible admissible and κ satisfying (166), introduced only in §8.3.1 (p. 126). (166) is genuinely needed: m_{a_w} − m_n = Σ_σ(κ_{σ,a_w}+κ_{σc,b_w}−n), and if this is −1 the corrected character |κ_norm|_pδ_w^{1/2} has equal exponents at t_{a_w} and t_n, so it is fixed by the transposition x = (a_w n); then β_x = β^x is unit-valued, and for π_w = Ind(α) irreducible with α^x ≠ α both α and α^x give ordinary eigenvectors, so the ordinary space is 2-dimensional. The classical instance is weight-one elliptic forms (n = 2), where both roots of X² − a_pX + χ(p) are units. Reducible π_p (e.g. ρ ⊕ ρ) are trivially excluded. Since the printed statement is false without these hypotheses (not merely unproved), the kind should be error (missing hypotheses) rather than gap. The same applies to the claim 'This space has dimension at most one' in §6.6.8 and to Lemma 6.6.10(i) for κ outside (166). Nothing downstream is affected: §§7–9 work with sufficiently regular κ, which satisfy (166). v4 p. 98 is identical (referring to 'Section 8.2 below'). Second, independent reading of the same mistake: For a reducible π_p = π′_p ⊕ π′_p with π′_p ordinary the ordinary eigenspace has dimension 2. The proof in §8.3 works with irreducible admissible π_w (Lemma 8.3.2), and the theorem is applied to local components of cuspidal π. (166) is genuinely needed: m_{a_w} − m_n = Σ_σ(κ_{σ,a_w}+κ_{σc,b_w}−n), and if this is −1 the corrected character |κ_norm|_pδ_w^{1/2} has equal exponents at t_{a_w} and t_n, so it is fixed by the transposition x = (a_w n); then β_x = β^x is unit-valued, and for π_w = Ind(α) irreducible with α^x ≠ α both α and α^x give ordinary eigenvectors, so the ordinary space is 2-dimensional. The classical instance is weight-one elliptic forms (n = 2), where both roots of X² − a_pX + χ(p) are units. Reducible π_p (e.g. ρ ⊕ ρ) are trivially excluded. Since the printed statement is false without these hypotheses (not merely unproved), the kind should be error (missing hypotheses) rather than gap. The same applies to the claim 'This space has dimension at most one' in §6.6.8 and to Lemma 6.6.10(i) for κ outside (166). Nothing downstream is affected: §§7–9 work with sufficiently regular κ, which satisfy (166). v4 p. 98 is identical (referring to 'Section 8.2 below'). Second, independent reading of the same mistake: For a reducible π_p = π′_p ⊕ π′_p with π′_p ordinary the ordinary eigenspace has dimension 2. The proof in §8.3 works with irreducible admissible π_w (Lemma 8.3.2), and the theorem is applied to local components of cuspidal π. - **Gap** at Lemma 6.6.10 (hypothesis on R), p. 102, and its uses in Lemma 6.6.12 and Lemma 6.7.1, pp. 103–105, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 99–101 (it affects a stated result). The source says `Let R ⊂ C be the localization of a finite extension of R(λ_π) at the prime determined by incl_p or the p-adic completion of such a ring. … S^ord_κ(K_r,R)_π is identified with an R-lattice in ⊕_{π′∈S(K_s,κ,π)} π′^{,ord}_p ⊗ (π′_S)^{K_S}.`; it should be `Require R to be p-adically complete (or Henselian), or large enough to contain the Hecke eigenvalues of every π′ ∈ S(K_r,κ,π); otherwise replace the localization at m_π by the corresponding direct factor after completion.`. If R is a non-complete discrete valuation ring, T^ord_{K_r,κ,R} need not be a product of local rings: e.g. if some Hecke eigensystem λ_{π′} has values in a quadratic extension F of Frac(R) in which p splits, with one prime above p giving λ̄_π and the other not, then T^ord_R contains an order of F with two maximal ideals, its localization at m_π is not finitely generated over R, and S^ord_κ(K_r;R)_π is not an R-lattice; moreover its ⊗E would contain the π″-component with λ̄_{π″} ≠ λ̄_π. When all eigenvalues lie in Frac(R), T^ord_R ⊂ ∏R contains all idempotents of its completion and is a product of local rings, so the statement holds. Defence: from §6.7.8 on R is ‘a sufficiently large finite flat p-adic integer ring’ and in §7 R = O_π is complete; Lemma 6.7.1’s proof uses finiteness (‘H^{d,ord} … are finite R-modules’). Independent check: Checked on the page image (p. 102). Lemma 6.6.10 allows R to be the localization, not completed, of a finite extension of R(λ_π) at the prime given by incl_p. The lemma has no proof. T = T^ord_{K_r,κ,R} is finite over the DVR R, but it need not be a product of local rings unless R is Henselian. Its localization at m_π can then fail to be finitely generated over R. Example of the mechanism: Z_(p)[i] with p ≡ 1 mod 4 has two maximal ideals, and its localization at one of them contains 1/π̄^k for all k. This happens whenever some π′ ≡ π modulo one prime of F′ = F(λ_{π′}) above 𝔭 = the prime of R does not satisfy the congruence at another prime above 𝔭. S_π⊗E then contains the components of the Galois conjugates of π′ whose reductions differ from λ̄_π, so it is not a lattice in ⊕_{π′∈S(K_r,κ,π)}(…). When R contains all Hecke eigenvalues (so T ⊂ ∏R), or R is complete, T contains the idempotents of its completion and the statement holds. The [π]-part is unaffected: for x ∈ S(E)[λ_π] and s ∉ m_π, s acts on x by the unit λ_π(s), so S_π ∩ S(E)[λ_π] = S(R) ∩ S(E)[λ_π] is a lattice. Downstream: Lemma 6.7.1 only pairs against H_{π^♭}, and localizing at s ∉ m multiplies the pairing by units, so the image is the same as for H(R). From §6.7.8 on and throughout §7, R is complete. The defect is a missing hypothesis in a result stated without proof. I keep 'gap' and not 'error' because the failing configuration is generic but no explicit automorphic example is exhibited. Identical in v4 (pp. 99–100). Note also the misprint S(K_s,κ,π) for S(K_r,κ,π) in the same display. Reach: a stated result (stated results (Lemma 6.6.10(ii), 6.6.12(ii)–(iii), 6.7.1 for non-complete R); nothing downstream). - **Error** at Lemma 6.6.12(iii), p. 104 (first pairing), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 100 and in v2 at p. 101 (Lemma 6.5.12(iii)) (it affects a stated result). The source says `(iii) Normalized Serre duality induces perfect T^ord_{K_r,κ,R}-equivariant pairings (with respect to the isomorphisms of Lemma 6.6.7) S^ord_κ(K_r;R)[π] ⊗_R H^{d,ord}_{κ^D}(K_r;R)[π] → R and S^ord_κ(K_r;R)_π ⊗_R H^{d,ord}_{κ^D}(K_r;R)_π → R`; it should be `Only the pairing of the localizations S_π ⊗ H_π → R is perfect. The pairing of the saturated λ_π-isotypic lattices S[π] ⊗ H[π] → R is perfect after ⊗E but its image is the congruence ideal C(π) (Definition 6.7.2, Lemma 6.7.3), so it is perfect over R iff C(π) = R (no congruences).`. Take 𝕋 = {(a,b) ∈ O×O : a ≡ b mod ϖ^n}, S_π = 𝕋 (free of rank one, as under the Gorenstein hypothesis), H_π = Hom_O(𝕋,O) with the perfect evaluation pairing, λ_π = first projection. Then S[π] = 𝕋 ∩ (E×0) = O·(ϖ^n,0) and H[π] = O·λ_π (λ_π is primitive since λ_π(1,1) = 1), and ⟨(ϖ^n,0),λ_π⟩ = ϖ^n, so the pairing S[π]×H[π] → O has image ϖ^nO. The paper itself uses this: Lemma 6.7.3 (c(π) = Q[π]/Q_π generates C(π); if the [π]-pairing were perfect, L[π] = L_π and c(π) would be a unit) and Lemma 7.5.2 (L_φ restricted to S[π] takes values in C(π)). Defence: harmless downstream — no later argument uses perfectness of the [π]-pairing; the statement is a slip for the localized pairing only. Independent check: Quotation checked on the page image (p. 104). The paper's [π]-parts are saturated λ_π-isotypic lattices, not localizations. Lemma 6.6.10(ii) (p. 102) defines S^ord_κ(K_r;R)[π] := S^ord_κ(K_r;R)_π ∩ S^ord_κ(K_r;E)[λ_π], and Lemma 6.6.12 (p. 103) defines H^{d,ord}(K_r;R)[π] := H^{d,ord}(K_r;R)_π ∩ H^{d,ord}(K_r;E)[λ_π], 'where the notation [λ_π] again denotes the λ_π-isotypic component'. H^{d,ord}_{κ^D}(K_r;R) is by definition the R-dual of S^ord_κ(K_r;R) under the normalized pairing (p. 103), and the localizations are direct factors (R complete), so the second pairing S_π ⊗ H_π → R is perfect. The first is not. By T-equivariance the λ_π-part is orthogonal to the other eigen-components. Hence H[π] is the annihilator in H_π of S' := S_π ∩ (⊕_{π'≠π} components), i.e. H[π] = Hom_R(S_π/S', R). So S[π] × H[π] → R is perfect iff S[π] → S_π/S' is onto, i.e. iff S_π = S[π] ⊕ S', i.e. iff π has no congruences; the cokernel is the congruence module. The first reading's rank-one example checks: S[π] = O·(ϖ^n,0), H[π] = O·pr_1, pairing image ϖ^nO. The paper contradicts the statement itself: Lemma 7.5.2 (p. 120) says the restriction of L_φ = ⟨·,φ⟩_{κ,K_r} (φ ∈ H^{d,ord}(K_r,O)[π]) to S^ord(K_r,O)[π] takes values in the congruence ideal C(π), and Lemma 6.7.3/Remark 6.7.4 treat C(π) as non-trivial in general. The perfectness of the [π]-pairing is not used later: Lemma 6.6.12 is cited again only in the list of modifications in Remark 9.3.2. Versions: v4 p. 100 identical; v2/v3 Lemma 6.5.12(iii) reads 'Serre duality induces perfect …'. Reach: a stated result (Lemma 6.6.12(iii), first half); nothing downstream). - **Gap** at §6.7, definition of C(π,M), p. 105, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 102. The source says `More generally, the congruence ideal C(π,M) can be defined for any T^{♭,ord}_{K^♭,κ^♭,R}-module M as the annihilator of M_{π^♭}/(M[π^♭]+M[π]^⊥), where the notation has the same meaning as above.`; it should be `M[π]^⊥ requires a pairing of M with a dual module; for M = 𝕋 (as used for C(π,𝕋) and (153)) it must be read as ker λ_π = 𝕋 ∩ ⊕_{π′≠π}𝕋_E[λ_{π′}], i.e. the annihilator of Hom(𝕋,R)[λ_π] under evaluation.`. In Definition 6.7.2, [π]^⊥ is the orthogonal complement for Serre duality between H^{d,ord} on V and on −V; a general module M carries no such pairing. With the reading above, C(π,𝕋) = Ann(𝕋/(𝕋[λ_π]+ker λ_π)), which is what (153) computes. Defence: the intended meaning (the usual congruence module) is standard. - **Misprint** at Lemma 6.7.6, display, p. 106, in arXiv v5; absent in v4 (§6.7.5 and Lemmas 6.7.6–6.7.7 are new in v5) (it affects a stated result). The source says `L[π] = (1/Vol(I_{V,r} ∩ I_{−V,r}))⟨H^{d,ord}_{κ,V}(K,ψ,R)[π], H^{d,ord}_{κ^♭,−V}(K^♭_r,ψ^{-1},R)[π^♭]⟩^Ser_κ, L_π = (1/Vol(I_{V,r} ∩ I_{−V,r}))⟨H^{d,ord}_{κ,V}(K,ψ,R)[π], H^{d,ord}_{κ^♭,−V}(K^♭_r,ψ^{-1},R)_{π^♭}⟩^Ser_κ are rank one R-submodules of C, generated by positive real numbers Q[π,χ] and Q_{π,χ}, respectively.`; it should be `L[π,χ] = Vol(I_{V,r} ∩ I_{−V,r})^{-1}⟨H^{d,ord}_{κ,V}(K,ψ,R)[π], H^{d,ord}_{κ^♭,−V}(K^♭_r,ψ^{-1},R)[π^♭]_χ⟩^Ser_{κ,χ}. L_{π,χ} is defined the same way, with the second argument replaced by the localization at π^♭⊗χ^{-1}∘det of H^{d,ord}_{κ^♭⋆χ,−V}(K^♭_r,ψ^{-1},R). These are generated by Q[π,χ] and Q_{π,χ} respectively.`. The display is a verbatim copy of Lemma 6.7.1 (p. 104): neither the twisted lattice H[π^♭]_χ just defined in §6.7.5 nor the twisted pairing (147) appears, so as printed Q[π,χ] = Q[π] and Q_{π,χ} = Q_π, contradicting the Note that the twisted structure ‘is not a simple algebraic twist … even the rational structure is modified by a CM period’. Intended meaning clear from the preceding paragraph (‘We reformulate Lemma 6.7.1 in this framework’). Independent check: Checked on the page image (p. 106). The display of Lemma 6.7.6 is a verbatim copy of Lemma 6.7.1's display (p. 104). The labels are still L[π] and L_π. The pairing is still ⟨·,·⟩^Ser_κ, not the twisted pairing ⟨·,·⟩^Ser_{κ,χ} of (147) (p. 97). The second argument is H^{d,ord}_{κ^♭,−V}(K^♭_r,ψ^{-1},R)[π^♭] (resp. its localization at π^♭), not the module H^{d,ord}_{κ^♭,−V}(K^♭_r,ψ^{-1},R)[π^♭]_χ := H^{d,ord}_{κ^♭⋆χ,−V}(K^♭_r,ψ^{-1},R)[π^♭⊗χ^{-1}∘det] that is defined just above. Yet the generators are named Q[π,χ] and Q_{π,χ}. As printed, the modules would force Q[π,χ] = Q[π] and Q_{π,χ} = Q_π, which contradicts the Note on the same page ('Even the rational structure is modified by a CM period corresponding to χ'). The intended statement is clear from 'We reformulate Lemma 6.7.1 in this framework' and from the use of H^{d,ord}(…)_χ and Q[π′,χ] in Lemma 8.5.3 (p. 139). The twisted periods enter the Main Theorem 9.2.2 through Ω_{π′,χ} and P_{π′,χ}. The passage is new in v5: v4 has no §6.7.5. Reach: a stated result (Lemma 6.7.6 display); the twisted periods enter Main Theorem 9.2.2). The display of Lemma 6.7.6 is a verbatim copy of Lemma 6.7.1's display (p. 104). The labels are still L[π] and L_π. The pairing is still ⟨·,·⟩^Ser_κ, not the twisted pairing ⟨·,·⟩^Ser_{κ,χ} of (147) (p. 97). The second argument is H^{d,ord}_{κ^♭,−V}(K^♭_r,ψ^{-1},R)[π^♭] (resp. its localization at π^♭), not the module H^{d,ord}_{κ^♭,−V}(K^♭_r,ψ^{-1},R)[π^♭]_χ := H^{d,ord}_{κ^♭⋆χ,−V}(K^♭_r,ψ^{-1},R)[π^♭⊗χ^{-1}∘det] that is defined just above. Yet the generators are named Q[π,χ] and Q_{π,χ}. As printed, the modules would force Q[π,χ] = Q[π] and Q_{π,χ} = Q_π, which contradicts the Note on the same page ('Even the rational structure is modified by a CM period corresponding to χ'). The intended statement is clear from 'We reformulate Lemma 6.7.1 in this framework' and from the use of H^{d,ord}(…)_χ and Q[π′,χ] in Lemma 8.5.3 (p. 139). The twisted periods enter the Main Theorem 9.2.2 through Ω_{π′,χ} and P_{π′,χ}. The passage is new in v5: v4 has no §6.7.5. Reach: a stated result (Lemma 6.7.6 display); the twisted periods enter Main Theorem 9.2.2). - **Gap** at §6.7.5, paragraph after Lemma 6.7.7, p. 106, in arXiv v5 (and ‘as noted above, does not actually depend on χ’, p. 107); absent in v4 (it affects a stated result). The source says `However, since the family of p-adic Hecke characters is smooth, it is easy to see that C(π,χ) and c(π,χ) do not depend on χ.`; it should be `Give an argument, or state the independence as an expectation. A sketch: twisting by χ∘det gives an isomorphism of Hecke algebras 𝕋 ≅ 𝕋_χ carrying λ_{π^♭} to λ_{π^♭⊗χ^{-1}}. It carries the integral lattices to each other up to a single scalar (the CM period), so the congruence modules agree: C(π,χ) = C(π), and c(π,χ) = c(π)·unit. This requires that the twist be integral at p, i.e. that the p-adic CM period be a unit.`. C(π,χ) is only defined ‘by analogy’, and the lattices H[π^♭]_χ are defined through the coherent cohomology of the twisted weight κ^♭⋆χ with its own rational/integral structure; smoothness of the family of characters does not by itself compare integral structures of different coherent cohomology groups. Defence: the claim is plausible (scalar changes of lattice do not affect the ratio Q[π,χ]/Q_{π,χ}), and it is exactly what Main Theorem 9.2.2 needs to state c(π′,χ) uniformly. Independent check: Checked on the page image (p. 106): 'However, since the family of p-adic Hecke characters is smooth, it is easy to see that C(π,χ) and c(π,χ) do not depend on χ'. It is repeated on p. 107 ('as noted above, does not actually depend on χ'). C(π,χ) is only defined 'by analogy'. It is the congruence module of the π^♭⊗χ^{-1}∘det-component of the coherent cohomology H^{d,ord}_{κ^♭⋆χ,−V}. That is a different weight with its own integral structure, which the paper says differs from the untwisted one even rationally by a CM period. Smoothness of the character family says nothing about these integral structures. A real argument is needed. For example: (a) twisting by χ∘det gives an isomorphism of Hecke algebras (T ↦ χ(det T)T) and, up to a scalar, of the integral lattices; or (b) under the Gorenstein hypothesis, C(π,χ) = C(π,𝕋_χ) ≅ C(π,𝕋) as in Lemma 6.7.10. The claim is plausible but not proved. Correction to the first reading's note on reach: Main Theorem 9.2.2 does not depend on this claim. It keeps χ in c(π′,χ), and c(π′,χ)·Ω_{π′,χ}/P_{π′,χ} = ⟨φ,φ^♭_χ⟩_χ / Vol(I^0_{r^1,V} ∩ I^0_{r^1,−V}) because Q[π′,χ] = c(π′,χ)Q_{π′,χ} (Lemma 6.7.7 and the proof on p. 145). So the gap affects only the stated independence claim and the motivation in Remark 6.7.12; nothing downstream. New in v5. Reach: a stated result (independence of χ); used in the formulation of Main Theorem 9.2.2). - **Error** at Theorem 7.1.1, p. 108, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 104 (it affects a stated result). The source says `Theorem 7.1.1. For any pair of characters κ_1, κ_2 of T_H, there is a canonical isomorphism T^ord_{K^p,κ_1,R} ⥲ T^ord_{K^p,κ_2,R}.`; it should be `For any pair of sufficiently regular characters κ_1, κ_2 of T_H (in the range of Hida’s classicality theorem (32)), there is a canonical isomorphism T^ord_{K^p,κ_1,R} ⥲ T^ord_{K^p,κ_2,R}.`. T^ord_{K^p,κ,R} := lim_r T^ord_{K_r,κ,R} is built from classical ordinary cusp forms of weight κ (§7.1). For κ the trivial character, S_κ(K_r;R) consists of holomorphic cusp forms of weight 0, which vanish on a non-compact Shimura variety, so T^ord_{K^p,0,R} = 0, while for regular κ the big Hecke algebra is a non-zero finite free Λ^o-algebra (Theorem 7.2.1). Weight independence holds for the Hecke algebra of p-adic forms and for classical forms only in the range where Hida’s control/classicality theorem applies. Defence: the paper only uses the theorem for sufficiently regular weights (Proposition 7.4.10: ‘if κ^1 is a second sufficiently regular character’), and Remark 7.1.2 refers to Hida’s theorems which carry such a hypothesis. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 108 (v5): 'Theorem 7.1.1. For any pair of characters κ_1, κ_2 of T_H, there is a canonical isomorphism T^ord_{K^p,κ_1,R} ⥲ T^ord_{K^p,κ_2,R}.' Here T^ord_{K^p,κ,R} := lim_r T^ord_{K_r,κ,R} (p. 108), and T^ord_{K_r,κ,R} = e_κ T_{K_r,κ,R} is the ring obtained by restricting Hecke operators to S^ord_κ(K_r;R) (§6.6.6, p. 101), a submodule of the CLASSICAL cusp forms S_κ(K_r;R) = H^0(M^tor_K, ω_κ(−D_∞)) (§2.6.5; p. 98: T_{K_r,κ,R} ⊂ End_C(S_κ(K_r;C))). So the objects are built from classical forms of the single weight κ, not from p-adic forms of all weights, and there is no standing regularity hypothesis in §7.1 (Theorem 7.2.1(ii) and 7.3.1(ii) impose 'κ sufficiently regular' explicitly, which shows 7.1.1 lacks it). 'Characters of T_H' include dominant non-regular ones: κ with all κ_{σ,i,j} = 0 satisfies (16), and on a non-compact Shimura variety S_0(K_r) = 0 (holomorphic cusp forms of scalar weight 0 vanish), so T^ord_{K^p,0,R} = 0, whereas for regular κ with an ordinary π the big algebra is non-zero (finite free over Λ^o, Theorem 7.2.1(i)). Likewise, below Hida's bound classical ordinary forms of level K_r do not exhaust the family (GL_2 analogue: Hida's lim_r h^ord_k(Np^r) ≅ h^ord(N;Λ) holds for k ≥ 2, not k = 1). Remark 7.1.2 cites Hida's theorems and mentions only (G1)–(G3), not the weight bound of (32) under which those theorems are proved. The missing hypothesis is harmless downstream: the theorem is invoked only for sufficiently regular weights (Proposition 7.3.5 via §7.3.4, Proposition 7.4.10 'if κ^1 is a second sufficiently regular character', Hypothesis 7.3.3 comment). Versions: v4 p. 104 identical ('of T = T_H'); v2/v3 Theorem 7.1.1 'For any pair of characters κ, κ_1' also without hypothesis. Reach: a stated result (as printed); nothing downstream). Remark 7.1.2 cites Hida's theorems and mentions only (G1)–(G3), not the weight bound of (32) under which those theorems are proved. The missing hypothesis is harmless downstream: the theorem is invoked only for sufficiently regular weights (Proposition 7.3.5 via §7.3.4, Proposition 7.4.10 'if κ^1 is a second sufficiently regular character', Hypothesis 7.3.3 comment). - **Error** at Theorem 7.2.1(ii), p. 109, and Theorem 7.3.1(ii), p. 110, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 105 (with Λ_R, Λ_π instead of Λ^o) and in v2/v3 (Theorem 7.1.3(ii)) (it affects a stated result). The source says `(ii) (Control theorem) Let I_κ ⊂ Λ^o_R be the kernel of the map Λ^o_R → R ⊂ C_p defined by the character κ. Suppose κ is sufficiently regular. Then the natural homomorphism T_{K^p,R} ⊗_{Λ^o_R} Λ^o_R/I_κ → T_{K^p_r,κ,R} is an isomorphism. [7.3.1(ii): 𝕋_π ⊗_{Λ^o_π} Λ^o_π/I_κ → 𝕋_{K^p_r,κ,O_π}]`; it should be `The isomorphism holds at level r = 1 (target T_{K_1,κ,R}, all nebentypes tame), or at level r for a fixed nebentypus: T_{K^p,R} ⊗_{Λ_R} Λ_R/I_{κψ} ≅ T_{K_r,κ,ψ,R} for ψ of level r (I_{κψ} the kernel of κψ on Λ_R); equivalently T_{K^p,R} ⊗_Λ Λ_{r,κ} ≅ T_{K_r,κ,R} with Λ_{r,κ} = Λ/𝓘_{r,κ} — which is the form actually used in Proposition 7.4.12 (‘T ↠ T ⊗_Λ Λ_{r,κ} = T_{r,κ}’) and in Hida’s (33).`. The left side does not depend on r, while T_{K_r,κ,R} acts on S^ord_κ(K_r;R) ⊇ ⊕_ψ S^ord_κ(K_r,ψ;R) over all characters ψ of T_H(Z_p/p^r), whose rank grows with r (for κ sufficiently regular each ψ-part has the rank of the corresponding Λ^o-component). Moreover elements t − κ(t), t in the pro-p part of T, do not act by zero on forms whose nebentypus is non-trivial on the pro-p part, so for r ≥ 2 the natural map T_{K^p,R} → T_{K_r,κ,R} does not factor through Λ^o/I_κ. Defence: ‘K^p_r’ is unspecified; with r = 1 or with the nebentypus built into κ (κ read as a locally algebraic character κψ and the target as the ψ-part) the statement is Hida’s theorem. Independent check: Quotations checked on the page images (Theorem 7.2.1(ii), p. 109; Theorem 7.3.1(ii), p. 110). The target T_{K^p_r,κ,R} is the Hecke algebra of S_κ(K_r;R), which by p. 99 contains the subspaces S_κ(K_r,ψ) for every nebentypus ψ of T_H(Z_p/p^rZ_p); T_{K_r,κ,ψ,R} are its quotients. The source T_{K^p,R} ⊗_{Λ^o_R} Λ^o_R/I_κ does not depend on r. By Hida's control theorem as the paper itself states it ((34), p. 35), each ψ of W trivial on W^{p^{r−1}} gives S^ord_κ(K_r,ωω_κψ,R[ψ]) ≅ 𝒮^ord_ω ⊗ R[ψ]/p_{κψ}, of the same rank as the ψ = 1 part. Since T_{K_r,κ,R} contains the diamond operators separating these ψ, its rank for r ≥ 2 exceeds rank_{Λ^o} T_{K^p,R} = rank_R(T ⊗ Λ^o/I_κ). Moreover t ∈ W acts on the ψ-part through κψ(t), not κ(t), so the natural map does not even factor through Λ^o/I_κ. The statement is correct for r = 1, or at level r with Λ^o/I_κ replaced by Λ/𝓘_{r,κ} (𝓘_{r,ρ} the annihilator of C_r(T,O)·ρ^υ, p. 114). The paper later uses exactly that form in Proposition 7.4.12 ('T ↠ T ⊗_Λ Λ_{r,κ} = T_{r,κ}', p. 118). But §7.3.4 (p. 111) and hence Proposition 7.3.5 invoke part (ii) as printed at level r. Versions: v4 p. 105 same (over Λ_R, Λ_π); v2/v3 Theorem 7.1.3(ii) same. Reach: a stated result (Theorems 7.2.1(ii), 7.3.1(ii)); used in §7.3.4 and Proposition 7.3.5 at level r, where the nebentypus form is needed). - **Gap** at §7.3.4, first two displays, p. 111, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 106 (it affects the proof). The source says `By part (ii) of Theorem 7.3.1, tensoring over Λ_π with Λ_π/I_κ gives an isomorphism 𝕋_{K^p_r,κ,O} ⊗_O Î_π ⥲ Hom_O(S^ord_κ(K_r,O)_{m_π},O) = H^{d,ord}_{κ^D}(K_r,O)_π.`; it should be `Also invoke control for the module of ordinary forms (Hida’s (33): (S^ord_ω ⊗ R[ψ])/p_{κψ} ≅ S^ord_κ(K_r,ωω_κψ,R[ψ])), in the level-r/nebentypus form, and tensor over Λ^o_π with Λ^o_π/I_κ; κ must be sufficiently regular.`. Theorem 7.3.1(ii) only identifies 𝕋_π ⊗ Λ^o_π/I_κ with the finite-level Hecke algebra; the right-hand side requires Hom_O(lim_r S^ord_κ(K_r,O)_{m_π},O) ⊗ Λ^o/I = Hom_O(S^ord_κ(K_r,O)_{m_π},O), a separate control statement for forms. Also Theorem 7.3.1 is over Λ^o_π, not Λ_π. Defence: (33) (Hida) provides it for regular weights. Independent check: Quotation checked on the page image (p. 111). Tensoring 𝕋_π ⊗ Î_π ≅ M := Hom_O(lim_r S^ord_κ(K_r,O)_{m_π},O) with Λ/I gives (𝕋_π/I) ⊗ Î_π ≅ M/IM. Theorem 7.3.1(ii) identifies only 𝕋_π/I with the finite-level Hecke algebra. The step also needs M/IM ≅ Hom_O(S^ord_κ(K_r,O)_{m_π},O). The restriction map M → Hom(S_r,O) is surjective (Lemma 6.6.14), but injectivity modulo I is a rank statement about the space of forms. That is Hida's control theorem for forms ((33)–(34), p. 35), used in dual form and at level r with nebentypus (cf. sourceIssues E117). It does not follow from control for the Hecke algebra. For unitary groups there is no perfect q-expansion duality between T and S that would make it follow. The input is available in the paper, but it is not invoked. Minor: Theorem 7.3.1 is over Λ^o_π, while §7.3.4 tensors over Λ_π. Versions: v4 p. 106 identical. Reach: the proof (of the finite-level isomorphisms in §7.3.4 and Proposition 7.3.5). The step also needs M/IM ≅ Hom_O(S^ord_κ(K_r,O)_{m_π},O). The restriction map M → Hom(S_r,O) is surjective (Lemma 6.6.14), but injectivity modulo I is a rank statement about the space of forms. That is Hida's control theorem for forms ((33)–(34), p. 35), used in dual form and at level r with nebentypus (cf. sourceIssues E117). It does not follow from control for the Hecke algebra. For unitary groups there is no perfect q-expansion duality between T and S that would make it follow. The input is available in the paper, but it is not invoked. Minor: Theorem 7.3.1 is over Λ^o_π, while §7.3.4 tensors over Λ_π. Versions: v4 p. 106 identical. Reach: the proof (of the finite-level isomorphisms in §7.3.4 and Proposition 7.3.5). - **Gap** at Proposition 7.3.5 and the sentence before it, pp. 111–112, in arXiv v5; v4 p. 106 (‘a simple rephrasing of the preceding discussion’) (it affects a stated result). The source says `In view of the comment following Hypothesis 7.3.3, the following consequence of Hypotheses 7.3.2 and 7.3.3 follows from the preceding discussion and Theorem 7.1.1. Proposition 7.3.5. (Minimality Hypothesis) For every pair (κ^1, r^1), there is an isomorphism of 𝕋_{K^p_{r^1},κ^1,O,π}-modules …`; it should be `The derivation (specializing 𝕋_π ⊗ Î_π ≅ Hom_O(lim_r S^ord_κ(K_r,O)_{m_π},O) via the control theorem) gives the finite-level isomorphism only for κ^1 sufficiently regular, and needs the control theorem for the module of forms (Hida’s (33)) in its level-r/nebentypus form, not just Theorem 7.3.1(ii) for the Hecke algebra. The statement should read ‘for every pair (κ^1,r^1) with κ^1 sufficiently regular’.`. Theorem 7.3.1(ii) is stated only for κ sufficiently regular and only concerns 𝕋_π; the step ‘tensoring over Λ_π with Λ_π/I_κ gives 𝕋_{K^p_r,κ,O} ⊗ Î_π ≅ Hom_O(S^ord_κ(K_r,O)_{m_π},O)’ (p. 111) also requires Hom_O(lim S,O) ⊗ Λ/I = Hom_O(S_{r},O), a control statement for forms. For non-regular κ^1 the finite-level Hecke algebra need not be a specialization of 𝕋_π at all. Defence: Hida’s (33) supplies module control in the regular range, and the paper only uses sufficiently regular weights. Note also that the v5 Main Theorem 9.2.2 still lists ‘Proposition-Hypothesis 7.3.5’ as a hypothesis, while Propositions 7.4.13 and 7.4.15 no longer assume it. Independent check: Quotation checked on the page images (pp. 111–112). Proposition 7.3.5 is asserted 'for every pair (κ^1, r^1)' and derived from §7.3.4 and Theorem 7.1.1. §7.3.4 gets the finite-level isomorphism from Theorem 7.3.1(ii), which requires κ sufficiently regular. The derivation also needs control at level r (sourceIssues E117) and control for the module of forms (sourceIssues E118). There is no standing regularity hypothesis in §7.3. Elsewhere the paper adds 'sufficiently regular' explicitly (Proposition 7.4.10, Definition 7.4.11, Lemma 7.4.14, Proposition 7.4.15). For non-regular κ^1 the classical finite-level Hecke algebra need not be a specialization of 𝕋_π (cf. sourceIssues E115), so the argument does not cover those pairs. It is not known whether the statement fails there, hence 'gap'. Nothing downstream is affected, since the proposition is used only at sufficiently regular weights. Overlaps with sourceIssues E118, which concerns the proof step. Also note that Main Theorem 9.2.2 still lists 'Proposition-Hypothesis 7.3.5' among its hypotheses. Versions: v4 pp. 106–107 ('a simple rephrasing of the preceding discussion'); v2/v3 Hypothesis 7.1.7. Reach: a stated result (Proposition 7.3.5 as printed, for all (κ^1,r^1)); nothing downstream if restricted to regular weights). - **Error** at §2.3.2, p. 18, lines 6–8 of §2.3.2, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 16–17. The source says `"Suppose 𝒦_1, …, 𝒦_r are finite CM extensions of 𝒦 with Σ_{i=1}^r [𝒦_i : 𝒦] = n. … Let V′_i = 𝒦_i, viewed as a 𝒦-space of dimension [𝒦_i : 𝒦]. Each V′_i can be given a 𝒦_i-hermitian structure such that ⊕_i V′_i is isomorphic to V as an hermitian space over 𝒦."`; it should be `This must be a hypothesis on (𝒦_1, …, 𝒦_r) ('Suppose each V′_i can be given …'); it holds e.g. when all 𝒦_i = 𝒦, but not for arbitrary CM extensions.`. Counterexample: 𝒦 = Q(i), p ≡ 1 mod 4, n = 2, r = 1, 𝒦_1 = Q(i, √2) (CM, 𝒦_1⁺ = Q(√2)), V = 𝒦² with ⟨x, y⟩_V = x_1ȳ_1 + 3x_2ȳ_2 (definite, admissible in §2.3). The 𝒦-hermitian forms on 𝒦_1 for which 𝒦_1 acts by ⟨ax, y⟩ = ⟨x, āy⟩ are Tr_{𝒦_1/𝒦}(αxȳ), α ∈ Q(√2)^×; in the 𝒦-basis {1, √2} their Gram matrix is [[2a_0, 4a_1],[4a_1, 4a_0]] (α = a_0 + a_1√2), of determinant 8N(α). Hence ⊕V′_i ≅ V would force 3 · 8N(α) ∈ N_{𝒦/Q}(𝒦^×). At the place 3 (inert in Q(i) and in Q(√2)), norms from Q_3(i) and from Q_3(√2) have even 3-adic valuation, while 24N(α) has odd valuation: impossible. Equivalently, 𝒦_1 ⊗_{Q} Q_3 splits over 𝒦 ⊗ Q_3 with the involution swapping the factors, so every such trace form is hyperbolic at 3, whereas V ⊗ Q_3 is anisotropic (−3 is not a norm from Q_3(i)). Defence: the only case used for the standing assumption is 𝒦_i = 𝒦 (always possible by diagonalization), and §3.2.4 only uses CM pairs (J_0′, h_0) that exist. Independent check: The quote on p. 18 is accurate. It is stated as a fact for arbitrary CM extensions K_i/K. I verified the counterexample. The K-hermitian forms on K_1 = Q(i, √2) = Q(ζ_8) (with K_1^+ = Q(√2)) compatible with the K_1-action are Tr_{K_1/K}(αxȳ), α = a_0 + a_1√2 ∈ Q(√2)^×. In the basis {1, √2} the Gram matrix is [[2a_0, 4a_1],[4a_1, 4a_0]], of determinant 8N(α). An isometry with V = ⟨1, 3⟩ over Q(i) needs 24N(α) ∈ N(Q(i)^×). But 3 is inert in both Q(i) and Q(√2), so v_3(24N(α)) is odd while local norms from Q_3(i) have even valuation. Equivalently, K_1 ⊗_K K_3 ≅ Q_9 × Q_9 with the involution swapping the factors, so every such form is hyperbolic at 3, whereas V ⊗ Q_3 is anisotropic. V (with δ = i, lattice O², p ≡ 1 mod 4, p ≠ 3) satisfies the §2.3 set-up. The sentence must be a hypothesis on (K_i). The only case the paper needs is K_i = K, where it holds by diagonalisation. Present in v1 (p. 15) and v4 (p. 17). - **Misprint** at Proposition 7.3.5, second diagram, p. 112, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 107. The source says `Moreover, the specialization of this isomorphism at the O-valued point λ_π (tensoring both sides over 𝕋_{K^p_{r^1},κ^1,O,π} with 𝕋_{K^p_{r^1},κ^1,O,π}/ker(λ_π) ≃ O) … Hom_O(S^ord_{κ^1}(K^p_{r^1},O)_{m_π},O) ⊗_{𝕋_{K^p_r,κ^1,O,π}} 𝕋_{K^p_{r^1},κ,O,π}/ker(λ_π)`; it should be `The specialization at λ_π only makes sense for κ^1 = κ (the weight of π): tensor over 𝕋_{K^p_{r^1},κ,O,π} with 𝕋_{K^p_{r^1},κ,O,π}/ker(λ_π).`. λ_π is a character of the weight-κ Hecke algebra; ker(λ_π) is not an ideal of 𝕋_{K^p_{r^1},κ^1,O,π} for κ^1 ≠ κ. The printed subscripts mix r and r^1, κ and κ^1 (the right-hand factor already has κ). Intended meaning clear. - **Misprint** at Lemma 7.4.2(1), p. 114, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 108; absent in v2/v3 (Lemma 7.2.2(i), p. 108) (it affects a stated result). The source says `1. 𝒱-valued measures φ on T satisfying φ(t·f) = ρ^υ(t)·φ(f), f ∈ C(T,O), t ∈ T;`; it should be `φ(t·f) = ρ^υ(t)^{−1}·(t·φ(f)) for f ∈ C(T,O), t ∈ T, where t acts on 𝒱 through its Λ-module structure (with the translation convention (t·f)(x) = f(xt); with (t·f)(x) = f(t^{−1}x) the scalar is ρ^υ(t)). This is what the stated equivalence φ(f) = φ_{r,ρ}(f·ρ^υ) with Λ-linear φ_{r,ρ} requires. Alternatively keep the v2/v3 condition φ(t·f) = υ(t)·φ(f) and replace the equivalence by φ_{r,ρ} = φ|_{C_r(T,O)·ρ^υ}.`. As printed the right side is a scalar multiple of φ(f). Taking f = ψ a finite-order character (t·ψ = ψ(t)^{±1}ψ) gives (ψ(t)^{±1} − ρ^υ(t))φ(ψ) = 0 for all t, so φ(ψ) = 0 unless ψ^{±1} = ρ^υ; since finite-order characters span the locally constant functions (over O with enough roots of unity), φ = 0 whenever ρ^υ has infinite order (e.g. ρ algebraic). Condition (2) (Λ-linear maps into the Λ-module 𝒱) shows the T-action on 𝒱 must appear. The v2/v3 version φ(t·f) = υ(t)·φ(f) was changed in v4 to the degenerate form. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 114 (v5) and p. 108 (v4): condition 1 reads φ(t·f) = ρ^υ(t)·φ(f), f ∈ C(T,O), t ∈ T, with ρ: T → O^× fixed, so the right side is the scalar ρ^υ(t) ∈ O^× times φ(f); 𝒱 = V^{ord,cusp}_3(K^p,O) is O-torsion-free and p-adically separated. As printed only φ = 0 qualifies, for every ρ (simpler than the first reading's argument): if f ∈ C_r(T,O) and t ∈ T_r then t·f = f, so (1 − ρ^υ(t))φ(f) = 0; if ρ^υ is non-trivial on every T_r (e.g. ρ algebraic, the case of interest since κ = ρ·α(χ) is sufficiently regular) this gives φ(f) = 0 for all locally constant f; if ρ^υ is trivial on some T_r, summing translates gives φ(1_{aT_r}) = [T_r:T_s]·φ(1_{aT_s}) for all s ≥ r, so φ(1_{aT_r}) ∈ ∩_k p^k𝒱 = 0. By density φ = 0 in both cases, while condition 2 (Λ-linear maps C_r(T,O)·ρ^υ → 𝒱) has non-zero solutions, so the equivalence fails. The printed condition drops the action of t on 𝒱. However, the first reading's correction (revert to the v2/v3 form φ(t·f) = υ(t)·φ(f)) does not fit the v4/v5 lemma, which adds 'The equivalence is such that φ(f) = φ_{r,ρ}(f·ρ^υ)': with (t·g)(x) = g(xt) one has t·(fρ^υ) = ρ^υ(t)·(t·f)ρ^υ, so Λ-linearity of φ_{r,ρ} is equivalent to ρ^υ(t)·φ(t·f) = t·φ(f). The v2/v3 form matches instead the older reading φ_{r,ρ} = φ|_{C_r(T,O)·ρ^υ} (no such formula in v2/v3). Intended meaning recoverable from condition 2 and §5.2.2; downstream arguments use condition 2. Versions: v2/v3 Lemma 7.2.2(i) φ(t·f) = υ(t)·φ(f); v4 p. 108 = v5. Reach: a stated result (Lemma 7.4.2(1) as printed is degenerate); nothing downstream, which works with condition (2). - **Gap** at Proposition 7.4.10, ‘Moreover’ part and proof, p. 117, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 112 (it affects the proof). The source says `Moreover, if κ^1 is a second sufficiently regular character, then L(φ_κ) and L(φ_{κ^1}) are identified with respect to the identifications 𝕋 ⥲ 𝕋_{K^p,κ,O_π} ⥲ 𝕋_{K^p,κ^1,O_π} of Theorem 7.1.1 (after localization at π). … PROOF. This is a consequence of Lemma 7.4.9 and follows by unwinding the definitions.`; it should be `An argument is needed that the elements built at weights κ and κ^1 agree: one must show that the Gorenstein isomorphisms G_r and the identifications Ŝ_{r,V} ≅ 𝕋_{r,κ} ⊗ Î_π at different weights are specializations of the single Λ-adic isomorphisms of Hypothesis 7.3.2 and §7.3.4, and that φ_{r,κ}, φ_{r,κ^1} are specializations of the same Λ-linear measure.`. Lemma 7.4.9 concerns change of level at fixed weight and gives the existence of L(φ_κ) as an inverse limit; it says nothing about comparing weights. The comparison is the heart of the construction of a two-variable (Hida-family) p-adic L-function. Defence: it is a standard consequence of Λ-adic duality once all identifications are chosen Λ-adically (as §7.3.4 does), so the gap is expository. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 117 (v5): Proposition 7.4.10's 'Moreover, if κ^1 is a second sufficiently regular character, then L(φ_κ) and L(φ_{κ^1}) are identified with respect to the identifications 𝕋 ⥲ 𝕋_{K^p,κ,O_π} ⥲ 𝕋_{K^p,κ^1,O_π} of Theorem 7.1.1', with 'PROOF. This is a consequence of Lemma 7.4.9 and follows by unwinding the definitions.' Lemma 7.4.9 (p. 117) only says that ι_r^* is the trace map K_{r+1} → K_r at a FIXED weight κ, i.e. it gives the compatibility in r that makes L(φ_κ) ∈ lim_r 𝕋_{r,κ} ⊗ I_{π^♭} ⊗ I_π well defined. It says nothing about changing weight. L(φ_κ) is obtained from φ_{r,κ} ∈ Hom_{𝕋_{r,κ}}(C_r ⊗ Ŝ^ord_{r,V}, S^ord_{r,−V}) through the chosen isomorphisms 𝕋_{r,κ} ⊗ Î_π ≅ Ŝ^ord_{r,V}, 𝕋̂_{r,κ} ⊗ I_{π^♭} ≅ S^ord_{r,−V} (§7.3.4, Proposition 7.3.5) and G_r. These choices are unique only up to units of 𝕋_{r,κ} and automorphisms of Î_π, and p. 115 admits 'These isomorphisms depended on certain choices'. So L(φ_κ) = L(φ_{κ^1}) needs the weight-κ and weight-κ^1 isomorphisms to be specialisations of one Λ-adic isomorphism. The paper never supplies this. §7.3.4 fixes the Λ-adic isomorphism only for lim_r S^ord_κ(K_r,O) at one weight κ. Proposition 7.3.5 asserts isomorphisms for every (κ^1,r^1) with commutative diagrams for change of level only, with no compatibility across weights. Theorem 7.1.1 identifies Hecke algebras, not the modules of forms. The missing input is Hida's Λ-adic control for the modules ((33)–(34)) together with choosing all finite-level isomorphisms and G_r as specialisations of the Λ-adic ones (for G_r this is how Hypothesis 7.3.2 reads). With the measure φ fixed (Lemma 7.4.2, same φ for every ρ), the claim then does follow by unwinding. So the gap is expository and the result is standard, but it is needed for Lemma 7.4.14 and for Propositions 7.4.13 and 7.4.15 (specialisation at λ ∈ X(κ,r,R) for any sufficiently regular κ). Versions: v4 p. 112 identical; v2/v3 Proposition 7.2.13 same, with proof citing Lemma 7.2.12. Reach: the proof (of Proposition 7.4.10’s weight independence, hence of Propositions 7.4.13, 7.4.15). - **Error** at Lemma 7.5.3, p. 121, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 115; v2 (Lemma 7.3.3) had no volume factor (it affects a stated result). The source says `L_φ(h) = (1/(Vol(I^0_{r,V})Vol(I^0_{r,−V}))) ∫_{G(Q)Z_G(R)\G(A)} [h(g),φ(g)]||ν(g)^{−a(κ)}||dg.`; it should be `L_φ(h) = ⟨h,φ⟩_{κ,K_r} = Vol(I^0_{r,V})^{-1} ∫_{G(Q)Z_G(R)\G(A)} [h(g),φ(g)]·||ν(g)||^{−a(κ)} dg, by (136)–(137). The product of the two volumes is the normalization for the doubled group G_3 used in Proposition 9.1.7.`. Lemma 7.5.2 defines L_φ(h) := ⟨h,φ⟩_{κ,K_r}, and (136) sets ⟨·,·⟩_{κ,K_r} = Vol(I^0_{r,V})^{-1}⟨·,·⟩^Ser_κ with ⟨·,·⟩^Ser given by the integral (133); (137) states exactly the one-volume formula. By (125), I^0_{r,−V} = δ_p^{-1}Ī^0_{r,V}δ_p has the same volume, so the printed formula is off by the factor Vol(I^0_r)^{-1}, a non-unit rational number depending on r. The lemma calls itself ‘just a restatement of (133)’, which has no volume at all. Defence: Proposition 9.1.7 applies the formula ‘doubled’, i.e. on G_3 ⊂ G_1 × G_2, where a product of two volumes is natural; the printed G_1 version seems to anticipate that. Whether Proposition 9.1.7/Corollary 9.1.8 carry the correct factor is not settled here. Independent check: Quotation checked on the page image (p. 121). Lemma 7.5.2 (p. 120) defines L_φ(h) := ⟨h,φ⟩_{κ,K_r}. By (136)–(137) (p. 94), ⟨·,·⟩_{κ,K_r} = Vol(I^0_{r,V})^{-1}⟨·,·⟩^Ser_κ = Vol(I^0_r)^{-1}∫_{G(Q)Z_G(R)\G(A)}[φ(g),φ'(g)]·||ν(g)||^{−a(κ)}dg. The identification 'as in Equation (114)' (p. 87) is the plain identification of coherent cohomology with (𝔓_h,K_h)-cohomology and introduces no volume. So the extra factor Vol(I^0_{r,−V})^{-1} in Lemma 7.5.3 is unjustified. By (125), I^0_{r,−V} = δ_p^{-1}Ī^0_{r,V}δ_p has the same volume as I^0_{r,V}, so the printed value is Vol(I^0_r)^{-1} times the correct one, an r-dependent non-unit. The lemma calls itself 'just a restatement of (133)', which has no volume at all. Nothing downstream is affected. Proposition 9.1.7 'doubles' the lemma on G_3 ⊂ G_1 × G_2 with the factor [Vol(I^0_{r,V})Vol(I^0_{r,−V})]^{-1}, one volume per factor. That is what doubling the corrected one-volume formula gives, not the printed one. Versions: v4 p. 115 identical; v2 Lemma 7.3.3 has no volume factor. Reach: a stated result (Lemma 7.5.3); possibly the volume factor in Proposition 9.1.7. - **Gap** at §8.1, Corollary 8.1.2, p. 122, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 117 (it affects the proof). The source says `The following corollary is the p-adic version of the last part of Corollary 4.4.9. Corollary 8.1.2. Under the hypotheses of the previous proposition, for all κ† ≤ κ there are differential operators … such that θ(κ, χ) = Σ_{κ†≤κ} res_3 ∘ θ(κ, κ†) ∘ θ^hol(κ†, χ).`; it should be `Add a proof: θ(κ,χ), θ^hol(κ†,χ) and θ(κ,κ†) are the p-adic operators attached to the polynomials p(r̃,s̃), P^hol(κ†,χ) and δ(κ,κ†) ∈ U(p_3^+) ⊂ Sym(p_4^+) underlying Corollary 4.4.9 and Proposition 8.1.1(d); the polynomial identity underlying Corollary 4.4.9 transfers because the assignment polynomial ↦ p-adic operator is multiplicative and commutes with res_3 for elements of U(p_3^+) (with a reference, e.g. to [EFMV18]).`. No argument is given, and it is an input to Proposition 8.1.3 (hence to Corollary 8.2.4 and the Main Theorem). Defence: the p-adic operators are attached to the same polynomials as the C^∞ ones (Proposition 8.1.1(a), (d)), so polynomial identities transfer; this is routine in Eischen's framework. Independent check: p. 122: Corollary 8.1.2 is introduced only by 'The following corollary is the p-adic version of the last part of Corollary 4.4.9' and has no proof; it is used as the first step of the proof of Proposition 8.1.3 (p. 123), hence feeds Corollary 8.2.4. Corollary 4.4.9 (p. 73) is an identity D(κ,χ) = Σ δ(κ,κ†)∘D^hol(κ†,χ) of C^∞ operators with δ(κ,κ†) ∈ U(p_3^+), derived from the (g,K)-module decomposition and holomorphic projection. The mechanism for transfer is indicated in the proof of Proposition 8.1.1(d) ('one lets θ^hol(κ,χ) be the differential operator on p-adic modular forms attached to the same polynomial'), but the transfer of the identity additionally needs that the assignment polynomial ↦ p-adic differential operator is compatible with composition and with restriction res_3 to G_3 (δ(κ,κ†) acts on G_3, while the formula applies θ(κ,κ†) on G_4 before res_3), which is neither stated nor referenced. The statement is surely correct and the missing argument routine in Eischen's framework, so this is a minor expository gap. (The symbol θ(κ,λ) and the domain V_χ(G_4,…) in the statement are misprints for θ(κ,κ†) acting on V(G_4,K^p,O); that is recorded separately, sourceIssues E126.) v4 p. 117 is identical. - **Gap** at §8.1, Corollary 8.1.2, p. 122, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 117 (it affects the proof). The source says `The following corollary is the p-adic version of the last part of Corollary 4.4.9. Corollary 8.1.2. Under the hypotheses of the previous proposition, for all κ† ≤ κ there are differential operators … such that θ(κ, χ) = Σ_{κ†≤κ} res_3 ∘ θ(κ, κ†) ∘ θ^hol(κ†, χ).`; it should be `Add a proof: θ(κ,χ), θ^hol(κ†,χ) and θ(κ,κ†) are the p-adic operators attached to the polynomials p(r̃,s̃), P^hol(κ†,χ) and δ(κ,κ†) ∈ U(p_3^+) ⊂ Sym(p_4^+) underlying Corollary 4.4.9 and Proposition 8.1.1(d); the polynomial identity underlying Corollary 4.4.9 transfers because the assignment polynomial ↦ p-adic operator is multiplicative and commutes with res_3 for elements of U(p_3^+) (with a reference, e.g. to [EFMV18]).`. No argument is given, and it is an input to Proposition 8.1.3 (hence to Corollary 8.2.4 and the Main Theorem). Defence: the p-adic operators are attached to the same polynomials as the C^∞ ones (Proposition 8.1.1(a), (d)), so polynomial identities transfer; this is routine in Eischen's framework. Independent check: p. 122: Corollary 8.1.2 is introduced only by 'The following corollary is the p-adic version of the last part of Corollary 4.4.9' and has no proof; it is used as the first step of the proof of Proposition 8.1.3 (p. 123), hence feeds Corollary 8.2.4. Corollary 4.4.9 (p. 73) is an identity D(κ,χ) = Σ δ(κ,κ†)∘D^hol(κ†,χ) of C^∞ operators with δ(κ,κ†) ∈ U(p_3^+), derived from the (g,K)-module decomposition and holomorphic projection. The mechanism for transfer is indicated in the proof of Proposition 8.1.1(d) ('one lets θ^hol(κ,χ) be the differential operator on p-adic modular forms attached to the same polynomial'), but the transfer of the identity additionally needs that the assignment polynomial ↦ p-adic differential operator is compatible with composition and with restriction res_3 to G_3 (δ(κ,κ†) acts on G_3, while the formula applies θ(κ,κ†) on G_4 before res_3), which is neither stated nor referenced. The statement is surely correct and the missing argument routine in Eischen's framework, so this is a minor expository gap. (The symbol θ(κ,λ) and the domain V_χ(G_4,…) in the statement are misprints for θ(κ,κ†) acting on V(G_4,K^p,O); that is recorded separately, sourceIssues E126.) v4 p. 117 is identical. - **Gap** at §8.1, proof of Proposition 8.1.3, p. 123, last sentence ('Part (1) above now follows from …') and the proof of Lemma 8.1.4, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 117 (it affects the proof). The source says `The condition κ† < κ is equivalent to the condition that the p-adic valuation of ∏_{w,j} κ′^{,−1}·κ^{†,′}(t_{w,j}) is positive. … Part (1) above now follows from the fact that the ordinary projector commutes with the differential operators.`; it should be `State and justify (or cite) the commutation U_{w,j,κ}∘θ(κ,κ†) = θ(κ,κ†)∘(|κ'^{−1}κ†'(t_{w,j})|_p U_{w,j,κ†}) on p-adic forms (together with res_3∘θ(κ,κ†) = θ_3(κ,κ†)∘res_3); in Lemma 8.1.4 read 'κ† < κ implies that ∏_{w,j}κ'^{−1}κ†'(t_{w,j}) has negative p-adic valuation (so its |·|_p is a positive power of p)', with κ' = κ_norm as in (30), not 2.6.11.`. On p-adic modular forms the (unnormalised) U-operators do not commute with the differential operators on the nose (for elliptic forms U_pθ = pθU_p); the needed statement is that they commute after the weight-dependent normalisations |κ′(t)|_p^{−1}, i.e. that the power of p produced by θ(κ, κ†) is exactly the ratio of normalising factors used in Lemma 8.1.4 — this is asserted, not checked. The 'equivalence' in Lemma 8.1.4 is also more than true in general: the valuation is one linear functional (pairing with the strictly dominant cocharacter ∏_j t_{w,j}), positive on κ − κ† when κ† < κ, but not conversely. Defence: the conclusion (the κ† < κ terms are killed by e_κ) is the standard 'ordinary projection kills θ-images' phenomenon and is correct. Independent check: p. 123 (zoomed). Part (1) of the proof of Proposition 8.1.3 is dispatched by 'the ordinary projector commutes with the differential operators', together with Lemma 8.1.4. What is needed is e_κ∘θ(κ,κ†) = θ(κ,κ†)∘lim U_{p,κ}^{N!}, where on weight-κ† forms U_{p,κ} = ∏|κ'^{−1}κ†'(t_{w,j})|_p U_{w,j,κ†}, i.e. that the p-adic U-operators and θ(κ,κ†) commute up to exactly the ratio of weight normalisations (for elliptic forms U_pθ = pθU_p, so 'commutes' is only true after renormalisation). This is asserted without proof or reference; it also requires moving res_3 past θ(κ,κ†). The first reading's second point (the 'equivalence' is more than true) is minor: only the implication is used, and within the index set κ† ≤ κ of Corollary 8.1.2 the converse is harmless. I found one more slip in the same proof, which supports the verdict: if the p-adic valuation of y = ∏κ'^{−1}κ†'(t_{w,j}) is e > 0 as printed, the scalar |y|_p = p^{−e} has p-adic norm p^{e} > 1, so 'Thus U_{p,κ} has p-adic norm strictly less than 1' does not follow; the argument needs v_p(y) < 0 (equivalently, the rational number |y|_p has positive valuation). A sample computation with p⁺-weights e_{σ,i} + e_{σc,j} in the κ_norm coordinates of p. 129 does give v_p(y) = j − (n − i + 1) < 0. Also 'κ' defined as in 2.6.11' is a wrong cross-reference: 2.6.11 defines the twist κ' = (κ_0 + a,(κ_{σ,i})), whereas the normalisation is by κ_norm as in (30) (cf. p. 98 'κ' related to κ as in (30)'). The conclusion (e_κ kills the κ† < κ terms) is the standard phenomenon and is correct. v4 p. 117 is identical. - **Error** at §2.3, p. 18, lines 3–5, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 16. The source says `"More precisely, the elements of ker¹(Q, G) classify isomorphism classes of hermitian tuples 𝒱′ = (V′_j, ⟨·,·⟩_{V′_j})_{1≤j≤m} that are locally isomorphic to 𝒱 at every place of Q."`; it should be `They classify tuples that are locally similar to 𝒱 at every place (V′_j ⊗ Q_v ≅ c_v·(V_j ⊗ Q_v) with a common c_v ∈ Q_v^× for all j), up to global similitude with a common factor c ∈ Q^×.`. G is a similitude group, so H¹(Q, G) and H¹(Q_v, G) classify hermitian tuples up to similitude, not up to isometry. Read literally, the printed sentence makes ker¹(Q, G) trivial: by Landherr's theorem (Hasse principle for hermitian forms over a CM extension), hermitian spaces that are isomorphic at every place are globally isomorphic, so there would be a single class — contradicting the next paragraph, which says the Hasse principle fails in general when dim V_1 is odd. Defence: the intended statement is Kottwitz's [Kot92, §7–§8], which the paper cites. Independent check: The quote on p. 18 is accurate. G = G_P is the similitude group with a common factor ν. From 1 → U → G → G_m → 1 and H¹(Q, G_m) = 1 we get H¹(Q,G) = H¹(Q,U)/Q^×, and likewise locally. So ker¹(Q,G) classifies tuples that are locally similar everywhere, with a common c_v at each v, modulo a common global similitude. With the standard meaning of 'isomorphic' (isometric), tuples locally isometric to 𝒱 everywhere are globally isometric by Landherr's Hasse principle for hermitian forms over K/K^+. The set would then be a singleton, which contradicts the next paragraph: ker¹ ≠ 0 in general when dim V_1 is odd or m > 1. The paper never says that isomorphisms are similitudes. The intended statement is Kottwitz's, and nothing downstream is affected. Present in v1 (p. 14) and v4 (p. 16). - **Gap** at §8.2, Theorem 8.2.2, p. 125 (and the identification of sections on p. 124), in arXiv v5; present in v4 as Theorem 5.4.1 at pp. 84–85 (without the Y^class_H qualifier) (it affects a stated result). The source says `From the p-adic q-expansion principle and the description of the q-expansion coefficients given in [Eis14, Section 3], we obtain the following theorem (similar to [EFMV18, Theorem 7.2.3]). Theorem 8.2.2 (The Eisenstein Measure). … There is a measure Eis_{a,b} … that satisfies ∫ χ̃ψ·ρ^υ Eis_{a,b} = θ^{(κ,a,b)}(G_{k,ν,χ_unitary,ψ}) whenever (χ, c = ψ·ρ^υ) ∈ Y^class_H.`; it should be `Give the proof, or a precise reference for general signature: define Eis_{a,b} by the q-expansion coefficients of G_{k,ν,F} for the §4.3 Schwartz data at p (checking the Kummer congruences, Lemma 5.1.3) together with the action of θ^{(κ,a,b)} on q-expansions [EFMV18], and verify that the §4 sections f(χ,c), including the 'minor changes' at p of §4.3.1, are the sections underlying G_{k,ν,χ_unitary,ψ}.`. The theorem is only 'obtained', with a pointer to a similar theorem; in the definite case it is [Eis15, Theorem 20] (Remark 8.2.3), but for general signature neither cited source states it, and the identification of the Eisenstein series of the §4 sections with (a normalisation of) G_{k,ν,χ_unitary,ψ} is asserted on p. 124 without verification. Defence: the construction is standard (Katz–Hida–Eischen) once q-expansions are known, and [EFMV18, Thm 7.2.3] is the analogous statement. Independent check: Quotation checked on the page image (p. 125). The theorem is only 'obtained', with a pointer to a result that is 'similar'. The first reading's 'neither cited source states it for general signature' is too strong. The arXiv version of [EFMV18] (1511.06771, Theorem 7.2.4 there) constructs a signature-dependent measure μ_{G'} on X_p × T(Z_p) for the sections F_{χ_u,ψ}(x,y) = χ_u(x)φ_ζ(N(x)ᵗy). What is genuinely unverified is the step connecting that measure to the data of this paper. §4.3.1 (p. 49) says the Siegel–Weil section at p agrees with that of [Eis15, Eis14] only 'with a few minor changes'. Yet p. 124 and Remark 8.2.1 assert without argument that the Eisenstein series of the §4 sections f(χ,c) is (a normalization of) G_{k,ν,χ_unitary,ψ}. Also, θ^{(κ,a,b)} is applied on G_4 before restriction, not res∘Θ^κ as in [EFMV18]. So the Kummer-congruence/q-expansion argument for these modified sections, and the matching of sections, are left to the reader. p. 85 claims the existence 'is proved in [Eis15, Eis12]; see Theorem 8.2.2'. That holds in the definite case (Remark 8.2.3) but not literally in general. Versions: v4 Theorem 5.4.1 (pp. 84–85) is the same apart from the Y^class_H qualifier. - **Misprint** at §8.3, p. 126, definition of the modulus character δ_w, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 118. The source says `δ_w(t) = |t_1^{n−1} ⋯ t_{a_w}^{b_w−a_w} t_{a_w+1}^{1−n} ⋯ t_n^{b_w−1−a_w}|_p.`; it should be `δ_w(t) = |t_1^{n−1} ⋯ t_{a_w}^{b_w−a_w+1} t_{a_w+1}^{1−n} ⋯ t_n^{b_w−1−a_w}|_p, i.e. exponent n+1−2i for i ≤ a_w and 2i−n−2a_w−1 for i > a_w.`. Count roots in Lie(B^u_w): for i ≤ a_w the root e_i − e_k occurs for i < k ≤ a_w and for all k > a_w (n−i roots with +e_i), and e_k − e_i for k < i (i−1 roots), giving exponent n+1−2i; at i = a_w this is b_w − a_w + 1. Checks: GL_2 with a_w = 2, b_w = 0 (standard upper Borel) has δ(diag(t_1,t_2)) = |t_1/t_2|, while the printed formula gives |t_1 t_2^{−2}|; with a_w = 1 the printed formula assigns t_1 both n−1 and b_w−a_w = n−2. The exponents sum to 0 only with the correction. Case for the defence: the i > a_w exponents are right and the proof of Lemma 8.3.2 only uses that the exponents strictly decrease/increase in blocks, which holds for the corrected values. - **Gap** at §8.2, proof of Corollary 8.2.4, p. 126, in arXiv v5 (the proof is new in v5; v4 Corollary 5.4.3, p. 85, has no proof) (it affects the proof). The source says `Proof. We need to compare the expression in Theorem 8.2.2 with the specifications required in Definition 5.3.2. Bearing in mind the translation mentioned in Remark 8.2.1, this comes down to comparing the action of e_κ ∘ res_3θ^{(κ,a,b)} with e_κ ∘ ∘D^hol(κ, χ). But this follows from Proposition 8.1.3.`; it should be `Also verify the remaining requirements of Definition 5.3.2: the local sections of G_{k,ν,χ_unitary,ψ} at v ∉ S, v ∈ S, v | p and ∞ are those prescribed; the normalising factor D(n, K, 𝔟, p, k) of [Eis15, Prop. 13] matches D_S(χ) (or D(χ)) of (108) as required in the last bullet; and the shift (1, χ) condition (109).`. Only the differential-operator part of the last bullet of Definition 5.3.2 is addressed; the normalisations and local-section conditions are left to 'the translation mentioned in Remark 8.2.1'. Defence: these are bookkeeping facts about Eischen's construction. Independent check: Quotation checked on the page image (p. 126). The local-section bullets of Definition 5.3.2 hold by the choice made on p. 124 ('We choose f(χ,c) to be a factorizable Siegel section meeting the conditions of Definition 5.3.2'). They transfer to G_{k,ν,χ_unitary,ψ} only through the identification discussed in sourceIssues E130 (overlap). What the proof leaves out is the rest of the last bullet. That bullet requires e_κ∫(χ,c)dEis = D^S(χ)·e_κ∘res_3E_{f(χ,c)}, whereas Remark 8.2.1 says the Eisenstein series is normalized by D(n,K,𝔟,p,k) of [Eis15, Prop. 13]. The equality of these factors (or the passage between normalized and unnormalized measures) is not checked. Nor is the claimed shift (1,χ) of (109). The proof reduces everything to Proposition 8.1.3 'bearing in mind the translation mentioned in Remark 8.2.1'. The conclusion is standard bookkeeping, but it is not supplied. - **Misprint** at §8.3.1, proof of Lemma 8.3.2, p. 129 (display 'β_x/β^x(t) = …', the definition of θ, the formula for θ(diag), the chain of inequalities, and the definition of m_i), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 120 (it affects the proof). The source says `β_x/β^x(t) = |κ_norm(xtx^{−1}t^{−1})|_p^{−1} δ_w(xtx^{−1}t^{−1})^{−1/2} … That is, the character θ = |κ_norm|_p δ_w^{−1/2} satisfies θ^x = θ. … m_i = … −Σ_{σ,𝔭_σ=𝔭_w}(κ_{σc,i} − a_w) (i > a_w) … θ(diag(t_1, ..., t_n)) = |t_1^{m_1+(n−1)/2} ⋯ t_{a_w}^{m_{a_w}+(b_w−a_w)/2} t_{a_w+1}^{m_{a_w+1}+(1−n)/2} ⋯ t_n^{m_n+(a_w−2−b_w)/2}|_p^{−1}. … m_1 + (n−1)/2 > ⋯ > m_{a_w} + (b_w−a_w)/2 > m_n + (b_w−2−a_w)/2 > ⋯ > m_{a_w+1} + (1−n)/2.`; it should be `β_x(t)/β^x(t) = |κ_norm(xtx^{−1}t^{−1})|_p δ_w(xtx^{−1}t^{−1})^{1/2}; the invariant character is θ = |κ_norm|_p δ_w^{1/2} (equivalently its inverse |κ_norm|_p^{−1}δ_w^{−1/2}, which is what the θ(diag) display computes); m_i = −Σ_{σ,𝔭_σ=𝔭_w}(κ_{σc,i−a_w} − a_w) for i > a_w; θ(diag(t)) = ∏_i |t_i|_p^{m_i + e_i/2} with e_i = n+1−2i (i ≤ a_w), 2i−n−2a_w−1 (i > a_w), so the t_{a_w}-exponent is m_{a_w} + (b_w−a_w+1)/2 and the t_n-exponent m_n + (b_w−a_w−1)/2; the chain reads m_1 + (n−1)/2 > ⋯ > m_{a_w} + (b_w−a_w+1)/2 > m_n + (b_w−a_w−1)/2 > ⋯ > m_{a_w+1} + (1−n)/2. Also 'Weil group' should be 'Weyl group'.`. With β = |κ_norm|_p^{−1}δ_w^{−1/2}α and β_x = |κ_norm|_p^{−1}δ_w^{−1/2}α^x, one gets β_x(t)/β(xtx^{−1}) = (|κ_norm|_p^{−1}δ_w^{−1/2})(t)/(|κ_norm|_p^{−1}δ_w^{−1/2})(xtx^{−1}) = (|κ_norm|_pδ_w^{1/2})(xtx^{−1}t^{−1}), the inverse of the printed value (harmless: a p-adic unit iff its inverse is). The printed θ = |κ_norm|_pδ_w^{−1/2} would have exponents m_i − e_i/2, which need not be distinct (e.g. m_1 = m_2 + 1 makes the t_1- and t_2-exponents equal), so the regularity argument needs the corrected θ; the displayed θ(diag) is in fact the corrected character (up to inversion) with the δ-exponent misprints of the previous issue, and the misprinted constants (b_w−a_w)/2, (b_w−2−a_w)/2 differ from the correct ones by the same 1/2, so every inequality of the chain is unaffected (m_{a_w} + (b_w−a_w+1)/2 > m_n + (b_w−a_w−1)/2 ⇔ m_{a_w} ≥ m_n). The t_n-exponent (a_w−2−b_w)/2 in θ(diag) is inconsistent even with the chain. Index: κ_{σc} has b_w entries and the κ_norm formula just above uses κ_{σc,j} for t_{a_w+j}. Defence: the logic (unit ⇒ trivial ⇒ θ^x = θ ⇒ x = 1 by regularity) is sound with the corrected character, and (166) (read as κ_{σ,a_σ} + κ_{σc,b_σ} ≥ n) gives m_{a_w} ≥ m_n. Independent check: Checked on 300-dpi zooms of p. 129 (and p. 126 for δ_w, B_w). With β = |κ_norm|_p^{-1}δ_w^{-1/2}α, β_x = |κ_norm|_p^{-1}δ_w^{-1/2}α^x and β^x(t) = β(xtx^{-1}) (by analogy with α^x), the α-factors cancel and β_x(t)/β^x(t) = |κ_norm(xtx^{-1}t^{-1})|_p·δ_w(xtx^{-1}t^{-1})^{1/2}: the printed value is its inverse (harmless, a unit iff its inverse is). The invariant character is therefore |κ_norm|_pδ_w^{1/2} (or its inverse), not the printed θ = |κ_norm|_pδ_w^{-1/2}; the printed θ has exponents m_i − e_i/2, which coincide at t_1,t_2 when m_1 = m_2 + 1 (a_w ≥ 2), so it would not be regular. Root count for B_w (A upper, D lower triangular) gives δ_w exponents e_i = n+1−2i (i ≤ a_w) and 2i−n−2a_w−1 (i > a_w), i.e. b_w−a_w+1 at t_{a_w} (p. 126 prints b_w−a_w, cf. sourceIssues E131) and b_w−a_w−1 at t_n. The κ_norm display σ(t_{a_w+j})^{−κ_{σc,j}+a_w} gives m_i = −Σ(κ_{σc,i−a_w} − a_w) for i > a_w (printed κ_{σc,i} is out of range for i > b_w). The θ(diag) display, |∏t_i^{m_i+e_i/2}|_p^{-1}, is exactly |κ_norm|_p^{-1}δ_w^{-1/2}, i.e. the corrected character up to inversion, with the t_{a_w} exponent inheriting the δ_w misprint and the t_n exponent (a_w−2−b_w)/2 wrong under any reading (the chain itself has (b_w−2−a_w)/2). All constants in the chain are off by the same 1/2 on the relevant comparison, so the inequalities are unaffected: m_{a_w}+(b_w−a_w+1)/2 > m_n+(b_w−a_w−1)/2 ⇔ m_{a_w} ≥ m_n, which is Σ_σ(κ_{σ,a_w}+κ_{σc,b_w}−n) ≥ 0, i.e. (166). 'Weil group' should be 'Weyl group'. The logic (unit ⇒ trivial ⇒ θ^x = θ ⇒ x = 1) is sound with the corrected character. v4 p. 120 is identical. - **Misprint** at §8.3.5, pp. 131–132, normalisation of the anti-ordinary Hecke operators, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 122 (it affects the proof). The source says `p. 131: 'the Hecke operators u^−_{w,j} = |κ_norm(t_{w,j})|_p U^−_{w,j}'; p. 132: 'the Hecke operator u^{GL,−}_{w,j} = |κ_norm(t_{w,j})|_p^{−1} U^{GL,−}_{w,j}'`; it should be `p. 131: u^−_{w,j} = |κ_norm(t_{w,j})|_p^{−1} U^−_{w,j} (the same scalar as u_{w,j} and u^{GL,−}_{w,j}).`. (170) and (171) use ⟨u^{GL,−}_{w,j}φ, φ′⟩_w = ⟨φ, u^GL_{w,j}φ′⟩_w; since [I t^{−1} I] is the adjoint of [I t I] for the invariant pairing, this holds exactly when both operators carry the same scalar |κ_norm(t_{w,j})|_p^{−1}; with the p. 131 normalisation the identity is off by |κ_norm(t_{w,j})|_p^{2}. Case for the defence: for n = 1 the p. 131 normalisation makes 'anti-ordinary' coincide with 'ordinary', in line with Lemma 9.0.1, so the authors may intend a different weight normalisation on the anti-holomorphic side; the paper does not make this explicit, and the local analysis of §8.3.5 is written with the p. 132 convention. Independent check: Zoomed pp. 131–132. p. 131: 'u^−_{w,j} = |κ_norm(t_{w,j})|_p U^−_{w,j}'; p. 132, in the next sentence of the same paragraph: 'u^−_{w,j} acts on π_p^{I_r} = ⊗π_w^{I_{w,r}} via the action of the Hecke operator u^{GL,−}_{w,j} = |κ_norm(t_{w,j})|_p^{−1}U^{GL,−}_{w,j}'. U^−_{w,j} = I_r t^{−1}_{w,j} I_r and U^{GL,−}_{w,j} = I_{w,r}t^{−1}_{w,j}I_{w,r} are the same operator (t^+_{w,j} has trivial similitude component, (23)), so the two normalisations differ by |κ_norm(t_{w,j})|_p^2 and contradict each other. The p. 132 one is the one the proofs need: for the G_w-invariant pairing π_w × π_w^∨, (1/vol I)∫_{ItI}⟨π(x)v,v'⟩dx = ⟨v,[It^{−1}I]v'⟩, so [It^{−1}I] on π_w is exactly adjoint to [ItI] on π_w^∨ = (π^♭)_w (the ||ν||^{a(κ)} twist in (141) only affects μ_p); (170)/(171) (⟨u^{GL,−}φ,φ'⟩ = ⟨φ,u^{GL}φ'⟩ with u^{GL} = |κ_norm(t)|_p^{−1}U^{GL}, p. 127) hold only if both carry the same scalar |κ_norm(t_{w,j})|_p^{−1}, and only then does 'anti-ordinary' correspond to ordinarity of π^♭_w for the weight κ, as Lemma 8.3.6(i) asserts. p. 131 copies the shape of the §6.6 convention U^−_{w,j,κ} = |κ'(t_{w,j})|_pU^−_{w,j} (p. 98), which there is used with the Serre-dual subscript κ^D (e^−_{κ^D}, p. 101), but applies it to the holomorphic weight κ of π^♭. The global definition of anti-ordinarity (p. 132, e^−·φ = φ) uses the p. 131 operator, so the slip is in a definition, but the intended meaning is fixed by p. 132 and (170). v4 p. 122 is identical. - **Misprint** at §8.3.5, Lemma 8.3.6(ii), p. 132 (statement), in arXiv v5; present in v4 (Lemma 8.2.6(ii)) at p. 123 (it affects a stated result). The source says `it is characterized by ⟨φ^{a-ord}_{w,r}, φ^{∨,ord}_w⟩_w ≠ 0 and ⟨φ^{a-ord}_{w,r}, φ⟩_w = 0 for all φ ∈ π_w^{I_{w,r}} belonging to a generalized eigenspace of some u^{GL,−}_{w,j} with non-unit eigenvalue.`; it should be `… for all φ ∈ π_w^{∨,I_{w,r}} belonging to a generalized eigenspace of some u^GL_{w,j} with non-unit eigenvalue.`. ⟨·,·⟩_w pairs π_w with π_w^∨, so the second argument must lie in π_w^∨; the proof establishes exactly ⟨φ^{a-ord}_{w,r}, V_i⟩_w = 0 for the joint generalized u^GL_{w,j}-eigenspaces V_i ⊂ π_w^{∨,I_{w,r}} with a non-unit eigenvalue. Intended meaning clear from the proof. Independent check: Zoomed p. 132: Lemma 8.3.6(ii) reads '⟨φ^{a-ord}_{w,r}, φ⟩_w = 0 for all φ ∈ π_w^{I_{w,r}} belonging to a generalized eigenspace of some u^{GL,−}_{w,j} with non-unit eigenvalue'. ⟨·,·⟩_w is the pairing π_w × π_w^∨ → C (Lemma 8.3.4, and 'Let ⟨·,·⟩_w : π_w × π_w^∨ → C' in the proof), and φ^{a-ord}_{w,r} ∈ π_w, so the second slot must be in π_w^∨; the proof (p. 133) decomposes π_w^{∨,I_{w,r}} = Cφ_w^{∨,ord} ⊕ V_1 ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ V_t into simultaneous generalized u^{GL}_{w,j}-eigenspaces and shows ⟨φ^{a-ord}_{w,r}, V_i⟩_w = 0, which is valid: ℓ = ⟨φ^{a-ord},·⟩ satisfies ℓ∘(u^{GL}_{w,j} − a(j,r)) = 0 by (170), and u^{GL}_{w,j} − a(j,r) is invertible on a generalized eigenspace with non-unit eigenvalue. v4 Lemma 8.2.6(ii), p. 123, is identical. - **Gap** at §8.3.5, proof of Lemma 8.3.6(i), pp. 132–133 (induction on j after (170), and 'as in the preceding proof' after (171)), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 123 (it affects the proof). The source says `Let V_{j−1} ⊂ π_w^{∨,I_{w,r}} be a maximal subspace that is a simultaneous eigenspace for u^GL_{w,1}, …, u^GL_{w,j−1} with respective eigenvalues a(1, r), …, a(j−1, r). Then by the commutativity of the u^GL_{w,j}s, the identity (170) holds for all φ ∈ V_{j−1}. In particular, there is a non-zero (maximal) subspace of V_j ⊂ V_{j−1} which is an eigenspace for u^GL_{w,j} with eigenvalue a(j, r).`; it should be `Work with joint generalised eigenspaces: ℓ = ⟨φ^{a-ord}_{w,r}, ·⟩_w satisfies ℓ∘(u^GL_{w,i} − a(i,r)) = 0, hence vanishes on every generalised u^GL_{w,i}-eigenspace for eigenvalues ≠ a(i,r); so ℓ ≠ 0 on the joint generalised eigenspace W_{j−1} for (a(1,r), …, a(j−1,r)); u^GL_{w,j} preserves W_{j−1} and u^GL_{w,j} − a(j,r) is not surjective there, so W_j ≠ 0; finally commuting operators on W_n have a common eigenvector.`. The step needs ℓ|_{V_{j−1}} ≠ 0, which is not shown and can fail for true eigenspaces: on ℂ² with u = [[a,1],[0,a]], ℓ(x,y) = y satisfies ℓ∘(u − a) = 0 but vanishes on the eigenspace ℂe_1. Defence: the conclusion is standard linear algebra and holds by the corrected argument. Independent check: p. 132–133: after (170), the first step is justified (ℓ = ⟨φ^{a-ord}_{w,r},·⟩_w is non-zero on π_w^{∨,I_{w,r}} since the pairing of I-invariants is perfect, and ℓ∘(u − a) = 0 forces u − a to be non-surjective, hence a is an eigenvalue). The induction step 'the identity (170) holds for all φ ∈ V_{j−1}. In particular, there is a non-zero subspace V_j ⊂ V_{j−1} which is an eigenspace for u^{GL}_{w,j} with eigenvalue a(j,r)' needs ℓ|_{V_{j−1}} ≠ 0, which is not shown and fails in general for true eigenspaces: on C² with u = [[a,1],[0,a]] and ℓ(x,y) = y one has ℓ∘(u − a) = 0 but ℓ vanishes on ker(u − a) = Ce_1 (checked). The conclusion is nevertheless true (the first reading's generalized-eigenspace argument works; in fact V_{j−1} ∩ W_j ≠ 0 where W_j is the joint generalized eigenspace), so this is a gap in the argument, not an error. v4 p. 123 is identical. In particular, there is a non-zero subspace V_j ⊂ V_{j−1} which is an eigenspace for u^{GL}_{w,j} with eigenvalue a(j,r)' needs ℓ|_{V_{j−1}} ≠ 0, which is not shown and fails in general for true eigenspaces: on C² with u = [[a,1],[0,a]] and ℓ(x,y) = y one has ℓ∘(u − a) = 0 but ℓ vanishes on ker(u − a) = Ce_1 (checked). The conclusion is nevertheless true (the first reading's generalized-eigenspace argument works; in fact V_{j−1} ∩ W_j ≠ 0 where W_j is the joint generalized eigenspace), so this is a gap in the argument, not an error. v4 p. 123 is identical. - **Misprint** at §8.5, proof of Lemma 8.5.3, p. 139 ('The remaining claims of the lemma are consequences of the definition of Q[π′, χ]'), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 129 (it affects a stated result). The source says `The ratio ⟨φ_{r′}(v_S, π′), φ_{r′}(v^♭_S, (π′)^♭)_χ⟩_{π′,χ} / Vol(I^0_{r′,V} ∩ I^0_{r′,−V}) … its value is in R·Q[π′, χ] … The remaining claims of the lemma are consequences of the definition of Q[π′, χ].`; it should be `In Lemmas 6.7.1 and 6.7.6 and in the normalization of the orthogonal complement before Definition 6.7.2 (pp. 104–106), replace Vol(I_{V,r} ∩ I_{−V,r}) by Vol(I^0_{r,V} ∩ I^0_{r,−V}). Lemma 8.5.3 and the Main Theorem then hold as stated.`. I^0 ∩ ᵗI^0 (diagonal mod p^r) contains I ∩ ᵗI (≡ 1 mod p^r) with index ∏_w #T_w(𝒪_w/p^r), which is divisible by p for r ≥ 2; so 'value in R·Q[π′, χ]' with the §6.7 normalisation requires an extra divisibility that is not addressed. Moreover, by Lemma 8.4.9 the pairing of the trace-compatible anti-ordinary vectors grows like Vol(I^0 ∩ ᵗI^0), so a period defined with Vol(I ∩ ᵗI) would depend on r, contradicting 'these periods are independent of r ≫ 0 … (see also Lemma 8.4.9)' (p. 105) — which suggests §6.7 intends I^0. Defence: with I^0 in §6.7 the claims are indeed immediate from the definitions. Independent check: The inconsistency is real (checked on pp. 104, 106, 137–139, 145). §6.7 normalizes the periods by Vol(I_{V,r} ∩ I_{−V,r}): five occurrences, in Lemmas 6.7.1 and 6.7.6 and before Definition 6.7.2, all without superscript 0 (zoomed image of p. 104). Everything downstream uses I^0: Remark 4.6.2, Lemma 8.4.9, Lemma 8.5.3, Proposition 9.1.7 and the Main Theorem's Ω_{π′,χ} = ⟨φ,φ^♭_χ⟩_χ/(Vol(I^0_{r^1,V} ∩ I^0_{r^1,−V})·Q[π′,χ]). The index [I^0 ∩ ᵗI^0 : I ∩ ᵗI] = ∏_w #T_w(O_w/p^r) is divisible by p for r ≥ 2. So, taken literally, for lattice vectors the ratio in Lemma 8.5.3 lies in (∏#T_w(O_w/p^r))^{-1}·R·Q[π′,χ], not in R·Q[π′,χ]. Likewise Ω is neither p-integral nor r^1-independent, contrary to the last sentence of Main Theorem 9.2.2. With I^0 in §6.7, everything is consistent. The paper's own claim (p. 105) that the periods 'are independent of r ≫ 0 … (see also Lemma 8.4.9)' only holds with the I^0 normalization of Lemma 8.4.9. So the fault is a notational slip in §6.7 (a dropped superscript 0), not a missing argument in Lemma 8.5.3, whose 'consequences of the definition' are then immediate. Versions: same in v4 (§6.7 with Vol(I_{V,r} ∩ I_{−V,r}); I^0 elsewhere). - **Error** at §2.5, p. 20, last lines before (14), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 18–19. The source says `"and M̄_{K_r/F} (resp. M̄_{K_r,L/F}) is the normalization of M^tor_{K/F} (resp. M^tor_{K,L/F}) in M_{K_r/F} (resp. M_{K_r,L}/F)."`; it should be `M̄_{K_r/F} is an open subscheme of that normalization (dense, containing M_{K_r/F}), in general a proper one: the normalization is finite over M^tor_{K/F}, whereas M̄_{K_r/F} is not.`. The normalization of M^tor_{K/F} in M_{K_r/F} is finite over M^tor_{K/F}. The paper itself says M̄_{K_r} is étale and quasi-finite but not finite over M^tor_K, and this already holds in characteristic 0: over a boundary point, 𝒜^∨ has a non-trivial torus part and 𝒜^∨[p^r] has fewer geometric points than over M_K, so there are fewer injections L⁺ ⊗ μ_{p^r} ↪ 𝒜^∨[p^r]. Since M̄_{K_r/F} is normal (étale over a smooth scheme) and quasi-finite over M^tor_{K/F}, Zariski's main theorem makes it an open subscheme of the normalization, missing the boundary points where the level structure does not extend. Modular-curve case: over X(1) with the Tate curve at ∞, μ_p ↪ E[p] has p² − 1 geometric choices generically but only p − 1 over the cusp (those onto the canonical μ_p); the normalization X_μ(p) has in addition the (p − 1) cusps ramified of index p, which are not in M̄. Defence: later sections use M̄_{K_r} as defined (sections of ω_{r,κ} over M̄_{K_r}, §2.6.6), not the normalization, and the Koecher principle (20) compares with sections over M_{K_r}; the claim is not used in an essential way, though the definition of cusp forms S_κ(K_r, ψ; R) via D_{∞,r} = M̄_{K_r} − M_{K_r} only imposes vanishing at the boundary present in M̄_{K_r}. Independent check: The quote on p. 20 is accurate; the printed text has 'M_{K_r,L/F}'. The same paragraph says that M̄_{K_r} (resp. M̄_{K_r,L}) is étale and quasi-finite but not finite over M^tor_K. A normalization of the excellent scheme M^tor_{K/F} in M_{K_r/F} is finite over it. So the two statements are incompatible unless M̄_{K_r/F} is finite. It is not finite, even over F. At a boundary point, 𝒜^∨ has a torus part, so 𝒜^∨[p^r] has fewer geometric points. Injections L^+⊗μ_{p^r} ↪ 𝒜^∨[p^r] that do not land in the toric part do not specialise. In the modular-curve analogue, μ_p ↪ E[p] over the Tate curve has p² − 1 generic choices but only p − 1 at the cusp, and the normalization has p − 1 further cusps with ramification index p. M̄_{K_r/F} is normal, quasi-finite and separated over M^tor_{K/F}, and it contains M_{K_r/F} densely (étale maps are open). By Zariski's main theorem it is a dense open subscheme of the normalization, in general a proper one. The paper works with M̄_{K_r} as defined, so the sentence itself carries no weight. A caveat not decided here: the cusp forms S_κ(K_r,ψ;R) = H⁰(M̄_{K_r}, ω(−D_{∞,r})) only require vanishing at the boundary strata present in M̄_{K_r}. §2.6.7's identification of them with classical cusp forms of level K_r therefore cannot rest on this sentence.
