- **Gap** at §9, proof of Lemma 9.0.1, p. 140, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 130. The source says `The property of being ordinary is preserved under complex conjugation, and by twist by a power of the similitude character. On the other hand, duality exchanges ordinary with anti-ordinary representations, by Lemma 8.3.6. Since π is essentially unitary, it follows that it is both ordinary and anti-ordinary.`; it should be `A proof that ordinarity (with the paper's weight normalisations) is preserved under π ↦ π̄, or a different argument.`. Complex conjugation replaces the U_{w,j}-eigenvalues by their complex conjugates, and for a fixed embedding incl_p: Q̄ → Q̄_p complex conjugation need not preserve p-adic absolute values (e.g. for n = 1 a CM Hecke character of infinity type z^k with p split: one of χ(ϖ_w), χ(ϖ_w)‾ is a p-adic unit and the other is not). Since π̄ ≅ π^∨ ⊗ (similitude twist) by essential unitarity, the first sentence is essentially equivalent to the conclusion; the weight normalisations (κ_norm for π̄ versus π) are not discussed. Defence: the lemma is presented as reassurance and is not used — §9 assumes anti-ordinarity and the Main Theorem assumes ordinarity separately. The source says `(179): '= D(χ) · L_{φ⊗φ^♭}(res_3 D(κ, m, χ_0) E^holo_{χ_0,ψρ^υ}(m))'; Prop. 9.1.7: '= D(χ) · 1/(Vol(I^0_{r,V})Vol(I^0_{r,−V})) I(φ′, φ′^♭, D(κ, m, χ_0) f^holo(χ_u, ψρ^υ), m)' with 'π′ ∈ S(K_{r^1}, κ^1, π), for some r^1 and κ^1'`; it should be `As in (113): D(κ, m, χ_u) E^holo_{χ_u,ψρ^υ}(m); and the volumes at level r^1 (as in Corollary 9.2.1), with κ the weight of π′ (κ^1).`. (113) — of which (179) is an instance — reads D(κ, m, χ_u) E^holo_{χ_u,c}(m); §8.0 uses χ_0 for the algebraic part of χ = ||•||^m χ_0, a different factorisation from χ = ||•||^m χ_u, and the proposition itself mixes χ_0 (operator) with χ_u (section). - **Gap** at §9.1.6, proof of Proposition 9.1.7, p. 143, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 133 (it affects the proof). The source says `Abbreviate [G_3] = G_3(ℚ)Z(ℝ)\G_3(𝔸), dg^χ_2 = χ(det(g_2))^{−1}dg_2. By doubling the formula in Lemma 7.5.3 … = 1/(Vol(I^0_{r,V})Vol(I^0_{r,−V})) ∫_{[G_3]} D(κ, m, χ_0)E^holo_{f(χ_0,ψρ^υ)}((g_1, g_2), m) φ′(g_1)φ′^♭(g_2) ||ν(g_1)^{a(κ)}|| dg_1 dg^χ_2. Comparing this with Equation (179) and the definition of the zeta integral, we obtain the equality.`; it should be `Spell out the comparison: Lemma 7.5.3 has the factor ||ν(g)^{−a(κ)}|| (sign of the exponent flipped here) and is over G(ℚ)Z_G(ℝ)\G(𝔸); the zeta integral I(φ, φ′, f, s) (p. 142) has no ν-factor and is over Z_3(𝔸)G_3(ℚ)\G_3(𝔸). The central characters and the ||ν||^{±a(κ)} twist (π^♭ = π^∨ ⊗ ||ν||^{a(κ)}) have to be reconciled to identify the two integrals.`. The 'comparison' is asserted in one line although the two integrals differ by a character of the centre and by the integration domain. Defence: these are normalisations of the twist by the similitude character, presumably absorbed into the identification of π^♭ with π^∨ ⊗ ||ν||^{a(κ)}; the final formula is unaffected up to such a normalisation. Independent check: Quotation checked on the page image (p. 143). The 'comparison' is a single sentence, but the two integrals visibly differ. (a) The doubled Lemma 7.5.3 carries ||ν(g_1)^{a(κ)}||, with the sign of the exponent opposite to Lemma 7.5.3's ||ν(g)^{−a(κ)}|| (p. 121). (b) It is integrated over G_3(Q)Z(R)\G_3(A), while the zeta integral I(φ,φ′,f,s) (p. 142; (51), p. 45) is over Z_3(A)G_3(Q)\G_3(A), with χ^{-1}(det g_2) and no ν-factor. (c) The proof uses E^holo_{f(χ_0,ψρ^υ)}, while the statement has f^holo(χ_u,ψρ^υ). Matching requires tracking the central characters and the twist π^♭ = π^∨ ⊗ ||ν||^{a(κ)} (141). A quick check of Z(R)-invariance suggests the forms alone require ||ν||^{−a(κ)}, not +a(κ), unless the Eisenstein series compensates. None of this is written. The final formula is presumably right up to such normalizations, so this is a gap in the proof. The volume factor itself is consistent (see sourceIssues E125). Versions: v4 p. 133 same. - **Gap** at §9.2, Main Theorem 9.2.2 (and Corollary 9.2.1), statement, pp. 144–145, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 133–134 ('for any π′ congruent to π') (it affects a stated result). The source says `For any classical χ = ||•||^m χ_u : X_p → R^×, and for any π′ ∈ S(K_{r^1}, κ^1, π) for some r^1, the image of L(Eis, φ ⊗ φ^♭) … equals …`; it should be `'… for any classical χ = ||•||^m χ_u with m ≥ n and any π′ ∈ S(K_{r^1},κ^1,π) with κ^1 sufficiently regular (and satisfying (166)) such that (χ,ψρ^υ) ∈ Y^class_H, i.e. κ^1_σ ∈ C_3(χ_σ) for all σ, with ρ, ρ^υ determined by κ^1 and χ via (95), (97) …'`. The interpolation formula is derived from Proposition 9.1.7, which assumes (χ, ψρ^υ) ∈ Y^class_H and m ≥ n; I_∞(χ, κ^1) (Proposition 4.5.6) and the local computations at p are only available for such pairs. The Main Theorem quantifies over all classical χ and all π′ in the family, with only the preceding sentence 'Let the algebraic characters κ, ρ, ρ^υ determine one another, relative to a given χ, as in (95) and (97)' hinting at the constraint. Defence: 'classical' may be read as 'the pair (χ, κ^1) is classical', i.e. lies in Y^class_H; and the anti-ordinarity is a stated standing assumption of §9 (p. 140). Independent check: Quotation checked on the page images (pp. 144–145). The interpolation formula comes from Proposition 9.1.7 and Corollary 9.1.8, which assume (χ,ψρ^υ) ∈ Y^class_H and m ≥ n. It also relies on Proposition 7.4.15, which needs λ ∈ X(κ,r,R) with κ sufficiently regular, and on Proposition 8.5.1/Lemma 8.5.3 (κ satisfying (166)). 'Classical χ' in the paper means only that χ is the p-adic avatar of an algebraic Hecke character (§5.3.1, p. 83). The sentence before the theorem ('Let … κ, ρ, ρ^υ determine one another, relative to a given χ, as in Inequalities (95) and Equation (97)') arguably imposes κ^1_σ ∈ C_3(χ_σ), i.e. the Y^class_H condition. It does not impose m ≥ n or the regularity of κ^1, and the theorem quantifies over all classical χ and all π′ ∈ S(K_{r^1},κ^1,π). So the stated range exceeds what is proved. Whether the formula holds outside it (e.g. m < n) is not addressed, hence 'gap'. The anti-ordinarity clause of the first reading's correction is unnecessary: it is a stated standing assumption of §9 (p. 140). Versions: v4 pp. 133–134 same ('for any π′ congruent to π'). - **Misprint** at §9.2, Main Theorem 9.2.2 and Corollaries 9.1.8, 9.2.1 (pp. 144–145): meaning of the partial L-function L^S, in arXiv v5; present in v4. The source says `… I_S L_p(m, ord, π′, χ_u) L^S(m + 1/2, π′, χ_u)/P_{π′,χ} …, with S (§8.5, p. 138) 'the set of finite primes, not dividing p, at which K^p is not hyperspecial maximal'`; it should be `L^S(s, π′, χ_u) must be the standard L-function with the Euler factors at v ∈ S, at the places above p and at ∞ removed (the p-part being the modified factor L_p(·, ord, …)).`. In Theorem 4.6.1 the unramified computation produces Euler factors only at places where the test vectors are spherical; at p the local integral is I_p (a ratio of L- and ε-factors times volumes), so the global identity D(χ)·I = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ I_p I_∞ I_S L^S(s + 1/2, π, χ_u) forces L^S to omit the p-factor. With S defined as in §8.5 (excluding primes above p) the notation L^S literally includes the Euler factor at p. Theorem 4.6.1 ('local components at finite places outside S = S_π are unramified') implicitly puts p into S_π. Meaning clear from the construction (Coates–Perrin-Riou shape). - **Gap** at §2.5, p. 20, lines 5–3 from the bottom before (14), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 18. The source says `"The choice of a basis of Z_p(1) naturally identifies M_{K_r/F} (resp. M_{K_r,L}) with M_{I_rK^p/F} (resp. M_{I_rK^p,L/F} = S_{I_rK^p}(G, X_P))"`; it should be `The identification induced by a basis of Z_p(1) (i.e. μ_{p^r} ≅ Z/p^r) is defined over F(μ_{p^r}) (in particular on C-points), not over F. Over F, M_{K_r/F} corresponds to the level group I_r′ ⊂ I_r^0 that acts on L⁻ unipotently and on L⁺ with diagonal ν, rather than to I_r.`. For (A, α) ∈ M_{I_rK^p}, π_1-stability of the I_r-orbit of α_t: L ⊗ Z/p^r ≅ A_t[p^r] means σ∘α_t = α_t∘g_σ with g_σ ∈ I_r, and I_r acts unipotently on L⁺; so α_t(L⁺/p^r) is a subgroup with trivial Galois action on its graded pieces (constant type), while L⁻ carries the cyclotomic character through ν. For M_{K_r}, φ(L⁺ ⊗ μ_{p^r}) is a μ-type subgroup. These moduli problems agree after trivializing μ_{p^r}, which requires μ_{p^r} ⊂ base; μ_p ⊄ F for p odd since p is unramified in F ⊂ 𝒦′. (Compare Y_μ(N) and Y_1(N) over Q.) Defence: all later uses compare classical forms with automorphic forms over C (or over rings containing μ_{p^∞}), where the identification is valid; v1–v3 wrote 'a basis of Z(1)', suggesting the analytic identification over C was meant. 'S_0 = K′ if □ = ∅'). For □ = ∅, Λ_0 is an F-vector space and a Z_(p)-valued pairing on it is meaningless. Defence: for □ = {p}, the case used in all p-adic arguments, the printed text is correct. - **Misprint** at §2.6.5, p. 24, statement of (19) and footnote 2, arXiv v5. The source says `except when F_0 = Q and G^der/Q has an irreducible factor isomorphic to SU(1,1)`; it should be `except when K^+ = Q (K imaginary quadratic) and G^der/Q has an irreducible factor isomorphic to SU(1,1)`. - **Error** at §2.6.9, p. 26, 'Note that t^+_{w,i,j} has the property that t^+_{w,i,j} I_r^0 t^{+,−1}_{w,i,j} ⊂ I_r^0', arXiv v5. The source says `t^+_{w,i,j} I_r^0 t^{+,−1}_{w,i,j} ⊂ I_r^0.`; it should be `t^+ N^+(Z_p) (t^+)^{−1} ⊂ N^+(Z_p) and (t^+)^{−1} N^−(p^rZ_p) t^+ ⊂ N^−(p^rZ_p), with N^+ the unipotent radical of B^+ and N^− that of the opposite Borel (equivalently, I_r t^+ I_r = ⊔_{u∈N^+(Z_p)/t^+N^+(Z_p)(t^+)^{−1}} u t^+ I_r).`. Counterexample: in one GL_{n_i}(O_w)-factor take j ≤ a_{w,i}, j < n_i, and g = 1 + p^r E_{j+1,1} ∈ I_r^0 (the (j+1,1) entry lies in the strictly lower part of the A-block or in the C-block, both ≡ 0 mod p^r for elements of I_r^0; the other components of g are 1 and ν = 1, allowed by (9)). Then t^+ g (t^+)^{−1} = 1 + p^{r−1}E_{j+1,1}, which is not in B^+ mod p^r. Similarly for a_{w,i} < j < n_i with g = 1 + p^rE_{a+1,1}. Conjugation by t^+ divides the entries (k,l) with t_k/t_l = p^{−1} by p, and these are lower-left entries. The inclusion holds only for j = n_i (t^+ central in that factor). Defence: the intended meaning (t^+ is 'positive', contracting N^+ and expanding N^−) is standard and is what the definition of U_{w,i,j} needs; the inclusion is not used in any proof. Independent check: The quote on p. 26 is accurate. I_r^0 = {g ∈ G(Z_p) : g mod p^r ∈ B^+(Z/p^r)} with B^+ as in (14): A upper-triangular, D lower-triangular, C ≡ 0. Conjugation by t = t^+_{w,i,j} multiplies the (k,l) entry by t_k/t_l. Take j ≤ a, j < n_i, and g = 1 + p^rE_{j+1,1} ∈ I_r^0 in one GL_{n_i}(O_w) factor. Then tgt^{-1} = 1 + p^{r−1}E_{j+1,1}. Its (j+1,1) entry lies in the strictly lower part of A or in C, where elements of I_r^0 must be ≡ 0 mod p^r. So tgt^{-1} ∉ I_r^0. The case a < j < n_i is analogous (entry (a+1,1), or an upper entry of D when a = 0). The reverse inclusion t^{-1}I_r^0t ⊂ I_r^0 also fails: it divides free upper entries by p. What holds is the standard positivity, which is what the definition of U_{w,i,j} (23) needs: t contracts N^+(Z_p) and t^{-1} contracts N^−(p^rZ_p). The printed inclusion is used nowhere. Same in v1 and v4 (p. 23). - **Misprint** at §2.7.2, p. 28, lines 17–18 from the bottom, arXiv v5. The source says `Let g = Lie(G(R))_C, and let g = p^− ⊕ k ⊕ p^+ be the Cartan decomposition for the involution h(√−1): ad h(√−1) acts as ±√−1 on p^±.`; it should be `Ad h(√−1) is the Cartan involution, acting as +1 on k and −1 on p = p^+ ⊕ p^−; p^± are the subspaces of p on which Ad h(z) acts by (z/z̄)^{±1} (equivalently the ±√−1-eigenspaces of the complex structure Ad h(e^{π√−1/4}) on p, or the ±2√−1-eigenspaces of ad(dh(√−1))).`. With h(z) acting by z on V^{−1,0} and z̄ on V^{0,−1} (as for h_σ(z) = diag(z1_r, z̄1_s) in §2.3), Ad h(i) acts on Hom(V^{0,−1}, V^{−1,0}) by i·(−i)^{−1} = −1 and on Hom(V^{−1,0}, V^{0,−1}) also by −1. The text itself calls h(√−1) an involution, which is incompatible with eigenvalues ±√−1. Harmless: p^± are standard and only the characterisation 'holomorphic iff p^− ∗ f = 0' is used. - **Misprint** at §2.8, p. 29, lines 3–4, arXiv v5. The source says `Let k > 0 be so large that the kth-power of the Hasse invariant has a lift to a section E ∈ M_{det^k}(K; Z_p).`; it should be `E ∈ M_{det^{k(p−1)}}(K; Z_p)`. The Hasse invariant is a section of det(ω)^{⊗(p−1)} mod p (cf. [Lan18, §6.3.1]), so its k-th power has weight det^{k(p−1)}. Defence: only the existence of some lift E of a power of the Hasse invariant matters for defining S_m = M^tor_{K,L}[1/E] mod p^m, so the weight label is immaterial. - **Misprint** at §2.9.2, p. 30, display, arXiv v5. The source says `these actions give an action of G(A_f^p) on lim_{←K^p} V(K^p, R) and lim_{←K^p} V_κ(K^p, ψ, R)`; it should be `lim_{→K^p} V(K^p, R) and lim_{→K^p} V_κ(K^p, ψ, R) (direct limits over shrinking K^p, as in §2.6.7)`. For K′^p ⊂ K^p the pullback V(K^p, R) → V(K′^p, R) is injective and the natural object carrying a G(A_f^p)-action is the union (direct limit); the next sentence ('The submodules fixed by K^p are just the p-adic modular forms ... of level K^p') makes sense for the direct limit. §2.6.7 uses lim_→ for the classical analogue. - **Misprint** at §2.9.4, p. 32, the two displayed formulas for f_{p-adic} and t·f_{p-adic}, arXiv v5. The source says `f_{p-adic}(A, φ) = lim_{←m} f(A_m, φ_{m,m,r}, (Lie(φ_{m,m,r})^∨, id)) ... Lie(φ) was defined only for φ ∈ T_{n,m}(S) with n ≥ m; for m > r, Lie of φ_{m,m,r} : L^+ ⊗ μ_{p^r} → A^∨[p^r]° over a Z/p^m-scheme is L^+ ⊗ O_S[p^r] → Lie A^∨, not an isomorphism, so (Lie(φ_{m,m,r})^∨, id) is not a point of E. - **Gap** at §2.9.4, p. 32, justification of injectivity of (28), arXiv v5. The source says `– these are injective because, as already noted, S_1 is dense in the special fiber of M^tor_{K,L} –`; it should be `Injectivity of M_κ(K_r, ψ; R) → V_{κ_p}(K^p, ψ, R) needs (for R flat over Z_p): every connected component of \overline{M}_{K_r,L/R} meets the special fibre, plus p-adic separatedness of H^0. Density of the ordinary locus in the special fibre of M^tor_{K,L} gives this at level K, not directly at level K_r.`. The special fibre of \overline{M}_{K_r} already lies over the ordinary locus (a closed immersion L^+ ⊗ μ_{p^r} ↪ A^∨[p^r] in characteristic p forces ordinarity under Hypothesis 2.2.1), and \overline{M}_{K_r} is only quasi-finite over M^tor_K, so the density of S_1 in the special fibre of M^tor_{K,L} does not by itself rule out components of the generic fibre of \overline{M}_{K_r,L} whose closure misses the special fibre (sections supported there would have f_{p-adic} = 0). Defence: the needed fact is standard in Hida's theory (e.g. via the q-expansion principle or irreducibility of Igusa towers, [Hid04, Ch. 8], [Lan18]), and the statement is true; only the justification is too brief. - **Misprint** at §1.4.3, p. 13, lines 1–3 after Hypotheses 1.4.4, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 12. The source says `"let Z ⊂ Z_G(A) be any closed subgroup such that Z_G(A)/Z is compact; for example, one can take Z to be the group of real points of the maximal F-split subgroup of Z_G"`; it should be `"such that Z · Z_G(F)\Z_G(A) is compact".`. For G = GL_1 over Q, Z_G(A)/Z = A^×/R^× (or A^×/R_{>0}) is not compact, since Q^× is an infinite discrete subgroup; the paper's own example Z = A(F ⊗ R) (A the maximal F-split central torus) satisfies the corrected condition (Z_G/A is F-anisotropic and F^×F_∞^×\A_F^× is compact) but not the printed one. The pairing (3) is over Z·G(F)\G(A), so the corrected condition is what is used. Defence: obvious slip; intended meaning clear. - **Misprint** at §2.9.6, (32), p. 33, arXiv v5. The source says `V^{ord,cusp}_{κ_p}(K^p, ψ, R) = S^ord_κ(K_r, ψ; R) ... if κ_{σ,i,a_{σ,i}} + κ_{σc,i,b_{σ,i}} ≫ n_ir_i ∀σ ∈ Σ_K, 1 ≤ i ≤ m.`; it should be `if κ_{σ,i,b_{σ,i}} + κ_{σc,i,a_{σ,i}} ≫ 0 (classical weight κ, κ_{σ,i} ∈ Z^{b_{σ,i}}); equivalently (κ_p)_{σ,i,a_{σ,i}} + (κ_p)_{σc,i,b_{σ,i}} ≫ 0`. For the classical weight, κ_{σ,i} has length b_{σ,i} and κ_{σc,i} has length b_{σc,i} = a_{σ,i}, so κ_{σ,i,a_{σ,i}} and κ_{σc,i,b_{σ,i}} are out of range whenever a_{σ,i} > b_{σ,i} (resp. b_{σ,i} > a_{σ,i}). The printed indices are those of the p-adic weight (§2.9.1), inherited from v1–v3 where the theorem was stated as V^{ord,cusp}_κ = S^ord_κ with a single κ; since (κ_p)_{τ,i} = κ_{τc,i}, the printed expression evaluated on κ_p is exactly κ_{σc,i,a_{σ,i}} + κ_{σ,i,b_{σ,i}}, the sum of the smallest entries of κ_{σ,i} and κ_{σc,i}. The symbol r_i in 'n_ir_i' is not defined in the paper (the bound is vague anyway: '≫'; v1 had '≫ 0'). - **Error** at §2.9.6, pp. 33–34, arXiv v5. The source says `Let R be as in Equation (32) and let O^+ denote the integral closure of Z_(p) in R. The fraction field Frac(O^+) of O^+ is a number field over which S_κ(K_r, ψ; R) ⊗ Q has a rational model`; it should be `Let O^+ be the localisation at the prime above p (determined by incl_p) of the ring of integers of a number field E_0 ⊂ Frac(R) over which S_κ(K_r, ψ; ·) has a rational model (e.g. E_0 containing K′ and the values of ψ); equivalently, the integral closure of Z_(p) in E_0.`. R is a finite O′[ψ]-domain, e.g. R = Z_p or O′. The integral closure of Z_(p) in Z_p is Z_p ∩ \overline{Q}, whose fraction field Q_p ∩ \overline{Q} has infinite degree over Q (it contains √(1 + p^2 k) for all integers k, p odd, hence infinitely many quadratic fields). So Frac(O^+) is never a number field. Defence: any sufficiently large number field works for the definition of 'ordinary complex cusp forms relative to ι' that follows, and O^+ is not used elsewhere in the paper. Independent check: The quote on pp. 33–34 is accurate. R is a finite O′- or O′[ψ]-domain, where O′ is the ring of integers of the finite extension L′ of Q_p (p. 30). So R ⊃ Z_p. The integral closure of Z_(p) in R contains Z_p ∩ Q̄. For odd p, √(1 + p²k) ∈ Z_p for every integer k, and these generate infinitely many quadratic fields. So Frac(O^+) ⊇ Q_p ∩ Q̄ has infinite degree over Q and is never a number field. The intended object is the p-integers of a suitable number field E_0 carrying the rational model. O^+ is used only in this paragraph, to define 'ordinary complex cusp forms relative to ι'. Present in v1–v4 (v4 p. 30). - **Gap** at §2.10.2, p. 35, lines 1–5, arXiv v5 (it affects a stated result). The source says `Let Δ ⊂ T_H(Z_p) be the torsion subgroup. Since p is unramified in K by hypothesis, (12) induces an identification Δ ≅ ∏_{w|p} ∏_{i=1}^m (k_w^×)^{a_{w,i}} ... In particular, Δ has order prime-to-p`; it should be `Add 'p odd' to the standing hypotheses of §1.4.1, or restrict to p > 2 here.`. The standing hypotheses (§1.4.1: p unramified in K, every place of K^+ above p split in K) allow p = 2 (e.g. K = Q(√−7)); then O_w^× ⊃ {±1} and for O_w = Z_2 the torsion of O_w^× is {±1} while k_w^× = 1, so the displayed isomorphism fails and |Δ| is a power of 2, and the decomposition into ω-isotypic pieces over O′ is not available. Defence: p odd is presumably implicit through the cited results of Hida ([Hid02], [Hid04]) and elsewhere in the paper, and all later statements are about p odd in practice; but it is never stated. Independent check: The quote on p. 35 is accurate. The only hypotheses on p (§1.4.1, p. 11) are 'unramified in K, every place of K^+ above p split in K'. p odd is never stated; I searched the text layer. For p = 2, K = Q(√−7) satisfies them (2 splits, K^+ = Q). Then O_w = Z_2, the torsion of O_w^× is {±1} while k_w^× = 1, so the displayed Δ ≅ ∏(k_w^×)^{a_{w,i}} fails. Δ is then a nontrivial 2-group, so it does not have order prime to p. The decomposition of S^ord over O′ into ω-isotypic parts, which needs |Δ| ∈ O′^×, is unavailable. For p odd and unramified the statement is correct: the torsion is the Teichmüller lift of k_w^×. p odd is implicitly needed elsewhere too, e.g. the 1/2 in V_d ⊕ V^d and in (58), but the paper never says so. Present in v1–v4 (v4 p. 31). - **Misprint** at §2.10.2, (34), p. 35, arXiv v5. The source says `μ ↦ μ(κψ) : ... → S^ord_κ(K_r, ωω_κψ, R[ψ]) ... and ω_κ ∈ Δ̂ is κ|_Δ.`; it should be `S^ord_{κ^cl}(K_r, ωω_κ^{−1}ψ, R[ψ]) with κ the p-adic weight of §2.9.1, ω_κ = κ|_Δ and κ^cl the classical weight with (κ^cl)_p = κ; equivalently keep ωω_κψ but define ω_κ as the restriction of the classical weight to Δ via t ↦ (1, t) ∈ T_{H_0}, which is κ_p^{−1}|_Δ.`. By §2.9.4, t·f_{p-adic} = ψ(t)κ_p(t)f_{p-adic} for f ∈ M_κ(K_r, ψ; R); so a classical form of nebentypus χ has Δ acting on its p-adic avatar by χ|_Δ·κ_p|_Δ. If μ lies in the ω-isotypic piece (Δ acting by ω through μ(t·f) = t·μ(f)), then μ(κψ) has Δ-character ω, whence χ|_Δ = ω·(κ_p|_Δ)^{−1} = ωω_κ^{−1}. The printed ωω_κψ differs by ω_κ^2. Case for the defence: the sign depends on which of the two dual characters (κ on T_{H_0} versus κ_p on T_H, related by κ(1, t) = κ_p(t^{−1})) is called κ|_Δ; the paper's text says 'κ as in 2.9.1', which gives the discrepancy. Also S^ord_κ is written with the p-adic weight κ although S_κ requires a classical weight (v1–v3 wrote κ*). This is a cited result of Hida, so only the transcription is at stake. In v5 no isomorphisms are described in §§3.1–3.2 (res_2, res_4 are only 'maps'), and 'similitude components' are not defined (v1–v3 had §2.11 'Similitude components' and §3.1.5). - **Gap** at Proposition 3.2.5(ii), proof, p. 41, arXiv v5. The source says `Note that V^ord_{κ_p}((G, X); K^p, R) is the R-dual to a finite rank module over an appropriate Iwasawa algebra, by Hida theory; thus f belongs to a finite rank R module. Point (ii) follows from the Zariski density of the ordinary locus in the integral model of S(G, X) [Wed99], provided we know there are enough CM points in the ordinary locus. But every point on the ordinary locus over a finite field lifts ... to the generic fiber (see for example [Moo04, Proposition 2.3.12]).`; it should be `A complete argument: every F̄_p-point of the ordinary locus is the reduction of an ordinary CM point (Serre–Tate canonical lift) and the Igusa tower over it is covered by the Igusa towers (46) of CM pairs and their prime-to-p Hecke translates; hence f mod p vanishes at all F̄_p-points of the reduced Igusa varieties T_{n,1}, so f ≡ 0 mod p; since T_{n,m} is flat over Z/p^m and the value of p·g at a canonical lift depends only on g mod p, induction on m gives f ≡ 0 mod p^m for all m (for R flat over Z_p; general R by the same dévissage), so f = 0.`. The printed proof invokes the density of the ordinary locus in the integral model, which is irrelevant for a p-adic form (a function on the formal Igusa tower over the ordinary locus), and never explains how vanishing at the (discrete) set of CM points forces a function on a formal scheme to vanish; the finite-rank remark is not used. Also the Igusa tower of S(J′_0, h_0) must meet every point of each fibre of the Igusa tower, which needs the CM pairs to be taken with all their Hecke translates. Defence: the conclusion is true and the ingredients cited (canonical lifts) suffice once the p-adic dévissage is added; ordinarity of f is not needed for this route. - **Error** at §4.1.4, p. 45, lines 5–12 (the paragraph after the definition of I(φ, φ^♭, f, s)), in arXiv v5. The source says `“Moreover, it follows from the unfolding in [GPSR87] that, for any pair π, π′ of automorphic representations of G_1, the map (φ, φ′) ↦ I(φ, φ′, f, s) defines a G_1(𝔸)-invariant pairing between π and π′. The multiplicity one hypothesis 7.3.3 implies that the space of such pairings is at most one-dimensional, and is exactly one-dimensional provided π′ = π^∨ (upon restriction to U(V). Thus: If ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ = 0 then I(φ, φ^♭, f, s) = 0 for all s.”`; it should be `For fixed f the map (φ, φ′) ↦ I(φ, φ′, f, s) is not G_1(𝔸)-invariant. Only the trilinear form in (f, φ, φ′) is invariant, and f transforms by the diagonal translation. What is true, using Hypothesis 7.3.3: after unfolding, I depends on (φ, φ′) only through the L² pairings ⟨π(u)φ, φ′⟩, so I ≡ 0 unless π′ ≅ π^∨ (on U(V)). The implication ‘⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ = 0 ⇒ I(φ, φ^♭, f, s) = 0’ is false in general.`. By the unfolding (p. 45), I(π(h)φ, π′(h)φ′, f, s) = ∫ f((huh^{-1}, 1))⟨π(u)φ, φ′⟩ du, which differs from I(φ, φ′, f, s) unless f((huh^{-1},1)) = f((u,1)). Concretely, I = c·∏_v Z_v, where Z_v(φ_v, φ^♭_v, f_v) = ⟨π_v(F_v)φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩ with F_v(u) = f_v((u,1)). Take v ∈ S_π (or v = ∞), where the statement allows arbitrary f_v and φ_v. Sections supported in the open cell P_v(U_{1,v} × 1) give arbitrary F_v ∈ C_c^∞(U_{1,v}), for instance F_v = char(g_0K′). Then one can choose φ_v, φ^♭_v with ⟨φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩ = 0 but ⟨π_v(F_v)φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩ ≠ 0, which gives ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ = 0 while I ≠ 0 for Re(s) ≫ 0. Uniqueness of invariant pairings π × π′ → ℂ comes from Schur's lemma, not from multiplicity one. Hypothesis 7.3.3 (π′ occurs with multiplicity one in the cuspidal spectrum) is what makes the L² pairing between π and π′ vanish unless π′ is the realisation of π^∨. Defence: the paper immediately assumes ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ ≠ 0 and uses only (51), which is correct under that assumption. For the specific ramified sections of §4.2.2 one does have Z_v = vol(𝒰_v)⟨φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩. Independent check: The quote on p. 45 is accurate. Replace φ, φ′ by π(h)φ, π′(h)φ′ and change variables (g_1,g_2) ↦ (g_1,g_2)(h,h)^{-1}. This moves (h,h) onto f by right translation, and f is not right-invariant. Equivalently, after unfolding, I(π(h)φ, π(h)φ^♭) = ∫ f((huh^{-1},1))⟨π(u)φ,φ^♭⟩du. Here (h,h) ∈ P, since it stabilises V^d, so f((huh^{-1},1)) = χ(det h)f((u,1)(h,h)^{-1}), which is not f((u,1)) in general. So for fixed f the map is not G_1(A)-invariant. For factorizable data, I = c∏_v⟨π_v(F_v)φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩ with F_v(u) = f_v((u,1)). u ↦ P(u,1) is an open embedding (the paper cites [HLS06] for openness; injectivity holds because (u,1) ∈ P forces u = 1). So at v ∈ S_π or at ∞, F_v can be any function in C_c^∞. Wherever π_v has dimension > 1, one can take ⟨φ_v,φ^♭_v⟩ = 0 and ⟨π_v(F_v)φ_v,φ^♭_v⟩ ≠ 0. That gives ⟨φ,φ^♭⟩ = 0 but I ≠ 0 for Re s ≫ 0, so the displayed implication is false. Uniqueness of invariant pairings on irreducible π × π′ is Schur's lemma, not Hypothesis 7.3.3. The paper then assumes ⟨φ,φ^♭⟩ ≠ 0, and (51), Theorem 4.6.1 and the rest do not use the implication. Same argument in v4 (p. 40); absent in v1. - **Gap** at §1.4.3, p. 13, formulas (4)–(6), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 12–13. The source says `"Assume moreover that we are given non-degenerate pairings of G(F_v)-spaces ⟨,⟩_{π_v}: π_v ⊗ π_v^∨ → C for all v. Then there is a constant C = C(dg, fac_π, fac_{π^∨}, ∏_v⟨,⟩_{π_v}) such that … ⟨φ, φ^∨⟩_Z = C(…) ∏_v ⟨φ_v, φ_v^∨⟩_{π_v}."`; it should be `Add the hypothesis that for almost all v the local pairings satisfy ⟨φ_v^0, φ_v^{∨,0}⟩_{π_v} = 1 for the distinguished vectors used to form the restricted tensor products ⊗′π_v, ⊗′π_v^∨ (implicit in fac_π, fac_{π^∨}); only then is ∏_v ⟨φ_v, φ_v^∨⟩_{π_v} a finite product and (6) meaningful.`. For factorizable φ = ⊗φ_v, φ_v = φ_v^0 for almost all v; with arbitrary non-degenerate local pairings the factors ⟨φ_v^0, φ_v^{∨,0}⟩ are arbitrary non-zero numbers and the infinite product need not converge. With the normalization, existence of C follows from Schur's lemma (Hom_{G(A)}(π ⊗ π^∨, C) is one-dimensional). Defence: the standard local pairing (7) with spherical vectors normalized by f(1) = 1 satisfies the normalization automatically (vol K_v = 1), and this is what the paper uses later. - **Misprint** at Remark 4.1.6, pp. 45–46 (last two sentences of p. 45 and first sentence of p. 46), in arXiv v5; the remark is absent in v4. The source says `“Thus for φ_1 ∈ π, φ_2 ∈ π⊗χ^{-1}∘det we define ⟨φ_1, φ_2⟩_χ to be the L_2 pairing of φ_1 with φ_2 ⊗ χ∘det.” and “… integral with respect to a structure native to the space π ⊗ π ⊗ χ^{-1}∘det”`; it should be `“φ_2 ∈ π^♭ ⊗ χ^{-1}∘det” and “π ⊗ π^♭ ⊗ χ^{-1}∘det”.`. The remark defines φ^♭_χ := φ^♭ ⊗ χ^{-1}∘det ∈ π^♭ ⊗ χ^{-1}∘det and concludes ⟨φ, φ^♭_χ⟩_χ = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩. The pairing must therefore be defined on π × (π^♭ ⊗ χ^{-1}∘det), and φ ⊗ φ^♭_χ lies in π ⊗ π^♭ ⊗ χ^{-1}∘det. The printed π in place of π^♭ makes the L² pairing of φ_1 ∈ π with φ_2 ⊗ χ∘det ∈ π vanish identically. - **Error** at §4.2.1, pp. 46–47, the displayed identity “d_{n,v}(s, χ_v) I_v(φ_v, φ′_v, f_v, s) = L_v(s + 1/2, π_v, χ_v)” with (53), in arXiv v5 (it affects a stated result). The source says `“In either case, we have d_{n,v}(s, χ_v) I_v(φ_v, φ′_v, f_v, s) = L_v(s + 1/2, π_v, χ_v), where d_{n,v}(s, χ_v) = d_{n,v}(s) = ∏_{r=0}^{n−1} L_v(2s + n − r, χ_v|_{𝒦^+} η_v^r)” and “L_v(s, π_v, χ_v) = L_v(s, BC(π_v) ⊗ χ_v∘det)”`; it should be `d_{n,v}(s, χ_v^{-1}) I_v(φ_v, φ′_v, f_v, s) = L_v(s+½, π_v, χ_v^{-1}), with L_v(s, π_v, χ) = L_v(s, BC(π_v) ⊗ χ∘det). Alternatively, keep the printed identity and replace χ by χ^{-1} in the definition of I(χ,s) (inducing from χ^{-1}(det∘Δ(·))δ_P^{-s/n}|ν|^{sn/2}, with the paper's δ_P = |det∘Δ|^n). The first reading's alternative 'χ^{-1}(det∘Δ)δ_P^{s/n}' is right only if δ_P means the true modulus character |det∘Δ|^{-n}. With the paper's δ_P it also flips s ↦ −s.`. Right versus left action. Under the right action p acts on V^d by v ↦ vp, the inverse of the left action g·v := vg^{-1}. So χ(det Δ(p))|det Δ(p)|^{-s} = χ^{-1}(det Δ_left(p))|det Δ_left(p)|^{s}, and the paper's I(χ, s) is the left-action induced representation for χ^{-1} used in [GPSR87], [Li92], [HKS96]; the cited computations then give L(s+½, π, χ^{-1})/d(s, χ^{-1}). Direct check for n = 1 at a split unramified v: U(1)(𝒦_v^+) ≅ 𝒦_w^× via the action on V_w, and π_v = β. In (V_d, V^d)-coordinates (u, 1) = ((u+1)/2, (u−1)/2; (u−1)/2, (u+1)/2). The spherical section of Ind(ψ_{w,s}) takes value χ_w(d)χ_{w̄}^{-1}(a)|a/d|^{s+1/2} at a matrix with bottom row (γ, δ), where |d| = max(|γ|, |δ|) and ad = det. Hence f((u,1)) = χ_{w̄}^{-1}(u)|u|^{s+1/2} for |u| ≤ 1 and χ_w(u)|u|^{-s-1/2} for |u| ≥ 1, and ∫ f((u,1))β(u) d^×u = L(s+½, βχ_{w̄}^{-1}) L(s+½, β^{-1}χ_w^{-1}) / L(2s+1, (χ_wχ_{w̄})^{-1}). Equivalently, with Φ = char M_{1×2}(O_w) in (55), f^Φ(1) = L(2s+1, (χ_wχ_{w̄})^{-1}), and the substitution z_1 = xu, z_2 = x factors ∫ f^Φ((u,1))β(u) d^×u into these two Tate integrals. The printed formula predicts L(s+½, β^{±1}χ_w)L(s+½, β^{∓1}χ_{w̄}) / L(2s+1, χ_wχ_{w̄}), which is different for generic unramified χ_v. The corrected characters are exactly those in the p-adic factor of Theorem 4.3.10, L(s+½, π_b ⊗ χ_{2,w}) = L(s+½, π_b ⊗ χ_{w̄}^{-1}) and L(s+½, π̃_a ⊗ χ_{1,w}^{-1}) = L(s+½, π̃_a ⊗ χ_w^{-1}), so the p-adic computation agrees with the corrected unramified formula and the printed one is the odd one out. Defence: the identity is quoted from sources that use left actions, and the discrepancy is the relabelling χ ↦ χ^{-1} (complex conjugation for unitary χ), under which the construction is unchanged in substance. Independent check: The quotes on pp. 46–47 are accurate. I checked independently at n = 1, v = ww̄ split and unramified. I(χ,s) (§4.1.2) with Δ(p) = the V^d-block D restricts on the w-component to Ind(ψ_{w,s}): the w̄-part of Δ(p) is ᵗA^{-1}, so ψ_{w,s} = χ_w(D)χ_{w̄}^{-1}(A)|A/D|^s, and the normalised f(pg) = ψ δ^{1/2}f(g) with δ^{1/2} = |A/D|^{1/2}. This agrees with (55). In polarization coordinates (§4.1.1: (a,b) ↦ (a+b, b−a)), (u,1) = ½[[u+1, u−1],[u−1, u+1]]. So the spherical f with f(1) = 1 gives f((u,1)) = χ_{w̄}^{-1}(u)|u|^{s+1/2} for |u| ≤ 1 and χ_w(u)|u|^{-s-1/2} for |u| ≥ 1. With π_v = β, (51) gives I_v = Σ_{k≥0}X^k + Σ_{k≥1}Y^k, where X = χ_{w̄}^{-1}β(ϖ)q^{-s-1/2} and Y = (χ_wβ)^{-1}(ϖ)q^{-s-1/2}. This sums to (1−XY)/((1−X)(1−Y)) = L(s+½, βχ_{w̄}^{-1})L(s+½, β^{-1}χ_w^{-1})/L(2s+1, (χ_wχ_{w̄})^{-1}). The printed formula predicts denominator d_{1,v}(s,χ_v) = L(2s+1, χ_wχ_{w̄}) and numerator L(s+½, β^{±1}χ_w)L(s+½, β^{∓1}χ_{w̄}). These agree with the computation only when χ_wχ_{w̄}(ϖ) = 1, i.e. χ|_{K^+} is trivial at v, whatever identification of U(1) or BC is used. So the identity holds with χ_v^{-1}. The cause is the right action: the paper's I(χ,s) is the left-action I(s, χ^{-1}) of [Li92]/[GPSR87]. The p-adic factors of Theorem 4.3.10 (L(s+½, π_b ⊗ χ_{w̄}^{-1}), L(s+½, π̃_a ⊗ χ_w^{-1})) match the corrected form. This propagates to the statement of Theorem 4.6.1 (D(χ), L^S(s+½, π, χ_u)), up to the relabelling χ ↦ χ^{-1} = χ̄. Identical in v4 (p. 41) and v1 (p. 39). - **Gap** at Lemma 4.2.3 and its proof, §4.2.2, p. 48, first display of the proof (“for g ∈ U_{1,v} × 1_n, f^-_{L_v}(g) = δ_{−1_n·𝒰_v×1_n}(g)”), in arXiv v5 (it affects a stated result). The source says `“The support of f^-_{L_v} in U_{1,v} × 1_n is −1_n·𝒰_v × 1_n, and for g ∈ U_{1,v} × 1_n, f^-_{L_v}(g) = δ_{−1_n·𝒰_v×1_n}(g) … I_v(φ_v, φ′_v, f_v, χ) = volume(𝒰_v).”`; it should be `Add to the conditions on L_v in §4.2.2 that χ_v(det(1_n − x)) = 1 for all x ∈ L_v, which is possible by shrinking L_v. Fix w := (−1_n, 1_n), or normalise f_{L_v} so that f^-_{L_v}(1) = 1. Then f^-_{L_v}|_{U_{1,v}×1_n} is the characteristic function of −1_n·𝒰_v × 1_n and I_v = vol(𝒰_v).`. In (V_d, V^d)-coordinates (u, 1) = p^-·n(X), with p^- block lower triangular with upper-left block (u+1)/2 and X = (u+1)^{-1}(u−1), the Cayley transform. So (−u, 1) = (−1_n, 1_n)(u, 1) = (wp^-w^{-1})·w·n(X), with w = (−1_n, 1_n) and Δ(wp^-w^{-1}) = (u+1)/2 = (1_n − X)^{-1}. Hence f^-_{L_v}((u,1)) = f_{L_v}((−u,1)) = χ_v(det(1_n − X))^{-1}·|det(1_n − X)|^{s+n/2}·δ_{L_v}(X) = χ_v(det(1_n − X))^{-1}δ_{L_v}(X). The paper's two conditions on L_v (𝔘_v ⊇ N(L_v) and P_vwN(L_v) ⊆ P_v(−1_n K_v × 1_n)) do not make χ_v∘det trivial on 1 − L_v. If χ_v is ramified, I_v = ∫_{−𝒰_v} χ_v^{-1}(det(1 − X(u))) du can differ from vol(𝒰_v) and can even vanish. The paper never fixes w: it only says P_vw = P_v(−1_n, 1_n). If w = p_0(−1_n, 1_n) with p_0 ≠ 1, a constant character value χ_s(p_0) also appears. Defence: L_v is only asked to be ‘small enough’, so the extra condition changes nothing else, and later arguments only need I_v to be a nonzero constant. Independent check: The quotes on pp. 47–48 are accurate. The mistake is real. In polarization coordinates, (−1_n,1_n) = [[0,−1],[−1,0]] and (−u,1) = p·(−1_n,1_n)·n(X), where X = (1+u)^{-1}(u−1) and p has V^d-block Δ(p) = (1+u)/2 = (1−X)^{-1}. So with w = (−1_n,1_n), f^-_{L_v}((u,1)) = χ_v(det((1+u)/2))|det((1+u)/2)|^{…}δ_{L_v}(X) = χ_v(det(1−X))^{-1}δ_{L_v}(X) on the support. This is the characteristic function of −𝒰_v × 1 only if χ_v∘det is trivial on (1 − L_v)^{-1}. Neither stated condition on L_v (𝔘_v ⊇ N(L_v); P_vwN(L_v) ⊆ P_v(−1_nK_v × 1_n)) gives that, and K_v is chosen from φ_v, not from χ_v. For v ∈ S_χ ⊂ S′, I_v = ∫_{−𝒰_v} χ_v(det((1+u)/2))du, which can differ from vol(𝒰_v) and can vanish. A choice of w other than (−1_n,1_n) (the paper only has P_vw = P_v(−1_n,1_n)) adds a constant χ_s(p_0). Reach, changed from 'the proof': Lemma 4.2.3 itself asserts I_v = volume(𝒰_v) for L_v as constructed, and Theorem 4.6.1 states I_S = ∏_{v∈S}D_v(χ)·volume(𝒰_v). So stated results are false for some admissible L_v when χ_v is ramified. Both are repaired by the extra smallness condition (possible since L_v is at the authors' disposal) together with fixing w, or f^-_{L_v}(1) = 1. Same in v4 (p. 43) and v1 (p. 40). In (V_d, V^d)-coordinates (u, 1) = p^-·n(X), with p^- block lower triangular with upper-left block (u+1)/2 and X = (u+1)^{-1}(u−1), the Cayley transform. So (−u, 1) = (−1_n, 1_n)(u, 1) = (wp^-w^{-1})·w·n(X), with w = (−1_n, 1_n) and Δ(wp^-w^{-1}) = (u+1)/2 = (1_n − X)^{-1}. - **Error** at §4.3.1, (54), p. 50, and the sentence following it (“Then, as explained in [Eis15], f_p ∈ I_p(χ_p, s).”), in arXiv v5. The source says `“f_{p,s}(g) = |ν|_p^{sn/2} ⊗_{w∈Σ_p} f_{w,s}(g_w), g = (ν, (g_w)) ∈ G(ℚ_p). (54) Then, as explained in [Eis15], f_p ∈ I_p(χ_p, s).”`; it should be `(54) lies in I_p(χ_p, s) only after restriction to U_4(ℚ_p). To lie in I_p(χ_p, s) on all of G(ℚ_p), the factor |ν|_p^{sn/2} must be replaced by ∏_{w∈Σ_p} χ_{w̄}(ν)^n, reading the absolute values of §4.1.2 as the idelic module of 𝒦 (which makes the centre act unitarily). If |ν| is read as |ν|_{𝔸_ℚ}, the factor is instead |ν|_p^{sn/2}∏_{w∈Σ_p} χ_{w̄}(ν)^n |ν|_w^{-ns}.`. For p = (ν, ((A_w, B_w; 0, D_w))_w) ∈ P(ℚ_p), the w̄-component of Δ(p) has determinant ν^n/det A_w, because V^d_{w̄} pairs with V_{d,w} and A_w·ᵗD_{w̄} = ν. Hence χ_p(det Δ(p)) = ∏_w χ_w(det D_w) χ_{w̄}^{-1}(det A_w) χ_{w̄}(ν)^n, while |det Δ(p)|_{𝒦_p}^{-s}|ν|_{𝒦_p}^{sn/2} = ∏_w |A_w^{-1}D_w|_w^{-s}. So I_p(χ_p, s) is induced from ∏_w ψ_{w,s}(p_w)·∏_w χ_{w̄}(ν)^n, whereas (54) transforms by |ν|_p^{sn/2}∏_w ψ_{w,s}(p_w). Test at s = 0 with a central element t = (t_w, t_{w̄}): I_p requires the factor χ_w(t_w)^n χ_{w̄}(t_{w̄})^n, and (54) gives χ_w(t_w)^n χ_{w̄}(t_w)^{-n}. These differ as soon as χ_{w̄}(t_w t_{w̄})^n ≠ 1. Defence: §4 only uses f_U, the restriction to U_4 (see (51)), where ν = 1 and (54) is correct. The similitude part matters only for the Eisenstein series on G_4 via [Eis15]. Independent check: The quote on p. 50 is accurate. For p = (ν,(p_w)) ∈ P(Q_p), unitarity of the similitude gives Δ_{w̄}(p) = ν·ᵗA_w^{-1}, since V^d_{w̄} pairs with V_{d,w}. Hence χ_p(det Δ(p)) = ∏_{w∈Σ_p} χ_w(det D_w)χ_{w̄}^{-1}(det A_w)χ_{w̄}(ν)^n. The factor χ_{w̄}(ν)^n cannot come from |ν|_p^{sn/2}. A decisive test at s = 0 with a central z = (z_w, z_{w̄}), ν = z_wz_{w̄}, which does not depend on how |·| is read: I_p needs the factor χ(z)^n = ∏χ_w(z_w)^nχ_{w̄}(z_{w̄})^n, while (54) gives ∏χ_w(z_w)^nχ_{w̄}(z_w)^{-n}. The ratio is ∏_wχ_{w̄}(ν)^n, which is nontrivial in general. So (54) is not in I_p(χ_p,s) on G(Q_p). It is in I_p after restriction to U_4 (ν = 1), which is all §4 uses through f_U and (51). The first reading's correction checks out: with |·| read as the K-idelic module, |det Δ|^{-s}|ν|^{sn/2} = ∏_w|A_w^{-1}D_w|^{-s}. Versions: v1 prints −sn/2 both globally and in (54). v4 prints +sn/2 globally and −sn/2 in (54). v5 prints +sn/2 in both. Recorded as `PAPER-EISCHEN-HARRIS-LI-ETAL-20/E43`; looked for an existing correction in: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: v4 (4.3.1), p. 44 and v1–v3 print |ν|_p^{−sn/2}, also inconsistent. The global I(χ,s) had |ν|^{−sn/2} in v1–v3 and |ν|^{+sn/2} in v4–v5. With r ≥ 2t this also bounds the conductors of the μ′_{i,w}.`. Lemma 4.3.2(i) and the support bounds in (ii) need every ν_{i,w} = χ_{1,w}^{-1}χ_{2,w}μ_{i,w} = χ_w^{-1}χ_{w̄}^{-1}μ_{i,w} to be trivial on 1 + 𝔭_w^t. The extension claim in §4.3.4 needs μ′_{i,w} = χ_{w̄}μ_{i,w}^{-1} (i ≤ t(w)) to be trivial on 1 + 𝔭^r. At split p, χ_w and χ_{w̄} are independent, and (56) does not bound cond(χ_{w̄}). Counterexample to Lemma 4.3.2(i): take n = 2, a_w = b_w = 1, so t(w) = 1, r(w) = 2, Γ_w(t) is the set of γ ∈ GL_2(O_w) diagonal mod 𝔭^t, and φ_ν((A, B; C, D)) = ν_1(A)ν_2(D) on 𝔛. With γ_1 = 1 and γ_2 = (1, ϖ^t; 0, 1), φ_ν(Xγ_2) = ν_1(A)ν_2(D + ϖ^tC) = ν_2(1 + ϖ^tC/D)φ_ν(X), while the right side of (i) is φ_ν(X) because μ_w(γ_2) = det γ_2 = 1. Suppose χ_w and μ_2 have conductor ≤ 𝔭^t and χ_{w̄} has conductor 𝔭^{t+1}. Then ν_2 is nontrivial on 1 + 𝔭^t and (i) fails for suitable C. Lemma 4.3.2(i) and the support bounds in (ii) need every ν_{i,w} = χ_{1,w}^{-1}χ_{2,w}μ_{i,w} = χ_w^{-1}χ_{w̄}^{-1}μ_{i,w} to be trivial on 1 + 𝔭_w^t. The extension claim in §4.3.4 needs μ′_{i,w} = χ_{w̄}μ_{i,w}^{-1} (i ≤ t(w)) to be trivial on 1 + 𝔭^r. At split p, χ_w and χ_{w̄} are independent, and (56) does not bound cond(χ_{w̄}). Counterexample to Lemma 4.3.2(i): take n = 2, a_w = b_w = 1, so t(w) = 1, r(w) = 2, Γ_w(t) is the set of γ ∈ GL_2(O_w) diagonal mod 𝔭^t, and φ_ν((A, B; C, D)) = ν_1(A)ν_2(D) on 𝔛. With γ_1 = 1 and γ_2 = (1, ϖ^t; 0, 1), φ_ν(Xγ_2) = ν_1(A)ν_2(D + ϖ^tC) = ν_2(1 + ϖ^tC/D)φ_ν(X), while the right side of (i) is φ_ν(X) because μ_w(γ_2) = det γ_2 = 1. Suppose χ_w and μ_2 have conductor ≤ 𝔭^t and χ_{w̄} has conductor 𝔭^{t+1}. Then ν_2 is nontrivial on 1 + 𝔭^t and (i) fails for suitable C. Likewise φ(diag(α, 1)) need not be invariant under α ↦ α + 𝔭^tM, so supp Φ^{(1)} ⊆ 𝔭^{-t}M can fail. Defence: t (and r) are free, ‘sufficiently large’ parameters, so enlarging t repairs everything; possibly χ_w was meant to range over all w | p. Independent check: The quote of (56) on p. 51 is accurate. ν_{i,w} = χ_{1,w}^{-1}χ_{2,w}μ_{i,w} = χ_w^{-1}χ_{w̄}^{-1}μ_{i,w}, with χ_{w̄} viewed on K_w via K_w = K^+_{w+} = K_{w̄} (p. 49). (56) bounds cond(μ_{i,w}) and cond(χ_w) for w ∈ Σ_p only. I checked the counterexample. n = 2, a = b = 1, Γ_w(t) = matrices diagonal mod 𝔭^t, φ_ν((A B; C D)) = ν_1(A)ν_2(D) on 𝔛. γ_2 = (1 ϖ^t; 0 1) gives φ_ν(Xγ_2) = ν_2(1 + ϖ^tC/D)φ_ν(X), while the right side of Lemma 4.3.2(i) is φ_ν(X) (μ_w(γ_2) = 1, det γ_2 = 1). If cond χ_{w̄} = 𝔭^{t+1} and the other conductors are ≤ 𝔭^t, then ν_2 is nontrivial on 1+𝔭^t and (i) fails. The 𝔭^{-t} support bounds in (ii) fail with it. Likewise μ′_{i,w} = χ_{w̄}μ_{i,w}^{-1} (i ≤ t(w)) need not be trivial on 1+𝔭^r, so the extension of μ′_w to Γ_R, ᵗΓ_R on p. 55 is not justified by (56) and (60). Enlarging t repairs everything, since t and r are free. Identical in v4 ((4.3.3), p. 45) and v1. - **Error** at §1.4.3, p. 14, sentence after (7), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 13. The source says `"In situation (2) of Hypotheses 1.4.4, we take K_v = ∏_i GL(n_i, O_i); however, the pairing (7) does not depend on the choice of K_v."`; it should be `Replace 'however, the pairing (7) does not depend on the choice of K_v' by 'changing K_v to bK_vb^{-1} (b ∈ B) multiplies the pairing (7) by δ_B(b); we fix K_v as stated'.`. Computation: ∫_{gK_vg^{−1}} F = ∫_{K_v} F(gkg^{−1})dk = ∫_{K_v} φ(gk)dk with φ = F(·g^{−1}); writing g = bk_0 this is δ_B(b)∫_{K_v} φ = δ_B(b)∫_{K_v} F by the G-invariance of ∫_{K_v}. Explicit case: G = GL_2(Q_p), B upper triangular, K = GL_2(Z_p), K′ = diag(p,1)K diag(p,1)^{−1} (hyperspecial, volume 1 for the same Haar measure), F(bk) = δ_B(b) the K-spherical vector with F(1) = 1. For k′ = (a, pb; c/p, d) ∈ K′, F(k′) = |det k′|/max(|c/p|,|d|)² equals 1 if p | c and p^{−2} if c ∈ Z_p^× (probability p/(p+1)), so ∫_{K′} F = 1/(p+1) + p^{−1}/(p+1) = p^{−1} = δ_B(diag(p,1)) ≠ 1 = ∫_K F. Defence: the discrepancy is a constant absorbed into C of (6), so nothing breaks if one K_v is used consistently. Independent check: The quote on p. 14 is accurate. It is also in v4 (p. 13, (1.4.5)) and absent from v3, where the sentence stops at 'we take K_v = ∏_i GL(n_i, O_i)'. For F(bx) = δ_B(b)F(x), the functional Λ_K(F) = ∫_K F dg is G-invariant. If K′ = gKg^{-1} with g = bk_0 (Iwasawa), then ∫_{K′}F dg = ∫_K F(gkg^{-1})dk = ∫_K φ(gk)dk with φ = R(g^{-1})F, which equals δ_B(b)Λ_K(φ) = δ_B(b)Λ_K(F). Here vol(K′) = vol(K) because G is unimodular. I checked the first reading's GL_2(Q_p) example directly. Take K′ = diag(p,1)GL_2(Z_p)diag(p,1)^{-1} and let F be the K-spherical δ_B-function with F(1) = 1 (this is f·f^∨ for the normalised spherical vectors). Then F(k′) = 1 when p | c and p^{-2} when c is a unit; the second case has proportion p/(p+1). So ∫_{K′}F = 1/p ≠ 1 = ∫_K F. The pairing (7) therefore depends on K_v through the positive scalar δ_B(b). The claim is false as stated. It is harmless because the scalar is absorbed into C of (6) once K_v is fixed, which the paper does. The quotation of this finding is a displayed formula which neither PDF's text layer reproduces faithfully, so it could not be located mechanically in the published version; the surrounding prose is unchanged there, but the formula itself was not re-read in print, and the finding stands as recorded against arXiv v5, the accepted version..
- **Error** at §4.3.6, p. 59, display “So Φ((Xg, X)) = Vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}(Z′_1, Z″_2)Φ_{2,w}(Z′_2, Z″_1)”, read against the definition (58) of Φ_w on p. 52, in arXiv v5. ; the same mistake at §4.3.6, p. 58 (first paragraph, definition of Z_w) and p. 59 (evaluation of Φ), in arXiv v5; also in v4 pp. 51–52 (it affects a stated result). The source says `p. 52: “For X = (X_1, X_2) ∈ Hom_{𝒦_w}(V_w, W_w) = Hom_{𝒦_w}(V_w, V_{d,w}) ⊕ Hom_{𝒦_w}(V_w, V^d_w), let Φ_w(X) = Φ_{χ,μ,w}(X_1, X_2) = vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}(−X_1)·Φ_{2,w}(2X_2).” p. 58: “With respect to this new decomposition [W_w = V_w ⊕ V_w], 𝐗 no longer consists of elements (0, X) but instead elements (X, X).” p. 59: “So Φ((Xg, X)) = Vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}(Z′_1, Z″_2)Φ_{2,w}(Z′_2, Z″_1)”`; it should be `In the V_w ⊕ V_w coordinates, an element of Hom(V_w, W_w) with components (Y_1, Y_2) has polarization components X_1 = (Y_1 − Y_2)/2 and X_2 = (Y_1 + Y_2)/2. So the function (58) is Φ_{χ,μ,w}(Y_1, Y_2) = vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}((Y_2 − Y_1)/2)Φ_{2,w}(Y_1 + Y_2). At (Y_1, Y_2) = (Xg, X)γ_V = ([Z′_1, Z″_2], [Z′_2, Z″_1]) this is not Vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}(Z′_1, Z″_2)Φ_{2,w}(Z′_2, Z″_1). One of two fixes is needed. Either §4.3.1 should define Φ_w := vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}(Y_1)Φ_{2,w}(Y_2) in V ⊕ V coordinates (for which §4.3.6–§4.3.10 are the correct computation), and its compatibility with the Eisenstein measure ([Eis15, Lemma 10], §5) must be re-established. Or §4.3.6–§4.3.10 must be redone for the section (58).`. Coordinates: ι_d(a) + ι^d(b) = (a, −a) + (b, b) = (a + b, b − a), with V_d, V^d identified with V by the first projection (§4.1.1). Test case n = 1, a_w = 1, b_w = 0 (so γ_V = 1), with χ unramified at w and w̄, μ = μ_{1,w} ramified of conductor 𝔭^c (1 ≤ c ≤ t), β = π_w with β|_{O^×} = μ′ = μ^{-1}, and ν = μ on O^×. For the section (58), f((u,1)) = χ_2(u)|u|^{1/2+s} ∫ Φ_1(x(1−u)/2)Φ_2(x(1+u)) χ_1^{-1}χ_2(x)|x|^{1+2s} d^×x (up to vol(Γ_w)^{-1}). Since supp Φ_1 = O^× and supp Φ_2 = ϖ^{-c}O^×, the integrand vanishes unless |1 − u| = q^{-c}. Substitute z_1 = x(1−u)/2 ∈ O^× and z_2 = x(1+u) ∈ ϖ^{-c}O^×, so that d^×x d^×u = dz_1dz_2/|z_2|^2 and u = (z_2 − 2z_1)/(z_2 + 2z_1) ∈ 1 + 𝔭^c, on which βχ_2 = μ^{-1} is trivial. This gives Z_w = c′·∫_{O^×} μ(z_1) dz_1 · ∫ Φ_2(z_2)(χ_1^{-1}χ_2)(z_2/2)|z_2|^{2s−1} dz_2 = 0. The p. 59 formula instead gives Z_w = Vol^{-1}·vol(O^×)·∫ Φ_2(z)χ_1^{-1}β^{-1}(z)|z|^{s+1/2} d^×z = (nonzero constant)·(Gauss sum)·q^{c(s+1/2)} ≠ 0, in agreement with Theorem 4.3.10 (Z_w = ε(½ − s, π_a ⊗ χ_{1,w})·V_w·⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩, the L-factors being 1). So Theorem 4.3.10 does not compute the zeta integral of the section defined in (58). Defence: the paper is explicit that the V ⊕ V identification differs from the polarization one and rewrites 𝐗 correctly, and the §4.3.6–§4.3.10 computation is correct for the product function in V ⊕ V coordinates, which is presumably the intended section. The factor 2 in Φ_{2,w}(2X_2) turns into Φ_{2,w}(Y_1 + Y_2), so the authors may have had the coordinate change partly in mind. Marcil (arXiv:2311.05466, §4.1) makes the same step with his (37). Independent check: The quotes on pp. 52, 58 and 59 are accurate. §4.1.1 (p. 42): V_d = {(x,−x)} and V^d = {(x,x)}, identified with V by the first projection, and p. 50 builds the basis of W_w from these identifications. So an element with V⊕V components (Y_1,Y_2) has polarization components X_1 = (Y_1−Y_2)/2 and X_2 = (Y_1+Y_2)/2. This is consistent with p. 58's rewriting of 𝐗 = {(0,X)} as {(X,X)}. (58) is therefore Φ_w(Y_1,Y_2) = vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}((Y_2−Y_1)/2)Φ_{2,w}(Y_1+Y_2). From (73), (Xg,X)γ_V = ([Z′_1,Z″_2],[Z′_2,Z″_1]) (checked), so p. 59 evaluates Φ as vol^{-1}Φ_1(Y_1)Φ_2(Y_2). That is a different function, and no linear identification of V_d, V^d with V can make the two agree. I redid the n = 1, a_w = 1, b_w = 0 test (γ_V = 1; χ unramified at w and w̄; μ of conductor 𝔭^c, 1 ≤ c ≤ t; π_w a character equal to μ^{-1} on O^×). Φ_1 = μ·1_{O^×}, and Φ_2 is a Gauss-sum function supported on ϖ^{-c}O^×. For (58), Z_w ∝ ∫∫Φ_1(x(1−u)/2)Φ_2(x(1+u))χ_1^{-1}χ_2(x)|x|^{1+2s}χ_2π_w(u)|u|^{1/2+s}d^×xd^×u. On the support, |1+u| = 1 and u ∈ 1+𝔭^c, where π_wχ_2 = 1. The substitution z_1 = x(1−u)/2, z_2 = x(1+u) (Jacobian |x|) is a bijection onto O^× × ϖ^{-c}O^×, and the integral factors through ∫_{O^×}μ(z_1)dz_1 = 0. So Z_w ≡ 0. The p. 59 formula instead gives vol^{-1}·vol^×(O^×)·∫Φ_2(z)χ_1^{-1}π_w^{-1}(z)|z|^{s+1/2}d^×z ≠ 0. This agrees with Theorem 4.3.10, whose value is an ε-factor times 𝔙_w⟨φ_w,φ̃_w⟩, with trivial L-factors. So Theorem 4.3.10, and hence I_p in Theorem 4.6.1, does not hold for the section defined in (58). It is correct for the product section in V⊕V coordinates, whose relation to the Eisenstein measure ([Eis15, Lemma 10], partial Fourier transform in X_2) would have to be re-established. Versions: definition in v4 (p. 46) and v1 (p. 43). The evaluation in v4 (p. 52) and v1 (p. 47) is printed 'Φ((Xg, g))', so v4 also has that misprint. I did not check the first reading's remark about Marcil (arXiv:2311.05466). Second, independent reading of the same mistake: Toy case n = 1, a_w = 1, b_w = 0 (so γ_{V_w} = 1), K_w = Q_p with p odd, all finite-order characters trivial, t = 1, π_w unramified with π_w(p) = α, X := q^{−(s+1/2)}. Then Φ_1 = char(O^×) and Φ_2 = char_O − q^{−1}char_{p^{−1}O}. With the product function Φ' one gets Z = (1 − αq^{−1}X^{−1})/(1 − α^{−1}X) = L(s + 1/2, π̃)/L(1/2 − s, π), as Theorem 4.3.10 predicts. With the literal Φ_w of §4.3.1 one gets Z = (1 − q^{−1})[α^{−1}X/(1 − α^{−1}X) + αX/(1 − αX) + (q − 2)/(q − 1)] − q^{−2}X^{−2}, which also has the pole of L(s + 1/2, π). I confirmed both closed forms by exact enumeration modulo p^5 for p = 3. So the two sections really differ, and Theorem 4.3.10 is about the translated section. Even if Φ is read in the new coordinates, the p. 59 formula also drops the unit constants coming from −X_1 and 2X_2 (∏_iμ_{i,w}(−1)^{n_{i,w}} and ∏_iν_{i,w}(2)^{−n_{i,w}}) and the factor χ_{2,w}(det γ_{V_w}) = χ_{2,w}(−1)^{b_w}. Case for the defence: the authors say explicitly that they switch decompositions ('often convenient … e.g. in [GPSR87]'). v1 (p. 46, (4.3.10)) put an extra change-of-basis-type matrix (½·1_n, −½·1_n; 1_n, 1_n) into the translation, so the need for a translation was recognised. The discrepancy is a right translation of the section by a fixed group element together with unit constants, so the shape of the Euler factor is unaffected provided the Eisenstein measure is built from the matching section. Marcil (arXiv:2311.05466, (37) and p. 23) repeats the same step, also dropping the sign −X_1. Independent check: Quotations checked on the page images (pp. 50, 52, 58-59). By §4.1.1 (p. 42), V^d = {(x,x)} and V_d = {(x,-x)}, and both are identified with V by the first projection (p. 50 uses the same identification for the matrices X_1, X_2). So a homomorphism with V+V components (Y_1,Y_2) has polarization components X_1 = (Y_1-Y_2)/2 and X_2 = (Y_1+Y_2)/2. Then (58) is Phi(Y) = vol^-1 Phi_1((Y_2-Y_1)/2) Phi_2(Y_1+Y_2). It is not the product vol^-1 Phi_1(Y_1)Phi_2(Y_2) that the p. 59 display uses. The block bookkeeping (Xg,X)gamma = ([Z_1',Z_2''],[Z_2',Z_1'']) is itself correct. I re-derived the toy case by hand: n=a=1, b=0, K_w=Q_p with p odd, trivial characters, t=1, pi unramified with pi(p)=alpha, and X=q^-(s+1/2). The product function gives (1-alpha q^-1 X^-1)/(1-alpha^-1 X) = L(s+1/2,pi~)/L(1/2-s,pi), as Theorem 4.3.10 predicts. The literal (58) needs |z_2-z_1|=1 and splits into four cases: v(z_1)=0<v(z_2); v(z_2)=0<v(z_1); z_1,z_2 units with z_1 !≡ z_2 mod p; and v(z_1)=v(z_2)=-1 with z_1≡z_2 mod p but not mod p^2. These give (1-q^-1)[alpha^-1X/(1-alpha^-1X)+alphaX/(1-alphaX)+(q-2)/(q-1)] - q^-2 X^-2. I reran the exact-enumeration check (p=3, mod 3^5), and it matches both closed forms up to truncation (-3.9487 vs -3.9487; -4.798 vs -4.793). A second test, the ramified case of sourceIssues E52 (n=a=1, b=0, chi unramified, mu of conductor p^c): the supports force u=z_1/z_2 in 1+p^c, and the literal zeta integral then contains the factor ∫_{O^x} mu = 0. Theorem 4.3.10 instead gives eps(1/2-s, pi_a⊗chi_1)·Vol·<phi,phi~>, which is nonzero. Theorem 4.3.10 is stated for Z_w built from the translate (73) of the section (58), and (58) is the p-adic section fed into Definition 5.3.2 (p. 85: 'choices ... 4.3 (local choices for v | p)'). So the theorem is false as stated for the section the paper defines. This is an error in a stated result, not only a gap in the proof, and it agrees with sourceIssues E52. The §4.3.6-4.3.10 computation is correct for the product Schwartz function in V_w+V_w coordinates. Whether the Main Theorem survives depends on the Eisenstein measure ([Eis15], Theorem 8.2.2) being built from that section. In the ramified test the literal section would make the p-adic L-function vanish at those characters. Smaller slips: the unit constants from -X_1 and 2X_2 and the factor chi_2(det gamma) = chi_2(-1)^{b_w} are also dropped (p. 58 writes chi_2(g), not chi_2(det g·gamma)). Versions: v4 p. 52 prints 'Phi((Xg,g))'. v1 (4.3.10) puts an extra matrix (1/2, -1/2; 1, 1) into the translation, but v1 (4.3.12) still evaluates Phi((Xg,X)gamma) without it, so v1 was already inconsistent. Reach: a stated result (whether the section whose zeta integral is computed is the section (58) used in the Eisenstein measure). Recorded as `PAPER-EISCHEN-HARRIS-LI-ETAL-20/E52`; looked for an existing correction in: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: Present in v4 (definition p. 46; evaluation p. 52) and in v1 (definition p. 43; evaluation p. 47, printed ‘Φ((Xg, g))’). v4 pp. 51–52: same text (v4 p. 52 prints 'Φ((Xg, g))', corrected in v5 to (Xg, X)); v2/v3 §4.3.7: same; v1 p. 46, (4.3.10): the translation is g ↦ f_w^{χ,μ}(g·(½·1_n, −½·1_n; 1_n, 1_n)·γ_V), with the same expansion Φ((Xg, g)) = volume(Γ_w)^{−1}Φ_{1,w}(Z_1', Z_2'')Φ_{2,w}(Z_2', Z_1'') on p. 47; the extra matrix was removed in v2.; Crossref record of doi:10.1017/fmp.2020.4 (published online 6 May 2020): no update-to, relation or updated-by entry; the Cambridge Core article page links no correction or erratum. The published PDF itself could not be retrieved (www.cambridge.org returned 404/HTML on 2026-09-23), so the correction was checked against arXiv v5, the accepted version; Michael Harris's annotated publication list with errata (https://www.math.columbia.edu/~harris/website/content/12-errata-publications-list-links-here/errata.pdf, dated 7 December 2021): no entry for this paper; zbMATH Open (Zbl 1473.11118) and a web search for an erratum, corrigendum or correction to the paper: none found; Later work building on the paper, read for reported corrections: Marcil, arXiv:2311.05466 and arXiv:2310.09110; Eischen–Liu, arXiv:2006.04302 (J. reine angew. Math. 2024); Z. Liu, arXiv:1904.07121; Eischen, arXiv:2101.01879; Wan, arXiv:1908.07205; Eischen–Fintzen–Mantovan–Varma, arXiv:1511.06771. None reports a mistake in the paper (Marcil, Remark 3.4, notes only a different Fourier-transform convention at p, which is harmless here).

So a homomorphism with V+V components (Y_1,Y_2) has polarization components X_1 = (Y_1-Y_2)/2 and X_2 = (Y_1+Y_2)/2. Then (58) is Phi(Y) = vol^-1 Phi_1((Y_2-Y_1)/2) Phi_2(Y_1+Y_2). It is not the product vol^-1 Phi_1(Y_1)Phi_2(Y_2) that the p. 59 display uses. The block bookkeeping (Xg,X)gamma = ([Z_1',Z_2''],[Z_2',Z_1'']) is itself correct. I re-derived the toy case by hand: n=a=1, b=0, K_w=Q_p with p odd, trivial characters, t=1, pi unramified with pi(p)=alpha, and X=q^-(s+1/2). The product function gives (1-alpha q^-1 X^-1)/(1-alpha^-1 X) = L(s+1/2,pi~)/L(1/2-s,pi), as Theorem 4.3.10 predicts. The literal (58) needs |z_2-z_1|=1 and splits into four cases: v(z_1)=0<v(z_2); v(z_2)=0<v(z_1); z_1,z_2 units with z_1 !≡ z_2 mod p; and v(z_1)=v(z_2)=-1 with z_1≡z_2 mod p but not mod p^2. These give (1-q^-1)[alpha^-1X/(1-alpha^-1X)+alphaX/(1-alphaX)+(q-2)/(q-1)] - q^-2 X^-2. I reran the exact-enumeration check (p=3, mod 3^5), and it matches both closed forms up to truncation (-3.9487 vs -3.9487; -4.798 vs -4.793). A second test, the ramified case of sourceIssues E52 (n=a=1, b=0, chi unramified, mu of conductor p^c): the supports force u=z_1/z_2 in 1+p^c, and the literal zeta integral then contains the factor ∫_{O^x} mu = 0. Theorem 4.3.10 instead gives eps(1/2-s, pi_a⊗chi_1)·Vol·<phi,phi~>, which is nonzero. Theorem 4.3.10 is stated for Z_w built from the translate (73) of the section (58), and (58) is the p-adic section fed into Definition 5.3.2 (p. 85: 'choices ... 4.3 (local choices for v | p)'). So the theorem is false as stated for the section the paper defines. This is an error in a stated result, not only a gap in the proof, and it agrees with sourceIssues E52. The §4.3.6-4.3.10 computation is correct for the product Schwartz function in V_w+V_w coordinates. Whether the Main Theorem survives depends on the Eisenstein measure ([Eis15], Theorem 8.2.2) being built from that section. In the ramified test the literal section would make the p-adic L-function vanish at those characters. Smaller slips: the unit constants from -X_1 and 2X_2 and the factor chi_2(det gamma) = chi_2(-1)^{b_w} are also dropped (p. 58 writes chi_2(g), not chi_2(det g·gamma)). Versions: v4 p. 52 prints 'Phi((Xg,g))'. v1 (4.3.10) puts an extra matrix (1/2, -1/2; 1, 1) into the translation, but v1 (4.3.12) still evaluates Phi((Xg,X)gamma) without it, so v1 was already inconsistent. Reach: a stated result (whether the section whose zeta integral is computed is the section (58) used in the Eisenstein measure). The source says `“When all of the above conditions are met, we have the following factorization at each prime w ∈ Σ_p: Φ_{1,w}(Z_1', Z_2'')Φ_{2,w}(Z_2', Z_1'')⟨π_w(Z_1)φ_w, π̃_w(Z_2)φ̃_w⟩_{π_w} = Vol(Γ_{a_w,b_w})·J_1·J_2” (conditions: A_1 ∈ Γ_{a_w,w}(t), C_1 ∈ p_w^t M, D_2 ∈ Γ_{b_w,w}(t), B_2 ∈ p_w^t M, …); proof: “π_w(Z_1)φ_w = π_w((1 0; C_1 D_1))μ'_w((A_1 0; 0 1))φ_w, π̃_w(Z_2)φ̃_w = π̃_w((A_2 B_2; 0 1))(μ'_w)^{−1}((1 0; 0 D_2))φ̃_w” and, on p. 61, “A = 1 − B_2C_1 ∈ 1 + p_w^{2t}M_{a_w}(O_w) … D = (1 + CB_2)D_1 ∈ (1 + p^{2t}M_{b_w}(O_w))D_1. Therefore, applying the invariance conditions (66) and (69) we obtain ⟨π_w((1 0; C_1 D_1))φ_w, π̃_w((A_2 B_2; 0 1))φ̃_w⟩ = ⟨π_w((1 −B_2; 0 1)(1 0; C_1 D_1))φ_w, π̃_w((A_2 0; 0 1))φ̃_w⟩ = ⟨π_w((1 0; C_1 1)(1 0; 0 D_1))φ_w, π̃_w(A_2 0; 0 1)φ̃_w⟩ = …”`; it should be `(77) holds only under the extra conditions A_1 in Gamma_{a_w,w}, D_2 in Gamma_{b_w,w} (level p^r) and r = 2t (or with the factors A = 1-B_2C_1 and 1+CB_2 carried along). State Proposition 4.3.7 in that form, and prove Corollary 4.3.8 by first using the Gamma_w(t)-invariance of the integrand of (74) to reduce to that case, as in the first reading's steps (i)-(iii).`. (66) and (69) give equivariance only under Γ_{R,w}, ᵗΓ_{R,w}, which have level p^r with r ≥ 2t (60). The support of Φ_{1,w} = Γ_w(t) gives only level p^t. So diag(A_1, 1) with A_1 ∈ Γ_{a_w,w}(t) \ Γ_{a_w,w} need not act on φ_w by μ'_w. For example, for u lower unipotent with entries in p^t \ p^r, π_{a_w}(u)φ_{a_w} ≠ φ_{a_w}, since the model function of φ_{a_w} is supported on B_{a_w}Γ_{a_w,w}. In the p. 61 chain the second equality silently replaces (1 0; C 1)(A 0; 0 D) by (1 0; C_1 1)(1 0; 0 D_1). Carrying the factors through gives ⟨φ_w, π̃_w(diag(A^{−1}A_2, D_1^{−1}(1 + CB_2)^{−1}))φ̃_w⟩. Removing A^{−1} and (1 + CB_2)^{−1} needs diag(A, 1) ∈ Γ_{R,w} and diag(1, 1 + CB_2) ∈ ᵗΓ_{R,w}, i.e. 1 + p^{2t}M ⊂ Γ(r), i.e. r ≤ 2t. The next step (levi-coefficient-factorization) needs r ≥ 2t (D_1CA_2 ∈ O for C ∈ p^r). So the printed argument covers exactly r = 2t. Case for the defence: the final formulas (Corollary 4.3.8, Theorem 4.3.10) do hold, and the missing steps are routine once noticed. Marcil 2023 (Lemma 4.1, Lemma 4.2, Proposition 4.3) takes Φ_{1,w} of level p^r and handles the elements γ_0 = (A, AB; 0, 1), γ̃_0 = (1, 0; C, 1 + CB_2) explicitly, which avoids the issue. Independent check: Quotations checked on pp. 60-61. First step of the proof: it applies (66) to diag(A_1,1). But Prop. 4.3.7 only gives A_1 in Gamma_{a_w,w}(t) (level p^t, from supp Phi_{1,w} = Gamma_w(t), p. 51), while (66) holds on Gamma_{R,w} (level p^r, r >= 2t). Second step: the second equality of the p. 61 chain needs diag(A,1) in Gamma_R and diag(1,1+CB_2) in tGamma_R, where A = 1-B_2C_1 = (1+B_2C)^-1 is in 1+p^{2t}M. That requires r <= 2t, while the Levi step needs D_1CA_2 integral, i.e. r >= 2t. So the printed argument covers at most r = 2t, and even there the A_1 problem remains. Beyond the proof, (77) itself is false as stated. Counterexample: b_w=0, a_w=n=2, partition 1+1, K_w=Q_p, all characters trivial, pi_{i,w} unramified, t=1, r=2. Let phi = char(B·Iw_2), where Iw_2 has lower-left entry in p^2. Let phi~ be supported on B·tIw_2 with phi~(k) = [k_22 in O^x] on GL_2(O); it satisfies (67) and (69). Take A_1 = u = (1 0; p 1), which is in Gamma_{a,w}(1), and A_2 = diag(p^-1, p), which is in p^-1 M_2(O). Then Phi^(1)(A_2) = -(1-1/p)/p ≠ 0. Next, <pi(u)phi, pi~(A_2)phi~> = ∫_{k_22 unit} phi(k A_2^-1 u) dk = 0: the bottom row of kA_2^-1u is (p k_21 + k_22, p^-1 k_22), whose ratio has valuation 1. On the other hand <phi, pi~(A_2)phi~> ≠ 0 (the ratio is p^2k_21/k_22). So the left side of (77) is 0, while the right side Vol·Phi^(1)(A_2)·<phi_a, pi~_a(A_2)phi~_a> is nonzero. Corollary 4.3.8 survives. The integrand of (74) is invariant under (Z_1,Z_2) -> (uZ_1,uZ_2) for unipotent u in Gamma_w(t), by Lemma 4.3.2(i) (for Phi_2) and the definition of Phi_1, and this reduces A_1 to level p^r. I checked this step (the first reading's step (i)); steps (ii)-(iii) for the A and 1+CB_2 factors are plausible but I did not check them. Independent check: Quotation checked (p. 64; Remark 4.3.11, p. 65). With a_w = 1, I_2 (p. 62) is a Tate integral: I_2 = <phi,phi~> Z(Phi^(1), xi, s+1/2) with xi = (beta chi_1)^-1 = pi~_a ⊗ chi_1^-1. Phi^(1) is the e_w(-tr)-Fourier transform of phi_nu on O^x, so its psi = e_w transform is phi_nu (the analogue of (85)). Also beta chi_1 nu_1 = beta chi_2 mu_1 = 1 on O^x, because beta|O^x = mu'_1 = chi_2^-1 mu_1^-1. So the dual integral is vol(O^x) with no sign. Tate's functional equation then gives I_2 = L(s+1/2,xi)/(eps(s+1/2,xi,e_w) L(1/2-s,xi^-1))·vol·<,>. Since eps(s+1/2,xi)^-1 = xi(-1) eps(1/2-s,xi^-1), this is I_2 = omega_{pi_a⊗chi_1}(-1) × (printed I_2). The same computation for I_1 (b_w=1) reproduces the printed I_1 exactly with psi = e_w. With psi = e_w^-1 each eps changes by the character's value at -1: I_2 then comes out as printed, but I_1 is off by omega_{pi_b⊗chi_2}(-1). For general characters no single psi makes both formulas right, so Z_w, (83), (86) and Remark 4.3.11 are off by ±1. Remark 4.3.11 has a further slip: the identity eps(1/2-s,pi_a⊗chi_1) eps(1/2+s,pi~_a⊗chi_1^-1) = omega(-1) involves the central character of pi_a⊗chi_1, i.e. omega_{a_w}(-1)chi_{1,w}(-1)^{a_w}, not omega_{a_w}(-1). The sign varies continuously with chi, so it is harmless for p-adic interpolation. v4 p. 57 is the same. Reach: a stated result (by a sign ±1). Recorded as `PAPER-EISCHEN-HARRIS-LI-ETAL-20/E57`; looked for an existing correction in: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: v4 p. 57 same; v2/v3 Theorem 4.3.11 same; v1 (Theorem on pp. 53–54 and Remark 4.3.5) same.; Crossref record of doi:10.1017/fmp.2020.4 (published online 6 May 2020): no update-to, relation or updated-by entry; the Cambridge Core article page links no correction or erratum. The published PDF itself could not be retrieved (www.cambridge.org returned 404/HTML on 2026-09-23), so the correction was checked against arXiv v5, the accepted version; Michael Harris's annotated publication list with errata (https://www.math.columbia.edu/~harris/website/content/12-errata-publications-list-links-here/errata.pdf, dated 7 December 2021): no entry for this paper; zbMATH Open (Zbl 1473.11118) and a web search for an erratum, corrigendum or correction to the paper: none found; Later work building on the paper, read for reported corrections: Marcil, arXiv:2311.05466 and arXiv:2310.09110; Eischen–Liu, arXiv:2006.04302 (J. reine angew. Math. 2024); Z. Liu, arXiv:1904.07121; Eischen, arXiv:2101.01879; Wan, arXiv:1908.07205; Eischen–Fintzen–Mantovan–Varma, arXiv:1511.06771. None reports a mistake in the paper (Marcil, Remark 3.4, notes only a different Fourier-transform convention at p, which is harmless here); The published version was obtained on 23 September 2026 and compared with arXiv v5. - **Error** at Theorem 4.3.10, (83), p. 64, in arXiv v5; propagates to Remark 4.3.12 (p. 66), Theorem 4.6.1 and Remark 4.6.2 (p. 78); present in v4 p. 57 ((4.3.30)); the same mistake at §9.1.6 Corollary 9.1.8 (p. 144), §9.2 Corollary 9.2.1 (p. 144) and the proof of Main Theorem 9.2.2 (p. 145), in arXiv v5; inherited from Theorem 4.6.1 / Remark 4.6.2 (p. 78); present in v4 at pp. 133–134 (it affects a stated result). The source says `“and thus I_w = L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w) · 𝔙_w · ⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w}, (83)” and, in Theorem 4.6.1, “I_p = L_p(s, ord, π, χ) × ∏_w[𝔙_w · ⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w}]”`; it should be `I_w = Z_w/⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w} = L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w) · 𝔙_w (up to the sign of sourceIssues E57); I_p = ∏_w L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w)𝔙_w.`. By (51), I_w is the zeta integral Z_w divided by ⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w}, and the theorem's own formula gives Z_w = L(…)·𝔙_w·⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩. The proof says 'the consequence for I_w then follows from Corollary 4.3.8 and Equations (71) and (51)', and those give L·𝔙_w. Remark 4.3.11 writes 'I_w/𝔙 = [ratio]' without the pairing. Main Theorem 9.2.2 (whose proof invokes Remark 4.6.2) has Ω = ⟨φ, φ^♭_χ⟩/(Vol(I^0_{r_1,V} ∩ I^0_{r_1,−V})Q[π', χ]) with no ∏_w⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩, consistent with the correction. Marcil 2023, Theorem 4.6, states I_p = E_p(s + 1/2, …)·Vol(I^0_{P,r})Vol(ᵗI^0_{P,r})/Vol(I^0_{P,r} ∩ ᵗI^0_{P,r}), also without the pairing. Case for the defence: if (83) is read as a formula for Z_w the statement is right, and the Main Theorem is unaffected. Independent check: Checked (51) on p. 45: I_v = Z_v/<phi_v, phi_v^flat>_{pi_v}, and at w|p phi^flat_w = phi~_w. Theorem 4.3.10 (p. 64) gives Z_w = L(s+1/2,ord)·V_w·<phi_w,phi~_w>, so I_w = L(s+1/2,ord)·V_w. (83) and Theorem 4.6.1 (p. 78) print the pairing a second time, and by (72) it is not 1 (it equals Vol(Gamma_R) prod <phi_i,phi~_i>). The proof itself cites (51). Remark 4.3.11 (I_w/V without the pairing) agrees with the corrected formula. Main Theorem 9.2.2's Omega contains no prod_w <phi_w,phi~_w>, even though its proof cites Remark 4.6.2, which does contain it. So the Main Theorem matches the corrected I_p = prod_w L·V_w. v4 (4.3.30) and v4 p. 69 are the same. Reach: a stated result (83), Remark 4.3.12, Theorem 4.6.1, Remark 4.6.2); the Main Theorem 9.2.2 matches the corrected version). Second, independent reading of the same mistake: (1) Remark 4.6.2 gives I_p/(Vol(I^0_{r,V})Vol(I^0_{r,−V})) = L_p · ∏_w⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w} / Vol(I^0_{r,V} ∩ I^0_{r,−V}), so Corollary 9.2.1 equals [Main Theorem value] × ∏_{w|p}⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w}; the proof of the Main Theorem drops this factor without comment. (2) With the trace-compatible normalisations (Remarks 8.3.9, 8.4.7) Lemma 8.4.9 gives ⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w} = Vol(I^0_{w,r} ∩ ᵗI^0_{w,r}) · Vol(I^0_{w,r}ᵗI^0_{w,r}), which depends on r; and Lemma 8.5.3 shows ⟨φ, φ^♭_χ⟩_χ / Vol(I^0_{r,V} ∩ I^0_{r,−V}) is r-independent. Hence the right side of Corollary 9.2.1 depends on the choice of r^1 (any r^1 at which π′ ∈ S(K_{r^1}, κ^1, π) is allowed), whereas the left side — the specialisation of a fixed element at χ ⊗ λ_{π′} — does not; likewise the left side of Corollary 9.1.8 is r-independent by trace compatibility (174). The Main Theorem's value is r^1-independent. (3) Source of the double count: (51) (p. 45) defines I_v = Z_v/⟨φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩_{π_v}; Theorem 4.3.10 (p. 64) computes Z_w = [ratio of L- and ε-factors]·𝔙_w·⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w} and then says 'and thus I_w = L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w)·𝔙_w·⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w}' (83) — the right side is Z_w, not I_w — and Theorem 4.6.1 multiplies this by the global ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ as well. Defence: the Main Theorem, the paper's endpoint, has the right shape; only the intermediate corollaries (and §4.6) carry the extra factor. Independent check: Checked on the page images (pp. 45, 57–58, 64–66, 78, 137–138, 143–145). (51) gives I(φ,φ^♭,f,s) = ⟨φ,φ^♭⟩∏_v I_v with I_v = Z_v/⟨φ_v,φ^♭_v⟩_{π_v}. At w|p, Z_w is the zeta integral with the pair (φ_w,φ̃_w) (p. 58: 'the numerator of the local factor I_{w+} … defined in (51)'), and φ̃_w = φ^{♭,a-ord}_{w,r} (Remark 8.4.8). Theorem 4.3.10 computes Z_w = [ratio of L- and ε-factors]·𝔙_w·⟨φ_w,φ̃_w⟩_{π_w} from Corollary 4.3.8 and (71). So I_w = [ratio]·𝔙_w, as Remark 4.3.11 itself writes ('I_w/𝔙 = [ratio]'). But (83) prints 'I_w = L(s+1/2,ord,π_w,χ_w)·𝔙_w·⟨φ_w,φ̃_w⟩_{π_w}', which is Z_w. Theorem 4.6.1 then uses I_p = L_p·∏_w[𝔙_w⟨φ_w,φ̃_w⟩] together with the global ⟨φ,φ^♭⟩, and Corollaries 9.1.8 and 9.2.1 inherit this. By Remark 4.6.2, Cor. 9.2.1's value equals the Main Theorem's value times ∏_{w|p}⟨φ_w,φ̃_w⟩_{π_w}. The proof of the Main Theorem drops this factor without comment. The local pairings are not normalized to 1 at p: the normalization ⟨φ_{v,0},φ^♭_{v,0}⟩ = 1 on p. 44 is only for v ∉ S_π. By Lemma 8.4.9 and its proof (pp. 137–138), ⟨φ^{a-ord}_{w,r},φ^{♭,a-ord}_{w,r}⟩_w = Vol(I^0_{w,r} ∩ ᵗI^0_{w,r})·Vol(I^0_{w,r}ᵗI^0_{w,r}), which depends on r. Since ⟨φ,φ^♭⟩/Vol(I^0_{r,V} ∩ I^0_{r,−V}) is r-independent (Lemma 8.5.3), the right side of Cor. 9.2.1 depends on the auxiliary r^1 (any r^1 at which π′ has level may be used), while the left side does not. So Cor. 9.1.8/9.2.1 are wrong as printed. Redoing the computation with I_w = Z_w/⟨φ_w,φ̃_w⟩ gives exactly the Main Theorem's formula, which is the consistent one. Root cause: (83)/Theorem 4.6.1 (cf. sourceIssues E58); this item records its propagation to §9. Also misprint on p. 145: 'Vol(I^0_{r^1,V}) and Vol(I^0_{r^1,V})' should have −V in the second. Versions: same in v4 (pp. 133–134; Theorem 4.6.1/Remark 4.6.2 on p. 69). So we may rewrite I_2 as I_2 = ω_{a_w}(−1)L(1/2 + s, π̃_{a_w} ⊗ χ_{1,w}^{−1}) / [ε(s + 1/2, π̃_{a_w} ⊗ χ_{1,w}^{−1}) L(−s + 1/2, π_{a_w} ⊗ χ_{1,w})] · Vol(𝔛^{(1)}), and hence I_w/𝔙 as …”`; it should be `ω_{a_w}(−1) should be the value at −1 of the central character of π_{a_w} ⊗ χ_{1,w}, i.e. ω_{a_w}(−1)χ_{1,w}(−1)^{a_w}. (Given sourceIssues E57, the true I_2 and I_w/𝔙_w are these expressions without the sign.)`. ε(s, Π, ψ)ε(1 − s, Π̃, ψ) = ω_Π(−1) with Π = π_{a_w} ⊗ χ_{1,w}, whose central character is ω_{a_w}χ_{1,w}^{a_w}. - **Misprint** at §2.1, p. 15, last lines (equivalence of quadruples), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 14. The source says `"two quadruples (A, λ, ι, α) and (A′, λ′, ι′, α′) are equivalent if there exists a prime-to-□ isogeny f : A → A′ such that λ equals f^∨∘λ′∘f up to some positive element in Z_(□)^×, ι′(b)∘f = f∘ι(b) for all b ∈ O_B, and α′ = f∘α."`; it should be `"prime-to-□ quasi-isogeny" (a Z_(□)^×-isogeny as in Lan's isogeny-class formulation), or 'the equivalence relation generated by' the printed relation.`. With genuine isogenies the relation is not symmetric: for □ = {p}, if f has degree prime to p and g: A′ → A satisfies g∘f = [N] (N prime to p), then g∘α′ = g∘f∘α = N·α, which is not in the K^□-orbit of α in general (N·1 ∉ K^□ when K^□ ⊂ G(Ẑ^p)). Defence: 'isogeny' for 'quasi-isogeny' is a common abuse and the reference to Lan's representability theorem fixes the meaning. - **Error** at Remark 4.3.12, pp. 65–66, in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 58 (it affects a stated result). The source says `“From this we conclude that I_w/(Vol(Γ_{R,w})·Vol(ᵗΓ_{R,w})) = L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w)⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w}/Vol(Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w}). The right-hand side (and hence the left-hand side) is easily seen to be independent of r.”`; it should be `The quantities independent of r are 𝔙_w = Vol(Γ_{R,w})Vol(ᵗΓ_{R,w})/Vol(Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w}) (the volume of the big cell ᵗΓ_{R,w}Γ_{R,w} = N^-_R(O)L_R(O)N_R(O)) and I_w = L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w)𝔙_w. Neither side of the displayed identity is independent of r: with (72), the right side equals L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w) · q_w^{r·dim N_{R_w}} · ∏_{i=1}^{r(w)}⟨φ_{i,w}, φ̃_{i,w}⟩ (and, with the corrected (83), the left side equals L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w)/Vol(Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w}), which also grows with r).`. By (72) (with the product over all i ≤ r(w)), ⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩ = Vol(Γ_{R,w})∏_i⟨φ_{i,w}, φ̃_{i,w}⟩, with the φ_{i,w} independent of r. Also Vol(Γ_{R,w})/Vol(Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w}) = [Γ_{R,w} : Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w}] = |N_{R_w}(O_w/p_w^r)| = q_w^{r·dim N_{R_w}}, since Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w} is the set of matrices that are in the Levi L_{R_w} mod p^r. This is positive-dimensional unless R_w = GL_n. Case for the defence: the claim becomes true if the test vectors are renormalized so that ⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩ is proportional to Vol(Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w}), which may be what the global normalization of §8–§9 achieves (Main Theorem 9.2.2 asserts that Ω_{π',χ} = ⟨φ, φ^♭_χ⟩/(Vol(I^0_{r_1,V} ∩ I^0_{r_1,−V})Q) is independent of r_1). As stated with the vectors of §4.3.4, it is false. Independent check: Checked pp. 65-66. The phi_{i,w} do not depend on r, and by (72) (product over all i <= r(w)) <phi_w,phi~_w> = Vol(Gamma_{R,w}) prod_i <phi_i,phi~_i>. Gamma_R ∩ tGamma_R is the preimage of the Levi L_R(O/p^r), and tR is the opposite parabolic, so Vol(Gamma_R)/Vol(Gamma_R ∩ tGamma_R) = |N_R(O/p^r)| = q^{r·dim N_R}. The right-hand side of the remark is therefore L·q^{r dim N_R}·prod<phi_i,phi~_i>, which depends on r unless N_R = 1. The left-hand side (by (83) as printed, or as corrected in sourceIssues E58) also depends on r. What is independent of r is V_w = Vol(tGamma_R Gamma_R) = Vol(N^-(O)L(O)N(O)) (Iwahori factorization), and hence the corrected I_w = L·V_w. v4 p. 58 is the same. Reach: a stated result (remark). - **Misprint** at §4.4.1, p. 66, lines 3–4, in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 59 and v2/v3 p. 59. The source says `“we let G* = GU_1^+ = R_{K/Q}GU^+(V) where GU^+(V) denotes the full unitary similitude group of V. Thus G*(R) = ∏_{σ∈Σ_{K^+}} G_σ, with G_σ = GU^+(V)_{K^+_σ}”`; it should be `G* = R_{K^+/Q} GU^+(V)`. GU^+(V) is a reductive group over K^+ (the fixed field of c), and the decomposition of G*(R) over Σ_{K^+} with factors GU^+(V)_{K^+_σ} is that of a restriction of scalars from K^+. Thus G*(R) = ∏_{σ∈Σ_{K^+}} G_σ, with G_σ = GU^+(V)_{K^+_σ}”`; it should be `G* = R_{K^+/Q} GU^+(V)`. GU^+(V) is a reductive group over K^+ (the fixed field of c), and the decomposition of G*(R) over Σ_{K^+} with factors GU^+(V)_{K^+_σ} is that of a restriction of scalars from K^+. - **Error** at §4.4.2, definition of J_{χ_σ} and Remark 4.4.3, p. 69, in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 61. The source says `“ι(χ_σ)(v(χ_σ)) = J_{χ_σ}(g) := j(g)^{−m+a(χ_σ)} · j'(g)^{−m+b(χ_σ)}ν(g)^{n(m+a(χ_σ)+b(χ_σ))}” and “Remark 4.4.3. Note that J_{χ_σ} depends only on the archimedean character χ_σ = ||•||^m_σ χ_{0,σ}.”`; it should be `The claim holds for the restriction of J_{χ_σ} to U(n, n) (ν = 1). On the similitude group the ν-exponent n(m + a(χ_σ) + b(χ_σ)) depends on the factorization χ = ||•||^m χ_0.`. Replacing (m, χ_0) by (m − k, ||•||^k χ_0), which gives a(χ_σ) − k and b(χ_σ) − k, leaves −m + a and −m + b unchanged but changes m + a + b by −3k. Case for the defence: similitude factors are ignored throughout (Remark 4.5.3), and the ν-exponent may itself be a slip. Definition 5.3.2 cites Remark 4.4.3 to say that f_σ does not depend on the factorization. Independent check: Checked p. 69. At sigma, ||z|| = z zbar, so chi_sigma = z^{m-a} zbar^{m-b}. The factorization (m, chi_0) -> (m-k, ||·||^k chi_0) gives a' = a-k and b' = b-k, so -m+a and -m+b are unchanged while m+a+b drops by 3k. Hence J_{chi_sigma}, which is defined on G_sigma = GU(n,n) (p. 68), depends on the factorization through nu(g)^{n(m+a+b)}, and Remark 4.4.3 is false on the similitude group. On U(n,n) it is true. The nu-exponent is probably itself a slip: on the centre, J(t) = t^{n(3a+3b)}, which is not a function of chi_sigma|R^x = t^{2m-a-b}. v4 p. 61 is the same. Reach: nothing (similitude factors are ignored, Remark 4.5.3). - **Gap** at Corollary 4.4.9, last statement, and its proof, p. 73, in arXiv v5; present in v4 pp. 64–65 (it affects the proof). The source says `“Then for all κ† ≤ κ there exist unique elements δ(κ, κ†) ∈ U(p^+_3), defined over algebraic number fields, such that D(κ, χ) = Σ_{κ†≤κ} δ(κ, κ†) ∘ D^{hol}(κ†, χ); δ(κ, κ) is the scalar ∏_σ P_{κ_σ,χ,σ}.” … “The remaining statements are formal consequences of the decomposition (93) and the fact that the decomposition is rational over an appropriate reflex field, cf. Lemma 7.3.2 of [Har86].”`; it should be `An argument is needed that the component of D(κ, χ)v(χ) in each summand D(κ†) ⊗ D(κ†^♭ ⊗ χ) lies in U(p^+_3)·(v_{κ†} ⊗ v_{κ†^♭⊗χ}). Alternatively, δ(κ, κ†) should be allowed to be vector-valued differential operators, i.e. elements of U(p^+_3) composed with maps between K_3-types.`. Each summand is U(p^+_3) ⊗ (minimal K_3-type), and U(p^+_3)·(v ⊗ v) consists of the vectors whose K_3-type component is the highest-weight line. The component of δ(r̃, s̃)·v(χ) in the κ†-summand is a K_3-highest-weight vector of weight κ in S(p^+_3) ⊗ W_{κ†}. When W_{κ†} has dimension > 1 such a vector is in general a combination Σ p_i ⊗ w_i with w_i of lower weight, not of the form p ⊗ v_{κ†}, so neither existence nor the meaning of 'δ(κ, κ†) ∘ D^{hol}(κ†, χ)' follows formally. Case for the defence: with vector-valued operators the decomposition is immediate from (93). The only use, in §8.1 (Proposition 8.1.3 and the proof of Corollary 8.2.4, 'by induction on the size of κ'), needs just that the terms with κ† ≠ κ are killed by the ordinary projector, which holds for such operators as well. The meaning of the order κ† ≤ κ is not explained either. I did not settle this. Independent check: Checked p. 73. The kappa†-component of D(kappa,chi)v(chi) is a K_3-highest-weight vector of weight kappa in D(kappa†)⊗D(kappa†^flat⊗chi), which is S(p_3^+)⊗W_{kappa†}⊗W_{kappa†^flat} as a K_3-module. Writing it as delta(kappa,kappa†)·(v⊗v) with delta in U(p_3^+) requires it to lie in S(p_3^+)⊗(highest-weight line). This is automatic when the minimal K-types are 1-dimensional (e.g. a_sigma, b_sigma <= 1). In general it is not a formal consequence of (93), and for non-Cartan constituents it is not expected. The paper itself stresses, just before, that delta(r~,s~)v(chi) need not lie in the highest-weight space. So 'formal consequences' does not prove the statement as formulated. With vector-valued operators the decomposition does follow, and the first reading reports that the §8.1 uses need only that the terms with kappa† ≠ kappa are killed by the ordinary projector; I did not re-check those uses. v4 pp. 64-65 is the same. Reach: the proof (of the last statement of Corollary 4.4.9 as formulated).
