- **Gap** at Corollary 4.4.9, last statement, and its proof, p. 73, in arXiv v5; present in v4 pp. 64–65 (it affects the proof). The source says `“Then for all κ† ≤ κ there exist unique elements δ(κ, κ†) ∈ U(p^+_3), defined over algebraic number fields, such that D(κ, χ) = Σ_{κ†≤κ} δ(κ, κ†) ∘ D^{hol}(κ†, χ); δ(κ, κ) is the scalar ∏_σ P_{κ_σ,χ,σ}.” … “The remaining statements are formal consequences of the decomposition (93) and the fact that the decomposition is rational over an appropriate reflex field, cf. Lemma 7.3.2 of [Har86].”`; it should be `An argument is needed that the component of D(κ, χ)v(χ) in each summand D(κ†) ⊗ D(κ†^♭ ⊗ χ) lies in U(p^+_3)·(v_{κ†} ⊗ v_{κ†^♭⊗χ}). Alternatively, δ(κ, κ†) should be allowed to be vector-valued differential operators, i.e. elements of U(p^+_3) composed with maps between K_3-types.`. Each summand is U(p^+_3) ⊗ (minimal K_3-type), and U(p^+_3)·(v ⊗ v) consists of the vectors whose K_3-type component is the highest-weight line. The component of δ(r̃, s̃)·v(χ) in the κ†-summand is a K_3-highest-weight vector of weight κ in S(p^+_3) ⊗ W_{κ†}. When W_{κ†} has dimension > 1 such a vector is in general a combination Σ p_i ⊗ w_i with w_i of lower weight, not of the form p ⊗ v_{κ†}, so neither existence nor the meaning of 'δ(κ, κ†) ∘ D^{hol}(κ†, χ)' follows formally. Case for the defence: with vector-valued operators the decomposition is immediate from (93). The only use, in §8.1 (Proposition 8.1.3 and the proof of Corollary 8.2.4, 'by induction on the size of κ'), needs just that the terms with κ† ≠ κ are killed by the ordinary projector, which holds for such operators as well. The meaning of the order κ† ≤ κ is not explained either. I did not settle this. Independent check: Checked p. 73. The kappa†-component of D(kappa,chi)v(chi) is a K_3-highest-weight vector of weight kappa in D(kappa†)⊗D(kappa†^flat⊗chi), which is S(p_3^+)⊗W_{kappa†}⊗W_{kappa†^flat} as a K_3-module. Writing it as delta(kappa,kappa†)·(v⊗v) with delta in U(p_3^+) requires it to lie in S(p_3^+)⊗(highest-weight line). This is automatic when the minimal K-types are 1-dimensional (e.g. a_sigma, b_sigma <= 1). In general it is not a formal consequence of (93), and for non-Cartan constituents it is not expected. The paper itself stresses, just before, that delta(r~,s~)v(chi) need not lie in the highest-weight space. So 'formal consequences' does not prove the statement as formulated. With vector-valued operators the decomposition does follow, and the first reading reports that the §8.1 uses need only that the terms with kappa† ≠ kappa are killed by the ordinary projector; I did not re-check those uses. v4 pp. 64-65 is the same. Reach: the proof (of the last statement of Corollary 4.4.9 as formulated). - **Misprint** at §4.4.10, p. 74, last paragraph (before (105)), in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 66 and v2/v3 p. 66. The source says `“Suppose Σ_σ[Σ_i r̃_{i,σ} + Σ_j s̃_{j,σ}] = d. Then we define p(r̃, s̃) = ∏_σ p(r̃_σ, s̃_σ) … δ^d_χ(r̃, s̃) = δ^d_χ(p(r̃, s̃))”`; it should be `Σ_σ[Σ_i i·r̃_{i,σ} + Σ_j j·s̃_{j,σ}] = Σ_σ[Σ_i r_{i,σ} + Σ_j s_{j,σ}] = d`. Δ_i and Δ'_j have degree i and j, so deg p(r̃_σ, s̃_σ) = Σ_i i r̃_{i,σ} + Σ_j j s̃_{j,σ}, which telescopes to Σ_i r_{i,σ} + Σ_j s_{j,σ}. The printed sum equals r_{1,σ} + s_{1,σ}. Independent check: Checked p. 74 against (100) on p. 72. Delta_i and Delta'_j are the i-th and j-th leading minors, of degrees i and j, so deg p(r~_sigma,s~_sigma) = sum_i i r~_i + sum_j j s~_j = sum_i r_i + sum_j s_j (telescoping, with r_{a+1} = s_{b+1} = 0). The printed sum_i r~_i + sum_j s~_j telescopes to r_1 + s_1. d must be the total degree for delta^d_chi(p) to make sense. v4 p. 66 is the same. Reach: nothing (d is determined by (r̃, s̃) anyway). - **Error** at §4.4.12, p. 75, first sentence, in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 66 and v2/v3 p. 66. The source says `“If π is a cuspidal automorphic representation of GU(V) whose component at σ is an anti-holomorphic discrete series representation of the form D_c(τ_σ), then its base change Π to an automorphic representation of GL(n)_K (ignoring the split center) is cuspidal, cohomological, and satisfies Π^∨ ≅ Π^c”`; it should be `Π is an isobaric sum of conjugate-self-dual cuspidal representations (cohomological, Π^∨ ≅ Π^c). It is cuspidal only for π with stable (non-endoscopic) parameter.`. Endoscopic cuspidal representations of unitary groups, e.g. those whose parameter is a sum of two conjugate-self-dual parameters, have non-cuspidal base change (Mok, KMSW). Case for the defence: the passage is motivational ('in most cases'), and the Hodge types (106) depend only on the archimedean component. Independent check: Checked p. 75. Base change of a cuspidal representation of a unitary group is in general only an isobaric sum of conjugate-self-dual cuspidal representations. Endoscopic cuspidal representations can have discrete series at infinity: for example, holomorphic CM forms on U(1,1) have base change Ind of characters, and Rogawski's endoscopic packets on U(2,1) contain holomorphic discrete series members. The paper itself writes in Remark 9.3.2 'an automorphic representation ... whose base change to GL(n) is cuspidal', which acknowledges that this is an extra condition. v4 p. 66 is the same. Reach: nothing (expository). - **Misprint** at §2.2, p. 16, definition of the signature of h, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 15. The source says `"The homomorphism h determines a pure Hodge structure of weight −1 on V = L ⊗ C. Let V^0 ⊂ V be the degree 0 piece of the Hodge filtration; this is an O_B ⊗ C-submodule. For each σ ∈ Σ_𝒦, let a_{σ,i} = dim_C e_i(V^0 ⊗_{O⊗C,σ} C)."`; it should be `V^0 should be V^{−1,0} ≅ V/V^{0,−1} (the summand on which h(z) acts by z; Lan's V_0, the Lie-algebra side of the Kottwitz determinant condition), not the degree-0 Hodge filtration step F^0V = V^{0,−1}.`. Convention-free check against §2.6.1/§2.6.3 (p. 21–22): there W = V/V^{0,−1}, Λ_0 ⊗ C = W, and 'e_iΛ_{0,σ} and e_iΛ^∨_{0,σ} are free S′_0-modules of respective ranks a_{σ,i} and b_{σ,i}'. But dim e_i(V/V^{0,−1})_σ = n_i − dim e_i(F^0V)_σ, which with the printed definition is b_{σ,i}, not a_{σ,i} (the weight −1 Hodge filtration is F^{−1} = V ⊃ F^0 = V^{0,−1} ⊃ F^1 = 0). Second check (Deligne's sign convention, h(z) acts on V^{p,q} by z^{−p}z̄^{−q}, the one compatible with weight −1 for an R-algebra homomorphism h): in §2.3, for σ ∈ Σ, h(z) acts on the σ-component V_{i,σ} by diag(z 1_{r_{i,σ}}, z̄ 1_{s_{i,σ}}), so F^0 = V^{0,−1} (h(z) = z̄) has dimension s_{i,σ}, contradicting '(a_{σ,i}, b_{σ,i}) equals (r_{i,σ}, s_{i,σ}) if σ ∈ Σ'. With V^0 = V^{−1,0} both statements hold. Likely origin: Lan's notation V_0 (subscript) for the h(z) = z part read as a Hodge degree. Defence: the symmetry (a_{σc}, b_{σc}) = (b_σ, a_σ), the reflex field formula and all later uses are consistent with the corrected reading. - **Misprint** at §4.4.14, p. 76, and §4.5.4, p. 76 versus Proposition 4.5.6, p. 77, in arXiv v5; present in v4 pp. 67–68. The source says `§4.4.14: “with φ_v a vector in the minimal U_σ-type 1 ⊗ W^∨_{τ_σ} of D_c(κ) … φ_{κ,+} (resp. φ_{κ,−}) is an eigenvector for T_σ of weight −w_0(κ) (resp. of weight −κ).” §4.5.4: “Let φ_σ ⊗ φ^♭_σ be an anti-holomorphic vector in the highest weight subspace of the minimal K_σ-type of π_σ ⊗ π^♭_σ.” Proposition 4.5.6: “where φ_σ = φ_{κ_σ,−}, φ^♭_σ = φ_{κ^♭_σ,−}”`; it should be `By (90) and §4.4.1, the minimal U_σ-type of D_c(κ) is 1 ⊗ W_{τ_σ}. Either §4.4.1/(90) or §4.4.14 must be adjusted, together with the weights. The vector used in Propositions 4.5.5 and 4.5.6 should be described consistently: the lowest weight vector φ_{κ,−} in Proposition 4.5.6 and (50), but 'highest weight subspace' in §4.5.4.`. (90) gives D_c(τ_σ) = U(𝔤_σ) ⊗_{U(k_σ⊕p^+_σ)} W_{τ_σ}, and p. 67 states that its minimal U_σ-type is 1 ⊗ W_{τ_σ}. The weights −w_0(κ), −κ quoted in §4.4.14 are the highest and lowest weights of W^∨_{τ_σ}. For the pairing in Proposition 4.5.5 to be non-zero the anti-holomorphic vector must be dual to the highest weight vector v_κ ⊗ v_{κ^♭⊗χ} of the holomorphic side, i.e. the lowest weight vector of the dual type, consistent with φ_{κ,−}. Case for the defence: the inconsistency is between two dual conventions and the intended vector is clear from (50) and Proposition 4.5.6. - **Gap** at Lemma 4.5.2 and §4.5.4, (107), p. 76, in arXiv v5 (with §4.4.2, p. 69); present in v4 p. 67 (it affects the proof). The source says `Lemma 4.5.2: “ι(m, χ_σ)(D²(m, χ_σ)) ⊂ I_σ(m − n/2, χ).” §4.5.4: “f_σ = f_σ(χ_σ, c) ∈ I(χ_{u,σ}, m) … f_σ(χ_σ, c, g) = B(χ_σ, κ_σ)D(κ_σ, m, χ_{u,σ})J_{m,χ_{u,σ}}(g) … where J_{m,χ_{u,σ}} ∈ C^∞(G_4) is the canonical automorphy factor introduced in Section 4.4.2”`; it should be `Fix one parametrization. J_χ and D²(m, χ_0) of §4.4.2 use χ = ||•||^m χ_0 with χ_{0,σ}(z) = z^{−a}z̄^{−b} algebraic, whereas §4.5.4 and §4.6 use χ = ||•||^m χ_u with χ_u unitary. The two m differ by (a(χ_σ) + b(χ_σ))/2; §5.3.1 calls the first one μ. Say which induced representation, I(χ, s) or I(χ_u, s), and which s contains the image of ι.`. With the same letter m used for both factorizations and the argument order of I_σ(·, ·) swapped relative to §4.1.2, one cannot tell which section (107) denotes. Lemma 4.5.2 (proof omitted: 'an easy computation, similar to that in [Har97]') places the image in I_σ(m − n/2, χ), while §4.5.4 and Definition 5.3.2 place f_σ in I(χ_{u,σ}, m). I could not reconcile these without the paper's sign conventions for the tube-domain realization, so I did not verify Lemma 4.5.2. Case for the defence: §5.3.1 explicitly separates μ from m ('We omit the expression of μ and χ_0 in terms of m and χ_u'), so the authors were aware of the two normalizations. Independent check: Checked pp. 69, 76, 83-84. §4.4.2 defines J_{chi_sigma} = J_{m,chi_0} for chi = ||·||^m chi_0 with chi_{0,sigma} = z^-a zbar^-b algebraic. Lemma 4.5.2 puts the image of iota(m,chi_sigma) in I_sigma(m - n/2, chi), with the arguments in the reverse order to §4.1.2's I(chi,s). §4.5.4, (107) and Definition 5.3.2 instead put f_sigma = B·D(kappa,m,chi_{u,sigma})J_{m,chi_{u,sigma}} in I(chi_{u,sigma}, m), where chi = ||·||^m chi_u with chi_u unitary; so J_{m,chi_u} is used with a unitary chi_u, although J was defined for algebraic chi_0. I(chi,s) and I(chi_u,s') differ by a shift of s depending on the factorization, so the two placements cannot both hold with the same m. §5.3.1 introduces mu to separate the two normalizations and says 'We omit the expression of mu and chi_0 in terms of m and chi_u'. The global identity (Theorem 4.6.1) needs all local sections in the same I(chi_u,m), and the proof of Lemma 4.5.2 is omitted, so which section (107) denotes is not established. v4 p. 67 is the same. Reach: the proof (identification of the archimedean section). - **Gap** at Proposition 4.5.6, p. 77, in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 68 (it affects a stated result). The source says `“In the meantime, we will be satisfied with the following result, due to Garrett [Gar08]. Proposition 4.5.6. … Then I_σ(χ_σ, κ_σ) is a non-zero algebraic number.”`; it should be `Non-vanishing follows from Proposition 4.5.5. For algebraicity the text itself only reports that [Gar08] proves the integrals 'algebraic up to a predictable power of the transcendental number π, which can be normalized away', for F imaginary quadratic (Remark 4.5.7). The statement needs the normalization (Haar measure at σ and/or the constant B(χ_σ, κ_σ) of (107)) that removes this power of π, and a reference or proof for general CM K.`. The paragraph before the proposition says Garrett shows algebraicity 'up to a predictable power of … π', and explicit values are known only when one factor of the extreme K-type is one-dimensional ([Gar08, p. 12]). Remark 4.5.7 says the computation in [Har08, §5] is for imaginary quadratic F and 'the same reasoning applies in general'. B(χ_σ, κ_σ) is only required to be a non-zero algebraic scalar, so it cannot absorb a power of π. Case for the defence: only non-vanishing (and algebraicity up to an explicit normalization) is needed for the construction, and Eischen–Liu (arXiv:2006.04302) later computed these integrals. Independent check: Checked p. 77. The paragraph before the proposition says that Garrett shows the integrals are 'algebraic up to a predictable power of the transcendental number pi, which can be normalized away', gives exact values only when one factor of the extreme K-type is one-dimensional, and gives non-zero algebraic values when both are scalar. Remark 4.5.7 relies on [Har08] for imaginary quadratic F ('the same reasoning applies in general'). The proposition asserts plain algebraicity without fixing the Haar measure or normalizing constant that removes the power of pi. B(chi_sigma,kappa_sigma) is now required to be algebraic (v5 p. 76; v4 said only 'non-zero scalar'), so it cannot absorb a power of pi. Non-vanishing follows from Proposition 4.5.5. Reach: a stated result (the algebraicity part of Proposition 4.5.6). - **Gap** at Proposition 4.5.6, p. 77, in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 68 (it affects a stated result). The source says `“In the meantime, we will be satisfied with the following result, due to Garrett [Gar08]. Proposition 4.5.6. … Then I_σ(χ_σ, κ_σ) is a non-zero algebraic number.”`; it should be `Non-vanishing follows from Proposition 4.5.5. For algebraicity the text itself only reports that [Gar08] proves the integrals 'algebraic up to a predictable power of the transcendental number π, which can be normalized away', for F imaginary quadratic (Remark 4.5.7). The statement needs the normalization (Haar measure at σ and/or the constant B(χ_σ, κ_σ) of (107)) that removes this power of π, and a reference or proof for general CM K.`. The paragraph before the proposition says Garrett shows algebraicity 'up to a predictable power of … π', and explicit values are known only when one factor of the extreme K-type is one-dimensional ([Gar08, p. 12]). Remark 4.5.7 says the computation in [Har08, §5] is for imaginary quadratic F and 'the same reasoning applies in general'. B(χ_σ, κ_σ) is only required to be a non-zero algebraic scalar, so it cannot absorb a power of π. Case for the defence: only non-vanishing (and algebraicity up to an explicit normalization) is needed for the construction, and Eischen–Liu (arXiv:2006.04302) later computed these integrals. Independent check: Checked p. 77. The paragraph before the proposition says that Garrett shows the integrals are 'algebraic up to a predictable power of the transcendental number pi, which can be normalized away', gives exact values only when one factor of the extreme K-type is one-dimensional, and gives non-zero algebraic values when both are scalar. Remark 4.5.7 relies on [Har08] for imaginary quadratic F ('the same reasoning applies in general'). The proposition asserts plain algebraicity without fixing the Haar measure or normalizing constant that removes the power of pi. B(chi_sigma,kappa_sigma) is now required to be algebraic (v5 p. 76; v4 said only 'non-zero scalar'), so it cannot absorb a power of pi. Non-vanishing follows from Proposition 4.5.5. Reach: a stated result (the algebraicity part of Proposition 4.5.6). - **Misprint** at Theorem 4.6.1, p. 78, definition of I_p and L_p (and Remark 4.6.2), in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 69 and v2/v3 p. 68–69 (Proposition 4.6.1); the same mistake at §9.2, Main Theorem 9.2.2, p. 145 (interpolation formula), in arXiv v5; inherited from Theorem 4.6.1 (p. 78); present in v4 at p. 134 (it affects a stated result). The source says `“I_p = L_p(s, ord, π, χ) × ∏_w[𝔙_w · ⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w}], … L_p(s, ord, π, χ) := ∏_{w|p} L(s, ord, π_w, χ_w).” and “D(χ) · I(φ, φ^♭, f, s) = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ · I_p(χ, κ)I_∞(χ, ρ^υ)I_S L^S(s + 1/2, π, χ_u) … I_∞(χ, κ) = ∏_σ I_σ(χ_σ, κ_σ)”`; it should be `I_p = L_p(s + 1/2, ord, π, χ) × ∏_w 𝔙_w (see also sourceIssues E58); I_∞(χ, ρ^υ) and I_∞(χ, κ) denote the same product.`. By (83), the local factor at w is L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w). The global identity is evaluated at the same s as L^S(s + 1/2, …). Main Theorem 9.2.2 inherits the shift ('L_p(m, ord, π', χ_u) L^S(m + 1/2, π', χ_u)'). Marcil 2023, Theorem 4.6, writes E_p(s + 1/2, P − ord, π_p, χ_p). Case for the defence: this is a pure naming shift, and L_p(s, ord) could be read as 'the ord-factor attached to the value at s + 1/2'. Independent check: Checked p. 64 and p. 78. (83) says 'L(s+1/2, ord, pi_w, chi_w) is the ratio ... that appear in the formula for Z_w', which defines L(·,ord) with the shift built in. Remark 4.3.11 also calls prod_w L(s+1/2,ord,...) the Euler factor at p. Theorem 4.6.1 instead sets I_p = L_p(s,ord) := prod_w L(s,ord,pi_w,chi_w), in the same identity as L^S(s+1/2). Main Theorem 9.2.2 inherits this as 'L_p(m,ord,pi',chi_u) L^S(m+1/2,...)'. Also I_inf(chi,rho^upsilon) and I_inf(chi,kappa) denote the same product. v4 p. 69 is the same. Reach: a stated result (by a shift of 1/2 in the argument of the p-factor). Second, independent reading of the same mistake: (83) (p. 64) gives the p-adic zeta integral as I_w = L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w)·𝔙_w·⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩, and (86) displays this ratio with arguments s + 1/2 and −s + 1/2; Theorem 4.6.1 (p. 78) nevertheless sets L_p(s, ord, π, χ) := ∏_{w|p} L(s, ord, π_w, χ_w) and uses it in I_p at the same s, a half-unit shift; specialising s = m produces L_p(m, …) in the Main Theorem, next to L^S(m + 1/2, …). Defence: the Main Theorem is consistent with Theorem 4.6.1's own (misprinted) definition; the intended meaning is clear from (83), (86) and the parallel L^S(m + 1/2). Independent check: Checked on the page images (pp. 64–65, 78, 145). (83) defines L(s+1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w) as the ratio of L- and ε-factors in Z_w, whose arguments are s+1/2 and −s+1/2 ((86)). Remark 4.3.11 calls ∏_{w|p}L(s+1/2,ord,π_w,χ_w) 'the Euler factor at p'. Theorem 4.6.1 nevertheless defines L_p(s,ord,π,χ) := ∏_w L(s,ord,π_w,χ_w) and puts L_p(s,…) into I_p at the same s as L^S(s+1/2,π,χ_u), a half-unit shift. Specializing at s = m gives L_p(m,ord,π′,χ_u) next to L^S(m+1/2,π′,χ_u) in the Main Theorem. The intended value is L_p(m+1/2,…), i.e. ∏_w L(m+1/2,ord,π′_w,χ_{u,w}). Intended meaning clear from (83), (86) and the parallel L^S(m+1/2). Versions: v4 same; v2/v3 also have I_p = L_p(s,ord,π,χ) and L_p(m,ord,π,χ_u) in the Main Theorem. - **Error** at Theorem 4.6.1, p. 78, in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 69 and v2/v3 (Proposition 4.6.1) (it affects a stated result). The source says `“Assume the local components at finite places outside S = S_π are unramified vectors … assume the Siegel–Weil section f_s ∈ I(χ, s) … Write χ = ||•||^m χ_u. Then we have the equality D(χ)·I(φ, φ^♭, f, s) = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ · I_p(χ, κ)I_∞(χ, ρ^υ)I_S L^S(s + 1/2, π, χ_u) where I_S = ∏_{v∈S} D_v(χ)·volume(𝒰_v)”`; it should be `D(χ) · I(φ, φ^♭, f, m) = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ · ∏_{v|p}D_v(χ) · I_p · I_∞ · I_{S'} · L^{S'∪Σ_p}(m + 1/2, π, χ_u), for f ∈ I(χ_u, m) (equivalently D^{Σ_p}(χ)·I = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ I_p I_∞ I_{S'} L^{S'∪Σ_p}(m + 1/2, π, χ_u)), where S' ⊇ S_π ∪ S_χ ∪ S_K is the set of places of §4.2 and I_{S'} = ∏_{v∈S'}D_v(χ)vol(U_v).`. The unfolding gives I = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩∏_v I_v. For v ∉ S' ∪ Σ_p, d_{n,v}(s, χ_v)I_v = L_v(s + 1/2, π_v, χ_v) (§4.2.1), and d_{n,v}(s, χ_{u,v}) = D_v(χ) only at s = m (definition (108): D_v(χ) = d_{n,v}(m, χ_v)). So the identity holds at s = m for sections in I(χ_u, m), the parametrization used in Definition 5.3.2 and Corollary 9.1.8, not for f_s ∈ I(χ, s) with variable s. For v | p, I_v = I_w is given by Theorem 4.3.10, which contains no standard Euler factor and no D_v. So the D_v(χ) (v | p) contained in D(χ) = D^∅(χ) have no counterpart on the right, and L^S (S = S_π, which does not contain p when π_p is unramified) wrongly includes the Euler factors at p. Moreover the unramified computation needs v ∉ S_ram = S_π ∪ S_χ ∪ S_K, and Lemma 4.2.3 is stated for v ∈ S', so S should be S', not S_π. If instead p ∈ S_π, then I_S would include p-adic places with the §4.2.2 value D_v·vol(U_v), which is not what is computed at p. Case for the defence: it is plausible that the intended statement omits the places above p from both D(χ) and L^S (the natural shape for a p-adic L-function, with the modified factor L_p(ord) replacing the Euler factor at p). But the printed formula does not say so, and Corollary 9.1.8 and Main Theorem 9.2.2 reproduce it (with D(χ) and L^S). Independent check: Checked p. 78, p. 47 ((53)), §4.2 (p. 46), Corollary 9.1.8 and Main Theorem 9.2.2 (pp. 144-145). (i) The s-dependence. D_v(chi) = prod_r L_v(2m+n-r, chi^+ eta^r) = d_{n,v}(m, chi_{u,v}) is fixed by m. For f in I(chi,s) with chi = ||·||^m chi_u, the unramified factor is L_v(s+1/2,pi,chi) = L_v(s+m+1/2,pi,chi_u) over d_{n,v}(s,chi) = d_{n,v}(s+m,chi_u). So the printed identity (D(chi) on the left, L^S(s+1/2,pi,chi_u) on the right) can hold only at s = m for sections in I(chi_u,m), which is the parametrization of Definition 5.3.2 and Corollary 9.1.8. (ii) The places above p. D(chi) = D^∅(chi) runs over all finite v, including v|p (108). The factor I_p of Theorem 4.3.10 contains no D_v, and at v|p the section is not unramified. S = S_pi need not contain p (§4.2 even requires p not in S), so L^S wrongly keeps the Euler factor at p. The printed identity is off by prod_{v|p} L_v(m+1/2,pi,chi_u)/D_v(chi), which is not 1 when chi is unramified at p. (iii) At places of S_chi ∪ S_K outside S_pi the sections are those of §4.2.2, with I_v = vol(U_v), so the set should be S' as in §4.2. Main Theorem 9.2.2 reproduces D(chi) (via Corollary 9.1.8) and L^S. v4 p. 69 is the same. Reach: a stated result (Theorem 4.6.1; through Corollary 9.1.8, the form of Main Theorem 9.2.2). The unfolding gives I = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩∏_v I_v. For v ∉ S' ∪ Σ_p, d_{n,v}(s, χ_v)I_v = L_v(s + 1/2, π_v, χ_v) (§4.2.1), and d_{n,v}(s, χ_{u,v}) = D_v(χ) only at s = m (definition (108): D_v(χ) = d_{n,v}(m, χ_v)). So the identity holds at s = m for sections in I(χ_u, m), the parametrization used in Definition 5.3.2 and Corollary 9.1.8, not for f_s ∈ I(χ, s) with variable s. For v | p, I_v = I_w is given by Theorem 4.3.10, which contains no standard Euler factor and no D_v. So the D_v(χ) (v | p) contained in D(χ) = D^∅(χ) have no counterpart on the right, and L^S (S = S_π, which does not contain p when π_p is unramified) wrongly includes the Euler factors at p. Moreover the unramified computation needs v ∉ S_ram = S_π ∪ S_χ ∪ S_K, and Lemma 4.2.3 is stated for v ∈ S', so S should be S', not S_π. If instead p ∈ S_π, then I_S would include p-adic places with the §4.2.2 value D_v·vol(U_v), which is not what is computed at p. Case for the defence: it is plausible that the intended statement omits the places above p from both D(χ) and L^S (the natural shape for a p-adic L-function, with the modified factor L_p(ord) replacing the Euler factor at p). But the printed formula does not say so, and Corollary 9.1.8 and Main Theorem 9.2.2 reproduce it (with D(χ) and L^S). Independent check: Checked p. 78, p. 47 ((53)), §4.2 (p. 46), Corollary 9.1.8 and Main Theorem 9.2.2 (pp. 144-145). (i) The s-dependence. D_v(chi) = prod_r L_v(2m+n-r, chi^+ eta^r) = d_{n,v}(m, chi_{u,v}) is fixed by m. For f in I(chi,s) with chi = ||·||^m chi_u, the unramified factor is L_v(s+1/2,pi,chi) = L_v(s+m+1/2,pi,chi_u) over d_{n,v}(s,chi) = d_{n,v}(s+m,chi_u). So the printed identity (D(chi) on the left, L^S(s+1/2,pi,chi_u) on the right) can hold only at s = m for sections in I(chi_u,m), which is the parametrization of Definition 5.3.2 and Corollary 9.1.8. (ii) The places above p. D(chi) = D^∅(chi) runs over all finite v, including v|p (108). The factor I_p of Theorem 4.3.10 contains no D_v, and at v|p the section is not unramified. S = S_pi need not contain p (§4.2 even requires p not in S), so L^S wrongly keeps the Euler factor at p. The printed identity is off by prod_{v|p} L_v(m+1/2,pi,chi_u)/D_v(chi), which is not 1 when chi is unramified at p. (iii) At places of S_chi ∪ S_K outside S_pi the sections are those of §4.2.2, with I_v = vol(U_v), so the set should be S' as in §4.2. Main Theorem 9.2.2 reproduces D(chi) (via Corollary 9.1.8) and L^S. v4 p. 69 is the same. Reach: a stated result (Theorem 4.6.1; through Corollary 9.1.8, the form of Main Theorem 9.2.2). - **Error** at §5.1, p. 79, after the definition of Λ_{X,R}, in arXiv v5. The source says `Λ_{X,R} = lim_i R[X/X_i]. This is a compact topological ring.`; it should be `This is a topological ring, compact when R is compact (e.g. R finite over Z_p).`. For a general p-adic ring R (e.g. R = O_{C_p}, or R = Z_p[[T]] with its p-adic topology, both allowed in §5.1) R[X/X_i] ≅ R^{#(X/X_i)} is not compact, and neither is the inverse limit. Defence: compactness is never used. Independent check: Checked p. 79. R is any 'p-adic ring' (p-adic topology). For R = O_{C_p}, allowed since R ⊂ C_p is used throughout, R itself is not compact (its residue field is infinite), and Lambda_{X,R} for X trivial is R. Compactness holds when R is compact, e.g. finite over Z_p, and it is never used. v4 is the same. - **Gap** at §5.3.1, p. 84, paragraph after Definition 5.3.2, in arXiv v5 (it affects the proof). The source says `One obtains a measure normalized at S from an unnormalized measure by multiplying by the appropriate product of local Euler factors at S.`; it should be `Multiplying by chi -> prod_{v in S} D_v(chi) gives a pseudo-measure; it is a measure when the elements 1 - eta^r(varpi_v) q_v^{r-n}[varpi_v] (v in S, 0 <= r <= n-1) are units in Lambda_{X_p}. Otherwise state the Main Theorem with the unnormalized measure (I_S = prod_{v in S} vol(U_v)), or in the localized Iwasawa algebra.`. For v ∈ S (v ∤ p) at which χ is unramified, D_v(χ) = ∏_r (1 − η^r(ϖ_v) q_v^{r−n} χ(ϖ_v))^{-1}, the evaluation at χ of the inverse of an element of the Iwasawa algebra Λ_{X_p}; that element is a unit only if its reductions at all maximal ideals are non-zero, which fails e.g. for r = n−1 when q_v ≡ ±1 (mod p) and the residual image of [ϖ_v] allows η^r(ϖ_v) q_v^{-1}ζ ≡ 1. Defence: the paper mostly uses D^?(χ) as notation. Independent check: Checked p. 84. For v in S with chi unramified at v, D_v(chi) = prod_r (1 - eta^r(varpi_v) q_v^{r-n} chi(varpi_v))^-1 is the inverse of an element of Lambda_{X_p}, and that element is a unit only if 1 - c_r psi([varpi_v]) is nonzero in every residue field. This fails, for example, for r = n-1 when eta^{n-1}(varpi_v) q_v^-1 ≡ 1 mod p. So multiplying by the Euler factors at S gives in general only a pseudo-measure. The reach is wider than 'nothing'. Corollary 9.1.8 is written with the normalized measure (D(chi)·prod_v I_v), and Main Theorem 9.2.2 keeps prod_{v in S} D_v(chi) inside I_S while asserting that L(Eis, phi⊗phi^flat) lies in Lambda_{X_p,R}⊗T. If the measure of Theorem 8.2.2/Corollary 8.2.4 is the unnormalized one (Corollary 8.2.4 does not say which), integrality in those exceptional cases rests on this unproved sentence. v4 p. 82 is the same. Reach: the proof (of Corollary 9.1.8 / Main Theorem 9.2.2 in the exceptional cases). For v ∈ S (v ∤ p) at which χ is unramified, D_v(χ) = ∏_r (1 − η^r(ϖ_v) q_v^{r−n} χ(ϖ_v))^{-1}, the evaluation at χ of the inverse of an element of the Iwasawa algebra Λ_{X_p}; that element is a unit only if its reductions at all maximal ideals are non-zero, which fails e.g. for r = n−1 when q_v ≡ ±1 (mod p) and the residual image of [ϖ_v] allows η^r(ϖ_v) q_v^{-1}ζ ≡ 1. Defence: the paper mostly uses D^?(χ) as notation. Independent check: Checked p. 84. For v in S with chi unramified at v, D_v(chi) = prod_r (1 - eta^r(varpi_v) q_v^{r-n} chi(varpi_v))^-1 is the inverse of an element of Lambda_{X_p}, and that element is a unit only if 1 - c_r psi([varpi_v]) is nonzero in every residue field. This fails, for example, for r = n-1 when eta^{n-1}(varpi_v) q_v^-1 ≡ 1 mod p. So multiplying by the Euler factors at S gives in general only a pseudo-measure. The reach is wider than 'nothing'. Corollary 9.1.8 is written with the normalized measure (D(chi)·prod_v I_v), and Main Theorem 9.2.2 keeps prod_{v in S} D_v(chi) inside I_S while asserting that L(Eis, phi⊗phi^flat) lies in Lambda_{X_p,R}⊗T. If the measure of Theorem 8.2.2/Corollary 8.2.4 is the unnormalized one (Corollary 8.2.4 does not say which), integrality in those exceptional cases rests on this unproved sentence. v4 p. 82 is the same. Reach: the proof (of Corollary 9.1.8 / Main Theorem 9.2.2 in the exceptional cases). - **Gap** at Definition 5.3.2, first condition, p. 84, in arXiv v5. The source says `If v is a finite place outside S – so in particular χ_v is unramified for all χ ∈ Y_H^class – then f_v(χ_v,c) is the unramified vector in I_v(χ_{u,v},m) with f_v(χ_v,c)(1) = 1.`; it should be `If v is a finite place with v ∤ p and v ∉ S, then …; and one must assume that S contains the primes dividing N_0 (and those ramified in K/K^+), so that χ_v is unramified outside S ∪ {p} for all χ ∈ Y_H^class.`. S is defined as the set of primes at which K_4^p, K_3^p (subgroups of G_i(A_f^p)) are not hyperspecial, so p ∉ S and the condition literally applies to v | p, contradicting the fourth condition and the ramified p-adic sections of §4.3. Moreover characters of X_p = X_{p,N_0} may ramify at primes dividing N_0, where K_4^p may well be hyperspecial; then I_v(χ_{u,v},m) has no unramified vector. The 'so in particular' is therefore an extra hypothesis, which in §4.2 is built into the definition of S (S ⊇ S_ram = S_π ∪ S_χ ∪ S_K). Defence: the intended meaning is clear from §4.2. - **Error** at §5.3.1, (113), p. 85 (with Definition 5.3.2, third condition, p. 84), in arXiv v5 (it affects a stated result). The source says `e_κ ∘ ∫_{X_p×T_H(Z_p)} (χ,c) dEis = D^?(χ) · e_κ ∘ res_3 D(κ,m,χ_u) E^holo_{χ_u,c}(m)`; it should be `e_κ ∘ ∫ (χ,c) dEis = D^?(χ) · (∏_{σ∈Σ} B(χ_σ,κ_σ)) · e_κ ∘ res_3 D(κ,m,χ_u) E^holo_{χ_u,c}(m) — or impose B(χ_σ,κ_σ) = 1 in Definition 5.3.2.`. Definition 5.3.2 requires f_σ(χ_σ,c,g) = B(χ_σ,κ_σ) D(κ_σ,m,χ_{u,σ}) J_{m,χ_{u,σ}}(g) with B(χ_σ,κ_σ) ∈ Q̄^× arbitrary, while f^holo of (112) has archimedean components J_{m,χ_{u,σ}} only; hence E_{f(χ,c)} = ∏_σ B(χ_σ,κ_σ) · D(κ,m,χ_u) E^holo, and the 'rewriting' (113) drops the scalar. Defence: B is an algebraic scalar that can be normalised to 1, and §9 uses (113) as printed (effectively B = 1). Independent check: Checked pp. 84-85. Definition 5.3.2 and (107) put an arbitrary B(chi_sigma,kappa_sigma) in Qbar^x into f_sigma, while f^holo of (112) has archimedean components J_{m,chi_u,sigma} only. So E_{f(chi,c)} = prod_sigma B · D(kappa,m,chi_u) E^holo, and the 'rewriting' (113) drops prod B. The mismatch reaches the final formula: I_sigma in Proposition 4.5.6 is computed with f_sigma from (107), which includes B, while Corollary 9.1.8 uses D(kappa,m,chi_0)f^holo, which does not. The constant is algebraic and can be normalized to 1. v4 (5.3.3) is the same. Reach: a stated result (113) as a reformulation of Definition 5.3.2); harmless if B ≡ 1). The subscripts χ_u vs χ and χ_{0,σ} vs χ_{u,σ} are inconsistent within the same display. Also D(κ_σ,m,χ_{u,σ}) is written D(κ_σ,χ_σ) in Corollary 4.4.9. - **Gap** at §6.1.2, (114), p. 87, in arXiv v5. The source says `Then over C there is a natural identification of G(A_f)-modules: H^i_!(Sh(V), ω_κ) = H^i(P_h, K_h; A_0(G) ⊗ W_κ). - **Error** at §6.1.3, p. 88, lines 12–16 (the characters κ_h^±), in arXiv v5 (it affects a stated result). The source says `The action of h = (h_0,(h_σ)) ∈ H_0(C) on Hom_C(∧^d p_h^±, C) is just multiplication by h_0^{∓d} ∏_{σ∈Σ_K} det(h_σ)^{±2a_σ}; this is just the character κ_h^± = (∓d, (κ^±_{h,σ})), κ^±_{h,σ} = (±2a_σ, …, ±2a_σ).`; it should be `h_0^{∓d} ∏_{σ∈Σ_K} det(h_σ)^{±a_σ}, i.e. κ^±_{h,σ} = (±a_σ, …, ±a_σ) (with the paper's sign pattern; the overall sign depends on which of p_h^± is identified with the nilradical of Lie P_0, cf. sourceIssues E90).`. (1) The centre acts trivially on p_h^±. Under (15) (H_0 → G_m × GL(Λ_0^∨), first factor ν), t ∈ R^× ⊂ G(R) maps to (t^2, (t·1_{b_σ})), so the printed character takes the value t^{∓2d}·t^{±2Σ_{σ∈Σ_K} a_σ b_σ} = t^{±2d} ≠ 1, while with a_σ it is t^{∓2d ± 2d} = 1. (2) Direct computation: p_h^± ≅ ⊕_{σ∈Σ} Hom between Λ_{0,σ} (rank a_σ, h acting by h_0 ᵗh_{σc}^{-1}) and Λ^∨_{0,σ} (rank b_σ, h acting by h_σ); the determinant on Hom(Λ_{0,σ}, Λ^∨_{0,σ}) is h_0^{-a_σ b_σ} det(h_σ)^{a_σ} det(h_{σc})^{a_{σc}}, and the product over σ ∈ Σ is h_0^{-d} ∏_{σ∈Σ_K} det(h_σ)^{a_σ}. (3) Modular curve (U(1,1) over imaginary quadratic K, d = 1): the canonical bundle has parallel weight 1 in σ and σc (classical weight 2) and similitude −1, i.e. (−1,(1,1)); the printed formula gives (−1,(2,2)) (weight 4). Defence: κ^D is only used through the intrinsic W_{κ^D} = Hom(∧^d p_h^+, W_{κ^⋆}) in §§6.2–6.5, so the arguments there are unaffected. Independent check: Checked p. 88, with (15) on p. 22, (17) on p. 23 and d = (1/2) sum_{sigma in Sigma_K} a_sigma b_sigma on p. 86. (1) The centre acts trivially on p_h^±. Real scalars t act on Lambda_0^vee by t, with nu(t) = t^2, so under (15) t -> (t^2,(t·1)). The printed character then takes the value t^{∓2d ± 2 sum_{Sigma_K} a_sigma b_sigma} = t^{±2d} ≠ 1; with exponent a_sigma it takes the value 1. (2) Direct computation: h acts on Lambda^vee_{0,sigma} by h_sigma and on Lambda_{0,sigma} by h_0 th_{sigma c}^-1, so the determinant of h on Hom(Lambda_{0,sigma}, Lambda^vee_{0,sigma}) is h_0^{-a_sigma b_sigma} det(h_sigma)^{a_sigma} det(h_{sigma c})^{a_{sigma c}}. The product over the CM type is h_0^-d prod_{Sigma_K} det(h_sigma)^{a_sigma}. So the exponent is ±a_sigma, not ±2a_sigma. The overall sign depends on which of p_h^± is the nilradical (sourceIssues E90). The explicit kappa^D also enters the normalization U^-_{w,j,kappa^D} = |kappa^D'(t_{w,j})|_p U^-_{w,j} in §6.6 (p. 98). Same in v4 and v2. Reach: a stated result (the explicit characters kappa_h^± and kappa^D = kappa* + kappa_h^+). - **Gap** at §2.3, p. 17, construction of P from hermitian pairs, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 15–16 (it affects a stated result). The source says `"Let δ ∈ O be totally imaginary and prime to p, and put ⟨·,·⟩_i = trace_{𝒦/Q} δ⟨·,·⟩_{V_i}. … let h_{i,σ} : C → End_R(V_{i,σ}) be h_{i,σ}(z) = diag(z1_{r_{i,σ}}, z̄1_{s_{i,σ}}). Let Σ = {σ ∈ Σ_𝒦 : p_σ ∈ Σ_p}. … Then P = (B, ∗, O_B, L, 2π√−1⟨·,·⟩, h) is a PEL datum of unitary type"`; it should be `δ must also satisfy a sign condition tied to the CM type Σ: Im σ(δ) > 0 for all σ ∈ Σ if ⟨·,·⟩_{V_i} is 𝒦-linear in the first variable (Im σ(δ) < 0 for all σ ∈ Σ if linear in the second). Such δ exist (weak approximation), so the fix is to choose δ after Σ.`. Positivity axiom of a PEL datum: −√−1 · 2π√−1⟨x, h(√−1)x⟩ = 2π Σ_{σ∈Σ} 2Re(σ(δ) H_σ(x_σ, h(i)x_σ)). With H linear in the first variable: on the r-part (H_σ(x,x) = |x|² > 0, h(i)x = ix) the summand is 2|x|² Im σ(δ); on the s-part (H_σ(x,x) = −|x|², h(i)x = −ix) it is again 2|x|² Im σ(δ). So the form is positive definite iff Im σ(δ) > 0 for every σ ∈ Σ with V_{i,σ} ≠ 0. Σ is determined by the p-adic datum Σ_p and δ only by 'totally imaginary and prime to p', so for a general δ the positivity fails on some V_{i,σ}. The text never states such a condition later (δ reappears in §4.1 only as ⟨·,·⟩_1 = trace δ⟨·,·⟩_V). Defence: the requirement is implicit in the claim that P is a PEL datum and is trivially arranged; alternatively one could flip h_{i,σ} at the offending σ, but that would change the stated relation between (a, b) and (r, s). Independent check: The quote on p. 17 is accurate. δ is only required to be totally imaginary and prime to p, and it is chosen before Σ = {σ : p_σ ∈ Σ_p} is defined. The positivity axiom (p. 14) for the pairing 2π√−1⟨·,·⟩ reads 2π⟨x, h(√−1)x⟩ > 0. On V_i ⊗ R = ⊕_{σ∈Σ} V_{i,σ} we have ⟨x, h(i)x⟩_i = Σ_{σ∈Σ} 2Re(σ(δ)H_σ(x_σ, h_{i,σ}(i)x_σ)). Take H linear in the first variable. On the r-part, h(i)x = ix and H(x,x) = |x|². On the s-part, h(i)x = −ix and H(x,x) = −|x|². In both cases the summand is 2 Im σ(δ)|x|². So positivity holds iff Im σ(δ) > 0 for every σ ∈ Σ with V_{i,σ} ≠ 0 (the reverse sign if H is linear in the second variable). The compatibility ⟨h(z)x, y⟩ = ⟨x, h(z̄)y⟩ holds for every δ, but positivity does not. Replacing δ by −δ, which is allowed, destroys it. Flipping h at the offending σ would contradict the stated equality (a_{σ,i}, b_{σ,i}) = (r_{i,σ}, s_{i,σ}) for σ ∈ Σ. So 'P is a PEL datum' can fail for admissible δ. The fix is trivial: choose δ after Σ with the right signs. Present in v1 (p. 14) and v4 (pp. 15–16). - **Gap** at §2.3, p. 17, construction of P from hermitian pairs, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 15–16 (it affects a stated result). The source says `"Let δ ∈ O be totally imaginary and prime to p, and put ⟨·,·⟩_i = trace_{𝒦/Q} δ⟨·,·⟩_{V_i}. … let h_{i,σ} : C → End_R(V_{i,σ}) be h_{i,σ}(z) = diag(z1_{r_{i,σ}}, z̄1_{s_{i,σ}}). Let Σ = {σ ∈ Σ_𝒦 : p_σ ∈ Σ_p}. … Then P = (B, ∗, O_B, L, 2π√−1⟨·,·⟩, h) is a PEL datum of unitary type"`; it should be `δ must also satisfy a sign condition tied to the CM type Σ: Im σ(δ) > 0 for all σ ∈ Σ if ⟨·,·⟩_{V_i} is 𝒦-linear in the first variable (Im σ(δ) < 0 for all σ ∈ Σ if linear in the second). Such δ exist (weak approximation), so the fix is to choose δ after Σ.`. Positivity axiom of a PEL datum: −√−1 · 2π√−1⟨x, h(√−1)x⟩ = 2π Σ_{σ∈Σ} 2Re(σ(δ) H_σ(x_σ, h(i)x_σ)). With H linear in the first variable: on the r-part (H_σ(x,x) = |x|² > 0, h(i)x = ix) the summand is 2|x|² Im σ(δ); on the s-part (H_σ(x,x) = −|x|², h(i)x = −ix) it is again 2|x|² Im σ(δ). So the form is positive definite iff Im σ(δ) > 0 for every σ ∈ Σ with V_{i,σ} ≠ 0. Σ is determined by the p-adic datum Σ_p and δ only by 'totally imaginary and prime to p', so for a general δ the positivity fails on some V_{i,σ}. The text never states such a condition later (δ reappears in §4.1 only as ⟨·,·⟩_1 = trace δ⟨·,·⟩_V). Defence: the requirement is implicit in the claim that P is a PEL datum and is trivially arranged; alternatively one could flip h_{i,σ} at the offending σ, but that would change the stated relation between (a, b) and (r, s). Independent check: The quote on p. 17 is accurate. δ is only required to be totally imaginary and prime to p, and it is chosen before Σ = {σ : p_σ ∈ Σ_p} is defined. The positivity axiom (p. 14) for the pairing 2π√−1⟨·,·⟩ reads 2π⟨x, h(√−1)x⟩ > 0. On V_i ⊗ R = ⊕_{σ∈Σ} V_{i,σ} we have ⟨x, h(i)x⟩_i = Σ_{σ∈Σ} 2Re(σ(δ)H_σ(x_σ, h_{i,σ}(i)x_σ)). Take H linear in the first variable. On the r-part, h(i)x = ix and H(x,x) = |x|². On the s-part, h(i)x = −ix and H(x,x) = −|x|². In both cases the summand is 2 Im σ(δ)|x|². So positivity holds iff Im σ(δ) > 0 for every σ ∈ Σ with V_{i,σ} ≠ 0 (the reverse sign if H is linear in the second variable). The compatibility ⟨h(z)x, y⟩ = ⟨x, h(z̄)y⟩ holds for every δ, but positivity does not. Replacing δ by −δ, which is allowed, destroys it. Flipping h at the offending σ would contradict the stated equality (a_{σ,i}, b_{σ,i}) = (r_{i,σ}, s_{i,σ}) for σ ∈ Σ. So 'P is a PEL datum' can fail for admissible δ. The fix is trivial: choose δ after Σ with the right signs. Present in v1 (p. 14) and v4 (pp. 15–16). - **Misprint** at §6.1.3, p. 88, 'The identification of G(C) with G_0(C) in 2.6.1 identifies Lie(P_0(C)) with P_h and Lie(H_0(C)) with k_h', versus §2.7.2, p. 28, in arXiv v5. The source says `p. 88: 'identifies Lie(P_0(C)) with P_h' (P_h = p_h^- ⊕ k_h, p. 87); p. 28: 'The identification of G(C) with G_0(C) identifies Lie(P_0(C)) with k ⊕ p^+, and so f corresponds to a holomorphic form if and only if p^- ∗ f = 0.'`; it should be `One convention throughout; §6 consistently uses Lie(P_0(C)) ↔ P_h = p_h^- ⊕ k_h (holomorphic = annihilated by p_h^-, holomorphic tangent space p_h^+, Ω^d ↔ Hom(∧^d p_h^+, C)), so the §2.7.2 phrase 'k ⊕ p^+' is the likely slip.`. The two identifications are incompatible. The sign pattern of κ_h^± on p. 88 (∓d on Hom(∧^d p_h^±,C)) matches the §2.7.2 version: with P_0 = Stab(Λ_0) (§2.7.1), the nilradical of Lie P_0 is Hom(Λ_0^∨, Λ_0)^{sym}, whose ∧^d has character (d, (−a_σ)). Independent check: Checked p. 28 ('identifies Lie(P_0(C)) with k ⊕ p^+, and so f corresponds to a holomorphic form if and only if p^- * f = 0') and p. 87-88 (P_h = p_h^- ⊕ k_h; 'identifies Lie(P_0(C)) with P_h'). The two statements contradict each other. By my computation in sourceIssues E89, the nilradical Hom(Lambda_0^vee, Lambda_0) of Lie P_0 (P_0 = Stab(Lambda_0)) has ∧^d-character (d, (-a_sigma)), so the printed sign pattern of kappa_h^± matches the p. 28 convention, as the first reading says. Which of the two statements is the slip is therefore unclear. Either way it is a local inconsistency. v4 p. 25 and p. 87 are the same. Reach: nothing (sign conventions for kappa_h^±; cf. sourceIssues E89). The source says `Let δ_p = (1, D ᵗβ_w^{-1} β_w^{-1})_{w∈Σ_p} ∈ Q_p^× × ∏_{w∈Σ_p} GL_n(K_w) ≅ G(Q_p) … Then δ̄_p = δ_p^{-1}, δ_p^{-1} conj(G(Z_p)) δ_p = G(Z_p), and δ_p^{-1} Ī^0_{r,V} δ_p = I^0_{r,−V}. For M = D ᵗβ^{-1}β^{-1}: w-component of δ̄_p = D^{-1} ᵗM^{-1} D = D^{-2} β ᵗβ D, which equals M^{-1} = β ᵗβ D^{-1} iff D^2 commutes with β ᵗβ; and δ_p^{-1} ḡ δ_p = ν(g)·β[u ᵗg'^{-1} u^{-1}]β^{-1} with u = ᵗβ D^{-2} ᵗβ^{-1}, which need not normalize ᵗI^0. With D^{-1} in place of D, u = 1. The paper gives no proof ('Then'). Defence: the printed formula is right if D is the matrix of the dual pairing or G acts on row vectors, and whenever β_w is diagonal; the convention for 'the hermitian pairing is given by D' is not specified. The middle identity holds in all cases (δ_p ∈ G(Z_p) when the d_i are p-units). Independent check: Checked p. 90 (D = diag(d_i), d_i in K^+, is the Gram matrix of <·,·>_V in the fixed K-basis) and p. 91. The paper's action convention is fixed: §2.1 (<g(v),g(v')> = nu<v,v'>, <gx,gy> = nu<x,y>) is a left action. With that convention and either Gram convention, t g D gbar = nu D gives (gbar)_w = nu D^-1 t g_w^-1 D in each w-component. For delta_p = (1, M): the w-component of delta_pbar is D^-1 tM^-1 D. With M = D tbeta^-1 beta^-1 this is D^-2 beta tbeta D, which equals M^-1 = beta tbeta D^-1 only if D^2 commutes with beta tbeta. Also delta^-1 gbar delta = nu·beta[u tg'^-1 u^-1]beta^-1 with u = tbeta D^-2 tbeta^-1 in GL_n(O_w), which does not normalize tI^0 in general. With M = D^-1 tbeta^-1 beta^-1 one gets u = 1 and all three identities of (125) hold. beta_w is an arbitrary change of O_w-basis of L_w and D is not scalar, so the printed element fails in general. The fix is one symbol (D -> D^-1), and later arguments use only the three properties, so this is a misprint rather than a gap. The printed formula would be right for a right action on row vectors, but that is not the paper's convention for G_1 on V. v4 (6.2.9) is the same. Reach: nothing (convention-dependent; the later arguments only need an element with the three properties). - **Gap** at §6.2.3, p. 91, lines after the definition of g^†, in arXiv v5. The source says `Given K ⊂ G(A_f) we let K^† be the image of K under †. As a consequence of (125), if K = G(Z_p)K^p, then K^† = G(Z_p)K̄^p`; it should be `K^† = G(Z_p)·{ν(k)^{-1} k̄ : k ∈ K^p}, which equals G(Z_p)K̄^p when K^p contains the scalars ν(k)^{-1}, k ∈ K^p (e.g. principal congruence subgroups); or define K^† := G(Z_p)K̄^p.`. g^† = ν(g)^{-1} δ_p^{-1} ḡ δ_p contains the central factor ν(g)^{-1}. For K^p of Γ_1(N)-type (k ≡ (1 ∗; 0 ∗) mod N), the corresponding entry of ν(k)^{-1}k̄ is ν(k)^{-1}, not ≡ 1 mod N in general, so (K^p)^† ≠ K̄^p. Defence: the level actually matched by g ↦ ḡδ_p (the map used on Shimura varieties) and by the moduli description α ↦ α∘I in Proposition 6.2.4 is K̄^p, so the text is correct with K^† := G(Z_p)K̄^p. The source says `If (π_∞ ⊗_C W_κ)^{K_h} ≠ 0 (for example, if π is holomorphic of type (κ,K)), then ξ_{π,∞}(t) = t^{a(κ)} for t ∈ R^×. / The function g ↦ ||ν(g)||^{-a(κ)} defines a global section of L(κ)^∨`; it should be `With the conventions of §§2.6.3 and 2.7.2 (W_κ = functions on H_0 with right-translation action; forms f with f(gu) = u^{-1}·f(g), i.e. diagonal K_h-invariants), ξ_{π,∞}(t) = t^{−a(κ)}, g ↦ ||ν(g)||^{-a(κ)} is a section of L(κ), and the factors ||ν||^{-a(κ)} in (133), (137), (146), (147) and ||ν||^{a(κ)} in (141) change sign. Alternatively, keep §6 as printed and declare that K_h acts on W_κ contragrediently to §2.7.2.`. Under (15), t ∈ R^× maps to (t^2, (t·1)) ∈ H_0, which lies in B_{H_0} and acts on W_κ by κ(t) = t^{a(κ)} (this is how (116) is designed). A diagonal K_h-invariant in π_∞ ⊗ W_κ then forces ξ_{π,∞}(t)·t^{a(κ)} = 1. Likewise, with sections of L(χ) satisfying s(gu) = χ(u)^{-1}s(g), g ↦ ||ν(g)||^{-a(κ)} is a section of L(ν^{a(κ)}) = L(κ). Defence: §§6.3–6.5 are internally consistent with ξ_{π,∞}(t) = t^{a(κ)} (π^♭ = π^∨ ⊗ ||ν||^{a(κ)}, φ'_i·||ν||^{-a(κ)} ∈ π^∨ in (146)), so this is a sign-convention clash between Part I and §6 rather than a failure of an argument. Independent check: Checked p. 28 (f(gu) = u^-1 f(g), U_inf acting on W_kappa by right translation), (17) and (116), pp. 93-94 and p. 96. A central t in R^x maps to (t^2,(t)) in T_{H_0} and acts on W_kappa by kappa(t) = t^{2kappa_0 + sum kappa_{sigma,j}} = t^{a(kappa)}. A diagonal K_h-invariant in pi_inf ⊗ W_kappa (the §2.7.2 and §6.1.2 identification) therefore forces xi_{pi,inf}(t) = t^-a(kappa), not t^a(kappa). Check with (133): under §2.7.2 conventions [phi(gt),phi'(gt)] = t^-2a [phi,phi'](g), so Z_G(R)-invariance of the integrand needs ||nu||^{+a(kappa)}. §6 is internally consistent with the contragredient convention (xi(t) = t^a, pi^flat = pi^vee ⊗ ||nu||^a, (133), (146)). ### Ellenberg–Venkatesh–Westerland, "Homological stability for Hurwitz spaces and the Cohen-Lenstra conjecture over function fields", Annals of Mathematics 183 (2016), no. 3 (`PAPER-ELLENBERG-VENKATESH-WESTERLAND-16`)

- **Misprint** at Published Annals 2016 version, after Conjecture 1.5, p.733. The source says `equal to 1`; it should be `The reference to delta^± of Theorem 1.2 cannot be literal: these densities have CL masses. Identify the intended Malle/moment normalization before deriving any claim from this sentence.`. Distinct class-group isomorphism events are disjoint and their probabilities cannot each tend to one. Theorem1.2 itself gives c_ell/|Aut A|. The marked set can be used for component orbits only after proving that −I∈Sp(V) makes their Sp-orbit sets identical.`. For V=F3²,A=F3 there are8 surjections but4 sign classes. - **Gap** at Published Annals 2016 version, Theorem 1.2, p.730; §§8.6–8.8 (it affects a stated result). The source says `q≠1(modℓ)`; it should be `The proof supplied in this extraction supports odd q with ell∤q(q−1). Either state those restrictions or supply the missing characteristic2 and characteristicell arguments before claiming the broader written domain.`. The Kummer quadratic parametrization needs odd q; the Hurwitz/torsion comparison and Theorem8.8 exclude characteristicell. This is a supported-domain gap, not a proof that the broader assertion is false. (cc-442dc5) Reclassified to affect a stated result. Theorem 1.2 asserts convergence 'as q → ∞ with q ≢ 1 (mod ℓ)', which includes q = 2^k and q = ℓ^k. §8, however, works under the standing hypothesis 'ℓ an odd prime not dividing q' (§8.6), uses tame A ⋊ Z/2-covers and K(√f), and Theorem 8.8 assumes ℓ ∤ q(q − 1). So the stated limit is established only along odd q prime to ℓ (item 109). ### Esnault–Groechenig, "Rigid connections and F-isocrystals", Acta Mathematica (2020) (`PAPER-ESNAULT-GROECHENIG-20`)

- **Misprint** at Published p. 106, the last display of the introduction; compare §7, p. 148 (it affects a stated result). The source says `An irreducible flat connection (E,∇) with torsion determinant L is called cohomologically rigid, if [(E,∇)] is a reduced isolated point of M_dR(X,L,r). This is equivalent to vanishing of H¹_dR(X,(End(E),∇)) = 0, and hence explains the nomenclature.`; it should be `H¹_dR(X,(End⁰(E),∇)) = 0, the trace-free endomorphisms, as §7 (p. 148) writes it: "Recall that an irreducible connection (E,∇) with determinant L on X over C is called cohomologically rigid if H¹(X,End⁰(E,∇))=0". ("equivalent to vanishing of … = 0" is also one "vanishing" too many.)`. M_dR(X,L,r) is the moduli of connections with the determinant fixed, so its Zariski tangent space at an irreducible point is H¹_dR(X,End⁰(E,∇)) — which is exactly what p. 148 says. In characteristic zero the trace splitting gives End(E) = End⁰(E) ⊕ O_X as flat bundles, so H¹_dR(X,(End(E),∇)) = H¹_dR(X,End⁰(E,∇)) ⊕ H¹_dR(X,(O_X,d)) and the second summand is H¹(X,C), of dimension b₁(X). For every X with b₁(X) > 0 — every curve of positive genus, and every variety the paper is really about — the printed condition therefore holds for no connection at all, and the notion it defines would be empty. Read on the rendered page: the display carries an underlined "End" with no superscript. The source says `It is clear that there is at most one such a∈A_{Z′,r}(S) with this property, since a and b are monic polynomials. … By uniqueness of solutions to the equation a^{p^d}=b in Sym^• Ω¹_{Z′×S/S}[λ], we obtain a∈A_{Z′,r}(S) with the required property.`; it should be `Both claims fail as soon as S is non-reduced, and so does the essential-image half of the statement of Theorem 2.17. The invariant that is canonical is the one the proof has just built: the characteristic polynomial of the Morita-reduced Higgs sheaf π′_*F, which is independent of the splitting because F is unique up to unique isomorphism. Theorem 2.17 should require of M that this reduced invariant equal a, rather than only that M be supported on Z′_a with π′_*M of characteristic polynomial a^{p^d}; the descent of a should be deduced from that canonicity, not from uniqueness of p^d-th roots.`. Sym^• Ω¹_{Z′×S/S}[λ] is a commutative F_p-algebra, so x ↦ x^{p^d} is a ring endomorphism of it, and it is injective only when the algebra is reduced. Witness for the two printed claims (r=2): let k be a field of characteristic p > 0, Z′ an elliptic curve over k with a nowhere-vanishing ω ∈ H⁰(Z′,Ω¹), and S = Spec k[ε]/(ε²). Then a = λ² + εω² and a₀ = λ² are distinct monic elements of A_{Z′,2}(S) with a^{p} = λ^{2p} + ε^pω^{2p} = λ^{2p} = a₀^{p}, so b = λ^{2p} has two monic degree-2 roots. Witness for the statement (r=3, d=1): take a = λ³ + εω²λ and a₀ = λ³, again with a^p = a₀^p. Since a vanishes on the zero section, Z′ ×_k S ⊂ Z′_a, so the D_{Z′}-module M of the constant family (F^*V,∇_can) with V of rank 3 — whose p-curvature is zero — is scheme-theoretically supported on Z′_a, and π′_*M is locally free of rank 3p with characteristic polynomial λ^{3p} = a^{p}. M therefore satisfies every condition on the right-hand side of Theorem 2.17 for this a, while the connection it corresponds to has Hitchin invariant a₀ ≠ a: the asserted equivalence of groupoids fails. Over reduced S the printed argument is correct and nothing changes. The correspondence is applied over non-reduced bases exactly where it matters — the Artinian deformations in the proof of Proposition 3.5, and the divided-power thickenings of Appendix A — so the repair is needed, but no main theorem depends on the defective half: §3 uses the equivalence C_a supplied by [OV, Corollary 2.9] for an OV-admissible a, and the forward assignment (E,∇) ↦ (χ_dR(E,∇),M) is unaffected. The source says `Since there are infinitely many prime numbers p such that there exists a good closed point s∈S (Lemma 5.11), we conclude that the Kodaira–Spencer class vanishes everywhere on X_S.`; it should be `Apply Lemma 5.11 after inverting a non-zero coefficient of gr(∇_S) — equivalently, after shrinking S — which its own proof allows, since the finitely generated ring R₁ ⊂ C chosen there may be enlarged at will and Cassels's theorem then sends the adjoined inverse to a p-adic unit. The good points of Lemma 5.11(c) are closed points of S of pairwise distinct residue characteristics, and such a family need not meet every non-empty open subset of a positive-dimensional arithmetic base: in Spec Z[t] the closed points (p,t), p prime, realise every residue characteristic and all lie in V(t), where the non-zero section t vanishes. The vanishing of a section at all of them therefore does not make it zero. What is true, and is what the proof needs, is this: gr(∇_S) is a section of a coherent sheaf on the integral scheme X_S, so it is non-zero if and only if it is non-zero on the generic fibre; if gr(∇_C) ≠ 0 there is a non-empty open V ⊂ S over which it is non-zero, and a good point inside V contradicts the vanishing established for every good s. The rest of the proof is unaffected: on the reduced fibre X_s the identity gr(∇_s) = ω·id together with nilpotency does force ω = 0. ### Fakhruddin–Khare–Patrikis, "Lifting and automorphy of reducible mod p Galois representations over global fields", Inventiones Mathematicae (2022) (`PAPER-FAKHRUDDIN-KHARE-PATRIKIS-22`)

- **Misprint** at Proof of Lemma 7.1, p. 32 (arXiv v5). - **Misprint** at Forum of Mathematics, Pi 12 (2024), §6.2.1 (Assumptions). Theorem 1.5 for all λ ∈ Z_p^r follows from [AW14, Ths. 4.6 and 5.4], which the paper cites after Theorem 1.5, and Theorem 1.4 needs genericity only at induced parameters (the closure of the λ_k).`. Preserve the direct induced-character proof separately. For the all-integral theorem adjoin the roots in a finite coefficient extension and use the affinoid-Verma annihilator and faithfulness theorems, with explicit faithful scalar-extension comparisons. AW14 allows n=0; this was checked on its page image. The continuation spells out finite-free coefficient descent and the AW14 n=0 application in the central-scalar-descent proofSteps. - **Gap** at §7.1, proof of Theorem 7.2, (7.5)–(7.7), p. 21 (it affects the proof). The source says `(7.5) tr(Frob_z, V(Π,V)) = tr(Frob_z^n, V(Π,𝔳_1)) = Σ_j tr(Frob_z^n, L_j) = Σ_j tr(Frob_1^n, L_j)·tr(m_z^{−n}, L_j). … (7.6) tr(m_z, L_j) = μ(z)^{⟨α,β_j⟩} … 0 = Σ_{z∈k^×} μ(z)^{−2}·tr(Frob_z, V(Π,V)) = Σ_{z∈k^×} μ(z)^{−2}·Σ_j tr(Frob_1^n, L_j)·μ(z)^{⟨α,β_j⟩} = … = (q − 1)·Σ_{j : ⟨α,β_j⟩ ≡ 2 mod (q−1)} tr(Frob_1^n, L_j). (7.7)`; it should be `By (7.6), tr(m_z^{−n}, L_j) = μ(z)^{−n⟨α,β_j⟩}, so constancy of z ↦ tr(Frob_z, V(Π,V)) gives Σ_j A_j ν(z)^{c_j} = const with ν = μ^{−n} and c_j = ⟨α,β_j⟩ ∈ {−2, …, 2}. Pairing with ν^{−2} isolates the highest-root term exactly when ν^2 differs from ν^c for c ∈ {−2, −1, 0, 1}, that is when d = (q − 1)/gcd(n, q − 1) ≥ 5 (always true for n = 1 and q > 5, where the printed argument works up to a sign). For d ≤ 4 another argument is needed, for example reducing a Weil restriction Res_{k_n/k} G′ to G′ over k_n((t)), or choosing χ_k on T(k) = T′(k_n) through a faithful character of k_n^× instead of μ ∘ α.`. Over k_n, Lemma 4.7 applies to Frob_z^n and to the inertia element acting on T^{1/(q^n−1)} by z, which acts on T^{1/(q−1)} by z^n; so the exponent is −n⟨α,β_j⟩, as (7.5) itself records with tr(m_z^{−n}, L_j), but (7.7) substitutes μ(z)^{⟨α,β_j⟩}. The case n ≥ 2 is in scope: after the reduction of Theorem 7.1, G is k-simple, and the tensor induction over the W_k-orbit 𝔳_1, …, 𝔳_n is there precisely to handle n > 1. Example: q = 7, n = 2, G = Res_{F_49/F_7} SL_3. Then ν = μ^{−2} has order 3, and the values of c on 𝔳_1 are 2, 1, 1, 0, 0, −1, −1, −2. Its inverse matrix I − J/4 gives the printed q on cocharacters. With the roots (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (−1, 1, 1) and the printed coroots, the Cartan matrix is [[2, −1, 0], [−1, 2, −1], [0, −2, 2]], of type C_3. ### Gan–Savin, "The Local Langlands Conjecture for G_2", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2023) (`PAPER-GAN-SAVIN-23-B`)

- **Gap** at §3.5, proof of Proposition 3.2, pp. 14–15 (it affects the proof). The source says `One has a projective system (relative to G_2-conjugacy) of centralizer subgroups Z_{G_2}(φ) which are finite of order 3, and thus identified with the component groups S_φ. We denote this projective system of local component groups by S_[φ] and set C_[φ] = Z_{G_2}(S_[φ]): this is a projective system of subgroups of G_2(C) which are simply-connected of type A_2.`; it should be `Restrict this construction to the φ = ι′ ∘ ρ with ρ not self-dual, where Z_{G_2}(φ) = μ_3. For self-dual ρ (S_φ ≅ S_3) a separate parametrisation is needed; Theorem 9.1(i) predicts it: the two characters of S_3 trivial on μ_3 go to the lifts from PGL_3 ⋊ Z/2Z, the 2-dimensional representation to the lift from PD^×.`. Lemma 2.4(i) (p. 9) states S_{ι′_*(φ)} = S_3 when φ ∈ Φ_ds(PGL_3) is self-dual, and its proof (p. 10) says the centraliser in G_2(C) is μ_3 or S_3 according as φ ≇ φ^∨ or φ ≅ φ^∨. Self-dual discrete φ exist for every p: for φ trivial on W_F and 3-dimensional irreducible on SL_2, ι′ ∘ φ is the subregular SL_2 of G_2(C), which the proposition itself names, and its component group is S_3. For such φ, S_[φ] does not have order 3; C_[φ] = Z_{G_2}(S_3) is the fixed group of an outer involution of SL_3(C), isomorphic to SO_3(C), not simply connected of type A_2; and Irr(S_3) has three elements, so the bijection j : Irr(S_[φ]) → Z/3Z and the map η ↦ π_η of (b)–(c) are not defined. The count is right (three members; PAPER-GAN-SAVIN-23's desiderata list π_gen[1], π_deg[1], π_sc[1], indexed by 1, r, ε of S_3, for the subregular unipotent parameter), so the statement is plausible, but the 'natural bijection' of Proposition 3.2 and Main Theorem (vii) is not constructed for these φ. ### Groechenig–Wyss–Ziegler, "Mirror symmetry for moduli spaces of Higgs bundles via p-adic integration", Inventiones Mathematicae (2020) (`PAPER-GROECHENIG-WYSS-ZIEGLER-20`)

- **Error** at §2.5, Definition 2.16(c), p. 525 (it affects the proof). The source says `Since two choices s and s′ of roots of p differ by an element σ of Gal(Q̄/Q), we see that for X, Y ∈ K_0(Var_G/R)[(L^{1/r})_{r≥2}] we have #^{s,χ}_{F_q}(X) = #^{s,χ}_{F_q}(Y) if and only if #^{s′,χ}_{F_q}(X) = #^{s′,χ}_{F_q}(Y). Hence we obtain a well-defined relation #^χ_{F_q}(X) = #^χ_{F_q}(Y)`; it should be `This holds when q = p is a prime not dividing the order m of the values of χ: x^N − p is Eisenstein at every prime of Q(ζ_m) above p, so for each N some σ ∈ Gal(Q̄/Q(ζ_m)) sends s_N to s′_N, and by compactness one σ works for all r. ### Hacon–Witaszek, "On the relative minimal model program for fourfolds in positive and mixed characteristic", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2023) (`PAPER-HACON-WITASZEK-23`)

- **Error** at Lemma 2.2, second paragraph, p.5 of the published version (arXiv v2 Lemma 2.2, p.6) (it affects a stated result). The source says `index of K_X`; it should be `m should be the Cartier index of K_X + S at P, the log index. For the plt surface germ obtained by localising at P, this equals the order of the local class group, and the conclusions then hold.`. Counterexample. Take X = Spec k[x,y,z]/(xy − z²), the A1 surface singularity with char k > 5, S = V(x, z), Δ = S and P the vertex. Then X is Q-factorial, (X, S) is plt and hence dlt, and P is a codimension-one point of the curve S. The minimal resolution (charts (x,z,y) = (u,uv,uv²) and (st²,st,s)) is crepant, so K_X is Cartier and m = 1. But div(x) = 2S and the ideal (x, z) is not principal at P, so S is not Cartier. Since f*S = S′ + E/2, adjunction gives (K_X + S)|_S = K_S + ½P, not K_S. With m = index(K_X + S) = 2 every clause holds. For a threefold example, multiply by A¹. The only other use is Lemma 4.2 (p.16), which needs only that the different of a plt pair with standard coefficients has standard coefficients; that is unaffected. Checked on the page image. - **Error** at §2.1(a), p. 9, with Corollary 9, p. 12, Theorem A/§0.3, p. 3, and §5.2, p. 20 (both versions) (it affects a stated result). The source says `(a) Each θ-twisted conjugacy class of W̃ intersects only finitely many W_a cosets. [Justified by: 'Since the action of θ on V is of finite order, each θ-orbit on Ω is a finite set.']`; it should be `The statement needs a hypothesis: that (1 − θ)Ω is finite — equivalently, that the fibres of Ω → Ω_θ are finite. It holds automatically for θ = id and whenever Ω is finite (for instance G semisimple), but not in general.`. The image in W̃/W_a ≅ Ω of the θ-twisted conjugacy class of w′ is κ(w′) + (1 − θ)Ω, not the θ-orbit of κ(w′), because w ·_θ w′ = w w′ θ(w)^{-1} changes the W_a-coset by ω − θ(ω). Two instances. (i) G = G_m and θ inversion: W̃ = Ω = Z, W_a = 1, all lengths are 0, twisted conjugation sends m to m + 2k, so each of the two classes 2Z and 1 + 2Z meets infinitely many W_a-cosets; every element is of minimal length in its class, so Corollary 9 fails and X_ν is the set of elements of F^× of a fixed parity of valuation, which is not compact. (ii) The case the paper is written for: G = GL_n with the twisted-endoscopy automorphism g ↦ J·(ᵗg)^{-1}·J^{-1} that preserves the standard Iwahori. Then Ω ≅ Z through the valuation of the determinant, θ acts on it by −1, and the twisted class of 1 contains τ^{2k} for every k, where τ generates Ω; all of these have length 0, hence are of minimal length, and all have the same invariants π = (0,0). So again Corollary 9 and the compactness of X_ν fail. The Newton decomposition of Theorem 3 itself is unaffected, and the compactness can be restored by replacing X_ν with a compact core inside one chosen Ω-coset, which the items of this extraction do (see C17 and N20): every minimal element of a Newton fibre is θ-conjugate by an element of Ω into that coset. Lifting a σ-fixed coset to a σ-fixed representative is the vanishing of a nonabelian first cohomology H^1(σ, Ĭ_n ∩ gĬ_ng^{-1}), which is not implied by the abstract pro-p condition: for a finite p-group with an automorphism the twisted classes need not be trivial. What makes it work is that these groups are k̄-points of connected pro-unipotent groups, which is where Lang's theorem applies; the paper itself gives the product decompositions Π_{a∈Φ̆′} X_{α_a+n} × T_n ≅ Ĭ_n that a proof would use, two paragraphs later. ### He, "Cordial elements and dimensions of affine Deligne–Lusztig varieties", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2021) (`PAPER-HE-21`)

- **Gap** at §6.3, p. 14 (published version; the same sentence is in arXiv:2001.03325) (it affects the proof). The source says `By [He15, Theorem 2.27], X_{at^γ}(τ̇) ≠ ∅, where τ ∈ Ω with κ(w) = κ(t^γ) = κ(τ).`; it should be `The basic seed has to be taken from a criterion that does not assume a shrunken alcove — [GHN15, Theorem A] (Corollary 3.6.1 with Theorem 4.4.7), which is stated for every element of W̃ — or proved for a t^γ directly; [He15, Theorem 2.27] cannot be quoted as printed.`. The cited theorem reads (arXiv:1511.01386, Theorem 2.27, the numbering of the published survey, cross-checked through its Theorems 2.28, 2.30 and 2.34, which this paper cites for the results they carry): 'Assume that G is simple. Let w ∈ W̃ such that wσ(a) is contained in a Shrunken Weyl chamber. Then for any basic σ-conjugacy class [b], Ĭ ẇ Ĭ ∩ [b] ≠ ∅ if and only if κ(w) = κ(b) and η_σ(w) is not contained in W_M for any proper standard ς-stable Levi M.' The element it is applied to is the a t^γ produced by Theorem 5.5, and that element is not shrunken whenever γ is not regular: if ⟨γ, α⟩ = 0 for a root α, then every point v of the alcove a t^γ(a) satisfies ⟨v, a(α)⟩ = ⟨u, α⟩ for a point u of the base alcove, so 0 < |⟨v, a(α)⟩| < 1 and v lies in the critical strip of ±a(α). Non-regular γ is the normal case, not an edge case: the proof of Theorem 5.5 introduces K = {s ∈ S; s(γ) = γ} and y′ ∈ W_0^K for exactly this reason, and §6.4 discusses λ_w = nω^∨ for a fundamental coweight ω^∨, where γ lies on the walls. A worked instance in split adjoint type A_2: λ = ω_2^∨, y = 1, x = s_2s_1 give J = ∅, J′ = {s_1}, x′ = s_2, z = s_1, γ = λ, y′ = 1 and a = s_1 ∗ s_2 = s_1s_2; on the base alcove {u < 0, v < 0, u + v > −1} the element w = x t^λ y is outside every critical strip, while a t^γ sends (u,v) to (1−u−v, u), whose second coordinate lies in (−1,0), so a t^γ is not shrunken although both finite parts have full support. The conclusion is not contradicted — [GHN15, Theorem A] is available for every w — but the step as written applies its source outside its hypothesis. - **Gap** at Proposition 5.1 with its proof, p. 8 (both versions) (it affects the proof). The source says `Then the set {μ'; μ' is dominant, μ' + λ' ≥_Z λ} contains a unique minimal element with respect the dominance order ≥_Z. … [proof] The statement is proved.`; it should be `Two steps have to be added: that the set is nonempty, and that it has a minimal element at all.`. What the printed proof establishes is that the set is lower directed: for any two of its elements μ'_1, μ'_2 it produces a dominant μ in the set with μ'_1 ≥_Z μ and μ'_2 ≥_Z μ. Directedness gives uniqueness of a minimal element once one exists, but not existence. Both missing steps are standard: μ' = λ − λ' + NΣ_{α∈Δ}α^∨ is dominant and feasible for N large, which gives nonemptiness; and for a fixed feasible μ'_0 the dominant coweights μ with μ'_0 ≥_Z μ form a finite set, so a minimal element exists. The statement is correct as it stands. The source says `As discussed in [GHN15, §2], the study of the nonemptiness pattern and dimension formula of affine Deligne–Lusztig varieties for an arbitrary reductive group may be reduced to simple and quasi-split groups over F. From now on, we assume that G is simple and quasi-split over F.`; it should be `The reduction must also carry 'of adjoint type', as the cited section does: [GHN15, p. 648] reduces 'to the case where G is quasi-split and semisimple of adjoint type' (§2.2 Reduction to adjoint groups, §2.3, §2.4).`. Adjointness is what makes §5 well defined. §5.2 introduces ρ^∨_J, the dominant coweight with ⟨ρ^∨_J, α_s⟩ = 1 for s ∈ J and 0 otherwise — that is, Σ_{s∈J} ω^∨_s — and §5.4 uses the elements w_1 = x z^{-1} t^{λ_w − ρ^∨_J} y' and w_2 = (y')^{-1} z t^{ρ^∨_J} y of W̃ and the element a t^γ of W̃. These require ρ^∨_J ∈ X_*(T)_{Γ_0}, which fails as soon as that lattice is smaller than the coweight lattice: for G = SL_3, split, X_*(T) is the coroot lattice of A_2, and y = s_1 gives J = {s_1} and ρ^∨_J = ω^∨_1 = (2α^∨_1 + α^∨_2)/3 ∉ X_*(T), so t^{ρ^∨_J} is not an element of W̃ at all. The twisted case shifts γ itself out of the lattice: in unramified simply connected ²A_2, with P^∨/Q^∨ = Z/3 and σ acting by −1, taking λ = 3ρ^∨, x = 1, y = s_1 gives J = {s_1}, σ^{-1}(ρ^∨_J) = ρ^∨_{σ^{-1}(J)} = ω^∨_2, and the class of γ in P^∨/Q^∨ is that of ω^∨_2 − ω^∨_1 ≠ 0, so no W_0-translate of it is a coweight of G. That this is a slip in summarising the reduction, and not a restriction the author intends, is clear from §1.2, which describes W̃ as 'the semidirect product of the coweight lattice with the relative Weyl group' — the coweight lattice being X_*(T) exactly for adjoint groups. Two consequences are worth recording: the cited reduction to adjoint groups holds under char k ∤ |π_1(G_ad)| and, after the authors' erratum, only component by component (see E13), and the descent of Theorem 6.1 from G_ad back to G is not written out. For n = 2 and F imaginary quadratic, the left side of [45, (1.2)] is 16 + 3(a_1 − a_2) + (b_1 − b_2) for λ_τ̃ = (a_1, a_2), λ_τ̃c = (b_1, b_2); its minimum over regular weights is 20, at λ = ((1,0),(1,0)), which is the footnote's ℓ > 20. ### Uwe Jannsen, "Hasse principles for higher-dimensional fields", Annals of Mathematics 183 (2016), no. 1 (`PAPER-JANNSEN-16`)

- **Misprint** at §2, discussion of the weight spectral sequence (2.1), p. 17, and the paragraph before Proposition 2.2, p. 18 (published); same in arXiv v2. The source says `"Moreover, for r > 3, the differentials d_r^{p,q} : E_r^{p,q} → E_r^{p+r,q−r+1} are morphisms between Galois Q_ℓ-representation of different weights (viz., p + 2q and p + 2q − r + 2) and hence vanish, so that E_∞^{p,q} = E_3^{p,q}." … "in the Q_ℓ/Z_ℓ-analogue of (2.1) the differentials d_1^{p,q} will not in general vanish for r ≥ 3."`; it should be `"for r ≥ 3, the differentials … vanish", and "the differentials d_r^{p,q} will not in general vanish for r ≥ 3".`. The weights p + 2q and p + 2q − r + 2 differ exactly when r ≠ 2, so every d_r with r ≥ 3 vanishes, which is what E_∞ = E_3 needs; with only r > 3, d_3 is not covered. In the second sentence the subscript 1 is a slip for r, as the following 'for r ≥ 3' shows. ### Kisin–Madapusi Pera–Shin, "Honda-Tate theory for Shimura varieties", Duke Mathematical Journal (2022) (`PAPER-KISIN-MADAPUSIPERA-SHIN-22`)

- **Misprint** at (1.1.2.2), p.6, in the author PDF https://math.berkeley.edu/~swshin/HT.pdf (41 pp., created 27 January 2021, SHA-256 fd22990b…52db), the named version independently rechecked on 23 September 2026; the published text, Duke Math. J. 171 (2022), 1559–1614, was not collated; the older author version newton2.pdf (18 August 2018) on M. Kisin's page retains the same defect. The source says `"There exists c ∈ G(L) and an integer r ∈ Z_{>0} such that rν_b factors through a cocharacter G_{m,L} → G_L, that c(rν_b)c^{−1} is defined over the fixed field of σ^r on L, and that c b σ(b) σ²(b) ··· σ^r(b) σ^r(c)^{−1} = c(rν_b)(p)c^{−1}."`; it should be `c b σ(b) ··· σ^{r−1}(b) σ^r(c)^{−1} = c(rν_b)(p)c^{−1}.`. The r-th power of bσ is b σ(b) ··· σ^{r−1}(b) σ^r, with r factors. The printed left side contains r+1 factors. For G=G_m, b=p and any c∈L×, its p-adic valuation is r+1, because v(c)=v(σ^r(c)); the right side has valuation r. Thus no choice of c repairs the assertion. J. 171 (2022), 1559–1614, was not collated; the older author version newton2.pdf (18 August 2018) on M. Kisin's page retains the same defect (it affects a stated result). The source says `"Corollary 1.1.15. Let G be an arbitrary connected reductive group over Q_p with a Q_p-rational Levi subgroup M. Let μ: G_m → M be a minuscule cocharacter and [b_M] ∈ B(M)_b such that ([b_M], {μ}) is G-admissible. Then there exists w ∈ W(G, M) := N_G(M)/M such that ([b_M], {w·μ}) is M-admissible." Proof: "(1.1.13) implies that there exists w* ∈ W(G*, M*) such that ([b_{M*}], {w*·μ*}) is M*-admissible."`; it should be `Use the absolute geometric Weyl group W(G,T) for a maximal torus T of M containing a representative of μ, with compatible choices under the inner twisting, rather than N_G(M)/M. Equivalently, some G(Q̄_p)-conjugate μ′ of μ factoring through T makes ([b_M], {μ′}) M-admissible. No Q_p-rationality of μ or of a chosen Weyl representative is asserted.`. The printed statement fails already for split G. Take G = GL_3, M = GL_1 × GL_2 (blocks of sizes 1 and 2), μ = (0,1,0) and b_M = diag(p,1,1), which is basic in M. Then ([b_M], {μ}) is G-admissible: its Newton point (1,0,0) equals the dominant μ̄, and both have κ_G = 1. But κ_M(b_M) = (1,0), while κ_M(μ) = (0,1). Since the blocks have different sizes, N_G(M) = M, so W(G, M) is trivial and no w in it helps. The permutation of the first two coordinates, in W(G, T) = S_3, does. The proof transports to the quasi-split inner form and applies Proposition 1.1.13. That proposition gives w* in the absolute Weyl group W(G*, T*), not in N_{G*}(M*)/M*, so the proof establishes the corrected statement. The only use is in the proof of Corollary 1.1.17, p.13, for G not necessarily quasi-split. It cites "Lemma 1.1.13" (the quasi-split Proposition 1.1.13) in the form w ∈ W(G, T). The corrected Corollary 1.1.15 is exactly what that step needs, so this particular downstream step is repaired; this is not a verification of every later result. Checked on the page images. Noted by the extraction (source discrepancy 2, items N29 and N32), which also verified the Weyl-group computation by machine. J. 171 (2022), 1559–1614, was not collated (it affects the proof). The source says `"Let G′ = G × T, equipped with the symplectic representation V′ = V ⊕ V. Let X′ = X × {h_T}. Then we have (G′, X′) ↪ (G_{V′}, H_{V′}). … Restricting the action of I_{s′_0} to A_T induces a map of Q-groups I_{s′_0} → T, and we consider the composite I_{s′_0} → T → G^ab. By Corollary 2.1.9, I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0} is surjective, so the map I_{s′_0} → G^ab factors through I_{s_0}, as this is true over Q_ℓ for any ℓ ≠ p."`; it should be `Replace G′=G×T by G′=G×_{G^ab}T. This is a connected reductive central-torus extension of G: its kernel is 1×(T∩G^der). The similitude character factors through G^ab, so the two blocks have equal multipliers. Since h^ab is constant on X, X×{h_T} factors through G′. After constructing the lift and its CM factor as in the proof, Corollary 2.1.9 identifies the ℓ-adic groups with Frobenius centralizers. Their projection is surjective and its kernel lies in 1×(T∩G^der), which maps trivially to G^ab. Faithfully flat descent then gives I_s→G^ab. The written proof must include this kernel argument; surjectivity alone is insufficient.`. The direct-product construction is false as written, not merely an unexplained descent: already for G=GSp_2 and a CM maximal torus T, (1,2·1)∈G×T scales the two blocks of ψ⊕ψ by 1 and 4. Thus it is not a symplectic similitude. Independently of that failed Shimura construction, on the proposed direct-product group the composite G×T→T→G^ab is nontrivial on the kernel 1×T of projection to G, so it cannot descend. The original errata's unconditional claim about I_{s′} is replaced by this group-level obstruction, since the proposed Shimura embedding has already failed. In the repaired fibre product, projection to G has central torus kernel, so geometric Frobenius centralizers surject: after splitting off the connected center up to isogeny, centralizing a semisimple element is unchanged on the derived factor. Corollary 2.1.9 then gives surjectivity on the I-groups; over Q_ℓ the kernel is killed by T→G^ab, hence over Q as well. Read Lemma 2.2.8, Corollary 2.1.9 and the preceding lifting construction. This repairs the identified local construction/descent; it is not a global certification of Proposition 2.2.2, whose preceding construction has the related E13 defect. Take G = GL_2, α = e_1 − e_2 and ϖ = (p, 0). The Weyl module V(ϖ) has basis v_0, …, v_p with v_i of weight (p − i, i) and X_α v_i = (p − i + 1) v_{i−1}, so X_α v_1 = p·v_0 = 0 although (p − 1, 1) and (p, 0) are weights. Proposition 4.2.10(2) for general λ ≼ μ, and the equalities with l_α in (4.2.12), Proposition 4.2.13, Remark 4.2.16 and Corollary 4.2.19, rest on the printed step and are not established by it in characteristic p. The results used later need only k_α = j_α. ### Klevdal–Patrikis, "Compatibility of canonical ℓ-adic local systems on adjoint Shimura varieties", Inventiones Mathematicae (2025) (`PAPER-KLEVDAL-PATRIKIS-25`)

- **Gap** at Journal §2 p312, after Lemma2.1; v2 §2 p8 (it affects the proof). The source says `There exists an open (dense) immersion`; it should be `Add quasi-projectivity of X_F, or make the existence of the stated smooth projective SNC compactification an explicit hypothesis as v1 did.`. The preceding hypothesis is only smooth geometrically connected finite type. An open subscheme of a projective scheme is quasi-projective, whereas smooth proper nonprojective varieties exist (for example the split smooth complete toric threefolds of Fujino–Payne, https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0510679). A proper open immersion into a projective compactification would make such a variety projective. Shimura varieties here are quasi-projective, so this does not change that application. FIMR's Proposition 5.2 needs (5.6) for every ideal d. §3 bounds only the part coprime to F for m coprime to F and to all σ(m). The missing cases are easy, as above, but the paper states (2.5) in general without them. - **Gap** at Proof of Lemma 3.2, (3.16), p.13 (arXiv v1). The source says `"By Lemma 3.1 we conclude that for all A > 0 and ǫ > 0, |{β ∈ M : |β^{(i)}| ≤ x^{1/n}, g₁ > A}| ≪_ǫ x^{(n−1)/n+ǫ}A^{−1/2+1/ord(σ)}."`; it should be `"By the proof of Lemma 3.1 (summing the bound x^{r/n}/g^{r/n} over squarefull g > A, and passing from M′ to M as in (3.22))". Lemma 3.1 as stated controls the radical g₀ > Z, not the squarefull part g₁ > A. Since Σ_{g>A, g squarefull}g^{−r/n} ≪ A^{1/2−r/n} with r/n = 1 − 1/ord(σ), the proof gives exactly A^{−1/2+1/ord(σ)}.`. A squarefull integer g₁ > A can have a tiny radical (for example a large power of 2), so g₁ > A does not give g₀ > A^c for any c > 0, and the statement of Lemma 3.1 does not apply. The exponent −1/2 + 1/ord(σ) written in (3.16) is what summing over g₁ > A yields. The paper also passes from M′ to M silently. The conclusion of Lemma 3.2 is unaffected. Recorded as `PAPER-KOYMANS-MILOVIC-21/E4`; looked for an existing correction in: arXiv 1809.09597: only v1 (25 September 2018, 23 pages) exists; Duke Mathematical Journal 170 (2021), 1723–1755 (10.1215/00127094-2020-0068): the published version (33 pages in print) was not accessible (Project Euclid blocks scripted access), so these issues are recorded against arXiv v1 and may have been corrected in print; Crossref metadata for 10.1215/00127094-2020-0068: no update or correction relation.
- **Misprint** at Lemma 4.1 (P3), p.20, and its verification, p.21 (arXiv v1). The source says `"(P3) for all non-zero w ∈ O_K, if z₁, z₂ ∈ O_K satisfy z₁ ≡ z₂ mod N(w), then we have γ(w, z₁) = γ(w, z₂); moreover, if |N(w)| is not squarefull in ℤ, then Σ_{ξ mod w} γ(w, ξ) = 0."`; it should be `Quantify over w ∈ S_f (the domain of γ) and sum over ξ mod N(w): "if |N(w)| is not squarefull, then Σ_{ξ mod N(w)} γ(w, ξ) = 0". The verification needs the degree-one prime p with p ∥ N(β) to be unramified. That holds for w ∈ S_f, since f = (F) contains D_K.`. γ(w, ·) is periodic modulo N(w), not modulo w: φ(ξ, β) = (ξ/ϕ(β)) with ϕ(β) = ∏_{σ∈S}σ(β)σ^{−1}(β). So "Σ_{ξ mod w}" is not well defined, and the verification itself sums modulo N(β). For a ramified degree-one prime all conjugates σ(p) coincide, and ∏σ(p)σ^{−1}(p) = p^{2|S|} is a square, so the argument needs p unramified. Recorded as `PAPER-KOYMANS-MILOVIC-21/E5`; looked for an existing correction in: arXiv 1809.09597: only v1 (25 September 2018, 23 pages) exists; Duke Mathematical Journal 170 (2021), 1723–1755 (10.1215/00127094-2020-0068): the published version (33 pages in print) was not accessible (Project Euclid blocks scripted access), so these issues are recorded against arXiv v1 and may have been corrected in print; Crossref metadata for 10.1215/00127094-2020-0068: no update or correction relation.
