### Land–Mathew–Meier–Tamme, "Purity in chromatically localized K-theory", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2024) (`PAPER-LAND-MATHEW-MEIER-ETAL-24`)

- **Misprint** at §4.5, the paragraph introducing Corollary 4.31, last sentence (page 25 of the arXiv v5 PDF); the LaTeX source has \Cref{remark:tstructure} at line 1484 of Purity-in-K-theory.tex. The source says `For another proof of this result, cf. ??.`; it should be `the cross-reference should resolve to Proposition 3.12`. The label remark:tstructure is never defined anywhere in the source: the only labels containing "tstructure" are prop:tstructure on Proposition 3.12, the alternative proof due to Ishan Levy that §3.3 introduces with the words "an alternative proof of the implication (i) ⇒ (ii) in Proposition 3.6". A mechanical check of the source found this to be the only undefined \ref or \Cref among all cross-references, and the text of the content streams of the v5 PDF prints the sentence literally as "For another proof of this result, cf. ??.". The intended target is unambiguous: Proposition 3.12 states in its own proof that it reproves L_{T(i)}K^add(𝒞) ≃ L_{T(i)}K(𝒞) for i ≥ 2, "this fact is also proved as Corollary 4.31 below", so the two statements point at each other and only one of the two pointers resolves. Recorded as `PAPER-LAND-MATHEW-MEIER-ETAL-24/E1`; looked for an existing correction in: arXiv:2001.10425, all five versions listed on the abstract page; v5 of 18 December 2023 is the latest and is described there as the accepted version, and no erratum is announced; the published article at https://www.ams.org/jams/2024-37-04/S0894-0347-2024-01043-X/, which is paywalled and returned HTTP 403, so it is not known whether copy-editing removed this; the publication lists on the home pages of Akhil Mathew and Lennart Meier, which link only to the arXiv version and record no corrigendum.
- **Misprint** at Corollary 4.34, first sentence (page 26 of the arXiv v5 PDF); line 1578 of Purity-in-K-theory.tex. The source says `Let R be any ring spectrum, and let G be any group, and let 𝒪_𝒞(G) be as in Proposition 4.33.`; it should be `𝒪_𝒞(G) should read 𝒪_𝒞yc(G)`. Proposition 4.33 defines 𝒪_𝒞yc(G), written \mathcal{O}_{\mathscr{Cyc}}(G), and the assembly map displayed inside Corollary 4.34 itself is indexed by 𝒪_𝒞yc(G); only the introducing sentence writes \mathscr{C} in place of \mathscr{Cyc}, so the corollary names a symbol that the proposition it refers to does not define. The clash is with §4 alone: §1 separately introduces 𝒪_𝒞(G) for the same orbit category before Corollary F, and the two sections were evidently written with different notations. The source says `Let τ be a 3-generic type with lowest alcove presentation (s, µ) and let 𝔐̄ ∈ Y^{[0,h],τ}(F′) be semisimple of shape w̃ = (w̃_j) ∈ W̃^∨. … Then W?(ρ̄, τ) … = {σ^{(s,µ+η)}_{(ω,a)} : (ω, a) ∈ Σ_{w̃^*}}`; it should be `Add the hypothesis w̃ ∈ Adm^∨(η) (e.g. 𝔐̄ ∈ Y^{η,τ}(F′)), or more generally w̃* ∈ W̲_a t_η as Corollary 2.3.11 requires. An arbitrary X⁰(T̲)-twist is not enough, because it changes the central character of W?(ρ̄) but not Σ_{w̃*}.`. The proof invokes Corollary 2.3.11, which requires w̃^* ∈ W̲_a t_η. For other shapes the statement fails. Take f = 1, s = 1, μ 4-deep, and the semisimple Kisin module with A = v^{(1,0,0)} (height ≤ 1, shape t_{(1,0,0)}). Then ρ̄ = T^*_dd(𝔐̄) is 3-generic with ρ̄|_{I_K} ≅ τ̄(1, μ+(1,0,0)+η). The central character of W?(ρ̄) is that of F(μ+(1,0,0)), which differs from that of JH(σ̄(τ)) = JH(R̄_1(μ+η)) (F(μ+1̲)) by N(x)^2 ≠ 1, so W?(ρ̄,τ) = ∅. But Σ_{t_{ε_1}} = Σ_0 ∩ t_{ε_1}(r(Σ_0)) = {(ε_2,1), (ε_1,0), (ε_1+ε_2,0), (ε_1,1)} ≠ ∅, so the right-hand side is nonempty. Defence: the paper only ever uses shapes in Adm^∨(η), Table 2 lists only Adm(η), and the surrounding text (§3.4 introduction, Prop. 3.4.4) makes the intended scope clear. Independent check: Quote checked on p. 35. The hypothesis allows any semisimple 𝔐̄ ∈ Y^{[0,h],τ}(F′) of shape w̃ ∈ W̲̃^∨. The proof is 'follows from Corollary 2.3.11 and Proposition 3.4.1', but Corollary 2.3.11 requires w̃ ∈ W̲_a t_η. I rechecked the counterexample. Take f = 1, s = 1, μ deep, A = v^(1,0,0) = diag(v,1,1). This matrix is in Mat_3(F[[v]]) and upper triangular mod v, so by [LLHLM18, Prop. 2.13, Lemma 2.14] it defines 𝔐̄ ∈ Y^{[0,h],τ}(F) for h ≥ 1, semisimple of shape t_(1,0,0), with w̃* = t_(1,0,0). By Prop. 3.4.1 and Def. 2.3.6, V(ρ̄|_{I_K}) = R_1(μ+η+(1,0,0)), which is 3-generic for μ deep. All Jordan–Hölder factors of R̄_w(λ) have the central character given by λ restricted to Z, and W?(ρ̄) = R(JH(V(ρ̄|_{I_K}))) with R shifting the central character by a fixed amount. Compare the admissible shape t_1̲ (Table 2, 'Id' row, 6 weights), where V = R_1(μ+η+(1,1,1)) and the intersection is nonempty, so the central characters match there. For t_(1,0,0) the central character of W?(ρ̄) differs from that case by x ↦ x², which is nontrivial because p > 3. Hence W?(ρ̄,τ) = ∅. But Σ_{t_(1,0,0)} = {(ε1,0), (ε1,1), (ε2,1), (ε1+ε2,0)} ≠ ∅ (recomputed; W̃ acts through W̃^der). The same failure occurs inside Adm(η)X⁰(T). For example, A = v²·Id has shape t_(2,2,2), and Σ_{t_(2,2,2)} = Σ_{Id} has 6 elements. But ρ̄|_{I_K} is the t_1̲ case twisted by a character that changes the central character by x³ ≠ 1, so the left side is again empty. The reader's weaker fix 'w̃* ∈ W̲_a t_η X⁰(T̲)' therefore does not suffice. The applications (Prop. 3.4.4, Lemma 3.5.4, proofs of Lemma 3.5.9 and Thm 3.5.3) all use shapes in Adm^∨(η). By Remark 3.4.3 these have w̃* ∈ Adm(η) ⊂ W̲_a t_η, so no result downstream is affected. Versions: identical in v3 and v4 (p. 27). - **Misprint** at §3.5.1, Definition 3.5.1(2), published p. 37; arXiv v4 p. 28. The source says `(2) If M_∞(R_1(µ)) is nonzero, then ρ̄_ṽ has a semistable lift of type τ_ṽ(1, µ_ṽ) for all ṽ ∈ S.`; it should be `'If M_∞(R_1(μ)°) is nonzero for an O-lattice R_1(μ)° ⊂ R_1(μ), then each ρ̄_ṽ has a potentially semistable lift of Hodge type η_ṽ and inertial type τ_ṽ(1, μ_ṽ).'`. M_∞ is defined on Rep_K(O) (finitely generated O-modules), and R_1(μ) is an E-representation, so M_∞(R_1(μ)) is undefined. By exactness and p-torsion-freeness (axiom (1)), nonvanishing does not depend on the lattice. 'Semistable lift of type τ(1,μ)' must mean potentially semistable (semistable over a tame extension) with the Hodge type (2,1,0), which is left implicit. This is the input to [Enn, Axiom (WE)] in Proposition 3.5.6. Defence: the conventions are standard and the intended axiom is clear. - **Gap** at Proposition 4.1.1 and its proof, and the phrase 'directed acyclic graph Γ(M)', published p. 76; arXiv v4 pp. 57–58. The source says `By replacing σ by σ′ repeatedly, we can assume, without loss of generality, that σ′ does not point to σ for all σ′ ∈ JH(N). … If M is multiplicity free, we can attach a directed acyclic graph Γ(M)`; it should be `(i) State and prove that Γ(M) is acyclic: if σ₁ → ⋯ → σ_k → σ₁ were a cycle, take N minimal with σ₁ ∈ JH(N) and N′ ⊂ N maximal; then σ_k ∈ JH(N′) and closedness of JH(N′) forces σ₁ ∈ JH(N′), a contradiction. (ii) Add injectivity of N ↦ JH(N): for multiplicity-free M, JH(N₁ ∩ N₂) = JH(N₁) ∩ JH(N₂), so JH(N₁) = JH(N₂) implies N₁ ∩ N₂ = N₁ = N₂.`. The repeated-replacement step terminates only if there is no directed cycle. Acyclicity is asserted afterwards ('directed acyclic graph') without proof, and it is used again in the proof of Theorem 4.2.7(3), condition (2). The proof shows only that N ↦ JH(N) lands in closed sets and is surjective; injectivity is not addressed. In the paper's defence, both facts are elementary, and the fixes above use only what the proof already establishes. For G of type A (here λ+η ≡ w(η)+pν with ν ≠ 0 weakly decreasing), this gives ⟨λ,α0^∨⟩ ⩾ 2(p−h+1) ⩾ 2(h−1), contradicting ⟨ω_κ,α0^∨⟩ < 2(h−1). For GL3 with p ⩾ 5 one may instead note that ⟨ω_κ+η,α0^∨⟩ ⩽ 3+2 ⩽ p, so ω_κ lies in the closure of C0, which meets W_p·0 only in X⁰(T); then apply the linkage principle.`. The lemma assumes only p ≥ 2(h−1), and for p ∈ {2h−2, 2h−1} (e.g. h = 3, p = 5) one has 2(h−1) > p−2. For h = 3, p = 5 and ω_κ = (3,0,0), ⟨ω_κ, α^∨⟩ ≤ 3 < 4 for all positive coroots but ⟨ω_κ+ρ, α₀^∨⟩ = 5 = p, so ω_κ is on the upper wall and not in the lower alcove. For h ≥ 4, even p ≥ 2h does not put ω_κ in the lowest alcove, since that needs ⟨ω_κ, α₀^∨⟩ ≤ p−h. In the paper's defence, the conclusion (no extensions with characters) is true under the stated hypotheses by the argument above, and the paper only applies the lemma to GL₃ with p ≥ 5 and large genericity. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 83 (page image). §4.2.1 works with a general G of Coxeter number h (p. 79), and Lemma 4.2.4 assumes only p ⩾ 2(h−1). Alcoves are open (p. 9: connected components of the complement of the hyperplanes), and C0 is 'the p-restricted lower alcove' (p. 11). p-bounded means ⟨κ,α^∨⟩ < 2(h−1)p (p. 81), so ⟨ω_κ,α^∨⟩ ⩽ 2h−3. For GL3 (h = 3) with p = 5, which is allowed by the lemma and by p > 3 (§1.4), 2(h−1) = 4 > p−2 = 3. Take κ = pω_κ with ω_κ = (3,0,0). It is p-bounded (⟨κ,α0^∨⟩ = 15 < 20), but ⟨ω_κ+η,α0^∨⟩ = 5 = p, so ω_κ lies on the wall H_{α0,1} and not in C0. For general h, lying in C0 needs ⟨ω_κ,α0^∨⟩ ⩽ p−h, i.e. p ⩾ 3h−3. The conclusion (4.8) is still true in type A, the only case the paper uses. Suppose Ext¹_G(L(ω_κ),L(ω)) ≠ 0 with ω ∈ X⁰(T). Then λ := ω_κ−ω is dominant, nonzero and in W_p·0 (mod X⁰). Write λ+η ≡ w(η)+pν with ν a nonzero element of the root lattice. Dominance of λ+η and p > h−1 force ν to be weakly decreasing, so ν1−νn ⩾ 2 and ⟨λ,α0^∨⟩ ⩾ 2p−2(h−1) ⩾ 2(h−1). This contradicts ⟨ω_κ,α0^∨⟩ < 2(h−1). So a false intermediate claim sits in the proof of a true lemma. The lemma is only applied under large genericity, where p is large. Versions: the same sentence is in v3 and v4 (v4 p. 62); v2 has the analogous '< 2(n−1) ⩽ p−2'. - **Error** at Proposition 4.2.9, published p. 91; arXiv v4 p. 67 (it affects a stated result). The source says `Then Ext¹_G(L(θ), L(λ)) is at most one-dimensional, and it is one-dimensional if and only if λ and θ are linked and lie in adjacent alcoves (that is, there exists i₀ ∈ 𝒥 such that λ_i = θ_i for all i ≠ i₀ and λ_{i₀} and θ_{i₀} lie in different alcoves sharing a face).`; it should be `Replace 'lie in different alcoves sharing a face' by the actual Ext¹ pattern (as in [And87, §4.1] and Table 6). In Table 5 labels the nonzero pairs among {A,…,G} are A–B, A–E, A–F, B–C, B–D, C–E, C–F, D–E, D–F, E–G, F–G. Alternatively, state only what is used: Ext¹ ≠ 0 forces λ_i = θ_i for i ≠ i₀, and dim Ext¹ ≤ 1.`. Counterexample from the paper's own results. Take f = 1 and λ 6-deep in A, and let θ := w̃_E·λ = (12)t_{α₂}·λ, which lies in E and is 6-deep. By Lemma 4.2.6's proof and Table 5 (row E), L(θ) is a summand of gr₁Q₁(λ). By (4.8) (ξ = 0), Q₁(λ) is injective among p-bounded modules, so Ext¹_G(L(θ), L(λ)) ≅ Hom_G(L(θ), gr₁Q₁(λ)) ≠ 0. But A ⊂ (0,p)³ and E ⊂ (0,p)×(p,2p)×(2p,3p) (pairings with α₁^∨, α₂^∨, α₀^∨) share no face, not even a vertex. Table 6 likewise draws arrows A–E, A–F, C–F and D–E between non-adjacent alcoves. In the paper's defence, the proof of Proposition 4.2.12 (p. 94) uses the correct pattern ('λ_{i₀} ∈ D ⇒ θ_{i₀} ∈ E or F; λ_{i₀} ∈ F ⇒ θ_{i₀} ∈ C, D or G', matching Table 6), and the other uses (uniqueness of M, existence of i₀) only need dim ≤ 1 and the Künneth reduction, so the downstream results are unaffected. Independent check: Statement checked on p. 91. Encode an alcove by (⌊⟨x+η,α1^∨⟩/p⌋, ⌊⟨x+η,α2^∨⟩/p⌋, ⌊⟨x+η,α0^∨⟩/p⌋). Table 5 and Table 6 then give: A = (0,0,0), B = (0,0,1), {C,D} = {(1,0,1),(0,1,1)}, {E,F} = {(1,0,2),(0,1,2)}, G = (1,1,2). With Table 6's own weights, C = (1,0,1), D = (0,1,1), E = (1,0,2), F = (0,1,2); Table 5's permutation convention swaps the letters but not the geometry. Two of these alcoves share a face iff their triples differ in exactly one entry by 1. So A shares a face only with B, and A–E, A–F, C–F and D–E are non-adjacent pairs. The closures of A and E are disjoint (α0-pairings in (0,p) and (2p,3p)). The paper itself gives nonzero Ext¹ for these pairs. On p. 93, 'gr₁Q₁(λ⁰_{i₀}) is the direct sum of three irreducible modules in alcoves … B, E, and F if λ⁰_{i₀} is in alcove A'. Table 6 (second diagram) puts A = L(μ) in the socle of V(μ^op+pη′) ⊂ Q₁(μ) with E and F in the next layer, and the first diagram has edges A–E, A–F, C–F and D–E. Since Q₁(λ) has simple socle L(λ), each L(θ) ⊂ gr₁Q₁(λ) gives a nonsplit extension, so Ext¹_G(L(θ),L(λ)) ≠ 0. This holds for 6-deep λ ∈ A and θ = w̃_E·λ ∈ E, so the 'only if' direction is false. Every face-sharing pair in {A,…,G} is an edge of Table 6, so the 'if' direction and dim ⩽ 1 are not contradicted. The proof of Proposition 4.2.12 (p. 94) cites 4.2.9 for 'λ_{i₀} in D (resp. F) ⇒ θ_{i₀} in E or F (resp. C, D, or G)'. That is the Table 6 pattern, not face-sharing (D shares a face with only one of E, F, and F none with C), so the downstream arguments are unaffected. The source says `Let τ'_S be τ_S(s(w')^{−1}, μ + s(w̃')^{−1}(0)) … Then M_∞(V) is a cyclic R_∞(τ'_S)-module by Lemma 5.1.3. / If we change the type τ_S so that w̃_i^* is replaced by w̃'_i, but w̃_{i'}^* are unchanged for i' ≠ i, there is still a surjection σ̄(τ_S)^σ ↠ V by (5.5) and Theorem 4.1.9.`; it should be `Either assume τ_S is 15-generic in Theorem 5.1.1 (and propagate this to §5.2–§5.3), or show that Theorem 4.1.9 and Proposition 4.3.7 hold for the 11-generic auxiliary types σ(τ′_S) used in Lemmas 5.1.4–5.1.5.`. τ_S has lowest-alcove parameter μ + s(w̃^*)^{−1}(0) − η and τ'_S has μ + s(w̃')^{−1}(0) − η; their difference s((w̃')^{−1}(0) − (w̃^*)^{−1}(0)) pairs with coroots by up to 2 in the cases actually used. Computed: for w̃^* = α and the triple (ε1−ε2, 0, ε2−ε1), (5.5) forces w̃' = γ^+α; in the n = 0 base case with w̃^* = id and σ_i = (ε1,1), the only admissible w̃' are γ^+β, βγ^+, βγ^+β; in both situations the translation parts differ by (1,2,0) or (1,−1,0), of spread 2. So τ'_S may be only (13−2)-generic. Lemma 5.1.3 uses Proposition 4.3.7 and Theorem 4.1.9 for σ(τ'_S), both stated for 13-generic representations, and the proof of Theorem 4.1.9 through Prop. 4.3.7 needs 13 to produce an auxiliary 10-generic ρ̄ (13 − 3). Defence: the constant 13 may have slack, and ρ̄_S is already 10-generic here; but the paper does not address the genericity of τ'_S at all. Independent check: Quotations checked on pp. 113–114. The auxiliary type τ′_S = τ(s(w′)^{−1}, μ+s(w̃′)^{−1}(0)) has lowest alcove parameter shifted from that of τ_S by δ = s((w̃′)^{−1}(0)−(w̃*)^{−1}(0)). This δ lies in the root lattice mod X⁰, because Adm(η) ⊂ t_ηW_a and η ≡ η′ = α0 mod X⁰. A nonzero element of the A2 root lattice pairs with some coroot to absolute value at least 2. So whenever the parameter moves, a 13-generic τ_S only guarantees that τ′_S is 11-generic (take μ exactly 13-deep on the relevant wall). The parameter does move in cases the proof needs. Example: in the n = 0 case of Lemma 5.1.4 with w̃*_i = id and σ_i = (ε1,1), a finite w′ of length ⩾ 2 cannot work, because (ε1,1) ∈ w′^{−1}(Σ0) forces w′(ε1) ∈ {0,ε1,ε2} ∩ Wε1 = {ε1}, hence w′ ∈ {1,β}. So w̃′ has a nonzero translation part mod X⁰. The readers' enumeration (checked by rerunning it and against the definitions on pp. 18–20, including that W̃ acts only on the first factor of Λ_W×A) gives γβ, βγ, βγβ with shift of spread 2, and for (5.5) with w̃* = α it forces γα with spread 2. Lemma 5.1.3 for τ′_S uses Proposition 4.3.7 and Theorem 4.1.9 for σ(τ′_S). Both are stated for 13-generic R, and their proofs need 13 − 3 = 10-generic auxiliary ρ̄ to exist (p. 101, via Proposition 3.4.5). The paper never addresses the genericity of τ′_S. Salvaging part of this with the given 10-generic ρ̄_S is possible for Proposition 4.3.7 but not obviously for Theorem 4.1.9. - **Gap** at §5.1, proofs of Lemma 5.1.4 (n = 0) and Lemma 5.1.5, published pp. 113–114; arXiv v4 pp. 85–86 (it affects the proof). The source says `there is still a surjection σ̄(τ_S)^σ ↠ V by (5.5) and Theorem 4.1.9.`; it should be `V is defined as a quotient of σ̄(τ_S)^σ. To apply Lemma 5.1.3 (resp. the induction) for another type τ'_S one needs V to be isomorphic, as a G-module, to a quotient of σ̄(τ'_S)^σ. Theorem 4.1.9 and Proposition 4.1.1 only give that the quotient of σ̄(τ'_S)^σ with Jordan–Hölder set JH(V) exists and has the same pointing graph. An argument that the two multiplicity-free modules (same cosocle, constituents and extension graph, coming from lattices in different Deligne–Lusztig representations) are isomorphic is missing.`. Two multiplicity-free modules with the same constituents and the same Γ need not be isomorphic in general (e.g. a 'diamond' σ over κ1 ⊕ κ2 over κ carries a gluing parameter when the relevant Yoneda products in Ext^2 vanish). So 'by Theorem 4.1.9' does not suffice as stated. Defence: the claim is very plausibly true for these specific modules, for instance via multiplicity-one statements in projective envelopes as in Lemma 4.2.14, or via the Weyl-module embedding of §4.2.4. EGS15 handles the analogous GL2 step at the level of patched modules (proof of their Lemma 10.1.12). Independent check: Checked on pp. 111–114. Lemma 5.1.3 (applied to τ′_S in the n = 0 case of Lemma 5.1.4) and the induction after the type change in Lemma 5.1.5 both need V itself to be a quotient of σ̄(τ′_S)^σ. V is given as a quotient of σ̄(τ_S)^σ. Theorem 4.1.9 with Propositions 4.1.1–4.1.2 yields only a quotient V″ of σ̄(τ′_S)^σ with JH(V″) = JH(V) and the same graph Γ. I found nothing in the paper showing that a multiplicity-free module with cosocle σ is determined by JH and Γ; a search for such a uniqueness statement came up empty. In general it is not: in a 'diamond' σ over κ1⊕κ2 over κ with vanishing Yoneda products in Ext², the two extension classes glue with a free parameter. Lemma 3.6.2 does not rescue the argument either. It makes M∞(V) ≅ R∞/I(V) depend only on JH(V) once M∞(V) is cyclic, but cyclicity is the point at issue, and two MCM modules with the same reduced support need not both be cyclic. For f = 1 the small V's in the n = 0 case are determined (Ext¹ is one-dimensional), so the problem arises from f ⩾ 2 or larger V. EGS15 (Lemma 10.1.12) identify the lattice explicitly for the analogous GL2 step, but only in length 2. The claim is very plausible, but the justification 'by (5.5) and Theorem 4.1.9' is incomplete. The standing assumption (p. 111: 'we assume that the weight σ satisfies the conditions of Theorem 5.1.1', and p. 112) is that V is a quotient of σ̄(τ_S)^σ with σ satisfying (5.1), i.e. a_i = 1 whenever ℓ(w̃_i^*) ⩽ 1 (Proposition 2.1.3(1): Tr_μ(ω,a) lies in alcove π^{−1}(a)). - **Gap** at Proof of Lemma 2.1, p.9 (published version) (it affects the proof). The source says `"Let t_i := Σ_{v|w_i} x_v. Then since |x_{v_{i,j}} − x_{v_{i,j′}}| ≤ 2, we have x_{v_{i,j}} = t_i/k_i + O_k(1). We have Σ_i t_i = 0, since u, α_r, and α_s all have norm 1. Thus Σ_{i,j} max(x_{v_{i,j}}, 0) = Σ_i t_i + O_k(1) = O_k(1)."`; it should be `Normalise the α_i first. Their relative norms η_i = Nm_{L/K}(α_i) are units of K, since the ideal (α_i) has trivial relative norm. Pigeonhole the α_i by the class of η_i in O_K^*/(O_K^*)^d, which has at most d^{[K:ℚ]} = O_{[L:ℚ]}(1) classes. Within one class, η_i = η₀e_i^d with e_i ∈ O_K^*; replace α_i by α_i/e_i, which leaves the ideal unchanged. Then Nm_{L/K}(uα_r/α_s) = 1, so every t_i = log|Nm_{L/K}(uα_r/α_s)|_{w_i} vanishes, and the stated height bound follows. The loss is a factor O_{[L:ℚ]}(1) in N + 1, so (2.1) is unchanged.`. The boxes control only PUL(α_i), i.e. the differences of coordinates within each block, because P drops the block sums t_i. Units u ∈ O* = ker(Nm_{L/K}) have t_i = 0, but an arbitrary generator α_i of ℘_i^{ℓa_i}℘̄_i^{−ℓb_i}℘₀^{−ℓa₀}℘̄₀^{ℓb₀} has t_i(α_i) = log|Nm_{L/K}(α_i)|_{w_i}, the logarithm of a unit of K, which need not be bounded. "Norm 1" in the absolute sense gives only Σ_i t_i = 0. The step Σ max(x_v, 0) = Σ_i t_i + O(1) needs each t_i = O(1) (for example t₁ = T, t₂ = −T gives Σ max ≈ T). So the claimed bound on H(uα_r/α_s) is not justified as written, though the repair costs only a constant depending on [L : ℚ]. ### Yingkun Li, "Algebraicity of higher Green functions at a CM point", Inventiones Mathematicae (2023) (`PAPER-LI-23`)

- **Error** at Lemma 2.8, p. 394 (it affects a stated result). The source says `"Let θ1, …, θN ∈ R be Q-linearly independent irrational numbers, M ∈ N and b an integer with 0 ≤ b ≤ M − 1. For any α1, …, αN ∈ R, there exists an infinite subsequence {ni} ⊂ N such that lim e((Mni + b)θj) = e(αj) for all 1 ≤ j ≤ N."`; it should be `Assume that 1, θ1, …, θN are Q-linearly independent.`. As printed the lemma is false. θ1 = √2 and θ2 = 1 − √2 are irrational and Q-linearly independent, but e(nθ1)e(nθ2) = 1 for every n, so (e(1/2), e(0)) is never approached. The proof cites Kronecker's theorem (Apostol, Thm. 7.10), which needs the stronger hypothesis. The only application, in the proof of Lemma 2.9, chooses θj with 1, θ1, …, θN linearly independent, so nothing downstream is affected. Recorded as `PAPER-LI-23/E1`; looked for an existing correction in: the published article, Invent. Math. 234 (2023), 375–418 (doi 10.1007/s00222-023-01205-5, CC BY 4.0), read in full; arXiv 2106.13653 v1 (June 2021) and v2 (June 2023, 'final version'); a word-level diff of v2 against the published text shows only layout changes; Crossref metadata for 10.1007/s00222-023-01205-5, which records no correction or erratum.
- **Error** at Lemma 2.9, p. 394 (it affects a stated result). The source says `"Suppose αi, ci ∈ C for i ∈ N satisfy the condition that the series defining φ(s) := Σ αi ci^s converges absolutely for s = s0 ∈ R and equals to 0 for all but finitely many s ∈ Z_{>s0}. Then we have Σ_{ci = c} αi = 0 for any c ∈ C^×."`; it should be `Add the hypothesis that for every ε > 0 only finitely many i have |ci| ≥ ε (equivalently, the moduli |ci| can be listed in decreasing order with finite multiplicities). The proof, which starts by arranging |c1| = |cm| > |c_{m+1}| ≥ …, then works.`. Without the hypothesis the lemma is false. Let F(x) = ∏_{k≥1}(1 − x/2^k), an entire function with Taylor coefficients αi, and let ci = 2^i and s0 = 0. Then Σ|αi| < ∞ and φ(s) = F(2^s) = 0 for every s ≥ 1, yet α0 = 1 with c0 = 1 unique (checked numerically). The applications are unaffected: in Corollary 2.11 with s0 > 0 the hypothesis follows from absolute convergence, and in Lemmas 3.2–3.3 the ci are values c(β, τ0)^{−𝔯}, which tend to 0 because the Eisenstein series converge. The source says `"By the discussion and Lemma 31.32.4(3) in [Stacks, Tag 01OF] and Lemma 29.38.2 in [Tag 01VL], we know that O_X̃(−E) = O_X̃(1) is π-relatively ample."`; it should be `Replace the boundary divisor E by the exceptional Cartier divisor D = V(I·O_X̃) of the (normalized) blow-up. In Proposition 4.2 take ℓ0 ≥ n0·k·max aσ, so that g^{ℓ0}, which vanishes to order ≥ ℓ0 along every boundary component, gives a section twisted by −n0k′D.`. In particular, Int(L) only depends on the isometry class of L."`; it should be `A lift g̃ ∈ J(F) of g ∈ SO(V)(F) has spinor norm η(g̃) = sn(g) in F^×/(F^×)², so η(g̃) = 1 forces sn(g) = 1. What the argument needs is only val η(g̃) = 0, since g̃ carries RZ^{(ℓ)}_G to RZ^{(ℓ + val η(g̃))}_G (§4.5) and N = RZ^{(0)}_G; that is available exactly when some isometry carrying L′ to L has spinor norm of even valuation, which the remark does not establish.`. There are isometric pairs for which every isometry has spinor norm of odd valuation. Take m even and ε = −1: for m even and U unimodular, ϵ(ϖU) = χ(U), so V^−_m ≅ ϖ·H^−_{m,F}. Write H^−_m = M ⊥ ⟨w⟩ with M self-dual of rank n = m − 1, and let L ⊆ V be M with the scaled form, so that all its fundamental invariants are 1 and val(w) = 1. An element of SO(V)(F) stabilizing L preserves L_F and the line L^⊥_F, hence is a product of an even number of reflections in vectors of L or of L^⊥_F (for p odd the orthogonal group of a unimodular lattice is generated by the reflections in its vectors of unit norm, O'Meara 92:4); each such reflection has spinor norm of valuation 1, so the stabilizer has spinor norms of even valuation. Since V is isotropic, sn : SO(V)(F) → F^×/(F^×)² is surjective; choosing h with val sn(h) odd and L′ = hL gives isometric lattices such that every g ∈ SO(V)(F) with gL′ = L has val sn(g) odd. Remark 4.11.5 is the invariance input for Lemma 9.2.2 (i) (the O(W)(F)-invariance of Int^⊥_{L^♭,V}), hence for Proposition 9.2.3 and Theorem 9.3.2. The conclusion is presumably true — Theorem 4.15.1 asserts it, and for m = 4, ε = −1 it follows from Terstiege's explicit formulas (Remark 4.15.2) — and an automorphism of RZ_G outside J(F) shifting the components would supply it; but no such argument is given here, and this extraction did not settle it. Hence the commutant is Q_5[F]≅Q_5[X]/(X²+5), a field and therefore a division algebra. In companion coordinates F=[[0,−5],[1,0]], every commuting matrix is xI+yF with determinant x²+5y²; unequal parity of valuations prevents a nonzero zero determinant. The proposition is not disproved: the preceding invariant proof is valid, and a field is split over its own center. F(m)=F(m)+=F(ζ3); its degree over F+ is four, so u remains a noncube (use the fundamental-unit description of Q(√5)). FS=F(m)(cuberoot(u)) has cyclic cubic kernel. This covers every instance of Theorem 1.1.1 (R = (Sym^{n₀−1}H¹(A₀)⊗Sym^{n₁−1}H¹(A₁))(n)|_{Γ_F}) and base-change pairs in Theorems 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9. Then so does στ, for τ ∈ Gal(F̄/F_rflx) with ρ_{A₀}(τ) ≡ −1, ρ_{A₁}(τ) ≡ 1 and ε(τ) ≡ 1 mod ℓ^m (such τ exists by Serre's open image theorem): h_γ and ξ are unchanged, and the sign flips because n₀−1 is odd. For the hypothetical S that the proof by contradiction must exclude, lying in one eigenspace, one of these two admissible choices of γ gives loc_𝔭(S) = 0 at every γ-associated 𝔭. Then no abundant Ψ exists, ⟨s₁,c₁⟩_𝔭 = 0, and no contradiction follows. So the proofs of Theorems 8.2.2 and 8.3.2, and hence of Theorems 1.1.1, 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9, have a gap in the self-conjugate case. For Theorem 1.1.1 the gap is repairable for all but finitely many ℓ: take S in one eigenspace and γ of matching sign. In rank one, if the Selmer group meets both eigenspaces, no single γ gives an abundant pair, so use γ at 𝔭₁ and γτ at 𝔭₂ (conditions (PI)/(PII) depend only on h_γ and ξ). For general admissible λ (Definition 8.1.1) and base-change pairs, (L5-2) supplies only one γ, and nothing in (L1)–(L7) guarantees one of the opposite sign. There the proofs of Theorems 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9 are incomplete as written. No main theorem is shown false. The defect only makes a particular γ useless, and the statements remain consistent with BBK: e.g. a rank-one configuration with Selmer rank one in each eigenspace would violate parity. Theorems 8.2.2 and 8.3.2 apply Proposition 2.6.6, and so this lemma, with [F:F⁺] = 2, R = R₀⊗R₁ and j = 1. The γ comes from (L5-2) via Lemma 2.7.1 and is chosen after S, with no condition tying it to S (page images pp. 310, 317–319). Nothing in the Rankin–Selberg setup, the 1-polarization or Definition 8.1.1 rules out the failure. Case R_ℚ ≅ R_ℚ^𝔠. This covers all of Theorem 1.1.1 (A and A′ are over F⁺: Lemma 8.1.3, Prop. 2.7.2) and base-change instances of 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9. The lattice R is then Γ_{F⁺}-stable (call it R⁺), ℓ is odd, and H¹(F,R̄^{(m)}) = H¹(F⁺,R̄⁺) ⊕ H¹(F⁺,R̄⁺⊗η), with the local conditions preserved. For S in the χ-eigenspace, F_S is Galois over F⁺, and a cocycle computation gives θ_S(σ₀xσ₀⁻¹) = χ(σ₀)ρ⁺(σ₀)∘θ_S(x). Hence G_{S,γ} = θ_S⁻¹Hom(S,(R̄^{(m)})^{χ(σ₀)ρ⁺(σ₀)=1}). The module (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} is a line (Lemma 2.7.1(c)), and ρ⁺(σ₀) acts on it by a sign ε₀. So G_{S,γ} is either all of θ_S⁻¹Hom(S,(R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) or {1}. In the second case θ_S(Ψ_w)(s) = 0 at every γ-associated w. Restriction from F_w to F^{(m)}_{w^{(m)}} has degree g, which is prime to ℓ, so loc_w(s) = 0 in H¹_ns(F_w,R̄^{(m)}) ≅ R̄^{(m)}/(h_γ−1). Consequence for 8.2.2. The prime 𝔭 is γ-associated, so ⟨s₁,c₁⟩_𝔭 = 0 and no contradiction arises: the argument does not bound that eigenspace. Nothing controls the sign. For example, with n = 2 and the element g^{[F′:F⁺]}𝔠 of Prop. 2.7.2 (taking ρ̄(g) to commute with ρ⁺(𝔠)), one finds ε₀ = −c₁, where c₁ = ±1 is the eigenvalue of 𝔠 on the a-eigenvector of ρ̄_{A₀}(g). The paper leaves this free, and both choices satisfy (a)–(e). Consequence for 8.3.2. Suppose the hypothetical rank-2 S is ⟨s₊,s₋⟩, with one class in each eigenspace. Then every element of θ_S(G_{S,γ}) kills s₋ or kills s₊, for every γ, so no abundant pair exists. The paper uses a single γ for both 𝔭₁ and 𝔭₂. Repair. In rank 0, choose γ according to the eigenspace of S. In rank 1, use γ's of opposite signs at 𝔭₁ and 𝔭₂, as Bertolini–Darmon do when they choose ε_p. Changing the sign keeps h_γ and ξ, so conditions (a)–(e) and (PI)/(PII) are unaffected, since those are stated through Satake parameters at inert primes. For Theorem 1.1.1 both signs exist when ℓ ≫ 0: choose g in Prop. 2.7.2, or multiply by ρ̄₊(τ) with ρ̄(τ) = (−1)⊗1, which lies in the image since the image contains SL₂×SL₂ (Serre). So Theorem 1.1.1 survives with a modified proof. Not covered. For 1.1.5 and 1.1.9 at an arbitrary admissible λ, Definition 8.1.1 guarantees only one element satisfying (a)–(e). For 1.1.7, Lemma 8.1.4 supplies only ρ̄₊(φ_𝔭) at one prime 𝔭. So in the base-change case those proofs are incomplete unless a γ of the other sign is shown to exist, by an added hypothesis or a large-image argument. Case R_ℚ ≇ R_ℚ^𝔠. F_S and its 𝔠-conjugate should be linearly disjoint over F^{(m)} up to bounded index, because Hom_{Γ_F}(R,R^𝔠) = 0. A version of the lemma that loses only a bounded power of λ is then plausible, but the paper does not prove it. No main theorem is shown false. What fails is a proof by contradiction about a hypothetical Selmer class, and the statements are what Bloch–Kato predicts. Let γ̃ run over lifts of γ to Gal(F̃_S/F⁺) and let 2g be the order of γ on F^{(m)}. For a γ-associated place, Ψ_{w^{(m)}} = γ̃^{2g}|_{F_S}, which commutes with γ̃; so G_{S,γ} is contained in the restriction of the σ-fixed part of Gal(F̃_S/F_+^{(m)}), σ = conjugation by γ̃. This is the mechanism of E1's example (R = ℤ_3(1), S from a unit of F⁺, γ = complex conjugation). Nothing in Lemma 2.7.1(a)–(e), which is all the proof requires of γ, relates b to the c-sign of S, and γ is chosen without regard to S. Defence: when ρ̄ ≇ ρ̄^c, F_S and F_{S^c} are essentially independent over F_+^{(m)} and G_{S,γ} is as large as Lemma 2.6.4 claims (up to a bounded defect); in the elliptic case of Corollary 8.2.3 (both ranks) the sign can be corrected by the central element as indicated, and in rank 0 a suitable generator of S can be chosen instead. In a base-change situation without a central −1 in the image (e.g. Π_α base changes in Corollary 8.2.5, where (L5-1) comes from Lemma 2.3.5(b)), the rank-one argument, in which s is fixed by the cycle, needs a further idea. The printed proofs address none of this. Independent check: Checked on pp. 133–137, 310, 317–319. The mechanism is correct and hits the printed proofs. Let σ ∈ Γ_{F⁺} be a Frobenius above a γ-associated place, so Ψ = σ^{2g}|_{F_S} (g the order of h_γ). Suppose s ∈ H^1(F, R̄) satisfies c·s = εs for an extension r̄ of ρ̄ to Γ_{F⁺}; r̄ factors through Gal(F₊^{(m)}/F⁺) since ker ρ̄₊ ⊆ ker ρ̄. The cocycle relation on ker r̄ gives s(σ^{2g}) = εr̄(σ)s(σ^{2g}), and by (c) R̄^{r̄(σ)²} is a free rank-one line on which r̄(σ) acts by b = b(γ) = ±1. If εb = −1 then θ_S(Ψ)(s) = 0 for every Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ}; since H^1_ns(F_w, R̄) → R̄ (evaluation at Ψ) is injective, loc_w(s) = 0 at every γ-associated w, and no abundant element exists. In the elliptic setting of Corollary 8.2.3, both signs are admissible. On R̄₁ = Sym^{2r₁}H^1(A₁)(r₁) the fixed line is the middle weight and b₁ = +1. On R̄₀ = Sym^{2r₀−1}H^1(A₀)(r₀), replacing σ by σz with (ρ̄_{A₀}, ρ̄_{A₁}, ε̄)(z) = (−1, 1, 1) (such z exists in Γ_{FF′} for large ℓ) negates r̄(σ), since n₀ − 1 is odd. The element z is central in im ρ̄₊ with z² = 1, so h_γ, ξ, the prime-to-ℓ orders and (a)–(e) of Lemma 2.7.1 are unchanged, while b flips. Since the proofs pick γ from (a)–(e) alone, after S, one of the two admissible choices fails for S in an eigenspace. In rank 0 the hypothetical S may lie in either eigenspace. In rank 1 the Abel–Jacobi class s lies in the eigenspace of the vanishing L-factor when the other Selmer part vanishes. So the reliance on Proposition 2.6.6 is a genuine hole. Repairs. Rank 0: take S c-stable inside one eigenspace and replace γ by γz if needed. Rank 1: a single γ does not suffice when S meets both eigenspaces (then s₂ is invisible at every γ-associated place), but the argument permits different elements at the two primes: take 𝔭₁ γ-associated with b(γ) matching the component of s with unit coefficient, and 𝔭₂ γz-associated. Then loc_{𝔭₁}(s₂) = 0 automatically, loc_{𝔭₂}(s₂) is large, and (PI)/(PII) depend only on h_γ and ξ. The first reading's alternative (a generator with both components) works only if both eigenspaces of the Selmer group are nonzero. When R̄ ≇ R̄^c as Γ_F-modules, F_S and its conjugate are disjoint up to bounded defect (Goursat), and Lemma 2.6.4 holds up to that defect, so the problem is confined to essentially self-dual (e.g. base-change) R. In base-change cases without a central −1 in the image (the setting of Corollary 8.2.5, where (L5-1) comes from Lemma 2.3.5(b)), no repair is available from the paper. Lemma 4.2.4 is a specialization isomorphism for p-coprime coefficients and gives only unramifiedness at w ∤ ℓ. At w | ℓ one needs the torsion class loc_w(c₁) to lie in H^1_ns(F_w, R̄^{(m)c}) in the sense of Definitions 2.2.4–2.2.5, i.e. its extension must be a quotient of lattices in a crystalline representation. Lemma 2.2.6 does not give this, since c₁ is a torsion class obtained through Υ_i and the quotient by (𝔫₀, 𝔫₁). The fact is standard but not in the paper. Faltings' comparison for the good-reduction pair (X, Z) over O_{F_w} (F_w/Q_ℓ unramified, degree 2n − 1 ⩽ ℓ − 2 by (L1)) makes the torsion Abel–Jacobi extension torsion-crystalline. Torsion-crystalline modules in the sense of Definition 2.2.4 are closed under subquotients and direct sums, so the pushout along Υ_i stays crystalline. Same sentence in v1 ('Lemma 4.1.4') and v3. In particular, π is a blow-up along DL(V♯)′, for which we denote by E ⊆ D̃L(V) the exceptional divisor.”`; it should be `Describe D̃L(𝒱) as the closed subscheme of the ℙ^{r−1}-bundle of hyperplanes H_2 ⊂ H^⊨ over DL(𝒱♯) cut out by H_2 ⊆ 𝒱, i.e. by the vanishing on H_2 of the projection ℓ: H^⊨ → O·1. This needs H^⊨ handled as a subbundle, e.g. through the F_{p²}-structure. Then show that ℓ, as a section of (H^⊨)^∨ (rank r) on the smooth r-dimensional DL(𝒱♯), has as zero scheme exactly the reduced set DL(𝒱♯)′: a transversality check at the (p+1)(p³+1)⋯(p^{2r−1}+1) special points. The standard description of the blow-up along the zero scheme of a regular section then identifies π with Bl_{DL(𝒱♯)′}, gives E as the exceptional divisor and gives O_E(E) ≅ O_E(−1).`. A proper morphism that is an isomorphism away from finitely many smooth points and has fibres P^{r−1} over them need not be the blow-up (D̃L(V) could a priori be non-reduced or non-normal along E); the blow-up structure is used for ℒ|_E ≃ O_E(−E) = O_E(1) and for c_1(O(E))|_E = −η in (A.3)–(A.4), which determine the value of the integral. Case for the defence: the deformation argument of Proposition A.1.3(2) presumably adapts to show D̃L(V) smooth, all other steps of (A.1)–(A.5) check out, the case r = 1 is confirmed directly (−p = d•_{1,p}), and the numbers d•_{r,q} are exactly those making Proposition B.3.5(3) factor, so the stated result is very likely correct. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 328. The inference 'In particular, π is a blow-up along DL(𝒱♯)′' is drawn only from the fibre data: π is an isomorphism off the special points, with fibre ℙ^{r−1} over each. That data does not determine a blow-up. Counterexample: take X a smooth surface and Z the curvilinear length-2 point (x, y²). Then Bl_Z X = {xt = y²s} is an isomorphism off the point with reduced fibre ℙ^1 over it, but it is singular and its exceptional Cartier divisor is 2·ℙ^1. Intersection numbers like those in (A.3)–(A.5), which use O_E(E) ≅ O_E(−1) and c_1(O(E))|_E = −η, would change. The paper gives no scheme-theoretic analysis of D̃L(𝒱). Note also that H^⊨ is a left orthogonal for a pairing σ-linear in the first variable, and in families over non-perfect bases this need not be a subbundle, so the functor as written needs care. A correct route is in the correction. Case for the defence: the result is very likely true. The first reading reports that r = 1 checks directly (−p = d•_{1,p}) and that the numbers d•_{r,q} are the ones that make Proposition B.3.5(3) factor. I did not independently recheck these. The remaining steps (A.1)–(A.5) follow once the blow-up structure is established. The source says `For every (S, γ)-abundant r-tuple (Ψ₁, …, Ψ_r), one can choose a basis {s₁, …, s_r} of S such that θ_S(Ψ_i)(s_j) = 0 if i ≠ j and exp_λ(θ_S(Ψ_j)(s_j), (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) ⩾ m − m₀ − 𝔣(r)r_R. … Proof The first part is obvious from Definition 2.6.5.`; it should be `Assume 𝔣(r)r_R = 0 (e.g. R̄ absolutely irreducible and r_R minimal), or weaken to: there are elements s_j := Ce_j with AC = λ^c·I (a submodule containing λ^cS), or state it for a suitably chosen tuple rather than every abundant one. The application needs only one good pair, which exists when the O_λ-span of θ_S(G_{S,γ}) is large (cf. E1). At Proof of Theorem 8.3.2, (8.11), published pp. 317–318: Use only what abundance gives: after possibly interchanging Ψ1 and Ψ2, exp_λ θ_S(Ψ1)(λ0^{m_Σ−m_per}s) ⩾ m − m_Σ − 4𝔯_R, and there is a primitive t ∈ S with θ_S(Ψ1)(t) = 0 and exp_λ θ_S(Ψ2)(t) ⩾ m − m_Σ − 4𝔯_R; replace s2 by t in the rest of the proof.`. Over O/λ^m with m>4, A=[[λ,1],[0,λ]] has image containing λ²O² and hence λ⁴O². Its total image has index |k|² but its two coordinate projections have indices 1 and |k|; a diagonal matrix with those projections would have index |k|. Right multiplication by a basis change preserves the image, so cannot diagonalize it. Thus the claimed implication from Definition 2.6.5 is false for general linear maps. This example is not presented as a realized Selmer evaluation system, so the finding is a proof gap rather than a counterexample under every global hypothesis. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): revised — confirmed that the inference is invalid, but it is an error in the stated first part of Proposition 2.6.7 (asserted for EVERY abundant tuple), not only a proof gap; the counterexample matrix is realizable whenever θ_S(G_{S,γ}) is all of Hom(S, (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}). Locator is Proposition 2.6.7 (not 2.6.6). Over O_λ/λ^n with n ⩾ 2, A = [[λ,1],[0,λ]] has det λ², image {(λx+y, λy)} ⊇ λ²(O_λ/λ^n)², of index |k|²; its coordinate projections have indices 1 and |k|, so a diagonal matrix with the same image would have index |k|. Column operations (change of basis of S) preserve the image, so no basis diagonalizes A. This A is abundant as soon as 𝔣(2)r_R = 4r_R ⩾ 2, i.e. r_R ⩾ 1 (r_R is any bound from Lemma 2.3.3, and is ⩾ 1 whenever R̄ is reducible). It is realized by actual Frobenius elements whenever θ_S(G_{S,γ}) = Hom(S, (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) (e.g. [F:F⁺] = 1, where Lemma 2.6.4 holds, and θ_S surjective). Reach: a stated result (first part of Proposition 2.6.7; the second part depends on it); the proof of Theorem 8.3.2 (Theorem 1.1.9), which uses it with r = 2). Independent check 1: Quotation checked on p. 135 (PDF p. 29): 'For every (S,γ)-abundant r-tuple … one can choose a basis {s₁,…,s_r} of S such that θ_S(Ψ_i)(s_j) = 0 if i ≠ j and exp_λ(θ_S(Ψ_j)(s_j), (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) ⩾ m − m₀ − 𝔣(r)r_R' with proof 'The first part is obvious from Definition 2.6.5'. The statement is universally quantified over abundant tuples. Definition 2.6.5 (p. 134) asks only that the image of s ↦ (θ_S(Ψ_i)(s))_i contain λ^{m₀+𝔣(r)r_R}((R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ})^{⊕r}. Normalizing by λ^{m₀} (the values lie in λ^{m₀}O/λ^m because S is killed by λ^{m−m₀}), this says: the matrix A ∈ M_r(O/λ^n), n = m − m₀, has image ⊇ λ^c(O/λ^n)^r with c = 𝔣(r)r_R. A change of basis of S acts by A ↦ AC and preserves the image, so a diagonalizing basis exists iff im A is a product of coordinate submodules. Checked: A = [[λ,1],[0,λ]] has Smith form diag(1,λ²), image of index |k|² containing λ²(O/λ^n)², while its coordinate projections are O/λ^n and λO/λ^n (a product would have index |k|). So it is abundant when c ⩾ 2 and not diagonalizable. Also A = [[1,0],[1,λ]] with image {(a,b): a ≡ b mod λ} ⊇ λ(O/λ^n)² is abundant as soon as c ⩾ 1. Does Definition 2.6.5 allow such matrices? It needs c = 𝔣(r)r_R ⩾ 1, i.e. r_R ⩾ 1, and rows that lie in θ_S(G_{S,γ}). r_R is only 'an integer' from Lemma 2.3.3 (any upper bound works), and even the minimal one is ⩾ 1 whenever R̄ is reducible, which the hypotheses of Prop. 2.6.6 allow (R_ℚ irreducible; Lemma 2.3.5(a) or (b), and (b) allows semisimple reducible R̄). The rows are available whenever θ_S(G_{S,γ}) contains Hom(S,(R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) up to less than c: e.g. [F:F⁺] = 1, which §2.4–2.6 allow, where Lemma 2.6.4 holds, with θ_S surjective. So the first part is false as stated. It is TRUE when 𝔣(r)r_R = 0: abundance then means A invertible, and C = A^{−1} works with exponent m − m₀. It is also trivially true for r = 1. The second part is derived from the first. Column operations preserve im A, and the image of a diagonal matrix is the product of its coordinate projections. Counterexample. Take A = [[λ,1],[0,λ]] with n ≥ 2. Its image {(λx+y, λy)} contains λ²(O_λ/λ^n)² and has index |k|². Its projections have indices 1 and |k|, so no diagonalizing basis exists. A is abundant once c ≥ 2, i.e. r ≥ 2 and 𝔯_R ≥ 1. Let S be generated by κ(1+√2) and κ((1+√5)/2); these are independent modulo cubes (take norms to the two quadratic subfields), so S is free of rank 2. Take γ = 1 (h_γ = 1). Then K ≅ (ℤ/3^m)², θ_S is bijective, and G_{S,γ} = K by Chebotarev. Choose Frobenii Ψ₁, Ψ₂ with rows (3,1) and (0,3). With 𝔯_R := 1, which is a legitimate bound in the sense of Lemma 2.3.3 ('at most 𝔯_R'), the pair is abundant (λ⁴ ⊆ λ²), yet no basis diagonalizes it. If 𝔯_R is instead read as the exact depth, this R gives 𝔯_R = 0. In that case abundance forces A to be invertible and the first part holds. The statement is then false exactly when R̄ is not absolutely irreducible and θ_S(G_{S,γ}) contains the two rows, which is automatic wherever Lemma 2.6.4 holds and θ_S is onto. With the basis x^a y^{k−a}, the natural map to the divided powers is multiplication by a!(k−a)!. So the lattices are homothetic iff every binomial coefficient C(k,a) is prime to ℓ. Choose ρ̄_{A_α}(g) diagonal in eigenbases where ρ̄_{A_α}(𝔠) = diag(1,−1); this is possible because the image is all of {det g₀ = det g₁ = ξ^{−1}} and is conjugation-stable. Then h_{γ₀} has eigenvalues a^{2ti} for −r₀ ⩽ i ⩽ r₀−1 and h_{γ₁} has eigenvalues (ab²)^{2tj} for |j| ⩽ r₁. My sign convention gives i ↦ −i relative to the first reading's range 1−r₀ ⩽ i ⩽ r₀; every condition (a)–(e) is invariant under inverting the eigenvalues, so this is immaterial. The printed second bullet is right. The first, third and fourth bullets do not match (a), (d), (e): they should read 𝒫(−a^{−t}) ≠ 0, a^{2ti} ≠ −1 and (a(ab²)^{2j})^t ≠ 1. I checked both counterexamples by hand for r₀ = r₁ = t = 1 and 𝒫 = T²−1. (i) a of order 4 with b⁴ ∉ {±1, ±a} satisfies every printed bullet, yet a² = −1 is an eigenvalue of h_{γ₀}, violating (d). (ii) With b⁴ = a^{−1} and a ∉ μ₄ ∪ μ₃, all printed bullets hold, yet (ab²)^{−2} = a^{−1} = −ξ, violating (e). The conjugacy class alone also does not determine h_{γ₀}: if 𝔠 swaps the eigenlines, then ρ̄_{A₀}(y²) = a^t·I and h_{γ₀} is scalar, so (c) fails. The statement survives, with the corrected conditions, for ℓ ≫ 0 when 𝒫 ≠ 0. Versions: same in v1 (Prop. 2.6.3) and v3. Take g ∈ Gal(F̄/F′) with image (γ′₀, γ′₁, ξ′) lifting (γ₀, γ₁, ξ). For (c), h has order prime to ℓ, so ker(h−1) is the image of the averaging idempotent: a free direct summand whose rank is the residual multiplicity 1. The source says `"This is equivalent to that for every prime q of F+ above p that is inert in F, [F+q : Qp] is odd."`; it should be `Delete the footnote or replace it with a correct criterion. Let M be the Galois closure of F, σ the Frobenius at 𝔭 (for ι_p inducing 𝔭), and H ⊆ Gal(M/ℚ) the subgroup generated by the stabilizers of the CM types of F. Then 𝔭 is very special inert iff σc ∈ H. The footnote's condition is equivalent to something else: that some CM type Φ ∋ τ_∞ satisfies σ²Φ = Φ, i.e. ℚ_p^Φ = ℚ_{p²}, which is condition (P3)/(PI3) of §§6–7.`. (i) The footnote's condition does not imply very special. Take F = ℚ(√(−(3+√2))) (minimal polynomial x⁴ + 6x² + 7, Galois group D_4, F^+ = ℚ(√2)) and p = 17. Then 17 = 𝔭𝔮 in F^+, with √2 ≡ 6 at 𝔭. At 𝔭, −3 + √2 ≡ 3 is a non-square mod 17, so 𝔭 is inert in F. At 𝔮, −3 + √2 ≡ 8 = 5², so 𝔮 splits in F. 17 is odd and unramified in F (the polynomial discriminant is 2^{10}·7), and 𝔭 has degree 1, so 𝔭 is special inert. The only prime above 17 that is inert in F is 𝔭, of odd degree 1, so the footnote declares 𝔭 very special. But the CM types of F are primitive with reflex fields of real quadratic subfield ℚ(√7) (√7 = √(−3+√2)·√(−3−√2)), so ⋂_Φ F_Φ = ℚ(√7). Hence F_rflx = F(√7) = M and F^+_rflx = ℚ(√2, √7). Since (7/17) = −1, 𝔭 is inert in F^+_rflx/F^+ and is not very special. (ii) Very special does not imply the footnote's condition. Take F a CM octic field with Gal(M/ℚ) = W(B_4) = (ℤ/2)^4 ⋊ S_4 (a generic F = F^+(√−δ) with F^+ an S_4-quartic). Then H = {(ε, π) : Σε_i even}, which has index 2 and contains c, so 𝔭 is very special iff the number of primes of F^+ above p that are inert in F is even. A Frobenius σ = ((1,1,0,0), (2 3)) (it exists by Chebotarev) gives 𝔭 inert of degree 1, 𝔮 inert of degree 2 and 𝔮′ split of degree 1. There are two inert primes, so 𝔭 is very special, but 𝔮 has even degree. Moreover σ² interchanges τ and τ^c for the embeddings above 𝔮, so no CM type is σ²-stable and (P3) fails. Defence: no proof uses the footnote. Lemma 8.1.4 uses only 'φ_𝔭 ∈ Gal(F̄/F^+_rflx)', which is the definition. In the cases of Remark 1.1.8 (F Galois or containing an imaginary quadratic field) the definition and the footnote both reduce to 'special inert'. The footnote does mislead anyone checking hypothesis (a) of Theorem 1.1.7. Independent check: Footnote 11 and the definitions were checked on the image of p. 147. Let M be the Galois closure of F, σ the Frobenius at 𝔭, and H = ⟨Stab Φ⟩, which is normal. Then Gal(M/F_rflx) = Gal(M/F) ∩ H, so a special inert 𝔭 is very special iff σc ∈ H. The footnote's condition is equivalent to the existence of Φ ∋ τ_∞ with σ²Φ = Φ, i.e. (P3). I checked all of this by machine: I enumerated every σ with σ(τ_∞) = τ_∞^c in D₄ and in W(B₄). There the footnote condition is always equivalent to (P3), while 'very special' differs in both directions. (i) D₄: x⁴+6x²+7 has discriminant 2¹⁰·7. Mod 17 it factors as (x−5)(x+5)(x²−3), H = V₄ ∋ c, and ⋂F_Φ = ℚ(√7). Since (7/17) = −1, the degree-one prime inert in F is not very special, though it meets the footnote. Small slip: for F = ℚ(√(−(3+√2))), the inert prime is the one with √2 ≡ −6 mod 17 (−3−√2 ≡ 3); at √2 ≡ 6, −3−√2 ≡ 8 = 5², which splits. The conclusion is unchanged after relabelling. (ii) Explicit W(B₄) instance: F⁺ = ℚ(α) with α⁴−4α²−α+1 = 0, which is totally real with disc 1957 and group S₄, and F = F⁺(√−(α+4)). Since N(α+4) = 197 is not a square in ℚ(√1957), Gal = W(B₄); Frobenius cycle-type frequencies for p < 20000 match. H is the even-sign subgroup, M^H = ℚ(√197) and F⁺_rflx = F⁺(√197). At p = 43, f ≡ (x−3)(x−11)·(quadratic), and the degree-8 polynomial has type [1,1,2,4]. 𝔭 = (43, α−11) is special inert, since −(α+4) ≡ 28 is a non-square, and it splits in F⁺_rflx because 197 ≡ 5² mod 43. So 𝔭 is very special, but the degree-2 prime above 43 is inert in F: the footnote fails, and no CM type Φ ∋ τ_∞ has ℚ_43^Φ = ℚ_{43²}. No proof cites the footnote. The source says `(2) The restriction of ι to B_{s⋆} is locally on B_{s⋆} a closed immersion, with a canonical isomorphism for its normal bundle … / Proof: … It is clearly injective, with cokernel canonically isomorphic to ℋom(ω_{𝒜^∨,τ∞}, im α_{*,τ∞}). Thus, (2) follows. / p. 180: 'By Theorem 4.3.5, we know that ι_sp is locally for the Zariski topology on the source a closed immersion'`; it should be `(2) The restriction of ι to B_{s⋆} is unramified (i.e. étale-locally on B_{s⋆} a closed immersion), with normal bundle ℋom(ω_{𝒜^∨,τ∞}, im α_{*,τ∞}); it is a closed immersion when it is injective on geometric points, e.g. when K^p is sufficiently small (Remark 4.3.6).`. The proof only shows that the tangent map T_{B_{s⋆}} → ι^*T_M is injective, i.e. that ι|B_{s⋆} is unramified. Zariski-locally a closed immersion fails whenever ι|B_{s⋆} is not injective on geometric points: B_{s⋆} is proper and irreducible (Theorem 4.3.5(3)), so any Zariski open U ∋ x is dense and ι(U) ∩ V must equal ι(B_{s⋆}) ∩ V for ι|U to be a closed immersion into an open V; if x′ ≠ x has ι(x′) = ι(x) = y, then ι(B_{s⋆}) has two branches at y (or ι is generically non-injective), while U is smooth at x, so U → ι(B_{s⋆}) ∩ V is not an isomorphism. Non-injectivity does occur: for N = 3 each superspecial point of M_𝔭 lies on p + 1 components ι(B_{s⋆}) indexed by the p + 1 neighbouring vertex lattices, and these p + 1 lattices give points of S_𝔭(V, K^p)(F̄_p) over one point of T_𝔭(F̄_p), a set in bijection with Sh(V⋆, (iK^p)K⋆_p) (Proposition 4.4.4); if p + 1 exceeds |Sh(V⋆, (iK^p)K⋆_p)|, two of them coincide and the corresponding B_{s⋆} passes twice through the superspecial point. Remark 4.3.6 (closed immersion for K^p sufficiently small) is consistent with this. Defence: 'locally' can be read étale-locally, which is what the proof gives; every later use (pure codimension ⌊N/2⌋, the normal bundle, the Gysin maps ι_! in Construction 4.4.9, transversality in Theorem 4.6.2) needs only unramifiedness, and in Proposition 4.5.5 the reduction still works: an unramified morphism from a smooth scheme that is bijective on geometric points and on tangent spaces is étale and universally injective, hence an isomorphism. Independent check: Quotation checked on pp. 166, 168, 180 (and Remark 4.3.6, p. 169: closed immersion only 'when K^p is sufficiently small'). The proof of (2) only shows T_{B_{s⋆}} → ι^*T_M injective, i.e. ι|B_{s⋆} unramified; p. 180 then uses (2) as 'locally for the Zariski topology on the source a closed immersion'. That reading is false as soon as ι|B_{s⋆} is not injective on geometric points. Independent proof: let x ≠ x′ in B := B_{s⋆} (over κ = F̄_p) with ι(x) = ι(x′) = y, and suppose U ∋ x is open with ι|U an immersion onto Z. B is proper and irreducible, so U is dense, Z is open in the closed set ι(B), Z = ι(B) ∩ V with V ⊆ M open, and W := B ∩ ι^{-1}(V) → Z is proper. The inverse Z ≅ U ⊆ W is a section of the separated map W → Z, so U is closed in W; it is also open and W is irreducible, hence U = W ∋ x′, contradicting injectivity of U → Z. Non-injectivity occurs: for N = 3 (Vollaard–Wedhorn picture) each superspecial point lies on p + 1 curves ι(B_{s⋆}) indexed by the p + 1 neighbouring vertex lattices, which share the prime-to-p component; if two are equivalent under U(V⋆)(F⁺) (γΛ₁ = Λ₂, γ ≠ 1 by neatness), the curve of Λ₁ passes through the superspecial point twice (at v and γ^{-1}v ≠ v). By pigeonhole this happens when p + 1 > |Sh(V⋆, (iK^p)K⋆_p)|, and for a fixed away-from-p level this cardinality does not grow with p (for odd N, K⋆_p is hyperspecial and the totally definite unitary group of rank 3 is independent of p up to isomorphism), so it happens for all large inert p. Case for the defence: read étale-locally, (2) is true (unramified ⇒ étale-locally a closed immersion, Stacks 04HJ); all later uses (codimension, normal bundle, Gysin maps, transversality) need only unramifiedness, and in Proposition 4.5.5 the reduction still works (a morphism of smooth schemes bijective on geometric points and on tangent spaces is étale and universally injective, hence an isomorphism). So the statement is wrong in the sense the paper itself uses, with no downstream damage. In L=F5×F5 use the three roots (1,2),(2,1),(3,3). Componentwise the polynomial is (T−1)(T−2)(T−3), which has the required odd reciprocal identity. No root has square one in L, so no root can occupy the middle of a reciprocal ordering. This does not obstruct the usual field-valued construction. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): revised: the gap is real (the counterexample checks) and occurs also in the split case (2), but every use of Construction 3.1.8 is over ℂ or with an ordered tuple given, so it affects nothing (previous record: 'the proof'). Inert case (previous record, rechecked): L = 𝔽_5 × 𝔽_5, α = {(1,2), (2,1), (3,3)}: both components give (T−1)(T−2)(T−3) = T³ + 4T² + T + 4 over 𝔽_5, which equals (−T)³P(T^{−1}) because 2·3 = 1; but no element squares to 1 (so none can be the middle entry) and (1,2)(2,1) = (2,2) ≠ 1. Split case (new): L = 𝔽_5 × 𝔽_5, α_1 = {(1,2), (2,1)}, α_2 = {(1,1), (3,3)}: P_{α_1} = (T−1)(T−2) and T²P_{α_2}(T^{−1}) = (1−T)(1−3T) = 3(T−1)(T−2) over 𝔽_5, so α is unitary with c = 2; the inverses (1,3), (3,1) of the elements of α_1 do not lie in α_2, so no orders with α_{1,i}α_{2,N+1−i} = 1 exist. Defence: over a field or domain the orderings exist, and when they exist the value of φ_α is independent of the choice (valid orderings give Weyl-conjugate characters). The construction is used only in Construction 3.1.10 with L = ℂ, and Notation B.2.5 starts from an ordered tuple. Independent check: Construction 3.1.8 (pp. 141–142) and Definition 3.1.3 (p. 139) were checked on the images: L is an arbitrary ℤ[‖v‖^{±δ(v)/2}]-ring. Both counterexamples recomputed over 𝔽₅×𝔽₅. Inert case: each component of P_α is (T−1)(T−2)(T−3), and (−T)³P(T^{−1}) = (T−1)(T−2)(T−3), so α is unitary. No element squares to (1,1), and (1,2)(2,1) = (2,2), so no admissible ordering exists. Split case: P_{α₁} = (T−1)(T−2), and T²P_{α₂}(T^{−1}) = (1−T)(1−3T) = 3(T−1)(T−2), so α is unitary with c = 2. But (1,3) and (3,1) are not in α₂, so no ordering with α_{1,i}α_{2,N+1−i} = 1 exists. Over a domain the multisets are inversion-stable and orderings exist. When orderings exist, φ_α is independent of the choice: inverses in a ring are unique, so two orderings differ by a Weyl element. The construction is used only with L = ℂ: Construction 3.1.10, and Definition 6.1.8 via φ_{α(BC(π_v))}. Notation B.2.5 starts from an ordered tuple. The first reading's alternative is also sound over any ring: for N odd, a_i = −a_{N−i} forces P_α(1) = 0 without inverting 2. Versions: same in v1 and v3. The middle term H^i_𝔗(𝐌^η_{n₀} ×_{𝐓^η} 𝐌^η_{n₁}, L(j)) is the arithmetic generic fibre over Q_p^Φ. The chain has no arrow from the generic fibre to 'H^i_𝔗(M ×_T M, RΨL(j))', and under every reading one link fails. With RΨ the geometric nearby cycles, there is no canonical map from arithmetic generic-fibre cohomology to arithmetic special-fibre cohomology. With the arithmetic version i^*Rj_*L, the map exists, but 'L ≃ RΨL' is false (i^*R^1j_*L = L(−1)). For X smooth proper over Z_p^Φ, purity and the vanishing of c₁(O(X_s)) give 0 → H^i(X_s, L(j)) → H^i(X_η, L(j)) → H^{i−1}(X_s, L(j−1)) → 0, so the only canonical map runs from special to generic and has nonzero cokernel in general (Kummer class of p). For n even, B_sp = S_sp ×_{S_n} B_n and (id × π_{n₁}) ∘ b_△ = (b_↓, s_↑ ∘ π_sp): B_sp → B_n ×_{T_𝔭} S_{n+1} is the base change of (s_↓, s_↑): S_sp → S_n ×_{T_𝔭} S_{n+1} along π_n × id, so its pushforward of [B_sp] is (π_n × id)^*((s_↓, s_↑)_*1), which counts multiplicities. Under the uniformizations (Proposition 4.5.9), (s_↓, s_↑) is (sh⋆_↓, sh⋆_↑) × id, and this map need not be injective: the fibre of sh⋆_↓ over a point has p + 1 elements (Lemma 4.5.2(2), (4.13)), which are distinct points of Sh(V⋆_n, K⋆_{sp}) (a common image in Sh(V⋆_n, K⋆_n) plus equality would need an element of U(V⋆_n)(F⁺) fixing the prime-to-p class and Λ⋆_{n,𝔭}, trivial by neatness), and their images under sh⋆_↑ lie in Sh(V⋆_{n+1}, (i_{n+1}−_{n+1})K⋆_{n+1,p}); if p + 1 exceeds the number of points of that Shimura set — the typical situation for fixed K^p and large p — two of them coincide by pigeonhole. At such a point the characteristic function of the image subset is 1 while the left-hand side of the displayed identity is ⩾ 2, so the identity, and hence Theorem 4.6.2 with the literal 'subset' reading, fails. For n odd, sh⋆_↓ = id and both readings agree. Defence: the proof proves the pushforward version, and the only application (proof of Theorem 7.3.4, which applies Theorem 4.6.2 at level (K_sp, K_{n+1}) 'followed by pushforward') uses the pushforward reading, which it states explicitly. Independent check: Checked on pp. 186–188. The correspondence is not injective in general. The p + 1 points of a fibre of sh⋆_↓ are distinct (neat level) and share their prime-to-p component. Their images lie in Sh(V⋆_{n+1}, K_♯K⋆_{n+1,p}), whose level at 𝔭 is hyperspecial (n + 1 odd, (Λ⋆)^∨ = pΛ⋆), so its cardinality is bounded independently of p for a fixed away-from-p level; pigeonhole then applies for large p. The theorem itself (not just the proof step) fails under the literal 'subset' reading. The last step of the proof (p. 188, via Theorem 4.4.10) gives LHS − RHS = (ι_{n₀} × id)_!(π_{n₀} × id)^*(T⋆_{n₁,𝔭}(f − 𝟙_△)). Take n = 2, F⁺ ≠ Q so that everything is proper, and L = Z_ℓ. Then B_2 = S_2, and ι_{2!} sends a point to its cycle class, whose degree is 1. Applying the total-degree map H^2_𝔗(M_2 ×_T S_3, L(1)) → L gives d·(|Sh(V⋆_2, K⋆_sp)| − |△|) per point of T. Here d is the common column sum of T⋆_{3,𝔭} = d_{1,p} + d_{0,p}·deg T_{3,𝔭;1} = (−2p² − p + 1) + p(p³ + 1) = (p² − 1)² ≠ 0 (Notation 1.3.1; T_{3;1} has degree p(p³ + 1)). So the difference is nonzero whenever the correspondence is non-injective. The pushforward reading, which §7.3 states explicitly and which is the only one used downstream, makes the theorem and its proof correct. Near P^{†,†}, 𝐏 is x0y0 = x1y1 (= p) with M°_{nα} = {xα = 0}, and the ideal of P^{°,°} is pr_0^*O(−M°_{n0}) + pr_1^*O(−M°_{n1}). So 𝐐 embeds in P(pr_0^*O(−M°_{n0}) ⊕ pr_1^*O(−M°_{n1})). A chart computation (x0 = u·x1, y1 = u·y0, p = u·x1·y0) shows σ^{-1}(P^{†,†}) = {x1 = y0 = 0} is reduced, smooth and meets each fibre in a whole P¹, hence σ^{-1}(P^{†,†}) = P(pr_0^*N_0 ⊕ pr_1^*N_1). Since O(M°+M•) = O(div p) ≅ O, O(−M°)|_{M†} ≅ O_{M°}(M†)|_{M†} = N_{M†/M°}, which by Theorem 5.3.4 and Corollary 5.3.5 is O(p+1) restricted to the degree-(p+1) Fermat hypersurface DL(V_{s°}) ⊂ P(V_{s°}). Over a connected proper base, P(A ⊕ B) ≅ base × P¹ iff A ⊕ B ≅ M ⊕ M for a line bundle M (P(E) ≅ P(E′) iff E′ ≅ E ⊗ M), hence, by Atiyah's Krull–Schmidt theorem, iff A ≅ B. Also I ⊗ O_{P^{†,†}} is free on x0, x1, because the relation y0x0 − y1x1 dies modulo the maximal ideal. Hence Q^{†,†} = ℙ(pr_0^*O(−M°_{n0}) ⊕ pr_1^*O(−M°_{n1}))|_{P^{†,†}}. Since O(M° + M•) = O(div p) ≅ O, O(−M°)|_{M†} ≅ O_{M°}(M†)|_{M†} = N_{M†/M°}. By Corollary 5.3.5 (p. 198) this is (m^{†°})^*O_{M°}(p+1), i.e. O(p+1) on each Fermat fibre, a degree-(p+1) hypersurface in ℙ^{n−1} (Lemma A.1.4(1)). A ℙ^1-bundle ℙ(A ⊕ B) over a connected proper base is trivial iff A ≅ B. Restrict to {z} × C, with C a component of a fibre of M†_{n1} (dimension n1 − 2 ⩾ 1 since n1 = 2r1+1 ⩾ 3). There pr_0^*N_0 is trivial while pr_1^*N_1 = O(p+1)|_C is ample. For n1 = 3 this gives the ruled surface ℙ(O ⊕ O(p+1)|_C) over a Fermat curve, which has a section of self-intersection −(p+1)^2 and so is not C × ℙ^1. The bundle is therefore not trivial over any connected component. Uses: Lemma 5.11.3(3)–(5) feed Lemma 7.2.5(2),(4),(6) (pp. 289–291) and Theorem 7.2.8(1a)–(1d) (pp. 293–295). No argument uses f² = 0 or independence of f from the section. So nothing downstream is affected. Defence: with the reading above the isomorphism holds and gives (3): the eigenvalues of r^♮_ram(φ_p²) on R_1 are p^{1−2r}α_i^{±1} (i ≠ the level-raising index), and twisting by ε_ℓ(φ_p²)^r = p^{2r} gives pα_i^{±1}, avoiding 1 and p². Independent check: Quote checked on p. 285: 'Part (3) is a consequence of (1) and (P4) … In fact, we have an isomorphism H^{2r−1}_𝔗(M̄•_N, O_λ(r)) ≃ H ⊗_{R^ram} R_1(r) of O_λ[Gal(F̄_p/F_{p²})]-modules.' In the text layer of pub/v1/v2/v3, R_1 occurs only in this line, so it is never defined. The left side also lacks the localisation at 𝔪 that part (3) concerns. The displayed isomorphism is all the proof of (3) has, and it is not immediate. By Lemma 5.9.3(1), E_1^{0,2r−1} = H^{2r−1}_𝔗(M̄•_N, L(r)) and the odd-degree terms of M°, M† vanish, so H^{2r−1}_𝔗(M̄•_N)_𝔪 = E_2^{0,2r−1} = Gr_0 of H^{2r−1}_𝔪 ≅ H ⊗ (R^ram)^{⊕N}(r) (p. 282). To identify Gr_0 with H ⊗ (complement of R^ram v ⊕ R^ram v′)(r) one needs three things. (i) Frobenius eigenvalues. E_2^{−1,2r} ⊆ H^{2r−2}(M̄†, L(r−1)) and E_2^{1,2r−2}, a quotient of H^{2r−2}(M̄†, L(r)), have Frobenius eigenvalues 1 and p² (Lemma 5.6.2). By (P4) these are separated modulo λ from the eigenvalues p·α_i^{±1} (i ≠ the level-raising index) on the complement, so the complement lies in Gr_0. (ii) The {1, p²}-block H ⊗ (R^ram v ⊕ R^ram v′)(r) contributes nothing to Gr_0. This needs a further argument. For example: at every characteristic-zero point of R^ram ≅ T^ram_𝔪, the monodromy x is nonzero (nontrivial monodromy at 𝔭, cf. p. 277), so the block has no Gr_0 rationally, and Gr_0 is O_λ-free by (2). (iii) The complement on which inertia acts trivially must actually be named. The first reading's reading (R_1 = the φ²-stable complement, i.e. M_1 of [51]) makes the isomorphism true, and (3) then follows. But the paper supplies neither the definition nor steps (i)–(ii), so this is a gap, not a misprint. Versions: the same line is in v1/v2 p. 120 and v3 p. 119. - **Error** at Proof of Theorem 6.3.4(5), published pp. 285–286 (it affects a stated result). The source says `We claim that O_λ/λ^m = R^ram/𝔫 … Since 𝔫 satisfies 𝔫 ∩ O_λ = λ^m O_λ, the structure homomorphism O_λ → R^ram induces an equality O_λ/λ^m = R^ram/𝔫.`; it should be `Add to Theorem 6.3.4(5) the hypothesis that P_{α(Π_v)} mod λ^m is level-raising special at v (Definition 3.1.5) for every v ∈ Σ⁺_lr. Equivalently, ρ̄^{(m)}_{Π,λ,+} satisfies 𝒟^ram at Σ⁺_lr; this holds vacuously if Σ⁺_lr = ∅. In the proof, read 𝔫 O_λ-linearly, as the kernel of O_λ ⊗ T^{Σ⁺∪Σ⁺_p}_N → O_λ/λ^m. With these, ρ_{Π,λ,+} mod λ^m is of type 𝒮^ram, and so R^ram/𝔫 = O_λ/λ^m. The added hypothesis holds in both applications: Theorem 8.2.2 (Σ⁺_lr = ∅) and Theorem 8.3.2 (Σ⁺_lr = {𝔭_1}, by (PII4)).`. As defined in Notation 6.1.3, 𝔫 is an ideal of the ℤ[‖v‖^{±1/2}]-algebra T^{Σ⁺∪Σ⁺_p}_N; read literally, λ^m need not lie in 𝔫R^ram when E_λ is ramified over the field generated by the Hecke eigenvalues. Read O_λ-linearly, R^ram/𝔫 is a quotient O_λ/λ^j of O_λ/λ^m, and j = m requires an O_λ-algebra map R^ram → O_λ/λ^m compatible with φ_Π, i.e. (Chebotarev and Carayol) that ρ_{Π,λ} mod λ^m be a lifting of type 𝒮^ram. At 𝔭 this is (P4) (mod λ^m); but at v ∈ Σ⁺_lr the local condition is 𝒟^ram, which demands P_0(T) = (T − ‖v‖^{−N})(T − ‖v‖^{−N+2}) exactly ([51, Definition 3.5.1]), whereas the hypotheses of Theorem 6.3.4 (rigidity (b), §6.1) only give this modulo λ. If Π_v is level-raising special only modulo λ^j with j < m, then R^ram/𝔫 = O_λ/λ^{j′} with j′ ⩽ j, H^{2r−1}/𝔫 ≅ H ⊗ (R^ram/𝔫)^{⊕N}(r) is killed by λ^{j′} (and nonzero since d_ram > 0), and the conclusion (R̄^{(m)c})^{⊕μ} with μ ⩾ 1 fails. Defence: in the applications (§8, pp. 318–319) Σ⁺_lr is either ∅ or {𝔭_1} with 𝔭_1 a previously chosen prime satisfying (PII4), i.e. level-raising special modulo λ^m, so the main theorems are unaffected; Theorem 6.3.4(4) is unaffected. Independent check: Quote checked on pp. 285–286. The problem is real, but the asserted step is false in general rather than merely unjustified, and so is Theorem 6.3.4(5) as stated. So the kind should be 'error'. The argument: 𝔫 is read O_λ-linearly, which is clearly the intended reading. R^ram/𝔫 = T^ram_𝔪/𝔫 is then a quotient O_λ/λ^j of O_λ/λ^m. j = m iff φ_Π mod λ^m factors through T^ram_𝔪 ≅ R^ram. By Chebotarev and Carayol (Assumption 6.1.6), that happens iff ρ_{Π,λ,+} mod λ^m is a lifting of type 𝒮^ram. At v ∈ Σ⁺_lr the local condition is 𝒟^ram, i.e. s = ‖v‖^{−N} exactly: the paper itself writes R^ram = R^mix/(s − p^{−2r}) on p. 281. But Π_v is unramified, since Σ⁺_lr is strongly disjoint from Σ⁺_min ⊇ Σ⁺_Π. The hypotheses of Theorem 6.3.4 constrain Π_v only through rigidity (Definition 6.3.3(2): generalized eigenvalues of r̄♮_v(φ_w) in F̄_ℓ, i.e. modulo λ) and through ℓ ∤ ‖v‖(‖v‖²−1) (p. 264). (P4) is mod λ^m but only at 𝔭, and (P6)/(d) are congruences with no local content at v. So if P_{α(Π_v)} is level-raising special modulo λ^j but not λ^{j+1} with j < m, then R^ram/𝔫 = O_λ/λ^{j′} with j′ ⩽ j. In that case H^{2r−1}_ét(Sh(V′_N,…)_F̄, O_λ(r))/𝔫 ≅ H ⊗ (R^ram/𝔫)^{⊕N}(r) is nonzero (d_ram > 0) and killed by λ^{j′}. It therefore cannot be isomorphic to (R̄^{(m)c})^{⊕μ} with μ ⩾ 1, and (5) is false. The literal (ℤ-linear) reading of 𝔫 fails too, independently, when E_λ is ramified over the field of Hecke eigenvalues; that part is only a notational slip. Reach: §7 never invokes (5). §7.2 uses 6.3.4(1)–(3) (Lemma 7.2.5, pp. 289–291) and 6.3.4(4) (Theorem 7.2.8(2), p. 295). §8 invokes (5) explicitly only in the proof of Theorem 8.2.2 ((8.6), p. 312), where Σ⁺_lr,I = ∅ (p. 310). It invokes (5) implicitly in the proof of Theorem 8.3.2 ('exactly same argument for the parallel claim in the proof of Theorem 8.2.2', p. 319), where Σ⁺_lr,I = {𝔭_1}. There 𝔭_1 satisfies (PII4), 'P_{α(Π_{0,𝔭})} mod λ^m is level-raising special' (p. 298), with the same m, which is exactly the missing hypothesis. So the main theorems are unaffected. Part (4) does not use R^ram/𝔫 = O_λ/λ^m. Versions: the wording '𝔫 ∩ O_λ = λ^m O_λ' is in v1/v2 p. 120 and v3 p. 119. For u < 0, Theorems 5.15, 6.2 and 7.4–7.5 evaluate µ_u on Borel sets V_{𝒞,H} and integrate against µ_u. That requires µ_u to extend to a Borel measure, which is proved (Theorem 5.12, with Carathéodory extension) only for u ≥ 0 as printed. The main Theorems 1.2 and 1.4 use u = 1 and are unaffected. With the hypothesis dropped the statements hold. For example, at u = −1 and Γ = Z/2 the formula gives measure 0 to every finite abelianization, consistent with the free rank-one abelianization of 𝓕_n/(n−1 relations). ### Maulik–Shankar–Tang, "Picard ranks of K3 surfaces over function fields and the Hecke orbit conjecture", Inventiones Mathematicae (2022) (`PAPER-MAULIK-SHANKAR-TANG-22`)

- **Misprint** at §7, in the proof of Proposition 7.17, the non-superspecial supersingular case (accepted version of 25 December 2021; the same expression is in arXiv:2011.08887v1). The source says `≤ (h/(p-1)) · 2(p² − p + 1)/(p(p² − 1)) ≤ (11/12)(h/(p-1)) for all p ≥ 3`; it should be `the middle expression is 2(p² + p − 1)/(p(p² − 1)); the two summands of the numerator are transposed`. The displayed series is (2/(1-p^{-2}))(h(p^{-1}+1)/p² + hp/p⁴ + hp²/p⁶ + ···). Summing the geometric tail, the bracket is h((p+1)/p³ + 1/(p²(p-1))) = h(p²+p-1)/(p³(p-1)), and multiplying by 2p²/(p²-1) gives exactly (h/(p-1))·2(p²+p-1)/(p(p²-1)). At p = 3 this is 22/24 = 11/12, which is where the constant 11/12 comes from and shows the bound is sharp there; numerically, with h = 1 and p = 3 the series is (9/4)(4/27 + 1/18) = 0.4583… = (11/12)·(1/2), confirming it. The printed 2(p²-p+1)/(p(p²-1)) equals 7/12 at p = 3, so as printed the first inequality of the chain is false, although the final bound 11/12 that the proof uses is correct. The same computation carried out for the two superspecial cases of the same proof reproduces the printed constants exactly, 61/62 at p = 5 in case (1) and 17/20 at p = 5 in case (2), which confirms the method. ### Nelson–Venkatesh, "The orbit method and analysis of automorphic forms", Acta Mathematica 226 (2021) (`PAPER-NELSON-VENKATESH-21`)

- **Gap** at Proof of Lemma 27.3, p. 182 (also arXiv v3) (it affects a stated result). The source says `G=SOn: in this case, the spinor norm injects G(Fv)/G(Fv)+ into Fv× modulo squares, and our assertion follows from the surjectivity of the spinor norm on SOn−1 (for n−1⩾2).`; it should be `The spinor norm is surjective on SO_{n−1} only when n − 1 ≥ 3 (or the binary space is split). For (G, H) = (SO3, SO2), allowed by §25.7, the claimed surjectivity of H(A) onto ε = G(F)G∞⁺U\G(A) fails for small U, and Theorem 27.1 (hence Lemma 30.4, Theorems 30.1 and 31.11) needs another argument. The argument still works when Π ≇ Π ⊗ (η_{K/F}∘θ), K = F(√−disc V_H): then ∫_{[G]}[a]·(η_{K/F}∘θ) = 0 (multiplication by the automorphic character carries Π into the orthogonal Π ⊗ η∘θ), so the G∞⁺-components that [H] meets carry the average mass. For Π ≅ Π ⊗ (η_{K/F}∘θ) (Π dihedral with respect to K) that integral need not vanish and the proof gives nothing.`. For SO2 = SO(V_H) with V_H an anisotropic plane (as it is here, G being anisotropic), θ(SO2(F_v)) = N(K_v^×)F_v^{×2}, of index 2 in F_v^×/F_v^{×2} wherever K_v is a field. Globally the spinor norms of G(F)H(A)G(A)⁺ lie in F^×N(A_K^×)(A^×)², which is the kernel of η_{K/F} (class field theory), while θ(SO3(F_v)) = F_v^×/F_v^{×2} contains a uniformizer at any inert v. So η_{K/F}∘θ is a non-trivial character of G(A) trivial on G(F)H(A)G(A)⁺, and G(F)H(A) → G(A)/G(A)⁺ is not surjective. It stays non-trivial on ε whenever θ(U) ⊆ ker η_{K/F}, e.g. for U small, and then [H] meets only half of the G∞⁺-orbits. Checked on the page image of p. 182. ### Nikolaus–Scholze, "On topological cyclic homology", Acta Mathematica 221 (2018) (`PAPER-NIKOLAUS-SCHOLZE-18`)

- **Error** at Proposition II.3.4 and its proof, p. 259 (also arXiv v2) (it affects a stated result). The source says `There is a natural functor Cyc Sp^gen → Cyc Sp = Sp^{BT} ×_{∏_{p∈P} Sp^{BC_{p^∞}}} ∏_{p∈P} Cyc Sp_p. … The induced functor Cyc Sp^gen → ∏_{p∈P} Sp^{BC_{p^∞}} lifts to a functor Cyc Sp^gen → Sp^{BT} by looking at the underlying spectrum with T-action`; it should be `Drop the identification. Cyc Sp (Definition II.1.6(i)) asks each φ_p to be T ≅ T/C_p-equivariant, while the fibre product only records φ_p as a C_{p^∞}-equivariant map. The natural functor Cyc Sp^gen → Cyc Sp does exist: it is the one of §II.6, Cyc Sp^gen ⊆ CoAlg_{(Φ^{C_p})}(TSp_F) → CoAlg_{(−^{tC_p})}(Sp^{BT}) ≃ Cyc Sp (Lemma II.5.8), where the residual T/C_p-action on Φ^{C_p}X makes each Frobenius T-equivariant. On bounded below objects X^{tC_p} is p-complete (Lemma I.2.9) and C_{p^∞} → T is a p-adic equivalence, as the proof of Theorem II.4.11 uses, so there the two notions of Frobenius agree.`. Both sides are categorical fibrations over Sp^{BT}, so an equivalence would give equivalences of fibres. Over X = KU with trivial T-action the fibres are ∏_p Ω^∞W_p^{hT} and ∏_p Ω^∞W_p^{hC_{p^∞}}, with W_p = map(KU, KU^{tC_p}). W_p is a rational KU-module, as KU^{tC_p} is rational (Example I.2.3(iii)), so W_p^{hC_{p^∞}} ≃ W_p, BC_{p^∞} being rationally a point. The fibre of W_p^{hT} → W_p is Σ^{−2}W_p^{hT} (Gysin sequence; W_p is complex oriented), and W_p^{hT} ≠ 0 because the non-zero map KU → KU^{hC_p} → KU^{tC_p} is T-equivariant (as in Example II.1.2(ii)). Being 2-periodic, Σ^{−2}W_p^{hT} has non-zero homotopy in non-negative degrees, so Ω^∞W_p^{hT} → Ω^∞W_p is not an equivalence. The authors' Remark II.1.3 notes the same difference between T- and C_{p^∞}-equivariant Frobenius maps outside the p-complete bounded below case. The theorem is true, by the argument above. - **Misprint** at Theorem 5.3.8, p. 65. The conclusion of Theorem 5.2.6 is not in doubt: the proof opens by deducing it from [Pan22, Theorem 4.2.7] through the embedding of the height-zero Lubin-Tate space into a modular curve, and that route is complete. So the reach is nothing for the paper's results, but a blueprint that follows the conceptual route inherits an unproved step. ### Paškūnas–Quast, "On local Galois deformation rings: generalised reductive groups", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2026) (`PAPER-PASKUNAS-QUAST-26`)

- **Error** at §11, Proposition 11.5 and its proof, pp. 55–56 (published version; arXiv v2, Proposition 11.5, p. 62) (it affects a stated result). The source says `§11: 'Let G be a generalised reductive group over an algebraically closed field κ.' Proposition 11.5: 'Let ρ : Γ_F → P(κ) be a representation such that (1) ρ(Γ_F) is not contained in an R-Levi of P; (2) the G-semisimplification of ρ is not contained in H_0; (3) h⁰(Γ_F, (Lie(G′_1)_sc)^*(1)) = 0. Then h⁰(Γ_F, (Lie G′_sc)^*(1)) = 0.' Proof: 'If ψ = ω or ψ = ω^{−1} then ψ^{p−1} = 1.'`; it should be `Add the hypothesis char κ = p (as in its only application, Proposition 14.5, which works on the special fibre X̄^gen); in characteristic 0 the proposition must also exclude ψ = ω^{±1}, e.g. by replacing condition (2) with 'ψ ≠ ω^{±1}' as in Lemma 11.4.`. The step ψ = ω^{±1} ⇒ ψ^{p−1} = 1 uses ω = χ_cyc ⊗ κ of order dividing p − 1, true only in characteristic p. Counterexample in characteristic 0: G = PGL_2, P = B_2, L = T_2 (dim U = 1, G_1 trivial, H_0 = μ_{p−1} ⊂ T_2), κ = ℚ̄_p, ρ̃ = (1 b; 0 χ_cyc) a non-split extension (H¹(Γ_F, ℚ̄_p(χ_cyc^{±1})) ≠ 0 by the Euler characteristic), so ψ = χ_cyc^{−1} = ω^{−1}. Then (1) holds (non-split), (2) holds (ψ has infinite order, so the G-semisimplification is not in μ_{p−1}), (3) is vacuous; but the line ē_{12} of (Lie SL_2)^*(1) has character ωψ = 1 (the computation in the proof of Lemma 11.4), so h⁰ ≥ 1.
