### Pilloni, "Higher coherent cohomology and p-adic modular forms of singular weights", Duke Mathematical Journal (2020) (`PAPER-PILLONI-20`)

- **Misprint** at §1 Introduction, p. 2 of the author version (17 June 2019), last lines of the paragraph before Theorem 1.1. This defines the T used in Thm 1.1(2), Remark 1.1 and the p. 4 control theorem. HAL v3 (6 Jan 2018) does not have this sentence. Its introduction names only U ('an Hecke operator U at p associated to the double classe K_Kli(p)diag(1,p,p,p^2)K_Kli(p)', v3 p. 2), and its Thm 1.1 uses a bare 'ord'. So the sentence is new in the author version. HAL v3 §7 also lacks the comparison T = T_{p,1} + (1+p+p^2+p^3)T_{p,0} that the author version gives on p. 37.. The source says `There is also a corresponding Hecke operator T at p associated to the double coset K_p diag(p^2, p, p, 1)K_p which acts on the cohomology of X_K.`; it should be `Suggested rewording: 'There is also a corresponding Hecke operator T at p, a modification of the double coset operator T_{p,1} = K_p diag(p^2,p,p,1)K_p, which acts on the cohomology of X_K. T is the normalized composite of the parahoric double cosets GSp4(Z_p)diag(p,p,p,1)GSp4'(Z_p) ⋆ GSp4'(Z_p)diag(p,1,1,1)GSp4(Z_p) (§7). It acts as p^{3-r}(T_{p,1} + (1+p+p^2+p^3)T_{p,0}), with T_{p,0} = pK_p. For r = 2 and k ≥ 2 it is congruent to pT_{p,1} mod p, so its ordinary part is that of the normalized double coset operator.' Besides the Hecke-algebra identity, the normalization p^{3-r} (a factor p when r = 2) is needed. K_p diag(p^2,p,p,1)K_p and K_p diag(1,p,p,p^2)K_p are indeed the same double coset: the two matrices are Weyl-conjugate with the same similitude p^2.`. Checked on the page images of pp. 2, 3, 4, 37 and 38.
(1) The discrepancy is real. §7, p. 37 says 'The Hecke operator T is related to the classical Hecke operator T_{p,1} = GSp4(Z_p)diag(1,p,p,p^2)GSp4(Z_p) … This suggests to replace T_{p,1} by a composition (denoted T) of two double cosets', and 'an elementary computation reveals that T = T_{p,1} + (1+p+p^2+p^3)T_{p,0}'. p. 38: 'The Hecke operator T that we use acts like p^{3-r}(T_{p,1} + (1+p+p^2+p^3)T_{p,0})'. The body then works only with T = T1∘T2 (p. 39 'We let T = T1 ◦ T2'; §8; §11.1.1).
(2) I checked the identity by counting degrees, using footnote 8's chains G → G/H1 → (G/H1)/H2. There are 1+p+p^2+p^3 choices of H1 and p+1 of H2. H2 ≠ G[p]/H1 gives L = ker of type (1,p,p,p^2), each counted once, so deg T_{p,1} = p(1+p+p^2+p^3). H2 = G[p]/H1 gives multiplication by p, counted 1+p+p^2+p^3 times. The eigenvalue formula on p. 38 also checks out: p^{3-r}[p^{-1}Σ − p^{-3}αδ + (1+p+p^2+p^3)p^{-3}αδ] = p^{2-r}Σ + p^{1-r}(1+p+p^2)αδ.
(3) The p. 2 sentence is written in parallel with the one for U, where 'associated to' is meant literally: §10, p. 57 says U 'corresponds to the operator p^{3-r}U_{Kli(p),1}'. Read the same way, the sentence identifies T with the normalized double coset operator, and that is inaccurate. The difference p·(1+p+p^2+p^3)·T_{p,0} is nonzero.
(4) Case for the defence. The sentence says 'associated to', not 'equal to'. The introduction itself, on p. 4, says T is built from the factorization diag(p^2,p,p,1) = diag(p,p,p,1)·diag(p,1,1,1) as T1 and T2. §7 gives the exact definition and states the relation. So the intended meaning is clear from context, which makes this a slip or imprecision (misprint class), not a false statement.
(5) Consequences: none. For r = 2, v(αδ) = k+1, so the normalized term p(1+p+p^2+p^3)T_{p,0} has eigenvalue (1+p+p^2+p^3)p^{-2}αδ, of valuation k−1. The paper itself notes (p. 38) 'T and pT_{p,1} are congruent modulo p for k ≥ 2'. Integrally, this term is p^{k-1} times an automorphism, because the central element p acts through a prime-to-p central automorphism of X_K. Theorem 1.1(2) and Remark 1.1 assume k > p+1 ≥ 3. So the T-ordinary part equals the pT_{p,1}-ordinary part, and both results are true under either reading. Nothing later in the paper uses the intro sentence; every proof uses the T of §7. Recorded as `PAPER-PILLONI-20/E1`; looked for an existing correction in: The author's version on V. Pilloni's homepage (https://www.imo.universite-paris-saclay.fr/~pilloni/complexhidatheorygsp4.pdf, 17 June 2019, 113 pp., SHA-256 4c05724efeab1dbbb108f980ec9a722127d2a8cd2abf6e8c2a6a2251cf0f9f58), which is post-referee but precedes the journal's final revision (15 October 2019), and HAL hal-01393374v3 (6 January 2018) at the same place; the published Duke text is paywalled and could not be compared; Crossref for doi:10.1215/00127094-2019-0075 (no relation, update-to or updated-by record; no update records), the errata and addenda of Duke Math. J. since June 2019, the Project Euclid article page, zbMATH 07226649 (Zbl 1481.11051) and the author's homepage: no erratum or correction; Later work citing the paper, searched for reported errors: Boxer–Calegari–Gee–Pilloni (arXiv:1812.09269v3), Boxer–Pilloni, Higher Hida theory for Siegel modular forms (Invent. Math. 2026) and Higher Coleman theory (arXiv:2002.06845v2), Loeffler–Pilloni–Skinner–Zerbes (arXiv:1905.08779v5), Loeffler–Zerbes (arXiv:2003.05960v4, arXiv:2106.14511v2, arXiv:2110.13102v3, ICM 2022), Grossi (arXiv:2106.05666v4), Calegari–Geraghty (arXiv:1907.08691v1), and the citing works listed by Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and OpenCitations; none reports a mistake in the paper.
- **Error** at §3.1, proof of Proposition 3.1.1, second paragraph, p. 12 of the author version (PDF p. 12). HAL v3 has the same sentence word for word ("There is a surjective map of coherent sheaves over X : OX → OX̄red and we denote by IX its kernel"), but it sits in the paragraph just before Proposition 3.1.1 on printed p. 10 (PDF p. 11), followed by "If X has reduced special fiber then IX = mOk OX".. The source says `There is a surjective map of coherent sheaves over 𝔛 : 𝒪_𝔛 → 𝒪_{X̄^{red}} and we denote by 𝔍_𝔛 its kernel.`; it should be `Delete "coherent" and read: "There is a surjective map of sheaves of 𝒪_𝔛-modules 𝒪_𝔛 → 𝒪_{X̄^{red}}; we denote by 𝔍_𝔛 its kernel." The two sheaves are coherent over 𝔛 only when k is discretely valued. The rest of the proof stands as printed.`. I transcribed the sentence from the page rendered at 250 dpi. §3.1 lets k be "a complete non-archimedean field" with no discreteness assumption. The section's results are also used later over non-discretely valued fields: Corollary 3.1.1 is applied "over the non-archimedean field (k(x), k(x)+)" for a maximal rank-1 point x (proof of Prop. 3.4.1, p. 15).

Counterexample: take k = C_p and X = Spa(C_p, O_{C_p}), which is separated and of finite type. It has the formal model 𝔛 = Spf O_{C_p}, whose underlying space is a single point. Then X̄ = Spec(O_{C_p}/m) = Spec F̄_p, which is already reduced. So the printed map is O_{C_p} → F̄_p on global sections, and its kernel is 𝔍_𝔛 = m_{C_p}.

For 𝒪_{X̄^{red}} to be a coherent 𝒪_𝔛-module, the kernel of 𝒪_𝔛 → 𝒪_{X̄^{red}} must be of finite type. On a one-point space that means m_{C_p} must be a finitely generated O_{C_p}-module. It is not. In a valuation ring every finitely generated ideal is principal. If m = (π), then |π| would be the largest absolute value below 1. But |p^{1/n}| = p^{-1/n} tends to 1, so no such largest value exists. Equivalently, F̄_p = O_{C_p}/m is not finitely presented. The claim that this is a map of coherent sheaves is therefore false for non-discretely valued k. For discretely valued k it is true, because 𝔛 is then noetherian.

The mistake is harmless. The proof uses only two facts, and neither needs coherence:
1. 𝒪^{++} = colim 𝔍_𝔛.
2. Čech cohomology equals cohomology for 𝔍_𝔛 on separated models.
Fact 2 follows because H^i(𝔘, 𝔍) = 0 for i > 0 on an affine 𝔘 = Spf A. This comes from the exact sequence 0 → 𝔍 → 𝒪_𝔛 → 𝒪_{X̄^{red}} → 0. Both 𝒪_𝔛 and the quasi-coherent sheaf 𝒪_{X̄^{red}} on the affine scheme have no higher cohomology. Also A → (A/mA)_red is surjective on sections, so H^1(𝔘, 𝔍) = 0 as well. The colimit result cited as [19] prop. 3.1.10 applies to arbitrary sheaves. So this is a false side remark, not a failed step. I class it as an error rather than a misprint because the word states a property that fails, rather than being a typing slip. The defence fails. §3.1 says "Let k be a complete non-archimedean field" and puts no discreteness hypothesis on k. The paper uses §3 over non-discretely valued fields: Corollary 3.1.1 is applied over completed residue fields k(x) in the proof of Prop. 3.4.1 (p. 15), and Lemma 3.2.2 is applied to cohomology over C_p in §13.3 (p. 89). No convention makes 𝒪_{X̄^{red}} coherent over 𝔛. It is generated by one section, 1, whose annihilator is 𝔍_𝔛, so coherence would need 𝔍_𝔛 to be of finite type.

Simplest counterexample: 𝔛 = Spf O_k. Then 𝔍_𝔛 = m_{O_k}. For a non-discrete valuation, m_{O_k} is not finitely generated, because a finitely generated ideal of a valuation ring is principal. So k̃ = O_k/m is finitely generated but not finitely presented over the coherent ring O_k, and is not coherent.

The same failure happens on every formal model 𝔛 of every non-empty X. Suppose 𝔍_𝔛 = (f_1,…,f_r) on an affine Spf A. Each f_j has some power in mA, so its sup norm on the generic fibre is below 1. Every element of (f_1,…,f_r)A then has sup norm at most max_j |f_j|_sup < 1. But m ⊂ 𝔍_𝔛 contains constants a with max_j |f_j|_sup < |a| < 1, which is a contradiction. The HAL v3 sentence "𝔍_𝔛 = m_{O_k}𝒪_𝔛" shows the same thing directly. When O_k is a DVR, A is noetherian and the statement is true.

Why this is harmless: the proof never uses coherence. Repeating the proof of the first isomorphism needs only three facts.
(a) 𝒪_𝒳^{++} = colim_𝔛 𝔍_𝔛. Elements of 𝔍_𝔛 have a power in m𝒪_𝔛, so they have |f| < 1. Conversely, a section with |f| < 1 on an affinoid is topologically nilpotent, so it lies in 𝔍_𝔛 on a suitable model.
(b) [19] prop. 3.1.10 and the reduction to finite coverings. These are purely topological statements.
(c) H^i(𝔘, 𝔍_𝔛) = 0 for i > 0 on affine opens 𝔘 = Spf A (so H^i = Ȟ^i on the separated 𝔛). This follows from 0 → 𝔍 → 𝒪_𝔘 → 𝒪_{Ū^{red}} → 0. Here 𝒪_𝔘 is acyclic on affines (it is lim 𝒪/ϖ^n, with Mittag-Leffler), 𝒪_{Ū^{red}} is quasi-coherent on the affine scheme Ū^{red}, and A → (A/mA)_red is surjective.

Consequences: Proposition 3.1.1 is correct for arbitrary k with the word "coherent" deleted. Deleting that word is the right, minimal correction. Prop. 3.1.1 itself is never cited later in the paper; a search of the whole author version finds no citation. Prop. 3.4.1 uses Corollary 3.1.1, whose proof relies on [26] and Theorem 3.1.1, not on Prop. 3.1.1. The mistake is nonetheless real, because Prop. 3.1.1 itself is stated for arbitrary k. It is a false descriptive claim rather than a typographical slip, so I class it as an "error" with affects "nothing". Some readers might call it a misprint, since the intended meaning ("surjective map of sheaves") is clear. - **Misprint** at §12.7.2, paragraph before Lemma 12.7.2.2 and the statement of Lemma 12.7.2.2, p. 78. The source says `p. 78 (checked on the page image at 110 and 250 dpi): "Let us denote by 𝓕𝓛^+ → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n, e_1)^+ the moduli space of flags (a locally direct summand of rank 1 in this case) Fil ω_G of ω_G together with a trivialization ρ ∈ Grω_G = ω_G/Filω_G^(18)." and "Lemma 12.7.2.2. — The space 𝓕𝓛^+_{n,ε,w,w'} descends to an open-subspace of 𝓕𝓛^+ → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n, e_1)^+ that we denote by 𝓕𝓛^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'}. This is the space of flags Filω_G ⊂ ω_G and trivialization ρ ∈ Gr_{ω_G} which satisfy the following conditions : — (Filω_G ∩ ω_G^{mod,+})_w = Fil^{can}_w, — The trivialization ρ belongs to ω_G^{mod,+}/(Filω_G ∩ ω_G^{mod,+}) and reduces to the element HT_4(1) of Gr^{can}_{w'}." In both places the second argument is an italic e with subscript 1 (e_1), not ε.`; it should be `Replace 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n, e_1)^+ with 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n, ε)^+ in both places.`. The page image confirms the printed e_1 in both places; this is not a text-layer artefact. Under the paper's own notation the second argument of 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n, ·) is the rational number ε ∈ [0, n−1/(p−1)] ∩ Q. See §12.7.1, p. 77: "We denote by 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε) ⊂ 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n) the quotient of 𝒳(p^n,ε) by 𝔎𝔩𝔦(Z/p^n) and by 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε)^+ ⊂ 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n)^+ the quotient of 𝒳(p^n,ε) by 𝔎𝔩𝔦(Z/p^n)^+". e_1 is the first basis vector of (Z/p^nZ)^4 (§12.2.2). The only spaces indexed by basis vectors are 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i) for i ∈ {2,3}, which take three arguments. No 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n, e_1) is defined anywhere: a search of the text finds only these two occurrences. ε is the right base, for three reasons. (1) FL^+_{n,ε,w,w'} lies over 𝒳(p^n,ε), which is the space that is quotiented to give 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε)^+. (2) The second condition uses HT_4(1). On p. 78 this map is defined only "Over 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε)^+ … obtained via the map ψ", where ψ is the universal trivialization of H_n^D. So the base has to be the '+' space at level ε. (3) The companion Lemma 12.7.2.1, immediately before, descends to FL → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε). The notation cannot be read charitably. P_Kli is the stabiliser of ⟨e_1⟩ (§5.1.2, p. 20), but that is already encoded in the subscript "Kli", and "e_1" is not an admissible value for the ε slot. Even if one read it as 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n)^+, the notation is still undefined; ε is the reading that agrees with everything around it. Nothing downstream uses 'e_1'. On p. 79 the projection is π : FL^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'} → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), the composite through the '+' space, followed by T_{w',n}-invariants. Corollary 13.2.2.1 (p. 86) uses only FL^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'}. The proof of Lemma 13.3.2.1 (p. 89) defines its own FL^+ as the G_m-torsor over FL → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε). That is a separate minor inconsistency ('+' vs no '+'), not part of this finding. So the slip changes no statement or argument. HAL v3 has the same text: PDF p. 68 (printed p. 67), "Let us denote by 𝓕𝓛^+ → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n, e_1)^+ the moduli space of flags …" and "Lemma 12.7.2.2. — The space 𝓕𝓛^+_{n,ε,w',w} descends to an open-subspace of 𝓕𝓛^+ → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n, e_1)^+ …". The v3 lemma has a different subscript order and a condition "ρ reduces to the element HT(1)", but the e_1 slip is the same. - **Misprint** at §12.8.2, proof of Proposition 12.8.2.1, p. 79 (author version, 17 June 2019); in HAL v3 it is the same proposition number on printed p. 68 (PDF p. 69). The source says `"The 𝒰-Čech complex of the sheaf ℒ^{κ_A} ⊗ ω^r is a bounded complex of projective Banach A[1/p]-modules which computes RΓ(𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), 𝒢^{κ_A,w} ⊗ ω^r). The group 𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^nℤ) acts on this complex and the direct factor of invariants computes the cohomology RΓ(𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), ℱ^{κ_A,w} ⊗ ω^r)." (checked on the page rendered at 300 dpi: the subscript "Kli" is clearly printed on 𝒳 in the first RΓ)`; it should be `"... which computes RΓ(𝒳(p^n,ε), 𝒢^{κ_A,w} ⊗ ω^r) (= RΓ(ℱℒ_{n,ε,w}, ℒ^{κ_A} ⊗ ω^r))". The subscript Kli should be dropped from 𝒳.`. The paper puts 𝒢^{κ_A,w} on the full level space, not on the Klingen quotient. On p. 78 it says: "We denote by 𝒢^{κ_A,w} the Banach sheaf generic fiber of 𝔊^{κ_A,w} over 𝒳(p^n,ε) × Spa(A[1/p],A)". Here 𝔊^{κ_A,w} = (π_2)_* ℒ^{κ_A} over X(p^n,ε) × Spf A (§12.6.2, p. 76). The Klingen-level sheaf is the separate sheaf ℱ^{κ_A,w} = ((π_3)_* 𝔊^{κ_A,w})^{T_{w,n}}, with π_3 : X(p^n,ε) → X_{Kli}(p^n,ε) (p. 77). The display just above the proposition (p. 79) is exactly the corrected identity: RΓ(𝒳(p^n,ε), 𝒢^{κ_A,w}⊗ω^r) = RΓ(ℱℒ_{n,ε,w}, ℒ^{κ_A}⊗ω^r). The proof takes a covering 𝒰 of ℱℒ_{n,ε,w}, so its Čech complex computes RΓ(ℱℒ_{n,ε,w}, ℒ^{κ_A}⊗ω^r), which equals RΓ(𝒳(p^n,ε), 𝒢⊗ω^r). The next sentence takes 𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^nℤ)-invariants to reach the Klingen level. That step only makes sense if the complex is still at full level 𝒳(p^n,ε), which matches the second display, RΓ(𝒳_{Kli}, ℱ⊗ω^r) = RΓ(𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^nℤ), RΓ(ℱℒ_{n,ε,w}, ℒ⊗ω^r)). The same pattern appears in Corollary 12.9.2.1 on p. 80: H^i(𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), ℱ⊗ω^r(−D)) = H^0(Kli(ℤ/p^n), H^i(𝒳(p^n,ε), 𝒢⊗ω^r(−D))). One charitable reading is RΓ(𝒳_{Kli}, (π_3)_*𝒢), which gives the same thing because π_3 is finite. But the paper always writes that pushforward explicitly, so as printed the formula names a space the sheaf does not live on. It is a subscript slip, not a mathematical error: the corrected argument goes through unchanged. HAL v3 (printed p. 68, PDF p. 69) has the identical sentence ("𝒰-Chech complex ... computes RΓ(𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), 𝒢^{κ_A,w} ⊗ ω^r)"), so the slip was there in 2018 and was not fixed by June 2019. Whether the Duke version fixes it cannot be checked because that text is paywalled. Recorded as `PAPER-PILLONI-20/E101`; looked for an existing correction in: The author's version on V. - **Misprint** at §12.9.1, Lemma 12.9.1.3, in both the statement and the last line of the proof, p. 81 of the author version. HAL v3 (Lemma 12.9.1.2, printed p. 70 = PDF p. 71) has the same '⋆−mod' in the statement. Its proof's final equality instead reads '𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^⋆ = 𝔛(p^n)^{⋆−mod} ×_{𝔛(p^n)^{⋆−HT}} 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^{⋆−HT}'. So the revision spread the undefined notation into the proof.. The source says `Lemma 12.9.1.3. — The formal scheme 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^{⋆−HT} is affine and the map 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^{⋆−mod} → 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^{⋆−HT} is a projective map and is an isomorphism on the generic fiber. […] The final claim follows from the obvious equality 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^{⋆−mod} = 𝔛(p^n)^{⋆−mod} ×_{𝔛(p^n)^{⋆−HT}} 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^{⋆−HT}.`; it should be `Read 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^⋆ in place of 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^{⋆−mod}, both in the statement (𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^⋆ → 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^{⋆−HT}) and on the left of the displayed equality.`. The symbol 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^{⋆−mod} is not defined anywhere. The only occurrences of '⋆−mod' attached to (p^n,ε,e_i) are these two. The paper defines 𝔛(p^n)^{⋆−mod}, the space 𝔛(p^n,ε)^⋆ ⊂ 𝔛(p^n)^{⋆−mod} (p. 80), and the opens 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^⋆ ⊂ 𝔛(p^n,ε)^⋆ (p. 81, top).

The fibre product on the right is the locus of 𝔛(p^n)^{⋆−mod} where s_{i,4} generates and s_{1,j} ∈ p^ε det ω^{mod}. Since s_{i,j} ≡ HT(e_i)∧HT(e_j) mod p^ε, this is exactly 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^⋆: the condition HT(e_1)∧HT(e_j) ≡ 0 mod p^ε plus the requirement that HT(e_4)∧HT(e_i) generates.

The lemma is used, through Theorem 12.9.2.1, in the proof of Lemma 12.9.2.1 (p. 83) for affine coverings of 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^⋆. HAL v3's proof also writes 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^⋆. The intended object is therefore clear. Recorded as `PAPER-PILLONI-20/E102`; looked for an existing correction in: The author's version on V. - **Misprint** at §12.9.2, first sentence of the proof of Proposition 12.9.2.1, p. 82 of the author version. The same text is in HAL v3 (printed p. 70 = PDF p. 71).. The source says `Proof. The formal scheme 𝔛(p^n,ε) carries a stratification indexed by a subset of the set of all Lagrangian locally direct factors W of V = ℤ^4. […] The case W = {0} corresponds to the open and dense stratum with complement the boundary D. […] We now deal with the case W is one-dimensional. […] In the case W is two dimensional, …`; it should be `'… indexed by a subset of the set of all totally isotropic locally direct factors W of V = ℤ^4.'`. V = ℤ^4 carries a symplectic form of rank 4, so a Lagrangian direct factor has rank exactly 2. The strata listed immediately afterwards, however, are W = {0}, W one-dimensional and W two-dimensional. Only the last of these are Lagrangian.

The paper's own boundary index set is 'the set of totally isotropic direct factors W ⊂ V' (§6.1.5.2, p. 27; see also §5.1.2). The standard stratification of a toroidal compactification of a Siegel threefold is indexed the same way. The word 'Lagrangian' is therefore a slip for 'totally isotropic', and the intended meaning is clear from the list that follows. Here ^∧ is the formal completion along 𝔷_W(p^n,ε)/Γ_W, and D is the whole boundary 𝔐̄_W∖𝔐_W, which is where O_𝔛(−D) restricts to. The printed ideal of 𝔷_W/Γ_W is the wrong sheaf. This is exactly AIP's H^q(Z̃_{V'}, O(−D)). Two smaller slips: item 2 needs "= 0", and the hat-M^x there should be defined as the completion of 𝔐̄_W(p^n,ε), not of itself, along the fibre. The arguments of [3] Prop. 8.2.2.4 and [51] §4 need not be redone for the models 𝔐̄_W(p^n,ε): neither the level p^n, nor ω^mod, nor the Hodge–Tate condition enters the local models in a way that breaks them. Pointing to the argument of [3] Prop. 8.2.2.4 and [51] §4 is an adequate proof, because the needed local models are stated on p. 82, so no gap needs recording. Minimal fix: correct item 1 as above and add "= 0" in item 2.`. I rendered pp. 82–83 at 130 and 250 dpi. Item 1 has no hat, while item 2 has one.

(a) The missing completion in item 1 is a notational slip. The theorem on formal functions computes the completion of the coherent sheaf R^iπ_*𝒪(−D) along the image of ℨ_W/Γ_W, which is finite over Spf 𝒪. The toroidal fibre over a 0-dimensional cusp is the union of strata whose cones meet the interior of the positive cone. That union is closed and equals ℨ_W/Γ_W. So the completion equals H^i of the completion of 𝔛 along ℨ_W/Γ_W. By the p. 82 sentence, that is the completion of 𝔐̄_W/Γ_W along ℨ_W/Γ_W. The paper itself separates 𝔐̄_W/Γ_W from this completion on p. 82. Moreover, the uncompleted quotient is not a reasonable object: Γ_W acts on the torus part M_W by group automorphisms and fixes the identity section, so it does not act freely or properly there. AIP's own version ([3] p. 678) says "it suffices to prove that H^q(Z̃_{V'}, 𝒪_{Ẑ}(−D)) = 0", with Z̃_{V'} = Ẑ_{V'}/Γ, the completed object. So the intended meaning is clear from context: a misprint. The same applies to the self-referential definition under item 2.

(b) The "repeat the arguments" step is not a genuine gap. The "equivalent to" step is correct once the completions are read in. The two local statements depend only on the local structure that Pilloni records from [63] thm 4.1:
- Two-dimensional W: this stratum lies in the ordinary locus, where 𝔛(p^n,ϵ) → 𝔛(p^n) is an open immersion. The local model is the completion along ℨ_W of a relative torus embedding for a torus isogenous to Hom(Sym²V/W^⊥, G_m), divided by a neat Γ_W. This is exactly AIP's situation with trivial abelian part. Their Kempf-type argument (Γ-admissible polarization function h, the finite flat maps Φ_ℓ, and the round-down ⌊ℓ^{-1}sD_h⌋ = −D) needs only the fan and the lattice. Replacing the lattice by an isogenous one (adjoining p^n-th roots of the q-parameters) rescales h and changes nothing.
- One-dimensional W: the fan is R_{≥0} and Γ is trivial, since GL_1 is {±1} and the level is neat. 𝔐̄_W is a line-bundle total space over the elliptic curve 𝔅_W (a G_m-torsor with 0 adjoined). The completed cohomology is ∏_{k≥1} H^i(𝔅_{W,x}, N^k), where N is the conormal bundle, which is isogenous to 𝒪(2O) and has positive degree. Hence H^1 = 0 by cohomology and base change on an elliptic curve, which is the [Mum70]-vanishing step of AIP's proof.

§12.9.1 says openly that it "follows [3] section 8 closely". Deferring a verbatim-applicable argument to one's own earlier paper is not an unproved step. Neither the level p^n, nor ω^mod, nor the Hodge–Tate condition enters the local models in a way that breaks the argument. Checked against AIP [3] (author PDF, pp. 46–50). Its proof of 8.2.2.4 reads: "By the theorem of formal functions it suffices to prove that H^q(Z̃_{V'}, O_{Ẑ_{V'}}(−D)) = 0." In AIP, Ẑ is the formal completion and Z̃ = Ẑ/Γ. D sums D_ρ over all rays ρ, explicitly "not simply over the set Σ(1)^o as in the definition of W_Σ". Pilloni's 𝔷_W is a "closed codimension 1" subscheme and its quotient by Γ_W is the closed W-stratum, so it is AIP's W (the interior-ray part), not D. The divisor D_ρ of a boundary ray, such as ρ = x², meets 𝔷_W: the orbit of the cone ⟨x²,y²⟩ lies in both. So O(−𝔷_W) differs from O(−D) on the completion, and item 1 as printed is the wrong group. Also, 𝔐̄_W/Γ_W without completion is not even defined, because Γ_W does not act properly on the torus part; the preceding sentence uses the completion. The intended object is clear from context, since the proposition is about O(−D) and item 2 correctly uses O(−𝔅_W), the full complement. So this is a misprint.

Defence of the "repeat the arguments" step:
(i) W two-dimensional. Pilloni states on p. 82 that the boundary lies in the ordinary locus, where 𝔛(p^n,ε) → 𝔛(p^n)^mod is an open immersion and 𝔛(p^n)^mod → 𝔛(p^n) is an isomorphism. So ω^mod and the HT condition play no role there. The model is the normalisation of the toroidal compactification at full level p^n: a torus embedding with the character lattice uniformly rescaled, which is still smooth for the fan. AIP's own 8.2.2.4 already treats such a normalised level-p^n model, X_1(p^n)(v). Its inputs all survive a finite normalisation: a smooth admissible decomposition, a polarisation function h, the [C-S] splitting, freeness of Γ, and ampleness of O(D'_h) (from FC V.5.8, or AIP's alternative argument via the boundary).
(ii) W one-dimensional. The torus has rank 1 and Γ_W is trivial. The completion is a line bundle over the elliptic curve 𝔅_W completed along its zero section. The cohomology of O(−𝔅_W) is then the product over k ≥ 1 of H^i(𝔅_W, L^k), with L isogenous to O(2O) and hence ample. This vanishes by Mumford §16, which is the argument AIP use in their first proof of Thm 8.2.2.3.
One caveat the text does not address: §12.1 takes O = O_{C_p}, which is not noetherian, so EGA III formal functions needs a routine descent to a finite extension. Everything is finitely presented, so this is standard.

Downstream use: Lemma 12.9.2.1 (p. 83) → Cor. 12.9.2.1 → Prop. 12.9.1 (vanishing of H^i_cusp for i > 1) → §13. The intended statement is right and the proof goes through with the corrected item 1, so nothing downstream is affected. - **Gap** at §12.9.2, proof of Lemma 12.9.2.1, last paragraph, p. 83 of the author version (17 June 2019). HAL v3 has the same text, with "Chech" for Čech. The proof is on printed pp. 71–72 there (PDF pp. 72–73), and this passage is on p. 72. (it affects the proof). The source says `We deduce from thm 12.9.2.1 that Čech(𝔘_i, 𝔏^{κ_A}⊗ω^r(−D))[1/p] is concentrated in degree 0. We now consider the Čech complex associated to the covering 𝔘 = 𝔘_2∪𝔘_3 of 𝔉𝔏_{n,ε,w} for the sheaf 𝔏^{κ_A}(−D)). Then Čech(𝔘, 𝔏^{κ_A}⊗ω^r(−D))[1/p] computes RΓ(ℱℒ_{n,ε,w}, ℒ^{κ_A}⊗ω^r(−D)). But this Čech complex is quasi-isomorphic to the complex: H^0(𝒳(p^n,ε,e_2)^⋆, π_⋆𝒢^{κ_A}⊗ω^r(−D)) ⊕ H^0(𝒳(p^n,ε,e_3)^⋆, π_⋆𝒢^{κ_A}⊗ω^r(−D)) ⟶ H^0(𝒳(p^n,ε,e_2)^⋆ ∩ 𝒳(p^n,ε,e_3)^⋆, π_⋆𝒢^{κ_A}⊗ω^r(−D)) and has therefore cohomology in degree 0 and 1.`; it should be `Add the missing step. Write 𝔛_2, 𝔛_3 for 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_2)^⋆, 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_3)^⋆. The intersection 𝔛_2 ∩ 𝔛_3 is the inverse image in 𝔛_2 = 𝔛(p^n)^{⋆−mod} ×_{𝔛(p^n)^{⋆−HT}} 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_2)^{⋆−HT} of the locus in the affine 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_2)^{⋆−HT} = Spf A⟨s_{1,j}/(s_{2,4}p^ε)⟩ where s_{3,4}/s_{2,4} is a unit. That locus is again affine: it is the locus where s_{2,4} and s_{3,4} are both invertible and s_{1,j} ∈ p^ε det ω^mod. Projectivity and the isomorphism on generic fibres are preserved by this open base change, so Theorem 12.9.2.1 also applies to 𝔛_2 ∩ 𝔛_3 with the small sheaf π_⋆𝔊^{κ_A,w}⊗ω^r(−D) restricted to it. Hence the Čech complex of the mixed intersections 𝔘_2 ∩ 𝔘_3, after inverting p, is also concentrated in degree 0. Only with this does the Mayer–Vietoris total complex reduce to the displayed two-term complex. This correction is right and essentially minimal. As a separate harmless misprint, the display writes 𝒢^{κ_A} for 𝒢^{κ_A,w}.`. The proof only establishes acyclicity for the two pieces. It says "We deduce from thm 12.9.2.1 that Čech(𝔘_i, …)[1/p] is concentrated in degree 0" for i ∈ {2,3}. That rests on Lemma 12.9.1.3, which gives each 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^⋆ a projective map to an affine that is an isomorphism on generic fibres. The Čech complex of 𝔘 = 𝔘_2 ∪ 𝔘_3 is quasi-isomorphic to the Mayer–Vietoris total complex [Čech(𝔘_2) ⊕ Čech(𝔘_3) → Čech(𝔘_2∩𝔘_3)]. Acyclicity on the pieces alone gives exact sequences 0 → H^0 → H^0(X_2)⊕H^0(X_3) → H^0(X_23) → H^1 → 0 and H^{j+1}(FL) ≅ H^j(X_23) for j ≥ 1. So the claimed concentration in degrees 0 and 1 is equivalent to H^j(X_2∩X_3, π_⋆𝒢⊗ω^r(−D)) = 0 for j ≥ 1, and the text never states or proves this.

Defence attempted. The intersection is not affine, because the pieces themselves are only projective over affines, not affine. It is affinoid on the generic fibre, but π_⋆𝒢 is a Banach sheaf on the minimal compactification, not a coherent sheaf. Being affinoid therefore gives no acyclicity; Theorem 12.9.2.1 with a formal model is what supplies it. The strategy in the §12.9 introduction ("covered by two affines") shows this is what the author meant. The analogous argument in §14 (proof on p. 91 onward) has no such gap, because there the covering opens are genuinely affine and D(s_1)∩D(s_2) = D(s_1 s_2). Here the gap is filled by one line, since Theorem 12.9.2.1 applies to the intersection exactly as to the pieces (see the correction). So the step is asserted without justification, but it is true.

- **Misprint** at §13.1.1 (Slope decomposition), condition 4 in the definition of an h-slope decomposition, p. 84 of the author version (17 June 2019). HAL v3: §13.1.1, printed p. 72 (PDF p. 73), same wording.. The source says `4. For any polynomial Q with roots of valuation strictly greater than h, the restriction of Q^⋆(U) to M^{>h} is an invertible endomorphism. Here Q^⋆ is the reciprocal of Q.`; it should be `Minimal fix: replace "with roots of valuation strictly greater than h" by "with roots of valuation ≥ −h". This is Urban's "Q of slope ≤ h" ([81] §2.3.1), whose reciprocal Q^⋆ has all its roots of valuation ≤ h. An equivalent form: P(U)|_{M^{>h}} is invertible for every nonzero polynomial P whose roots (in k̄) all have valuation ≤ h. Variants of this correction that add the side condition "Q(0) a unit" or "Q(0) ≠ 0" are also right and equivalent; these side conditions are harmless but not needed. Rescaling Q does not affect invertibility, and a root 0 (valuation +∞ ≥ −h) only lowers the degree of Q^⋆.`. The printed text matches the page image at 150 dpi exactly. In HAL v3 condition 4 is word-for-word the same; only condition 3 differs, lacking "(in an algebraic closure of k)". The text layers of HAL v1 and v2 give the same condition 4.

Why the printed condition fails:
- The paper uses "reciprocal" in the standard sense, X^d Q(1/X) (compare §5.1.5, p. 23: "the roots of the reciprocal of Θ(Q_ℓ(X))").
- For Q = c∏(X−α_i) this gives Q^⋆(U) = c∏(1−α_i U). Its invertibility only says that U − β is invertible for β = 1/α_i, and these have v(β) < −h. That is the wrong condition.

Counterexample: k = Q_p, M = k^2, U = diag(1,p), h = 1/2.
- Decomposition A: M^{≤h} = 0 and M^{>h} = M. Condition 3 is vacuous. For condition 4, Q^⋆(U) = diag(c∏(1−α_i), c∏(1−pα_i)). Here v(α_i) > 1/2, so 1−α_i and 1−pα_i are units, and a root α_i = 0 gives a factor 1.
- Decomposition B: M^{≤h} = ke_1 (eigenvalue 1, valuation 0 ≤ 1/2) and M^{>h} = ke_2. It also satisfies conditions 1–4 as printed.
- So the uniqueness asserted right after the definition ("By [81], coro. 2.3.3 ... it is unique") is false under the printed definition.
- Reading "reciprocal" as 1/Q does not rescue it. Then Q(U) must be invertible when v(root) > h, and Q = X−p kills e_2, so neither A nor B qualifies and no decomposition exists at all.

Checked against [81] (Urban, Ann. of Math. 174 (2011), §2.3.1, from the Annals PDF):
- Urban says Q is of slope ≤ h "if Q(0) ∈ O_L^× and if the roots of Q^*(X) := X^d Q(1/X) ... have their slope ... less or equal to h".
- His condition (4) reads: "For any polynomial Q of slope ≤ h, the restriction of Q^*(u) to M_2 is an invertible endomorphism of M_2".
- So Urban requires roots of Q of valuation ≥ −h, not > h, and the proposed correction states exactly that.
- Equivalence with the P(U) form: P ↦ P^⋆ is a bijection, up to scalars, between polynomials with P(0) ≠ 0 and roots of valuation ≥ −h and polynomials with roots of valuation ≤ h, and P^⋆⋆ = P.
- Under the corrected condition, uniqueness holds even with Pilloni's condition 3. Take P = the characteristic polynomial of U on M_1. P(U) kills M_1 and is invertible on M_2'. This forces M_1 ⊂ M_1', and M_2 ⊂ M_2' follows the same way.
- In the counterexample the correction rules out A: Q = 1−X gives Q^⋆(U) = diag(0, p−1).

Why it affects nothing:
- The intended notion is clear from the citation of [81] and from the use of Serre [72] and Coleman [14] for existence.
- The later uses all rely on the standard notion: Prop. 13.1.3.1, §13.2–13.3, Lemma 14.7.1, Rem. 14.8.1 (H^{>0} = (1−f)H) and "0-slope decomposition is functorial" (§14, near p. 107).
- The Duke version was not available to compare. The printed text matches the page image at 130 dpi. The paper defines "reciprocal" as X^d Q(1/X). This is its only meaning in the paper: the Hecke polynomial Q_ℓ(X) = 1 − T_{ℓ,2}X + … has "reciprocal" with roots the Hecke parameters (§5.1.5, p. 23; also p. 32).

Defence attempts, all failing:
(a) Literal reading. For Q = c∏(X−α_i) with v(α_i) > h, Q^⋆(U) = c∏(1−α_iU). Its invertibility only excludes eigenvalues 1/α_i, which have valuation < −h, so this is the wrong condition.
(b) "Roots" read as roots of Q^⋆ (valuation > h). Then eigenvalues of valuation > h are excluded from M^{>h}, the opposite of what is wanted.
(c) Reading Q(U) in place of Q^⋆(U) gives the same opposite condition.
No sign convention rescues it: v(p) = 1 is fixed on the same page.

Counterexamples to the uniqueness claimed in the next line (I checked both):
- M = k, U = 1, h = 0. Both (M^{≤0}, M^{>0}) = (M, 0) and (0, M) qualify, since Q^⋆(1) = c∏(1−β_j) is a unit when v(β_j) > 0.
- M = k², U = diag(1, p), h = 1/2. Both (0, M) and (ke₁, ke₂) qualify.
Under the printed definition, existence also fails for h < 0. Take M = k, U = 1, h = −1. Condition 3 forces M^{≤−1} = 0, and Q = X − 1 (root of valuation 0 > −1) gives Q^⋆(U) = 1 − U = 0. So the claim in §13.1.3 that [72] gives a slope decomposition would also fail as printed.

Urban's definition, checked in the local copy of Ann. Math. 174, §2.3.1: Q is of slope ≤ h if Q(0) ∈ O_L^× and the roots of Q*(X) := X^d Q(1/X) have valuation ≤ h. His condition (4) is "For any polynomial Q of slope ≤ h, the restriction of Q*(u) to M_2 is an invertible endomorphism". This is exactly the correction.

Uniqueness holds under the corrected definition together with Pilloni's condition 3. Let P be the characteristic polynomial of U on M₁. Its roots are nonzero, since condition 3 excludes eigenvalue 0 (valuation +∞). P(U) kills M₁ and is invertible on M₂', which gives M₁ ⊂ M₁'. The argument is symmetric, and M₂ ⊂ M₂' follows the same way.

Later uses, all of which import the standard notion from its sources:
- the uniqueness sentence ([81] Cor. 2.3.3) and the definition of M^{=h} and M^{<h} (p. 84);
- existence via [72] and Prop. 13.1.3.1 via [14] Part A (pp. 84–85);
- the finite slope part in Cor. 13.2.4.2 (p. 87);
- (M^•)^{≤h} for a compact operator in Lemma 14.7.1 and Thm 14.7.1 (p. 99);
- "0-slope decomposition is functorial" (p. 102), which is [81] Lemma 2.3.2.
Nothing in the paper argues from condition 4 as printed. Every claim is right for the intended notion, which the citation of [81] identifies. So this is a sign or inequality slip in the definition ("≥ −h" printed as "> h"), not a failing step. It affects nothing, though a formaliser must use the corrected definition. It is not an "error" affecting "a stated result": the uniqueness claim after the definition is false only under the literal misprinted definition; it is true under the intended one. - **Misprint** at §13.2.1, proof of Lemma 13.2.1.1, last paragraph of p. 85 of the author version. HAL v3 (printed p. 74 = PDF p. 75) has the same sentence. Its preceding sentence is worded '(In case G and G_1 have bad reduction, …)'.. The source says `In case G and G_1 are semi-abelian scheme, one can interpret T_p(G) and T_p(G_1) as the Tate modules of the corresponding 1-motives. We take a basis of T_p(G) ≃ ℤ_p^4 and T_p(G_1) ≃ ℤ_p^4 lifting the basis of G[p^n] and G_1[p^n] provided by the moduli problems. For suitable basis of ω_G and ω_{G_1} respecting the canonical filtration, this diagram is isomorphic to`; it should be `Choose bases e_1,…,e_4 of T_p(G) and f_1,…,f_4 of T_p(G_1), adapted to ξ, so that ξ = diag(1,p,p,p^2) (i.e. f_1 = ξ(e_1)) and e_1 lifts a generator of H_n ⊂ G[p^n]. Then f_1 lifts a generator of the level subgroup H_{n+1} = t_2-image ⊂ G_1[p^{n+1}].`. The moduli problems here are the Klingen-level ones. By p. 77, 𝒳_Kli(p^n,ε) 'parametrizes pairs (x,H_n)', and t_2 lands in 𝒴_Kli(p^{n+1}). So no basis of G[p^n] is provided, only the cyclic subgroup H_n. For G_1 the relevant level is p^{n+1}, not p^n: the next page speaks of 'the group generated by the image [1,p,p,p^2](e_1) in G_1[p^{n+1}]'.

Moreover, if bases of G[p^n] and G_1[p^n] were both prescribed independently, ξ could not in general be put in diagonal form. The subsequent computation needs exactly the diagonal form plus the fact that e_1 lifts a generator of H_n, which gives p_1(e_1) ∈ p^ε.

The intended choice exists. Write T = T_p(G) ⊂ T_1 = T_p(G_1) with T_1/T ≅ L. The vector e_1 is primitive in T_1, because p^{-1}e_1 mod T lies in H_n[p] \ {0} and L ∩ H_n = 0. Take elementary-divisor bases (p,p,p^2) of T/ℤ_p e_1 ⊂ T_1/ℤ_p e_1, lift them, and correct the lifts in T by multiples of e_1. This gives ξ = diag(1,p,p,p^2) with f_1 = e_1.

A charitable reading is also possible: lift the geometric point to full level 𝒳(p^n), resp. 𝒳(p^{n+1}). Under it the sentence is merely loose rather than false. Either way, the intended argument is clear from the rest of the proof. Hence this is a misprint (imprecise wording), not a gap. Confidence is medium because the classification between an imprecision and a misprint is a judgement call. - **Misprint** at §13.2.1, definition of the correspondence and proof of Lemma 13.2.1.1, p. 85 of the author version. The same text is in HAL v3 (printed pp. 73–74 = PDF pp. 74–75), apart from the wording '(G,H_n) ∈ 𝒴_Kli(p^n)'.. The source says `p. 85: 'There is a Hecke correspondence t_1 : C|_{𝒴_Kli(p^n)} → 𝒴_Kli(p^n) where C|_{𝒴_Kli(p^n)} is the moduli space of (G, H_n, L) where (G, H_n) is a point of 𝒴_Kli(p^n) and L ⊂ G[p^2] is a totally isotropic subgroup which is locally for the étale topology isomorphic to (ℤ/pℤ)^2 ⊕ ℤ/p^2ℤ and L ∩ H_n = {0}. The map t_1 sends (G, H_n, L) to (G, H). There is a map t_2 : C_n|_{𝒴_Kli(p^n)} → 𝒴_Kli(p^{n+1}) defined by mapping (G, H_n, L) to (G/L, p^{−1}H_n + L/L).' Proof of Lemma 13.2.1.1: 'Let (K, 𝒪_K) be a rank one point of C_n corresponding to an isogeny ξ : G → G_1.'`; it should be `t_1(G,H_n,L) = (G,H_n). The map is t_2 : C|_{𝒴_Kli(p^n)} → 𝒴_Kli(p^{n+1}), (G,H_n,L) ↦ (G/L, ([p]^{-1}(H_n) + L)/L). In the proof, read 'a rank one point of C_ε'.`. (1) 'H' is not defined in §13; the level subgroup here is H_n. '(G,H)' is a leftover from the Klingen-level-p correspondence of §10 ('The construction is parallel to section 10').

(2) 'C_n' is not defined in §13. There the objects are C|_{𝒴_Kli(p^n)}, its compactification C, and C_ε = C ×_{t_1} 𝒳_Kli(p^n,ε), which is the space Lemma 13.2.1.1 is about. The parallel proof of Lemma 13.2.2.1 (p. 86) says 'a rank one point of C_ε'. The symbol C_n is later defined in §14.2 for a different object (the n-fold iterate of the correspondence over 𝒳_Kli(p)).

(3) 'p^{-1}H_n + L/L' is shorthand with missing parentheses for the image in G/L of [p]^{-1}(H_n) + L. I checked that this is the right level-p^{n+1} subgroup. L ≅ (ℤ/p)^2 ⊕ ℤ/p^2, so L[p] has order p^3. Since L ∩ H_n = 0, L[p] ⊕ H_n[p] = G[p]. Then L ∩ [p]^{-1}(H_n) = L[p], because pL ⊂ L meets H_n trivially. The image therefore has order p^{n+4}/p^3 = p^{n+1}.

The image is generated by the class of any y with py generating H_n. That class has order p^{n+1}, because p^n y ∈ H_n \ {0} is not in L. So the image is cyclic, as a Klingen p^{n+1} structure must be. It agrees with p. 86, 'the group generated by the image [1,p,p,p^2](e_1) in G_1[p^{n+1}]'.

All of these are notational slips with clear intended meaning. Recorded as `PAPER-PILLONI-20/E109`; looked for an existing correction in: The author's version on V. The source says `There is an isomorphism in the category of locally ringed spaces (𝒳, O^+_𝒳) = lim_𝔛(𝔛, O_𝔛) where 𝔛 runs over all formal models of 𝒳 (see [69], thm. 2.22). It writes 'lim' for inverse limits: lim_n in §3.2, and lim_𝔛(𝔛, O_𝔛) for the space itself. Cohomology is contravariant in 𝔛, so the groups H^i(𝔛, O_𝔛) form a direct system. For a limit of quasi-compact quasi-separated spaces, cohomology of the colimit of pulled-back sheaves is the colimit of the cohomologies; that is the cited result. An inverse limit is not the right object. The next step, Čech cohomology computed with finite coverings, also commutes with filtered colimits. - **Misprint** at §13.3.1, proof of Proposition 13.3.1.1, p. 88 (author version, 17 June 2019); HAL v3: same proposition number, printed pp. 76–77 (PDF pp. 77–78). The source says `"By proposition 14.4.1.1^{(22)} we have that R^i(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = 0 for all i > 0. Finally, the trace map Tr : (t_1)_⋆𝒪_{C_ε} → 𝒪_{𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε)} restricts to Tr : (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} → 𝒪^{++}_{𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε)}" (author version p. 88, read from the page image at 110 and 250 dpi; (22) is a footnote mark)`; it should be `R(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε}, i.e. R^i(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = 0 for all i > 0. This is exactly the form Proposition 14.4.1.1(2) states (p. 94): "R(t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪_{C_n} = (t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪_{C_n} and R(t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_n} = (t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_n}".`. I checked the page image (p. 88). The printed chain "R^i(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = 0 for all i > 0" is what is on the page; it is not a text-layer artefact. The middle term has no index i, so read literally the chain says two things: the pushforward (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} is 0, and R^i equals R^0. Both are wrong. The pushforward is not zero: the very next sentence defines the restricted trace Tr : (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} → 𝒪^{++}_{𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε)} on it, and that trace is what builds p^3U on the ++ complexes. The cited result, Proposition 14.4.1.1(2) (p. 94), says R(t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪^{++} = (t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪^{++}. That means the higher direct images vanish; it does not mean the pushforward itself vanishes. Also, on p. 85 (§13.2.1) the paper recalls "the map (t_1)_⋆𝒪_C → R(t_1)_⋆𝒪_C is a quasi-isomorphism." So the author meant R^i(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = 0 for i > 0 and ran together two ways of writing it. The proposed correction fits the paper's own conventions. - **Gap** at §13.3.1, proof of Proposition 13.3.1.1, p. 88 of the author version (the citation of Prop. 14.4.1.1 with footnote 22). The cited Prop. 14.4.1.1(2) is on p. 94 (§14.4.1). HAL v3 has the same citation, without the footnote, on printed p. 76, and states Prop. 14.4.1.1(2) the same way (still only at level p) on printed pp. 81–82. (it affects the proof). The source says `p. 88 (proof of Prop. 13.3.1.1): "By proposition 14.4.1.1 ⁽²²⁾ we have that R^i(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = 0 for all i > 0." Footnote 22: "We again use a result that is only proved in the next section, the proof of this proposition depends only on results obtained in section 3.4, so there is no circularity in our arguments." The cited result, p. 94, Prop. 14.4.1.1(2): "Let t_{n,1} : C_n → 𝒳_{Kli}(p). Then we have R(t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪_{C_n} = (t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪_{C_n} and R(t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_n} = (t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_n}."`; it should be `Minimal fix: state Prop. 14.4.1.1(2) for any Klingen level p^n (n ≥ 1), for the map t_1 : C_{Σ'} → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n)_Σ of §13.2.1, with Σ' chosen smooth, because Prop. 3.4.1 needs that and §13.2.1 does not say it. The conclusion is R(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_C = (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_C, i.e. R^i(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_C = 0 for i > 0. The proof is word for word the same. The 𝒪-version is the "standard computation" already recalled on p. 85. The ++-version comes from the local toroidal charts (Kuga–Sato variety times a torus), Props. 3.4.1 and 3.3.1, the p-dévissage, and the factorisation of t_1 as C_{Σ'} → C_Σ → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n)_Σ (a change of cone decomposition, then a finite map). Restricting over 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε) needs no extra work: higher direct images are local on the target and C_ε = t_1^{-1}(𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε)).`. I rendered pp. 85, 88, 92 and 94 and checked the text. In §13 the correspondence depends on n. On p. 85, C|_{Y_Kli(p^n)} is 'the moduli space of (G, H_n, L) where (G, H_n) is a point of Y_Kli(p^n)', and t_1 : C_{Σ'} → 𝒳_Kli(p^n)_Σ. The proof of 13.3.1.1 uses t_1 : C_ε → 𝒳_Kli(p^n, ε) and needs R^i(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = 0 for i > 0.

Prop. 14.4.1.1 is stated only for t_{n,1} : C_n → 𝒳_Kli(p), the n-fold iterate of the U-correspondence at Klingen level p. §14.1 says: '𝒳_Kli(p) is the analytic Siegel threefold of Klingen level at p'. In the remark on p. 92, the author identifies C_1 with 'the correspondence C|_{Y_Kli(p)} considered in section 13.2.1', which is §13's C in the case n = 1 only.

The case n > 1 cannot be avoided. On p. 55, ε lies in [0, n − 1/(p−1)], and §13.2.2 requires w ≤ ε. A w-analytic κ may need w ≥ 1, which forces n > 1. Cor. 13.2.4.2 allows changing (n, ε, w) only among admissible triples.

As stated, 14.4.1.1 does not formally imply the level-p^n claim. On the abelian locus, C^{(p^n)} = C_1 ×_{Y_Kli(p)} Y_Kli(p^n): because H_n is cyclic, L ∩ H_n = 0 exactly when L ∩ H_n[p] = 0. But no base-change result is available for the ++ sheaves or across the toroidal boundary. So the cited proposition does not cover the step as written.

The step is nonetheless very likely true. The proof of 14.4.1.1 uses nothing specific to level p. The author also 'recall[s]' the non-++ statement (t_1)_⋆𝒪_C ≅ R(t_1)_⋆𝒪_C at level p^n on p. 85, without a reference. So this is a minor gap: the cited result is stated for a different space. The proof is affected, but the stated result is not.

Footnote 22 only addresses circularity. It does not address the level. Lemma 14.3.1(2), cited in the same sentence, is fine: it is a pointwise statement about L alone, so it transfers via (G, H_n, L) ↦ (G, H_n[p], L).

A separate, unrelated slip: the printed '(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = 0' should read 'R(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++} = (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}, i.e. R^i = 0 for i > 0'. Defence first.
(i) For n = 1 the citation is literally correct. §14.2 (p. 92) says C_n|_{𝒴_Kli(p)} is "obtained by iterating n times the correspondence C_1|_{𝒴_Kli(p)} (which is the correspondence C|_{𝒴_Kli(p)} considered in section 13.2.1)". So the author treats the §13.2.1 correspondence as the level-p^n member of the same family.
(ii) Nothing in the proof of 14.4.1.1 (pp. 94–95) depends on the level. On the interior t_1 is finite. The boundary input is the toroidal chart computation (Prop. 3.4.1, Prop. 3.3.1) plus a finite map g. Footnote 22 points the reader to that proof.
(iii) §13.2.1 (p. 85) already "recall[s] that the map (t_1)_⋆𝒪_C → R(t_1)_⋆𝒪_C is a quasi-isomorphism" at level p^n.
So the mathematics is not in doubt.

The defence still does not make the text literally right.
- The ++-statement is stated and proved only for t_{n,1} : C_n → 𝒳_{Kli}(p). Here it is applied to the level-p^n map t_1 : C_ε → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), and no level-p^n ++-statement appears anywhere.
- Taking n = 1 does not cover the use. §13 needs general n: w-analytic κ needs w ≤ ε ≤ n − 1/(p−1), and §13.4 takes n, ε, w large.
- Base change from level p does not give it formally either. On the interior, C at level p^n is C_1 ×_{Y_Kli(p)} Y_Kli(p^n), because H_n is cyclic, so L ∩ H_n = 0 exactly when L ∩ H_n[p] = 0. But the content sits at the boundary, and R(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++} does not formally commute with that finite base change.
So a reader must redo the proof at level p^n. That makes it a genuine but minor gap: a citation used beyond its stated scope, filled routinely.

Consequences. The vanishing is needed to identify RΓ(C_ε, t_1^⋆(−)^{++}) with RΓ(𝒳, (t_1)_⋆t_1^⋆(−)^{++}), so that the ++-trace can define p^3U on the ++ complexes. That gives slopes ≥ −3 in all degrees in Prop. 13.3.1.1. The degree-0 bound (slopes ≥ 0) uses a separate q-expansion argument and is unaffected. Downstream: Prop. 13.3.1.1 → Cor. 13.3.3.1 (pp. 90–91) → Cor. 14.7.1 (p. 100) and Lemma 14.8.4 (p. 102, "with equality if k ≥ 3 by corollary 13.3.3.1") → the main classicity and dimension results. The extension is routine, so no stated result is affected, and affects = the proof. Confidence is medium only because it is a judgement call whether a verbatim-transferable citation counts as a gap. At Klingen level it is the Kli(Z/p^n)-invariants of its pushforward along the finite map π_3. - Bartenwerfer's constant (Thm 3.1.1) works uniformly for completed direct sums: reduce mod p^m, commute cohomology with direct sums on qcqs spaces, then take R lim as in §3.2. - O^{++} differs from m·O^+ by torsion killed by p. - Taking invariants under a finite group of order N costs at most N-torsion. It also needs bounded torsion for R^iπ_⋆L^{κ,++} along π : FL_{Kli,n,ε,w} → X_Kli(p^n,ε), or p^3U rebuilt on RΓ(FL, L^{κ,++}). (1) Lemma 3.2.2 is proved under the standing assumption on p. 12: "Let F be a locally free sheaf of O_X-modules. We assume that there exists F^+ ⊂ F a locally free sheaf of O_X^+-modules such that F = F^+ ⊗ O_X". Its statement on p. 13 needs "a finite affinoid covering of X, such that F^+|_U is trivial". Its conclusion is about F^+ and F/p^nF^+, not about a ++-lattice. On p. 89 it is applied to F^{κ,w,++} ⊗ (ω^{++})^r, where F^{κ,w} = (π_⋆O_{FL^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'}} ⊗̂ A)^{T_{w',n}} is a Banach sheaf (p. 79). That sheaf is not locally free, and it is a ++-lattice, not an O^+-lattice. The covering is chosen only so that FL_{Kli,n,ε,w} is affinoid over each U. At Klingen level, triviality on U is not established: Fil^can is only étale-local, and FL descends from X(p^n,ε) (Lemma 12.7.2.1). The proof of 3.2.2 bounds H^k(U_J, F^+) by Thm 3.1.1 applied to a finite free sheaf, so it does not literally cover this case.

(2) Prop. 14.4.1.1(2) (p. 94) says: "Let t_{n,1} : C_n → X_Kli(p). Then we have ... R(t_{n,1})_⋆O^{++}_{C_n} = (t_{n,1})_⋆O^{++}_{C_n}". Here C_n (§14.2) is the n-fold iterate of the correspondence at Klingen level p. On p. 88 it is applied to t_1 : C_ε → X_Kli(p^n,ε), the level-p^n correspondence of §13.2.1. The O-version at level p^n is "recalled" in §13.2.1, but the ++-version is nowhere stated at that level. This is the only explicit citation of 14.4.1.1 in the paper. Constructing p^3U on RΓ(F^{κ,w,++} ⊗ (ω^{++})^r) also needs the corresponding vanishing for the completed pullback t_1^*F^{κ,w,++}, which is not covered either.

Both uses go beyond the hypotheses of the cited results, and the paper gives no argument for the extensions. So this is a genuine, if minor, gap in the proof as printed, not a text-layer artefact. The fix in the correction is sound: Bartenwerfer's constant is uniform on completed direct sums, and invariants under a finite group cost bounded torsion. The proofs of §3.2 and §14.4.1 adapt without new ideas, so the statement is not in doubt.

Dependence: Prop. 13.3.1.1 (slopes ≥ −3 in all degrees) is used in the proof of the sheaf-level classicity theorem on pp. 90–91 ("This follows from proposition 13.3.1.1, proposition 13.3.3.1, and corollary 13.3.2.1"), and through it in the later classicity results. Because the gap can be filled routinely, no stated result is affected. The degree-0 claim (slopes ≥ 0) uses a separate q-expansion argument and does not depend on these citations. HAL v3 (printed pp. 76–77) has the same text: "We now deduce from lemma 3.2.2 that the map ... has kernel and co-kernel of bounded p-torsion", with the same citation of Prop. 14.4.1.1, whose statement there (p. 82) is identical. I rate confidence medium only because it is a judgement call whether a routine extension of a cited lemma counts as a gap. I checked this on page images of pp. 12–13, 76–79, 85–95 and 99, and of HAL v3 pp. 11, 76–77 and 82.

Defences I tried, and why each fails:

(1) Lemma 3.2.2 under its own hypotheses. p. 12: "Let F be a locally free sheaf of O_X-modules. We assume that there exists F^+ ⊂ F a locally free sheaf of O_X^+-modules such that F = F^+ ⊗ O_X". p. 13: "Let U be a finite affinoid covering of X, such that F^+|_U is trivial." The conclusions concern F^+ and F/p^nF^+.
- Here F^{κ,w} = (π_⋆O_{FL^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'}} ⊗̂ A)^{T_{w',n}} (p. 79) is a Banach sheaf. Locally it is a completed direct sum, not a direct sum, so it is not locally free even in the infinite-rank algebraic sense.
- The lattice used is F^{κ,w} ∩ O^{++} (p. 88), not an O^+-lattice.
- The covering is chosen only so that FL_{Kli,n,ε,w} is affinoid over each U, not so that the lattice is trivial. At Klingen level, analytic-local triviality is not even established: Fil^can is étale-local (p. 78), and FL_Kli is obtained by descent (Lemma 12.7.2.1).
- The proof of 3.2.2 bounds H^k(U_J, F^+/p^n) by Thm 3.1.1 for a finite free sheaf, so it does not literally apply. For completed sums, a uniform bound needs the R lim arguments of §3.2, because Bartenwerfer's c(X) depends on the affinoid.

(2) Is the step avoidable? No. The argument needs the cokernel of H^i(C^{•,++}) → H^i(X, F^{++}⊗…) to be bounded, so that the p^3U-stable image of H^i(X, F^{++}⊗…) in H^i(C^•)^{=a} is bounded. The kernel bound is not needed. Building p^3U directly on Čech complexes would need the same comparison on C_ε, since t_1 is not finite on the compactification.

(3) Prop. 14.4.1.1(2) under its own hypotheses. It is stated for t_{n,1} : C_n → X_Kli(p). §14.2 says that C_1 is the correspondence of §13.2.1, so the citation is literally correct only when the Klingen level is p^1. Proposition 13.3.1.1 needs level p^n with n large (w-analyticity forces w ≤ ε ≤ n − 1/(p−1)). Deducing it by base change along X_Kli(p^n) → X_Kli(p) is not automatic: the map is not known to be flat at the boundary, and this is the ++ lattice. The proof does carry over word for word, so this half is a citation stretch. The completed-pullback vanishing for t_1^*F^{κ,w,++} is also unstated.

Conclusion: the paper as printed supplies no argument, but the missing pieces follow routinely from §3.2, §3.4 and §14.4.1. So this is a genuine but minor gap, and Proposition 13.3.1.1 is not in doubt.

What uses the passage: Prop. 13.3.1.1 (slopes ≥ −3 in all degrees) is cited in the proof of Cor. 13.3.3.1 on p. 91 (the "<k−2" isomorphism in item 1). That corollary feeds Cor. 14.7.1 (p. 100) and Lemma 14.8.4 (p. 102, "with equality if k ≥ 3 by corollary 13.3.3.1"), and through them §14.8 and the main theorems. Since the gap can be filled, none of these stated results is affected. The degree-0 claim (slopes ≥ 0) uses a separate q-expansion argument and does not depend on either citation. Confidence is medium only because deciding whether an unstated routine extension counts as a gap is a judgement call. The facts about the hypotheses are certain. Further occurrences: - p. 101, proof of Lemma 14.8.2: "the analytic adic space over Spa(ℂ, O) attached to 𝔛*_{Kli}(p)". - p. 101, footnote 25: "the ℂ-vector space". - p. 102: "d_i(k) = dim_ℂ fH^i(...)" and "d_i^{†,'}(k) = dim_ℂ H^i_cusp(†,k,2)". - p. 102, Prop. 14.9.1: "⊗_{ℤ_p} ℂ"; Cor. 14.9.1: "⊗ ℂ". - p. 103: "Let f ∈ H^i(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗ ℂ be an eigenclass".`; it should be `Throughout §§13.3.1–14.9, ℂ should be ℂ_p = Frac(O), where O is the ring of integers of ℂ_p fixed in §12.1 for all of Part III. So it should read "tensored with ℂ_p", "dim_{ℂ_p}", "roots a of P in ℂ_p" (HAL v3 has Q̄_p here), "Spa(ℂ_p, O)", "⊗^L_{ℤ_p} ℂ_p" and "ℂ_p-vector space". The page images show a real inconsistency in notation; the text layer is not the cause. §12.1 (p. 73) makes Part III work over "O the ring of integers of ℂ_p", and §12.2.1, §12.9.2 and §13.4 write Spa(ℂ_p, O). The paper never defines ℂ to mean ℂ_p in Part III. Elsewhere ℂ means other things:
- the complex numbers in §5.1 (the Satake isomorphism into ℂ[X*(T)]^W, and GSp4(ℂ)) and in §15 ("Siegel threefold of level K over ℂ", "H^i(p,K_∞;…) = ℂ", and "We fix an isomorphism Q̄_p ≃ ℂ" on p. 108);
- on p. 48 (§7.4) a locally defined ℂ, "the completion of an algebraic closure of W(l)[1/p]".

Read as the complex numbers, "Spa(ℂ, O)" with O = O_{ℂ_p} is not a Huber pair. Even with §15's fixed isomorphism Q̄_p ≃ ℂ it fails, because Q̄_p is not complete and does not contain O. The GAGA-type identification in Lemma 14.8.1 and footnote 25 (the p-adic topology defined through ⊗̂_{ℤ_p} O) only make sense if ℂ = Frac(O) = ℂ_p. The mix is visible inside single passages: on p. 89 "ℂ_p vector spaces" and "tensored with ℂ" sit in the same proof, and §13.4 has "α^{-1} ∈ ℂ_p^×" followed immediately by dim_ℂ of the same ℂ_p-spaces. The correction to ℂ_p is right.

For Cor. 14.6.2, ℂ_p is also more precise than HAL v3's Q̄_p, since P has coefficients in O = O_{ℂ_p}. The author's change from Q̄_p to ℂ suggests ℂ was meant as shorthand for ℂ_p but was never declared.

Comparison with HAL v3 (6 Jan 2018):

- Cor. 14.6.2 printed "roots a of P in Q̄_p" (v3 printed p. 86).

- v3's §14.8 is a different proof using ⊗ Q_p and [1/p], with no Spa(ℂ, O) and no Lemma 14.8.1.
- v3 has no §14.9.
So most of the ℂ occurrences were added in the 2019 revision.

The source says `Proposition 13.3.3.1. — The following diagram is commutative: [top row] RΓ(𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), 𝓕^{k,w^-} ⊗ ω^r) --U--> RΓ(𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), 𝓕^{k,w^-} ⊗ ω^r); [both vertical arrows] d_1; [bottom row] RΓ(𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), 𝓕^{-2-k,w^-} ⊗ ω^{k+r+1}) --p^{-k-1}U--> RΓ(𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), 𝓕^{-2-k,w^-} ⊗ ω^{k+r+1}). That is, d_1∘U = p^{k+1}·U∘d_1, or equivalently U∘d_1 = p^{-k-1}·d_1∘U. The printed factor p^{-k-1} is correct only with the two sides swapped. The fix is to change the sign of the exponent. Corollary 13.3.3.1 and the results built on it (Corollary 14.7.1, Lemma 14.8.4) are stated correctly and follow from the corrected diagram.`. I redid the computation.

(1) §13.2.3 (p. 87, checked on the image) defines U on 𝓕^{κ,w}⊗ω^{r'} for any κ and r' as (1/p^3)Tr ∘ (1/p^{r'})ξ*. Here ξ* is the transport of structure along (ξ*)^{-1}: ω_G → ω_{G_1} (Corollary 13.2.2.1: ξ*s(Fil,ρ) = s((ξ*)^{-1}Fil, (ξ*)^{-1}ρ)), tensored with the natural map on ω^{r'}. So the top row carries p^{-r} and the bottom row carries p^{-(k+r+1)}.

(2) d_1: 𝓕^{k}⊗ω^r → 𝓕^{-2-k}⊗ω^{k+r+1} is a canonical O_X-linear relative operator. It is (d/dY)^{k+1} ⊗ (det)^{k+1} in a flag coordinate Y. It is GL(ω)-equivariant by Bol's identity, (d/dz)^{k+1}((cz+d)^k f(gz)) = det(g)^{k+1}(cz+d)^{-2-k} f^{(k+1)}(gz). That identity is exactly what forces the twist ω^{+(k+1)} that the paper prints. So d_1 commutes with the unnormalised transport along any isomorphism of ω, including the rational one ξ*. It also commutes with t_i^* and with Tr.

Hence d_1∘U_top = p^{-r}·p^{k+r+1}·U_bottom∘d_1 = p^{k+1}U_bottom∘d_1.

Scalar check: for ξ* = c·Id, the top transport is c^{k+2r}p^{-r} and the bottom transport is c^{-2-k}c^{2(k+r+1)}p^{-(k+r+1)} = c^{k+2r}p^{-(k+r+1)}. Their ratio is p^{k+1}.

Coordinate check: from Lemmas 13.2.1.1 and 13.2.2.1, ξ* = diag(p,1) in the basis (HT(e_2), HT(e_4)). The flag coordinate goes Y ↦ pY and det ξ* = p. So (d/dY)^{k+1} picks up p^{k+1}, and the det normalisations cancel to 1 on both rows. Again the factor is p^{k+1}.

With the printed p^{-k-1}, the square would force (p^{k+1} - p^{-k-1})·U∘d_1 = 0, i.e. U∘d_1 = 0, so it is false as printed.

The paper's own Corollary 13.3.3.1 uses the corrected factor. Proposition 13.3.1.1 gives U slopes ≥ -3 in all degrees and ≥ 0 on H^0. So p^{k+1}U_bottom has slopes ≥ k-2 in all degrees and ≥ k+1 on H^0. Through the long exact sequence of Corollary 13.3.2.1, this gives exactly the thresholds <k-2 (isomorphisms in all degrees), <k+1 (H^0 isomorphism) and <k+1 (H^1 injective) in the corollary. With p^{-k-1}, the bound would only be slopes ≥ -k-4, and the corollary would not follow.

I classify this as a sign misprint in the exponent rather than a mathematical error: the downstream statements (Corollary 13.3.3.1, and through it Corollary 14.7.1 and Lemma 14.8.4) are correct and consistent with p^{k+1}. It still 'affects a stated result', because the displayed statement of Proposition 13.3.3.1 is false as printed. HAL v3 has the same p^{-k-1}. I tried to defend the paper and could not.

(1) Normalisations (checked on the images of pp. 86–88). By §13.2.3, U on 𝓕^{κ,w}⊗ω^{r'} is p^{-3}Tr ∘ p^{-r'}ξ^* ∘ res, where ω^{r'} = det^{r'} ω_G (§6: 'we sometimes write ω^r instead of Ω^{(0,r)}'). So the top row carries p^{-r} and the bottom row carries p^{-(k+r+1)}. By Corollary 13.2.2.1, ξ^*s(Fil,ρ) = s((ξ^*)^{-1}Fil, (ξ^*)^{-1}ρ). By Lemma 13.2.2.1, the flag HT(e_2)+αp^w HT(e_4) goes to HT(e_2)+αp^{w+1}HT(e_4). So in the basis (HT(e_2), HT(e_4)) we have ξ^* = diag(p,1), with det of valuation 1, as p. 88 uses ('ξ^*: t_2^*(ω^{++})^r → p^r t_1^*(ω^{++})^r').

(2) Computation. Write sections in a flag coordinate Y and a Gr-trivialisation t:
- top: t^{-k}P(Y)⊗E^r;
- bottom: t^{k+2}Q(Y)⊗E^{k+r+1}, with E the basis of det.

The canonical d_1 is P ↦ P^{(k+1)}. I checked by hand that this formula is invariant under diagonal changes of basis; Bol's identity covers the unipotent ones. After normalisation, transport sends P(Y) to P(pY) on the top row and Q(Y) to Q(pY) on the bottom row. The det factors p^r and p^{k+r+1} cancel exactly. Since (d/dY)^{k+1}[P(pY)] = p^{k+1}P^{(k+1)}(pY), and Tr and restriction commute with the O_X-linear d_1, we get d_1∘U_top = p^{k+1}·U_bot∘d_1. A monomial check in python agrees. So does a scalar check: for ξ^* = c·Id, both unnormalised transports are c^{k+2r}, and the normalisations differ by p^{k+1}. No normalisation in the paper produces p^{-k-1}.

(3) The printed square is false. It would force (p^{k+1} − p^{-k-1})·U∘d_1 = 0. But take a finite-slope class f that is not classical (Uf = αf with α ≠ 0 and d_1f ≠ 0). Then U(d_1f) = p^{-k-1}α·d_1f ≠ 0.

(4) The cited source does not rescue the statement; it explains where the slip came from. [3] is Andreatta–Iovita–Pilloni, Annals 2015; I read the homepage PDF. Its Prop. 7.2.3 (p. 35) prints Θ_αU_{p,i} = α(d_{g−i})^{⟨κ,α∨⟩+1}U_{p,i}Θ_α, with d_i = diag(p^{-1}1_{g−i}, 1_i) (p. 10). For g = 2 and α = t_1/t_2 this gives ΘU = p^{-(k+1)}UΘ, which is exactly Pilloni's p^{-k-1}. But [3] itself uses the other direction elsewhere:
- its §2.5 formula δ_iΘ_α = α(d_i)^{⟨κ,α∨⟩+1}Θ_αδ_i has δ on the left;
- its proof of Prop. 7.3.1 uses U_{p,g−i}Θ_α(f) = p^{k_{i+1}−k_i−1}Θ_αU_{p,g−i}(f).
Both mean ΘU = p^{k+1}UΘ, which agrees with the correction.

(5) Consequences. Proposition 13.3.3.1 is used only in the proof of Corollary 13.3.3.1. With the corrected factor, the bottom operator p^{k+1}U has slopes ≥ k−2 in every degree (Prop. 13.3.1.1 gives U slopes ≥ −3) and ≥ k+1 on H^0. The triangle of Corollary 13.3.2.1 then gives parts 1–3 with exactly the printed thresholds <k−2, <k+1 and <k+1. With the printed p^{-k-1}U, the bottom slopes are only ≥ −k−4 and nothing follows. Corollary 13.3.3.1 then feeds Corollary 14.7.1 (p. 100) and Lemma 14.8.4 (p. 102; 'equality if k ≥ 3', i.e. slope 0 < k−2), and both are right with p^{k+1}.

- **Misprint** at §3.2, proof of Proposition 3.2.1 (injectivity when 𝒳 is proper), p. 13 (author version, 17 June 2019). The source says `Author version p. 13, checked on the rendered page: "Take a normal proper formal model 𝔛 of 𝒳 such that the sheaf ℱ⁺ comes from a locally free sheaf ℱ on 𝔛. We can obtain such a model as follows. By Raynaud's theory, we can find a model 𝔛′ of 𝒳 which admits an affinoid covering 𝔘′ whose generic fiber refines 𝒰. We can replace 𝔛′ by its normalisation 𝔛 in 𝒳. This is still a formal model. The sheaf ℱ⁺ comes from a locally free sheaf ℱ on 𝔛′. By [52], lemma 2.6, this model is automatically proper. Let 𝔙 be an affine covering of 𝔛 and 𝒱 be its generic fiber. ... The cohomology Ȟⁱ_𝒱(𝒳, ℱ⁺) is identified with the cohomology Hⁱ(𝔛, ℱ) and it is a finite 𝒪_k-module since 𝔛 is proper."`; it should be `"The sheaf ℱ⁺ comes from a locally free sheaf ℱ on 𝔛", where 𝔛 is the normalisation of 𝔛′ in 𝒳. This matches the paragraph's opening sentence ("a normal proper formal model 𝔛 ... a locally free sheaf ℱ on 𝔛") and the later use of Hⁱ(𝔛, ℱ).`. The printed text is exactly as quoted. The symbol is a fraktur X with a prime (𝔛′), so this is not a text-layer artefact. Four points support a misprint.

(1) It contradicts the framing sentence of the same paragraph, which asks for a normal model 𝔛 with ℱ⁺ coming from a locally free ℱ on 𝔛. The rest of the proof uses ℱ on 𝔛: the affine covering 𝔙 of 𝔛, Ȟⁱ_𝒱(𝒳, ℱ⁺) = Hⁱ(𝔛, ℱ), and finiteness because 𝔛 is proper.

(2) As mathematics, the claim on 𝔛′ is false in the sense the proof needs, which is ℱ(𝔙) = ℱ⁺(𝔙_η), i.e. sp_*ℱ⁺ = ℱ. On an affine piece Spf A of a model with reduced generic fiber, O⁺(Spf A_η) = A°, the integral closure of A in A[1/p]. This equals A exactly when A is integrally closed there. So on a non-normal 𝔛′ we get sp_*O⁺ = ν_*O_𝔛 ≠ O_𝔛′. This is not even invertible. Suppose A° = A·a. Since 1 ∈ A°, we have 1 = ba with b ∈ A, and a² = ca with c ∈ A. Cancelling the unit a gives a = c ∈ A, so A° = A. Already for ℱ⁺ = O⁺, the sheaf on 𝔛′ is therefore not locally free. On the normal 𝔛, O_𝔛(𝔙) = O⁺(𝔙_η). So the gluing matrices in GL_r(O⁺) descend, and ℱ is locally free on 𝔛. This is why the normalisation is taken.

(3) HAL v3 (p. 11) had the sentences in the other order and without "locally free": "The sheaf ℱ⁺ comes from a sheaf ℱ on 𝔛′. We can then replace 𝔛′ by its normalisation 𝔛 in 𝒳. This is still a formal model." The 2019 revision moved the sentence after the normalisation step and added "locally free", but did not change 𝔛′ to 𝔛. That is a leftover from editing.

(4) The intended argument is correct once 𝔛 is read, so no gap remains. The only later use I found, in the construction of the map "ext" ("by proposition 3.2.1, this defines the map ext", p. 100), relies on the statement of Proposition 3.2.1, which is unaffected. I rendered p. 90 at 110 and 300 dpi. The last argument of C inside the colimit is plainly an unprimed w, while the colimit index is w′<w. Two lines above, the paper defines F^{k,w^−} := colim_{w′<w} F^{k,w′}, with the prime in the right place. §12.8.1 (p. 79) defines C(n, ϵ, w, κ, r) := RΓ(X_Kli(p^n, ϵ), F^{κ,w} ⊗ ω^r), with transition maps for w1 ≥ w. So colim_{w′<w} C(n, ϵ, w′, k, r) is a directed colimit. On the quasi-compact space X_Kli(p^n, ϵ) it equals RΓ(F^{k,w^−} ⊗ ω^r). Corollary 13.3.2.1 then follows by applying RΓ to the exact sequence of Proposition 13.3.2.1. Read literally, the printed formula is the colimit of a constant diagram over a nonempty directed set, which is just C(n, ϵ, w, k, r). Corollary 13.3.2.1 would then become the fixed-w statement that the proof of Prop. 13.3.2.1 calls a 'minor error' in [3] ('the colimit is necessary because integration changes the radius of convergence'). So the printed line is not correct under the paper's own conventions. The meaning is unambiguous, so this is a misprint. The text layer shows the same thing ('colimw0 <w C(n, , w, k, r)'), so this is not an extraction artefact. HAL v3 (PDF p. 79, printed p. 78) has the identical line, and I checked it on the rendered image. The w^− version of C appears only in this definition and in Corollary 13.3.2.1. That corollary is used in the proof of Corollary 13.3.3.1, which is stated with F^{k,w}. With the obvious reading, nothing downstream changes, so affects = nothing. - **Error** at §13.4 (The spectral variety), displayed formula in the second paragraph, just before Proposition 13.4.1, p. 91 (author version). HAL v3 has the same text on printed p. 79 (PDF p. 80).. The source says `"Moreover, for all κ : Spa(C_p, O) → Spa(A_l[1/p], A_l) and α^{−1} ∈ C_p^× providing a point (κ, α^{−1}) : Spa(C_p, O) → Spa(A_l[1/p], A_l) × G_m , we have isomorphisms : H^i((κ, α^{−1})^⋆ C_cusp(A_l)) = H^i_cusp(κ, r)[U = α]." (checked on the rendered page image, author version p. 91)`; it should be `There are two faults. (i) Notation: 'H^i_cusp(κ, r)' should read 'H^i_cusp(†, κ, 2)'. The complex is built from C_cusp(n,ε,w,κ_{A_l},2), and r is not defined in §13.4. (ii) Mathematics: the fibre at the point does not compute the eigenspace. The correct statement localises at α^{−1} instead of taking the fibre there: H^i(Lκ^*C_cusp(A_l))_{(α^{−1})} ≅ H^i_cusp(†,κ,2)_{(α)}, the generalised α-eigenspace of U. Equivalently, for the support: (κ,α^{−1}) lies in Supp H^•(C_cusp(A_l)) iff α is a U-eigenvalue on H^•_cusp(†,κ,2). That support statement is all the definition of Z_l needs. If a pointwise formula is wanted, for x = (κ,α^{−1}) there is an exact sequence 0 → coker(U−α | H^i_cusp(†,κ,2)_{(α)}) → H^i(Lx^*C_cusp(A_l)) → ker(U−α | H^{i+1}_cusp(†,κ,2)_{(α)}) → 0. Another proposed reading gives the same correction, but with the exact sequence shifted by one (that is the x^! form); its example (α only on H^0) fails only in degree −1 under the standard derived x^*. The passage is a false statement, not just an unproved one, so it is an error, not a gap.`. I transcribed the formula from the page image, and HAL v3 prints the same formula. In §13.1.2 the G_m/A^1 coordinate X is inverse to the eigenvalue (det(1−XŨ)), and the sheaf over the spectral variety is the slope part N^• with X acting as U^{−1}. My own check: the derived pullback along κ is N^•_κ, which computes the generalised eigenspaces (base change, since N^• is perfect over O_V). Pulling back further to X = α^{−1} tensors with the Koszul complex in degrees −1 and 0. That gives the long exact sequence above: H^i(fibre) is an extension of ker(U−α | H^{i+1}) by coker(U−α | H^i). So the printed equality fails in general. If α is a U-eigenvalue on H^0_cusp, then H^{−1}(fibre) = ker(U−α|H^0) ≠ 0, while the right side is 0 in degree −1. If α occurs on H^1 but not on H^0, then H^0(fibre) ≠ 0 = H^0[U=α]. The underived, termwise reading also fails. It depends on the representative Ũ. Explicit counterexample: N^0 = C_p^2 with U a Jordan block at α, N^1 = C_p with U = α, and d(e2) = 1. Then H^0 = ⟨e1⟩ with U = α, but the termwise fibre is acyclic. Another proposed reading has a long exact sequence with an index shift: the cocone/x^! version, 0 → coker(H^{i−1}) → H^i → ker(H^i) → 0. With the standard derived tensor, its example (α on H^0 only) gives H^{−1}(fibre) ≠ 0 rather than H^1(fibre) ≠ 0. The conclusion still holds, in degree −1. What the text actually uses does hold. By derived Nakayama, the support of H^•(C_cusp(A_l)) is the set of pairs (κ,α^{−1}) with α a U-eigenvalue on H^•_cusp(†,κ,2), so the definition of Z is fine. Proposition 13.4.1 ('corollary of the discussion above and proposition 13.1.3.1') needs only Prop 13.1.3.1 with h = 0 applied to C_cusp(n,ε,w,κ_{A_l},2), plus independence of n,ε,w. It does not use the fibre formula. Its only later use is in Lemma 14.8.4 (p. 102), where it enters only through local constancy of the Euler characteristic. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED. In §13.1.2 (p. 84) the paper sets up a complex of coherent sheaves 𝓜^• over Z̃ ⊂ A^1 × Spa(A,A^+), 'the universal eigenspace of M^• for the action of Ũ'. The coordinate X satisfies P̃(X) = det(1 − XŨ), so X acts as U^{−1}, and the point (κ,α^{−1}) corresponds to the eigenvalue α. Nothing in §13.1–13.2 or in the cited sources ([14] Coleman, [9] Buzzard, [81] Urban) identifies the fibre at a point with an eigenspace. Buzzard's machine gives the fibre as the eigenspace quotient coker(U−α), not the eigenspace itself. I tested every reading of '(κ,α^{−1})^⋆':
(a) Derived fibre. Lx^*N = N ⊗^L O/(X−α^{−1}) = cone(U^{−1}−α^{−1} : N → N), where N = Lκ^*C_cusp(A_l) is the finite-slope part of C_cusp(n,ε,w,κ,2). This gives the exact sequence in the correction. Toy check, computed by hand: take N = C_p in degree 1 with U = α. The map U^{−1}−α^{−1} is 0, so the cone is N[1] ⊕ N and H^0(fibre) = C_p. But H^0[U=α] = 0. In general, in degree 0 the fibre has dimension dim H^0[U=α] + dim H^1[U=α]. So the formula fails at every α that is a U-eigenvalue on H^1_cusp(†,κ,2), which is the case the paper is about. It also fails in degree −1 whenever α occurs on H^0. Another way to see it: every derived fibre has Euler characteristic 0, while dim H^0[U=α] − dim H^1[U=α] is not 0 in general.
(b) Termwise fibre of the complex. This depends on the representative Ũ and fails the same way.
(c) Fibre x^*H^i(C) of the cohomology sheaves. For i = 1 this is coker(U−α | H^1_{(α)}), whose dimension equals that of H^1[U=α]. For i = 0 base change fails wherever H^1(C) has κ-torsion, i.e. where the dimensions jump. Lemma 14.8.4 exists precisely to rule out such jumps.
(d) '[U=α]' read as the generalised eigenspace. This is right only for the localisation, not for the fibre at the point.
So no faithful reading makes the display true. Separately, the r is a leftover of the general-r notation H^i_cusp(†,κ_A,r) (p. 83), and the † is missing.
CONSEQUENCES. 'Z_l' is defined as the support of H^•(C_cusp(A_l)). That, and 'quasi-finite and locally finite', need only the support description and Z_l ⊂ Z̃; the support description holds by derived Nakayama. Proposition 13.4.1 ('corollary of the discussion above and proposition 13.1.3.1') follows from Prop. 13.1.3.1 with h = 0, applied to C_cusp(n,ε,w,κ_{A_l},2), together with Cor. 13.2.4.2 (independence of n,ε,w on the finite-slope part). Neither step uses the display. The only later reference to §13.4 is Lemma 14.8.4 (author p. 102: 'by theorem 11.3.1 and proposition 13.4.1'), and it uses only the local constancy of the Euler characteristic. I searched the text: the glued Z → W and H^•(C_cusp) are never used again. Remark 1.2 mentions the finite-slope theory in passing, but no numbered result depends on this display. So the mathematics as intended (support, generalised eigenspaces) is right, and no result or proof is damaged. - **Misprint** at §14.2 (The correspondences C_n), definition of C_n|_{𝒴_Kli(p)}, p. 92 of the author version (HAL v3: same passage, printed p. 80 = PDF p. 81). The source says `where (G, H) ∈ 𝒴_{Kli}(p) and L_n ⊂ G[p^n] is a totally isotropic subgroup which is locally for the étale topology isomorphic to (ℤ/p^nℤ)^2 ⊕ ℤ/p^{2n}ℤ and L_n ∩ H = {0}.`; it should be `L_n ⊂ G[p^{2n}] (a Lagrangian subgroup: its order p^{n}·p^{n}·p^{2n} = p^{4n} is half the order p^{8n} of G[p^{2n}]).`. The printed text contradicts itself. A group scheme locally isomorphic to (ℤ/p^n)^2 ⊕ ℤ/p^{2n} has sections of order p^{2n}, so for n ≥ 1 it cannot lie in G[p^n]. For n = 1 it would require a ℤ/p^2 inside G[p]. The paper's own later text uses G[p^{2n}]: (1) the same paragraph says C_1 is the correspondence C of §13.2.1 (p. 85), which reads "L ⊂ G[p^2] ... isomorphic to (ℤ/pℤ)^2 ⊕ ℤ/p^2ℤ", and G[p^2] matches G[p^{2n}] at n = 1. (2) The proof of Corollary 14.3.1 (p. 94) says "L_i locally isomorphic to ℤ/p^{2i} ⊕ (ℤ/p^i)^2 and totally isotropic in G[p^{2i}]". (3) The proof of Lemma 14.6.1 (p. 97) says "|m_i|_x ≥ |p^{2n}|_x since L_n ⊂ G[p^{2n}]". (4) The ordinary-case analogue in the proof of Lemma 11.1.1.4 (p. 68) says "L_n ⊂ G[p^{2n}] is a totally isotropic subgroup". The order count also works: L_n has order p^{4n}, exactly Lagrangian in G[p^{2n}], which fits the double coset diag(1, p^n, p^n, p^{2n}) = U^n that comes from iterating C_1 n times. - **Misprint** at §14.1, proof of Lemma 14.1.1, p. 92 (author version, 17 June 2019); same sentence in HAL v3, p. 80 (PDF p. 81). The source says `"The group H_n has degree at least n − 2(n − ϵ + 1/(p−1)). Morover the maps p^{k−1} : H_n[p^k]/H_n[p^{k−1}] → H_n[p^{n−1}] = H_1 are morphisms which are isomorphisms on the generic fiber. Therefore, using [20], coro. 3 on p. 13, we deduce that deg H_1 ≥ (1/n) deg H_n ≥ 1 − (2/n)(n − ϵ + 1/(p−1))." (checked on the page image at 110 and 250 dpi, author version p. 92)`; it should be `p^{k−1} : H_n[p^k]/H_n[p^{k−1}] → H_n[p] = H_1 (the same as p^{n−1}H_n on the generic fiber)`. This is a real misprint. By §12.7.1 (p. 77), X_Kli(p^n, ϵ) parametrizes pairs (x, H_n), where H_n ⊂ G_x[p^n] is locally isomorphic to Z/p^nZ and is generated by e_1. The map to X_Kli(p) sends H_n to its subgroup of order p. So H_1, the Klingen subgroup whose degree is v_x(δ_H), is H_n[p] = p^{n−1}H_n, which has order p. H_n[p^{n−1}] has order p^{n−1}, and it is the level-p^{n−1} group H_{n−1}, not H_1. The two agree only when n = 2.

Checking the step myself: on the generic fiber, H_n[p^k]/H_n[p^{k−1}] ≅ Z/p. Multiplication by p^{k−1} maps it isomorphically onto H_n[p], which is also ≅ Z/p. For n ≥ 3 it cannot be an isomorphism onto H_n[p^{n−1}], a group of order p^{n−1}. So the sentence as printed is false.

With H_n[p] the argument works. Fargues [20], coro. 3 says that a morphism of finite flat group schemes that is a generic isomorphism does not decrease degree. Hence deg(H_n[p^k]/H_n[p^{k−1}]) ≤ deg H_1 for each k. Since degree is additive along the filtration 0 ⊂ H_n[p] ⊂ … ⊂ H_n[p^n] = H_n, we get deg H_n ≤ n·deg H_1. Also deg H_n + deg H_n^D = n and deg H_n^D ≤ 2(n − ϵ + 1/(p−1)). Together these give deg H_1 ≥ 1 − (2/n)(n − ϵ + 1/(p−1)), exactly as printed.

The error is only the exponent in one target group. The rest of the proof, the statement of Lemma 14.1.1 and Remark 14.1.1 are unaffected, and later uses of the lemma depend only on the bound, which is correct. HAL v3 (p. 80) has the same "H_n[p^{n−1}] = H_1", there with the phrase "are generic isomorphisms". It also has the separate slip "deg H_1 ≥ (1/n) deg H_n^D", which the author version fixes to deg H_n.
