- **Error** at §15.2 (Euler characteristic), first paragraph, just before Theorem 15.2.1, p. 107 of the author version (17 June 2019). HAL v3 has the same sentence word for word, including the typo "Fob_ℓ", in §15.2, printed p. 89 (PDF p. 90).. The source says `"We let 𝔪 be the associated maximal ideal of the abstract Hecke algebra ℋ^{Np} and Θ_𝔪 : ℋ^{Np} → F̄_p the corresponding morphism. The map Θ_𝔪 is thus defined by the rule Θ_𝔪(Q_ℓ(X)) = det(1 − X ρ̄(Fob_ℓ))." (The definition in §5.1.3, p. 21, reads: "H_ℓ ... isomorphic to Z[T_{ℓ,0}, T_{ℓ,0}^{-1}, T_{ℓ,1}, T_{ℓ,2}]" and "Q_ℓ(X) = 1 − T_{ℓ,2}X + ℓ(T_{ℓ,1} + (ℓ²+1)T_{ℓ,0})X² − ℓ³T_{ℓ,2}T_{ℓ,0}X³ + ℓ⁶T_{ℓ,0}²X⁴".)`; it should be `Minimal fix: say that m is any maximal ideal of H^{Np} whose character satisfies Θ_m(Q_ℓ(X)) = det(1 − Xρ̄(Frob_ℓ)) for all ℓ ∤ Np, and that Theorem 15.2.1 holds for each such m. This matches how Theorem 1.2 in the introduction is stated. To keep "the" maximal ideal, add the rule Θ_m(T_{ℓ,0}) = ℓ^{-3} ν(ρ̄(Frob_ℓ)), where ν is the similitude character of ρ̄. This agrees with Lemma 5.1.5.1 (T_{ℓ,0} ↦ ℓ^{-3}αδ, with αδ = βγ = ν) and with the X³ and X⁴ coefficients, so the rule then determines T_{ℓ,2}, T_{ℓ,0} and T_{ℓ,1}. The same line has a separate misprint: "Fob_ℓ" should read "Frob_ℓ".`. I rendered pp. 21 and 107, and HAL v3 p. 89, and checked them directly.

1. The rule is compatible with the local theory. I computed with exact fractions: the eigenvalues in Lemma 5.1.5.1 (ℓ^{-3}αδ; ℓ^{-1}(αβ+αγ+αδ+βδ+γδ) − ℓ^{-3}αδ; α+β+γ+δ) with αδ = βγ give exactly the coefficients of det(1−X·diag(α,β,γ,δ)). So under Θ the coefficients of Q_ℓ(X) are: −Θ(T_{ℓ,2}); ℓ(Θ(T_{ℓ,1}) + (ℓ²+1)Θ(T_{ℓ,0})); −ℓ³Θ(T_{ℓ,2})Θ(T_{ℓ,0}); ℓ⁶Θ(T_{ℓ,0})².

2. When it fails. If Θ(T_{ℓ,2}) = tr ρ̄(Frob_ℓ) ≠ 0, the X³ coefficient fixes Θ(T_{ℓ,0}), and then the X² coefficient fixes Θ(T_{ℓ,1}). If tr ρ̄(Frob_ℓ) = 0, only Θ(T_{ℓ,0})² is fixed. The substitution T_{ℓ,0} ↦ −T_{ℓ,0}, T_{ℓ,1} ↦ T_{ℓ,1} + 2(ℓ²+1)T_{ℓ,0} leaves every coefficient unchanged; I checked this for 200 random rational inputs. For p odd and ℓ ≠ p, the two characters are different.

3. The case really occurs. A ρ̄ that shows up in this cohomology is odd, so complex conjugation has eigenvalues (1,1,−1,−1), trace 0 and ν = −1. By Chebotarev there are infinitely many ℓ ∤ Np with ρ̄(Frob_ℓ) in that class. For ℓ = 5, both Θ(T_{ℓ,0}) = +ℓ^{-3} and −ℓ^{-3} (with the matching T_{ℓ,1}) give Θ(Q_ℓ(X)) = 1 − 2X² + X⁴ = det(1 − X·ρ̄(c)). So the rule allows infinitely many characters of ℋ^{Np}. The sentence "Θ_𝔪 is thus defined by the rule" is therefore false, and "the associated maximal ideal" is not pinned down by what is printed. Nothing in the paper excludes odd p.

4. Why no result is affected. The intended meaning (the natural character attached to ρ̄ in GSp4, including its similitude) is clear. The proof in 15.2.3–15.2.5 uses Θ_𝔪 only through "Θ_{π_f} congruent to Θ_𝔪". It uses this to see, by comparing characteristic polynomials, that the Galois representation of π_f reduces to the irreducible ρ̄, which rules out the Yoshida and Saito–Kurokawa cases and the Eisenstein-type contributions. That argument works for every 𝔪 that satisfies the printed rule, so Theorem 15.2.1 holds for each of them.

Classification: I call it an error, meaning a false claim that the rule determines Θ_𝔪, with no effect on the results. It could also reasonably be recorded as a gap in the definition. I checked the rendered pages 21 and 107 and HAL v3 p. 90. §5.1.3 gives Q_ℓ(X) = 1 − T_{ℓ,2}X + ℓ(T_{ℓ,1}+(ℓ²+1)T_{ℓ,0})X² − ℓ³T_{ℓ,2}T_{ℓ,0}X³ + ℓ⁶T_{ℓ,0}²X⁴, and H_ℓ = Z[T_{ℓ,0}^{±1}, T_{ℓ,1}, T_{ℓ,2}]. Write det(1 − Xρ̄(Frob_ℓ)) = 1 − a1X + a2X² − a3X³ + a4X⁴. For g in GSp4, a3 = ν·a1 and a4 = ν². Comparing coefficients gives Θ(T2) = a1, ℓΘ(T1) + ℓ(ℓ²+1)Θ(T0) = a2, ℓ³a1Θ(T0) = a3 and ℓ⁶Θ(T0)² = a4.

If a1 ≠ 0, the rule fixes Θ(T0) = ℓ^{-3}ν and then Θ(T1). If a1 = 0, only Θ(T0)² is fixed. The substitution T0 ↦ −T0, T1 ↦ T1 + 2(ℓ²+1)T0 then leaves Θ(Q_ℓ) unchanged, which I checked numerically. So for p odd there are two distinct characters at that ℓ, because Θ(T0) is a unit. Example: p = 3, ℓ = 5, eigenvalues (1,1,−1,−1) with ν = −1. The solutions (T0,T1,T2) mod 3 are (1,0,0) and (2,1,0).

This is not a rare edge case. When ν(c) = −1, as for the Galois representations of Siegel forms, ρ̄(complex conjugation) has eigenvalues ±1,±1 and trace 0. By Chebotarev, infinitely many ℓ ∤ Np then have tr ρ̄(Frob_ℓ) = 0. So for p odd, "thus defined by the rule" is false, and "the associated maximal ideal" is not well defined. For p = 2 the two choices coincide.

Defence tried: Lemma 5.1.5.1 does supply the natural choice T_{ℓ,0} ↦ ℓ^{-3}αδ, but §15.2 never states it and calls the rule alone a definition. The problem is harmless for the results, which is why affects is "nothing". Theorem 1.2 in the introduction (p. 3) starts from a maximal ideal m with an associated absolutely irreducible ρ̄. That direction is unambiguous. The proof of Theorem 15.2.1 uses m only through "Θ_{π_f} is congruent to Θ_m", which appears in Corollary 15.2.3.1, the boundary argument on p. 109 (ρ_f ⊕ ρ_f is not congruent to ρ̄), Proposition 15.2.4.1 (the irreducibility of ρ̄ excludes Yoshida and Saito–Kurokawa packets) and §15.2.5. Each of these needs only that the Q_ℓ-values match det(1 − Xρ̄(Frob_ℓ)), via Brauer–Nesbitt and Chebotarev. So the theorem and its proof hold for every m satisfying the rule. I class this as an error rather than a gap because the assertion is false, not merely unproved. This correction is right and is consistent with Lemma 5.1.5.1. - **Misprint** at §15.2.1 (Limits of discrete series), first sentence, p. 107 of the author version (17 June 2019). The source says `15.2.1. Limits of discrete series. — Given λ = (λ_1, λ_2; c) ∈ X^⋆(T) + (2, 1; 0) ⊂ X^⋆(T)_ℂ which satisfies −λ_1 ≥ λ_2 > −λ_1 and a Weyl chamber C positive for λ we have a (limit of) discrete series π(λ, C) (see [28], 3.3).`; it should be `−λ_1 ≥ λ_2 > λ_1, i.e. drop the minus sign on the last λ_1. This is the exact image of HAL v3's "λ_1 > λ_2 ≥ −λ_1" under λ ↦ −λ. An alternative correction, "−λ_1 ≥ λ_2 ≥ λ_1" (as in §5.1.6), is close but not quite right: it also admits the compact wall λ_2 = λ_1.`. I checked the page at 300 dpi. The line reads "which satisfies −λ1 ≥ λ2 > −λ1", with a clear minus before both outer λ1's, so this is not a text-layer artefact. The condition asks for λ2 ≤ −λ1 and λ2 > −λ1 at once, so no λ satisfies it.

HAL v3 (PDF p. 90, printed p. 89, §15.2.1) has a different text: "λ1 > λ2 ≥ −λ1", and continues "The case of interest to us is λ2 = 0 and λ1 > 0". The author version switched this section to λ ↦ −λ throughout:
- "λ2 = 0 and 0 > λ1"
- the character (λ1+1,2;c) became (−λ1+1,2;−c) in §15.2.2
- k = λ1−1 became k = −λ1−1 in §15.2.3

Applying λ ↦ −λ to λ1 > λ2 ≥ −λ1 gives −λ1 > −λ2 ≥ λ1, i.e. −λ1 ≥ λ2 > λ1. The printed line keeps exactly this pattern of ≥ and > but has a stray "−" on the last term.

The strict ">" is the right choice. By §5.1.1 (p. 20), the compact root is α1 = e1−e2, so λ2 = λ1 is singular for the compact root and gives no (limit of) discrete series. The next paragraph also says that if λ2 ≠ 0 and λ2 ≠ −λ1 then λ determines C uniquely, and that only works if λ2 = λ1 is excluded. So the alternative correction, copied from §5.1.6 (p. 22, which does print "−λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ λ1" and then "0 ≥ λ2 > λ1" for the holomorphic case), is slightly too weak. Both versions agree on the case actually used.

Why "affects: nothing": the next sentence fixes λ2 = 0 and λ1 < 0. That point satisfies either corrected inequality, and §§15.2.2–15.2.5, including the proof of Theorem 15.2.1, use only this case. So no stated result depends on the general inequality.

- **Misprint** at §15.2.1 (Limits of discrete series), p. 107 of the author version. HAL v3 p. 89 has 'By Harris-Chandra isomorphism, ℨ ≃ ℂ[Y(T)]^W' and 'Si λ_2 ≠ 0'. The author version corrected both slips in §5.1.6 (p. 22: 'By Harish-Chandra isomorphism …', 'If λ_2 ≠ 0 …') but not here.. The source says `Let ℨ be the center of the enveloping algebra U(𝔤). By Harris-Chandra isomorphism, ℨ ≃ ℂ[X_⋆(T)]^W where W is the Weyl group. … Si λ_2 ≠ 0 and λ_2 ≠ −λ_1, λ determines uniquely C and π(λ, C) is a discrete series.`; it should be `By the Harish-Chandra isomorphism, ℨ ≃ ℂ[X_⋆(T)]^W (to be read as the polynomial algebra S(X_⋆(T) ⊗ ℂ)^W = S(𝔱)^W) … If λ_2 ≠ 0 and λ_2 ≠ −λ_1, …`. The page image confirms 'Harris-Chandra' and the French 'Si'. Both are clear slips: the name is spelled Harish-Chandra and the sentence starts 'If' in the parallel §5.1.6 on p. 22, and in the abstract. The notation ℂ[X_⋆(T)]^W is not a separate slip. The same notation appears in the author's revised §5.1.6, and it has a consistent reading as the symmetric algebra of X_⋆(T) ⊗ ℂ = 𝔱. Its characters are then W-orbits in X^⋆(T)_ℂ = 𝔱^*, which matches 'the infinitesimal character of π(λ, C) is the Weyl group orbit of λ'. It clashes with the group-algebra meaning of ℂ[X_⋆(T)] in the twisted Satake isomorphism on p. 21, so it is an abuse of notation. The parenthetical reading S(X_⋆(T) ⊗ ℂ)^W in the correction is a correct clarification but optional. The source says `p. 107, §15.2.2 (checked on the page image at 110 and 250 dpi): "For λ = (λ_1, λ_2; c) with λ_2 = 0, 0 > λ_1, consider the character (−λ_1 + 1, 2; −c) ∈ X^⋆(T). ... It is defined with highest weight (−λ_1+1,2;−c) but labelled V_{(λ_1+1,2;−c)}, which drops the minus on λ_1. The next sentence calls the same object "the representation V_{(−λ_1+1,2;c)}", which drops the minus on c. Theorem 15.2.2.1 then uses V_{(−λ_1+1,2;−c)} throughout. HAL v3 (§15.2.2, printed p. 90 = PDF p. 91, checked on the image) has no inconsistency. There λ_1 > 0 and k = λ_1 − 1, and it writes highest weight (λ_1+1,2;c) and V_{(λ_1+1,2;c)} everywhere: in the definition, in the "can also be viewed" sentence and in Theorem 15.2.2.1. The author version replaced λ_1 by −λ_1 and c by −c. Each faulty label carries exactly one of those two changes: the first changes only c, the second only λ_1. This indicates that they are leftovers of the edit.

Affects nothing: the symbol V_… is not used anywhere after Theorem 15.2.2.1 (grep over the whole text). The theorem itself, Theorem 15.2.3.1 (which only uses the constant R), Corollary 15.2.3.1 and the proof of Theorem 15.2.1 all use the correct notation or do not use V at all.

Related leftovers of the same edit, outside this entry: §15.2.1 prints the impossible condition "−λ_1 ≥ λ_2 > −λ_1" (v3 has "λ_1 > λ_2 ≥ −λ_1"). Theorem 15.2.2.1(2) keeps "λ_1 ≥ R" even though λ_1 < 0 now. Theorem 15.2.3.1's condition "k ≥ R − 1", with k = −λ_1 − 1, corresponds to −λ_1 ≥ R. - **Misprint** at §15.2.2, pp. 107–108: the Cartan decomposition is on the last lines of p. 107, the "(𝔭, K∞)-cohomology" at the top of p. 108; the same symbol is used throughout Theorem 15.2.2.1, p. 108. HAL v3 p. 90 has the same text, citing [28].. The source says `p. 107: "We let 𝔤 be the complex Lie algebra of GSp4. We have the Cartan decomposition 𝔤 = 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭. Since 𝔨 is also the complex lie algebra of M_Si, the representation V_{(−λ1+1,2;c)} can also be viewed as a representation" p. 108: "of 𝔨 and K∞. Let W be a (𝔤, K∞)-module. Then one can define the (𝔭, K∞)-cohomology of W, denoted by H^•(𝔭, K∞; W) (see [30], sect. 4.1.1)." Theorem 15.2.2.1 then uses H^i(𝔭, K∞; π(λ)^h ⊗ V_{(−λ1+1,2;−c)}) etc.`; it should be `The cohomology meant is H^•(𝔓, K∞; W), the (𝔓, K)-cohomology of Harris [30] and of Blasius–Harris–Ramakrishnan [4]. Here 𝔓 ⊃ 𝔨 is the parabolic subalgebra 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭^± of the Hodge decomposition. In this paper's notation this is presumably 𝔭_h = 𝔤^{(0,0)} ⊕ 𝔤^{(1,−1)} of Remark 5.2.1.1, which is conjugate to 𝔭_Si. It should not be denoted by the Cartan complement 𝔭 just introduced, and Theorem 15.2.2.1 should be read with the same change.`. Checked on the page images. The Cartan complement 𝔭 in 𝔤 = 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭 is not a Lie subalgebra ([𝔭,𝔭] ⊂ 𝔨) and does not contain 𝔨 = Lie(K∞). So relative Lie algebra cohomology H^•(𝔭, K∞; W) is undefined with this 𝔭. Reading it as the complex Hom_{K∞}(∧^•𝔭, W) would give (𝔤, K∞)-cohomology, which cannot be meant. The coefficient V_{(−λ1+1,2;−c)} is only a P_Si-module, viewed as a 𝔨-module, not a 𝔤-module. The statements of Theorem 15.2.2.1 (H^0 for π(λ)^h, H^1 for π(λ)^g) are those of [4] Thm 3.2.1 for coherent (𝔓, K)-cohomology. The citation of [30] §4.1.1 and the parabolic 𝔭_h of Remark 5.2.1.1 make the intended object clear, so this is a notation clash (𝔭 used for two things), not a mathematical error. Whether 𝔓 is 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭^+ or 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭^− depends on the holomorphy convention, which I could not check against [30] (not accessible); hence the ± in the correction. - **Misprint** at §15.2.3, Corollary 15.2.3.1, second display ("Similarly, H^1(...)"), p. 108 of the author version (17 June 2019). HAL v3 (hal-01393374v3) has the same text on printed p. 91 (PDF p. 92), Corollary 15.2.3.1.. The source says `Corollary 15.2.3.1. — For k ≥ R − 1, we have H^0(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_𝔪 = ⊕_{π_f}(π_f^K)^{m^h(π_f)} where π_f runs over all irreducible admissible representations of GSp_4(𝔸_f) such that π_f ⊗ π(λ)^h is cuspidal automorphic and m^h(π_f) is the multiplicity of π_f ⊗ π(λ)^h and the character Θ_{π_f} : ℋ^{Np} → ℂ is congruent to Θ_𝔪. Similarly, H^1(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) = ⊕_{π_f}(π_f^K)^{m^g(π_f)} where π_f runs over all irreducible admissible representations of GSp_4(𝔸_f) such that π_f ⊗ π(λ)^g is cuspidal automorphic and m^g(π_f) is the multiplicity of π_f ⊗ π(λ)^g and the character Θ_{π_f} : ℋ^{Np} → ℂ is congruent to Θ_𝔪.`; it should be `H^1(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_𝔪 = ⊕_{π_f}(π_f^K)^{m^g(π_f)}, with the same index set: π_f ⊗ π(λ)^g cuspidal automorphic and Θ_{π_f} congruent to Θ_𝔪. The subscript 𝔪 is missing on the left side, as it is present in the H^0 display just above.`. I checked this on the page images, not the text layer. At 300 dpi, p. 108 of the author version shows the H^0 display with the subscript 𝔪 ("…(−D))_𝔪 = ⊕…") and the H^1 display without it ("…(−D)) = ⊕…"). HAL v3, printed p. 91, has the same two displays.

As printed, the H^1 statement is false in general. Its right side depends on 𝔪, since it keeps only the π_f with Θ_{π_f} ≡ Θ_𝔪. Its left side does not depend on 𝔪. Two maximal ideals whose sets of contributing π_f are non-empty and disjoint would therefore give the same group two different values. Also, without localisation, H^1(Ω(−D)) can contain boundary classes: the image of H^0(Ω^{(k,2)} ⊗ O_D) is the kernel of the map to H^1(Ω^{(k,2)}).

The intended meaning is clear from the context:
- The sentence just before the corollary introduces "the localized cohomology groups H^i(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_𝔪".
- The parallel H^0 display carries the subscript 𝔪.
- The proof opens by saying it must show that "the natural map H^1(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_𝔪 → H^1(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}) is injective". It does this by showing H^0(Ω^{(k,2)} ⊗ O_D)_𝔪 = 0: boundary eigenforms have reducible Galois representations, and ρ̄ is irreducible.

I redid the deduction. Localisation is exact, so the kernel of H^1(Ω(−D))_𝔪 → H^1(Ω)_𝔪 is a quotient of H^0(Ω ⊗ O_D)_𝔪 = 0. So H^1(Ω(−D))_𝔪 ≅ (interior H^1)_𝔪. By Theorem 15.2.3.1, taking 𝔪-parts of the Hecke-module decomposition keeps exactly the π_f with Θ_{π_f} ≡ Θ_𝔪. This proves the localised statement.

The only later use is §15.2.5 (p. 109), the proof of Theorem 15.2.1, and it applies the corollary to the localised groups f H^i(X_Kli(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_𝔪 ⊗ Q̄_p. The misprint does not reach any later result.

On 'affects': PROTOCOL.md §18 defines "nothing" as "the mathematics is right as intended". That is the case here, so it affects nothing, not a stated result. Only the printed H^1 formula of the corollary is wrong, and the intended statement is what is proved and used.

- **Misprint** at §15.2.3, proof of Corollary 15.2.3.1, p. 108 (last lines of the page). HAL v3 p. 91 has the same passage, also with S^{tor}_K; its display reads Ω^{(k,r)} / Ω_{(k,r)} where the author version has Ω^{(k,2)}.. The source says `Proof. In order to deduce the corollary from theorem 15.2.3.1, we need to prove that the natural map H^1(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_𝔪 → H^1(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}) is injective. We have a short exact sequence : H^0(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}) → H^0(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)} ⊗ 𝒪_D) → H^1(S^{tor}_K, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)).`; it should be `We have an exact sequence, part of the long exact cohomology sequence of 0 → Ω^{(k,2)}(−D) → Ω^{(k,2)} → Ω^{(k,2)} ⊗ 𝒪_D → 0: H^0(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}) → H^0(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)} ⊗ 𝒪_D) → H^1(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) → H^1(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}). It stays exact after localisation at 𝔪. Localising the target of the injectivity statement is optional: the printed version is correct as it stands.`. Checked on the page image at 250 dpi. Two of the three sub-claims hold. (1) The displayed three-term sequence is only exact in the middle. It is not a short exact sequence: that would need H^0(Ω) → H^0(Ω⊗𝒪_D) to be injective and the map onto H^1(Ω(−D)) to be surjective, i.e. H^1(Ω(−D)) → H^1(Ω) to be zero. The argument needs the next term. The kernel of H^1(Ω(−D)) → H^1(Ω) is the image of H^0(Ω⊗𝒪_D), so the vanishing of H^0(Ω⊗𝒪_D)_𝔪, proved next, gives the injectivity. The intended long exact sequence is clear. (2) The third term is printed S^{tor}_K with no Σ, while the other two terms have S^{tor}_{K,Σ}. S^{tor}_K is not defined, so the Σ was dropped. (3) Not a mistake: the unlocalised target is fine. H^1(Ω(−D))_𝔪 is a Hecke direct factor of H^1(Ω(−D)), and the map is Hecke-equivariant. So the kernel of H^1(Ω(−D))_𝔪 → H^1(Ω) is (ker)_𝔪 = image of H^0(Ω⊗𝒪_D)_𝔪, and injectivity into H^1(Ω) is equivalent to injectivity into H^1(Ω)_𝔪. The group is a genuine misprint, but the correction should not insist on the localised target. The proof goes through as intended. - **Misprint** at §15.2.2, Theorem 15.2.2.1(2), p. 108 (author version, 17 June 2019). The source says `2. There is a constant R such that if λ_1 ≥ R and π_∞ in an irreducible, essentially unitary representation of GSp_4(ℝ) and : — if H^0(𝔭, K_∞; π_∞ ⊗ V_{(−λ_1+1,2;−c)}) ≠ 0 then π_∞ ≃ π(λ)^h, — if H^1(𝔭, K_∞; π_∞ ⊗ V_{(−λ_1+1,2;−c)}) ≠ 0 then π_∞ ≃ π(λ)^g.`; it should be `"if −λ_1 ≥ R" (equivalently k = −λ_1 − 1 ≥ R − 1). This matches the "k ≥ R − 1 (see thm. 15.2.2.1, 2.)" in Theorem 15.2.3.1 and Corollary 15.2.3.1.`. I checked the page image at 110 and 300 dpi. It prints "λ_1 ≥ R" with no minus sign, so the text layer is right. The author version flipped the sign convention. §15.2.1 (p. 107) says "The case of interest to us is λ_2 = 0 and 0 > λ_1". §15.2.2 fixes "λ = (λ_1, λ_2; c) with λ_2 = 0, 0 > λ_1" and uses the character (−λ_1+1, 2; −c). §15.2.3 (p. 108) sets "k = −λ_1 − 1". Theorem 15.2.3.1 then assumes "For every integer k ≥ R − 1 (see thm. 15.2.2.1, 2.)", and Corollary 15.2.3.1 assumes "For k ≥ R − 1".

Redoing the computation: k ≥ R − 1 ⇔ −λ_1 − 1 ≥ R − 1 ⇔ −λ_1 ≥ R. As printed, with λ_1 < 0, "λ_1 ≥ R" picks out the bounded band R ≤ λ_1 < 0 of small weights. If R > 0 it is empty. The theorem needs the reverse: sufficiently regular weights, |λ_1| large. As printed it does not give "k ≥ R − 1", so the cross-reference fails. Within the paper's own conventions the printed text is a sign misprint.

HAL v3 (p. 90, PDF p. 91) has the same words "if λ_1 ≥ R". There it is consistent, because v3 has "λ_2 = 0 and λ_1 > 0", "V_{(λ_1+1,2;c)}" and "k = λ_1 − 1", so k ≥ R − 1 ⇔ λ_1 ≥ R. The author version changed the signs everywhere except this line. The same section has other sign leftovers, which are separate issues. Proposition 15.2.4.1 (p. 109) still says "with λ_1 > 0". Page 107 prints "V_{(λ_1+1,2;−c)}" and "V_{(−λ_1+1,2;c)}" next to "(−λ_1+1,2;−c)". The inequality "−λ_1 ≥ λ_2 > −λ_1" in §15.2.1 is self-contradictory. I could not check the published Duke text.

Effect: none downstream. Theorem 15.2.2.1 is quoted from [4] (Blasius–Harris–Ramakrishnan). Its only users are Theorem 15.2.3.1 and Corollary 15.2.3.1. Both state their hypothesis correctly as k ≥ R − 1, and the proof of Theorem 15.2.1 (§15.2.5) only specializes "at a very large weight k". The intended meaning is clear from the cross-reference. We first observe that the result holds true after inverting p by classical results on toroidal embeddings (see [40], coro. 1 on page 44) and the comparison theorem stated in [70], thm. 9.1. It follows easily that O^{++}_{T^an_Σ} ≃ f_⋆O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}} and we are left to prove that R^i f_⋆O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}} = 0 for all i > 0. It suffices to show that R^i f_⋆O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}}/p = 0 for all i > 0 since this will imply that multiplication by p is surjective on R^i f_⋆O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}} for all i > 0 and we know that this sheaf is torsion.`; it should be `What the argument actually needs is that O^{++}_{T^an_Σ}/p → Rf_⋆(O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}}/p) is a quasi-isomorphism, including in degree 0. Then multiplication by p is bijective on R^i f_⋆O^{++} for every i > 0, and a torsion sheaf on which p is injective is 0. - For i ≥ 2 the printed vanishing is already enough: R^{i−1}f_⋆(O^{++}/p) = 0 makes p injective on R^i f_⋆O^{++}. - For i = 1 one must add the degree-0 step f_⋆(O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}}/p) = O^{++}_{T^an_Σ}/p. Together with f_⋆O^{++} = O^{++}, this makes f_⋆O^{++} → f_⋆(O^{++}/p) surjective. That surjectivity is equivalent to p being injective on R^1 f_⋆O^{++}. - Alternatively, a bound on the p-power torsion of R^1 f_⋆O^{++} would do, but the paper proves none. The degree-0 step comes from the proof's own fibre computation: - H^1(f^{−1}(U_n), O^{++}) = 0 gives H^0(f^{−1}(U_n), O^{++}/p) = H^0(f^{−1}(U_n), O^{++})/p. - H^0(f^{−1}(U_n), O^{++}) = H^0(U_n, O^{++}), by the degree-0 part of [40] Coro. 1 through Cor. 3.1.1. - Pass to the colimit, then use Prop. 3.3.1 and Lemma 3.3.1 for i = 0, and the same generisation argument at non-maximal points. The correction is minimal: the fix changes "surjective" to "bijective" and adds the i = 0 case to the fibre computation. Nothing else changes.`. I transcribed the text from a 220 dpi render of p. 15. Proposition 3.3.1's proof shows that 'R^i f_⋆O^{++}/p' in this paper means R^i f_⋆(O^{++}/p). The fibrewise computation later in the proof indeed gives H^i(f^{−1}(U_n), O^{++}/p) = 0 for i > 0. Since p is invertible on the analytic space, 0 → O^{++} →p O^{++} → O^{++}/p → 0 is exact. The long exact sequence then gives only what the proof says: p is surjective on R^i f_⋆O^{++} for i > 0. But a p-divisible torsion sheaf need not vanish (Q_p/Z_p is an example), and the proof proves no bound on the torsion. So 'surjective + torsion ⇒ 0' is a non sequitur. Injectivity is what is needed. For i ≥ 2 it follows from R^{i−1}f_⋆(O^{++}/p) = 0. For i = 1, the p-torsion of R^1 f_⋆O^{++} is coker(f_⋆O^{++} → f_⋆(O^{++}/p)), and the proof never controls it: its fibre computation only treats i > 0 and never compares f_⋆(O^{++}/p) with O^{++}/p. The author makes exactly this degree-0 step explicitly in Prop. 14.4.1.1, p. 95: 'We look at the sequence for i = 0. Since (π)_⋆O^{++}/p = O^{++}/p … the map … is surjective. This implies that for all i > 0, multiplication by p is an isomorphism'. That confirms the argument in §3.4 is incomplete as printed and that the proposed fix is the right one. The correction is sound: the isomorphism f_⋆(O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}}/p) = O^{++}_{T^an_Σ}/p together with f_⋆O^{++} = O^{++} gives the surjectivity. It uses only ingredients already present. The statement of Prop. 3.4.1 is true. Its only later use is the statement, in the proof of Prop. 14.4.1.1 (pp. 94–95), so no stated result is affected. HAL v3 (p. 14) has word-for-word the same argument. The published Duke version could not be checked. I transcribed the passage from a 130 dpi render of author p. 15 and compared it with a render of HAL v3 PDF p. 14.

Notation: in this paper 'R^i f_⋆O^{++}/p' means R^i f_⋆(O^{++}/p). The proof of Prop. 3.3.1 on p. 14 says so ('R^k f_⋆O^{++}/p^n is the sheaf associated to the presheaf U ↦ H^k(f^{−1}(U), O^{++}/p^n)'). The fibre computation also gives exactly this: H^i(f^{−1}(U_n), O^{++}) = 0 for i > 0 implies H^i(f^{−1}(U_n), O^{++}/p) = 0 for i ≥ 1.

The failing step: p is invertible on the analytic space, so 0 → O^{++} →p O^{++} → O^{++}/p → 0 is exact. The long exact sequence, with R^i f_⋆(O^{++}/p) = 0 for i > 0, gives what the text says: p is surjective on R^i f_⋆O^{++} for i ≥ 1, and bijective for i ≥ 2. But 'p-surjective + torsion ⇒ 0' is false in general; Q_p/Z_p is p-divisible torsion. For i = 1 the kernel of p on R^1 f_⋆O^{++} is coker(f_⋆O^{++} → f_⋆(O^{++}/p)), and the proof never controls it. In fact R^1 f_⋆O^{++} = colim_n R^1 f_⋆O^{++}[p^n] = coker(O → f_⋆(O/O^{++})). So its vanishing is exactly a degree-0 statement about f_⋆(O/O^{++}), and the proof omits it.

Defences tried, all of which fail:
1. Reading 'R^i f_⋆O^{++}/p' as the cokernel of p only makes the sentence a tautology. The inference 'surjective + torsion ⇒ 0' is still invalid.
2. 'Torsion' comes only from inverting p ([40] + [70] Thm 9.1). That gives unbounded torsion. No bounded-torsion or derived-completeness result is cited, and derived Nakayama would also need the degree-0 mod-p statement.
3. The integral statement f_⋆O^{++} = O^{++} ('it follows easily') says nothing about f_⋆(O^{++}/p).

The author supplies the missing step himself when he reuses the result. In Prop. 14.4.1.1 (p. 95) he writes: 'We look at the sequence for i = 0. Since (π_{Σ′,Σ})_⋆O^{++}/p = O^{++}/p and O^{++} ↪ (π_{Σ′,Σ})_⋆O^{++}, we deduce that the map … is surjective. This implies that for all i > 0, multiplication by p is an isomorphism'. That is exactly the correct argument, and it confirms that the one on p. 15 is incomplete.

Consequences:
- The statement of Prop. 3.4.1 is true. The fix uses only ingredients already in its proof.
- A grep of both versions finds only one other citation of Prop. 3.4.1: p. 95 (HAL v3 p. 89), where the proof of Prop. 14.4.1.1 uses its statement ('By proposition 3.4.1, we deduce that Rπ_⋆O^{++}_{M_{σ∩Σ}} = O^{++}_{M_σ}').
- No stated result is affected.

- **Gap** at §15.2.4, proof of Proposition 15.2.4.1, p. 109. HAL v3 p. 91 has the same text.. The source says `Proof. Assume that π_f ⊗ π(λ)^h is automorphic (the argument would be the same if we assumed that π_f ⊗ π(λ)^g is automorphic). Let Π be the associated global A-packet. We claim that Π is of generic type in the sense of [1], classification theorem on p. 78. Hence Π is stable and tempered. The conclusion follows.`; it should be `"We claim that ψ is of general type ([1], p. 78, case (a): stable, semisimple). Hence S_ψ = 1 and ψ is trivial on Arthur's SL(2,ℂ), so the local packet Π∞ = Π_{ψ∞} is the L-packet of the archimedean L-parameter. Since it contains the limit of discrete series π(λ)^h, this parameter is tempered and Π∞ = {π(λ)^g, π(λ)^h} ([4], prop. 5.3.7)." Temperedness of the whole global packet should not be claimed.`. I checked Arthur [1], Clay library copy, pp. 77–78. The six families on p. 78 are headed "(a) Stable, semisimple (general type)", with S_ψ = 1. Remark 2 on p. 77 says explicitly: "if ψ belongs to Ψ_{ss,2}(G, χ), the generalized Ramanujan conjecture (applied to the groups GL(2) and GL(4)) implies that the representations in the packet Π_ψ are tempered". So Arthur says semisimple (general type) parameters give tempered packets only conditionally on the generalized Ramanujan conjecture. For these non-regular weights (π∞ a limit of discrete series) Ramanujan was not known, so the assertion "Π is ... tempered" is unproved. It is not needed. The next step ("Π∞ is an L-packet") follows from ψ being semisimple (trivial on SL2), which general type gives. The archimedean parameter is tempered because the packet contains π(λ)^h. Multiplicity one follows from S_ψ = 1. The paper also writes "generic type" where Arthur says "general type", a naming slip. The conclusion of the proposition is unaffected, given Arthur's classification as announced, on which the paper explicitly relies. - **Misprint** at §15.2.3, proof of Corollary 15.2.3.1, p. 109 (author version, 17 June 2019), paragraph starting "Let ℓ be a prime that is prime to the level K", lines 3–4. The source says `One computes that π_⋆Ω^{(k,2)}|_D = ω^{k+2}(−cusp) if k ≠ 0 and ω^2 when k = 0, where ω^{k+2} is the usual sheaf of modular forms of weight k + 2 on the modular curve. [...] On H^0(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)} ⊗ 𝒪_D) ≃ H^0(S_K^{(1),⋆}, ω^{k+2}(−cusp)) (resp. ≃ H^0(S_K^{(1),⋆}, ω^2) if k = 2), we have the formula T_{ℓ,2} = 2T_ℓ by [22], IV, satz 4.4.`; it should be `(resp. ≃ H^0(S_K^{(1),⋆}, ω^2) if k = 0)`. I checked the rendered p. 109 at 250 dpi, so this is not a text-layer artefact. The page does print "(resp. ≃ H^0(S_K^{(1),⋆}, ω^2) if k = 2)". The sentence just before it sets out two cases: π_⋆Ω^{(k,2)}|_D = ω^{k+2}(−cusp) if k ≠ 0, and ω^2 when k = 0. The "resp." clause must therefore cover the second case, k = 0. That is the only value where ω^{k+2} = ω^2, and the only case with no (−cusp) twist. With k = 2 the paper's own formula gives ω^4(−cusp), not ω^2.

I also checked that the preceding sentence, not the "resp." clause, is the correct one, using the paper's convention. By p. 1402 of the text layer (the definition Ω^{(k,r)} = Sym^k ω_G ⊗ det^r ω_G), Ω^{(k,2)} = Sym^k ω ⊗ det^2 ω, which is classical weight (k+2, 2). Near a 1-dimensional cusp ω_G restricts to ω_E ⊕ (torus part). The Siegel Φ-operator keeps the top component, giving ω_E^{k+2}. For a vector-valued weight (k > 0), Φ(f) is cuspidal, which explains the (−cusp) twist. For k = 0 (weight (2,2)) the result is ω^2 with no twist. This matches the preceding sentence. There is no reading of the paper's conventions under which "k = 2" is right, so it is a misprint for k = 0.

Effect: the corollary assumes k ≥ R − 1 with R a large constant, and its only use (§15.2.5, proof of Theorem 15.2.1) specialises "at a very large weight k". So the k = 0 case never arises there. The argument (T_{ℓ,2} = 2T_ℓ, giving a reducible ρ_f ⊕ ρ_f that is not congruent to ρ̄) is also the same in both cases. Nothing downstream depends on the parenthetical.

(1) Theorem 11.3.1 (p. 71) covers only two things:
- point 3: the p-rank ≥ 1 formal scheme 𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p). For all k ≥ 0 it gives fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ≃ fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ⊗ω²(−D)) ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Z_p.
- point 4: the spherical-level eH^i(𝔛, ·). For k ≥ C this map is bijective only for i = 0 and injective for i = 1.
Neither point mentions the classical Klingen-level scheme X_{Kli}(p).

(2) The comparison with X_{Kli}(p) is Theorem 14.8.1 (p. 100): fRΓ(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗^L_{Z_p} Q_p → fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗^L_{Z_p} Q_p is an isomorphism for all k ≥ 0. The author says this himself on p. 73, right after proving Theorem 11.3.1: "In order to complete the proof of theorem 1.1 of the introduction, we still have to obtain a control theorem for characteristic 0 classes of weight k ≥ 0. This will be obtained at the end of the next part of this work in theorem 14.8.1." So Theorem 11.3.1 alone cannot justify the equality in §15.2.5.

(3) The right-hand side is missing ⊗Q_p. X_{Kli}(p) lives over Z_p (the intro has X_K → Spec Z_p, and Theorem 14.8.1 needs ⊗_{Z_p} Q_p). As printed, a Q_p-complex is set equal to a Z_p-complex. The next display does add "⊗ \bar Q_p".

(4) The equality is true once ⊗Q_p is added: combine 11.3.1(3), localised at 𝔪 and tensored with Q_p, with Theorem 14.8.1. This is exactly Theorem 1.1(1). So the mathematics holds and the proof of Theorem 15.2.1 goes through; only the citation and notation slipped.

(5) Comparing with HAL v3 shows how this happened. There the right-hand side was eRΓ(X_K, ·)_m, and even that version was not fully covered by 11.3.1(4), which is only injective for i = 1. The author moved the comparison to Klingen level but kept the old reference.

This is a misprint, not an error: a wrong or incomplete cross-reference plus a missing ⊗Q_p. The statement itself is correct, and the right justification is stated in the paper and flagged by the author on p. 73.

Side remark: Corollary 15.2.3.1 is stated for S_K at spherical level, but here it is used at level K^pKli(p). The underlying result [30] holds at any level, so this is harmless. Checked on rendered page images: author p. 109, p. 71 (Thm 11.3.1), p. 100 (Thm 14.8.1), and HAL v3 PDF p. 93.
(1) The citation is incomplete. Theorem 11.3.1 is only about the formal scheme 𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p) (the p-rank ≥ 1 locus). Point 3 gives fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ≅ fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ⊗ω^2(−D)) ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Z_p. Point 4 concerns eH^i(𝔛, ·) at spherical level, is surjective only for i = 0, and does not concern X_{Kli}(p) at all. The author himself says, just after the proof of 11.3.1 (p. 73): "In order to complete the proof of theorem 1.1 ... we still have to obtain a control theorem for characteristic 0 classes of weight k ≥ 0. This will be obtained ... in theorem 14.8.1." Theorem 14.8.1 (p. 100) is exactly fRΓ(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗^L_{Z_p} Q_p ≅ fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗^L_{Z_p} Q_p. So 11.3.1 alone does not give the printed equality, and the missing input is 14.8.1.
(2) The right-hand side is missing ⊗Q_p. Here X_{Kli}(p) (roman) is the toroidal compactification over Spec Z_p (§6.1, §7.1: "normal and lci over Spec Z_p"), the same object as in Theorem 14.8.1. So the right-hand side is a Z_p-complex, which may have p-torsion, while the left-hand side is a Q_p-complex.
Defence tried: no reading makes 11.3.1 by itself cover the classical Klingen-level cohomology, so the printed justification is inadequate. However, the intended statement is clear: it is Theorem 1.1(1) localised at 𝔪, which the paper proves. The missing ⊗Q_p is repaired by the very next display, which tensors both H^0 and H^1 with Q̄_p. So this is a slip in the cross-reference and in the notation, not a false step. It is a misprint (a wrong name/reference with clear intended meaning), not an error; "gap" would be the most one could argue for.
Consequences: the passage is used only in this proof of Theorem 15.2.1. That theorem, which is Theorem 1.2 of the introduction (Euler characteristic of M_𝔪 is 0), follows because χ(M_𝔪) = χ(M_𝔪 ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Q_p) and the next display gives dim fH^0 = dim fH^1. With the corrected references the argument goes through unchanged. Stated results are unaffected. Recorded as `PAPER-PILLONI-20/E164`; looked for an existing correction in: The author's version on V. - **Gap** at §15.2.5, proof of Theorem 15.2.1 (= Theorem 1.2 of the introduction), p. 109 of the author version (17 June 2019). I checked the rendered page. HAL v3 has the same opening sentence word for word in §15.2.5, printed p. 92 (PDF p. 93). There the right-hand side of the specialisation is eRΓ(X_K, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_m and the display uses e instead of f. The gap is the same. (it affects the proof). The source says `15.2.5. Proof of theorem 15.2.1. — In order to prove the theorem, we can specialize at a very large weight k. Then fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ ⊗ ω^2(−D))_m ⊗_{Λ,k} Q_p = fRΓ(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_m by theorem 11.3.1. The cohomology is concentrated in degree 0 and 1. Extending the scalars to Q̄_p we can express the cohomology in automorphic terms using corollary 15.2.3.1 and proposition prop 15.2.4.1 : fH^0(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_m ⊗ Q̄_p = ⊕_{π_f} f(π_f^{K^p Kli(p)}) = fH^1(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_m ⊗ Q̄_p [...]`; it should be `Minimal fix: replace "specialize at a very large weight k" with "specialize at every sufficiently large weight k". It is enough to take one such k in each residue class mod p−1, which is one point on each of the p−1 connected components of Spec Λ, Λ = Z_p[[Z_p^×]] ≅ ∏_{p−1} Z_p[[T]], for p odd. For p = 2 the ring Λ is local and one k is enough. The rest of the argument applies unchanged to every such k. The proof should then conclude: χ(M_m) restricted to the component of k equals Σ(−1)^i dim H^i(M_m ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Q̄_p) = dim fH^0 − dim fH^1 = 0, so χ(M_m) = 0. An alternative fix needs more work. One shows that M_m is supported on the single component singled out by ρ̄. The central operator T_{ℓ,0} ∈ H_{Np} acts through the group element of ℓ in Λ times a tame character, and the tame character cannot absorb ω^{i−j}, which is ramified at p. One then takes k in that class. The printed text does neither of these.`. Defence attempted. Λ = Z_p[[Z_p^×]] (§1 and §9.3; §13.4 again: "Λ = Z_p[[Z_p^×]] is the one-dimensional Iwasawa algebra"). The paper fixes an arbitrary prime p (§6.1). For p odd, Z_p[μ_{p−1}] ≅ Z_p^{p−1}, so Λ ≅ ∏_{p−1} Z_p[[T]] and Spec Λ has p−1 connected components. The Euler characteristic of a perfect Λ-complex is a locally constant rank function, i.e. an element of K_0(Λ) = Z^{p−1}. The paper itself treats Euler characteristics this way in the proof of Lemma 14.8.4: "are locally constant functions of k ∈ Z_{≥0} by theorem 11.3.1". The map k: Λ → Z_p sends ζ ∈ μ_{p−1} to ζ^k, so it lands on the component e_{ω^k}. One specialisation M_m ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Q_p therefore gives χ(M_m) on the component of k mod p−1 only.

The charitable reading "any large k" is not what the text says. The defence that M_m sits on one component does hold, but only through an unstated Hecke/Galois argument. T_{ℓ,0} acts on 𝔉^κ through κ(ℓ), so Θ_m fixes the character ψ̄·ω^{±i}, and ψ̄ is unramified at p. Even then, the single weight k has to be chosen in the right class, and the printed proof never says so. For p = 2, Z_2[C_2] is local, so Spec Λ is connected and the printed argument is complete. The flaw is therefore real only for odd p.

The fix is right and minimal. Theorem 11.3.1(3) holds for all k ≥ 0, Theorem 15.2.3.1 and Corollary 15.2.3.1 for all k ≥ R−1, and Proposition 15.2.4.1 for all admissible λ. None of these depends on k mod p−1, so the displayed equality dim fH^0 = dim fH^1 holds for every large k. In a class that does not support M_m, both sides are 0. The missing last line "hence χ = 0" is an immediate consequence of the display and is not a separate gap.

Consequences: Theorem 15.2.1 (= Theorem 1.2) is the last result of the paper, and nothing later uses it. The stated result stays true, and only the written proof is incomplete for odd p. - **Gap** at §3.4, proof of Proposition 3.4.1, p. 15 (paragraph "First assume that x is a maximal point ..."). HAL v3 (hal-01393374v3) has the same Proposition 3.4.1 and word-for-word the same sentence on its p. 13. (it affects the proof). The source says `Set U_0 = x′ × T^{rig}_{2,σ}. Fix an isomorphism T_2 ≃ G^s_m for some integer s. Let p̲ = (p, ···, p) ∈ T^{an}_2(Q_p). Then the {U_n = p̲^n U_0}_{n∈N} form a fundamental system of neighborhoods of x in x′ × T^{an}_{2,σ}. It is enough to prove that H^i(f^{-1}(U_n), O^{++}_{x′×T^{an}_{2,Σ″}}) = 0 for all i > 0 and all n ≥ 0. Using the action of p̲ we are reduced to the case of U_0.`; it should be `Tie the choice of p̲ to σ. Take a cocharacter λ ∈ X_*(T_2) in the interior of σ, for example the sum of the primitive generators of the rays of σ. This lies in the interior because σ spans X_*(T_2)_R. Put p̲ = λ(p). Equivalently, choose the isomorphism T_2 ≃ G_m^s so that (1,…,1) lies in the interior of σ. Such an isomorphism exists because GL_s(Z) acts transitively on primitive vectors. With the opposite sign convention for σ^∨, use −λ instead. Then ⟨χ,λ⟩ ≥ 1 for every nonzero χ ∈ σ^∨ ∩ X^*(T_2). Let χ_1,…,χ_r generate σ^∨ ∩ X^*(T_2) and let N = max_j ⟨χ_j,λ⟩. Then {|χ_j| ≤ |p|^{nN} for all j} ⊂ U_n ⊂ {|χ_j| ≤ |p|^n for all j}. So the U_n are cofinal among the neighbourhoods of the rational point 0 in the fibre x′ × T^{an}_{2,σ}. The rest of the proof is unchanged, because translation by λ(p) is an automorphism of the whole situation: f_2′ is T_2-equivariant and automorphisms preserve O^{++}.`. I checked the printed text on the rendered page (p. 15 at 130 and 220 dpi). The page has p̲ with an underline, and the quote above is accurate.

Setup (p. 15): σ spans X_*(T_2), T_{2,σ} = Spec Z[σ^∨ ∩ X^*(T_2)], and U_0 = x′ × T^{rig}_{2,σ} = {|χ| ≤ 1 for all χ ∈ σ^∨}. For t = λ(p) we have y ∈ t^n U_0 ⇔ |χ(t^{-n}y)| ≤ 1 ⇔ |χ(y)| ≤ |p|^{n⟨χ,λ⟩}. So the U_n shrink to the closed-orbit point 0 exactly when ⟨χ,λ⟩ > 0 for every nonzero χ ∈ σ^∨, that is, when λ ∈ int σ. Here p̲ = (p,…,p) means λ = (1,…,1) in the chosen coordinates. The paper says only "Fix an isomorphism T_2 ≃ G_m^s" and never ties the choice to σ. Note that σ need not be smooth: only Σ′ is assumed smooth, so there is no canonical identification with (1,…,1) ∈ σ.

There is already a counterexample with s=1. With σ = R_{≥0}(−1) and T_{2,σ} = Spec Z[t^{-1}], we get p^nU_0 = {|t^{-1}| ≤ |p|^{-n}}, which increases. That example depends on the direction of the action, so I also checked a stronger one that fails under either sign convention. Take s=2 and σ = cone(e1, e1−e2). Then σ^∨ is generated by u = (0,−1) and v = (1,1), and T_{2,σ} ≅ A^2. The pairings are ⟨u,(1,1)⟩ = −1 and ⟨v,(1,1)⟩ = 2. So p̲^{±n}U_0 = {|u| ≤ |p|^{∓n}, |v| ≤ |p|^{±2n}}, and neither family is a neighbourhood basis of 0. The printed claim is therefore false for some admissible choices of the isomorphism. This is a genuine but minor gap, not a text-layer artefact.

Proposition 3.4.1 itself is true and the fix is immediate. The later use of Proposition 3.4.1, on p. 95 in §13 (Rπ_⋆O^{++}_{M_{σ∩Σ′}} = O^{++}_{M_σ}, independence of the toroidal compactification), relies only on the statement, so it is unaffected. I checked the printed text on the rendered page (p. 15 at 130 and 220 dpi). The page has p̲ with an underline, which the text layer drops. HAL v3 p. 13 has the same passage.

Setup (p. 15). X_*(T_2) = X_*(T) ∩ σ_R, and σ spans X_*(T_2). So T_{2,σ} = Spec Z[σ^∨ ∩ X^*(T_2)] has a unique fixed point 0, and U_0 = {|χ| ≤ 1 for all χ ∈ σ^∨}. For t = λ(p) we have y ∈ t^n U_0 ⇔ |χ(t^{-n}y)| ≤ 1 ⇔ |χ(y)| ≤ |p|^{n⟨χ,λ⟩}. The printed choice p̲ = (p,…,p) means λ = (1,…,1) in coordinates that the paper fixes with no reference to σ. The U_n shrink to 0 exactly when ⟨χ,λ⟩ > 0 for all nonzero χ ∈ σ^∨, i.e. when λ lies in the interior of σ.

Defences I tried, none of which works:
(1) Sign convention. Take s = 2 and σ = cone(e1, e1−e2). This σ is even smooth, and only Σ′ is assumed smooth anyway. Its dual σ^∨ is generated by (0,−1) and (1,1), and T_{2,σ} ≅ A^2. The pairings with (1,1) are −1 and 2. So p̲^{±n}U_0 = {|u| ≤ |p|^{∓n}, |v| ≤ |p|^{±2n}}, and neither family is a neighbourhood basis of 0. Reversing the convention for σ^∨ only swaps the two signs, so it does not help. Also, neither (1,1) nor (−1,−1) lies in σ = {(a+b, −b) : a, b ≥ 0}.
(2) Charitable reading, "an isomorphism suitably adapted". The text says only "Fix an isomorphism ... for some integer s", with no condition. The decomposition T = T_1 × T_2 is itself an arbitrary choice, so no canonical coordinates exist.
(3) Other statements in the paper or cited sources. The proof cites [40] only for the cohomology of the toroidal embedding, not for this step.
So the sentence as written is false for some admissible choices. Because the choice is the author's to make and a good one always exists, this is a local gap in the proof, not an error in the result.

Consequences. Proposition 3.4.1 is true: the corrected choice restores the argument without changing anything else. Its only later use is on p. 95, in the proof of Proposition 14.4.1.1 (§14.4, independence of the toroidal compactification: "By proposition 3.4.1, we deduce that Rπ_⋆O^{++}_{M_{σ∩Σ′}} = O^{++}_{M_σ}"). That proof uses only the statement. This use is in §14.4, not in §13 as said above. The correction is right and minimal, in either of its two equivalent forms. The s = 1 counterexample above depends on the direction of the sign convention; the s = 2 example above fails under either convention. - **Misprint** at §4.1.3, Proposition 4.1.3.1, p. 16 (author version, 17 June 2019); the same text is in HAL v3, printed p. 14 (PDF p. 15). The source says `Proposition 4.1.3.1. — If h : X → S is an embeddable morphism and a local complete intersection of pure relative dimension n, then f^!𝒪_X = ω_{X/S}[n] where ω_{X/S} is the determinant of the cotangent complex 𝕃_{X/S}. [Proof: "This follows from the very definition of f^! given in thm 8.7 of [32]."]`; it should be `h^!𝒪_S = ω_{X/S}[n]. Two symbols are wrong: the letter f should be h, and 𝒪_X should be 𝒪_S. The proof's "definition of f^!" is the generic functor from §4.1.2, applied here to h.`. I checked the rendered page image, not the text layer (page 16 at 150 dpi, and HAL v3 PDF p. 15). The statement is in italics and reads "then f^!𝒪_X = ω_{X/S}[n]". Inside the proposition only h : X → S is named. By §4.1.2 on the same page, f^! for f : X → Y is a functor D^+_qcoh(𝒪_Y) → D^+_qcoh(𝒪_X), so it takes objects on the target. That makes h^! a functor from D^+_qcoh(𝒪_S) to D^+_qcoh(𝒪_X), and h^!𝒪_X has the wrong type. Reading f as h does not fix it; the argument also has to be 𝒪_S. The slip probably comes from the paragraph just before, which defines lci for a generic "f : X → S". The corrected statement is the standard one. For a smooth h of relative dimension n, h^!𝒪_S = Ω^n_{X/S}[n]. For an lci h, 𝕃_{X/S} is perfect in degrees −1 and 0 with virtual rank n, and its determinant ω_{X/S} = det(L^0) ⊗ det(L^{−1})^{−1} generalises Ω^n. The paper uses exactly this form on p. 17: the proof of Corollary 4.1.3.1 opens "We have h^!𝒪_S = ω_{X/S}[n]" (image checked) and then computes h^!𝒪_S = f^!(g^!𝒪_S) = f^!(ω_{Y/S}[n]) = f^!(𝒪_Y) ⊗ f^*ω_{Y/S}[n]. HAL hal-01393374v3 has the same wrong text word for word (Proposition 4.1.3.1, with [29] cited in place of [32]). I could not check the published Duke text. - **Misprint** at §4.2.3, proof of Lemma 4.2.3.1, top of p. 18 (author version). HAL v3 has the identical sentence (§4.2.3, pp. 15–16 printed).. The source says `The morphism f_⋆ det 𝕃_{X/Y} = Hom(f_⋆𝒪_X, 𝒪_Y) → 𝒪_Y is the residue map which associates to ω ∈ f_⋆Ω^1_{X/S} and to (t_1, ···, t_n) local generators of the ideal ℐ_X over Y the function Res[ω, t_1, ..., t_n].`; it should be `… which associates to ω ∈ f_⋆Ω^n_{X/S} = f_⋆ω_{X/S}, where n is the relative dimension, and to (t_1, …, t_n) … the function Res[ω; t_1, …, t_n].`. X ↪ X ×_S Y is a regular immersion of codimension n into a smooth Y-scheme of relative dimension n, and the ideal has n local generators t_1, …, t_n. Hartshorne's residue symbol Res[ω; t_1, …, t_n] ([32] III.9) is defined for relative n-forms ω ∈ Ω^n_{X×_S Y/Y}, whose restriction to X is Ω^n_{X/S}. This matches the determinant ω_{X/Y} of the rank-n complex [Ω^1_{Y/S} ⊗ 𝒪_X → Ω^1_{X/S}] used in the same paragraph. A 1-form is only right when n = 1. The paper writes ω_{X/S} for the determinant and never uses Ω^1 for top forms, so this is a slip with clear intended meaning. - **Misprint** at §1 (Introduction), p. 2, the paragraph that sets up Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 (author version, 17 June 2019). HAL v3 (p. 2) has the same omission, worded slightly differently: "a toroidal compactification of the Siegel threefold of level some open subgroup K = ∏ K_ℓ ⊂ GSp4(A_f) such that K_p = GSp4(Z_p)". That version also drops "compact".. The source says `We denote by X_K → Spec Z_p a toroidal compactification of the Siegel threefold of level given by an compact open subgroup K = ∏_ℓ K_ℓ ⊂ GSp4(A_f) such that K_p = GSp4(Z_p).`; it should be `Read "given by a neat compact open subgroup K = ∏_ℓ K_ℓ ⊂ GSp4(A_f) such that K_p = GSp4(Z_p)". This is the standing hypothesis of §5.2.1 (p. 23) and §6.1.1 (p. 26). A second option, also adding "for a good polyhedral cone decomposition", is not needed. Theorem 1.1 is about cuspidal cohomology, and by Theorem 6.1.5.1(2) (Rπ_*O = O and, in the form corrected in sourceIssues E40, (Rπ)_*I_Σ' = I_Σ, plus the projection formula and common refinements) that cohomology does not depend on which toroidal compactification is chosen. So the minimal correction is the single word "neat".`. The omission is real. I checked the page images of p. 2 of the author version and of the HAL v3 intro. The list of conditions on K is only "compact open, K = ∏K_ℓ, K_p = GSp4(Z_p)", and "neat" does not appear. Everything the proof uses is built for neat K. The only occurrences of "neat" in the paper are p. 23, §5.2.1 ("Let K ⊂ GSp4(A_f) be a neat compact open subgroup. We let S_K = …") and p. 26, §6.1.1 ("Let K ⊂ GSp4(A_f) be a neat compact open subgroup. We assume that K = K^p K_p and that K_p = GSp4(Z_p)"). Y_K, the compactifications of Theorem 6.1.5.1, the Hecke correspondences and all later sections rest on §6.1.1. That includes Theorems 11.2.1 and 11.3.1 and Theorem 14.8.1, which together give Theorem 1.1 (p. 73: "In order to complete the proof of theorem 1.1 …"), and Theorem 15.2.1, which gives Theorem 1.2. The paper has no descent to non-neat level; no text mentions stacks, coarse spaces or taking invariants.

The defence is partial but substantial. (i) In the paper's own terminology, "the Siegel threefold of level K" is only ever defined for neat K (§5.2.1, §6.1.1). The same intro sentence also speaks of "the semi-abelian scheme" over X_K and "the relative Cartier divisor of the boundary", which assume a fine moduli scheme. A careful reader therefore infers neatness, and the intended meaning is clear from context. §15.1 and §15.2 (pp. 106–107) likewise reintroduce "K = ∏K_ℓ … a compact open subgroup. We assume as usual that K_p = GSp4(Z_p)" without saying "neat". There it plainly means the standing assumption of §6.1.1. (ii) Read literally for a non-neat K, such as level 1 with X_K taken as a Faltings–Chai stack, the claims are not proved. When p divides the order of the finite quotient K/K', taking invariants is not exact. The perfect amplitude-[0,1] claim of Theorem 1.1 and the integral statement in point 2 would then need an argument the paper does not give. When p does not divide that order, a descent argument works easily, but none is written.

So this is a genuine slip in the printed statement, not a mathematical failure. It is a misprint rather than a gap, and it affects nothing rather than a stated result, because under the intended hypothesis the proved results are exactly Theorems 1.1 and 1.2. Nothing later relies on the intro passage with non-neat K; the only back-reference, on p. 6, just uses the complex M. - **Error** at §5.1.1 (The dual group of GSp4), p. 20. The source says `(p. 20, checked on the page image) "We make the following choice of positive roots {e1 − e2, −2e1 + e3, −e1 − e2 + e3, −2e2 + e3}. Set α1 = e1 − e2 and α2 = −2e2 + e3. The simple positive roots are ∆ = {α1, α2}. The compact root is α1. We let ρ = (−1, −2; 0) be half the sum of the positive roots. This choice of positive roots is related to the Shimura datum (see remark 5.2.1.1). [...] The coroot of α1 is α1^∨ = f1 − f2 and the coroot of α2 is α2^∨ = f2. We let ∆^∨ = {α1^∨, α2^∨}. [...] By [65], lemma 2.3.1 there is an isomorphism of roots datum between (X*(T), ∆, X_*(T), ∆^∨) and (X_*(T), ∆^∨, X*(T), ∆). It is given by a map i : X*(T) → X_*(T) whose matrix in the basis e1, e2, e3 and f1, f2, f3 is (1 1 1 / 1 0 1 / 1 1 2)". Earlier on the page: e1 = (1,0;1), e2 = (0,1;1), e3 = (0,0;2); f1 = (1,0;0), f2 = (0,1;0), f3 = (−1/2,−1/2;1/2).`; it should be `The correction that fits the rest of the paper is to take the positive system of the lower-triangular Borel, which is the negative of HAL v3's system. The changes in §5.1.1 are: - positive roots {e2−e1, −2e1+e3, −e1−e2+e3, −2e2+e3}; - α1 = e2 − e1 (the compact root); - α2 = −2e2 + e3 (unchanged); - α1^∨ = f2 − f1 and α2^∨ = −f2; - ρ = (−2, −1; 0). The matrix of i stays as printed: i(α1) = −f2 = α2^∨ and i(α2) = f2 − f1 = α1^∨, and the matrix is symmetric and unimodular. The coset X*(T) + (−1,−2;0) in §5.1.6 needs no change, because (−1,−2;0) − (−2,−1;0) = (1,−1;0) lies in X*(T). An alternative correction keeps the printed list and ρ and changes α2 to −2e1+e3, α2^∨ to −f1 and the matrix. That makes §5.1.1 consistent on its own, but it leaves §5.1.6 and §15.2.1 wrong. For holomorphic λ (λ1 < λ2 ≤ 0), λ is not in the closure of the printed dominant chamber. So that fix is not the right one for the paper as a whole, and it changes the matrix for no reason.`. I redid the computation. A character (a1,a2;c) pairs with a cocharacter (b1,b2;d) as a1b1 + a2b2 + cd, and I checked that the f_i are dual to the e_i.

**Positive roots and ρ.** In (t1,t2)-exponents the printed positive roots are t1/t2, t1^−2, (t1t2)^−1 and t2^−2. They form a positive system; λ = (−1,−2) is regular dominant for it. Half their sum is (−1,−2;0), so ρ is right.

**The printed ∆ is wrong.**
- −e1−e2+e3 = (e1−e2) + (−2e1+e3), and −2e2+e3 = (e1−e2) + (−e1−e2+e3). So −2e2+e3 is a sum of two positive roots and is not simple.
- The coroot of −2e2+e3 = (0,−2;0) is −f2, not f2: ⟨−2e2+e3, f2⟩ = −2.
- ⟨ρ, −f2⟩ = 2, which is its height. The simple coroots f1−f2 and −f1 both pair with ρ to give 1.
- ⟨e1−e2, −f2⟩ = +1 > 0, so {e1−e2, −2e2+e3} is not a base of any positive system.

**The printed matrix.** It is symmetric, so rows and columns read the same way. It gives i(e1) = f1+f2+f3, i(e2) = f1+f3, i(e3) = f1+f2+2f3. So i(e1−e2) = f2, which is the printed α2^∨ but a negative coroot for the printed positive system. And i(−2e2+e3) = f2−f1, which is not in the printed ∆^∨. For the correct base, i(−2e1+e3) = −f1−f2. So the printed i is not a based isomorphism for the author-version choices.

**Images in ∆^∨.** The image f2 does lie in the printed ∆^∨ (it is the printed α2^∨); only f2−f1 does not. Neither image lies in the correct ∆^∨ = {f1−f2, −f1}. This does not change the conclusion.

**HAL v3.** HAL v3 had the upper-triangular positive system on printed p. 17 (PDF p. 18): positive roots {e1−e2, 2e1−e3, e1+e2−e3, 2e2−e3}, α2 = 2e2−e3 and α2^∨ = f2. The same matrix is on printed p. 18 (PDF p. 19). There everything is consistent: i(e1−e2) = f2 = α2^∨ and i(2e2−e3) = f1−f2 = α1^∨. HAL v3 has a different typo, e2 = (1,0;1). The revision negated the three non-compact roots and added ρ, but left ∆, the coroot of α2 and i as they were. So the inconsistency was introduced by the revision; HAL v3 itself was consistent (its matrix is on printed p. 18).

**Affects nothing.** ∆, α1, α2, α2^∨ and ∆^∨ appear only in §5.1.1; I grepped the whole text. The printed i still sends every root to a coroot and satisfies the transpose condition, so it is an unbased root-datum isomorphism, and a based one for the upper-triangular Borel. The identification of the dual group with GSp4(C) is therefore still valid. It is used only through semisimple conjugacy classes c_Θ in §5.1.3 and §5.1.5, which do not depend on the choice of base. ρ and 'our choice of positive roots' are used later (§5.1.6), and both are printed correctly. I checked this by hand and by direct computation. The pairing is (a1,a2;c)·(b1,b2;d) = a1b1 + a2b2 + cd, and the f_i are dual to the e_i.

**No reading makes the printed §5.1.1 consistent.**
- The printed Δ = {e1−e2, −2e2+e3} is not a base of any positive system: ⟨e1−e2, (−2e2+e3)^∨⟩ = ⟨(1,−1), (0,−1)⟩ = +1 > 0.
- In the printed list, −2e2+e3 = (e1−e2) + (−e1−e2+e3), so it is not simple. The simple roots of the printed list are e1−e2 and −2e1+e3.
- α2^∨ = f2 is wrong in every system: ⟨−2e2+e3, f2⟩ = −2, so the coroot is −f2.
- The printed i sends α1 to f2 and α2 to f2 − f1. The pair {f2, f2 − f1} is not the printed Δ^∨ = {f1−f2, f2}. So the stated based isomorphism fails for the printed data.

**Defence attempt.** The printed list and ρ = (−1,−2;0) do agree with each other, and Remark 5.1.2.1 holds for them. But the paper's only later uses of "our choice of positive roots" require e2−e1 to be positive:
- §5.1.6 (p. 22) says: "0 ≥ λ2 > λ1 and C is the dominant chamber corresponding to our choice of positive roots". The same range for holomorphic λ appears on p. 24, and the embedding into H^0(Ω^(λ2−λ1−1, 2−λ2)) gives λ = (1−k−r, 2−r; ·).
- For λ = (−5, −2), λ pairs with the coroots of the printed positive roots as (−3, 5, 7, 2). The signs are mixed, so λ is neither dominant nor antidominant under either sign convention.
- For the lower-Borel system the same pairings are (3, 5, 7, 2), all positive.
- The normalizing region "−λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ λ1" in §5.1.6 lies in the half-plane λ2 ≥ λ1, where e2−e1 is non-negative on λ.
- In §15.2.1 (λ2 = 0 > λ1), both chambers positive for λ contain e2−e1. For λ = (−5, 0) the printed pairings are (−5, 5, 5, 0). So the printed chamber is not one of the "two choices for C", and π(λ)^h would be ill-defined as written.
- The printed α2 = −2e2+e3 and the printed matrix are exactly right for the lower-Borel system.
- On the other side, §15.2.2 says "(−λ1+1, 2; −c) is dominant for the Levi M_Si". That is the standard upper-Borel convention for GL2 highest weights, and the same phrase appears in HAL v3. It does not refer to "our choice".
So no charitable reading rescues the printed list.

**How the error arose.** HAL v3 used upper-triangular conventions throughout, with holomorphic λ1 > λ2 ≥ 0. The revision negated λ but updated §5.1.1 only in part: it negated the non-compact roots, kept e1−e2, computed ρ from that mixed list, and kept the old α1^∨, α2^∨ and matrix.

**Consequences.** Δ, Δ^∨ and i only fix the identification of the dual group with GSp4(C). That identification is used only through semisimple conjugacy classes (c_Θ in §5.1.3 and §5.1.5), which do not depend on the base. In §5.1.6 and §15.2.1 the intended holomorphic chamber is clear from the stated range of λ. No stated result or proof changes once the correction is made, so this affects nothing downstream.

**On §5.1.6.** The statement in the "Affects nothing" paragraph that ρ and 'our choice of positive roots' are used later (§5.1.6) and both are printed correctly is wrong for §5.1.6. The correct §5.3 formula is λ = (1−k−r, 2−r; k+2r). The main text on p. 24 actually prints (1−k+r, …), which is a separate slip; the correct form appears in Remark 5.3.1. - **Misprint** at §5.1.6 (Discrete series), first sentence, p. 22 of the author version (17 June 2019). The source says `5.1.6. Discrete series. — Given λ = (λ1, λ2; c) ∈ X⋆(T) + (−1, −2; 0) ⊂ X⋆(T)_C which satisfies −λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ λ1 and a Weyl chamber C positive for λ we have a (limit of) discrete series π(λ, C) (see [28], 3.3). [...] If λ2 ≠ 0 and λ2 ≠ −λ1, λ determines uniquely C and π(λ, C) is a discrete series. It is natural to normalize the central character c by c = −λ1 − λ2 + 3. If 0 ≥ λ2 > λ1 and C is the dominant chamber corresponding to our choice of positive roots, then π(λ, C) is called a holomorphic (limit of) discrete series.`; it should be `Read '−λ1 ≥ λ2 > λ1', making the inequality strict on the compact wall λ1 = λ2. This is exactly v3's 'λ1 > λ2 ≥ −λ1' after the sign change. The one-symbol fix repairs both sentences: once λ2 > λ1, the only root walls left in the region are λ2 = 0 and λ2 = −λ1. An alternative correction instead adds 'λ2 ≠ λ1' to the uniqueness sentence. That also works but is less minimal, because it leaves the first sentence claiming that a (limit of) discrete series exists for λ1 = λ2. That claim holds only if one lets the zero coherent continuation count as a 'limit', which the text does not do.`. Checked on page images (pdftoppm at 300 dpi, crop of p. 22): the printed text is '−λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ λ1', with both signs non-strict. The holomorphic condition two sentences later is '0 ≥ λ2 > λ1', which is strict.

Conventions (§5.1.1, pp. 20–21): (a1, a2; c) = a1e1 + a2e2 + ((c−a1−a2)/2)e3, and f1, f2 are dual to e1, e2. So a weight λ = (λ1, λ2; c) pairs with the coroot α1∨ = f1 − f2 of the compact root α1 = e1 − e2 to give λ1 − λ2. The line λ1 = λ2 is therefore the compact wall, whichever sign convention is used for positivity.

The set of admissible λ modulo the order-4 group {id, s_α1, −1, −s_α1} is cut out by λ2 ≥ λ1 and λ1 + λ2 ≤ 0. That is the printed inequality. But a (limit of) discrete series needs λ to be regular for the compact root. The next sentence confirms this: it lists only the non-compact walls λ2 = 0 and λ2 = −λ1 as the limit cases. So the equality λ2 = λ1 has to be excluded.

Counterexample: take λ = (−1, −1; 5). Then λ − (−1, −2; 0) = (0, 1; 5), and 5 ≡ 0 + 1 (mod 2), so λ is in X⋆(T) + ρ. Also c = 5 = −λ1 − λ2 + 3 matches the paper's normalization. The inequality holds: 1 ≥ −1 ≥ −1. And λ2 = −1 ≠ 0, λ2 ≠ −λ1 = 1. So as printed, λ 'determines uniquely C' and gives a discrete series. In fact λ lies on the wall between two chambers, and no (limit of) discrete series has this parameter.

HAL v3 (§5.1.4, printed p. 18, checked on the page image) has 'λ1 > λ2 ≥ −λ1' with shift (2, 1; 0) and a strict compact inequality. The author version changed conventions by negation. v3 holomorphic 'λ1 > λ2 ≥ 0' becomes '0 ≥ λ2 > λ1', exactly as printed, but the strict sign in the region was lost. So this is not an artefact of the text layer.

Side notes, not part of this item:
- §15.2.1 on p. 107 prints '−λ1 ≥ λ2 > −λ1', which describes an empty set, together with the stale shift (2, 1; 0). This is a separate misprint, probably meant to read the same as the corrected §5.1.6.
- The stated positive system {e1−e2, −2e1+e3, −e1−e2+e3, −2e2+e3} with ρ = (−1, −2; 0) has dominant chamber 0 ≥ λ1 ≥ λ2. Its simple roots are e1−e2 and −2e1+e3, not −2e2+e3. That does not match '0 ≥ λ2 > λ1, C dominant'. This separate sign problem does not affect the correction, because the compact wall is λ1 = λ2 in every convention.

The published Duke version could not be checked. Printed text, checked on a 300 dpi crop of p. 22: '−λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ λ1', with both inequalities non-strict. The holomorphic condition on the same page, '0 ≥ λ2 > λ1', is strict.

The walls are convention-independent. §5.1.1 (p. 20) writes (a1, a2; c) = a1e1 + a2e2 + ((c−a1−a2)/2)e3, with f1, f2, f3 dual to e1, e2, e3. The coroots of the roots e1−e2, −2e1+e3, −2e2+e3 and −e1−e2+e3 are proportional to f1−f2, f1, f2 and f1+f2. So the walls in the λ-plane are λ1 = λ2, λ1 = 0, λ2 = 0 and λ1 + λ2 = 0. The compact root is α1 = e1−e2, so its wall is λ1 = λ2. This holds under any sign convention for positivity.

A separate sign inconsistency in §5.1.1 does not change this. The stated coroots α1∨ = f1−f2 and α2∨ = f2 are left over from v3, and the dominant chamber of the stated positive system is 0 > λ1 > λ2, which does not match '0 ≥ λ2 > λ1'.

Strongest defence tried: in the Knapp–Zuckerman / Harris [28] §3.3 framework, a (limit of) discrete series needs λ to be nonsingular for the compact roots. When λ is singular for a compact root, the coherent continuation is 0, not a representation. So the printed sentence 'we have a (limit of) discrete series π(λ, C)' fails for λ1 = λ2. The later sentence is false outright: λ then lies on the wall between two chambers exchanged by s_α1, so C is not unique, and there is no discrete series. The defence fails.

These points are attainable in the paper's lattice. For any a < 0, λ = (a, a; −2a+3) satisfies λ − (−1, −2; 0) = (a+1, a+2; −2a+3), and the parity condition c ≡ a1 + a2 (mod 2) holds. So λ ∈ X⋆(T) + ρ, and it has the paper's normalized c.
- Example λ = (−1, −1; 5): 1 ≥ −1 ≥ −1 holds, λ2 ≠ 0 and λ2 ≠ −λ1 = 1, so the printed text calls π(λ, C) a discrete series.
- Another example, (−2, −2; 1), also checks: (−1, 0; 1) ∈ X⋆(T) since 1 ≡ −1 (mod 2).
- Cross-check: Theorem 5.1.7.1(3) would give Hodge–Tate weights (0, −λ2, −λ1, −λ1−λ2) = (0, 1, 1, 2), which are not distinct. This fits with no discrete series existing there.

The intended meaning is clear from context:
- v3 has the strict sign.
- The next sentence lists only the non-compact walls λ2 = 0 and λ2 = −λ1 as the degenerate cases.
- The holomorphic condition is strict.
So this is a misprint rather than a mathematical error.

Consequences: nothing later in the paper uses the case λ1 = λ2.
- Theorem 5.1.7.1 assumes π∞ is in the discrete series, which forces λ to be regular.
- §5.3 (pp. 24–25) uses holomorphic λ = (1−k−r, 2−r; ...) with k ≥ 0, so λ2 − λ1 = k + 1 > 0, strictly.
- §15.2.1–15.2.2 (p. 107) use λ2 = 0 > λ1, which lies inside the corrected region.
§15.2.1 has its own misprint, the empty region '−λ1 ≥ λ2 > −λ1' with the stale shift (2, 1; 0), and should read like the corrected §5.1.6. That is a separate item. - **Misprint** at §5.1.5, unnumbered paragraph between Proposition 5.1.5.1 and Proposition 5.1.5.2, p. 22 (author version, 17 June 2019). The source says `Let π_ℓ be an irreducible complex smooth admissible representation of GSp_4(Q_ℓ) and assume that π_ℓ^{Kli(ℓ)} ≠ 0. Then there is a quadruple (α, β, γ, δ) ∈ C^4 satisfying αβ = γδ such that π_ℓ^{Kli(ℓ)} ≠ 0 contains an eigenvector for U_{Kli(ℓ),0}, U_{Kli(ℓ),1} and U_{Kli(ℓ),2} with eigenvalues ℓ^{−3}αδ, ℓ^{−1}αβ, α + β. The W-orbit of (α, β, γ, δ) ∈ C^4 is still called the Hecke parameters of π_ℓ.`; it should be `"satisfying αδ = βγ" in place of "satisfying αβ = γδ". The rest of the sentence, including the eigenvalues ℓ^{−3}αδ, ℓ^{−1}αβ, α+β, stays as printed.`. I checked the printed text on a 250 dpi render of p. 22, and it does read "αβ = γδ". This does not fit the paper's own conventions:

(1) The maximal torus. §5.1.1 (p. 20) defines it as diag(st1, st2, st2^{-1}, st1^{-1}), so diag(a,b,c,d) lies in GSp4 exactly when ad = bc. §5.1.5 (p. 21) matches this: it orders the Hecke parameters "in such a way that αδ = βγ, so that diag(α,β,γ,δ) represents the semi-simple conjugacy class". The Weyl group W acts on quadruples by keeping αδ = βγ. It does not keep αβ = γδ: for example, swapping α and δ turns it into δβ = γα.

(2) Lemma 5.1.5.1 (T_{ℓ,0} ↦ ℓ^{−3}αδ, T_{ℓ,1} ↦ ℓ^{−1}(αβ+αγ+αδ+βδ+γδ) − ℓ^{−3}αδ, T_{ℓ,2} ↦ α+β+γ+δ). I checked it against the Hecke polynomial Q_ℓ(X) = 1 − T2X + ℓ(T1+(ℓ²+1)T0)X² − ℓ³T2T0X³ + ℓ⁶T0²X⁴ = ∏(1−ξX), both by hand and numerically. The formulas hold only under αδ = βγ, which makes αδ the similitude and gives αβγδ = (ℓ³T0)².

(3) Proposition 5.1.5.1 (p. 22) gives the eigenvalues as the W-orbit of ℓ^{−3}αδ, ℓ^{−1}αβ, α+β. The central eigenvalue ℓ^{−3}αδ stays the same across the orbit only because αδ = βγ. The orbit {αβ, αγ, βδ, γδ} is the 4-element set that appears in Lemma 5.1.5.2.

(4) Proposition 5.1.5.2 concludes that π_ℓ is generic spherical "with Hecke parameters (α,β,γ,δ)". By the definition on p. 21, such parameters must satisfy αδ = βγ. So the Klingen-level parameters must be normalised the same way.

(5) Later use. In the proof of Lemma 14.8.3 (p. 102), Corollary 14.9.1 is invoked for the Klingen-level Hecke parameters of this paragraph, together with Proposition 5.1.5.2 and Lemma 5.1.5.2. Corollary 14.9.1 (p. 102) says those parameters have valuations (0,0,k+1,k+1). That is impossible under αβ = γδ: the unit ℓ^{−1}αβ would force Σv = 2v(αβ) = 0. It holds under αδ = βγ, where αβ is a unit and v(αδ) = v(βγ) = k+1.

Also, "αβ = γδ" does not occur anywhere else in the text. HAL v3 has no such passage: its §5.1 goes straight from the spherical Hecke algebra to discrete series, and its §5.1.5 is about Galois representations. Where HAL v3 orders Hecke parameters (printed p. 57), it uses "α_p δ_p = β_p γ_p". The slip was therefore introduced in the revision. As a bare existence claim the printed sentence is not false, because the quadruple is underdetermined. But the "Hecke parameters" it defines are the wrong ones for every later use, so this is a genuine misprint rather than an artefact of the text layer. - **Misprint** at §5.1.6 (Discrete series), p. 22 (author version). HAL v3 §5.1.4 has the same statement: 'By Harris-Chandra isomorphism (recalled in [16], p. 229 for instance), Z ≃ C[Y(T)]^W'.. The source says `Let ℨ be the center of the enveloping algebra U(𝔤). By Harish-Chandra isomorphism (recalled in [18], p. 229 for instance), ℨ ≃ ℂ[X_⋆(T)]^W where W is the Weyl group. The infinitesimal character of π(λ, C) is the Weyl group orbit of λ.`; it should be `ℨ ≅ Sym(X_⋆(T) ⊗ ℂ)^W = S(𝔥)^W, i.e. the W-invariant polynomial functions on X^⋆(T)_ℂ = 𝔥^*.`. One paragraph earlier (§5.1.3, p. 21) ℂ[X_⋆(T)]^W is the target of the twisted Satake isomorphism, so it denotes the W-invariants of the group algebra of the cocharacter lattice, i.e. regular functions on the dual torus. With that meaning the displayed isomorphism is false. ℨ is a polynomial algebra with only constant units. ℂ[X_⋆(T)]^W contains the non-constant unit given by the similitude ν^{±1} of the dual GSp_4. The Harish-Chandra isomorphism is ℨ ≅ S(𝔥)^W with 𝔥 = X_⋆(T) ⊗ ℂ. Its characters are W-orbits in 𝔥^* = X^⋆(T)_ℂ, which is what the next sentence uses: the orbit of λ ∈ X^⋆(T)_ℂ. The intended meaning is clear and nothing depends on the notation. The misprint is milder if one reads ℂ[X_⋆(T)] loosely as the polynomial algebra on the lattice, but that clashes with the paper's own notation. - **Error** at §5.1.7, Theorem 5.1.7.1, item 5, p. 23 (with Remark 5.1.7.1, p. 23). HAL v3: Theorem 5.1.5.1, item 5, printed p. 19 (PDF p. 20). (it affects a stated result). The source says `Thm 5.1.7.1, item 3 (p. 23, from the page image): "The representation ρ_{π,λ} is de Rham at p with Hodge-Tate weights (0, −λ2, −λ1, −λ1−λ2)." Item 5: "ρ_{π,λ} ≃ ρ^∨_{π,λ} ⊗ χ_p^{−λ1−λ2} ω_{π,λ} for some finite character ω_{π,λ} and the cyclotomic character χ_p." Remark 5.1.7.1: "We use geometric Frobenii, the Artin reciprocity law is normalized by sending p to the geometric Frobenius at p, and the Hodge-Tate weight of the cyclotomic character is −1. [...] The Hodge cocharacter is given by t ↦ diag(1, t^{−λ1}, t^{−λ2}, t^{−λ1−λ2}). The central character of π ⊗ |ν|^{−3/2} is |.|^{−λ1−λ2} ⊗ ω_π for some finite character ω_π."`; it should be `Item 5 should read ρ_{π,λ} ≃ ρ^∨_{π,λ} ⊗ χ_p^{λ1+λ2} ω_{π,λ}. Equivalently, ν∘ρ_{π,λ} = χ_p^{λ1+λ2}·(finite), which is χ_p^{3−k−2r}·(finite) for λ = (1−k−r, 2−r; k+2r). This is the minimal fix: it keeps item 3, the Hodge cocharacter, geometric Frobenius and HT(χ_p) = −1. The Remark's sentence "central character of π⊗|ν|^{−3/2} is |.|^{−λ1−λ2}⊗ω_π" is tied to item 5. The link goes through Lemma 5.1.5.1 (T_{ℓ,0} = ℓ^{−3}αδ), item 2 and the stated reciprocity normalisation, where |·|_A corresponds to χ_p. For consistency that sentence must also change, to |.|^{λ1+λ2}⊗ω_π (or ω_{π,λ} must be matched with ω_π^{−1}). This second change is right under the standard convention that T_{ℓ,0} acts by π_ℓ(ℓ). It is less certain than the fix to item 5, because the author version's automorphic-side central normalisation (c = −λ1−λ2+3) is itself hard to reconcile with §5.3.`. I rendered p. 23 at 200 dpi and read it off the image. The exponent in item 5 is −λ1−λ2 as quoted, so this is not a text-layer artefact.

(1) Hodge-Tate weights. If ρ ≃ ρ^∨⊗χ_p^m⊗(finite) and HT(χ_p) = −1, then the multiset {h_i} must equal {−h_i − m}. With h = (0, −λ2, −λ1, −λ1−λ2), pairing the largest weight with the smallest forces m = λ1+λ2. The printed m = −λ1−λ2 would need λ1+λ2 = 0, which the theorem's discrete-series hypothesis excludes (λ2 ≠ −λ1). The Hodge cocharacter has similitude t^{−λ1−λ2}. Under the paper's own map i (p. 20), i(λ1,λ2;−λ1−λ2) = diag(1, t^{−λ2}, t^{−λ1}, t^{−λ1−λ2}), which gives the same answer.

(2) Frobenius check, which does not depend on the HT convention. Lemma 5.1.5.1 gives T_{ℓ,0} = ℓ^{−3}αδ. In §5.3, T_{ℓ,0} = ℓ^{−6}T′_{ℓ,0}, where T′_{ℓ,0} is the differential of the isogeny [ℓ] acting on Sym^k⊗det^r ω, i.e. ℓ^{k+2r}. So T_{ℓ,0} = ℓ^{k+2r−6} and αδ = ℓ^{k+2r−3} = ℓ^{−λ1−λ2}, using λ = (1−k−r, 2−r; k+2r) from the proof of Thm 5.3.1. Thus ν(ρ(Frob_geom)) = ℓ^{−λ1−λ2} up to a root of unity. Since χ_p(Frob_geom) = ℓ^{−1}, this gives ν∘ρ = χ_p^{λ1+λ2}·(finite). The printed character would give ℓ^{λ1+λ2} instead. This agrees with item 4 and with Remark 5.3.2: slopes 0, r−2, k+r−1, k+2r−3, so v_p(αδ) = k+2r−3.

(3) Abelian surface. Take (k,r) = (0,2), so λ = (−1,0). Item 3 gives weights (0,0,1,1), which is H^1(A), and αδ = ℓ. The Weil pairing gives H^1 ≅ (H^1)^∨ ⊗ χ_p^{−1} = χ_p^{λ1+λ2}. The printed formula gives χ_p^{+1}, which is right for V_pA = H_1, not for H^1.

HAL v3 prints the same formula χ_p^{−λ1−λ2}, with no convention remark. But v3 uses the opposite λ: holomorphic means λ1 > λ2 ≥ 0 and λ = (k+r−1, r−2; −k−2r+6). There χ_p^{−λ1−λ2} = χ_p^{3−k−2r}, which is correct, and it is the same character as the corrected author-version χ_p^{λ1+λ2}. So the error came in when the author version negated λ (and made HT(χ_p) = −1 explicit) without flipping the sign in item 5. The new Remark's |.|^{−λ1−λ2} carries the same leftover sign.

Impact: this is a false statement inside a theorem quoted from the literature. Nothing later uses item 5. Theorem 5.3.1 uses only the Frobenius characteristic polynomials (item 2), and §15 uses only Θ_m(Q_ℓ(X)). The correction above is right. Its supporting numbers αδ = ℓ^{k+2r−3} and T_{ℓ,0} = ℓ^{k+2r−6} check out. I checked the text on the rendered page images (author pp. 20–26 and 38; v3 PDF pp. 19–22), not only in the text layer. I tried to defend the paper and could not.

(1) HT check, independent of the Frobenius convention. Item 3 gives weights {0, −λ2, −λ1, −λ1−λ2}. For a GSp4-valued ρ we have ρ ≅ ρ^∨⊗(ν∘ρ), and the weights pair to the weight of ν∘ρ. Other pairings would force λ1 = 0 or λ2 = 0, which the discrete-series hypothesis excludes. So HT(ν∘ρ) = −λ1−λ2, which is also the similitude t^{−λ1−λ2} of the stated Hodge cocharacter. With HT(χ_p) = −1 this gives ν∘ρ = χ_p^{λ1+λ2}·(finite). The printed χ_p^{−λ1−λ2} would need λ1+λ2 = 0, i.e. λ2 = −λ1, and that is excluded.

(2) Crystalline check, independent of both the Frobenius and the HT conventions. D_crys(χ_p^n) has φ = p^{−n}. By item 4, φ on D_crys(ν∘ρ) is α_pδ_p. §5.3 (p. 25) sets T_{ℓ,0} = ℓ^{−6}T'_{ℓ,0}, where T' is the differential of the isogeny [ℓ] acting on Sym^k⊗det^r ω, so T' = ℓ^{k+2r}. Lemma 5.1.5.1 (T_{ℓ,0} = ℓ^{−3}αδ) then gives αδ = ℓ^{k+2r−3} = ℓ^{−λ1−λ2}. This agrees with Remark 5.3.2 and p. 38, where the Hodge slopes are 0, r−2, k+r−1, k+2r−3 with the same endpoints, so v_p(α_pδ_p) = k+2r−3. The printed character gives slope λ1+λ2 = 3−k−2r instead. The ℓ-adic check with geometric Frobenius (χ_p(Frob_ℓ) = ℓ^{−1}) gives the same exponent, λ1+λ2.

(3) Small cases, checked by direct computation over λ = (1−k−r, 2−r). For (k,r) = (0,3), λ = (−2,−1), the weights are (0,1,2,3). The HT, Frobenius and crystalline routes all give ν = χ_p^{−3}; the printed formula gives χ_p^{3}. For (0,2), H^1 of an abelian surface: the Weil pairing gives χ_p^{−1}; the printed formula gives χ_p^{+1}.

Defences tried:
(a) The HT convention is the misprint. Flipping it breaks check (2).
(b) "Geometric" should read "arithmetic". Then item 5 would agree with item 2 and §5.3, but it would still contradict item 3 (check (1)) and item 4 (check (2)).
(c) Cited sources. The printed exponent k+2r−3 = k1+k2−3 is the twist in the arithmetic-Frobenius statement of the cited literature (Weissauer/Taylor style), so it does not fit the geometric normalisation this paper declares. That attribution is from memory: I did not check the cited papers.
(d) HAL v3 prints the same formula. Its value there is χ_p^{3−k−2r}, and it is consistent with v3's non-positive weights under HT(χ_p) = +1.

So the error entered in revision. The author negated λ and flipped the HT sign convention, which keeps item 3 describing the same representation. Item 5 was not updated, and the new Remark was written to match item 5.

Uses later in the paper: none. Theorem 5.3.1 uses only item 2 (Frobenius characteristic polynomials). p. 38 uses Remark 5.3.2's weights and slopes. §15 uses Arthur's classification and reducibility. No later passage cites ρ^∨, the twist, or ω_π. The false statement is therefore confined to item 5 of the recalled theorem (and the matching Remark sentence), so 'affects' is "a stated result" with no downstream consequence. One could record 'nothing' because nothing downstream uses item 5; I use 'a stated result' because item 5 itself is false as printed. The source says `As a replacement of H^0(X_K, Ω^{(0,2)}(−D) ⊗ Q_p/Z_p), we suggest to use H^0(M ⊗^L_{Λ,2} Q_p/Z_p) where M is the complex provided by theorem 1.1. The point is that p-divisible classes in H^0(M ⊗^L_{Λ,2} Q_p/Z_p) do come from cohomology classes in H^0(X_{Kli}(p)_K, Ω^{(0,2)}(−D)) and thus from classical automorphic forms.`; it should be `Both occurrences should read H^0(M ⊗^L_{Λ,0} Q_p/Z_p), i.e. specialise M at k = 0 (weight (0,2)), not at k = 2 (weight (2,2)).`. I checked the printed text on a 300 dpi page render. Both occurrences clearly show the subscript "Λ,2" under ⊗^L; this is not an artefact of the text layer.

The paper's own conventions:
- p. 3 says: "For each integer k, there is a map k : Λ → Z_p extending the character z ↦ z^k of Z_p^×".
- Theorem 1.1(1) says: M ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Q_p = RΓ(X_{Kli}(p)_K, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D) ⊗_{Z_p} Q_p)^{U−ord}, where Ω^{(k,2)} comes from Sym^k St ⊗ det^2 St.
- p. 3 also says M is the U-ordinary part of the cohomology of F^κ ⊗ Ω^{(0,2)}(−D).
- §9.4 (p. 56) gives F^{n,n}_k ≅ (ω_{H_n})^k, which is the highest-weight quotient of Ω^{(k,0)}.
- Theorem 11.3.1(3) (p. 71) gives f RΓ(X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ≃ f RΓ(X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), F^κ ⊗ ω^2(−D)) ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Z_p.

So ⊗_{Λ,2} specialises to Ω^{(2,2)} (Sym^2 ⊗ det^2). The paragraph is about Ω^{(0,2)} = det^2, the abelian-surface weight, which is k = 0.

I redid the check that the claim holds after the correction. Let M_0 = M ⊗^L_{Λ,0} Z_p. It is perfect over Z_p with amplitude [0,1], so there is an exact sequence 0 → H^0(M_0) ⊗ Q_p/Z_p → H^0(M_0 ⊗^L Q_p/Z_p) → H^1(M_0)[p^∞] → 0. The last term is finite, so the maximal p-divisible subgroup is H^0(M_0) ⊗ Q_p/Z_p. Also H^0(M_0) ⊗ Q_p = H^0(X_{Kli}(p)_K, Ω^{(0,2)}(−D) ⊗ Q_p)^{U−ord} by Theorem 1.1(1) at k = 0. This is exactly the stated claim, and with k = 2 it would concern Ω^{(2,2)} instead. Part (2) of Theorem 1.1 (k > p+1) plays no role here.

The slip may come from BCGP-style notation, where abelian surfaces have weight (2,2). In this paper, however, the weight is Ω^{(k,r)} = Sym^k ⊗ det^r and specialisation is written ⊗_{Λ,k}, so the text is wrong under its own conventions.
