The source says `"We now prove by descending induction on i that H^i(C(f)) = 0. Assume this holds for i ≥ n + 1. Using the spectral sequence E_2^{p,q} = Tor^R_{−p}(H^q(M^•), R/m_R) ⇒ H^{p+q}(M^• ⊗_R R/m_R) we see that H^n(C(f))/m_R ↪ H^n(C(f)/m_R) = 0. By Nakayama's lemma, we deduce that H^n(C(f)) = 0." (Checked on the page image at 110 and 220 dpi; the page has the subscript R on ⊗, i.e. ⊗_R.)`; it should be `Replace M^• by C(f) in the displayed spectral sequence. It should read: "Using the (Künneth) spectral sequence E_2^{p,q} = Tor^R_{−p}(H^q(C(f)), R/m_R) ⇒ H^{p+q}(C(f) ⊗_R R/m_R) we see that H^n(C(f))/m_R ↪ H^n(C(f)/m_R) = 0."`. In Prop. 2.2.2, M^• is the source of f : M^• → N^•. The displayed formula is copied word for word from the display in the proof of Prop. 2.2.1, where M^• was the complex of that proposition. As printed, it is the spectral sequence of the source complex, and that says nothing about H^n(C(f)). I redid the argument. C(f) is a bounded complex of flat modules, so C(f) ⊗_R R/m_R computes the derived tensor product, and the Künneth spectral sequence (Weibel 5.6.4, which the paper cites as [83]) gives E_2^{p,q} = Tor_{−p}(H^q(C(f)), k) for p ≤ 0. The term E_2^{0,n} = H^n(C(f))/m_R has no outgoing differentials, because they land in columns p > 0, which are zero. Its incoming differentials are d_r from E_r^{−r, n+r−1}, which are subquotients of Tor_r(H^{n+r−1}(C(f)), k) with r ≥ 2. These vanish by the induction hypothesis, since n+r−1 ≥ n+1. So the edge map H^n(C(f))/m_R → H^n(C(f)/m_R) is injective, and its target is 0 because the cone of f⊗1 is acyclic. H^n(C(f)) is finite by Prop. 2.2.1, so Nakayama gives H^n(C(f)) = 0. The descending induction can start because C(f) is bounded. So the argument is correct once C(f) replaces M^•. The index Tor_r(H^{n+r−1}(C(f))) used above is right. - **Error** at §9.1.1, proof of Lemma 9.1.1.1 (the affineness part, case n = 1), p. 55 of the author version (17 June 2019). HAL v3 has the same text on printed pp. 45–46 (PDF p. 46), where "Verschiebung" is misspelt "Vershiebung". (it affects the proof). The source says `"Let us denote by Z′ the closed subscheme of Z where C[p^{m−1}] = H_{m−1}. The group scheme C/H_{m−1} is connected of order p over Z′. Its co-normal sheaf is ℒ, an invertible sheaf over Z′ and the differential of the Verschiebung map V : (C/H_{m−1})^{(p)} → C/H_{m−1} provides a section s ∈ H^0(Z′, ℒ^{(p−1)}). The non vanishing locus of this section is the open subscheme (Z′)^m of Z where C/H_{m−1} is of multiplicative type. The map (Z′)^m → X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^{m−1})_1 is affine as the composite of the affine open immersion (Z′)^m ↪ Z′ and the finite map Z′ → X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^{m−1})_1."`; it should be `For m ≥ 2, replace the definition of Z′. In all cases, give the reason why ℒ is invertible. (It is enough to treat n = 1, as the paper does.) m = 1. Here H_0 = 0, so Z′ = Z. C ⊂ G[F] is killed by F. So locally C ≅ Spec R[x]/(x^p − ax) with a = 0, and ℒ ≅ R/aR = R is invertible. With this sentence added, the printed argument is correct. m ≥ 2. Let Z′ be the closed subscheme of Z where H_{m−1} ⊂ C and F kills C/H_{m−1}; in Oort–Tate terms, a = 0. Both conditions are closed, so Z′ is finite over X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1. On Z′ the conormal sheaf ℒ of C/H_{m−1} is ≅ R/aR = R, so it is invertible. The differential of V gives s ∈ H^0(Z′, ℒ^{⊗(p−1)}), and its non-vanishing locus (Z′)^m is where C/H_{m−1} is multiplicative. So (Z′)^m → Z′ → X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1 is affine. The map H_m ↦ C = H_m embeds X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 in Z, because μ_{p^m} is killed by F^m. The image lies in (Z′)^m: C/H_{m−1} ≅ H_{m−1}[p] is multiplicative, hence killed by F. On (Z′)^m, C is multiplicative of order p^m. There, the three conditions "C is étale-locally μ_{p^m}", "C[p] has order p" and "C[p^{m−1}] = H_{m−1}" are equivalent, and they cut out an open and closed subscheme. That subscheme is X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1, since both represent the subgroups H_m with H_m[p^{m−1}] = H_{m−1}. So the map X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 → X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1 is affine. Two alternative fixes: - Keep Z′ = {H_{m−1} ⊂ C}, write C/H_{m−1} = G^L_{a,b} in Oort–Tate form, and replace s by the section b of L^{⊗(1−p)}. Its non-vanishing locus is the multiplicative locus, and a = 0 there. - Replace {H_{m−1} ⊂ C} by its reduction. On a reduced base, a connected group of order p has a nilpotent, hence a = 0. X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 is reduced, being étale over the smooth X^{≥1}_1, so it lies in the reduction. The same change repairs the proof of Lemma 9.5.1.`. What the step claims. The affineness half of Lemma 9.1.1.1 is reduced to n = 1. Z → X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1 is the finite scheme of subgroups C ⊂ G[F^m] of order p^m. Z′ is defined as "the closed subscheme of Z where C[p^{m−1}] = H_{m−1}". The proof then makes two claims.
(a) Z′ is closed in Z, so Z′ is finite over X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1.
(b) C/H_{m−1} is connected of order p over Z′, and its conormal sheaf ℒ is invertible; no other reason is given. The differential of V then gives s ∈ H^0(Z′, ℒ^{⊗(p−1)}), whose non-vanishing locus (Z′)^m is the multiplicative locus.
From these, (Z′)^m → Z′ → X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1 is affine, and X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 is open and closed in (Z′)^m.
Connectedness is true: H_{m−1} ⊂ G[F^{m−1}] ⊂ G[F^m], and G[F^m] is infinitesimal. So C and C/H_{m−1} are connected wherever H_{m−1} ⊂ C.

Why "connected of order p" gives no reason. Over an F_p-algebra R, a group of order p is locally Oort–Tate: Spec R[x]/(x^p − ax) with ab = 0. Its conormal module is I/I² = Rx/(ax) ≅ R/aR. Connectedness says only that a vanishes at every point, i.e. that a is nilpotent. If a is nilpotent and non-zero, R/aR is not invertible. Such a group is still killed by F^m once a^{1+p+⋯+p^{m−1}} = 0. The paper knows only that Z is finite over a smooth base; it does not claim Z is reduced. Invertibility holds exactly where a = 0, i.e. where F kills the group. On a reduced base, connectedness does imply a = 0.

m = 1. Here H_0 = 0, so Z′ = Z under any reading. C ⊂ G[F] is killed by F, so a = 0 and ℒ is invertible. The step is correct and only the reason is missing.

m ≥ 2, literal reading. Suppose C_T[p^{m−1}] = H_{m−1,T}. Since C ⊂ G[F^m] ⊂ G[p^m], multiplication by p^{m−1} induces a monomorphism C/H_{m−1} ↪ H_{m−1}[p]. Both are finite flat of order p, so C/H_{m−1} ≅ H_{m−1}[p] is multiplicative. Then C is multiplicative with C[p] of order p, so C is étale-locally μ_{p^m}. Conversely, every H_m gives such a C. So the literal locus is X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 itself. On it, ℒ is invertible, s is nowhere zero, and (Z′)^m = Z′.

This locus is not closed in Z; Remark 9.1.1.2 itself says it is not finite over the base. The usual argument that equality of two finite flat subgroups of the same order is a closed condition does not apply here. The reason is that C[p^{m−1}] is not flat over Z: the literal condition is the closed condition H_{m−1} ⊂ C together with the open condition that C[p^{m−1}] has order p^{m−1}.

Suppose the locus were closed. Then it would be finite over the base. The map is étale (first half of the lemma), so it would be finite locally free of locally constant rank. But the rank is p at ordinary points: the lifts of a cyclic H_{m−1} ⊂ μ_{p^m}² are the p points of P¹(Z/p^m) over a point of P¹(Z/p^{m−1}). The rank is 1 at points of p-rank 1, where the multiplicative part is μ_{p^m} (Remark 9.1.1.2). The ordinary locus is dense, being the complement of the Hasse divisor in a scheme étale over the smooth X^{≥1}_1. This is a contradiction.

The missing points can be identified. Let x be a geometric point of X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1 of p-rank 1, over k. Write E for the local-local p-divisible group of height 2 and dimension 1 at x. Then G_x[F^m] = μ_{p^m} × E[F^m] and H_{m−1} = μ_{p^{m−1}} × 0. Over k, the only order-p subgroups of G_x[F^m]/H_{m−1} = μ_p × E[F^m] are μ_p × 0 and 0 × E[F]. Indeed, such a subgroup is μ_p or α_p. Hom(μ_p, E[F^m]) = 0 and Hom(α_p, μ_p) = 0. And E[F] is the only subgroup of order p of E[F^m], since E is one-dimensional. So {H_{m−1} ⊂ C} has two points over x.
- C = μ_{p^m} lies in the literal locus.
- C = μ_{p^{m−1}} × E[F] is killed by p^{m−1}, so it does not.
The literal locus is open in {H_{m−1} ⊂ C} and étale over the base. Hence, along a trait from an ordinary point to x, at most one of the p lifts can specialise into it. The others specialise to μ_{p^{m−1}} × E[F].
So under the literal reading, claim (a) is false, and the step assumes the finiteness it was meant to supply.

m ≥ 2, closed reading. The last sentence of the proof ("X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 is the open and closed subscheme of (Z′)^m where C ≅ μ_{p^m}") only has content if (Z′)^m can be strictly larger than X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1. That holds for Z″ = {H_{m−1} ⊂ C}. For example, take H_{m−1} = μ_{p^{m−1}} × 0 and C = μ_{p^{m−1}} × μ_p at an ordinary point. Z″ is closed and finite, but ℒ is not invertible on it.

Counterexample. Take x as above, and let E_0 be a supersingular elliptic curve over k, so that E ≅ E_0[p^∞]. Let Spec A be the scheme of order-p subgroups of E[p]. This is the fibre over E_0 of the finite flat degree-(p+1) Γ_0(p) map of Katz–Mazur. Its only k-point is E[F]. So A is Artin local with residue field k and length p+1. Let D ⊂ E[p]_A be the universal subgroup, D ≅ Spec A[t]/(t^p − at). The locus V(a) where F kills D is where D = E[F]_A, which is the closed point. So aA = m_A ≠ 0, and ω_D ≅ A/aA = k is not free over A. Since E[p] = E[F²] ⊂ E[F^m], the group C = μ_{p^{m−1}} × D ⊂ G_x[F^m]_A is flat of order p^m, contains H_{m−1}, and has C/H_{m−1} ≅ D. The conormal sheaf commutes with base change. So the conormal sheaf of C/H_{m−1} on Z″ is not invertible at C = μ_{p^{m−1}} × E[F]. Under this reading, claim (b) is false.

Conclusion. For m ≥ 2 the printed step fails under both readings. The literal Z′ is not finite over the base, and the closed Z′ does not carry an invertible ℒ. The argument works as written only on a closed subscheme the text does not define. Examples are the locus where F also kills C/H_{m−1}, or the closure of X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 in Z, which is reduced. So this is an error in the proof. The lemma itself is still true, with the fix given in the correction.

What is affected. Lemma 9.5.1 (p. 57) is proved as "Similar to the proof of lemma 9.1.1.1", for G′ over X_par. Its p-rank-1 points have the same shape, so it has the same flaw, and the same fix repairs it. The affineness is used in three places:
- in §9.1.2, where the vertical maps are "étale and affine";
- in §9.2, to form 𝔛^{≥1}_Kli(p^∞) ("It exists because the transition maps are affine");
- in Remark 9.3.1.
All of these still hold. No stated result changes. Recorded as `PAPER-PILLONI-20/E70`; looked for an existing correction in: The author's version on V. The source says `By Illusie's deformation theory ([37], thm VII, 4.2.5) , the map ψ_T admits a unique extension ψ_{T'} : G̃^D[p^m]|_{T'} → H^D_m|_{T'}. … [37] Luc Illusie, Complexe cotangent et déformations I Lecture Notes in Mathematics, Vol. 239. Springer- Verlag, Berlin, 1971.`; it should be `Chapter VII ("Déformations équivariantes de G-schémas et déformations de schémas en groupes") is in L. - **Misprint** at §10.1 (Definition of the correspondence), definition of ℭ_𝔜(p^m) just before Lemma 10.1.1, p. 57 of the author version (17 June 2019). The printed symbol is fraktur C, ℭ_𝔜(p^m).. The source says `Let ℭ_𝔜(p^m) be the moduli over 𝔜^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m) of triples (G, H_m, L) where L ⊂ G[p²] is totally isotropic, L[p] is of rank p³ and L∩H_m = {0}. We recall that H_1 = H_m[p]. In the following lemma the orthogonal is taken for the Weil pairing inside G[p].`; it should be `"... of triples (G, H_m, L) where L ⊂ G[p^2] is a totally isotropic subgroup of rank p^4 (that is, a Lagrangian of G[p^2]), L[p] is of rank p^3 and L ∩ H_m = {0}." The condition L[p] of rank p^3 is still needed, because it rules out Lagrangians of type (Z/p^2)^2. Saying "maximal totally isotropic, of order p^4" is right and minimal. The extra clause "étale-locally ≅ (Z/pZ)^2 ⊕ Z/p^2Z" of an alternative correction should not go into this definition over 𝔜, where p is nilpotent. At an ordinary F̄_p-point the intended L contains a copy of μ_p, for example L = μ_p b ⊕ Z/p^2 e ⊕ Z/p f. Lemma 10.1.1 itself says L ∩ H_1^⊥ is a BT_1 of dimension 1, so L is not étale there. That wording, used in §13.2.1, only fits the adic generic fibre.`. I checked the rendered p. 57, and the text matches the quote above, with the symbol ℭ_𝔜 (fraktur C). The definition does not bound the order of L.

In detail:
(1) Every subgroup of G[p] is totally isotropic in G[p²]. Take x, y ∈ G[p] and write x = p·x̃. Then e_{p²}(x, y) = e_{p²}(x̃, y)^p = e_{p²}(x̃, py) = 1.
(2) Suppose L is totally isotropic with |L[p]| = p³. Then |L| = p³·|pL| ≤ p⁴, so |L| is p³ or p⁴. Order is locally constant for finite flat L, so the literal ℭ_𝔜(p^m) has an extra open and closed piece where L ⊂ G[p] has order p³.
(3) This piece is not empty. Take an ordinary point with G[p] = μ_p a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ Z/p e ⊕ Z/p f, where a pairs with e and b pairs with f. Let H_1 = μ_p a and L = μ_p b ⊕ Z/p e ⊕ Z/p f. Then L ∩ H_m ⊂ L ∩ H_1 = 0. Also H_1^⊥ = μ_p a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ Z/p f, so L ∩ H_1^⊥ = μ_p b ⊕ Z/p f. That gives L/(L ∩ H_1^⊥) ≅ Z/p, not Z/p², so the second claim of Lemma 10.1.1 fails. More generally, L ∩ H_1 = 0 forces L ≠ H_1^⊥, so the quotient always has order p on this piece.
(4) The proof of Lemma 10.1.1 needs |L| = p⁴ for "pL = L[p]^⊥". The inclusion pL ⊂ L[p]^⊥ always holds, and |L[p]^⊥| = p, so equality holds exactly when |pL| = p.
(5) Proposition 10.2.1 fails literally. Its proof needs "the kernel of G/L[p] → G/L is étale of order p". Also, ℭ(p^m) = ℭ² ×_{𝔛^{m-et}_{par,Kli}(p^m)} ℭ¹ only parametrises isogenies G → G' → G'' of degree p³·p = p⁴, while on the extra piece G → G/L has degree p³.

The intended meaning is clear from the paper itself. Footnote 16 on p. 60 (in the proof of Lemma 10.3.2) says "the universal rank p⁴ subgroup L". The proof of Proposition 10.2.1 uses an étale kernel of order p for G/L[p] → G/L. The parallel definitions on p. 44 (§7, the correspondence D: "an extension of an étale group scheme locally isomorphic to Z/pZ ⊕ Z/p²Z by ... µ_p") and in §13.2.1 ("locally ... isomorphic to (Z/pZ)² ⊕ Z/p²Z") both state the isomorphism type. So this is an omitted condition, not a real mathematical error.

Effect: ℭ_𝔜(p^m) is only used on pp. 57–60. It appears in Lemma 10.1.1, Proposition 10.2.1 and Lemmas 10.3.1–10.3.2, where the 1/p³ trace normalisation and the deformation computation assume |L| = p⁴. As literally stated, Lemma 10.1.1 and Proposition 10.2.1 are false. The U-operator itself is built from ℭ(p^m) via ℭ¹ and ℭ², which never mention L, so the operator and everything after §10.3 are unaffected once the obvious correction is made.

HAL v3 (p. 47, §10.1) has different text: "Let ℭ_𝔜(p^m) be the moduli over 𝔜_{Kli}(p^m) of triples (G, H_m, L) where L ⊂ G[p²] is totally isotropic L ∩ H_m = {0}, and pL ∩ H_m^⊥ = {0}", with the matrix diag(1,p,p,p²). That definition also has no order condition. It is even weaker, since L = {0} satisfies it. So the defect was already there in v3, in a different form. Defence attempted and failed.
(a) The paper's own convention does not make "totally isotropic" mean Lagrangian. §5.1.2 calls W = <e1> a "totally isotropic direct factor". §6.1.4 says "totally isotropic direct factors L ⊂ V1 of rank 2", giving the rank separately. In §6.1.5.2 the set C contains isotropic factors of every rank.
(b) The conditions do not force the order. For x ∈ L and y ∈ L[p], e_p(px, y) = e_{p^2}(x, y) = 1, so pL ⊂ L[p]^⊥, which has order p. Hence |L| is p^3 or p^4, and every subgroup of G[p] is isotropic for e_{p^2}. The case |L| = p^3 (L = L[p]) does occur. Take an ordinary point with G[p] = μ_p a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ Z/p e ⊕ Z/p f, H_m = μ_{p^m} a and L = μ_p b ⊕ Z/p e ⊕ Z/p f. Then L ∩ H_m ⊂ L ∩ H_1 = 0.
(c) Brute force for p = 2 on (Z/4)^4 with the standard symplectic form and H_1 = <2a>, by a short computer enumeration. There are 16 = p^4 subgroups of order p^4, each with L/(L∩H_1^⊥) ≅ Z/4. There are also 8 = p^3 extra subgroups of order p^3, each with quotient of order p.
(d) On this extra piece the literal statement of Lemma 10.1.1 fails, because the quotient has order p and is not Z/p^2. Its proof uses "pL = L[p]^⊥", which needs |pL| = p. Worse, G/L = G/H^⊥ with H = L^⊥ is the paramodular quotient of the Klingen chain in §6.1.2–6.1.3. The polarization descended from p^2λ has degree p^2, so t_2(G, H_m, L) = (G/L, ...) does not lie in 𝔜^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m). In fact this piece is just ℭ^1(p^m)|_𝔜. Proposition 10.2.1 is also false as printed: ℭ(p^m) = ℭ^2 ×_{𝔛^{m-et}_{par,Kli}} ℭ^1 only gives composite isogenies of degree p^3·p = p^4.

So the literal definition is wrong. The intended meaning is still clear from the context:
- U is "associated to the matrix diag(p^2,p,p,1)", which is U_{Kli(p),1} of §5.1.4.
- The statement of Lemma 10.1.1 forces |L| = p^4.
- The proof of Proposition 10.2.1 factors G → G/L[p] → G/L, where the second map has an étale kernel of order p.
- Footnote 16 on p. 60 speaks of "the universal rank p^4 subgroup L".
- The parallel definitions state the type: D in §11.1.1 (p. 67; the "p. 44, §7" given above is a wrong locator), Lemma 11.1.1.4 on p. 68 (L_n of type Z/p^n ⊕ Z/p^{2n} by μ_{p^n}), and §13.2.1 on p. 85.
This is an omitted condition in a definition, not a step asserted without proof, so "misprint" fits better than "gap".

Consequences: ℭ_𝔜(p^m) is used only on pp. 57–60, in Lemma 10.1.1, the maps t_1 and t_2, Proposition 10.2.1, and Lemmas 10.3.1–10.3.2. All of these hold once the definition is corrected. The operator U = U_1 ∘ U_2 of §10.4 is built from ℭ^1 and ℭ^2 and the traces of Lemmas 10.3.3–10.3.4, which never mention L. §11.1.1 and §13.2.1 state the kernel type again explicitly. So no later result depends on the defective wording. Following PROTOCOL §18 ("nothing (the mathematics is right as intended)"), I set affects = nothing. If the register records printed statements that are literally false, it should instead say "a stated result": Lemma 10.1.1 and Proposition 10.2.1 are false as printed. - **Misprint** at §10.1, proof of Lemma 10.1.1 (the 'classical fact' paragraph), p. 57 of the author version (17 June 2019). The source says `Proof. We start by recalling the following classical fact^(14). Let S be a scheme over which p is nilpotent, and let M → S be a finite flat group scheme. Then M → S is a truncated Barsotti-Tate group scheme of level n if and only if M is killed by p^n and for all s ∈ S, M_s → s is a truncated Barsotti-Tate group scheme of level n. We give the argument when n = 1 (a similar argument works for arbitrary n). By definition, we can suppose that S is a scheme over Spec F_p. By assumption, G is killed by p and it follows that the Frobenius map F : G → G^(p) factors into a map G → Ker(V : G^(p) → G). We have to prove that the morphism G → Ker(V : G^(p) → G) is faithfully flat. By assumption, it is surjective. By the criterion for flatness by fiber it is flat.`; it should be `Write M for G in the two sentences that prove the classical fact: "By assumption, M is killed by p and it follows that the Frobenius map F : M → M^(p) factors into a map M → Ker(V : M^(p) → M). We have to prove that the morphism M → Ker(V : M^(p) → M) is faithfully flat." That is all nine occurrences of G/G^(p) in those two sentences. "Throughout" must stop there. In the next paragraph of the same proof ("L[p] ⊕ H1 = G[p]"), G correctly means the universal abelian surface and should stay as it is.`. I rendered p. 57 at 150 dpi, and the page image confirms the printed text word for word. The paragraph states the fact for an arbitrary finite flat M → S, but the proof then says "G is killed by p" and works with F : G → G^(p), V : G^(p) → G. In §10.1, G is the abelian scheme in the triples (G, H_m, L) with L ⊂ G[p^2]. That abelian surface is not killed by p. It is also not the object the fact is about: the fact is applied to L and its subquotients to reduce Lemma 10.1.1 to geometric points. The same proof uses G for the abelian surface again a few lines later (G[p]). So the letter G here is a slip for M. With M in place of G I redid the argument and it is correct. If M is killed by p, then V∘F = [p] = 0, so F factors through Ker V. Surjectivity onto Ker V is a fiberwise statement: fibers of a BT_1 satisfy Im F = Ker V, and taking kernels commutes with base change. Faithful flatness then follows because M is flat and finitely presented over S and each fiber map M_s → (Ker V)_s is a surjective homomorphism of finite group schemes over a field, hence flat (fiberwise flatness criterion, EGA IV 11.3.10). The proof of the other half, Ker F = Im V, is left to "a similar argument" in the paper and is not considered here. Nothing downstream uses the letter G in this paragraph, so the statement and logic of Lemma 10.1.1 and everything built on it (the U-correspondence in §10.2 onwards) are unaffected. HAL v3 (6 Jan 2018, §10.1, pp. 48–49) does not have this text. There the exact sequences are stated inline with no proof, and the 'classical fact' / footnote-to-Fargues paragraph does not appear, so it was added between v3 and the June 2019 version. - **Gap** at §10.3, proof of Lemma 10.3.1, p. 60 (author version, 17 June 2019). Lemma 10.2.2 is on p. 59. The definition ℭ(p^m) = ℭ²(p^m) ×_{r_1, 𝔛^{m-et}_{par,Kli}(p^m), q_2} ℭ¹(p^m) is on p. 59, and Prop. 10.2.1 (ℭ(p^m) restricted to 𝔜 is ℭ_𝔜(p^m)) is on p. 60. (it affects the proof). The source says `Lemma 10.3.1. — The map t_1 : ℭ_𝔜(p^m) → 𝔜^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m) is finite flat. Proof. The map is proper. The quasi-finiteness follows from the fact that an abelian surface over a field of characteristic p and of p-rank at least 1 has only finitely many subgroups of order p. Therefore the map is finite. We prove the flatness. The formal scheme 𝔜^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m) is regular and ℭ_𝔜(p^m) is Cohen-Macaulay by lemma 10.2.2. Flatness follows from [53], chap. 23, thm. 2.3.1. [The cited lemma, p. 59: "Lemma 10.2.2. — The structural morphisms ℭ^i(p^m) → Spf Z_p for i ∈ {1, 2} are local complete intersection morphisms^(15). Proof. The morphism 𝔛_Kli(p) → Spf Z_p is a local complete intersection morphism. There are étale morphisms ℭ^i(p^m) → 𝔛_Kli(p) by construction. So the proposition follows."]`; it should be `Add one step saying why ℭ(p^m) (and hence ℭ_𝔜(p^m)) is lci. The shortest fix keeps the proof of Lemma 10.2.2. (a) The map q'_2 : ℭ(p^m) → ℭ^2(p^m) is the base change of q_2 : ℭ^1(p^m) → 𝔛^{m-et}_{par,Kli}(p^m), and q_2 is étale. The reason: on ℭ^1, Ker(G'→G) is the image of H_1, so it equals K(λ')^m. On that open-closed piece, p_2 : 𝔛_{Kli}(p) → 𝔛_par is an isomorphism onto 𝔛^{m-et}_par, since G = G'/K(λ')^m. So ℭ^1 and 𝔛^{m-et}_{par,Kli}(p^m) are both étale over 𝔛^{m-et}_par. It follows that the composite ℭ(p^m) → ℭ^2(p^m) → 𝔛_{Kli}(p) is étale. The argument of Lemma 10.2.2 then gives: ℭ(p^m) is lci over Spf Z_p, so ℭ_𝔜(p^m) is Cohen–Macaulay. (b) Another route, the one HAL v3 takes, also works. Over the interior, r_1 is finite flat of degree p: its fibre is the set of order-p subgroups C ⊂ K(λ') with C ∩ K(λ')^m = 0, which is a torsor under Hom(K^et, K^m), locally μ_p. So r'_1 : ℭ → ℭ^1 is finite flat with lci fibres, and ℭ_𝔜 is lci by Lemma 10.2.2 for i = 1. An alternative correction gets r_1 flat by miracle flatness. That needs 𝔛^{m-et}_{par,Kli}(p^m) to be regular, which the paper never establishes, so the direct torsor description is preferable. The statement of Lemma 10.3.1 is unchanged.`. I checked the page images for pp. 58–61 of the author version. The text layer matches the page.

As printed, the justification is inadequate. Lemma 10.2.2 is stated and proved only for ℭ¹(p^m) and ℭ²(p^m). ℭ_𝔜(p^m) is the restriction of the fibre product ℭ² ×_{r_1,q_2} ℭ¹ (Prop. 10.2.1). A fibre product of lci formal schemes is not lci in general unless one of the two maps is flat or étale. The author version never proves the step that is needed: it states neither that r_1 is flat nor that q_2 is étale. That makes this a gap in the sense of PROTOCOL §18: a step asserted without an adequate proof.

The conclusion is true, and I redid it both ways. Along the way I recomputed the fibres.
- r_1 has degree p: its fibre is the splittings torsor.
- q_1 has degree p^3: it parametrizes hyperplanes H^⊥ ⊂ F_p^4 not containing H_1, and there are p^3+p^2+p+1−(p^2+p+1) = p^3 of them.
- So t_1 has degree p^4. This agrees with the rank p^3 of each Serre–Tate component on p. 60 times the p components counted in footnote 16. On the ordinary locus it also agrees with t_2 being étale.

One might think CM needs an extra flatness step, because the composite is not étale over ℭ¹. But ℭ(p^m) is étale over ℭ²(p^m), since q_2 is étale. So the lemma's own "étale over 𝔛_Kli(p)" argument extends directly, and flatness of r_1 is one sufficient fix, not a necessary one. The flatness route (b) of the correction is still mathematically valid.

HAL v3 (hal-01393374v3, pp. 49–50) does not have this text. It has no Lemma 10.2.2, and its proof of Lemma 10.3.1 argues instead that "This boils down to the flatness of the maps r_1 and q_1 over the interior". It proves r_1 finite flat as "a standard fact". Its q_1 step has a weakness: it deduces flatness from "the fiber is flat". So the gap was introduced by the rewrite into the miracle-flatness argument (Matsumura, CRT Thm 23.1, printed as "chap. 23, thm. 2.3.1"). The published Duke text could not be compared.

Dependence: Lemma 10.3.1 is used only in Lemma 10.3.2 (the normalized trace (1/p^3)Tr_{t_1} over the interior). Neither lemma is cited later by number. The U-operator is built from Lemmas 10.3.3 and 10.3.4, which use Lemma 10.2.2 only for ℭ^i. So only this proof is affected.

Side observation, outside this issue and not fully checked: q_2 is étale but seems not finite. Over the open-closed locus {H'_1 = K(λ')^m}, for m = 1 its fibres have p points at ordinary points and 1 point at p-rank-1 points. That suggests the parenthetical "q_2 and q_1 are proper" (p. 58) is wrong for q_2. U_1 does not need q_2 to be proper. I checked the page images for pp. 57–61 of the author version and pp. 49–50 of HAL v3. The text layer matches the pages.

Defence attempted. The best charitable reading is "by (the proof of) Lemma 10.2.2": the object is lci because it is étale over 𝔛_{Kli}(p). That reading does not hold up. Lemma 10.2.2 is stated and proved only for ℭ^1 and ℭ^2, and its only input is "étale morphisms ℭ^i(p^m) → 𝔛_{Kli}(p) by construction". ℭ(p^m) is a fibre product, not one of the ℭ^i. Its natural map through ℭ^1 is not étale in characteristic p: r'_1 has μ_p-torsor fibres. Its map through ℭ^2 is étale only because q_2 is étale. The author version never states that q_2 is étale or that r_1 is flat. HAL v3 did prove r_1 finite flat, but that argument was removed in the rewrite. A fibre product of lci formal schemes is not lci in general. So the citation does not justify the step. The missing step is small but not a slip of notation, so "gap" (PROTOCOL §18) is the right kind, not "misprint".

The conclusion is true. I checked both routes:
- (a) q_2 is étale, because source and target are étale over 𝔛^{m-et}_par. That uses the open-closed component of 𝔛_{Kli}(p)|_{𝔛^{m-et}_par} where C = K(λ')^m, which p_2 maps isomorphically onto 𝔛^{m-et}_par.
- (b) r_1 is finite flat of degree p over the interior, as a splitting torsor.

The degrees are consistent: q_1 has degree p^3 (p^3+p^2+p+1 − (p^2+p+1) = p^3), r_1 has degree p, and t_1 has degree p^4. This matches the normalisations 1/p^2 (Lemma 10.3.3) · 1/p (Lemma 10.3.4) = 1/p^3 (Lemma 10.3.2). It also matches the rank-p^3 local rings on p. 60 times the p components of footnote 16. The other inputs of miracle flatness in Matsumura, CRT Thm 23.1 (printed as "chap. 23, thm. 2.3.1") are fine: 𝔜^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m) is étale over the smooth 𝔜, so it is regular, and t_1 is finite between equidimensional schemes.

Consequences. Lemma 10.3.1 is used only in Lemma 10.3.2, the normalized trace (1/p^3)Tr_{t_1} over the interior. Neither lemma is cited by number later. U = U_1∘U_2 is built from Lemmas 10.3.3 and 10.3.4, which rely on Lemma 10.2.2 only for ℭ^i and are unaffected. So only this proof is affected, and no stated result changes.

On "affects": since the printed justification does not cover the object and a new argument is needed, "the proof" is more accurate than "nothing". The underlying facts are solid. Confidence is medium only because the omission is small, and a reviewer could treat it as an implicit extension of Lemma 10.2.2. The image reads "Flatness follows from [53], chap. 23, thm. 2.3.1." with a bold [53], so this is not a text-layer artefact. [53] is Matsumura's Commutative Ring Theory. That book has chapters 1–11 and numbered sections §1–§33, and its theorems are numbered by section (Theorem 23.1, 23.2, …). No result anywhere in it is numbered with three parts like "2.3.1". "Chap. 23" is loose wording for §23 "Flatness and fibres", which sits in Chapter 8 "Flatness revisited". Theorem 23.1 is the miracle-flatness criterion, and a web search agrees: the standard citation for miracle flatness is "Matsumura, CRT, §23, Theorem 23.1". This is exactly the tool the proof needs: a finite (so quasi-finite) map from a Cohen–Macaulay source to a regular target. So the citation as printed points to a theorem that doesn't exist, and the intended one is Theorem 23.1. The paper has no numbering convention of its own that would make "thm. 2.3.1" correct. The bibliography names CRT, and Matsumura's other book, Commutative Algebra, uses (n.X)/Theorem-N numbering, so it doesn't match either. HAL v3 (6 Jan 2018, p. 50, Lemma 10.3.1) does not have this text. There the flatness is proved directly, by showing that the fibres of q1 are torsors under a group étale-locally isomorphic to the finite flat H1^⊥ and that r1 is finite flat. Matsumura ([49] in v3) is listed in the v3 bibliography, but I found no citation of it in the text layer. So the misprint was introduced when this proof was rewritten for the 2019 version. The published Duke text could not be checked. Side remarks, not part of this item: Theorem 23.1 also needs dim O_{ℭ,x} = dim O_{𝔜,y}, which the paper leaves implicit. Lemma 10.2.2 as stated covers ℭ^1(p^m) and ℭ^2(p^m) (lci over Spf Z_p), not the composite ℭ(p^m) directly. Neither point bears on the citation misprint. The exponents on X′ and Z′ are swapped in print. The diagram on p. 61 is correct as printed.`. I redid the computation from the moduli problem.

**Setup.** C_Y(p^m) (§10.1, p. 57) parametrises triples (G, H_m, L) where:
- L ⊂ G[p^2] is totally isotropic;
- L[p] has rank p^3 and L ∩ H_m = 0;
- L has rank p^4 (footnote 16).

At an ordinary point, write G[p^∞] = T^∨⊗μ_{p^∞} ⊕ T⊗Q_p/Z_p, with dual bases f_i and e_i. Here L^m = ℓ⊗μ_p for a line ℓ, and isotropy forces L^et = {t ∈ T/p^2 : ⟨ℓ,t⟩ ≡ 0 mod p}. In a basis with ℓ = f_2 this gives L^et = ⟨e_1/p^2, e_2/p⟩. Lemma 10.1.1 (p. 57) confirms this: L∩H_1^⊥ is (p,p) and the remaining part is Z/p^2.

**The vertical maps.** On Tate modules, T → T′ = Z_p e_1/p^2 ⊕ Z_p e_2/p, so A = diag(p^2, p). On multiplicative parts, M → M/(f_2⊗μ_p), so B = diag(1, p). These are exactly the matrices printed on p. 61. Since p^2λ = f^∨λ′f, the bases e_i′ and f_i′ are dual for the principal polarisation of G′ = G/L. So Q′ is symmetric, as printed.

**The compatibility condition.** For the extension model G = (T^∨⊗Ĝ_m ⊕ T⊗Q_p)/graph(−q), a morphism exists only if q′∘A = B∘q. Entrywise this reads Q′_ij^{a_j} = Q_ij^{b_i}. The transposed convention, which is the one that makes the p. 39 diagram consistent, gives the same result for the diagonal entries and for a symmetric Q′:
- entry (1,1): (1+X′)^{p^2} = 1+X;
- entries (1,2) and (2,1): (1+Z′)^p = 1+Z;
- entry (2,2): Y′ = Y.

**Direct count of lifts.** I also counted the lifts of L directly:
- the lift x_1 = (m_1, e_1/p^2) needs a p^2-th root of Q_11 (p^2 choices);
- the f_1-component of x_2 = (m_2, e_2/p) needs a p-th root of Q_12 (p choices);
- isotropy then fixes the f_2-component of m_1;
- the condition that L[p] has rank p^3 forces px_2 = 0, so Y′ = Y.

**No relabelling saves the printed ring.** Whatever the ordering, the off-diagonal parameter gets exponent p and the diagonal entries get p^2 and 1. So no relabelling gives Z′ the exponent p^2. The printed ring also contradicts the diagram printed right under it, whose (1,1) entries force the exponent p^2 on X′. The text layer agrees with the image, so this is not a pdftotext artefact.

**HAL v3.** HAL v3 (PDF p. 51, printed p. 50) has the same error. There it is written with "=" signs: "((1 + X′)^p − 1 = X, (1 + Z′)^{p^2} − 1 = Z, Y′ = Y)". It has the same diagram: (p^2,0;0,p), (1,0;0,p), (X′,Z′;Z′,Y′).

**Why nothing else changes.** Write u = 1+X′ and v = 1+Z′. For R[u,v]/(u^a − (1+X), v^b − (1+Z)), the basis u^i v^j has trace 0 unless i = j = 0. So Tr(R′) = ab·R with ab = p^3 in both versions, and dividing by p^3 still preserves integrality. The lemma and everything built on it stand.

The ring appears only in this proof. The other similar displays (pp. 39 and 61, both exponents p) belong to Lemma 7.1.1 and C^1, and they are correct. HAL v3 (p. 50) instead says "since the intersection of the boundary and the non-ordinary locus is of codimension 2", which is correct for the special fibre. The "codimension 1 in the special fiber … boundary is flat" wording was introduced in the revision.. The source says `Actually, it is enough to see that it is well defined over the entire ordinary locus since the intersection of the boundary and the non-ordinary locus is of codimension 1 in the special fiber and the boundary is flat over Spf Z_p (in other words, in the spectrum of the local rings Spec O_{ℭ^1(p^m),x} at closed points x of ℭ^1(p^m), the intersection of the boundary and the non-ordinary locus is of codimension at least 2).`; it should be `"… is of codimension 1 in the special fiber of the boundary (codimension 2 in the special fiber of ℭ^1(p^m)), and the boundary is flat over Spf Z_p …"`. Printed text confirmed. Dimension count: the special fibre of ℭ^1(p^m), finite over X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m) away from the boundary, has dimension 3. Its boundary D_s has dimension 2. On the toric-rank-1 stratum, p-rank = 1 + p-rank of the elliptic abelian part, so non-ordinary means that elliptic curve is supersingular, a codimension-1 condition in D_s. The toric-rank-2 strata are ordinary. So D ∩ (non-ordinary) has dimension 1: codimension 1 in D_s but codimension 2 in the ambient special fibre. Read as the special fibre of ℭ^1(p^m), which is the natural reading, "codimension 1" is false. The appeal to flatness of the boundary shows the author meant D_s: codimension 1 in D_s and D flat give codimension 2 in D, hence at least 2 in Spec O_{ℭ^1(p^m),x} (in fact 3). The parenthetical conclusion, codimension ≥ 2 in the 4-dimensional local rings, is true either way, so the Hartogs-type extension of Θ is unaffected. This is a wording slip, not an error. Confidence is only medium because a charitable reader can take "the special fiber" to mean the boundary's. (1) The correspondence 𝔥 in the proof of Lemma 11.1.1.3 is defined only with the projections s_1 and s_2, and the same sentence gives Θ the target s_1^!. So "p_1^!" is a leftover from the notation of §7.1 (Lemmas 7.1.1 and 7.1.2 use p_1, p_2). This part is an unambiguous misprint.

(2) L is an extension of Z/p⊕Z/p^2 by μ_p. Its étale quotient has exponent p^2, so L is not contained in G[p], and G[p]/L is not literally defined. The intended group is the image of G[p] in G/L. On the mod-p ordinary locus (X_1^{ord}, where the reduced base forces L[p] = L∩G[p] to be flat of order p^3), I recomputed:
- L[p] maps onto G[p]^{et}, and L[p] ∩ G^m = L^m, which is μ_p.
- Hence G[p]/L[p] = G[p]^m/L^m ≅ μ_p, which is multiplicative of order p.
The author's revisions support this reading. HAL v3 wrote "L′ ∩ G[p]/L ≠ {0}" and "G[p] ⊂ L+L′". The author version changed these to "L′ ∩ (G[p]/(L∩G[p])) ≠ {0}" and "G[p]/L ⊂ L′", but left the other occurrences of "G[p]/L" unchanged.

(3) "(G/L[p])/L′", read literally as G/(L[p]), is an abelian scheme, not a subgroup of (G/L)/L′. The intended group is the image of (G/L)[p]. HAL v3 already wrote "G/L[p^2]" for (G/L)[p^2]. The author version added the parentheses in "(G/L)[p^2]" but not here.

The mathematics works with the intended meanings:
- H′ is the image of G[p] and has order p. Since L′∩H′ ≠ 0, we get H′ ⊂ L′.
- So the composite G → G/L → (G/L)/L′ kills G[p] and factors through [p].
- Its multiplicative kernel has order p^2, so on ω it is p times an isomorphism. This gives p^{k+2r} on Ω^{(k,r)}.
- With p^6 from the fundamental classes and the normalization p^{-(3+r)} twice, the normalized operator is divisible by p^k. It is therefore 0 mod p for k ≥ 1, exactly as stated.

A caveat: "G[p]/L" is used consistently (three times) and its meaning is clear, so one could call it an abuse of notation rather than a misprint. The p_1^! and the missing parentheses are genuine misprints either way.

- **Error** at §11.1.1, proof of Lemma 11.1.1.4, p. 68 (author version, 17 June 2019) (it affects the proof). The source says `(we have T^{1,et} = T′). We now observe that any isogeny G → G/L occuring in T^{n,m} will factor through multiplication by p on G. So we deduce, reasoning as in the proof of lemma 11.1.1.3, that T^{n,et} = T^n mod p^k. It is clear that Tr ∘ U^n ∘ i = pT^{n,et} and the factor p arises from the fact that given L_n, we can find p different subgroups H of order p and multiplicative type such that H ∩ L_n = {0}. [Lemma 11.1.1.4 as printed: "For all n ≥ 0, we have Tr ∘ U^n ∘ i = pT^n mod p^k as endomorphisms of H^0(𝔛^{ord}, Ω^{(k,r)})."]`; it should be `Replace "will factor through multiplication by p on G" with "has kernel L ⊇ G[p]^m, the multiplicative part of G[p]". Then do the count step by step instead of copying Lemma 11.1.1.3. Why L ⊇ G[p]^m holds for every chain in T^{n,m}: - A T1^m step has H1 ⊇ G_i[p]^m. - A T1^et∘T2^m step has kernel G_i[p]. - A chain made only of T′ = T1^et∘T2^et steps whose L^m is not cyclic already contains G[p]^m. - If L^m is cyclic, then |L^m| = p^n and L is Lagrangian, so L has the T^{n,et} type (μ_{p^n}; Z/p^n ⊕ Z/p^{2n}). The count uses Lemmas 7.1.1 and 7.1.2. Write M_i for a step's multiplicative-order exponent, F_i for its fundamental-class exponent, and δ = F_i + rM_i − 3 − r. The four step types give: - T1^et T2^et: δ = 0 - T1^et T2^m: δ = r−1 - T1^m T2^et: δ = r−2 - T1^m T2^m: δ = 2r−3 A chain's normalized coefficient is then divisible by p^{Σδ + k·min(j1,j2)}, where (p^{j1}, p^{j2}) are the elementary divisors of L^m, and min(j1,j2) ≥ 1 on T^{n,m}. So T^{n,et} ≡ T^n mod p^k when r ≥ 2. That is the standing hypothesis of §11.1.1, and the lemma should state it. An equivalent alternative correction: - T ≡ T′ mod p^k when r ≥ 2, since the other three pieces carry p^{k+r−1}, p^{k+r−2} and p^{k+2r−3}. - Inside T′^n the printed claim is literally true: L ⊇ L_1[p], and L_1[p] + G[p]^m = G[p]. How this compares with another proposed correction: - The equivalent fix above is right and complete. - The other proposed correction names the right fact (L ⊇ G[p]^m) but understates the rest: it takes divisibility of the differential by p to be all that the argument of Lemma 11.1.1.3 uses. Lemma 11.1.1.3 also takes p^3 per step from fundamental classes, and T1^m and T2^m steps do not supply that. Only det^r makes up the difference, and that needs r ≥ 2. Aside: the lemma itself only needs pT^{n,m} ≡ 0 mod p^k. The same count seems to give this already for r = 1, because each T1^m step makes the whole differential divisible by p. So r ≥ 2 is needed for the proof's intermediate claim, not necessarily for the lemma. The requirement n ≥ 1 (the lemma fails at n = 0) is a separate item, sourceIssues E85.`. The page image of p. 68 matches the quoted text. Read literally, the sentence is false. I checked the counterexample myself. Take an ordinary G, for example the canonical lift, with G[p^∞] = μa ⊕ μb ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)e ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)f, where a pairs with e and b pairs with f. Let L = μ_{p²}a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ (Z/p)f.
- L is isotropic for e_{p²}: e_{p²} is trivial on G[p]×G[p], ⟨a,f⟩ = 0, and the annihilator of L^m in G^et[p²] is exactly (Z/p)f. Its order is p^4, so L is Lagrangian.
- L[p] = μ_p a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ Z/p f has order p^3, with K = L[p]^⊥ = μ_p a. So L is the T_{p,1} chain T1^m ∘ T2^m, and it lies in T^{1,m}.
- G[p] ⊄ L, since e is missing.
There are other counterexamples: the T1^m T2^et chains H1 + ⟨e + αã⟩ with α ≠ 0 also lie in T^{1,m} and do not contain G[p].

The true statement is weaker: every T^{n,m} chain satisfies L ⊇ G[p]^m, so the differential is still divisible by p. But the appeal to "reasoning as in lemma 11.1.1.3" does not transfer. That proof gets p^6 from two T‴-type steps, each with fundamental class p^3. On T1^m and T2^m steps the fundamental class is an isomorphism (Lemmas 7.1.1 and 7.1.2). The missing powers are recovered only through extra det^r factors, which needs r ≥ 2. For example, T1^m T2^et has normalized coefficient p^{k+r−2}, and that hypothesis is not in the lemma.

I recomputed the coefficients p^{k+r−1}, p^{k+r−2}, p^{k+2r−3} of the pieces T1^et T2^m, T1^m T2^et and T1^m T2^m of T and confirmed them. I also found that T1^et T2^m consists only of the T_{p,0} chains L = G[p]. The corrected argument is sound.

The conclusion holds for n ≥ 1 and r ≥ 2. Its only use is Corollary 11.1.1.2 (r ≥ 2, k ≥ 2, n large), which then feeds Proposition 11.1.3/Theorem 11.2.1, so no stated downstream result is affected.

HAL v3 does not have this lemma. There, Corollary 11.1.1.2 (r ≥ 2, k ≥ 1) proves injectivity by a different argument, a local representation-theoretic p-stabilisation. So this passage is new in the 2019 version. The printed claim is false even for n = 1. Take an ordinary G with G[p^∞] = μ a ⊕ μ b ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)e ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)f, where a pairs with e and b with f.

First counterexample: L = μ_{p²}a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ (Z/p)f.
- L is Lagrangian in G[p²], and L[p] = (μ_p a)^⊥.
- It is the chain T1^m∘T2^m. This is the same L as in the counterexample above.
- Its multiplicative part is μ_{p²} ⊕ μ_p, so it lies in T^{1,m}.
- The e-direction is missing from G[p], so G → G/L does not factor through [p].

Second family: the T1^m∘T2^et chains (μ_p a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ Z/p f) + ⟨e + αã⟩ with α ≠ 0 also lie in T^{1,m} and do not contain G[p].

I checked this by a short computer enumeration with p = 3, over all 40 order-p lines H, with H1 = H^⊥ and H1 ⊂ L ⊂ p^{-1}H:
- 108 T1^et T2^et chains, each with L^m = μ_p. These are exactly T^{1,et}.
- 36 T1^et T2^m chains, all with L = G[p].
- 12 T1^m T2^et chains: 4 with L = G[p] and 8 with G[p] ⊄ L.
- 4 T1^m T2^m chains, each with |L^m| = p³ and G[p] ⊄ L.
- All 48 chains of T^{1,m} contain G[p]^m. Of these, 12 do not contain G[p].

The defence fails.
- If T meant T′, the claim would be true. But the proof itself writes T^{1,et} = T′, so T^{1,m} = T − T′ is nonzero over 𝔛^ord.
- The paper identifies T with T′ only on H^0(X_1^ord), that is mod p, through Lemma 11.1.1.1. It never does so mod p^k.
- No nearby statement supplies T ≡ T′ mod p^k. That congruence follows from the local computations in the proofs of Lemmas 7.1.1 and 7.1.2 (T1^m: p^{k+2r} with the fundamental class an isomorphism; T2^m: p^r with the fundamental class an isomorphism), but it holds only for r ≥ 2, and the paper does not state it.
- "Reasoning as in 11.1.1.3" does not transfer either, because that proof takes p^6 from two T′′′-type fundamental classes.

The conclusion does hold with r ≥ 2, by the corrected count.

- **Error** at §11.1.1, Lemma 11.1.1.4, p. 68 (author version, 17 June 2019) (it affects a stated result). The source says `Lemma 11.1.1.4. — For all n ≥ 0, we have Tr ◦ U^n ◦ i = pT^n mod p^k as endomorphisms of H^0(𝔛^ord, Ω^(k,r)). [Just above it, p. 68: "The morphism 𝔛^ord_Kli(p) → 𝔛^ord is finite étale of rank p+1. We let Tr : H^0(𝔛^ord_Kli(p), Ω^(k,r)) → H^0(𝔛^ord, Ω^(k,r)) be the trace map." End of the proof: "It is clear that Tr ◦ U^n ◦ i = pT^{n,et} and the factor p arises from the fact that given L_n, we can find p different subgroups H of order p and multiplicative type such that H ∩ L_n = {0}."]`; it should be `Replace "For all n ≥ 0" with "For all n ≥ 1". At n = 0 the correct identity is Tr ∘ i = (p+1)·Id. Other hypotheses the lemma may need, such as r ≥ 2 for T^{n,et} ≡ T^n mod p^k, are a separate issue and not part of this correction.`. I checked the page image at 220 dpi, and the statement reads "n ≥ 0". Take n = 0. Then U^0 = Id and T^0 = Id, so the left side is Tr ◦ i. Here i is pullback along 𝔛^ord_Kli(p) → 𝔛^ord, and the paper says just above the lemma that this map is finite étale of rank p+1. This matches §9.1.1: H ⊂ G[p] is étale-locally μ_p, and on the ordinary locus G[p]^mult ≅ μ_p^2 has p+1 such lines. The trace of a pullback along a finite étale map of degree p+1 is multiplication by p+1, so Tr ◦ i = (p+1)·Id. The right side is p·T^0 = p·Id. The difference is Id. That is not ≡ 0 mod p^k for k ≥ 1, the standing range in §11.1.1 (Lemmas 11.1.1.1–3 need k ≥ 1, Corollary 11.1.1.2 needs k ≥ 2), because H^0(𝔛^ord, Ω^(k,r)) is a nonzero p-adically separated module. The printed statement is therefore false at n = 0. No normalisation convention rescues it: T^0 = Id whatever the normalisation of T, and renormalising Tr by 1/(p+1) would break the case n ≥ 1. The proof's count fails at the same place. L_0 ⊂ G[p^0] is 0, so all p+1 multiplicative H satisfy H ∩ L_0 = {0}, not p of them. For n ≥ 1 the count p is right: L_n ∩ G[p]^mult is the line μ_p ⊂ μ_p^2, and H must avoid it, which leaves p of the p+1 lines. The lemma is used only in the proof of Corollary 11.1.1.2, "Applying lemma 11.1.1.4 for n large enough"; a grep finds no other citation. So the fix to n ≥ 1 changes nothing downstream. HAL v3 (hal-01393374v3) does not contain this lemma or the rank-(p+1) sentence. Its §11.1.1 stops at Lemma 11.1.1.3 and Corollaries 11.1.1.1–2 (Corollary 11.1.1.2 there assumes k ≥ 1), and it proves injectivity by a p-stabilisation / Hecke-polynomial argument. The published Duke version could not be checked. On 'affects': I would record 'a stated result', not 'nothing'. The printed Lemma 11.1.1.4 is itself a stated result that is false in its n = 0 case, and its proof fails there too. The reach stops at that lemma: no later result depends on the n = 0 case. I checked this against the page image at 250 dpi. The statement reads "n ≥ 0".

**Why n = 0 fails.** U^0 = Id and T^0 = Id, so the claim at n = 0 says Tr ∘ i ≡ p·Id mod p^k. Here i is pullback along 𝔛^ord_Kli(p) → 𝔛^ord. The paper says in the sentence just before the lemma that this map is finite étale of rank p+1. That matches §9.1.1, where H ⊂ G[p] is étale-locally μ_p: on the ordinary locus G[p]^0 ≅ μ_p², which has p+1 lines. Ω^(k,r) on the Klingen space is pulled back from 𝔛^ord, so Tr ∘ i = (p+1)·Id. The difference from p·Id is Id. Now M = H^0(𝔛^ord, Ω^(k,r)) is nonzero, p-torsion-free and p-adically separated. So M ≠ p^k M for every k ≥ 1, and Id is not ≡ 0 mod p^k. The statement is vacuous only for k = 0, and the lemma sets no condition on k.

**The proof fails at the same place.** L_0 ⊂ G[p^0] is 0 and T^{0,et} = Id, so all p+1 multiplicative H satisfy H ∩ L_0 = {0}, not p of them. For n ≥ 1 the count of p is right: L_n ∩ G[p]^0 is the line μ_{p^n}[p] = μ_p inside μ_p², and H must avoid it, which leaves p choices.

**Defences tried, none works:**
- Normalisations: the powers U^0 and T^0 are the identity whatever normalisation U and T carry (p^{3−r}U_{Kli(p),1} and p^{−3−r}).
- Tr: it is the plain trace map, as stated. Rescaling it by 1/(p+1) would break the cases n ≥ 1.
- i: it is the canonical pullback from p. 67.
- The rank: the paper's own count of p+1 is correct.
- k in "mod p^k" is the weight, so the congruence has content for every k ≥ 1.

**Who uses the lemma.** A grep finds a single citation, in the proof of Corollary 11.1.1.2: "Applying lemma 11.1.1.4 for n large enough, we find that Tr(f∘(i))(F) = pF = 0 mod p^k". This passes to the limit f = lim U^{n!}, e = lim T^{n!}, which only needs n ≥ 1. Corollary 11.1.1.2 is later used in Corollary 11.1.3.1 (the left vertical map), again without the n = 0 case. So "n ≥ 1" is the right and minimal fix, and it changes nothing downstream.

**On 'affects'.** The printed Lemma 11.1.1.4 is a stated result that is false as printed (its n = 0 case), and its proof fails there too. So I record "a stated result", with the reach stopping at the lemma itself; no later result depends on n = 0. This is an error rather than a misprint because the proof's own count shows the author did not treat n = 0; it is not an evident typographical slip. The module is killed by p and T is locally finite on it (Prop. 7.4.1.1). So for x ∈ (1−e)M we have T^{N!}x = 0 when N ≫ 0, which gives U^{N!} f i x = 0 and therefore f i x = 0. Defence attempts:
(a) Lemma 2.1.4, which says maps commute with ordinary projectors, needs the same operator T acting equivariantly on source and target. Here the map i goes from T on H^0(X_1^{ord}) to U or T''' on H^0(X_Kli^{ord}(p)_1), so the lemma does not apply.
(b) The element x = T''U^{-1}G is not known to lie in eM already. We have T^n T'' = T'' T'''^n, but the paper never shows that T''' preserves the f-part. So e cannot simply be deleted.
(c) No statement anywhere in the paper gives the intertwining relation f∘i∘T = U∘f∘i. I searched for "◦ i", "i ◦" and "equivariant".

The missing step is still true and follows in two lines from facts on pp. 67–68 (the diagram, Lemma 11.1.1.3, Lemma 2.1.3). I checked each step of this argument:
- T'''∘i = i∘T∘... more precisely T'''∘i = i∘T''∘i = i∘T.
- U f T''' = f U U = U f U, and U is injective on fM, so f T''' = f U.
- By induction, f i T^n = U^n f i.
- On (1−e)M with M killed by p, Lemma 2.1.3 gives T^{N!} = 0 locally.
- So U^{N!} f i x = 0, and f i x = 0.
Nothing is false; the argument is only incomplete. So this is a genuine minor gap, not a misprint and not an error.

- **Misprint** at §11.2, Theorem 11.2.1, point 6, p. 70 (author version, 17 June 2019); HAL v3: Theorem 11.2.1, point 6, printed p. 60 (PDF p. 61). The source says `6. For all k ≥ C, eH^i(𝔛, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) → eH^i(𝔛^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,r)}(−D)) is bijective for i = 0 and injective if i = 1.`; it should be `eH^i(𝔛, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) → eH^i(𝔛^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)): the weight on the target should be (k,2), not (k,r).`. I checked the page image at 200 dpi, and the printed text is as quoted: the source has weight (k,2) and the target has weight (k,r).

The r in point 6 is not unbound: the theorem opens with "For k > p + 1 and r ≥ 2 :", so r is the theorem's general r ≥ 2. The misprint still stands, for these reasons:

(a) Ω^{(k,r)} = Sym^k ω_G ⊗ det^r ω_G (p. ~27). The map in point 6 is the natural restriction from 𝔛 to 𝔛^{≥1}, and restriction cannot change the sheaf. For r ≠ 2 there is no natural map Ω^{(k,2)} → Ω^{(k,r)} (multiplying by Ha^m would only reach r = 2 + m(p−1), and the paper never uses it here). With general r, the i = 0 bijectivity would compare ordinary forms of different weights.

(b) Point 6 is the r = 2 complement of point 5 (r ≥ 3). Its proof, "The point 6 also follows by induction on n from corollary 11.1.3.1" (p. 71), relies on Cor 11.1.3.1(4) (p. 69): "eH^i(X_1, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) → f H^i(X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p)_1, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) is bijective for k ≥ C and i = 0 and injective ... i = 1". That in turn comes from Prop 8.2.1 (p. 53): "For all k ≥ C, eH^0(X_1^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) = eH^0(X_1, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) and the map eH^1(X_1, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) → eH^1(X_1^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) is injective." Both have weight (k,2) on both sides.

(c) The later use is also at r = 2. Theorem 11.3.1(4) (p. 71) states "eH^i(𝔛, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) → H^i(fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ ⊗ ω^2(−D)) ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Z_p) is bijective for i = 0 and injective for i = 1". Its proof (p. 73) says "proposition 2.2.2 and theorem 11.2.1 imply directly the points 3 and 4". Section 11.3 says "We specialize to r = 2".

HAL v3 has the identical point 6 (printed p. 60). In HAL v3, Corollary 11.2.1 had the same kind of mismatch: eH^0(X, Ω^{(k,2)}...) → fH^0(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,r)}...). The author version corrected that corollary to (k,2) on both sides (p. 71) but left point 6 unchanged. This supports reading point 6 as a leftover typo.

- **Misprint** at §11.2, end of the proof of Theorem 11.2.1, p. 71 (author version). HAL v3 has the same text (printed p. 60).. The source says `The points 4 and 5 follow from corollary 11.1.3.1 using proposition 2.2.2. The point 6 also follows by induction on n from corollary 11.1.3.1. Finally, we deduce 7 by another application of proposition 2.2.2.`; it should be `Finally, 7 follows from Proposition 2.2.1 applied to fN^•. fN^• is in C^{flat}(Z_p), concentrated in degrees [0,1], and fN^• ⊗ F_p computes fRΓ(X^{≥1}_Kli(p)_1, Ω^{(k,r)}(−D)). By Corollary 11.1.3.1(5) that complex is perfect of amplitude [0,1] (so it has finite cohomology) for r ≥ 2 and k ≥ C.`. Proposition 2.2.2 (p. 9) is Nakayama's lemma for complexes: a map in C^{flat}(R) that is a quasi-isomorphism mod m_R is a quasi-isomorphism. Using it requires a map to or from a complex already known to be perfect. For r ≥ 3, point 7 follows from points 4 and 5 by composing quasi-isomorphisms with eRΓ(𝔛, …). For r = 2, point 6 gives only a bijection for i = 0 and an injection for i = 1, so no such quasi-isomorphism is available. Proposition 2.2.1 is the perfectness criterion: M^• in C^{flat}(R) in degrees [a,b] with M^• ⊗ R/m_R of finite cohomology is quasi-isomorphic to a perfect complex in degrees [a,b]. Its hypotheses are exactly those of Corollary 11.1.3.1(5), with the same range k ≥ C and r ≥ 2 as point 7. The mod-p reduction of fN^• is f(N^•/p) by Lemma 2.1.4. So the intended argument is clear and complete once the reference is corrected to 2.2.1. The printed 'another application of proposition 2.2.2' is a wrong cross-reference, not a gap. The source says `where 1_{I'×I'} is the identity matrix of size I' × I', C = (c_{i,j})_{(i,j)∈I'×I''} ∈ M_{I'×I''}(R) and B ∈ M_{I'',J''}(m_R).`; it should be `B ∈ M_{J''×I''}(m_R): rows indexed by J'', the target basis {h_j}, and columns by I'', the source basis.`. The paper's own indexing puts rows first and columns second. C = (c_{i,j}) ∈ M_{I'×I''} has row index i ∈ I' = J' (target) and column index l ∈ I'' (source). This matches the change of basis e_l ↦ e_l − Σ_{i∈I'} c_{i,l} e_i, since f(e_l) = Σ_{i∈I'} c_{i,l} h_i + Σ_{j∈J''} b_{j,l} h_j. It also matches the statement that columns tend to 0, which is what makes f(e_l) converge. So the lower-right block B has rows J'' and columns I''. The printed M_{I'',J''} has the two index sets swapped; J'' and I'' need not even have the same size. The slip is harmless. (Separately, C actually has entries in m_R, since ē_l ∈ ker for l ∈ I''; the printed M(R) is only weaker, not wrong.) Rendered pp. 70–72 and checked the text. HAL v3 is identical.

(1) The cited theorem is not limited to automorphic vector bundles at spherical and paramodular level. That description fits only the paper's restatement, Thm 6.2.2.1. I downloaded Lan's paper [50] (kwlan.org/articles/cpt-ram-nbl.pdf). Its Thm 8.6 applies to any quasi-coherent sheaf E on M^tor_{H,Σ} that is "formally canonical (resp. formally subcanonical) over R" (Def. 8.5). It works at any neat level H and over any O_{F_0,(p)}-algebra R. So Ω^{(k,r)}(−D) on the Klingen-level compactification is covered. The paper itself uses this for X_Kli(p) → X*_Kli(p) in §14, where it shows that X^{≥1}_Kli(p) is the preimage of X*^{≥1}_Kli(p). Colimits and the quotients by Ha^l then follow from the long exact sequence. So the citation in the proof of Thm 11.2.1 is not a gap.

(2) For Thm 11.3.1 the citation does not apply as written. Lan's Def. 8.5(2) requires, at each boundary point x̄, a finite filtration of E_{0,x̄} whose graded pieces are pullbacks of finite R-modules. So E must be of finite type near the boundary.
- As an O-module, F^κ_{m,n} is the pushforward along X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_n → X^{≥1}_Kli(p)_n (and the finite Igusa torsor). That map is affine, étale and quasi-finite but not finite: Remark 9.1.1.2 says it is an isomorphism over the p-rank-1 locus and has degree p or p+1 over the ordinary locus. The p-rank-1 locus meets the boundary (toric rank 1 with supersingular abelian part). There, for m ≥ 2, F^κ_{m,n}⊗ω^2(−D) is not of finite type, because an affine quasi-finite map with a coherent pushforward would be finite. So it is not formally subcanonical.
- The Ha-torsion right-hand sheaves do not have the form in Def. 8.5(2) either.
- The paper checks none of this, and F^κ_{m,n} exists only on the p-rank ≥ 1 open.

The conclusion that is actually needed is very likely true and can be recovered as described in the correction. So this is a gap in the proof, not an error in any stated result. Defence, part 1. The citation in the proof of Thm 11.2.1 is not a gap. The cited theorem is not only about automorphic vector bundles on the spherical and paramodular compactifications; that describes only the paper's own restatement, Thm 6.2.2.1 on p. 30. [50] itself (Lan, IMRN 2017; author's compilation read from kwlan.org) is much more general:
- Thm 8.6 reads: "Suppose R is an O_{F0,(p)}-algebra, and suppose that E is a quasi-coherent sheaf over M^tor_{H,Σ} that is formally canonical (resp. formally subcanonical) over R ... Then R^i(∮_{H,Σ})_* E(−nD′) = 0 for all i > 0 and n > 0 (resp. n ≥ 0)."
- The introduction states that the models work "when the image H^p of H under G(Ẑ) → G(Ẑ^p) is neat ... regardless of the levels and ramifications involved at p."

The paper's proof of Thm 6.1.5.1 (p. 29) says that X_Kli(p) is built in [49] and [50] by normalisation, and on p. 101 the paper itself applies [50] to X_Kli(p) → X*_Kli(p). (There it cites "thm. 8.9", but 8.9 is a Remark in [50].) Ω^{(k,r)}(−D) is the subcanonical extension of an automorphic bundle, which is the intended case. Three further points are formal:
- X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p) is the preimage of the open X^{*,≥1}_{Kli}(p) (p. 101), and relative vanishing is local on the target.
- Reduction mod p^n follows from flatness.
- R^iπ_* commutes with the Ha-colimit, and the quotient term follows from the long exact sequence.

So the p. 71 claim, and its implicit use in Cor. 11.1.3.1, is covered by the cited source.

Part 2, what remains. On p. 72 the sheaf F^κ_{m,n} = (π_{m,n})_*(O_{IG(p^m)_n} ⊗ Λ_n)[κ_{m,n}] is a pushforward along a non-finite affine étale map, so it is not coherent. It exists only on the open X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p)_n, whereas Thm 8.6 is stated for sheaves on all of M^tor, where H_1 need not be multiplicative at the boundary. The paper never checks Def. 8.5 for it, and Lan's proof via [17, Thm 3.9] works with formal completions along fibres; for a non-coherent sheaf that step does not follow formally. The paper itself takes a separate argument for the analogous non-finite sheaves in Part III: Prop. 12.9.2.1, plus smallness via [3] A.1.3.1 in Lemma 12.9.2.1. That contrast suggests the one-line citation on p. 72 is not enough. My local analysis (see the correction) indicates the vanishing is true, so this is an omitted verification rather than an error.

Consequences. The acyclic resolutions give the two-term flat complexes behind Thm 11.3.1 (U locally finite; fRΓ perfect over Λ in degrees [0,1]; the control maps 3 and 4). These feed Thm 1.1 and §14.8. Because the missing step can be filled, only the proof is affected.

Repair: only the Thm 11.3.1 citation needs one. Affineness from Lemma 9.1.1.1 plus the local structure at the boundary is the right approach and close to minimal, but it needs to be combined with [50] Def. 8.5, as described above. (ii) For p odd, write Λ = Z_p[μ_{p−1}] ⊗ Z_p[[1+pZ_p]] ≅ ∏_{i mod p−1} Λ_i, using the idempotents of Z_p[μ_{p−1}]. Each Λ_i ≅ Z_p[[T]] is complete local noetherian with residue field F_p. For p = 2, Λ ≅ Z_2[C_2][[T]] is already local. (iii) For each i, choose k ≡ i mod p−1 with k ≥ C. Then e_i fM• ⊗ Λ_i/m_i = fM• ⊗_{Λ,k} F_p. That complex has finite cohomology by Cor. 11.1.3.1(5), or by Thm 11.2.1(7) together with point 3. (iv) Prop. 2.2.1 over Λ_i then shows that e_i fM• is quasi-isomorphic to a perfect complex in degrees [0,1]. Taking the product over i, fM• is perfect over Λ in degrees [0,1]. Only finiteness of the cohomology mod m_i is needed. The amplitude [0,1] comes from the representative itself.`. I read the rendered pp. 69–73, 56 and 7, and checked the HAL v3 text. The proof of Theorem 11.3.1 builds the acyclic resolution. It proves the mod-p quasi-isomorphism fRΓ(X_1, Ω^{(k,r)}(−D)) → fRΓ(X_1, 𝓕^k_{1,1}⊗ω²(−D)) for k > p+1, then the identity f colim_m RΓ(X_1, 𝓕^k_{m,1}⊗ω²(−D)) = fRΓ(X_1, Ω^{(k,r)}(−D)). Lemma 2.1.2 then gives point 1, and the case k > p+1 is removed. The only closing sentence covers "the points 3 and 4". Point 2 (perfectness over Λ, amplitude [0,1]) is never mentioned. The tools it needs, Prop. 2.2.1 and Cor. 11.1.3.1(5) (or Thm 11.2.1(7)), are not cited in the proof. Prop. 2.2.2, which is cited, is a quasi-isomorphism criterion and does not give perfectness. So a stated result is asserted with no proof: this is a gap in the sense of PROTOCOL §18.

There is also a second problem. §2 is set up only for a complete local noetherian R with finite residue field. Λ = Z_p[[Z_p^×]] ≅ Z_p[μ_{p−1}] ⊗ Z_p[[1+pZ_p]] ≅ ∏_{p−1} Z_p[[T]] is only semi-local for p odd. So "locally finite" (Def. 2.1.1), Lemma 2.1.2 and Props 2.2.1–2.2.2 do not literally apply over Λ. Working over R = Z_p instead fails: the ordinary part mod p is a finite F_p[[T]]-module, not a finite F_p-module. The fix is routine: decompose by the idempotents and work factor by factor. Every ingredient of the repair is already in the paper, so the result stands and 'affects' is 'nothing'. My confidence is medium only because this is a minor omission in the write-up rather than a failing step. Defence attempted and failed.

(a) The proof establishes point 1: "We deduce from lemma 2.1.2 that U is locally finite …". Its only other conclusion is the closing sentence, which names points 3 and 4 only. Point 2 is never mentioned. The proof does not cite Prop. 2.2.1, which is the only perfectness criterion in §2. Unlike the proof of Thm 11.2.1 ("They are objects of C^flat(Z_p) by construction"), it also never says that the limit complex is Λ-flat and complete.

(b) A charitable reading does not rescue it. The proof of Thm 11.2.1 itself gets its perfectness point 7 "by another application of proposition 2.2.2", which should be 2.2.1. So "proposition 2.2.2" in the closing sentence might loosely stand for §2.2 as a whole. Even so, that sentence claims only points 3 and 4.

(c) The intended argument is the one given in the correction. The introduction (p. 3) says the integral control theorem for k ≫ 0 is used "to show that M is a perfect complex". It is not carried out anywhere else in the paper. Footnote 24 on p. 101 cites "theorem 11.3.1, point 2" as the place where the degrees [0,1] are established.

(d) The fix works, so the statement is true. For each maximal ideal of Λ one picks k ≥ C in the matching class, which is always possible. Reduction modulo that ideal gives fRΓ(X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p)_1, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)), by the mod-p comparison proved in the text on pp. 72–73. That complex is finite by Cor. 11.1.3.1(5), and Prop. 2.2.1 applies.

(e) The semi-local point is correct. For p odd, μ_{p−1} ⊂ Z_p and p−1 is prime to p, so Z_p[μ_{p−1}] ≅ Z_p^{p−1} and Λ ≅ Z_p[[T]]^{p−1}. This ring is not local, while §2 assumes a complete local noetherian ring. Applying §2 factor by factor is routine. The same issue affects the use of Lemma 2.1.2 for point 1; this overlaps with sourceIssues E5.

Downstream uses of point 2:
- Thm 1.1 (M is perfect of amplitude [0,1]).
- Lemma 14.8.4 (Euler characteristics are "locally constant functions of k … by theorem 11.3.1").
- Footnote 24.
- §15.2: the Hecke-generated subalgebra is a finite Λ-algebra, the localisation uses [41] lem. 2.12, and Thm 15.2.1 concerns the Euler characteristic of the perfect complex, hence Thm 1.2.

All of these stand once point 2 is supplied as above. I set 'affects' to 'the proof' rather than 'nothing': as written, the proof of Thm 11.3.1 does not prove one of its four points, although no stated result fails. The source says `H^0(X_{Kli}(p)^{≥1}_1, colim𝓕^k_{1,1} ⊗ ω^{2+l(p−1)}(−D)/Ha^l)`; it should be `H^0(X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p)_1, colim 𝓕^k_{1,1} ⊗ ω^{2+l(p−1)}(−D)/Ha^l). Only the index placement changes. Adding the subscript 'colim_l' is optional: every row of the printed diagram writes plain 'colim'.`. The other two right-hand entries of the same diagram, and the surrounding text, use X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p)_1. X_{Kli}(p)^{≥1}_1 is not notation defined in the paper, but it plainly means the same space. - **Misprint** at §12.2.2, proof of Lemma 12.2.2.1, p. 74 (author version, 17 June 2019); HAL v3 §12.2.2, Lemma 12.2.2.1, PDF p. 64. The source says `Author version p. 74, checked on the page image: "Let us assume that c, f are units for example. We deduce that HT(e_2) = \frac{a}{c} HT(e_3) and that Fil^{can}_ε is generated by HT(e_2), a direct factor is provided by the submodule generated by HT(e_4). □". Earlier in the proof the matrix of HT is the 2×4 matrix with rows (0 a c e) and (0 b d f), and the proof gives "ad − bc = 0" and "cf − de is a unit in R_ε". HAL v3 (hal-01393374v3, PDF p. 64, checked on the page image) has the same text word for word, except that it writes "sub-module" and says "the matrix of Hodge-Tate".`; it should be `"... We deduce that HT(e_2) = (a/c) HT(e_3) and that Fil^{can}_ε is generated by HT(e_3), a direct factor is provided by the submodule generated by HT(e_4)."`. I redid the computation. The columns of the printed 2×4 matrix are HT(e_1) = 0, HT(e_2) = (a,b), HT(e_3) = (c,d) and HT(e_4) = (e,f). The relation ad − bc = 0 agrees with J from §5.1: J = [[0,A],[−A,0]] with A antidiagonal, so e_1 pairs with e_4 and e_2 pairs with e_3. A Lagrangian kernel containing e_1 therefore lies in ⟨e_1,e_2,e_3⟩. Suppose c is a unit. Then b = ad/c, so HT(e_2) = (a, ad/c) = (a/c)·HT(e_3), as printed. Hence Fil^can_ε = ⟨HT(e_2), HT(e_3)⟩ = R_ε·HT(e_3). This is free of rank one because c is a unit. HT(e_3) and HT(e_4) form a basis of R_ε^2 because det[[c,e],[d,f]] = cf − de is a unit, so HT(e_4) spans a direct complement. HT(e_2) = (a/c)HT(e_3) generates Fil only when a is a unit, and nothing forces that. So the printed "generated by HT(e_2)" is wrong under the stated assumptions; the correct generator is HT(e_3). The same holds in the other case (d, e units), where HT(e_2) = (b/d)HT(e_3). The paragraph right after the proof supports this reading: X(p^n,ε) is covered by X(p^n,ε,e_2) and X(p^n,ε,e_3), where HT(e_2), respectively HT(e_3), generates Fil. The case the proof treats (cf − de a unit) is exactly the HT(e_3) chart. The HT(e_2) chart corresponds to af − be being a unit; minors that use column 1 vanish, and ad − bc = 0. This is not a text-layer artefact: the page images of both versions clearly print HT(e_2). The lemma's statement still holds (locally free of rank one, locally a direct summand), because the corrected argument proves it. The later uses at pp. 81–84 (the X(p^n,ε,e_2)^?, X(p^n,ε,e_3)^? covering and the Mayer–Vietoris-type sequence) depend only on the lemma and the covering, both of which are correct. So the misprint is a one-symbol slip (e_2 for e_3) and affects nothing downstream. Recorded as `PAPER-PILLONI-20/E96`; looked for an existing correction in: The author's version on V. Pilloni's homepage (https://www.imo.universite-paris-saclay.fr/~pilloni/complexhidatheorygsp4.pdf, 17 June 2019, 113 pp., SHA-256 4c05724efeab1dbbb108f980ec9a722127d2a8cd2abf6e8c2a6a2251cf0f9f58), which is post-referee but precedes the journal's final revision (15 October 2019), and HAL hal-01393374v3 (6 January 2018) at the same place; the published Duke text is paywalled and could not be compared; Crossref for doi:10.1215/00127094-2019-0075 (no relation, update-to or updated-by record; no update records), the errata and addenda of Duke Math. - **Misprint** at §12.4 (Group action), p. 75, 2nd paragraph, first line (author version). This is not in HAL v3: HAL v3 (printed p. 64 = PDF p. 65) reads 'We let 𝔗_{w'} be the formal scheme in groups defined by ...' with no range for w'. The slip was introduced in the author version.. The source says `"For all rational numbers w' ≥ 0, we let 𝔗_{w'} be the formal group scheme defined by 𝔗_{w'}(R) = Z_p^×(1 + p^{w'}R) for all R in Adm. We let 𝔗^0_{w'} be the connected component of the identity in 𝔗_{w'}. For all R in Adm, 𝔗^0_{w'}(R) = 1 + p^{w'}R."`; it should be `For all rational numbers w' > 0`. For w' = 0 the definition does not give a group. Take R = O ∈ Adm: 1 + p^0 R = 1 + O = O, which contains 0, so 𝔗_0(O) = Z_p^× · O = O is not a subgroup of O^×. Formally, 1/(1+X) does not converge in O⟨X⟩, so R ↦ 1 + R is only a formal monoid. For w' > 0, p^{w'}R is topologically nilpotent in the p-adically complete R, so 1 + p^{w'}R is a group. Every later use has w' > 0: §12.3 says 'positive rational numbers w' ≤ w', and §12.6.2 says '0 < w' ≤ w ≤ ε', which governs §§12.6–14. The intended range is therefore clearly w' > 0. The source says `"Using a covering as in section 12.5, 𝔉𝔏^+_{n,ε,w,w'}|_{Spf R} is identified with the set of matrices (1 0; p^w𝔅(0,1)_R 1) × (1 + p^{w'}𝔅(0,1)_R). The action of 𝔗^0_w is on the right term. It follows that 𝔊^{κ_A,w}(Spf R × Spf A) ≃ R⊗̂A⟨X⟩."`; it should be `The action of 𝔗^0_{w'} is on the right term.`. - **Misprint** at §12.6.2, paragraph after the proof of Lemma 12.6.2.2 (definition of 𝔉^{κ_A,w}), p. 77 of the author version. HAL v3 is different (printed p. 65 = PDF p. 66): it reads '(π_3)_⋆𝔊^{κ_A,w} is 𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^nℤ)-equivariant. We define a Banach sheaf 𝔉^{κ_A,w} = ((π_3)_⋆𝔊^{κ_A,w})^{𝔗_{w,n}}', with no second expression. HAL v3 also defined 𝔏^{κ_A} using 𝔗^0_w invariants, which explains the leftover w.. The source says `We let π_3 : 𝔛(p^n,ε) → 𝔛_Kli(p^n,ε) be the finite projection. The sheaf (π_3)_⋆𝔊^{κ_A,w} is 𝔗_{w,n}-equivariant. We define a Banach sheaf 𝔉^{κ_A,w} = ((π_3)_⋆𝔊^{κ_A,w})^{𝔗_{w,n}} = (π_⋆𝒪_{𝔉𝔏^+_{n,ε,w,w'}} ⊗̂ A)^{𝔗_{w,n}} over 𝔛_Kli(p^n,ε) × Spf A.`; it should be `Replace 𝔗_{w,n} by 𝔗_{w',n}, as defined in §12.4. This is essential in the second expression, (π_⋆𝒪_{𝔉𝔏^+_{n,ε,w,w'}} ⊗̂ A)^{𝔗_{w',n}}. It is harmless but consistent in the other two places. This matches the analytic definition on p. 79, (π_⋆𝒪_{𝓕𝓛^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'}} ⊗̂ A)^{𝒯_{w',n}}.`. §12.4 (p. 75) defines 𝔗_{w',n} = 𝔗_{w'} ×_{𝔗_{w'}/𝔗^0_{w'}} 𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^nℤ). It says that the 𝔗^0_{w'}-action on 𝔉𝔏^+_{n,ε,w,w'} (a 𝔗^0_{w'}-torsor over 𝔉𝔏_{n,ε,w}) extends to an action of 𝔗_{w',n}. With the dummy variable renamed, 𝔗_{w,n} is a subgroup of 𝔗_{w',n} that contains only 𝔗^0_w ⊆ 𝔗^0_{w'}.

First expression: 𝔗^0_{w'} already acts trivially on 𝔊^{κ_A,w} = (π_2)_⋆((π_1)_⋆𝒪 ⊗̂ A)^{𝔗^0_{w'}}, and 𝔗_{w,n} maps onto 𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^n). So ((π_3)_⋆𝔊)^{𝔗_{w,n}} equals the 𝔎𝔩𝔦-invariants, which equal ((π_3)_⋆𝔊)^{𝔗_{w',n}}. That expression is therefore correct even as printed.

Second expression: this one is wrong for w' < w. In the local chart of §12.5, 𝔉𝔏^+ = 𝔉𝔏 × (1 + p^{w'}𝔅(0,1)). Invariants of 𝒪 ⊗̂ A under the diagonal action of 𝔗^0_w = 1 + p^w(·) only impose κ_A-equivariance along the smaller group. They give a strictly larger sheaf, namely functions on the 𝔗^0_{w'}/𝔗^0_w-torsor 𝔉𝔏^+/𝔗^0_w, not π_⋆𝔏^{κ_A}. With 𝔗_{w',n} one gets the intended sheaf, as in the p. 79 definition.

The cause is a leftover from HAL v3, where w and w' played swapped roles (𝔏^{κ_A} was defined with 𝔗^0_w). A separate minor point, not part of this issue: π in the second expression is the map to 𝔛(p^n,ε) (p. 76), so strictly one means π_3∘π. The source says `is maximally nilpotent`; it should be `Add v(t)<0 at the local place in the statement, as used in its proof and in §4; item071 has this hypothesis.`. The source says `"We use that f := supp Z(M^der)(𝔽̄_p) < +∞."`; it should be `f := sup_p #Z(M^der)(𝔽̄_p) < +∞.`. f is a uniform bound on the order of the finite group Z(M^der)(𝔽̄_p), used to raise to the power f!. Recorded as `PAPER-RICHARD-YAFAEV-25/E5`; looked for an existing correction in: arXiv 2111.11216 versions (v4, 20 October 2023); Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS 141 (2025), 249–331 (open access): no correction notice; Crossref metadata for 10.1007/s10240-025-00154-4: no update or correction relation.
- **Gap** at Lemma 5.12 and its proof, pp.285–287 (published version) (it affects the proof). The source says `"Let m ∈ M(𝔽̄_p) such that m̂ := ad_M(m) belongs to Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(U)). … Since #F | e, by construction of U[e], we have φ_m(U[e]) = {1}. Equivalently m ∈ Z_M(U[e]). This proves the Lemma with U′ = U[e] and c(N) = e^{k(N)}."`; it should be `The argument proves the inclusion Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(U)) ⊆ Z_M(U[e])/Z(M). This is what the applications use, and it suffices there. In Lemma 5.11 the Tate hypothesis gives Z_M(V[e]) = Z(M), hence Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(V)) = 1 and so Z_{M^ad}(Û) = 1. Either restate Lemma 5.12 as this inclusion, or supply a separate argument for the equality on U′.`. The lemma asserts Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(U′)) = Z_M(U′)/Z(M) for U′ = U[e]. That needs, for every m with ad_M(m) centralising ad_M(U[e]), that m centralises U[e]. The proof takes m centralising the image of the larger group U. Then φ_m is a homomorphism U → F killed by U[e]. For m only centralising ad_M(U[e]), φ_m is a homomorphism U[e] → F, and U[e] need not lie in its kernel, because homomorphisms of U[e] to F need not extend to U. The inclusion needed for the stated equality is therefore not established. - **Misprint** at Lemma 1.1, p. 5 (arXiv v3, identical to the author version of 19 July 2022; the published pagination was not seen). ### Ananth Shankar–Arul Shankar–Tang–Tayou, "Exceptional jumps of Picard ranks of reductions of K3 surfaces over number fields", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2022) (`PAPER-SHANKAR-SHANKAR-TANG-ETAL-22`)

- **Gap** at Lemma 5.3, Proposition 5.2, Theorems 5.7 and 5.8, pp.25–31 (it affects the proof). The source says `Proposition 5.2: "Let m ∈ Z_{>0} such that Z(m) ≠ ∅; and if b is odd, we further assume that for a fixed D, √(m/D) ∈ Z, as in Theorem 2.4." Lemma 5.3 likewise, with the proof "we conclude by [BK03, Theorem 4.11, (4.73), (4.74)], since both d_0 and k are independent of m." But: "Theorem 5.7. For every m representable by (L, Q) …" and "Theorem 5.8. For every positive integer m, we have the following bounds …", proved from Proposition 5.2.`; it should be `For b odd and m/D not a square, add this to the proof of Lemma 5.3. In [BK03, Thm. 4.11(ii)] (r odd), the m-dependence through d_0 = d_0(m) enters as log|4m/D_0²| − 2L′(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ)/L(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ). By the functional equation of L(s, χ_{D_0}), this is log m + 2L′(χ_{D_0}, κ − 1/2)/L(χ_{D_0}, κ − 1/2) + O(1): the log|D_0| terms cancel. The logarithmic derivative at κ − 1/2 ≥ 2 is bounded by |ζ′/ζ(2)|, and the χ_{d_0}-factors of σ_m(s) are bounded uniformly as in the proof of Proposition 5.2. So Lemma 5.3 (with O(1) uniform in m) and Proposition 5.2 hold for every m with Z(m) ≠ ∅. That is what Theorems 5.7–5.8 assert, and what Proposition 6.4 and Lemma 7.6 use.`. Theorem 5.8 is proved from equation (3.1), Proposition 3.2 and Proposition 5.2, so for b odd its proof covers only m ∈ D·(Q^×)². It is then applied to arbitrary integers:
- in Proposition 6.4 to M = Q(λ) for a difference λ of two lattice vectors ("Theorem 5.8(i) implies X^{b/2} ≪ −log|Q(λ_x)| ≪ A(M) ≪ M^{b/2} log M");
- in Lemma 7.6 to m = a_1(n)², a square but not in general D times a square.
Both feed Theorem 6.1 and Theorem 7.1, hence the main theorem for every odd b ≥ 3. For b even, d = (−1)^{r/2}det(L) does not depend on m and there is no gap. BK03 Theorem 4.11 was read in arXiv:math/0204100v2 (p.27): its r-odd formula contains log|4m/D_0²| and −2L′(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ)/L(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ). Recorded as `PAPER-SHANKAR-SHANKAR-TANG-ETAL-22/E1`; looked for an existing correction in: Forum Math. Pi 10 (2022), e21, DOI 10.1017/fmp.2022.14: Crossref (checked 2026-09-22) records no update or correction relation, and a title search finds no correction notice; arXiv 1909.07473: v3 of 29 August 2022 ("Final version. To appear in Forum of Mathematics, Pi") is the latest version; the published text was read.
- **Error** at §7.3, construction of μ, p.43 (it affects the proof). The source says `"We define the a_i as follows: suppose that a_n ≠ 0; we define a_i = 0 for n + 1 ≤ i ≤ e^{e^{p^n}}, and we then define a_i = 1 for i = ⌈e^{e^{p^n}}⌉. This implies that Σ_{i≤n} a_ip^i ≡ μ mod p^N with N ≥ e^{e^{p^n}} – that is, there is an integer x_n of size O(p^n) that approximates μ mod p^N, with N double-exponential in the size of x_n. … the lattice Λ created this way must also have property 2."`; it should be `Make the gaps double-exponential in the discriminant rather than in x_n: after a_n ≠ 0, set a_i = 0 for n < i < exp(exp(C·p^{2c(n+1)})) with C depending only on L (so that exp(C·p^{2c(n+1)}) exceeds the discriminant of L_n below). Then property (2) of Lemma 7.11 holds with L_n = span_Z{e_j + x_nf_j}, and the example stands.`. Property (2) of Lemma 7.11 needs N_i ≥ e^{e^{D_i}}, where D_i is the discriminant of the approximating sublattice L_i. Here L_i = span_Z{e_j + x_nf_j : 1 ≤ j ≤ c}, with e_j, f_j orthogonal and Q positive definite. So D_i ≍ Π_j (Q(e_j) + x_n²Q(f_j)) ≥ x_n^{2c} ≥ p^{2cn}, because a_n ≠ 0 forces x_n ≥ p^n. The printed choice gives only N ≈ e^{e^{p^n}}, which is far below e^{e^{D_i}}, so the proof of Lemma 7.11 (m_i < e^{D_i} and (Y_Λ.Z(m_i)) > N_i ≥ e^{e^{D_i}} > e^{m_i}) does not apply. "Double-exponential in the size of x_n" is not double-exponential in D_i ≍ x_n^{2c}. The example is illustrative and not used for the main results. - **Misprint** at §9.2, pp.45. The source says `"… A^+ is isogenous to B^{2^n}, where B is an abelian variety with dim B = 2^n." and, in the proof of Theorems 1.4 and 1.6, "Since s_B is not a scalar multiplication, ker(s_B − [Dm]) is a nontrivial simple factor of B_𝔓, and hence B_𝔓 is nonsimple."`; it should be `"dim B = 2^{n−1}"; "ker(s_B − [Dm]) contains a nonzero proper abelian subvariety of B_𝔓".`. dim A = 2^{b+1} (the paper's own 2^{2+3−1} = 16 for b = 3), so dim A^+ = 2^b = 2^{2n−1}, and A^+ ~ B^{2^n} forces dim B = 2^{n−1}. For b = 3, n = 2, B is the abelian surface (A^+ ~ B^4 of dimension 8), not a 4-fold. The PDF text layer shows the superscript n on 2 in both M_{2^n}(Q) and dim B = 2^n. The support of R1 + R2 + R∩ has h⁰ = 1, so the argument goes through whenever all total weights, which are at most 2g − 2, are nonzero in k. With it the contour estimate of p. 31 gives #Θ_n(F_q)/#J(F_q) = q^{n−g} + O(q^{−g/2+εg+o(g)}), for every q. So the discrepancy affects nothing. - **Error** at Published Lemma 3.14 pp. 701–703 (it affects a stated result). The source says `2^d H^(d+1)/(Ω^d φ(Ω)) · 1(gcd(R(k),Ω)=1) + O_A(H^(d+1)/(log H)^A)`; it should be `Count both signs: Σ Λ(|P(k)|) (equivalently Σ log|P(k)| over |P(k)| prime) has the printed main term and error, which is what the proof proves (item 34). Theorem 1.9 and everything after it stand.`. For d = k = ℓ = 1, P(t) = at + b with 1 ≤ a ≤ H, |b| ≤ H, and the positive-prime sum is Σ_{a≤H} θ(H + a) = (3/2)H² + o(H²), not 2H² (the triangle a + b ≤ 0 has area H²/2). The proof counts k₁ | P(k) in progressions, which does not see the sign of P(k). Lemma 4.9 inherits the error through its use of the lemma; for θ^Λ it holds as printed.
