### Treumann–Venkatesh, "Functoriality, Smith theory, and the Brauer homomorphism", Annals of Mathematics 183 (2016), no. 1 (`PAPER-TREUMANN-VENKATESH-16`)

- **Misprint** at arXiv:1407.2346v1 (9 July 2014), §12.2, the second unnumbered Proposition after Proposition 12.3, part (2). The source says `$\LL_G(U^2)$ is the Levi obtained by adjoining the roots to $\TT$ the roots ±x_1, ±y_3, ±y_1, ±y_3`; it should be `The four root pairs are ±x_1, ±x_3, ±y_1, ±y_3: the second entry should be ±x_3, not a second ±y_3.`. As printed the list names only three distinct root pairs, which cannot give the derived group SL_2^4 asserted two lines later. Computing directly in the E_8 root system with the simple roots of (12.1) and the roots x_1, x_2, x_3, y_1, y_2, y_3 of (12.3): U is orthogonal, has order 4 and equals s_{x_1}s_{x_2+x_3}s_{-x_1-x_2}s_{y_1}s_{y_2+y_3}s_{-y_1-y_2} exactly, L_G(U) has 24 roots, and the centraliser of the identity component of T^{U^2}, that is the set of roots orthogonal to the fixed space of U^2, consists of exactly eight roots, namely ±x_1, ±x_3, ±y_1, ±y_3. These four are orthogonal and satisfy U^2 v = -v, so they span the (-1)-eigenspace of U^2 and give SL_2^4. The deleted proof in the source file makes the same statement: 'x_1, x_3, y_1, y_3 are orthogonal and generate the (-1)-eigenspace of U^2'. The sentence and the two sentences after it argue about Out(H) and about the image of Γ in Out(H), and conclude 'that Γ → Out(H) has image of size ≤ 2 follows from §11.1', so they establish (ii). The exception named, the first-listed pair so_{2n+1} ⊃ so_{2u+1} x so_{2v} with v = 4, is exactly the case where Out(so_{2v}) = Out(D_4) has six elements rather than two, again a statement about (ii); π_1 of the fixed groups in the list is a 2-group throughout, with nothing to check. - **Gap** at Theorem 1.2, p.3, and the last assertion of Theorem 4.8, p.23, with its proof, pp.24–25, in arXiv 1702.04644v2 (13 July 2018, the latest version; its source file is Duke_Final_Revision.tex; PDF SHA-256 2eacf07f…e1bd); now collated with the published journal: Theorem 1.2 p.379; Theorem 4.8 pp.406–407; proof pp.408–410 (especially p.409) (it affects a stated result). The source says `lim_{q→∞} Ẽ^±/|H₂(G′,c)[q−1]|`; it should be `For G′ not good, replace lim by liminf: liminf_{q→∞, (q,|G′|)=1} Ẽ^±_{F_q(t),q^{2n}}(G,G′)/|H_2(G′,c)[q−1]| ≥ w_G n^{N_{G′}−1}, and likewise with E^± and a smaller constant in Theorem 1.2.`. The proof bounds the ratio from below for each large q. It keeps only the multidegrees n in a set 𝒞 (all n_i large, with prescribed parities) on which the number of Frobenius-fixed components is |H_2(G′,c)[q−1]|, and discards the other components as nonnegative. That gives a lower bound for the liminf. It does not show the limit exists: the discarded components with small n_i and their Frobenius-fixed counts may depend on q, and nothing in the argument controls them. The good cases, where the limits are computed exactly, are unaffected. In Theorem 1.2 the passage from Ẽ to E divides by the positive constants of §2.1, |Aut_{G′}(G)| and A(G,G′), so the lower bound transfers with a smaller constant. The proof's remark that "the second statements of both theorems are the same" should be read that way. Noted by the extraction (items 97, 141 and 143). The continuation makes the remaining obligation precise: by /307–/309 the ordinary limit exists iff the total normalized fixed-component profile is eventually constant. Stable parity fibers themselves require the obstruction test /300–/304; do not assume all stable fibers are independent of q without that test. No admissible-type counterexample is asserted. (cc-442dc5) Rechecked in the published text (pp.406–409): the proof ends 'by dividing both sides by |H_2(G′,c)[q−1]| and then letting q → ∞', after a lower bound valid for each large q, so only the liminf is established. The good cases and the lower-bound content are unaffected. For example, for p ≥ 5 the tame fundamental group of P¹ ∖ {0, 1728, ∞} has as quotients the groups PSL₂(F_ℓ), ℓ ≠ p, of modular covers X(ℓ) → X(1), ramified with indices 2, 3, ℓ, and these orders are divisible by p for suitable ℓ. The definition and the proof of Theorem 3.13 only use homomorphisms to F and its lift F̃_c, whose orders are prime to p. These factor through the prime-to-p quotient, so nothing changes. Noted by the extraction (item 56). - **Error** at §1.2.9(i), (1.2.9.1), p = 2 line, p. 6 (it affects a stated result). The source says `(Σ_{x∈F_q^×} ψ(Tr(x + a/x)))² − q = −(1/√q) Σ_{x_1,x_2∈F_q^×} ψ(Tr(x_1 + x_2 + a/(x_1x_2))), p = 2`; it should be `(Σ_x ψ(Tr(x + a/x)))² − q = Σ_{x_1,x_2} ψ(Tr(x_1 + x_2 + a/(x_1x_2))) for p = 2, with no factor −1/√q.`. In the paper's normalisation Kl(2; a) = −S_2(a)/√q and Kl(3; a) = S_3(a)/q, so Carlitz's identity Kl(3; a) = Kl(2; a)² − 1, which the appendix states and reproves, reads S_2(a)² − q = S_3(a). A brute-force computation over F_q for q = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and every a ∈ F_q^× gives S_2(a)² − q = S_3(a) exactly. The printed right-hand side is −S_3(a)/√q, which is not even rational for q = 2, 8, 32. The p > 2 line, S_2(a)² − q = G(ψ^{−1}, ρ^{−1})^{−1} Σ_{x_1x_2x_3=4ay} ψ(Tr(x_1 + x_2 + x_3 − y))ρ^{−1}(y), holds, as the same computation confirms for q = 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 and a = 1, 2. ### Xinyi Yuan, "Arithmetic bigness and a uniform Bogomolov-type result", Annals of Mathematics 203 (2026), no. 1 (`PAPER-YUAN-26`)

- **Error** at Theorem 4.19, p. 101, read together with the definition of maximal variation in section 1.6, p. 16 (author manuscript dated 21 August 2024; identical in arXiv:2108.05625v4) (it affects a stated result). The source says `Theorem 4.19. Let K be either a number field or a function field of one variable. Let S be a quasi-projective variety over K. Let pi : X -> S be a smooth relative curve over S of genus g > 1 with maximal variation. [...] Then the following morphisms satisfy the relative Bogomolov conjecture: (1) the S-morphism i^m_alpha : X^m_{/S} -> J^m_{/S} for any m >= dim S + 1. [...] -- where section 1.6 defines: "Let S be a quasi-projective integral scheme over a noetherian base ring R [...] We say that pi : X -> S has maximal variation (or maximal variation of moduli) if the moduli morphism S -> M_{g,R} associated to pi is generically finite"`; it should be `In the function-field case the hypothesis must be maximal variation over the field of constants k, not over K: the moduli morphism must be generically finite on a projective model of S over k, equivalently the family must not become isotrivial over the constant field. The number-field case needs no change.`. As stated the theorem is false in the function-field case. Because S is a quasi-projective variety over K, the base ring in the section 1.6 definition is R = K, so 'maximal variation' means that S -> M_{g,K} is generically finite. Take k any field, K = k(t), and S = Spec K, so that dim S = 0. Let C be a smooth projective curve of genus g >= 2 over k and let X = C x_k K be the constant family, with alpha any line bundle of positive degree. The hypothesis is then satisfied vacuously: S = Spec K is its own dense open and Spec K -> M_{g,K} is quasi-finite, so the family has maximal variation over K. Part (1) with m = 1 >= dim S + 1 therefore asserts the relative Bogomolov conjecture for i_alpha : X -> J. But that fails: by the definition recalled on p. 100 the canonical height is the one attached to the adelic extension of L over k, and every point of C(kbar), viewed in X(Kbar), is a constant section of a constant family and so has canonical height 0; C(kbar) is infinite, hence Zariski dense in the curve X_{Kbar}. So for every epsilon > 0 the set of points of height at most epsilon is Zariski dense, contradicting the conclusion. The defect is only in the hypothesis, and the paper's own proof shows what the hypothesis should be: it states 'Similar to Proposition 4.18, we need the bigness of the adelic line bundles over k instead of over K, where k = Z if K is a number field and k is the field of constants if K is a function field of one variable', and the bigness input it invokes, Theorem 4.5, requires maximal variation over that same k. Proposition 4.18, on p. 100, is stated correctly and carries bigness on S/k as an explicit hypothesis; it is Theorem 4.19 that fails to upgrade 'maximal variation' to match. The number-field case is unaffected: there k = Z, and for S a variety over a number field K generic finiteness of S -> M_{g,K} is equivalent to that of the induced morphism on a Z-model, since passing to the model adds one to the dimension of the source and of the image alike. Consistently with this, the paper's main uniform theorem is stated with an explicit non-isotriviality condition of its own (section 4.3.2), so the isotrivial case is excluded there and that theorem is not affected. With dim T throughout, the term is the degree of Theta|_Y on the generic fibre of Y -> T times (pi_{T*}<omega_a,omega_a>)^{dim T}, which is positive by Theorem 3.2 applied over T - which is exactly what the hypothesis on T buys. So the complement of Z_y contains no point with h_{L_m} strictly less than the threshold, but the boundary case of equality is not excluded, and the set as written with <= is therefore not contained in Z_y. Since epsilon is an arbitrary positive rational, halving it repairs the step; but it is a genuine off-by-boundary slip and it occurs twice, in the two parallel proofs. The source says `The condition is equivalent to (i/pi) ddbar g_D = dmu_Ar - delta_D as currents on C`; it should be `(i/pi) ddbar g_D = deg(D) dmu_Ar - delta_D`. The paper's own normalization makes mu_Ar a probability measure: dmu_Ar = (i/2g) sum_j alpha_j wedge alpha_j-bar for an orthonormal basis of the pairing <alpha,beta> = (i/2) integral alpha wedge beta-bar, so its total mass is (1/g) times g, namely 1; and delta_D has total mass deg(D). The factor is also forced by the two neighbouring definitions: admissibility of a metric is defined three lines earlier as c_1(L,||.||) = deg(L) dmu_Ar, and Poincare-Lelong for ||1|| = exp(-g_D), the paper's own convention, gives c_1(O(D),||.||) = (i/pi) ddbar g_D + delta_D, so substituting admissibility produces the deg(D). The non-archimedean twin, Proposition A.2 on p. 108, correctly carries deg(L). Nothing downstream breaks, because every subsequent use is for a divisor D = x_0 of degree 1. - **Misprint** at Section 3.3.1, p. 49 (the base-change recipe for delta). The source says `If C has split semistable reduction, delta(C) is also the total number of nodes on the minimal regular model of C over O_K; in general, if K' is a finite extension of K such that C has split semistable reduction over K', then delta(C) = delta(C_{K'})/[K' : K]`; it should be `delta(C) = delta(C_{K'})/e(K'/K), with e the ramification index (equivalently, K'/K must be required totally ramified)`. False as printed, and the two halves of the one sentence contradict each other. Let C already have split semistable reduction over K and let K'/K be unramified of degree f > 1. By the first half, delta(C) is the number of nodes of the minimal regular model over O_K. Over O_{K'} the reduction is still split semistable and the minimal regular model base-changes etale-locally, so it has the same nodes and delta(C_{K'}) = delta(C). The second half then gives delta(C) = delta(C)/f, forcing delta(C) = 0 for every such curve. The recipe is not even well defined as printed, since taking K' = K and K' unramified quadratic give answers differing by a factor 2. With the ramification index it is consistent: a node with local equation t_1 t_2 = pi^m becomes t_1 t_2 = pi'^{em} after a degree-e ramified extension, so delta scales by exactly e. That delta is the raw uniformizer-normalized length, with no residue-degree factor, is fixed by the paper's own conventions: p. 47 normalizes the local Green functions by log e_v, and section 4.5.1, p. 86, writes the global invariants as delta(C) = deg(Delta_S) and phi(C) = sum_v phi_v(C) deg(v), carrying the residue degree separately in deg(v). This is an internal inconsistency in one sentence and is independent of how the conventions of [Zha3] compare with this paper's. The source says `By Theorem 3.6, there is an adelic divisor Phi-bar in Div^(M/Z) with underlying divisor 0 on M, such that the value g~_{Phi-bar}(v) of the total Green's function g~_{Phi-bar} at any discrete or archimedean valuation v in S^an_v is equal to phi(X_{H_v})`; it should be `at any discrete or archimedean valuation v in M^an is equal to phi(C_{H_v}), and the citation is to section 3.3.2 rather than to Theorem 3.6`. The sentence was transplanted from section 3.3.2 without renaming its objects, and picked up a stray subscript on the way. Three things are wrong and all three are visible on the page. First, 'v in S^an_v' is self-referential, v occurring as both the element and the subscript; the source sentence in section 3.3.2, p. 50, correctly reads 'at any discrete or archimedean valuation v in S^an'. It is reduced with only ordinary double points, so semistable by the paper's own definition, and its arithmetic genus is 0 + 2 = 2 > 1. It is a stable curve in the standard sense - its only component is singular, so the Deligne-Mumford condition on nonsingular rational components is vacuous, and omega_C is ample - and it is a point of the boundary of Mbar_2. But its unique component is rational and meets OTHER irreducible components in 0 < 3 points, so the printed condition fails. The paper treats its own section 1.6 and [DM, section 1] as interchangeable, saying on p. 41 'We refer to [DM, Sec. 1] (or our Sec. 1.6) for quick definitions of stable curves', and then defines Mbar_g as the moduli of stable curves, whose boundary contains exactly the curves the printed definition rules out. Section 3.3.4 confirms the intended notion by counting nodes 'of type 0', where the partial normalization is connected, i.e. self-nodes of a single component. Every later use is the Deligne-Mumford notion, so nothing downstream is affected. ### Zhiwei Yun–Wei Zhang, "Shtukas and the Taylor expansion of L-functions", Annals of Mathematics 186 (2017), no. 3 (`PAPER-YUN-ZHANG-17`)

- **Misprint** at Proposition B.1, p. 902, and §B.2, p. 903 (published; also arXiv v3) — both verified on rendered page images, since a text layer drops the superscript. The source says `"φ^{(r)}(0) := (d/ds)|_{s=0}φ(s) ≥ 0" (Proposition B.1) and "Λ^{(r)}(π, 1/2) := (d/ds)|_{s=1/2}Λ(π, s)" (§B.2)`; it should be `(d/ds)^r|_{s=0}φ(s) and (d/ds)^r|_{s=1/2}Λ(π, s).`. The superscript (r) on the left-hand side is the r-th derivative — this is the whole point of "super-positivity", and both statements quantify over all r ≥ 0 and compare φ^{(r_0)} with φ^{(r_0+2i)}. As printed, the definitions say that every φ^{(r)}(0) is the first derivative. The proofs use the genuine r-th derivative (the Taylor coefficients of the product expansion in the proof of Proposition B.1, and the even-degree coefficients of A_i(s) in Remark B.4).
